# Active server bar

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/active_server_bar.htm

## Active server bar

The active server bar, which is located in the bottom right corner of the 
main window, displays information about the active Pipeline Pilot Server connection.
When connected to an on-prem server, it shows the address, port number,
resource level, and the version of the DS component collection.
When connected to a cloud server, it shows the name of the connected
user in the format USER@Cloud. To change to a different server, click the active server bar to launch the Change Server dialog .

When connected to an on-prem server, the resource level of a server or
grid/cluster is indicated by one of the colored icons:

| Availability | Server | Cluster/Grid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Excellent | | |
| Good | | |
| Medium | | |
| Poor | | |
| Critical | | |
| Inaccessible | | |

If your server is running at a critical or poor resource level,
it is heavily loaded and is running low on memory, and jobs may not be able to run. 
Free up memory on the server to improve the resource level.

### Collection License

When connected to an on-prem server, hovering over the active server bar
will display a tooltip containing a license expiration date for the collections. For more information on the license expiration dates please open the
Pipeline Pilot Administration Portal and 
navigate to the Reports/Installed Packages page. For more information about licenses, see Licenses .

# Installing and configuring a grid

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/config_para-grid.htm

## Installing and configuring a grid

A set of Linux machines with a shared disk can be configured as a
grid. In this configuration, load balancing can be performed using
queue management software such as PBS Pro or Slurm. For details about supported grid systems, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

In this
configuration, a parameter on the protocol (Run On Grid) can be used
to distribute a protocol on the grid. This parameter is set for a
number of slow running protocols from Discovery Studio by default.
Parallel protocols may also be run across the nodes of a grid. All
coarse-grained parallel protocols in Discovery Studio have been
configured to be distributed using a grid if one is configured.

* Install Discovery Studio on a shared disk with a network path that all the machines in the grid can access.

* The installer starts the server on the machine you installed on. You only need to start a single server on a single machine in the grid configuration.

* Use a web browser to open the Administration Portal: http://hostname:port/admin . See Pipeline Pilot help for more information.

* Click Setup . Under Grid , select a Grid Engine Type (for example SLURM ). Click the help icon on this page for further information.

* Set the Grid Engine Path to the path on the server containing your
grid implementation. This path should be valid on all the nodes of
the grid. For example, /opt/slurm .

* By default grid-enabled protocols and parallel jobs will be
submitted to the default queue. You can use a different queue by
default by changing the Grid Engine Default Queue . You can also
provide additional options using Grid Engine Submit Options .

* By default, the maximum number of simultaneous jobs that are started by any protocol is four. For clusters, which typically have more
than four CPUs, you can increase this using the Maximum number of simultaneous parallel processing subprotocol jobs allowed setting on the Server tab. For more information, see the following topic in the Pipeline Pilot Help Center: Administrators > Setup and Configuration > Server Deployments > Grids .

For more information, see the following topic in the Pipeline Pilot Help Center: Administrators > Setup and Configuration > Server Deployments > Grids .

#### Further information

Distributed grid computing Run a parallel calculation

# Distributed computing

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/distributed_computing.htm

## Distributed computing

Discovery Studio and Pipeline Pilot Server support a number of configurations
that may be termed High Performance Computing (HPC), or Distributed
Computing.

A Linux cluster is defined by us as any set of Linux machines with a
shared disk and http access. The Pipeline Pilot Server is
installed on that disk and it is used to share data for running parallel
jobs. When running a large number of jobs, the performance of the shared disk
becomes an important factor in the overall speed.

An important consideration is whether to use Pipeline Pilot to distribute and load balance the jobs (Cluster mode), or use
a 3rd party queue management system (Grid mode). Consider the following when deciding which method to use:

| Cluster mode | Grid mode |
| --- | --- |
| Runs on a Linux cluster | Runs on a Linux cluster |
| Always available | Requires 3rd party software: SGE, PBS, or LSF |
| Basic load balancing (Job Leveling, Round Robin) | Advanced load balancing |
| No sharing of resources with other applications | Resources shared with other applications |
| Jobs start immediately | Jobs submitted to a queue |
| No limit on number of jobs submitted simultaneously | Number of simultaneous jobs controlled by queue configuration |
| All protocols are distributed on the cluster | Only configured jobs are distributed on the grid |

When multiple jobs are submitted to a server, they are distributed
according to the load balancing scheme in place. Coarse-grained parallel
jobs can also be submitted where parts of the workflow are distributed
across multiple CPUs. On a Cluster, all protocols are distributed in this
way. On a Grid, you have control over which jobs are distributed. Several slow-running Discovery Studio protocols have been
configured to be run on a grid by default. All
coarse-grained parallel protocols have also been configured to be run on a
grid.

For more information about installing and configuring a cluster or grid, see Installing and configuring a cluster and Installing and configuring a grid .

#### Further information

Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Change Server dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/dl_change-server.htm

## Change Server dialog

The Change Server dialog allows you to change the current a Pipeline Pilot Server that your client is connected to, specify the default server, and test a connection. The dialog has an editable dropdown list that displays the current Pipeline Pilot Server name and up to nine of the most recent servers that have been accessed by the client.

Server name: By default, the server is set to a local instance, https://localhost:9943 . You can change this field to point to a different server on your network. The syntax to specify a server is [https:// | http://]<server name>:<port> , where <server name> is the machine name (alias) or IP address of a host running a Pipeline Pilot Server , and <port> is the port number for the host. If the protocol identifier is omitted, the secure http protocol https:// is used by default. If the port number is omitted, the default port will be used (9943 for https and 9944 for http).

Test: This performs a series of tests that check the connection and determine if a server with the specified name and port is running. The Result column will indicate OK or FAIL for individual tests.

If all tests are successful, clicking the OK button will close the Change Server dialog and the specified server connection is established. Otherwise, an error message will appear.

If you are unable to make a successful server connection, you can send this information to your system administrator for further analysis.

If your selected Pipeline Pilot Server is equipped with a General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) data privacy policy, you must give consent (on the Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page) before you can connect to this server.

### Server connection troubleshooting tips

* The server name is how your client machine is able to address the Pipeline Pilot Server . To test a server's name and accessibility status, type "ping servername" in a command line window. In most cases, the server name is a simple machine name, such as "mainserver".

* If the server is configured to use a port number other than the default (9943), you need to specify the port number directly after the server name, separated by a colon. For example, mainserver:61143 .

* If the ping test fails and/or if your network service does not allow you to specify a server name, use the IP address instead. Examples of IP addresses include 192.168.73.108 and 192.168.73.108:50043 .

* When using an IP address, ask your system administrator if the IP address will change at a later time. If it changes, you need to update the server's address in your Pipeline Pilot Client . (A network name automatically maps to the current IP address, even if the address changes, so you do not need to worry about this when using machine names).

### Access methods

| Menu | File \| Change Server... |
| --- | --- |
| Active server bar | Left-click |

When the application starts, it attempts to restore the connection to the default server. If the server is unavailable, it will ask you to specify another server. You can specify a new server or choose not to connect to a server. To avoid being prompted to connect each time you start the application, open this dialog and delete the server name.

| Menu | File \| Change Server... |
| --- | --- |
| Status bar | Click the Active Server Bar . |

Managing Pipeline Pilot Server

## Login to Server dialog

The Login to Server dialog allows you to enter username and password login 
information when running a protocol on a Pipeline Pilot Server that requires 
authentication. This dialog is displayed when you connect to an a Pipeline Pilot Server through the Change Server dialog .

If your selected Pipeline Pilot Server is equipped with a General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) data privacy policy, you must give consent (on the Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page) before you can connect to this server.

Username: Enter your username for the Pipeline
Pilot server.

Password: Enter the appropriate password
for the Pipeline Pilot Server .

Save password: Check this box if you wish to save 
your login information so that the Login to Server dialog is not displayed when 
using this server in the future. If the application is restarted and the login 
information is not saved, this dialog is displayed when you open a protocol 
from the Protocols Explorer .

* The Login to Server dialog 
is only displayed if authentication is enabled on the Pipeline Pilot Server . 
Refer to the Pipeline Pilot help for guidance on enabling authentication 
methods.

* The password will not be saved if the Pipeline Pilot Server is a cloud server.

Click the OK button to submit the specified authentication 
details to the Pipeline Pilot Server .

# Installing and configuring a cluster

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/inst_cluster_support.htm

## Installing and configuring a cluster

This section describes how to install and configure a cluster of Pipeline Pilot Server s for use with Discovery Studio .

For more information, see the following topic in the Pipeline Pilot Help Center: Administrators > Setup and Configuration > Server Deployments > Clustering .

Any set of Linux machines with a shared disk can be configured as a cluster. In this configuration, load balancing can be performed such that
any protocol launched on the primary server is distributed to one of the secondary machines. Two load balancing methods can be used, Round Robin or
Job Leveling. The cluster can also be used for running parallel protocols. For more information about grid computing in Discovery Studio , see Distributed grid computing .

To install Discovery Studio with Pipeline Pilot Server on a cluster

* Log onto the primary node as a non-root user. This does not
allow configuring user impersonation for running jobs or the automatic restart of the
server upon reboot. These facilities require root permissions and can be configured independently if needed.

This does not
allow configuring user impersonation for running jobs or the automatic restart of the
server upon reboot. These facilities require root permissions and can be configured independently if needed.

* Perform a Discovery Studio installation , using the Complete or Custom options, on the server. Ensure that the
software is installed on a file system that is shared by all servers on the cluster, using a
file path that is valid for all servers.

* Once the installation is complete, check that you can connect to the server portal by 
opening a browser and typing http://<servername>:<portnumber>/ to open the Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page.
The default port number is 9944. You can specify an alternate port during installation.
From the Home Page, run the Server Diagnostics Tests to verify that you can run a simple job.
At this point, all jobs run on the primary node only.

* After this initial installation, you can configure the other (secondary) nodes on the cluster. This
task is performed by starting additional Pipeline Pilot Server s on each of the secondary nodes, and then
configuring the primary node to use these servers.
For the secondary servers: Login to each machine and change to the directory where the Pipeline Pilot Server is located.
This should be on the shared file system. Go into the linux_bin directory and type startserver to start the Pipeline Pilot Server on the secondary node. Repeat for each additional server you want to include.

* Login to each machine and change to the directory where the Pipeline Pilot Server is located.
This should be on the shared file system.

* Go into the linux_bin directory and type startserver to start the Pipeline Pilot Server on the secondary node. Repeat for each additional server you want to include.

* Now configure the primary node so it can use the servers running on the secondary nodes: Open the Administration Portal on the primary server using the link on the Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page. From the Setup tab, click Server , and then turn on the Load Balancing Server option. Click Clustering , and add the names and ports 
of the secondary servers to the list of cluster nodes using the form <servername>:<portnumber> .
For each secondary server, <servername> is the hostname of that machine. Each should
be visible to the primary node using this name. The <portnumber> will typically be the same port as
that of the primary server. If the client machines only have HTTP access to the primary node, but not the secondary nodes, 
you need to turn on the private cluster option. From the Setup tab, click Clustering , 
and then enable the Private Cluster option.

* Open the Administration Portal on the primary server using the link on the Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page.

* From the Setup tab, click Server , and then turn on the Load Balancing Server option.

* Click Clustering , and add the names and ports 
of the secondary servers to the list of cluster nodes using the form <servername>:<portnumber> .
For each secondary server, <servername> is the hostname of that machine. Each should
be visible to the primary node using this name. The <portnumber> will typically be the same port as
that of the primary server.

* If the client machines only have HTTP access to the primary node, but not the secondary nodes, 
you need to turn on the private cluster option. From the Setup tab, click Clustering , 
and then enable the Private Cluster option.

* After adding all of the secondary nodes and configuring the primary server, re-run the initial installation checks on the primary 
node to ensure that the secondary nodes can run jobs. From the Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page, run the Server Diagnostics Tests again and
check that the server name for each job varies.

* If you intend to run with impersonation and authentication enabled in the cluster, 
then you need to propagate the primary node's "/etc/pam.d/scitegic" folder the secondary nodes. Also, when running on servers with impersonation, ensure that the temporary folder belonging to the server owner is writable by all impersonated users.

#### Further information

Installing Discovery Studio

# Folder locations

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/inst_folders.htm

## Folder locations

The location of important folders can vary depending on your operating system and configuration. This section describes the folders used by Discovery Studio :

Traditionally, file paths on Windows use the
backslash character "\" to separate folders. On Linux, a forward slash "/" is
used. In this documentation, we use a forward slash. Most recent Windows applications allow either separator.

### Discovery Studio client installation

Depending on your installation options,
other programs may also be installed in this location.

Although you can modify the location during
installation, the following is the default path: C:/Program Files/BIOVIA/ Discovery Studio 2026 . Throughout the Discovery Studio documentation the client installation location is abbreviated as <DS_client_install> .

### Pipeline Pilot installation

This is the folder containing the Pipeline Pilot Server including the DS Component Collection. Although you can modify the location during

# License Pack

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationmanagement

Source file: applicationmanagement/licensing_server.htm

## License Pack

This application is licensed using the License Pack. The License Pack is a system for managing BIOVIA software at your site. Licensing is provided as a service to help you access all the features of our software that your users require and to comply with your software purchase agreement. It is also designed to protect BIOVIA software from unauthorized use.

Because the License Pack is used for other BIOVIA products, you can share licenses, including license tokens, with products, such as Materials Studio.

The Linux installation location of BIOVIA License Pack 2026 has changed from earlier versions, the default location now uses a BIOVIA_LicensePack folder. Installing License Pack in the presence of License Pack 7.6.14 or earlier on Linux will no longer perform an in-place upgrade of the previous version. If you need to continue to use your previous license, you may need to perform some additional installation steps. Refer to the License Pack documentation for more information.

Licenses are made available when the software is purchased. If you need further assistance relating to licenses you should initially contact your account manager.

### Users with current maintenance

No license installation necessary: If your BIOVIA software maintenance is current and you have already installed the corresponding license file, no new license is necessary. You will be able to use the Discovery Studio software once it is installed as long as it is configured to use the currently installed license. On Linux, BIOVIA recommends that you restart the FLEXlm license manager running on the license server machine after upgrading License Pack on your license server to ensure that you are using the most recent version of the license manager program. To restart the license manager program use the license administration tools.

### New users or users adding new products with this release

Install license file : Once you have received your BIOVIA software license file, you need to configure it correctly. To install the license, use the license administration tools.

Use a remote license server : PCs and Linux 
gateways without NFS support must be configured to use a remote license server via a TCP/IP connection. To connect to a remote license server use the license administration tools.

### Wait functionality

Servers check out licenses when they are launched. If the server is unable to check out a 
license due to unavailability, the server will wait for a license to become available. If there are insufficient licenses, 
the process will exit with an error. To determine if a process is waiting for a license, view the details section of the job manager.

### Coarse-grained parallelization licensing

Coarse-grained parallelization licensing is supported. A job that requires multiple processes to be executed to complete will use the appropriate 
calculation for parallel processing. When a job requiring coarse-grained parallelization is launched, the total number of floating or token licenses 
needed for the job is checked out and shared among all of the processes. For fine-grained parallelization, the number of floating or token licenses 
checked out for jobs is performed only by the parent process and held until all child processes complete. Refer to the 
License Pack Help documentation for details about the calculation process for both floating and token 
licenses.

### Linux clustering

Linux cluster support is available. Linux clusters that are configured as private Linux clusters 
without TCP/IP access to nodes outside the cluster (except for the head node) require the location of the 
license server to be on the head node or for the cluster to be configured to forward communication to the license server through the
head node. Refer to the License Pack Help documentation for additional information.

#### Further information

Accessing License Pack Help Licensing on Windows Licensing on Linux Starting the License Administrator

# Working with ADMET

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_admet.htm

## Working with ADMET

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

ADMET refers to the Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity properties 
of a molecule within an organism. Optimizing these properties during early drug discovery is 
crucial for reducing ADMET problems later in the development process. ADMET descriptors allow 
you to eliminate compounds with unfavorable ADMET characteristics early on to avoid expensive 
reformulation later, and to evaluate proposed structural refinements that are designed to 
improve ADMET properties, prior to resource expenditure on synthesis.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to run a ADMET Descriptors protocol and how to analyze 
the results.

This tutorial covers:

* Running an ADMET Descriptors job

* Inspecting the results of ADMET Descriptors

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | pk-test.sd .

This opens 20 pyruvate kinase inhibitors in a Molecule Window.

Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click ADMET Descriptors... to open the ADMET Descriptors dialog. Set the Input Ligands to pk-test:All .

By default it is set to pk-test:Visible if the pk-test Molecule Window is active and has a visible molecule in it.

Keep the ADMET Descriptors parameter as default.

This will calculate all ADMET descriptors included in this protocol.

Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

After the job completes, a dialog asks if you want to display the ADMET plot. Click Yes to open pk-test.sd in a new Molecule Window, and an ADMET plot. The ADMET plot is a 2D chart of 
ADMET_PSA_2D versus ADMET_AlogP98. The two sets of ellipses are for the prediction confidence space (95% and 
99%) for the Blood Brain Barrier Penetration and Human Intestinal Absorption models, respectively.

If you do not see four ellipses in the plot, from the menu bar, choose Edit | Preferences... | Charts | ADMET Plot to check both Blood Brain Barrier and Absorption .
If the legend is not shown, right-click on the plot and choose Display Style to open the display style page, click the Axis and Font tab, then check 
the Show legend box.

Drag the pk-test plot tab and drop it to the side of the viewing area to create a side-by-side split view with the pk-test Molecule Window. Click a point outside the blue ellipse (99% Blood Brain Barrier confidence).

The molecule corresponding to this point is highlighted in the pk-test Molecule Window. Since the molecule 
is outside of the 99% BBB model confidence ellipse, the prediction is considered unreliable and no BBB prediction is made for this ligand.

You can select more than one molecule by pressing SHIFT+clicking, or by drawing a circle around the chart with the select tool. You can also select molecules in the Molecule
Window to highlight the corresponding points on the chart.

# Analyzing allosteric motion with Analyze Trajectory tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_allosteric_motion.htm

## Analyzing allosteric motion with Analyze Trajectory tools

Time: 30 minutes + MD simulation time (16+ hours depending upon resources)

### Introduction

Allosteric communication is a fundamental mechanism by which proteins transmit 
signals from one site to another, often resulting in functional conformational changes 
that modulate activity. Identifying these allosteric pathways is critical for 
understanding protein function and for the rational design of allosteric modulators. 
Molecular dynamics simulations provide a powerful approach for capturing the dynamic 
behavior of proteins in both the apo (unbound) and holo (bound) states, allowing 
researchers to analyze how binding events alter structural communication networks.

In this tutorial, you will simulate the PDZ domain in both its apo and holo states 
using the Standard Dynamics Cascade and Dynamics NAMD protocols. 
These simulations will generate two sets of trajectories: one for the unbound PDZ domain, 
and another for the peptide-bound PDZ complex. Following the simulations, you will use the Measure Trajectory Features protocol to extract distance features between specific residue pairs that are in contact 
in each state. The resulting data is saved as CSV files, serving as input for subsequent analyses.

Next, you will use the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol to calculate the cross-covariance of these distance pairs, allowing 
you to identify dynamic couplings that are altered between the apo and holo states. This analysis 
helps to pinpoint residue pairs that exhibit significant changes in coordinated motion, 
revealing potential allosteric communication pathways and how they are modulated by peptide binding.

In addition, you will learn how to incorporate pocket feature data generated by the Detect and Analyze Pockets protocol 
into the cross-covariance analysis. This approach provides further insights into how the dynamics 
of pockets and binding sites are functionally linked to structural changes elsewhere in the protein, 
offering a more comprehensive view of peptide-induced allosteric communication.

Throughout this tutorial, you will learn how to prepare simulations, extract feature data, and interpret 
cross-covariance results to uncover peptide-induced allosteric pathways in PDZ domains, leveraging 
both residue pair distances and pocket feature data for comprehensive allosteric analysis.

The tutorial covers:

* Examining and preparing the protein structures

* Solvating the protein structures

* Running the molecular dynamics simulations

* Preparing the trajectories for feature analysis

* Setting up and running Measure Trajectory Features

* Setting up and running Analyze Trajectory Features

* Understanding the Analyze Trajectory Features results

* Alternative workflow: Detect and Analyze Pockets for allosteric motion detection

The details of this tutorial might not match what you observe as some of the
protocols covered here are not deterministic, unless you use the provided files. However, it does cover the
steps for using the tools and describes which aspects of the results are important.

The PDB code for the PDZ domain from synaptic protein PSD-95 with a short peptide 
used is 1BE9 [Doyle et al., 1996] . 
The file was downloaded from the RCSB website.

You will prepare two systems: one peptide-bound PDZ, and one peptide-free PDZ. 
The provided PDB file contains the peptide already bound to the PDZ domain.

#### Prepare the holo state

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | 1BE9.pdb file. Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if
it is not visible. Expand the <Cell> grouping and double-click on 1BE9 . Rename the molecule to 1BE9_holo to distinguish between the holo and the apo structures for the rest of the tutorial. Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tool panel 
and click Prepare Proteins... . Expand the Protonate parameter group and specify
the pH for Protonation parameter to 7.0 to match the
simulation conditions in Steiner et al. (2012) . Click Run .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send
the job to the background. Sending a job to the background closes the
status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio Simulation
while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job by
opening the Jobs Explorer.

The Prepare Proteins protocol removes all water 
molecules from the structure by default.

When the job completes, double-click the completed job in the Jobs Explorer to open the report. Click View Results to open a new Molecule window named 1BE9_holo_prep , containing the prepared protein structure named 1BE9_holo . Click Detailed Report in the table to view details of what has been modified in the structure. Close the Report window.

#### Prepare the apo state

Start by removing the peptide and preparing for the apo state simulation.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | 1BE9.pdb file. A dialog will appear indicating that the file has been modified and asking if you want to revert to the saved version. Click Yes to proceed with loading the original file from the folder. Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if
it is not visible. Expand the <Cell> grouping and double-click on 1BE9 . Rename the molecule to 1BE9_apo to distinguish between the holo and the apo structures for the rest of the tutorial. Under the 1BE9_apo grouping, click on the first B chain to select
that group, and then press the Delete key.
This will delete the bound peptide. Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tool panel 
and click Prepare Proteins... . Expand the Protonate parameter group and specify
the pH for Protonation parameter to 7.0 to match the
simulation conditions in Steiner et al. (2012) . Click Run .

When the job completes, double-click the completed job in the Jobs Explorer to open the report. Click View Results to open a new Molecule window named 1BE9_apo_prep , containing the prepared protein structure named 1BE9_apo . Click Detailed Report in the table to view details of what has been modified in the structure. Close the Report window.

After this point, the following four sections of this tutorial will walk you through the steps for the holo state. You will be instructed to repeat the steps in each section for the apo state.

You will specify the charmm36 forcefield for the system, which is optimized for protein and peptide simulations. For more information about this forcefield, see Change Forcefield tools .

Click the 1BE9_holo_prep tab to make it active. Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel and change the Forcefield to charmm36 . Click Apply Forcefield .

You will now solvate the system for the simulation, 
adding enough water molecules to allow the protein to interact 
with the solvent naturally, but not so much that the system becomes 
too big to simulate using the available computing power.

Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and click Solvation... . Set Input Typed Molecule to 1BE9_holo_prep:1BE9_holo . Expand the Solvation Model parameter group and change the Minimum Distance From Boundary parameter to 12 . This creates a water layer of 12 angstroms on all sides of the protein. This distance is chosen to ensure that the protein doesn't interact with its periodic images and has sufficient solvent for natural dynamics. Leave the rest of the parameters set to their default values and click Run .

When the job completes, double-click the completed job in the Jobs Explorer to open the report. Click View Results to open the solvated Molecule window named 1BE9_holo .

When you have completed this section for the holo structure, repeat the steps for the apo structure.

You will use Standard Dynamics Cascade to minimize and equilibrate the systems.

The molecular dynamics simulations ( Standard Dynamics Cascade and Dynamics (NAMD) ) can take several hours to run. 
If you do not have the time to run it, you can continue with the tutorial using the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | 1BE9_tutorial_apo.dcd and 1BE9_tutorial_holo.dcd file 
provided when the output DSV and DCD are required below. In this case, you can skip this step and continue with the Preparing the trajectories for feature analysis section.

From the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel, click Standard Dynamics Cascade... . Click on the window for the solvated holo system to make it active. Make sure that Input Typed Molecule is 1BE9_holo:1BE9_holo . Expand the Equilibration parameter group and set the Simulation Time (ps) time to 100 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and leave the job to complete.

When the job completes, double-click the completed job in the Jobs Explorer to open the report. Click View Results to open the Molecule window named 1BE9_holo .

Now that the system is equilibrated, run the production simulations using Dynamics NAMD to leverage the GPU-resident mode, depending on your resources.

From the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel, click Dynamics (NAMD)... . Click on the window for the equilibrated holo system to make it active. Make sure that Input Typed Molecule is 1BE9_holo:1BE9_holo . Set Simulation Time (ps) parameter to 50000 , which equals 50 nanoseconds. Set Save Results Interval (ps) parameter to 1000 to save 1 frame per nanosecond. Specify the restart files by expanding the Restart Files parameter group and clicking the ... at the CHARMm Restart File parameter. Navigate to rst file generated by the Standard Dynamics Cascade job. Under the Results folder, navigate to the corresponding
Standard Dynamics Cascade jobs Output folder and choose the 1BE9_holo_prod.rst restart file. Leave the remaining parameters at their default values and click Run . Click Background and leave the job to complete.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link to see the details of the simulation.

Before analyzing the trajectories, prepare the system by selecting only the central portion of the protein and removing the C and N-terminal flexible regions. This selection will reduce computational cost and minimize noise in the analysis by focusing on the most structurally stable part of the protein, excluding flexible terminal regions that can introduce variability unrelated to the core protein dynamics.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and
open Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | 1BE9_holo.dsv .

This opens the structure of the peptide-bound PDZ domain in a new Molecule Window 
if it is not already on your screen from running the simulations.
The Measure Trajectory Features protocol accepts Groups as Input Atoms
so you create a new Group consisting of all residues except for the C and N-termini.

Open the Data Table View (CTRL+T if it is not visible) 
and select the Group tab. 
Deselect Hetatm to hide water and ions. Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if
it is not visible. Expand the <Cell> and 1BE9_holo grouping. To select the central part of the protein and the peptide, expand the chain A grouping. While pressing the Shift key; click on PRO311 , scroll down, and click on ALA402 . All residues between 311 and 402 (inclusive) should be selected and highlighted in yellow. To add the bound peptide, while pressing the ctrl key, click on chain B . Now both the central part of the protein and the bound peptide should be selected and highlighted in yellow. Right-click and select Group . Name the group central .

Your atom selection appears under the Group tab of the Data Table View .

When you have completed this section for the holo structure, repeat the steps for the apo structure, excluding the selection of the bound peptide.

Adding the bound peptide to the holo structure feature extraction is optional, since the effect of the bound peptide is already captured in the protein's conformational changes. Including the peptide is useful when protein-peptide interactions are of interest.

Now that you have prepared your Input Atoms (the Group named "central"), you will configure and run the Measure Trajectory Features protocol to analyze the trajectory. The Measure Trajectory Features protocol offers five available Feature Type s: RMSD, SASA, Dihedral, Distance, and Pocket Detection.

For this tutorial, you will extract and use the Distance feature to analyze allosteric communication. Specifically, you will measure distances between residues that are in proximity to each other (within 2.5 angstroms) to identify any correlated motion between residue pairs with and without the bound peptide. Note that for your own research, you can choose different features or feature combinations depending on which aspects of molecular motion you want to analyze.

With the 1BE9_holo Molecule Window open (make sure nothing is selected), go to Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tool panel and under the Analyze tools, click Measure Trajectory Features to open the
dialog. Expand and set Feature Type to Distance . Make sure Distance Type parameter is set to All Contacts and Distance Cutoff parameter is set to 2.5 to define the residue distance measurement as explained above. Set Input Molecule to 1BE9_holo:1BE9_holo . Click the ... at the Input Trajectory parameter and navigate to either Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | 1BE9_tutorial_holo.dcd or the dcd file generated by the Dynamics(NAMD) job that you have run. Expand Input Molecule and set Input Atoms to 1BE9_holo:central . Click Run to start the feature extraction
process from the trajectory.

If you ran a longer simulation that resulted in multiple DCD files, you can select multiple files as input for Measure Trajectory Features.

Repeat the previous steps in this section for the apo state, specifying the Input Molecule to 1BE9_apo:1BE9_apo and opening Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | 1BE9_tutorial_apo.dcd or the dcd file generated by the Dynamics(NAMD) job that you have run.

* Dihedral and Distance features are particularly useful for detailed allosteric analysis because they provide residue-level data that can capture localized dynamic changes throughout the trajectory. These feature types enable cross-covariance calculations between specific residues, allowing detection of allosteric couplings between different parts of the protein.

* In contrast, RMSD, SASA, and Pocket Detection features represent overall simulation values for each frame rather than individual residue measurements. When using these features, the protocol performs auto-correlation analysis instead of cross-correlation/covariance analysis. While these are valuable analysis options, they are beyond the scope of this tutorial.

After the jobs complete, navigate to each Output folder and rename the simulation_data.csv files to simulation_data_holo.csv and simulation_data-apo.csv . Now that you have extracted the desired features from the trajectories, the 
distances between residues that are within 2.5 angstrom of each other, you will set up and run 
the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol to calculate cross-covariance
and cross-correlation of the distance between the apo and holo structures.
You can use the CSV file outputs from the Measure Trajectory Features protocol as inputs to run the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol.

After the jobs complete, navigate to each Output folder and rename the simulation_data.csv files to simulation_data_holo.csv and simulation_data-apo.csv .

The extracted number of features (columns in the output CSV from Measure Trajectory Features ) between two simulations are expected to be different for two reasons. First, you included the peptide in the analysis for the holo structure, which introduced more residues in the vicinity of each other. Second, the simulations are different and the 2.5 angstrom threshold can include more or fewer residue pairs that are in proximity to each other. The key is to have the same number of frames to compare.

#### When to use normalization and periodicity conversion

You can enable normalization using the Normalize parameter under each input data selection.

Normalization is recommended when your data has features with very different scales or when a few measurements have much larger values that might overshadow smaller but important changes. For example, if some distance measurements are consistently much larger than others, normalization ensures all features contribute equally to the analysis rather than letting the large values dominate.

In this tutorial, the protein is relatively small and the conformational changes are stable, so normalization is not required.

Periodicity conversion is applied to handle angular data that exhibits cyclical behavior, 
such as dihedral angles, using the Convert Angular Data parameter
under each input data selection. When using custom files with an angular feature, make sure the unit is in radians. In this tutorial, you are using the distance feature, so angular conversion is not required.

When using custom files with an angular feature, make sure the unit is in radians.

For details on the theory, see Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance .

#### Introducing time lag to cross-comparison calculations

In cross-comparison calculations, time lag introduces a delay between two data points, allowing the detection of 
time-dependent relationships between feature pairs. Adjusting the time lag parameters ( Minimum Time Lag , Maximum Time Lag , and Time Lag Stride ) can reveal dynamic coupling 
patterns that may not be evident when only considering simultaneous data points. 
By configuring these parameters, you can explore how residue pairs respond to each other over different timescales, 
identifying potential allosteric communication pathways or time-dependent structural relationships within the 
system. In this tutorial, the input features are extracted from separate simulations of the apo and holo states of the protein, 
meaning there is no direct temporal continuity between them.

These options are available for applying a time 
lag to independent datasets, as the frames are not sequentially related in time. You can set all the time lag parameters to 0 to run non-time-lagged 
calculations. Alternatively, you can specify Maximum Time Lag to be (number of frames − 5) to cover all possible time delay comparisons. 
As an example, you will use a time lag of 10 frames. Note that, 
in scenarios where a single continuous simulation is run and a ligand binds to the protein partway through the trajectory, 
introducing a time lag can be particularly informative. By applying a time lag, you can detect how dynamic coupling between 
residue pairs evolves as the ligand interacts with the protein and potentially drives conformational changes.

For more information about these parameters, see Analyze Trajectory Features Parameter Help .

#### Run the protocol

Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory | Analyze tools and click Analyze Trajectory Features to open the
dialog. Under Comparative Analysis Type , 
select both Cross-covariance and Cross-correlation check boxes. Select the Input Data by either navigating to the corresponding 
Output folder from the previous section, and selecting the CSV file named simulation_data-apo.csv , 
or choose the file from Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | simulation_data-apo.csv . Expand the Input Data parameter group and set Convert Angular Data to False and Normalize to False . Select the Additional Data by either navigating to the corresponding 
Output folder from the previous section, and selecting the CSV file named simulation_data_holo.csv , 
or choose the file from Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | Allostery | simulation_data-holo.csv . Expand the Additional Data parameter group and set Convert Angular Data to False and Normalize to False . Set the Maximum Time Lag to 10 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run .

#### Cross-Covariance versus Cross-Correlation

Cross-covariance and cross-correlation both measure dynamic coupling between feature pairs over time. 
Cross-covariance retains information about absolute fluctuation magnitudes, making it sensitive to 
structural rearrangements, while cross-correlation normalizes values between -1 and 1, highlighting 
relative coupling strength. For more details on these metrics, see Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance .

Here, you will use cross-covariance to detect changes in dynamic coupling between residue pairs 
in apo and holo PDZ structures. While cross-correlation reveals the relative strength of coupling, 
cross-covariance retains information on absolute fluctuation magnitudes, making it more sensitive to 
structural rearrangements.

Open the report when the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol completes:

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the Report in
an HTML Window. Click Cross-covariance Analysis to open the HTML Window
with interactive plots showing details of the cross-covariance calculations.

#### Using the report

You can choose the areas to zoom in
with your mouse, double-click to zoom back out or use the zoom controls on the 
top right corner of the window:

##### Max Covariance tab

This tab provides a heat map of the feature pairs 
(distance between residue pairs in this case) 
that exhibit the highest covariance or anticovariance across the entire 
trajectory. This plot is particularly useful for quickly identifying which pairs of features 
are most dynamically coupled within the provided trajectory(ies).
The x-axis represents the residue pairs of holo state ( Additional Data is Feature 2 ), while the y-axis 
represents the residue pairs of apo state ( Input Data is Feature 1 ). 
Each element in the heat map 
has the maximum covariance values observed across the trajectory and across each
calculated time lag. Positive values indicate coordinated 
fluctuations, while negative values indicate anticorrelated dynamics.
You can hover over each element in the heat map plot to see details such as the feature pairs,
time lag values and the covariance values.
The Max Covariance tab includes the following useful views:

* Hierarchical clustering in the heat map: The Hierarchical Clustering view organizes 
features based on their covariance profiles. This clustering allows you to easily identify 
groups of features that exhibit similar dynamic coupling patterns across the simulation. 
Clustering is performed using a distance metric that considers the covariance values between 
each pair of features, resulting in a heat map where similar features are grouped together.

* Value-based sorting in the heat map: The Value-based Sorting view allows 
you to sort the heat map based on the 
magnitude of covariance values, making it easier to identify the most significant dynamic 
couplings or anticorrelations in the data set. The most significant covariance and 
anticovariance values are positioned in the top-left corner, gradually decreasing
toward the bottom-right corner.

##### Pairwise Covariance tab

This tab provides a line plot showing how the covariance (y-axis) between two selected features 
evolves over time lags (x-axis). This view is crucial for detecting changes in dynamic coupling 
between specific residue pairs over time delays.

##### Feature Plot tab

This tab displays the raw data of the corresponding feature over the course 
of the simulation. This time-series view allows you to inspect how each feature fluctuates 
independently over time, providing context for the covariance and correlation analyses.
The x-axis shows the simulation frames, while the y-axis represents the 
raw feature values (for example, dihedral angle, pocket volume) with an option to
view two different y-axes if selected features have different units or 
scales. Monitoring these 
time-series data can reveal trends such as structural relaxation or ligand-induced stabilization 
in specific regions.

By integrating information across these three tabs, you can comprehensively assess how specific 
residues, residue pairs, and pocket features contribute to dynamic coupling and potential 
allosteric communication in the PDZ domain under apo and holo conditions.

#### Interpreting the cross-covariance results

In the analysis of the provided trajectory, the strongest covariance is observed between the distances of Glu331 - Arg399 in the apo state and Ser339 - Glu401 in the holo state. 
This interaction is particularly significant because the salt bridge between Glu331 in the β2-β3 loop 
and Arg399 in the α3 helix has been identified in Steiner et al. (2012) as a stabilizing interaction 
in the apo state. Upon peptide binding, this salt bridge interaction is disrupted, and a new dynamic 
coupling emerges between Ser339 in the β3 strand and Glu401 in the α3 helix, reflecting a shift 
from loop-helix interaction to a more localized stabilization of the binding groove. 
This shift in dynamic 
coupling is a textbook example of allosteric motion, where the binding event triggers a redistribution of 
dynamic interactions.

Another trajectory analysis tool, aside from Measure Trajectory Features, that can be used for detecting allosteric motion is Detect and Analyze Pockets . 
The combination of pocket feature analysis with cross-covariance or cross-correlation provides a powerful 
approach to detect dynamic coupling between pockets, allowing you to map out allosteric pathways that are 
functionally relevant to ligand binding, protein stability, or conformational changes. 
The feature_data folder generated by the Detect and Analyze Pockets protocol contains 
detailed analysis data of each feature for all detected pockets. Each CSV file in this folder provides 
information such as pocket volume, surface area, hydrophobicity, polarity, and charge distribution 
over time. These features help you understand how pocket properties change throughout 
a simulation and how they correlate with conformational dynamics.

You can use the CSV files as input to the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol to identify how specific pocket features fluctuate in response to ligand binding or other 
structural events. This analysis helps detect potential allosteric communication pathways by 
highlighting feature pairs whose dynamics are correlated or anti-correlated between apo and holo states.

This workflow involves running the Detect and Analyze Pockets protocol on your trajectory data, 
then using the generated CSV files from the feature_data folder as input for the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol. 
You can select specific pocket features such as volume, polar surface area, and charge score for analysis. 
The cross-covariance and cross-correlation calculations between selected features across apo and holo states 
can reveal pairs of pocket features whose dynamic coupling changes upon ligand binding, indicating potential 
allosteric pathways.

### Conclusion

In this tutorial, you explored how to use the Discovery Studio
Simulation Analyze Trajectory tools, Measure Trajectory Features , Analyze Trajectory Features and Detect and Analyze Pockets protocols 
to detect allosteric communication in PDZ domains by comparing distance 
fluctuations between the apo and holo states. You prepared the MD systems,
ran simulations and from the trajectories, extracted distance features, 
calculated cross-covariance, and identified key residue pairs with altered 
dynamic coupling due to peptide binding. This workflow provides insights 
into the structural pathways that mediate allosteric signaling, 
offering a foundation for further investigation and potential therapeutic targeting.

#### Further information

Standard Dynamics Cascade Dynamics NAMD Measure Trajectory Features Analyze Trajectory Features Detect and Analyze Pockets Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance

# Analyze ligand poses

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_analyze.htm

## Analyze ligand poses

Time: 20 minutes.

### Introduction

Non-bond interactions that form between two partner molecules are the basis of molecular recognition in biological systems. A detailed and comprehensive perception of non-bond interactions is crucial in structure-based design where identifying and optimizing the molecular interactions between ligands and their host receptor is a fundamental process.

In this tutorial, you will use a thermostabilized adenosine A2A receptor in complex with a selective inverse agonist ZM241385 [Dore et al., 2011] . The adenosine A2A receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor of particular interest as a drug target for Parkinson's disease. In this tutorial you will analyze ligand poses docked to the receptor.

### Calculating non-bond interactions with the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol

You will now run the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol to calculate non-bond interactions. Fifty diverse ligands, including 20 control ligands with a CHEMBL prefix and 30 decoy ligands with a ZINC prefix, are selected from a published docking study [Desaphy et al., 2013] .
They are docked into the prepared adenosine A2A receptor using the Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) protocol . The interaction properties calculated will be used to analyze the important interactions involved in binding inhibitors to the receptor target.

The study of screening results happens at different stages of a drug discovery project. It is necessary during a validation to optimize a virtual screening workflow where there are known control and decoy ligands, and also during a larger scale screening of unknown ligands. You may have no knowledge about the significant residues involved in ligand binding to the receptor, or you may have mutagenesis data revealing conserved active site residues or those crucial for high affinity binding. You may want to base your analysis, and further criteria to filter and prioritize screening results on non-bond interactions, or also incorporate scoring functions and energy calculations. Depending on your circumstance, project objective, and available information, the steps and interpretation of your analyses may differ from the example in this tutorial.

In this example, the CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY property from the docking is used as a score to filter poses before analysis of the possible significant non-bond interactions. The Calculate ROC Curve protocol identified an area under the curve of 0.908 for this property, indicating that it may serve as a good scoring function to prioritize active ligands ahead of inactive ligands. The mechanism of GPCR activation by native ligands or synthetic agonists is a fundamental question that remains largely unsolved [Xu et al., 2011] , and there are few crystal structure ligands available to characterize a distinct binding motif or identify essential required protein residues. So in this tutorial you will proceed with these assumptions to identify which non-bond interactions may further help enrich the virtual screen results after analyses and filtering.

Open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 3pwh_dockedposes.dsv . Click Analyze Ligand Poses... on the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tool panel to open the protocol dialog. Change the Input Ligands parameter to 3pwh_dockedposes:All . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

After the run, the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of poses processed.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. Click the View Interaction Histogram (Residues) link.

Frequency histograms summarize the different interactions calculated for the docked poses. For each major interaction category, you can see which protein residue forms the greatest number of interactions for those poses. The residue axis is the same for all of the histograms so that it is easy to compare the different interactions.

Hover the mouse over one of the columns of the frequency histograms to see the count of ligand poses that form that type of interaction with that residue. Click Go Back on the Smart Tools toolbar to return to the report window. Click the View Statistical Information link.

The Statistical Residue Analysis report summarizes the interaction count and lists the most frequently encountered residues for each interaction type. You can view the raw data of the residue interaction counts by clicking the Frequency Data (Residues) link in the report.

Notice in the second table (Top 5 Residues with Favorable Interactions) that ILE274 and PHE168 form the most favorable interactions with the docked poses, and these are hydrophobic interactions. The most hydrogen bonds are formed with residue GLU169. If you look at the Top 5 Residues with HydrogenBond Interactions table you can see GLU169 listed first and also SER67 as the second most common residue forming hydrogen bonds with the docked poses.

Scroll down further to see the Simultaneously Interacting Residues table. This is a useful summary of the number of ligands that form favorable interactions with simultaneously occurring residues. The table begins with the five most common combinations of five concurrently occurring residues, ordered by ligand count, and concludes with the five most common combinations of two simultaneously occurring residues. Notice that the ligand counts and percentages increase further down the table with less simultaneously interacting residues.

Look at the first row of two residues simultaneous interactions and notice that >75% of the poses (~380 poses) make favorable interactions with both PHE168 and ILE274 at the same time. This is not the same as knowing that ILE274 and PHE168 are the two most commonly occurring residues forming favorable interactions with the docked poses (Top 5 Residues with Favorable Interactions), as these two residues may be in different parts of the binding site, representing two dissimilar binding modes

You can think of these simultaneously interacting residues as a pattern, or binding motif, and the more specific the pattern (more residues), the fewer the ligands that match the pattern. Bear in mind that this analysis has been done on screening results with both control and decoy ligands, so these motifs are unlikely able to distinguish the control ligands from the decoy ligands. However, the later steps of this tutorial focus on how to identify combinations of residues that will enrich the virtual screen results after analysis and filtering.

Next you will open a heat map script to visualize the favorable ligand interactions with the receptor.

Click Go Back on the Smart Tools toolbar to return to the report window Click the View Heat Map (Favorable) link in the report window.

This opens the SD file of all 500 ligand poses with non-bond interaction properties calculated and an interactive heat map of the favorable interactions with specific residues that you can investigate.

From these types of heat maps, you would hope to be able to identify which residues predominantly interact with the active/control ligands (in this example the ligands with a CHEMBL prefix), but not the decoy ligands (ZINC prefix ligands), or vice versa. Unfortunately, such simple patterns are not always easy to identify. In this heat map of favorable interactions, you can see all of the significant residues involved in favorable non-bond interactions with the ligand poses such as PHE168, and ILE274.

By default only the favorable heat map script is created. However, the Analysis Options | Create Heat Maps parameter allows you to include other interactions as well.

You can see the non-bond interactions between the receptor and ligand poses presented as molecular properties in the Data Table View, which you can easily filter and use to generate charts. The interaction properties are added and sorted by interaction category, which makes charting easy. Note that these properties can also be sorted by scope, such as by residue sequence.

You will now generate heat maps to analyze some specific interaction properties of the docked control and decoy ligands for a subset of poses in the Data Table View. As −CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY was already identified as a suitable property to prioritize and filter the docking poses, you will focus on the top scoring pose for each ligand.

Go to the Molecule Window with the Analyze Ligand Poses results, right-click in the Data Table View and choose Filter . Set Choice for the -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY column to Top (#) and set Value to 1 . Check the Apply filter to each group of identical values option, choose Name , and then click OK. Choose Chart | Heap Map from the menu bar. Set Y to Name and X to Hydrophobic A:TYR9 . SHIFT+select HydrogenBond A:HIS278 , and then click OK .

In this heat map of the hydrophobic and hydrogen bond interactions you can see that all of the control ligands make a hydrophobic interaction with ILE274. While many of the decoy ligands also make hydrophobic interactions with this residue, you can see that this is persistent in all of the control ligands. It is not easy to identify a second interaction that could further differentiate control and decoy ligands, but in the next step you will see how using ILE274 and a second interaction can reduce the screening set of ligands to those of most interest.

Return to the Molecule Window with the filtered Analyze Ligand Poses results. In the Data Table View, choose the first row, SHIFT+select the last row, and then press CTRL+C. Open a new Molecule Window and paste in the ligands. In the new Molecule Window right-click in the Data Table View and choose Filter . For Hydrophobic A:ILE274 , change Choice to Greater than or equal and set Value to 1 . For HydrogenBond A:SER67 , change Choice to Greater than or equal and set Value to 1 . Click OK . Sort the table by the Control column.

You now have 19 ligands that meet the criteria of being the highest scoring pose based on the CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY property, forming a hydrophobic interaction with ILE274, and forming a hydrogen bond interaction with SER67. Thirteen of the original 20 control ligands, and 6 of the original 30 decoy ligands are not filtered out by this criteria. This may be a satisfactory object for this validation study, which you can then use to process and filter the results of a larger scale screening of unknown ligands. However, you may be less concerned about false negatives not filtered out by these interactions and desire an increase in the true positives retained by a different set of non-bond interactions.

In this step it was necessary to create a copy of the highest scoring pose based on the −CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY property for each ligand in a new Molecule Window. If you had used the ILE274 and SER67 filters in the previous Molecule Window, you would have a different number of final ligands. This is because the filtering tool would have acted on all ligands poses, identified those that formed a hydrophobic interaction with ILE274 and a hydrogen bond interaction with SER67, and then selected the single highest value pose based on −CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY from these poses because the filtering logic used for multiple properties is AND .

At this point you could return to the heat map of the hydrophobic and hydrogen bond interactions and try to identify another residue that filters your validation study ligands to increase your true positives as well as reducing or managing your false positives. Alternatively, you could rerun the Analyze Ligand Poses using only the control active ligands and study the Simultaneously Interacting Residues table in the statistical information reported to quickly identify motifs of multiple residues thatsimultaneously interact with as many control ligands as possible. The subtle difference to the analysis you have just performed here is being able to see the effect on the decoy ligands.

Finally, you may want to study the interactions in the adenosine A2A ZM241385 receptor-ligand complex to select interactions to filter the virtual screening results with (see Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating results ) . However, these interactions may reflect the binding for a single chemotype and could be too restrictive for a virtual screening program that is attempting to identify new active scaffolds for this receptor.

If you know of essential required interactions for a particular receptor, or once you have identified interactions you want to use as you have done in this tutorial, you can utilize the filtering tools in the Data Table View to screen out ligand poses that do not form those interactions. Alternatively, you can use the Interacting Residues parameter in the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol, which allows you to specify protein residues which ligands must form a favorable interaction with, specifying whether any or all interactions are required.

#### Further information

Receptor-Ligand Interactions tools Analyze Ligand Poses Non-bond Interactions Ligand preparation Using the Hierarchy View Data Table View
