# Creating a 3D model of an antibody Fv domain from a sequence

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_antibody.htm

## Creating a 3D model of an antibody Fv domain from a sequence

Time: 30 minutes + model building time.

### Introduction

The structures of antibodies and antibody-antigen complexes are routinely solved to understand the action mechanisms of antibody-based drugs, and to help in antibody engineering. While X-ray crystallography is the favored method for antibody structure determination, it is expensive and time-consuming relative to computational modeling.

The Second Antibody Modeling Assessment (AMA-II) [Almagro et al., 2014] , organized by Pfizer and Janssen (Johnson & Johnson), follows an initial antibody modeling assessment [Almagro et al., 2011] to assess the state of the art in 3D structure modeling of the variable regions of antibodies. A number of high-resolution X-ray Fv crystal structures covering a wide range of antigen-binding site conformations were used in a blind study to assess structure prediction. The results of AMA-II, benchmarking a number of different software applications [Teplyakov et al., 2014] as well as a study of the performance of Discovery Studio Tools in AMA-II [Fasnacht et al., 2014] are published in a special AMA-II issue of Proteins: Structure, Function and Bioinformatics.

In this tutorial you will start with a synthetic human fragment variable (Fv) sequence from AMA-II and use it to create a 3D antibody model, and optionally assess the quality of the model versus an X-ray crystal structure. With the large number of known antibody Fv and fragment antigen binding (Fab) structures, and the high degree of structural conservation, antibody structures are modeled using homology modeling methods. A typical workflow to model an antibody Fv or Fab region is to first model the framework from known antibody template structures and then refine the complementarity determining regions (CDRs) using additional templates when necessary. In this tutorial the following tasks are covered:

The templates selected for the framework and loops may be different depending on the version of the antibody database. The details of this tutorial may not match what you observe. However, it does cover the steps for using the tools and describes which aspects of the results are important.

* Identifying structural templates

* Modeling the antibody framework

* Modeling antibody loops

* Aligning the model to an X-ray crystal structure (optional)

The first few steps in this tutorial of annotating the antibody sequences are not strictly necessary in the creation of the antibody homology model. However an analysis of the sequence is useful to see the structural elements of your antibody to be modeled. The Annotate Antibody Sequence protocol identifies and annotates domains and CDRs of antibody sequences using several pre-computed Hidden Markov Models (HMMs).

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | MA5_H.bsml and MA5_L.bsml files in separate windows. Close the DS Welcome page if it is open to make room and select the MA5_L Sequence Window to make it active. Open the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel and click Annotate Antibody Sequence . Check that the Input Sequences parameter is set to MA5_L:All . Leave the parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete in the foreground.

The Sequence Window is updated and a Sequence Annotation Window automatically opens after the calculation completes. The blue colored carets in the Sequence Window indicate this sequence has been identified and annotated as a variable light chain, with the CDR loops highlighted with bold pink colored font. The Sequence Annotation Window shows the domains and loop regions, with the same coloring. If you select a loop in the Sequence Annotation Window the corresponding residues are selected in the Sequence Window, and vice versa. The Report available in the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer tabulates this information.

Right-click in the Sequence Window ruler and select Residue ID to display the sequence numbering based on your chosen annotation method (in your case this is IMGT). This is particularly useful if you are changing from one method to another.

Go to the MA5_H Sequence Window . Click Annotate Antibody Sequence from the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel again. Check that the Input Sequences parameter is set to MA5_H:All . Leave the parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete in the foreground.

In this second sequence the green carets indicate that this has been identified and annotated as a variable heavy chain, with the CDR loops highlighted with bold red font. Notice that the H3 loop (labeled as heavy_cdr3_imgt in the Sequence Annotation Window), which plays a particularly important role in antigen specificity, is ten residues long.

You will now identify suitable framework template structures that you can use to model your antibody sequence. Based on the same HMM models used in previous steps to annotate your input sequence, the input VL and VH domains are matched to the corresponding template sequences provided with Discovery Studio . If your input is a Fab region, CL and CH1 domains will be matched to the corresponding templates as well.

From the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel click Identify Framework Templates . Set the Light Chain Sequence parameter to MA5_L:MA5_L . Set the Heavy Chain Sequence parameter to MA5_H:MA5_H . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run.

When finished, the final dialog and the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 25 templates have been identified.

Click the Report button on the dialog.

The report includes four tables summarizing the templates identified. The first lists the top template for the overall input sequence and the light and heavy chains individually. The best hit for the overall sequence may not be the best hits for the individual chains, so the ranking and similarity of the individual chain hits are also shown for the overall hit.

The remaining three tables list the top template hits for the overall sequence and for the light and heavy chains, sorted by percentage sequence similarity. For hits with identical sequence similarity, the percentage sequence identity and then the resolution of the corresponding structure are used as secondary sorting criteria.

There are two common methods for building antibody models: a chimeric method and a single template method. In the chimeric method, different templates are used for the light and heavy chain and an overall interface template is required to define the relative orientation of the individual domains. A chimeric template is built by structurally superimposing the light chain template onto the light chain domain of the interface template and the heavy chain template onto the heavy chain domain of the interface template. The superimposed light chain template and heavy chain template are merged into one structure, which results in the chimeric template for modeling. The advantage of a chimeric template is that it can use the best available templates to model structural details of the light and heavy chain domains, while preserving the overall orientation of the domains specified by the interface template. The drawback to the chimeric method is that basing the spatial orientation and interaction of two chains from two different proteins on that of a third known complex may not be accurate. Whether you use a single template or the chimeric template often depends on the sequence similarity of your input sequence to the overall interface template and the individual light and heavy chain templates. The similarity of the CDR regions also plays an important role when choosing templates.

In this tutorial you will use the single template method, where a single reference template is used to model the antibody.

Template 4M6M_LH is the best matching template shown in the Best Matching Templates summary table and is the first entry in the Overall Templates table, with a similarity and identity of 100%. This is the self hit. 
For the purpose of this tutorial, the self hit is excluded from the framework modeling step.

The second and the third best hit in the Overall Template table are 4WUU_DE and 3MLW_LH. The latter has a similarity of 96.1%, an identity match of 84.9% and a resolution of 2.7 Å.

Click twice on the Identity (%) column header in the Overall Templates table (second table) to sort in descending order.

The second best template is now 2XWT_BA with a similarity of 94.4%, an identity match of 89.4% and a resolution of 1.9 Å. If you sort the templates by the Similarity (%) (including CDRs) and Identity (%) (including CDRs) properties, you will notice that 2XWT_BA is a better hit than 4WUU_DE or 3MLW_SH. The Organism property reports that this is a human antibody, which is suitable for a synthetic human Fv sequence. You can set the Identify Framework Templates parameters to pre-filter the identified templates to only include those that match an organism name or NCBI taxonomy ID, or have a resolution better than a desired value for X-ray structures.

The greatest variability in antibodies is found in the CDRs that form the antigen binding sites and define the specificity of the antibody. The percentage similarities and identities of your templates, excluding and including the CDRs, are reported to help you compare the results. As expected, the percentage values including the hypervariable CDRs are lower than when these regions are excluded. Studies have shown that CDRs are sometimes oriented by the framework and choosing a template that better accommodates your CDRs reduces the risk of losing affinity and decreasing stability [Honegger et al., 2009] . You can also choose to include CDR regions from the sequence similarity calculation used to rank the templates by setting the Exclude CDR Regions parameter to False when running the Identify Framework Templates protocol.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the output for the Identify Framework Templates protocol and click the Overall Framework Hits Alignment link.

This opens a Sequence Window with the aligned sequences for the hits listed in the table. Compare the H3 loop for both 2XWT_BA and 3MLW_LH (alignment index 213-232) with your sequence. Notice that the loop in 2XWT_BA is more similar to the query sequence in length.

Return to the report and click 2XWT_BA in the Name column of the Overall Templates table (second table). Click 3MLW_LH .

A new Molecule Window named Overall Framework Hits opens with the two templates you have selected. These structures have been prepared from the RCSB, with only the required domains used and superimposed so that no further preparation is required. Notice that the biggest structural difference is the H3 loop. The Molecule Window is linked and interactive with the Sequence Window named OverallHits you have previously opened, so you can make selections in one or the other and see the corresponding sequence or 3D structure highlighted.

Based on this examination of the templates and comparison of the X-ray structure resolutions, you will now use the 2XWT_BA template to build your antibody structure. It has high sequence similarity and identity, similar H3 loop length compared to 3MLW_LH, and the structure is well resolved with high resolution.

Close the Identify Framework Templates report window, the MA5_L and MA5_H annotation windows, and the OverallHits sequence window.

In this part of the tutorial you will use the Model Antibody Framework protocol to build a homology model for your antibody Fv based on its sequence. This protocol can also be used for Fab antibodies.

From the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel click Model Antibody Framework . Set the Light Chain Sequence parameter to MA5_L:MA5_L . Set the Heavy Chain Sequence parameter to MA5_H:MA5_H . Set the Interface Template parameter to Overall Framework Hits:2XWT_BA_FV . Set the Number of Models parameter to 3 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 3 models have been built.

If you had wanted to use the chimeric method to build your antibody model then you would additionally specify a Light and Heavy Chain Template; their domains are superimposed onto the corresponding domains in the Interface Template and used to construct the chimeric framework template. The Interface Template determines the overall orientation of the domains in the model.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. In the report, click the View Results button.

The Report lists the three models that have been built, sorted by ascending PDF Total Energy, PDF Physical Energy, and DOPE Score for each model. Smaller PDF energy indicates that the model satisfies the homology restraints better. A lower DOPE Score also indicates a better model. These properties are also available for sorting and filtering in the Molecule tab in the Data Table View of the Molecule Window that opens. A Sequence Window with your models aligned to the template also opens.

In the Hierarchy View, turn on the visibility for the second and third models by clicking on the check box of those models.

You can see that the models are all very similar with minor differences in the loops.

Back in the Hierarchy View, turn on the visibility for the template, and turn the visibility off for all models except the first model.

Notice how structurally similar to the template your models are.

For a more detailed visual analysis of the structural differences between the models, use Display Style and set the Atom tab to Line, colored by Element, and the Protein tab to Ca wire, colored by Secondary Type.

Close the Model Antibody Framework Report , the Overall Framework Hits Molecule Window and the Sequence Windows .

In this tutorial you will use the first model to further model the important CDR loops.

The selectivity of antibody binding with an antigen is determined by the CDR loops on the variable domains of the antibody. Each of the variable domains, VL and VH, have three hypervariable loops, L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, and H3, that form the antigen binding site. In this part of the tutorial you will use the Model Antibody Loops protocol to identify templates for the CDRs in your antibody structure and build models for these loops using these templates.

From the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel click Model Antibody Loops . Set the Input Protein Molecule parameter to the top model from your Model Antibody Framework results. Set the Number of Models parameter to 1 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run. Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that one model has been built.

The Model Antibody Loops protocol uses HMMs to identify variable antibody domains and corresponding CDR loops in your antibody structure and performs a similarity search against pre-compiled antibody database to identify the three most suitable templates for each CDR loop. A sequence alignment is created that aligns each loop template to the corresponding CDR loop region of your original antibody structure. MODELER is then used to generate homology models of the structure based on the hits.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report.

The report has tables for each CDR region that list the loop residues and identified templates with the template loop scores. Because the antibody structure has multiple chains, the loops are listed for each chain. You can see three templates for each loop as this is the default value for the Maximum Templates per Loop parameter.

The tables also report the resolution, similarity, identity, and organism of the templates identified and used in the loop building.

(Advanced) If you want to explicitly determine which templates to use to build each loop, set the Build Models parameter to False , and then use the sequence alignments and superimposed templates and structures provided to build your own loops using the Build Homology Models protocol. See the "Selecting specific templates to rebuild CDR loops" section in Model Antibody Loops .

In the report, click the View Results link.

The opened Molecule Window contains the original antibody structure, the model that were built, and all the templates that were used. Each structure has a corresponding (and linked) sequence in the Sequence Window that also opens.

Go to the Sequence Window . Right-click in the Sequence Window ruler and choose Residue ID .

In the Molecule and the Sequence Window, the CDR model just built with _M.M000# extensions in the name is followed by the framework model MA5_L_MA5_H_M000#. The CDR model sequence is aligned in the framework region with the framework model and de-aligned in the CDR regions. The CDR loops are only aligned and modeled by the identified loop templates.

Notice the VL_LAMBDA_CDR1 loop beginning at SER27. The sequences for templates 4M6M_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR1, 5OCC_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR1 and 5USH_E_VL_LAMBDA_CDR1 are aligned to the CDR model sequence with the hit loop aligned and other loops completely shifted. The next loop VL_LAMBDA_CDR2 beginning at GLY56 has the sequences for templates 4M6M_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR2, 4M1D_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR2 and 4M1D_M_VL_LAMBDA_CDR2 aligned to the model sequence.

Because one template structure may be used to model more than one CDR loop, the template will appear as multiple entries in the Sequence Window if this occurs (each with a corresponding structure in the Molecule Window). Each entry is named by the template domain name appended by the CDR number. Notice that template 4M6M_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR2 is used to model the CDR2 loop in addition to the CDR1 loop.

Go to the Molecule Window that corresponds to the Sequence Window. In the Hierarchy View select the first model, right-click and choose Show Only . Turn on the visibility for 5OCC_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR1, 5USH_E_VL_LAMBDA_CDR1, and 4M6M_L_VL_LAMBDA_CDR1 . Click on the arrow next to Display Style on the Standard toolbar and select the last pre-set display style (protein displayed as line, and ligands as ball-and-stick). Expand the first model in the Hierarchy View and then expand the CDR Loops group in this first model. Select the VL_LAMBDA_CDR1 group. Right-click in the Graphics View and click the Fit to Screen icon.

Notice the template structures used to model the CDR1 loop. The alignment of these structures in the Molecule Window is generated using the sequence window alignments.

There are numerous ways that homology models can be analyzed, including scrutinizing the PDF Total Energy, PDF Physical Energy and DOPE scores; running the Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) protocol to calculate the compatibility of each residue in a sequence with its predicted 3D environment; and studying Ramachandran plots. However, you will often find that the first model will be the best compromise of multiple elements considered in model building.

In this optional part of the tutorial you will use the protein superimposition tools to compare the final antibody model you have built and refined to a high-resolution X-ray Fv crystal structure of your sequence (PDB ID: 4M6M).

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | Ab05.pdb file. From the previous Molecule Window with the Model Antibody Loops protocol results, select the first model and copy and paste it into the Ab05 Molecule Window. Click the arrow next to Display Style on the Standard toolbar and choose the first pre-set display style (protein displayed as ribbon). Click in the Molecule Window to deselect the model. From the Macromolecules | Superimpose Proteins tool panel click Create... next to Sequence Alignment.

This opens a Sequence Window for your two structures and automatically opens the Align Sequences protocol.

Leave all the parameters set to their default values and click Run .

A pop-up dialog will report the sequence identity (99.6%) and similarity (99.6%) for the structures. The Molecule Window remains the active window.

Click OK to close the results dialog. From the Macromolecules | Superimpose Proteins tool panel click Superimpose , and then Show Report .

The antibody model will be aligned to the X-ray crystal structure in the molecule window, and a Superimpose by Alignment report opens reporting the Cα atom RMSD of approximately 0.9 for the 227 residues compared to the built model to the X-ray structure.

Close the report window.

Notice biggest structural difference in some of the loops of the superimposed structures in the Molecule Window are VL_LAMBDA_CDR3 and VH_CDR3.

Go to the Ab05 Sequence Window . From the menu bar, choose Edit | Select... . Set Residue Property: Secondary structure to Sheet . Click OK. Right-click in the Sequence Window and choose Extend Aligned Selection . Click the Ab05 Molecule Window tab to make it active. From the menu bar, choose Structure | RMSD | Biopolymer Structures... . Set the Reference molecule to Ab05 . Select the model you have built for Calculate RMSD for molecules . Select the Selected residues option. Select the C-Alpha checkbox and deselect the Main-chain checkbox under Amino acids, and click OK.

An RMSD report opens and reports a lower Cα atom RMSD for the residues forming the sheets in the structures. This indicates how well the antibody framework was modeled, versus the more flexible CDRs.

Make the Ab05 Molecule Window active. Click CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View. Expand the built antibody model in the Hierarchy View and then expand the CDR Loops group. Select the VH_CDR3 group. Right-click in the Ab05 Sequence Window and choose Extend Aligned Selection . Make the Ab05 Molecule Window the active window again by clicking on the tab. From the menu bar, choose Structure | RMSD | Biopolymer Structures... . Set the Reference molecule to Ab05 . Select the model you have built for Calculate RMSD for molecules list. Select the Selected residues option. Select the C-Alpha checkbox and deselect the Main-chain checkbox under Amino acids, and then click OK.

The RMSD report that opens shows the Cα atom RMSD for the H3 loop. In this case, since one of the templates 4M6M_LH is a self hit, the RMSD for the loops is low. However, in most cases, the H3 loop is the most flexible region of the antibody and may result in higher RMSD compared to other parts of the model. Sometimes an ab initio refinement method is used to refine the H3 loop. The ab initio Loop Refinement protocol uses the LOOPER algorithm to optimize the structure of any loop region, based on systematic conformational sampling of the loop backbone and CHARMm energy minimization. Loop refinement becomes more difficult as the loops become longer, especially for those longer than 12 amino acids.

You may want to now return to modeling the antibody framework and try generating a model using the chimeric approach, or 
use the Antibody Modeling Cascade which automates the model building.

#### Further information

Macromolecules tools Annotate Antibody Sequence Identify Framework Templates Model Antibody Framework Model Antibody Loops

# Assigning forcefield types

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_assign_ff_type_protocol.htm

## Assigning forcefield types

Time: 25 minutes

### Introduction

In molecular mechanics simulations, an essential step is to first assign a forcefield to the input molecule. The Discovery Studio client uses a charmm-style residue topology file (RTF)
to match a residue to its corresponding template in the forcefield. The match is performed by comparing the residue
name and atom name from the input structure to the residue template in the RTF file. In the case of biopolymers which 
consist of well-defined monomers in a linear form, such as a protein or nucleic acid, this task is relatively straightforward.

However, residue names and atom names are much more variable for other types of molecules, including carbohydrates, lipids, 
and small molecule ligands. Additionally, each of the supported forcefields may include some residue patches to allow
variations of the residues. A typical example is the use of a patch to define the connection between
different carbohydrate monomers to form either linear or branched connections. The client typing only allows a limited
number of patches to be applied, such as those related to capping of the termini of protein chains or nucleic acid chains.
Other types of patching are not supported by the client typing methods.

Most of the Discovery Studio forcefields, including charmm19, charmm22, and charmm27 mainly support the standard biopolymers
and work well with the client typing mechanism. Additionally, the client can also automatically estimate atom types and 
parameters for CHARMm forcefields where they are missing from the forcefield.

The charmm36 forcefield supports additional functional forms that are not suitable for the client typing method. To support these moieties, the Assign Forcefield protocol works by matching each residue to its template structurally. It also recognizes where residue patches need to be applied to match the structure and applies them automatically. The assigned forcefield types are saved in the molecule DSV format so that they are automatically used in subsequent simulation calculations.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to apply the charmm36 forcefield to a few different inputs, including a protein with a ligand
and a protein with carbohydrates. For advanced users, you will also learn how to include user-defined residue patches and parameters 
that are missing in the existing charmm 36 forcefield.

* Applying charmm36 to a protein that contains a retinol molecule

* Applying charmm36 to a protein with bound carbohydrate moieties

* Typing an unnatural amino acid using a customized patch and parameters

As this protocol uses structure mapping to find a matching template in the forcefield, you need to make sure that the structure is complete and has the correct bond order, formal charge, and so on. However, residue names and atom names do not need to match.

Choose File | Open URL... from the menu bar and type 1RBP in the ID field. Click Open .

This opens a human serum retinol binding protein in a new Molecule Window. It contains a retinol molecule as the ligand.

Choose Macromolecules | Prepare Protein | Clean Protein from the tool panel. Click Show Clean Report to see what clean actions have been taken.

The Complete Residues section should report that A:ASP175 has been patched for backbone and side-chain.

In the Hierarchy Window, select the Ligand Groups and then click to focus on the retinol ligand.

The double bond perception is incorrect for the retinol structure, and must be modified before the structure can be typed.

In the Molecule Window, select a bond and type 1 to change it to a single bond or type 2 to change it to a double bond.

Alternatively, you can use Scripts | Structure Editing | PDB Ligand Bond Orders to automatically apply bond orders from PDB ideal ligand definitions.

The final structure of retinol should have five conjugated double bonds:

Retinol with atom numbering

Now choose Simulation | Change Forcefield | Assign Forcefield from the toolpanel. Make sure Input Molecule is set to 1RBP:1RBP and Forcefield Name is set to charmm36 . Click Run to start the job.

The template library will be saved on the server and a later run will take significantly less time.

After the job finishes successfully, the molecule window will be updated automatically.

You can inspect the Residue and Atom tabs of the data table. The ForcefieldTemplate property for the retinol ligand residue RTL183 should have a value of RTOL and all atoms should have a ForcefieldType value assigned.

You can now optionally run Calculate Energy using the typed structure.

* If the data table is hidden, press Ctrl + T to turn it on.

* If you use the Apply Forcefield command with the charmm36 forcefield, an error message would have indicated that your structure could not be typed with that forcefield and that no matching template could be found for the retinol ligand.

* If you had not corrected the topology of the retinol ligand, the protocol would have returned an error that a template was not found, and the ForcefieldTemplate property would show a ‘?’ value.

Next you will try to type a full length antibody structure with carbohydrate moieties.

Close all open windows. Choose File | Open URL... from the menu bar and type 1IGT in the ID field. Click Open .

This structure does not require any cleaning steps before being typed. You can try the Clean Protein action, but no modification will be performed if the defaults are used.

Choose Simulation | Change Forcefield | Assign Forcefield from the toolpanel. Make sure Input Molecule is set to 1IGT:1IGT and Forcefield Name is set to charmm36 . Click Run to start the job.

The Molecule Window will be updated automatically when the job finishes. You can inspect the Residue and Atom tabs of the data table. The ForceFieldTemplate for each of the mannose (MAN) residues in the Residue tab is assigned as AGLC which stands for α-glucose. 
This is because α-mannose has the same structure as α-glucose except the stereochemistry. The protocol 
ignores stereochemistry in structure matching. This is consistent with the charmm36 forcefield, which treats carbohydrates with different stereochemistry in the same way and assigns them the same atom types and parameters. The protocol has applied the appropriate patches based on the connectivity of the carbohydrates and these are listed in the residue Patch property.

If you use the Apply Forcefield command with the charmm36 forcefield in this case, there would be estimated parameters for the carbohydrates rather than the published charmm36 parameters.

The next example shows how to use a custom RTF and parameter file to type a structure with an unnatural amino acid.

Close all open windows. Choose File | Open URL... from the menu bar and type 4GES in the ID field. Click Open . Choose Macromolecules | Prepare Protein | Clean Protein from the tool panel. Click Show Clean Report to see what clean actions have been taken.

It should contain the following actions:

* Alternate conformations of 10 residues have been deleted.

* Backbone patched for B:SER65 , Side-chain completed for B:ASP190 and B:HIS231 .

* 1 terminal residue(s) adjusted.

Close the clean report. Press Ctrl + T to show the data table. In the Residue tab, click on the first cell of the first line to select residue 0WZ151 , and then click to focus on it. Press Ctrl + D to open the Atom Display Style dialog. Change the display style to Stick and click OK to dismiss the dialog.

Residue 0WZ151 is an unnatural amino acid, a tyrosine derivative. The standard charmm36 forcefield does not have a residue definition for this. You will have to use a custom patch to modify the TYR to allow it to be matched.

Choose Simulation | Change Forcefield | Assign Forcefield from the toolpanel. Make sure Input Molecule is set to 4GES:4GES and Forcefield Name is set to charmm36 . Expand the Advanced parameter group. Click the Custom RTF File parameter, and then click the button. On the File Open dialogue, navigate to Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | PYZ.rtf , and then click Open . Repeat for the Custom Parameter File parameter and use file Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | PYZ.prm . Click Run to start the job.

The Molecule Window will be updated automatically when the job finishes. You can inspect the Residue and Atom tabs of the data table. The ForceFieldTemplate for 0WZ151 is assigned as TYR with a patch of PYZ .

The custom RTF and parameter files are examples that should not be used for production. You can open these files in a text editor to inspect the content. For more information on how to make your own custom RTF and parameter files, see Forcefield Development .

If your molecular system includes carbohydrates, lipids, or non-standard amino acids, and you want to use one of the charmm22, charmm27, or charmm36 forcefields, this protocol allows you to easily type the system using the published forcefield parameters rather than using non-validated approximations.

# Creating pharmacophore queries

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_basic-pharmacophore.htm

## Creating pharmacophore queries

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

Discovery Studio provides several methods for creating pharmacophore models:

* Automatically create a model from a receptor-ligand complex using the Interaction Pharmacophore Generation protocol.

* Automatically create a model from a set of ligands using the 3D QSAR
Pharmacophore Generation or Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol.

* Enumerate a collection of pharmacophore features from ligand(s) using the Feature Mapping protocol and then manually generate a pharmacophore from a
subset of features.

* Use the Interaction Generation protocol to generate a collection of pharmacophore features in an active site of a protein.

Additionally, you can use the Edit and Cluster Features tool to selectively
display, cluster, and edit a set of pharmacophore features.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to build a basic 
pharmacophore starting from a single conformation of a ligand. The following tasks are covered:

* Opening and viewing a ligand

* Adding pharmacophore features using ligand atoms

* Adding location constraints to the pharmacophore features

* Adding a shape constraint

In this lesson you will build a pharmacophore starting with the X-ray 
structure of staurosporine complexed with Cyclin-Dependent Protein Kinase 2 (CDK2). The PDB code for this ligand-protein complex is 1AQ1. The file was 
downloaded from the PDB web site and the ligand was extracted and exported 
to 1aq1_lig.mol .

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | 1aq1_lig.mol .

This opens 1aq1_lig.mol in a Molecule Window. Typically, only the Data Table View is displayed when opening small molecules. Since interaction with the molecule is required for adding pharmacophore
features, you will need to ensure the Graphics View and Hierarchy View are displayed.

From the menu bar, choose View | Graphics , and then View | Hierarchy .

You can add pharmacophore features based on selected ligand atoms
by using one of the following methods:

* Choose Structure | Query Feature... from the menu bar.

* Use the Query toolbar.

* Use the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Manually tool panel.

Both enable appropriate options based on the type of atom(s) selected. This tutorial demonstrates the Query toolbar.

From the menu bar, choose View | Toolbars | Query .

This displays the Query toolbar:

You will use several buttons from this toolbar to add hydrogen bond 
acceptor, donor, and hydrophobic features based on atoms in staurosporine. 
The following illustrates the desired pharmacophore features:

First, add the hydrophobic features.

In the Graphics View , select the methyl carbon (atom C7). In the Query toolbar , click the Point Feature button .

This places a selected hydrophobic feature at the methyl carbon.

It is easy to change the type of this
feature if desired. With the feature still selected, right-click in the 
Graphics View and choose Attributes of Point... . Select
an appropriate Type to 
change it. For example, you could choose Hydrophobe_Aliphatic to change this feature to a Hydrophobic Aliphatic feature.

In the Graphics View , select all the heavy atoms in one of the aromatic rings (atoms C25, C26, C27, C28, C29, C30). Click the Point Feature button to add a hydrophobic feature.

Notice that the type is automatically set to Hydrophobic Aromatic. 
Change this to a generic Hydrophobic group.

Right-click in the Graphics View , and choose Attributes of Point... . Set the Type to Hydrophobe . Repeat the previous step for the other aromatic ring (atoms C15, C16, C17, C18, C19, C20).

Add the hydrogen bond acceptor features.

In the Graphics View , select the double bonded Oxygen (atom O24). Click the Acceptor Feature button on the Query toolbar. With the feature selected, right-click in the Graphics View and choose Attributes of Acceptor... . Set the Orientation to First Lone Pair and click OK .

If none of the choices give you the right
location for the projection point, you can change the projection point to 
free and put the point wherever you want by selecting it and dragging it.

Add the hydrogen bond donor features.

In the Graphics View , select the Nitrogen atom N22. Click the Donor Feature button . Repeat the previous step for the Nitrogen atom N34.

So far in this tutorial, pharmacophore features have been added 
based on the atoms of a ligand.
However, you must add some type of constraints to define the relative
location of the features. Without constraints of some kind, this query
will map any ligand that has three hydrophobic, one acceptor, and two
donor groups no matter where they are in space. Typically, location
constraints are used to define pharmacophore features. Roughly speaking,
a location constraint ensures that a matching atom will be in the tolerance
sphere of the corresponding feature. You can add location constraints 
to individual features or to all features.

In the Hierarchy View , select the QueryRoot node to select all of the pharmacophore features. From the Query toolbar , click the Location Constraint button .

You can also set location constraints for selected features by choosing Structure | Query Feature... from the menu bar, and then choosing Location from the Feature list.

The pharmacophore you created in the previous steps is a valid 
pharmacophore and can be used, as is, in several of the Pharmacophore
protocols that use a pharmacophore as input. However, you may want 
to add steric information to the pharmacophore to make it more selective.
You can do this using two different methods:

* Select atoms that are regions
that ligands atoms are forbidden to go and add excluded volumes using
the Exclusion Constraint button . For example, you could import the PDB code, select atoms on the protein that are within a certain distance of the ligand, and add excluded volumes.

* Convert the ligand molecule to a shape using the Shape Feature button on the Query toolbar.

In the Hierarchy View , select the 1aq1_lig node to select all of the atoms in the ligand. From the Query toolbar , click the Shape Feature button .

This adds a shape to the pharmacophore. A ligand will match all 
features of the pharmacophore if a matching atom is found in the right
location for the hydrophobic, acceptor, and donor features and if the overall
shape of the molecule after being aligned is similar to the
staurosporine shape:

# Creating homology models from a protein sequence

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_build_homology-model.htm

## Creating homology models from a protein sequence

Time: 1 hour.

### Introduction

Homology modeling is the most reliable computational method for predicting protein
structure from its sequence when templates with sufficient sequence homology are available. This typically involves several steps, including:

* Identifying templates using sequence similarity search methods BLAST or PSI-BLAST

* Aligning and superimposing the templates using structure alignment methods

* Aligning the model sequence with template sequences using sequence alignment methods

* Creating a model using MODELER

When identifying the templates and aligning the model sequence with the template sequences, 
the strategy used depends on the similarity between the model sequence and the templates:

* When high homology exists between templates and model (typically
sequence identity above 60%), BLAST can easily identify the correct template and simple 
multiple sequence alignment between the model sequence and the templates works well.

* When the sequence similarity is not very high, but still well above the twilight zone,
(typically between 25% and 60% sequence identity), BLAST can still effectively identify
the correct templates. However, simple multiple sequence alignment may not produce the
best alignment for model building. The sequence alignment can be improved by creating 
sequence profiles using homologous sequences from a non-redundant sequence database. This is
probably the most common workflow and this tutorial will show you an example of how
to use this approach.

* When the sequence similarity is low between model sequence and template (below 25%
sequence identity), an iterative searching method (PSI-BLAST) should be used to identify 
the templates and sequence profile should be used in aligning the sequence with the templates.

In this tutorial, you will use an extracellular amylase protein to create a homology
model using the second approach mentioned above. The following tasks are covered:

* Identifying templates

* Aligning the model sequence to templates

* Building a 3D model using MODELER

* Assessing the validity of the 3D structure

The first step in building a homology model is to identify one or more templates 
from known protein structures based on sequence similarity. The sequence similarity
searching program BLAST is commonly used for this purpose, which searches against 
a sequence database constructed from proteins deposited in the PDB repository. Although two 
sequence databases, PDB and PDB_nr95, are available, it is common to search against 
the non-redundant sequence database PDB_nr95 to find the templates.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | P41131.fasta .

The P41131 sequence is opened in a Sequence Window.

You will now search the PDB_nr95 database using the BLAST Search tool.

Open the Macromolecules | Search Sequences by Similarity tools and click BLAST Search... to open the BLAST Search dialog. Click the Input Sequence parameter and choose P41131:P41131 .

The name of the Input Sequence is a combination of 
the name of the Sequence Window, P41131, and the name of the sequence in that window, P41131.

Click the Input Database parameter and
choose PDB_nr95 .

This specifies that the PDB_nr95 database, non-redundant at
95% sequence identity, is to be used for the BLAST search.

The PDB_nr95, PDB and Swiss-Prot 
sequence databases are installed with the DS Server installation.
To use other sequence databases in BLAST searches, you would need
to install these databases prior to running the protocol.

Click Run and wait for the job to finish.

When the job completes, the sequences found by the BLAST search are automatically displayed in a BLAST Window . A message box indicates the number of hits found e.g. "P41131 found 66 BLAST hits".

The details of number of sequences and hits found will change due to updates to the PDB_nr95 database.
Using different parameters or the PDB database will also produce different results.

Dismiss the message box. In the BLAST Window , click the Table View tab at the bottom of the window.

The Table View displays the hits, with one line per sequence.

In Discovery Studio , gray cells cannot be edited.

The hits are
initially ranked according to the E-value (the probability of a
gapless alignment sequence occurring by chance alone), with the
best, lowest value first.

Click the Map View tab.

The Map View displays the coverage of the hits in a map, with
one line per sequence. The bars are colored according to the bit
score of the hits (with above 400, red, being the best hits). The
query sequence, P41131 in this case, is displayed at the top of
the Map View represented as a line 443 residues long.

You can hover the cursor over a hit on the Map View to display the
following:

* description of the database sequence

* sequence accession number

* organism

* start and end position of the query sequence

* start and end of the database sequence of the hit

* length of the hit

* scores for the hit

When a database sequence matches the query sequence in multiple regions (multiple
hits), the matches are displayed as different bars in the same
line (i.e., one line per sequence). Select any hit in the
Map View to select the corresponding row in the Table View.

Use the mouse wheel to zoom in on the Map View. If your mouse has no wheel, you can choose View | Transform | Zoom In from the menu bar.

This allows you to see the residue display on the ruler at the
top of the window. You may have to zoom in several times to see
the residue display.

The order of
the hits in the Map View is the same as in the Table View, with
initially the best hits colored orange and appearing at the top
of the view.

In this tutorial, you will create a 3D model of the protein
sequence P41131. To achieve this, one or more suitable homologs or templates
must be found. An ideal homolog covers the entire sequence
length, has a fairly high sequence identity, and has a good
E-value (< 1 x 10 -5 ). This limits the number of
qualifying candidates obtained from the BLAST Search run.

It is often desirable to choose multiple templates if the templates
all have similar homology to the query sequence, but are not highly similar to 
each other. They usually have high structure similarity at the core, but
may have different length for some of the loops and different
loop conformation. The query sequence may align best to one template in
one loop region and another in another loop region. Therefore, by using multiple 
templates it will be possible to model each part of the structure using the best 
template for that region.

Click the Blast Window to make it active. Click the Map View tab. Hover the mouse over each of the orange bars representing homologs which cover most of the target length, and check that they have an appropriately low Expect value. While pressing and holding SHIFT, click these hits to select them all. Right-click and choose Load Structure and Alignment .

This opens a Molecule Window named from the top selected hit, which in the version of the database used to create this tutorial is 1ig94, and a Sequence Window named P41131(1).
The Molecule Window has structures for each selected homolog along with any ligands and waters. The Sequence Window
has the sequence alignment between the query sequence P41131 and the selected templates 
produced by the BLAST program.

Click the P41131(1) to make it active. From the menu, choose Sequence | Secondary Structure | Visibility... to open the Secondary Structure Visibility dialog. Check Kabsch-Sander and PDB and click OK .

This allows you to view the PDB and Kabsch-Sander secondary structure
of the templates under their sequences in the Sequence Window. Red
bars indicate alpha helices and blue arrows indicate beta strands.

Examine the alignment between the query sequence and the templates.
There are about 50 residues at the C-terminal end that are not aligned. This
alignment is not suitable for homology modeling and sequences should be
realigned. The next step shows you how to align the model sequence to
the templates.

The following approaches can be used when aligning a model sequence to templates:

* Align the model sequence to templates directly by aligning multiple sequences.

* Align template structures using structure alignment, and then add the model sequence to
the template alignment by aligning a sequence to a sequence profile.

* Use structure alignment to align template structures, create a sequence profile for the model
sequence, and then align the sequence profile to the structure alignment by aligning two profiles.

In the following step, you will use the Align Sequence to Templates tool to
align the model sequence with the selected templates. You can use any of the approaches discussed 
above. In this example, you will use the last approach for the following reasons:

* Sequence conservation and structure conservation are often slightly different, which leads to different results.
For homology modeling purposes, it is best to align the template structures based
on their structure similarity before they are aligned to the query sequence.

* As discussed in the introduction, when aligning a sequence to templates, better alignment can be
obtained by creating a sequence profile and aligning the sequence profile to the pre-aligned structures.
A good sequence profile is a sequence alignment that contains a large set of homologous, but non-redundant
set of sequences. You can obtain the sequence alignment by searching the Swiss-Prot
sequence database using the BLAST search method, and then aligning the sequences with the multiple sequence alignment method.

Click the Sequence Window labeled P41131 (1) , which contains the template sequences. Open the Macromolecules | Create Homology Models tools and click Align Sequence to Templates... to open the Align Sequence to Templates dialog. Set Input Model Sequence to P41131-(1):P41131 . Set Input Template Structures to 1g94A::All to ensure that all template structures 
loaded from the previous step are specified. Set Create Sequence Profile to True . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job completes, the alignment between the model sequence and the 
templates opens in a Sequence Window labeled P41131_templates, as well as a Molecule Window 1g94A (1) containing the superimposed template structures. A message box shows the sequence identity and similarity of the aligned model and template sequences.

Click the Report button in the message box to display a table of the pairwise backbone RMSD between all superimposed templates and number of 
overlapping residues.

In this section, you will build a 3D model of your original protein
sequence using the alignment you just created and the template structures.
You will also compare the model structure with the
template and evaluate the model score generated by the MODELER
program.

Click the Molecule Window labeled 1g94A (1) to activate it.

Note that the Molecule Window and Sequence Window P41131_templates are linked.

Open the Macromolecules | Create Homology Models tools and click Build Homology Models... to open the Build Homology Models dialog. Click the Input Sequence Alignment parameter
and choose P41131_templates:All . Make sure all template structures are selected in the Input Template Structures parameter. Set Input Model Sequence to P41131 . Click the Number of Models parameter and change the value to 2 . Click the Optimization Level parameter and choose Low .

Changing the Optimization Level parameter 
from the default setting allows the protocol to run faster, but will produce less accurate models.

Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job finishes, a Molecule and Sequence Window open showing two models. The Molecule Window shows the PDF Total Energy of the best model.

Click Report on the message box.

In the Summary section of the report that opens, review the scores of all the 
models. The models are sorted
by PDF Total Energy . A model is better optimized against the homology restraints
when it has lower PDF Total Energy and models with the least violation to homology
restraints are preferred. However, if the models all have similar PDF Total Energy, you can use the DOPE score based on statistical
potential as a measure of the model quality (the lower the score, the better the model).

Click the Molecule Window labeled P41131 to 
activate it.

The best model structure, defined by the PDF Total Energy ,
is shown with the templates in the Molecule Window.

The ranking of the model may change depending on the version of MODELER used
or templates selected so may be P41131.M0001 rather than P41131.M0002.

The model is superimposed to the templates, and the display style set to 
C-alpha trace. The templates and any other models are hidden. You can identify areas of the structure with large violations of the homology restraints by examining a line plot.

Click the AminoAcid tab and scroll towards the right side of
the table to the PDF Total column. Click the PDF Total column header
to select it. Choose Chart | Line Plot from the menu bar.

This opens a line plot containing the PDF Total value for each residue in the sequence. You can select peaks from the plot and then examine the selected residues in the Molecule Window.

Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if it is not open. 
Expand the top molecule P41131.M0002 and expand Modeler Groups under it.

Four groups are shown: Identical , 
which consists of residues having identical type to one of the templates, and Non-Identical , which consists of residues different from the template residues
based on the input alignment. If there are residues not aligned to any of the template residues, they are placed in groups named Insertion<i> (<i> = 1,2,...), where each insertion consists of consecutive residues
that are not aligned to any template residues.

Use the same method to examine model P41131.M0001.

The model structure can be further evaluated using the Verify
Protein (Profiles-3D) protocol, which assesses the compatibility
of the 3D structure of a protein model with the sequence of
residues it contains.

Select molecule P41131.M0002 and then
open the Macromolecules | Create Homology Models tools and click Verify Protein (Profiles-3D)... to open the Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) dialog. Click Input Protein Molecules and select P41131:Selected . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job finishes, a message box shows the protein score.

The message indicates the per-residue scores have been added to the AminoAcid tab in the Data Table.

Activate the Molecule Window labeled P41131 .

The Molecule Window has been updated with results from the Verify Proteins job.
The structure is now displayed as a C-alpha trace with its
color based on the Verify score (the higher the score, the
better the structure). The color varies from blue to white to red,
with blue corresponding to high scores, white to average scores, and red
to low scores. 
Be aware that the color of the ribbon is relative
to this particular model. You are looking for significant
variations from the remainder of the ribbon.

In the Data Table View , click the Molecule tab and scroll to the end
of the table to the Verify Expected High Score , Verify Expected Low Score , 
and Verify Score columns.

If the Verify Score result of the
model protein is higher than the Verify Expected Low Score value, 
then the model is of acceptable quality. The closer the Verify Score result is to the Verify Expected High Score value, the better the
quality of the model.

Click the AminoAcid tab and scroll to end of
the table to the Verify Score column. Click the Verify Score column header 
to select it. From the menu choose Chart | Line Plot .

This opens a plot containing the score for each amino acid residue in the model structure. Note
the low scoring region is at the C-terminal end of the protein.

Arrange the Line Plot Window, Molecule Window, and the Sequence Window 
side-by-side. Click and drag around the low score peak to select the residues with the lowest scores in the Line Plot.

The selected residues are highlighted in the Graphics View of the Molecule Window and the Sequence Window, 
allowing you to see the low scoring region of the alignment.

## Ligand docking with CDOCKER

Time: 15 minutes.

### Introduction

CDOCKER is a powerful CHARMm-based docking method that has been shown to generate highly accurate docked poses [Wu et al., 2003] .

In this tutorial, a random conformation of the native ibuprofen ligand is docked backed into the COX-1 
receptor binding site.
The native x-ray pose is overlaid to the docked poses for comparison.
This tutorial covers:

* Preparing Inputs

* Launching CDOCKER

* Analyzing CDOCKER Results

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions| 1EQG.dsv .

The protein opens with the site sphere at the center of 
the receptor active site. See the Preparing a Receptor Binding Site tutorial for more information on how to create a binding site sphere.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools. Click Show/Hide Residues Outside Sphere and Show/Hide Sphere . From the menu bar, select View | Transform | Fit To Screen or click Fit To Screen on the View toolbar to center and zoom into the binding site.

This will hide the residues outside the binding site sphere and the sphere itself, which will make viewing the results easier.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions| 1EQG-ibuprofen-conf.sd .

This opens a random conformation of the ibuprofen structure.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools and click Dock Ligands (CDOCKER)... to open the Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) dialog. Ensure that the Input Receptor parameter is set to 1EQG:1EQG . Set Input Ligands to 1EQG-ibuprofen-conf:All Click the Input Site Sphere parameter and choose 
the coordinates of the sphere from the dropdown list.

To ensure the docked poses are diverse we will set an RMSD threshold of 0.5 Å.

Expand the Top Hits parameter
and set the Pose Cluster Radius to 0.5 . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

The results are automatically opened in a Molecule Window that contains the
docked ligand poses and the 1EQG receptor.

Before you step through the docked ligand poses, you will use the Receptor-Ligand Interactions tools to
add monitors to visualize non-bond interactions.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools and click Ligand Interactions .

This displays the non-bond interactions between the receptor and the ligand as well as any intramolecular interactions in the ligand.

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions toolpanel to navigate through the ligands.

Notice that the non-bond interactions are updated when stepping through the docked poses. Only the residues that have an interaction with the ligand are displayed.

See the Analyze Ligand Poses tutorial for more information on how to analyze the docked poses for non-bond interactions.

In the next step, you will compare the docked ligands to the native ibuprofen X-ray ligand structure.

Expand the job in the Jobs Explorer , and then click the Docked Ligands link.

This opens the docked ligands in a new Molecule Window.

Press CTRL+G to open the Graphics View. Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1EQG-ibuprofen.sd . In the Data Table , navigate to the last entry (Ibuprofen) and set the Visibility to True . Lock the visibility by setting Visibility Locked to True .

This will lock the visibility of the native ligand when stepping through the docked poses.

Select the Data Table and press CTRL+Down repeatedly to step through the docked ligands.

Notice that the top scoring CDOCKER pose, with the highest -CDOCKER_ENERGY value,
aligns very well with the native X-ray structure.

# Creating charts

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_charts.htm

## Creating charts

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

The Molecule Window provides powerful features for visualizing 3D molecular structures
and related property data. In addition to this, there is a range of viewers in
which you can chart molecular data properties. The following types of charts are supported:

* Line Plot

* Point Plot

* 3D Point Plot

* Heat Map

* Bar Chart

* Histogram

All charts are fully interactive. You can select data in a chart, and the same data will be selected in other windows. As multiple charts are generated from a data set, selections in one chart update the parent data
and any other dependent charts.

In this tutorial, you will use a sample set of drug molecules with precalculated properties to generate a Point Plot, a 3D Point Plot, and a Heat Map:

* Create a simple Point Plot

* Create a 3D Point Plot

* Create a Heat Map

From the menu bar, choose Edit | Preferences... . Open the Molecule Window | Import preferences page. Set Number of molecules to show when opening files to 0 and click OK . Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Quick Start Tutorials | NCI Drug Sample.sd .

This file contains a set of 2000 ligands, with several precalculated properties. In addition, a principal 
component analysis has been performed on the data, and the first eight principal components (PCATempModel_PC1, ..., PCATempModel_PC8), explaining 75% 
of the variation in the molecules, are included in the data file.

The data set will open in the Data Table View of the Molecule Window.

From the menu bar, choose Chart | Point Plot .

This opens the Choose Plot Axes dialog. This dialog allows you to select the variables
to be plotted. The X-axis variable is selected with a radio button in the X column. Multiple Y-axis variables can be
selected using check boxes in the Y column.

You can also select the X-axis variable and the Y-axis variable or variables to be plotted by selecting the corresponding columns in the Data Table View. The plot will then be generated directly when choosing Chart | Point Plot from the menu bar.

Choose Plot Axes Dialog

For Choose Plot Axes click the radio button in the X column next to
the Minimized_Energy row. Select the Molecular_Volume check box in the Y column. Click OK .

A new window is created containing the point plot.

Drag the plot window tab to the right side of the application
workspace so that it displays next to the Molecule Window.

All of the standard viewing controls can now be used to interact with the plot. For example, you can zoom in and out by turning the mouse wheel. Alternatively, to translate
the plot, press the wheel and drag the plot within the axes.

Alternatively, if you do not have a mouse wheel, use the tools on
the View toolbar to perform these actions.

Clicking Home from the toolbar allows you to go back to the original settings.

Once a chart is generated, the appearance is easily customized using the Display Style 
dialog.

From the toolbar, click Display Style... .

Press CTRL+D or right-click in 
the Point Plot Window and choose Display Style... . You can also 
choose View | Display Style from the menu bar.

Point Plot Window Display Style dialog

On the Display Style dialog, click the General tab and, with the Show chart title check box checked, set the chart title to "Volume versus Energy". Click the Advanced tab and select the Filled Circle shape from the Point marker list. Click the Axis and Font tab and ensure that the Show legend check box is checked. Click OK to update the display.

The chart now shows the point plot with title and legend displayed, and uses filled circles for shapes.

From the toolbar, click Display Style... . On the Display Style dialog, click the General tab and uncheck the Show chart title check box in order to turn off the chart title display. Click the Advanced tab and select the Circle shape from the Point marker list. Click the Axis and Font tab and uncheck the Show legend check box in order to turn off the legend display. Click OK to update the display.

The chart now shows the point plot without displaying title or legend, and uses hollow circles for shapes.

A common use of the charts is to identify specific points of interest in the original data (e.g., clusters of related properties or individual outliers). Selections made in the plot are also reflected in the Molecule Window, and vice versa. Once the 
selection has been made, the corresponding molecule can be quickly located using the filtering functionality 
in the Molecule Window.

Locate the outlier data point at the top of the plot with a molecular volume of ~950. Hover over the point to 
get more information about its value. Select the point using the Select tool. Select the Molecule Window . In the Data Table View , click Show selection tool.

The 3D structure of the selected molecule is now displayed in the Graphics View.

Click on the blank area in the Graphics View to deselect the molecule. In the Data Table View , right-click and choose List Only Visible Objects .

The Data Table View is now filtered and only the single visible molecule is shown. At this point it is easy 
to inspect properties or view the molecular structure in the Graphics View.

The range of chart types supported in the application makes it possible to view different sets of variables 
simultaneously. In this tutorial's data set, a principal component analysis has been performed, and the eigenvalues for the different eigenvectors are stored in the file.

Turn off the filter in the Data Table from the previous step to ensure all molecules are listed.

Click the Molecule Window . In the Data Table View , right-click and deselect List Only Visible Objects .

All molecules are now listed in the Data Table View.

From the menu bar, select Chart | 3D Point Plot .

This opens the Choose Plot Axes dialog.

In the Choose Plot Axes dialog, choose PCATempModel_PC1 for the X axis and PCATempModel_PC2 for the Y axis. For the Z axis, choose PCATempModel_PC3 and select Molecular_Volume in the Color by Data Series dropdown list. Click OK .

A 3D point plot is generated and displayed in a new window. This plot is fully interactive with the original data and
with the previously generated Point Plot. This plot can be rotated as well as scaled and translated.

Drag the 3D Point Plot Window tab beneath the Point Plot window. Locate the outlier point in the corner opposite the origin. Hold the mouse over the point; the tooltip indicates "22.2606 : 11.9444 : -0.000104738 : 956.28"; select it.

Another useful chart type provided in Discovery Studio is the Heat Map. Heat maps are a valuable way of inspecting 
multiple sets of variables to identify patterns. Any set of tabular data can be plotted as a heat map whether it comes 
from a molecule file or a comma separated value file.

From the menu bar, choose Window | Close All . Do not save anything when prompted. From the File Explorer , open Samples | Tutorials | Quick Start Tutorials | 1fvv_conformations.sd .

This file contains a set of conformations and associated RMSD values for the conformations relative to the original 
ligand structure.

From the menu bar, choose Chart | Heat Map .

You will generate a heat map to show the different RMSD values for some of the conformations.

Choose conformation for the Y axis. In the Choose Plot Axes dialog, click the check box for conformation 1 for the X axis. Scroll down the list to conformation 145 and hold SHIFT while clicking the check box for it. Click OK .

Click on individual cells to select the corresponding molecules in the Molecule Window.

# Generating conformations using the toolbar

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_conf_toolbar.htm

## Generating conformations using the toolbar

Time: 30 minutes

### Introduction

Conformation analysis of small molecules is required in many situations. Discovery Studio provides an intuitive and interactive method for exploring conformational space of a set of molecules with flexible controls for search methods, selecting rotatable bonds, and changing torsion grids. For instance, you can select a particular rotatable bond and generate a set of conformations by changing the torsion angle of that rotatable bond, and then view the conformation energy profile. You can also view all of the generated conformations in a Molecule Window to check the overall conformation coverage.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to use the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel to generate conformations. The following tasks are covered:

* Searching for conformations

* Reviewing the conformations in the Molecule Window

* Searching conformations with selected rotatable bonds

* Showing all conformations in the Molecule Window

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Benzenesulfonamide.dsv .

This will display the benzene sulfonamide in the Molecule Window. With the ligand now visible in the Graphics View, the next task will be to use the Search Small Molecule Conformations tools to analyze the ligand.

Open the Small Molecules | Search Small Molecule Conformations tools and click Generate Conformations... to open the Generate Conformations dialog.

There are six conformation search methods in Discovery Studio : FAST, BEST, CAESAR, Systematic Search, Random Search and Boltzmann Jump. Accept the default setting, and click Run to begin the conformation search.

By default, the job will run in foreground. However, if this is a long-running job with many molecules, you can move the job to the background.

When the search is complete, the generated conformations are automatically opened in a Molecule Window:

To visually check the overall conformation distribution of a molecule, it is convenient to use the Molecule tab of the
Data Table View. For example, you can review the conformations using the navigation controls to compare the different variants
with the lowest energy conformation.

In the Data Table View , double click the Relative Energy column to ensure that the conformations are sorted by energy. Check both the Visible and the Visibility Locked checkbox in the first row to make sure it remains visible. Use the Previous and Next .

The Previous and Next buttons display each conformation individually while the lowest energy conformations remains visible. This way you can compare the conformations.

Discovery Studio provides a convenient way to do conformation search around the selected rotatable bonds. This applies to the torsion search methods, including CAESAR, Systematic Search, Random Search and Boltzmann Jump.

This will display the benzene sulfonamide in the Molecule Window.

With the molecule visible in the Graphics View, you can select the 
bonds for torsion search in the Conformation generation.

Select two rotatable bonds near the center of the molecule. From the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel, click Add rotatable bonds .

In the Graphics View, torsion monitors are added to the selected rotatable bonds. Note that torsion monitors are not added to any of the selected bonds that are not rotatable.

If some torsion monitors are removed from the Molecule Window by editing, make sure that the ROTBONDS properties of the modified molecules are updated. To update them, click Add Rotatable Bonds after editing.

From the Search Small Molecule Conformations panel, click Generate Conformations , which opens the Generate Conformations protocol dialog. Set Conformation Method to CAESAR and 
set Energy Threshold to 100 . Click Run .

Torsion monitor constraints are only used by the following conformation methods: CAESAR, Systematic Search and Random Search and Boltzmann Jump.

When the search is complete, the generated conformations are automatically opened in a Molecule Window.

You can review the overall conformation distribution of a molecule by showing all conformations in the same window.

Click the top navigation button , to make the first conformation visible. Right-click in the Graphics view and choose Show All .

This shows all conformations in the same window:

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_create-binding-site.htm

## Preparing a receptor binding site

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

The receptor binding site is important for docking and scoring applications.
It defines a region in a protein cavity where binding interactions can occur.

For most protocols, a sub-section of the binding site is defined by a sphere that encloses part of the binding site volume.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to find binding sites and define a search sphere. This tutorial covers:

* Finding a Binding Site from receptor cavities

* Defining a Binding Site Sphere from a selection

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1kim.pdb .

The protein opens in a new Molecule Window.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools. If not already defined, click Define Receptor and set it to 1kim .

This defines the receptor molecule as a receptor. You can now run the site finding algorithm.

From the Tools Explorer, under Define Site tools group, click From Receptor Cavities .

Green grid points now show the location of the first receptor binding site, which is engulfed by a red site sphere.

Click either Show Previous Site or Show Next Site arrow
from the Display tools group to navigate through the sites.

The binding site changes as you click through the navigation buttons.

Now you will learn how to define a site sphere from a residue selection.

If the Hierarchy View in the Molecule Window is not visible, press Ctrl+H . In the Hierarchy View , expand 1kim .

Now there are nine sites created from the receptor cavities.

Select all the sites and press Delete on the keyboard to remove them. Expand chain A and select residues HIS58 and VAL70 . From the Tools Explorer, click From Current Selection under the Define Site tools group.

A binding site sphere is created that engulfs the two selected residues.

You can use any atom or object selection to define a binding site sphere. 
You can change the radius of the search sphere and the size of the binding sites 
using + Expand or - Contract in the Define and Edit Binding Site | Change Site Size tools.
