# Creating a tool panel

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_create-tool-panel.htm

## Creating a tool panel

Time: 20 minutes.

### Introduction

The Discovery Studio Client offers considerable flexibility for configuring and customizing
the user interface. New toolbars and script commands can be easily created to provide easy access to
commonly used features.

The most flexible parts of the interface for providing custom access to functionality are tool
panels. The Discovery Studio Client provides a wide number of tool panels that host pre-configured
functionality. Most of the tool panels contain features that can be used to perform advanced analysis
tasks on different types of data.

However, you can easily create new tool panels designed to satisfy specific tasks. One use for this
customizability is to create a tool panel that can aggregate all the steps required for a particular task and provides instructions to walk the user through the task. In the
following tutorial you will create a tool panel that exposes all the steps necessary to generate a set of
conformations, calculate their RMSDs relative to the starting molecule, and plot the results.

The tool panel that is generated in this tutorial is also
available in Samples | Customizations | GenerateCompareConformations.panel.

In this tutorial you will learn how to:

* Create a new tool panel

* Exporting and importing a tool panel

### Creating a new tool panel

Choose the My Tools tool set from the toolbar.

In the next step, you will create a new tool panel named "Generate and Compare
Conformations".

There may be a delay while the Tool Panel Editor dialog opens, as it updates the list of available protocols. This could be significant if you are connected to a remote server. The following example does use a protocol, but in other cases you could disconnect from the server to avoid the delay.

Right-click on one of the tool panels and choose Insert New Panel... .

This opens the Create Tool Panel... dialog which will prompt you for a name.

In the Create Tool Panels dialog, type
"Generate and Compare Conformations" for the name.

Once you create the new tool panel, the Tool Panel Editor dialog will automatically open, allowing you to add tools and text.

In this tutorial, you will create a tool panel that can be used to
generate a set of conformations and then compare the reference molecule with the conformations by
computing the RMSDs:

* Generate conformations

* Visualize conformations

* Calculate RMSDs

* Display RMSDs in a chart

In the Tool Panel Editor dialog, drag a Header to the left pane.

This inserts an html snippet that creates a header element.

Double-click the html snippet and add "Generate Conformations" between the <b> tags.

Drag a Static text item to the left pane.

Enter some additional text to explain the purpose of the step.

Double-click the snippet and enter the following text between the <font>
tags: "Select a conformational search method and then select Generate Conformations to start the search."

Now add a button to access the Generate Conformations protocol.

Open Protocols | Discovery Studio | Small Molecules | Conformations node. Drag the Generate Conformations tool to the left pane. Click OK .

The new tool panel appears:

Next you will reopen the Tool Panel Editor dialog and add two additional groups to view and analyze
the conformations.

Right-click the tool panel and choose Edit... . Drag a Header to the left pane. Double-click the html snippet and add "View Conformations" between the <b> tags. Drag a Static text item to the left pane. Double-click the snippet and enter the following text between the <font>
tags: "Select Show All to make all conformations visible. Select Tile Molecules in View to arrange the molecules and compare them." Open View node. Drag the Visibility | Show All and Tile Molecules in View tools to the left pane.

Repeat the previous steps to add a group for calculating the RMSD.

Drag a Header to the left pane and name the section "Calculate RMSD". Drag a Static text item to the left pane and add the following text: "Select the original molecule and choose Set Reference. Select All Atoms to compute RMSDs." Open the Structure | RMSD node. Drag the Set Reference and All Atoms tools to the left pane.

Repeat the previous steps to add a group for plotting the data.

Create another header named "Plot Data" Add the following static text: "Use the point plot to compare the RMSD and Relative Energy values."

You can increase the size of the Tool Panel
Editor dialog by clicking and dragging the bottom-right corner.

Open the Chart node. Drag the Point Plot tool to the left pane. Close the dialog and review the Tool Panel

It is possible to share your new tool panel with other users by exporting it to
a .panel file that they can import.

In the Tools Explorer, right-click Generate and Compare Conformations and choose Export... . Navigate to a writable folder. In the File name: input box type GenerateCompareConformations .

Click Save .

The .panel file is now saved and can be shared with other users.

# Fragment docking using De Novo Evolution

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_denovo-evolution.htm

## Fragment docking using De Novo Evolution

Time: 15 minutes.

### Introduction

Structure-based design is an established method for using the structures of biological targets to discover novel ligands.
Examples of successful applications are abundant in the literature, particularly for HIV protease inhibitors.
The increasing understanding of target receptors through experimentally determined structures of protein-ligand complexes
makes structure-based design accessible to all modelers.

The De Novo design tools employ the Ludi algorithm [Böhm, 1992a] , which provides tools for suggesting new templates and modifying existing scaffolds in the search for
new and potentially improved ligands. Robust design tools allow you to simulate screening before performing experimental assays, which helps to
prioritize lead candidates before synthesis or purchase. De Novo design can facilitate the exploration of libraries of commercially available ligand scaffolds
or the development of existing ligands by scoring candidate derivatives in the receptor binding site.

In this tutorial, you will use a De Novo design method to investigate the inhibition of the cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2), a positive regulator of eukaryotic cell cycle
progression. The structure that will be used for this tutorial, 1fvv_protein.dsv, is supplied with your Discovery
Studio installation and was retrieved from the Protein Data Bank.

You will try to improve the binding of the ligand to the receptor by finding suitable fragments which increase binding. 
The De Novo Evolution creates novel ligands from the starting scaffold by successively covalently 
linking new Ludi fragments to the 
scaffold core. The binding is iteratively improved to obtain new ligands from a starting scaffold.
You will use the Full Evolution mode to link a maximum of up to three fragments to the scaffold core.

This tutorial covers:

* Preparing De Novo Evolution

* Launching a De Novo Evolution run

* Analyzing De Novo Evolution results

Choose File | Open... from the menu and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1fvv_protein.dsv .

The protein opens with site sphere at the center of 
the receptor active site.
See the Preparing a Receptor Binding Site tutorial for more information on how 
to create a binding site sphere.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools. Click Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres and Show/Hide Site Spheres .

This hides residues outside the binding site sphere and the sphere itself.

Choose View | Transform | Fit To Screen from the menu bar or click on the View toolbar to center and zoom into the binding site.

Next we open the ligand scaffold.

Choose File | Open... from the menu and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1fvv_ligand.dsv .

The ligand carbon atoms are colored green for better viewing.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Fragment Based Design tools and click De Novo Evolution... to open the De Novo Evolution dialog. Ensure that the Input Receptor parameter is set to 1fvv_protein:1fvv_protein . Set Input Ligand Scaffold to 1fvv_ligand:1fvv_ligand . Set Input Fragment Libraries to the fragment_link.inp link library. Click the Input Site Sphere parameter and choose -9.42369, 207.623, 113.547, 8 from the list.

The De Novo Evolution protocol uses a pre-generated library of fragments 
for docking. These libraries can be generated using the De Novo Library Generation protocol. 
A library always consists of two files: the structure file, and the target file. 
Although both need to be present, you only need to specify one. 
The second library file is located automatically by the protocol.

To decrease the run time for this tutorial, you will now change the default parameters.

Expand the Advanced | Fitting group and set Maximum RMSD to 0.3. Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job finishes, the receptor and all the ligands open
in a new Molecule Window.

From the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tool panel click Ligand Interactions to monitor the receptor-ligand non-bond interactions. Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions tool panel to navigate through the remaining ligands.

Notice that the input scaffold ligand has grown at different positions.

You can
easily see where the fragments were added by superimposing the initial scaffold structure.

Choose File | Insert From | File from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1fvv_ligand.dsv . In the Data Table View , set the Visibility Lock to Yes for 1fvv_ligand .

Notice that the table contains GENERATION and FAMILY columns, which indicates how many generations
or fragments were added, and how it ranked at each docking step.

For this tutorial, you ran the protocol in the Full Evolution mode. In this mode only one fragment is added at 
each generation. However, in Quick mode, multiple fragments are linked at each generation.
You can re-run the tutorial by setting the Evolution Mode to Quick and compare the results.

## Fragment docking using De Novo Link

### Introduction

Structure-based design is an established method for using the structures of biological targets to discover novel ligands.
Examples of successful applications are abundant in the literature, particularly for HIV protease inhibitors.
The increasing understanding of target receptors through experimentally determined structures of protein-ligand complexes
makes structure-based design accessible to all modelers.

The De Novo protocols employ the Ludi algorithm [Böhm, 1992a] , 
which provides tools for suggesting new templates and modifying existing scaffolds in the search for
new and potentially improved ligands. Robust design tools allow you to simulate screening before performing experimental assays, which helps to
prioritize lead candidates before synthesis or purchase. De Novo can facilitate the exploration of libraries of commercially available ligand scaffolds
or the development of existing ligands by scoring candidate derivatives in the receptor binding site.

In this tutorial, you will investigate the inhibition of the cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2), a positive regulator of eukaryotic cell cycle progression, using a De Novo Method. The structure file used for this tutorial ( 1fvv_protein.dsv ), is supplied with your Discovery Studio installation and was retrieved from the Protein Data Bank.

This tutorial covers:

* Preparing De Novo Link

* Launching a De Novo Link run

* Analyzing De Novo Link results

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1fvv_protein.dsv .

The protein opens with the site sphere at the center of 
the receptor active site.
See the Preparing a Receptor Binding Site tutorial for more information on how 
to create a binding site sphere.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools. Click Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres and Show/Hide Spheres .

This will hide the sphere and the residues outside the binding site sphere.

From the menu bar, choose View | Transform | Fit To Screen or click Fit To Screen on the View toolbar to center and zoom into the binding site.

Next, open the ligand scaffold.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1fvv_ligand.dsv .

The ligand carbon atoms appear green for better viewing.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Fragment Based Design tools and click De Novo Link... to open the De Novo Link dialog. Ensure that the Input Receptor parameter is set to 1fvv_protein:1fvv_protein . Set Input Ligand Scaffold to 1fvv_ligand:1fvv_ligand . Click the Input Site Sphere parameter and choose 
the coordinates of the sphere from the list. Set Input Fragment Libraries to the fragment_link.inp link library.

The De Novo Receptor protocol uses a pre-generated library of fragments 
for docking. These libraries can be generated using the De Novo Library Generation protocol.
A library always consists of two files: the structure file, and the target file. 
Although, both need to be present, you only need to specify one. The second library file is located automatically by the protocol.

Ensure that Link Points parameter is set to Use all hydrogen atoms .

All available ligand hydrogen atoms are potential targets for fragment linking. For this tutorial, you will change the default values to decrease the run time.

Expand the Advanced | Fitting group and set Maximum RMSD to 0.3 . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job completes, the docked fragments, ligand scaffold, and the receptor file open in a Molecule Window.

From the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tool panel click Ligand Interactions to monitor the receptor-fragment non-bond interactions.

Non-bond interactions will be displayed for the receptor and the ligand scaffold.

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions tool panel to navigate through the remaining fragments.

Notice that the non-bond interactions are updated when stepping through the fragments. Only the residues that have an interaction with the fragment are displayed.

The placement of the fragments can be further investigated by superimposing
the interaction map generated by the protocol onto the Graphics View ( Ludi.interactionmap.mol2 file in the Output Files section).

Notice that the terminal docked fragment atoms are aligned with the ligand scaffold hydrogens.
This indicates that the scaffold binding can be improved by covalently linking the docked fragments.

# Customizing an existing protocol

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_dev-client_append-min.htm

## Customizing an existing protocol

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

You can create and customize protocols with the combined capabilities of Discovery Studio and Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications .
Using Pipeline Pilot , 
you can access the individual DS/PP components and parameters directly, 
modifying and promoting parameters to the top level of the protocol, and publish the custom protocol for the use in Discovery Studio .

The Standard Dynamics Cascade (SDC) protocol is a Discovery Studio protocol. It runs a CHARMm simulation 
cascade including minimization and dynamics stages. In this custom protocol example tutorial, you will use Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications to customize the protocol by adding another pipeline that selects the N lowest potential energy conformations 
from the trajectory frames generated from the SDC protocol, minimize those conformations, and write them out to 
a .mol2 file.

* Opening a protocol

* Building a pipeline

* Setting parameters

* Promoting parameters

* Testing the protocol and publishing in Discovery Studio

Open Pipeline Pilot Client . In the Protocols tab, navigate to BIOVIA Discovery Studio | Discovery Studio | Simulation | Dynamics | Standard Dynamics Cascade . Double-click the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol to open it.

The Standard Dynamics Cascade (SDC) protocol is displayed in the workspace, shown as pipeline 1.

The remaining pipelines are used for adding a table to the report and are not required in this implementation. Select and delete them.

For this tutorial, insert a new second pipeline to select a number of low energy conformations from the MD trajectory file generated by the first pipeline (the SDC protocol), minimize those conformations, and write them out to a .mol2 file. The pipeline will look like the following after it is completed.

Switch to the Components tab in the Protocols Explorer. Open the Chemistry | Data Access and Manipulation | Readers | Discovery Studio folder. Double-click (or drag and drop) to open the DS Molecule Reader component into the workspace, it is shown as the first component of pipeline 2.

You should use the DS Molecule Reader component because this reader component includes the Read Conformations parameter that you can use to read the conformations of the .dsv file.

While still in the Components tab, search and double-click to open the Count and Index Data component to append to the pipeline. Start typing 'count' in the search bar at the top, and hit F3 key repeatedly until you see the Count and Index Data component. Double click it to add it.

It will be automatically connected to the DS Molecule Reader component.

Similarly, search and open the Top N Filter component.

It will be automatically connected to the Count and Index Data component.

Search and open the CHARMm Minimization component.

It will be automatically connected to the Top N Filter component.

Search and open the DS Mol2 Writer component.

It will be automatically connected to the CHARMm Minimization component.

This completes the second pipeline. Notice that three components are shown in red, which means required parameters have yet to be specified.

The rest of the tutorial steps involves editing the parameters in each component to specify appropriate parameter values, and promoting the parameters up to expose them at the protocol level.

Click the Update Discovery Studio File component in the workspace.

The purpose of this component is to update the .dsv file after the SDC run.

In the Parameters Explorer window, the Output File parameter is set to 
$(RunDirectory)/$(Input Molecule).dsv. This is the file path that you will use as the Source parameter for the DS Molecule Reader component.

Copy and paste this file path to the Source parameter of the DS Molecule Reader component. Open the Source parameter in the Parameters Explorer and set the parameter Read Conformations to True .

The following picture shows the parameters settings:

Click the next component, Count and Index Data .

This component will put a property named "Index" on the data stream to hold the data record count. The data record in our case is the frame number (conformation number) of the trajectory .dsv file. Nothing needs to change in this component.

Click the next component, Top N Filter . Enter the following in the Expression parameter: Property('Potential Energy') Specify a default value for Number to Keep of 10 .

This specifies that the Potential Energy property value will be used as criteria to select the data records sent out to the Pass port.

Change the Max or Min parameter to Min .

Now promote the Number to Keep parameter in this component to the top level of the protocol, so that the user can have access to change this parameter value at the protocol level.

Right-click on the Number to Keep parameter and select the Edit Component... command from the context menu.

This launches the Edit dialog:

Click the Number to Keep parameter and click the Promote Parameter button in this dialog.

This brings up the Promote Parameter to Parent dialog.

Click the OK button to accept the default parameter name. Click OK again to close the Edit dialog.

The Number to Keep parameter has been promoted to the parent protocol level.

Next, click the DS Mol2 Writer component. Enter the following for the Destination parameter: $(RunDirectory)/$(Input Molecule)_min.mol2

This specifies the .mol2 file name for saving the final minimized conformations.

Notice components are no longer colored in red, indicating that all required parameters are specified.

Click the white space of the protocol workspace.

The protocol level parameters currently are those parameters from pipeline 1 (the SDC protocol) and the parameter Number to Keep that was promoted from the Top N Filter component in pipeline 2. None of the parameters from the CHARMm Minimization component of pipeline 2 are promoted to the protocol level.

If you want the user to be able to access these parameters for this final minimization at the protocol level, you can promote the parameters in this CHARMm Minimization component to the top protocol level, with a different procedure for promotion.

Right-click on the white space of the protocol workspace and select Edit Protocol... .

This brings up the Edit dialog.

Click the Promote tab.

The top panel lists the parameters for the protocol, and the bottom panel lists the parameters 
from each component.

Click the Next>> button to navigate to the CHARMm Minimization component.

See that there are five parameters under the Minimization group parameter: Minimization Algorithm, Minimization Max Steps, Minimization RMS Gradient, Minimization Energy Change, Minimization Save Results Frequency. If desired, you could promote the whole parameter group, but in this case we will omit the last parameter for consistency with the existing Minimization options.

Select the Minimization Algorithm parameter and click the Promote button. In the dialog shown below enter a name for the parameter. As there is already a top-level 'Minimization Algorithm' parameter, change the name to Final Minimization Algorithm Click OK .

Similarly, promote the other parameters: Minimization Max Steps , Minimization RMS Gradient , and Minimization Energy Change , renaming each by prepending 'Final'.

Next you will create a new parameter called Final Minimization , where the Parameter type is set to Group Type , and then drag those promoted parameters into it.

Still in the Edit dialog, click the Parameters tab. Click the Add Parameter button. In the Add Parameter dialog, fill in the appropriate selection as shown in the picture below. Click OK .

In the Edit dialog, move up the Final Minimization parameter to beneath the Minimization2 group, and drag and drop those promoted parameters into it.

They may, by default, have been placed in the Minimization group.

When you select a parameter and drag it around, notice the horizontal bar that is displayed. It moves up and down as you drag an item in the list. Use it as a visual Indicator of where the item will be placed in the list when you release the mouse button. Parameter name may be highlighted when you drag an item up and down the list, when you release the mouse button when the parameter is highlighted, the parameter you are moving is placed as a child of that highlighted parameter.

You can use Pipeline Pilot Server Home Page > Help Center (User Resources) for online documentation. Search for 'parameter group' and read more details of the sections Parameter Groups, Dragging and Dropping to Group Parameters.

The following illustrates the new parameter grouping:

You can use the same procedures to promote other parameters in the CHARMm Minimization component to the protocol level.

In the Edit dialog, click the Help Text tab and enter text to describe how the protocol or component works. Click OK .

To test run a protocol from the Pipeline Pilot Client

Enter the required parameters and click the now active Run Protocol (green) button. If you want to save a working copy of the protocol .ppxml file to a local directory, use the File > Export Protocol command from the menu.

To publish the custom protocol in Discovery Studio

Choose the File > Save Protocol As command from the menu and use the Up One Level button several times to browse to your User Name folder. Name the protocol SDC with Final Minimization . Click OK .

This will save the protocol to your user protocols folder.

Start up Discovery Studio . Connect to the Pipeline Pilot Server server. If you are already connected, switch to the Protocols tab and press the F5 key or select Refresh from the context menu to refresh the view.

The new protocol should appear in your user folder in the Protocols tab and is ready to be used just like the other Discovery Studio protocols.

# Creating a custom protocol - Calculate Molecular Properties

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_dev-client_calc-mol-prop.htm

## Creating a custom protocol - Calculate Molecular Properties

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

You can take advantage of the combined capabilities of Discovery Studio and Pipeline Pilot to 
create and customize protocols. Using the Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications application, you can access the individual DS/PP components and parameters directly, modifying and exposing the 
appropriate parameters, and publishing the custom protocol for use 
in the Discovery Studio Client.

Accessing the Discovery Studio components through the Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications also makes it possible 
to combine several different steps into a single workflow. In this example, you will use the Search 3D Database component to extract the lowest energy conformation from a 
Catalyst database, and then use these structures to calculate some 3D molecular properties using the components 
in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol.

The Calculate Molecular Properties protocol in the General Purpose folder calculates 
various molecular properties ranging from traditional molecular descriptors, semi-empirical 
QM descriptors, and density functional QM descriptors, to user-built models. Some of these descriptors 
are two dimensional, but others are three dimensional descriptors. The input ligands for the protocol can be specified either from an open molecule window or from an external .sd file.

This tutorial illustrates how this protocol can be modified to use the lowest energy conformation 
from an existing Catalyst database. A Catalyst database is a multi-conformational 
database, which allows you to sort the compounds according to their energies and extract only the lowest 
energy conformation. These compounds can then be used as input for calculating molecular properties.

* Opening a protocol

* Replacing components

* Exposing parameters

* Ranking structures and retaining the lowest energy conformation

* Testing the protocol and publishing in Discovery Studio

Launch Pipeline Pilot Client and open the Protocols tab. Open BIOVIA Discovery Studio | Discovery Studio | Small Molecules | General Purpose | Calculate Molecular Properties .

Notice that the protocol consists of several pipelines 
and each pipeline consists of several different components and subprotocols. The components and subprotocols 
are labeled so they describe briefly their functions.

The first pipeline specifies the input ligand that will be used by the DS Ligand 
Reader component for the property calculation.

In this tutorial, you will modify the input ligands for the property calculation, so 
the modifications will occur in this pipeline.
The rest of the steps in this protocol will be unchanged.

You will use structures stored in a Catalyst database and extract the lowest energy conformation as input for the property calculation. To access data in a Catalyst database, you can 
use the 3D Database Search component, which will search and extract structures from a specified database using the catSearch program.

Open the Explorer Window for Components and open Chemistry | Pharmacophore | Database . Drag and drop the 3D Database Search component to the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol.

You can also type "3D Database Search" in the search box of the Explorer Window for Components as shown here.

In the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol, delete the DS Ligand Reader , Set Up Run and Add Error Message components. Replace them with the 3D Database Search component by connecting its green output port to the input port of the Count and Index Data component. Add a Create Empty Data component before the 3D Database Search component. This needs to be done because the 3D Database Search component has 
an input port, so data has to be sent to trigger it. Alternatively, you could select the component, 
right-click and choose Toggle Ports | Input to remove the input port.

Parameters must be promoted to the protocol level to be exposed to users who run the protocol from Discovery Studio .
Notice that there are no new parameters from the 3D Database Search component exposed to 
the protocol's top level for now. You must individually promote the parameters you want to expose.

Right-click on the workspace and select Edit Protocol... .

Click the Promote tab. The parameters from the protocol are listed
on the top panel, and the bottom panel lists the parameters from each individual component. Click Next to navigate to the 3D Database Search component.

Select the Input Database parameter, and then click the Promote button. Click OK .

To be able to search a subset of compounds from the Catalyst database and also specify the number 
of compounds to extract from the database, you need to add one more parameter. The Maximum Hits parameter will allow the user to enter the number 
of compounds returned from the database.

Expand the Limit Hits parameter to see the Maximum Hits parameter. Repeat the steps used to promote the Input
Database parameter to promote the Maximum Hits parameter. Click the Parameters tab. Click the Input Ligands parameter, and then click Delete (red cross icon) to remove it.

The Input Ligands parameter is no longer exposed.

Drag the Input Database parameter to the top of the other parameters.

This makes the Input Database parameter the first parameter in the list.

Drag the Maximum Hits parameter and drop it under the Input Database .

You could also drag it so it is a level below 
the Input Database parameter.

The protocol uses the Input Ligands parameter to name the output file, check for success, and write summary help. 
Since you have removed that parameter, you need to make changes to the components that rely on this name. You will change the output .sd file in the DS Molecule Viewer component at the end of the fourth pipeline, the Success? check in the 5th pipe, and the file name in the Generate DS Report in the 6th pipe.

Select the DS Molecule Viewer component and set the Output File Name parameter in the Advanced group to low_energy_confs_withProperties.sd . Set the Action parameter to Open in a new Window . Select the Success? filter component and set the Expression to FileExists(@'RunDirectory'."/low_energy_confs_withProperties.sd") Select the Generate DS Report component and set the File Name to low_energy_confs_withProperties.sd

If you run this protocol it its current state, it will only take 
one conformation of all the compounds from the database and 
return the calculated properties, but it will not select only the lowest energy conformation.

To add an option to consider only the lowest energy conformation, the protocol needs to extract all of the 
conformations contained in the database for each compound and sort them by energy and keep only the lowest energy conformation.

On the 3D Database Search component, set the Limit Hits parameter to First N and set the What to Output parameter to All Conformations .

This ensures that the Maximum Hits parameter works and all the conformations are extracted for each compound from the database.

To be able to rank the structures and retain only the lowest energy conformation, you need to add additional
steps after the Search 3D Database component before the data is passed to the Cache Writer component in this pipeline. As there are multiple conformations 
for each structure being extracted from the database, the first step is to group the molecules by 
"Name" using the Group Data by Tag component.

From the Component tab, begin typing "Group Data by Tag" to find this component quickly. Drag and insert it between the Search 3D Database component and the Count and Index Data component. Click the component and set the Group Using parameter to Name on the Parameters Explorer .

After grouping the structures according to name to process them, the structures are ungrouped and their energies compared.

Add the following components to the pipeline after the Group Data by Tag component: Ungroup Data , Conformation Generator , and Top N filter .

On the Conformation Generator component, set the Maximum Conformations to 0 .

This enables the protocol to access only the energies for each conformation but not generate any further 
conformations for the structure.

Check that the Discard Existing Conformations parameter is set to False .

The Top N Filter component can be used to sort the data records according to a 
specific property and pass only a set number of records at the top or bottom of the list. On the Top N Filter component in the Expression Line , you can specify the property on which to base the selection. In this case the Relative Energy value is used because when the relative energy of the conformation is 0, it is the lowest energy conformation.

These steps need to be carried out for each compound separately, so you must set them to "Run to Completion" in the RunTime Tab. This option causes the subprotocol to be re-initialized and executed in its entirety for each record.

Set the Expression parameter to RelativeEnergy . Set the Number to Keep property to 1 and 
the Max or Min parameter to Min . Select these three components, right-click and select Collapse to Subprotocol .

This groups the components into a single subprotocol, which allows you to use the RunToCompletion option in the RunTime Tab. Notice that all three components are now represented 
as a single icon.

Rename the subprotocol to reflect the tasks that it carries out: Compute and 
extract lowest energy conf. Click this subprotocol, and open the RunTime tab on the Parameters Explorer . In the RunTime Tab , set the RunToCompletion parameter to True - For Each Data Record .

After these changes the pipeline should look like this:

To test run a protocol from the Pipeline Pilot Client

To thoroughly test this protocol, you should run it in both Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications and Discovery Studio . To run 
the protocol in Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications you must specify a Catalyst database.

For the Input Database parameter, use the default DruglikeDiverse [5384 mol] .

This will search the DruglikeDiverse database, which is shipped with Discovery Studio .

For test purposes, reduce the Maximum Hits parameter to 10 .

Run the protocol.

To publish the custom protocol in Discovery Studio

Set the Maximum Hits parameter to the desired default value e.g. 300 instead of its test value. From the File menu, choose Save Protocol As command. Use the Up One Level button several times to browse to your User name folder. Name the protocol Molecular Properties Lowest Energy Conformation . Click OK .

This saves the protocol to your user protocols folder.

Start Discovery Studio . Connect to the Pipeline Pilot Server server. Open the Protocols Explorer and choose Refresh from the context menu or press F5 to refresh the view.

The new protocol appears in your user folder in the Protocols tab and is ready to be used like other Discovery Studio protocols.

You can also add this protocol to a tool panel to run the protocol interactively. See Tools Explorer for more information.

# Optimizing and running a docking validation for a virtual screening target

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_docking_opt.htm

## Optimizing and running a docking validation for a virtual screening target

Time: 30 minutes plus docking time

### Introduction

Docking is one of the most commonly used virtual screening methods and involves two separate steps:

* positioning ligands into a protein active site

* scoring and ranking these docked ligands

Both steps require some form of examination to determine the best parameters and scoring function for an individual protein target to maximize the probability of success. Optimizing and validating a docking method for a particular protein target can be done in a number of different ways and in this tutorial you will use a dataset of known active and inactive ligands to determine the best conditions before embarking on a larger-scale screening of unknown compounds.

CDOCKER [Wu et al., 2003] is a grid-based molecular docking method that employs CHARMm. Random ligand conformations are generated from the initial ligand structure through high temperature molecular dynamics, followed by random rotations. The random conformations are refined by grid-based simulated annealing and a final grid-based or full forcefield minimization with the rigid receptor. Poses are ranked by the CHARMm energy.

For virtual screening projects involving thousands to tens of thousands of compounds, CDOCKER is an excellent docking method. If you wish to screen hundreds of thousands of ligands or more, then the LibDock method [Diller and Merz, 2001] will be more suitable, as it uses a rapid hotspots matching algorithm to place the ligand in the active site. LibDock uses a Piecewise Linear Potential-like scoring function which is less accurate than CHARMm. The docking protocol you should use will depend on the scale of your virtual screening project and the computational resources available. However, the principles of optimization and validation detailed in this tutorial are the same, regardless of the docking method used.

In this tutorial the following steps are covered:

* Preparing the protein active site

* Optimizing the docking parameters and calculating X-ray RMSD

* Docking with a small validation set

* Scoring and ROC calculations

The PDB code for the epidermal growth factor receptor erbB1 protein-ligand complex used is 2RGP [Xu et al., 2008] . The sample file used in this tutorial was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared with the Prepare Proteins protocol.

In this first step you will define a binding site sphere which CDOCKER uses to first place the ligand conformation. This is an important step as a poor initial placement may mean that the docking does not reposition the ligand sufficiently to a good docking pose.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 2RGP_prep.dsv . Select the HYZ1 ligand in the second A chain in the Hierarchy View. Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel and click From Current Selection .

In this example a crystallized ligand makes it easy to define the binding site. If you do not have a protein-ligand complex, or you are exploring alternative binding sites then you can use the From Receptor Cavities functionality to identify other possible binding sites.

Some PDB files include active site definitions which can also be useful in defining the binding site, using the From PDB Site Records option.

Expand the Active Sites group and select the Active Site AC3 group.

You can see that nearly all of these residues are within the defined red site sphere. If there are important residues not inside, or very close to, the site sphere you may want to use another selection to define the binding site, or increase the binding site sphere radius.

If you have a small site sphere you can increase the radius of the search sphere using the + Expand button, as the radius of the sphere may affect the docking results due to the location of the energy grid.

Click Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres and then Show/Hide Site Spheres . Select the HYZ1 ligand again and press the Delete key. Right-mouse click and select Fit to Screen .

In this step of the tutorial you will try to select the best parameters to use for the virtual screening by docking the native X-ray ligand and determining how well you can reproduce the X-ray ligand pose. You will use a randomized starting conformation of the X-ray ligand structure which will act as an arbitrary starting point for an impartial docking. A more thorough way to optimize the docking parameters would be to dock a set of known active and inactive ligands for the protein target, as these would represent more than a single chemotype. However, this would be much more time consuming.

The default parameters for protocols in Discovery Studio are always a good starting point for your project. Typically you would run several jobs to optimize the docking parameters if the default parameters did not immediately give good results. One of the most commonly modified parameters to suit a virtual screening project is the Ligand Partial Charge Method parameter, and in this tutorial you will change this to better suit the 2RGP complex you are using.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 2rgp_random.sd . From the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tool panel click Dock Ligands (CDOCKER)... . Set the Input Receptor parameter to 2RGP_prep:2RGP and the Input Ligands parameter to 2rgp_random:All . The Input Site Sphere parameter will be automatically updated. Expand the Advanced parameter group and change the Ligand Partial Charge Method parameter to CFF . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background on the job dialog and wait for the job to complete.

The job should take a few minutes to run. The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 10 poses have been saved.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the Report in an HTML Window. Click View Results .

CDOCKER calculates an energy for each pose which includes an internal ligand strain energy and the receptor-ligand interaction energy. The docked poses are returned ranked by the negative of this energy (that is, -CDOCKER_ENERGY) to enable it to be used like a score where a higher value indicates a more favorable binding. The negative of the receptor-ligand interaction energy is also reported as -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY.

As a general rule, the -CDOCKER_ENERGY is most useful for comparing the multiple poses of a ligand due to the inclusion of the internal ligand strain energy, and the -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY more effective when comparing different ligands.

In the Data Table View, click the first navigation arrow to see the first docking in the Graphics View. Scroll through the ten docked poses. Right-click in the Molecule View and select Show All . Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and insert Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 2rgp_xrayligand.sd . Select 2rgp_xrayligand from the Hierarchy View and select Structure | RMSD | Set Reference from the menu bar. Select the first 2rgp_random pose and then SHIFT-select the last 2rgp_random pose. Select Structure | RMSD | Heavy Atoms from the menu bar.

In the 2rgp_xrayligand - RMSD Report you can see the root-mean-square-deviation of each pose from the X-ray ligand; these values are also added as a molecular property to each pose in the Molecule Window. Ideally, the top scoring pose should have the smallest RMSD value, and should be lower than the resolution of the crystal structure of 2 Å. However, if you examine some of the docked poses and the X-ray ligand pose more closely, you can see that the largest deviation in the structures is mainly in the piperidine substructure, which is also located at the solvent exposed portion of the binding site. The isotropic displacement (B-factor) values of the PDB X-Ray ligand in the complex are quite large for this piperidine substructure (>50), indicating that there is a high flexibility. The image below shows the PDB ligand pose colored by B-factor in the active site.

If your ligand is larger and more flexible than in this example you may find that increasing the Random Conformations and Orientations to Refine parameters is necessary to better sample the conformational space of the ligand and binding site. Increasing the radius of the site sphere may also help to expand the search space during docking. However, increasing those parameters will increase the docking time.

You may now want to repeat this docking with different parameters to see if you can improve the RSMD of the top scoring pose, which you can use for the next part of the tutorial, or continue with these new values for the next stage of your screening validation.

In the next part of the tutorial you will dock a small validation set of known active and inactive ligands to identify the scoring function(s) which best discriminate or prioritize the active ligands over the inactive ligands.

There are numerous chemical databases accessible online providing ligands for docking, including screening compounds available to purchase and ligands known to be active against a particular protein target. Decoy ligands are more commonly available than true inactive ligands, as data for the latter for a particular protein target is often not published. In addition, when inactive ligands are available there may be too few to constitute a sufficiently large dataset for validation. The active and inactive ligands in this tutorial come from the Database of Useful Decoys: Enhanced ( http://dude.docking.org/ ) [Mysinger et al., 2013] . A small diverse selection of 15 active and 45 inactive epidermal growth factor receptor erbB1 ligands was chosen for this tutorial.

The ligand preparation for docking is, unfortunately, not as simple as the protein preparation step and can be dependent on the source and quality of the ligands to be docked. The fundamental issue is identifying the most likely chemical state(s) of the ligand at physiological conditions. Ligands can be represented in multiple ionization, tautomeric and isomeric forms. Charged functional groups may either be ionized or neutral, and with multiple charged functional groups you may need several representations of how the ligand may reasonably exist when binding to the protein. Different tautomers have different charge and hydrogen bond distributions, and missing some tautomers may mean that you miss some important binding modes in docking. Some researchers choose to consider stereoisomers as different ligands, however, when working with racemic compounds you may prefer to consider the many stereoisomers of a ligand as different chemical representations of the one compound.

Exhaustively representing all of the chemical states of your ligands may drastically increase the number of ligands to dock. Using the Prepare Ligands protocol with default parameters on these 60 ligands will generate 414 presentations of the ligands. The different ionization states, tautomers and isomers of each ligand will retain the same name as the original ligand to simplify latter analysis. For a reasonable docking performance it is necessary to reduce the chemical representations and you may do this by modifying the parameters in the Prepare Ligands protocol. In this tutorial the ligands have already been prepared.

The Filter by SMARTS and Filter by Lipinksi and Verber Rules protocols can also be very useful in preparing a ligand library for docking by removing compounds that are not likely to be "drug-like" or "lead-like", and retaining those that have a higher probability of good oral bioavailability.

Open a new Molecule Window and insert Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | egfr_actives15.sd . Right-mouse click in the Data Table View and select Add Attribute… . Enter the attribute Control for Name and 1 for Value . Change the Type dropdown from String to Integer , and click OK . Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and insert Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | egfr_inactives45.sd . From the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tool panel click Dock Ligands (CDOCKER)... . Set the Input Receptor parameter to 2RGP_prep:2RGP and the Input Ligands parameter to Molecule:All . Expand the Advanced parameter group and change the Ligand Partial Charge Method parameter to CFF .

If you have appropriate hardware available you can parallelize the docking by setting the Parallel Processing parameter to "True" and specifying the number of processes you want to use. You may also want to adjust the Batch Size value to suit the number of processes you are using.

Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background on the job dialog and wait for the job to complete.

The job may take a while to run, depending on the number of processors you have available. When finished, the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer should report the number of poses which have been saved.

Select Window | Close All from the menu bar to close all the molecule windows. In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the Report in a HTML Window. Click View Results .

The second phase of any docking involves scoring and ranking docked ligands to determine those which will have more favorable interactions and higher binding affinity. No single scoring function is suitable for all protein targets, and before undertaking a larger-scale virtual screening it is necessary to select the scoring function(s) which best discriminates and prioritizes the actives from the inactive ligands for your docking project. There are numerous empirical and knowledge-based scoring functions available in Discovery Studio for this purpose.

From the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tool panel click Score Ligand Poses... . Set the Input Receptor parameter to 2RGP:2RGP and the Input Ligands parameter to 2RGP:All . Click on the button for the Scoring Functions parameter. Choose Ludi Energy Estimate 3 from the left hand column and click the >> button to select, click OK . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background on the job dialog and wait for the job to complete.

The job is short and will report the number of poses scored. The scores calculated are always reported as positive values to ensure that a higher score indicates more favorable binding.

Receptor flexibility is automatically included if the ligands are the result of a Ligand Minimization , Flexible Docking , or Dock Ligands (GOLD) protocol.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the Score Ligand Poses job and click the Scored Ligands link. Select Chart | Hit Rate Plot from the menu bar. CTRL-select the calculated scoring functions: -CDOCKER_ENERGY -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY -PLP1 -PLP2 -PMF -PMF04 Jain LigScore1_Dreiding LigScore2_Dreiding Ludi_3 Click OK .

This hit rate plot gives a qualitative indication of the performance of the scoring functions in ranking all of the poses of the actives in the docking. A better way to determine and compare scoring functions is to calculate Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves which show the fraction of true positive ligands versus the fraction of false positive ligands. For each scoring function, the highest scoring pose for each ligand is used for the calculation of the enrichment of the actives, rather than all poses.

Return to the Molecule Window with the scored ligand poses and from the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties Ligands tool panel click Calculate ROC Curve... . Set the Input Ligands parameter to 2RGP-(1):All . Click the button for the Scores parameter grouping and select all of the available items except Control , POSE_NUMBER , and TopHits from the left hand column. Click the >> button to select and click OK . Choose Name for Group Using and Control for Control Property . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run .

The Advanced parameter grouping in the Calculate ROC Curve protocol allows you to set the total number of records and positives. This is in the event that if some of your ligands had fail to dock, the calculated ROC scores will be incorrect, as the number of records and actives are determined from the dataset.

The job is short and a Calculate ROC Curve report should open on completion. The results table lists the scoring functions and provides a quantitative area under the curve value and evaluation. A docking or scoring method can be evaluated by the area under the ROC curve (AUC). A value closer to 1 indicates good selectivity, whereas a value closer to 0.5 indicates random selection.

This analysis shows that the scoring function -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY, -PLP1, -PLP2, and LigScore2_Dreiding provide good ranking of the actives over the inactive ligands and you may want to choose one of these scoring functions to prioritize ligands when screening datasets of unknown ligands.

At this point you can reasonably begin your larger-scale screening of unknown compounds, as you know which parameters are most suitable for your protein target, and you know which scoring function(s) to use to rank your compounds. To further help enrich the virtual screening results many modelers will also study the non-bond interactions which may be significant in driving ligand binding and distinguishing active ligands from inactive ones.

Discovery Studio includes simple and powerful tools to investigate non-bond interactions and you can learn more about them in the following tutorials:

Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating results

Analyze Ligand Poses

#### Further information

Receptor-Ligand Interactions tools Ligand preparation Using the Hierarchy View

# Calculating protein ionization and residue pK

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_electrostatics_pk.htm

## Calculating protein ionization and residue pK

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

Modeling of the protein ionization is important because the variation of protonation states of ionizable amino acid residues
at different solution pH can affect protein biological function, stability, solubility, and viscosity. 
The calculations of the protein ionization and residue pKas in Discovery Studio are based on a 
fast and accurate computational approach [Spassov and Yan, 2008] to pH-dependent electrostatic effects in protein molecules.

In this tutorial you will learn how to calculate the titration characteristics of a protein molecule and how to predict the pK values of the individual sites of titration on a lysozyme structure.
All calculations are carried out using Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK .

At a selected pH, the protocol also generates a structure where all acidic and basic atomic groups are protonated according to the 
predicted pKa values of each residue and the positions of all hydrogen atoms are correspondingly optimized. 
Optionally, the protocol creates a fully protonated structure with all hydrogen atoms added to the sites of titration. 
Instead of the original force field partial charges, the fully protonated acidic and basic groups are assigned
with mean atomic charges that are derived from the fractional protonation of the corresponding groups at the selected pH. 
The protonated structure represents a single protonation state with each titration site either protonated or deprotonated
according to the titration curve of the site at the selected pH, while the fully protonated structure represents 
the average properties of the protein charge multipole at the given pH.

Based on the fully protonated structure, the protocol calculates the pH-dependence of a number of average electrostatic properties, 
such as:

* Molecular dipole moment

* Net charge square

* Electrostatic contribution to the solvation transfer energy, ddGsolv, calculated as the difference between the 
solvation energies of the molecule embedded in the water solvent and in a condensed (crystalline) phase.

These properties are of interest to study the effect of the environment on 
the protein solubility, aggregation, and viscosity. For example, it is well known that the solubility is minimal and the viscosity increases at a pH close 
to the isoelectric point. The solubility increases sharply
with the net charge of the molecule due to electrostatic repulsion between molecules. However, the dipole moment, as a measure of the charge asymmetry, 
has an opposite effect and increases the attraction between molecules. Also, the more negative values of ddGsolv correspond to a decreased solubility.

Furthermore, the fully protonated model, with mean atomic charges at a given pH can be used as input for the Calculate Electrostatic Potential protocol to study the change in the 3-D distribution of the electrostatic potential with changing the acidicity and the ionic strength of the solution.

The tutorial covers:

* Preparing the molecule and running the calculations

* Analyzing the predicted pK values of the individual amino acid residues

* Activating the plots of pH-dependent protein properties

* Analyzing the total charge of a molecule as a function of pH

* Analyzing the pH-dependence of protein stability

* Analyzing the pH-dependence of electrostatic properties related to protein solubility

* Analyzing the protonation of individual residues as a function of pH

* Analyzing the hydrogen structure at given pH

* Analyzing the fully protonated structure at given pH

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Electrostatics | 2lzt.pdb .

In the Hierarchy View, select the second chain A (nitrate ions) and the Water chain. Press the Delete key to remove them.

The calculation of the ionization of individual residues is important because it enables the derivation of all other pH-dependent characteristics of a protein molecule.
A pK value of an amino acid reported in this protocol is defined as the pH value at which the titratable group is half protonated.

When the interactive job finishes, a molecule window Proteins with Ionization Properties should open automatically, containing the output structures for all input molecules. To open the Report, expand the results in the

The predicted pK values are stored in three columns as Predicted

Click the 2lzt link in Details column in the Summary Table.

The protocol provides an estimation of the pH-dependent electrostatic contribution to free energy of protein folding.

Inspect the ddGsolv , Net Charge Square and Protein Dipole Moment curves.

The transfer energy (ddGsolv), the net charge squared and the dipole moment are average physical properties that can be used to determine the pH-range for optimal solubility. 
The more positive values of ddGsolv and bigger values of net charge squared correspond to increased solubility. 
A higher molecular dipole moment due to larger asymmetry of protein charge distribution could decrease the solubility of the protein molecule and
increase the viscosity of the solution, especially when solution pH is close to the isoelectric point where the charge-charge repulsion between solvated molecules is minimal. 
If you look at the ddGsolv and Net Charge Square curves, you can see that the minimum of ddGsolv and the minimum of Net Charge square is quite close to the calculated isoelectric point pI=11.4.

# Generating ensemble pharmacophores from large data sets

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_epg.htm

## Generating ensemble pharmacophores from large data sets

Time: 20 minutes plus pharmacophore generation time.

### Introduction

In the early days of pharmacophore generation [Barnum et al., 1996] , datasets of active ligands were relatively small. In recent years, significantly more data for a vast number of targets have become available from databases such as ChEMBL [Gaulton et al., 2017] .

To address this, the Ensemble Pharmacophore Generation protocol has been created. The protocol automates and enhances the HipHop algorithm used in the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol. It allows users to quickly identify clusters of ligands within datasets larger than those that can be managed by the existing pharmacophore generation protocols, and it generates one pharmacophore model for each cluster. Taken together, these pharmacophore models form a single ensemble pharmacophore of different hypotheses which effectively represents that target.

The active and inactive ligands in this tutorial were obtained from the Database of Useful Decoys: Enhanced (DUD-E) for the AKT1 dataset (see http://dude.docking.org/ and [Mysinger et al., 2012] ). AKT1 is one of three closely related serine/threonine-protein kinases (AKT1, AKT2, and AKT3). The AKT kinases regulate many processes including metabolism, proliferation, cell survival, growth, and angiogenesis.

The DUD-E ligands were prepared by removing ligands with duplicate names and structures. To keep the running time of this tutorial short, a diverse subset of 300 inactive ligands was selected from the 16400+ AKT1 decoys with the help of the Find Diverse Molecules protocol.

This tutorial covers:

* Generating an ensemble pharmacophore

* Rescuing a failed cluster

* Using the ensemble pharmacophore for virtual screening

The 293 active ligands in the AKT1 dataset would traditionally have required users to manually select a maximum of 32 active ligands as input to the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol. The Ensemble Pharmacophore Generation protocol automates this by clustering the large input active dataset using a pharmacophoric fingerprint, and selecting the top 5 ligands from each cluster to generate common feature pharmacophores. The 10 pharmacophores for each cluster are validated with active and inactive ligands to choose the best hypothesis to model that cluster chemotype.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | akt1_actives.sd and akt1_decoys.sd files. Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Automatically tool panel and click Ensemble Pharmacophore Generation . Set the Input Active Ligands parameter to akt1_actives:All and the Input Inactive Ligands parameter to akt1_decoys:All . Expand the Pharmacophore Generation parameter group and select the Features parameter to open the Select Features dialog. Check the boxes for the HYDROPHOBIC_aliphatic and NEG_IONIZABLE features to add to those already selected, and then click OK . Expand the Advanced parameter group and change the Pharmacophore Target Prefix to akt1 . If you have a multi-processor server you can set the Parallel Processing parameters to complete the protocol more quickly. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Running this job on a single processor may take about two hours.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 15 clusters have been analyzed.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. Click View Results .

This opens tabulated results showing the validation of the clusters and the pharmacophores.
On the first Intra-Cluster Validation with Cluster Actives/Inactives tab you can see that a pharmacophore was generated for each cluster with an ROC score greater than 0.85, which is set by the Minimum AUC ROC parameter. The table includes the details of a confusion matrix for each pharmacophore validation within the cluster that the pharmacophore was generated from. Ideally, we want pharmacophore models that have a high number of True Positives and a low number of False Positives. Pharm 1 maps 82 of the 96 ligands from Cluster 1, and incorrectly maps only 1 of 300 inactive ligands.

Move the cursor over Pharm 1 to see the features of the pharmacophore.

The Cutoff Score in the table is the pharmacophore FitValue that has been determined to give the best discrimination of the active ligands from the inactive ligands based on balanced accuracy:

Open the Validation with All Actives/Inactives tab.

The validation performance of the same pharmacophores from the first tab is shown. However, in this table their performance against the entire data set of 293 original active ligands is presented, rather than only those within the cluster they have been generated from. The Sensitivity metric for the model has decreased, but this is not surprising as there are now many more active ligands with different chemotypes from different clusters.

Open the third tab labeled Intra-Cluster Validation with Cluster Actives/Inactives .

The clusters in which none of the default 10 common feature pharmacophores generated produced a model whose ROC score was greater than 0.85 are shown. The ROC score and other metrics are provided so that if a pharmacophore model has statistical values close to the cutoff, or suits your project criteria in a different way, you can still include it in your ensemble of pharmacophores for this target.

The first cluster amongst these validation failures includes 90 active ligands, of which only 59 are retrieved. This may be because the 5 ligands selected as leads for the pharmacophore elucidation do not well characterize the entire cluster. You may decide to try another selection method on this cluster to generate a pharmacophore model that represents the chemotypes of this cluster.

Clusters 6–15 contain less than 10 ligands each, and as expected, no pharmacophores were generated for them. At this point, you may want to combine some of the failed clusters and select a different representative training set to model them.

In this step you will take the ligands from the failed first cluster and see if you can select different input ligands for pharmacophore generation. You will use an automated method to select 5 ligands, but could peruse the ligands and manually select a training set for the cluster.

Click SD 2 to open a molecule window with the 90 ligands of the first failed cluster. From the Small Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tool panel click Find Diverse Molecules . Set the Input Ligands parameter to cluster_2:All and the Subset Size parameter to 5 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run .

The job should complete within seconds.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 5 diverse ligands have been selected.

In the Jobs Explorer, click View Results to open the 5 diverse ligands. Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Automatically tool panel and click Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation . Set the Input Ligands parameter to diverse-ligands:All . Select the Features parameter to open the Select Features dialog. Select the checkbox for the HYDROPHOBIC_aromatic , HYDROPHOBIC_aliphatic , POS_IONIZABLE , and NEG_IONIZABLE features, and then click OK . Change the Validation parameter to True . Expand the parameter group and set the Active Ligands parameter to cluster_2:All and the Inactive Ligands parameter to akt1_decoys:All . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job should complete in less than 15 minutes.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 10 hypotheses have been generated.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report.

The Summary section of the Report.html shows a similar validation table to the output from the Ensemble Pharmacophore Generation protocol. The primary difference between the results of the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol and the previous protocol is that 10 models are returned for this cluster rather than one, and the Cutoff Scores (FitValue) that produce the best AUC are not incorporated in these models.

Analyzing this table, you might select pharmacophore 6 as the best performing model based on its ROC score.

You can now use the ensemble AKT1 pharmacophore for virtual screening. You will use a database of ligands from the scPDB ( http://bioinfo-pharma.u-strasbg.fr/scPDB/ ) for identifying new potential leads for AKT1.

From the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation Report.html table click Pharmacophore 6 to open it in its own window. In the Jobs Explorer, right-click the Ensemble Pharmacophore Generation job and choose Locate . In the Files Explorer expand the Clusters folder and Ctrl+select all the ds_chm files . These were the successful pharmacophores from the ensemble pharmacophore generation. Drag the selected pharmacophores into the same molecule window as Pharmacophore 6. In the Hierarchy View double click diverse-ligands_06 and change the model name to akt1_CFG_06 . Open the Pharmacophores | Search, Screen and Profile tool panel and click Ligand Profiler. Click the Input File Pharmacophores parameter and select the four akt1 pharmacophores from the active molecule window. Expand the Advanced parameter group and change the Input Type parameter to Database . Expand the Input Type parameter group and select scPDB [7622 mol] from the Input Database parameter. Expand the Input Database parameter group and change the Limit Hits parameter to All . Set the Scale Fit Values parameter to False . If you have a multi-processor server you can set the Parallel Processing parameters to complete the protocol more quickly. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Running this job on a single processor may take about 70 minutes.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the number of ligands retrieved for the 4 pharmacophores.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. Click Fits Organized by Molecule to open the Fits by Molecule report. Click the FitValue column header twice to sort the table.

Many of the highest FitValues will correspond with AKT1 protein-ligand complex. However, what may be more interesting for your lead identification objective are other ligands not already known as AKT1 binding ligands, that may be repurposed as AKT1 binders.
