# Adding an explicit membrane to a transmembrane protein

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_explicit-membrane.htm

## Adding an explicit membrane to a transmembrane protein

Time: 20 minutes (with equilibration 7 hours)

### Introduction

Transmembrane proteins play broad roles in biological processes such as cell signaling and drug transport, which make them important drug targets. It is estimated that about half of all available drugs interact with membrane proteins. Molecular dynamics simulations that include membranes can provide insights into the structure and function of transmembrane proteins.

Membranes are composed of double layers of phospholipids and can be treated in simulations either implicitly or explicitly. Explicit membrane simulations are usually more accurate and may offer greater insights into protein behavior, solvation effects, and the biomolecular interactions and conformational changes within a protein system under various conditions. Unfortunately, the calculation times for explicit membrane simulations are significantly longer than for implicit membrane simulations.

Discovery Studio supports both implicit and explicit membrane simulations with the tools on the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel and the Solvate with Explicit Membrane protocol, respectively. In this tutorial you will use this protocol to position a transmembrane protein within an explicit membrane bilayer, solvate the protein-membrane complex in water, optionally equilibrate the solvated system, and then analyze the results. The equilibrated system may then be the starting point for further dynamic simulations.

The transmembrane protein used in this tutorial is EmrD [Yin et al., 2006] , a multidrug transporter from E. coli, which is involved in the efflux of amphipathic compounds from the cytoplasm. It is typically found in the inner membrane of E. coli, which can be best approximated with a 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) lipid membrane.

The following tasks are covered in this tutorial:

* Preparing the input protein

* Adding an explicit membrane to the protein

* Optionally equilibrating the solvated system

* Analyzing the results

The PDB code for the EmrD transporter used is 2GFP [Yin et al., 2006] . It contains two copies of the biomolecule; you will only need one of these for the simulation.

Choose File | Open URL … and enter 2GFP in the ID field. Click Open . Open the Hierarchy View, select chain B from molecule 2GFP and select Edit | Delete from the menu bar to remove chain B . Right-click and choose Fit to Screen to center the view on the protein structure.

#### Typing the input molecule

The input molecule must be typed with the charmm36 forcefield.

Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel. Set Forcefield to charmm36 , and then click Apply Forcefield .

The molecule is now typed with the charmm36 forcefield and related forcefield properties have been added to the molecule, residues, and atoms.

You can also use the Assign Forcefield… protocol to type the molecule. It has advanced capabilities such as the ability to recognize residues with different names, and supports patched residues and custom RTF files.

In general, it is good practice to run Prepare Protein when using files from the PDB, however this example structure did not require that preparation and you can directly go to the more necessary step of minimizing the input structure. This is important as it will take the simulation longer to resolve bad contacts after lipids and water are added.

Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and click Minimization . Click Run .

The job should take less than a minute to run, and the molecule window is updated with the minimized protein if the job is run in the foreground mode.

#### Pre-positioning the input molecule

The input structure needs to be reoriented so that its z-axis is aligned with the normal of the explicit membrane that will be subsequently added, and to position it at the center of the membrane. The following options are available to reorient your membrane protein:

* Run the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol to automatically add an implicit membrane and optimize its position.

* Use the Macromolecule | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins | Create and Edit Membrane tool to manually add an implicit membrane and adjust the position. For details, see the Modeling Transmembrane Proteins tutorial.

* Download the protein from the Orientations of Proteins in Membranes (OPM) database ( https://opm.phar.umich.edu/ ). The structure will be properly positioned.

In this tutorial, you will use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. The two planes of the implicit membrane are always placed in the z=L/2 and z=-L/2 plane, where L is the thickness of the membrane. The protein is reoriented accordingly so that the explicit lipid bilayers can be added in the correct orientation and location in the next stage.

Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel and click Add Membrane and Orient Molecule… . Set Input Typed Molecule to 2GFP:2GFP . Change Membrane Thickness to 25 (the DMPC bilayer has a thickness of 25 Å at 300 K). Leave the remaining parameters set to their default settings and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Running this job on a single processor should take less than 8 minutes.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that a membrane has been added.

Close the current 2GFP molecule window. In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. Click View Results .

The molecule window that opens has the EmrD transporter protein with the planar implicit membrane represented by two rectangular objects that correspond to the boundaries of a hydrophobic slab. The schematic blue plane represents the membrane plane oriented to the cytosolic space.

In the next step, the implicit membrane bilayer is used to orient and position the explicit DMPC lipid bilayer, embedding the protein in the explicit membrane and also adding water and salts to each side of the membrane. The protocol allows you to select one of several common lipid types:

* POPC: 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine

* POPE: 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine

* DPPC: 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine

* DMPC: 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine

* DLPC: 1,2-dilauroyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine).

Alternatively, you may use your own custom lipid type obtained from a source such as CHARMM-GUI ( http://www.charmm-gui.org/ ) [Jo et al., 2008] . This should be supplied as a pre-equilibrated membrane box in crd format.

Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and click Solvate with Explicit Membrane . Set Input Typed Molecule to 2GFP:2GFP . Set Lipid Type to DMPC . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default settings and click Run .

The job should take less than a minute to run, and a molecule window with the 2GFP structure within a DMPC double layer as the explicit membrane is opened if the job is run in the foreground. Water and counterions (Na + and Cl - ) are also added to the top (extracellular) and bottom (intracellular) domains of the protein.

This is a quick way to check the approximate structure of your membrane protein within the explicit membrane. However, the system will require further optimization before you can run the Molecular Dynamics Production protocol. You can set this up using the Dynamics (Equilibration) protocol, or optionally repeat the Solvate with Explicit Membrane protocol with the optional equilibration step enabled.

In this optional step of the tutorial you can repeat the protocol, enabling the equilibration step when adding the explicit membrane to the transmembrane protein. This will significantly increase the job run time.

Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and click Solvate with Explicit Membrane again. Set Input Typed Molecule to 2GFP:2GFP and Lipid Type to DMPC . Set Equilibration to True . If your machine has more than one core, set Number of Processors to the number of cores you want to use. Expand the Equilibration parameter group and change the run time for Stage 1 , Stage 2 , and Stage 3 to 200 , 200 , and 500 , respectively. Click Run , and then click Background .

Running this job on a machine with 8 cores can take several hours.

Once the job has finished the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer will report that the explicit membrane has been added. You can double-click the completed job to open the report.

When the job finishes, double click on the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report.htm .

The report has three plots for the last stage of the equilibration: Temperature, Total Energy, and Density vs Time. The temperature fluctuates within 299 ± 3 K because it is controlled by the Langevin Dynamics thermostat.

The total energy gradually decreases and levels off.

The density gradually increases over the course of the simulation and stabilizes. This indicates that the system is well packed at the end.

In the Results section of the report, click View Results .

The protein structure with the solvated membrane opens and you can inspect the equilibrated structure.

If the results indicate that the system is not fully equilibrated, further equilibration can be performed using the Dynamics (NAMD) protocol.

# Calculating relative binding free energies with alchemical free energy perturbation

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_fep.htm

## Calculating relative binding free energies with alchemical free energy perturbation

Time: 30 minutes

### Introduction

The ability to understand and quantify the strength of interactions between a ligand and protein is essential in drug discovery projects to discern how changes to a ligand might alter affinity. Reliable estimation of binding affinity would improve selection of ligands in the lead optimization process. During early stage lead optimization tens of thousands of ligands, of diverse scaffold families, may be considered and thus computational methods such as docking and MM-GBSA are suitable for the throughput required. Later stage lead optimization involving small, sequential chemical modifications needs to be much more accurate and likely require explicit solvent modeling and rigorous free energy methods.

Alchemical free energy perturbation (FEP) is based on a thermodynamic cycle.

The horizontal physical processes describe the free energy change from the unbound ligand in solvent to the bound state in the protein complex. In the vertical alchemical processes, ligand 1 is transmuted to ligand 2 in the unbound and bound states. This is performed computationally via a series of unphysical intermediate states. The calculation of the alchemical relative binding free energy of ΔG complex – ΔG free is equivalent to ΔG 2 – ΔG 1 but is computationally less expensive.

In this tutorial the following tasks are covered:

* Preparing analogs and ligand pairs

* Setting up the relative FEP calculations

* Running the FEP calculations

* Collating and analyzing the FEP results

The FEP dynamics simulations require all the ligands of interest to be positioned in the protein active site. In this first step you will use the Generate Analog Conformations protocol to align your ligands to the lead ligand in the protein active site. The protocol detects the common and different atoms between each analog and the lead compound by the maximum common substructure (MCS) method. It assigns the coordinates of the common atoms of the analog directly from the corresponding lead atoms, and generates new coordinates for the atoms that differ.

The PDB code for the heat shock protein 90 protein-ligand complex used is 4YKR. The sample file used in this tutorial was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared with the Prepare Proteins protocol. When preparing your protein, particular attention should be given to crystal waters to determine if they should be retained as conserved water molecules. Water molecules deeply buried in the core of the protein may play a role in maintaining the folded structure and often make strong hydrogen bonds to polar groups. In this tutorial, we retained three water molecules in the binding site that are known to form important interactions with the lead compound and use the same protein structure throughout the workflow. However, in prospective applications where the relevance of particular water molecules may not be known initially, it is recommended that the Generate Analog Conformations protocol be run without any crystallographic water molecules present in the protein and the FEP setup be with the protein structure retaining all water molecules.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 4YKR_prep.dsv file. Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | hsp90_analogs.sd and hsp90_lead.sd files. Open the Simulation | Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel and click the Generate Analog Conformations link from the descriptive text at the top of the tool panel. Set the Input Lead Ligands parameter to hsp90_lead:All , and the Input Analog Ligands parameter to hsp90_analogs:All . Set the Input Receptor parameter to 4YKR_prep: 4YKR_protein . Expand the Input Receptor parameter grouping and then the In-situ Minimization parameter grouping. Delete the value for the Radius of Flexible Residues parameter, to keep the protein rigid during the in-situ minimization and reduce the run time for the job. Expand the Advanced parameter grouping and ensure the Implicit Solvent Model parameter is set to Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job should take a couple of minutes to run. The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 7 analogs have been processed and 8 conformations generated.

The Generate Analog Conformations protocol can be used to quickly position and optimize analogous ligands in the protein active site based on a lead ligand’s binding mode [Raman, 2019] . The MM-GBSA methods can then be used to rank order the analogs. For some protein systems, MM-GBSA methods can be accurate and effective at a fraction of the computational cost of some other methods. However, these approximate methods are not always reliable. Therefore, when resources are available and datasets are small enough, methods such as FEP must be considered.

If you wish to calculate MM-GBSA energies independently, or for structurally dissimilar ligands, you can use the Calculate Binding Energies protocol.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an HTML Window. Click View Results .

This opens two molecule windows - one with the 8 conformations generated and another with only the top scoring conformation for each analog. You will now use the top scoring conformation for each analog to identify ligand pairs for the FEP calculations.

In the Top_Scoring_Analog_Conformation molecule window ensure that all of the ligands are visible in the graphics view. Right-click and select Show All from the shortcut menu. Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel. Check that the Forcefield list is set to CHARMm and click Apply Forcefield .

The FEP algorithm supports both the CHARMm and charmm36 forcefields. You can use the Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) protocol to type your ligands if using the charmm36 forcefield. This protocol uses the Multipurpose Atom-Typer for CHARMM (MATCH) algorithm [Yesselman et al., 2012] for the automated assignment of atom types and forcefield parameters for the latest generation of forcefields.

Return to the Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel and click Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP... . Set the Input Typed Ligands parameter to Top_Scoring_Analog_Conformation:All . In the Lead Ligand Name parameter enter hsp90_12 and click Run .

This protocol calculates a similarity matrix of all of the ligands to identify connections between them, such that the most similar ligands (based on chemical and topological similarity) are connected to the best extent possible. If you are only working with two ligands, or wish to define your own ligand pairs you can use the Pair Ligands for FEP command.

The job should take a few seconds to run. The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 6 ligand pairs have been generated.

This opens a molecule window containing the generated ligand pairs, and a 2D window displaying a network plot. The ligand pairs in the molecule window are defined as assemblies where the first ligand will be alchemically changed to the second ligand. The network plot displays the relationship between the ligand pairs, where the nodes are the ligands and the edges show the pairings. The edges are labeled with the similarity score of the pair, and the arrow head indicates the direction of the alchemical change.

You can optionally specify a lead ligand and in that case the ligands in each pair are arranged based on their distance from the lead, where distance is measured by the number of intervening nodes between the ligand and the lead. The hsp90_12 ligand is the same ligand as crystallized in the 4YKR.pdb complex, and with the network plot you can start with the lead and move unidirectionally outward to analogs that are more and more dissimilar.

In this step of the tutorial you will prepare the structures to run the FEP calculations. For each ligand pair a merged dual topology molecule is generated, based on the identified common and different sets of atoms in the topologies and nonbonded parameters. A solvated ligand system and a solvated protein-ligand complex for this merged dual topology molecule are also generated.

Return to the PairsForFEP molecule window. From the Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel click Set Up Relative FEP Calculations... . Set the Input Ligand Pairs parameter to PairsForFEP:All and the Input Receptor parameter to 4YKR_prep: 4YKR_protein . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

In alchemical FEP calculations one ligand is transformed into the second ligand by the use of a merged dual topology molecule. This chimeric molecule is generated by first detecting the common and different atoms between the ligands by a maximum common substructure (MCS) method. Common atoms are those that are considered identical in terms of topology, atom-types and partial charges. All other atoms are designated as the different set.

The job should take several minutes to run. The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 6 solvated complex systems have been generated.

This opens two molecule windows. One contains each of the merged dual topology molecules in a cubic shaped box with water molecules and counterions. The other molecule window contains the complexes of each of the dual topology molecules with the protein in similarly solvated boxes.

This tutorial describes a CPU based FEP workflow. If you have GPU resources, you can use the CHARMm Relative FEP Calculations (GPU) protocol from this step onwards, and skip the remaining. This protocol also embeds the functionality from Collate FEP Simulation Results protocol.

In the next part of the workflow you would normally run the FEP calculations for the solvated ligand systems and the solvated protein-ligand complexes for each ligand pair. However, these calculations can be time consuming and computationally expensive, and are beyond the reasonable time frame for a tutorial. Hence, some of the results of these calculations are only discussed in the next steps of this tutorial. If run this calculation on a 32-core server using the default parameters, each solvated protein-ligand system used in this tutorial would require about 12 hours.

The Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol should be run with the SolvatedLigands molecule window, and again with the SolvatedComplexes molecule window, to run all of the ligand pair calculations. This protocol allows you to run the calculations in parallel and, if available, on a server with a grid engine enabled.

There are a few key parameters that may affect the time, accuracy, and statistical confidence of your results and should be considered when planning FEP calculations. These include the Number of Lambda Windows parameter which determines the number of intermediate states that are simulated. The interactions involving the initial state or groups unique to Ligand 1 are "turned off", and the same for Ligand 2 are "turned on" by tuning the non-bonded interactions off and on. A smaller number of lambda windows will reduce calculation time, but may also affect accuracy. The default value of 16 is a good compromise of time and accuracy, and recommended for most situations.

The Simulation Time per Lambda Window (ps) parameter specifies the dynamics simulation time length per lambda window. Hence the total simulation time is equal to the Number of Lambda Windows parameter multiplied by the value of this parameter, which by default is 16 × 500 ps, totaling 8 ns. The Equilibration Time per Lambda Window (ps) parameter specifies how much of the simulation time per lambda window is considered for equilibration; the remaining time is for the dynamics production and it is this data which is used for the free energy calculation. The Save Results Interval (ps) parameter specifies how often the coordinates are saved to the trajectory file. Changing the values of these parameters can greatly affect how long FEP calculations take, as well as the size of the trajectory files, and should be considered carefully.

At the end of this stage of the workflow you would have the results from the two runs of the Free Energy Perturbation FEP) protocol - one for the solvated ligand systems and one for the solvated protein-ligand complexes. In each of the Output folders you would have six folders with the results for each of the ligand pairs. The Report.htm summarizes the simulations results, with links to the simulation trajectories, with and without solvent. Tabulated and plotted free energy values for each lambda window in a simulation, individually and cumulatively for each ligand pair are also reported.

In the next part of the workflow you would typically calculate the relative binding free energy for each ligand pair. The files required for this are too large to provide with this tutorial, and hence an explanation of the steps to set up the protocol and the analysis is detailed instead.

If the experimental absolute free energy value of one ligand in the data set is available, then the absolute free energies for all of the ligands can be determined. The starting hsp90_analogs.sd input included experimental absolute free energy values [D3R] so that you can assess how well FEP is able to rank and predict binding free energies. The hsp90_12 ligand will be the reference ligand in your calculations; it is also the crystallized ligand from the 4YKR.pdb complex.

From the Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel click Collate FEP Simulation Results... .

The FEP Data Directory Ligand and FEP Data Directory Complex parameters are where you set the parent directories for the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol runs with the solvated ligand systems and solvated protein-ligand complexes, respectively. The results in these folders contain a simulationinfo.xml file and a free energy data file ( .fepout ) for each ligand pair. The simulationinfo.xml file specifies the names of ligands involved in each perturbation and whether the simulation involves the free ligand or the complex. The .fepout file is produced during the NAMD FEP production run and contains the raw free energy data.

Set the FEP Data Directory Ligand parameter to the results location for the NAMD FEP calculation on SolvatedLigands. Set the FEP Data Directory Complex parameter to the results location for the NAMD FEP calculation on SolvatedComplexes. Expand the Absolute Free Energy parameter group and in the Lead Ligand Name parameter enter hsp90_12 . In the Lead Ligand Free Energy parameter field enter a value of -10.27 . Set the Input Ligands parameter to Top_Scoring_Analog_Conformation:All .

The protocol is now ready to run, collating and analyzing the FEP simulation results.

An example of the results of running the Collate FEP Simulation Results protocol is shown and discussed below.

The Report.htm from this protocol displays a table of the calculated relative free energy values for the ligand pairs, and a table of the absolute free energies for the ligands. The latter table is only generated when you have provided a lead ligand and free energy value. Both tables are also graphically represented by bar charts.

You will notice that the absolute free energy for hsp90_52 has been marked as being "likely unreliable" in the table and colored red in the charts. This is because empirical observations have shown that the magnitude of relative free energy values within a congeneric series is rarely larger than 3 kcal/mol. The Extreme Value Threshold parameter allows you to flag these possibly unreliable predictions, which may be due to inaccuracies in the simulation such as non-convergence due to insufficient sampling or the forcefield. For certain datasets containing inactive molecules, it is possible that a threshold value of 3 kcal/mol may flag a large number of predictions. In such cases, it would be useful to test the sensitivity of the results to the threshold value by raising it to 4 or 5 kcal/mol.

Return to the Top_Scoring_Analog_Conformation molecule window and observe the exp_dg molecular property for each ligand.

If you compare these values to the computed absolute ΔG values in the report you will see that, with the exception of the unreliable hsp90_52 prediction, the free energy perturbation calculations are able to reasonably predict the absolute values.

Perhaps more significantly than reproducing accurate absolute free energy predictions the FEP method was able to rank order the ligands. When absolute free energy predictions cannot be calculated for rank ordering you can still use the relative values for analysis. Look at the ΔΔG value of 2.864 for the ligand pair hsp90_40 - hsp90_4, and look at the value of -0.482 for hsp90_4 - hsp90_3. You can use this to infer that hsp90_40 has a better binding energy than hsp90_4 but also that hsp90_3 has a better binding energy than hsp90_4. The ΔΔG value of 2.746 for the ligand pair hsp90_4 - hsp90_5 means that hsp90_5 has the poorest binding energy.

The Collate FEP Simulation Results protocol also generates a network plot (pictured) that graphically presents the ΔΔG values of the ligand pairs. The edges are labeled and color-coded with the relative free energy of the ligand pair, and the arrow head indicates the direction of the alchemical change.

In this tutorial you have used relative alchemical free energy perturbation to rank order a congeneric series of ligands for late-stage lead optimization. The computational cost of the simulations required restricts this method to small datasets, but its potential to provide more accurate quantitative estimates of binding energies makes it an invaluable tool for rational structure-based drug design.

# Calculating relative binding free energies with OpenFE alchemical free energy perturbation

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_fep_openfe.htm

## Calculating relative binding free energies with OpenFE alchemical free energy perturbation

Time: ~16 to 35 hours (depending on GPU resources)

### Introduction

Understanding and quantifying the strength of ligand-protein interactions is essential in drug discovery for predicting how chemical modifications affect binding affinity. Reliable estimation of binding affinity improves selection of ligands in the lead optimization process. During early stage lead optimization, tens of thousands of diverse scaffolds could be considered, and thus, computational methods such as docking and MM-GBSA are suitable for the throughput required. Later stage lead optimization involves small, sequential chemical modifications that require much higher accuracy to reliably predict subtle differences in binding affinity between closely related compounds. Free energy perturbation (FEP) methods, with their explicit solvent modeling and rigorous statistical mechanics framework, are well suited for meeting these demanding accuracy requirements. However, FEP is not well suited for early stage optimization because of its high computational cost and the need for careful setup when dealing with structurally diverse compounds.

Alchemical free energy perturbation (FEP) is based on a thermodynamic cycle:

The horizontal physical processes describe the free energy change from the unbound ligand in solvent to the bound state in the protein complex. In the vertical alchemical processes, ligand 1 is transmuted to ligand 2 in the unbound and bound states. This is performed computationally by means of a series of unphysical intermediate states. Calculating the alchemical relative binding free energy (ΔG complex – ΔG free ) is thermodynamically equivalent to calculating ΔG 2 – ΔG 1 , but is computationally more tractable.

In this tutorial the following tasks are covered:

* Preparing input ligands

* Generating and analyzing the ligand perturbation network

* Running the FEP calculations

* Analyzing the FEP results

### Preparing input ligands and input receptor

The FEP dynamics simulations require all the ligands of interest to be positioned in the protein active site. In this first step, you will use the Generate Analog Conformations protocol to align your ligands to the lead ligand in the protein active site. The protocol uses the maximum common substructure (MCS) method to identify common and differing atoms between each analog and the lead compound. Common atoms are mapped from the target ligand to the lead ligand, inheriting their positions directly from the corresponding atoms in the lead. The positions of differing atoms are then generated to preserve the relative spatial arrangements of atoms in the target ligand, ensuring that bond lengths, angles, and overall molecular geometry remain appropriate.

For this tutorial, the input receptor is TYK2, a tyrosine-protein kinase. The protein in the sample file was prepared using the Prepare Proteins protocol. When preparing your protein, pay attention to crystal waters to determine if you should retain them as conserved water molecules. Water molecules deeply buried in the core of the protein may play a role in maintaining the folded structure and often make strong hydrogen bonds to polar groups. For prospective applications where water molecule importance is uncertain, run the Generate Analog Conformations protocol without crystallographic waters, then include relevant water molecules when running the Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | tyk2_prep.dsv file. Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | tyk2_subset.sd and tyk2_lead.sd files. Open the Simulation | Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel and click the Generate Analog Conformations link from the descriptive text at the top of the tool panel. Set the Input Lead Ligands parameter to tyk2_lead:All , and the Input Analog Ligands parameter to tyk2_subset:All . Set the Input Receptor parameter to tyk2_prep:tyk2 . Expand the Input Receptor parameter grouping and then the In-situ Minimization parameter grouping. To keep the protein rigid during the in-situ minimization and reduce the run time for the job, delete the value for the Radius of Flexible Residues parameter, to keep the protein rigid during the in-situ minimization and reduce the run time for the job. Expand the Advanced parameter grouping and ensure the Implicit Solvent Model parameter is set to Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values, and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job should take a couple of minutes to run. Once complete, the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 3 analogs have been processed and 8 conformations generated.

You can use the Generate Analog Conformations protocol to quickly position and optimize analogous ligands in the protein active site based on a lead ligand’s binding mode [Raman, 2019] . The MM-GBSA methods can then be used to rank order the analogs. For some protein systems, MM-GBSA methods can be accurate and effective at a fraction of the computational cost of some other methods. However, these approximate methods are not always reliable. Therefore, when resources are available and datasets are small enough, methods such as FEP should be considered.

If you want to calculate MM-GBSA energies independently, or for structurally dissimilar ligands, use the Calculate Binding Energies protocol.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an HTML Window. Click View Results .

This opens two molecule windows: one window with the 8 conformations generated and another window with only the top scoring conformation for each analog. In the next step, you willuse the top scoring conformation for each analog to generate the ligand perturbation network for the FEP calculations.

You will now generate atom mappings for the alchemical transformation of the ligands from the previous step and construct the ligand perturbation network required to run the FEP calculations. A merged dual topology molecule is generated for each ligand pair, based on the identified common and differing sets of atoms between the two ligands. Nonbonded parameters from the specified force field are then assigned to the atoms in this dual topology, with special treatment for atoms that will be alchemically transformed.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | tyk2_prep.dsv file. Make sure the Top_Scoring_Analog_Conformation molecule window was active and then from the Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel click Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE)... . Set the Input Ligands parameter to Top_Scoring_Analog_Conformation:All which we already generated. Expand the Input Ligand parameter grouping and ensure that Refine Alignment is set to True . This option performs a shape-based alignment to further improve the alignment of the input ligands and is generally recommended. Set the Atom Mapper parameter to LOMAP and Kartograf , to generate both types of atom mappings. Set the Ligand Network parameter to Minimal spanning tree and Minimal redundant network , to generate the corresponding networks. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values, and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete, which should take a few minutes. In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the Report in an HTML Window. Click View Results . In the Report you will see several files are returned. Click Ligand networks to open an interactive report of the constructed ligand perturbation networks. Enlarge this window for better viewing.

In the interactive report above you will see buttons for choosing the type of network and the type of atom mapping, clicking through them will change the graph that is rendered in the panel below.

The nodes represent the input ligands. You can click and drag the nodes to reposition them as required. Clicking on the edges between nodes will allow you to view the atom mapping and proposed transformation between the two corresponding ligands as seen here:

In this example, the transformation between lig_ejm_44 and lig_ejm_55 is depicted. The score is a measure of the quality of the mapping and is utilized in the construction of the ligand perturbation networks. The score ranges from 0 (a bad mapping) to 1 (a great mapping). In the 2D depiction of the ligands, atoms and bonds that are deleted in the transformation are highlighted in red while atoms and bonds that undergo transformations (element change or bond order change) are highlighted in blue.

When analyzing the networks and atom mappings, your goal is to select an appropriate network topology and atom mapping strategy for your system.

In this tutorial, you generated a minimal spanning tree and a minimal redundant network. The minimal spanning tree here is constructed with as few edges as possible while maximizing total score (score here reflects the difficulty and quality of each ligand transformation). This network will typically reduce the number of total calculations needed, but it may not be very accurate as there isn't enough statistical redundancy. The minimal redundant network is also constructed with as few edges as possible while maximizing total score, but it also ensures that every node has at least two edges for statistical redundancy. This increases the number of calculations, but greatly improves accuracy.

After choosing a network of interest, you will choose an atom mapping. This involves visually inspecting the proposed atom mappings and score for each individual edge. Generally, you would choose a mapping with a higher score, but also consider that Kartograf and LOMAP have complementary strengths: LOMAP is less sensitive to input ligand alignment and constructs the Maximal Common Substructure, but may struggle with stereoisomers and molecular symmetries. Kartograf takes into account the 3D coordinates of the ligands, and therefore is more sensitive to the alignment of the input ligands, but can handle stereoisomers and molecular symmetries better. Scores alone should not guide your decision—a mapping can have a high score yet still map atoms incorrectly.

In the following figures, notice that the LOMAP mapping (the first figure) and the Kartograf mapping (the second figure) are close in scores with LOMAP doing slightly better. But if you view the actual atoms being mapped, you can see that the Kartograf mapping is not correctly mapping a methyl group, and is suggesting that the methyl group will be deleted as part of the transformation. In this case, LOMAP is a better choice.

With the Ligand Networks interactive report as the active window, click the Go Back button or right-click on the page and click Back to go back to the Report. Click Aligned Ligands .

This opens a molecule window containing the input ligands after a refined alignment. This is only available when the Refine Alignment parameter is True. It is recommended to view the ligands here in the context of the input receptor to confirm that the refined alignment of the ligands did not introduce any steric clashes.

Now that you have constructed the ligand perturbation networks and analyzed them, you can continue with the production FEP protocol. In this tutorial you will use the minimal redundant network with LOMAP atom mapping. On the report page, this is represented as the GraphML file named network_lomap_minimal_redundant.graphml . The GraphML file encodes all information relevant to the ligands and also the proposed alchemical transformations needed to move forward with the production simulations in the Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol.

The Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol takes the prepared protein receptor and the generated ligand perturbation network GraphML file as inputs. Alchemical free energy calculations are carried out using the OpenFE framework and the OpenMM simulation engine. During the simulation, the input system is solvated with TIP3P waters and 0.15 M NaCl around the solute. In addition, the input protein is parametrized with the Amber ff14SB force field [Maier et al., 2015] , the ligands are parametrized with OpenFF Sage 2.1.1 [Boothroyd et al., 2023] , and then all are minimized. Equilibration and production simulations are carried out using Hamiltonian Replica Exchange (HREX) as the multistate lambda sampling method under NPT conditions using the Langevin Middle Integrator [Zhang et al., 2019] and a Monte Carlo Barostat.

With the tyk2_prep molecule window active, from the Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel, click Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE)... Specify the chosen ligand perturbation network GraphML file from Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE)
protocol run for the Ligand Perturbation Network . Under the Results folder, navigate to the corresponding
Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) job's Output folder, and then choose the network_lomap_minimal_redundant.graphml GraphML file. Set Number of Simulations to 2 . For realistic scenarios it is recommended to set this to at least 2 or 3 for statistical accuracy, but for testing it can be set to 1.

There are a few key parameters that may affect the time, accuracy, and statistical confidence of your results and should be considered when planning FEP calculations. Key parameters include Equilibration Time , which sets the duration for system relaxation before data collection begins. This is a single period for the entire simulation system, which includes all lambda states running in parallel. Production Time specifies the duration of the simulation phase that occurs after the equilibration phase is complete. During this period, data is collected from all lambda windows for the final free energy analysis. Lambda Windows defines the number of discrete steps in the lambda schedule for the alchemical transformation. This schedule controls the transformation from the starting state (lambda=0) to the final state (lambda=1). It also controls the number of replicas utilized. Parameters prefixed with Charge Change typically use doubled values to accommodate the increased complexity of charge-changing transformations. This is because charge change transformations can be more complex and require more sampling and lambda windows. In general the default settings are recommended unless you run into issues for a particular set of ligands.

Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Upon completion, the Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol provides comprehensive results in the Report.htm file. The report summarizes the simulation results. Tabulated free energy values for each ligand transformation, individually and cumulatively, are reported, as well as the estimated absolute free energy (ΔG).

The FEP Simulation Results table shows ligand pairs, the computed relative free energy change ΔΔG between them, and the associated uncertainty for each transformation. The Estimated Absolute Free Energies table presents each ligand along with its calculated absolute free energy and corresponding uncertainty. These values represent maximum likelihood estimates derived from the mean and standard deviation of ΔΔG replicas. The MLE estimates are centered at 0.0 and can be adjusted to align with experimental data. The Detailed FEP Report in the Output links to the Raw Free Energies table, which contains the unprocessed results from individual repeat simulations (without any aggregation of redundant runs). The table also includes runtime information and links to the corresponding MBAR convergence/overlap matrix plots.

This plot evaluates whether the simulated lambda states have adequate energetic overlap. Each matrix element shows the probability that a sample from the row state could be observed in the column state. Since MBAR estimator accuracy requires sufficient overlap between lambda states, this is a critical diagnostic. The goal is a matrix displaying a diagonal pattern with some "width," ensuring connectivity between the two end states, with off-diagonal elements adjacent to the main diagonal being at least 0.03. The color scheme indicates:

* Light Gray: Very low probabilities (< 0.025), minimal transitions

* Sky Blue: Low probabilities (0.025 – 0.100), infrequent transitions

* Dark Blue: Medium probabilities (0.100 – 0.300), moderate transitions

* Green: High probabilities (0.300 – 0.800), frequent transitions

* Gray: Very high probabilities (>= 0.800), dominant transitions

The figure above is from the first simulation of the complex leg of the lig_ejm_44 to lig_ejm_42 transformation. Notice that the main diagonal elements show good overlap (above 0.03), with the off-diagonal elements suggesting the reliability of the free energy estimate.

Finally, revisiting the values from the Estimated Absolute Free Energies table, notice that lig_ejm_55 is suggested to be the most favorable, followed by lig_ejm_42, and then lig_ejm_44. Note that this tutorial uses a subset of the larger TYK2 benchmark dataset. Production calculations would require the full dataset with appropriate statistical redundancy for accurate estimates.

In this tutorial, you employed relative alchemical free energy perturbation to rank a congeneric series of ligands for late-stage lead optimization. This method's ability to provide accurate quantitative binding energy estimates makes it an invaluable tool for rational structure-based drug design.

# Docking into a flexible receptor

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_flex-docking.htm

## Docking into a flexible receptor

Time: 25 minutes.

### Introduction

Flexible docking allows greater realism than other docking formalisms in that flexibility of the ligand and receptor side-chains is
permitted during the docking procedure. In general, only a limited number of side-chains undergo conformational changes during docking.
Since the computational effort increases exponentially with the number of flexible residues selected, it is recommended that you only enable flexibility for residues within the vicinity of the binding site.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to dock a ligand into a receptor with flexible amino acid side-chains
using the Flexible Docking protocol. The input parameters for this tutorial
have been adjusted to reduce calculation time by considering
fewer protein conformations from ChiFlex and fewer ligand poses
from LibDock than would be typically used.

In this tutorial, you will perform a cross-docking of the ligand from PDB ID 1fk9 into a different HIV-RT receptor structure. The following steps are covered:

* Preparing Flexible Docking

* Launching a Flexible Docking run

* Analyzing Flexible Docking results

* Calculating RMSD of the docked poses

for the superimposition.

# Preparing and analyzing a Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics simulation

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_gamd.htm

## Preparing and analyzing a Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics simulation

Time: 30 minutes + simulation time

### Introduction

While molecular dynamics simulations can provide key insights into the behavior of biomolecules and small molecules, such systems are prone to oversampling local energy minima. Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) is an enhanced sampling technique that flattens free energy landscapes to lower energy barriers for conformational transitions without the need to define a collective variable. In addition, harmonic boost potentials from GaMD follow a Gaussian distribution, facilitating accurate reweighting of free energy landscapes. Thus, GaMD is a useful technique to probe free energy landscapes of molecules with less simulation time than conventional molecular dynamics.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to perform and analyze GaMD simulations as covered by the following tasks:

* Preparation

* Running GaMD Equilibration

* Running GaMD Production

* Estimating a free energy landscape (with statistical reweighting)

The PDB code for the folded Chignolin peptide (GYDPETGTWG) is 1uao. However, for this tutorial, you will begin from a Chignolin peptide in an extended conformation.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | GaMD | Chignolin.dsv file. On the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel check that the Forcefield Status is set to charmm36 .

You can either use the provided tutorial file ( Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | GaMD | Chignolin.dsv ) that contains the Chignolin peptide in an extended conformation, or you can prepare your own before starting this tutorial. Chignolin in the tutorial file was built using the Build and Edit Protein tools. The molecule was then typed with the charmm36 forcefield, solvated in a water box, and subject to energy minimization. Finally, chignolin was equilibrated with a standard run of the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol and a 5ns equilibration run of Dynamics (NAMD) .

To run a GaMD simulation, the system must be equilibrated by the GaMD Equilibration protocol. The primary goal of this simulation is to equilibrate parameters that determine how boost potentials are applied to flatten the free energy landscape and accelerate sampling. Before running GaMD Equilibration , you should consider what time scales you want to sample and how accurately you need to correct any free energy landscape from the simulations for the biasing potentials being applied. Specifically, you will need to select what kind of boost potential to apply, how to select the threshold energy for applying the boost potential, and how much to limit the standard deviation of each potential. In conventional molecular dynamics, Chignolin folding can occur over several hundred nanoseconds—thus, you should try to equilibrate quickly over 1 to 10 nanoseconds to allow for production runs of 50 to 200 nanoseconds.

For the purposes of the tutorial, the following parameters are used:

* Boost Potential: Dual

* We wish to boost both the dihedral and total potentials to accelerate conformational sampling. The alternative option is to only boost the dihedral potential or only boost the total potential. Choosing a single type of boost will decrease the total amount of acceleration you achieve with GaMD; however, there may be cases where boosting a single type of potential is preferred.

* Boost Potential Threshold: Vmax

* This parameter determines how to calculate the boost potential threshold.

* The choice of Vmax or Vmin determines if the threshold is calculated from Vmax or Vmin, respectively. Note that in the case that Vmin is selected, the threshold energy is not exactly Vmin. In fact, threshold energies for well-equilibrated systems tend to be similar regardless of whether Vmax or Vmin is used in the calculation of the energy threshold.

* Boost Potential Standard Deviation: 6.0

* Higher values increase acceleration while decreasing the accuracy of statistical reweighting.

* Lower values increase the accuracy of reweighting while decreasing the degree of acceleration.

* For this tutorial, higher acceleration is preferred over reweighting accuracy, so the boost potential standard deviation is increased to 6.0 from the default value of 3.0.

You are only able to configure these GaMD parameters during the GaMD Equilibration protocol. When you proceed to the next protocol, GaMD Production , or resume a previous run of GaMD Equilibration , restart information and GaMD parameters are extracted from the input molecule.

With the type and duration of simulation considered, you can now begin to set up a GaMD Equilibration run.

Open the Simulation | Enhanced Sampling Dynamics tool panel and click GaMD Equilibration . Set the Input Typed Molecule parameter to Chignolin:Chignolin . Expand the Simulation parameter group and set the Time (ps) parameter to 10,000 and the Report Interval (ps) parameter to 10 . Expand the Boost Potential parameter group and set the Boost Potential Standard Deviation parameter to 6.0 . Expand the Restart Files parameter group, select the Velocities Restart File at Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | GaMD | Chignolin_restart.vel , and select the Extended System restart file at Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | GaMD | Chignolin_restart.xsc . Click Run to start the simulation, and then click Background and wait for the job to complete.

GaMD Equilibration is performed in phases:

* Phase I requires 10% of simulation time and performs conventional molecular dynamics without collecting statistics about boost potential parameters.

* Phase II requires 40% of simulation time and performs conventional molecular dynamics while collecting statistics about boost potential parameters. At the end of Phase II, the threshold energy below which a boost potential is applied and a boost potential scaling factor are determined.

* Phase III requires 10 % of simulation time and applies boost potentials using the threshold energy and scaling factor determined from phase II.

* Phase IV requires 40 % of simulation time and applies boost potentials while updating the threshold and scaling factors every step.

The simulation should take several hours to finish, but, once complete, you should inspect the report to check for convergence of GaMD parameters. As with the Dynamics (NAMD) protocol, you should observe temperature and total energy time-series remain relatively stable for the duration of the simulation. Approximately halfway into the simulation, you may observe some increase in total energy associated with the first application of the biasing potentials. However, the total energy should stabilize during the later parts of the simulation. When you inspect the report, it is also important to observe that the average boost potential converges to some value, and that the distribution of boost potentials follows a normal distribution. Finally, for each boost potential that is applied, the standard deviation of the corresponding potential should converge to a particular value.

#### Options and Best Practices

* Where possible, providing restart information will greatly enhance the stability of simulations.

* Restart files can only be provided for the first run of the GaMD Equilibration protocol.

* If you resume/extend a GaMD Equilibration run or start a GaMD Production simulation, then restart information is automatically extracted from the input molecule.

* If any GaMD parameters appear to be unconverged, you can extend the initial GaMD Equilibration simulation to allow additional time for these parameters to converge. To do this, follow these: Open the Output Molecule from the prior run of GaMD Equilibration . Open the Simulation | Enhanced Sampling Dynamics tool panel and click GaMD Equilibration . With the output molecule from the previous GaMD Equilibration run as the active window, set the Input Typed Molecule parameter to the output molecule. Expand the Simulation parameter group and set the Simulation Time (ps) and Report Interval (ps) parameters to appropriate values respectively. Set the Resume Equilibration parameter to True . Click Run to start the simulation. After the simulation completes, inspect the report again as described previously.

Open the Output Molecule from the prior run of GaMD Equilibration . Open the Simulation | Enhanced Sampling Dynamics tool panel and click GaMD Equilibration . With the output molecule from the previous GaMD Equilibration run as the active window, set the Input Typed Molecule parameter to the output molecule. Expand the Simulation parameter group and set the Simulation Time (ps) and Report Interval (ps) parameters to appropriate values respectively. Set the Resume Equilibration parameter to True . Click Run to start the simulation. After the simulation completes, inspect the report again as described previously.

When the simulation from GaMD Equilibration is complete and all GaMD parameters have converged, the system is ready for GaMD Production . You can begin one or more GaMD Production simulations from a single molecular system prepared by GaMD Equilibration as the simulation is stochastic in nature due to the Langevin pressure and temperature control. However, since multiple replicates begin from the same conformational state, initial motions may be highly correlated between simulations. You can avoid this by running sufficiently long simulations.

To begin running GaMD Production , perform the following steps:

Open the Output Molecule from the prior run of GaMD Equilibration . Open the Simulation | Enhanced Sampling Dynamics tool panel and click GaMD Production .
With the output molecule from the previous GaMD Equilibration run as the active window, set the Input Typed Molecule parameter to the output molecule that corresponds to the end state of the prior simulation. Expand the Simulation parameter group and set the Simulation Time (ps) parameter to 100,000 and the Report Interval (ps) parameter to 100 . Click Run to start the simulation, and then click Background and wait for the job to complete.

After the simulation completes, inspect the report to make sure that the average boost potential remains relatively stable throughout the simulation and that the boost potentials follow a normal distribution. If desired, you can also view the simulation by using the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory | Load Trajectory protocol and selecting the output trajectory from GaMD Production as the input.

Once GaMD Production has completed, you should analyze the trajectory in a manner appropriate for the types of molecular behavior of interest. In this tutorial, you are measuring the folding of Chignolin as the simulation progresses. Then, you will view the free energy along the folding reaction coordinate. For this purpose, you will measure root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of Chignolin in the simulation from the folded state (PDB: 1uao).

Measuring features of a trajectory can be performed within the Estimate Free Energy Landscape and the Measure Trajectory Features protocols. Both of these protocols measure features in the same way—inn this tutorial you will use the Estimate Free Energy Landscape protocol:

Open the Output Molecule from the prior run of GaMD Production . Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | GaMD | 1uao.dsv file. Open the Estimate Free Energy Landscape protocol. If the protocol opens in an undocked window, press the minimize button in the upper-right corner to dock the protocol. Select the Chignolin Output Molecule output from GaMD Production as your active window.

Now you will make some atom selections to correctly calculate the RMSD of each trajectory frame from the reference structure of 1uao .

Select the drop down menu next to Chignolin and chain A to display all residues in Chignolin. Select residues GLY1 through GLY10 by clicking GLY1 with the left mouse button then shift left-clicking GLY10 . Create a group from the selection by right-clicking the selection and selecting Group . Give the group the name Peptide . Select residues ASP3 through THR8 and create a new group from the selection and name it Peptide 3-8 . Select the folded state of Chignolin 1auo as the active window. Select residues GLY1 through GLY10 and create a group from the selection and name it Peptide . Select residues ASP3 through THR8 and create a new group from the selection and name it Peptide 3-8 .

At this point you have configured all necessary selections to correctly configure Estimate Free Energy Landscape .

Estimate Free Energy Landscape can either accept an input dataset in CSV format, or you can configure how to measure data from one or more simulation trajectories. This tutorial demonstrates the latter option. However, you could use Measure Trajectory Features to generate the dataset in CSV format and then pass the CSV file directly to Estimate Free Energy Landscape .

Select the Chignolin Output Molecule output from GaMD Production as your active window and set it as the Input Molecule parameter. Expand the Input Molecule parameter group and set the Input Trajectory parameter to the output trajectory file in DCD format from the GaMD Production protocol. Set the Input Atoms parameter to the selection group Peptide . Set the Input Bias Potentials parameter to the energy table with boost potentials output by GaMD Production . If this parameter is not provided, statistical reweighting to correct for the biasing potentials will not be performed. Select the folded state of Chignolin 1auo as the active window and set it as the Reference Molecule parameter. Expand the Reference Molecule parameter group and set the Reference Atoms parameter to the selection group Peptide . Set the Superpose Frames on Reference parameter to True . Expand the Superpose Frames on Reference parameter group and set the Mobile Atoms parameter to the selection group Peptide 3-8 and the Fixed Atoms parameter to the selection group Peptide 3-8 . Set the Feature Type parameter to RMSD . Click Run to start the analysis, and then click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Once the Estimate Free Energy Landscape protocol completes, you can view the Potential of Mean Force associated with different RMSD from the folded state. Lower RMSD values indicate a conformation that is more similar to the folded state, and you should see an energy well in the landscape that corresponds to a folded state as seen in the following image at an RMSD value of 1.25 angstroms:

# Optimizing lead compounds from a scaffold in a protein active site

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_grow-scaffold.htm

## Optimizing lead compounds from a scaffold in a protein active site

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

Lead optimization is the complex, iterative process of refining the chemical structure of promising compounds and scaffolds in order to improve biochemical potency, selectivity, bioavailability, and pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters, and reduce toxicity, with the goal of producing a preclinical drug candidate. This stage frequently represents the bottleneck of a drug discovery program. Effective and practical computational tools for lead optimization need to be able to rapidly propose synthetically feasible candidates from realistic reagents representing accessible chemistry. Structure-based lead optimization focuses the chemical design within the binding site of a protein target. The Grow Scaffold tool uses a reaction-based in situ enumeration approach to identify and prioritize which reagents are most likely to produce potential optimized leads for that protein binding site.

In this tutorial, you will study the lead optimization of a diaryl urea lead candidate to produce a p38α drug candidate ( Figure 1 ). This was first studied by Boehringer Ingelheim [Pargellis et al., 2002] , and then subsequently by Pfizer [Millan et al. 2011] . p38α is a member of the well characterized mitogen activated protein kinase family of serine/threonine protein kinases. It is widely expressed in endothelial, immune, and inflammatory cells and plays a central role in the regulation of pro-inflammatory cytokine production including tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-1. Selective blockade of any one of these cytokines has proven efficacious for a variety of inflammatory and immunological disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, septic shock, and osteoporosis.

Figure 1: p38α lead and optimized candidates

In this tutorial, you will use the Grow Scaffold lead optimization tool to reproduce one of the structural optimizations identified by Boehringer Ingelheim, and explore additional modifications published by Pfizer. The following tasks are covered:

* Generating optimized lead compounds by a reaction-based in situ enumeration

* Using a custom reaction to generate optimized lead compounds

The PDB code for the protein-ligand complex used is 1KV2 [Pargellis et al., 2002] . The sample file used in this tutorial was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared with the Prepare Proteins protocol.

Open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1kv2_complex.dsv .

Boehringer Ingelheim reported three major structural changes to the initial diaryl urea lead candidate that conferred increases in binding affinity [Pargellis et al., 2002] : replacement of the methyl substituent on the pyrazole ring with a tolyl group (~140-fold enhancement in affinity), replacement of the chlorophenyl group with the naphthyl moiety (~15-fold) and the introduction of an ethoxymorpholine substituent on the naphthyl ring (~11-fold).

The crystallized ligand displayed (1kv2_xrayligand) is BIRB 796, was the first reported inhibitor of p38α which did not bind to the canonical ATP site, opening up the prospect of allosteric inhibition of kinases as a viable approach to identifying novel drug candidates. In this tutorial you will model the introduction of the ethoxymorpholine substituent on the naphthyl ring which produced BIRB 796.

In the Hierarchy View , uncheck the visibility checkbox 1kv2_xrayligand and turn on the visibility for the 1kv2_scaffold . Select the naphthyl hydrogen para to the urea group (H31). Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tool panel and click Grow Scaffold... to open the protocol dialog. Set Input Receptor to 1kv2_complex:1kv2_protein . Check that Input Ligand Scaffold is set to 1kv2_complex:1kv2_scaffold . Click Scaffold Grow Points and choose Create New Group From Selection... . Click the Reactions parameter to uncheck the Amide Synthesis reaction and check the Williamson Ether Synthesis reaction. Click the Reagents parameter and check Halides and Alcohols . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of enumerated ligands (~500).

The Williamson Ether Synthesis reaction scheme ( Figure 2 ) was not the actual reaction pathway used to synthesize BIRB 796 [Regan et al., 2003] . But in this tutorial, it illustrates how a reaction and the associated reagents for that reaction can be used to explore possible ligand enumerations that can potentially fit into the protein active site.

Figure 2: Williamson Ether Synthesis reaction scheme

The Grow Scaffold protocol allows you to specify a generic scaffold and consider the reaction of the scaffold to either potential reagent types: alcohols or halides. If only alcohol reagents are selected for the enumeration, the Grow Point of the scaffold would act as if this were a halide to react with the alcohol to create the ether product (first reaction in Figure 3 ). Alternatively, halide reagents react with the scaffold as if there were a hydroxy substituent at the Grow Point.

Figure 3: How the scaffold reacts with the reagents

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link. Click View Results .

The report includes a summary of the enumeration at the Grow Point within the protein active site. The table summarizes the number of reagents in each library, the number of unique reagents from each library that can be enumerated in the protein active site, and the actual enumerated reagents. Some reagents may contain more than one instance of the reactive substructure (e.g., the reagent may have two alcohol substituents) and thus two enumerated products may be possible from this single reagent.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools
and click Ligand Interactions .

This displays the non-bond interactions between the receptor and the ligand as well as any intramolecular interactions in the ligand.

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions tool panel to browse through the ligands.

The final list of enumerated ligands are returned pareto sorted by the number of interactions formed with the protein (maximized), Lipinski violations (minimized), receptor bumps (minimized), and fragment 'novelty' (maximized). The interactions of the ligand with the protein are reported, and details of the interaction type, protein residues, and interaction distances are included.

In the Data Table View, double-click the Fragment Name R1 column header. Use the Data Table View scroll bar to find 2-MORPHOLINOETHANOL , and then select the row. Locate 2-MORPHOLINOETHANOL in the Fragment Name R1 column.

Another option is to apply a filter to the table.

Right-click in the Data Table and choose Filter... . In the Filter dialog, locate the column named "Fragment Name R1", and then change the Choice to Contains . Set Value to MORPHO . Note that this field is case-sensitive.

The Data Table now shows only rows that match this filter.

Select the 2-MORPHOLINOETHANOL row. SHIFT+click the Show selection icon to the left of the Data Table to view this ligand only.

This ligand is the BIRB 796 structure ( Figure 1 ). If you compare this structure to the crystal structure conformation (1kv2_xrayligand) in the 1kv2_complex Molecule Window, you will find that they are not necessarily the same, as running this protocol is not the same as performing docking. However, the Grow Scaffold protocol does include parameters to allow you to further optimize the enumerated ligands in the protein active site by performing an in situ minimization (this is covered in the second part of the tutorial).

Despite BIRB 796 progressing to late stage clinical trials as a potential therapy for acute and chronic inflammatory diseases, elevations of liver transaminases were observed and Boehringer Ingelheim is no longer developing this compound.

Grow Scaffold comes with a default list of reaction schemes that represent many of the common reactions used by medicinal chemists. However, you can easily add your own reactions. In this part of the tutorial you will optimize another p38α scaffold with a reaction scheme not included by default.

Additionally, you will set up this lead optimization to target residue MET109, which plays an essential role in the linker beta strand that connects the alpha and beta domains of p38 kinase. Only new ligands that interact with this residue will be returned.

Open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | diverse_sulfides.sd . Return to the 1kv2_complex Molecule Window . Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and insert Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 2yis_scaffold.sd . In the Hierarchy View, uncheck the visibility checkbox for 1kv2_scaffold and turn on the visibility for 2yis_scaffold .

The PF-03715455 structure ( Figure 1 ) arose from an optimization of p38 inhibitors as inhaled agents for the treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [Millan et al., 2011] . The optimization focused on potency and selectivity for p38, as well as slow enzyme dissociation kinetics, high intrinsic clearance, low oral bioavailability, high CYP mediated clearance and glucuronidation, and multiple routes of clearance to minimize drug-drug interactions. The 2yis_scaffold you will be optimizing is similar in chemistry and orientation to the 1kv2_scaffold. However, as the linker is a thioether substructure, you will use a custom thioether synthesis reaction scheme instead of the Williamson Ether Synthesis:

Figure 4: Thioether synthesis reaction scheme

Reaction schemes in the Grow Scaffold tool are written as half-reactions, with one reactant and the product. The advantage of half-reactions is that they can be used individually or together to define the complete reaction scheme for greater control. So if you are using a mixed reagent library (e.g., a library containing both sulfide and halide reagents), the use of only the sulfide half-reaction of the thioether synthesis would allow you to extract solely those reagents with sulfide substituents for the enumeration. The sulfide half-reaction you will use is illustrated in the following figure. The X in the half-reaction represents the scaffold that acts as the halide reagent in the complete reaction.

Figure 5: Sulfide half-reaction of the thioether synthesis reaction scheme

If you use RXN files to define your custom reaction, atom-atom mapping is required as this specifies which reactant atom becomes which product atom through the reaction.

If you want to enumerate the complete reaction scheme, like the default reactions, you can specify both halide and sulfide half-reactions.

In the 2yis_scaffold , select the phenyl hydrogen ortho to the methylurea group on the open side of the receptor surface (H19). Open Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tool panel, and the click Grow Scaffold... to open the protocol dialog. Set Input Receptor to 1kv2_complex:1kv2_protein . Expand the Input Receptor parameter group, and set Interacting Residues to the predefined MET109 group. Set Input Ligand Scaffold to 1kv2_complex:2yis_scaffold . Click Scaffold Grow Points and choose Create New Group From Selection... . Expand the Reactions group. Set Custom to Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | sulfide_halfreaction.rxn . Return to the Reactions parameter, uncheck the Amide Synthesis reaction and check the Custom: sulfide_halfreaction option, which now appears at the bottom of the list of reactions. Expand the Reagent group and set the Custom parameter to diverse_sulfides:All . Return to the Reagents parameter and check the Custom: diverse_sulfides option. Set Minimization to True . Expand the Advanced parameter group and set Torsion Step Size to 10 . Set Generate Reagents Conformations to True , and then expand the group and set Maximum Conformations to 10 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of enumerated ligands; you should get back about 10 ligands.

The parameters in this example of the Grow Scaffold enumeration have been changed to illustrate how you can tailor this tool to more closely mimic the optimization in the protein that occurs during docking and thoroughly sample conformations and torsional positioning of reagents, which may be more flexible than fragment-centric reagents. Also, you were able to target residue MET109, which plays an essential role in the linker beta strand that connects the alpha and beta domains of p38 kinase.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link. Click View Results . Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools
and click Ligand Interactions .

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions tool panel to navigate through the ligands.

None of the new ligands will be the same as PF-03715455 ( Figure 1 ) as no reagents in the diverse_sulfides.sd file include the required hydroxyethylsulfanylphenyl triazolopyridinyl substructure.

However, you will notice several interesting new substituents, including benzothiazole, benzoxazolinone, indazole, benzimidazole, and imidazopyridine substructures. You may also notice that these new ligands do not have as many, if any, bump interactions with the protein (shown as Receptor Bumps in the Molecule tab) compared to the previous ligands you generated.
