# Humanizing an antibody Fv sequence

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_humanization.htm

## Humanizing an antibody Fv sequence

Time: 30 minutes + model building time.

### Introduction

Humanization is the process of engineering an antibody that retains the antigen binding specificity and affinity of a non-human antibody, yet exhibits low human immunogenicity and does not compromise stability. 
Predicting such an antibody structure entails mutating residues in the framework regions of the variable domain to make them more similar to the types found in human antibodies (for example, those found in germline genes and in a large antibody sequence database).
Native CDR regions that confer the desired specificity are retained, along with the Vernier residues, which are framework residues important for stabilizing CDR conformation [Almagro and Fransson, 2008] . 
Additionally, humanizing mutations can be suggested by a machine learning (ML) method [Marks et al., 2021] . 
The mutations can then be assessed for their effects on stability.

In this tutorial, you will start with the sequence of a murine monoclonal antibody, which specifically inhibits proliferation of human tumor cells that over-express p185 HER2 , and predict and assess humanizing mutations. The following tasks are covered:

* Prepare the input structure

* Predict humanizing mutations

* Examine the interactive reports

* Examine suggested mutations

* Analyze mutation energies

* Assess formulation properties

The Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol requires a structure if you want to assess the effects of the suggested mutations on protein stability, preferably a crystal structure of the Fv or Fab domain of the antibody that you want to humanize. The input structure must be typed by CHARMm Polar H forcefield for energy calculations. The protocol will type the protein if an untyped structure is provided, but it is recommended that you perform this step separately. Providing the input structure is optional. When no structure is provided, the protocol will automatically generate the structure from the query sequence. However, this is only allowed if the query sequence is a complete Fv or Fab domain as stability calculations will not be valid for a single light or heavy chain.

Open the Samples\Tutorials\Protein Modeling\4D5_FV.fasta file. This contains the sequence of the entire FV region of the antibody with no chain breaks. With the 4D5_FV Sequence Window active, click Antibody Modeling Cascade... on the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel. Check that the Input Sequences parameter is set to 4D5_FV:All . Leave the parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The model generation takes a few minutes. The Job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 1/1 models were built.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. In the report, click the View Results button.

A molecule window opens that contains the 4D5 model structure, and a sequence window displaying an annotated copy of the input sequence.

If you have a structure from another source, for example a PDB file, you should use Macromolecules | Prepare Protein | Prepare Proteins to ensure it is valid before typing.

Activate the Antibody Cascade Models window. Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel. Set the Forcefield to CHARMm Polar H , and then click Apply Forcefield . Choose File | Save As... from the menu and save the structure as 4D5.dsv .

You now have a typed protein structure suitable for mutation energy calculations.

A copy of this file can be found in the Samples folder for reference.

With the 4D5_FV sequence window active, click Predict Humanizing Mutations... on the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tool panel. Set the Query Sequence parameter to 4D5_FV:4D5 . Set the Query Structure parameter to 4D5:4D5 . Expand the Predict using Machine Learning group and set the Target Scores parameter to 0.9. Expand the Calculate Mutation Energy group and set the Germline and Frequent Residues and Machine Learning Prediction parameters to True . If you wish, set Parallel Processing to True and its sub-parameters appropriately for your server. Leave the other parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The initial single mutations can be run in parallel, but the other sets of combined mutations each have to be run sequentially which can take some time.

The Job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports when Humanizing Mutation Prediction finishes.

The report tabulates the results of mutation energy calculations. It also includes a table of the similarity and identity of the various substituted sequences compared to the query sequence, and also the "humanness" scores for each chain. These scores are calculated using the random forest classifiers in the ML method. The View Results button will open the Interactive Residue Analysis Report for the heavy and light chain variable domains, the Residue Substitutions sequence alignment, and the Multiple Mutations molecule window.

The Interactive Residue Analysis Report for each of the variable domains contains a legend that defines the color and style that denote residue characteristics in the table. There is also a legend for the details that you can display by hovering the cursor over each residue cell.

Activate the VL_KAPPA Interactive Residue Analysis Report window. Hover over an orange hotspot residue to display its details. For example, the methionine at position 11 (in both the Kabat and IMGT numbering). Observe that this is a residue that does not match the germline type (leucine) and has a low frequency in the human residue statistics database for the IGKV1 gene. The types found with frequency >5% are leucine and valine. Examine other residues of interest, and then the VH Interactive Residue Analysis Report .

The Residue Substitutions alignment contains various mutations suggested by the protocol:

* Best_Single_Mutations sequence : The residue type found in the germline sequence, ML models, or with frequency > 5%, which produces the most stabilized structure.

* Frequent_Residue_Substitutions sequence : Residues substituted where appropriate to the type found most frequently at that position in human antibodies.

* Germline_Substitutions sequence : Residues mutated where appropriate to type found in best-matching human germline sequence.

* ML_Prediction_1 : Residues mutated using the ML method. If multiple Target Score values are entered then a corresponding number of predicted sequences will be created.

Activate the ResidueSubstitutions sequence alignment window. Observe that the first sequence is the query annotated with the normal antibody annotation styles and that hovering over individual residue shows the IMGT residue ID. Observe that the second sequence is also the query but with Vernier residues denoted by a blue caret, hotspots in orange, and the combined Kabat and IMGT CDR regions in magenta or red depending on domain. The next three sequences show various mutations for hotspot residues that are not excluded from substitution (by default, CDR, Vernier, and where the query residue matches the germline type are excluded). The ML_Prediction sequences show mutations predicted by the ML method, which always excludes IMGT CDR positions. In the current example, with humanness score setting at 0.9 as used in Marks' ML paper [Marks et al., 2021] , the number of mutations suggested by ML model is less than other approaches. This is similar to what's reported by the original ML paper and during a humanization process, it is desirable to keep the mutations minimum to conserve the function and properties of the antibody.

This alignment can be used to calculate the mutation stability energy for the combined Best Single Mutations , Germline Substitutions, Frequent Residue Substitution, or ML_Prediction mutations.

Activate the Predict Humanizing Mutations Report window. The first table shows the sequence identity, similarity and "humanness score" for the various sequences.

Note that the second table contains the energies of all single mutations.

Examine the third table, which lists the four combined mutations as shown in the Residue Substitutions alignment.

The combined mutations result in four sequences. The Best Single Mutations shows stabilization, whereas Germline Mutations, Frequent Residue Mutations, and ML_Prediction_1 turn out to be nearly neutral (the exact values may vary a little depending on the server OS). 
The single mutation models results in the second table show that 
several of the individual mutations suggested by the various methods are destabilizing. This demonstrates the importance of considering stability rather than accepting the most frequently found types. 
The destabilizing single mutations could be removed from the alignment and the stability of the remainder assessed using the Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) protocol.

From the VL_KAPPA Interactive Residue Analysis Report window, position 83 (IMGT numbering 99) is LEU in the query sequence, ILE in the Germline sequence, PHE in ML_Prediction_1,
and the Percentages of Human Ab Statistics at this position are shown F=76, I=10, and V=7. View the Predict Humanizing Mutations report window. The second table (Single mutation models) lists the Mutation Energy for these three single mutations: L:LEU99>ILE, L:LEU99>PHE, and L:LEU99>VAL.

L:LEU99>PHE has the best (lowest) mutation energy. Therefore, this mutation is chosen to be included in the model for the final Best_Single_Mutations, as shown in the second table (Multiple mutation models).

With the Multiple Mutations molecule window active, use File | Insert From | File to open the previously saved 4D5.dsv into the same window. In the Macromolecules | Predict Protein Formulation Properties tool panel, click the Calculate Protein Formulation Properties link. Set the Input Protein Molecules parameter to Humanization Prediction - Multiple Mutations:All . If you wish, set Parallel Processing to True and its sub-parameters appropriately for your server. Leave the other parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete.

The Report should show that the structure with the suggested Best Single mutations is predicted to have a higher solubility score, lower viscosity and somewhat decreased tendency to aggregate compared to the native 4D5 structure.

The Sample\Tutorials\Protein Modeling folder contains the alignment and structures for the 4D5 sequence with all the suggested substitutions and also Trastuzumab ( 4D5_and_Mutations_and_Trastuzumab.dsv/bsml ). Trastuzumab is the therapeutic antibody derived from the native 4D5 sequence, which is marketed as Herceptin. You may want to further examine and compare these. It can be seen that many of the mutations suggested by the Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol are found in Trastuzumab.

# Introduction to the Discovery Studio Client

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_introduction.htm

## Introduction to the Discovery Studio Client

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

Discovery Studio is a comprehensive software suite for analyzing and modeling 
molecular structures, sequences, and other data of relevance to life 
science researchers. The product includes functionality for viewing and editing data along
with tools for performing basic data analysis.

The Discovery Studio Client is a desktop application that can be used to access all the functionality in Discovery Studio .

The Discovery Studio Visualizer is a free viewer that can be used to open data
generated by other software in the Discovery Studio product line.

It is designed to offer an interactive environment for viewing and 
editing molecular structures, sequences, X-ray reflection data, scripts, and other data. It 
also provides a rich set of viewers for displaying plots and other graphical 
representations of data. The application runs on Windows and is a fully 
integrated desktop environment that provides access to standard operating system features 
such as the file system, clipboard, and printing services.

To get the most from the product it is useful to understand some of the key 
concepts and features behind the program design. This lesson provides a basic overview of 
how to work with the application by introducing the following basic concepts:

* Application Workspace

* Tools

* Protocols

* Preferences

* Display Style

* Status Bar

* Scripts

The application workspace occupies the main screen area when the application is opened. By default, 
a Welcome page is displayed in this space when the application is first started. As subsequent windows
are opened they can be easily arranged to either tile them or arrange them on top of each other.

The application offers several ways of organizing and switching 
between windows. You can move a Window by clicking and dragging its tab to the desired 
position. In this way you can arrange windows on top of each 
other or organize them to view them simultaneously. You can
also open windows outside of the
main application window by clicking on the Undock button on 
the right side of the window header. 
This feature is useful when working with multiple monitors.

It is also possible to work with the explorer windows in autohide mode to increase the viewable area. To set this mode,
click the Pushpin button at the top of an explorer dock. This causes the dock to
collapse. When you subsequently click on the tab of an explorer, the
window is temporarily revealed.

Discovery Studio offers a wide variety of tools for working with and visualizing data. Tools 
can be accessed from menus, toolbars and tool panels. In addition you can create your own tools using 
scripting or by linking to protocols and expose 
them anywhere in the application. Of all of the methods for accessing 
the tools, tool panels are the most flexible. Tool panels group tools based on specific tasks 
you want to perform. Furthermore, tool panels are grouped into large sets for working in areas 
such as Pharmacophores and Receptor-Ligand Interactions. You 
can also create your own custom tool panels that contain commonly used tools. For details, see Creating a tool panel .

A useful feature for most buttons and menu items is the tool tip. Hover your cursor over a 
feature to display a small note that offers basic information about it. In many cases, 
the tool tip includes a link to more detailed help or related functionality such as 
preferences.

Another valuable resource for finding information about the application is the Feature Search Box in the upper-right corner of the application. To locate a feature, begin typing
its name, or some term that relates to its
functionality. A list of associated features appears in a dropdown
list. The Feature Search Box matches text in the short descriptions of features so matches are obtained
even if you do not specify the precise name of a tool. Click on it in the list to present
the corresponding menu item, toolbar button, tool panel, or protocol.

#### Menus

The main menu of the application window provides access to basic tools for
accessing, editing, and viewing data. The following menus provide access to related
sets of functionality:

* File

* Edit

* View

* Chemistry

* Structure

* Sequence

* Charts

* Window

* Help

Individual tools on menus, toolbars and tool panels are enabled and disabled depending on the data being viewed. 
Help for the tool, including information about what type of data is needed to enable the command, can be displayed by hovering over the tool to view a tooltip. Click the help link in the tooltip for more detail.

#### Toolbars

Toolbars are useful for providing quick access to commonly used, quick-running tools.
A large set of toolbars are provided, which can be shown or hidden
depending on the current task. By default, a set of general purpose toolbars such as
Standard, Search Product Features and the Smart Tools are shown when you start the application for the first time. However,
as you start to work with the application you can add additional toolbars by right-clicking on an existing toolbar or the menu bar and selecting from the list.

#### Tool Panels

Tool panels are another way of invoking tools to analyze data. Tool panels are graphical
palettes that contain buttons, dropdowns, and other controls that provide
access to related sets of functionality. The tools exposed on tool panels typically operate
directly on a selected object in the current window, and like other tools, are
enabled and disabled depending on whether the appropriate data is selected.

Tool Panels are located in the Tools Explorer. Custom tool panels can be created 
from the Tools Explorer or using the Tool Panels preferences page.

Discovery Studio uses Pipeline Pilot Server to run complex scientific tasks. Pipeline Pilot uses data pipelining technology that makes it possible to connect different data sources with applications 
and rapidly process data through a branching network of computational steps. Points of data are 
processed independently via components, and multiple data points can be processed simultaneously 
via protocols.

Pipeline Pilot Server is tightly integrated with Discovery Studio so that data being viewed or edited in
the application can be used as input to an Pipeline Pilot protocol. However, you can also edit and run 
protocols with the Pipeline Pilot Client . You can also run Discovery Studio protocols outside of the 
application using other Pipeline Pilot Client s such as the Pipeline Pilot Web Port.

In Discovery Studio , protocols are typically used to perform more complex multi-stage tasks, often
taking significant computational time.

Application customization and settings are available in the Preferences 
dialog, which can be accessed from the Edit menu. The dialog contains a tree control
that lists the different preferences categories. By clicking on the area of interest, the main 
preference page displays the available options.

### Display Style Dialog

While the Preferences dialog provides access to application-wide settings, the Display Style
dialog is used to change the settings that affect the appearance and behavior of specific data
opened in different windows. When data is opened in the application, you can access this dialog by right-clicking the view
or from the View menu. This dialog provides access to settings that control particular aspects of the appearance of data or
the way the display is configured. Any changes made in the display style dialog
are stored with the data if it is saved in a Discovery Studio file format ( .dsv ).

The Status Bar at the bottom of the application window displays useful information relating to your current activity in
the Visualizer. During the execution of some operations, it will display a Progress Bar that shows status of the current operations. Clicking the Close icon stops the operation. In addition,
when working with molecules or sequences, the Status Bar often displays information about the state of
the selected object.

Discovery Studio provides a Perl Application Programming Interface (API) to allow development of 
custom scripts. This powerful feature enables the creation of Perl scripts that automate commonly used
tasks in the application. In addition, because the API provides full access to the underlying data 
models in the application (e.g. the Molecular Data Model, the Sequence Data Model), you can create scripts that perform advanced analysis routines if desired.

Another powerful feature of scripting in the Discovery Studio Client

Visualizer

is that the API provides functions
for accessing data already in memory. This enables the creation of scripts that process molecules,
sequences, or other data that you happen to be editing. In this way it is possible to create new tools
that can be invoked through menus, toolbars, or tool panels. For details, see Working with scripts .

# Generating interaction pharmacophores from a protein-ligand complex

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_ipg.htm

## Generating interaction pharmacophores from a protein-ligand complex

Time: 40 minutes.

### Introduction

In the early days of pharmacophore generation, [Barnum et al., 1996], pharmacophore features were defined in a ligand-centric view, which has not changed significantly over the years, even though users gained the ability to modify and customize feature definitions. In a recent release of Discovery Studio, the non-bond interaction definitions were updated and improved to better represent the wealth and complexity of potential interactions between proteins and ligands.

The Interaction Pharmacophore Generation protocol generates a set of selective pharmacophore models from a receptor-ligand complex. The models are generated from features that correspond to the receptor-ligand interactions. Compared with its predecessor, it uses new pharmacophore feature types, which correspond more closely to the modern understanding of non-bond interactions. It automatically generates a set of pharmacophore models from them, which can then be used for fast pharmacophore searching and mapping of ligands into a protein active site.

The protein complex used in this tutorial is the serine/threonine kinase B-Raf protein [Hansen et al., 2008] that plays a role in regulating the MAP kinase/ERK signaling pathway, which affects cell division, differentiation, and secretion. Mutations in this gene are the most frequently identified cancer-causing mutations in melanoma and have been identified in various other cancers as well, including non-Hodgkin lymphoma, colorectal cancer, thyroid carcinoma, non-small cell lung carcinoma, hairy cell leukemia, and adenocarcinoma of lung.

The active and inactive ligands in this tutorial come from the Database of Useful Decoys: Enhanced (DUD-E) for the BRAF dataset (see http://dude.docking.org/ and [Mysinger et al., 2012] ). The DUD-E ligands were prepared by removing ligands with duplicate names and structures. To keep the running time of this tutorial short, the Find Diverse Molecules protocol was used to select a diverse subset of 150 inactive ligands from the almost-10000 BRAF decoys.

This tutorial covers:

* Generating interaction pharmacophores

* Modifying parameters to improve performance

The PDB code for the B-Raf receptor-ligand complex used is 3D4Q [Hansen et al., 2008] . The file was downloaded from the PDB website and the protein was prepared using the Prepare Proteins protocol.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | 3d4q_complex.dsv , braf_actives.sd , and braf_decoys.sd files. Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Automatically tool panel and click Interaction Pharmacophore Generation . Set the Input Receptor parameter to 3d4q_complex:3d4q_protein , and the Input Ligand parameter to 3d4q_complex:3d4q_ligand . Set the Validation parameter to True . Expand the parameter group and set the Active Ligands parameter to braf_actives:All , and the Inactive Ligands parameter to braf_decoys:All . Expand the Advanced parameter group and click the Non-bond Interactions parameter to open the dialog listing the types of interactions to consider. You will make no changes to this default selection. If you have a multi-processor server you can set the Parallel Processing parameters to complete the protocol more quickly. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Running this job on a single processor should take less than 8 minutes.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 10 pharmacophores have been generated.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report. Click View Results .

You can now see the detailed report of the resulting validated pharmacophores, and a 3D window with the protein, ligand, and the 10 generated pharmacophores.

The first part of the report tabulates the generated pharmacophores, reporting the number of features and the feature types. The 10 pharmacophores include 5 that have 6 features and 5 that have 5 features each.

Notice that the algorithm has identified 18 non-bond interactions between the protein and ligand. The next part of the report shows the performance of each of the pharmacophores in mapping ligands from the actives and decoys datasets. Amongst them, Pharmacophore 7 has the best overall AUC ROC, the highest Sensitivity, and a reasonable Specificity. This model maps 83 of the 152 possible actives, while also fitting to 15 false positives from the 150 decoys. If minimizing false positives is key to your project then Pharmacophore 2 may be preferred even though it only maps to 29 of the active ligands. The ROC curves in the next section of the report illustrate that the pharmacophores are considered poor in their screening performance with these validation datasets.

Scroll to the bottom of the report to see another listing of the generated pharmacophores, which reports the number of features and the feature types. The 10 pharmacophores include 5 that have 6 features and 5 that have 5 features each.

In the Jobs Explorer, right-click the Interaction Pharmacophore Generation job entry line and choose Locate . In the Files Explorer, drag the AllFeatures.ds_chm file into the 3D window with the pharmacophore results. Click the arrow next to the Non-bond Interactions toolbar and choose Ligand Interactions . Note that this context-sensitive toolbar appears when a Molecule Window with a protein-ligand complex is active. In the Hierarchy View, uncheck the 3d4q_ligand_01 pharmacophore so that it is no longer visible.

You can now see how all the pharmacophore features representing the protein-ligand interactions correspond to the non-bond interactions between the ligand and the protein active site. You may want to toggle the visibility of the all features pharmacophore (3d4q_ligand_all) on and off to see the interactions.

Open the Data Table View with the CTRL+T shortcut and open the Non-bond tab. If this tab is not visible, use the arrow to the right of the visible tabs to access it.

On this tab you can see each of the interactions summarized in detail, including the distance, category and type of the interaction, and the chemistry and atoms that form the interaction.

There are 18 interactions listed, while the pharmacophore only has 10 features. This is because interactions 3–5 are Carbon Hydrogen Bonds and the carbonHBondType feature was not selected from the Non-bond Interactions parameter when the pharmacophores were generated, and because some features make multiple interactions.

When the protein-ligand complex has a large number of interactions and features, the default protocol values may mean that you have not explored all of the combinations of pharmacophores that will give the best performance to match your project criteria. With a 10 feature pharmacophore there are 672 possible combinations of models with a minimum of 4 and a maximum of 6 features; there are 210 possible pharmacophores that have only 4 features. A smaller number of features may improve the number of retrieved actives.

Now you will repeat the pharmacophore generation, modifying the parameters to see if smaller subsets of features can improve the screening performance with these validation datasets.

Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Automatically tool panel and click Interaction Pharmacophore Generation . As before, set the Input Receptor parameter to 3d4q_complex:3d4q_protein and the Input Ligand parameter to 3d4q_complex:3d4q_ligand . Change the Maximum Features parameter from the default 6 to 4 . Set the Validation parameter to True . Expand the parameter group and set the Active Ligands parameter to braf_actives:All , and the Inactive Ligands parameter to braf_decoys:All again. If you have a multi-processor server you can set the Parallel Processing parameters to complete the protocol more quickly. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

Running this job on a single processor should take about 8 minutes.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the report.

This opens a report of the resulting validated pharmacophores. The validation table and ROC curves show improved screening performance. Pharmacophore 5 maps 134 of the 152 possible actives to give a better Sensitivity. The Specificity is only marginally reduced by the model fitting to 27 false positives from the 150 decoys, and the overall AUC ROC has also improved.

You can now determine for yourself which pharmacophore from those generated suits your screening or profiling objectives and use it as input for one of the protocols found on the Search, Screen, and Profile tool panel.

# Ligand docking with LibDock

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_libdock.htm

## Ligand docking with LibDock

Time: 15 minutes.

### Introduction

LibDock is an algorithm for docking small molecules into an active 
receptor site. Initially, a hotspot map is calculated for the receptor 
active site which contains polar and apolar groups. This hotspot map is subsequently used 
to rigidly align the ligand conformations to form favorable interactions. 
After a final energy-minimization step (allowing the ligand poses to be flexible), the top scoring ligand poses are saved.

In this tutorial, you will dock a set of ligands into the thymidine kinase receptor.
This tutorial covers:

* Creating a binding site and preparing LibDock

* Launching LibDock

* Analyzing the docking results

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1kim_prot.dsv .

The protein opens in a new Molecule Window showing the site sphere at the center of 
the receptor active site. See the Preparing a Receptor Binding Site tutorial for more information on how to create a binding site sphere.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools. Click Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres and then Show/Hide Site Spheres . Choose View | Transform | Fit To Screen from the menu bar to center and zoom into the binding site.

This will hide the residues outside the binding site sphere and the sphere itself, which will make viewing the results easier.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | kinase_ligands.sd .

This opens a new Molecule Window containing several ligands.

Click the tab of the 1kim_prot window to activate it and then open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools and click Dock Ligands (LibDock)... to open the Dock Ligands (LibDock) dialog. Ensure that Input Receptor is set to 1kim_prot:1kim and Input Ligands is set to kinase_ligands:All .

This docks all ligands in the window.

Ensure that Input Site Sphere is set to 48.6808, 82.5963, 54.0744, 9 . If not, click the field and choose 
the coordinates of the sphere from the list. Set the Docking Preferences to User Specified . Expand the Docking Preferences parameter and set Max Hits to Save to 10 .

For this tutorial, the default setting is 
lowered to reduce the number of top scoring poses reported.

Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

After the run finishes, the results are automatically opened in a new Molecule Window.
Both the protein (showing binding site residues only) and the docked ligand poses are loaded in
the same window. The visibility of the protein is locked so that it remains visible when you step 
through the docked ligand poses.

In the Data Table , step through the ligand poses using the Navigation Keys or
by pressing CTRL+Down .

Each ligand pose is shown in the binding site in turn.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools 
and click Ligand Interactions .

This displays the non-bond interactions between the receptor and the ligand as well as any intramolecular interactions in the ligand.

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions toolpanel to navigate through the ligands.

Notice that the non-bond interactions are updated when stepping through the docked poses. Only the residues that have an interaction with the ligand are displayed.

Use the Rotate tool 
in the View toolbar to rotate the molecule for better viewing of the pose and bonds.

See the Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating results tutorial for more information on interpreting the non-bond interactions.

See the Analyze Ligand Poses tutorial for more information on how to analyze the docked poses for non-bond interactions.

## Working with library analysis tools

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

The library analysis tools allow you to perform a variety of tasks with a ligand library, such as selecting 
a diverse set of ligands, clustering the library into subsets, finding outliers, and finding similar molecules. These methods
are useful when a known lead compound is identified and you want to expand it into a larger set of ligands for screening.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to perform a selection of compounds that are similar to a known lead compound.

The following tasks are covered:

* Prepare a lead compound

* Search for similar molecules in a library

* Inspect the returned molecules

There are several ways to import a structure into Discovery Studio Client. If you have the 
structure in .sd format, you can open it directly. In this tutorial, you will import the structure from a SMILES string.

From the menu bar, choose File | New | Molecule Window .

This open a blank Molecule Window.

In the menu bar, choose File | Insert From | SMILES... . Enter CCC(CC)O[C@@H]1C=C(C[C@@H]([C@H]1NC(=O)C)N)C(=O)OCC , and then click OK .

This imports the molecule Oseltamivir into the Molecule Window.

You can copy and paste the text above to perform this step.

In the Hierarchy View, click Molecule 1 to select the molecule. In the Graphics View, right-click and select Attributes of Molecule 1... .

This opens the Molecule Attributes dialog.

Click the Value box corresponding to Name and change it to Oseltamivir . Choose File | Save As... from the menu and save it as "Oseltamivir.sd".

The title of the Molecule Window changes to Oseltamivir.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Sample Drug Molecules.dsv .

This opens the file in a new Molecule Window.

Open the Small Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tools and click Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints... to open the Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints dialog.
If the Small Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tools are hidden, right-click
on Tools and click Select Subset Libraries . Set Input Ligands to Sample Drug Molecules:All and
set Input Reference Ligand to Oseltamivir:All . Keep the remaining default settings. Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the protocol finishes, the returned molecules are opened automatically in a new Molecule Window.

Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open the file you saved previously: Oseltamivir.sd . Press CTRL+G to turn on the Graphics View.

# Working with library design tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_library-design.htm

## Working with library design tools

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

A common task when designing libraries of ligands is the
selection of small subsets of ligands from a large library. These
subset libraries must adequately represent the chemical diversity
of the original library and satisfy additional property
criteria. The challenge of this task is to find subset library
choices that satisfy the competing goals of small size, high
diversity, and defined chemical properties.

Pareto optimization is useful when you have more than one
property you wish to optimize. Unlike other optimization methods
that generate a single solution, a Pareto optimization generates
multiple solutions to give the best possible tradeoffs among the
properties being optimized. The optimal solutions are those for
which it is not possible to improve on one property without
degrading at least one other property.

In this tutorial, you will select a diverse subset of ligands
from a combinatorial library and optimize that selection for
diversity and some Lipinski properties. The original
combinatorial library is defined by a generic reaction, an amide
formation involving 35 different amines and 45 different
carboxylic acids. The subset library will be a combinatorial
selection of the amides from seven different amines and eight different
carboxylic acids, with maximal diversity and an optimal range of
some Lipinski properties.

This tutorial covers:

* Defining the combinatorial library

* Defining the Pareto optimization

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Library Design | amines_35.sd . Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Library Design | acids_45.sd . Open the Small Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tools and click Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method... to open the 
Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method dialog. If the Small 
Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tools are hidden, right-click Tools and click Select Subset Libraries . Click the Input Library Type parameter and choose Reaction from the dropdown list.

The previously unavailable parameters (gray) Input Reactants and Input Reaction File are now required (red). 
The Input RG File parameter is no longer available.

Click the Input Reactants parameter, 
and choose amines_35:All from the dropdown list. Click the Input Reaction File parameter, then click
the button.

This opens the Input Reaction File dialog.

On the dialog, navigate to Samples | Tutorials |
Library Design | AmideFormation.rxn ,
then click Open .

This assigns it to the Input Reaction File parameter.

Click the Library Dimensions parameter and enter 7,8 .

The default value is changed in this step because it assumes three reactants or R-groups and there
are only two reactants in this example. This parameter setting defines that 7 amines and 8 acids
will be selected for the subset library.

Click the Optimization Property 1 parameter, then click the button.

This opens the Calculable Property dialog.

On the dialog, in the search textbox, enter FCFP for the value, 
then choose FCFP_12 from the list. Click OK .

This sets the diversity of a functional class
extended-connectivity fingerprint to a maximum diameter of 12.

Expand the Optimization Property 1 parameter. Click
the What to Optimize parameter and choose Unique Value Count from the list.

These parameters maximize the number of distinctly
different fingerprint features in the subset.

Click the Optimization Property 2 parameter, then click .

On the dialog, in the search textbox, enter Molecular_Weight for the value,
then choose Molecular_Weight from the list. Click OK .

This sets the molecular weight of the ligands as an optimization property.

Expand the Optimization Property 2 parameter. Click
the What to Optimize parameter, 
and choose Range Penalty from the dropdown list. Expand the What to Optimize parameter. Click the Range Minimum parameter and 
enter 100 for the value. Click the Range Maximum parameter and
enter 500 for the value. Click the Goal parameter and change its value to Minimize .

These parameters minimize the selection of ligands that
have a molecular weight less than 100 or greater than
500.

Click the Optimization Property 3 parameter, then
click .

On the dialog, in the Search textbox, enter num for the value, 
then choose Num_H_Donors_Lipinski from the list. Click OK .

This sets the number of hydrogen bond donors as an
optimization property.

Expand the Optimization Property 3 parameter.
Click the What to Optimize parameter and choose Range Penalty from the dropdown list. Expand the What to Optimize parameter. Click the Range Minimum parameter and
enter 0 . Click the Range Maximum parameter and
enter 5 . Click the Goal parameter and change its value to Minimize .

These parameters minimize the selection of ligands that
have more than 5 hydrogen bond donors.

Click Run and wait for the job to complete. When the protocol finishes running, a report is automatically opened in an HTML Window .

In the Summary section, the results of the optimization of each of
the 20 subset libraries are listed.

The CrowdingDistance value
indicates the relative distance (in terms of the optimization
properties) to other subsets on the same Pareto front.
Subsets at the extremes are assigned an infinite crowding
distance (1.0e99).

The ParetoFront value indicates how optimal each of the solutions is.
A value of 1 means that there are no other solutions that are better.

The table also lists the values of the optimized objectives and the composition of each reactant's R1
and R2.

The Pareto Plots show the optimization properties of the
20 subset libraries relative to the first property (i.e.,
the function class extended-connectivity fingerprints). Each
subset solution is equal to any other subset. However, some
are better optimized for one property (or goal) than another.
Compare the subsets:

* A subset in the top-right
corner of the plot has a higher overall fingerprint diversity,
but includes more ligands that have been penalized because
they were outside of the molecular weight range (100 - 500).

* A subset in the bottom-left corner has a lower
overall fingerprint diversity but most compounds are within
the specified molecular weight range.

In the Results section of the report that opens, 20
possible subsets of the original library are listed. Each
subset contains 56 ligands, composed of 7 amine and
8 carboxylic acid combinations.

# Fragment docking using MCSS

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_mcss.htm

## Fragment docking using MCSS

Time: 15 - 20 minutes.

### Introduction

MCSS is a fragment docking methodology that can be used to characterize and analyze binding sites.
Multiple fragment copies are randomly distributed in a binding site sphere and 
CHARMm minimizations are performed to find the most favorable fragment positions.
The placed fragments are sorted by the MCSS_Score.

In this tutorial, ibuprofen fragments are docked into the COX-1 receptor binding site.
The docked fragments are overlaid to the native ibuprofen pose from the x-ray crystal structure.

This tutorial covers:

* Preparing MCSS

* Launching MCSS

* Analyzing MCSS Results

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1EQG.dsv .

The protein opens in a new Molecule Window showing the site sphere at the center of 
the receptor active site. See the Preparing a Receptor Binding Site tutorial for more information on how to create a binding site sphere.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools and click Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres , 
and then Show/Hide Site Spheres . Select View | Transform | Fit To Screen or click on the View toolbar to center and zoom into the binding site.

This will hide the residues outside the binding site sphere and the sphere itself, which will 
make it easier to view and analyze the results.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1EQG-fragments.sd .

The Molecule Window shows two fragment entries: isobutyric acid and isopentane .

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tools and click Dock Fragments (MCSS)... to open the Dock Fragments (MCSS) dialog. Ensure that the Input Receptor parameter is set to 1EQG:1EQG , and the Input Fragments parameter is set to 1EQG-fragments:All . If not, click the 
value field to select the correct entry from the list.

This prepares all the fragments in the 1EQG-fragments Molecule Window for docking into the receptor active site.

Ensure that the Input Site Sphere parameter is set to
"26.6899, 33.8694, 200.361, 10". If not, click the value field to choose the correct coordinates of the sphere from the list. Expand the Number of Replicas and the Number to Keep parameter. Set Number to Keep to 20 and is to Percentage .

This will limit the number of fragments reported to the top scoring 20%.

The time required to execute the protocol can be reduced by running it in parallel .
If your computer has multiple processors or cores, set the Parallel Processing parameter to True . Expand the Parallel Processing parameter and 
set the Batch Size to 1 .

By setting the Batch Size to 1, each processor will handle one fragment.

Click the Run and wait for the job to complete.

The job status is displayed while the job is running.

The docked result is automatically opened in a new Molecule Window. 
The receptor and the docked fragment poses are displayed in the same window. The 
visibility of the receptor is locked so that it stays visible when you step through
each of the docked fragment poses.

Select the Data Table and using the Navigation Keys or 
press CTRL+Down repeatedly 
to step through the docked ligand poses in the Molecule Window.

You will see that the fragments are mainly centered around two main regions in the receptor binding site.

In the next step, you will compare the docked fragment positions with the native ibuprofen X-ray ligand structure.

Double click Dock Fragments (MCSS) in the Jobs Explorer . If the Jobs Explorer is hidden, click View | Explorers | Jobs to open it.

This opens a report in a HTML Window.

From the report, in the Results section, click the Top Scoring Fragments in Cluster link.

is set to Yes . Lock the visibility by setting Visibility Locked to Yes .

This will lock the visibility of the native ligand when stepping through the docked fragments.

Select the Data Table and press CTRL+Down repeatedly to step through the docked fragments.

Notice that the docked fragments are closely aligned with the native ibuprofen structure, indicating that MCSS was able to
find the hydrophobic (isopentane) and hydrophilic binding positions (isobutyric acid).

# Calculate relative binding free energies using Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_msld.htm

## Calculate relative binding free energies using Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics

Time: 30 minutes (optionally 24 hours)

### Introduction

The ability to understand and quantify the strength of interactions between ligands and a protein is essential in drug discovery projects to discern how changes to a ligand might alter binding affinity. Reliable estimation of binding affinity improves ligand selection in the lead optimization process. During early stage lead optimization, tens of thousands of ligands from diverse scaffold families may be considered. Thus computational methods such as docking and MM-GBSA are suitable for the throughput required. Later stage lead optimization involving smaller chemical modifications needs to be more accurate if the predictions are to be used to determine prioritization for expensive and time-consuming chemical synthesis.

Free energy perturbation (FEP) and Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) fall into the category of alchemical free energy methods. The rigorous physical nature of these methods in combination with explicit solvent modeling makes them the most accurate binding affinity predictors. While FEP involves pairwise estimation of free energies by simulating a transformation between two ligands, MSLD models multiple ligands in a simulation and can be substantially more efficient.

The MSLD method is best positioned to calculate the relative binding affinities of a combinatorial library, which is expanded upon a lead ligand. In this method, you provide a target protein structure, and specify the lead or the core ligand, the attachment points or “sites” on it, and a set of chemical groups or “substituents” that you want to decorate the core with. With these inputs, the MSLD method calculates the binding affinities of the combinatorial library.

In MSLD, two simulations are required: the multi-site ligand system alone and in complex with the protein. Both are solvated to complete the thermodynamic cycle, which allows for the calculation of the relative binding affinities of the set of ligands.

The following tasks are covered in this tutorial:

* Enumerating ligands for MSLD setup

* Setting up MSLD calculations

* Running MSLD bias optimization and production calculations

MSLD simulation setup requires the core ligand to be positioned in the protein active site. In this first step you will use the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol to generate the set of ligands for the subsequent setup of the MSLD simulations. Each generated ligand represents an R-group substitution to the core ligand specified in the protocol. The figure below shows two sites selected in the core ligand, which represent the sites of the attachment of the R-groups.

The input core ligand should be in the frame of reference of the protein binding site. You can verify the correct positioning of the ligand by copying both the ligand and protein into a new window and viewing the structures.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | hsp90_core.dsv file. On the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel check that the Forcefield Status is set to CHARMm .

The MSLD algorithm supports the CHARMm and charmm36 forcefields. When using the charmm36 forcefield, you can use the Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) protocol to type your ligands. This protocol uses the Multipurpose Atom-Typer for CHARMM (MATCH) algorithm [Yesselman et al., 2012] for the automated assignment of atom types and forcefield parameters for the latest generation of forcefields.

Open the Simulation | Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel and click Enumerate Ligands for MSLD . Set the Core Structure parameter to hsp90_core:4YKR_core . Set the MSLD Sites parameter to Group . Set R1 Groups parameter to select Methyl , Alcohol , Amino , and Methoxy groups. Set R2 Groups parameter to select Methyl , Alcohol , Fluoro , and Chloro groups. Click Run .

You can optionally add more substituents by editing the Custom Substituents parameter.

The job should take less than a minute to run.

For specifying sites of modifications on a core ligand, you can select hydrogen atoms and set the MSLD Sites parameter in the protocol to “Create New Group From Selection”. This will add the R labels to the molecule and use those sites for enumeration.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open the Report in an Html Window. Click View Results .

This opens the Enumerated_Ligands file which contains the core ligand and 8 ligands typed with CHARMm. Each of the enumerated ligands represent one modification with respect to the core structure at one site. While each ligand only models a single change, the multi-topology molecule generated later models the combinations of modifications from each site. Including the core ligand, which models a hydrogen at each site, the set of ligands generated represent 5 substituents at each site, thus representing 25 unique ligands. In the data table view, each ligand has a property named “MSLD Site,” which indicates the index of the site of modification. For the core ligand, this property is zero. You will now use these ligands to set up the MSLD calculations.

In this step you will prepare the structures for the MSLD calculations. For the entire set of typed ligands, a single multi-topology molecule is generated based on the identified common and different sets of atoms in the topologies, partial charges, and non-bonded parameters. A solvated ligand system and a solvated protein-ligand complex for this merged multi-topology molecule are also generated.

The protocol requires a protein structure. The PDB code for the heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) protein-ligand complex used is 4YKR. The sample file in this tutorial was downloaded from the PDB and the protein was prepared with the Prepare Proteins protocol. When preparing your protein, decide if crystal waters should be retained as conserved water molecules. Water molecules deeply buried in the core of the protein may play a role in maintaining the folded structure and often make strong hydrogen bonds to polar groups. In this tutorial, three water molecules in the binding site that are known to form important interactions with the core compound are retained and the same protein structure is used throughout the workflow.

Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 4YKR_prep.dsv file. Make sure Forcefield is set to CHARMm . Select the Enumerated_Ligands molecule window as the active window. Open the Simulation | Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel and click Set Up MSLD Calculations . Set the Input Typed Ligands parameter to Enumerated_Ligands:All . Set the Input Receptor parameter to 4YKR_prep:4YKR_protein . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

#### Options and Best Practices

* You can provide additional ligands as input to the protocol that include additional modifications. The need for this may arise because the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol only supports modifications that involve substitution of a hydrogen atom with another group. Some modifications, for example changing a carbon atom in a phenyl ring to a nitrogen, do not involve a hydrogen transformation. To model these groups: Copy the core ligand from the hierarchy view. Make the modification using the Small Molecules tool panel. Add the MSLD Site property for the new ligand and set its value based on the site of modification. Type the ligand with the same forcefield as the rest of the ligands. Core changes or changes in topology of the molecule are not supported.

To model these groups:

* Copy the core ligand from the hierarchy view.

* Make the modification using the Small Molecules tool panel.

* Add the MSLD Site property for the new ligand and set its value based on the site of modification.

* Type the ligand with the same forcefield as the rest of the ligands.

Core changes or changes in topology of the molecule are not supported.

* MSLD simulations can be run on CPU or GPU. When run on CPU, there is a minimum system size requirement—set the Minimum Distance from Boundary parameter to 15.0 or more for a ligand system. There is no such requirement for the protein-ligand complex system because it is already large. When running on GPU, you can run using a much smaller system. GPU is recommended because it is substantially faster.

* You can reduce the system size. By default, the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol generates an orthogonal shaped solvated box for the protein-ligand complex system. To avoid the rotation and translation of the protein in the subsequent simulations and prevent potential interactions of the protein with its own periodic image, soft restraints are applied on protein backbone C-alpha atoms. By default these restraints are weak and involve a force constant of 0.01 kcal/mol, such that intramolecular protein dynamics is minimally perturbed. Additionally, restraints are not applied to binding site residues that are identified based on proximity to the ligand. If you intend to avoid these restraints, change the Set Up MSLD Calculations > Cell Shape parameter for the Protein-ligand complex to Cubic . In this case restraints are not applied in subsequent simulations, but there will be an increased computation time because of the larger system size.

#### Viewing the Results

In alchemical MSLD calculations, the multiple ligands are represented by a multi-topology molecule. This chimeric molecule is generated by first detecting the common and different atoms between the ligands and the core by a maximum common substructure (MCS) method. Common atoms are those that are considered identical in terms of chemical nature, topology, forcefield atom-types and partial charges. All other atoms are designated as the different set.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an Html Window. Click View Results to open the solvated ligand and complex files.

This opens the solvated ligand and complex files in one molecule window.

* The Ligand molecule contains the merged dual topology molecule in a cubic shaped box with water molecules and counterions.

* The Complex molecule contains the complex of the multi-topology molecule with the protein also in a solvated box.

* The Vacuum molecule contains only the multi-topology molecule. This is not used unless a hydration free energy calculation is desired.

You will now use the Complex and Ligand molecules to run MSLD bias optimization and production calculations.

In the next part of the MSLD workflow you will run the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production calculations for the solvated ligand system and the solvated protein-ligand complex system. If you run this calculation on the system used in this tutorial using the following parameters on a machine or grid with three or more NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti cards, the calculation may take between 17-24 hours.

Select the MSLD_systems molecule window as the active window, and make the Complex and Ligand systems visible. Open the Simulation | Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel and click MSLD Bias Optimization and Production . Expand the Input MSLD Systems grouping and set the Solvated Complex parameter to MSLD_systems: Complex . Set the Solvated Ligand parameter to MSLD_systems: Ligand . If running on a grid enabled server with multiple GPUs, set Parallel Processing to True , expand Server , and set Run on Grid to True . Then set Grid Options to specify resources for each simulation. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run .

* The system used in this tutorial models only 25 combinatorial ligands and involves substituents that only differ by a few heavy atoms. For larger combinatorial libraries or systems that involve chemically and structurally diverse substituents, enabling Phase 3 of bias optimization may result in improved accuracy. For such systems, increasing the Number of Simulations parameter under the Production group to 6 and Number of Simulations to Combine parameter to 2 would also result in better sampling and therefore more accurate predictions.

* When running on GPU platform, increasing the Number of Cores per Simulation from 1 to 2, 4, or 8 will typically result in better performance. Before running production-scale calculations, it is recommended that you run a short benchmark on your computing infrastructure to ensure the performance does not degrade with increasing the Number of Cores per Simulation . A short benchmark can be run by setting Maximum Number of Iterations under Bias Optimization > Phase 1 to 1, and then disabling Bias Optimization > Phase 2 , Bias Optimization > Phase 3 , and Production .

The goal of bias optimization is to optimize the parameters used in bias functions added to the energy of the system in MSLD to enhance transitions between the different substituents on each site. A large number of transitions at each site are required in the subsequent MSLD production calculations to obtain reliable estimates of the free energies. To achieve this, the bias optimization protocol iteratively optimizes bias potentials that are added to the energy of the system to flatten the free energy landscape of the transformations. The later phases of bias optimization are run with an increasing amount of sampling per iteration to allow for refined adjustment to the biases. For details see [Raman et al., 2020] and [Hayes et al., 2017] .

By default, the first phase of bias optimization runs 100 iterations, with each iteration involving 100 ps of MSLD simulation followed by an evaluation of the free energy landscape and corresponding adjustment of the bias potentials. Free energy landscapes are computed for each substituent on each site separately and all pairs of substituents on a site. The second phase involves 10 iterations of 1 ns each, and the third involves 5 iterations of 2 ns each. The overall flatness is monitored by Average RMSD and Average Pair RMSD, which capture the average flatness observed for transitions. Ideally, these values should reach below 0.5 and 1.0, respectively, which corresponds with a high degree of flatness and consequently a high number of transitions during subsequent simulations. At the end of each phase, a set of biases that results in the most even sampling of all substituents is chosen from the last few iterations.

Following bias optimization, the solvated ligand and protein-ligand complex systems are subjected to MSLD production simulations. During these simulations, the substituents on each site of the ligand are sampled, and the probabilities of each unique ligand are recorded. These probabilities are analyzed from each independent trajectory, and the corresponding free energy of each combinatorial ligand is calculated. An average of the free energies and standard deviation over all the independent simulations is also calculated.

When the production simulations are finished, the relative binding free energies for the ligands are calculated by combining the results from the free ligand and the protein-ligand complex simulations. The report from the protocol displays the calculated relative free energy values for each ligand in the combinatorial library. A table lists the average free energy in the ligand and complex states, and a difference of these free energies as the average relative binding free energy, which are normalized with respect to the free energy of the first ligand that models the core substituents on all sites. An associated standard deviation is also reported. Per this analysis, combination 3,5 is predicted to be the best binder with a relative free energy of -2.24 kcal/mol with respect to the core. Note that owing to the stochastic nature of the simulation, you may get slightly different results when you run the tutorial.

An additive free energy table is also displayed that lists approximate free energies that neglect the cooperativity between the two sites. In challenging systems involving a large number of ligands, the free energy table may not be fully populated because of insufficient sampling of substituents at multiple sites simultaneously. In those cases the additive free energy table provides approximate estimates for most combinatorial ligands.

Relative free energies are also reported for each site separately. These values also neglect the cooperative effects between sites, except that they allow the assessment of different substituents at each site.

Another method for sampling certain ligands where it is lacking is to lower the value of the Lambda Threshold parameter from its default of 0.99. You can do this by post-processing the simulations using the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol. However, large deviations from unity may lead to inaccurate estimates.

Bias optimization results are reported in the MSLD Bias Optimization Results table. The linked report associated with each system and phase presents the Average RMSD and Average Pair RMSD values and shows how the free energy landscape flatness has evolved over the iterations. For example, the following are the phase 2 bias optimization results for the Complex system:

Rough estimates of free energies can be obtained from the bias optimization stage itself. These estimates are listed in the Calc Bias ddG columns in the Estimated Bias report, which you can access from the MSLD Bias Optimization Results table. However, production simulation results are expected to be significantly more accurate.

In this tutorial you have used multi-site lambda dynamics to estimate relative binding affinities of a combinatorial library of ligands for late-stage lead optimization.

# Creating and validating a 3D QSAR pharmacophore

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_pharm-3dqsar.htm

## Creating and validating a 3D QSAR pharmacophore

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

3D Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) pharmacophore generation is designed to produce predictive pharmacophores from a set of ligands with known activity values against a given biological target. The algorithm produces pharmacophore models that are common among the active ligands but not among the inactive ligands, and then optimizes these using simulated annealing. These hypotheses can be used to predict the activity of new candidate ligands and guide lead optimization to improve the activity of existing ligands.

In this tutorial, you will use a training set of ligands with activity values to derive 3D QSAR pharmacophore models for prediction. The following tasks are covered:

* Generating and validating 3D QSAR pharmacophores with a training and test set

* Analyzing generated pharmacophores (alignment and cost analysis)

* Designing with a 3D QSAR pharmacophore

In this lesson, you will use a number of related selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) [Brogi et al., 2009] to develop a 3D QSAR pharmacophore to use to predict the activities of new ligands.

SERMs are potential drugs that act as either an agonist or antagonist depending on the tissue type and hormonal milieu. Their estrogen-like properties may help prevent the loss of bone density in postmenopausal women. However, SERMs may cause bone loss in premenopausal women. Their antiestrogen activity may help reduce the risk of breast cancer by blocking the effects of estrogen on breast tissue.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | serm_ligands.sd .

The ligands in the data set have the Activ and Uncert properties pre-defined.
Activ is the ligand's tested biological activity. Data such as IC50 values should be used instead of logarithmic values. Ideally, the data should span four orders of magnitude as demonstrated in this training set.

The ligands' Activ property is inhibitory IC50 (μM) data on MCF7 human breast adenocarcinoma cell line proliferation. MCF7 is a well characterized positive control cell line that can be used to approximate the binding of a ligand to estrogen receptor-alpha.

Uncert is the uncertainty in the activity value. It is a ratio of the reported value to the minimum and maximum values and must be greater than 1.0. If you do not specify a value, a default of 3.0 is used. For example, if Activ is 0.001 and the Uncert is set to 3.0, the Activ is considered to be between 0.001/3.0 = 0.00033 and 0.001×3.0 = 0.003.

The Uncert value can affect which ligands in a data set are defined as active and inactive, and used during the constructive and subtractive phases of the pharmacophore generation respectively. See the 3D QSAR pharmacophore generation algorithm in the Pharmacophore Theory documentation for details. The Uncert value will also affect the regression fitting of the generated pharmacophores during the Optimization phase. A value of 1.5 has been used as these settings were taken from Brogi et al. [Brogi et al., 2009] .

In the Data Table View, right-click and choose Color By Activity . Double-click the Activ column to sort the ligands.

Notice the two ligands that are identified as active according to the definition used by the 3D QSAR pharmacophore generation algorithm and from which the pharmacophore domain will be generated. You can visually inspect these ligands one at a time to determine which pharmacophore feature types should be considered during the pharmacophore generation. Alternatively, you can use the Feature Mapping tool to do this quickly.

Click on the First button in the Data Table View to display the most active ligand, (serm-40) , in the Graphics View. Select the visibility checkbox for the second most active ligand, (serm-34) . In the Tools Explorer, open the Pharmacophores | Edit and Cluster Features tool panel. Click Feature Mapping and select the desired features from the Select Features dialog. Use the default features 
for this tutorial. Click Run .

The Feature Mapping function identifies all possible locations of the selected pharmacophore features on the visible molecules. Note that only solvent accessible features can be mapped, so be sure to start with ligands represented by reasonable starting conformations.

In the Edit and Cluster Features tool panel, click Current Feature: All Features to see the list of pharmacophore feature types represented in your training set.

Both of the active ligands include positive ionizable features, but not negative ionizable features. They also have the RING_AROMATIC feature mapped. However, for the pharmacophore generation you will use the HYDROPHOBIC_aromatic feature instead. It is a less restrictive feature type because it is only a point feature without the plane and vector constraints of RING_AROMATIC.

Once the pharmacophores have been generated, you would normally determine the best models by assessing their ability to estimate the activity of a test set of ligands with similar receptor binding that have not been used to derive the pharmacophores. The pharmacophore generation protocol can perform this 
validation automatically.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | test_serm_ligands.sd .

Now you will set up the protocol to generate the 3D QSAR pharmacophores for this training set and validate with the test set.

In the Tools Explorer, open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophores Automatically tool panel. Click 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation . In the Parameters Explorer, ensure that Input Ligands is set to serm_ligands:All . Expand the Validation parameter group and set it to True . Ensure that the Input Test Ligands is set to test_serm_ligands:All . Expand the Conformation Generation parameter group. Set Energy Threshold to 10 . Click on the button for Features to open the Select Features dialog. Add HYDROPHOBIC_aromatic and POS_IONIZABLE to the default selection. Change Minimum Interfeature Distance to 1.5 . Leave the remaining default values, then click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

These parameters will generate up to 255 conformations to represent each ligand. Only conformations within a 10 kcal/mol energy range will be retained.

The job takes approximately 10 minutes to finish.

After the job finishes, double click on the job in the Jobs Window to open the Report.

The report lists the top ten 3D QSAR pharmacophores ranked by cost value in the results section. For each pharmacophore there is a corresponding SD file of the input ligands aligned to that pharmacophore model. For each pharmacophore, the report summary includes the validation statistics and a plot of the LogActiv versus LogEstimate for the test ligands. This allows you to quickly determine which pharmacophores best predict the activities of new ligands, which were not used to derive the models. The summary indicates that the best hypotheses are pharmacophore 2, 5, 7, and 8. You can focus on those pharmacophores when looking at the cost analysis in the next step.

The overall cost of each hypothesis is calculated by summing three cost factors: a weight cost, an error cost, and a configuration cost. The first pharmacophore is not necessarily the best pharmacophore model, so you will need to analyze all of them.

Choosing the best 3D QSAR pharmacophore model involves more than considering the ranking from the pharmacophore generation. In addition to the cost analysis of the models, you should look at the alignment of the training set ligands to the pharmacophores and see how this may explain the activity of the ligands. Finally, and most importantly, you should also use a test set of ligands whose biological activity you know.

As assessments of the alignments of the training set ligands against all the hypotheses can be time consuming. In this tutorial you will only briefly look at how the training set ligands map to the pharmacophores. The primary assumption of 3D QSAR pharmacophores is that active ligands should map more features than inactive ligands. In other words, a ligand is inactive because it doesn't have an important feature, or the feature is present but cannot be oriented correctly in space. Hence it is important that you agree with the alignment and orientation of the training set ligands when explaining the range of biological activity in the pharmacophore models that you chose.

From the report, click the View Aligned Ligands 01 link to load the training set aligned to the highest ranked pharmacophore. Click the First button in the Data Table View to display the highest predicted active ligand (serm-40) in the Graphics View.

The actual activity of this ligand is 0.02 μM, while the estimated activity is 0.015 μM. All of the features of the ligand are mapped by the pharmacophore.

Click the Last button to display the lowest predicted active ligand (serm-49) in the Graphics View.

The actual activity of this ligand is 235 μM, while the estimated activity is 172 μM. This is still an acceptable prediction as all reasonable estimates should be within one order of magnitude of the actual activity. You can see that this inactive ligand maps only two of the possible five pharmacophore features, which could explain its low activity against the biological target.

Next, you will analyze how all ten pharmacophore models represent the training set and then look at some basic aspects of the log file.

From the report, click the Detailed Analysis Report link to load a graphical cost analysis report.

The report is organized into three sections:

* Summary of common significant parameters and the features considered

* Digest of the cost analysis

* Graphical and tabular display of how the training set ligands fit each of the pharmacophore models

The 3D QSAR pharmacophore produces three significant cost values: hypothesis, fixed, and null. In terms of hypothesis significance, what really matters is the magnitude of the difference between the cost of any returned hypothesis and the cost of the null hypothesis. If a returned hypothesis has a cost that differs from the Null hypothesis by 40-60, there is a high probability (75%-90%) that it represents a true correlation to the data. As the difference becomes less than 40, the likelihood of the hypothesis representing a true correlation in the data rapidly drops below 50%.

A brief look at the ten graphical and tabulated models reveals that the first pharmacophore provides the best estimated activities for the training set ligands, with the smallest deviations from the actual biological activity:

The last column of the training set summary table includes useful feature mapping information from the log file. Notice that the serm-34 ligand includes an asterisk (*) in the mapping summary against the first pharmacophore. This means that highest fitting map of serm-34 to this pharmacophore model was not able to map the hydrogen bond acceptor feature.

A general guideline for evaluating 3D QSAR pharmacophores is that the two most active ligands should map to all features of the pharmacophore. In this example, only hypotheses 2 and 8 meet this criteria. Pharmacophores 2 and 8 were also amongst the best hypotheses based on prediction of the external test set, so you will focus on these further in the next step. However, this is only a guideline and you may want to focus on a pharmacophore in which the two most active ligands do not map all features because the alignment is more fitting and/or the correlation better for your significant ligands of interest. Choose the elements of analysis most appropriate to your situation.
