(Alternatively, you can select all of the models). Ensure that any other listed pharmacophores which may be open in the client are unchecked. Expand the Conformation Generation parameter group. Change Energy Threshold to 10 . Expand the Advanced parameter group and set Maximum Omitted Features to -1 . Set Scale Fit Values to False and Save Aligned Ligands to True . Leave the remaining default values and click Run to run the protocol.

The Ligand Profiler protocol is useful because it allows you to map a set of ligands against multiple pharmacophores and quickly determine the matches. Changing the Maximum Omitted Features parameter in this protocol is particularly important as the assumption is that a ligand is less active when it lacks an important feature, or the feature is present but cannot be oriented correctly in space. The setting of -1 allows partial mapping of the pharmacophore features.

A Heat Map will be displayed when the job is finished.

To view more data produced by the protocol, find the job in the Jobs Explorer and double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an Html Window.

In the report, click serm_ligands_02_view.pl to view the ligands aligned to pharmacophore 2.

The highest FitValue and lowest Estimate for each of the 29 test set ligands are mapped to the second pharmacophore. The estimated activity is derived from regression parameters computed during the optimization phase. These parameters are derived by regression of a geometric fit versus -log(Activity).

Check the visibility checkbox for the testserm-38 ligand, and then CTRL-select testserm-38 and the serm_ligands_02 pharmacophores. Copy and paste these into a new Molecule window.

The actual activity of testserm-38 is 63 μM, while the estimated activity is around 143 μM. The ligand maps two of the five possible pharmacophore features (click on the First button in the Data Table View to refresh the mapping information). The relative energy of the conformation in this case is low and not a concern, but may be a consideration in some situations if it is high.

From a brief study of the pharmacophore features not mapped by testserm-38, you can make two simple modifications to attempt to improve the biological activity of this lead ligand.

In the Hierarchy View, turn off the visibility checkbox for the serm_ligands_02 pharmacophore. Edit testserm-38 to include a para hydroxyl group on the benzaldehyde phenyl. Add a meta hydroxyl and para methyl amine to the other aromatic ring.

Your modified lead should look like this:

In the Hierarchy View, turn on the visibility checkbox for the serm_ligands_02 pharmacophore. In the Tools Explorer, open Pharmacophore | Search, Screen and Profile | Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping . Check that Input Pharmacophore is set to the Molecule:serm_ligands_02 pharmacophore in the current window. Ensure that Input Ligands is set to the current window with your edited Molecule:Visible ligand. Expand the Input Ligands | Conformation Generation parameter group. Set Energy Threshold to 10 . Set Best Mapping Only to False and Maximum Omitted Features to -1 . Leave the remaining default values and run the protocol.

The mapping results will be appended to the Data Table.

Click the Next button in the Data Table View to display the highest predicted mapping in the Graphics View.

The estimated activity of this modified lead ligand is now less than 1 μM. Four of the five features of the pharmacophore now map and the relative energy of the conformation is still low.

Notice how the para hydroxyl maps to the hydrogen bond acceptor feature.

Use the Next button to scroll the mappings.

Notice the two aromatic rings reverse their mappings and the para hydroxyl substituent maps to the hydrogen bond donor feature for some mappings. Studying the different possible mappings of a ligand to a pharmacophore may reveal a more relevant binding mode and identify alternative alignment relationships between ligands.

You may now want to see if different modifications to the original testserm-38 ligand further improve on this estimated activity, or try starting with another lead ligand. Alternatively, you can start the optimization from the mapping of the test ligands to pharmacophore 8.

If you often use the same settings to run any protocol and do not want to reset them each time, set them as desired, and then choose Options | Save Protocol Settings before running the job.

# Creating customized pharmacophore features

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_pharm-customized-features.htm

## Creating customized pharmacophore features

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

Discovery Studio provides several default pharmacophore 
feature definitions that are used during pharmacophore 
modeling. These pharmacophore features are essentially
a collection of complex substructure mappings. When
one of the substructures is found on a ligand, it 
is a potential mapping for that feature. The language
that describes these pharmacophore features in Discovery Studio is rich and powerful. It is possible 
to assign several attributes to each atom 
(for example, hydrogen count, multiple-elements, possible 
formal charges) and each bond in a substructure. It is also
possible to define exclusions for each substructure.
In addition, it is possible to define the atom or 
the region (such as a centroid of atoms), where the 
actual feature mapping on the ligand will occur.

The 18 default pharmacophore features are sufficient for most projects.
However, occasionally it may be desirable to modify a default feature 
definition to address a specific need. For example, you may want to allow 
a particular functional group in a molecule to be recognized as a
pharmacophore feature. Discovery Studio provides an interactive environment for
modifying and creating pharmacophore features. You can extend
or modify an existing pharmacophore feature or you can create
an entirely new feature definition.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to customize
pharmacophore features using the Customize Pharmacophore Features
tool panel by modifying an
pharmacophore feature. The following tasks are covered:

* Modifying the default positive ionizable feature

* Mapping the feature to the fragment

* Adding custom features

The following 18 feature definitions are available in Discovery Studio :

* hydrophobic

* hydrophobic aliphatic

* hydrophobic aromatic

* hydrogen bond acceptor

* hydrogen bond acceptor heavy atom only

* hydrogen bond acceptor projection only

* hydrogen bond acceptor lipid

* hydrogen bond donor

* hydrogen bond donor 1 (same as hydrogen bond donor but includes aromatic carbons with a hydrogen)

* hydrogen bond donor heavy atom only

* hydrogen bond donor projection only

* negative charge

* positive charge

* negative ionizable

* positive ionizable

* positive ionizable 1 (will also match a pyridyl group)

* ring aromatic

* zinc binder

A detailed description of these feature definitions is
available in the Discovery Studio help .

The Customize Pharmacophore Features tool panel allows you to modify existing feature definitions as well as to create new feature types. In this tutorial, you will customize the positive ionizable
feature to map pyridyl and imidazolyl groups (the default positive ionizable feature
does not map pyridyl or imidazolyl groups).

From the menu bar, choose File | New | Molecule Window .

This opens a new Molecule Window.

Open the Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features tools. In the Feature Dictionary tools 
group, click Add Feature From Dictionary... .

This opens the Add Feature From Dictionary dialog.

On the dialog, click POS_IONIZABLE to select it. Click OK .

A single red sphere appears that defines the positive ionizable group. It is possible to see more details of the definitions 
using the Hierarchy View and some of the tool buttons. See the tip below for more information.

You can use
the Hierarchy View to turn on the display of
substructure definitions associated with 
this feature. You can also use the Show Mappings button to identify which
atoms or collection of atoms are used for
the mapping. The Simplify Customized 
Feature View button will improve the 
visualization of the substructures. 
To view only the red sphere again, click
on the check box of the top node in the 
Hierarchy labeled POS_IONIZABLE to turn
off the display of everything, then click
the check box again. Only the red sphere
will be displayed.

Now add the new fragments to be included in the definition

Open the Small Molecules | Build Fragment tools. Expand Aromatics in the listbox. Select 2-Imidazolyl and click Add Fragment . Select 2-Pyridyl and click Add Fragment . Press CTRL+A .

This adds the fragments to the same Molecule Window and selects all the objects in the Molecule Window.

Open the Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features tools. Click Map ANY Selected .

This adds the two new substructures to the definition. Notice that the bond types are conveniently set to aromatic by default and the hydrogen counts are reset:

With the substructures added to the positive ionizable
definition, you can now choose the atoms or region of the new
substructures that will be responsible for the mapping. In this case, the
most appropriate mapping location is the centroid of the ring.

In the Graphics View , select the 2-Imidazolyl fragment by double-clicking any atom in the molecule. From the menu bar, choose Structure | Query Features... .

This opens the Create Feature dialog.

On the dialog, choose Centroid from the list. Click OK .

This creates the required association for the point at which the feature mapping will take place.

Repeat these steps for the 2-Pyridyl fragment.

The two centroids are displayed in the Graphics View. The mapping can now be created.

In the Graphics View , select both centroids and the red positively ionizable feature object. In the Customize Pharmacophore
Features tool panel, click Create Mapping .

The modified positive ionizable feature is complete and
you can save it as a new DS_CHM file or add it to
the dictionary using Add Feature To Dictionary... in the Customize Pharmacophore Features tool panel. Customized 
pharmacophore features that are added to the 
dictionary can be used in many of the pharmacophore protocols.

In the Customize Pharmacophore Features tool panel, click Add Feature To Dictionary .

This opens the Add Feature To Dictionary dialog.

On the dialog, enter POS_IONIZABLE_MOD in the Function name textbox. Click OK .

This adds the feature to the dictionary and makes it available for use 
with many of the pharmacophore protocols.

Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Automatically tools and click Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation... to open the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation dialog. Click the Features parameter, then click .

This opens the Select Features dialog. The dialog contains the added feature 
POS_IONIZABLE_MOD, which is now available as one of the possible features for 
building pharmacophore models.

# Creating and validating a common feature pharmacophore

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_pharm-hiphop.htm

## Creating and validating a common feature pharmacophore

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

Common feature pharmacophore generation is designed specifically for finding the chemical features shared by a set of ligands and for providing the ligands' relative alignments with a pharmacophore expressing these common features. Common feature pharmacophores can also be useful for stimulating ideas about structure-activity when you have only a few molecules that have similar activity, but dissimilar and/or flexible structures.

In this tutorial a training set of six active ligands will be used to derive common feature pharmacophores for lead identification. The following tasks are covered:

* Generating common feature pharmacophores with a training set

* Validating generated pharmacophores with a test set

* Identifying new leads

In this lesson, you will take a number of known 5-HT2c ligands (1,2) and develop a common feature pharmacophore to use for lead identification. The 5-HT2c receptor belongs to the seven-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor superfamily and offers interesting therapeutic opportunities for the treatment of schizophrenia, migraine headaches, and Parkinson's disease.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | 5HT2c_ligands.sd .

The ligands in the dataset have two properties already defined, Principal and MaxOmitFeat. Common feature pharmacophore generation uses these values to determine which molecules should be considered when building the pharmacophore space and which molecules should map to all or some of the features in the final pharmacophores.

The Principal property indicates the activity level of the molecule:

| Value | Activity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | Active | A reference molecule ensures that all of the chemical features in the molecule are considered in building pharmacophore space. |
| 1 | Moderately Active | Conformations of this molecule are considered when placing pharmacophore features. |
| 0 | Inactive | The molecule is not considered when placing pharmacophore features, and is considered as an inactive molecule when optionally attempting to place excluded volumes. |

The MaxOmitFeat property indicates how many features are allowed to miss for each molecule:

| Value | Description |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | All features in the generated pharmacophore must map to the compound. |
| 1 | All but one of the features in the generated pharmacophore must map to the compound. |
| 2 | No features in the generated pharmacophore need to map to the compound. |

In this tutorial, you assume that all molecules are equally active and set all of them as reference ligands. If your molecules have very different pharmacophore feature types and sizes, different Principal and MaxOmitFeat settings can significantly affect the pharmacophore models generated.

You can visually inspect your ligands one at a time to determine which pharmacophore feature types should considered during the pharmacophore generation. Alternatively, you can use the Feature Mapping tool to do this quickly.

In the Data Table View, click the First , and then right-click in the Graphics View and choose Show All . Open the Pharmacophores | Edit and Cluster Features tools and click Feature Mapping... to open the Feature Mapping dialog. Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

The Feature Mapping function identifies all possible locations of the selected pharmacophore features from the Select Features dialog on the visible molecules. This can be useful for manually deriving a pharmacophore from a set of aligned ligands. Bear in mind that only solvent accessible features can be mapped and therefore you should start with ligands represented by reasonable starting conformations.

Click Current Feature to see the list of pharmacophore feature types represented in your training set.

Notice that the training set includes ligands with positive ionizable features, but not negative ionizable features.

Now you will set up the protocol to generate the common feature pharmacophores for this training set [Micheli et al., 2006] .

Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Automatically tools and click Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation... to open the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation dialog. Ensure that Input Ligands is set to 5HT2c_ligands:All . For Features , click on the button to open the Select Features dialog. Add POS_IONIZABLE and RING_AROMATIC to the default selection as additional features to consider during the pharmacophore generation. Expand the Conformation Generation parameter group, and then change Conformation Generation to BEST . Change Maximum Conformations to 200 and Energy Threshold to 10 . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

This will generate up to 200 conformations to represent each ligand. Only conformations within a 10 kcal.mol-1 energy range will be kept for use. These settings were used by the reference paper [Micheli et al., 2006] .

Ten common feature pharmacophores are listed by ranking in an HTML Window. The ranking is a measure of how well the molecules map onto the proposed pharmacophores, as well as the rarity of the pharmacophore model. The first pharmacophore may not necessarily be the best pharmacophore model, and so it is necessary for you to analyze all of them.

For each pharmacophore there is a corresponding .sd file of the input ligands aligned to that pharmacophore model.

From the report, click the View Aligned Ligands 01 link to load the training set aligned to the highest ranked pharmacophore.

Notice the range of the FitValue property for the training set in this alignment of the ligands to this pharmacophore and the values for ligands such as 5HT2c_ligand4 and 5HT2c_ligand5.

Return to the Report Html window and click the View Aligned Ligands 10 link.

In this alignment, 5HT2c_ligand5 has a higher FitValue and fits to the pharmacophore better than 5HT2c_ligand4.

When analyzing the results from a Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol you should look at all ten of the alignments to see how they explain your training set.

Return to the Report Html window and expand the Details section of the Report.

This table allows you to quickly see the differences in the generated pharmacophore models.

Deciding which is the best pharmacophore model to represent your ligands, and generate possible new leads for the 5-HT2c receptor target, can be a subjective process. You may decide based on an analysis of the overlay of key chemical features in your ligands. You might also use a test set of ligands, including known negative compounds.

You can also set the protocol to perform validation automatically using the parameters under the Validation group. Each pharmacophore will be compared against a set of actives and inactives. ROC curves will be displayed in the report.

In this tutorial you will use a test set, including negative compounds, to perform a simple validation of your pharmacophore models and determine which one(s) to use to identify potential new scaffolds.

Select Windows | Close All from the menu bar to clear all the existing windows. Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | sulfonamide5HT2c_ligands.sd . Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | sampledrugs20.sd .

The first file contains eighteen sulfonamides with known 5-HT2c activity [Garzya et al., 2007] . The second file contains the twenty ligands from the Samples | Sample Drug Molecules.dsv small molecule library with the highest similarity to the six training set ligands (based on Lipinski properties and FCFP_6 fingerprints). These compounds will act as inactive ligands; ideally they would be true negative control ligands, known not to bind to this receptor.

Open the Pharmacophore | Search, Screen, and Profile tools and click Ligand Profiler... to open the Ligand Profiler dialog. Ensure that Input Ligands is set to sulfonamide5HT2c_ligands:All . For Input File Pharmacophores , click the button and browse to the Output folder of the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol that you ran. SHIFT+select the ten pharmacophore models and click OK . Expand the Conformation Generation parameter group, and then change Conformation Generation to BEST . Change Maximum Conformations to 200 and Energy Threshold to 10 . Change Save Conformations to True . Expand the Advanced parameter group, and then change Scale Fit Values to False and Save Aligned Ligands to True . Click Options and choose Save Protocol Settings . Note that you can return the original settings the next time you run the protocol by clicking the Options button and choosing Restore Original Settings. Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

The Ligand Profiler protocol is useful for validation as it allows you to map a set of ligands against a set of pharmacophores and quickly determine the matches.

When the protocol finishes, a new Molecule Window opens that contains the 13 ligands that mapped to eight of the pharmacophores and a Heat Map representing the best FitValues. If you sent the job to the background, click the View Results link in the Report to open the data.

On the Heat Map notice that pharmacophore models 6 and 10 do not map to any of the test ligands. The first pharmacophore fits to seven of the active test ligands compared to the second pharmacophore mapping six active test ligands. Two of the retrieved ligands are from your inactive ligands.

To open other files from the job, use the Jobs Explorer to find the run. Double click on the job to open the Report. From the Report, click the 5HT2c_ligands_01_view.pl script. Right-click in the Graphics View and choose Show All .

Seven ligands are aligned to the first pharmacophore. Some of the ligands may not map as well to the pharmacophore as you may expect; notice the low FitValues of the sulfonamide ligands. This is likely due to the Maximum Omitted Features parameter in the Ligand Profiler protocol being set to 0, which does not allow any of the pharmacophore features to be missed. Changing this parameter may allow a ligand that fits to all of the pharmacophore features to fit to fewer features, but with a better fit, resulting in a higher FitValue and more relevant alignment.

When the Maximum Omitted Features parameter is set to -1 all feature subsets of the pharmacophore are considered. For a pharmacophore with five features, -1 allows up to four features to miss when mapping the ligand to the pharmacophore.

Click the Ligand Profiler button again. Click Browse... in Input Ligands and navigate to sulfonamide5HT2c_ligands_BEST.sd in the Output folder of the Ligand Profiler protocol that you ran. Click Browse... in Input File Pharmacophores and navigate to the Output folder of the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol that you ran. SHIFT+select the ten pharmacophore models and click OK . Change the Conformation Generation parameter to NONE . Expand the Advanced parameter group, and then change Scale Fit Values to False , Save Aligned Ligands to True , and the Maximum Omitted Features parameter to -1 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete.

The job will complete faster because the conformation generation step does not need to be repeated.

This time, all 18 of the active sulfonamides were retrieved and 17 of the inactive ligands.

A brief visual analysis of the Heat Map shows that several of the ligands fitting to the first pharmacophore are represented by blue cells, indicating lower fit values. Alternatively, pharmacophore 5HT2c_ligands_04 shows more ligands with orange and red cells.

Find the job in the Jobs Explorer and double click on it. From the Report Html window, click the 5HT2c_ligands_04_view.pl script.

In the Data Table View the ligands are sorted by FitValue and you can see that the first 14 ligands are active sulfonamide ligands. Interestingly, 4 of the 17 inactive ligands that map have Antipsychotic listed in the activityclass property.

In the Hierarchy View, SHIFT+select the first 14 ligands (all sulfonamide5HT2c_n ligands), and then right-click in the Graphics View and choose Show .

Notice that the alignments of the sulfonamide ligands have improved from the previous Ligand Profiler results, as are the FitValues, and that all of the ligands miss mapping to the positive ionizable feature.

Further analyses of the generated pharmacophores would be required for a complete validation. However in this tutorial you will take the 5HT2c_ligands_04 pharmacophore forward to the final lead identification step.

Now you will perform a 3D pharmacophore search of the MiniMaybridge compound structure database in order to identify potential new leads.

# Creating a structure-based fragment pharmacophore to optimize a scaffold

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_pharm-struct-fragment-scaffold.htm

## Creating a structure-based fragment pharmacophore to optimize a scaffold

Time: 60 minutes.

### Introduction

Structure-based ligand optimization can involve a variety of different methods such as de novo design or fragment pharmacophores to introduce additional chemical functional groups or hop scaffolds in particular parts of the binding site.

In this tutorial, the optimization of a scaffold in a protein active site will focus on a fragment pharmacophore method where the pharmacophore features will be derived from information about the original bound crystal structure ligand and known interacting protein residues. The following tasks are covered:

* Analyzing the interactions of a bound crystal structure ligand in a protein

* Designing a fragment pharmacophore based on the crystal structure ligand, its interactions, and a positioned scaffold

* Searching a 3D compound database with the designed pharmacophore

* Enumerating the screened fragments with the scaffold

* Refining the enumerated library

In this lesson, you will take the top scoring pose from a Dock Fragments (MCSS) protocol run, derived from the inhibitor of a cAMP-dependent protein kinase (2VNW), and use this as a scaffold to attach additional fragments. The PDB code for the protein used is 1YDT. The file was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared with the Prepare Proteins protocol.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | 1ydt_2vnw_scaffold.dsv . Select File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | 1ydt_ligand.dsv .

The top scoring pose of the 2VNW scaffold overlays very closely on the isoquinonesulfonamide group of the 1YDT bound ligand. The six-membered rings are in the same position and the amine group is in a similar position to the sulfur.

The top scoring pose also makes a hydrogen bond to the backbone amide of Val123, as does the original inhibitor, and makes an additional hydrogen bond to the backbone carbonyl group of Glu121.

In the Hierarchy View turn off the visibility checkbox for the 2vnw_scaffold so that you can concentrate on the interactions of the bound crystal structure ligand in the protein. Select 1ydt_ligand in the Hierarchy View. Open the View Interactions tool panel from the Receptor-Ligand Interactions toolset. Click Define Ligand to set the ligand then click Ligand Interactions .

The cAMP-dependent protein kinase paper [Engh et al., 1996] reports bridging water molecules that make contacts between the inhibitor and the protein. For example, water HOH17 forms a hydrogen bond with the ligand, bridged to Glu127 and Leu49 (visible if you expand the shell). Additionally, there is a Pi-cation interaction between the aromatic ring of the bromocinnamoyl group and the terminal nitrogen of Lys72. In the Molecule Window, you can also see the interactions of the bromine group, which are also mentioned in the paper.

You will now install some custom scripts and a custom tool panel designed for structure-based pharmacophore analysis to help create your fragment-based pharmacophore.

If you haven't already added these scripts, choose Edit | Preferences from the menu bar to open the Preferences dialog. Select the General | Script Commands preference. Click Import... , and then click on the Samples shortcut . Open the Customization folder , and select StructureBasedPharmacophore.scripts . Click OK.

A folder called Structure Based Pharmacophore is now under the Scripts menu.

In the Tools Explorer, go to the Pharmacophores tool set. Right-click the Tools Explorer and choose Import... , and then click on the Samples shortcut . Open the Customization folder , and then select StructureBasedPharmacophore.panel .

This loads a custom tool panel that can be used to quickly create pharmacophores from protein-ligand complexes.

A fragment pharmacophore to optimize the MCSS-positioned scaffold can be designed in a number of different ways. You can base the pharmacophore on potential protein-ligand interactions identified using the Interaction Generation protocol. Alternatively, you can derive pharmacophore features from protein residues that you want to target. A third method would be to use the bound crystal structure ligand as a template to position pharmacophore features. The methods you use will depend on the information you have and want to use from your protein-ligand complex. In this tutorial you will use a combination of the latter two methods to create your fragment pharmacophore.

The X-ray crystal structure shows hydrogen bonds formed by the sulfonamide nitrogen and the aliphatic linker amine as being important to ligand-protein binding and stabilization of the protein structural features. It may be interesting to see what alternative chemistry may form hydrogen bonds in lieu of these features. The sulfonamide nitrogen and the aliphatic linker amine are hydrogen bond donors, and so you will place hydrogen bond donor projected point features where those ligand features are currently interacting.

Select the oxygen atom of HOH17 , which is hydrogen bonding to the sulfonamide nitrogen. From the Structure Based Pharmacophore tool panel, click Hydrogen Bond Donor Projected Point .

A purple caged sphere is now positioned on the water molecule, representing the location where a hydrogen bond donating ligand feature would interact with the protein, or in this case, a bound crystal water. This custom pharmacophore feature allows a greater degree of flexibility in the positioning of the hydrogen bond donor base point representing the ligand. New ligand features do not have to be in the same position as the current sulfonamide nitrogen; they only have to be positioned to have a similar projected point.

Select the carbonyl oxygen atom of Glu170 , which is hydrogen bonding to the aliphatic linker amine. From the tool panel, click Hydrogen Bond Donor Projected Point .

For the pharmacophore feature in this location you could have also chosen the oxygen atom of HOH10 instead.

Now you will add a couple of pharmacophore features based on the bound crystal structure ligand, rather than the protein residues.

Open the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Manually tool panel. Select the 6 carbons of the aromatic ring of the bromocinnamoyl group , and then click Query Features . In the Create Feature dialog, change Feature from Centroid to Point (Pharmacophore) .

Notice that Type changes automatically to Hydrophobe_Aromatic as it recognizes the selected chemistry.

Click OK to create the point feature. With the newly added feature still selected, click Location Constraint .

Select the bromine atom of the bromocinnamoyl group , and then click Query Features . In the Create Feature dialog, change Feature from Centroid to Point (Pharmacophore) . Change Type from Centroid to Hydrophobe .

This is an example of where it is better to use the tool panel or menu bar rather than the Query toolbar, as a bromine atom could also serve as a centroid feature.

Click OK to create the point feature. While the newly added feature is still selected, click Location Constraint .

The subsequent method used to enumerate the de novo fragments (identified by the pharmacophore screening) with the scaffold relies on the exact 3D location and chemical specifications of a selected link atom from the bound crystal ligand or, more ideally, the scaffold. You will now create and edit a linker query.

In the Hierarchy View turn on the visibility checkbox for the 2vnw_scaffold .

You can see that the amine of the 2vnw_scaffold is positioned very close to the sulfonamide of the bound crystal ligand. If you were working with the isoquinoline scaffold, you would likely choose the sulfur atom as the linker query.

Turn off the visibility checkbox for the 1ydt_ligand so that you can concentrate on the linker query. Select the amine nitrogen (N10) of the 2vnw_scaffold. From the Structure Based Pharmacophore tool panel, click Create Link Atom(s) .

This creates a copy of the nitrogen atom and converts it to a query atom at the exact 3D location of the N10 atom. This defines a link point between your existing scaffold and the fragments you will identify with your pharmacophore.

The query atom specifications control the chemistry of the ligand atom at the link atom location relative to the other pharmacophore features and the scaffold. You can use this to ensure that only molecules with atoms suitable for enumeration are returned by the 3D fragment pharmacophore screening.

In the Hierarchy View, expand the QueryRoot , Fit and And nodes and select the newly created query atom (it appears as an object with the name "Molecule"). From the same tool panel, click Query Atom Specification . On the Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog, check the Aliphatic and Exocyclic checkboxes. In the Elements list, enter C N O S (separated by spaces), or click the button to open the Select Elements dialog to select the same elements. Click OK to save the changes.

The Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog is a powerful tool that can control the diversity and chemical accessibility of the resulting fragment de novo libraries. The above specifications mean that the candidate fragments must possess an aliphatic exocyclic atom at the query location. You could have added further restraints (such as a hydrogen count of 1 or 2 to include fragments that contain hydroxyl but not ether fragments at the link point), but this relaxed definition will give you a reasonable number of fragments to work with.

You will now add a molecular shape constraint to the pharmacophore in order to increase the selectivity and ensure that reasonably sized fragments are identified. Alternatively, you could select atoms from the protein and place excluded volumes on these to enclose the pharmacophore and prevent fragments that are too large from being identified in the subsequent database search.

A third popular option is to use the binding site cavity and convert this to a shape. You can define the binding site with Define Site From Receptor Cavities on the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel (Receptor-Ligand Interactions tool set), and edit the site as desired. The custom Structure Based Pharmacophore tool panel includes a Binding Site to Shape Query command that creates the shape query from the binding site points. Note that if you create your shape query with this method, you may need to adjust the Minimum Similarity Tolerance (accessed via the Attributes for the Shape query) to retrieve reasonably fitting fragments in the database search.

Turn on the visibility checkbox for 1ydt_ligand and select the entire ligand, excluding the isoquinoline scaffold (atoms C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, N7, C8, C9, C10).

This is the portion of the bound crystal ligand now represented by your pharmacophore.

You may find it easier if you turn off the visibility for the 1ydt protein, the 2vnw_scaffold, and the QueryRoot.

Choose Structure | Query Features... from the menu bar. In the Create Feature dialog, change Feature from Centroid to Shape . Click OK to create the shape feature.

You have now completed your fragment query. You can click the visibility checkbox for the pharmacophore off and on to see it completely. You can also remove the labels for some of the features by choosing Structure | Labels | Remove from the menu bar.

Now you will perform a 3D pharmacophore search of the MiniMaybridge compound structure database to identify matching fragment hits. Later, you will use these hits to enumerate a de novo library.

Open the Pharmacophore | Search, Screen and Profile tools and click Search 3D Database... to open the Search 3D Database dialog. Set the Input Database to MiniMaybridge [2000 mol] . Check that Input Pharmacophore specifies the 1ydt_2vnw_scaffold:QueryRoot in the Molecule Window that you have been working in. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete.

A dialog indicates the number of hits.

In the dialog, click Report to open the report.

This tutorial demonstrated the Search 3D Database protocol because it is the fastest way to screen a 3D compound database with this query. Alternatively, you could have used the Screen Library protocol, which is ideal if you have more features in your pharmacophore and are interested in finding hits that fit to a subset of those features.

In this tutorial you have used a sample database of 2000 molecules from the MiniMaybridge database. Realistically, you would have used a database of fragments optimized for fragment-based design, as these have different ideal properties to whole molecules. The Generate RECAP Fragments protocol from the Small Molecules | Design and Analyze Libraries tool panel can be used to generate synthetically-accessible fragments, for fragment-based design, from whole molecules.

From the Report, click View Results to open a new Molecule window containing the fragment pharmacophore and fitted fragments ranked in order of FitValue.

Browse through the results using the arrows in the table and see how the retrieved hits meet each of the pharmacophore feature requirements. In particular, the linker query feature ensures that there is a linking atom at the same location as the amine from the 2VNW scaffold.

Not all of these fragments may be chemically suitable for linking to the 2vnw_scaffold amine. You could return to refine the pharmacophore to retrieve only amine substituents at this location, or you can see how the next enumeration step will handle these situations.

Return to the Molecule Window where you constructed your fragment pharmacophore. In the Hierarchy View, turn on the visibility checkbox for 2vnw_scaffold . Select it and press CTRL+C to copy it to the clipboard. Choose File | New | Molecule Window from the menu bar and press CTRL+V to paste the scaffold into the new Molecule Window. In the Protocols Explorer open the Discovery Studio | Pharmacophore | Search and Build Databases | Enumerate from Fragments protocol. Check that the Fragment A is set to the visible ligand in the Molecule Window containing the newly pasted 2vnw_scaffold. Set Fragment B to all ligands in the Molecule Window containing the results of the database search. Set the Library Name to 2vnw_scaffold_library . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run on the Smart Tools toolbar and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of enumerated ligands. You should get back around 12 ligands.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an Html Window. Click the Ligands that Failed to Enumerate link.

This will open an SD file of the ligands which failed to enumerate - these are molecules that are duplicates or likely to be poor candidates for high-throughput screening as they contain non-organic atom types, reactive substructures, molecular weights < 150, or high minimized energy. Depending on the reason for the failure you may wish to retain some of these ligands for further refinement.

Return to the Report Html window and click the Enumerated Ligands link.

This will open the SD file of the ligands which completed the enumeration. Expand the width of the Name column and you will see the naming convention used, and also that some of the fragments result in more than one enumerated ligand. This will be because the enumeration found multiple ways to link the scaffold to the fragment. Look at the two enumerated ligands for fragment RH 01071 - one ligand has an amine linking the purine and pyrimidine rings systems, while the second ligand has an ether functional group linking the two. This is because the RH 01071 fragment has a hydroxyl group at the linker query, and the enumeration will use the amine nitrogen from the 2vnw_scaffold fragment for one ligand and the hydroxyl oxygen from the RH 01071 fragment for the second ligand.

As you scrolled through the enumerated library you may have noticed that the original scaffold for all of the ligands is positioned slightly different. This is because the enumeration can change the geometries of one or both of the fragments, which in turn affects how the whole ligand may fit to the pharmacophore, and more importantly, to the protein.

It is important to refine the enumerated library in the protein, and this can be easily done by re-docking the ligands into the protein active site or performing an energy minimization with the protein present. If you would like to try re-docking the ligands, you can use the Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) protocol without defining an input site sphere, and this will use the starting pose of each ligand for the docking. Alternatively, you could also use the Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) protocol, and define the starting scaffold as the pharmacophore restraint - this will optimize the enumerated ligands in the protein active site, but ensure that the purine scaffold retains as much of its position identified by the MCSS run as possible. In the final part of this tutorial, you will re-dock with the scaffold as a restraint.

As a first step you will create the scaffold pharmacophore which will be restrained during the docking.

Return to the Molecule Window where you copied the 2vnw_scaffold for the enumeration of your library.

If you have closed this window or cannot find it, then return to the Molecule Window where you constructed your fragment-based pharmacophore. Turn on the visibility checkbox for 2vnw_scaffold and select it to copy and paste into a new Molecule Window.

Delete the amine substituent .

This is so that enumerated ligands that do not include a nitrogen atom (like 2vnw_scaffold-RH 01071-2) here are not automatically filtered.

Select the 2vnw_scaffold . From the Structure Based Pharmacophore tool panel, click Fragment to Query .

This creates the scaffold query which will act as a restraint during the docking.

Return to the Molecule Window where you constructed your fragment pharmacophore. Ensure the 1ydt protein is visible. Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Click Show/Hide Spheres and then toggle on and off Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres .

This will show all the atoms within the site sphere.

Click Show/Hide Site Spheres to hide the site sphere. In the Protocols Explorer, open the Discovery Studio | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Docking | Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) protocol. From the Parameters Explorer, check that Input Receptor is set to the 1ydt molecule in the original Molecule Window containing the 1ydt protein - 1ydt_2vnw_scaffold:1ydt. Set Input Ligands to the Molecule Window containing the enumerated library - 2vnw_scaffold_library:All. Set Input Pharmacophore to the Molecule window containing the newly created substructure query - Molecule:QueryRoot. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run on the Smart Tools toolbar and wait for the job to complete.

The job should take less than an hour to run.
In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an Html Window.

Click View Results to open a new Molecule window containing the re-docked ligands in the protein active site. Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools panel. Click Ligand Interactions to enable the non-bond interactions monitor. Use the Step through Ligands arrows to navigate through the results.

The purine moiety of all of the poses remains fairly constant through the poses because you have restrained it with harmonic restraints during the docking.

None of the ligands may make all of the interactions found in the bound crystal structure ligand, as the change in conformation due to the enumeration and the restraint of the purine scaffold may have made this infeasible. However, you may find some poses interacting with protein residues that you did not target previously.

Notice that the view changes when enabling the interactions monitor; only interacting residues are visible. The monitors indicate that some of docked poses 
retain the Pi-cation interaction of the original bound crystal structure, some make additional Pi-cation interactions, and some form a Pi-Sigma interaction.

You can use Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions | Display receptor-ligand interactions | Show Types to display the non-bond interaction types when stepping through the results.

# Creating a structure-based pharmacophore to screen a ligand library

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_pharm-struct-screen-ligand.htm

## Creating a structure-based pharmacophore to screen a ligand library

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

The Structure-Based Pharmacophore (SBP) method uses the known or suspected active site of a protein to select compounds that are likely to bind within that site, and can be seen as a complementary method to docking.

In this tutorial, the defined active site is first analyzed to create an interaction map of features that the ligand is expected to satisfy for a reasonable interaction with the protein. The feature interaction map is used to create an input pharmacophore model that, in turn, is used to enumerate several possible pharmacophores on the fly. This is used to screen an input set of ligands. The resulting hits can be viewed and further analyzed.

The following tasks are covered:

* Generating a structure-based pharmacophore

* Editing pharmacophore features

* Screening a ligand library

* Analyzing the screening results

In this lesson, you will generate the pharmacophore models based on the α-thrombin protein structure. The PDB code for the protein used is 1K22. The file was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared with the Prepare Proteins protocol.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | 1k22_protein_ligand.dsv .

α-Thrombin is a serine protease and a member of the chymotrypsin family, playing a prominent role in the blood clotting cascade. There are three principal binding pockets at the cleaving site, the specificity S1 pocket (residues in red), the proximal P pocket (residues in blue), and the distal D pocket (residues in green) (1,2).

Next you will define the active site to generate the structure-based pharmacophore.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools. The receptor is automatically set to 1k22_protein as it is the first protein in the active window. In the Hierarchy View select 1k22_ligand . From the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel, click From Current Selection in the Define Site section.

In the Graphics View, notice a red site sphere encompassing the crystallized 1K22 ligand.

If you do not have a bound ligand to use for the selection, you can select residues of the known active site, or use the binding site tools to identify cavities and binding sites.

In the Graphics View select the red site sphere, then right-click and choose Attributes of SBD_Site_Sphere . In SphereObject Attributes dialog enter 9 in the Radius textbox. Deselect the sphere.

You may need to increase the radius of the site sphere to include all the residues of the active site. However, this also increases the number of interactions identified and may include some that are not relevant.

Next, you will generate the interaction map and model consisting of hydrogen bond acceptors, hydrogen bond donors, and hydrophobic features within the receptor active site sphere.

Open the Pharmacophores | Edit and Cluster Features tools and click Interaction Generation... to open the Interaction Generation dialog. Ensure that Input Receptor is set to 1k22_protein_ligand:1k22_protein . Set Input Site Sphere to the 9 Å sphere just created. Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job finishes the features will be automatically inserted into the Graphics View.

The pharmacophore query has been created from a Ludi interaction map, and must be edited before it can be used for screening.

From the Hierarchy View , turn off the visibility of the SBD_Site_Sphere for clarity. From the Pharmacophores | Edit and Cluster Features tools and click Show/Hide Location Spheres .

Notice that multiple vectored features can represent a single interaction with an active site residue. The editing of a structure-based pharmacophore, to a reasonable number of features for screening, is a subjective process in which you would consider information about important amino acid residues and interactions with the bound ligand, if available. When first developing and validating an interaction model, twenty pharmacophore features is a reasonable number to work with for the subsequent screening step.

In this tutorial, you will try a number of different ways to select and edit the pharmacophore model, incorporating binding site and bound ligand information.

The 1k22_protein_ligand window contains the colored binding pockets, the bound ligand, and intermolecular interactions to help in the editing of the pharmacophore.

Set Current Feature to All Features and click Show/Hide All Features on the Edit and Cluster Features tool panel to hide all of the pharmacophore features. Set Current Feature to Acceptor and click Show/Hide Acceptor . Click Cluster Current Features .

This clusters the Acceptor features and opens a new Dendrogram Window.

Drag the Dendrogram Window tab and drop it in the right side of the window to place it side-by-side with the 1k22_protein_ligand Molecule Window.

Use the mouse wheel to zoom vertically and see all of the dendrogram.
As you move the slider in the Dendrogram Window, different cluster centers are highlighted based on the distance geometry of all the features used to create the dendrogram. What you may consider the best representative cluster center for a group of features may not always be highlighted. You may also want to increase the number of cluster centers to highlight more than one representative for a collection of features. A combination of automatic clustering and manual selection may be required to select the best features to represent your protein active site.

Move the slider in the Dendrogram Window to highlight 12 cluster centers , as reported in the bottom-right corner of the application window.

If you have trouble selecting 12 clusters, expand the width of the Dendrogram window to make this easier to select.

Click Keep Only Cluster Centers on the tool panel, and then close the Dendrogram Window.

Only the 12 cluster centers for the Acceptor feature are retained.

In the Hierarchy View expand QueryRoot and Fit Fit_1 . CTRL+select the acceptor features numbered 28, 46, 56, 77, and 97 , and then click Keep Only Current Feature Selections on the tool panel.

You select these features for inclusion as they correspond to residues of the active site. The remaining features may be too far from the relevant active site residues, or have vectors pointing away from the putative binding site.

Click Show/Hide Acceptor again to hide the acceptor features. Set Current Feature to Donor and click Donor under the Show/Hide tools group. In the Hierarchy View CTRL+select the donor features numbered 44, 63, 75, 76, 94, 101, 107, 141, 198, and 207 , and then click Keep Only Current Feature Selections .

These donor features have been manually selected as good representative centers of clusters that correspond with important residues of the active site, as well as interesting potential new features such as the Donor94 representing a Ser195 interaction. These features were selected predominantly based on interactions generated solely from protein structure information. You could also have manually selected features for a cluster based on the known hydrogen bond interactions between the current ligand and the protein.

Click Show/Hide Donor again to hide the donor features. Set Current Feature to Hydrophobe , and then click Hydrophobe under the Show/Hide tools group. Click Cluster Current Features .

The new Dendrogram Window for the Hydrophobe features opens next the Molecule window you are working in.

Move the slider in the Dendrogram Window to highlight 8 cluster centers . Click Keep Only Cluster Centers on the Edit and Cluster Features tool panel, and then close the Dendrogram Window. In the Hierarchy View, CTRL+select the hydrophobe features numbered 9, 48, and 81 , and then click Keep Only Current Feature Selections .

These three remaining hydrophobe features correspond well with the cyclohexyl and benzene features in the bound ligand, as well as the azetidine ring nestled between the residues of the P pocket (colored in blue).

Set Current Feature to All Features , and then click All Features under the Show/Hide tools group.

These eighteen features represent a pharmacophoric structural model of the protein active site, and have been chosen based on observed interactions between the bound ligand and the protein, as well as interactions structurally derived from only the protein.

Another useful tool for editing the pharmacophore model is the Average Pharmacophore Features command. Select several of the same feature type in what you determine to be a cluster and use this command to generate an average feature to represent that cluster.

The main determinant for the specificity of ligands toward proteins of the chymotrypsin family is the deep hydrophobic S pocket (shown in red). Both the P (blue) and the D (green) pockets are mostly hydrophobic, and the differences in their amino acid residues have been used in the past to enhance selectivity for thrombin.

You will be able to use some of this information to refine your screening in the next step.

In the Hierarchy View, CTRL+select the acceptor features numbered 28, 77, and 97 and the donor features numbered 63, 75, 141 and 198 , and then choose Edit | Group... from the menu bar. Name the group S-interactions.

These interactions should all be representative of residues composing, or close, to the hydrophobic S-pocket.

The last step in editing the structure-based pharmacophore is to add excluded volumes to represent the steric aspect of the protein. You can manually select these based on the protein structure, or use this quicker selection method.

In the Hierarchy View select QueryRoot , and then choose Edit | Select... from the menu bar. In the Select dialog change Selection Mode to Replace and Scope to AminoAcid . Set Radius to 2.00 Å. Click Apply . Change Selection Mode to Intersection and Scope to Atom . Select Property and enter CA in the text box next to Name and equals drop-downs.
Click Apply . Open the Pharmacophore | Create Pharmacophore Manually tools and click Exclusion Constraint .

You have now completed editing your structure-based pharmacophore.

Uncheck and recheck the visibility checkbox for the pharmacophore to see it completely.

Please verify in the Hierarchy View under the QueryRoot that Fit Fit_1 contains: 5 Acceptors, 10 Donors, 3 Hydrophobes, 16 Excluded Volumes, and 33 Location Features.

Before you use this pharmacophore to screen a library of compounds, similarly to docking ligands into a protein active site, it is necessary to first validate the model and understand which of the eighteen pharmacophore features are most significant. You may need to go back to the original interaction model and edit the pharmacophore using different criteria and information.

You will now screen a test set comprising a number of known thrombin inhibitors with a number of kinase inhibitors that are serving as unknown ligands. Ideally the kinase inhibitors would be true negative control ligands, known not to bind to this protein target.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Pharmacophore | thrombin_ligands.sd . Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | kinase_ligands.sd .

The active thrombin inhibitors have the "_ligand" suffix and can be easily distinguished from the kinase inhibitors.

Return to the 1k22 protein_ligand window. In the Hierarchy View, select the Hydrophobe81 feature. This will be used as a required feature during the screening. Open the Pharmacophores | Search, Screen and Profile tools and click Screen Library... to open the Screen Library dialog. Check that the Input Pharmacophore parameter specifies 1k22_protein_ligand:QueryRoot . Set the Input Ligands parameter to thrombin_ligands:All .

Previously, you have grouped some of the interactions which represent those occupying the thrombin S pocket (interactions colored in red). You can now specify the number of these which must be satisfied by the ligands screened, as well as any interactions that are required to be present in every pharmacophore screened. The required feature you will use is the hydrophobic feature near the center of the azetidine ring close to the three residues (shown in blue) representing the hydrophobic D pocket.

Expand the Input Pharmacophore parameter group. Set Required Features group to True and expand the group. Set the Required Features value to the hydrophobe feature you selected (18:Hydrophobe81). Set Features Group to True and expand the group. Set Feature Group 1 to the S-interactions group. Expand the Feature Group 1 parameter group, and change Maximum to 7 . Change Maximum Features to 8 .

With these settings, screened ligands must fit at least four features of the eighteen features of your edited pharmacophore. Of those four features, one must include the Hydrophobe81 feature and one must come from the group of features representing the S pocket.

Change Maximum Subset of Pharmacophores to 250 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job finishes, a Report will open in an Html Window.

Click the View All Results link to open a Molecule Window containing the structure-based pharmacophore and all the fitted hits (54 poses). 11 ligands of the 17 thrombin and kinase inhibitors are fitted to the pharmacophore.

The Screen Library protocol can be very versatile and provides much informative output for analysis. Next you will look at a couple of methods for analyzing the data. These methods are not mutually exclusive and can collectively provide different insights into the pharmacophore model you have edited.

Right-click in the Data Table View, select the Molecule tab, and choose Filter... to open the Filter dialog . Change Choice for the FitValue property to Top (#) and Value to 1 . Select the Apply filter to each group of identical value option, and then select Name for Group By .

Notice that seven of the original eight thrombin inhibitors were picked up by the screen, and four of the nine kinase inhibitors were also identified.

Right-click in the Data Table View and choose Remove Filters . Double-click the PharmprintFrequency column twice.

The first eight ligands (which all fit the same pharmacophore, as the Pharmprint property shows) all have a PharmprintFrequency of 8 and include four thrombin inhibitors, but also four kinase inhibitors.

If you scroll down to the five ligands with a PharmprintFrequency of 5, you can see that this subset of pharmacophore features fits five thrombin inhibitors but none of the kinase inhibitors.

Also notice that, generally, pharmacophores with higher frequencies have fewer features.

Double-click the Name column so that the thrombin ligands are sorted at the top of the table. Unselect the Name column. Choose Chart | Heat Map from the menu bar. For the Y column , select the Name property. For the X column , select Acceptor28 and then SHIFT+select Hydrophobe9 . Unselect the ConfNumber , FitValue , and all FeatureName_fit and FeatureName_atom properties

In the heat map, all of the mappings include Hydrophobe81, as you specified this as a required feature. Other features such as Donor107 and Hydrophobe48 map to different mappings of thrombin inhibitors, but not kinase inhibitors. Also observe features such as Donor94, which map very few inhibitors, and might be removed to simplify the pharmacophore when you are considering screening a much larger library.

Different analyses can be performed to help you determine how valid the pharmacophore model is, or whether you need to re-edit it before further use. After this validation you may identify different subsets of the edited pharmacophore, which can be used to search compound databases for new ligands that may potentially bind to the protein active site, or to screen larger ligand libraries.

If you have used the pharmacophore model to screen ligands as an alternative to docking, you may now wish to minimize the ligands within the context of the protein using the In Situ Ligand Minimization .

#### Further reading

* [Banner and Hadváry, 1991]

* [Kastenholz et al., 2000]

# Predict protein aggregation sites

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_predict-agg-sites.htm

## Predict protein aggregation sites

Time: 20 minutes.

### Background

Therapeutic proteins, such as antibodies, have a tendency to aggregate in high concentrations. This can lead to a decrease in activity as well as elicit immunological responses. 
Protein aggregation propensity is a measure of the tendency of surface residues to aggregate. Sites with a high aggregation propensity score on a protein surface specify regions that are prone to aggregation. Identifying these areas allows you to use targeted mutation to engineer therapeutic proteins with higher stability.

### Introduction

In this tutorial, you will perform a protein aggregation propensity score 
calculation on an antibody, and then examine the resulting sites.
A full length IgG1 antibody structure (PDB ID 1hzh) will be used.

This tutorial covers:

* Calculating Protein Aggregation Score

* Analyzing Protein Aggregation Sites

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | 1hzh.pdb .

This opens the protein in a new Molecule Window.

Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if it is not visible. Click Water to select this group, and then 
press the Delete key.

This removes water molecules from 1hzh.

Open the Simulation | 
Change Forcefield tools, set the Forcefield to 
CHARMm Polar H, and then click Apply Forcefield .

This types the protein to prepare for the calculation.

Open the Macromolecules | Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools and click Calculate Aggregation Scores... . Set Input Typed Protein to 1hzh:1HZH . Set the Cutoff Radius values to 5,7,10 . Click Run to start the job.

When the run finishes, the structure in the active Molecule Window is updated with the calculated protein aggregation propensity scores for the specified radii and the scores are added as atom properties to each protein atom and residue properties to each amino acid. The aggregation propensity score properties are labeled Aggr R5 etc. for each radius value used in the calculation. Aggregation sites are defined as groups containing adjacent exposed residues with high aggregation propensity scores, and groups are created in the Hierarchy View under an Aggregation Sites node.

A solvent surface is created covering all non-solvent residues, colored according to the atom aggregation propensity score at the largest cutoff radius used. Atoms with high aggregation propensity scores are colored red, through blue for lower scores. Additionally, a line plot of residue index versus aggregation propensity score and a point plot of site ID versus aggregation propensity score are created.

The structure is shown in the Graphics View with the entire surface for the 10 Å cutoff radius displayed.

Rotate the molecule and observe the areas where the surface is red. These are sites liable to aggregate. The Cutoff Radius is initially set to the highest value used in the calculation, in this case 10 Å. Click View at Cutoff Radius in the View Aggregation Sites tool group, change the radius to 5 Å, and observe the changes in the surface color.

This provides an overview of the aggregation sites. You will see that a smaller radius yields a greater number of localized aggregation sites, whereas a larger radius shows broader areas liable to aggregate. The next step is to examine the sites in more detail.

Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if it is not visible. Expand the Aggregation Sites node and then the sub-nodes to see the Site groups.

You can see more sites under the Radius 5 node than Radius 10, which typically contains fewer residues. You can also observe this in the point plot of Site ID versus aggregation propensity score.

In the tool panel, reset the Cutoff Radius to 10 Å. Click the First Site tool, and then click Show Details of Site 1 . Use the Fit To Screen tool and rotate as needed to view the site.

The first aggregation site is colored red, with the remainder of the surface pale green. An annotation box connected to the center of the site lists the residues that constitute the site. This site contains the exposed residue with the highest aggregation propensity score.

Click Hide Surface to turn off the display of the surface and allow the underlying residues to be examined.

To view the individual residues, it is useful to change the display style of the
structure to an atomistic representation using the Display Style control
on the Standard toolbar.

Click the arrow to the right of the Display Style button and choose the style in the bottom right of the preview page.

The appearance of the structure beneath the surface is now updated to show the atoms in line mode.

The atoms in the site are colored by their aggregation score with the highest scoring atoms in red.

In the Hierarchy View, click the first site group to select the residues of the site in the Graphics View, which also selects the 
corresponding residues in the line and point plots.

Notice that one of the residues in the first site has the highest aggregation score in the line plot. Some of
the residues with high aggregation scores are not part of the site group since they are buried inside the protein.

Click Next to examine Site 2 in the same way; continue to browse the sites as desired. At any point, use the Reset Display tool to restore the surface to show all aggregation sites in red and non-aggregating areas in blue.

You should be able to identify sites liable to aggregation which are on the exposed surfaces of the protein. Residues within these sites may be good targets for mutation experiments.

### Introduction

Discovery Studio provides a range of viewers for working with molecular structures and properties. When working with proteins, the Molecule and Sequence Windows are of most value and can be used very effectively to explore different aspects of a molecule and make inferences about its functionality. For example, protein secondary structure predictions can be made on the sequences, and the corresponding regions can be highlighted in the Molecule Window.

In addition to these general views, the application provides access to more specialized viewers for studying violations and anomalies in protein structures. Specifically, the Ramachandran plots and Contact Plots provide the ability to analyze high-level structural properties in detail and identify residues that may be incorrectly modeled.

into a structure's function by looking at its sequence. The tutorial also covers the use of one of the more specialized views, the

# Working with QSAR - 3D QSAR

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_qsar-3d.htm

## Working with QSAR - 3D QSAR

Time: 20 minutes.

### Introduction

Drug design involves finding small molecules that are complementary in shape (steric) and charge (electrostatic) to a bio-molecular target. Regression models built from whole molecular steric and electrostatic fields can be useful for predicting activity and for visualizing favorable and unfavorable interactions. In this tutorial, a Partial Least-Squares (PLS) model is built using energy grids as descriptors. The energy grids are computed using two probe types designed to measure electrostatic and steric effects. A user model is then created that can be used to predict the activity of unknown ligands.

This tutorial covers:

* Building a 3D QSAR Model

* Viewing Results

* Predicting Activity Using 3D QSAR Model

* Interpreting a 3D QSAR Model

Before building a 3D QSAR model, it is important to have all training set molecules aligned. There is no general way to find the best alignment, but one of the following methods could be used:

* If the ligands are from crystal structures and bound to the same target, you can use the crystal structure conformations.

* You can use a common substructure as the core for the alignment.

* You can convert the common core into a substructure query, and then run a Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping protocol to align the training set.

* You could align the ligands to a pharmacophore.

* You could use the field fit method to align the ligands based on a combination of steric and electrostatic fields (Structure | Superimpose | Molecular Overlay...).

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | trainingset.sd .

This opens 14 pre-aligned training set molecules with activity data in a Molecule Window.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | testset.sd .

This opens eight pre-aligned test set molecules in another Molecule Window.

Open the Small Molecules | Create QSAR Model tools and click Create 3D QSAR Model... to open the Create 3D QSAR Model dialog. Set the Input Ligands to trainingset:All . Set Input Test Ligands to testset:All . Set Activity Property to arNCTRlogRBA . For Model Name , type in "GridBasedModel" . Keep the default settings for the remaining parameters. Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

The job should take about one minute on a 2.4 GHz CPU machine.

When the job finishes, a report opens in an Html Window.

In the Results section of the report, click View Results , and if prompted whether to show a plot of the model prediction respond Yes .

This opens the training set molecules in a new Molecule Window and a line plot of predicted activity vs. activity data:

The test data set provides a simple way to check the predictive power of the model.

From the report, click View Test Results .

This opens a plot of predicted activity versus test data:

You can find more details about the generated QSAR
model by viewing
the Model Description file in the Results section of the report. It contains information such as the regression statistics, the model's coefficients and variables, and the training data information. The result of 5-fold cross validation of the training set molecules can be found in the report:

In addition to the predictive power of the 3D QSAR model, the 3D grid representation of the model is also very useful. The grid includes two parts: one for electrostatic potential, and the other for van der Waals interactions.

From the report, click View Training Set Aligned to Model (EP) .

This opens the training set molecules aligned with the two isosurfaces of the 3D QSAR model coefficients on electrostatic potential grids:

Blue represents positive coefficients; red represents negative coefficients. The isovalues for both positive and negative coefficients are automatically determined from the mode in the histogram of the coefficients.

From the report, click View Training Set Aligned to Model (VDW) .

This opens the training set molecules aligned with the isosurface of the 3D QSAR model coefficients on van der Waals grids:

Green represents positive coefficients; yellow represents negative coefficients. The isovalues are selected using the same method as electrostatic potential.

### Predict Activity Using 3D QSAR Model

The generated 3D QSAR Model can be used to predict activity of new compounds. You can do this using the Calculate Molecular Properties tool.

Close all the windows. Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | testset.sd .

This opens the molecules in a new Molecule Window.

Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and
click Calculate Molecular Properties... to open the Calculate 
Molecular Properties dialog. Set Input Ligands to testset:All . Click the Molecular Properties parameter, then click
the button.

This opens the Molecular Properties dialog.

In the dialog, check and uncheck All to clear the selections.
Expand Other and check GridBasedModel . Click OK . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

It is important to have the new molecules aligned to the original training set molecules before applying the model. A practical way for doing this is to align all molecules, including training set, test set (if available), and the new compounds before building the model.

When the protocol finishes, a message box indicates that the calculated properties have been added to the Molecule Window.

Click OK .

3D QSAR model provides useful information about the correlation between the molecular fields and the activity. An obvious question is how to interpret the model and how to provide guidance for medicinal chemists about how to increase (or decrease) the activity by modifying the compounds.

By convention, the log units of concentration (e.g.,IC50) are used as a measure of activity. The more negative the log IC50 value is, the more active a compound is. The predicted activity of a compound is a linear summation of the model coefficients multiplied by their corresponding grid values:

where N EP is the number of descriptors of electrostatic potential (EP), C EP (i) is the model coefficient for EP descriptor i, and V EP is the electrostatic potential value on a grid point. Similarly, N VDW is the number of descriptors of van der Waals(VDW) interaction, C VDW (i) is the model coefficient for VDW descriptor i, and V VDW is the VDW interaction energy on a grid point.

From the above equation, notice that patterns of the 3D representation of the coefficients can provide useful information for designing compounds with enhanced
activity. For instance, the model coefficients of electrostatic potential interaction show a clear pattern. The red blocks show the top and bottom of the aligned molecules, while blue areas are shown in between.

To increase the activity (larger negative value of predicted activity), you should have a molecule that shows positive electrostatic potential in the red area and negative in the blue area. This can be achieved by strategically adding polar groups.

Note that it is usually difficult to determine the effects of a functional group on the electrostatic potential.
The best way to check this is to generate CHARMm grid files for the molecule and then visualize the grid file. For example, the 3D view of the electrostatic potential of molecule 12 in the training set is shown as follows:

The red area shows negative electrostatic potential, and the blue area shows the positive.

The 3D view of model coefficients of VDW interactions is also shown with two colors. Green indicates positive coefficients; yellow indicates negative coefficients. To increase activity, a new molecule should have strong VDW attraction in the green area and weak VDW attraction in the yellow area. In other words, the new molecule should be designed in such a way that in the green area, the molecule shape should have a better match with the target system.
