# Bayesian categorization

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_qsar.htm

## Bayesian categorization

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

A QSAR (quantitative structure-activity relationship) is a
mathematical relationship between a set of physicochemical
properties, known as descriptors, and the biological activity of
that set of molecules. The descriptors on which a QSAR is based
are derived from topological and 3D information for the
molecules.

QSAR protocols can be used to make informed decisions about
which candidate compounds should be considered (based on
estimates of biological activity), as well as to gain insight
into various underlying biological processes. QSAR can also be
used to provide basic insight into structure-property
relationships.

In this tutorial, you will use Bayesian categorization to create a QSAR model
to predict the activity of a molecule as a pyruvate kinase inhibitor, 
and then use the model to predict the activity of some test molecules.

This tutorial covers:

* Generating a Bayesian model

* Predicting the activity of new molecules

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | pk-400.sd .

This opens 400 pyruvate kinase inhibitors in a Molecule Window.

Open the Small Molecules | Create QSAR Model tools and click Create Bayesian Model... to open the Create Bayesian Model dialog. Set the Input Ligands to pk-400:All . Set the Property for Active parameter to Act_Tag .

This property is used to identify active molecules from the training set.
It is required to have a value of 1 for active molecules, and 0 for others. You can first 
add a tag property with default value of 0 in the Data Table, then use the Filter dialog to select the active molecules and change the value to 1 for
this property.

For Model Name , type pkBayesian . Keep the default settings for the remaining parameters. Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the job finishes, a Report automatically opens in an Html Window. The report contains the information
regarding the quality of the generated model, (for example, ROC score from leave-one-out cross validation, best cutoff 
for the Bayesian score). Because a 5-fold cross validation is performed by default, the statistics of the model such 
as the ROC score, rating, true positive, false negative, false positive, true negative, sensitivity, specificity,
and concordance rate are reported in a table. The ROC plot from the 5-fold cross validation
is also present. If an external test set is used, the result will be shown in the report.

The report also contains links to other files in the Results section. The Bin Assignment file contains statistics information used in Bayesian statistics, such as the frequency of each feature
appearing in the training set and the active subset (referred to as good in the model). The Good and Bad Fingerprints file contains the fingerprint features that are statistically significant in
the model. The Model Description file contains more detailed information such as
leave-one-out cross validation results, enrichment results (compared to random chance), etc. The Model Component file contains the model as an xml file that can be shared among
colleagues.

In the Results section, 
click View Training ROC Plot .

This opens pk-400.sd in a new Molecule Window, and a Line plot. The plot is a ROC plot, showing
the percentage of true positives against false positives.

This ROC plot uses prediction from the final model (no cross validation).

Once you have created a QSAR model, you can use it to
predict the activity of a molecule with unknown activity.
Models generated by the Create Bayesian Model and other QSAR
Model protocols are saved directly on the server and can be accessed
from the Calculate Molecular Properties tool.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | pk-test.sd .

This opens the molecule in a new Molecule Window.

Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click Calculate Molecular Properties... to open the Calculate Molecular Properties dialog. Set Input Ligands to pk-test:All . Click the Molecular Properties parameter, then click
the button.

This opens the Molecular Properties dialog.

In the dialog, clear the selections by checking and unchecking All . 
Expand Other and check pkBayesian . Click OK . Click Run and wait for the job to complete.

When the protocol run finishes, a message box pops up indicating the calculated properties have been added to the 
Molecule Window.

Click OK .

You can now inspect the predicted pyruvate kinase 
inhibition activity as a property pkBayesian Prediction. This can be compared to the experimental 
result (Act_Tag or Activity). The pkBayesian property is a Bayesian score derived internally in 
the Bayesian model. A molecule is predicted to be good or active if its Bayesian score is above a
cutoff value, which is determined in the leave-one-out cross validation during the model building process.
The pkBayesian Enrichment gives the increased likelihood (versus random) of this molecule being a
pyruvate kinase inhibitor. The pkBayesian EstPGood property gives the estimated probability of the 
molecule being an inhibitor based on the assumption of a normal distribution of the Bayesian score.

Recursive partitioning is a technique to classify members of the population based on several dichotomous 
dependent variables in a decision tree.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to create a recursive partitioning model using a training set of 
pyruvate kinase inhibitors, and then use the model to predict the activity class of some new compounds. 
The following tasks are covered:

* Create a recursive partitioning model

* Use the recursive partitioning model to make predictions

Partitioning Model dialog. Set the Input Ligands to pk-400:All

The model name will be used for registering a component in the Pipeline Pilot Server database,
and the properties the model can calculate will become calculable properties appearing in the Molecular Properties dialog launched by the Calculate Molecular Properties tool. The name should be illustrative and should not contain
non-alphanumeric characters (underscore is allowed).

Set Dependent Property to Activity .

The dependent property should be categorical data identifying the class of the molecules in the

# Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating results

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_rlinteractions-nonbond.htm

## Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating results

Time: 30 minutes

### Introduction

Non-bond interactions that form between two molecules are the basis of molecular recognition in biological systems. A detailed and comprehensive perception of non-bond interactions is crucial in structure-based design where identifying and optimizing the molecular interactions between ligands and their host receptor is a fundamental process.

In this tutorial, you will use a thermostabilized adenosine A2A receptor in complex with a selective inverse agonist ZM241385 [Dore et al., 2011] . The adenosine A2A receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor of particular interest as a drug target for Parkinson's disease. In this tutorial you will visualize the non-bond interactions between the protein and ligand, and then you will analyze ligand poses docked to the receptor. The following tasks are covered:

* Viewing non-bond interactions for a protein-ligand complex

* Viewing non-bond interactions for ligand poses

The PDB code for the adenosine A2A ZM241385 receptor-ligand complex used is 3PWH [Dore et al., 2011] . The file was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared using the Prepare Proteins protocol.

Open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 3pwh_complex.dsv . Click the arrow next to the Non-bond Interactions toolbar 
(also known as the Smart Tools toolbar ) and choose Ligand Interactions . Note that this context-sensitive toolbar appears when a Molecule Window with a protein-ligand complex is active.

# Understanding SAR trends using matched molecular pairs

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_sar-trends.htm

## Understanding SAR trends using matched molecular pairs

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

A considerable amount of a medicinal chemist's time may be committed to the process of lead optimization whereby the best balance between potency, off-target interactions, toxicity, and pharmacokinetic behavior is pursued to maximize the chance of progression to the candidate stage of the drug discovery pipeline. Structure-activity relationship (SAR) methods, which link chemical structure to molecular properties, are used extensively to determine which analogue should be synthesized next based on the knowledge that has been obtained thus far in the optimization. They are not always solely focused on increasing biological potency, but can be applied to an existing bioactive lead to yield analogues that might exhibit superior pharmacokinetic properties.

Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) analysis is an inverse SAR technique that is rapidly gaining popularity in the retrospective analysis of experimental datasets that is used to understand differences in properties between structurally related groups of existing compounds and to de-novo design novel structures ( [Griffen et al., 2011] , [Leach et al., 2006] , and [Warner et al., 2012] ). MMPs are pairs of molecules that differ only by a particular well-defined structural transformation, and when accompanied by large differences in biological activity can be considered activity cliffs ( [Hussain and Rea, 2010] and [Hu et al., 2012] ). When studying SARs, the activity responses to positional changes in biologically relevant chemical space can be conceptualized as an activity landscape, in which activity cliffs are discontinuities in the landscape where small changes in structure, corresponding to small steps in chemical space, lead to significant changes in the activity/potency hypersurface [Sisay et al., 2009] .

The use of MMPs in large heterogeneous datasets can particularly aid in the optimization of non-potency related properties by identifying structural trends that affect them and predicting what may happen when these transformations are applied elsewhere ( [Leach et al., 2006] and [Papadatos et al., 2010] ). The Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs protocol used in this tutorial identifies these structural trends within the dataset by identifying all possible MMPs and grouping them by common transformations. The frequency of the transformations gives an indication of the probability that the structural transformation will cause the property to change (or remain the same), and outliers may indicate potential ways of avoiding the general trend.

In this tutorial, a library of diverse ligands with cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitory data will be studied to identify structural trends, guide molecular design, and aid decision making in the lead optimization process. Cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) is a member of the large super-family of heme-containing enzymes responsible for oxidizing and reducing both endogenous and exogenous substrates, and plays a key role in the metabolism of drugs. Understanding CYP2D6 metabolism can improve the optimization of potential drugs to avoid or minimize metabolism and inhibition, which reduces their effectiveness.

In this tutorial, you will study trends where transformations can lead to increases or decreases in activity, and transformations that result in no change in activity.

### Analyzing Activity Effects Using Matched Molecular Pairs

The CYP2D6 ligands used were sourced from ChEMBL (http://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembldb/ [Gaulton et al., 2012] ) and have bioactivity data from the CHEMBL1614110 assay. The ligands were prepared by removing salts and retaining the largest fragment. Duplicate ligands were removed as analysis revealed substantial spreads in the duplicate activity values, which affected less than 8% of the data.

Open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | p450_2d6_chembl1614110.sd . Open the Small Molecules | Study SAR tool panel and click Analyze Activity Effects Using MMPs... to open the protocol. Check that Input Ligands is set to p450_2d6_chembl1614110:All . Check that Activity Property is set to pIC50 . Set Activity Change Threshold to 2 . Click Run , and then click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 16093 MMPs have been identified.

The activity change threshold is used to determine when the change in activity is considered an increase or decrease. Changes in activity between the negative of this value and this value are considered neutral. If the activity scales logarithmically, such as with pKi values, and a change in activity of two orders of magnitude is set as significant, the threshold should be set to 2.

pIC50 values can be easily calculated from original IC50 values using the Scale Data parameters in the Prepare Dependent Property protocol in the Create QSAR Model tool panel.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link.

The Report summarizes that the CYP2D6 dataset produced 16093 MMPs, of which there are 527 unique transformations.

In the Report, click the View Results link.

The Transformations summary page includes four tabs summarizing the MMP transformations identified. The Most Frequent tab lists the 15 most frequent MMP transformations across the entire dataset. Only transformations that occur more than 10 times (controlled by the Minimum Frequency parameter) are retained. The transformations are represented as SMILES, with a visual representation for ease of interpretation. The values in parentheses indicate the number of occurrences of that transformation. If a SMILES transformation is too long to see the occurrences (e.g., c1cccc(OC)c1 >> c1ccccc1OC), click the Transformations (SMILES) link to view the list of the cores with the transformation and the frequency.

The colored bars indicate the proportion of transformations that resulted in an increase (green), decrease (red), or no change (yellow) in CYP2D6 activity. Hover the cursor over the colored bars to see the percentage changes for the transformations.

Open the Most Frequently Change Activity tab.

This tab lists the 15 most frequent transformations that result in an activity change of more than two orders of magnitude.

Click the first transformation c1nccs1 >> c1ccccc1OC in the table to open a Molecule Window of the common cores that have the thiazole to methoxyphenyl transformation. Double-click the MMPEffect column header to sort the table. Use the Data Table View navigation arrows to step through these common cores in the Molecule Window.

The dark pink atom indicates the position of the transformation. Five of the fifteen transformation examples result in an increase in CYP2D6 activity, which is not desirable in drug design. This low propensity may not be enough to constitute a meaningful trend, but it is interesting to see that all of these transformations involve spiro compounds.
Observe the values in the ActivityChange property. The MMP noted as having a decrease in CYP2D6 activity has an activity change of -2.7. The MMPs with an increase in activity have values greater than 2 and those with values between 2 and -2 are defined as having a neutral effect on CYP2D6.

Notice that the reactant and product in the first transformation are essentially substructures of the second transformation. This is due to the inherent nature of MMP identification, which involves a size constraint on the chemical change between a pair of ligands [Hussain and Rea, 2010] .

Click the 7th transformation C(=O)c1cnccn1 >> S(=O)(=O)c1ccccc1 in the table to open a Molecule Window of the common cores that have the pyrazinecarbaldehyde to sulfonylbenzene transformation. Double-click the MMPEffect column header. Use the Data Table View navigation arrows to step through these common cores in the Molecule Window.

Notice that the first transformation, which has a decrease in CYP2D6 activity, is the only ligand that is not a spiro compound. However, a single occurrence of this type of core within this series of transformations is unlikely to be significant and should be treated with caution.

Return to the Transformations summary page and open the Most Frequently Do Not Change Activity tab.

This tab lists the 15 most frequent transformations that result in an activity change of less than two orders of magnitude.

There are more of these types of transformations compared to the previous page of transformations, which were associated with activity changes greater than two orders of magnitude. These transformations can be considered like bioisosteres, which are replacements of a part of a bioactive molecule with a substructure that is similar in size and exhibits similar properties [Griffen et al., 2011] .

You will now observe several transformations that include phenyl to thienyl substructures, with particular attention to the 8th transformation (c1ccccc1 >> c1cccs1). Thienyl is slightly less aromatic than phenyl, but can potentially be involved in hydrogen bond formation within a protein active site. The 7th transformation includes a trifluoromethyl substructure, which is a well-known bioisostere employed to lower basicity and modifies lipophilicity and solvation properties of ligands. In this context, you might consider these transformations when trying to increase the potency of a lead compound in an optimization project, or modify another pharmacokinetic property, but maintain the same level of CYP2D6 metabolism.

Click on the first transformation c1ccccc1OC >> c1cccs1 in the table to open a Molecule Window of the common cores which have the methoxyphenyl to thienyl transformation. Use the Data Table View navigation arrows to step through these common cores in the Molecule Window.

Notice the similarities of some of these cores. 19 of the 51 cores contain a quinazoline substructure and 24 of the remaining 32 contain a phenylpyrimidine substructure.

Open the All Transformations tab.

This last tab summarizes all of the transformations identified for the dataset. Notice the note that mentions that only 300 of the possible 527 transformations have been displayed. A large number of transformations may reduce performance when displaying all possible results. You may want to repeat this analysis with the Maximum MMPs to Display parameter blank to see all transformations summarized by frequency and affect (neutral, increase, and decrease).

To study matched molecular pairs and activity cliffs in further detail you can try using this dataset with the Find Activity Cliffs using MMPs protocol.

#### Further information

# Understanding SAR and activity cliffs using matched molecular pairs and Free-Wilson analysis

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_sar.htm

## Understanding SAR and activity cliffs using matched molecular pairs and Free-Wilson analysis

Time: 20 minutes.

### Introduction

Structure-activity relationships (SAR) are used ubiquitously in medicinal chemistry because the analysis of these relationships enables the identification of the chemical groups responsible for evoking a targeted biological effect. This knowledge can then be used to direct chemical modification of a lead candidate to improve biochemical potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters, and toxicity and bioavailability.

Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) analysis is an inverse SAR technique that is rapidly gaining popularity. It is used in the retrospective analysis of experimental datasets to understand differences in properties between structurally related groups of existing compounds and to de novo design new structures [Leach et al., 2006] [Warner et al., 2012] . MMPs are pairs of molecules that differ only by a singular, well-defined structural transformation. Activity cliffs can be defined as those MMPs that have a significant difference in biological activity ( [Sisay et al., 2009] and [Hu et al., 2012] ).

When studying SARs, the activity responses to positional changes in biologically relevant chemical space can be conceptualized as an activity landscape in which activity cliffs are discontinuities where small changes in structure, which correspond to small steps in chemical space, lead to significant changes in the activity/potency hypersurface [Sisay et al., 2009] . Activity cliffs are a particularly rich source of SAR information, but essentially unpredictable when using traditional SAR methods.

In this tutorial, you will study a library of cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) inhibitors to identify activity cliffs using MMPs and suggest possible new ligands to synthesize, exploiting the understanding derived from studying the SAR landscape. CDK2 is a member of the highly conserved serine-threonine family of protein kinases, which are key regulatory elements of the eukaryotic cell cycle. Loss of cell cycle control can result in aberrant cellular proliferation. It is hoped that inhibition of CDKs can provide an effective method for controlling tumor growth and be an effective weapon in cancer chemotherapy.

You will first identify the activity cliffs using matched molecular pairs in the dataset and then you may optionally perform a Free Wilson analysis with some of the ligands to generate new prioritized ligands to synthesize. The following tasks are covered:

* Finding Activity Cliffs Using Matched Molecular Pairs

* Creating a custom tool panel for Free-Wilson analysis (optional)

CDK2 ligands were sourced from the BindingDB , 
public, web-accessible database of measured binding affinities
( [Liu et al., 2007] ). Only CDK2 ligands for which explicit Ki measurements were available and which had at least 10 micromoles of potency were used [Hu et al., 2012] . In this instance, an activity cliff is defined as a potency difference of at least two orders of magnitude, ensuring that at least one member of the cliff was always potent in the nanomolar range.

Open Samples | Tutorials | QSAR | bindingdb_cdk2.sd . Open the Small Molecules | Study SAR tool panel and click Find Activity Cliffs Using MMPs... to open the protocol. Check that Input Ligands is set to bindingdb_cdk2:All . Check that Activity Property is set to pKi . Set Activity Change Threshold to 2 . Click Run , and then click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 27 activity cliffs have been identified.

The activity change threshold is used to determine whether a MMP is an activity cliff. If the activity scales logarithmically (e.g., as with pKi values) and a change in activity of two orders of magnitude is set as significant, the threshold should be set to 2. However, if the activity scales linearly (e.g., as with Ki values), a change in activity of two orders of magnitude would require a threshold of 100. You will use pKi in this tutorial as logarithmic values are more consistently used in other SAR techniques (e.g., the Free-Wilson analysis).

You can easily calculate pKi and pIC50 values from original Ki and IC50 values using the Scale Data parameters in the Prepare Dependent Property protocol (in the Calculate QSAR Model tools).

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link.

The Report summarizes that the CDK2 dataset produced 27 activity cliffs with 20 different core substructures, and over 600 MMPs (Matched Molecular Pairs) were filtered.

In the Report, click the View Results button.

The Activity Cliffs summary table lists the 27 activity cliffs identified (reactant and product), the activity change in each of those cliffs, and the core substructure of each cliff pair. All the columns, excluding the Reactant and Product columns, are sortable and can be hidden or displayed to simplify the display.

Click the arrow to the right of the Reactant Name column header and choose Sort Ascending .

This allows you to sort by the reactants and easily see all the multiple transformations that any one ligand may be involved in. Notice at the top that 2,4-Diamino-5-ketopyrimidine 23 is involved in three activity cliffs. However, as the activity threshold in the report is always positive, this means that in these three activity cliffs, 2,4-Diamino-5-ketopyrimidine 23 is the lower activity partner. If 2,4-Diamino-5-ketopyrimidine 23 was the higher activity partner, it would be listed in the Product Name column. Potential chains for activity improvement are more easily seen in the SD file from the Input Ligands, which you can open using the Activity Information link (which you will view later in this tutorial).

Scroll towards the bottom of the table and see the four activity cliffs involving CDK Inhibitor 2 and CDK Inhibitor 3 .

Notice that these cliffs are essentially the same transformation. The nature of MMP identification involves a size constraint on the chemical change between a pair of compounds [Hussain and Rea, 2010] . Therefore, transformations may be represented by substructures ranging from a minimum change (methyl to hydrogen) to substructures of the maximum size ( N-Ethyl-4-methyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine to N,4-Dimethyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine ). This allows additional methods for analyzing the activity cliffs data.

Click the arrow next to the Transformation column header and choose Sort Descending .

There are several interesting observations to note here:

* The first two transformations (Index 16 and 8) are N-Ethyl-4-methyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine to N,4-Dimethyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine and N,4-Dimethyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine to 4-Methyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine . Could the activity of CDK Inhibitor, 2 be improved by a transformation to a 4-Methyl-1,3-thiazol-2-amine substructure?

* Scroll further and notice several different transformations (Index 4, 3 and 27) which involve a nitro group. Twice these transformations are to sulfonyl-containing substructures. Additional sulfonyl contain transformations include Index 13, 14, 1, and 12.

* The last two transformations (Index 9 and 18) are identical. In this instance, it is not of much significance, but sometimes duplicates of a particular transformation in different environments, such as different scaffolds or at different substituent positions can reinforce the possible importance of that transformation.

Click the arrow next to the Core column header and choose Sort Ascending . Scroll down to Index 4 and 3, which include core 3.

In this instance, it represents 2-Anilino-4-(thiazol-5-yl)pyrimidine derivative 30 in cliff partnership with CDK Inhibitor, 3 and CDK Inhibitor, 6 respectively.

Scroll further to the three activity cliffs with core 17.

In this case, the reactants are two different ligands: 2-Anilino-4-(thiazol-5-yl)pyrimidine derivative 34 and 2-Anilino-4-(thiazol-5-yl)pyrimidine derivative 8 . Compare cliff index 20 with cliff index 23, which contain core 16 and 17 respectively. These activity cliffs are effectively duplicates, an artifact of the algorithm used to identify the MMP. The two seemingly different transformations simply correspond to cutting the parent structure at one or other side of the amine nitrogen.

Return to the Report and click on the Input Ligands with Activity Information link. Double-click twice on the Num_Cliffs column header.

This SD file allows you to see the original dataset with the additional properties that identify which ligands are involved in activity cliffs, the number of cliffs they are involved in, and the exact partners and transformations involved.

Highlight Index 91 to see the previously discussed ligand 2,4-Diamino-5-ketopyrimidine 23 . Scroll horizontally to view the three cliff partners and see that the activity change is a positive value, indicating that this ligand is the lower activity partner in each of these cliffs.

If you were to see a negative value with one of the cliff partners, it would indicate a potential chain of activity improvements for further study and may be usefully applied to different scaffolds and environments.

In the second part of the tutorial, you will analyze some of the related ligands in the CDK2 dataset further to generate possible new ligands to synthesize as potential CDK2 inhibitors. Free-Wilson analysis is a SAR method for incomplete congeneric series, which relates biological activity with the presence or absence of specific functional groups at specific locations on the core structure [Kubinyi, 1988] . A matrix is built summarizing every functional group at every position, and substituent constants are derived indicating their contribution and significance to activity. The Free-Wilson model can help understand and interpret substituent effects. However, the method assumes that the effects of substituents are additive, and its applicability is limited to series of substituted compounds. Additional substituents cannot be considered.

Discovery Studio includes a set of predefined tool panels presenting the most commonly used workflows within each tool set. However, the Discovery Studio client also allows you to create custom tools panels to aggregate all the steps required for your own particular task. These custom tool panels can be added to the existing tool sets or collected under your own tool set. Custom tool panels are also a simple and easy way to access custom protocols without using the Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications application.

With the Small Molecules tool set open, right-click the Tools Explorer and choose Insert New Panel... to create a custom tool panel. Enter Free-Wilson SAR as the panel name and click OK to open the Tool Panel Editor. Expand the Protocols | Examples | SAR group in the Commands column. Select the Create Free-Wilson Least Squares Model example protocol and click+drag the item to the left column. Click OK to complete the custom panel.

Custom tool panels can be elaborated with headings and text to provide instructions to walk the user through the task or workflow, and can be edited further once created. You can also export custom tool panels as .panel files and share them with other users. You can also drag the tool panel you have just created so that it appears below the default Study SAR tool panel.

Double-click twice on the Free-Wilson column header so that the 31 compounds with the value of 1 are at the top of the table. Select the first row of the table, and then scroll down and SHIFT+select the 31st row in the table, effectively selecting all 31 ligands with a value of 1 in the Free-Wilson property. Right-click in the Data Table View and choose Show in Graphics View . Open the Small Molecules | Free-Wilson SAR tool panel and click Create Free-Wilson Least Squares Model... to open the protocol. Check that Input Core Structure is set to methylthiazolpyrimidinamine: methylthiazolpyrimidinamine . Check that Input Ligands is set to bindingdb_cdk2:Selected . Check that Activity Property is set to pKi . Change Maximum Number of Virtual Molecules in Report to 200 . Note that this is more than the expected number of virtual molecules to be enumerated. Click Run , and then click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The 31 ligands with a value of 1 in the Free-Wilson property all contain the methylthiazolyl pyrimidinamine substructure (Figure 1) and are suitable for a Free-Wilson analysis.

Figure 1: Methylthiazolyl pyrimidinamine core structure

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the SAR Table Report link, and then click on the Report link.

The SAR Table Report summarizes the 31 ligands used in the Free-Wilson analysis in terms of the substituents at each of the two substituent points.

In the Report, click on the Coefficient-Variable Table tab in the Summary section.

The table lists the coefficients for all of the substituents at each substituent point; substituents with coefficients of zero are not included.

Notice the two largest equation coefficients:
Count<R2:[Z]c1cccc(c1)S(=O)(=O)C> 4.1141 and
Count<R2:[Z]c1cccc(c1)S(=O)(=O)N> 3.1591

Interestingly, these substituents are the same as those for CDK Inhibitor 6 and CDK Inhibitor 3 respectively, which were both involved in activity cliffs as the more active cliff partner, in both cases with 2-Anilino-4-(thiazol-5-yl)pyrimidine derivative 30 (Index 5 and 6).

Also notice that the largest equation coefficient for R1 is Count<R1:[Z]N> 0.93400 (amine).

In the Jobs Explorer click the Virtual Library Prediction Report link.

This report (and the accompanying Virtual Library Compounds with Model Prediction SD file) lists the complete virtual enumerated library that can be generated by the full matrix of substituents in the 31 ligands used in the Free-Wilson analysis, including their predicted activities from the least squares model regression: the combined R1 and R2 substituents results in a complete virtual library of 147 ligands.

In the Jobs Explorer click the Virtual Library Compounds with Model Prediction link. Double-click twice on the Free Wilson Predicted Activity column header.

The next three ligands have the same R2 substituent, but different R1 substituents (with lower R1 coefficients), which are predicted to contribute less to the predicted Free-Wilson activity of the ligand. The fifth highest predicted activity ligand also has the amine substituent at R1 and a benzenesulfonamide (c1cccc(c1)S(=O)(=O)N ) substituent at R2.

You can now analyze these virtual ligands to further corroborate your SAR analysis from the first part of this tutorial. Experimentally, you can decide which to synthesize to further understand and verify the SAR for these CDK2 ligands, or which to optimize to increase activity.

# Scaffold hopping to identify replacement fragments for lead optimization

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_scaffold-hopping.htm

## Scaffold hopping to identify replacement fragments for lead optimization

Time: 30 minutes.

### Introduction

Scaffold hopping is the replacement of the core framework of a ligand with new isofunctional chemotypes to improve the properties of the molecule or to find similar potent compounds that exist in novel chemical space [Langdon et al., 2010] . These replacements may offer medicinal chemists choice in terms of chemical accessibility and create new intellectual property for lead optimization.

In this tutorial, you will use the Replace Fragment protocol to identify replacement fragments for lisinopril (Figure 1), the third angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor introduced into therapy after captopril and enalapril. ACE catalyzes the conversion of the biologically inactive decapeptide angiotensin I to the octapeptide angiotensin II, a powerful vasoconstrictor, and degrades bradykinin, a potent vasodilator. The dual functionality plays a key role in the blood pressure regulating renin-angiotensin system (RAS) and makes this zinc-dependent dipeptidase a prominent target in treatment of conditions such as high blood pressure, heart failure, diabetic nephropathy, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Figure 1: Lisinopril

In this tutorial, you will identify alternative scaffolds for the acetylproline substructure of lisinopril. The following tasks are covered:

* Generating replacement fragments solely from a ligand structure

* Using the protein active site to refine potential replacement fragments

* Using different properties to identify novel scaffolds

In the first part of this tutorial, you will use the Replace Fragment protocol to identify alternative replacements for the acetylproline substructure of lisinopril using only the ligand structure. Lisinopril was developed [Patchett et al. 1980] before crystal structures of ACE became available for structure-based drug design [Natesh et al., 2003] , and often ligand scaffold hopping is performed in the absence of a protein structure.

Open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1o86_ligand.sd . Select the acetylproline substructure of the ligand, C15, O17, O22-C29 , with a lasso selection, or use the Hierarchy View (CTRL-H). Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tool panel and click Replace Fragment... to open the protocol. Check that Input Ligand is set to 1o86_ligand:1o86_ligand . Click on the Fragment to Replace parameter drop-down and choose Create New Group From Selection... . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of created ligands (~100).

In the Jobs Explorer , expand the completed job and click the View Results link. In the Data Table View , click the first navigation arrow to see the first ligand in the Graphics View.

As you have used only the ligand structure for the fragment replacement, the novel ligands generated are pareto sorted by Lipinski violations and fragment "novelty". The similarity of the replacement fragments to the original fragment is reported, and can be useful to prioritize the ligands to scroll through, and will be explored further in the last part of the tutorial.

The number of novel ligands generated may be too numerous for you to carefully consider each replacement. However, as the protein structure of ACE is available, this information can be incorporated into the protocol so that the protein active site is used to refine the fragments that are suggested and the novel ligands generated better reflect the environment in which they would potentially bind and be active. Alternatively, you can calculate ADMET and related properties for these larger libraries, and use this to filter and prioritize the ligands for further consideration.

You will now use the ACE X-ray crystal structure to refine the fragments returned as possible replacements for the acetylproline substructure.

The PDB code for the ACE-lisinopril protein-ligand complex used is 1O86 [Natesh et al., 2003] . The file was downloaded from the PDB web site and the protein was prepared using the Prepare Proteins protocol.

Open Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | 1o86_complex.dsv . Select the acetylproline substructure of the ligand, C1, O1, O4, O5, N2, C5-C9 .

When using the lasso selection, you may find it easier to turn off the visibility for 1o86_protein in the Hierarchy View, make the selection, and then turn the visibility back on. If you accidentally select part of the protein structure or the surface, these will be ignored when running the protocol.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tool panel and click Replace Fragment to open the protocol. Ensure that Input Receptor is set to 1o86_complex:1o86_protein . Expand the Input Receptor parameter group, and set Interacting Residues to the predefined 1o86_complex:interacting_residues group. Check that Input Ligand is set to 1o86_complex:1o86_ligand . Click Fragment to Replace and choose Create New Group From Selection... . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of created ligands (~45).

The setting used in this example of Replace Fragment allowed the steric restraint of the protein active site to refine the novel ligands generated. Also, you were able to target replacement fragments that interact with any one of the residues defined in the interacting_residues group. These residues include GLN281, HIS353, LYS511, HIS513, and TYR520, which are known to be involved in interactions with the lisinopril acetylproline substructure [Patchett et al. 1980] .

In the Jobs Explorer , expand the completed job and click the View Results link.

Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools
and click Ligand Interactions .

This displays the non-bond interactions between the receptor and the ligand as well as any intramolecular interactions in the ligand.

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions toolpanel to navigate through the ligands.

In this example, you have considered the protein active site when considering replacement fragments, and hence the novel ligands generated are returned pareto sorted by interactions formed with the protein (maximized), Lipinski violations (minimized), receptor bumps (minimized), and fragment "novelty" (maximized). The novel ligands now also include calculated properties reflecting the ligand-protein interactions including protein residues, interaction types, and interaction distances. All of the novel ligands should make interactions with at least one of the residues defined in the interacting_residues group. Using the Data Table View filtering tools, you can focus on ligands that interact with multiple residues simultaneously, including residues that you may not have considered.

The red colored bumps indicate that you would likely get improved results by selecting the optional minimization parameter. Scroll through and visualize some of the interesting alternative fragments suggested.

The Replace Fragment protocol identifies isosteric fragments from the default fragment libraries and the original fragment is automatically replaced to create novel ligands. Fragments are judged isosteric if they are similar to the original fragment, where similarity is user-definable by select molecular properties and fingerprints. By default the properties Num_Rings, Num_AromaticRings, and Molecular_SurfaceArea are used to calculate the similarity as an Euclidean distance. These properties have been shown to give the best balance between chemotype diversity and isofunctional similarity with the original lead compound.

In the final part of the tutorial, you will change the properties used to see the different fragments that can be returned.

Return to the Jobs Explorer and click the Report link. Expand the Parameters section and click the Protocol.pr_xml link to open the protocol with the parameters defined per the previous run. Expand Advanced | Fragment Search . Click the button in the Properties for Similarity parameter to open the dialog. Select the Num_Rings , Num_AromaticRings , and Molecular_SurfaceArea properties in the Selected Items column and click on the left arrows to clear the list. Select FCFP_4 from the Available Items column and click on the right arrows to select this property. Change Maximum Distance to 0.7 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and right-mouse click in the protocol panel to select Run (or press the F5 key) and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the total number of enumerated ligands (~85).

When working with fingerprint descriptors, the similarity of isosteric fragments is measured as a Tanimoto similarity, which can be regarded as the proportion of the "on-bits" shared between the two fingerprints. Two fragments that appear similar may actually have a low Tanimoto similarity. For example, the Tanimoto similarity using the ECFP_4 fingerprint between a phenyl and pyridine fragment is only 0.333. When using only fingerprint descriptors, you will likely need to increase the Maximum Distance parameter to return a reasonable number of interesting hits. You can filter all results by the reported Fragment Similarity property at a later point.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job, and then click the View Results link.

Use the First, Previous, Next Ligand buttons in the View Interactions tool panel to navigate through the ligands.

Notice some of the ligands contain linear fragments. These would not have been returned as possible hits using the Num_Rings, Num_AromaticRings, and Molecular_SurfaceArea properties. The properties for the similarity calculation should be selected considering the scaffold hopping objectives.

The default fragment libraries provided with the Replace Fragment protocol are extensive with over half a million fragments in the 1-attachment and 2-attachment libraries and almost 300,000 fragments in the 3-attachment library. Nevertheless these are not exhaustive in their chemical coverage and you may want to generate your own fragment libraries for focused lead optimization projects. An example protocol, Generate Fragment Libraries, which generates fragments from whole ligands is available via the Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications in the Examples | Receptor-Ligand Interactions folder. You can specify the use of custom fragment libraries with the parameters in the Fragment Libraries parameter grouping.

You can create a custom tool panel and add the Generate Fragment Libraries protocol to generate your own fragment libraries in Discovery Studio . See Tools Explorer .

Now you may want to try generating a focused ACE fragment library using the Samples | Tutorials | Receptor-Ligand Interactions | ace_inhibitors.sd , which includes numerous known ACE inhibitors. Alternatively, you can repeat this protocol using MyFragments-Cyclic-1R.smi as a custom fragment library pre-generated with the Generate Fragment Libraries custom protocol and the ace_inhibitors.sd file to see which novel ligands are generated and how similar they are to known ACE inhibitors.

#### Further information

Grow Scaffold Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration

# Working with scripts

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_scripts.htm

## Working with scripts

Time: 15 minutes.

### Introduction

Although Discovery Studio provides a rich set of functionality and viewers that assist
in the process of performing computational analysis of data, it is often desirable to be able to extend
these capabilities. For example, you may need to create an analysis tool that calculates some
property using a specific algorithm. You may also want to chain together a set of commonly used tasks so that they can be run as a single operation.

Discovery Studio uses scripting as one way of providing this extensibility. Scripts are 
sets of instructions written in a programming language. Discovery Studio uses Perl as its scripting
language because it is a simple and widely available programming language that is 
commonly used throughout the research community.

Discovery Studio provides programmatic access to much of its functionality through an Application 
Programming Interface (API). This API allows you to write scripts that can provide powerful functionality 
such as:

* Loading molecules and sequences from different file formats

* Set the display styles of objects in different Windows

* Create and execute multi-step tasks in a single operation

* Perform complex analyses of data

For additional information about Scripting and to access the API, see Working with scripts .

In addition to the API, you can easily create a new command that runs a script and expose it in the application as a menu item, toolbar button,
or tool on a tool panel. This makes it possible to extend Discovery Studio to suit specific needs. Scripts can also be run outside
of the client, at the command line or by Pipeline Pilot components.

In this tutorial you will learn how to write and execute scripts in Discovery Studio .

* Create and run a simple script

* Modify a script to process data in the Molecule Window

* Create a button to run a script

Discovery Studio provides a special window, the Script Window, for creating and running 
scripts. The Script Window contains a number of features that assist in the development
of valid Perl scripts, and simplify debugging and running them.

From the menu bar, choose File | New | Script Window . Remove the default template text.

The Script Window contains two primary views:

* Editor View: This is the region of the window into which you type your script. If you
open a script it also appears in the Editor View.

* Output View: As you perform operations in the Script Window, the Output View displays
any information generated by those operations. For example, if you run a script that 
writes output data, that data appears in the Output View as the script executes. Similarly,
when you check the syntax of a script, details about errors in your script are written 
to the Output View.

The next step is to write a simple script that prints a test string "Hello World!"

In the Editor View type the following line: print "Hello World!\n"; On the Scripting toolbar, click the Run button.

Notice that Hello World! is written in the Output View. The Run button launches the Perl executable, which interprets and executes the script. The executable is also referred to as the Perl interpreter.

Now write a script that utilizes the DiscoveryScript API. In this example, you will write a script that creates and displays an Ethene molecule. To incorporate the DiscoveryScript
API into a script, some additional set up is recommended when writing the script.

Delete the existing text in the Editor View. Type in the following lines: #!/usr/bin/perl -w use strict; use MdmDiscoveryScript;

The first line, #!/usr/bin/perl -w is required if the script is to be run outside of the 
application on Linux. It tells the Linux shell to locate the /usr/bin/perl program. The file is then passed 
to /usr/bin/perl for execution. The -w flag at the end of the line tells the Perl executable
to report suspicious statements
in the code that may prevent the script from executing successfully.

The second line, use strict; , is a Perl pragma command. This is a special type of command that tells the
Perl interpreter to handle the code execution in a particular way. It is not necessary to go into the details of this 
here, but the use strict; pragma tells the Perl interpreter to be strict about the way it interprets the code.
In particular, ambiguous statements that could normally be handled by the interpreter are not allowed so that correct 
execution is more likely.

The third line, use MdmDiscoveryScript; is another pragma that tells the interpreter that the
script uses the MdmDiscoveryScript module. This module is a library that implements functionality in the DiscoveryScript API. There
are several modules that make up the DiscoveryScript API, including:

* MdmDiscoveryScript: Contains functionality for accessing the Molecular Data Model (MDM).

* SdmDiscoveryScript: Contains functionality for accessing the Sequence Data Model (SDM).

* PharmacophoreDiscoveryScript: Contains functionality for working with pharmacophore data.

* SbdDiscoveryScript: Contains functionality for working with binding sites and other functionality
relevant to Structure Based Design (SBD).

For more information about available modules and their functionality, consult the Discovery Studio help.

Now add some code that will create a document to display the molecule. In this case, a document is a window, such as a Molecule Window, and the data it contains. Discovery Script supports several
document types such as MDM and SDM documents.

Add the following line to the script in the Editor Window: my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();

This line instructs the program to create an MDM document. If the script is being run within
the application, the result of adding this line will be to create a new Molecule Window. Otherwise, 
this script has no observable effect when run outside of the application (for example, in a standalone script).

The objective is to create a simple ethene molecule. The next line in the script
creates the molecule object. At this point, the molecule has no atoms, bonds, or other objects, so it
is effectively an empty container. There will be no update to the screen on executing this line.

Add the following line to the script in the Editor Window: my $molecule = $document->CreateMolecule();

At this point, the basic document and molecule object have been set up and it is possible to use MdmDiscoveryScript to create and assemble the objects that make up the molecule.

Add the following lines to achieve this: my $atom1 = $molecule->CreateAtom('C'); my $atom2 = $molecule->CreateAtom('C'); my $ccBond = $document->CreateBond($atom1, $atom2, Mdm::doubleBond); $document->AddHydrogenAtoms(); $document->Clean();

The first two lines create variables for the two carbon
atoms. The third line creates a double bond between the two atoms. The fourth line adds hydrogens to the 
carbon atoms. The final line invokes the Clean method, which uses a fast, Dreiding-like forcefield to 
improve the geometry of the selected atoms and results in an approximate 3D structure.

At this point, the molecule has been created and now you can add lines to report information about the bond length between the carbon atoms in the 3D structure.

Add the following two lines: my $ccBondlength = $ccBond->Length; print "The length of the C=C bond is $ccBondlength\n";

The Editor View should appear as follows:

Notice that the lines are numbered. Also
notice that text elements are colored differently. This is known as syntax highlighting. You can modify the fonts, tab spacing, and indentation
behavior by right-clicking the Script Window and choosing Display Style...

Before running the script, it is useful to review two important features of the Script Window: the Syntax Checker and
context sensitive help.

The syntax checking feature runs the Perl interpreter to identify any syntactic errors in a script. To 
illustrate this, edit the current script to introduce an error.

On line 12 of the script, delete the first parenthesis in 
the CreateBonds function call: my $ccBond = $document->CreateBond$atom1, $atom2, Mdm::doubleBond); Press the Check Syntax button on the Scripting toolbar.

The syntax checker will detect the error and report it in the Output View:

On line 12 of the script correct the error by re-inserting the first parenthesis in 
the CreateBonds function. To do this, press Ctrl+Z to undo the previous edit. This should change the code back to: my $ccBond = $document->CreateBond($atom1, $atom2, Mdm::doubleBond);

The script is ready to run.

On the toolbar, click the Run button. This results in the creation of a new Molecule Window containing the ethene 
molecule. Drag the tab on the Molecule window to position the Molecule Window next to the Script Window.

Inspect the molecule created in the Molecule Window to verify it is an ethene molecule. Also note that the bond length has been 
written in the Output Window.

At this point, you can save the script if desired.

The first section of this tutorial demonstrated how to create a new molecule in the application using
the DiscoveryScript API. However, a powerful feature of the API is the ability to reference
an object in memory and modify or analyze the data. For example, you can
write a script that accesses the data object corresponding to a molecule already displayed in the 
application and make changes to it (for example, modify the appearance). Similarly, you can write a script that 
references a sequence alignment and performs some analysis.

Now you will create and run a script that modifies a protein 
molecule loaded in the Molecule Window. The script will update the appearance of a protein 
structure to prepare it for publication.

From the main menu bar choose Window | Close All to close all open 
windows in the application workspace. Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Quick Start Tutorials | 1TPO.pdb .

This file is a raw pdb file. The default display shows the protein in solid ribbon style and the water molecules as atoms. You will now write a script to display the molecule using a Schematic Display for the protein chains.

From the menu bar select File | New | Script Window and remove the template text. Drag the tab on the Script window to position the Script Window next to the 
Molecule Window. Copy and paste the following script into the Script Window: #!/usr/bin/perl -w use strict; use MdmDiscoveryScript; # Create a document from the last active Molecule Window my $document = DiscoveryScript->LastActiveDocument(MdmModelType); # Ensure all view updates turned off so action seems atomic $document->EnableUpdateViews(False); # Define variables of the display styles that will be applied my $atomDisplayStyle = Mdm::styleAtomNone; my $proteinDisplayStyle = Mdm::styleProteinSchematic; # Turn off the display of atoms $document->SetAtomDisplayStyle($atomDisplayStyle); # Set the display style of proteins to schematic $document->SetProteinDisplayStyle($proteinDisplayStyle); $document->EnableUpdateViews(True);

This code snippet emphasizes a number of important features of scripting. Review line 7: my $document = DiscoveryScript->LastActiveDocument(MdmModelType);

The function LastActiveDocument() is a powerful command that cycles through the current
open windows and finds the last open document matching the model type, in this case MdmModelType .
The function then sets the $document variable to that Mdm object. At this point, the data 
object can be directly manipulated by the script by using the variable.

Now review line 10: $document->EnableUpdateViews(False);

The EnableUpdateViews() function turns on or off any updates to the display. This is useful when
a number of operations are to be performed that result in updates to the display, but the script is intended
to update the display in a single action (i.e., without any flickering and for improved performance). In this code snippet, the display updates are disabled until the display refresh is turned back on in line 22.

The main work of the script is done in lines 17 and 20. Here SetAtomDisplayStyle and SetProteinDisplayStyle apply the specified styles to all molecules in the document. If desired,
this section of the script could be enhanced to apply other display effects, but only these two operations are shown in this example.

Now save the script for use in the next section of this tutorial.

From the menu bar, choose File | Save As... . Save the script with the 
name ApplyProteinSchematic.pl .

Discovery Studio provides a powerful interface for creating tools from scripts that can be launched
from menus, toolbars, and tool panels. You can create these tools using the Script Commands preference page. This page enables you to select a script
that can run inside the application and assign attributes to it such as a tool tip, status message, 
and icon.

In this section, you will create a toolbar button that launches the script you just created.

From the menu bar, choose Edit | Preferences... to 
open the Preferences dialog. Open General | Script Commands .

Click Add Command to open the Choose Script dialog. Navigate to the location in which the ApplyProteinSchematic.pl script was saved and select it. Click Open .

This specifies ApplyProteinSchematic.pl as the source script for the command.

In the Tooltip input field enter: 
"Apply Protein Schematic Style". In the Status message input field
enter "Updates the display of a protein structure to render it in schematic style". In the Scripts menu tree view, double-click Script1 and 
type its name: "Apply Protein Schematic Style". Click OK .

By default, when a new script command is created it appears in the Scripts menu. When the application is installed
a set of toolbar folders are configured as shown in the screenshot below. The new script command can
be dragged into one of the existing toolbar folders. Alternatively, a new toolbar folder can be created and the script command moved
there.

Notice that the new script is now available from the menu.

You will now create a toolbar button to launch the script command. The Toolbar
preferences page will be used to create a new toolbar and button.

There may be a delay while opening this preference page, as it updates the list of available protocols. This could be significant if you are connected to a remote server, so unless you want to create a button for a protocol it may be advisable to disconnect before opening this page.

Choose Edit | Preferences... from the menu bar. Open General | Toolbar .

The Toolbar preference subpage enables the addition of new tools to any
of the preset toolbars. In addition, you can use it to create new toolbars. To expose the new Apply Protein Schematic Style tool, you will first create a new toolbar.

In the New toolbar field, type "Display". Click Add Toolbar .

This creates the new Display toolbar. The new toolbar is now selected
in the Toolbar list. At the bottom of the dialog a blank Toolbar Preview is displayed.

In the Commands hierarchy, expand Scripts . Scroll down and locate the Apply Protein Schematic Style . Click and drag it to Toolbar Preview . Click OK .

A new toolbar is now displayed in the application window. This toolbar has a single command, Apply Protein Schematic Style .

Reopen 1TPO.pdb . Click the new Apply Protein Schematic Style button to run the script.

# Opening and editing sequence alignments

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_seq-alignments.htm

## Opening and editing sequence alignments

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

Sequence alignments are usually created by alignment programs, such as ClustalW or Muscle.
Visualization of the sequence alignment provides useful insights into the relationships between
sets of homologous sequences. In addition, inspection of the automatically
generated sequence alignment and manual edits of the alignment are often
desirable. Discovery Studio provides an interactive environment for viewing, analyzing,
and editing sequence alignment.

In this tutorial you will learn how to manually edit the sequence alignment of
three highly homologous protein sequences.

* Opening and viewing the sequences

* Aligning the sequences

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Quick Start Tutorials | kinases.fasta .

This opens the kinases.fasta file in a Sequence Window with
three sequences, 1e2k , 1ki4 , and 1ki3 .

The background of the residues are colored according to sequence similarity.
The first 25 residues are identical in three sequences and are colored blue to indicate
this. The remaining sequence block is poorly aligned, with most positions not similar 
and the residue backgrounds colored white. The sequence identity 
and similarity of the three unaligned sequences are very low and are indicated 
on the status bar at the bottom of the application window.

The Sequence Window provides a number of tools and shortcuts for manually aligning and editing 
sequences. Inserting and removing multiple alignment gaps and dragging alignment blocks are supported, which are both useful for the kinase alignment.

Place the cursor before the Asp residue of 1ki4 at alignment position 26 as shown above and press the space bar twice.

This inserts two gaps in the 1ki4 sequence immediately before the Asp residue. This aligns the first 99 residues and their background turns blue. At the bottom of the application, the status bar shows
that the percentage of sequence identity and similarity has increased.

Select the two aligned Pro residues in the 1e2k and 1ki4 sequences as shown below.

Press the space bar three times to insert three gaps. Place the cursor in front of the previously selected Pro residue in the 1ki4 sequence and press the space bar once to insert another gap.

The residues are now aligned up to position 214.

Select the two aligned Pro residues in the 1ki4 and 1ki3 sequence as shown below.

Press the space bar twice to insert two gaps. Deselect all
sequences by clicking on white space in the Sequence Window.

Now the three sequences are aligned and most of the residues are identical.
The percentage sequence identity and similarity are well
over 90% as shown in the status bar.

# Finding orphan sequences using phylogenetics

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_sequence-analysis.htm

## Finding orphan sequences using phylogenetics

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

Sequence analysis is frequently a first step in characterizing a potential protein target. Because proteins
with the same or similar functionality almost always share high sequence similarity, you can use similarity 
search to identify homologous sequences that might provide clues about the functionality of a particular
target candidate. Comparative methods, such as multiple sequence alignment, can be used to make more specific
predictions of the significance of particular sequence regions.

Discovery Studio provides several tools for performing searches and comparative analysis. In this
tutorial, the following common tasks are covered:

* Opening and performing a BLAST sequence similarity search

* Performing a multiple sequence alignment

* Using bootstrap analysis of a phylogenetic tree to identify orphan sequences

The part of this tutorial demonstrates how to open a sequence file and run a BLAST search with it. A lysozyme protein is used for the analysis.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Sequence Analysis | Lysozyme.fa .

This opens the file in the Sequence Window.

Open the Macromolecules | Search Sequences by Similarity tools and click BLAST Search... to open the BLAST Search dialog. Click Run .

The selected data is automatically loaded. If no sequence is selected, it uses the
first sequence in the window to perform the search. While the search is running, a dialog displays the search status.

When the search completes, if any matches have been found, a BLAST window opens to display the 
results. By default, the Table View is selected and sorted by Identity. 
A message box reports the number of similar sequences found. Click OK to dismiss the message box.

At this point, the number of sequences displayed in the BLAST window varies depending on the 
particular database searched. Note that you can also use BLAST Search (NCBI Server) to perform the search. This has the advantage that the sequence database is always up to date.
However, the search requires internet connection and takes much longer than a local search.

Right-click and select all the sequences in the list. Right-click in the selected region and choose Load Selected Sequences .

This opens a new Sequence Window containing the corresponding sequences.

Now that you have retrieved a set of related sequences, you use the Align Sequences tool in the Align Sequences and Structures tool panel to perform a sequence alignment. It uses
Align123, a multiple sequence alignment method based on the ClustalW program.

Ensure that no sequences are selected in the Sequence Window. Open the Macromolecules | Align Sequences and Structures tools and click Align Sequences... to open the Align Sequences dialog. Click Run .

The sequence window is automatically loaded. If some sequences are selected, it uses the selected 
sequences for the alignment. Otherwise all sequences in the window are used. Only a single residue needs
to be selected for the whole sequence to be considered as selected in this case.

A dialog indicates the progress of the alignment. When the alignment job completes, the Sequence Window 
is updated with the alignment results automatically. A message box reports the sequence identity and
similarity. Click OK to dismiss the message box.

You will now use phylogenetic analysis to identify sequences in the alignment that do not 
cluster with other sequences. These sequences represent orphans that may be useful if you are trying to create
a diverse set of sequences for tasks such as structural homology modeling.

In the Analyze Sequences tool panel. Ensure that Mode is set to Best Tree . Click Create Phylogenetic Tree .

A Dendrogram Window opens with a Neighbor Joining tree for the sequence alignment. Note that the tree
indicates clustering within the sequences. However, the terminal branch lengths are very long compared to the basal
branch lengths, which may indicate that the sequences are too diverged to be reliably used to reconstruct a phylogeny.
To test this, perform a bootstrap analysis.

Activate the Sequence Window . In the Analyze Sequences tool panel, change the mode to Bootstrap . Click Create Phylogenetic Tree .

The Dendrogram Window is now updated to display a bootstrap tree. Notice that the tree contains a number of resolved nodes
for which the bootstrap confidence levels are greater than 80%. However, many of the other nodes are unresolved and show no clustering
pattern. This indicates that there is insufficient signal in the sequences to cluster them, and that they may represent orphan
sequences that can collectively be used to create a diverse sample of similar sequences.

#### Further information

Macromolecules BLAST search Analyze Sequences tools Phylogenetics
