# Preparing and analyzing an explicit solvation molecular dynamics simulation

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_simulation.htm

## Preparing and analyzing an explicit solvation molecular dynamics simulation

Time: 30 minutes + MD simulation time

### Introduction

Molecular dynamics simulations can help in the study of protein stability and folding, molecular recognition, conformational changes, and other critical aspects of protein function that involve small and large scale atomic movements. You can use molecular dynamics to generate a realistic model of a structure's motion, perform conformational searching, produce a time series analysis of structural and energetic properties, explore energy decay, and analyze solvent effects.

The protein system used is the Src-homology-3 (SH3) domain of the SEM-5 protein from Caenorhabditis elegans, which is involved in linking protein tyrosine kinase activity to Ras [Lim et al., 1994] . Sem-5 activates Ras signaling by binding to the PPPXPPR motifs found in the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Sos. SH3 domains participate in diverse signaling pathways by binding to unique proline-rich peptide motifs, and thus serve as important targets for drug design. The crystal structure used is of the carboxy-terminal SH3 domain from SEM-5 complexed to the mSos-derived amino-acid sequence PPPVPPRRR. The peptide is found to bind in two different orientations, and you will study the conformational changes of the RT loop (named for conserved arginine and threonine residues) that makes direct contact with the peptide, and may play an important role in the signaling specificity of pathways involving SH3 domains. In this tutorial the following tasks are covered:

* Examining and preparing the protein structure

* Solvating the protein structure

* Running the molecular dynamics simulation

* Analyzing the molecular dynamics trajectory

The PDB code for the carboxy-terminal SH3 domain from SEM-5 complexed with a short peptide used is 1SEM [Lim et al., 1994] . The file was downloaded from the RCSB web site.

The following steps assume that the short peptides have been perceived as ligands. In this case, this requires changing one of the default preferences. Before opening the data file, ensure that the maximum number of atoms in a ligand is set to 200.

From the menu bar, choose Edit | Preferences to open the Preferences dialog. In the navigation panel click Ligand Definition . Set the Maximum number of atoms to 200. Click OK to close the Preferences dialog. Open the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 1sem.pdb file. Close the Welcome tab. Open the Macromolecules | Protein Report and Analysis tool panel and click Protein Report .

When working with experimental structures, it is important to inspect the quality of the structure that will affect its use in further modeling [Cooper et al., 2011] . The Protein Report summarizes key information about the protein structure, making it easy to see what may need to be corrected before performing a molecular dynamics simulation. If the structure contains gaps in the chains (in comparison with PDB SEQRES records or from mmCIF _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme data), or incomplete or invalid residues, they are colored magenta in the Graphics View, and groups are created for them in the Hierarchy View. If available, the experimental pH is also reported, which you can use when protonating and ionizing the protein during the preparation steps for further modeling.

This X-ray structure includes two copies of the protein-peptide complex. In the next step you will determine the best copy of the subunit to use.

Click the 1sem tab to make it active again. Click the arrow next to Display Style on the Standard toolbar and select the bottom-right display style (protein displayed as line, and ligands as ball-and-stick). Click Display Style and change Color by to Isotropic Displacement . Click on the Colors... button and change the Spectrum to Blue-White-Red . Click OK to dismiss the Color Mapping and Display Style dialogs.

The isotropic displacement (also known as B factor or the temperature factor) of each atom can be used as an indicator of the uncertainty of its position:

* Higher values indicate a higher degree of variation of the atom's position, averaged over the different unit cells of the crystal and duration of the X-ray diffraction experiment. Atoms with large B-factors (colored red) generally belong to parts of the structure that are more flexible.

* Atoms with low B-factors (colored blue) belong to a part of the structure that is well-ordered, with lower values associated with smaller thermal vibrations and more precise positioning.

Observe the relative colors of the C and D peptide chains, which are complexed with the A and B SH3 protein chains, respectively. Chain C has several residues that are more pink-red than chain D, which is predominantly blue throughout. The protein report showed little difference between the two subunits in terms of gaps or incomplete or invalid residues, so in this example you can use the isotropic displacement to select the better subunit to use for the molecular dynamics simulation.

The final step in examining the structure is to briefly look at the non-bond interactions in the structure to identify extraneous molecular entities, such as water molecules that may require specific considerations. Additional molecular objects (for example, hetero groups like sulfates and non-functional counterions) are generally removed as they are often artifacts of the crystallization process.

Close the Protein Report. Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View. Select all of the A and C chains and delete them. Click the arrow on the Non-bond Interactions... toolbar button and choose Ligand Interactions . This context-sensitive command is available when a Molecule Window with a protein-ligand complex is active.

The peptide in the complex is automatically identified as a ligand and rendered in stick style, and the non-bond interactions between it and the protein are displayed as colored dashed lines. The amino acid residues that interact with the ligand are shown as thin sticks, with all other residues hidden. The View Interactions tool panel in the Receptor-Ligand Interactions tool set also opens automatically to allow access to additional related functionality.

For more information about working with non-bond interactions, run the following tutorial: Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating interactions from screening results .

When working with non amino-acid structures such as small molecule ligands, you should always check the chemistry as Discovery Studio perceives the bond order using geometric factors such as bond lengths and angles, and ring and group planarity, which may result in incorrect assignments.
Conserved water molecules are thought to be important for maintaining the structural architecture of biomolecules and are also involved in the functional activity of enzymes. However, the identification and treatment of conserved water molecules is open to debate and hence there are multiple ways in which you may want to treat them.

Notice the hydrogen bonds identified between the peptide and water molecules involved in non-bond interactions.

From the View Interactions tool panel, click +Expand under Interactions Options... to see if any of these are participating in bridging or stabilizing interactions between the protein and peptide, which are often considered significant. Right-click in the Molecule Window and choose Labels | Add... . Set Object to Residue , and then click OK. Move the mouse while right-clicking to rotate and use the mouse wheel to zoom the view until you see the water molecule HOH51.

Notice that there are bridging interactions, colored mid-blue, between residue ARG8 of the peptide and ASN166 of the protein.

Click Receptor to see the rest of the protein.

Water molecules deeply buried in the core of the protein are considered to be important in the folded structure and often make strong hydrogen bonds to polar groups. If these have a low B-factor, you can retain them for the later molecular dynamics simulation. However, you will not retain water molecules in this tutorial as the single bridging interaction has significant solvent exposure, and there are no other waters deeply buried in the protein.

Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tool panel and click Prepare Proteins... . Leave the parameters set to their default values and click Run .

The Prepare Proteins protocol allows you to set the pH value to protonate the protein, which you can set to the experimental value identified from the Protein Report. Also, all water molecules are removed from the structure by default, but you can retain all or selected waters if desired.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the prepared protein structure, which will be automatically displayed in a Molecule window named 1SEM_prep.

In the Jobs Explorer, double-click the completed job to open up the Report in an Html Window. Click the Detailed Report link in the table.

The Prepare Proteins protocol prepares experimental structures as a starting point for other modeling workflows, performing tasks such as inserting missing atoms in incomplete residues, modeling missing loop regions, deleting alternate conformations (disorder), removing waters, standardizing atom names, and protonating titratable residues using predicted pKs. Of particular significance may be gaps in the protein sequence, which are identified in the protein report. Depending on the objective of the simulation, and the location and length of the missing region, the correction to the protein may require particular attention to ensure optimal preparation of the structure. If the missing residues are significant to the study, you may want to choose the more extensive (but time-consuming) Looper algorithm (in the Build Loops parameter group of the Prepare Proteins protocol) to refine short to medium size loops that have already been built with MODELER.

Water molecules have a fundamental influence in governing biomolecules, aiding in the stabilization of three-dimensional structure, function, and thermodynamic properties, both locally and globally. Protein hydration plays an important role in biological processes, and hydration forces are responsible for the packing and stabilization of three-dimensional protein structures, with water molecules participating in many hydrogen-bonding networks. An accurate description of the solvent environment is essential for realistic biomolecular modeling, and the recent increase in hardware performance has provided means for modeling individual water molecules more tractably.

For extremely large biomolecular systems undergoing significant structural transitions, or for very long simulations, the more realistic explicit modeling of water may be too prohibitive, and you may want to use an implicit solvent model instead. In these solvent models, the polar and non-polar effects of the solvent are accounted for in an averaged way through a continuum dielectric medium, the solvent accessible surface area of the solute, and predefined parameters.

At this stage you should consider the forcefield that you want to use to describe the energy function of the molecular system of interest. Discovery Studio provides a large collection of forcefields that differ in the parameter coverage, accuracy, and computational efficiency. See Supported forcefields .

The Prepare Proteins protocol uses the CHARMm forcefield, which is a general-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids, and general organic molecules. In this example you will change the forcefield and use charmm36, which is a revised version of the protein and peptide focused charmm22/charmm27 forcefields. Charmm36 has optimized backbone CMAP (2D dihedral energy correction map for the Φ, Ψ energy surface) and side-chain torsion potentials ( [Best et al., 2012a] and [Best et al., 2012b] ) and is a highly accurate parameter set for both proteins and nucleic acids that has been well validated and extensively published.

Click the 1SEM_prep tab to make it active. Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel and change the Forcefield to charmm36 . Click Apply Forcefield . Click More... .

The Forcefield Status on the Change Forcefield tool panel reports that 1SEM is typed with the chosen forcefield. The Types and Parameters summary lists the residues that did not match the forcefield templates, and the atoms that could not be typed, or were assigned newly created types, and parameters that were estimated or missing are reported in additional tabs. The ACE1 residue in the peptide does not have a matching template in the charmm36 forcefield, and some of its parameters are estimated. However, this is expected as it is not a standard amino acid residue. Missing parameters require that you check the structure and provide the missing parameter manually before re-typing, and possibly reconsider which forcefield to use.

You will now create the explicit solvation for the simulation, adding enough water molecules to allow the protein to interact with the solvent naturally, but not so much that the system becomes too big to simulate using the available computing power. For a typical molecular dynamics simulation, the protein should be solvated in a water box, which allows the simulation to run using periodic boundary conditions to avoid surface artifacts, preventing the water molecules from diffusing away from the protein during the simulation and permitting a relatively small number of water molecules to act as a bulk solution. Thus a water molecule that exits to the right of the cell shape reappears on the left of the same cell.

You can optionally minimize the solvated system so that any possible van der Waals clashes and bad geometry in the input structure can be cleaned up. As you will be continuing on to a molecular dynamics simulation that includes a minimization step, it is not necessary to run the minimization during this solvation.

Close the 1sem, Report, and 1SEM-charmm36 tabs.
Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and click Solvation... . Leave the parameters set to their default values and click Run .

On completion, the solvated structure is displayed in a Molecule Window named 1SEM. The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 2275 water molecules, and 7 sodium and 6 chloride ions have been added. If you had chosen to optionally minimize the solvated system, the job would have taken longer to complete.

Expand the Hierarchy View until you see the groups under the molecule.

Notice three new chains in the Hierarchy View: water molecules (W), cations (SOD), and anions (CLA), which keep the system neutral and set the salt concentration of the system. Additionally, the water molecules are also defined in a group called Water. If you had retained any significant crystal water molecules from the protein preparation step, these would be included in the Water group, but they would be in a chain separate from the W chain added by the solvation processes.

A number of protocols allow you to run molecular dynamics simulations. You can run these as separate phases (i.e., Minimization, Heating, Equilibration, and Production) or you can use the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol, which concatenates the following set of defined simulation procedures:

* Minimization: An initial minimization stage, typically using the robust Steepest Descent algorithm to resolve any initial poor contacts within the system.

* Minimization2: A second minimization stage, typically using the Conjugate Gradient method to ensure that a low energy starting point is supplied to subsequent dynamics stages.

* Heating: A molecular dynamics simulation heating stage to add thermal energy to the system to reach a target temperature.

* Equilibration: A standard molecular dynamics simulation stage to equilibrate the system at a target temperature to ensure that the energy in the system is distributed appropriately among all degrees of freedom. This allows the system to achieve thermal equilibration at the target temperature.

* Production: A standard molecular dynamics simulation stage from which the data will be collected. The results of the Production stage are stored in the simulation trajectory, from which structural and energetic properties can be calculated and subsequently analyzed.

In a more complete study of the conformational changes of the RT loop of the SH3 domain, you might run molecular dynamics simulations of the protein with and without the PPPVPPRRR peptide present to see how the loop behaves. In this tutorial you will use the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol to run a molecular dynamics simulation with the peptide present, and then analyze the results.

The internal motions of biological molecules occur over a wide range of time scales. They range from local motions such as the vibrations of single atoms and torsional oscillations of side chains in a femtosecond to picosecond range, through rigid body motions such as helix, domain (hinge bending), and subunit motions on a nanosecond to microsecond time scale, to global fluctuations such as helix coil transitions, dissociation/association events, and folding and unfolding of protein structures, which require microseconds to seconds and longer. Thus it is extremely difficult to provide guidance on how long a molecular dynamics simulation should proceed to capture the desired protein motion. However, it is easy to restart a simulations run, so you may prefer to set relatively short time frames and restart frequently to monitor the simulation. In this tutorial you will set parameters to produce enough results for analysis, but may not be necessarily optimized for study. You may need to modify the parameters used depending on the time and hardware resources. In particular, if you have multiple processors, set the number of processors to a power of 2.

The molecular dynamics simulation can take several hours to run. If you do not have the time to run it, you can continue with the tutorial using the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 1SEM_nosolvent.dsv file provided when the Output Molecule Without Solvent link is required below.

From the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel, click Standard Dynamics Cascade... . Set Equilibration | Simulation Time (ps) parameter to 20 . Set Production | Simulation Time (ps) to 200 . Set Advanced | Number of Processors to 4 . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and leave the job to complete.

As the simulation is running, you will see the progression in the details in the Jobs Explorer. When finished, the job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports the final potential energy.

The total simulation time over the heating, equilibration, and production steps is 224 picoseconds. However only the production simulation time is provided in the results. The production simulation time of 200 picoseconds in conjunction with the production save results interval of 2 picoseconds results in a trajectory with 100 frames. The time step of 2 femtoseconds in the heating, equilibration, and production steps of the Standard Dynamics Cascade halves the number of steps required to reach the simulation time. This is enabled because the SHAKE constraint, which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens, is applied by default. The SHAKE constraint parameter is located in the Advanced parameter group.

Note that the Implicit Solvent Model parameter was set to None as you have explicit waters describing the solvent environment. The Electrostatics parameter was set to Automatic , which automatically recognizes the periodic environment and sets the electrostatic calculation to Particle Mesh Ewald (PME), otherwise a spherical non-bond cutoff would have been used. If the biomolecular system is extremely large, or if you want to run very long simulations, select an implicit solvent model, which represents the solvent as a continuous medium instead of individual "explicit" solvent molecules.

Depending on such variables as the size of the biomolecular system, the accuracy desired, time allowed, and the available hardware resources, different methods for estimating the electrostatic solvation energy are available. See Solvent models in biomolecular simulations .

Close the 1SEM tab. In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link.

The report includes a table summary of the molecular dynamics phases, and temperature and total energy time-dependent plots of the trajectory frames from the production phase. Temperature and energy versus simulation time plots are only shown for the heating and equilibration phases if the final temperature is off target by 10% or more. This would strongly suggest that you need to increase the simulation time for those affected phases to achieve stability in the protein system. If you want to monitor the entire progression of the protein during the heating, equilibration, and production phases, you can choose to save the Intermediate Directory for the protocol, which will contain the trajectory, energy, and restart files for each phase for further study and analysis.

The Results section of the report lists the most useful output from the protocol. The Energy Table (<molecule>_energy.csv file) allows you to analyze the energetic properties in the production phase (without loading all the conformations) and plot the energy terms against simulation time using the charting tools.

The Output Molecule Without Conformations section (<molecule>_noconfs.dsv) is useful if you want to extend the simulation and continue the production phase for longer using the Dynamics (Production) protocol. This file has the final coordinates of the dynamics simulation and can be used with the restart file (<molecule>_prod.rst) found in the Output folder.

You can click the View Results link to open the Output Molecule section (<molecule>.dsv), which contains the protein structure with the trajectory frames from the production phase stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order (that is, the first conformation corresponds to the first trajectory frame in the production phase saved by CHARMm). The time-dependent energy properties from the production phase are also stored with each conformation.

In this tutorial, you are specifically studying the conformational changes of the RT loop using explicit waters. As there were no conserved water molecule interactions that you wanted to monitor, you will use the Output Molecule Without Solvent file because it has all of the conformations of the trajectory, with the solvent molecules and counterions removed for easy visualization.

In the Report , click the Output Molecule Without Solvent link. If you chose not to run the long simulation, open Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 1SEM_nosolvent.dsv file . From the Hierarchy View, expand the <Cell> and 1SEM levels to see the conformations representing the trajectory frames. Open the Data Table View (CTRL+T if it is not visible) and select the Conformation tab.

The time-dependent energy properties for each frame of the trajectory are tabulated here for ease of analysis.

At this stage, you may also find it useful to change to the last pre-set display style (protein displayed as line, and ligands as ball-and-stick) again to distinguish the protein and peptide during the trajectory animation.

In the 1SEM_nosolvent tab, click the Maximize icon. Right-click in the toolbar area and select Animation to display the Animation toolbar if it is not already displayed. Click Start Animation . Click Slow Down Animation to achieve an appropriate speed. Click Stop Animation once you have viewed the complete trajectory.

You will now analyze a number of structural properties for this molecular dynamics trajectory using the Analyze Trajectory protocol. This allows you to calculate geometric properties such as distance, angle, and torsion, or the number of non-bond interactions for each simulation frame. You can also calculate the RMSD between different conformations and the RMS fluctuation (RMSF) from the average structure in the trajectory. You will calculate the RMSD of each trajectory frame against the X-ray crystal structure, and monitor the non-bond interactions formed between the peptide and protein.

From the Hierarchy View, select the D chain , and then click Non-bond Interactions... on the Smart Tools toolbar to open the Create Non-bond Interaction Monitor dialog. Change the Molecular Scope to Intermolecular (between molecules) and click OK. Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tool panel. Click Analyze Trajectory... . For the Analysis Type parameter, select the RMSD , RMSF , and Properties checkboxes. Note that the Properties parameter listing the Non-bond Monitor1 is now enabled and no longer grayed-out. Change RMSD Reference to Specify a Molecule and expand the parameter group. Set the Reference Molecule to 1SEM_prep:1SEM , which is the protein structure generated from the Prepare Proteins protocol typed with the charmm36 forcefield. If you are using the 1SEM_nosolvent.dsv file, then Reference Molecule should be set to 1SEM_nosolvent:1SEM instead. Set Atom Group and Atom Group to Fit parameters to 1SEM:Protein Groups:Backbone . Leave the remaining parameters set to their default values and click Run . Click Background and wait for the job to complete.

The job entry line in the Jobs Explorer reports that 100 frames have been processed.

* If you are working with a very large trajectory, you can minimize the memory required by loading the molecular structure without conformations in the Graphics View and then specifying the trajectory file (<molecule>.dcd) and the frames to be examined in the Analyze Trajectory protocol. With this method, you can also focus on the frames that show interesting structural and dynamic behavior by choosing the start frame, end frame, and interval size to create a new trajectory from the original.

* The Process Trajectory Files protocol can also be useful when working with a very large trajectory or a large protein system to process the trajectory files for specific frames (such as the final stages of a long simulation) or a subset of the molecular system (such as the active site) prior to running the Analyze Trajectory protocol.

The Atom Group parameter allows you to specify the atoms to use in the RMSD calculation, which is calculated for each conformation. The Atom Group to Fit parameter allows you to specify that each of the trajectory frames will be superimposed to the Reference Molecule before the calculation of the RMSD. This compensates for any rotational or translational motion of the protein complex during the simulation.

In the Jobs Explorer, expand the completed job and click the Report link.

The report contains a link to a data table which summarizes the number of non-bond interactions between the protein and the peptide in each frame of the trajectory. The interaction monitor created included hydrogen bonds and unfavorable bump interactions. However, in this case, only favorable interactions (i.e., hydrogen bonds) have been found in the trajectory. The report also contains links to plots of the RMSD of each trajectory frame against the prepared X-ray crystal structure and RMSF from the average structure for each residue.

The values in the RMSD plot are calculated based only on the backbone of the protein system as requested, and are reported for each conformation of the trajectory. You can calculate RMSD values per-chain or per-residue by changing the Scope parameter.

Depending on the objective of your simulation, you may expect different observations in these analyses. The RMSD plot allows you to visualize how much the conformations of the protein-peptide complex, which are generated in solvent and at room temperature (300 K), deviate from the X-ray crystal structure. You can also see how similar the conformations are to each other: whether they have reached a stable state ,or if any significant conformational changes occurred during the simulation. The backbone RMSD fluctuates from frame to frame around a mean value (~0.8 Å), indicating that the conformations have deviated to a small degree from the X-ray crystal structure, and although there are structural differences between the conformations, they are minor and the trajectory is stable.

The RMSF plot shows the fluctuation of the residues compared to the average structure across the production trajectory, and can be used to identify the regions of highest and lowest flexibility. Typically terminal residue and surface loop regions have the highest flexibility, while the mobility of the protein core is more restricted. Also, the flexibility of a region can be affected by the interactions that it makes with surrounding residues.

In the Analyze Trajectory report, click the Analyzed Trajectory link in the Results section. In the Data Table View select the AminoAcid tab. Choose Chart | Line Plot from the menu bar. For the X column, select Name . For the Y column, select the RMSF , Main-Chain RMSF , and Side-Chain RMSF properties. Click OK.

This generates a plot showing the magnitude of the fluctuation of the heavy atoms of each residue compared to the average structure. However, the residues of the RT loop (LEU162 to ASP179) are now easily seen, and it is easy to see the contribution of the side-chain and the main-chain to the residue value, with the side-chain more variable than the backbone. Depending on your server specifications, there may be some differences in your trajectory compared to the 1SEM_nosolvent.dsv file provided.

In the red main-chain RMSF plot there are five predominant peaks corresponding to THR156, SER170, ASP187, ASN212, and PRO7/ARG8. THR156 and ASN212 correspond to the C- and N-terminus of the protein, where you might expect the greatest degree of movement, and PRO7/ARG8 are the last two residues of the short peptide. Residues SER170 and ASP187 are in surface coil or turn structures in the protein, which are known to be more flexible than residues in sheets and helices. The green side-chain RMSF values of zero are for glycine residues that do not have a side-chain.

If you focus on the residues of the RT loop, you might expect to see more disorder and movement in a loop. However, if you compare this in the red main-chain RMSF plot to the green side-chain RMSF, you can see that the loop does not fluctuate very much. The greatest fluctuation is in ASN166, GLU169, and ARG177, where the side-chains also show more variability. To complete the analysis of the movement of the RT loop, and to confirm any observations you may make, you can compare these results to a similar molecular dynamics simulation with only the protein.

In the final part of this tutorial, you will analyze the hydrogen bonds formed between the peptide and the protein, which were calculated for each frame of the trajectory.

Return to the Analyze Trajectory report tab and click the Non-bond Monitor1 Data Table link. Choose Chart | Heat Map from the menu bar. For the Y column, select the Conformation property. For the X column, select all properties with exception of Row Index and Conformation. Click OK.

In the resulting heat map, you can see the hydrogen bonds between the protein and peptide in each conformation of the simulation, detailed at the atomic level. The top row of the heat map is the X-ray crystal structure (Reference Molecule).

The heat map is a useful tool for studying the persistence and variability in the hydrogen bond interactions formed over the course of the simulation. There are hydrogen bonding interactions that are present in all (or almost all) conformations (predominantly red columns in the heat map), which indicate that these hydrogen bonds are very persistent and are likely to be significant in the binding of the peptide. These hydrogen bonds involve GLU172 of the RT loop, and ASN206, TYR207, and TRP191 on the other side of the binding cleft. GLN168 of the RT loop also makes some less persistent hydrogen bonds to the side-chain of ARG8 of the peptide, which provides additional stabilization. The other hydrogen bonds in the heat map appear to be more transient, appearing in a smaller number of conformations, and are likely to be less important for binding. This type of analysis can be used to investigate which interactions are particularly important, and where mutations could possibly be made to improve the binding.

Because the hydrogen bond monitor is updated automatically for each frame, the dynamic behavior of hydrogen bonds can be viewed by animating the trajectory.
If desired, you can return to the protein you prepared in the first step, remove the bound peptide, and then repeat the solvation and molecular dynamics simulation to see how the RT loop behaves without a bound peptide.

#### Further information

Work with forcefields Forcefield Window Choose a Forcefield Type dialog

# Working with small molecule data sets

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_small-molecule.htm

## Working with small molecule data sets

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

Drug molecules are typically analyzed in two ways. The structures of individual molecules are often 
modeled in detail to understand their activity and interactions with potential protein targets. In addition, 
studying the 3D structure may give ideas about synthetic modifications to molecules that may improve their 
activity. Alternatively, large sets of molecules may be analyzed collectively to compare various properties 
and identify a subset of molecules to be studied further.

The Molecule Window, and in particular the Data Table View, is designed to make it easy to work with very large 
numbers of molecules simultaneously. Properties can be calculated for different molecules and compared and 
filtered to isolate sets of lead candidates. This tutorial introduces the basic features of the Molecule 
Window and demonstrates some of its broader capabilities. The following tasks are covered:

* Opening files

* Viewing 3D structures of selected molecules

* Viewing 2D structures

* Sorting and filtering properties

* Appending data sets

A useful feature is the ability to automatically calculate basic molecular properties when you open molecules in Discovery Studio . The properties that can be calculated include:

* Molecular Composition

* Molecular Formula

* Molecular Weight

* Number of Atoms

This feature is enabled in preferences. Before opening a data file, make sure this feature is turned on.

From the menu bar, choose Edit | Preferences... to open the Preferences dialog. In the navigation panel click Molecule Window . Ensure that the Calculate basic properties on import checkbox is checked.

Click OK to close the dialog.

When files are opened, the properties will now be calculated and displayed automatically.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Quick Start Tutorials | NCI Drug Sample.sd .

The contents of the file and the calculated properties are displayed in the Molecules tab in the Data Table View:

The Molecule tab is of special importance in the Molecule Window. Often, when working in the Molecule Window, the focus is on making comparisons between molecules or molecular properties. The Molecule tab has a number of features specifically designed to 
support this and facilitate browsing.

Open the Graphics View by pressing Ctrl+G , or selecting View | Graphics . In the first row of the Data Table View, click the Visible Column of the Molecule tab, check Yes .

The first molecule in the data is now visible:

Notice that when the molecule is made visible, two additional tabs appear at the bottom of the Data Table View. These tabs
display the corresponding 3D objects in a tabular format and allow you to inspect the details of the corresponding objects. If the
molecules being visualized have additional properties (for example, surfaces or chains), these also appear in their own tabs.

When you select objects in the different tabs, the objects are also selected in the Graphics View. Likewise, when you select objects in the Graphics View, they are selected in the tabs.

If you turn off the visibility of a molecule, all corresponding entries in the
tabs are removed. If you turn off visibility of all molecules, the tabs
containing those entries are removed as well.

In addition to viewing individual files, it is also useful to be able to inspect multiple structures at the same time. You can perform this by controlling their visibility in the Data Table View and then arranging the structures in the Graphics View for convenience.

In the Molecule tab, turn on the visibility of the second and third molecules in the table by selecting
the Yes checkboxes in the Visible column. In the Graphics View, right-click and select View | Tile Molecules in View .

The first three molecules are now visible:

One particularly useful property when working with small molecules is to be 
able to display a 2D depiction of the molecule.

In the Molecule tab, right-click and choose Show/Hide Chemistry .

The molecules are now depicted in two dimensions:

Once populated, you can navigate around the table with the horizontal and 
vertical scroll bars. Another powerful way to move 
around the table is to use the controls on the navigation panel in the top left side of the Data Table View. The four navigation keys allow you to move the top or bottom of the table, or to move up or down a row. These controls have the added advantage that they always clear the Graphics View of all 3D structures except for that of the selected molecule. This is useful when you are browsing a set of molecules, and wish to inspect 
one at a time.

Another way of navigating and exploring data in the Molecule tab is to use filters to reduce the data to sets of molecules
of particular interest. Once filtered, only the molecules that pass the filter are displayed in the table. Data is not permanently discarded by the filter and it is always possible to remove the filter and return to a view that shows all molecules.

There are two methods for filtering in this application:

* By visibility or selection status

* By specific properties

In the Molecule tab, right-click and select List Only Visible Objects .

Now only the visible molecules are shown in the table:

At this point it is possible to apply another filter that will reduce the filtered set of molecules further.

In the Molecule tab, right-click and select List Only Visible Objects again.

The filter is removed and all molecules are shown again.

Right-click and select Filter... .

This opens the Filter dialog .

In the Filter dialog, set the Choice cell for Molecular Weight to Top(#) .
Enter 25 in the Value column.

Click OK .

This will show only the 25 molecules with the highest molecular weight.

In the Molecule tab right-click and select Remove Filters .

The Molecule tab returns to displaying all molecules.

Another common task is to append one data set to another. This is easily achieved in the Molecule Window by dragging 
and dropping the file to be added from the Files Explorer into the window, or as follows:

Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Quick Start Tutorials | 1fvv_conformations.sd .

The 1fvv_conformations.sd molecules are appended to the Molecule tab. Scroll to the bottom of the view and observe
that the molecules are now included and that the unique columns for that data set have been added to the right of the 
Data Table view.

It is also possible to append macromolecules, pharmacophores or any other
data type supported in the Molecule Window.

#### Further information

Working with the Molecule Window Data Table View Supported file formats - MDL MOL/SD (SD, SDF, MOL, MDL)

# Calculate binding energy using steered molecular dynamics

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_smd_simulation.htm

## Calculate binding energy using steered molecular dynamics

Time: 30 minutes + SMD simulation time (~9 hours)

### Introduction

Steered Molecular dynamics (SMD) simulations can aid in the study of biophysical processes on a computationally feasible timescale. In SMD, processes such as protein unfolding, ligand unbinding, or conformational changes can be simulated by actively steering the event towards a chosen direction as opposed to passively waiting for the event to take place as in standard molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, biological events that occur on the millisecond or longer timescales can be simulated on the nanosecond timescale. The free energy of such a process can be calculated by analyzing the steering work done. Free energies calculated using this approach require that the steering process take place in equilibrium. However, the Jarzynski's equality [Jarzynski, 1997 a , b ] which is applicable to data generated in the non-equilibrium regime allows us to adopt rapid steering schedules, thereby further enhancing the efficiency of the SMD approach. In addition to free energy values, an analysis of SMD simulations can reveal atomic-level structural details into the biophysical process being investigated. For example, double-decoupling free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations while providing the free energy of protein-ligand binding, do not provide mechanistic details, whereas an SMD simulation can.

In this tutorial we illustrate the SMD method by using the T4-Lysozyme protein. The unbinding of the 2-propylphenol ligand from the binding pocket of the protein was simulated [Boyce et al, 2009] . It is assumed that you are familiar with setting up and running standard molecular dynamics simulations (see Preparing and analyzing an explicit solvation molecular dynamics simulation ).

This test system is particularly challenging because the SMD simulation involves the sequestration of the ligand from a buried binding pocket as seen below. Thus, pulling the ligand out of the pocket will be accompanied by the protein unraveling, followed by the extrusion of the ligand, and the closing back of the protein.

The tutorial covers the following topics.

* Preparing the protein-ligand system for simulation

* Setting up and running the SMD simulation

* Analyzing the SMD simulation

* Calculating Free Energy from multiple SMD runs

This step involves reading, cleaning, typing with a forcefield, solvating, and equilibrating the protein ligand system. It also specifies the pulling atom pair for the SMD run. You can skip this initial setup step by using the following file: Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 3HTB.dsv .

The PDB code of the protein-ligand complex is 3HTB. You will first retrieve the protein-ligand complex from RCSB site and open it in Discovery Studio.

Choose File | Open URL and type 3HTB into the ID box to open the PDB file. Open the Macromolecules | Protein Report and Analysis tool panel and click Protein Report .

This opens up a report that shows some basic information about the PDB file, where you can inspect for missing residues and other potential problems that may need correction.

Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tool panel and click Clean Protein .

Now delete the crystal waters and salts.

In the Hierarchy View , select Water group and press delete key. Select the phosphate residues and BME residue from the second chain A and press Delete . The protein and the ligand should remain.

Now that the system is appropriately prepared, you will assign force-field parameters and optimize the geometry of the complex. You will use a standard dynamics cascade to minimize the protein-ligand complex and run a short equilibration and production molecular dynamics simulation, such that the ligand adopts a stable conformation in complex with the protein, which is consistent with the presence of explicit solvent.

Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel. Choose the CHARMm forcefield, and the Momany-Rone partial charge, and click Apply Forcefield . This will assign the chosen force-field to the complex. In the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel, navigate to the Advanced section and click Solvation . Running with the default parameters will solvate the system for the simulation. In the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel, navigate to the Dynamics section and click Standard Dynamics Cascade .

Running using the default parameters will run a standard set of minimization, followed by equilibration and production runs as a preparatory step for the steering molecular dynamics simulation.

Once the job is done, double click on the Job in the Jobs Explorer, which will open up the results of the dynamics cascade. Click on the Output Molecule Without Conformations link in the Results section. This will open up the optimized and equilibrated solvated complex, which you can use to set up the simulation.

For more information about preparation for molecular dynamics simulations, run the following tutorial: Preparing and analyzing an explicit solvation molecular dynamics simulation .

The SMD protocol requires you to specify a pulling direction by selecting a pair of atoms. During the simulation, constant velocity is applied via a spring to those atoms, acting in opposite directions to pull them apart. For a protein-ligand system, one of the atoms should be from the protein and the other from the ligand. It is best to choose a relatively inflexible atom from the protein so that the direction of pulling is preserved relative to the two molecules.

Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and navigate to the Steered Molecular Dynamics section. In the 3D viewer, zoom in to the ligand and select the protein CA atom of ALA99 (atom number 1564) from the protein first. This will cause it to turn yellow. Holding the SHIFT key, select the C12 ring carbon attached to the propyl group from the ligand (atom number 2621). Click the now active Create Pulling Atom Pair button from the Steered Molecular Dynamics section of the tool panel to set the direction for SMD, which displays as a two headed arrow in the 3D View.

Before initiating a large number of SMD runs or trajectories, you should first run trial SMD runs until you are sure that the pulling atom pair defined is optimal for a good pulling direction, such that the desired transition occurs successfully.

In the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel, click Steered Molecular Dynamics .

Take a moment to understand the different parameters. Importantly, check the simulation time and pulling speed (in the Advanced section), as a product of these determines the rough distance the ligand will travel during the simulation. At the default simulation time of 1000 ps and pulling speed of 0.02 Å/ps, the ligand will travel about 20 Å, which is the typical distance required to pull a ligand out of a protein binding pocket.

The simulation run for this tutorial can take around 9 hours. You can increase the pulling speed to 0.2 Å/ps or higher for a faster run. Additionally, if you can run in parallel, you can set the Number of Processors to improve performance.

The pulling direction, pulling speed and simulation time should be set so as to ensure that none of the molecules being pulled exit the box. Otherwise, the simulation may stall.

On the dialog, decrease the Simulation Time (ps) to 200. (Optional) Change the Number of Processors to desired number to get a faster run. Hit Run to start the simulation.

The run will take roughly 9 hours on a single CPU or 3 hours on 4 CPUs. When the run finishes, open it from the Jobs Explorer and click on the Output Molecule in the Results section. Observe the trajectory to ensure that the ligand unbinding path is proper.

Note that this tutorial only generates a single trajectory. While the SMD method is efficient, the reliable calculation of free energies including absolute binding affinities from SMD simulations requires a large number of trajectories to obtain convergence. You should run at least 30 trajectories to check for convergence and more to further improve the estimate. In order to run multiple trajectories efficiently, you can open the Steered Molecular Dynamics from the Protocols Explorer. Once you have set the parameters, leaving the Random Number Seed parameter blank to ensure unique runs, you can initiate multiple runs by simply repeatedly pressing the Run Protocol button (the green button).

Another important point to note is that all runs must start from the same distance between the two atoms involved in pulling. This is because the analysis routine (below) normalizes the starting distance to be zero. Therefore, in order to calculate average properties using multiple trajectories it is best to start the different trajectories from the same conformation.

### Analyzing an SMD simulation

When the SMD job finishes, double click on the status row in the Jobs Explorer.

A report opens which shows a force-profile as a function of distance. The force is calculated at the interval of 5 ps (specified during the run), which translates to 0.1 Å at the speed of 0.02 Å/ps up to 4 Å for your 200 ps SMD simulation. The example profile below shows the distances of most and least resistance during a 1000 ps simulation. The free energy profile is calculated using tens of such force profiles obtained from multiple trajectories as discussed below.

A valuable set of information provided uniquely by the SMD approach is atomic-detail mechanistic insight into the process investigated. Here we touch on this aspect briefly by showing a few snapshots from the unbinding trajectory (below). Notice how the conformational change during and after the complete unbinding is captured. Comparing the first (top left) and last (bottom right) snapshots shows the changed conformation of a helix which is a consequence of an empty binding pocket. The second conformation (top right) captures the transition of the ligand from the pocket to the bulk solvent. An analysis of such conformations near the transition can provide qualitative insights into the interactions that hold the ligand in the pocket and consequently could be useful in generating ideas for optimizing the ligand to increase bound state residency time.

As mentioned above, calculating free energies reliably from SMD requires a large number of trajectories. For the purpose of the tutorial, we present an analysis of 40 pre-generated trajectories. The force-profile files from the 40 runs can be found in the Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | smd-force-profiles directory.

Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tool panel and navigate to the Steered Molecular Dynamics section. Click Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces to open the dialog. Choose the smd-force-profiles directory for Steering Force Profile Files parameter. Click Run .

You can select multiple trajectory folders in Steering Force Profile Files parameter. The protocol will automatically pick up the Force-profile files by navigating the sub-directories.

Typically the calculation takes a little over 5 minutes. Open the results from the Jobs Explorer when it finishes. The first plot in the Summary tab shows the Work (kcal/mol) integrated from the force-profile for each individual run as a function of distance (Å). The protocol considers the first distance as zero. Therefore it is important that all runs start from the same distance between the two atoms involved in pulling.

The second plot shows the calculated free energy as a function of pulling distance computed using three methods. F jarz is obtained through a straightforward application of the Jarzynski equality. For each value of the reaction coordinate F jarz is computed as an average over N trajectories, and is given by.

F lin and F ci result from two different ways of better estimating the free energy by applying extrapolation methods. Common to both methods, the Jarzynski equality is applied to compute the F jarz values for randomly chosen subsets or samples of the data. Further, an F jarz trend is obtained as a function of the sample size. F lin is obtained by the linear extrapolation of the tail of this average F jarz trend in the limit of infinite sample size. F ci uses the same sample data generated above, but adopts a cumulative integral extrapolation, where not just the tail of the curve, but the entire F jarz curve is used for estimation. For details, please see [Ytreberg and Zuckerman, 2004] .

In the plot below, F jarz is shown in red, F lin in blue, and F ci in green. The divergence between F jarz and the other two quantities is expected as the former involves a simplistic estimator. On the other hand, a large difference between F lin and F ci as seen here in the range 15-20 Å seems to suggest that a larger number of trajectories may be needed. In this context, it must be said that the chosen example of T4-lysozyme is a challenging test case because the unbinding of the ligand accompanies the local unfolding of the protein, followed by re-folding.

If we choose the more favorable F lin value to estimate the absolute binding free energy, the value obtained is approximately -7.5 kcal/mol, which is obtained by simply taking the difference between the bound state at zero distance and the plateaued value in the unbound state. This value is consistent with the experimentally measured value of -5.33 kcal/mol for this ligand. [Boyce et al, 2009]

# Using the storyboard feature to create a movie

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_storyboards.htm

## Using the storyboard feature to create a movie

Time: 15 minutes.

### Introduction

In this tutorial, you will record various scenes to visualize an interesting donor-donor-acceptor feature that could be exploited as an effective kinase inhibitor [Regan et al., 2003] . You will then fine tune the resulting movie and export it to share with colleagues.

The storyboard mechanism is designed to work by manipulating the display of pre-existing objects, so you should create these first and then set up the storyboard.

Open the 1kv2 complex and visualize hydrogen bonding between the protein and ligand.

Choose File | Open URL... from the menu bar. Set ID to 1kv2 , and then click Open . Choose Chemistry | Hydrogens | Add Polar from the menu bar. Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions tool set, and then open the View Interactions tool panel. Click the H-Bond surface button. Choose Structure | Monitor | Intermolecular HBonds from the menu bar.

You have now created the required objects. The next step is to adjust the display to create the first scene of the storyboard.

Using the hierarchy view, toggle off the visibility of the Solvent Hydrogen Bond Donor/Acceptor Surface and HBond Monitor 1 . Expand Interface Groups and select the Interface Pocket Atoms group. From the toolbar, click Display Style , and set the Atom display style to Off . Deselect the group. Click on the Home and Fit To Screen buttons on the View toolbar to remove any zooming or rotations.

You are now ready to create the first scene.

Press the Insert key.

This creates the first scene and opens the Storyboard dialog.

Double-click the ligand to select it. Choose View | Transform | Fit To Screen from the menu bar.

The view is now zoomed in and centered on the ligand.

Deselect the ligand. Rotate the structure to a desirable orientation of the ligand. Press the Insert key.

This creates a second scene focused on the ligand with polar hydrogens displayed.

Click the first scene in the storyboard dialog. Right-click the first scene and rename it "P38 with inhibitor" . Rename the second scene "Birb796 bound" . Toggle on the visibility of the Solvent Hydrogen Bond Donor/Acceptor Surface and HBond Monitor 1 . Rotate the molecule again for a better view of the surface and
interactions. Press the Insert key. Rename the scene "ActiveSite Surface" .

You are now visualizing the surface of the receptor for the ligand.

From the hierarchy view, select the Interface Pocket Atoms group. From the toolbar, click Display Style , and set the Atom display style to Stick and the Stick Size to 0.1 . Deselect the group. Zoom into urea group NC(=O)N (This can be done by selecting atom C1 of the ligand and clicking the Fit to Screen button). Rotate and scale as desired to get a good view of the hydrogen bonds to this group and press the Insert key. Rename the scene "DFG Urea" . Zoom to the Morpholino group. (This can be done by selecting atom O47 of the ligand and clicking the Fit to Screen button). Adjust the view as desired.

This is an unusual example of the classical acceptor-donor-acceptor motif in a kinase being altered to donor-donor-acceptor. This is a feature of the rotational freedom of the Glycine in protein backbones and its presence at this location in the hinge is vary rare across the kinase family. This rarity can be potentially exploited to create a highly selective kinase inhibitor.

Press the Insert key. Rename the scene "Novel H-bond pattern" . In the storyboard dialog, drag the "DFG Urea" scene to swap the order with "Novel H-bond pattern" . Click first scene. Choose File | Save As... from the menu bar. Save the file in DSV format: 1kv2movie.dsv .

This saves your work. However, the default play settings might not be useful for illustrating this feature.

Click the Play button on the storyboard dialog.

Notice that the transitions move too fast and the pauses on each scene are too short.

From the storyboard dialog, click the More button.

This exposes options for adjusting transitions and pauses.

Select the "Birb796 bound" scene, and then set the Transition to 3 seconds and Pause to 2 seconds. Select the "ActiveSite Surface" scene, and then set Pause to 2 seconds. Click the "Novel H-bond pattern" scene, and then set the Transition to 2 seconds and Pause to 5 seconds. Click the "DFG Urea" scene, and then set Pause to 5 seconds.

Click the first scene , and then click Play .

If you want the storyboard to open automatically choose the Show dialog automatically option in the storyboard dialog.

You can share the storyboard with colleagues who do not have access to Discovery Studio by exporting it as a movie.

From the storyboard dialog, click Export Movie . Save the movie as "1kv2movie.webm" . Wait until all the scenes have been replayed frame by frame while recording the movie before closing the storyboard.

The WebM format can be played in most browsers.

Fit To Screen , Show Polar Hydrogens , H-Bond Surface , and Add Scene are all available by right-clicking the Graphics View.

# Superimposing protein structures

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_superimpose-prot-struct_tools.htm

## Superimposing protein structures

Time: 10 minutes.

### Introduction

When comparing protein structures, a typical first step is to superimpose the structures
based on either their Cα or backbone atoms. Since different proteins have different numbers 
and types of residues, the residues to be used must be known
to map the coordinates from different protein structures.

Discovery Studio provides several methods for superimposing 
protein structures. One is to manually specify matching residues between two proteins using Protein Tethers
and superimpose them based on those matching residues. Another approach is to 
superimpose two or more protein structures based on their sequence alignment, and then the 
matching residues for superimposition are automatically identified based on the aligned 
residues in the sequence alignment. The latter approach can also be used to superimpose
the protein structures based on a subset of aligned residues, such as ligand binding
site residues.

In this tutorial you will learn how to superimpose a set of proteins based on their sequence alignment.

* Opening, viewing, and aligning the sequence of a set of proteins

* Superimposing protein structures based on their sequence alignment

* Selecting the ligand binding site residues

* Superimposing the protein structures using the binding site residues

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | CDK2 Structures and Sequences.dsv .

This file contains 50 cyclin-dependent protein kinase 2 (CDK2) structures and corresponding aligned sequences. 
The first protein 1AQ1 is shown in the 
Graphics View. The other 49 molecules are shown in the Hierarchy View and Data Table, but hidden 
in the Graphics View.

In the Data Table View, open the Molecule tab and select rows 2 through 10. Right-click
and choose Show In Graphics View .

The first 10 molecules will be shown in the Graphics View. Right-click and drag to rotate the molecules
and observe that they are not all superimposed.

Because the dsv file contains embedded sequence data, a Sequence Window showing all 50 sequences is automatically opened, which includes the molecules not displayed in the Graphics View.
The sequences in the Sequence Window are linked to the corresponding visible proteins in the Molecule Window.
Any residue selections in the Sequence Window are reflected in the Molecule Window and vice versa.
Drag over a few residues in the first sequence in the Sequence Window to observe this.

In the Tools Explorer, expand Superimpose Proteins to open the tool panel. 
If it is not visible, choose View | Tool Panels | Superimpose Proteins from the menu bar. By default the first protein listed in the Hierarchy View, 1AQ1 , will be defined as the reference protein.

To define a different reference protein, select it by clicking
the molecule name in the Hierarchy View, and then from the tool panel, click Reference Protein .

The sequence alignment CDK2 Sequences will be automatically defined as the sequence alignment to use because it contains a sequence linked to the reference protein.

These sequences have been pre-aligned and saved in the sample file. To perform sequence alignment yourself, click Sequence Alignment to open the Align Sequences dialog. If no sequence window is linked to the molecules, one will be created.

The reference protein onto which the others will be superimposed is defined as 1AQ1 and the sequence
alignment for superimposition is defined as CDK2 Sequences . On the tool panel, the value for Reference Protein is set to 1AQ1 and the value for Sequence Alignment is set to CDK2 Sequences .

First, ensure that no parts of the structure are selected by clicking empty space in the Hierarchy or Graphics view. From the Tools Explorer, select Sequence Alignment from the Superimpose by dropdown list
and then click Superimpose .

This superimposes proteins 2 through 10 over the 1AQ1 structure based on the aligned residues defined in the Sequence Window. 
The 10 structures in the Molecule Window are now superimposed on each other. The molecules that are not visible
in the Graphics View are not moved by superimposition.

Click the arrow to the right of the Display Style button on the Standard toolbar and select the
style in the bottom left of the preview page.

Ensure there are no selections. In the Graphics View, right-click and choose Display Style... to open the dialog. Open the Atom tab and set Display style to Off , and then click OK .

This changes the display of the protein to C-Alpha trace and hides any solvent and ligand molecules so you can see the 10 superimposed structures more clearly.

Click Show Report .

This opens a report that summarizes the RMSD of the superimposition and the number of residues used to superimpose the proteins.
Close this window after inspecting the results so that the Molecule Window and Sequence Window
are both available to work with for the next section.

From the Hierarchy View of the CDK2 Structures and Sequences - Molecule Window , expand the 1AQ1 molecule and click <Chain> under the 1AQ1 molecule to select this ligand. In the Graphics View, right-click and click the arrow on Atom Display tool bar button which is 
the first button on the context menu. Choose Ball and Stick from the dropdown list.

This displays and highlights the ligand of 1AQ1 in the Graphics View.

Choose Edit | Select... from the menu bar
to display the Select dialog. Set Scope to AminoAcid . Click the Radius radio button and Intramolecular from the first list. Enter 5 for the distance. Click Apply , and then Close .

This selects any residues in 1AQ1 that have an atom 
within 5Å of any of the selected ligand atoms. Those selected
residues are highlighted in both the Molecule Window and the Sequence
Window.

Click the CDK2 Structures and Sequences - Molecule Window tab to make it active. From the Superimpose Proteins tool panel, click Superimpose .

This superimposes the proteins 2 through 10 over the 1AQ1 structure based on the selected residues in the 1AQ1 protein. The
residues in the proteins 2 through 10, which are aligned to the
selected residues in 1AQ1 , will be used to superimpose the 10 proteins.

The 10 protein structures are superimposed tightly on top of each other around the ligand binding 
site. However, the rest of the proteins are shifted from the previous superimposition and not superimposed 
very well.

From the tool panel, click Show Report .

This displays the 10 proteins that are superimposed using 21 binding site residues and the RMSD of the
superimposed residues.

# Modeling transmembrane proteins

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_transmembrane-protein.htm

## Modeling transmembrane proteins

Time: 30 minutes

### Introduction

Transmembrane proteins are very important in pharmaceutical research since transmembrane proteins, such as the G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR), are the target for many existing drugs as well as for many drug candidates in development. This tutorial demonstrates how the set of tools and protocols available in Discovery Studio can be combined in a workflow to construct a homology model of the 
beta-1-adrenergic receptor based on the X-ray structure for the beta-2-adrenergic receptor.

The following tasks are covered in this tutorial:

* Locating and opening the input files

* Predicting Transmembrane regions of a protein

* Aligning the sequence to templates

* Building a homology model

* Adding an implicit membrane to the model structure

* Adjusting the position of the membrane

The sequence of the human beta-1-adrenergic receptor is provided in the samples folder. To open the sequence in a sequence window.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | ADRB1_HUMAN.fasta .

This opens the file in a new Sequence Window labeled ADRB1_HUMAN.

The first step in building a homology model for a target is to identify a suitable template. If a template with high sequence identity is available, it can often be identified with a simple BLAST search. In the case of transmembrane proteins, the number of X-ray structures available may be rather limited, so this tutorial does not include this step. For more details on identifying templates, see the Creating homology models from a protein sequence tutorial.

You will use a solved structure of the X-ray structure of the beta-2-adrenergic receptor, PDB code 2rh1 as a template.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | 2rh1.pdb .

This opens the file in a new Molecule Window labeled 2rh1.

A BLAST search on the PDB_nr95 database reveals there are now structures available with very high sequence identity to the target sequence which would be superior templates. However, this tutorial uses 2rh1 to highlight Discovery Studio functionality that would not be relevant in the case of a template with such high sequence identity.

The next step in the model building process is to align the target sequence with the template sequence. The first step is to combine both sequences in one Sequence window.

Click the ADRB1_HUMAN Sequence Window tab to make it active. Right-click in the window and choose Insert Sequence | From Windows ... .

This will open the Insert Sequence from Windows dialog.

Select 2rh1 and click OK .

This will insert the sequence of 2rh1 into the ADRB1_HUMAN Sequence Window. The status bar displays the similarity 
and identity between the two sequences.

Note that the sequences are not aligned and the Sequence Identity and Sequence Similarity scores shown in the status bar (~ 7.0 % , ~ 27.4% ) are very low.

The Align Sequences Protocol allows use of secondary structure information to improve the quality of the alignment. Secondary structure prediction methods, such as DSC, are based on the solvent exposure patterns of globular proteins. A large part of the surface of transmembrane proteins is exposed to the hydrocarbon environment of the membrane interior, rather than water. This results in a different pattern of hydrophilic and hydrophobic residues in the amino acid sequence which causes standard secondary structure prediction methods to become unreliable. In this tutorial the TransMem method, which is designed to predict helical regions in transmembrane proteins, is used.

Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools. Click Predict Transmembrane Helices .

This adds secondary structure cartoons in the ADRB1_HUMAN Sequence Window. Notice that the TRANSMEM prediction for 2rh1 has a long region (residues A:ASN1002-A:TYR1161 ) for which TRANSMEM predicts no helical regions. This region corresponds to the sequence of lysozyme, which was fused into the beta-2-adrenergic receptor in order to facilitate crystallization. Standard structure prediction methods will predict secondary structure in this region. Such a large insertion will confound the alignment algorithm if secondary structure predictions are used to guide the alignment.

Open the Macromolecules | Align Sequences and Structures tools and click Align Sequences... to open the Align Sequences dialog. Verify that the Input Sequence Set parameter is set to ADRB1_HUMAN:All . Click the Use Secondary Structures parameter and choose TRANSMEM . Click Run and wait for the job to complete. When the job completes, the ADRB1_HUMAN Sequence Window is automatically updated with the sequence alignment and a dialog reports 
the Sequence Identity and Sequence Similarity scores (~ 42.1% , ~ 53.3% ) for the calculated alignment. Click OK to close the dialog.

The Sequence Identity and Sequence Similarity scores (~ 42.1% , ~ 53.3% ) are
now higher. You should also note that there are now more residues
colored dark turquoise, indicating strong similarity in those
regions.

Open the Macromolecules | Create Homology Models tools and click Build Homology Models... to open the Build Homology Models dialog. Click the Input Sequence Alignment parameter
and choose ADRB1_HUMAN:All from the list. Click the Input Template Structures parameter and select 2rh1 . Click the Input Model Sequence parameter and choose ADRB1_HUMAN . Expand the Copy From Templates parameter. Click the Ligands parameter and check 2rh1:A:CLR412 , 2rh1:A:CLR413 , 2rh1:A:CLR414 , and 2rh1:A:PLM415 .

This will copy palmitic acid and cholesterol molecules from the template to the model. These molecules help in determining the position of the membrane with respect to the model structure.

Click the Number of Models parameter and change the value to 1 . Click the Optimization Level parameter and choose Low .

Changing the Optimization Level parameter from the default setting allows the protocol to run faster, but the resulting model is less accurate.

Click Run and wait for the job to
complete. When the job is complete, the model opens in a Molecule Window named ADRB1_HUMAN and a separate dialog reports the PDF Total Energy of the model. Click OK to close the dialog box.

Discovery Studio provides tools to add and manipulate an implicit membrane to a structure. The position of this membrane can be used in simulation protocols to specify solvation properties in implicit solvent models.

From the menu bar, choose Edit | Preferences... to display the Preferences dialog. In the Transmembrane Protein page, verify that the value for the Membrane Thickness is set to 30 Å. Click OK to close the Preferences dialog.

The membrane thickness specified here refers to the hydrophobic region of the membrane, excluding the region occupied by the polar headgroups of the lipids.

Click the ADRB1_HUMAN Molecule Window tab to activate it. Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel. In the Create and Edit Membrane group, click Add .

This adds a membrane to the protein structure. The membrane is represented by two parallel planes in the Graphics View.

The Add command determines the position of the membrane by optimizing a very simple solvation model. It is optimized for speed rather than accuracy. Often the membrane position needs to be fine tuned.

Click the dropdown arrow of the Display Style button in the Standard toolbar. Select the second predefined display style so that the protein is rendered in ribbon and ligands are displayed as lines.

The cholesterol and palmitic acid molecules copied from the template are now visible in the Molecule Window.
Notice that the polar regions of the palmitic acid and cholesterol molecules lie inside the hydrophobic region of the membrane defined by the two planes. This indicates that the position of the membrane needs to be adjusted.

This can be done automatically by using the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol, which performs a full optimization of the membrane position using a Generalized Born solvation model. Since this computation requires more time than allotted for this tutorial, you will use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel to adjust the position of the membrane.

In the Hierarchy View, expand ADRB1_HUMAN.M0001 , then click chain A of the molecule to select it. In the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel,
in the Create and Edit Membrane group, click Add Orientation Monitor .

This adds a membrane orientation monitor to the ADRB1_HUMAN Molecule Window that indicates the shift as well as the tilt and rotation angle of the membrane with respect to the principal axis of the protein.

Click Modify... .

This opens the Edit Membrane dialog.

In the dialog, set Shift to 4.8 Å, Tilt to 15.5 degrees, and Rotation to 30.0 degrees. Click OK . Click anywhere in the Graphics View to de-select the protein.

This adjusts the position of the membrane such that the polar regions of the cholesterol and palmitic acid molecules come to lie outside the hydrophobic region of the membrane.
