# Working with Forcefield tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_typing.htm

## Working with Forcefield tools

Time: 15 minutes

### Introduction

In molecular mechanics simulations, an essential step is to first assign a forcefield to the input molecule. For novice users, the CHARMm forcefield with automatic parameter estimation can be used to automatically assign complete forcefield parameters for almost any type of molecule. However, advanced users may find it desirable to modify and define their own forcefield parameters for certain residues. In addition, some other forcefields, such as charmm19 or charmm27, do not have automatic parameter estimation capability built in, so you must create new residue and atom types for systems other than common biomolecular monomers. For these forcefields, nonstandard residues may not be assigned forcefield parameters successfully, and manual customization of the residues is necessary to ensure complete forcefield assignment of the molecule. In Discovery Studio , you can use Forcefield tools to help the customization of residues during the forcefield assignment process.

In this tutorial, you will learn how to apply the charmm27 forcefield to proteins containing HEME residues, which cannot be typed automatically by charmm27. The following tasks are covered:

* Applying charmm27 to a protein that contains a HEME residue

* Customizing the HEME residue

* Adding the customized HEME residue template to the charmm27 forcefield

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 1hho.pdb .

This opens the protein 1hho in the Molecule Window. The protein has an amino acid chain and a chain containing the HEME residue.

Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools. From the Forcefield list, choose charmm27 . Click Apply Forcefield .

This applies charmm27 forcefield to the 1hho protein. Since charmm27
does not contain all parameters necessary, the following message appears: "1hho could not be typed with the
current forcefield. See the Change Forcefield toolpanel for more information."

Click OK to dismiss the message.

The Forcefield Status tool panel displays "1hho is not fully typed with 1hho-charmm27". This is because the charmm27 forcefield does not have a residue template for the HEME residue.

Click More... .

This brings up a Forcefield Window that details why 1hho cannot be fully typed with the charmm27 forcefield.

The Forcefield Window has two tabs: Residues and Atoms . The Residues tab lists all residues that cannot be typed by the standard residue template. For example, HEM143 is listed with a status of "No matching template" because it does not match any residue template of the charmm27 forcefield.

Click the Atoms tab.

The Atoms tab in the Forcefield Window lists all the atoms that do not have a forcefield type assigned. There are four atoms (NA, NB, NC, and ND) with a status of "Missing". Their forcefield type is unknown and listed as "?" in the table, as charmm27 forcefield failed to find an appropriate forcefield type for them.

Now you can modify the HEME residue so it can be completely typed by charmm27 for use in simulation protocols. Begin by hiding everything except the HEME residue.

You can drag the
tab of the Forcefield Window to the right side of
the application to display the Molecule Window and the
Forcefield Window side-by-side.

Click on the 1hho molecule window tab. Press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View if it is not already showing. Expand the second chain A and select the HEM143 residue under the chain. Right-click the Hierarchy View and choose Show Only .

Now only the HEME residue is shown in the Molecule Window.

Expand the HEM143 residue and select the NA, NB, NC, and ND atoms.
You can also make this selection by clicking the row numbers in the Atom tab of the Forcefield Window, which causes the corresponding items in the Molecule Window to be
selected, then click the Molecule Window tab to make it active again.

These are the four atoms in the Atoms tab of the Forcefield Window that do not have a forcefield type.

From the Forcefield Customization group of the Change Forcefield tool panel, click Modify Atom Type .

This opens the Choose a Forcefield Type dialog. This dialog allows you to either assign an existing or new forcefield type to the selected atoms.

Choose NPH as the Forcefield type for the four atoms, and then click OK .

In the Choose a Forcefield Type dialog, the Description field for type NPH is "heme pyrrole N", which matches the chemical environment for the four nitrogen atoms.

Alternatively, you may also define a new atom type by filling in the Type and Description fields.

If you think the assigned atom type is incorrect, or you want to use your own parameters, you can choose a different forcefield type or define a new atom type for any atoms in the molecule. You can also modify the partial charges for the atoms in the Atoms tab.

Now all atoms have an assigned forcefield type and the Forcefield tool will automatically calculate the forcefield parameters needed for the molecule. Please check the Forcefield Window for any missing or estimated parameters that are not in the original forcefield.

The Forcefield Status tool panel now shows "1hho typed with 1hho-charmm27" since all atoms have forcefield type assigned, and all parameters are either provided or estimated by the charmm27 forcefield.

In the Forcefield Window, each of the four atoms in the Atoms tab now have the forcefield type as NPH . Notice that the Forcefield Window now has a few more tabs. In the Bonds , Angles , Torsions , and Improper tabs, estimated parameters associated with the HEME residue are listed. You can either accept these estimated parameters as is, or modify them appropriately based on other sources, such as accurate quantum mechanical calculations.

Once all parameters are acceptable, you can use the 1hho protein with charmm27 forcefield as input to Simulation protocols such as Minimization, or Standard Dynamics Cascade.

Once you have modified the HEME residue, you can also add it as part of your own forcefield library, so you do not have to manually assign the missing atom types each time when applying the charmm27 forcefield to HEME containing proteins.

In the Hierarchy View of the typed 1hho protein, select the HEM143 residue. From the Change Forcefield tool panel, click Add Residue Template in the Forcefield Customization group.

This adds the HEME residue template along with any estimated parameters to your forcefield library.
You can now use the template to type any other HEME containing proteins by charmm27 forcefield in the future.

You can check the residue template file (HEM143.rtf) and parameter file (HEM143.prm) for the HEME residue under your user's forcefield folder. The folder is stored in:

```text
<Settings Folder>/Forcefield/charmm27
```

For details about locations of folders in different operating systems, see Installation folders .

If you are an advanced user who is familiar with the CHARMm file format, you can manually modify the RTF files under your Forcefield folder. You can also copy any new RTF and PRM files that are compatible with the corresponding forcefield to this folder. Any residue templates and parameter files placed under this folder will be used by the Forcefield engine after restarting the application. Be aware that a residue template will only be matched if the atom labels, order, and bonds of the residue are exactly the same as the RTF file.

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Simulation | 2hhb.pdb . From the Tools Explorer , click Apply Forcefield to apply the charmm27 forcefield.

The typing now complete without any messages and the Forcefield Status now displays "2hhb typed with 2hhb-charmm27".

Although the HEME residue could not be typed by the original charmm27 forcefield, this molecule is now typed successfully because HEM has been added to the charmm27 forcefield's residue template library in the previous step. The Residues tab lists these as Matches custom template in the Status column of the Forcefield Window.

# Working with ZDOCK

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tut_zdock.htm

## Working with ZDOCK

Time: 1 hour 30 minutes.

### Background

ZDOCK is a rigid-body protein-protein docking algorithm based
on the Fast Fourier Transform correlation technique that is used
to explore the rotational and translational space of a
protein-protein system. RDOCK is a CHARMm-based energy
minimization procedure for refining and scoring docked poses
using energy scoring functions.

### Introduction

In this tutorial, you will perform protein docking with ZDOCK,
analyze the docked poses, and refine a set of selected poses with
RDOCK. A bovine beta-trypsin structure (PDB ID 2ptn) will be used
as the receptor protein, and a trypsin inhibitor CMTI-I (PDB ID
2sta, I chain) as the ligand protein. The X-ray crystal structure
of the bovine beta-trypsin and inhibitor CMTI-I protein complex
is known (PDB ID 1ppe).

This tutorial covers:

* Setting up a ZDOCK run

* Analyzing ZDOCK results

* Refining docked poses with RDOCK

* Analyzing the binding interface residues using RMSD

Choose File | Open... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | 2ptn.pdb .

This opens the protein in a new Molecule Window.

Choose File | Insert From | File... from the menu bar and open Samples | Tutorials | Protein Modeling | 2sta_I.pdb . If the new molecule is not visible, go to the Hierarchy View and click the checkbox next to 2sta_I to make the molecule visible.
If the two molecules are not both fully in view, reset the view using View | Transform | Fit To Screen . Open the Macromolecules | Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools and click Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)... to open the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) dialog. Set Input Receptor Protein to 2ptn:2ptn . Set Input Ligand Protein to 2ptn:2sta_I . Click the Angular Step Size and set the value to 15 .

ZDOCK can
run with two Euler angle sampling sizes: 6 degrees or 15
degrees. The 6 degrees search provides more accurate
predictions because it samples 54,000 poses. Although the 15
degrees search is not as accurate because it samples only
3,600 poses, it finishes faster than the 6 degrees search. For this tutorial, the speed of the protocol run is more important than sampling size.

Expand the Clustering parameter group. Click the RMSD Cutoff parameter and enter 6.0 for
the value. Click the Interface Cutoff parameter and enter 9.0 for
the value. Click the Maximum Number of
Clusters parameter and enter 60 for the value.

For this small protein inhibitor, a small cluster radius
of 6.0 Å for the RMSD Cutoff and a smaller Interface Cutoff of 9.0 Å produces better
clustering results. In this tutorial, a single processor
ZDOCK job is performed without specifying blocked residues or
filtering binding site residues.

Set the ZRank parameter to False .

The ZRank option can be used to rerank initial-stage ZDOCK predictions with detailed electrostatics, van der Waals, and desolvation energy terms. We will not make use of this functionality in this tutorial. For more details on ZRank, see Rerank Docked Proteins (ZRANK) .

ZDOCK can
be run with blocking and/or filtering options: If there is evidence that suggests certain residues are not likely to
appear in the protein-protein interface, select those
residues on the receptor protein, and then set the Receptor Blocked Residues parameter
to Create New Group from selection . Similarly, select residues to be blocked on
the ligand protein for input in the Ligand Blocked Residues parameter. If there is evidence that suggests that certain residues would appear in the
protein-protein interface, select them. Then expand the Filter Poses parameter group and set
the Receptor Binding Site Residues parameter and the Ligand Binding Site
Residues parameter to Create New Group from selection . The Filter Poses function can also
be performed separately after a ZDOCK run, using the Process
Poses (ZDOCK) protocol.

Click Run to start the job and observe the job status displayed in a dialog.
Click Background to send the job to background.
You can continue to monitor the progress of the job in
the Jobs Explorer . When the run finishes, double click on the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report.htm . Review the Summary section of the report and click View Results to open the docking poses in a Molecule Window.

Begin by visualizing the clustering of poses. The input receptor and ligand proteins are shown in the Graphics View.

If the view is not centered to show both proteins, choose View | Toolbars | View if necessary to display the View toolbar, and click Fit To Screen on the view toolbar. The top ranking pose of each cluster is displayed as a dot surrounding the receptor protein. In the Hierarchy View, expand Docked Poses and Clusters .

This displays the groups of clusters and poses. Cluster_1 is the largest cluster, followed by progressively smaller
clusters.

In the Hierarchy View, close the Docked Poses and Clusters groups.
In the Data Table, click the ProteinPose tab.

This displays the following data from the ZDOCK run:

* ZDock Score - contains the ZDOCK score (PSC scoring
function) of each pose. Pose1 has the highest (best) ZDOCK
score.

* Cluster - contains the cluster group number for each
pose.

* ClusterSize - reports the size (number of poses) of a
cluster.

* Density - represents the number of neighboring poses within the Clustering | RMSD Cutoff distance.

For details about the clustering algorithm, see Clustering and analysis of docked protein poses .

The following steps illustrate several ways to use plots
and the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools to help view the poses and select a smaller number of
ZDOCK poses for further RDOCK refinement.

In the Macromolecules | Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools,
set Browse to Top Poses in Largest Clusters .

This shows the 100 best scoring poses in the 10 largest clusters.

Click the first arrow to show the ligand molecule of the first pose.

This creates a ligand molecule with the name Pose1_Cluster2_2sta_I to indicate the pose number and the cluster number of the pose.

In the Calculate Ligand Interface RMSD group, click Calculate Binding Site RMSD .

This adds a column named RMSD to Pose1_Cluster2_2sta_I to the ProteinPose tab, which shows the RMSD of each ligand pose
to the defined ligand pose. The RMSD values are calculated based on the binding site residues from 
the ligand molecule of the defined ligand pose. Note that Define Ligand is automatically set to the name of this first pose.

Click Select Binding Interface .

This selects the receptor and ligand binding interface
residues and you can visually inspect the residues on the binding interface.

Click Lock Visibility to keep the ligand molecule of this pose and visible while clicking through the poses. Click to view the ligand molecule of the next pose, which
is pose 3 in cluster 2.

Observe that this pose is similar to the first pose.

Click twice to show Pose7_Cluster5_2sta_I .

Observe that this pose docks to a similar location on the receptor, but the docking interface
on the ligand is differs substantially.

Continue to click to browse other poses and click Lock Visibility to keep the ligand
molecule of the poses that you want to keep. In the Data Table, click the ProteinPose tab to make it active. Right-click and choose List Only Visible Objects . From the menu bar, choose Chart | Point Plot .

This opens the Choose Plot Axes dialog.

On the dialog, choose ZDock Score for the X
axis and Cluster for the Y axis . Click the OK button.

This opens a 2D Point Plot. It is clear from the plot that cluster 2 contains most top ranking poses (i.e., poses with best
ZDock Scores).

Click the ZDockResults Point Plot tab and drag the window so that you can also view the ZDockResults Molecule Window side by side. In the View toolbar, click the Select tool and lasso the
poses that have Zdock score higher than 12.0 in the plot.

This selects 11 poses, 5 poses in cluster 2, 4 poses in cluster 1, 1 pose each in cluster 3 and 5. 
The poses you select in the plot are also selected in
the Molecule Window.

Click on ZDockResults Molecule Window tab to make it active while retaining the selection. Open the Macromolecules | Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools and click Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK)... to open the Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK) dialog. Click the Input Receptor Protein parameter and choose ZDockResults:2ptn from the list. Click the Input Ligand Protein parameter and choose ZDockResults:2sta_I from the list. Click the Input Poses parameter and choose Create New Group From Selection... from the list.

The new group is named Group by default and includes the 11 poses selected previously.

Leave the Dielectric Constant parameter set to 4.0 . This will be the dielectric
value used in the RDOCK CHARMm energy calculation.

Click Run to start the job and observe the job status displayed in the dialog.

When the job finishes, double click on the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report.htm . In the Results section, click View Results .

Refined poses appear in a Molecule Window with the top refined 
pose visible in the Graphics View and the energies 
calculated by RDOCK for all the refined poses listed in the Data Table View:

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| E_elec1 and E_elec2 | The electrostatic energy of the protein complex after the first and second CHARMm minimizations. |
| E_vdw1 and E_vdw2 | van der Waals nonbond energy of the protein complex after the first and second CHARMm minimizations. |
| E_sol | The desolvation energy of the protein complex calculated by the ACE method. |
| E_RDock | The RDOCK score defined as: E_sol + beta × E_elec2 . |

The table also contains properties of the poses from the ZDOCK run, such as the ZDock Score and the clustering information, which can be helpful in interpreting the results.

The poses with the best RDock score are from cluster 2, then cluster 1, followed by the remaining clusters. This confirms that poses in
cluster 2 are the best docking poses and are likely to be near native docking conformation.

The RDock score may differ when the calculation is run on different platforms.

Use the Navigation Keys to the left of the Data Table View to navigate through the structures of the docked poses.

Check the
pose checkbox in the Hierarchy View to turn the molecule
display on or off in the Graphics View.

In this section, you will compare docked poses with the
crystal structure of the protein complex PDB 1ppe.

Click on the Poses Molecule Window tab to activate it. From the menu bar, choose File | Insert From | URL... .

This opens the Insert From URL dialog.

Enter 1ppe in the ID textbox. Check that Site is set to Default RCSB Structures . Click the Open button.

This inserts the protein complex in the Graphics View of the Poses Molecule Window.

Right-click in the Poses Molecule Window and choose Show All to show all poses. In the Hierarchy View, expand <Cell> , then expand 1PPE . Click Water to select it, and then click Delete .

This removes the water chain from 1PPE.

Before running the RMSD calculation, the poses and 1PPE
should be superimposed based on the receptor protein.

Right-click in the Graphics View and choose Show Sequence from the list.

This opens a Sequence Window.

Click the Poses Molecule Window tab to make the window active. In the Hierarchy View, click on chain E of 1PPE to select it.

This selects the receptor chain of 1PPE.

Open the Macromolecules | Superimpose Proteins tools. Click Reference Protein to choose the selected chain of 1PPE as reference for the superposition. Set Superimpose by to Sequence Alignment .
Note that Sequence Alignment is set to Poses by default. In the Molecule Window, check that the 1PPE receptor chain E is
still selected. In the Superimpose Proteins tool panel
click Superimpose .

This will superimpose the receptor chains of the docked poses onto chain E of 1PPE.

Select chain I from protein 1PPE from the hierarchy view. In the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tool panel, click Define Ligand . Click Select Binding Interface .

This selects the interface residues.

Finally, calculate the binding interface
residues RMSD values.

From the menu bar, choose Structure | RMSD | By Sequence
Alignment... .

This opens the RMSD by Sequence Alignment dialog.

On the dialog, set Reference molecule to 1PPE . Click the Selected residues radio
button. Clear the Report at
residue level checkbox. Click OK .

This opens the RMSD Report using the selected residues for
poses in an Html Window.

Compare the E_RDock scores of the docked poses with the
RMSD values in the RMSD report. The poses with the lowest RMSD
also have the lowest (best) E_RDock scores; all are in cluster 2.

Macromolecules Working with protocols

# Tutorials

Source type: HTML

Source section: applicationtutorials

Source file: applicationtutorials/tutorials.htm

## Tutorials

To begin using Discovery Studio Visualizer, work through the following Quick start tutorials. They provide a good foundation for working with various parts of the application:

Tutorials are available in the following areas:

* Quick Start

* Macromolecules

* Simulation

* Receptor-Ligand Interactions

* Pharmacophores

* Small Molecules

* Advanced Tutorials

BIOVIA offers a wide range of training workshops. See BIOVIA Product Training for details.

| Category | Tutorial | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quick Start tutorials | Introduction to the Discovery Studio Client | Basic overview of key concepts and how to work with basic features. |
| Opening and editing a molecular structure | Overview of working with protein structure data. | |
| Working with small molecule data sets | Introduces the basic features of the Molecule Window and demonstrates some of its broader capabilities. | |
| Working with protein structures and sequences | Overview of functionality that enables you to gain insights into a structure's function by looking at its sequence. The tutorial also covers the use of the Ramachandran Plot. | |
| Superimposing protein structures | Learn how to superimpose a set of proteins based on their sequence alignment. | |
| Opening and editing sequence alignments | Learn how to manually edit sequence alignment of three highly homologous protein sequences. | |
| Using the storyboard feature to create a movie | Create and edit scenes and share a movie with colleagues. | |
| Creating charts | Use a sample set of drug molecules with precalculated properties to generate a Point Plot, 3D Point Plot, and Heat Map. | |
| Working with scripts | Learn how to write and execute scripts to control Discovery Studio . | |
| Macromolecules | Creating homology models from a protein sequence | Use an extracellular amylase protein to create a homology model by aligning and superimposing the templates using structure alignment methods. |
| Modeling transmembrane proteins | Demonstrates a workflow for constructing a homology model of the beta-1-adrenergic receptor based on the recently solved X-ray structure for the beta-2-adrenergic receptor. | |
| Working with ZDOCK | Perform protein docking with ZDOCK, analyze the docked poses, and refine a set of selected poses with RDOCK. | |
| Finding orphan sequences using phylogenetics | Open and perform a BLAST sequence similarity search, perform a multiple sequence alignment, and use bootstrap analysis of a phylogenetic tree to identify orphan sequences | |
| Calculating protein ionization and residue pK | Learn how to calculate the titration characteristics of a protein molecule and how to predict the pK values of the individual sites of titration on a lysozyme structure. | |
| Predict protein aggregation sites | Learn how to calculate protein aggregation scores and analyze aggregation sites. | |
| Creating a 3D model of an antibody Fv domain from a sequence | Demonstrates the workflow to create a 3D model of an antibody fragment variable (Fv) domain and refine its CDR loops from an antibody sequence. | |
| Humanizing an antibody Fv sequence | Learn how to predict mutations for antibody humanization. | |
| Simulation | Working with Forcefield tools | Learn how to apply the charmm27 forcefield to proteins containing HEME residues, which cannot be typed automatically by charmm27. |
| Preparing and analyzing an explicit solvation molecular dynamics simulation | Learn how to solvate a protein in explicit water, run a dynamics simulation of the solvated system, and analyze the resulting trajectory. | |
| Adding an explicit membrane to a transmembrane protein | Demonstrates adding an explicit membrane to a transmembrane protein and analyzing the results. | |
| Assigning Forcefield Types | Learn how to use the Assign Forcefield protocol to type more complicated structures. | |
| Calculate binding energy using steered molecular dynamics | Learn how to use the Steered Molecular Dynamics protocol and the subsequent analysis protocol Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces to estimate the free energy of ligand binding. | |
| Calculating relative binding free energies with alchemical free energy perturbation | Learn how to calculate the relative ligand binding free energies with FEP. | |
| Calculate relative binding free energies using Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics | Assess ligands in late-stage lead optimization with Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) simulation tools. | |
| Calculating relative binding free energies with OpenFE alchemical free energy perturbation | Learn how to calculate the relative ligand binding free energies with FEP using OpenFE. | |
| Preparing and analyzing a Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics simulation | Learn how to perform and analyze enhanced sampling simulations with Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulation tools. | |
| Analyzing allosteric motion with Analyze Trajectory tools | Learn how to identify potential allosteric pathways using cross-comparison analysis of molecular dynamics trajectory features. | |
| Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Visualizing non-bond interactions and evaluating results | Learn how to use the non-bond interaction tools. |
| Analyze ligand poses | Learn how to run the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol to calculate and analyze non-bonded interactions between a receptor and a set of docked ligands. | |
| Preparing a receptor binding site | Learn how to find binding sites and define a search sphere. | |
| Ligand docking with LibDock | Dock a set of ligands into the thymidine kinase receptor. | |
| Ligand docking with CDOCKER | Dock a random conformation of the native ibuprofen ligand into the COX-1 receptor binding site. | |
| Docking into a flexible receptor | Learn how to dock a ligand into a receptor with flexible amino acid side-chains using the Flexible Docking protocol. | |
| Fragment docking using MCSS | Dock ibuprofen fragments into the COX-1 receptor binding site. | |
| Fragment docking using De Novo Receptor | Investigate the inhibition of the cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2), a positive regulator of eukaryotic cell cycle progression, using a De Novo method. | |
| Fragment docking using De Novo Link | | |
| Fragment docking using De Novo Evolution | | |
| Optimizing lead compounds from a scaffold in a protein active site | Perform lead optimization for a member of the well characterized mitogen activated protein kinase family of serine/threonine protein kinases using the Grow Scaffold protocol. | |
| Scaffold hopping to identify replacement fragments for lead optimization | Use Replace Fragment to identify replacement fragments for lisinopril, the third angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor introduced into therapy after captopril and enalapril. | |
| Optimizing and running a docking validation for a virtual screening target | Learn how to run a virtual screening experiment using CDOCKER. | |
| Pharmacophores | Creating a structure-based fragment pharmacophore to optimize a scaffold | Optimize a scaffold in a protein active site using a fragment pharmacophore method where the pharmacophore features will be derived from information about the original bound crystal structure ligand and known interacting protein residues. |
| Creating and validating a common feature pharmacophore | Use a training set of six active ligands to derive common feature pharmacophores for lead identification. | |
| Creating and validating a 3D QSAR pharmacophore | Use a training set of ligands with activity values to derive 3D QSAR pharmacophore models for prediction. | |
| Generating ensemble pharmacophores from large data sets | Demonstrates using the Ensemble Pharmacophore Generation protocol to generate an ensemble pharmacophore, rescue a failed cluster, and use the ensemble pharmacophore for virtual screening. | |
| Generating interaction pharmacophores from a protein-ligand complex | Demonstrates using the Interaction Pharmacophore Generation protocol to generate interaction pharmacophores and modify parameters to improve performance. | |
| Creating a structure-based pharmacophore to screen a ligand library | Use a known or suspected active site of a protein to select compounds that are likely to bind within that site using the Structure-Based Pharmacophore (SBP) method. | |
| Creating customized pharmacophore features | Learn how to customize pharmacophore features using the Customize Pharmacophore Features tool panel by modifying an pharmacophore feature. | |
| Creating pharmacophore queries | Learn how to build a basic pharmacophore starting from a single conformation of a ligand. | |
| Small Molecules | Working with ADMET | Learn how to run a ADMET Descriptors protocol and how to analyze the results. |
| Generating conformations using the toolbar | Learn how to use the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel to generate conformations. | |
| Working with library analysis tools | Learn how to perform a selection of compounds that are similar to a known lead compound. | |
| Working with library design tools | Learn how to select a diverse subset of ligands from a combinatorial library and optimize that selection for diversity and some Lipinski properties. | |
| Bayesian categorization | Use Bayesian categorization to create a QSAR model to predict the activity of a molecule as a pyruvate kinase inhibitor, and then use the model to predict the activity of some test molecules. | |
| Recursive partitioning | Learn how to create a recursive partitioning model using a training set of pyruvate kinase inhibitors, and then use the model to predict the activity class of some new compounds. | |
| Working with QSAR - 3D QSAR | Build a Partial Least-Squares (PLS) model using energy grids as descriptors. | |
| Understanding SAR and activity cliffs using matched molecular pairs and Free-Wilson analysis | Identify the activity cliffs using matched molecular pairs in the dataset and then optionally perform a Free Wilson analysis to generate new prioritized ligands to synthesize. | |
| Understanding SAR Trends using matched molecular pairs | Study a library of diverse ligands with cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitory data to identify what structural trends can be observed, to guide molecular design, and to aid decision making in the lead optimization process. | |
| Advanced tutorials | Creating a tool panel | Create a tool panel that exposes all the steps necessary to generate a set of conformations, calculate their RMSDs relative to the starting molecule, and plot the results. |
| Customizing an existing protocol | Use the Pipeline Pilot Client to customize an existing protocol. | |
| Creating a custom protocol - Calculate Molecular Properties | Illustrates how this protocol can be combined using the lowest energy conformation from an existing Catalyst database. | |

# Working with charts

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/chart.htm

## Working with charts

Discovery Studio allows you to create a rich variety of charts from numerical data generated
within the application. All charts are fully interactive with their source data, allowing you to
explore the origin of particular data points (e.g., outliers), and investigate the relationship 
between different points within the data.

### Common charts

The following table summarizes the different chart types that can be generated within Discovery
Studio:

| Chart Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Line Plot | Displays data points as a series of connected/disconnected line segments in a two-dimensional area |
| Point Plot | (Also called a scatter plot). Compares two or more sets of related quantitative data by plotting points in a 2D area |
| 3D Point Plot | Compares three or more sets of related quantitative data by plotting points in a 3D area |
| Histogram | A bar chart that shows the distribution of data. |
| Bar Chart | Displays data using rectangular bars with lengths that are proportional to the values they represent. |
| Heat Map | Represents values in a two-dimensional color map |
| Hit Rate Plot | Specialized plot useful in analyzing results from docking/scoring protocols where control ligands (i.e., ligands known to have significant binding affinity to the target receptor) have been specified along with a set of input ligands |
| Ramachandran Plot | Indicates low energy conformations for Φ (phi) and Ψ (psi), the conventional terms used to represent the torsion angles on either side of alpha carbons in peptides |
| Hydrophobicity Plot | Plots amino acids in a protein against their hydrophobicity index |
| Contact Plot | Shows the relationship between pairs of residues in a protein structure |
| Dendrogram | Tree diagram used to illustrate the arrangement of the clusters produced by a clustering algorithm |

You can customize many of the plot attributes including the data
associated with each axis, the color of most of the graphical
elements, the range of the axes, and the legends.

In addition, the Chart Window is highly interactive,
allowing you to select, zoom, and reposition a plot. Any selection
made in a Chart Window is reflected in any other view or window opened with the same data.

See Mouse and keyboard actions to learn how to work with charts efficiently.

#### Further information

# Context menu - Files Explorer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/contextmenu_file.htm

## Context menu - Files Explorer

The context menus for the Files Explorer are accessed by right-clicking a file or a folder 
in the Files Explorer. Both the file and the folder context menu contain commands found on the Edit menu 
(Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete) and on the File menu (Properties). The commands unique to the Files Explorer 
context menu are described in this topic.

### Context menu - files

When you right-click a file in the Files Explorer, the context menu contains the following unique commands:

Open: Opens the file in the current window.

Refresh: Updates the contents of the Files Explorer.

Open With: Opens the file into a specific window type. This option is only available for file types that 
are ambiguous and can contain data that can be handled in different ways (e.g. .dat files).

Rename: Makes the file name of the selected file editable. Type the new file name over the highlighted file 
name and press ENTER.

### Context menu - folders

When you right-click a folder in the Files Explorer, the context menu contains the following unique commands:

Add Root Node...: Sets a top-level root folder that provides access to defined storage locations accessible 
from your computer. For more information about adding root folders, see Mounting a folder 
as root .

Set Default: Sets the selected folder as the default location for saving data files. A blue triangle appears on 
the top right corner of the folder icon to indicate that this folder is now the default.

New Folder: Displays the New Folder dialog , which allows you to create and 
name a new subfolder within the selected folder.

### Context menu - root folders

When you right-click a root folder in the Files Explorer, the context menu contains the following unique commands:

Remove Root: Removes the root folder from the Files Explorer.

### Undo / Redo Support

Some of the commands of the File Explorer context menu support the Undo/Redo feature. To Undo/Redo a command, use the Edit menu. The commands that support Undo/Redo are:

* Set default folder

* Add root node

* Remove root

* Copy/Paste

* Cut/Paste

* Rename

* New Folder

# Create and view storyboards

Source type: HTML

## Create and view storyboards

You can use storyboards to save, navigate, manage, and animate multiple views of the same structure. You can access the storyboard options from the View | Storyboard menu. Storyboards are saved in .dsv files.

The following actions are supported:

| To | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Add scenes | Open a structure in the Molecule Window. Adjust the display style and position to the first scene you want to add. Press INSERT. The Storyboard dialog opens with the first scene displayed in a thumbnail. Continue adjusting the view and adding scenes as desired. If you capture a scene while an animation is playing or while the structure is spinning, the action is saved with the scene. |
| Rename or delete scenes | From the Storyboard dialog , right-click the scene you want to rename or remove and choose Rename or Delete <scene name> . |
| Rearrange scenes | From the Storyboard dialog , click and drag the thumbnails as desired. |
| Animate scenes | From the Storyboard dialog , click the Play button. You can check the Loop option to play the animation continuously. To change the transition length between scenes, or time paused at each scene, click More and set the Transition and Pause time (in seconds) as desired. Select all of the scenes before setting the values to apply them to all scenes. |
| Export storyboard as a movie | From the Storyboard dialog , click Export Movie to create a .webm file. For details, see Export and use storyboard movies . |
| Open the dialog automatically | You can enable the dialog to open automatically whenever you open a dsv file that has a storyboard. From the Storyboard dialog , choose Show this dialog automatically . |
| Navigate scenes | Use the options in the View \| Storyboard menu or open the Storyboard dialog and click individual thumbnails. When using the Storyboard dialog, you can press CTRL + HOME to return to the first scene. |

* Open a structure in the Molecule Window.

* Adjust the display style and position to the first scene you want to add.

* Press INSERT. The Storyboard dialog opens with the first scene displayed in a thumbnail.

* Continue adjusting the view and adding scenes as desired.

If you capture a scene while an animation is playing or while the structure is spinning, the action is saved with the scene.

* From the Storyboard dialog , click the Play button. You can check the Loop option to play the animation continuously.

* To change the transition length between scenes, or time paused at each scene, click More and set the Transition and Pause time (in seconds) as desired. Select all of the scenes before setting the values to apply them to all scenes.

When using the Storyboard dialog, you can press CTRL + HOME to return to the first scene.

# Customizing protocols

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/custom_protocols.htm

## Customizing protocols

With access to the Pipeline Pilot Client and Discovery Studio , you can
take advantage of the combined capabilities of the two products
to customize existing protocols or create entirely new ones. To learn more about this functionality, see About Pipeline Pilot .

This topic discusses basic information specific to working with custom protocols in Discovery Studio and extensively covers modifying parameters. More detailed help is available in the Pipeline Pilot Help Center . Additionally, the following tutorials walk you through creating and customizing protocols:

* Creating a custom protocol - Calculate Molecular Properties

* Customizing an existing protocol

The following subjects are covered in this topic:

* Protocol basics

* Pipeline Pilot help

* Protocol folders

* Modifying protocols

* Working with parameters

* Discovery Studio custom parameter types

* Reserved parameter names

Protocols are composed of components connected by pipes. A basic protocol begins with components that read data from a source. These components then send the data through pipes that connect to various filter and data processing components that are arranged to complete the desired task. Writer and viewer components are placed at the end to output the results. The following is an example of a simple pipeline:

You can customize protocols in the Pipeline Pilot Professional Client by adding or removing components and/or exposing or changing parameters and their default values.

Pipeline Pilot has an extensive help system. Although this topic covers the basics with regards to modifying Discovery Studio protocols, it is recommended you refer to the Pipeline Pilot help for details.

You can access the help from the Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server Home Page. Enter the following as an address in your browser: http://hostname:port , where hostname is the name of the host machine for the Pipeline Pilot server you want to access and port is the port number that Pipeline Pilot has been configured to use. In a default installation, the following link will open the Pipeline Pilot homepage: https://localhost:9943 . From there, click the Help Center (Client Users) link.

Protocols are available from the Protocols Explorer and are organized into two folders: "Discovery Studio" and "<user name>'s protocols". The Discovery Studio folder contains the standard Discovery Studio protocols which are available to all users. The <user name> protocols are protocols that you have customized using the Pipeline Pilot Professional Client and are only available to you.

The protocols that are installed into the Discovery Studio folder cannot be updated. However, you can make a copy of an existing protocol and customize it as needed before exposing it in Discovery Studio . You can also use one of the example protocols available from the Pipeline Pilot Client .

To customize a protocol in Pipeline Pilot
Professional Client

* Open the protocol in Pipeline Pilot: In Discovery Studio , navigate to the protocol you want to customize in the Protocols Explorer and choose View Protocol . Note that you need to specify a Pipeline Pilot Client Setting path to the client in the Protocols page - Preferences dialog . From the Pipeline Pilot Client , use the Protocols Explorer to navigate to the protocol you want to customize and double-click it. You can also use the Search protocol database feature to quickly find a protocol.

* In Discovery Studio , navigate to the protocol you want to customize in the Protocols Explorer and choose View Protocol . Note that you need to specify a Pipeline Pilot Client Setting path to the client in the Protocols page - Preferences dialog .

* From the Pipeline Pilot Client , use the Protocols Explorer to navigate to the protocol you want to customize and double-click it. You can also use the Search protocol database feature to quickly find a protocol.

* Make changes to parameters as described below in Working with Parameters. You can also make more complex customizations by adding and removing components. For details, refer to the Pipeline Pilot Help.

* Save the protocol with a new name.

#### Exposing and Hiding Parameters

Components generally have many parameters that affect how they manipulate data.
However, only a limited number of the parameters are exposed in the Parameters
Explorer (i.e., promoted to the protocol) when you run the protocol in Discovery Studio .
With the Pipeline Pilot Professional Client, you can
choose to expose hidden parameters to increase the flexibility, or hide them
to make them easier to use.
For details about how to expose component parameters by promoting them to the
protocol level, search for "Promoting Parameters" in the Pipeline Pilot help.

#### Default Parameter Values

In some circumstances, it may be useful to modify parameters in one of the Discovery Studio protocols (e.g., a particular project involves repeatedly analyzing data with a protocol initialized with a set of non-default parameters). You can do this from Discovery Studio by changing the parameter values as desired and then right-clicking and choosing Save Protocol Settings. However, these default values are only available to you.

If you want to set different default values for a protocol and make the protocol
with the new default values available to everyone, you can make a copy of the
protocol and set the default values as desired.
You can then expose the custom protocol in the Discovery Studio folder to share with everyone or add it to your <user name>'s protocols folder as discussed in Modifying Protocols above.

#### Custom Parameter Types

Parameters in Pipeline Pilot Professional Client are classified by specific types such as StringType, LongType, DoubleType, BoolType, URLType, etc., which can be used in Discovery Studio . In addition to this set, Discovery Studio also provides an enhanced level of integration with Pipeline Pilot protocols through the use of custom parameter types. These additional types provide an enhanced interface when opened in Discovery Studio . For example, a parameter of LigandsType allows you to select a Molecule Window, or an .sd file, and will convert the selection to a URL.

You can see the type of an existing parameter by selecting it in the Parameters Explorer and viewing the help in the Parameter Help Explorer.

Generally, you do not need to modify these custom types. The parameter types are already set in the Discovery Studio components, and are inherited when promoting parameters to the protocol level. For example, if you add the DS Ligand Reader component to a protocol and promote the Source parameter, then you will automatically inherit the LigandsType parameter in the Discovery Studio user interface. However, if you want to create a new component that uses one or more Discovery Studio parameter types, you must manually specify the parameter type in your component and promote it to the protocol level (as shown below).

There are two ways to specify a custom type in Pipeline Pilot Professional Client. You can set the parameter type in the Pipeline Pilot Professional Client directly, or you can specify a custom Discovery Studio type by adding an additional comment to the parameter help text. For example adding the following line to the help text will set the parameter to a Discovery Studio URL type.

```text
<!-- <DSClientParameterType=URLType> -->
```

For other Discovery Studio types please replace the URLType in the above example with one of the types shown in the table below. When working with custom parameter types, it is important to ensure that both the interface and the conversion to a standard Pipeline Pilot parameter type meets the users' needs.

The table below lists some of the commonly used customized parameter types in Discovery Studio . If you want to use them in a custom protocol, we suggest that you study the protocols that come with Discovery Studio to see how they are used. Additional customized types are available but are currently not documented.

Some parameters depend
on the values of others. These types contain the word "Of" (e.g., PropertiesOfLigands). If you have several
parameters with the same type, you can distinguish them by adding a numbered tag prefix (e.g., T1, T2, etc.). For example, if you make the type of one of the properties
"T1LigandsType" then a parameter of type "T1PropertiesOfLigandsType" will
depend on that one type, not on any other LigandsType properties you may
have defined in the protocol.

| Type | Editor | Converted Parameter value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copyurl | Select a file using the File Browser. The file is copied into the Input directory. | URL to the file |
| URL | Select a file using the File Browser. If the file is visible on the server, a link is created in the Input directory. Otherwise, the file is copied into the Input directory. | URL to the file or its copy |
| Alignment | Select from an open Sequence Window. Writes the sequences to a .bsml format file. | URL to the .bsml file containing the sequences |
| AtomgroupOfStructure | Select a Group defined in the same window as the Structure. | String containing a space separated list of the atom indices in the group. |
| Features | Select from a list of all pharmacophore feature types in the dictionary. | String containing a comma separated list of the selected features (the implementation parameter CustomDictionary will also be set to a URL to the dictionary file if the list contains a customized feature). |
| Ligands | Select all molecules in an open Molecule Window, or all molecules from an .sd format file. | URL to an .sd format file created from the window (if a file is selected, either a link or a copy is created following the same rules for a URL) |
| PropertiesOfLigands | Select multiple properties of the associated Ligands. If the Ligands are from a file, a simple text box is provided to enter the property names. | String containing an array of the selected properties |
| Proteinstructure | Select from a list of all protein molecules in all Molecule Windows. The selection is written to a .dsv format file. | URL to the .dsv file |
| Query | Select from a list of all pharmacophore queries in all Molecule Windows, or browse to a .ds_chm format file. Writes a .ds_chm format file to the Input directory if required. | URL to the .ds_chm file |
| ReceptorsphereOfStructure | Select a sphere in the same window as the associated structure. | String containing a comma separated list of the X, Y, Z coordinates, and the radius of the selected sphere |
| Structurewithforcefield | Select a molecule that has been successfully typed from a Molecule Window. Writes a .dsv file of the selected typed molecule to the Input directory. | URL to the .dsv file |
| Structure | Select from a list of all molecules in all Molecule Windows. Writes a .dsv format file for the selected molecule to the Input directory. | URL to the .dsv file |
| Aasequence | Select a sequence from all Sequence Windows. Writes out a .bsml format file that contains the selected amino acid sequence(s). | URL to the .bsml file |
| Nasequence | Select a sequence from all Sequence Windows. Writes a .bsml format file that contains the selected nucleotide sequences. | URL to the .bsml file |
| Numericproperty | Lists all numeric properties in a Molecule Window. | A string array with the selected numeric properties. |
| Property | Lists all properties in a Molecule Window. | A string array with the selected properties. |
| Proteinstructurewithforcefield | Select from a list of all typed protein molecules in every Molecule Window. The selection is written to a .dsv format file. | URL to the .dsv file |
| Structurewithconformations | Select from a list of all typed protein molecules that contain conformations. The selection is written to a .dsv format file. | URL to the .dsv file |
| Calculableproperties | Brings up a dialog with all calculable molecular properties. | A comma-separated list of selected molecular properties. |
| Constraint | Select one or more restraints/constraints from a list of all constraints and restraints defined using Setup Constraints tools . It also has option to bring up the file browsing dialog to select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. | A string that lists the restraint/constraint MDM object names and separated by comma. |
| Chains | Select one or more chains from a list of all chains in the selected molecule. | A string that lists all the selected chains defined as [molecule name]:[chain name]_[chain number] and separated by comma. |
| Centerofmass | Select either a molecule, a chain in a molecule, or a binding site defined using Define and Edit Binding Site tools . | A string of the molecule name, the chain name in form of [molecule name]:[chain name]_[chain number], or the coordinates of the center of the selected binding site. |
| Mutants | Brings up a dialog with selected or all residues from the selected protein molecule. Select some or all of the residues in the dialog and specify what type of residue to mutate into. | A string that lists all the mutations in the form: [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code][new residue name] and separated by comma. |
| MutantsMulti | Brings up a dialog with selected or all residues from the selected protein molecule. Select some or all of the residues in the dialog and specify what type of residues to mutate into. | A text that lists all the mutations in the form: [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code][greater than sign][substitutions separated by comma]. The mutations of each residue is listed in a new line. |

#### Parameter handlers

When working with a specific parameter type it is useful to have a customized graphical interface for modifying a parameter's value. For example, if a parameter is a URL type it useful to be able to specify a corresponding file using an interface such as the File Open dialog. Similarly if you are specifying a parameter that stores a date, it is useful to be able to use a calendar style interface to enter the date and ensure that the correct format is used.

A series of specialized parameter handlers have been created in Discovery Studio that deal with custom types. The parameter handlers work in two ways. For many protocols, the parameter handlers appear as drop down controls in the Parameters Explorer that show the list of available values. The other type of specialized parameter handlers are launched by clicking a launch button embedded in the Parameters Explorer which in turn opens a specialized input dialog.

# Customizing the visualizer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/customize_client.htm

## Customizing the visualizer

The Discovery Studio interface is flexible and allows you to customize it to suit any task at hand. You can change the location of toolbars, windows, and explorers to increase your productivity, or to maximize the screen area for a particular viewer. You can also customize tool panels or even create new ones for tools that you commonly use.

### Toolbars

The client contains a collection of toolbars that provide quick access to functionality. By default, only the View and Standard toolbars are displayed at the top of the window. You can
turn on the visibility of the other toolbars by either right clicking on the toolbars and selecting from
the drop down list, or selection from the View | Toolbars menu.

You can also move toolbars around dragging them to the desired location. Note that toolbars can be docked to any edge of the client window.

In addition to changing the location and visibility of Toolbars, it is also easy to create new Toolbars
that other frequently used functionality in the application. To add new toolbars, or to modify the specific buttons in an existing toolbar, you can use the Toolbar preferences .

### Docks

The client is organized into three areas (Docks) that are used to organize the explorers and windows you will work with.

By default, the Files, Protocols, and Tools Explorers are available from in the left dock, while the Jobs, Parameter Help, and Parameters Explorers are in the bottom dock. The client is flexible and allows you to drag the tab for an explorer between the left and bottom docks. You can use this feature to organize the explorers for convenient access and to control the amount of available viewing area. The right dock is reserved for the various windows supported by the application.

In addition to customizing which explorers appear in the dock, you can also control the visibility of the docks and explorers from the View menu.

Some docks include an autohide feature (pushpin icon) that causes the dock to be hidden when not in use. To use a feature in a dock that is hidden, click the tab to temporarily expand the dock.

To exit autohide, click on a tab to expand it, and then click the pushpin icon again.

### Tool Panels

A powerful feature of the application is the Tools Explorer. Tool panels are arranged in tool sets for working 
in specific domains such as Macromolecules or Pharmacophores. You can choose the tool sets from the toolbar.

The choice of tool sets displayed on the toolbar can be customized using the context menu. Toggle the check
boxes in the menu to control the visibility of different buttons. You can also use this menu to access the Create
tool set dialog which enables you to add custom tool sets.

You can also navigate to different tool sets from the Tools menu. Additionally, you can create your own tool panels. For 
details, see Creating a tool panel .

#### Further information

Working with windows Working with menu tools Working with toolbars

# Structure Based Pharmacophore tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/customize_samples-pharm.htm

## Structure Based Pharmacophore tools

This example tool panel allows you to create pharmacophores from the 
binding site of a protein. You must import the tool panel and custom scripts before you can use it.

To display the tool panel

* Import the associated example scripts and tool panels: StructureBasedPharmacophore.scripts and StructureBasedPharmacophore.panel . See Working with customization sample files and Sample Customization Files for details about how to find sample files and import them.

* Choose View | Tool Panels | Structure Based Pharmacophore from the menu bar.

### Tool Commands

Create Link atom(s): When creating a 
pharmacophore to search fragment databases that should be linked, use this
tool to define the linking atom.

Query Atom Specification...: Launches
the Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog, which can be used to modify 
the properties of the linking atom.

Hydrogen Bond Donor Projected Point: Creates a hydrogen bond donor projected point feature based on the protein. Select the protein heavy atom(s) that will form
the hydrogen bond interaction with the ligand before using this tool.

Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Projected Point: Similar
to Hydrogen Bond Donor Projected Point , but using a hydrogen bond acceptor projection point instead.

Hydrogen Bond Donor Or Acceptor Projected Point: Similar to Hydrogen Bond Donor 
Projected Point and Hydrogen Bond Acceptor 
Projected Point , but can match either a
donor or acceptor projected point.

Invert HbondDonor/Acceptor: After using 
the Query toolbar to create a hydrogen bond acceptor or donor on 
a protein atom, use this command to convert it to the ligand
compliment. Acceptors are converted to donors, the projected
point and heavy atom locations are inverted, and
donors are converted to acceptors.

Fragment to Query: Converts
a fragment into a substructure query. This can be useful when using
the Dock Ligands 
(Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) protocol to constrain poses 
to a substructure.

Define Receptor: Creates a group named
"SBD_Receptor"
that defines the selected molecule as the receptor. Receptors should have hydrogens and complete valence shells so that they
can be atom typed .
They also cannot have alternate conformations . The Data Table functionality depends on the
receptor being defined, including receptor-ligand hydrogen bonds.
For further information, see Define a receptor .

From Receptor Cavities: Derives binding sites from cavities within the structure of the previously defined receptor
molecule. The first binding site
found is displayed. If there is a ligand chain within the receptor
molecule, the binding site will not be detected.
For further information, see Site finding and Reparenting .

Binding Site to Shape Query: Once a 
binding site cavity has been defined using From Receptor Cavities , use this command to create
a shape query from this cavity. The default tolerance for the 
shape queries should be edited depending on the size of the ligands
in the database and the size of the cavity.

Merge Hypotheses: Performs 
a simple merge of two or more hypotheses.

# Attributes dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_attributes.htm

## Attributes dialog

The Attributes dialog displays the properties of the selected object.
Every object type (atoms, bonds, residues, etc.)
has a particular set of object attributes. For example, with an atom
selected, attributes such as Name , Color , Element , Formal Charge , and Oxidation State are displayed. For a molecule, additional attributes such as Number of Atoms and Molecular Formula are displayed, but attributes that do not apply such as Element do not display.

You can modify many of the attributes. Some attributes of objects cannot be edited (e.g., Index , Number of Atoms , Molecular Weight , etc.) Changes do not take effect until you click OK or Apply .

You can edit object names directly in the Hierarchy View .

* Atomic formal charges must be entered as rational numbers if you want to edit them. For example, +1/2 , -1/2 , 1 , -1 . Values such as 0.5 are not valid.

* Molecular Weight uses average atomic masses.

* Exact Mol. Weight uses the masses of the most abundant isotopes (for example 1 H in the case of hydrogen and 12 C in the case of carbon).

* Molecular Volume is estimated as 0.95×(A - B), where A is the sum of the volumes of atomic spheres having van der Waals radii and B is the volume of all intersections of those atomic spheres for bonded pairs of atoms.

* Calculate Charges controls whether cleaning the geometry of a molecule, calculating the Dreiding energy, adding a surface to a molecule, or calculating the dipole moment of a molecule will automatically calculate Gasteiger charges for the molecule. The Chemistry | Charge | Calculate command will always calculate Gasteiger charges for this molecule, regardless of the Calculate Charges setting.

* XYZ contains the 3D coordinates of the selected object if the object supports such an attribute. The value of the XYZ attribute can be edited directly without having to go through a separate Edit Coordinate dialog . For example, this makes it possible to modify the XYZ value by pasting 3D coordinates from the clipboard.

Copy: Copies selected attribute names and/or values to the clipboard. If nothing is selected, all names and values are copied.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Attributes... |
| --- | --- |
| Context menu | Right-click (Graphics or Hierarchy View) \| Choose Attributes of <object name>... |

# Clipping Planes dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_clipping-planes.htm

## Clipping Planes dialog

The Clipping Planes dialog allows you to control the visibility of objects through the 
use of adjustable planes. Two types of
clipping planes are supported:

* Front and back clipping planes for the current Graphics View

* Custom clipping planes

Front and back clipping planes are invisible planes parallel to the plane of the screen. 
Only objects and parts of objects between the front and back clipping planes are displayed in the Graphics View. 
You can use them to reveal the interior of structures by either adjusting the position of the
front and back clipping planes or translating objects in the z-direction relative to the 
front and back clipping planes. The clipping planes can be adjusted with the mouse wheel (refer to Mouse and keyboard actions )

Custom clipping planes can be oriented manually using your mouse like any other objects (refer to Mouse and keyboard actions ). 
A custom clipping plane applies either to the current selection or, if no objects are selected, 
to all current objects. To clip the surface of a protein and not its atoms, select the surface
and add a custom clipping plane. Adjust the position of the custom clipping plane to reveal the 
desired protein features by clipping away the protein surface.

In addition to creating individual custom clipping planes, you can create custom clipping plane 
slabs with defined thicknesses. This allows you to progressively reveal or cloak objects for an 
arbitrary planar region in the Graphics View.

Front clipping plane: Adjust this slider to change the position of the 
front clipping plane. You can see the change interactively in the current Graphics View.

Back clipping plane: Adjust this slider to change the position 
of the back clipping plane. You can see the change 
interactively in the current Graphics View.

Front and back clipping planes may be positioned differently in the perspective and orthographic projections.

Add Custom Clipping Plane Add a new custom clipping plane to the current 
Graphics View.

Add Custom Clipping Slab Add a new custom clipping plane slab to the current 
Graphics View. Additionally, set the width in angstroms by entering a number in the text box.

To change the position and rotation of a custom clipping plane, select it from the Hierarchy View .
Hold CTRL and rotate or move it using the appropriate tool as described in Mouse and keyboard actions .

To edit a custom clipping plane, including changing the name, color, or precise position, select it, 
and then right-click and select Attributes of PlaneObject... from the context menu. Use the PlaneObject attributes dialog to set the values.

Clipping plane is not supported when Tile Molecules in View is turned on.

# Color Mapping dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_color-mapping.htm

## Color Mapping dialog

The Color Mapping dialog allows you to specify how to map values onto a color spectrum when displaying
objects such as atoms, isosurfaces, surfaces, and proteins.

Histogram: Displays how the range of values available for the chosen criterion are colored
using the selected spectrum. Click and drag the vertical bars (or the cyan colored arrows below them) in the
histogram window to control what subset of the histogram is mapped to the spectrum (see Min/Max sliders below).
The entire spectra is mapped to the region between the left and right histogram sliding bars. For example, if using
the Red-White-Blue spectra with a full histogram data range of -100 to +50, but with the left slider bar (minimum) is
at -1 and the right slider bar (maximum) at +2, values less than or equal to -1 will be displayed with the color
on the left of the spectrum (pure red) and values of +2 or greater will be mapped with the color of the right side
of the spectrum (pure blue). Note that this means that if you want the center color of the spectrum to correspond
to a value of zero, the left value should be the negative of the right value (for example -2 and 2).

The active spectrum is displayed beneath the histogram. You can choose the number of bands in the
spectrum to be displayed. If a color band is off, that band has a small black rectangle beneath
it, and any objects currently displayed using colors within the band are not displayed. If a color band is
on, that band will have a small white rectangle beneath it, and any objects displayed using colors within that
band are displayed.

To turn a color off or on, click the color in the spectrum bands. To turn a range of colors off or on,
click and drag across a range of colors in the spectrum. The initial click before the drag is what determines
if all subsequent colors are turned off or on.

Spectrum: Spectra that can be applied to the
chosen criterion. The selected spectrum is displayed at the bottom of the histogram.

Bands: Number of bands of color in the spectrum.
The default number of bands depends on the property that is being mapped onto the spectrum. The minimum number of bands that can be displayed is 2 .
The maximum number of bands that can be displayed is 128 .

Clip outside range: Controls how objects that fall outside the current defined
range are displayed. When this box is unchecked, values outside the range are assigned the leftmost and
rightmost colors within the range. When this box is checked, values outside the defined
range are not displayed.

Min/Max sliders: Sets the minimum and maximum thresholds of the histogram
data to be mapped to the selected color spectrum. The minimum and maximum values can be set by
dragging the cyan sliders on the histogram to the required value, or by entering a value directly
into the Min or Max fields.

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Display Style... \| Atom ... \| Colors... |

# Create Feature dialog

Source type: HTML

## Create Feature dialog

The Create Feature dialog can be used to add a Catalyst pharmacophore feature, an Isentris 3D feature, or an interaction point for docking to a 3D structure document. In addition to the Create Feature dialog,
features can be added using the Query toolbar.

You can use the Create Feature dialog to add a feature with specified attributes and name.

Feature: The dropdown list contains the features which are available for the current selection in the Graphics View .

The features which can be created from the Create Feature dialog are:

* Angle - Catalyst constraint, Isentris 3D feature

* Centroid - Catalyst standard feature, Isentris 3D feature

* Dihedral - Catalyst constraint, Isentris 3D feature

* Distance - Catalyst constraint, Isentris 3D feature

* ExclusionSphere - Catalyst constraint, Isentris 3D feature

* Line - Isentris 3D feature

* Location - Catalyst constraint, Isentris 3D feature (fixed atoms)

* Normal - Isentris 3D feature

* RingAromatic - Catalyst standard feature

* Plane - Catalyst feature, Isentris 3D feature

* Point (Pharmacophore) - Catalyst feature, Isentris 3D feature

* InteractionPoint (Docking) - Interaction point for docking

* PointOffset - Isentris 3D feature (point)

* Acceptor - Catalyst standard feature

* Donor - Catalyst standard feature

* Shape - Catalyst constraint

* QueryAtom - Catalyst, Isentris atom attributes

* QueryBond - Catalyst, Isentris bond attributes

* Vector - Catalyst feature

For example, when a single atom is selected, the available features from the dropdown include:

* Centroid

* ExclusionSphere

* Location

* Point

* Acceptor

* Donor

* Shape

* QueryAtom

When a single bond is selected, the available features include:

* PointOffset

* QueryBond

When two atoms are selected, the available features include:

* Distance

* Line

* Plane

The feature selected from the dropdown list determines the feature attribute that can be specified through the dialog.

List: Specify the element list of a query atom, or the list of bond types of a query bond.

Radius: Specify the radius of an exclusion sphere or location feature.

Range: Specify the allowed range of values for a distance, angle or dihedral constraint.

RMS Deviation: Specify the allowed RMS deviation for a line or plane constraint.

Type: Specify the type of a point feature.

Name: Specify the name for the feature to be added.

# Create Metal Template dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_create-metal-template.htm

## Create Metal Template dialog

You can use this dialog to use to sketch a metal atom using a set of pre-defined geometries.

Metal coordination complexes and hypervalent main group compounds often
adopt more complex geometries, the most common of which are square-planar,
trigonal-bipyramidal, and octahedral. Higher order geometries are any
atom geometries other than sp (linear), sp2 (trigonal planar), and sp3
(tetrahedral). The distinguishing feature of higher order geometries
is that not all pairs of attachments have the same ideal angle. For example,
in the square-planar and octahedral cases, ideal angles can be 90 or
180 degrees. In the trigonal-bipyramidal case, ideal angles can be 90,
120, or 180 degrees.

Central Atom: Click the arrow on the dropdown list to choose from a list of metals more
commonly found in organometallic compounds, such as Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Mn,
Ni, Sc, Ti, V, and Zn.

Table...: Alternatively, click this button to select an element of your choice from the periodic table. The symbol of the selected element is displayed in the edit box. Refer to Central Atom dialog for more information.

Geometry: Click the arrow on the dropdown list to choose from the following geometric templates:

2-C2v Bent (H 2 O) 2-Dih Linear (sp) 3-C3v Pyramidal (NH 3 ) 3-D3h Trigonal (sp 2 ) 4-D4h Square planar (cis-platin) 4-Td Tetrahedral (sp 3 ) 5-D3h Trigonal bipyramidal 5-D4h Square pyramid 6-D3d Trigonal antiprismatic 6-D3h Trigonal prismatic 6-Oh Octahedral 7-D5h Pentagonal bipyramidal

Each template name consists of two parts. 
The first part (for example 2-C2v) is a descriptor made up of the coordination number 
(the number of ligands attached to the central atom) and the Schoenfliess symbol for the group of 
symmetry operations of the respective geometry. 
The second part (for example, Bent) consists of a textual description of the geometry.

The templates corresponding to higher order geometries are:

* 4-D4h

* All geometries with a coordination number larger than 4 (5-D3h, ..., 7-D5h)

### Access methods

| Menu | Chemistry \| Metal Templates... |
| --- | --- |
