# Create Surface dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_create-surface.htm

## Create Surface dialog

The Create Surface dialog allows you to construct a molecular surface from the atoms currently selected in the Graphics View . If no atoms are selected, the surface that is constructed includes 
all atoms in the current Graphics View. Note that surfaces are not displayed when molecules are tiled in the Graphics View.
See the Tile Molecules in View menu item in the View menu help for more information about tiling.

To create receptor surfaces quickly with just a few clicks, use the View Interactions tool panel.

### Display style

Select the display style for the surface to be created. Available options are:

Solvent: Creates a solvent surface, similar to a Connolly solvent surface.

Soft: Creates a soft surface, similar to a solvent surface. This method employs a faster, 
more approximate algorithm than that used for creating a solvent surface. For large molecules, a soft surface provides 
better performance, as it can be redrawn faster.

VDW: Creates a surface, based on the van der Waals (VDW) radius of each atom in the molecule.

### Surface rendering

Select the surface rendering option for the surface to be created. Available options are:

Solid: Creates a solid surface.

Wire mesh: Creates a surface that is displayed as a wire mesh.

Probe radius: Allows you to change the size of the probe atom when calculating a solvent surface,
the default is a radius of 1.4 Å. This is only available when creating a solvent surface.

Transparency: Specify the level of transparency for a solid surface using the slider control. 
Moving the slider to the right increases the opacity of the surface, while moving it to the left increases the transparency.

Setting the transparency level to maximum transparency will cause the surface to 
disappear and prevent it from being easily selected.

Reverse Side: Check this box to enable the transparency control for the reverse side of the surface. For example,
you can set higher surface
transparency and lower reverse side transparency, which would let you see the internal side of the surface better. Uncheck
this box if you want the reverse side of the surface to have the same transparency as the front side.

### Coloring

Select the coloring options for the surface to be created. Available options are:

Color by: The following options are available:

* Parent color - Colors the surface according to the color of its parent object

* Interpolated Charge - Maps the interpolated partial atom charge to the surface 

(for more information, refer to Color surfaces using electrostatic potential )

* Atom charge - Maps the interpolated partial atom charge of nearest neighbors to the surface

* Atom color - Maps the atom colors to the surface

By grid: The surfaces are colored using the values of a 3D grid associated with either an isosurface or a density map. The surface coloring is derived from linear interpolation of the 3D grid values at the surface vertices and mapping the interpolated values to colors using a spectrum. The details of this mapping can be specified in the color mapping dialog.

Custom: Click the color box to open the Select Color dialog , which allows 
you to select a predefined color or define a color of your choice.

Custom Reverse Side: Assign a custom color to the reverse side of the surface, if the surface has some transparent
character, this is the color which shows through the surface color. Click the color box to display the Select Color dialog .

### Type

Select the type of surface to be created. Available options are:

Open: Select this radio button to include breaks in the created surface where it contacts other atoms. 
This choice is only available if a subset of atoms is selected in the Graphics View.

Closed: Select this radio button to create a surface that completely encloses all of the selected 
atoms in the Graphics View. This is the only option when no atoms are selected in the Graphics View or if all atoms are selected. 
When a subset of atoms is selected, the surface that is created completely encloses the atoms as if they constitute a standalone 
structure.

### Properties

In the SolidSurface tab of the Data Table View , the surface area values for each surface are listed in the SurfaceArea column, whereas the surface volume values are listed in the Volume column.

The surface is represented as a triangle mesh. The surface area is obtained as the sum of the areas of all triangles in the mesh.

The surface volume of an open surface measures the volume of a closed surface obtained as the union of the open surface with all surface patches which were buried by other atoms.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Surface \| Add... |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Structure menu Structure | Surface | Add.../Remove Construction of molecular surfaces View Interactions Color surfaces using electrostatic potential

## Cell Parameters tab - Crystal Builder dialog

The Cell Parameters tab of the Crystal Builder dialog allows you to specify 
values for the unit cell parameters of a crystal cell.

Unit cell parameters determine the length and orientation of unit cell vectors
in space. Any translation of an atom by an integer multiple of
a unit cell vector results in that atom reaching the position of another 
identical atom in the crystal.

Lengths (angstroms): Specify the values of 
the lengths A , B , and C of the unit cell vectors in angstroms.

Angles (Degrees): Specify the angles Alpha , Beta , 
and Gamma between the unit cell vectors.

Preserve Fractional Positions: Check this option to fix the fractional coordinates of atoms when changing
the unit cell parameters.

# Preferences tab - Crystal Builder dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_crystal-builder_preferences.htm

## Preferences tab - Crystal Builder dialog

The Preferences tab of the Crystal Builder dialog allows you to specify the options used in the display of crystal 
cells. Use this tab to:

* Choose the symmetry style used in creating crystal cell displays

* Specify the tolerance used to test for proximity to special positions

* Calculate bonds between symmetry related atoms based on proximity

* Determine the number of unit cells in each of the crystallographic directions displayed for the cell

Symmetry Style: Determines which set of atoms from the infinite crystal will be used for the basic display. This is 
then modified using the View Range setting. Available options are:

* Default: Gives a representation that should be suitable for most crystals. In particular, for a molecular crystal, 
whole fragments are shown. No repeats are made for fragments that extend across unit cell boundaries.

* One Cell: Shows just one translational copy of each of the asymmetric unit and symmetry copy atoms. This copy is the 
one that lies within the unit cell. No repeats are made for atoms that lie on a face, edge, or corner.

* Original: Applies all symmetry operations (without any translational portion) to the atoms in the asymmetric unit.

* Positions: Shows just the asymmetric unit atoms with no translational offset.

The Original setting creates symmetry copies of molecules. If there are N symmetry operations (ignoring primitive translations) in the space group, building a single unit cell will create N molecules. The Default setting creates symmetry copies of fragments. If a molecule contains multiple fragments, it is possible that more than N symmetry copies of molecules contribute fragments to a single unit cell, and consequently, some of the molecules are built with only a subset of fragments. Finally, the One Cell setting creates symmetry copies of individual atoms. Again, it is possible that more than N symmetry copies of molecules contribute atoms to a single unit cell, and as a consequence, some of the molecules are built with only a subset of atoms.

Special Position Tolerance: Determines how close two atoms can be after symmetry operators are applied before they are considered the same atom, which is then assumed to lie in a special, rather than a general position. Such atoms are constrained to obey symmetry constraints in atom or fragment movement.

Proximity Bonding: Attempts to bond atoms within their covalent radii after symmetry operators are applied.

View Range: Determines how the unit cell is replicated in the A , B and C directions. For instance, the default View Range of 1 , 1 , 1 displays only a single unit cell. If the View Range is changed to 3 , 2 , 1 , the unit cell is replicated three times along the A-axis and twice along the B-axis.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Crystal Cell \| Edit Parameters... \| Preferences |
| --- | --- |

The Atom tab on the 2D Window Display

Line: Displays atoms using a traditional 
wire frame display. Non-bonded atoms are displayed as jacks.

Disc: Displays atoms using discs 
and bonds using lines. The discs are sized using the Ball size parameter.

Stick: Displays bonds using solid cylinders.

Ball and stick: Displays atoms using balls 
and bonds using cylinders. The balls and sticks sizes are controlled by the Ball size and Stick size parameters.

Color by: Color atoms using predefined color schemes:

Element: Colors each atom by element. You can element color definition by choosing Chemistry | Element Properties... from the menu bar.

dialog to apply a custom color to selected atoms.

Show SAS (solvent accessible surface): Select the checkbox to display the 
solvent accessible surface. Click the button to launch the Select Color dialog and set the solvent accessible surface colors of selected atoms.

The radius of the solvent accessible surface is the calculated value scaled by 0.015. Radii
less than 0.1 are not displayed.

### More controls

Ball size, Stick size: Scale features as desired.

None: Hides selected residues so they are not

Disc: Displays selected residues using discs

Plate: Displays residues using plates

### Coloring

Color by: Colors atoms according to predefined color schemes, including:

Interaction: Colors each residue by the type of interaction as shown in the table.

| Interaction | Color |
| --- | --- |
| Metal | Light gray |
| Water | Light blue |
| van der Waals | Green |
| Polar | Magenta |
| Hydrogen bond | Magenta |
| Charge | Magenta |

An atom-residue pair may have multiple interactions. Only the predominant interaction is retained. The precedence rules are as follows:

* Charge

* Hydrogen bond with amino acid side-chain

* Hydrogen bond with amino acid main-chain

* Hydrogen bond with non amino acid

* polar

* van der Waals

Custom: Select the radio button and click the color box to display the Select Color 
dialog .

Solvent accessible surface: Displays the 
difference in SAS of residues with and without the ligand present. 
Select the color button to launch the Select Color dialog and set the SAS colors of selected residues.

For Disc and Ball representations,
the displayed radius is the residue radius extended by the difference in SAS 
scaled by 0.01. 
Radii extended by less than 0.075 are not displayed. 
The color depth is also proportional to the radius.

For the Plates representation,
the plate height and width are also extended with
scaling factors of 0.01 and 0.005 respectively.

# Atom tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_atom.htm

## Atom tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Atom tab on the Graphics View Display Style dialog controls the graphical representation of atoms and bonds.

### Display style

Off: Blanks selected atoms so they are not displayed on the screen. You can use this style to simplify a complex 
molecule by displaying only atoms of interest, or hiding atoms when displaying a protein as a ribbon.

Line: Displays atoms using a traditional wire frame display. Nonbonded atoms are displayed as jacks.

Stick: Displays bonds using solid cylinders. Nonbonded atoms are displayed as jacks as in a Line style. The Stick size parameter changes the thickness of the sticks.

Ball and stick: Depicts bonds using cylinders for bonds and balls for atoms. The balls and sticks are sized using the Ball size and Stick size parameters.

Scaled ball and stick: Depicts bonds using cylinders and atoms using balls scaled to the van der Waals (VDW) radii. The 
balls and sticks are sized using the Ball Size and Stick Size parameters. You can customize the 
default VDW radius for each element by choosing the Chemistry | Element Properties... command from the menu bar.

CPK: Displays spheres sized to the van der Waals (VDW) radii. The CPK scale setting multiplies 
the VDW radii by the given factor. You can customize the default VDW radii for each element using the Chemistry | Element Properties... command.

Polyhedron: Displays coordination polyhedra around atoms. This style is used primarily for materials and inorganic 
molecules. The Polyhedron style creates polyhedra for atoms having four or more bonds. The resulting effect on polymers 
resembles beads in a chain. Atoms with fewer than four bonds are displayed as lines, and atoms with no bonds are not displayed.

### Coloring

Color by: you can color atoms in a number of ways. The Color by list has a variety of predefined 
color schemes, including:

Element: Colors each atom with the color defined for its element. You can change the basic elemental colors by choosing 
the Chemistry | Element Properties... command from the menu bar.

Parent Color: Colors each atom by the color of the parent object containing the atom. For instance, if an atom is 
contained in an amino acid, the atom is colored by the amino acid's color.

Molecule Color: Colors each atom by the color of the molecule to which the atom belongs.

Partial Charge: Colors each atom by its partial charge. The color is taken from a gradient that runs from red for 
negative charges to blue for positive charges.

<others>: A number of additional color schemes are automatically added to the available choices depending on the 
atomic and molecular attributes calculated on the molecule and the hierarchical structure of the model. These color schemes are named by the molecular 
object in the hierarchy that contains the atom and the color is based on how many of those objects are in the model. For instance, Molecule , AminoAcidChain , and AminoAcid schemes are added to the 
color options if a protein is loaded that contains multiple chains. If you use the Molecule scheme, all of the atoms in a 
molecule are a single color (typically there is only one molecule in the document). If you color by AminoAcidChain , all of 
the atoms in one chain are colored one color, and all of the atoms in the second chain are another color.

Any column in the Data Table that contains numbers can be used as a color criterion.

Colors...: This button launches the Color Mapping dialog .

Custom: Select the radio button and click the color box to display the Select Color 
dialog . After you have defined a color, click the Apply button or the OK button to apply the 
your custom color to the selected atoms.

Carbon atoms only: Check this box to apply the custom color only to Carbon atoms.

### More controls

Show bond order: This checkbox controls whether multiple bonds display differently than single bonds. The option affects 
the Line , Stick , and Ball and Stick display styles.

Ball size, Stick size, CPK scale: Use these fields to custom scale the appropriate features.

## Bootstrap tab - Dendrogram Display Style dialog

The Bootstrap tab of the Dendrogram Display Style dialog allows you to adjust the appearance of 
Bootstrap labels for an active Dendrogram Window. This tab is only displayed when the phylogenetic 
tree in the Dendrogram Window has been generated using the bootstrap mode.

Adjusting the values in this tab may be useful depending on the type of data set you have used to 
generate the tree. If many nodes are recovered with high confidence, you may wish to only collapse all 
nodes above 95%. Alternatively, if your sequences are highly diverged, it may be necessary to use a 
low filter level (e.g. 60%) to identify the more strongly supported nodes.

### Bootstrap Labels

Display absolute numbers: Displays the number of bootstrap 
replicates that support the corresponding node.

Display percentages: Displays the percentage of bootstrap 
replicates that support the corresponding node.

### Bootstrap Filters

Collapse nodes: Only shows nodes if bootstrap support exceeds the cutoff 
value.

Label nodes: Labels nodes with bootstrap value if support level 
exceeds cutoff value. This value must be greater than the Collapse nodes: value.

For the Bootstrap Labels and Label nodes options to take effect, you must enable the Show branch labels option in the General tab of the Dendrogram Display Style dialog.

# DNA/RNA tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_dna.htm

## DNA/RNA tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The DNA/RNA tab of the Graphics View
Display Style dialog provides several display styles that emphasize
the higher level structure of DNA/RNA molecules when a DNA or RNA strand
is in the current model. The display of DNA/RNA has two parts, the
backbone, which can be displayed as Arrows or Tubes , and the base pairs,
which can be displayed as a Ladder or as Rings .

### Backbone

Off: Select this option to turn off any special display of the backbone.

Arrows: Displays only the arrow along the backbone pointing toward the C3' end
(this is a subset of the Rings display style).

Tubes: Displays the backbones of each strand as continuous tubes.

Individual DNA/RNA strands are listed under the NucleicAcidChain tab in the Molecular Data Table. The Tube Size property of each strand controls the width of the tubes used to display the DNA/RNA backbone.

### Backbone coloring

Color by residues: Check this option to color the backbone according to the color
of the closest residue. This option requires to display the backbone as arrows or tubes.

Custom: Check this option to assign a custom color to the backbone. 
This option requires to display the backbone as arrows or tubes.
Click the color box to display the Select color dialog .

### Base pairs

Off: Select this option to turn off any special display of the base pairs.

Ladder: Represents nucleic acid structures as tubes along the phosphate backbone, and tubes 
along the major axis of the base groups.

Rings: Represents nucleic acids as an arrow along the backbone pointing toward the C3' end, 
and sugar groups and bases as boxes.

### Base pair coloring

These controls allow you to select from a variety of predefined styles by which to color the DNA/RNA representations.

Color by: Colors nucleic acids and nucleic
acid chains using one of a variety of predefined color schemes for
coloring the DNA/RNA representations, including:

Residue - Colors each residue differently.

Base Type . Colors residues according to
the base type of the residue.

NucleicAcidChain - The NucleicAcidChain color scheme is added automatically, and colors residues 
according to the nucleic acid chain that they are contained by. For example, if there are two chains, the residues in the first 
chain are colored one color, and in the second chain are colored another.

Molecule - The Molecule color scheme is added automatically, and colors residues according to the 
molecule that they are contained by. For example, if there are two molecules, the residues in the first molecule
are colored one color, and in the second molecule are colored another.

Cell - The Cell color scheme is added automatically, and colors residues according to the cell that 
they are contained by. For example, if there are two cells, the residues in the first cell
are colored one color, and in the second cell are colored another. If there are no cells in the model, this choice will not appear 
in the dialog.

Hydrophobicity - Colors residues on a gradient from red (negative hydrophobicity) to blue, passing 
through white at a hydrophobicity of zero.

Avg. Isotropic Displacement - Colors residues according to the average of the residue's atoms 
isotropic displacements.

ID - Colors residues in a continuous gradient
from blue at the 3-prime end through white to red at the 5-prime end.
You can change the color mapping for this scheme using the Color Mapping dialog .

Additional color schemes are automatically added to the available choices for properties shown as columns in the Molecular 
Data Table (see Data Table for more information) that contain numbers. 
These schemes color nucleic acids or nucleic acid chains by mapping the corresponding value in the Molecular Data Table. 
The color mapping of these properties can be modified using the Color Mapping dialog .

Colors...: This button launches the Color Mapping dialog . The Color 
Mapping dialog controls the mapping of colors onto values in the Molecular Data Table.

Custom: Colors nucleic acids or nucleic acid chains using a single color. Click the color bar to 
display the Select Color dialog and choose a single color for nucleic acids or nucleic acid chains.

# Graphics tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_graphics.htm

## Graphics tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Graphics tab on the Graphics View Display Style dialog allows you to set
general graphics properties for the current Molecule Window. This tab is always available, and settings specified here are
saved with the rest of the data when you save your file. The settings in this window are a subset of the 
global applications settings accessed through the Molecule Window | Graphics 
preferences page.

### Projection

These options allow you to set the display of molecules in different projection modes:

Orthographic: Orthographic projection produces a
view in which objects appear to be of the same size regardless of
their distance from the observer. Orthographic projection is typically used in
engineering graphics and is associated with higher precision reproduction.

Perspective: Perspective projection produces a
view in which objects that are further from the observer appear smaller than objects
closer to the observer. This is similar to the way the human eye views the world
and cameras produce photographs. Perspective projection usually provides a more
realistic representation of a model by emphasizing depth instead of size in the
model.

Angle: The perspective angle controls the amount
of foreshortening that occurs in a perspective projection. A smaller angle reduces
the foreshortening and a larger angle increases the foreshortening. The angle is
limited to values between 1 and 60 degrees. The default is 20.00° .

### Quality

The quality setting controls the coarseness of 3 dimensional
objects used to display proteins and DNA/RNA. A lower quality setting will improve
rendering performance by increasing coarseness. A higher quality setting improves the visual appearance.

For regular use, choose the setting that gives the best combination of performance and quality. If you are exporting an image , choose Ultra-high to get the best quality available.

### Background

Color: This opens the Select Color dialog where you can choose the background color of the current window.

Image: This opens a dialog that you can use to browse for a background image. Note that the image will be resized to fit the view. A set of background images is available in the Samples | Background Images folder .

### Other options

Line width: Controls the thickness of lines used to
render objects such as molecules in line display style and cell boundaries.

Depth cue: When switched on, objects further from the
observer gradually blend into the background, while objects closer to the observer are
displayed in full, bright colors. This feature allows a better feel for the depth of
field by lighting close objects more brightly while more distant objects fade into the
dark. With Depth cue off, object colors are full and bright regardless
of their apparent distance from the observer.

Depth cue and background image cannot be used at the same time. Setting the Depth cue clears the Background and vice versa.

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Display Style... \| Graphics tab |
| --- | --- |
| View toolbar | Display Style \| Graphics tab |
| Context menu | Display Style... \| Graphics tab |

# Isosurface tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_isosurface.htm

## Isosurface tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Isosurface tab on the Graphics View Display Style dialog is available only when the current 
structure contains one or more isosurfaces generated from a 3D grid.

### Display style

Off: Turns off the isosurface display.

Solid: Displays the isosurface as a solid
surface and enables the Transparency slider.

Triangle mesh: Displays the isosurface
data as a wire mesh divided into triangular planes and enables the Line Width control.

Quad mesh: Displays the isosurface data
as a wire mesh divided into rectangular planes and enables the Line Width control.

Volume: Displays the isosurface data
using a specified color spectrum. The histogram in the lower left corner
shows the data distribution and the spectrum applied to the data. This control enables the Spectrum , Bands , Transparency , and Clip outside range options.

### Coloring

By grid: When two or more surfaces created from different grids are loaded, choose from a list of all of the currently
loaded grids. This option is enabled when the Display Style is set to Solid , Triangle Mesh ,
or Quad Mesh .

The list of grids excludes the grids from which the isosurfaces were created. It also excludes un-named grids.

Colors...: Opens the Color Mapping dialog .

Custom: You can assign a custom color to the Solid , Triangle Mesh , and Quad Mesh display styles. Click the color box to choose the color.

Custom Reverse Side: Assign a custom color for the reverse side of an isosurface if its display style is set to Solid . Click the color box to choose the color.

### Other controls

Isovalue: Changes the geometry of the Solid , Triangle Mesh and Quad Mesh isosurface displays.

Line Width: Controls the thickness of the lines when isosurfaces are displayed as Triangle Mesh or Quad Mesh .

Histogram: Displays the range of isosurface
data contained in the file. Move the sliders to control the distribution of the spectrum.
Values below the left slider are assigned the left-most color. Values
above the right slider are assigned the right-most color. If the Clip outside range option is checked, these values are not displayed.

Show box: Check this option to cause the bounding box of the isosurface to be displayed.

Spectrum: Contains the various spectra that can be applied to the Volume isosurface displays. The selected spectrum is displayed at the bottom of the histogram.

Bands: Controls whether the spectrum is displayed in 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 (default), 64 , or 128 bands of color.

Transparency: Controls the transparency of the Volume isosurface.

Clip outside range: Controls the display
of the isosurface information when the values are limited in the Histogram.
When this box is unchecked, values outside the range are assigned the
left-most and right-most colors, respectively. When this box is checked,
values outside the range are not displayed.

# Lighting tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_lighting.htm

## Lighting tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Lighting tab on the Graphics View Display Style dialog allows you to set lighting
properties for the current Molecule Window . This tab is always available, and any settings specified here are
saved with the rest of the data when you save the file. The settings in this window are a subset of the 
global applications settings accessed through the Molecule Window | Lighting 
preferences page.

The settings on this page control the color and
source direction of the lighting. There are
four lights that you can control. For the best performance, by
default only one light is turned on. The light direction and color
are only apparent when you work with space-filling display styles such
as CPK or Ball
and Stick ), or molecules with surfaces. The lights do not affect lines.

On/Off: The numbered check boxes turn on or off each light (numbered one through four).

Color: Indicates the current color of the light numbered one through four. 
To change the light color, click the Color button corresponding to a light number to display the Select Color dialog , and choose a new color.

[Light direction control]

The Light Direction Control is displayed on the right side of the Lighting page and initially appears to 
be a blue sphere with a numbered white dot in the center. When you adjust the position of this dot by clicking and dragging it, it appears as a solid arrow pointed directly at the sphere. You can add three additional light direction arrows for a total of four light sources.

The default light colors are successive shades of gray. The grayness, or luminosity of the light color, effectively controls the 
intensity of the light.

Ambient Shadow: Controls the amount of shadows from neighboring elements.

Direct Shadow: Controls the intensity of shadows cast from the first direct light source.

Depth Blur: Improves realism by reducing focus with distance. 
The depth blur is at minimum at the center of the view and is at maximum at the front and back Clipping Planes .

Atom Outline: Helps visualize atoms by applying an edge to them.

Ambient and direct shadows, depth blur and atom outline require graphics acceleration hardware.
Some video cards do not support one or more of these features. For more information, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

# Materials tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_materials.htm

## Materials tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Materials tab on the Graphics View Display Style dialog allows you to set
material display properties for the current Molecule Window. This tab is always available, and any settings specified here are
saved with the rest of the data when you save the file. The settings in this dialog are a subset of the 
global settings in the Molecule Window | Materials 
preferences page.

Five sliders affect the display of objects
in the Molecule Window. Move the slider to the left to reduce the effect, and to the right increase it. The sliders
control the following settings:

* Ambient: A unique lighting setting in that it does not have a direction and affects the entire view.

* Diffuse: Controls the intensity of the light source.

* Specular: Used to produce highlights on an object. The location of the specular highlight is determined by the direction of the light.

* Emission: Allows the object to emit light, which gives the object a specular highlight that is determined by the direction of the light.

* Shininess: Controls how an object reflects light. Notice how the specular highlights
change while manipulating this control.

### Presets

Use the presets buttons to apply default display settings corresponding to the following materials:

* Chalk

* Metallic

* Plastic

* Rubber

### Trendline and correlation options

These options allow you to configure and control the trendline and correlation values.

Display R-squared value: Displays the R-squared value. It is an indicator of how closely the estimated 
values for the trendline correspond to the actual data. A trendline is most reliable when its R-squared value is at or near 1. Checking 
this option displays R-square value for all the trendlines in the plot.

Display trendline equation: Displays the equation for the least squares linear fit trendline. 
The equation is represented in the slope intercept format (y = mx + c). Checking this option displays the equation for all the 
trendlines displayed on the plot.

Show correlation: Toggles the display of the correlation value on the plot.
Check the checkbox to enable the list. The correlation value is determined for the two data sets selected from the list and is displayed 
in the bottom, left corner of the plot window.

# Protein tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_protein.htm

## Protein tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Protein tab of the Graphics View Display Style dialog allows you to control the representation 
of amino acids and amino acid chains in the Graphics View .

There are several representations available that highlight key characteristics of protein molecules to 
allow higher-level structural information to be examined.

This tab is only available if the Molecule Window contains amino acid chains, with either no selection or at least three amino acids selected. For most styles, it is best to select entire chains or long contiguous sections.

### Display style

Off: Hides the display of amino acids or amino acid chains.

Ca wire: Represents the protein backbone
by drawing a line that joins the alpha (α) carbon atoms in a polypeptide
molecule.

Ca stick: Represents the protein backbone
by drawing a cylinder that joins the alpha (α) carbon atoms in
a polypeptide molecule.

Line ribbon: Represents the protein backbone
as a ribbon of closely-spaced lines.

Flat ribbon: Represents the protein backbone
as a completely flat ribbon.

Solid ribbon: Represents the protein backbone
as a solid, 3D ribbon.

Tube: Similar to the Ca
Stick display style but gives a smoother representation of the protein.

Schematic: Represents the protein secondary structure motifs in cartoon form. 
Helical structures are represented as wide cylinders, beta-sheets as arrows pointing in the direction of the C-terminus, and coil 
and turn regions as tubes.

### Coloring

Color by: Colors amino acids and amino
acid chains using one of a variety of predefined color schemes. The following
color schemes are available:

Residue: Colors each residue differently.

CAlpha: Colors residues according to the color of the C-alpha atom of that residue.

Secondary Type: Colors according to secondary structure. Helices are red, beta sheets are cyan, 
turns are green, and coils are white.

N-to-C Terminal: Colors residues in a continuous gradient from blue at the N-terminus through white to 
red at the C-terminus.

AminoAcidChain: Colors residues according to the amino acid chain which contains the residue.

Molecule: Colors residues according to the molecule which contains the residue.

Cell: : Colors residues according to the cell that contains the residue. If there are no cells in the 
model, this choice will not appear in the dialog.

Hydrophobicity: Colors residues on a gradient from red (negative hydrophobicity) to blue, passing 
through white at a hydrophobicity of zero.

pKa: Colors residues according to pKa value.

Avg. Isotropic Displacement: : Colors residues according to the average isotropic displacement for 
the atoms that comprise the residue.

ID: Similar to the N-to-C Terminal color scheme, although with this scheme you can change the color map 
using the Color Mapping dialog .

Ribbon Size: Colors residues according to their assigned ribbon size.

Visible: A plain colored scheme is used, without reference to any of the attributes
listed above.

Additional color schemes are automatically added from appropriate properties that are contained in the Data Table . These schemes color amino acids or amino acid chains by mapping the corresponding 
value in the Data Table to a color. The color mapping of these properties can be modified using the Color Mapping dialog .

Colors...: This button launches the Color Mapping dialog , 
which controls the mapping of colors onto values in the Data Table.

Custom: Colors amino acids and amino acid chains using a single color. 
Click the color bar to display the Select Color dialog and select a single color.

### Other dialog controls

Display size: Enter a value in the text
box to change the thickness of the resulting display. The Display
size option is only enabled for the Ca Stick , Line , Flat ribbon , Solid
ribbon , and Tube display styles. The Display
size can be changed for individual residues by selecting individual
amino acids, and then changing the Ribbon size property.

Ribbon size: Check this option to map the
visible size of the Line ribbon , Flat
ribbon , Solid ribbon , or Tube display
styles to a built-in numeric property or a user-defined numeric property.
The Ribbon size option is not available if the Off or Ca
Wire display styles are selected.

### Access methods

| Context menu | Display Style... \| Protein tab |
| Keyboard shortcut | CTRL+D \| Protein tab |

# Color Scheme tab

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_sequence-color-scheme.htm

## Color Scheme tab

The Color Scheme tab on the Sequence Window Display Style dialog
controls the background and text coloring of residues of an active Sequence Window. It
can also be used to color objects in the Graphics View for molecules linked to sequences.

### Color alignment

Color scheme: Specifies how residues in the Sequence
Window are colored. The color schemes available are discussed below.

Apply to: Specifies whether to apply the scheme to the Background or Foreground . These options do not apply when setting a Custom scheme.

[table]: The table describes the color scheme. The following columns are included:

* Description: A description of one of the groupings for the specified color scheme.

* Residues: A list of residues belonging to the property group. The column is populated only
color schemes having a specific residue mapping.

* Color: Set the color. Click in a cell to open the Select Color dialog.

#### Color scheme options

The color schemes available depend on what is displayed in the Sequence Window. You can also define custom coloring schemes.

Coloring aligned residue properties: Residues are colored based on a
property's similarity to other residues in the aligned column. The following options are available:

* Aligned sequence similarity - Applicable to both proteins and nucleic acid sequences. For protein sequences, residues in one of the following groups are defined as having strong similarity: STA, NEQK, NHQK, NDEQ, QHRK, MILV, MILF, HY, FYW. Residues which fall into the following groups are defined as having weak similarity: CSA, ATV, SAG, STNK, STPA, SGND, SNDEQK, NDEQHK, NEQHRK, FVLIM, HFY.

For protein sequences, residues in one of the following groups are defined as having strong similarity: STA, NEQK, NHQK, NDEQ, QHRK, MILV, MILF, HY, FYW.

Residues which fall into the following groups are defined as having weak similarity: CSA, ATV, SAG, STNK, STPA, SGND, SNDEQK, NDEQHK, NEQHRK, FVLIM, HFY.

* Aligned secondary structure similarity - Applicable to proteins only.

* Aligned hydrophobicity similarity - Applicable to proteins only.

* Aligned charge similarity - Applicable to proteins only.

* Aligned residue frequency Residues are colored by the frequency of the residue types -
Colors for 100%, 50%, and 0% frequencies are specified by the color table. Colors for other frequencies are interpolated from these colors.

* Aligned match to 1st sequence -
Residues are colored based on their identity with the aligned residue in the first sequence.

* Aligned evolutionary trace (if available) - Applicable to proteins.

Color protein residue properties: Residue are colored based on the properties of the amino acids. The following options are available:

* Secondary structure

* Hydrophobicity

* Charge

* 3D structure-CA atom - available for linked sequences.

* 3D structure-protein display - available for linked sequences.

* Clustal W Default Groups

* Functionality

* Alpha-Helix

* Alpha-Helix + P450

* Hydrophobicity + Charge

* Acidity + Basicity

* Smooth Scaling

* Structural Position

* Steric Bulk

* Chou-Fasman Alpha Helix

* Chou-Fasman Beta Sheet

* Levitt Alpha Helix Forming

* Levitt Beta Sheet Forming

* Levitt Turn Forming

* Dayhoff Matrix

* Helix Terminators

* Gascuel and Golmard

* Chemical Type

Color nucleotide properties: Residue are colored based on the properties of the nucleotide. DNA Residues is the only option available

Custom coloring: Choose the Custom option to color selected residues (or all the residues if
none is selected). Custom colors are static and will only change upon selecting a new
color scheme.

### Percent match

This option is available for the following color schemes:

* Aligned sequence similarity

* Aligned secondary structure similarity

* Aligned hydrophobicity similarity

* Aligned charge similarity

When the value is 100%, all aligned residue properties must be the same for a match to occur. For example:

```text
EF
T
GHLIE
DF
T
LKLMN
SY
T
ARSLQ
```

Alternatively, identity can be 
determined for a user-defined percentage of the sequences. For example, 50% means that 
for an aligned position, just 50% (or more) of the residues in that position must be 
identical. Other residues in that position need not be identical. In the following example,
which includes five sequences, a residue must be identical in three or more 
sequences to be considered identical. Those three or more residues are marked as 
identical. Other residues in that position are marked as non-identical. 
In this example, the second, third, and last positions have identical residues.

```text
E
FT
GHLI
E

D
FT
LKLMN
SY
T
ARSLQ
S
FT
AKIT
E

T
FT
PHRS-
```

In the last column
there are effectively only four sequences because
there is a gap in this position.
This means that only two or more residues need be identical. You must have at
least two sequences to assess identity or similarity.

In the following example there is only one sequence:

```text
E
FT
GH---
D
FT
LK---
SY
T
AR
I
LQ
S
FT
AK
I
--
T
FT
PH---
```

LQ in the middle sequence is not marked as "identical" (to
itself). Note that the I residues in the third-to-last column
are identical.

### Color molecule to match sequence

Color molecule objects: Allows you to color protein structures as per linked protein sequence colors (this option is only available for sequences linked to molecules in a Graphics View). You can choose to color Atoms or the Protein display .

### Default Settings

Defaults: Choose Apply Current Settings as Defaults to set the current options to be the default settings or Reset To Factory Defaults to reset the options to the values set when the application was installed.

# Surface tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_display-style_surface.htm

## Surface tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog

The Surface tab on the Graphics View Display Style dialog allows you to display a variety of surfaces.

### Display style

Off: Hides the surface.

Solvent: The solvent surface is similar to a Connolly solvent surface. The Probe radius setting on this tab controls the size of the probe atom that is used to describe the surface.

Soft: The soft surface is similar to a solvent surface, but uses a faster, more approximate algorithm. This option offers better performance for large molecules because the surface is rendered faster.

VDW: The surface is based on the van der Waals (VDW) radius of each atom in the molecule.

The Display style radio buttons, coloring controls, and the Probe radius text box are disabled when the atoms used to build a surface have been deleted.

### Surface rendering

Solid: Makes the surface opaque.

Wire mesh: Makes the surface a wire mesh.

Probe radius: Size of the probe atom used when displaying a solvent surface.

Transparent/Opaque: Transparency of the surface. Note that setting the transparency level to maximum transparency will cause the surface to disappear and would not be easily selected.

Reverse Side: Enables the transparency control for the reverse side of the surface. For example,
you can set higher surface
transparency and lower reverse side transparency, which would let you see the internal side of the surface better. Uncheck
this box if you want the reverse side of the surface to have the same transparency as the front side.

### Coloring

Color by: Choose from the following predefined styles for coloring the protein representations:

* Parent Color: Colors the surface according to the color of its parent object

* Interpolated Charge: Maps the interpolated partial atom charge to the surface

* Atom Charge: Maps the interpolated partial atom charge of nearest neighbors to the surface

* Atom Color: Maps the atom colors to the surface

Legend: Toggles the display of the color legend.

By grid: Colors the surface using the values of a 3D grid associated with either an isosurface or a density map. The surface coloring is derived by linear interpolation of the 3D grid values at the surface vertices and mapping the interpolated values to colors using a spectrum. The details of this mapping can be specified in the color mapping dialog.

Colors...: Opens the Color Mapping dialog .

Custom: Click the color box to choose a color.

Custom Reverse Side: Assign a custom color to the reverse side of the surface. If the surface is partially transparent, this color shows through the surface color.

### Access methods

# Feature Editor dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_feature-editor.htm

## Feature Editor dialog

The Feature Editor dialog allows you to create and modify sequence features. A feature is an item of information about a sequence that is 
associated with a specific position within that sequence. The position may be a single residue, the gap between two residues, or a contiguous 
series of residues.

Keyword: From the dropdown list, you can select the keyword that describes the type of feature you are editing. 
Different sets of predefined keywords are provided for amino acid and nucleic acid sequences. These keyword sets are based on the keywords used 
in the SWISSPROT and GenBank file formats respectively. For a complete list of feature types click on the dropdown menu.

In addition to selecting a predefined keyword you can also add custom keywords to a feature. To do this, click the cursor inside the keyword 
dropdown listbox and type the name of the keyword you wish to create. After you have typed the keyword and pressed return, a * character will be 
prepended to the keyword to indicate that it is a user defined feature.

### Domain

The Domain group allows you to create and modify information about the location of a feature. Many types of features require only a start and 
stop coordinate to define their location. However, other more complex feature types (for example nucleic acid CDS features containing multiple 
introns and exons) have composite coordinate information. This application enables you to create and edit such locations using the controls in 
the Domain group.

Start: The residue number at which the feature starts.

Start point: If the feature extends beyond the Start coordinate, indicate this by selecting the appropriate Start Point value. If the feature is completely defined by the start value, leave the selection empty. If the feature actually begins before the 
start coordinate specify this by selecting the < operator from the dropdown list.

Stop: The residue number at which the feature ends.

Stop point: If the feature extends beyond the Stop coordinate, indicate this by selecting the appropriate Stop 
Point value. If the feature is completely defined by the stop value, leave the selection empty. If the feature actually ends after the stop
coordinate specify this by selecting the > operator from the dropdown list.

Complementary strand: Check this box if the feature is on the complementary strand of a nucleic acid sequence. 
This option is not available for protein sequences.

More...: Select this button to open the Location Editor dialog . Use the 
Location Editor if you need to create or edit features that contain multiple segments.

### Table

As well as location information, features can also contain comments that provide additional information about their structure or function. 
The Comments Table allows you to create and edit feature comments.

Qualifier: Use the qualifier dropdown to select the type of comment you wish to enter from a list. The list 
presents a predefined set of qualifiers that differs for amino acid and nucleic acid sequences. These qualifier sets are based on the qualifiers 
used in the SWISSPROT and GenBank file formats respectively. For a complete list of qualifier types click on the dropdown menu.

In addition to selecting a predefined qualifier you can also create custom qualifiers for a comment. To do this, click the cursor inside the 
qualifier dropdown listbox and type the name of the qualifier you wish to create.

Comments: Enter any descriptive text you wish to add to your comment in the Comments column. This column can be 
left blank if desired.

# Find dialog - Regular Expressions

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_find-regular-expressions.htm

## Find dialog - Regular Expressions

You can use the Find dialog - Sequence to select sequences by name or select sequence segments by regular expression. Regular expressions interpret the use of special characters, [\^$.|?*+() , to define complex match criteria. This topic covers basic regular expressions. More in-depth treatment can be found online.

#### Escaping special characters

Since special characters ( [\^$.|?*+() ) are interpreted differently than regular characters, you must escape them with a backslash if you want to match one. For example, to match "How?", you must escape the question mark by using a backslash: How\? .

#### Single character wildcard

A dot ( . ) character is used as a wildcard that can match any single character. For example, S.T could potentially match "SAT", "SET", "SIT", etc.

#### Character sets

Enclose in square brackets to match against more than one possible character. For example, [ND] matches an N or a D, which is useful for finding segments containing similar residues. Additionally, you can use a dash to specify ranges, which is useful for numeric strings that might be present in sequence names.

For example, to find segments with strong similarity to SNGLV, knowing that the grouping of strongly similar residue types STA, NEQK, NHQK, NDEQ, QHRK, MILV, MILF, HY, and FYW, you could set the Type to Segment and use:
[STA][NEQHDK]G[MILFV][MILV]

You can also specify multiple ranges, so [a-zA-Z] would match any lower or upper-case letter, and [a-zA-Z0-9_\-] would match any letter, number, underscore, or dash.

#### Repeats

The asterisk ( * ) requires zero or more matches for the preceding token/value. The plus ( + ) matches requires one or more matches for the preceding token/value.

For example, set the Type to Sequence name and use the regular expression .*HUMAN.* to find all sequences with names containing HUMAN

#### Alternative patterns

You can use the ( | ) character to include more than one set of criteria for matching. For example, set the Type to Sequence name and use the expression .*MOUSE.*|.*RAT.* to find all sequences with names containing "MOUSE" or "RAT".

#### Further information

Edit menu Find dialog

## Filter dialog

The Filter dialog allows you to select molecules in the Data Table based on 
specific criteria. The dialog also allows you to organize filtered data.

an AND operator.

The bottom section of the dialog allows you to create groups based on column selections
in the property list.

For example, if you group by molecule name, then all molecules with same name are grouped together. The molecules are not filtered unless you specify a filter in the top part of the dialog.
To filter for one molecule per group similar to previous Table Browser functionality, you set the filter to top # of items for a column (e.g., activity), and set the number of items to 1.
If the property values are identical, all molecules with the same value would be included. For example for molecules A, A, A, B, B, and B with activities of 100, 100, 20, 50, 40, and 30, group by name (A, B) and top # = 1 for activity to return (A, 100), (A, 100), and (B, 50).

# Hardware Acceleration dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_hardware-acceleration.htm

## Hardware Acceleration dialog

This dialog will appear before you open a Molecule Window if you have an unsupported graphics configuration with hardware acceleration enabled, or if you have hardware acceleration disabled while running on a supported graphics configuration.

If you are remotely accessing the client from a different machine (that is, Remote Desktop, VNC, remote display), the graphics card of the remote machine will not be used, so you may be warned despite having a supported card. Hardware acceleration is not available for remote displays.

The Discovery Studio Molecule Window is a graphically demanding
application. It makes use of 3D hardware acceleration and OpenGL features present in recent (more than three
years old) graphics cards. A number of NVIDIA and ATI graphics cards and
drivers are supported and fully tested to be compatible with Discovery
Studio. Generally, these cards are professional level cards with full
support for OpenGL. These cards are typically more expensive than lower end or gaming-level cards that do not come
with supported drivers. However, the lower end cards that are supported are fairly inexpensive.

For more information, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

Although a small number of cards and drivers are supported, many
users have success running Discovery Studio on other cards and drivers.
However, users have also reported issues on these unsupported
systems including slow performance, incorrect rendering, and occasional 
crashes.

Before you open a Molecule Window, the application checks if you
are running a supported card. You should also ensure that your driver is
the correct version. Typically more recent drivers do not introduce new
issues, but have been known to. If the card is supported, and hardware
acceleration is turned on; no messages appear.

If your configuration is not supported, you will be prompted to run
graphics tests. Click Yes to open the Optimize Graphics Settings window , which renders various images to test whether specific graphics functionality is supported. After the tests run, you can click OK to disable graphics functionality not supported by your card. If a critical error occurs, the test may not run at all, in which case hardware acceleration is disabled.

You can ignore this dialog and try using acceleration, but the issues described above are more likely
to occur. If you turn hardware acceleration off, you are less likely to
run into serious graphics issues, though performance and features will be limited.

If the configuration is supported, but hardware acceleration is turned off, this
dialog allows you to enable hardware acceleration, which provides performance
benefits and graphics features not available otherwise. The following features are not available or are limited when hardware acceleration is disabled:

* Hardware accelerated graphics

* Ambient shadows

* Direct shadows

* Atom outlines

* Depth blur

* Antialiasing

* The quality of spheres and tubes is reduced, even at ultra-high
quality

When running without hardware acceleration, set the following preferences to improve performance:

* Choose Edit | Preferences... from the menu bar.

* Open Molecule Window | Graphics .

* Select Use fast refresh . This uses a screenshot of the window which can make selections or moving windows faster if the 3D window is slow to render. It can also introduce update issues so is off by default.

* Deselect Antialiasing , and Depth cue .

* In the Quality section, choose Medium or Low . This controls the number of graphic objects created. Lower settings are faster, but with coarser graphics.

* In the Rendering on move , choose Fast or Simplified .

* Click OK .

* Consider using a simple representation of the molecule. Without
hardware acceleration, lines, CA trace etc. can often be rendered
faster than CPK, Ball and Stick, ribbons, or surfaces. This is
not necessarily true if hardware acceleration is enabled.

# Interaction Filters subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_i-filter-prefs.htm

## Interaction Filters subpage - Preferences dialog

The Interaction Filters subpage of the Binding Site page of the Preferences 
dialog allows you to set the preferences for defining interactions with receptor atoms that can be used during docking.

### Docking

Maximum distance (Å): The maximum distance between acceptor and hydrogen atoms for them to be involved in hydrogen bonding.

Acceptor maximum angle (°): The maximum angle between lone pair vectors at the acceptor atom and the hydrogen for hydrogen bonding.

Donor minimum angle (°): The minimum angle between donor and acceptor atoms for hydrogen bonding.

Linear acceptor angle (°): If Allow linear acceptor is enabled, this value
specifies the maximum angle between the co-linear vector of two lone pairs
with sp2 hybridization (carbonyl-like groups).

Allow linear acceptor: Enables the use of co-linear vectors to specify hydrogen bonds to acceptor atoms
with sp2 hybridization (carbonyl-like groups).

### GOLD Docking

Constraint weight: A penalty applied to the scoring function for each missing hydrogen bond.

Threshold H-bond geometry: This weight determines if a hydrogen bond is of suitable quality. This
term is a convolution of distance and angle between a donor and an acceptor.
Depending on how far a hydrogen bond deviates from ideal geometry, it's
energy is attenuated by a factor between 0.0 and 1.0. In simple terms,
one can say a higher value defines a more stringent hydrogen bond.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences \| Binding Site \| Interaction Filters |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Binding Site page - Preferences dialog

# Location Editor dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_location-editor.htm

## Location Editor dialog

The Location Editor dialog allows you to create and edit feature location segments. A location segment provides information about the start 
and stop coordinates of a specific sequence region. Features may consist of one or more location segments. Multiple segments are most commonly 
associated with composite nucleic acid features but can also be used to describe amino acid sequence features (for example binding sites).

The Location Editor dialog allows you to enter information about location segments in a table format, where individual rows correspond.

### Table

Start point: Use this to indicate that the 5' range end point either corresponds to the provided start position 
(in which case leave blank) or is before and does not include the specified start position (in which case specify the > operator).

Start: Indicates the 5' base or N-terminus amino acid position of the segment.

Operator: Use this to indicate whether the 5' segment corresponds to a range of residues between the start and 
stop position ('...') or corresponds to a specific site between adjacent start and stop positions ('^').

Stop point: Use this to indicate that the 5' range end point either corresponds to the provided stop position 
(in which case leave blank) or is beyond and does not include the specified stop position (in which case specify the < operator).

Stop: Indicates the 3' or C-terminus position of the segment.

Complement: Indicates whether the segment is on the sense strand ( No ) 
or the complementary strand ( Yes ).

### Other controls

Join: This control allows you to indicate what must be done to the sequence to find or construct the location. 
Although this information is not used elsewhere in the program, it is important if you are annotating a complex sequence and wish to export 
the annotation for use elsewhere.

If the checkbox is selected, this indicates that the selected segments should be joined (placed end-to-end) to form one contiguous sequence. 
If the box is unchecked this corresponds to the GenBank order operator which indicates that the selected elements can be found in the specified 
order but that there is no firm evidence to support the ordering when the segments are joined in (for example) a transcript.

Location in GenBank format: This text box displays the location information as it would appear in a GenBank 
feature table. This may be useful if you are intending to submit the sequence annotation to a public database or are already familiar with 
this format.

### Access methods

| Menu | Sequence \| Features \| Add... \| More... |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Sequence \| Features \| Edit... \| More... |
| Context Menu | Features \| Add... \| More... |
| Context Menu | Features \| Edit... \| More... |

## Navigation Keys

The Navigation Keys are a set of buttons located on the left side of the Molecules tab in the Molecule Window. They make it easy to visually browse through a set of molecules:

| Name | Description | Shortcut |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Display the first molecule and hide the others | CTRL+Left |
| Previous | Display the previous molecule and hide the others | CTRL+Up |
| Next | Display the next molecule and hide the others | CTRL+Down |
| Last | Display the last molecule and hide the others | CTRL+Right |
| Tag Selection | Toggles the tag status of selected rows. | CTRL+N/SHIFT+CTRL+N |
| Show selection | Turns on the visibility of selected molecules. Press the SHIFT key while clicking the mouse to show only the selected molecule. | CTRL+Space |

The Navigation Keys are particularly powerful when used in combination with the Visibility Locked feature. For example, if you are working with a receptor-ligand system, it is useful to browse through different poses of a ligand to see how they are docked into a particular binding site.

To lock the visibility of a receptor (or any molecule), locate the row for the receptor in the Data Table, and then check the Visible and Visibility Locked checkboxes. Now you can use the Navigation Keys to examine each pose within the binding site.

The Navigation Keys can also be used to step through different groups of
ligands. If the ligands have been grouped using the Filter
dialog , holding the shift key while clicking on the buttons (or
activating the keyboard shortcuts) allow you to step through the different
groups. Pressing CTRL-Shift-G will go back to showing all groups.

# Create Non-bond Interaction Monitor dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_nonbondmonitor_custom.htm

## Create Non-bond Interaction Monitor dialog

The Create Non-bond Interaction Monitor dialog allows you to construct a custom non-bond monitor.
By default, the monitor is set up to create a hydrogen bond and steric bump monitor.
The scope of interactions monitored can be further constrained using the Molecular Scope and Selection Scope options.
If there are selected atoms in the Molecule Window, then only the selected atoms are
monitored. Otherwise all atoms are monitored. 
For more information about non-bond interaction monitors in general, 
see Non-bond Interactions .

### Favorable Interaction Types

Hydrogen Bond: Show hydrogen bond interactions.

Electrostatic: Show charged interactions.

Hydrophobic: Show hydrophobic interactions.

Other: Show all other interactions.

### Unfavorable Interaction Types

Bumps: Show steric bumps.

Other: Show all other unfavorable interactions.

Unsatisfied: Show all unsatisfied interactions. This option is only available when the Hydrogen Bond or the Electrostatic option is selected because only unsatisfied strong hydrogen bond acceptors, strong hydrogen bond donors, and charged atoms are reported. This option is not available when Molecular Scope is set to Intermolecular or Selection Scope is set to Outside selection .

### Molecular Scope

The Molecular Scope can used to constrain the set of interactions monitored to be within or between molecules. See the Selection Scope option to further constrain the set of monitored interactions.

Intramolecular (within molecules): Show only non-bond interactions within molecules or chains.

Intermolecular (between molecules): Show only non-bond
interactions between molecules or chains.

Any atom-atom interaction: Show all non-bond interactions.

### Selection Scope

The Selection Scope can be used to further constrain the set of interactions monitored
based on a selected set of atoms. Atoms must be selected for this option to be enabled.

Within selection: Show only non-bond interactions between
selected pairs of atoms.

Outside selection: Show only non-bond interactions
between a selected and unselected pair of atoms.

Any interaction: Show non-bond interactions regardless of selection.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Monitor \| Non-bond Interactions... |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Non-bond Interactions Non-bond interaction strength

# Interaction Options dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_nonbondmonitor_display.htm

## Interaction Options dialog

The Interaction Options dialog allows you to control the 
display of non-bond interactions while editing the complex. The following 
controls are available. Note that some options may be disabled depending on the available interaction types.

The visibility options you choose will remain selected for new windows that you open. Click Reset to remove them.

Toggle Interaction Visibility (non-bond categories): Display non-bond interactions that match the specified categories.
Note that if an interaction matches multiple non-bond types, it will remain displayed if
at least one non-bond type is visible. The checkbox filters allow for coarse or fine
grain controls. For example, all Hydrogen Bonds or 
a specific type of hydrogen bond (e.g., Conventional ) can be shown or hidden.

| Favorable Interactions | Category | Help |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Classical | Hydrogen-bond perception based on earlier DS releases (prior to 4.1) between strong donor and acceptor atoms. |
| Non Classical | Interactions between a carbon donor atom and an acceptor, or a Pi group and a donor atom. | |
| Water | Hydrogen bonds formed with water molecules. | |
| Salt Bridge | Hydrogen bonds between charged groups. | |
| Electrostatic | Charge | Interactions between pairs of oppositely charged groups. |
| Pi-Charge | Interactions between a positively charged atom and the electrons of a delocalized Pi system. | |
| Hydrophobic | Pi-Hydrophobic | Hydrophobic interactions with delocalized Pi systems (such as Pi-Pi). |
| Alkyl Hydrophobic | Hydrophobic interactions with alkyl groups. | |
| Mixed Pi/Alkyl Hydrophobic | Weak Pi-Sigma interactions between a C-H and a Pi ring system, or interactions of other alkyl groups and Pi rings. | |
| Halogen | Fluorine | Interactions with fluorine atoms. |
| Cl, Br, I | Interactions with chlorine, bromine, or iodine atoms. | |
| Miscellaneous | Metal | Metal interactions between metal cations and hydrogen bond acceptors. |
| Sulfur | Interaction with sulfur atoms. | |
| Lone Pairs | Lone pair interaction with positively polarized Pi rings. | |

| Unfavorable Interactions | Help |
| --- | --- |
| Steric Bumps | Unfavorable steric interactions between atom pairs in close contacts. |
| Charge Repulsion | Repulsive charge interactions between atoms with the same formal charge sign. |
| Acceptor/Donor Clash | Pairs of acceptor or donor atoms within a close distance. |
| Metal Repulsion | Interaction between a metal ion and a donor. |

| Unsatisfied Interactions | Help |
| --- | --- |
| Unsatisfied | Hydrogen bond donor, hydrogen bond acceptor, and charged atoms that are not participating in non-bond interaction. |

Show Distance: Display distance labels with the non-bond interactions (?).

default visibility settings. Note that the visibility options set using this dialog are used for

# Open URL/Insert From URL dialogs

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_open-internet-location.htm

## Open URL/Insert From URL dialogs

The Open URL/Insert From URL dialogs allow you to access files on a
network-accessible resource such as a file server on your local area network
or a web server on the internet.

You cannot open a URL when another URL is in the process of opening. You will be prompted to cancel one of the two requests.

URL: Enter the uniform resource locator (URL) to the file or choose from recently opened files. You can also use the Generate URL using options to create the URL. For details, see Entering a URL .

### Generate URL using

These fields allow you to
download protein, nucleic acid or ligand structure files or protein or nucleic acid
sequence files from a site chosen from the Site list.
By default, protein and nucleic acid structures are downloaded from the
RCSB Protein Data Bank ( http://www.rcsb.org/ ) and protein and nucleic acid sequences are downloaded from the
NCBI National Center for Biotechnology Information ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ ).
Enter the structure identifier or sequence identifier in the ID text box.
For example, enter the PDB id (for example, 1crn, 1hbb, 1a30, etc.) of the structure file
or enter a valid locus ID, gi number or PDB chain ID (for example, CA73700, 1CRN_A, y13252 etc.) of the sequence file
you want to load.

ID: Enter the ID for the structure or sequence to be downloaded.

Site: Choose the site to download the structure or sequence from.

* You can add your own sites, including local databases, to access files by using the URL Location subpage - Preferences dialog . You can also view and update the default sites there. For details, see Add sites to the Open URL dialog .

* You can further edit generated URLs if required. For example, if downloading structures from the EBI AlphaFold DB, you could download a fragment other than F1, or from a different version of the database.

### Entering a URL

Enter or paste the desired URL into the text box at the top of the dialog.
You can also choose from a list of recent URLs or generate a URL
by choosing a download site from the Site list
and then specifying the structure or sequence identifier in the ID text box, which is usually the most convenient method.

The general format used for a URL is:

<protocol>://<server>:<port>/<dir/...>/<file>

where:

* <protocol> : Communication protocol employed to access the remote computer and download the specified file.
The application can obtain data from servers that support the following
protocols: http : web server https : secure web server file : local/network file system

* http : web server

* https : secure web server

* file : local/network file system

* <server> : Name of the remote computer.

* <port> is the port on the remote computer 
where the service is running. This field defaults to the correct value 
for all of the supported protocols and can be omitted under nearly all 
circumstances.

* <dir/../> : Sequence of directories 
that specify the location of the file on the remote computer.

* <file> : Name of the file to
load from the remote computer. The application determines the type
of the file by its extension. If no file extension exists for a given
file, the application reads the file to determine the file type.

### Sources of molecular and sequence data

There are many sites on the internet that allow the download of data in one of the Supported file formats . Some of these are predefined in the Site list, but others may be of interest. Some sites now only allow access from a browser, in which case data should be downloaded and saved to a file, which can be loaded using File/Open or File/Insert From/File .

Sites which at the time of writing allow downloads from Discovery Studio include:

| Type | Site | URL | Example ID |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Biological Assembly in PDB format | RCSB | https://files.rcsb.org/download/@.pdb3.gz | 4ins |
| PDB Structure (wwpdb) | wwpdb | https://files.wwpdb.org/pub/pdb/data/structures/divided/pdb/$/pdb@.ent.gz | 1crn |

where @ should be substituted with the appropriate ID, and the 3 in the biological assembly example can be any valid assembly number for that structure. The $ in the wwpdb example is automatically replaced with the correct subfolder.

While the data in some sources is freely available, others may be restricted to non-commercial use or require registration. This is solely the responsibility of the user.

### File location

Downloaded files are stored for the duration of the client session in the Transient temporary storage location for the process in a folder Navigator

For details about locations of temporary storage in different operating systems, see Temporary File Storage .

### Access method

| Menu | File \| Open URL... |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | File \| Insert From URL... |

#### Further information

URL Location subpage - Preferences dialog Add sites to the Open URL dialog Supported file formats File menu Files Explorer Edit menu

History: Click this button to view a list of recently opened documents.

Samples: Click this button to view a list of example data files and scripts.

text box.

# Molecular Overlay dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_overlay.htm

## Molecular Overlay dialog

The Molecular Overlay dialog allows you to align two or more 3D molecules
based on specified criteria.

You cannot run
molecular overlay if the molecule window contains a pharmacophore
query.

### Align by...

Field: Indicates that you wish to align the structures via the field fit method.

% steric: The percentage contribution of
the steric component in the forcefield estimate.

% electrostatic: The percentage contribution
of the electrostatic component in the forcefield estimate.

Tethers: Indicates that you wish to align
the structures via the RMS method. This option is active only if you
have defined tethers between your structures. Structures are overlaid
by a fitting function minimizing the sum of the squares of the distances
between the atoms to be superimposed.

If the Flexible torsions option is turned off, Align by 
Tethers is identical to the Structure | Superimpose | By Tether command.

### Align to...

Consensus: Aligns molecules according to best average overlay.

Target: Specify a target molecule to which all others are aligned.

### Alignment option

Flexible torsions: This option allows the
torsion angles of a subset of rotatable bonds, or of all rotatable bonds,
to be changed to achieve optimal alignment. The rotatable bonds are defined
using Structure | Superimpose | Add Rotatable Bonds and Structure | Superimpose | Remove Rotatable Bonds commands.

### Access methods

# Page Setup dialog

## Page Setup dialog

The Page Setup dialog provides two tabs of controls.

### Page Layout tab

Choose the Page Layout tab to modify margin settings, page orientation, borders, and view-specific settings that are used in Discovery Studio print-outs.

#### Margins

Left , Right , Top ,
and Bottom: Specifies the sizes of the left, right, top, and bottom margins. Measurement
units are those chosen at the operating system level, for example via
the Windows Control Panel | Regional Settings .

Symmetrical: Makes the margins symmetrical
by causing any change in the Right , Left , Bottom or Top fields
to be mirrored in all fields.

#### Preview

Displays a preview of page orientation, margins, and border settings.

#### Orientation

Portrait: Sets the orientation of the
printed page to portrait.

Landscape: Sets the orientation of the
printed page to landscape.

#### Content

Page border: Turns the page border on/off. The border is printed on the edge of the printable area, inside the margins. The left, right, top, and bottom borders can be individually turned on/off by clicking the border in the Preview .

### Header/Footer tab

Use the Header/Footer tab to edit the header and footer to be displayed on each printed page. Header and footer text appears within the margins at the top and bottom of each page.

#### Header

If checked, prints the header on each page.

#### Footer

If checked, prints the footer on each page.

The two edit fields contain the text to be printed. Use the tools in the toolbar above the edit field to apply formatting options to the text, and to insert variables for page number, page count, and the document title. Each item in the toolbar has a tooltip.

Using the three right-hand tools in the toolbar, you can include the
following variables:

| Variable | Expands to |
| --- | --- |
| %page% | The number of the page being printed. |
| %numpages% | The total number of pages in the document that is being printed. |
| %document% | The document's short name. It does not include path information, or a filename suffix. |

Additional variables and text can be added to headers and footers manually. Variables you can add include:

| Variable | Expands to |
| --- | --- |
| %date% | Date the document was printed. |
| %time% | Time the document was printed. |
