# Partition Site dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_partition-site.htm

## Partition Site dialog

The Partition Site dialog allows you to specify parameters that control the binding site 
partitioning operation. Its values are initially set according to the Site Partition preferences.

Maximum partition level: Specifies the number of partitions to use when constructing subsites.
A value of 5 creates 1+2+3+4+5 = 15 subsites. Partition 1 is the original unpartitioned site, 
partition 2 divides the original site into two parts (thereby producing two subsites), and so on. 
Partitioning a site is performed using a cluster analysis algorithm that involves use of random numbers. 
The default value set for the Maximum partition level option is 5 .

Use random seed: The cluster analysis algorithm requires a random 
list of numbers. If the Use random seed option is not checked, 
the default value 123,456 is used. 
To specify a different value, check Use random seed and change the seed value. Changes of the seed value will affect the shape of the site partitions.

### Access methods

| Tools Explorer | Menu \| View \| Tool Panel \| Define and Edit Binding Site (Advanced) \| Partition Sites... |
| --- | --- |

Define and Edit Binding Site tools

## Molecule Window page - Preferences dialog

The Molecule Window preferences can be used to change the behavior of
the window when opening files.

### General

These options allow you to set general properties of the behavior of the 3D
Window on opening different types of documents:

Show chemistry on import: When checked, any new Molecule Window opened shows a 2D
depiction of each molecule in the table. If not checked, new windows do not
contain the depiction.

Automatically fit structure in Graphics view: While browsing, structures shown in the Graphics View are
automatically centered and zoomed. If the center
of the next structure is close to the current center, and the size is
compatible with the current zoom level, no fitting is performed
to avoid disruptive resizing when browsing between structures of similar size.

Animate view changes: Changes to the view such as Fit to View or Center are
animated in the Graphics View. This includes animating automatic fits using the
preference above.

Show molecules with molecular weight below (g/mol): The 2D depiction for molecules whose structures have a weight
greater or equal to this value are not displayed. 
This option affects open Molecule Windows.

Ignore column titles when copying to the clipboard: When selected, the column titles are not copied to the clipboard along with the
selected cell values. This option affects open Molecule Windows.

Sort properties on import: When checked, file properties (column names) sorted when the file is opened. If
not checked, the columns names appear in the same order as the properties in the file.

Calculate basic properties on import: When checked, a set of basic properties are
computed for the molecules in a file when opened. Note that this does not apply to .dsv or .msv file formats. For those formats, molecular properties are only calculated if the molecules are visible. The calculated properties are described in more
detail in the Calculate Basic Properties topic.

### Special

Read protein flexibility from: Insert a comma-delimited list of column titles
within a .sd file of ligands. These columns specify per-atom flexibility
of receptor atoms such that, for each ligand placement, the specified
receptor atoms appear at a new set of coordinates.

Dim features that are not mapped: When checked, pharmacophore features that are not mapped are grayed out. If not checked, the unmapped features are hidden.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

# Auto Features subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_auto-features.htm

## Auto Features subpage - Preferences dialog

The Auto Features subpage of the Annotation Window page of the Preferences dialog 
allows you to specify which sequence annotation features are automatically calculated when you open a sequence in the Sequence Annotation Window. 
Auto features are a convenient way of quickly extracting summary information about potentially important properties of a sequence.

Automatically calculate features: Check this box to automatically calculate features when you open a sequence.

Maximum sequence length (bp/aa): Specify the maximum length of a sequence for which you calculate sequence 
features. Calculating the auto features for large sequences can have a detrimental effect on file opening performance. Depending on your hardware 
it may be desirable to limit the size of sequence for which you create auto features.

### Search site analysis

Site category: Predefined subsequences and enzyme cleavage sites can be included as auto features and this group 
allows you to specify the defaults. Click the dropdown arrow to choose from the following available options:

* Restriction Enzymes - Select a restriction enzyme file and specific enzymes for analyzing nucleic acid sequences.

* Nucleic Subsequences - Select a subsequence enzyme file and specific sites for analyzing nucleic acid sequences.

* Proteolytic Enzymes - Select a proteolytic enzyme file and specific enzymes for analyzing amino acid sequences.

* Protein Subsequences - Select a subsequence enzyme file and specific sites for analyzing amino acid sequences.

File: Shows the current reference file for the selected category.

Browse...: Click this button to select a new reference file for the selected category.

Selected Sites...: Click this button to select specific sites or subsequences in the reference file for the 
selected category. This launches the Sites dialog which allows you to select and de-select individual sites or 
subsequences.

### ORF search options

The ORF search options allow you to set the parameters for Open Reading Frame (ORF) computation. An ORF indicates a region of a nucleic acid 
sequences that can be translated to uninterrupted amino acid regions. ORFs are only computed for nucleic acid sequences.

Minimum ORF length (aa): Specify the minimum length of an ORF to display.

Genetic code name: Specify the genetic code to use for the protein translation.

5' ends are starts: Click this to indicate that the 5' end of a sequence can be considered a start codon when 
computing ORFs.

3' ends are stops: Click this to indicate that the 3' end of a sequence can be considered a stop codon when 
computing ORFs.

Codons after stops are starts: If this option is checked the program assumes that the first codon after a stop 
codon can be considered as a start codon when computing ORFs. If this option is unchecked, the program searches for the first start codon after a 
stop codon in a reading frame to compute ORFs.

# Protein Utilities page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_biopolymer.htm

## Protein Utilities page - Preferences dialog

The Protein Utilities page on the Preferences dialog contains controls that affect how the Build and Edit Protein tools work.

### Create peptides with hydrogen state

These controls specify how or whether you wish to create hydrogens on new peptides. For insertions, mutations, and capping operations, hydrogens are added or not to match the existing structure. 
The following options are available.

All: Peptides are created with all their hydrogens.

Polar: Peptides are created with just those hydrogens bonded to polar atoms, such as nitrogen and oxygen.

No hydrogens: Peptides are created with no hydrogens at all.

### Nomenclature of C-Terminus oxygens

You can apply alternative nomenclature for the oxygen atoms on the C-terminus by selecting from the following options (the default is the 
standard PDB convention, O/OXT):

* O/OXT (Standard PDB)

* OT1/OT2

* O/OT

* OCT2/OCT1 (CHARMm)

* OX1/OX2

* O/OE

### Other controls

Insertion without moving existing structure: When inserting residues into a chain, this option allows you to choose whether to keep the 
original structure rigid or to fit it onto the new section. Rigid insertion is particularly recommended 
when filling in a missing section of a structure or altering a loop region. The new section will be initially built in an extended conformation. Please note that it is best to specify the whole of the sequence 
to be inserted as one action (rather than one residue at a time) by using the Specify... dialog.

Temperature factor for new atoms: The temperature factor is a consequence of the dynamic disorder caused by 
the temperature-dependent vibration of the atoms in the structure. The temperature factor is related to the mean squared displacement of the 
atomic vibration. For example, the default value of 20.00 corresponds to an approximate 0.5 Å average displacement 
of an atom from the position indicated by the model. Increasing the temperature factor value corresponds to an increase in atom displacement.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the 
preferences you have changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Protein Utilities |
| --- | --- |

# Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_clean-protein.htm

## Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog

The Clean Protein subpage of the Protein Utilities page 
of the Preferences dialog allows you to specify how protein naming, alternate conformations, hydrogens, and 
other attributes are cleaned using the Prepare Protein tools .

### Correct problems

Check the checkbox for any or all of the following items to enable the option.

Nonstandard names: Nonstandard nomenclature is replaced by standard names: N-Terminal Nitrogen and Hydrogens: N, HT1, HT2, HT3 C-Terminal Carbonyl oxygen: O C-Terminal Carboxylate Oxygen: OXT Isoleucine Delta Carbon and Hydrogens: CD1, HD11, HD12, HD13 Amide Hydrogens: HN

Alternate conformations (retain one set): Corrects crystallographic disorder, 
removing all alternate conformations and resetting all occupancies to 1.0. The first conformer, as listed in the 
Hierarchy View, is retained.

The purpose of the Alternate Conformations (Retain one set) option is to quickly prepare a non-disordered 
structure suitable for use with tools and protocols in the application. You are not given the option of which 
conformer to retain; however, you can edit the conformers yourself using the Manage Conformers... tool on the Prepare Protein tool panel, or with the Select... and Delete commands on the Edit menu, and/or the Hierarchy View .

Incomplete residues: If an amino acid side-chain or backbone is incomplete, 
the missing atoms are added.

This option does not attempt to optimize bond lengths, bond angles, or completed side-chain conformations to avoid steric clashes. Therefore, further refinement may be required. Alternatively, you can use the Prepare Proteins protocol to automatically refine any side-chains it completes.

Standardize atom order in amino acids: Ensures that the atoms within each amino acid residue are in the standard order (i.e., N CA C O) followed by the sidechain heavy atoms in order of remoteness and number, followed by the OXT oxygen if present, followed by any hydrogen atoms again in order. Correct atom order is essential for some external software, for example CNX.

### Hydrogens

Modify hydrogens: Select this option to add or delete existing hydrogen atoms as necessary to create one of the following hydrogen representations:

* All : for use with most forcefields and modeling operations which require full atom representation.

* Polar : for use with the CHARMm Polar H forcefield.

* No hydrogens : for modeling operations not requiring forcefield calculations in which a reduced representation may be appropriate for performance reasons.

### Termini

Modify termini: Select this option and either Add or Remove to adjust the termini. If Add is specified, then all N-Termini will 
have an NH3+ group (or NH2 if the desired pH is set to at least 8.0) while all C-Termini will have a COO- group 
(or COOH if the pH is under 3.0). If Remove is specified then the N-terminal group will become NH 
and the C-Terminal carboxylate oxygen will be removed; capping groups will be unaffected. The C-Terminal nomenclature is defined using the Protein Utilities page of the Preferences dialog.

Merge capping groups: Select this option if you wish capping groups defined as separate non-amino acid residues to be incorporated within the terminal amino acid. This is appropriate if you perform simulations using the charmm36 forcefield.

### Other controls

Correct connectivity and bond orders: Select this option to correct errors in 
connectivity and bond orders.

Desired pH: The Modify Hydrogens and Modify Termini options use this setting to 
determine the protonation state of ionizable side-chains and terminal groups.

Use predicted pK: The Modify Hydrogens and Modify Termini options uses
this setting to determine whether to use the standard pKa or a predicted pK to set the protonation state of ionizable side-chains and terminal groups. If a predicted pK is not
available, the standard pKa value will be used. The Modify Hydrogens and Modify Termini options uses the standard pKa value.

Display report: Select this option to get a report of the clean function.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Protein Utilities \| Clean Protein |

Certain file types typically contain data that is primarily of interest for its structural 
content. For example, .pdb files are usually of interest because of the structure data they contain.
In this case, it is convenient to open the data with the Graphics View visible and maximized.

By contrast, other file formats typically contain data that contains information about properties.
For example, .sd files usually contain multiple molecules with calculated properties. In this
case, it is most convenient to work in the Data Table View, which is the default layout for this
file type.

After you make changes to the preferences, files of the specified type are subsequently opened
with the desired layout.

# Dreiding Minimize page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_dreiding-clean.htm

## Dreiding Minimize page - Preferences dialog

The Dreiding Minimize page on the Preferences dialog allows you to set preferences pertaining to a Dreiding [Mayo et al., 1990] minimization run from the Minimize Ligands tool panel .

### Minimization options

Number of iterations: Define the maximum number of iterations for a Dreiding minimization. One iteration of the 
Dreiding minimization entails calculating the Dreiding energy and first energy derivatives with respect to atomic positions, and deriving updated 
atomic positions.

Convergence criterion: If the absolute energy difference between two consecutive iterations falls below the 
specified convergence criterion and if the line search step length is 10 -6 or smaller, the Dreiding minimization is stopped.

### Options

Always replace inconsistent atom types: If checked, atom types are recalculated at the beginning of every 
minimization. If atom types have been assigned manually, this setting must not be checked.

If atom types have been assigned manually, they must be commensurate with the Dreiding forcefield. The current implementation supports 
the following types:

* H_ , covalently bonded hydrogen

* H__HB , hydrogen bonded to electronegative hydrogen bond donor (N,O,F)

* H___b , bridging hydrogen (for example as found in diborane)

* B_3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) boron

* B_2 , trigonal (sp 2 ) boron

* C_3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) carbon

* C_R , trigonal planar (sp 2 ) carbon involved in resonance

* C_2 , trigonal planar (sp 2 ) carbon

* C_1 , linear (sp) carbon

* N_3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) nitrogen

* N_R , trigonal planar (sp 2 ) nitrogen involved in resonance

* N_2 , trigonal planar (sp 2 ) nitrogen

* N_1 , linear (sp) nitrogen

* O_3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) carbon

* O_R , trigonal planar (sp 2 ) oxygen involved in resonance

* O_2 , trigonal planar (sp 2 ) oxygen

* O_1 , linear (sp) oxygen

* F_ , fluorine

* Al3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) aluminum

* Si3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) silicon

* P_3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) phosphorus

* S_3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) sulfur

* Cl , chlorine

* Ga3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) gallium

* Ge3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) germanium

* As3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) arsenic

* Se3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) selenium

* Br , bromine

* In3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) indium

* Sn3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) tin

* Sb3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) antimony

* Te3 , tetrahedral (sp 3 ) tellurium

* I_ , iodine

* Na , sodium (octahedral coordination)

* Ca , calcium (octahedral coordination)

* Fe , iron (octahedral coordination)

* Zn , zinc (tetrahedral coordination)

Include intermolecular forces: If checked, nonbond interactions between atoms belonging to different molecules 
are included in the energy calculation.

Show iterations every [number] steps: If checked, the 
minimization progress is reflected by reporting intermediate energy values in the application status bar, and by reporting intermediate geometries 
in the Molecule Window and the Data Table View.

Calculate Gasteiger charges: If checked, atom partial charges are calculated automatically for every molecule 
included in the energy minimization [Gasteiger and Marsali, 1980] . 
Specific molecules can be excluded from the automatic charge calculation by setting their Calculate Charges property to No .

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the 
preferences you have changed on any page of the preferences dialog, not just the current page.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences \| Dreiding Minimize |
| --- | --- |

# Dreiding Parameters subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_dreiding-parameters.htm

## Dreiding Parameters subpage - Preferences dialog

The Dreiding Parameters subpage of the Dreiding Minimize page of the Preferences 
dialog allows you to choose non-default parameters for the Dreiding 
forcefield. There are two tabs on the dialog: Valence contains valence 
interaction parameters, and van der Waals which contains nonbond interaction parameters.

### Valence tab

The Valence tab contains a table that 
lists the atomic Radius and 
central Angle for each of the 
atom types employed. The equilibrium bond distance for a bond 
A-B is given by the sum of the radii for the atom types 
assigned to atoms A and B. The equilibrium angle formed between 
two bonds A-B and B-C sharing the common atom B is given by the 
angle parameter for the atom type assigned to atom B.

### van der Waals tab

The van der Waals tab contains a 
table that lists the van der Waals bond length ( Radius ) 
and the van der Waals well depth ( Energy ) for each atom type. 
The parameters for an atom pair A,B with different atom types are obtained by 
using the arithmetic mean of the bond lengths and the geometric mean of the well depths.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences \| Dreiding Minimize \| Dreiding Parameters |
| --- | --- |

# Evolutionary Trace page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_evolutionary-trace.htm

## Evolutionary Trace page - Preferences dialog

The Evolutionary Trace page of the Preferences dialog
contains controls that affect how the Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools work.

### General

Treat conserved gaps as conserved positions: Treats 
a position as conserved for the sub-family if all the sequences in the sub-family 
have gaps at this position.

Treat a singleton sequence as a group: Allows 
use of a sequence which is in a group by itself in the trace residue calculation. The 
consensus sequence based on this group is the same as this sequence.

### Conserved residues

The controls in this group allow you to create and edit equivalent residue groups, 
where residue types in the same group are treated as a conserved position 
in the alignment. An equivalent residue group can be defined using one-letter amino 
acid codes. For example, you can create a group called "Positive" to include 
R(Arginine) and K(Lysine) residues by entering RK in the Residues column. When a position in the alignment has either R or K 
or a mixture of R and K, the position is considered conserved.

Enabled: Check the box in the Enabled column to enable individual groups. 
Uncheck the box to disable groups.

Name: Enter a name for the conserved residue group
in the existing or added row(s).

Residues: Enter the one letter code 
for the corresponding amino acids in the existing or added row(s).

Add: Click this button to create a conserved residue 
group by adding a new row in the Conserved residues table.

Remove: Select the row you want to delete in the Conserved residues table and 
click this button to remove that group.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

# Dendrogram Window page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_evolutionary-trace_dendrogram-calculation.htm

## Dendrogram Window page - Preferences dialog

The Dendrogram Window page of the Preferences dialog enables you to set preferences that control 
the way in which dendrograms are created. Dendrograms are calculated using the Unweighted Pair 
Group Method with Arithmetic mean (UPGMA) algorithm, and several options
allow you to fine tune the calculation.

### Tie breaking

These controls determine how sequences or residues are clustered when three or more distances are 
identical and must be arbitrarily resolved into a dichotomous tree.

Systematic: Sequences or residues are clustered together depending on the order 
and the proximity in which they appear in the original sequence alignment or molecule.

Random: A randomization procedure is used to determine which sequences or residues are grouped together.

### Negative branch lengths

These controls determine whether branches are displayed with negative lengths.

Collapse to zero: Branches with negative lengths are shown as if they had zero length.

Display as dashed line: Branches with negative lengths are drawn as dashed lines.

Clicking the OK or Apply buttons applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Dendrogram Window |
| --- | --- |

## Export subpage - Preferences dialog

The Export subpage of the Molecule Window page of the Preferences dialog contains controls 
that affect the exporting of molecular files.

### PDB export

Export selected molecules: Select this to export only 
the selected molecules when saving to the .pdb format. If unchecked, all molecules are exported.
Note, however, that it is not possible to export multiple molecules if they belong to different cells.

Export PDB header: Include the header information when exporting.

### SMILES export

Add molecule names: Select this to export 
the molecule names along with the SMILES strings when saving to the SMI format. 
In this case, each line of the file will contain the SMILES string of the molecule 
followed by the molecule name. If unchecked, only the SMILES strings are exported.

### MSV export

Export custom text annotations in ViewerPro msv format: Select this to export custom text annotations in msv format so that the custom
text annotations can be displayed by the BIOVIA ViewerPro application.

Beginning with Discovery Studio version 1.6, the msv format for custom text annotations
ceased to be compatible with older versions of Discovery Studio , all versions
of the Discovery Studio ViewerPro application. As a result of this break in compatibility,
the stored custom text annotations are not displayed.
If this option is checked, custom text annotations are exported in a format that
is compatible with the above mentioned applications.
However, this format is then no longer compatible with Discovery Studio versions
1.6 or later.

### MOL export

Assign Atom Stereo Parity: Select this to assign and include an odd or even atom stereo parity value for stereo centers when exporting MOL files in V2000 format. This applies only to molecules which have been made visible. If not checked, an already assigned stereo parity value will not be modified. Whether atom stereo parity values for stereo centers have been specified or not affects the results of protocols such as Prepare Ligands .

# Toolbar subpage - Preferences dialog

## Toolbar subpage - Preferences dialog

The Toolbar subpage of the General page of the 
Preferences dialog allows you to modify, add, and delete toolbars. You can also assign keyboard
shortcuts to often used commands.

There may be a delay while opening this preference page, as it updates the list of available protocols. This could be significant if you are connected to a remote server, so unless you want to create a button for a protocol it may be advisable to disconnect before opening this page.

To assign a command to a toolbar, drag that command
from the Command tree and drop in onto the currently selected toolbar at the bottom of the page.
If you want to remove a command from the toolbar, drag it from the toolbar and drop it onto the Command area.

Commands: This control is a listbox with a tree control that lists the actions that you can add to the 
toolbars and allows you to choose actions to assign shortcuts. The actions are listed in the order they appear in the menus.

Keyboard shortcut: Enter in this textbox a key combination to assign to the selected command
in the Command listbox. For example, if you want to assign CTRL+F10 to 
the Open URL command, select the File | Open URL in the Command tree,
move the cursor to the Keyboard shortcut entry field, press and hold CTRL, and then press F10.

To remove the assigned shortcut, press DELETE or BACKSPACE.

Shortcuts that are already assigned cannot be reassigned (for example ALT+F, ALT+E, ALT+V).

Toolbar: Click the dropdown arrow to select the Toolbar that you want to modify.

New toolbar: Enter a name for a new toolbar.

Add Toolbar: This button creates a new toolbar with the name entered in the New toolbar text field.

Delete Toolbar: This button deletes a previously created toolbar. Only toolbars that were created by 
you can be deleted.

# Script Commands subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

## Script Commands subpage - Preferences dialog

The Script Commands... subpage of the General page of the Preferences dialog allows you to add, 
modify, and delete custom scripting commands to and from the Scripts menu in the menu bar. Once 
you create a new script command, you can also add it to a toolbar or assign a shortcut as described in Toolbar page - Preferences dialog .

Scripts menu: To rename a script, double-click it and type a new name. Use the Add Submenu button and drag scripts between submenus to organize script commands. You can also use the Add Command , Delete , Export , and Import features described below to manage the Scripts menu.

Show scripts menu: Toggles the visibility of the Scripts menu.

Add Command: Creates a new command and prompts you to select a script file.

Add Submenu: Creates a new submenu. Drag and drop scripts from the Scripts menu , use Add Command , or use Import to add commands to the submenu.

Delete: Deletes the selected command or submenu.

Export...: Opens the Export

to a file that can be imported into another user's Discovery Studio Client.

Import...: Opens the Import Scripts dialog. 
This dialog enables you to specify a .scripts file created by another user containing 
one or more script commands.

Script file: Changes the path to the currently highlighted script. Type in the path or click Browse... to navigate to the new location of the script.

Icon: Type the path or click Browse... to navigate to a graphics file that will be displayed with the tool name.
The file must be in Portable Network Graphics format and have a .png extension. We recommend that the dimensions be no larger than 16 x 16 pixels.

Tooltip title: Title to be displayed when the cursor is hovered over the tool.

Tooltip text: Main text to be displayed when the cursor is hovered over the tool.

Requires: Specifies whether the script
command is enabled when a particular window is in focus. By default no window type is 
indicated, but you can require an Molecule Window or Protein Sequence Window 
for the script command to be enabled.

To create a scripting command

* Create a Perl script that you want to run from Discovery Studio . For details, see Working with scripts .

* Open the Script Commands subpage of the Preferences dialog.

* Click Add command to display the Choose a Script dialog.

* On the dialog, navigate to the desired Perl file and click Open .

menu control and assigns it the default name.

* To change the default name, double-click the name in the Scripts menu area and type a new one. Optionally, you can assign an icon, a tooltip title, and a tooltip text to the command.

# Graphics subpage - Preferences dialog

## Graphics subpage - Preferences dialog

The Molecule Window preferences can be used to change the appearance of
structures in the Molecule Window.

### Projection

These options allow you to set the display of molecules in two different projection
modes:

Orthographic: Orthographic projection produces a view in which objects appear to be of the same size regardless of their distance from the observer. Orthographic projection is typically used in engineering graphics and is associated with higher precision reproduction.

Perspective: Perspective projection produces a view in which objects that are further from the observer appear smaller than objects closer to the observer. This is similar to the way the human eye views the world and provides a more realistic representation of a model by emphasizing depth instead of size.

Angle: The perspective angle controls the amount of foreshortening that occurs in a perspective projection. A smaller angle reduces the foreshortening, which makes further objects seem closer. A larger angle increases the foreshortening. The angle is limited to values between 1 and 60 degrees. The default is 20.00° .

### Quality

The quality setting controls the coarseness of the spheres and cylinders used for CPK, Stick, and Ball and Stick representations of molecules, and for the solid objects used to display proteins and DNA/RNA. A lower quality setting will improve rendering performance by increasing coarseness. A higher quality setting improves the visual appearance.

For regular use, choose the setting that gives the best combination of performance and quality. If you are exporting an image , choose Ultra-high to get the best quality available.

Note that with the Low setting, depth cueing only applies to lines, not solid surfaces, and perspective projection is not available.

### Additional options

Background Color: Opens the Select Color dialog for choosing the background color of the current window.

Image: Allows you to browse for a background image. Note that the image will be resized to fit the view. A set of background images is available in the Samples | Background Images folder .

Line width: Controls the thickness of lines used to
render objects such as molecules in line display style and cell boundaries.

Hardware acceleration: Enables or
disables the hardware acceleration on the graphics board. Some graphics boards can accelerate OpenGL graphics drawing. However, these boards sometimes do not come with enough graphics memory to open up one or more large windows. Attempting to do so either gives an error, or results in nothing being displayed. Turn off this option when you experience such unwanted behavior. Disabling acceleration may result in slower graphics performance, but corrects many graphics rendering problems. For best performance, keep this option checked.

Use OpenGL Shaders: OpenGL shaders allow for faster rendering in many cases, but may not be supported on some older graphics cards. Some lighting techniques that require shaders will be unavailable if this option is turned off. Only disable this option if you experience problems with 3G graphics.

Use fast refresh: Enables or disables the fast refresh mode. In this mode, updates to the graphics window occur less frequently during operations like selection and resizing. This can speed up the performance when the graphics window is slow to render (e.g., when displaying a large number of atoms or a high quality surface). In general the use of fast refresh is only recommended, on some configurations, such as those that with slow graphics cards or no hardware acceleration. If you use an unsupported configuration, you may experience display refresh issues when using this setting.

Antialiasing: Transitions between colors are smoother and look more realistic. Turn off Antialiasing to improve performance.

Depth cue: Objects further from the observer gradually blend into the background, while objects closer to the observer are displayed in full, bright colors. This feature allows a better feel for the depth of field by lighting close objects more brightly while more distant objects fade to
dark. With Depth cue off, object colors are full and bright regardless of their apparent distance from the observer.

### Rendering on move

The rendering on move setting controls the quality of the molecule rendering
during rotation and translation.

Simplified: Molecules are rendered as lines, providing the fastest rendering performance and the lowest quality.

Fast: Molecules are rendered with lower quality and faster performance than Full .

Full: Molecules are rendered with the highest quality and the slowest performance.

This setting does not affect the quality of the molecule when it is not being moved.

Additional pages that affect the Molecule Window, or molecules displayed in the Molecule Window, include:

* Default Layout subpage - Preferences dialog

* Display Styles subpage - Preferences dialog

* Lighting subpage - Preferences dialog

* Materials subpage - Preferences dialog

* Stereo subpage - Preferences dialog

* Import subpage - Preferences dialog

* Export subpage - Preferences dialog

* Sketch and Clean subpage - Preferences dialog

* Query subpage - Preferences dialog

* Tools subpage - Preferences dialog

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have changed on any
page of the preferences dialog, not just the current page or subpage.

# Import PDB subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_import-pdb.htm

## Import PDB subpage - Preferences dialog

The Import PDB subpage of the Molecule Window page of the Preferences dialog contains preferences specific to the import of .pdb files.

### PDB import

Use first model only: If the .pdb file contains multiple models, only the first model is imported.

Remove crystal cell on import: If the .pdb file contains a crystal cell specification, it is removed on import. Otherwise, a cell is added to the model.

Merge chain segments with identical identifiers: If the .pdb file contains discontinuous chain segments with the same chain ID, the chain segments are merged into a single chain. If multiple models are imported, this process is performed for each.

Merging of chain segments may result in mixed chains that contain not only amino acids or nucleotides, but other types of residues. Not all functionality will perform optimally with mixed chains.

Create water chain on import and renumber water residues to start at 1: If the .pdb file contains water residues and this preference is set, the water residues are collected into a single, separate chain named "Water". To avoid residue ID collisions, the water residues are renumbered such that the water residue ID runs from 1 to N where N is the total number of water residues. If this preference is not set, water residues are collected in chains separate from the remaining residues, maintaining the chain ID and residue ID found in the .pdb file.

If the preference to merge chain segments with identical identifiers is set, water residues will still be collected into separate chains. All water residues with the same chain ID will be assigned to the same chain.

Respect CONECT records: If the .pdb file contains CONECT records and this preference is set, bonds between the specified atoms will be added without performing any validation. If the preference is not set, a bond will be created if (1) at least one of the atoms is not a metal atom and (2) if the interatomic distance D compared against the sum of the bonding radii S meets the conditions S 2 * 0.3 < D 2 and D < S.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Molecule Window \| Import \| PDB |
| --- | --- |

# Import subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_import.htm

## Import subpage - Preferences dialog

The Import subpage of the Molecule Window page within the Preferences dialog contains advanced molecule import options. 
These options control the behavior during and after reading a molecule file 
(except .dsv format files).

### On import

Convert 2D molecules to 3D: Converts a 2D molecule to 3D when a molecule file is opened in the product. A molecule is assumed to be 2D if all atom z-coordinates are zero. Conversion requires bond order information so is not applied to formats such as PDB which lack this.

If you do not perform the 2D to 3D conversion, a 3D molecule will be created with 2D coordinates.

Add hydrogens: Adds hydrogens after reading the molecule file. However, hydrogens are not added automatically upon import of .dsv files. To add hydrogens to an .dsv file, see Chemistry | Hydrogens | Add .

Display unit cell: Displays cell information contained in the file.

Use atom charges from file: With the exception of .pdb and .cif files, assigns atom partial charges based on the atom charges specified in the file. If the file format does not specify atom charges, the atom partial charges will be set to zero. If this option is not set, atom partial charges are assigned using the Gasteiger method.

Create animation from multiple molecules: Creates an Animation object if more than one molecule is detected when reading a file. The Animation object can be single-stepped or played using the Animation toolbar .

* More than one molecule must be visible for the animation to play.

* If an animation has been created for a collection of molecules, the animation results in at most one molecule from this collection to be displayed at a time. Only molecules marked as visible will be displayed, and a molecule will remain marked as visible although it may not currently be displayed by the animation.

Perceive aromaticity: Recognizes aromaticity in imported molecules and assigns aromatic bond orders where necessary.

Number of molecules to show when opening files: The number of molecules to make visible when you drag and drop, insert, or open files in a Molecule Window. Note that this preference only affects SD, MOL2, and PDB files. There are a few exceptions which apply if the number of molecules has been set to zero. Opening a PDB file will always make the molecule visible. Opening an SD or MOL2 file will always make at least the first molecule visible if the molecule window default layout preference for these file types specifies that the Graphics View is visible.

### Secondary structure

Use PDB secondary structure: Uses the secondary structure assignments defined in imported .pdb and macromolecular .cif format files. 
If this option is not selected, one of the two available secondary structure algorithms makes the assignments ( Kabsch & Sander or Discovery Studio described below).

If the .pdb file contains no HELIX, SHEET, or TURN records, secondary structure cannot be assigned. 
Likewise, a .cif file must contain _struct_conf and/or _struct_sheet_range records.

Kabsch & Sander: Uses an implementation of the Kabsch & Sander algorithm to determine the secondary structure assignments.

Discovery Studio : Uses an internal algorithm to determine the secondary structure assignments. This algorithm primarily uses hydrogen bonding to determine the secondary environments, and produces assignments which are slightly different to the Kabsch & Sander algorithm.

Predict turns: Allows the two secondary structure assignment algorithms to determine the location of turn structures.

## Internet Proxy subpage - Preferences dialog

The Internet Proxy subpage of the Files Explorer page of the Preferences dialog 
allows you to specify proxy settings.

You can choose to retrieve files from the internet using a proxy server.
A proxy server allows you to access the internet indirectly from another
computer and returns files requested to you.

Unless you specifically
know you need to access the internet with a proxy server, it is recommended
you leave Direct Connection to the Internet selected.
Consult your IT department for guidance if you are unsure whether your
computer should connect to the internet via a proxy server.

Normally, a proxy server URL and port number looks like the following:

http://www.proxy.org:8080

where, http:// is the protocol, www.proxy.org is the address, and 8080 is the port number.

### Proxy settings

Consult with the IT department for guidance if you are unsure if the
computer is connected to the internet via a proxy server.

Direct connection to the Internet: Select
this option if the computer has a direct connection to the internet.

Manual proxy configuration: Select this
option if the computer is connected to the internet via a proxy server.
The proxy server details for HTTP and FTP should also be supplied. This
option enables the following controls:

* Use same proxy for both HTTP and FTP: Check this box to use the same proxy for both HTTP and FTP.

* HTTP proxy: The URL of the proxy server (for example http://www.proxy.org ).

* Port: The Port number of the proxy HTTP server (for example 8080 ).

* FTP proxy: The URL of the FTP server (for example ftp://www.ftp.org ).

* Port: The port number of the proxy FTP server (for example 8080 ).

changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

## Lighting subpage - Preferences dialog

The Lighting subpage of the Molecule Window page of the Preferences dialog controls the color and source direction of the lighting in the view. There are four lights that you can control. By default, only one light is turned on for best performance. The light direction and color are only apparent when you work with space-filling display styles (such as CPK or Ball and Stick ), or molecules with surfaces. The lights do not affect lines.

On/Off: Enables up to four lights.

Color: Controls the color of the four available lights. Click the button corresponding to a light to open the Select Color dialog to choose a new color.

[Light direction control]

The Light Direction Control is displayed on the right side of the Lighting page and initially appears as a blue sphere with a numbered white dot in the center. Click and drag the pointer dot to control the lighting direction. An arrow is available for each light enabled.

The default light colors are successive shades of gray. The grayness, or luminosity of the light color, effectively controls the intensity of the light. By controlling the luminosity of the color, you can control the intensity of the light.

Ambient Shadow: Controls the amount of shadows from neighboring elements.

Direct Shadow: Controls the intensity of shadows cast from the first direct light source.

Depth Blur: Improves realism by reducing focus with distance. 
The depth blur is at minimum at the center of the view and is at maximum at the front and back Clipping Planes .

Atom Outline: Helps visualize atoms by applying an edge to them.

Ambient and direct shadows, depth blur and atom outline require graphics acceleration hardware.
Some video cards do not support one or more of these features.

# Phylogenetics page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_phylogenetics.htm

## Phylogenetics page - Preferences dialog

The Phylogenetics page of the Preferences dialog contains 
controls that allow you to configure the phylogenetic analysis methods in Discovery 
Studio. Phylogenetic capabilities are accessed through the Analyze Sequences tools .

### Gap treatment

The Gap treatment options specify how you treat gap characters in the alignments prior to computing the 
pairwise distance matrix for sequences. Gap positions often indicate uncertainty in an alignment and in such 
cases it may be desirable to exclude all gap positions. Conversely, when gaps have been inserted into an alignment
with high confidence it may be appropriate to only exclude gaps for specific pairs of sequences being compared.

Ignore all sites containing gaps: Prior to computing the distance matrix, exclude all 
alignment positions where a gap occurs in any of the sequences.

Ignore gaps in pairwise alignment: Only ignore the gap sites occurring between a pair 
of sequences for which a distance is being computed.

### Gamma correction

A gamma correction can be applied to sequence alignments where substitution rates vary between different alignment 
positions. The gamma parameter describes the shape of the distribution of substitution rates. Gamma correction is only 
applicable for certain nucleic acid distances: Jukes-Cantor, Kimura 2-parameter, and Tamura Nei. The gamma shape parameter 
setting is ignored for all other distances.

Enabled with shape: Select this option to specify the gamma shape parameter to be used 
for phylogenetic reconstruction. Use higher values (e.g., greater than 10 ) in cases where the 
distribution of substitution rates across alignment positions is more skewed.

### Transition: transversion ratio

The Kimura distance makes assumptions about the ratio of transversional to transitional nucleotide substitutions. You may
specify whether this ratio is estimated directly from the data or you can supply a specific value.

Estimated: Uses a transition: transversion ratio that is estimated from the current sequence 
alignment.

User defined: Select this to apply a user-defined transition: transversion ratio.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Phylogenetics |
| --- | --- |

# Validate Protein Structure page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_protein-health.htm

## Validate Protein Structure page - Preferences dialog

The Validate Protein Structure page of the Preferences dialog allows you to specify the parameters used for performing 
checks on a protein structure.

Display text report: Select this option to automatically display a text report when the Check Structure tool is used.

Fit view to Next/Previous violation: Select this option to automatically focus the view on the monitor selected 
by the Next/Previous tools.

Make structure gray after checking: Select this option to cause the atoms in the structure to be colored gray 
after the checks have been performed. By doing so, the subsequent highlighting of violations using the Color Atoms and display of monitors show 
up more clearly.

Select whole residues plus: Specifies to select whole residues and, in addition, the number of whole residues 
to select on either side.

Rotamer library: Allows the choice of rotamer library used for determining side-chain conformation violations. 
The Dunbrack library is main-chain conformation dependent, the others are independent of main-chain conformation.

* Ponder and Richards

* Sutcliffe

* Oldfield

* Lovell, Word, and Richardson

* Dunbrack

Chi angle tolerance: For the main-chain independent rotamer libraries, controls the deviation allowed for each 
chi angle from the defined rotamer value.

Dunbrack rotamers within: The Dunbrack library includes the standard deviations from the mean rotamer values. This 
preference determines how many standard deviations from the mean are allowed within which the observed conformation is deemed to match a rotamer.

Bond lengths within: Specifies how many standard deviations from the mean are allowed before the bond length is 
considered to be violating standard parameters.

Bond angles within: Specifies how many standard deviations from the mean are allowed before the bond angle is 
considered to be violating standard parameters.

Peptide planarity tolerance: Specifies the maximum deviation from either 0 or 180 degrees allowed before the 
peptide angle is considered to be nonplanar.

Cis peptide max deviation from zero: The peptide linkage is considered to be in the cis conformation if it is 
within this number of degrees either side of zero.

Exclude proline: If this option is checked, then a cis peptide bond from any amino acid to a proline is not 
reported as a violation.

CA-CA distance mean and tolerance: Specifies the mean value for C-alpha to C-alpha distances and the maximum 
deviation from this value allowed before a violation is reported. In the special case of cis-peptides, a mean distance of 2.9 is used as the distance is expected to be shorter.

## Protocols page - Preferences dialog

The Protocols page of the Preferences dialog 
allows you to configure various behaviors associated with running a protocol.

Number of jobs to display: Specify the number of jobs
to be displayed in the Jobs Explorer .

Maximum size for automatically downloading results (MB): Specify the maximum size for result files to be downloaded automatically.
If the size of the result files exceeds this value, click the View Results button in the Jobs Explorer or use the Collect Jobs Results button in the Protocols Toolbar to download the result files
for that job.
Leave this field blank to automatically download all results regardless of size.

This parameter does not apply when running jobs interactively
(in the foreground) from a tool panel, or when running on the Discovery Studio Server .

Close protocol tab on run: When this option is checked,
the Parameters Explorer tab
is automatically closed when a job is run.

Use default path to save a job: When this option is checked, 
the default folder name is used to save protocol data when you try to run or save
a protocol.
Uncheck this to specify the folder to save using the Save Protocol Data dialog .

You can set the default folder in the Files Explorer page - Preferences dialog .
You can also set it from the Files Explorer .
Navigate to the folder that you want to set as the default.
Right-click it and choose Set Default .

Save password: When this option is checked,
the username and password are saved for future logins.
Uncheck this option to change the username and password.

Save intermediate files when running protocols: Check this option to save files created and used internally by the application
during a protocol run. 
However, you are still able to change the protocol default in the Parameters Explorer context menu or,
if the Parameters Explorer is undocked,
in the Parameters Explorer Options pulldown menu.

The save intermediate files setting is saved in the protocol PR_XML data file and will override
the default setting when rerunning an experiment.

Server names list contains: Maximum number of recent servers that are listed in the Change Server dialog .

Path to the Pipeline Pilot Client used to view protocols: Path to the Pipeline Pilot Client executable.
When specified, a protocol can be opened in the Pipeline Pilot Client from the Protocols Explorer .

* This option is only available on Windows and requires a connection to an on-prem server.

* Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have changed on any page of the preferences dialog, not just the current page.

# Similarity subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_similarity.htm

## Similarity subpage - Preferences dialog

The Similarity subpage of the Sequence Window page of 
the Preferences dialog allows you to specify how sequence similarity is calculated and displayed.

### Multiple sequence alignment

Require match in all sequences: If this
option is selected, alignment
length is calculated (including all the gap positions) for multiple
selected sequences, or all sequences when none is selected. A position
is counted as identical only when all sequences at that position match.
A position with one or more gaps counts as a non-match.

Count partial match: When selected, the 
percentage identity is calculated as the total number 
of pairwise identities in the alignment divided by the total number of 
possible pairwise comparisons, including or excluding 
terminal regions where only one sequence has residues 
depending on whether Incl. unaligned 
terminal residues is checked. For example, when Require match in all sequences (selected by default) is selected, the 
following alignment:

```text
CDGWHIKL 
CD--HIKL 
CDGWHIKL
```

is 75% identical (6/8). This alignment:

```text
CDGWHIKL 
CD--HQK- 
CMG-HS-- 
CMGRQT--
```

is 12.5% identical (1/8).

Incl. unaligned terminal residues: When Count partial match is selected, the Incl. unaligned terminal residues checkbox 
is enabled, but unchecked by default. The following example illustrates how the calculation is performed:

```text
12345678 
CDGWHIKL 
CD--HQK- 
CMG-HS-- 
CMGRQT--
```

* Column 1: 6 identical pairs out of 6 possible

* Column 2: 2 identical pairs out of 6 possible

* Column 3: 3 identical pairs out of 6 possible

* Column 4: 0 identical pairs out of 6 possible

* Column 5: 3 identical pairs out of 6 possible

* Column 6: 0 identical pairs out of 6 possible

* Column 7: 1 identical pair out of 6 possible

* Column 8: ignore columns at the termini with no aligned residues in any other sequence
(because Incl. unaligned terminal residues is unchecked)

Total = 15 identical pairs out of 42 possible = 35.7%

With Incl. unaligned terminal residues checked, the calculation for Column 8 is:

* Column 8: 0 identical pairs out of 6 possible

Total = 15 identical pairs out of 48 possible pairs = 31.2%

The percentage similarity is calculated in the same way, 
except the number of identical positions is replaced by the number of 
similar positions. The definition of the similarity is the 
strong similarity used for sequence coloring.

### Calculate for

All sequences: Similarity is calculated for all sequences in the current Sequence Window.

Selected sequences: Similarity is calculated for the selected sequences only.

### Pairwise alignment

Include gaps: The alignment length is calculated
with or without gap positions depending on whether this option is checked.
Terminal gaps can be separately excluded from calculation when internal
gap positions are included. For example, for the following alignment:

```text
CDEFGWHIKL 
CDMM--HIKL
```

6 out of 10 positions (identity = 60%) are counted as identical if the Include gaps checkbox is checked. Six out of eight (identity = 75%) are counted as identical if the Include gaps checkbox is unchecked. Positions in which both sequences contain an aligned gap are not counted in either case.

Incl. unaligned terminal residues: Causes the alignment length to be 
calculated differently. In the following example:

```text
CDEFGWHIKLMPRST 
CDEFGWHIKL
```

The identity is 100% (10/10) with this option unchecked. But, the identity is 66.7% (10/15) with it checked.

### Secondary structure source

PDB secondary structure: Allows you to select PDB as the type of secondary structure for similarity 
calculations. If the PDB is not available, then Kabsch & Sander will
be selected for similarity calculations. If Kabsch & Sander is not
available, then DSC will be selected for similarity calculations.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Sequence Window \| Similarity |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Sequence Window page - Preferences dialog

## Sketch and Clean subpage - Preferences dialog

The Sketch and Clean subpage of the Molecule Window page of the Preferences dialog 
contains options that affect the behavior while you are building molecules.

### When Cleaning

Clean only selected atoms: Configures the software to use only the selected atoms in the clean 
algorithm. Check this option when you want to clean the side-chain of an amino acid without
cleaning the whole protein.

Include intermolecular forces: Configures
the clean algorithm to take into account intermolecular forces. Uncheck
this option when you want each molecule cleaned independently.

Perceive and update aromaticity: Configures
the software to try to determine whether a structure is aromatic,
and to change the appropriate bonds to aromatic bonds when the molecule
is cleaned. For example, if you sketch a cyclohexane molecule, draw
in three alternating double bonds and clean the structure. The Kekulé-type structure (alternating single and double
bonds) is converted to a ring with six equivalent aromatic bonds.

### When Sketching

Add and update hydrogens: Forces hydrogens to be sprouted or updated during sketching or editing. 
If you are more comfortable building molecules with hydrogens on the structure, check this option.

Default sketch style: Allows you to choose the default display style used when you sketch a molecule. 
From the dropdown list, select from the following options:

* Line

* Stick

* Ball and stick (default)

* Scaled ball and stick

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

# Stereo subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_stereo.htm

## Stereo subpage - Preferences dialog

The Stereo subpage of the Molecule Window page within the Preferences dialog controls 
the various ways that the Molecule Window can display molecules in stereo. For optimal stereo viewing, see Stereo Viewing Tips below.

Stereo capability is only available with specific video cards. For details, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

### Stereo Type

Hardware: Use shutter glasses for 3D viewing. This option is enabled only if your hardware is configured properly. Additionally, for many graphic cards, hardware stereo is 
not available.

On Linux, hardware stereo may not work unless you edit the XF86Config-4 file to 
include Option "Stereo" "3" in the screen section, for example: Section "Screen" Identifier "Screen0" Device "GeForce2" Monitor "Monitor0" DefaultDepth 24 Option "Stereo" "3" SubSection "Display" This should be included in addition to the other information on editing
this file.

Relaxed Eyes: Allows you to look beyond a rendering of two slightly skewed images of the same molecule 
to perceive its 3D shape.

Crossed Eyes: Produces a 3D perception when you look at the double image with crossed eyes.

Red/Cyan: Use red/cyan glasses for 3D viewing (anaglyph stereo).

In Red/Cyan stereo the colors are adjusted to provide a stereo effect when wearing red/cyan glasses. This results in any red objects becoming very dark. For an optimal 3D experience, you may want to alter red objects such as oxygen atoms or secondary structure helices to a different color. You can change the color of most objects by selecting, right-clicking, and then choosing Color from the menu.

### Parameters

Angle: Use this option to adjust the value
of rotation between the two renderings in the stereo image.

Separation: The interaxial separation is the distance between the virtual eye points in the Stereo 
Molecule Window. This is called the separation.

Skew: Offset projections for each eye in order to provide for a comfortable balance between positive 
and negative parallax in the Stereo Molecule Window. The amount of asymmetry adjustment is called the skew.

Calculations for optimal interaxial separation and stereo projection skew (asymmetry 
adjustment) values are based on the model size. The values for interaxial separation and projection skew that are calculated should 
be sufficient to produce good stereo depth perception and fusion for most users. Adjust these parameters to your liking. However, using 
scaling factors other than the default of 1 may result in uncomfortable viewing or may cause the model not appear in stereo at all. 
It is best to begin using the default scaling factors of 1, and then apply adjustments in small increments of 0.1 until you achieve 
the adjustments that work best for you.

Map colors for anaglyph stereo: Automatically alters colors of red objects when using Red/Cyan anaglyph stereo.

* The Reset button restores the settings on all
option Preferences dialog to those set when the software was installed.

* Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Stereo Viewing Tips

The following is a collection of tips to enhance the viewing of stereo images. These mainly focus on systems that use the alternating field-sequential method of displaying stereo pairs. There are many different types of systems for stereo viewing and each system has its own optimum methods. The alternating field-sequential method refers to a series of alternating left and right images where the view of the right eye is blocked while the left image is being shown and vice versa for the left eye. These systems often use a CRT monitor and a pair of polarized shutters either on a pair of glasses or on the CRT monitor.

Refresh rates: Left and right images are being
alternated constantly during the display of hardware stereo. This has the
effect of cutting the refresh rate of the monitor in half. That is, if the
refresh rate is set to 60 Hz, 30 images are shown each second to the left
eye and 30 images are shown each second to the right eye. Therefore, each eye
is effectively looking at a screen refresh rate of 30 Hz. This rate has a
noticeable flicker, and can cause eye strain and detract from the stereo
effect due to this distraction.

The solution is to increase the monitor refresh rate. Normally for stereo 
viewing a comfortable setting is 120 Hz. This gives each eye 60 images per 
second.

You must make sure your 
monitor is capable of handling a refresh rate this high. Overdriving your 
monitor can damage it. Likewise, the need for a high performance 
monitor is what makes most LCD monitors unacceptable for viewing stereo 
using a series of alternating images. Most LCD monitors are not capable 
of switching the required number of pixels on the screen this rapidly.

Perspective: Viewing the Molecule Window in perspective
mode is not common for most 3D modeling activities; however, for a 3D Stereo
window, the window must be in perspective mode for a more natural 3D effect.

Zoom levels: The zoom level for viewing a molecule

affects the perception of stereo on the screen. If the molecule 
is zoomed off into the distance it appears to be far from the user. This makes 
it harder to determine the relative distance for different parts of a molecule. 
This is similar to looking at two distant objects in real life. If the objects 
are too far away, it is hard to tell which one is the closest. The best zoom level 
is normally one where the molecule appears to be half in the screen and half 
out of the screen.

Depth cue: Almost anything that helps you visualize 
a 3D model also helps with viewing a stereo image. Turn on depth cueing for 
a more dramatic affect.

Movement: Normally, a moving image also helps 
to visualize a stereo image. Try rotating the molecule while viewing in stereo.

Distractions: When viewing stereo images, try 
to reduce the number of distractions. Any non-stereo image on the screen can 
cause a distraction. This includes dialogs, toolbars, and other windows and 
views. Try maximizing the stereo window by pressing F11.

If you are experiencing cross talk between the left and right stereo images 
(caused by phosphor afterglow in the monitor), try using a lighter background 
color.

A monitor with dust and fingerprints can distract from the quality
of the stereo image. Make sure your monitor is clean when viewing stereo
or 3D images.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Molecule Window \| Stereo |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

# Superimpose Proteins page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_superimposition.htm

## Superimpose Proteins page - Preferences dialog

The Superimpose Proteins page of the Preferences
dialog allows you to set options to control the macromolecular superimposition
methods.

### Superimpose by alignment using

These preferences control which atoms within aligned residues are used as matches.

Matches from pairwise alignments to reference: A series of independent pairwise superimpositions to the reference is performed, which is useful in the case where there is no common alignment.

Matches from residues aligned in all sequences: Only residues that align to the reference in all sequences are used, so that the superimposition is to a common framework.

C-alpha atom in each residue: Only the Cα atom of each residue is used for matching.

Main-chain atoms of each residue: All main-chain atoms (CA (Cα), N, 
C, and O) of each residue are used for matching.

### Superimpose by tether and C-Alpha pairs using

These preferences control which atoms are used for matching within the residues specified by tethers or close C-alpha atoms.

All atoms with matching names: Only atoms with matching names are superimposed.

### Other options

Generate matrix only: Instead of performing the superimposition directly, a transformation matrix is generated and stored as a property of the mover molecule. You can examine and apply this matrix by choosing Structure | Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix... and Structure | Superimpose | Apply Transformation Matrix... from the menu bar.

Matrix name: Specifies the name for this matrix.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Superimposition |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Superimpose Proteins tools Edit menu

# Surfaces subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_surfaces.htm

## Surfaces subpage - Preferences dialog

The Surfaces subpage of the Molecule Window page of the Preferences dialog contains controls that affect the creation of molecular surfaces.

### Display style

Select the display style for the surface to be created. Available options are:

Solvent: Creates a solvent surface, similar to a Connolly solvent surface.

Soft: Creates a soft surface, similar to a solvent surface. This method employs a faster, 
more approximate algorithm than that used for creating a solvent surface. For large molecules, a soft surface provides 
better performance, as it can be redrawn faster.

VDW: Creates a surface, based on the van der Waals (VDW) radius of each atom in the molecule.

### Surface rendering

Select the surface rendering option for the surface to be created. Available options are:

Solid: Creates a solid surface.

Wire mesh: Creates a surface that is displayed as a wire mesh.

### Probe radius

Probe radius: Allows you to change the size of the probe atom when calculating a solvent surface,
the default is a radius of 1.4 Å. This is only available when creating a solvent surface.

### Coloring

Select the coloring options for the surface to be created. Available options are:

Color by: The following options are available:

* Parent Color - Colors the surface according to the color of its parent object.

* Atom Color - Maps the atom color of the closest atom to the surface.

* Interpolated Charge - Maps the interpolated partial atom charge to the surface.
For more information, refer to Color surfaces using electrostatic potential .

* Atom Charge - Maps the partial atom charge of the closest atom to the surface.

* Hydrogen Bond Donor/Acceptor - Maps the classification of atoms as hydrogen bond donors or acceptors to the surface.
For details, see Surfaces Theory .

* Solvent Accessibility - Colors the surface according to residue solvent accessibility.
For details, see Surfaces Theory .

* Aromatic Edge/Face - Colors the surface based on proximity and orientation of aromatic rings. 
For details, see Surfaces Theory .

* Hydrophobicity - Colors the surface according to residue hydrophobicity.
For details, see Surfaces Theory .

* Ionizability - Colors the surface by mapping atom formal charges. 
For details of the formal charge assignment, see Surfaces Theory .

* pKa - Colors the surface according to residue pKa.

* Aggregation - Colors the surface based on the atomic contributions to the aggregation propensity score.
For details of the aggregation score calculation, see Theory - Calculate Aggregation Scores .

* Residue Properties

* Avg. Isotropic Displacement - Colors the surface by mapping residue average isotropic displacements.

* Default Ribbon Size - Colors the surface by mapping residue default ribbon sizes.

* Ribbon Size - Colors the surface by mapping residue ribbon sizes.

* Atom Properties

* Partial Charge - Colors the surface by mapping atom partial charges.

* ID - Colors the surface by mapping atom IDs.

* Isotropic Displacement - Colors the surface by mapping atom isotropic displacements.

* Occupancy - Colors the surface by mapping atom occupancies.

* X - Colors the surface by mapping atom X coordinates.

* Y - Colors the surface by mapping atom Y coordinates.

* Z - Colors the surface by mapping atom Z coordinates.

* Visibility Locked - Colors the surface by mapping atom visibility locked status. The values True and False for the Visibility Locked property are mapped to numerical values 1 and 0, respectively.

* Visible - Colors the surface by mapping atom visibility. The values True and False for the Visible property are mapped to numerical values 1 and 0, respectively.

* User-Defined Residue Properties

* User-Defined Atom Properties

A property which is a user-defined residue or atom property will be included in the Color by list
as soon as a surface colored by this property has been created.

If an atom property and a residue property have the same name, the atom property will be used for the color mapping.

Custom color: Click the color box to open the Select Color dialog , which allows 
you to select a predefined color or define a color of your choice.

Reverse side custom color: Assign a custom color to the reverse side of the surface, if the surface has some transparent
character, this is the color which shows through the surface color. Click the color box to display the Select Color dialog .

### Transparency

Transparency: Specify the level of transparency for a solid surface using the slider control. 
Moving the slider to the right increases the opacity of the surface, while moving it to the left increases the transparency of the surface.

Setting the transparency level to maximum transparency will cause the surface to 
disappear and prevent it from being easily selected.

Reverse side: Check this box to enable the transparency control for the reverse side of the surface. For example,
you can set higher surface
transparency and lower reverse side transparency, which would let you see the internal side of the surface better. Uncheck
this box if you want the reverse side of the surface to have the same transparency as the front side.

### Type

Select the type of surface to be created. Available options are:

Open: Select this radio button if you prefer to create a surface which encloses the selected atoms while including breaks where the surface contacts deselected atoms. When creating a surface, this choice will only be available if atoms are selected in the Graphics View.

Closed: Select this radio button if you prefer to create a surface which completely encloses atoms. If no atoms are selected in the Graphics View, the surface will enclose all of the atoms. If atoms are selected in the Graphics View, the surface will enclose only the selected atoms.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Molecule Window \| Surfaces |

# Tools subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_tools.htm

## Tools subpage - Preferences dialog

The Tools subpage of the Molecule Window page of the Preferences dialog contains controls that affect the Selection
and Rotation tools.

### Selection tool

Selection tools are used for multiple atom and bond selections. See the View | Toolbars | View topic
for more information on Selection tools.

Lasso: This tool allows a more accurate selection set to be chosen.

Rubber band box: This tool makes
it easier to draw a selection box.

Pick tolerance (pixels): This setting increases
the effective size of the Selection tool hit area. Increasing the Pick
tolerance (pixels) value makes it easier to select atoms; however,
for large molecules incorrect atoms may be selected. Reducing the Pick
tolerance (pixels) value increases the accuracy of the selection,
but requires more careful positioning of the mouse pointer.

### Rotation tool

See View | Toolbars | Standard for more information on the Rotation tool .

The Rotation tool has two different modes:

Track ball: This rotation models a virtual trackball so that rotations in all three axes can be 
achieved without a modifying key.

Track surface: This mode rotates the molecule in a combination of X- and Y-axis rotations. 
The molecule is rotated in the Z axis by holding the <SHIFT> key down while using the Rotation tool .

Rotation speed: Use the slider to adjust the rotation speed, and from Faster to Slower to decrease the speed. Increasing the rotation speed means the object rotates through a larger 
angle per unit of mouse movement.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

# Transmembrane Protein page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

## Transmembrane Protein page - Preferences dialog

The Transmembrane Protein page contains controls that affect the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools.

### Membrane

Membrane Thickness: Specifies the thickness (Å) of the low dielectric region of the lipid bilayer occupied by the hydrocarbon chains of the lipids.

### Orientation Monitor Placement

The Membrane Orientation Monitor measures the relative orientation of the membrane with respect to the principal axis of the monitored atoms. Depending on the representation of the atoms in the protein, you can adjust the position of the membrane to improve its visibility. The available options are:

Centered on Protein : The membrane orientation monitor is centered on the geometric center of the protein or atom selection.

Centered on Membrane : The membrane orientation monitor is centered at the center of the membrane, outside the protein or atom selection.

### Protein Reference Axis

You can specify which of the principal axis of the protein or atom selection should be used to define the tilt angle of the membrane. The available options are:

x: The shortest principal axis.

y: The middle principal axis.

z: The longest principal axis (default).
