# Forcefield page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_typing.htm

## Forcefield page - Preferences dialog

The Forcefield page of the Preferences dialog allows you to specify the options used when applying forcefields to 
molecules.

Adjust hydrogens to comply with the forcefield: Specify whether hydrogens in the molecular system are adjusted to 
comply with the current forcefield during typing. Different forcefields require the use of different types of hydrogen model. For example, charmm19 
is a polar hydrogen forcefield, while charmm22 is an all-atom forcefield. When this option is checked, the hydrogen atom names are also adjusted 
to comply with standard names in the current forcefield.

Localize bonds before typing: Specify whether partial bonds and partial formal charges are localized before typing.

### CHARMm

Partial charge estimation method: Choose a method to assign partial charges. By default, these charges are only applied to
atoms that do not match the residue templates: Momany-Rone , CFF , MMFF94 , or Use existing 
partial charges . The Momany-Rone option specifies that a set of bond-charge-increment rules are used for atom 
partial charges. The CFF option invokes the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. 
The MMFF94 option causes the atom partial charges to be determined by the charging rules in MMFF94 forcefield. The Use existing partial charges option specifies that existing atom partial charges are retained (only available for 
CHARMm forcefield).

By default, partial charge estimation methods in the CHARMm forcefield only apply to atoms that do not match residue templates. Any 
atom in a known residue will use a set of accurate charges in template files unless the preference Apply partial charges from residue templates is 
disabled.

Apply partial charges from residue templates: This option specifies whether the protein residue templates in the 
CHARMm forcefield should be used to assign atom partial charges on protein residues. When this option is disabled, different charges are used for residues than the charges that 
were used for the forcefield parameterization. This should be used with caution.

Use automatic parameter estimation: Specify whether automatic type generation and parameter estimation is performed 
during molecule typing. When this option is checked, typing automatically assigns unique types to all unrecognized atoms (only available for the 
CHARMm forcefield).
If parameters are missing 
for the molecular system, they are automatically estimated based on various system properties (available to all forcefields other than cff and MMFF). 
For the CHARMm forcefield, this option ensures that the molecular 
system is always successfully typed without requiring further input.

### XPROLIG

Automatically re-type on chemistry change: Specify whether the molecular system is automatically re-typed when the 
chemistry of the molecule changes. Existing types and parameters are remembered and reused wherever possible; however, you may be prompted to enter 
types and parameters for unrecognized atoms. This option is primarily used by the X-ray applications where the user is frequently modifying the 
molecular structure and always needs the molecule to be fully typed
(only available for the XPROLIG forcefield).

Clicking the OK or Apply button applies all the preferences 
you have changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Forcefield |
| --- | --- |

### Further information

Change Forcefield tools

# URL Location subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_url-location.htm

## URL Location subpage - Preferences dialog

The URL Location subpage of the Files 
Explorer page of the Preferences dialog allows you to create a set of templates for URL locations that can be used in the Open URL dialog . For an example of how to use these settings, see Add sites to the Open URL dialog .

Two of these templates, Default RCSB Structures and Default Sequences are used by applications that automatically download these types of files. You cannot delete or rename them.

Site Name: Specifies the site name that appears in the Open URL dialog .

URL Template: Specifies the URL template. The URL is generated by substituting the mandatory @ character with an ID. If the template is for PDB files arranged in subfolders, the $ character can be used to denote ID characters 2-3.

Add: Adds a new row to the table for a new template.

Remove: Removes the selected row from the table. Note that the first two rows, which specify the default macromolecular structure and sequence locations, cannot be removed.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences that you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

#### Site defaults

The default values of sites include:

* Default RCSB Structures: This is the URL
used by default for opening mmCIF format RCSB Protein Data Bank files; it cannot be removed or
renamed. By default, the RCSB server is used.

* Default Sequences: This is the URL
used by default for opening sequences files; it cannot be removed or
renamed. By default, the NCBI server is used.

* PDB Structures (pdb format): This URL downloads protein structures in pdb format from the RCSB server. As not all stuctures deposited in the RCSB Protein Data Bank are available in pdb format, this is no longer recommended as a default source of structures.

* RCSB Biological Units: This can be used to download biological assemblies specified by the RCSB.
Each structure may have multiple assemblies defined, so the number in the URL template should be edited as required.
For further information please refer to https://pdb101.rcsb.org/learn/guide-to-understanding-pdb-data/biological-assemblies .

* RCSB Ligands: Downloads the structure of any chemical component defined in the RCSB Chemical Component Dictionary, specified by its 3 or 5 letter identifier. 
This is returned in a .cif format file that includes standard atom nomenclature, bond orders and formal charges, and ideal coordinates.

* PDB-REDO: This site contains a database of updated and optimized crystallographic structures. In general, these should have more accurate coordinates than the originally deposited structures. 
Note that only a subset of PDB structures are present in this database, so this URL should not be used for the Default RCSB Structures preference. 
It should also be noted that the data may have variations from the original PDB structure other than just the conformation, which may not always be desirable. These variations can include, but are not limited to: Number of water molecules No SITE records, therefore no Active Site groups can be defined. No secondary structure records, so the PDB-defined secondary structure cannot be displayed. Different ordering of residues and/or placement of TER records yielding different chain definitions and sometimes different ligand definitions. There are cases where this results in residues which are bonded to each other being placed in different chains, which may not be ideal. A pragmatic solution may be to download and edit the file to remove unwanted TER records before opening.

* Number of water molecules

* No SITE records, therefore no Active Site groups can be defined.

* No secondary structure records, so the PDB-defined secondary structure cannot be displayed.

* Different ordering of residues and/or placement of TER records yielding different chain definitions and sometimes different ligand definitions. There are cases where this results in residues which are bonded to each other being placed in different chains, which may not be ideal. A pragmatic solution may be to download and edit the file to remove unwanted TER records before opening.

* EBI AlphaFold DB: Uses a UnitProt ID to download a structure predicted from a proteome sequence. The following limitations should be noted: These are theoretical models. Exercise caution in their use. In particular, note that structures derived from proteome sequences may be quite different from the biologically active entities. This URL template retrieves 'fragment 1' (denoted by -F1). AlphaFold2 currently supports sequences up to 2700 residues. Longer sequences are split into multiple fragments and are only available for human genes, and only by means of bulk download from EBI. You can edit the generated URL to retrieve other fragments or create additional templates if desired. The default URL retrieves the version denoted by _v6. The generated URL can be edited to retrieve other versions if available.

* These are theoretical models. Exercise caution in their use. In particular, note that structures derived from proteome sequences may be quite different from the biologically active entities.

* This URL template retrieves 'fragment 1' (denoted by -F1). AlphaFold2 currently supports sequences up to 2700 residues. Longer sequences are split into multiple fragments and are only available for human genes, and only by means of bulk download from EBI. You can edit the generated URL to retrieve other fragments or create additional templates if desired.

* The default URL retrieves the version denoted by _v6. The generated URL can be edited to retrieve other versions if available.

Whenever the AlphaFold database is upgraded to a new version, you should edit the template URL to use the new version.

* Nucleotide sequences: Allows you
to open a nucleotide sequence from the NCBI server.

To create a template to open a file on a local or shared disk, use the file protocol. For example, file:///C:/Users/<user name>/Documents/@.mol2 will open a mol2 format file from your documents folder given a valid ID, and file://host/path/$/pdb@.ent.gz will open a compressed PDB file from a pdb format RCSB mirror in 'divided' form on a windows UNC drive on a server called host .

# Build and Refine X-ray Structure subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_x-build.htm

## Build and Refine X-ray Structure subpage - Preferences dialog

The Build and Refine X-ray Structure subpage of the Edit X-ray Structure page of the Preferences dialog contains controls to configure commands in the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools panel Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools panel.

### Residue addition

This option applies to the Add Object | Amino Acid at Terminus command on the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel. After adding the specified amino acid, the geometry is defined using one of the following options:

Fit to electron density: The final geometry is determined by the best fit to the Density Map.

Alpha helix: After adding the amino acid, the phi angle is set to -60 degrees and psi is set to -40 degrees.

Beta strand: After adding the amino acid, the phi angle is set to -120 degrees and psi is set to 140 degrees.

Trans: After adding the amino acid, the phi and psi angles are set to 180 degrees.

### Regularization

Number of steps: The number of regularization steps. This preference is applied to the Regularize Selected Zone and Refine Selected Zone commands in the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel. Also, after the Move Atom and Regularize Zone monitor is completed, the selected zone is further regularized for this number of steps.

Phi/psi restraints: Defines the type of restraints to use for the phi and psi angles. Options include:

* None: Do not impose phi and psi restraints.

* Alpha helix: Restraint to alpha helix geometry with the phi and psi angles at -58 and -48 degrees, respectively.

* Beta strand: Restraint to beta strand geometry with the phi and psi angles at -115 and 120 degrees, respectively.

* Nearest: If the phi or psi angles are within allowed regions, their current values are restrained. If either of these angles are outside the allowed regions, it is restrained to the closest allowed angle.

### Loop and termination fit

Sets the number of Monte Carlo trials to perform in the Fit Loop and Fit Terminal commands on the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel.

Number of steps: The number of Monte Carlo steps. Sets a maximum number of steps for the loop fit algorithm. Upon reaching this limit, the search ends.

Clicking OK or Apply applies all the preferences you have
changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| X-ray \| Build and Refine X-ray Structure |
| --- | --- |

Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

# Edit X-ray Structure page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_preferences_x-ray.htm

## Edit X-ray Structure page - Preferences dialog

The Edit X-ray Structure page of the Preferences dialog contains controls to configure the display of Density Maps in the Molecule Window and commands in the Edit X-ray Structure tool panel.

### Maps

These options control the display and behavior of Density Maps in the Molecule Window:

Display contour levels without electron density scaling: Determines if contour levels for Density Maps are defined as unscaled electron density values or are defined relative to the RMSD ("sigma") of the electron density. This affects all Density Maps shown in the Molecule Window. If this box is checked, the contour values in the Molecule Window refer to the electron density. If this box is unchecked, the contour values in the Molecule Window refer to the electron density scaled by the inverse of its RMSD.

Disable map selection in 3D Structure View: Controls the ability to select Density Maps in the Molecule Window. If this box is unchecked, a map may be selected in any of the Molecule Window views. If checked, Density Maps cannot be selected. Disabling this selection can be helpful when other objects such as atoms and bonds need to be selected in the presence of Density Maps. When this option is checked, the 3D Pointer navigation tools in the Edit X-ray Structure tool panel can be used to navigate the structure.

### Add water at 3D pointer

The following options control the behavior of the Add water at 3D pointer tool in the Edit X-ray Structure tool panel by allowing you to specify the default naming and properties:

* Chain ID: The chain name for added water molecules.

* Residue name: The residue name for added water molecules.

* Avg. Isotropic Displacement: The B Factor or isotropic displacement for added water molecules.

* First residue number: The residue number for added water molecules. If the number defined here is already used, this number is incremented by 1 until an available residue number is found.

Click OK or Apply apply all the preferences you have changed on any subpage of the preferences dialog, not just the current subpage.

# Print dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_print.htm

## Print dialog

Use the Print dialog to send the active document to a printer.

The exact appearance of the Print dialog varies between operating systems (Windows, Linux) and 
different versions of specific operating systems (Windows 2000, Windows XP). Please use the following information as a guide, but be aware
that not all options may be available on all systems.

### Select Printer

Allows you to select a printer from a list of available printers.

Status : Reports whether the selected printer is ready.

Location : Describes the network location of the 
printer, or the port if the printer is connected directly to your computer.

Comment : If a comment is assigned to the selected 
printer, it is displayed here.

Print to file : Directs the output to a file instead of sending it to a printer. After 
the OK button is pressed, the Print to File dialog 
is displayed. Use this to specify the name and full path of the file to which 
you wish the output directed.

Preferences : Opens the Printing Preferences dialog, 
from where you can control options such as paper selection, copy count, orientation, 
duplex printing, use of color, and advanced printer options. The contents of 
this dialog vary depending on the actual printer selected.

Find Printer... : Click this button to access the 
Find Printers dialog. This provides a tool and search criteria for locating 
available printers.

### Page Range

The controls in this section of the 
dialog allow you to print all the pages in the active document or select a range 
of pages to be printed. Possible choices are:

All : Prints all pages.

Selection : Prints the currently highlighted selection 
in the document.

Current Page : Prints the currently displayed page only.

Pages : Prints the page range you specify in the text box (for example 1-5).

Number of copies : Allows you to enter or select 
the number of copies to print.

# Protocol dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_protocol.htm

## Protocol dialog

When you launch a protocol from a tool panel or toolbar, a parameter dialog may open that allows you to set values for key parameters.

When using the dialog, you are not able to make changes in the Molecule Window. To make changes to the Molecule Window and retain parameters you may have already set, click the Minimize icon to switch to the Parameters Explorer . Note that you can return to the dialog from the Parameters Explorer by clicking the Toggle window docking icon.

Minimize: Closes the protocol dialog and reopens the protocol in the Parameters Explorer . With the protocol open in the Parameters Explorer, the user can modify data windows (selections, visibility, grouping, etc.) and launch one or more instances of the protocol. This dialog can be reopened by selecting Maximize Protocol Dialog from the right click menu in the Parameters Explorer.

The Protocol dialog includes the following elements:

Title: The dialog title is the name of the protocol.

Parameter Name and Value: Click the value to edit. Depending upon the parameter type, it may provide a list of values to select from, a list of check boxes, a single numerical value, etc.

Show Help: Displays help for the protocol if no parameters are selected or help for the selected parameter. It may also indicate the legal values.

Run: Launches the protocol. If there are required parameters that are not satisfied, it is disabled.

Options: The following options are available:

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Run | Starts the job. |
| Save Protocol As... | Creates a copy of the protocol that you can customize . |
| Save Protocol Settings | Sets the current parameter settings to be the defaults. Use the Restore Original Settings option to reset them. Modifying the default parameter values in Discovery Studio does not affect the settings of the protocol on the Pipeline Pilot Server . Other users, including those sharing the same machine, must update their own settings to customize their client. |
| Restore Original Settings | Resets the saved protocol settings to the original settings. |
| Run in Foreground | The protocol will be run in the foreground, which locks the application and then automatically opens the results when the job finishes. If this option is not selected, the job will run in the background. You can monitor the job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer . |
| Debug Mode | Saves detailed debug messages generated during the run. Open the Output.log file in the Output folder to view the debug log. Additional progress messages may also display and the files are stored on the server for review. |
| Save Intermediate Directory | Saves the intermediate files generated during the run. These files may be useful when troubleshooting a run. The files can be found in the directory generated for the run in the default directory. |
| Use Default Path | Saves the files generated during the run in the default directory. You can change the default directory from the Files Explorer preferences . If this option is not selected, the Save Protocol Data dialog will open when you run the protocol that allows you choose the location for the generated files. |

Cancel: Cancels the protocol dialog without launching the protocol.

Help: Displays the help page for the protocol.

#### Further information

Working with protocols Protocols Explorer Protocol Progress dialog

==============================================================================================================
DOCUMENT 278
==============================================================================================================

Background: Switches the running protocol to background mode. This unlocks the user interface, allowing you to continue with other work while the protocol runs. When the protocol completes, use the Jobs Explorer to view the results.

Stop: Stops the running protocol. 
A message dialog will prompt you to download the current output that has been generated. The following options are available:

* Yes: Stop the job and download the current output. The Intermediate folder will be retrieved regardless whether the Save intermediate files when running protocols preference is set in the Protocols page - Preferences dialog .

# Save As dialog

Source type: HTML

Source file: client/dl_save-as.htm

## Save As dialog

The Save As dialog allows you to save an open document to a file of a specified type.

The Save As dialog functions in a similar manner to the Save As dialogs found in other desktop applications. 
A central file browser allows you to browse the file system and select the destination for the file to be saved.
Shortcut buttons allow you to go directly to one of the commonly used file system locations.

Path: Reports the path of the current directory viewed in the file browser view.

Look in: Provides access to file system locations which are one level above the current location. Click the arrow on the Look in dropdown list to display the list of locations.

Up one level: Click this button to navigate up one level.

Create New Folder: Click this button to create a new folder in the current location.

Views: Click this button to toggle between the Default and Detailed file browser views.

My Documents: Click this button to navigate to the My Documents folder.

Desktop: Click this button to navigate to the Desktop folder.

Default: This button allows you to navigate to 
the Default folder as specified in the Files 
Explorer Preferences .

History: Click this button to view a list of recently opened documents.

Samples: Click this button to view a list of example data files and scripts.

# Select dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_select.htm

## Select dialog

The Select dialog allows you to make complex selections in Discovery
Studio that would be time-consuming or impossible with the mouse alone.
Choose Edit | Select... from the menu bar to open the dialog. The dialog will open in Molecule Window mode or Sequence Window mode depending on whether a Molecule Window or Sequence Window is current.

### Molecule Window mode

The Select dialog for the Molecule window does not lock the rest of the application while it is displayed. This allows for full interactivity with the molecule including mouse-based selections alongside use of the dialog box.

#### Selection Mode

Specifies how the new selection should be combined with an existing selection.

* Add: Adds to existing selection.

* Replace: Replaces existing selection with the new one.

* Replace (New Only): Replace with new selection, excluding previously selected objects. This is useful for selecting an area around a structural feature.

* Intersection: Selects only objects that are in the existing selection that meet the criteria for the new selection.

* Remove: Removes objects that meet the criteria from the existing selection.

#### Scope

Specifies the type of object to select. The contents of the list varies depending on which objects are present in the current molecular structure (for example, for a simple protein, the list includes AminoAcid, AminoAcidChain, Atom, Bond, Cell, Group, and Molecule).

#### Select by

Selections may be made by property, radius, or by extension of a partial selection.

Property: This option allows selection according to various different properties. The list of available properties will depend on the current scope. After choosing a property, select the criterion (default equals ), and then the property value.

The following properties are available for all object types:

* Name: Selects objects by name.

* ID: Selects objects by ID number.

* Visibility: Selects objects by visibility.

Scope-dependent properties available are:

* Element: (Atoms) Selects by element name.

* Type: (AminoAcids, Nucleotides, and Bonds) Selects by residue or bond type.

* Secondary Type: (Amino Acids) Selects by secondary structure.

For all properties, the selection criteria equals and does not equal are available. There are additional choices for the Name property:

* Begins with/does not begin with: Selects any name which starts or doesn't start with the entered value. This allows for simple wildcarding. For example, if you have read a PDB file with active site definitions, then if you have the scope set to Group , choosing Name and begins with and entering Active in the value field will select all the active sites.

* Matches expression/does not match expression: Allows for UNIX-style regular expression pattern matching.

For some properties a list of valid possibilities will be presented, provided the list is not excessively long (>500 values). In all cases the desired value can be entered manually.

Radius: Selects objects within or outside the specified radius of the currently selected objects.
Hidden sub-molecular objects within this radius are included in the selection.

You may choose whether to select All objects, Intermolecular to limit the selection to objects that do not contain the currently selected objects, or Intramolecular to limit the selection to objects within the molecules that contain the currently selected objects.

Types that are collections (such as residues) are completely selected
if one or more of their atoms fall within the radius.

Extension of partial selection: This option fully selects objects belonging to the current scope that are only partially selected.
For example, use this option if you selected individual atoms by radius and want to select all of the objects that they belong to.

#### Apply

After making the desired choices, click Apply to make the selection.

#### Create Group

If you have made a selection that you want to re-use later, click Create Group... to open the Edit Group dialog. This creates a group that can be selected in the Hierarchy View .

#### Examples

To select by name

You can select all lysine residues in a protein by setting Scope to AminoAcid . Then choose to select by Property , and then set the selection parameters to Name , begins with , and LYS . You can use the does not equal operation to select all amino acids that are not lysine.

To select a specific lysine such as lysine 16 in the Heme.dsv sample, choose to select by Property , and then set Name , equals , and LYS16 .

To select by radius

You can select objects within a given radius of some
object with the Radius option.
First select the objects that are at the center of the radius of selection. Because the dialog box is does not lock the application, you can perform this by making a selection in the Molecule Window.
For instance, select a ligand such as the STU1 residue in the first molecule of the CDK2 Structures and Sequences.dsv sample.
In the Select dialog box, set the Scope to Atom , and choose to select by Radius . Set the selection parameters to All , within , and 10.00 . To include the ligand in the new selection, set the Selection Mode to Replace. The ligand and all atoms within 10 Å are selected. To make a selection that does not include the ligand, set the Selection Mode to Replace (New Only). This select all atoms within 10 Å without selecting the ligand.

### Sequence Window mode

#### Combine selection

Add: Adds the residues that satisfy the selection criteria to the current selection.

Replace: Replaces the current selection with residues which satisfy the selection criteria.

Remove: Removes the residues
that satisfy the selection criteria from the current selection.

Intersection: Selects the residues in
the current selection that also satisfy the new selection criteria. For example,
if you have the following sequence selected in the Sequence Window:

```text
G W
TSVVLDWNYRW
```

and you choose Intersection , set Residue to Trp , and click OK , only the following residues are selected:

```text
GWTSVVLD
W
NYR
W
```

Residue Property: For Protein Sequence Windows
you can select residues that meet criteria in the following properties. For each property, a varying
set of selection criteria are provided:

* Secondary Structure - Helix , Sheet , Other , or Non-matching

* Hydrophobicity - Hydrophobic , Hydrophilic , Neutral , or Non-matching

* Charge - Negative , Positive , Neutral , or Non-matching

* Sequence similarity - Identical , Strong , Weak , or Non-matching

* Secondary structure similarity - Helix , Sheet , Other , or Non-matching

* Hydrophobicity similarity - Hydrophobic , Hydrophilic , Neutral , or Non-matching

* Charge similarity - Negative , Positive , Neutral, or Non-matching

Residue Type: Select amino acids by their three-letter or one-letter abbreviations (for example, Ile or I, Ala or A, Trp or W, and so on) in the Protein Sequence Window or select nucleotides by their one-letter abbreviations (for example, A, C, G, T, U) in the Nucleotide Sequence Window.

For example, if you specify Val in the Residue field and click Apply or OK , all Valine amino acids are
selected in the current Protein Sequence Window.

Feature Type: Selects residues having a specified feature.

Organism: Selects sequences which are defined as being from a specified organism.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Select... |

# Regular Expressions

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_select_regular-expressions.htm

## Regular Expressions

In the Select dialog , you can use regular expressions to select by Name. Regular expressions interprets the use of special characters, [\^$.|?*+() , to perform complex match criteria. To use regular expressions in the Select dialog, Select by Property , and then set the select parameters to Name and matches expression , followed by the regular expression text. This topic covers very basic regular expressions. More in-depth treatment can be found online.

#### Escaping special characters

Since special characters, []\^$.|?*+() , are interpreted differently than regular characters, you must escape them with a backslash if you want to match one. For example, to match "How?", you must escape the question mark by using a backslash: How\? .

#### Single character wildcard

A dot ( . ) character is used as a wildcard that can match any single character. For example, S.t could potentially match "Sat", "Set", "Sit", etc.

#### Character sets

Enclose in square brackets to match against more than one possible character. For example, [AB] matches to an A or a B. Additionally, you can use a dash to specify ranges, which is useful with numeric strings.

For example, to match residues with IDs that range from 13 to 17, set Scope to AminoAcid , and then use the regular expression ...1[3-7] .
The three dots match to any 3-character residue name, the 1 matches to the tens position and the [3-7] matches the units range.

You can also specify multiple ranges, so [a-zA-Z] would match any lower or upper-case letter, and [a-zA-Z0-9_\-] would match any letter, number, underscore, or dash.

#### Alternative patterns

You can use the ( | ) character to include more than one set of criteria for matching. For example, to match residues in the range 13 to 45 and 50 to 58, you could use ...1[3-9]|...[23][0-9]|...4[0-5]|...5[0-8] .

#### Repeats

The asterisk ( * ) requires zero or more matches for the preceding token/value. The plus ( + ) matches requires one or more matches for the preceding token/value.

For example, to select all defined Groups, set the Scope to Group and use the regular expression .* .

To select all atoms with names ending in A, set the Scope to Atom and use the regular expression .*A . Because the asterisk allows the preceding token to not match, A all by itself would qualify.

To select atoms with names three or more characters long ending in A, use the regular expression ..+A . The first dot could be any single character, the second dot plus matches one or more of any character, and the final A matches a final A in the name.

Edit menu Select dialog

# Show Sequences Aligned by Structure dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_sequence_create-alignment-sup-proteins.htm

## Show Sequences Aligned by Structure dialog

The Show Sequences Aligned by Structure dialog allows you to automatically show two or more sequences aligned according to their structural superimposition. The alignments are performed pairwise against the reference molecule. For each pair of sequences, the longest aligned contiguous sections are found for which all Cα to Cα distances are within the cutoff distance. Each of these sections must not be shorter than the specified minimum section length. Finally, if more than one molecule has been aligned to the reference, the pairwise alignments are combined relative to the reference and a new Sequence Window is displayed.

Reference molecule: Choose the molecule against which the others are to be aligned.

Structures to align: Choose the molecule(s) to be aligned.

Distance cutoff: Specifies the maximum distance between pairs of Cα atoms from each sequence to be considered as being aligned. Note that this distance should not exceed the normal separation of Cα atoms along a peptide chain (~3.8 Å) as this tends to result in misalignment.

Homology weighting: If there are two possible alignments, then if this value is greater than 1 , the alignment with a greater number of matching residues is favored.

Minimum section length Specifies the shortest number of close residues pairs constituting an aligned section.

# Define and Edit Binding Site page - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_site-finding-options.htm

## Define and Edit Binding Site page - Preferences dialog

The Define and Edit Binding Site page of the Preferences dialog allows you to modify the
parameters used by the eraser algorithm to identify binding sites. See Define and Edit Binding Site tools for more
information on the eraser algorithm.

### Find site options

Site opening (Å): Determines the size of
the eraser, and thus the maximum size of the "mouth" 
of the site.

Grid resolution (Å): Specifies the
spacing of the grid points. The site-finding algorithm represents a site
as a 3D grid of points. A higher value for the resolution results
in a smaller number of grid points (that is, a coarser grid).

Minimum site size (points): Specifies the
number of grid points that the site must contain.

The minimum
site volume is the product of the cube of the grid resolution and the
minimum site size. If you change the Grid resolution, you may need to
change this value too.

Radius for receptor heavy atoms (Å): Specifies
the radius of non-hydrogen atoms in the receptor. Grid points within this 
radius of all heavy atoms in the receptor are marked as
"occupied". The cavity search eraser algorithm will then
identify neighboring cavities as potential binding sites.

Radius for receptor hydrogen atoms (Å): Specifies
the radius for the hydrogen atoms in the receptor. Grid points within
this radius of all hydrogen atoms in the receptor are marked as
"occupied". The cavity search eraser algorithm will then
identify neighboring cavities as potential binding sites.

Radius for ligand heavy atoms (Å): Specifies
the radius of non-hydrogen atoms in the ligand. This is used when finding
sites based on the ligand volume.

Radius for ligand hydrogen atoms (Å): Specifies
the radius for the hydrogen atoms in the ligand. This is used when
finding sites based on the ligand volume.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences... \| Define and Edit Binding Site |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Define and Edit Binding Site tools Site Partition subpage - Preferences dialog

# Site Partition subpage - Preferences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_site-partitioning-options.htm

## Site Partition subpage - Preferences dialog

The Site Partition subpage of the Binding Site page of the Preferences dialog 
allows you to specify parameters that affect the binding site partitioning operation.

Maximum partition level: Specifies the number of partitions to use when constructing subsites.
If a value of 5 is supplied for the maximum number of partitions, this
creates 1+2+3+4+5 = 15 subsites. Here, partition 1 is the original unpartitioned
site. Partition 2 divides the original site into two parts, thereby
producing two subsites, and so on. Partitioning a site is performed using
a cluster analysis algorithm that involves use of random numbers. The default value set for the Maximum partition level option is 5 .

Use random seed: The cluster analysis algorithm requires a random list of numbers. 
This list is generated using a random seed. If Use random seed is checked, the value specified 
will be used as the seed (the default value 123,456 can be edited). If Use random seed is not checked, a fixed internal random seed is used. Changes of the seed value will affect the shape of the site partitions.

Using
a different seed value may modify the way the site is partitioned.

### Access methods

| Menu | Edit \| Preferences \| Binding Site \| Site Partition |

# Solvent Accessibility dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_solvent-accessibility.htm

## Solvent Accessibility dialog

The Solvent Accessibility dialog calculates the solvent accessible surface 
of protein residues. The calculation is done for all/selected protein residues in the context of all/selected atoms excluding water. The results, including the total Solvent Accessible Surface
(SAS) for the whole protein, and the Residue Solvent Accessibility, Side-Chain 
Solvent Accessibility, and Percent Solvent Accessibility for each residue, 
are listed in the Data Table View .

Grid points per atom: Controls the accuracy
of a calculation. The higher the value, the finer the grid mesh and
the more accurate the surface accessibility calculation. For larger
structures, you may wish to use a coarser mesh, since calculation time
can be longer. Otherwise, higher per-atom grid point values are recommended.

Probe radius: Determines the radius of
the probing sphere (in Å), which is set to the size of a water molecule ( 1.4 Å) by default. The SAS is traced out by the center of the probe when the probe rolls over the protein surface, which, in turn, is defined by the van der Waals radii of the atoms.

Context is selected atoms only: Enables the calculation of solvent accessibility for the selected atoms while ignoring the presence of any others. If the option is not checked then the calculation will be performed for the selected atoms in the context of the whole structure.

Create residue groups: Check to create the Exposed and Buried residue groups.

"Exposed" for residues greater than: Creates the "Exposed"

# Optimize Graphics Settings window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/dl_test-graphics.htm

## Optimize Graphics Settings window

Discovery Studio uses many advanced features of graphics hardware to display three dimensional objects, such as molecules and charts. Since video card manufacturers may implement advanced features differently, and because of the large number of possible combinations of video cards and drivers, it is difficult to ensure that all graphics display features will work correctly on all systems.
For more information, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

The Optimize Graphics Settings feature runs a series of tests against graphics features, analyzes the results, and suggests changes to your settings that will maximize performance and compatibility. After the tests have completed, you have the option to accept the changes or continue with the default settings. Accepting the changes ensures stability and performance when running the client on the tested configuration. Declining the changes may reduce performance or introduce stability issues.
If a graphics test finishes abnormally, hardware acceleration will be turned off to avoid potential instabilities.

To optimize the graphics settings, choose Help | Optimize Graphics Settings from the menu bar.
When all tests are completed, click More to view the detailed results. Click OK to accept the suggested changes, or click Cancel to ignore the results of the tests (not recommended).

### Access methods

| Menu | Help \| Optimize Graphics Settings |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Configure your system and software for working with graphics Graphics subpage Stereo subpage

It is also possible to add text and headers:

Preferences are set to use Hardware Acceleration, the

the screen. However the size of the image that can be produced in
this manner is limited by the graphics card hardware. Additionally,
if the Antialiasing checkbox in the graphics preferences is
selected, the maximum image size is further reduced. If the
application cannot produce an image of the requested size, hardware
acceleration is disabled automatically, and shadows, depth blur,
and atom contours are not rendered in the resulting image. If the
saved image is blank or very different from how it appears on the
screen, temporarily disable hardware acceleration.

# Configure your system and software for working with graphics

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/faq_general_graphics.htm

## Configure your system and software for working with graphics

There are a very large number of graphics cards and
drivers available on the market. NVIDIA and
ATI provide access to a number of cards that allow us to
rigorously test our software. This results in a limited
number of officially supported cards. Typically, these
cards are from the NVIDIA Quadro, and ATI FireGL/FirePro
ranges. We test using a recent driver that is available
during our development cycle. For more information, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

Customer reports and
forum posts suggest many users have had success with
cards outside of our supported list. However it also
suggests that some cards and drivers perform poorly,
render incorrectly, and even cause system crashes. If you do not
have a supported card available, you are more likely to achieve
good results with cards of similar architecture to those we
support (i.e., NVIDIA Quadro and ATI FireGL/FirePro).

Limited testing has been run on Intel graphics cards on Windows. Some of these cards do not support all features used by Discovery Studio . The Optimize Graphics Setting startup option will detect this and disable those features.

Choose Menu | Check Graphics Card to open the Check Graphics Card window , which renders various images in order to test whether specific graphics functionality is supported. The window offers the ability to disable graphics functionality not supported by your card. If a critical error occurs, the test may not run at all, in which case the hardware acceleration will be disabled.

Given the large number of users, particularly of the
free visualizer, who do not have access to a supported
card, the application checks your configuration before you
open a Molecule Window and prompts you with a dialog if
your system is not supported. You may choose to continue or
to disable hardware acceleration. Disabling acceleration is
more likely to work on unsupported hardware, but has still
not been tested on all cards and driver versions. Disabling
hardware acceleration may also decrease the rendering
performance by more than an order of magnitude. For details
about graphics issues and working with unsupported
configurations, see Hardware Acceleration
dialog .

#### Further information

Prepare the content of the Graphics View for publication

Hardware Acceleration dialog

# Export and use storyboard movies

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/faq_general_movies.htm

## Export and use storyboard movies

Discovery Studio supports the ability to capture scenes of your structure and then export them as movies that can be shared with colleagues who may not have Discovery Studio . Movies are exported as Web Movies ( .webm ), which is a high-quality, freely available, open audio-video format designed for the web.

### Creating a movie

* Once you have created a storyboard , click the Export Movie button.

* The movie will play through from the beginning to the end,
recording the movie. Clicking the stop button or otherwise
modifying the window will stop the recording.

* The movies are compressed, and can easily be shared, uploaded, or played

### WebM files

There are a variety of methods for playing WebM files including Windows Media Player, web browsers, and YouTube. Various third-party tools, such as VLC ( http://www.videolan.org/ ), can also be used to view or convert WebM files.

For information about supported browsers, installing the WebM MF components, and other supported players, see the Play section at http://www.webmproject.org/ .

Microsoft Office does not currently support WebM files directly.

* To play WebM files using Windows Media Player, you need to install WebM MF components.

* Spin, Rock, and Wiggle animations can be exported with the movie. To include these animations, make sure that the Pause time for any scene which is to include Spin, Rock, and/or Wiggle animations is greater than zero.

#### Further information

Create and view storyboards Web Movie (WebM)

user interface and analysis settings in a set of XML files. To reset your 
application, delete the files as follows:

* Shut down the application if it is running.

* Locate your State folder. This is located here: <Settings Folder>/State

* Rename the State folder to State_old .

* Restart Discovery Studio . The application will reopen with the factory 
default settings.

For details about locations of folders in different operating systems, see Installation folders .

When the application restarts you 
will be prompted to copy your settings from the previous version of the 
application (if one was installed). To return to the factory defaults, decline 
this step.

# Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Plot Analysis

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/faq_general_roc.htm

## Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Plot Analysis

The Analyze Ligand Poses and Create Bayesian Model protocols allow you to
create ROC plots. These plots are an objective, quantitative measure of
whether a test (such as a Bayesian model, or a docking algorithm)
discriminates between two populations (typically active/inactive compounds).
The plots are similar to Hit-rate plots, but the results are more
quantifiable and can be compared between different data sets.

The curve is created by plotting (1-specificity) on the x axis against the sensitivity
on y. A random test that cannot distinguish between the groups will give a
straight line from (0,0) to (1,1). As the accuracy of the test improves, the
curve moves further towards the ideal situation where both sensitivity
and specificity is 1 (0,1). The accuracy of the test is assessed by
measuring the area under the curve (AUC). Typically, the results are
presented with the AUC ranging from 0.5 (a random model) to 1.0 (a perfect
model). Another interpretation of this score is: if you were given a true
positive and a true negative, and you used the model to determine which was
which, what proportion of the time would the choice be correct? A ROC score
of 0.5 is random, and means the model has no predictive value. 
The following guidance is often given to assess model quality:

| AUC | Quality |
| --- | --- |
| 0.9 - 1.0 | Excellent |
| 0.8 - 0.9 | Good |
| 0.7 - 0.8 | Fair |
| 0.6 - 0.7 | Poor |

Consider the four possible outcomes of making a prediction using a model
with two populations:

* TP = true positives, actives that are correctly predicted
active

* TN = true negatives, inactives that are correctly predicted
inactive

* FP = false positives, inactives that are incorrectly predicted
active

* FN = false negatives, actives that are incorrectly predicted
inactive

Sensitivity is defined as the power of a model to identify positives, for
example how well you can pick out active molecules from inactive, or the
fraction of your predicted actives that are actually active.

* Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN)

Specificity is conversely the ability of a model to determine negatives, or
the fraction of your predicted inactives that are correctly classified.

* Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)

Sensitivity and specificity in models trade against each other. If you
raise an arbitrary threshold of a test, for example the minimum score by
which you classify as active, then you will usually achieve better
sensitivity. The molecules you predict that are active will have fewer
inactives amongst them. However the specificity tends to go down, as the
molecules you predict as being inactive contain more active
molecules. ROC plots are a measure of both sensitivity and specificity
across all possible thresholds in your data, giving an overall score of a
predictive model.

Another simple concept to assess the overall performance of a model is the
concordance rate, which is defined as the fraction of correctly classified 
both positives and negatives in the prediction after using a preset cutoff value
in the classification.

* Concordance = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

#### Interpreting ROC Curve Data

A ROC curve demonstrates several other things including:

* It shows the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity
(any increase in sensitivity is accompanied by a decrease in
specificity).

* The closer the curve follows the left and then
the top of the ROC space, the more accurate the
model.

* The closer the curve comes to the 45-degree diagonal of the
ROC space, the less accurate the model.

* The slope of the tangent line at a given point gives the
likelihood ratio (LR) for the corresponding value of the
cutoff.

You can use the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol to generate a ROC curve from
any suitable data, including database search results and QSAR models. The
protocol allows ROC curves for multiple models to be plotted on the same
plot. Degenerate data, such as scores for several poses of the same ligand
can be grouped together giving the ROC for the best result of each group.
You can also set the total number of records and actives to get accurate AUC
values for a ranked list from a database search.

#### Further reading

[Triballeau et al., 2005]

#### Further information

Analyze Ligand Poses protocol Create Bayesian Model protocol Hit-rate plots

# Working with files

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/files.htm

## Working with files

Discovery Studio is able to work with data from a variety of diverse sources including local and 
remote databases and universal resource locators (URLs). However, the most commonly used data sources are 
files, and the application provides extensive support for working with different formats. The application 
works with a number of file formats that are specific to Discovery Studio , but also supports most commonly used
file formats used by applications designed for Life Sciences research.

Files can be opened in a variety of different ways from within the application. Common methods of 
opening files include:

* From the menu bar, choose File | Open .

* From the menu bar, choose File | Open URL .

* Use the Files Explorer to select and specify files.

* Drag and drop files from the Desktop into the application workspace.

* Specify file names as command line arguments to the application.

* Select a hyperlink to a file in an html page in the application.

Once you have opened a file, the data will be displayed in the appropriate visualizer window. For certain data 
types, it is possible to edit the data in the file directly. The types of data that can be 
modified and saved, and the corresponding windows, are as follows:

* Molecular data (in the Molecule Window).

* Sequence data (in the Sequence Window).

* X-ray Reflection data (in the Reflection Data Window).

* Scripts (in the Script Window).

You can change the default window type for specific file types. 
See File Associations subpage - Preferences dialog .

If you open a file in a Data Table View and use the open window to define input for a protocol, you will get an error if you move the file before running the protocol.

### Introduction to file support in Discovery Studio

In general, the application automatically determines the type of file that you select. Indeed, it
is possible to work effectively with the application without knowing anything about supported file formats. 
However, to understand how to persist data in the most appropriate format for a subsequent step, it is
useful to be aware of the basic data file categories supported by the application.

### Types of files

Discovery Studio provides comprehensive support for the most common file formats used for
storing molecular, sequence, or X-ray reflection data. In addition, generic file formats such as text, html,
and script files are also supported. Although the supported file formats are discussed in detail in Supported file formats , a number of categories of files 
are worth considering briefly.

#### Molecule files

When working in Discovery Studio , you will typically work with two general categories of molecular data
files:

* Macromolecular data containing one or more protein structures, sometimes bound to a small 
molecule ligand: Common file formats for handling this kind of data include Protein Data Bank 
(pdb) format files, Macromolecular CIF (mmCIF) files, and mol2 files.

* Small molecule data sets containing large numbers of molecules: The most common format used for 
such data is sd. However, mol2 format is also often used to persist small molecule data sets.

On opening a molecular data set, a typical task is to compute properties or customize the appearance 
of a property. If you wish to use such Discovery Studio specific data, it is recommended that you save to
the native Discovery Studio format, .dsv .

#### Sequence files

Many different file formats exist for storing molecular sequence data; Discovery Studio provides
support for the most commonly used formats. In general, there are two main types of sequence files 
used within the application.

* Raw sequence or sequence alignment data: Common formats include bsml, fasta, and pir.

* Annotated sequence data: Common formats used for annotated sequences include bsml, genbank, embl, and
SWISSPROT.

The application uses bsml format by default. This file type supports all data that can 
be viewed and edited in the application.

#### Reflection files

X-ray reflection data is used for generating and working with density maps of structural data. Although no
single standard exists for supporting this type of data, Discovery Studio supports many commonly used 
formats.

#### Script files

The application provides extensive support for creating and executing Perl scripts. Perl
scripts are stored in text files that usually have either a .pl or .pm extension.

#### HTML and text files

Many result files and reports generated by the application are stored as text or html files. Discovery Studio includes a Text Window for viewing such files. The application does not provide 
support for editing html files, but text files can be manipulated in the Script Window if required.

#### Further information

Files Explorer File menu Supported file formats Files Explorer page - Preferences dialog Open URL dialog URL Location subpage - Preferences dialog Add sites to the Open URL dialog

# Distributed grid computing

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/grid_hw.htm

## Distributed grid computing

### Background

Grid computing is a type of distributed computing in which CPU and/or GPU resources are shared across a computer network, allowing all connected machines to operate as a compute cluster. Discovery Studio , in conjunction with Pipeline Pilot Server , allows you to take advantage of Linux grid technologies such as PBS Professional and Slurm. For more information, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files. Distributed grid computing makes it possible to:

* Access extra computing power to work more efficiently

* Queue long-running jobs

* Efficiently distribute protocols and their subprocesses over cluster nodes

* Take advantage of improved capabilities for computer hardware administration and performance tuning

Pipeline Pilot can delegate management of protocol job distribution to a supported grid engine on Linux. Details of how to configure the Pipeline Pilot Server through the administration portal are provided in the Pipeline Pilot Administration Reference Guide.

Discovery Studio protocols can be classified into several typical types based on the computational intensity and method of parallelization :

* Short-running protocols that take less than a couple of minutes.

* Long-running protocols that take minutes or hours, but do not support parallelization by default.

* Protocols with coarse-grained parallelization where multiple subprocesses are spawned by the protocol at the same time, each taking a subset of the data records for processing. Example protocol: In Situ Ligand Minimization .

* Protocols with fine-grained parallelization or GPU where long running calculations are parallelized by the computational engine, such as NAMD or CHARMm. Example protocol: Dynamics (Production) .

* Protocols with combination of coarse-grained and fine-grained parallelization where each individual coarse-grained subprocess runs fine-grained parallelization calculation. Example protocol: Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) .

For short-running protocols, one may want to have the results returned immediately rather than risk them being queued on a grid system. The combined grid settings provided on the Pipeline Pilot administration portal and the protocol parameters allow the short-running protocols to bypass the queueing system. However, a protocol that is not submitted through the queueing mechanism will be run and consume resources on the head node. If a grid has limited resources on the head node, it is best set the grid options on the administration portal to force all protocols to run through a queueing system to prevent overloading the grid head node. In such case, the server is suitable for long running calculations and for short running job which immediate response is desirable, a separate server should be used.

Once the Pipeline Pilot Server is configured to work with a grid engine, you can take advantage of this by using protocols that are configured for grid computing by default, or by customizing a protocol that is not. The following sections cover this in detail:

* Using Protocols that Provide Grid Support For Coarse-Grained Parallelization

* Using 
Protocols that Provide Grid Support Without Coarse-Grained Parallelization

* Using Protocols that Provide Grid Support for Fine-Grained Parallelization or GPU

* Customizing Protocols to Work with Grid Systems

Mixed computing resources are not supported in the server list. You can only specify a single grid or cluster.

For more information, see the following topic in the Pipeline Pilot Help Center: Administrators > Setup and Configuration > Server Deployments > Grids .

The Discovery Studio protocols that supports coarse-grained parallelization will run on grid when the parallel option is turned on and when the server is configured to work with a grid engine .
To run these protocols through the grid engine, set the Parallel Processing parameter to True .

Some coarse-grained parallelized protocols also support fine-grained parallelization in each coarse-grained subprocesse. In this case, the resources to run each fine-grained parallelized job can be requested through the queueing system and passed on to the fine-grained calculation.

### Using Protocols that Provide Grid Support Without Coarse-Grained Parallelization

Some protocols are not suitable for coarse-grained parallelization, but are relatively long running and may still benefit from being run on a grid. The following protocols will be automatically submitted to the queue if the server is configured to support grid computing regardless if the Run on Grid parameter is set to True or False on the Administration portal.

Protein Modeling

* Add Membrane and Orient Molecule

Some of the protocols run computation engines, such as CHARMm and NAMD, with fine-grained parallelization. A subset of such protocols are able to reserve the specified number of cores with the queuing system and pass this resource to the fine-grained parallel calculation.

Simulation

* Dynamics (Equilibration)

* Dynamics (Heating or Cooling)

* Dynamics (Production)

* Dynamics (NAMD)

* Standard Dynamics Cascade

* Steered Molecular Dynamics

* Calculate Energy (QM-MM)

* Minimization (QM-MM)

From the protocol UI, set Run on Grid to True and use the Grid Options parameter to specify the number of cores to run the fine-grained parallelization on grid.

Ensure that the Number of Processors parameter is the same as the Number of Cores in the Grid Options parameter. The former parameter controls the number of threads for CHARMm or NAMD calculation and the latter parameter reserves the specified number of cores with the queuing system. The Number of Processors specified should be less or equal to the number of processors on a single computer node in the cluster because the applications are not compiled for cross-node purposes.

Both Dynamics (Production) and Dynamics (NAMD) protocols support running GPU calculation on a grid. Use the Grid Options parameter to request the GPU resource. Although it is possible to run a single GPU calculation using multiple GPU cards, it is recommended to run each job with single card since the calculation on GPU is much faster comparing to CPU and the scalability of using multiple GPU cards is not suffiently high.

The exact syntax to request the GPU resource on a grid is dependent on the grid engine setup. A typical example is ngpus=1. It is expected that the grid engine will set environment variable CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to the allocated GPU device indices.

Since there is some delay when submitting a job through the grid, this functionality may actually decrease performance for some of the fast-running protocols. That is why not all of the protocols are set up to use grid computing by default. However, if you think that a particular protocol would benefit from this feature, you can easily create a custom version of it using the Pipeline Pilot Client .

You may also modify a non-parallel protocol to be run on a grid queue.
This may be useful for efficient scheduling of relatively long running
protocols even if they are not able to be run in parallel.

To enable grid computing for coarse-grained parallelization

* Open the protocol in the Pipeline Pilot Client and use File | Save As to make a copy.

* Connect the Pipeline Pilot Client to the grid enabled server.

* Select the components in the protocol that should be parallelized.

* Right-click and choose Collapse to Subprotocol .

* Right-click the subprotocol and choose Edit .

* In the Implementation tab, set Run on Grid to True .

* Set Queue Name to the grid engine queue that you wish to use.

* Save your changes.

To enable grid computing for a protocol that does not support coarse-grained parallelization

* Create a new protocol, and then right-click and choose Edit.

* Open the Implementation tab and highlight the Run On Grid group
of parameters.

* Click Cancel and open to the
protocol you wish to run on a grid.

* Right-click the white space and choose Edit from the
context menu.

* In the Parameter tab, click Paste to add the grid
parameters.

* Set Run on Grid to True .

For additional information about customizing protocols and using them in Discovery Studio , see Customizing protocols .

### Some Commonly Used Grid Options

The following are some commonly used options for PBS and Slurm:

| Job Specification | PBS | Slurm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node Count | -l nodes=[count] | -N [min[-max]] |
| CPU Count | -l ncpus=[count] | -n [count] |
| GPU Count | -l ngpus=[count] | --gpus=[count] |
| Wall Clock Limit | -l walltime=[hh:mm:ss] | -t [min] OR -t [days-hh:mm:ss] |
| Memory Size | -l mem=[MB] | --mem=[mem][M\|G\|T] OR --mem-per-cpu=[mem][M\|G\|T] |
| Generic Resources | -l other=[resource_spec] | --gres=[resource_spec] |

#### Further information

Installing and configuring a grid Run a parallel calculation Run a GPU calculation Administering Pipeline Pilot

The workaround is to use the Clean and Aromaticity perception algorithms to update the aromaticity so that the system distinguishes between the nitrogens properly. |
| Partial Double | Change the type of the selected bonds to partial double. This type is typically used to indicate that there are several resonance structures in each of which the bond has different (integral) bond orders. However, there is no implication that these resonance structures represent an aromatic system. |
| Create Pi Bond | Create a pi bond between appropriate selected objects. For details, see Chemistry \| Bond \| Create Pi Bond . |
| Contract | Contract the selected bonds bond by one atom. For details, see Chemistry \| Bond \| Contract . |
| Fuse | Fuse the selected atoms or bonds of two different molecules. For details, see Chemistry \| Bond \| Fuse . |
| Bond Order From 3D | Calculate bond orders from the 3D geometry of the selected residues/molecules, or all molecules in the active window if no selection is made. For details, see Chemistry \| Bond \| Bond Order From 3D . |
| Localize | Localize the partial double bonds of the selected molecules, or all molecules in the active window if no selection is made. For details, see Chemistry \| Bond \| Localize . |
| Perceive Aromaticity | Perceive aromaticity for ring systems. For details, see Chemistry \| Bond \| Perceive Aromaticity . |

If the Add and update hydrogens option
is chosen under Edit | Preferences... | Molecule Window |
Sketch and Clean , hydrogens are updated when bonds are changed.

# Chemistry | Charge

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_chemistry_charge.htm

## Chemistry | Charge

These options set 
the formal charge of the selected atoms, or calculate Gasteiger
partial charges for all atoms in the molecules containing the selected atoms. 
If no atoms are selected, the calculation will be performed for all molecules.

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| +1 | Increase the formal charge of the selected atoms by 1. |
| 0 | Set the formal charge of the selected atoms to 0. |
| -1 | Decrease the formal charge of the selected atoms by 1. |
| Set | Open the Set Formal Charge dialog , which you can use to assign a specific formal charge to the selected atoms. |
| Calculate | Calculate the atomic partial charges using the Gasteiger method. |

### Formal charges

The formal charge Q of an atom in a molecule is given as Q = VE - LP×2 - B,
where VE is the number of the atom's valence electrons, LP is the number of 
the atom's electron lone pairs, and B is the sum of the bond orders of all 
bonds with other atoms. Changing the formal charge can be used to change 
the valence of an atom. For example, an aliphatic amine can be converted 
to an ammonium cation by changing the formal charge of the nitrogen atom 
from 0 to 1.

If the Add and update hydrogens option is chosen 
under Edit | Preferences... | Molecule Window | Sketch and Clean , 
then hydrogens are added or removed to conform with the formal charge.

#### Examples

The nitrogen in an ammonium ion R 1 R 2 R 3 NH + has a formal charge of +1.

The second oxygen in a carboxylate group (-COO - ) has a formal charge of -1. 
It is also possible to represent a carboxylate group by marking the carbon-oxygen bonds 
as partial double bonds and assigning formal charges of -1/2 to both oxygen atoms.

If a structure contains atoms with fractional formal charges, it cannot be saved to .mol files.

### Partial charges

If formal charges have been assigned to any of the atoms subjected to the partial charge calculation, 
they are added to the initial partial charges used in the Gasteiger-Marsili method. The sum of the 
final calculated partial charges will be equal to the sum of the formal charges.

If any atoms are selected, the calculation will include all of the atoms in the molecules 
that contain the selected atoms. It is not possible to calculate Gasteiger charges for a 
subset of atoms in a molecule.

### Access methods

| Menu | Chemistry \| Charge |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard shortcut | ALT+C, C |

Set Formal Charge dialog Chemistry menu Molecule Window page - Preferences dialog
