# Theory - Adding Hydrogens

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_chemistry_hydrogens_add_th.htm

## Theory - Adding Hydrogens

The Chemistry | Hydrogens | Add option adds hydrogen atoms to the selected atoms, or, if no selection is made, to any molecules in the active
window. The placement of the added hydrogen atoms depends on the element type and
formal charge of the central atom, and the types of any existing bonds. The (central
atom)-(hydrogen atom) bond distances are given by the sum of the covalent radii of the central atom and the hydrogen
atom.

This topic discusses the details of how the application adds hydrogens:

* Determining the number of hydrogens

* Determining the bond distance

* Placing the hydrogen atoms

The number of hydrogens added to an atom is derived from the element type of the atom, the number and types of bonds to other non-hydrogen
atoms, and the formal charge of the atom. The element type and formal charge of the atom together specify the valence of the atom, which is the
number of hydrogen atoms that could be added to the isolated atom. For example, the valence for a neutral, single carbon atom is 4, and the
number of hydrogen atoms which could be added to this atom is 4 (CH 4 ). The valence for a single nitrogen atom with a formal charge
of +1 is also 4 (NH 4 + ), whereas the valence for a single carbon atom with a formal charge of -1 is 3
(CH 3 - ). If the atom is already connected by bonds to other atoms, any single bond reduces the number of hydrogen atoms
added by one; every double bond reduces the number of hydrogen atoms added by two, and every triple bond reduces the number of hydrogen atoms
added by three.

The bond distance for any added bonds to hydrogen atoms is obtained from the sum of the covalent radii of two atoms. For hydrogen, the
covalent radius employed is 0.32 Å (32 picometers). The covalent radii employed for common element types are:

* Carbon: 0.77 Å

* Nitrogen: 0.75 Å

* Oxygen: 0.73 Å

* Fluorine: 0.72 Å

* Phosphorus: 1.06 Å

* Sulfur: 1.02 Å.

The placement of the hydrogen atoms added to an atom depends on whether there are already bonds to other atoms and the types of those bonds,
as well as on the total number of valence electrons of the atom. For example, the valence of a nitrogen atom is 3, but its number of valence
electrons is 5, resulting in one lone pair of electrons which is not involved in covalent bonds. If there are no bonds or all bonds are single
bonds, the hydrogen atoms should ideally be placed at the corners of a tetrahedron if the number of valence electrons is 4 or larger. If there
are no bonds or all bonds are single bonds and the number of valence electrons is 3, the hydrogen atoms should ideally be placed at the corners
of an equilateral triangle. If there are no bonds or all bonds are single bonds and the number of valence electrons is 2, the hydrogen atoms
and the central atom should be collinear. If there is one double bond and the number of valence electrons is 4 or larger, the hydrogen atoms
should ideally be placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle (example: CH 2 =NH 2 + ). If there is one triple
bond and the number of valence electrons is 4 or larger, the hydrogen atom should be placed so that the hydrogen atom is collinear with the
atoms of the triple bond (example: H-C≡N).

For all geometries, the coordinates for placing hydrogen atoms added to an atom A are calculated based on the number of existing bonds
involving atom A.

The coordinates of already existing hydrogen atoms are not altered when hydrogen atoms are added.

#### Linear geometry

In the case of a linear geometry where a hydrogen atom H is being added to an atom A already connected to one other atom B, and if the 3D
Cartesian coordinates of the atoms are denoted as r(H), r(A) and r(B), the algorithm placing the hydrogen atom first calculates the vector

v1 = r(A) - r(B)

which points from the atom B towards the atom A. The vector v1 is then normalized so that its length is 1. If atoms A and B
happen to be coincident, vector v1 is left unnormalized. In this case, vector v1 is zero (i.e. has zero length). The position of the hydrogen
atom is then obtained as

r(H) = d(HA)*v1

where d(HA) is the bond distance obtained from the sum of the covalent radii of atoms H and A (see above).

If the atom is not connected to other atoms, the hydrogen atoms are placed at r(A) + d(HA)*|i> for the first hydrogen atom and
r(A) - d(HA)*|i> for the second hydrogen atom. |i> is a vector of length 1 along the x axis of the 3D Cartesian coordinate system.

#### Trigonal geometry

In the case of a trigonal geometry, if no bonds exist, hydrogen atoms will be added at

(A) + d(HA)*|i> for the first hydrogen atom, r(A) - (1/2)*d(HA)*|i> + y*d(HA)*|j> for the second hydrogen atom and, r(A) - (1/2)*d(HA)*|i> - y*d(HA)*|j> for the third hydrogen atom,

where y = √(3)/2, d(HA), the bond distance and |j> is a vector of length 1 along the y axis of the 3D coordinate system.

If exactly one bond to another atom B exists, it is determined whether it is possible to specify a dihedral angle HABC by including an
additional atom C. If this is the case, it is also determined whether the bond AB is part of an allene system where three or more atoms are
connected by consecutive double bonds. A vector v1 is calculated as r(A) - r(B) followed by normalization as explained previously. If there is
no atom C, a vector v2 perpendicular to v1 is calculated. The calculation first defines a trial vector t with 3D coordinates (1,1,1). If the
x component of v1, v1.x, is not zero, then the x component of t, t.x, is replaced with the value -(v1.y + v1.z)/v1.x where v1.y and v1.z denote
the y and z components of vector v1, respectively. Otherwise, similar replacements are made for t.y and t.z. The resulting trial vector t is
then normalized to obtain v2. If v1 has a length of zero, v2 also has a length of zero. With v2 determined, the hydrogen atom positions are
obtained as

r(A) + d(HA)*(-(1/2)*v1 + y*v2) and r(A) + d(HA)*(-(1/2)*v1 - y*v2)

respectively, where y = √(3)/2.

If there is an atom C, a normalized vector v3 is calculated from the difference r(C) - r(B).

The atom C is chosen as the first atom connected to B which is not atom A; the order in
which atoms are connected to each other therefore effectively determines which atom is chosen. If no allene system is present of if the
allene system contains an even number of atoms, a vector v2 is calculated as the double 3D vector cross product [(v1 × v3) × v1]
which brings the resulting vector into the plane formed by v1 and v3. If an allene system is present and if it contains an odd number of
atoms, the vector v2 is calculated as the 3D vector cross product (v3 × v1). The final hydrogen atom positions are then obtained from
v1 and v2 as stated if no atom C is present.

If exactly two bonds to other atoms B and C exist, a normalized vector vb is calculated from the difference r(A) - r(B), and a
normalized vector vc is calculated from the difference r(A) - r(C). The two vectors are then combined to form a vector v1 = -(vb + vc). If the
length of v1 is 0.001 or less, v1 is replaced with a normalized vector which is perpendicular to the vector vb using the procedure described
earlier. Otherwise, v1 is normalized, and the hydrogen atom position is obtained as

r(H) = r(A) + d(HA)*v1.

#### Tetrahedral geometry

In the case of a tetrahedral geometry, if no bonds exist, hydrogen atoms will be added at positions
r(H i ) = r(A) + d(HA)*v i where the four vectors of unit length v i (i=1,2,3,4) are obtained by a pseudo-random
rotation of a tetrahedron. This prevents that if hydrogen atoms are added to more than one unbonded atom (for example, oxygen atoms of water
residues in protein structures obtained from X-ray crystallography), their bond vectors will in general not be parallel.

If exactly one bond AB exists, the vector v1 = r(B) - r(A) is calculated and normalized. A tetrahedron with corners at:

(1, 0, 0) (-1/3, √(8)/3, 0) (-1/3, - √(2)/3, √(2/3)) (-1/3, - √(2)/3, - √(2/3))

is rotated so that its first corner coincides with v1. If B is connected to another atom C, this atom is chosen to rotate the remaining
three corners around the A-B axis such that the vector from A to the second corner of the tetrahedron forms a dihedral angle of 180°
with the ABC plane. If the 3D coordinates of the rotated corners are c1, c2, c3 and c4, the hydrogen atoms will be placed at the following positions:

(A) + d(HA)*c2 r(A) + d(HA)*c3 r(A) + d(HA)*c4

If exactly two bonds AB and AC exist, the vectors vb = r(B) - r(A) and vc = r(C) - r(A) are calculated and normalized. The vectors are
combined to form a vector v1 = -(vb + vc) which is also normalized. The vector v1 is used to construct a 3D rotation matrix which will perform
a rotation by 90° with respect to the rotation axis defined by v1, followed by an inversion with respect to the origin. The matrix is
applied to the normalized vectors vb and vc. The resulting vector vb is then rotated with respect to an axis defined by the 3D vector cross
product (vc × vb). The rotation angle is given by half of the difference between the ideal tetrahedral angle (approximately 109.5°)
and the angle formed by vectors vb and vc.

A better approximation of the ideal tetrahedral angle can, for example, be obtained by using Google's built-in calculator function.

The resulting vector vc is rotated with respect to an axis defined by the 3D vector cross product (vb × vc), using the same rotation
angle. Hydrogen atoms will then be placed at positions r(A) + d(HA)*vb and r(A) + d(HA)*vc, respectively.

If exactly three bonds AB, AC and AD exist, the following vectors are calculated and normalized.

vb = r(B) - r(A) vc = r(C) - r(A) vd = r(D) - r(A)

Next, the vector v1 is calculated as the sum of the three cross products between pairs of vectors;

v1 = (vb × vc) + (vc × vd) + (vd × vb)

If v1 and vb form an angle of less than 90°, v1 is inverted. If the length of v1 is 0.001 or smaller, v1 is replaced with the cross
product (vb × vc). If the length of v1 is still 0.001 or smaller, v1 is replaced with the cross product (vc × vd). If the length of
v1 is still 0.001 or smaller, it is replaced with the cross product (vd × vb). If the length of v1 is still 0.001 or smaller, then it is
replaced with a vector perpendicular to vb. The resulting vector v1 is then normalized, and the position of the hydrogen atom added is given by

r(H) = r(A) + d(HA)*v1

#### Further information

Chemistry | Hydrogens

## Chemistry | Insert Atom

This option inserts a carbon atom adjacent to the selected bonds. Atoms can be inserted in rings 
and chains. If the rest of the molecule includes hydrogens, a CH 2 is inserted.

If there is more than one bond selected, an atom is inserted adjacent to each bond. If all of the bonds in a 6-membered are selected, 
the resulting ring will contain
12 atoms.

To make a 6-membered ring from a 5-membered ring, select a bond and choose Chemistry | Insert Atom from the menu.

# Chemistry | Stereochemistry

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_chemistry_stereochemistry.htm

## Chemistry | Stereochemistry

This menu allows you to assign chirality to chiral atoms. These chiral values are reflected in the Data Table :

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| S | Mark the atom chirality as S (left). |
| R | Mark the atom chirality as R (right). |
| Unknown | Mark the atom chirality as unknown (?). The geometric configuration of the atom is not changed. |
| Invert Center | If at least one molecule is selected, each selected molecule is inverted by reflecting the XYZ coordinates of all of its atoms across the XY plane which passes through the molecule's geometric center. If a selected double bond is not part of a ring system, a cis-trans transformation is performed by rotating the side of the double bond with the least number of atoms by 180 degrees along the bond axis. If a chiral atom is selected, it will be inverted by rotating two attached groups 180 degrees through an axis bisecting their attached bonds. |

* If at least one molecule is selected, each selected molecule is inverted by
reflecting the XYZ coordinates of all of its atoms across the XY plane which
passes through the molecule's geometric center.

* If a selected double bond is not part of a ring system, a cis-trans
transformation is performed by rotating the side of the double bond with the
least number of atoms by 180 degrees along the bond axis.

* If a chiral atom is
selected, it will be inverted by rotating two attached groups 180 degrees
through an axis bisecting their attached bonds.

Assigning Unknown chirality preserves the original chirality 
assignment. For example, R? represents an atom of R chirality which was subsequently marked 
as having Unknown chirality. The Unknown marker can only be removed by reassigning 
the same chirality.

| Keyboard shortcut | ALT+C, S |

## File menu

Direct connection is attempted unless a proxy has been configured in the Files Explorer Preferences dialog . Also, this option may not work if your firewall software blocks certain types of network traffic to the server. |

| Properties... | Open the Properties dialog , which you can use to view file or folder properties. |
| Recent Files | Reopen a recently opened file. The number of files listed can be set using the Files Explorer Preferences dialog . |
| Exit | Close the application. If you have made changes to any of the open documents, you will be prompted to save them. |

# Sequence | Chain and Domain

Source type: HTML

Source file: client/menu_sequence_chain.htm

## Sequence | Chain and Domain

These options allow you to insert or remove chain breaks in a sequence, shift a chain up and down the sequence alignment, 
swap the order of two chains, and copy chain breaks by alignment between two sequences.

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Swap Domains | Swap the order of two consecutive chains. This option is enabled when the Sequence Window is active and the layout is set to Chain view. Select at least one residue in each chain to be swapped before executing this command. |
| Insert Chain Break | Insert a chain break into a protein sequence. Place the cursor between two residues or select two residues to insert a chain break between the two residues. If the cursor is at a gap position, the chain break is inserted before the next residue (to the right of the cursor). |
| Remove Chain Break | Remove the selected chain breaks in the current Sequence Window. To select a chain break, select the two residues before and after the chain break. |
| Shift Domain Up | Shift the selected chain up a domain block. This option is enabled when the Sequence Window is active and the layout is set to Chain view. If the previous domain is empty for this sequence, the selected chain will fill the previous domain and the chains that follow will be shifted up a domain accordingly. Otherwise, all the previous chains will be pushed up a domain. |
| Shift Domain Down | Shift the selected chain to the next domain. This option is similar to Shift Domain Up . |
| Copy By Alignment | Open the Copy Chains By Alignment dialog , which allows you to copy the chain breaks from the source sequence to the selected sequence. |
| Remove Domain Boundaries | Remove the domain boundaries created by the View \| Chain View menu option. If the Sequence Window is in Chain View, it switches to wrapped view. |

When the protein sequence is linked to a structure in a Molecule Window,
the action will affect the linked structure (for example, split a chain into two, merge two chains into one, or
swap the order of two chains). You can see the effect on the structure by observing the chains in the 
Hierarchy view of the Molecule Window. For nucleic acid sequences, these actions will break any molecule links.

## Sequence | Link Sequence and Structure...

This option opens the Link Sequence and Structure dialog , which allows you to manually link a sequence with a structure 
when the two are not already linked.

After manually establishing the link, the selection in the Sequence Window and the Graphics View is synchronized. The coloring of the sequence and the structure can also
be synchronized for the linked sequence structure pair using the Sequence Window Display Style dialog .

When making the link, the link between the Sequence Window and the Molecule Window is first established and one 
Molecule Window can only link to one Sequence Window, and vice versa. Making a new link can potentially break another existing link.
In addition, the following rules apply when linking a sequence with a structure in the pair of linked Sequence and Molecule windows:

* The sequence must have same name as the structure.

* The sequence must have exactly the same sequence string as in the structure, including the chain break.

* A sequence can only link to one structure at a time and vice versa. If there is a link between
this sequence and another copy of the structure, making the new link will break the old one.

### Automatic linking between sequence and structure

When a Molecule Window is opened, it is linked to the first free Sequence Window (not linked to another Molecule Window) it finds
that contains one or more sequences that match the structures. When a Sequence Window 
is opened, it follows the same rule to link to a Molecule Window whenever it is possible.

# Sequence | Secondary Structure | Predict

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_sequence_secondary-structure-prediction-using-dsc.htm

## Sequence | Secondary Structure | Predict

This option, which is enabled for a protein Sequence Window, predicts the secondary structure 
of selected protein sequences, or all protein sequences if none is selected using the DSC method.

The prediction can be undertaken with or without a sequence alignment (as specified on the Sequence Window page of the Preferences dialog). When the 
prediction is completed, the DSC raw output is displayed in a Text Window . To see the secondary 
structure cartoon in the Sequence Window , right-click the Sequence Window and choose the Secondary Structure Cartoon command from the context menu.

The DSC raw output is displayed in a text window. The first section of the report shows 5 lines for each sequence:

* The sequence

* The predicted secondary structure type, DSC_SEC

* The probability of being helix, PROB_H

* The probability of being beta strand, PROB_E

* The probability of being coil, PROB_C

Values of PROB_H, PROB_E, and PROB_C are between 0 and 9, with 9 being the highest probability.

The second section of the report shows similar information for each residue, but the probabilities are shown in real number values for each residue; the sum of
probabilities of three secondary structure types equals 1.

The Secondary Structure Prediction command is disabled for the Nucleotide 
Sequence Window because nucleotides do not have any secondary structure.
As a result, the context menu option for displaying the secondary structure cartoon is also disabled.

### Access methods

| Menu | Sequence \| Secondary Structure \| Edit |

# Working with the Structure | RMSD menu

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_calculate-rmsd_hw.htm

## Working with the Structure | RMSD menu

The Structure | RMSD menu options allow you to calculate
the RMSD of structures relative to a specified reference structure.
The following topics are discussed here:

* Calculating RMSD for small molecules

* Calculating RMSD for biopolymers

* Calculating RMSD for sequence-aligned protein structures

The RMSD to the reference is calculated for all visible molecules in the Molecule Window .

The RMSD between a reference structure and a pose is calculated only if the following conditions are fulfilled:

* The number of atoms must match

* Each element must match

* The connectivity must match

* The molecules must be small molecules--defined as molecules that can be represented by a .sd file

If these conditions are met, it is said that the order of atoms in the two structures matches. The 
RMSD calculation uses the atom order to identify matching atoms from the reference pose and a test pose.

To calculate an RMSD against a pose or poses

* Load one or more poses of a structure into a Molecule Window.

* Select a molecule from one of the structures already present, or insert a reference pose of the same molecule into the Molecule Window 
and select it.

* Choose Structure | RMSD | Set Reference . The carbon atoms of the reference 
molecule are de-selected to indicate that the reference has been set.

* Choose Structure | RMSD | Heavy Atoms or All Atoms to 
perform the RMSD calculation.

Upon completion of the RMSD calculation, a RMSD Report opens showing the RMSD against the reference 
structure for each pose. If the order of atoms in any pose does not match the reference structure, 
a warning is shown at the bottom of the report.

This command allows the RMSD to be calculated for matching biopolymer structures and for different conformations of one structure. The 
structures are considered to match if they have all the same residues in the same order for the types of residue for which the calculation is 
being performed. For instance, if comparing cases of the same protein bound to different ligands, then the calculation will be performed so 
long as at least one of the Amino acid options has been chosen but the Other residues option 
is not selected.

To calculate an RMSD for biopolymer structures

* Load the structure(s) into the same Molecule Window.

* Open the Biopolymer RMSD Calculation dialog .

* Select All molecules selected from list below or
one reference molecule for the calculation from the Reference molecule dropdown list.

* Select one or more molecules from the list below.

* Choose whether to perform the calculation for all residues or for all pairs for which at least one residue is selected.

* Select one or more of the checkboxes controlling which atoms are used in the RMSD calculation.

* Choose whether to report the RMSD values in the Data Table per residue in addition to per molecule.

* Click the OK button to perform the calculation.

Upon completion of the RMSD calculation, a RMSD Report opens showing the RMSD against the reference structure for each structure. In 
addition, the values are added to the Molecule and/or Conformation tab of the Data Table. If Report At Residue Level is checked, then the per residue values will be added to the AminoAcid , NucleicAcid or Residue tab as appropriate.

This command allows the RMSD to be calculated for a set of sequence-aligned protein structures, either against one chosen reference 
structure or all-against-all.

To calculate RMSD for sequence-aligned protein structures

* Load one of the protein molecules into a Molecule Window.

* Use File | Insert From to insert one or more other protein molecules into the same view.

* Use Sequence | Show Sequence to display the Sequence View if it is not already present.

* Align the sequences or load an appropriate alignment.

* At this stage, it may be appropriate to perform a structural superimposition before performing the RMSD calculation.

* Open the RMSD by Sequence Alignment dialog .

* Select All Molecules or one reference molecule for the calculation from the Reference 
molecule dropdown list.

* If more than one alignment is available, choose which to use from the Sequence alignment dropdown list.

* Choose whether to perform the calculation for all aligned residues or for all pairs for which at least one residue is selected.

* Select one or more of the checkboxes controlling which atoms are used in the RMSD calculation. For RMSD by sequence alignment, 
only amino acid residues can be considered as only they are aligned.

Upon completion of the RMSD calculation, a RMSD Report opens showing the RMSD against the reference structure for each structure. In 
addition, the values are added to the Molecule tab of the Data Table.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| RMSD |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard shortcut | ALT+S, R |

#### Further information

Structure menu

# Structure | Clean Geometry

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_clean-geometry.htm

## Structure | Clean Geometry

This option uses a fast, Dreiding-like
forcefield [Hahn, 1995] to optimize the
geometry of all or selected structures in the Molecule Window .
The element, bond orders, number of bonds, and valence are taken into consideration when the terms of
the energy equation are calculated. The Clean Energy will be added as an property of the molecules.

If any atoms are selected, the molecules that contain the selected
atoms are cleaned. If multiple molecules are present but unselected,
each molecule is cleaned independent of the other molecules.
If multiple molecules are present and selected, the molecules are cleaned
with the VDW effects of the other selected molecules included in the
calculation.

The preferences set in Sketch and Clean subpage - Preferences dialog affect the calculation:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Perceive and Update Aromaticity | The molecule is first scanned for possible aromatic rings based on alternating single and double (Kekulé) bonds. |
| Include Intermolecular Forces | The forces between separate molecules in a document are included in the calculation. Otherwise, multiple molecules in a view are treated as if they were in separate views. |
| Clean Only Selected Atoms | Only the selected atoms are included in the calculation. |

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Clean Geometry |
| --- | --- |
| Toolbar | |

#### Further information

Structure menu Molecule Window page - Preferences dialog Sketch and Clean subpage - Preferences dialog

# Structure | Monitor | Angle

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_monitor_angle.htm

## Structure | Monitor | Angle

This option creates an angle
monitor. An angle monitor shows the angle between three atoms. If the
geometry of the molecule changes, the angle monitor automatically updates
the displayed angle.

Select any of the following before using this option:

* 3 atoms

* 2 adjacent bonds

* 1 atom and 1 bond not attached to that atom

You can change the angle monitored by editing the Orientation property in the Attributes dialog box for a selected angle monitor. You
can also change the Name , ID and Color attributes of an angle monitor, and the XYZ coordinates
of its label.

To launch the Attributes dialog for an angle monitor select the angle
monitor, then right-click over it and select Attributes
of [ angle monitor number ]. Alternatively, you can select the monitor and then choose Edit | Attributes... .

You can use an angle monitor to change the geometry of a structure by editing the value of the Angle property.

The Motion property of the angle monitor controls which part of the structure is being moved when the angle value is changed. For an angle formed by atoms A-B-C, the possible choices for motion are determined by which of the two legs B-A and B-C are moved. The choice No Leg leaves both legs fixed. The choice First Leg moves only the leg B-A. The choice Second Leg moves only the leg B-C. The choice Both Legs moves both legs B-A and B-C by equal amounts. If the atoms A-B-C are part of a ring, then only atoms A or C are moved respectively.

All monitors can be deleted by selecting Structure
| Monitor | Remove . You can also select an individual angle monitor
and press the DELETE key.

# Structure | Monitor | Chirality

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_monitor_chirality.htm

## Structure | Monitor | Chirality

This option creates a chirality
monitor displaying the stereochemistry of chiral atoms.

Chiral atoms are labeled either R or S ,
depending on their chirality. Atoms that are labeled with a ? are
indeterminate. In such cases, the center of chiral resolution is too far
away from the atom in question for the software to determine the
chirality. Hydrogens should be added to all atoms in the molecule for
the chirality monitor to be most effective. If a chiral center is created
by the addition or deletion of atoms, a label is created on the new chiral
center.

This option is available regardless
of whether a molecule has a chiral center. However, chirality labels
only appear if a molecule has one or more chiral centers.

For molecules and fragments with a number of heavy atoms which does not exceed the value specified by the Maximum number of atoms parameter on the Ligand Definition page of the preferences dialog, chirality perception is performed using the algorithm implemented in the Pipeline Pilot Chemistry Collection.

If atoms are selected when creating the chirality monitor, one chirality monitor is created for each molecule containing at least one selected atom, and the chirality monitor will show in the hierarchy view as being part of that molecule. If no atoms are selected when creating the chirality monitor, a single chirality monitor is created which will show in the hierarchy view as a top-level item.

When creating a chirality monitor, its name is initially set to "Chirality Monitor<N>" where <N> is the total number of chirality monitors. If chirality monitors are subsequently deleted, this can result in duplicate names.

To launch the Attributes dialog for a chirality monitor, select the chirality monitor,
then right-click and select Attributes of [ chirality monitor
number ]. Alternatively, you can select the monitor and then choose Edit | Attributes... .

Note that selecting a chirality monitor can be difficult. After you
have created a chirality monitor, choose View
| Data Table , select the Chirality Monitor tab on the Data
Table , and select the row in which
the chirality monitor you wish to select appears. Chirality monitors which were created without an atom selection can also be
selected by choosing View | Hierarchy and picking
the chirality monitor you wish to select from the objects listed at
the top-level of the hierarchy.

All monitors can be deleted by selecting Structure
| Monitor | Remove . You can also select an individual chirality

# Structure | Monitor | Dipole Moment

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_monitor_dipole.htm

## Structure | Monitor | Dipole Moment

This option displays the molecule dipole moment vector.
This vector is a measure of the polarity of a molecule and depends on the partial charge distribution.

The dipole moment is calculated as:

D × Σ i |q i |(R i - C)

where:

* the summation runs over all atoms

* q i is the partial charge of the i-th atom

* R i are the 3D coordinates of the i-th atom

* C is the 3D coordinates of the center of charge

* D is a unit conversion factor = Debye/(e Å); where: 1 Debye = 3.335641 10 -30 Cm (Coulomb-meters) 1 e = 1.602176 10 -19 C (Coulomb) 1 Å = 10 -10 m (meters)

* 1 Debye = 3.335641 10 -30 Cm (Coulomb-meters)

* 1 e = 1.602176 10 -19 C (Coulomb)

* 1 Å = 10 -10 m (meters)

# Structure | Monitor | Hydrophobic Moments

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_monitor_hydrophobic-moments.htm

## Structure | Monitor | Hydrophobic Moments

This option creates a HydrophobicMomentMonitor that displays hydrophobic moment vectors on the residues and secondary structure elements in selected amino acid chains. If no whole chains are selected then the monitor will be created for the entire protein structure.

You can change properties for hydrophobic moments monitors on the Attributes page. To launch the Attributes dialog for a hydrophobic moments monitor, select the monitor, then right-click and choose Attributes of [hydrophobic moments monitor number] . Alternatively, you can select the monitor and then choose Edit | Attributes... from the menu bar.

The following bump monitor properties are available:

* Show Labels: Displays the magnitude of the moments.

* Per Residue: Controls the display of the hydrophobic moment of each residue. Turn off if you wish to hide them and see only the secondary structure moments.

* Use DSSP class: Subclassifies contiguous sections of chain having the same secondary structure type into different structure elements.

You can also change the Name and ID attributes for a hydrophobic moments monitor.

All monitors can be deleted by choosing Structure
| Monitor | Remove . You can also select an individual hydrophobic moments monitor from the Hierarchy View or Molecular Data Table
and press DELETE.

### Hydrophobicity scale

The hydrophobicity scale used in Discovery Studio is taken from Kyte
and Doolittle [Kyte and Doolittle, 1982] .
The Kyte and Doolittle hydrophobicity values are as follows:

```text
PHE 2.8 SER -0.8
MET 1.9 PRO -1.6
ILE 4.5 TYR -1.3
LEU 3.8 HIS -3.2
VAL 4.2 GLN -3.5
CYS 2.5 ASN -3.5
TRP -0.9 GLU -3.5
ALA 1.8 LYS -3.9
THR -0.7 ASP -3.5
GLY -0.4 ARG -4.5
```

### Theory - Hydrophobic Moments

It is commonly observed that the side chains of hydrophobic residues are oriented towards the interior of a protein. The hydrophobic moment of a residue is a vector whose length is proportional to the hydrophobicity of the residue and whose direction is dependent on the side chain orientation. The hydrophobic moment will generally point to the interior of the protein. The hydrophobic moments of side chains of residues forming a secondary structure element can be summed to give some indication of the preferred orientation of the region of protein.

The hydrophobic moment vector of a residue is defined as having its origin at the position of the Cα atom.
The vector length is proportional to the hydrophobicity of the residue (as taken from standard amino acid hydrophobicity scales). The direction of the hydrophobic vector is found by averaging the vectors from the Cα atom to all the non-hydrogen atoms in the side chain. If the residue hydrophobicity is negative (that is, the residue is hydrophilic) the vector will point in the opposite direction to the side chain. The Hydrophobic Moment vector for a hydrophobic residue will be colored pale yellow, while that for a hydrophilic residue will be pale blue.

The hydrophobic moment of a secondary structure element is defined as the sum of the hydrophobic moments for all residues in the element and the vector origin is the center of the secondary structure vector. Secondary structure moments are colored red.

# Structure | Monitor | Valence

Source type: HTML

Source file: client/menu_structure_monitor_valence.htm

## Structure | Monitor | Valence

The Structure | Monitor | Valence option creates
valence monitors around atoms with under or over-filled valences. Atoms
with under-filled valences are indicated with a cyan frame and atoms
with over-filled valences are indicated with a red frame.

This command is available regardless
of whether a molecule has under or over-filled valences. However, valence
monitors only appear if a molecule has one or more such atoms. If a
group of atoms is selected before you issue the command, only the valence
monitors of the selected atoms are shown.

To make a structure containing only unfilled valences valid (cyan frames), you need only add hydrogens. 
If the structure contains atoms with over-filled valences (red frames), you should delete one or more bonds to that atom.

For unconnected metal ions, valence monitors show a valid valence state
when the formal charge equals the common valence of the atom. For instance,
+1 for sodium and potassium, +2 for magnesium and calcium.

You can turn off the display of under-valent atoms by setting the Show
under-valence attribute to No .
You can also label each valence monitor ("Under" or "Over") by setting
the Show labels attribute to Yes .
You can also change valence monitor Name , ID ,
and Color attributes.

To launch the Attributes dialog for a valence monitor, select the valence monitor,
then right-click and select Attributes of [ valence monitor
number ]. Alternatively, you can select the monitor and then choose Edit | Attributes... .

All monitors can be deleted by selecting Structure
| Monitor | Remove . You can also select valence monitors and delete
them with the DELETE key.

The action of valence
monitors is covered under U.S. Patents 6,582,233 and 6,758,677.

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Add tether | Associate selected atoms to use when superimposing molecules. For details, see Add Tether . |

| Add rotatable bonds | Add Rotatable Bond Attributes to the selected rotatable bonds or to all rotatable bonds if nothing is selected in the Graphics View. |

| By Center of Geometry | Calculate the geometric center of the selected molecule, repositions all other molecules not contained in a crystal cell to that center, and then executes the View \| Transform \| Fit To Screen command. Any molecule which is part of a crystal cell must have the cell removed using the Structure \| Crystal Cell \| Remove Cell command before it will be included. |
| By Tether | Perform an RMS (root mean squares) best fit on the objects connected by tethers to determine a rigid rotation and/or translation to overlay the structures. For details, see By Tether . |
| Edit Transformation Matrix | Edit transformation matrices. For details, see Edit Transformation Matrix... . |
| Apply Transformation Matrix | Transform the coordinates of the original molecule or create and transform a new chain containing a copy of the selected portion. For details, see Apply Transformation Matrix... . |
| Molecular Overlay | Overlay two or more molecules using a variety of techniques. For details, see Molecular Overlay... . |

# Structure | Superimpose | Apply Transformation Matrix

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_superimpose_apply-transformation-matirx.htm

## Structure | Superimpose | Apply Transformation Matrix

A transformation matrix can be stored as a property of a molecule. Structure | Superimpose | 
Apply Transformation Matrix... can be used to apply a matrix to all or selected parts of a molecule. This can either transform the 
coordinates of the original molecule or create and transform a new chain containing a copy of the selected portion.

While this tool can be used to simply transform a whole molecule, there
are more interesting uses for tasks such as:

* constructing biologically active units

* modeling non-crystallographic symmetry-related chains

* constructing repeat units for fiber structures

The following sections describe such tasks.

To construct a biologically active unit

Within some .pdb files there is a definition of how to generate the biologically
active unit by application of matrices to specific chains. The software
automatically stores the matrices for you, but you will need to refer to the .pdb file itself for the details of which matrix to apply to which chain.

* Open the .pdb file.

* In the text editor of your choice, display the .pdb file and search for REMARK
300. If this does not appear in the file then there is no definition of an
oligomeric biologically active unit.

* Following this will be a series of REMARK 350 records. These contain the transformation matrices, preceded by a list of 
chains to which to apply them.

* Select the first set of chains specified.

* Display the Apply Transformation Matrix dialog .

* From the dropdown list, select the correct matrix (for example BIOMT_1 for the first operation).

* Make sure that both the Selected Atoms Only and 
the Create Copy controls are checked on.

* Click OK to generate the new copy.

* Repeat as necessary for other chains and/or matrices specified.

To model a non-crystallographically related chain

* Determine the complete structure of one chain.

* Determine some residues from various points of the equivalent non-crystallographic 
symmetry-related chain. At this point both chains are in the same molecule and
assume the molecule name is ${mol1}

* From the Graphics View, select this partial second chain and drag it out of ${mol1} in the Hierarchy View to form a new molecule. 
Rename the molecule to ${mol1}_${chainID}.

* Use Superimpose by Tether commands on the Superimpose Proteins tools tool panel
to superimpose ${mol1} to ${mol1}_${chainID} using specified range(s).
Make sure to set ${mol1}_${chainID} as the reference protein and to generate a transformation matrix only.

* Alternatively, if you already have determined the NCS matrix by other means, 
you can add it to the molecule using Structure 
| Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix... .

* Select the full chain from ${mol1} and choose Structure | Superimpose | Apply Transformation Matrix... from the menu bar to display the Apply Transformation Matrix dialog .

* Select the matrix and ensure that both Selected Atoms Only and Create Copy are checked.

* Delete ${mol1}_${chainID} and rename the newly copied chain as desired.

To construct repeat units for fiber structures

A few .pdb files have structures determined by fiber diffraction methods. In some cases, the symmetry of the repeat units is specified in the same way as for biologically active units. For these, BIOMT matrices will be created when the file is opened, and the method shown above can be used. 
However, there are also some instances where the structure is an 'infinitely' long chain, and repeat units can be built by applying the correct translation vector if this information is present in the file.

* After importing the .pdb file, open it in a text editor

* Search for a keyword TVECT. The record should consist of the keyword, a serial number, the components of the translation vector, and optionally a comment, e.g.: TVECT 1 0.00000 0.00000 26.56000

* In Discovery Studio, open the Edit Transformation Matrix dialog and click Create Transformation Matrix .

* Enter a name for the matrix in the dialog box which is displayed and click on OK .

* Leave the default unit rotation matrix as it is and enter the correct values in the translation vector fields, then click OK .

* This matrix can then be applied as described above using the Apply Transformation Matrix dialog .

* The matrix may then be applied to the copy to create the next repeat unit in the chain, for as many times as required to build the desired length chain.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Superimpose \| Apply Transformation Matrix... |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

# Structure | Superimpose | By Tether

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_superimpose_by-tether.htm

## Structure | Superimpose | By Tether

The Structure | Superimpose | By Tether command performs an RMS (root mean squares) best fit on the 
objects connected by tethers to determine a rigid rotation and/or translation to overlay the structures.

To superimpose molecules using tethers

* Load the reference molecule into a Molecule Window. The top molecule in the Hierarchy View is considered the reference molecule.

* Use File | Insert From | File... to insert the molecules that you want to align to the reference molecule.

* Choose one atom in each molecule that you want to be superimposed,
and select the Structure
| Superimpose | Add Tether command.

* Repeat the previous step to define additional tethers. 
Having many tethers defined does not necessarily improve the alignment -- three or four tethers should be 
sufficient.

* Select the Structure
| Superimpose | By Tether command.

This does not fuse the
molecules together. If you wish to fuse two or more molecules into a
single molecule, use the Chemistry | Bond | Fuse command.

The Structure | Superimpose | Add Tether command
associates selected atoms to use when superimposing molecules.

To define a tether, select an atom in each molecule to be superimposed
and choose the Add Tether command. 
The associated atoms are labeled with a tether number [ N ]
in the Molecule Window. Note that the top molecule in the Hierarchy View is considered the reference molecule.

The tether is shown as Tuple[N] in

set using the Tether Attributes dialog. To open the Tether Attributes
dialog, select Tuple[N] in the 
Hierarchy View, right click to open the context menu and select
the Attributes of Tuple[N]... command.
Change the Show lines parameter in the Tether Attributes dialog to configure the
display of the tether line.

# Structure | Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_superimpose_edit-transformation-matirx.htm

## Structure | Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix

Transformation matrices that are stored as a property of a molecule
can be created using this command or Superimpose Proteins tools .
They may also be created
for imported .pdb format files from the contents of MtrIX records and
BIOMT remarks.

Structure | Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix... can be used to edit or delete such matrices or 
to add new matrices to the molecule. Such matrices may represent non-crystallographic symmetry and so are useful for model building.

To edit a transformation matrix

* Ensure the molecule containing the matrix is in the active Graphics View.

* If the view contains more than one molecule, select at least one atom in the relevant molecule.

* Open the Edit Transformation Matrix dialog .

* Select the matrix to be edited from the dropdown list.

* Edit the matrix as desired.

* Click Save to store the changes or click OK to save and exit the dialog.

To create a new transformation matrix

* Ensure the molecule to which the matrix is to be added is in the active Graphics View.

* Click Create Transformation Matrix .

* Enter a name for the matrix in the dialog box which is displayed and click on OK .

* Enter the rotation matrix and translation vector elements.

To delete a transformation matrix

* Ensure the molecule from which the matrix is to be deleted is in the active Graphics View.

* Select the matrix to be deleted from the dropdown list.

* Click Delete Transformation Matrix to delete the selected matrix.

# Structure | Superimpose | Molecular Overlay

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_superimpose_molecular-overlay.htm

## Structure | Superimpose | Molecular Overlay

Molecular Overlay command is used to overlay two or more molecules using a 
variety of techniques, including alignment by a combination of steric and 
electrostatic fields, alignment by atom-atom tethers, consensus 
alignment versus target alignment, and flexible alignment where the 
molecules being aligned are allowed to undergo conformational changes 
by modifying the dihedral angles of torsions with a low barrier of rotation.

From the menu bar, Structure | Superimpose | Molecular Overlay opens the Molecular Overlay dialog .

Alignment by tethers requires that interatomic 
tethers have been defined. This choice implies rigid alignment where 
molecules are translated and rotated so as to minimize the sum of 
the squared distances between the atoms in tethered atom pairs.

Alignment by field overlays molecules 
by maximizing steric and/or electrostatic repulsion between atoms. The relative 
weight of the steric and electrostatic contributions can be adjusted.

Consensus alignment will maximize the 
overlap between all pairs of molecules, whereas target alignment considers 
only those molecule pairs which have one molecule, the target molecule, in common.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Superimpose \| Molecular Overlay... |
| --- | --- |

# Structure | Update Coordinates

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_structure_update-coordinates.htm

## Structure | Update Coordinates

This option changes the coordinates of the structure in the 
Molecule Window to the current orientation.

Global rotations and translations in the Molecule Window are accomplished by applying
a transformation matrix to all 3D objects, without altering any coordinates. This option applies the matrix to the coordinates so that the current orientation is maintained for subsequent operations. 
For example, you might wish to set up a desired orientation and then update coordinates prior to superimposing other structures onto it.

Cells and Isosurfaces (for example electron Density Maps) cannot be transformed by this method,
so it is usually inadvisable to use this command if any such objects
are part of the system.

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Update Coordinates |
| --- | --- |

# View menu

Source file: client/menu_view.htm

## View menu

The View menu controls the way objects are displayed in application
views, which toolbars and explorers are exposed, and which side of the application Window to dock application
views. The options are organized into the following submenus:

| Submenu | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Display Style... | Open the Display Style dialog for the current view. |
| Color... | Open the Select Color dialog , allowing you to apply a color to the selected object. |
| Transform | Options for adjusting the view: Zoom In: Decrease the apparent distance of objects in the current view. Zoom Maximum: Magnify the view to show individual residues. Zoom Out: Increase the apparent distance of objects in the current view. Reset Zoom: Remove the zoom factor from views. Reset Rotation: Remove any rotation applied to the display of the objects in the active Graphics View . Fit To Screen: Scale and translate the selected objects to center and fit them inside the active Graphics View. If there are no selected objects, all objects will be fitted into the view. Center: Places the geometric center of the selected objects at the center of the active Graphics View. If no objects are selected, all objects will be centered in the View. |
| Storyboard | Options for working with storyboards. For details, see Create and view storyboards . Add: Take a snapshot of the current document and add it to the end of the list of scenes. You can recall the scene using the tools below. Rewind: Move to the first scene. Next Move to the next scene. Previous: Move to the previous scene. Story Board: Open the Story Board dialog that you can use to browse scenes of the visualization. |
| Spin | Options for controlling movement of the structure: Spin: Rotate the objects in the Graphics View clockwise. To stop the spin, click Spin again or click the Graphics View. The spin direction and speed can be adjusted by dragging and releasing in the desired trajectory. Rock: Rock the objects in the Graphics View along the Y axis. To stop the rocking, click Rock again. Wiggle: Small, slow oscillation in the Graphics View along the Y axis. To stop the wiggling, click Wiggle again. |
| Clipping Planes... | Open the Clipping Planes dialog allowing you to adjust both the front and back clipping planes. The visibility of objects is affected only in the 3D and Stereo Molecule Windows. |
| Stereo | Display stereo molecular data in 3D. By default, stereo molecular data will be displayed as a red/cyan anaglyph rendering which can best be viewed using red/cyan 3D stereo glasses. Stereo preferences are accessed from the Edit \| Preferences... \| Molecule Window \| Stereo from the top menu. See Stereo subpage - Preferences dialog . |
| Tile Molecules in View | Organizes all structures in the current Molecule Window by evenly spacing them into a table-like format. When multiple molecules are organized this way, you can rotate the molecules, each around its center of geometry, by holding down the CTRL key while rotating. |
| Full Screen | Displays the current window using the entire application window. The menus and the toolbars are not available in full screen mode. However, commands may still be executed using keyboard shortcuts and mouse actions. To exit the full screen mode, press the F11 key. |
| Visibility | Controls the visibility of objects in the Graphics Window. Hide: Makes selected objects invisible in the Graphics View (the objects are hidden but not deleted). Show: Makes selected objects visible in the Graphics View (this command is only available if there are hidden objects). Show All: Makes all objects visible in the Graphics View, whether or not they are selected (this command is only available if there are hidden objects). Show Only: Makes selected objects visible in the Graphics View, and makes all other objects invisible in the Graphics View. Lock: Locks the visibility of the selected objects so that their visibility in the Graphics View is unaffected by the Show and Show All commands. Unlock: Unlocks the visibility of the selected objects so that their visibility in the Graphics View is affected by the Show and Show All commands (this command is only available if there are locked objects). |
| Graphics | Toggles the display of the Graphics View in the current Molecule or Sequence Annotation Window. |
| Hierarchy | Toggles the display of the Hierarchy View in the current Molecule or Sequence Annotation Window. |
| Data Table | Toggles the display of the Data Table View in the current Molecule or Sequence Annotation Window. |
| Explorers | Toggles the display of explorers (for example, Tools Explorer). The Explorer windows can be reset to the default location with the Restore View Settings command. |
| Docks | Allows you to toggle between the display of docked windows. You can choose to show or hide All docked windows, or only a combination of the docked windows to the Left , Right , or at the Bottom . |
| Tool Panels | Controls the display of groups of tools. Refer to Working with tools \| Tools Explorer for more information. |
| Toolbars | Controls the display of toolbars. Refer to View \| Toolbars for more information. |

* Zoom In: Decrease the apparent distance of objects in the current view.

* Zoom Maximum: Magnify the view to show individual residues.

* Zoom Out: Increase the apparent distance of objects in the current view.

* Reset Zoom: Remove the zoom factor from views.

* Reset Rotation: Remove any rotation applied to the display of the objects in the active Graphics View .

* Fit To Screen: Scale and translate the selected objects to center and fit them inside the active Graphics
View. If there are no selected objects, all objects will be fitted into the view.

* Center: Places the geometric center of the selected objects at the center of the active Graphics View. If no objects are selected, all objects will be centered in the View.

* Add: Take a snapshot of the current
document and add it to the end of the list of scenes. You can recall

* Rock: Rock the objects in the Graphics View along the Y axis. To stop the rocking, click Rock again.

Display stereo molecular data in 3D.

# How to use the Query toolbar

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_view_toolbars_query-tools_hw.htm

## How to use the Query toolbar

You can use the Query toolbar to build Catalyst or Isentris database queries.

To query a particular feature, select an object in the Molecule Window and click the appropriate
button. The types of features and constraints to use in a given
query depend on the type of database you are going to search. Some of the query features
can be used for both Catalyst and Isentris-type queries; however, some are
specific to the type of search. Using an Isentris feature in a Catalyst search could yield unexpected
results.

You can specify the element type, bond order, structure,
shape, and many other properties of a molecule for purposes of locating molecules in a database
that have the same or similar features. The query operates like a search engine in that when more features are included in the
query, fewer and more specific results will be returned. Also, the choice of what features to include in a query affects the outcome of the
search. For example, searching for all molecules containing a particular element is likely to return far more results than searching for all molecules of a given shape.

In the Data Table View, in many cases you can change parameters of the features you create.

The following tools are available:

| Button | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| | Query Atom |
| | Query Bond |
| | Acceptor Feature |
| | Donor Feature |
| | Centroid Feature |
| | Point Feature |
| | Point Offset Feature |
| | Point Normal Feature |
| | Aromatic Ring Feature |
| | Vector Feature |
| | Location Constraint |
| | Exclusion Constraint |
| | Distance Constraint |
| | Angle Constraint |
| | Dihedral Constraint |
| | Plane Constraint |
| | Shape Feature |

To use the Query Atom tool:

A Query Atom Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query) allows a single
atom to be represented with several element types.

* To create a Query Atom Feature, select an atom and click the Query Atom button.

* To change the represented elements, select the Query Atom Feature, make sure the QueryAtom tab in the Data Table View is visible, and
edit the List property to contain the desired list of elements.

Each element symbol must be separated from other element symbols by a space.

To use the Query Bond tool:

A Query Bond Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query) allows a bond to
be associated with one or several bond orders (Single, Double, Triple, and Aromatic).

If just a single bond order is used in the list and the query is written to a .mol format file, the Query Bond Feature is lost, because .mol files do not support Query Bond Features
with only one type (they are considered as regular bonds).

* To create a Query Bond Feature, select a bond and click the Query Bond button.

* To change the represented bond orders, select the Bond query, make sure the QueryBond tab in the Data Table View is visible and edit the List property to contain the desired list of bond orders.

To use the Acceptor Feature tool:

The Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature (Catalyst type query) is a vector pointing
toward an atom that can serve as a hydrogen bond acceptor. For instance, a carbonyl oxygen
can serve as an acceptor. By default the Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature is oriented along
the vector that is the average of the lone pair vectors. This orientation is called the
Projection Orientation.

* To create a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature, select an atom or atoms that can serve as hydrogen
bond acceptors and click the Acceptor button.

* To change the length of the Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature, make sure the AcceptorFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible, and
edit the Length property.

* To change the Orientation property in the Acceptor Feature Properties
dialog box, select First Lone Pair , Second Lone Pair , 
or Third Lone Pair , or Projection (default). Note that 
because the default setting is Projection , if you select Third Lone Pair for a carbonyl oxygen (which only has two lone pairs), 
the Orientation property is reset to Projection .

To use the Donor Feature tool:

The Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature (Catalyst type query) is a vector pointing
toward an atom that can serve as a hydrogen bond donor. For instance, the hydrogen on a
hydroxyl group can serve as a donor.

* To create a Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature, select an atom that can serve as hydrogen bond donors, and click the Donor button.

* To change the length of the Hydrogen Bond Donor, make sure the DonorFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and edit the Length property.

To use the Centroid Feature tool:

The Centroid Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query) is placed
at the geometric center of the atoms you specify. A Centroid Feature is defined only by
atoms, unlike a Point Feature, which can be defined by any object.

To create a Centroid Feature, select a set of atoms and click the Centroid Feature button.

To use the Point Feature tool:

The Point Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query) is placed at the
geometrical center of the objects you specify.

* To create a Point Feature, select a set of objects and click the Point Feature button.

* To change the type of the Point Feature, and thus the nature of the query, make sure the PointFeature tab in the Data Table View is
visible, and choose one of the following types from the Type cell: Hydrophobe Hydrophobe_Aromatic Hydrophobe_Aliphatic Ionizable_Negative Ionizable_Positive Charged_Negative Charged_Positive

* Hydrophobe

* Hydrophobe_Aromatic

* Hydrophobe_Aliphatic

* Ionizable_Negative

* Ionizable_Positive

* Charged_Negative

* Charged_Positive

To use the Point Offset Feature tool:

The Point Offset Feature (Isentris type query) represents an offset location
from another object.

* To create a Point Offset Feature, select two atoms and click the Point
Offset Feature button.

* To change the amount of offset, select the Point Offset feature, make sure the PointOffsetFeature tab in the Data Table View is
visible and edit the Offset cell.

To use the Point Normal Feature tool:

The Point Normal Feature (Isentris type query) represents a vector normal
to a set of objects that define a plane.

To create a Point Normal Feature, select at least three atoms and click the Point Normal Feature button.

To use the Aromatic Ring Feature tool:

The Aromatic Ring Feature (Catalyst type query) represents an aromatic
ring.

To create a Aromatic Ring Feature, select at least three atoms in an aromatic ring and click the Aromatic Ring 
Feature button.

To use the Vector Feature tool:

The Vector Feature represents a vector between two objects.

To create a Vector Feature, select two objects in the Molecule Window and click the Vector 
Feature button.

To use the Location Constraint tool:

A Location Constraint Feature (Catalyst type query) is an object
that represents a location in space within a given radius.

* To create a Location Constraint Feature, select one of the following: an atom a Point Feature a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature a Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature a Centroid Feature a Point Offset Feature an Aromatic Ring Feature

* an atom

* a Point Feature

* a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature

* a Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature

* a Centroid Feature

* a Point Offset Feature

* an Aromatic Ring Feature

* To change the radius, select the Location Constraint Feature, make sure the LocationFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and
edit the Radius cell.

To use the Exclusion Constraint tool:

The Exclusion Constraint Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query)
is an object that represents an excluded volume in space, within a given radius.

* To create an Exclusion Constraint Feature, select an atom and click the Exclusion
Constraint button.

* To change the Exclusion Constraint Feature's radius, select the Exclusion Constraint Feature,
make sure the ExclusionFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and edit the Radius property.

To use the Distance Constraint tool:

The Distance Constraint Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query)
creates an object that uses a range to represent the distance between two other objects.

* To create a Distance Constraint Feature, select two atoms and click the Distance Constraint button.

* To change the distance range, select the Distance Constraint Feature, make sure the DistanceFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible
and edit the Range cell.

To use the Angle Constraint tool:

The Angle Constraint Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query)
uses a range to represent an angle between three other objects.

* To create an Angle Constraint Feature, select three atoms or two bonds and click the Angle Constraint button.

* To change the angle range, select the Angle Constraint Feature, make sure the AngleFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible, and
edit the Range cell.

To use the Dihedral Constraint tool:

The Dihedral Constraint Feature (Catalyst & Isentris type query)
uses a range to represent a dihedral between four other objects.

* To create a Dihedral Constraint Feature, select any set of atoms and bonds that define a contiguous set of four atoms or three bonds
and click the Dihedral Constraint button.

* To change the Dihedral Constraint Feature's range: select the Dihedral Constraint Feature,
make sure the DihedralFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and edit the Range cell.

To use the Plane Constraint tool:

The Plane Constraint Feature (Isentris type query) represents a planar
RMS fit of the atoms you specify.

To create a Plane Constraint Feature, select at least three atoms, and click the Plane Constraint button.

To use the Shape Feature tool:

The Shape Feature (Catalyst type query) represents atoms
contained within a surface. The Shape Feature uses a surface to represent the
shape of the molecule.

* To create a Shape Feature, select an entire molecule and click the Shape Feature button.

* To change the similarity tolerance, select the Shape Feature, make sure the ShapeFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and
edit the Tolerance property.

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Toolbars \| Query |
| --- | --- |

Toolbars Structure | Query Features...

# How to use the Sketching toolbar

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/menu_view_toolbars_sketching_hw.htm

## How to use the Sketching toolbar

The Sketching toolbar allows you to sketch structures directly in the Molecule Window .

The following tools are available:

| Button | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| | Torsion |
| | Sketch |
| | Chain |
| | Ring |
| | Text |
| | Text Box |
| | Text Callout |

You can delete objects such as bonds and atoms by selecting them and pressing DELETE. You can use the Select dialog , to fine tune your selection, or double-click objects multiple times to select the object, then its parent object, and so on.

To use the Torsion tool:

The Torsion tool is used to rotate atoms about a bond. When in use, the cursor changes to an arrow wrapping around a line.

To rotate a torsion, select the bond to be rotated, then click anywhere on the screen and drag to rotate. If there is more than one atom on both sides of the bond, the atoms involved in the rotation are labeled A, B, C (or B, C, D depending on which side is being rotated), a yellow circle indicates the plane of the rotation, and a green wedge and text box indicate the amount of rotation in degrees. By default, the Torsion tool moves the part of the molecule containing
fewer atoms. Click the bond again to move the other portion. A temporary torsion monitor is created (if there is no existing torsion monitor). The temporary torsion monitor is removed when the torsion tool is disengaged.
See Structure | Monitor | Torsion for more information about the torsion monitor.

To rotate the atoms of a peptide bond and all atoms immediately connected to them around the axis formed by the two C α atoms connected to the atoms of the peptide bond, use CTRL+drag.

To rotate the carbonyl group around the axis formed by the C α and N atoms connected to the carbon atom of the carbonyl group, use CTRL+SHIFT+drag.

To use the Sketch tool:

Use the Sketch tool to sketch atoms and bonds. The cursor changes to indicate which Sketch tool is in use.

* To sketch atoms and bonds, click in the Molecule Window, move the
cursor and click again. Double-click the mouse or move the mouse outside
the Molecule Window to end sketching.

* To change the element type while sketching, type a single-character
element (H, B, C, N, O, F, P, S, I) with one or more atoms selected. Alternatively, press the right
mouse button for a pop-up menu allowing you to change the given atom
or bond.

* To change the bond order from single to double, re-draw over an existing bond. You can also select one or more bonds and enter the desired bond order from the keyboard: 1, 2, 3, or 4 for an aromatic bond.

* To change the bond type from single to double to triple (then back to single), repeatedly click a bond with the Sketch tool.

To use the Chain tool:

Use the Chain tool to draw chains of atoms. When in use, the cursor changes to a pencil and line. An indicator appears to show how long the chain is.

* To create a chain, choose the Chain tool, hold down the left
mouse button and drag out a chain to the desired length. To flip the orientation
of the chain, hold down the CTRL key.

* To add a chain to an existing atom, click the Chain tool on that
atom and drag out the new chain.

To use the Ring tool:

Use the Ring tool to create rings of any size. The cursor changes to indicate the Ring tool is in use.

* To draw a single ring, click in the Molecule Window.

* To create a ring with more or fewer than six atoms, click while dragging.

* To create an aromatic ring, CTRL+click.

* To fuse a ring onto an existing ring, click
a bond in an existing ring, and then drag the mouse to draw a new ring of
the desired size.

* To spiro-fuse a ring onto an existing ring, click on an atom in the existing ring.

To use the Text tool:

Use the Text tool to add annotation text. When in use, the cursor changes to a pencil with the letter T.

To create annotation text, click in the Molecule Window at the location 
where the text should be placed. This opens the Annotation Text dialog , which allows you to enter the text.

To use the Text Box tool:

Use the Text Box tool
to add a box containing multi-line text in a paragraph-like format. The
cursor changes to a pencil with a text box to indicate that the Text
Box tool is in use.

* To create a text box, click in the Molecule Window at the location
where the text should be placed. To create a textbox with a custom width, click and drag
the box out to the desired width. You will then use the Annotation Text dialog to enter the text.

* To move a text box, choose the Translate tool,
select the text box, and then CTRL+drag it to a new location.

* To resize a text box, select it, and then click and drag the handle in the upper-right corner. The text is automatically reformatted to fit the resized text box.

To use the Text Callout tool:

Use the Text Callout tool to add a box containing multi-line text that is connected to a
3D object. The cursor changes to a pencil with a text box and a callout
to indicate that the Text Callout tool is in use.

* To create a text callout, click on a 3D object such as an atom, and then move the mouse and click to create the callout box. You can also click and drag to create a custom sized callout. You will then use the Annotation Text dialog to enter the text.

* To move a text callout, choose the Translate tool,
select the text box, and then CTRL+drag it to a new location.

* To resize a text callout, select it, and then click and drag the handle in the upper-right corner. The text is automatically reformatted to fit the resized text box.

* To make a text callout retain its position within the Molecule Window if the window is resized or the molecule is zoomed, set its Sticky attribute to Yes .

You can toggle the visibility of objects by right-clicking the view and choosing options ( Hide , Show , Show All , Show Only ) from the context menu.

See Mouse and keyboard actions to learn how to work with these tools efficiently.

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Toolbars \| Sketching |
| --- | --- |

# Status bar

## Status bar

The status bar, which is located along the bottom edge of the main window, displays information relating to current activity in the 
application. During the execution of some operations, it will display a Progress Bar that shows status of those 
tasks. For some operations, you can click the Close icon to stop the task.

The Active server bar , which appears to the right of the status 
bar, displays name, resource level, and version of the connected server. Click the Active server bar bar to open 
the Change Server dialog . The status bar also displays a graphical
resource monitor that indicates the state of the connected Pipeline Pilot Server . If the load on the server is heavy, for example
if CPU or memory usage is high, the monitor will reflect this. Hover the mouse over the resource monitor to view details 
in a tooltip.

# View toolbar

Source type: HTML

Source file: client/menu_view_toolbars_view.htm

## View toolbar

The View toolbar provides tools that manipulate the Molecule
Window or edit molecules in the document. For details about using these tools, see How to use the View toolbar .

The following tools are available:

| Button | Name | Description |

# How to use the View toolbar

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

## How to use the View toolbar

The View toolbar provides tools that manipulate the Molecule
Window or edit molecules in the document.

The following tools are available:

| Button | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| | Select |
| | Rotate |
| | Translate |
| | Zoom |
| | Home |
| | Fit To Screen |
| | Center Structure |
| | Measure |

To use the Select tool:

Use the Select tool to select one or more objects using the mouse.

You can use the Select dialog to perform complex selections or select objects that are difficult to locate or click.

* To select a single object (e.g. an atom or bond), click once.

* To select multiple objects (e.g. atoms or bonds), SHIFT+click or drag around the set of objects. The default drag behavior is Lasso , but you can set it to Rubber Band Box in the preferences. See Tools subpage - Preferences dialog .

* To add objects which have not already been selected to the current selection, or to remove objects which have already been selected from the current selection, use SHIFT+click or drag. To add objects to the current selection regardless of whether these objects have already been selected or not, use SHIFT+CTRL+click or drag. Click an empty region of the Molecule Window to unselect everything.

To use the Rotate tool:

Use the Rotate tool to change the viewing angle of the molecule. When in use, the cursor changes to a curved arrow. You can click without dragging to select atoms or bonds.

* To rotate a molecule: Drag in the direction of rotation. Hold the SHIFT key down while dragging the mouse to rotate around the z-axis. Use the up (↑), down (↓), left (←), and right (→) arrow keys.

* Drag in the direction of rotation. Hold the SHIFT key down while dragging the mouse to rotate around the z-axis.

* Use the up (↑), down (↓), left (←), and right (→) arrow keys.

* To rotate only the selected objects around their geometric center, use CTRL+drag.

* To rotate about the z-axis, you can use Track Surface or Track Ball mode. See Tools subpage - Preferences . For Track Surface mode, use SHIFT+drag to rotate about the z-axis. For Track Ball mode, a green circle appears around the molecule when you click. Drag inside the circle to rotate about the x- and y-axes. Drag outside of the circle to rotate about the z-axis

* For Track Surface mode, use SHIFT+drag to rotate about the z-axis.

* For Track Ball mode, a green circle appears around the molecule when you click. Drag inside the circle to rotate about the x- and y-axes. Drag outside of the circle to rotate about the z-axis

To use the Translate tool:

Use the Translate tool to move a molecule in the plane of the monitor. When in use, a four-way arrow appears next to the cursor. You can click without dragging to select atoms or bonds.

* To translate a molecule, drag it to the new location.

* To translate only selected objects, use CTRL+drag.

To use the Zoom tool:

Use the Zoom tool to zoom the view in or out. When in use, the cursor changes to a double
arrow. You can click without dragging to select atoms or bonds.

* To zoom with the mouse wheel, roll it forwards or backwards to zoom in or out.

* To zoom with the mouse, drag up or down to zoom in or out.

To use the Home tool:

Use the Home tool to undo all rotations and return the structure to the original orientation it was in when it was imported or created.
Note that centering ( Center Structure or Fit To Screen ) actions are not undone. This is the same functionality as View | Transform | Reset Rotation .

To use the Fit To Screen tool:

Use the Fit To Screen tool to scale and translate the selected objects to center and fit them inside the active Graphics View. If there are no selected objects, all objects will be fitted into the view.

To use the Center Structure tool:

Use the Center Structure tool to place the geometric center of the selected objects at the center of the active Graphics View. If no objects are selected, all objects will be centered in the View.

To use the Measure tool:

Use the Measure tool to measure the distance, angle, or torsion between selected objects.

* To measure the distance between two atoms, de-select all objects, select two atoms or one bond, and then click the Measure tool.

* To measure the angle between three atoms, de-select all objects, select three atoms or two connected bonds, and then click the Measure tool.

* To measure the torsion angle between four atoms, de-select all objects, select four atoms, two disconnected bonds, or three connected bonds, and then click the Measure tool.
