# Molecular Overlay - Theory

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/molecular_overlay_th.htm

## Molecular Overlay - Theory

Molecular overlay refers to methods which align two or more molecules 
to each other. The main differences between the various methods are outlined below.

#### Targeted and consensus alignment

When overlaying more than two molecules, two fundamental strategies are possible:

* targeted alignment: designates one molecule as the alignment target and aligns the remaining molecules to the target molecule

* consensus alignment: optimizes the alignment between all pairs of molecules from the original set

Optimization of the alignment is achieved by the minimization 
or maximization of an objective function, which provides a quantitative measure of 
the alignment quality. The objective function in targeted alignment 
is the sum over the objective functions for the alignment of the target 
molecule with each of the remaining molecules. The objective function 
in consensus alignment is the sum over the objective functions for the 
alignment of every pair of molecules in the set of molecules to be aligned.

#### Rigid and flexible alignment

In rigid alignment, the internal geometry of molecules is 
not allowed to change, and the optimization considers only translations and 
rotations of a whole molecule. In flexible alignment, the molecular 
geometry is allowed to change within limits. Changes are restricted 
to altering the dihedral angles formed by a connected chain of 
four atoms A-B-C-D, where the internal rotation barrier for the central 
B-C bond is assumed to be small. The current implementation of flexible 
alignment requires the identification of these rotatable bonds, 
which can be accomplished by adding rotatable bond monitors 
to the molecules to be overlayed.

#### Tethers and field fit

There are different choices for the objective function that 
measures the alignment quality. In alignment by tethers, the objective function 
is the sum of the squared distances between specific pairs of atoms in 
the two molecules to be aligned. Optimal alignment is achieved by minimizing 
the sum of the squared distances. The method requires the atom pairs to be 
specified, which is referred to as tethers.

In alignment by field fit, identification of atom pairs 
is unnecessary. The objective function is chosen as an energy expression that
includes a weighted mixture of an electrostatic and a steric (repulsive) 
contribution from the interactions of all pairs of atoms in 
the two molecules to be aligned. The optimal alignment is 
achieved if the energy is maximized. This method is similar to the 
SEAL (steric and electrostatic alignment) method [Kearsley and Smith, 1990] .

#### Results

Depending on the molecular overlay method, different sets of attributes 
measuring the quality of the alignment are added to the molecules being overlaid.

In alignment by tethers, attributes measuring the root mean square 
deviation (RMSD) between the pairs of atoms used in the alignment (in 
angstroms) are added to the aligned molecules. If there are N tethers 
corresponding to N atom pairs (a 1 , b 1 ), ..., 
(a N , b N ) between atoms a 1 , ..., a N in molecule A and atoms b 1 , ..., b N in 
molecule B, then the reported RMSD value for aligning molecule A to 
molecule B or vice versa is the average squared distance between the paired atoms:

where the summation includes the N atom pairs. r(x) 
represents the 3D vector whose components are the 3D coordinates of 
atom x, and (r(x) - r(y)) 2 is the squared distance of atoms x and y.

In targeted alignment by tethers, a single attribute Overlay RMS/[MoleculeName] is added to each molecule, 
where [MoleculeName] is the name of the target molecule. The attribute value 
is the RMSD between the molecule bearing the attribute and the target value.

In consensus alignment by tethers involving N molecules, N attributes 
named Overlay RMS/[MoleculeName#i] are added to 
each of the aligned molecules. [MoleculeName#i] is the name of the i-th 
molecule involved in the alignment. If the molecule names are not unique, 
[MoleculeName#i] is taken to be an automatically created unique name which 
is stored in the Overlay Label attribute. 
The attribute value of the attribute Overlay RMS/[MoleculeName#i] is the RMSD between the molecule bearing the attribute and the i-th molecule 
involved in the alignment.

In alignment by field fit, attributes measuring the similarity 
of the molecular fields are added to the aligned molecules. 
For each pair of molecules a and b, the similarity is calculated as:

where s is the weight of the steric contribution, e is the weight 
of the electrostatic contribution (defined as e = 1 - s ), S ij is the 
steric overlap of molecules i and j, and E ij is the electrostatic overlap 
of molecules i and j. S ij and E ij include 
contributions from all pairs of atoms of the two molecules.

The similarity coefficients are dimensionless, and can only assume 
values between -1 and 1.

In targeted alignment by field fit, a single attribute Overlay Similarity/[MoleculeName] is added to each of the molecules 
being aligned. [MoleculeName] is the name of the target molecule. 
The value of this attribute is the similarity of the molecule bearing 
the attribute with the target molecule.

In consensus alignment by field fit, N attributes named Overlay Similarity/[MoleculeName#i] are added to each of the 
molecules being aligned. [MoleculeName#i] is the name of the i-th molecule 
involved in the alignment. The value of each attribute is the similarity of 
the molecule bearing the attribute to the molecule indicated by the name 
of the attribute. If the molecule names are not unique, [MoleculeName#i] 
is an automatically created unique name which is stored in the Overlay Label attribute.

# Run a parallel calculation

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/para_hw.htm

## Run a parallel calculation

### Background

Discovery Studio servers allow several levels of parallelization and/or load balancing:

* You can switch between servers manually to distribute the jobs that you launch.

* You can configure a set of Linux machines sharing a disk (a Linux cluster) to distribute multiple jobs across computing resources automatically.

* You can use multi-processor servers to run a single job over several
CPUs in parallel.

Parallelization can occur in three modes, either using coarse-grained parallelization (splitting the inputs up and running several jobs), fine-grained parallelization (using multiple CPUs simultaneously to run a single job) or running the calculation on a graphics processing unit (GPU). Coarse-grained parallelization can be further combined with fine-grained CPU parallelization and GPU calculation where each coarse-grained parallel subprocess runs a fine-grained CPU calculation or a GPU calculation.

Coarse-grained parallel protocols typically operate on files containing a large number of records (for example, a .sd file). These types of files can be split 
up and the records processed on different machines. Coarse-grained 
parallelization is supported on a diverse set of configurations, including mixed networks of Windows and Linux machines. 
Fine-grained parallel protocols allow you to run single jobs on multiple CPUs using MPI (Message Passing Interface).

Parallel computations can be distributed across different Windows and
Linux machines. Frequently a single Linux cluster is used for distribution.
Linux clusters can be configured in two different ways for running
parallel protocols.
See Installing Discovery Studio on a Cluster for details about configuring Linux clusters to support parallel processing.

### Coarse-grained parallelization

Coarse-grained parallelization is enabled on a large number of protocols. These protocols all have a parameter group named Parallel Processing to enable running in parallel.

#### Implementation

Coarse-grained parallelization uses the parallel processing subprotocol functionality of Pipeline Pilot Server . This allows for input files to be split into individual data records (usually individual molecules). Each chunk is then run in parallel using separate servers defined by a list. The results of each job are then reassembled and returned.

A coarse-grained parallel protocol is run on the remote machine specified by the server that Discovery Studio is configured to use as the primary server. Refer to Change Server for more information.

The protocol then controls how the job is divided and distributed using the Parallel Processing options described below.

If the connection to a secondary server fails, it will be removed from the list and a connection to the next server is attempted. If 
no secondary servers are available, the job will fail.

When all the records have been processed, the results are made available in the Output folder. If the intermediate files are saved, then you
can also see the intermediate results for each chunk of the job.

The efficiency of the dispatcher has been shown to be better than 95% for suitable tasks. The efficiency depends on a balance between the 
speed of a job and the overhead of dispatching. For example, if you have a scoring job that runs in under a minute, you should not expect to 
see significant time savings by distributing the job. Long-running jobs, for example docking jobs, scale much better. Much of the overhead for parallel 
protocols is in reading and writing to the shared disk. When running a
large number of jobs, you may find the job performance depends on the
performance of the shared disk.

#### Settings

Coarse-grained parallel protocols contain several parameters within the Parallel Processing parameter group to 
control the parallel behavior:

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Parallel Processing | When set to False , the protocol will run in a single process on the primary server. When set to True , the protocol will be run in parallel, according to the other settings. |
| Batch Size | Where appropriate, this parameter is available to control the number of records in each batch that is sent to the secondary servers. The maximum number of processes started will be the total number of records divided by the batch size, rounded up to the next whole number. For maximum CPU use, ensure that the Chunk Size is sufficiently low to create at least as many jobs as the total number of CPUs you wish to use. |
| Server | This parameter contains a comma separated list of server URLs to use for the calculation. The default is typically localhost , meaning run on the primary server. This default is useful for running on multi-CPU or multi-core machines or Linux clusters. To distribute to a set of heterogenous servers, supply a list of each server you wish to use. If the remote servers use different ports aside from the defaults of 9944 and 9943, then specify the http port number (for example, remotehost:remoteport). Some protocols such as, Build 3D Databases and Search 3D Databases, may access large amounts of data. Distributing this large amount of data across networks to perform coarse-grained parallelization may not produce the desired time savings. Therefore, for these protocols the data is located on the current server. If the server has access to multiple CPUs, (for example, a grid, a cluster, a quad-core machine, etc.) then coarse-grained parallelization can be set by changing the Server Processes parameter. Since heterogenous servers can not be used, the Server parameter is not available in these protocols. |
| Processes | This parameter contains a comma separated list of the number of processes with one entry for each specified server. If there are fewer batches than the total number of processes specified here, only the first available servers will be used. Note that each server will only allow up to the number specified by the Maximum number of simultaneous parallel processing subprotocol jobs allowed parameter on the server administration page (see above). |
| Preserve Order | When set to True , the order of the jobs submitted for parallel processing is maintained. When False , the order of the results may be different, but the progress reporting may be more accurate because the protocol will not wait for slow batches to complete before continuing. |

Where appropriate, this parameter is available to control the number of records in each batch that
is sent to the secondary servers.

The maximum number of processes started will be the total number of records divided by the batch
size, rounded up to the next whole number. For maximum CPU use, ensure that the Chunk Size is sufficiently low to create at least as many
jobs as the total number of CPUs you wish to use.

Some protocols such as,
Build 3D Databases and Search 3D Databases, may access large amounts of
data. Distributing this large amount of data across networks to perform
coarse-grained parallelization may not produce the desired time savings.
Therefore, for these protocols the data is located on the current server. If
the server has access to multiple CPUs, (for example, a grid, a cluster, a quad-core
machine, etc.) then coarse-grained parallelization can be set by changing
the Server Processes parameter. Since
heterogenous servers can not be used, the Server parameter is not
available in these protocols.

#### Example Configurations

Single multi-processor machine

* Use the Change Server dialog to connect to the multi-CPU machine.

* Set the protocols parameters as required.

* Set Parallel Processing to True .

* Ensure Servers is set to localhost .

* Set Processes to the number of processes you want to use.

Combination of Linux and Windows servers with your local machine as the primary server

* Set Servers to a list of the servers you want to use (e.g., localhost, win-server, linux-box) .

* Set Processes to the number of processes on each machine you want to use (for example, 1, 1, 2 ). With the example in the previous step, 4 processes will be started on 3 servers.

Linux cluster (shared disk)

* Use the Change Server dialog to connect to the machine on which you performed the server installation.

* Set Servers to localhost .

* Set Processes to the number of processes you want to use. This number of process will be used along with the
load balancing cluster settings (or grid queue specified on the server) to start several jobs on the various nodes of the cluster.

### Fine-grained parallelization

Fine-grained parallelization is enabled on protocols where long-running tasks can be distributed across several processes on a 
multi-core or multi-CPU machine. These protocols all have an advanced parameter named Number of Processors . Fine-grained parallelization is also enabled for some parallel subprotocols. In this case a parameter, the name of which may vary in different protocols, is defined to set the number of processes for each parallel subprocess.

These protocols use a server configured to use multiple CPUs for some part of the computation using MPI. A version of HP-MPI is 
embedded within the server installations to enable running MPI jobs from Discovery Studio without additional configuration. 
For example, a Dynamics (Production) run
on a single molecule uses MPI to distribute some of the computation onto a set of processors on the server. Distributing fine-grained jobs to
processors on different machines is only possible when run on grid . However, it is not efficient and not recommended.

You can set Number of Processors to a value of 2 n , 
where n is a whole number, zero or greater (e.g., 1, 2, 4). For values other than 1, MPI is used to launch the 
computation.

### GPU computing

Similar to fine-grained parallelization, high performance computing on a GPU is supported by some computation engines, such as CHARMm. When a Discovery Studio server is installed on a machine with the supported graphics card, the protocols supporting GPU calculation can be run in GPU mode. For more information, see Run a GPU calculation .

#### Further information

Installing Discovery Studio Installing and configuring a cluster Distributed grid computing

# Opening a Protein Data Bank (PDB) file

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/pdb.htm

## Opening a Protein Data Bank (PDB) file

This topic covers the assignment of bond orders for ligand structures when
opening a Protein Data Bank (ENT, PDB) file in the legacy .pdb format.

The .pdb format was primarily designed for storage of biopolymer structures
such as proteins or nucleic acids for which bonding and bond orders are
known and can be accurately assigned. While the format does allow ligand
connectivity to be defined, there is no provision for defining the bond order.

The RCSB Protein Data Bank now uses macromolecular CIF (mmCIF) as its primary archival format. This does not have some of the limitations of the .pdb format. In particular, these files now include embedded Chemical Component definitions which allow correct assignment of bonds and bond orders to ligands.

When a .pdb file is opened, the application assigns bond orders for standard residues
such as amino and nucleic acids using a template-based approach. It then attempts to
automatically perceive the bond orders for other residues (typically ligands).
This process is not entirely straightforward, as ligand structures determined in
the context of a large molecule frequently have poor geometry and typically
have no hydrogen atoms defined. Therefore a combination of geometric factors (e.g., bond lengths and angles, ring and group planarity), and knowledge of chemical functional groups is employed to arrive at a plausible solution.

The following steps occur:

* Rings are perceived, and ring planarity is determined.

* Planar rings are analyzed to determine the hybridization of each ring atom. This process
includes the comparison of angles with average angles for the given ring size as
well as consideration of element type, planarity, and bond length of any substituents.

* Bond orders are assigned on the basis of atom hybridizations,
bond lengths, and chemical elements involved.

* For atoms that are not part of planar ring systems, hybridization is assigned
based on element type, numbers of bonds, bond distances, and where possible, bond angles 
and group planarity.

* Sulfate and phosphate groups are handled as special cases.

* Bond orders are assigned for bonds to sp3 and sp hybridized atoms.

* Bond orders are assigned to bonds between sp2 hybridized atoms.

* A "Water" group is created that contains all waters in the structure.

* At this stage, all bonds should have orders assigned, but for 
some atoms, the resulting sum of bond orders may exceed their atomic valence. 
Such atoms are subjected to checking for functional groups such as carboxyl, arginyl, and nitro.

As an alternative, a script has been provided which will retrieve the Chemical Component definitions for ligands from the PDB and use these to assign bond orders. This can be accessed from the Scripts | Structure Editing menu.

#### Further information

Import PDB subpage - Preferences dialog File menu Scripts | Structure Editing

The 3D Point Plot displays data as a 3D plot of points. 3D Point Plots can be used to explore relationships between different properties of 
molecular data displayed in Data Table View of
a Molecule Window .

The Point Plot and the Molecule Window are fully interactive and any selection you make in one is reflected in the other.

When the plot is created from a selected subset of data, it is not interactive if the molecular data has been modified.

To create a 3D Point Plot from the menu bar, ensure the Molecule Window is active, and then choose Chart | 3D Point Plot , which opens the Choose Plot Axes dialog .
You are prompted to select the data sets to be represented on the x, y and z axes. You can also set Color by Data Series to specify how the data
will be colored.

If you generate a 3D Point Plot from the Data Table View, you can choose a set of rows and choose Plot selected rows only in the Choose Plot Axes dialog to plot the selected rows only. Additionally, you can specify the variables to plot by selecting three or more columns in the Data Table View before generating the plot.

### Zooming

For easier distinction between points, use the standard Zoom button on the View toolbar. When this 
tool is selected, left-click and drag to change the axes maximal values, thus changing the stretch of the datasets along 
all axes. If you want to zoom along only one axis, left-click that axis and drag it. The Zoom tool does not change the grid size.

Rotating the mouse wheel to change the overall zoom of the chart, including grid.

### Repositioning

You can reposition the plot (for example to center on a section of interest) by clicking and dragging. You can also use 
the standard Translate button 
on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

You can also click and drag a single axis to limit the position change to that axis.

### Rotating

Right-click and drag to rotate the plot. You can also use the standard Rotate button on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect, or by using 
the ARROW keys. You can also press X , Y , and Z keys to control the plot along the corresponding axis.

### Selecting

Select regions of the plot using the selection tools in the View toolbar .

# Contact Plot

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/pl_contact-map.htm

## Contact Plot

Contact Plots show the relationship between pairs of amino acid residues. Contact Plots are classified into two categories.

* Distance Contact Plots

* Interaction Contact Plots

A Distance Contact Plot is a plot of mutual residue distances. Three types of distances can be shown on the plot: Cα-Cα distances, Cβ-Cβ distances,
and side-chain distances.

Distance between the atoms of residues i and j are shown on the upper left 
of the map and distances between residues j and i on the lower right. The two distances are commutative, 
so the two halves of the map are mirrored across a diagonal line of symmetry.

In a side-chain plot, the distance between the closest pair of side-chain atoms between the two residues is shown.

Residue pairs are included in the plot if the distance falls below a cutoff value which can be set on the Contact Plot subpage of the Preferences dialog. However, note that unless the selection contains three or fewer residues, the residues will not be shown if they are within two places along the amino acid chain. Such residues are necessarily close and are excluded to reduce clutter.

An Interaction Contact Plot is a plot of inter-residue interaction. Two types of interaction, 
Hydrogen bonds and residue types, can be plotted. The interactions between residues i and j are shown on the upper left of the map.

#### Hydrogen Bond Interaction Plots

Hydrogen Bond Interaction Plots indicate whether H-bond interactions are between main-chain atoms, 
side-chain atoms, or if multiple H-bonds exist within a single atom. The points are colored based on the type of 
H-bond the point represents:

* Main-chain - Main-chain

* Main-chain - Side-chain

* Side-chain - Side-chain

* Multiple

#### Residue Type

A Residue Type Interaction Plot is a plot of residues with atoms less than 6 angstroms apart.
The type of the pair of residues are indicated as:

* Hydrophobic-Hydrophobic

* Hydrophobic-Hydrophilic

* Hydrophilic-Hydrophilic

* Acidic-Basic

### Zooming

For easier distinction between points, you can use the mouse wheel or the keyboard
controls to zoom in and out on the plot. You can also use the standard Zoom button on the View toolbar
to achieve the same effect.

### Repositioning

You can reposition the plot (for example to center on a section of interest)
by holding the mouse wheel down and dragging, or by using the up, down,
left, and right ARROW keys. You can also use the standard Translate button on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Selecting

Select one or more points on the plot using the selection tools in the View toolbar . The corresponding points across the
line of symmetry are selected, and the constituent amino acids of each selected distance are selected in the Molecule Window.

### Hovering

To see which residue-residue distance is mapped by any given point,
hover your mouse cursor over the point until a pop-up appears displaying
the residue names and the distance between the residues in Ångstroms
(for example :CYS3-CYS40[5.62993] ).

For interaction plots, the pop-up displays only the residue names

# Hit Rate Plot

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/pl_hit-rate-plot.htm

## Hit Rate Plot

A Hit Rate Plot is a specialized plot useful in analyzing
results from docking/scoring protocols where control ligands 
(i.e., ligands known to have significant binding affinity to the target receptor) have 
been specified along with a set of input ligands. This is generally the case in virtual 
high-throughput screening, which typically employs random ligands and known 
actives. The Hit Rate Plot enables you to visualize the ranking of the 
known actives against the other ligands with respect to a given scoring function.

The following procedure is employed for generating a Hit Rate Plot.
First, the data in the Molecule Window should be prepared, 
to organize the entries (for example, by Name or MOL_NUMBER). For a given
scoring function, the highest scoring representative (typically the
best ligand pose) of each group (typically each group represents one
ligand) is retained, rejecting all other entries of that group. The
resulting representatives of each group are sorted in the order of the
respective scores. If a control ligand (i.e., an active molecule) is
encountered, it is considered a hit. A plot showing the number of hits
encountered on the y-axis plotted against the ligand/group rank on the
x-axis yields the Hit Rate Plot.

If there are n groups/ligands in the data set, the ligand rank
goes from 1 to n , where 1 corresponds to the highest scoring group/ligand while n is
the lowest scoring group/ligand. If there are m control ligands
in the set, the y-axis goes from 0 to m . The plot generally starts at y=0 (or y=1 if the highest ranking
ligand is a control ligand) and steps up by one count when a control
ligand is encountered. If a score (or any numeric) column is selected
from the table, the Hit Rate Plot is computed and displayed. If more
than one score is selected, multiple hit rate curves are generated in
the same plot using different colors to indicate the corresponding score
as shown by the color legend of the plot.

### Zooming

You can use the mouse wheel or the keyboard controls to zoom in and out on the plot. 
You can also use the standard Zoom tool from the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Repositioning

You can reposition the plot (for example to center a section of interest) by holding the 
mouse wheel down and dragging, or by using the up, down, left, and right ARROW keys. You 
can also use the standard Translate tool from the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Selecting

You can select regions of the plot using the selection tools in the View toolbar .

### Access methods

| Menu | Chart \| Hit Rate Plot |
| --- | --- |

# Hydrophobicity Plot

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/pl_hydrophobicity-plot.htm

## Hydrophobicity Plot

The Hydrophobicity Plot is a plot of the amino acids in a protein against their
hydrophobicity index. The hydrophobicity scale is taken from Kyte
and Doolittle [Kyte and Doolittle, 1982] . 
The Kyte and Doolittle hydrophobicity values are as follows:

```text
PHE 2.8 SER -0.8
MET 1.9 PRO -1.6
ILE 4.5 TYR -1.3
LEU 3.8 HIS -3.2
VAL 4.2 GLN -3.5
CYS 2.5 ASN -3.5
TRP -0.9 GLU -3.5
ALA 1.8 LYS -3.9
THR -0.7 ASP -3.5
GLY -0.4 ARG -4.5
```

Note that when creating the Protein Groups, residues with a hydrophobicity of 0.7 or more are considered to be hydrophobic and those under -2.4 are hydrophilic.

Hydrophobicity values are typically sequence based and have no 3D component.

### Smoothing

The Hydrophobicity Plot can be smoothed by averaging the hydrophobicity value of each 
residue with the neighboring residues. You can set the window size for including 
neighboring residues using the Edit | Preferences...| Charts command from the menu bar.

For example, if the Hydrophobicity Running Average Window 
is set to 5, the hydrophobicity of a residue is calculated as the average of the 
two residues before it, its own value, and the two residues after it.

### Zooming

To create a greater distinction between cells, use the mouse wheel or the keyboard
controls to zoom in and out on the plot. You can also use the standard Zoom tool on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Repositioning

You can reposition the plot (for example, to center on a particular section)
by clicking the mouse wheel and dragging, or by using the ARROW keys. You can also use the Translate tool on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Selecting

You can select peaks on the hydrophobicity plot by double-clicking them. Selecting 
a peak causes corresponding objects to be selected in related views (for example, 
the Data Table, Graphics View, Sequence View, and Hierarchy View). A range 
of peaks may be selected by clicking and dragging a lasso or box around the peaks.

### Hovering

Hovering the mouse cursor over a peak displays the chain ID, the 3-letter amino acid code and 
sequence number, and the hydrophobicity index. For example, in the following:

B:ILE3:4.5

B is the chain. ILE3 is the amino acid, and 4.5 is the hydrophobicity index.

### Access methods

| Menu | Chart \| Hydrophobicity Plot |

# Ramachandran Plot

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/pl_ramachandran.htm

## Ramachandran Plot

The Ramachandran Plot indicates low energy conformations for φ 
(phi) and ψ (psi), the conventional terms used to represent the
torsion angles on either side of alpha carbons in peptides. This plot
is often used as a first check to verify predicted
torsion angles in proteins.

The Ramachandran Plot provides a graphical representation
of the local backbone conformation of each residue in a protein. Each
point on the Ramachandran Plot represents the φ and ψ 
torsion angles of a residue. The plot also includes a representation
of the favorable and unfavorable regions for residues, so that you can
determine if individual residues are likely to be built correctly.
The Ramachandran plot computed here is as updated by Richardson and 
coworkers [Lovell et al. 2003] .

Ramachandran plot is fully interactive with the Graphics view

### Zooming

For easier distinction between points, you can use the mouse wheel or the keyboard
controls to zoom in and out on the plot. You can also use the standard Zoom button on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Repositioning

You can reposition the plot (for example to center on a section of interest)
by holding the mouse wheel down and dragging, or by using the up, down,
left, and right ARROW keys. You can also use the standard Translate button on the View toolbar to achieve the same effect.

### Selecting

Select one or more points on the Ramachandran Plot by using the selection tools in the View toolbar .
Selecting a point causes corresponding objects to be selected in related
views (for example, the Data Table, Graphics View, Sequence View,
and Hierarchy View).

Conversely, with the exception of terminal residues, any residues
that are selected in the Data Table, Graphics View, Sequence View,
or Hierarchy View are also automatically selected in the Ramachandran
Plot.

Double-clicking a point on 
the Ramachandran plot recenters the Graphics View onto the selected residue. 
This is useful for examining the problem area of a structure, such as 
Ramachandran violations.

### Hovering

Hovering over a point on the plot displays the chain ID, the 3-letter
amino acid code and sequence number, and the φ and ψ 
angles. For example, in the following:

A:SER216:-71.6:116

A is the chain, and SER216 is the amino acid. The value of φ is -71.6 and the value of 
ψ is 116 .

Amino Acid types are represented graphically as follows:
glycine as a triangle, proline as a square, and all other types as a circle.

### Access methods

| Menu | Chart \| Ramachandran Plot |
| --- | --- |

# BLAST XML report

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/prmo_bls_ar_op_blast-xml-report.htm

## BLAST XML report

BLAST results are stored in an .xml file in the protocol Output folder. The file is loaded automatically into the BLAST Results Window at the end of a protocol run. It can also be opened by clicking the .xml file in the Files Explorer. Refer to BLAST Results Window for more information.

#### Loading the hits

From the context sensitive menu of the Map View or Table View, choose a method to load the sequences, alignments, 
and structures into 
the Sequence Window and Molecule Window:

* Load Selected Sequences - loads the sequences 
of the selected hits into one Sequence Window.

* Load Selected Structures - loads the protein structures 
of the selected hits into one Molecule Window.

* Load Structure and Alignment - loads the protein
structures of the selected hits, extracts their sequences into one Sequence
Window, and aligns the sequences to the query sequence according to BLAST Search
or PSI-BLAST Search alignment.
If a protein contains multiple chains, only the protein chain associated with a hit will be kept, and this chain name will be appended to the protein name. 
Additionally, all ligand chains will be kept in the loaded structure.

* Load Aligned Regions - loads the alignments of
the selected hits from BLAST Search or PSI-BLAST Search output.

Additionally, the Get Structure Files option allows the retrieval of structure files for the selected hits without loading them in the Molecule Window. This is useful if you want to use them in a different protocol rather than viewing them.

Get Structure Files , Load Selected Structures , and Load Structure and Alignment commands are only valid when the
database searched is PDB_nr95 or PDB, or for hits recognisably derived from PDB structures in NCBI databases. For other databases, executing these 
commands prompts a message indicating that the selected hits have no associated structures.

These structure retrieval and loading commands download protein structures from an internet
RCSB Protein Data Bank site or from a local RCSB mirror. The location of the structure files is specified
on the URL Location subpage of the Preferences dialog by the Default RCSB Structures site.
This preference is shared with the Open URL command. The files can be in macromolecular cif (mmCIF) or pdb format and may be compressed. Note however that not all structures are available in the latter format so mmCIF is now preferred.

For example, if you have compressed PDB files installed in a mirror on your machine of the form C:\PDB\cr\pdb1crn.ent.gz , change the URL Template of the Default RCSB Structures to file:///C:/PDB/$/pdb@.ent.gz . For a mirror containing macromolecular cif format files on a shared drive, the URL template would be of the form file://servername/path/$/@.cif.gz

The downloaded structure files are copied to the Output folder of the BLAST search for subsequent reuse.

#### Loading multiple hits from one sequence

When there are multiple hits to the same database sequence, there are multiple
matching segments between the query sequence and the database sequence. Sometimes
the multiple hits overlap with each other, either on the query sequence or on
the database sequence. The behavior of the Table View and the Map View is different when alignments are loaded 
using the loading commands, Load Structure and Alignment ,
or Load Aligned Regions , depending on whether the hits are overlapping.

From the Table View, the three loading commands load one hit with the highest
bit score of that sequence. From the Map View, if multiple hits are selected,
multiple aligned regions are loaded if the hits are not overlapping with each
other. If they are overlapping, the alignment of the hit with the higher bit
score is loaded. When two hits are overlapping on the query sequence, it is
shown clearly by the bars in the Map View. To see if the two hits are overlapping
on the database sequence, use mouse fly-over to see the hit start and end positions
of the two hits.

## Example protocols

Included with the Discovery Studio component collection are a number of example protocols that demonstrate the use of Discovery Studio components in the Pipeline Pilot Client . These protocols are not available from the Protocols Explorer in Discovery Studio Client. However, you can add them to a custom tool panel (Discovery Guide).

To run an example protocol in Pipeline Pilot

* Open Pipeline Pilot Client and make sure it is connected to a Pipeline Pilot Server .

* From the Protocols Explorer, expand Discovery Studio | Examples .

* Double-click one of the examples in the subfolders to load it in the workspace.

* Click individual components to set parameter values for them.

* Click the run button in the tool bar to run the protocol.

To run an example protocol in Discovery Studio

* Open the Tools Explorer.

* Right-click the Tools Explorer and choose Insert New Panel...

* Type a panel name and click OK .

* In the Tool Panel Editor dialog, expand Protocols | Examples and then choose an example protocol from one of the subfolders. Click OK

* Click the protocol button in the tool panel to load it.

* Click the run button in the tool bar to run the protocol. Note that many example protocols do not have parameters available. You can set default parameter values for individual components by customizing the protocol in Pipeline Pilot. For more information, see Customizing protocols .

Not all example protocols available on the on-prem server are available on the cloud.

Sometimes you may need to share Discovery Studio output with non-licensed users. Although this is not a problem 
for some basic file formats such as TXT or CSV, there are some that are exclusive to Discovery Studio . BIOVIA offers a free solution for non-licensed users to visualize data. Users can download our free Discovery Studio Visualizer and view the 
data on their own.

You can request downloads from https://discover.3ds.com/discovery-studio-visualizer-download .

### Discovery Studio Visualizer

The Discovery Studio Visualizer is an integrated desktop application that provides extensive capabilities for viewing and editing
molecular structures and sequences. The Discovery Studio Visualizer does not provide many of the advanced analysis tools in the Discovery Studio Client. It also does not have the ability to connect to a Pipeline Pilot Server .

However, the Visualizer is able to read all structure and sequence formats output by the full Discovery Studio client. It is a convenient method for sharing results with collaborators who wish, for example, to 
view annotated results created in the Discovery Studio Client.

# Working with structures and surfaces

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/structures_and_surfaces.htm

## Working with structures and surfaces

Discovery Studio is designed for use in the Life Sciences, 
with focus on the study of biologically relevant structures. These range 
from small molecules, such as drugs and inhibitors, to larger molecules such as proteins and nucleic 
acid biopolymers.

Form typically determines function of molecular systems. A large body of 
experimentally determined and theoretically modeled structural information allows 
you to understand and predict molecular properties. In addition to atomistic 
representations, you can also create abstractions such as molecular surfaces 
to aid this process.

In the Discovery Studio Client, the following windows are available for working with molecular data:

* Molecule Window : Displays three dimensional structures , hierarchical organization , and data in a tabular form .

* 2D Window : Displays high quality graphical two dimensional representations
of molecular structures.

### Introduction to structural data

The molecular data used within the client can come from a variety of sources including:

* Macromolecular databases such as the Protein Data Bank [Bernstein et al., 1977]

* Files resulting from crystallographic or NMR structure determination, or modeled by other applications

* Small-molecule databases (which may contain 2D data which can be converted to 3D)

* Smiles strings, which are interpreted to provide 3D structures

* Structures built or modeled within the client

### Types of structural data

Depending on the particular focus of research, different aspects of molecular structure data may 
be of interest. For example, when working with small molecules, atomic level interactions
are usually of most interest, and it is important to view information about individual atoms
and bonds. On the other hand, when working with macromolecular data, it may be more 
useful to model systems at the level of chains and molecules.

To accommodate a wide variety of chemical and structural information,
The Discovery Studio Client provides a rich set of structural data types. These objects and the relationships between 
them are described by the molecular data model. This takes the form of a hierarchy of objects (e.g., a Cell contains Molecules, 
which contain chains of AminoAcids, which contain Atoms). A good way to begin understanding the hierarchy 
is to open a structure of interest and examine the Hierarchy View .

Data objects that model specific structural entities include:

| Level | Example data objects |
| --- | --- |
| Sub-molecular | Atom Bond Residue Pharmacophore Query |
| Molecular | Molecule Chain Conformation |
| Super-molecular | Cell Binding Site Conformation |

* Atom

* Bond

* Residue

* Pharmacophore Query

* Molecule

* Chain

* Conformation

* Cell

* Binding Site

In addition to the fundamental molecular objects that underlie a structural model, a variety
of other specialized data objects provide information, model additional data types,
or provide information about specific relationships. These include:

| Object Type | Example subcategories |
| --- | --- |
| Monitors | Distance Hydrogen Bond Bump Neighbor Valence |
| Constraint | |
| Containers | Groups Assemblies |
| Sphere | |
| Animation | |
| Density Map | |
| Text Annotation | |
| Clipping Plane | |

* Distance

* Hydrogen Bond

* Bump

* Neighbor

* Valence

* Groups

* Assemblies

The objects themselves have a variety of Properties (or Attributes) appropriate to their purpose. 
These can be viewed either in the Data Table View , 
or in the Attributes dialog .

### Introduction to Surfaces

The Discovery Studio Client can generate a variety of surface representations.
Molecular surfaces include:

* Solvent: Connolly-type surface created by rolling a "probe" around the molecule

* Soft: Similar to a solvent surface, but employing a faster, more approximate algorithm than that used for creating a solvent surface

* VDW: Surface based on the van der Waals radius of each atom in the molecule

In addition to molecular surfaces, isosurfaces such as electron density maps can also be displayed.

# Insight II files and Discover Cartesian Coordinate (CAR, COR, MDF)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_car-cor-mdf.htm

## Insight II files and Discover Cartesian Coordinate (CAR, COR, MDF)

Files with .car , .cor , and .mdf extension are Insight II /Discover Cartesian Coordinate files.

A single 3D structure is described by a .car and .mdf pair: the car file tends to contain information
that often changes, such as atomic coordinates, and the .mdf file contains more static information, such as
bonding. If an .mdf file is not available then Discovery Studio will create a 3D Model document from the .car file alone. The .car and .mdf files are key file formats used by the BIOVIA programs Insight II and Discover Cartesian Coordinate to save and retrieve structural
data and can represent a wide range of atomistic data
including:

* Atoms

* Bonds

* Polymers

* Surfaces

* Crystals

* Symmetry

Discovery Studio faithfully imports and
exports most information from .car / .mdf files and they should be used as the primary means of communicating
atomistic data between Discovery Studio and Insight II .

Data which are not transferred include:

* Helical structures

BIOVIA products also create files with a .cor suffix. These files contain the same data as .car files and are also associated with an .mdf file, and
usually contain the final result of a minimization or
dynamics simulation.

The .car file contains the Cartesian coordinates of
a molecular system, as well as related positional information. This
information is dynamic and can change during the course of a
calculation.

#### Description of .car file contents

The .car file consists of one file header (which
includes statements indicating what kinds of information are
present in the file), one coordinate section header, optional 2D or
3D periodicity records, one coordinate section for each molecule in
the file, and one end-of-file statement. All lines in the file are
exactly 80 characters long. The format of the .cor file is identical to that of the .car file. The
coordinate section(s) includes:

* Optional helix record

* Atom records

* End-of-section statement

The overall structure of a .car file for non-helical
systems is shown in Table 1 and that of a
file containing helix information is shown in Table 2 . Descriptions of the major parts follow.

Information
relating to 2D periodicity is indicated by bold type; italic type indicates contents that are replaced by
real data; plain type indicates actual contents.

Table 1. Structure of a Cartesian
Coordinate File for Systems Not Characterized by Helical
Symmetry

| line | columns | contents | comments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First: | | !BIOSYM archive 3 | |
| Second: | | PBC=ON, PBC=OFF, PBC=2D | one of these three choices must be present |
| The coordinate header begins with the third line: | | | |
| Third: | 1-64 | title for the system | if available--this line may be blank but must be present |
| | 65-80 | energy | |
| Fourth: | | ! DATE day month date time year | or just !DATE |
| Fifth line: PBC information if PBC=ON: | | | |
| | 1-3 | PBC | |
| | 4-13 | a | cell vector a in angstroms |
| | 14-23 | b | cell vector b in angstroms |
| | 24-33 | c | cell vector c in angstroms |
| | 34-43 | alpha | cell angle α in degrees |
| | 44-53 | beta | cell angle β in degrees |
| | 54-63 | gamma | cell angle γ in degrees |
| | 64-80 | space group name | |
| Fifth line: PBC information if PBC=2D: | | | |
| | 1-3 | PBC | |
| | 4-13 | k | plane vector k in angstroms |
| | 14-23 | l | plane vector l in angstroms |
| | 24-33 | gamma | plane angle γ in degrees |
| | 34-50 | plane group name | |
| Sixth-N (This section is repeated for each molecule in the system.): | | | |
| | 1-5 | atom name | |
| | 7-20 | x Cartesian coordinate of atom | in angstroms |
| | 22-35 | y Cartesian coordinate of atom | in angstroms |
| | 37-50 | z Cartesian coordinate of atom | in angstroms |
| | 52-55 | type of residue containing atom | |
| | 57-63 | residue sequence name | relative to beginning of current molecule, left justified |
| | 64-70 | potential type of atom | left justified |
| | 72-73 | element symbol | |
| | 75-80 | partial charge on atom | |
| Final line for a given molecule: | | | |
| | 1-3 | end | |
| Final line for the entire molecular system input: | | | |
| | 1-3 | end | |

Information
relating to helices and 2D periodicity is indicated by bold type; italic type indicates contents
that are replaced by real data; plain type indicates actual
contents.

Table 2. Structure of Cartesian
Coordinate File Containing Helix Information

| line | columns | contents | comments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First: | | !BIOSYM archive 3 | |
| Second: | | HELIX | |
| Third: | | PBC=OFF, PBC=2D | one of these two choices must be present |
| The coordinate header begins with the fourth line: | | | |
| Fourth: | 1-64 | title for the system | if available--this line may be blank but must be present |
| | 65-80 | energy | |
| Fifth: | 1 | ! DATE day month date time year | or just !DATE |
| Sixth line: PBC information if PBC=2D: | | | |
| | 1-3 | PBC | |
| | 4-13 | k | plane vector k in angstroms |
| | 14-23 | l | plane vector l in angstroms |
| | 24-33 | gamma | plane angle γ in degrees |
| | 34-50 | plane group name | |
| Seventh (This helix record is part of the section that repeats for each molecule in the system.): | | | |
| | 1-5 | HELIX | |
| | 6-15 | sigma | in degrees |
| | 16-25 | d | in angstroms |
| | 26-35 | kappa | angle between l axis and helix axis in degrees |
| | 36-45 | lambda | angle between k axis and helix axis in degrees |
| | 46-55 | Tk | fractional position of helix axis along k axis |
| | 56-65 | Tl | fractional position of helix axis along l axis |
| Eighth-N (This section repeats for each molecule in the system.): | | | |
| | 1-5 | atom name | |
| | 7-20 | x Cartesian coordinate of atom | in angstroms |
| | 22-35 | y Cartesian coordinate of atom | in angstroms |
| | 37-50 | z Cartesian coordinate of atom | in angstroms |
| | 52-55 | type of residue containing atom | |
| | 57-63 | residue sequence name | relative to beginning of current molecule, left justified |
| | 64-70 | potential type of atom | left justified |
| | 72-73 | element symbol | |
| | 75-80 | partial charge on atom | |
| Final line for a given molecule: | | | |
| | 1-3 | end | |
| Final line for the entire molecular system input: | | | |
| | 1-3 | end | |

#### File header

The first record of a .car file must be:

```text
!BIOSYM archive 
#
```

The ! must be the first character in the file.
The Discover program interprets this line as indicating an ASCII
file containing coordinate records as outlined in this section. The
string archive indicates that the contents of the
file are those of a .car file; the # identifies the file format. For example, 3 indicates that the file format is as specified
here for the Discover program, versions 2.9.5/3.2 and later.

If helix information is not present in the .car file, then the second line indicates whether the file contains PBC
information. If helix information is present, then the second line
of the .car file consists of the word HELIX and the
third line indicates whether the file contains PBC information.
Note that helical symmetry is not currently compatible with 3D
periodicity. So if the second line is HELIX and PBC=ON is found, an
error message is generated.

Valid file headers:

```text
!BIOSYM archive 3
HELIX
PBC=2D
!BIOSYM archive 3
HELIX
PBC=OFF
!BIOSYM archive 3
PBC=ON
!BIOSYM archive 3
PBC=OFF
!BIOSYM archive 3
PBC=2D
```

#### Coordinate section header

The coordinate section header consists of two lines. Both lines
must be present in the .car file. The first line,
which may be blank, usually contains a title and the energy. The
second line must contain the characters !DATE, optionally followed
by the full date when the file was written (see Tables 1 and 2 ).

#### Periodicity records

A periodicity record is present in the .car file
only if the entry PBC=ON or PBC=2D is present in the file
header.

For 3D periodicity, indicated by the file header line PBC=ON
(see Table 1 ). This line contains the word
PBC, followed by the a, b, and c unit cell lengths, the values of
the α, β, and γ angles, and 4he space group name. Please see the
About BCTL Help topics in the Discover module help for a discussion
of valid space group names.

For 2D periodicity, indicated by the file header line PBC=2D,
the PBC section (Tables 1 and 2 ) contains the word PBC, the k and l values, the
value of γ, and the plane group name. Currently, only the (P1)
plane group is supported.

Example PBC record for 2D periodicity:

```text
PBC 18.6200 18.6200 90.0000 (P 1)
```

#### Coordinate section

Coordinate records are present for each molecule in the system,
so this section is repeated as a whole for each molecule.

##### Helix records

If any helix information is present in a .car file,
the second line of the file must be the word HELIX.

If a molecule has helical symmetry (i.e., it is an infinite
helix), then an extra line is present in the relevant coordinate
section, just before the atom records for that molecule. Note that
each helical molecule has its own helix record. The new line in the
coordinate section contains the word HELIX, followed by the sigma and d
values, the kapp and lambda angles, and the Tk and Tl positions (see Table 1 ).

Example helix record:

```text
HELIX 143.3598 7.6194 90.0000 90.0000 0.5000 0.4500
```

The atom records (see Table 1 ) contain
information that identifies the complete Insight II name of each real
atom, some general properties of the atom, and its location in 3D
space. Ghost atoms are generated from real ones according to
symmetry and periodicity information.

##### End records

The coordinate section for each molecule in the system must end
with the word "end" in the first three columns of the last line of
the section. In addition, the entire file must end with the word
"end", also in the first three columns of the last line of the
file.

### Import/Export

CAR and COR files can be imported into Discovery Studio .

Working with files

# Crystallographic Information (CIF)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_cif.htm

## Crystallographic Information (CIF)

Files with a .cif extension are Crystallographic Information Files . This format is defined by the International Union
for Crystallography and is used for storing crystallographic and related structural science data [Hall et al., 1991] .

As CIF is a self-defining text archive (STAR) format, many
variations of CIF files exist in the structural chemistry and biology communities. Discovery Studio can read the following types, automatically deducing their content from the data categories they contain: Macromolecular CIF (mmCIF) files. This is the primary archival format for structural data used by the RCSB Protein Data Bank. It can accommodate structures that cannot be written in the original PDB format due to large numbers of atoms or residues, chain names greater than one character long and residue names more than three characters long. Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) files. These contain definitions including full bonding information for all residue and small molecule components found in RCSB entries. Small molecule crystallographic structure files.

* Macromolecular CIF (mmCIF) files. This is the primary archival format for structural data used by the RCSB Protein Data Bank. It can accommodate structures that cannot be written in the original PDB format due to large numbers of atoms or residues, chain names greater than one character long and residue names more than three characters long.

* Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) files. These contain definitions including full bonding information for all residue and small molecule components found in RCSB entries.

* Small molecule crystallographic structure files.

Additionally, CIF format Structure Factor files (named <PDB_ID>_sf.cif ) can be used as a source of reflection data in various of the X-Ray protocols but cannot be opened in Discovery Studio .

### Macromolecular CIF Files

Discovery Studio can import macromolecular CIF files conforming to the PDBx/mmCIF definitions (see Beginner’s Guide to PDB Structures and the PDBx/mmCIF Format for an introduction and PDBx/mmCIF Dictionary Resources for full information.)

The data which is read, if present, includes: Crystallographic information: Cell parameters, space group and resolution. Atom records: Atom positions and the hierarchical structure of the macromolecule in a similar way to the familiar PDB ATOM/HETATM records. Chemical component bond records: These allow automatic assignment of the correct bonding and bond orders to ligands. Connectivity records for inter-residue bonds. Active site definitions. Secondary structure definitions. Information about residues in the sequence that are not present in the resolved experimental structure. This is equivalent to the use of SEQRES records in the PDB format, allowing for missing sections to be built. Entity identifiers for protein and nucleic acid chains. These are unique numbers for each different sequence within a structure so can be useful information in multimers. Note that entity numbers refer to the full sequence rather than to the resolved residues.

* Crystallographic information: Cell parameters, space group and resolution.

* Atom records: Atom positions and the hierarchical structure of the macromolecule in a similar way to the familiar PDB ATOM/HETATM records.

* Chemical component bond records: These allow automatic assignment of the correct bonding and bond orders to ligands.

* Connectivity records for inter-residue bonds.

* Active site definitions.

* Secondary structure definitions.

* Information about residues in the sequence that are not present in the resolved experimental structure. This is equivalent to the use of SEQRES records in the PDB format, allowing for missing sections to be built.

* Entity identifiers for protein and nucleic acid chains. These are unique numbers for each different sequence within a structure so can be useful information in multimers. Note that entity numbers refer to the full sequence rather than to the resolved residues.

Macromolecular CIF files can also contain Biological Assemblies. These can be useful in cases where the biologically relevant entity is not identical to the crystallographic asymmetric unit. They can be obtained from RCSB and are named <PDB_ID>-assembly<N>.cif , where N is the assembly number.

Whereas in .pdb format files, the copies making up each assembly are stored as Models and read as separate molecules, in the mmCIF format they are stored and read as additional chains with labels A, A-2, A-3 etc.

### Chemical Component Dictionary Files

The Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) files contain the detailed descriptions of each
residue and small molecule found in RCSB PDB entries. Each chemical component has a unique 3 or 5 character alphanumeric identifier. 
They can be opened as small molecules in Discovery Studio using Open URL with the PDB Ligands (cif) Site. 
This information is now included in macromolecular cif files allowing correct bond order and formal charge assignments. 
See Chemical Component Dictionary for more information.

### Small Molecule Crystallographic Structure Files

Discovery Studio can import small molecule CIF files from two important sources: those specified to the minimum requirement (see Notes for Authors ) for submission to the journal Acta Crystallographica C: Crystal Structure Communications by the International Union of Crystallography and those generated by the Cambridge Structural Database (see the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre ) to their specification.

For import, the file must contain either of the following:

* Unit cell parameters

* Atom coordinates (Cartesian) and atom types (or atom
labels)

To utilize space group information, the file must include:

* Symmetry positions

* International Tables (IT) number

Discovery Studio reads:

* Cell setting

* Space group name

* Atom labels

* Atom types (if present - if not, get from atom labels and _atom_type_symbol , if present)

* Atom coordinates (fractional)

* Occupancies

* Isotropic temperature factors

* Isotropic/anisotropic flag

* Anisotropic temperature factors

* Connectivity

### Import/Export

These three types of CIF file can all be opened as molecular structures in Discovery Studio .
Macromolecular structures can be saved using Menus | Scripts | Export | Save as mmCIF .

# Comma Separated Value (CSV)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_csv.htm

## Comma Separated Value (CSV)

Files with a .csv extension are comma separated value
files. The application can open these files in the Molecule window.

A CSV file is a standard format providing a simple way of representing tabular or spreadsheet data. CSV files contain plain text that can be read and modified using any text editor as well as spreadsheet applications such as Microsoft Excel. Discovery Studio can load CSV files and will display their contents in the Data Table View . Additionally, data can be saved in this format.

All data on the same line in a CSV file appears on the same row in its spreadsheet form. Each comma on a line in the CSV file indicates a separation between adjacent columns. Thus, in reading a CSV file into a spreadsheet, each comma indicates to the program that the following data appears in a following cell.

However, should it be required to display a comma as part of the contents of a cell, it is necessary to enclose all of the contents of that element in double quotation marks (" "), so that the comma is not misinterpreted.

Finally, where it is necessary to display double quotation marks themselves as part of the contents of a cell, they should be represented in text by consecutive double quotes ("").

### Preferences

For import preferences, see Import CSV subpage - Preferences dialog .

### Import/Export

CSV files can be imported into and exported from Discovery Studio .

#### Further information

Working with files

DOCUMENT 514
==============================================================================================================

## CNX Reflection Data (CV, FOB, HKL)

# Protein Databank (ENT, PDB)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_ent-pdb.htm

## Protein Databank (ENT, PDB)

Files with a .ent or .pdb extension are RCSB Protein Data Bank files, which are best used for proteins and DNA structures. .pdb files do not contain bond order information, so they are not as useful for small molecules and should not be used for 2D representations. Discovery Studio can accurately assign bond orders to standard residues including amino and nucleic acids. However, for other species, it attempts to determine them based on geometry. See Opening a Protein Data Bank (PDB) file for further information.

The Protein Data Bank file format is a standard means of information exchange in macromolecular structure determination and is widely recognized by molecular modeling software

PDB files store Cartesian coordinates and element types of atoms
together with bonding connectivity and crystal unit cell parameters where appropriate.

PDB files consist of 80-character records, each with a left-justified keyword of up to six characters that indicates its record format type. The minimum requirement is that one ATOM or HETATM record is present. Of the many PDB record types in the complete specification, the most important read into Discovery Studio include:

* ATOM - atom, residue and chain information for amino and nucleic acids

* HETATM - atom, residue and chain information for nonstandard residues

* TER - marks the end of a chain

* CONECT - specifies connectivity for nonstandard groups

* CRYST1 - contains crystallographic information

* MODEL, ENDMDL - marks the start and end of models

These are sufficient to define the structure including correct chain breaks, and the unit cell for crystallographic structures or multiple models e.g. conformations determined by NMR. Other record types are also read if available to extract various useful information and for reporting. These include:

* REMARK - these contain information such as resolution, pH and biomolecule generation instructions

* SEQRES - used to determine missing residues in a sequence

* HELIX/SHEET/TURN - secondary structure definitions

* SITE - used to create the Active Site groups

* SSBOND - used to create the Disulfide Residues group

* CISPEP - used to create the Cis-peptide Residues group

* HEADER,TITLE,COMPND,SOURCE,KEYWDS,EXPDTA - displayed in the Protein Report

* MTRIXn - defines any non-crystallographic symmetry transformations

* SCALEn - orthogonal to fractional transformation matrix for nonstandard settings

Discovery Studio can also export structural data, both periodic
and non-periodic, in the .pdb format.

Further information on the .pdb file format can be found at www.wwpdb.org .

Protein Data Bank files with the .pdb1 extension contain Biological Assemblies. These can be useful in cases where the biologically relevant entity is not identical to the crystallographic asymmetric unit. Further information can be found at pdb101.rcsb.org .

### Preferences

For import preferences, see Import PDB subpage - Preferences dialog .

# Forcefield Markup Language (FFML)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_ffml.htm

## Forcefield Markup Language (FFML)

FFML files contain customized parameters for certain forcefields. Bond,
angle, torsion, and non-bonded parameters can be included. .ffml files can
be created by saving from the Forcefield Window, and can be used to type
molecules using the Browse option of the Forcefield selector from the Change Forcefield tools . Generally, you do not need to save or load ffml
files, as edits to the Forcefield window are applied to the current
molecule. However occasionally you may want to define some parameters for
one molecule and apply them to another, in which case you can store them
as a .ffml file and reuse them in the Simulate Structures tools.

For example, a bond between CT2 and NH2 atoms is:

```text
<bond atom1="CT2" atom2="NH2">
<quadratic
refValue="?"
forceConstant="?"/>
</bond>
```

Replace the unknown values ? with suitable values
for the force constant (forceConstant field, kcal/mol/Å) field and the equilibrium bond
length (refValue field, Å).

Similarly, an angle parameter for the angle CC-CT2-NH2 is listed as:

```text
<angle atom1="CC" atom2="CT2" atom3="NH2">
<quadratic
refValue="?"
forceConstant="?"/>
</angle>
```

Equilibrium bond angle (refValue field, degrees), force constant (forceConstant field, kcal/mol/degree)

A torsion parameter has more fields to complete (e.g., for the dihedral CC-CT2-NH2-H):

```text
<torsion atom1="CC" atom2="CT2" atom3="NH2" atom4="H">
<multiplecos
v1="?"
v2="?"
v3="?"
v4="?"
v5="?"
v6="?"
gamma1="?"
gamma2="?"
gamma3="?"
gamma4="?"
gamma5="?"
gamma6="?"/>
</torsion>
```

You can supply values for the fields v1 through v6 (kcal/mol), and the fields gamma1 through gamma6 (degrees), which describe
the torsional barrier height and the phase for each of the periodic term,
respectively. The energy is calculated as the sum over v1-v6 of v(n)×(1+cos(n×theta-gamma(n))).

A nonbonded parameter is specified as:

```text
<nonbond atom="h236">
<distanceDependent
minDistance="1.1"
minDistance14="1.1"
minEnergy="-0.05"
minEnergy14="-0.05"/>
</nonbond>
```

minDistance (Å) and minEnergy (kcal/mol) are used
to define the well depth in the 6-12 potential for non-bonded atom
pairs. minDistance14 and minEnergy14 are used the same way for 1-4
connected pairs.

### Import/Export

.ffml files can be imported into and exported from Discovery Studio .
When a .psf file is read, a companion .ffml file in the same folder will be read automatically.

#### Further information

Work with forcefields Change Forcefield tools Forcefield page - Preferences dialog

# Insight II Grid (GRD)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_grd.htm

## Insight II Grid (GRD)

Files with a .grd extension are Insight II Grid files that express 3D volumetric data such as energy grids.

The first line in a formatted file is a title or comment containing any combination of characters. All lines in a .grd file must not exceed 132 characters.

The standard grid file consists of five lines of parameters which precede the actual data. The first line is the title as described above. The second line is a format specifier (in FORTRAN style), enclosed in parentheses. This line must begin in column 1, and specify the number of values on a line in the file as well as the format of those values. An implicit single field causes errors. A single field must include the number 1. For example, (1F10.6).

The third line specifies the unit cell parameters associated with the grid: the cell lengths a, b, and c followed by the cell angles alpha, beta, and gamma. These six values must be floating-point numbers, separated by spaces (no commas). If the grid is not in the context of the molecule's unit cell, a, b, and c may be thought of as the distance the grid spans in each direction, x, y, and z. For example, if the grid spans the space from -20 to +10 in x, then a is entered as 30.0. Alpha, beta, and gamma are entered as 90.0 90.0 90.0.

The fourth line specifies the number of x, y, and z intervals which are actually contained in the file. Note that the width of an interval in x must be equal to the width of an interval in y, which must also be equal to the width of an interval in z; the grid is comprised of cubes. The fourth line also contains an optional set of three integers that describe which directions to contour if two-dimensional contouring is desired. By default, all directions are used. All numbers must be integers separated by spaces (no commas). The contour directions should be either 0 or 1, with 0 meaning no contour in this direction and non-zero (i.e., 1) meaning contour in this direction. The directions are x, then y, then z.

The final parameter line specifies which value, x or y, varies fastest in the file, and the starting and ending intervals in x, y, and z. The first number on the line is entered as a 1 or 3. The digit 1 specifies x is the fastest-varying coordinate. The digit 3 specifies y is the fastest varying coordinate. The next six numbers are entered in the order: x start, x end, y start, y end, z start, z end. The six numbers must be integer numbers, separated by spaces (no commas). Note that lines 3 through 5 are required to uniquely locate the starting and ending coordinates of the grid. The following expressions are used to calculate the starting and ending coordinates of the grid:

Similar computations are done for y and z.

### Example

```text
COMPLETE MINI MAP
(17I5) 
20.00000 1.25 1.25 90.00000 90.00000 90.00000 
16 1 1 
1 -8 8 -1 0 0 1
-6 14 0 -24 -31 -45 -48 -16 39 102 102 18 -38 -39 -42 -43 -44
-31 -21 -56 -50 -30 17 103 106 107 2 -37 -32 -29 -29 -27 -32 -36
-54 -54 20 95 90 74 62 11 -25 -25 -39 -50 -32 -19 -44 -51 -55
-56 -2 81 110 54 -25 -47 -41 -28 -33 -24 -16 -51 -42 108 215 230
```

This example specifies that there are 16 intervals in the x direction, 1 interval in the y direction, and 1 interval in the z direction contained in the file. The 16 x intervals span the coordinates -10.0 to 10.0, as calculated from:

20.0 * (-8/(8 - -8))

and:

20.0 * ((-8 + 16)/(8 - -8))

The interval in the y direction spans the coordinates -1.25 to 0.0, as calculated from:

1.25 * (-1/(0 - -1))

1.25 * ((-1 + 1)/(0 - -1))

The interval in the z direction spans the coordinates 0.0 to 1.25, as calculated from:

1.25 * (0/(1 - 0))

1.25 * ((0 + 1)/(1 - 0))

Note that the file contains 68 grid points, since there are 2 z planes, each having 2 y values and 17 x values:

2 * 2 * 17 = 68

### Import/Export

GRD files can be imported into Discovery Studio .

# BIOVIA MOL/SD (SD, SDF, MOL, MDL)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_mdl-mol-sd-sdf.htm

## BIOVIA MOL/SD (SD, SDF, MOL, MDL)

Files with a .mdl , .mol , .sd , or .sdf extension are BIOVIA MOL/SD files. BIOVIA MOL/SD files in V2000 format do not contain a definition for periodicity, protein, or nucleic acid residues, and are best suited for small molecules. The atom limit for these files is 999 for each individual molecular structure. BIOVIA MOL/SD files in V3000 format, however, do support the definition of protein or DNA residues, and allows to represent macromolecules with more than 999 atoms. The .sd file format supports multiple molecules and contains a separate section for each molecule. Each individual section can be in either V2000 or V3000 format.

### Import/Export

MDL, MOL, SD, and SDF files can be imported into and exported from Discovery Studio .

The following provides a brief summary of the main features of the two formats to represent individual molecules and the general structure of the SD and SDF file format to represent collections of molecules and their attributes.

#### The V2000 format

The molecular representation in V2000 format consists of a header block and a connection table. The header block contains four separate lines. The first line of the header block specifies the molecule name. The last line of the header block includes atom and bond counts, and the version information.

#### The V3000 format

The molecular representation in V3000 format also consists of a header block and a connection table. The header block has the same form as in the V2000 format, but the atom and bond counts are ignored. The specification of atoms and bonds no longer requires fixed field width, which allows it to exceed the atom limit imposed by the V2000 format.

Discovery Studio utilizes a subset of the information contained in the V3000 format connection table. In particular, this subset consists of the list of atoms and bonds, the definitions of 3D objects for a three-dimensional structure, and the definition of templates employed by the self-contained sequence representation (SCSR).

The self-contained sequence representation reduces the overall size of the molecular representation by defining the atoms and bonds in repeating groups of atoms such as proteins or nucleic acid residues only once, and by referring to these groups of atoms and bonds using one record per residue in the atom list, while the bond list is reduced to contain only bonds that link different residues.

#### SD and SDF files

SD and SDF files allow to store multiple molecules as well as molecular attributes. Each molecule is stored in V2000 or V3000 format.

The molecular attributes follow after the header block and connection table of the corresponding molecule. For each attribute, a single line contains the attribute name followed by one or more lines containing the attribute value. Each attribute specification is followed by a blank line.

Some molecular attributes in SD and SDF files may cause conflicts with molecular attributes used by Discovery Studio . Specifically, the SD and SDF file molecular attribute ID will not be preserved unless it is an integer value in the range from -2147483648 to 2147483647. The following property values are ignored: Number of Atoms , Molecular Formula , Molecular Composition , Molecular Weight , Net Partial Charge , and Net Formal Charge .

Each molecule section ends with a "$$$$" delimiter line.

#### Further reading

* Self-contained sequence representation: [Chen et al., 2011]

#### Further information

A detailed description of the V2000 and V3000 file formats is available on the BIOVIA web site. See https://discover.3ds.com/ctfile-documentation-request-form .

Working with files

## Cerius 2 Format (MSI)

Files with a .msi extension are Cerius 2 format files.

The .msi file extension may not be associated with Discovery Studio automatically. This is because of conflicts with
Microsoft Installer. As a result, .msi files may be
represented by Microsoft Installer icons in the Windows Explorer
and it may be necessary to right-click on a .msi file
and use the Open with... option on the
shortcut menu to open it using Discovery Studio .

The .msi file is the key file format used by the BIOVIA program Cerius 2 to save and retrieve structural
data and can represent a wide range of atomistic data
including:

* Atoms

* Bonds

* Polymers

* Organometallics

* Surfaces

* Crystals

* Symmetry

* Isosurfaces

* Morphologies

Discovery Studio only supports .msi files generated by
Cerius 2 2.0 and above.

This version of Discovery Studio will faithfully import and
export most information from version 2.0 .msi files
and they should be used as the primary means of communicating
atomistic data between Discovery Studio and Cerius 2 .

Data which is not transferred includes:

* Display styles and colors

* Element attributes such as color, radii, and mass

* Cerius 2 mixture atom compositions

The .msi file has a complex format but can be
viewed in text editors.

### Import/Export

MSI files can be imported into Discovery Studio .
