# POV-Ray (POV)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_pov.htm

## POV-Ray (POV)

The POV-Ray file format is used to specify the scene to be rendered by the Persistence of Vision Raytracer or POV-Ray program. The POV-Ray program
has to be downloaded from the POV-Ray web site: http://www.povray.org/ . The installed
program includes reference documentation and tutorials.

The file generated by the application starts with setting the viewing transformation, lighting, and background color, and then iterates over
all items displayed in the Molecule Window and generates the corresponding POV-Ray statements.

The viewing transformation is captured in the POV-Ray camera definition, which describes the position, projection type, and properties of the camera
viewing the scene.

Light sources are defined in the POV-Ray light_source definition, and the background color is specified in the POV-Ray background definition.

The items in the Molecule Window are displayed by creating lists of display elements such as lines, spheres, cylinders, cones, etc. These lists are saved
to the POV-Ray scene file, converting the item types used in the Molecule Window to item types recognized by the POV-Ray file format. For example, lines are
converted to spheres connected by cylinders since POV-Ray has no direct equivalent of lines.

POV-Ray uses a default
aspect ratio of 4:3 (width:height). For best results and to prevent
clipped images, make the 3D window approximately 4:3 when saving a POV-Ray file.

### Import/Export

POV files can be exported from Discovery Studio . For details, see Saving a file .

# CHARMm Structure (PSF)

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/supported_files_psf.htm

## CHARMm Structure (PSF)

Files with a .psf extension are CHARMm structure files. 
These are used in conjunction with CHARMm .crd files or .pdb files to represent molecular systems.

### Import/Export

PSF files can be imported into and exported from Discovery Studio .

When a PSF file is read, a companion .crd or .pdb file (in that order)
in the same folder is needed.
Forcefield information is taken from the PSF file.
The forcefield name should be present in the title lines of the PSF file.
If the forcefield name is not specified, the forcefield name is assumed to be CHARMm.
If a companion FFML file is present, it will also be read.
Connectivity information is taken from the PSF file as well instead of deriving it from the interatomic distances.

In most cases, PSF files created by Discovery Studio should already contain the forcefield information. For a PSF file 
created by another application, you can open the PSF file in a text editor and add a line such as "* GENERATED BY CHARMM USING 
CHARMM36 FORCEFIELD" in the header section (only the forcefield name will be scanned).

#### Further information

Working with files

The format is as follows:

```text
Number of Atoms
Title
AtomSymbol1 X1 Y1 Z1
AtomSymbol2 X2 Y2 Z2
...
AtomSymbolN Xn Yn Zn
```

# Temporary File Storage

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/temporary_file_storage.htm

## Temporary File Storage

The Discovery Studio Client stores temporary files in a temporary folder.

The location of the temporary folder can be specified in the General page - Preferences dialog .

* Temporary files are deleted at the end of a Discovery Studio Client session.

* Be sure to provide ample temporary storage capacity, especially when working with large or a large number of molecular models.

The default location is determined as the first path specified from the following list:

* The path specified by the TMP environment variable.

* The path specified by the TEMP environment variable.

* The path specified by the USERPROFILE environment variable.

* The Windows directory path.

For example, the user environment variable TMP may be set to %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Temp (this is equivalent to the default) where %USERPROFILE% is the value of the USERPROFILE environment variable.

### Implementation Details

In order to make it easier to identify temporary files created by Discovery Studio , temporary files are actually stored in a subfolder of the temporary folder. The location of the subfolder depends on whether a file is intended to be shared between consecutive client sessions or will be used only during a single client session.

For files to be shared between sessions, the location is given by [TMP]/ Discovery Studio _[USERNAME]/[VERSION]/Persistent/Cache .

For files not to be shared between sessions, the location is given by [TMP]/ Discovery Studio _[USERNAME]/[VERSION]/Transient/[HOSTNAME]/[PROCESS ID] .

Where:

* [TMP] is the location of the temporary folder as specified in General page - Preferences dialog

* [USERNAME] is the name of the user who launched the Discovery Studio client

* [VERSION] identifies the client version

* [HOSTNAME] is the name of the computer on which the Discovery Studio client is running

* [PROCESS ID] identifies the Discovery Studio client process.

An example of a file which is shared between client sessions is the PluginDescriptors.xml file which aggregates information about the Discovery Studio client user interface in order to accelerate the client startup.

#### Further information

General page - Preferences dialog

# Analyzing results with the Data Table View

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_analyzing-results-data-table.htm

## Analyzing results with the Data Table View

This discusses how the Data Table View can be used to efficiently perform common tasks such as:

* Viewing molecules

* Sorting molecules

* Filtering molecules

Many protocols generate structures that can be viewed in the context of another structure such as a receptor, an x-ray conformation, or a pharmacophore. When there are multiple molecules, it is useful to be able to view each separately. You can easily step through the different molecules using the Data Table View:

* Open the results from the View Results script generated by the protocol.

* If the Data Table View is not visible, press CTRL+T.

* In the Data Table View, set the Visible and Visibility Locked columns of the reference structure (e.g., receptor) to Yes .

* Use the navigation keys on the left side of the window to individually toggle the visibility of each molecule. This will toggle the visibility of any molecule for which the visibility has not been locked.

You can reduce the number of molecules to step through by tagging them and hiding the remaining molecules:

* Set the value in the Tagged column to Yes for the desired molecules, or use the Tag Selection icon on the left side of the window.

* Right-click in the Data Table View and choose List Only Tagged Molecules . Only the tagged molecules will be visible in the Data Table View. Now, when stepping through the molecules, non-tagged molecules are not displayed.

The initial order of the molecules in the Data Table View is determined by the input file or by the order in which they were added. You can easily adjust the order to suit your needs using the Sort dialog . Right-click and choose Sort... to open the dialog. You can choose to sort by a specific property, or perform more complex sorting with additional constraints. For example, to sort the Data Table View by molecular weight, set the Sort by field to Molecular Weight . The molecules will be sorted in the Data Table View showing the lightest molecules first.

You can perform a simple sort by double-clicking a column header.

Frequently, the number molecules can be quite large and it is helpful to work with a filtered subset:

* Right-click and choose Filter... to open the Filter dialog .

* Set the Choice and Value cells for one or more Column Names (properties).

* Click OK . Note that you can remove the filter by right-clicking and choosing Remove Filters .

For example, if only the 10 best scoring ligands are required, select the desired scoring function property (e.g., -PLP1) and chose Top(#) from the Choice and set the Value to 10.

If you want the best scoring pose for each ligand, you must enable grouping.
Set Top to 1, and check Apply filter to each group of identical values . This ensures that only the best scoring pose for each ligand is visible. Note that another property must be specified that uniquely identifies each ligand group (e.g., Name).

To filter a very large data set, consider using the General Purpose protocol Filter by Property as an alternative.

#### Further information

Working with the Molecule Window Sort dialog Filter dialog

# Change the orientation of an acceptor feature

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_change-orientation-acceptor-feature.htm

## Change the orientation of an acceptor feature

When an acceptor feature has been created, using the Create feature dialog , its 
orientation can be changed by altering the Orientation property on the Acceptor Feature tab of 
the Data Table.

To change the orientation of an acceptor feature

* Use the View | Data Table command to open the Data Table View.

* Select the Acceptor Feature tab.

* Change the Orientation property to Free .

* Edit the X , Y , and Z properties in the Data Table , on the Attributes dialog , or by selecting the point
feature and using the mouse to drag it across the Graphics View to change the orientation of the acceptor feature.

The orientation of the acceptor feature is defined by the position of the point
feature representing the head of the acceptor feature
relative to the position of the point feature representing the tail of the donor feature.

The distance between the head and tail point features is unchanged.

### Access methods

| Data Table | AcceptorFeature \| Orientation then X, Y and Z properties |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Change the orientation of the donor feature Change the orientation of the ring feature

# Change the orientation of a ring aromatic feature

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_change-orientation-ring-feature.htm

## Change the orientation of a ring aromatic feature

When an aromatic ring feature has been created, using the Create feature dialog , its 
orientation can be changed by altering the Normal Point Placement property on the RingAromaticFeature tab of 
the Data Table.

To change the orientation of a ring aromatic feature

* Choose the View | Data Table command to open the Data Table viewer.

* Select the RingAromaticFeature tab.

* Change the Normal Point Placement property from Above to Below or from Below to Above .

Other orientations are not possible, as the orientation of the feature is constrained to be perpendicular to the 
plane of the aromatic ring.

| | Root | Roots the tree on the selected node. This button is disabled if no node is selected or if the Dendrogram has been reconstructed using the UPGMA method, which determines a root as part of its algorithm. |
| | Midpoint Root | Applies the midpoint rooting method to root the tree. This button is disabled if the Dendrogram has been reconstructed using the UPGMA method, which determines a root as part of its algorithm. |

# Run a GPU calculation

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_gpucalculation.htm

## Run a GPU calculation

### Background

Graphics processing units (GPUs) in video cards were originally designed to render images, animations, and videos for computer screens. Since GPUs perform parallel operations on multiple data sets highly efficiently, they are suitable for many scientific calculations. Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), a high-level application programming interface developed by NVIDIA , made it feasible to develop GPU-based scientific calculations using C/C++. Since the introduction of CUDA, GPU computing has proven cost effective and has been widely adopted by the scientific community. Recently, Open Computing Language (OpenCL) has enabled cross-platform GPU acceleration. Molecular dynamics simulations of biomolecular systems are computationally intensive and many simulation packages take advantage of GPU computational resources.

### CHARMm OpenMM GPU

CHARMm supports GPU computing through the CHARMm/OpenMM interface or native DOMDEC kernels. In the current release, the Dynamics (Production) protocol can run CHARMm GPU through OpenMM [Eastman et al., 2017] .

The GPU option for the Dynamics (Production) protocol is only available on Linux.

CHARMm/OpenMM can run through CUDA (NVIDIA GPU cards) or OpenCL (non-NVIDIA GPU cards). OpenMM GPU computing has different precision models: single, double, and mixed. In single precision mode, nearly all calculations are done in single precision. This is the fastest option but will have the biggest fluctuation during the dynamics simulation. The Dynamics (Production) protocol is set to use mixed precision where forces are computed in single precision but integration is performed in double precision. The mixed precision model gives much better energy conservation with only a slight decrease (~10%) in speed.

GPU computing is highly efficient compared to its CPU counterpart. For example, the production dynamics of a typical solvated antibody Fab domain with approximately 35,000 atoms is about 30 times faster on a single GPU card in mixed precision mode compared to an 8 core CPU calculation running CHARMm MPI (the calculations used the default cutoff parameters defined in the Dynamics (Production) protocol).

OpenMM will only support CHARMm and CHARMm Polar H forcefields as well as charmm academic forcefields: charmm19, charmm22, charmm27, and charmm36.

#### Further information

Installing Discovery Studio Installing and configuring a cluster Distributed grid computing

# Add sites to the Open URL dialog

## Add sites to the Open URL dialog

The URL Location subpage of the preferences dialog allows you to configure your own locations to use when opening a URL from the Open URL dialog. These can be remote sites specified using https, or local and shared disks using the file protocol.
For example, you might have an RCSB database mirror consisting of compressed mmCIF files divided into subfolders under a folder called RCSB_Mirror on a shared disk or your own machine.

An RCSB mirror directory can be created and updated using an rsync command e.g. /usr/bin/rsync -rlpt -v -z --delete --port=33444 rsync.wwpdb.org::ftp_data/structures/divided/mmCIF/ MIRRORDIR > LOGFILE 2>ERRORFILE where MIRRORDIR is the path for the local mirror directory, LOGFILE is the path of a log file and ERRORFILE is the path for any errors.

To define this as a URL source, perform the following steps:

* Choose Edit | Preferences | Files Explorer | URL Location from the menu bar.

* Click Add to create a new row.

* In the Site Name field of the new row, add a descriptive name: "Local RCSB Mirror"
.

* For the URL Template , use the file: protocol and a path to the RCSB mirror folder: "file://<hostname>/<path>/RCSB_Mirror/$/@.cif", where <hostname> is the name of the server hosting the shared folder and <path> is the path to the mirror folder. The $ sign will be substituted with the second and third characters of the ID, and the @ sign will be substituted with the full ID. For a mirror on your local machine the template would be "file:///<path>/RCSB_Mirror/$/@.cif".

* Click OK to apply the changes and close the dialog.

* Choose File | Open URL... from the menu bar.

* Click the Site list and choose Local RCSB Mirror .

* Type in a 4 letter PDB code.

* Verify the URL is correct and click Open .

# Deploying script commands and custom tool panels

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_protocols_deploy-customization.htm

## Deploying script commands and custom tool panels

A valuable capability of Discovery Studio is the ability to create custom commands and custom tool panels .

Although it is relatively easy for individual users to import and export customized commands and tool panels , you may want to set up an easy system for deploying customizations efficiently to a group of users, which avoids errors and synchronization issues that might occur if individual users are required to import them on their own.

You can accomplish this by creating a protocol that installs .script and .panel files to individual clients, and then creating a custom tool that can launch the protocol from each client. Then, whenever a new customization is available, you only need to modify the protocol and then ask the users to run the tool, which will install it.

Discovery Studio provides a template protocol in the Examples folder that installs a .panel file. You can also customize it to install .script files. You will need to access Pipeline Pilot to copy it and modify it to suit your needs. For more information about Pipeline Pilot and customizing protocols, see About Pipeline Pilot and Customizing protocols .

To set up a customization protocol to run from a button on a tool panel

* Launch the Pipeline Pilot Client .

* From the Protocols tab, open BIOVIA Discovery Studio | Examples | Utilities | Customize Discovery Studio Template .
This protocol contains an example that writes a script and a .panel file that will
install a Tool Panel called Customize Structure Appearance.

* Select the Write Tool Panel file component and update the Tool Panel Definition parameter to contain the contents
of your .panel file.

* If you have more .panel and/or script files you want to deploy,
create corresponding copies of the Write Tool Panel File and Write Load Script components.
Be sure to change the values of the Destination and
the Tool Panel Definition parameters
of the Write Tool Panel File component
for each .panel file, and to change the values of
the Destination and the DSScript parameters of the Write Load Script component
for each script file.

* Save the protocol in the same folder and name it
"Customize Discovery Studio ".

* Open each client you want to deploy the customization to, and perform the following: Check you are connected to the server where you just saved the protocol. Open the Tools Explorer, then right-click it and choose Import... . Open Samples | Customization | ImportCustomizations.panel . Click OK . Click the Run Protocol button, then click Run (there are no parameters to set for this protocol).
The protocol will run and add import the script and .panel files to the client.

* Check you are connected to the server where you just saved the protocol.

* Open the Tools Explorer, then right-click it and choose Import... .

* Open Samples | Customization | ImportCustomizations.panel .

* Click OK .

* Click the Run Protocol button, then click Run (there are no parameters to set for this protocol).
The protocol will run and add import the script and .panel files to the client.

# Calculate molecular weight

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_structure_calculate-molecular-weight.htm

## Calculate molecular weight

The molecular weight of any molecule opened in the Molecule Window is automatically calculated and displayed
in the Data Table view. To view the value of the molecular weight:

* If the Data Table is not visible select View | Data Table or press
CTRL+T.

* Choose the Molecule tab of the Data Table. Use the horizontal scroll
bar to move to the Molecular Weight and Exact Mol. Weight columns.

The molecular weight and exact molecular weight for each molecule in the window is reported in Dalton units.
1 Dalton is defined as one twelfth of the mass of the 12 C isotope of Carbon.

### How are the molecular weights calculated?

The molecular weight is calculated by summing the average isotopic weights of every atom in the molecule.
The exact molecular weight is calculated by summing the isotopic weights of the most frequent isotope of every atom in
the molecule.

# Calculate the RMSD between conformations

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_structure_calculate-rmsd-between-conformations.htm

## Calculate the RMSD between conformations

You can calculate the symmetry minimized root mean squared deviation
(RMSD) between small molecule poses using the RMSD tools in the Structure menu.
However, the Analyze Trajectory protocol allows for a wider set of options,
including the ability to remove rotation and translation differences by
fitting the poses before calculating the RMSD.

* Ensure you have a single molecule with a set of conformations (see Convert a set
of identical molecules into a set of conformations ).

* From the Protocols Explorer, expand the Simulation folder and open 
the Analyze Trajectory protocol.

* Ensure the Input Molecule parameter is set to the correct molecule 
containing the conformations.

* Ensure the Analysis Type parameter is set to include the RMSD option and does not include any of the other options.

* Set the RMSD Reference parameter to All Frames . 
This option allows you to calculate a matrix of RMSD values and perform clustering
(if you have 3 or more conformations).

* Expand the RMSD Reference parameter group. The default values will calculate the RMSD using all atoms of the molecule. To act on heavy atoms only, from the menu bar,
choose Edit | Select... to open the Select dialog.
Choose Add from the Selection Mode dropdown menu.
Choose Atom from the Scope dropdown menu.
Click the Property radio button.
Choose Element , does not equal and Hydrogen from the dropdown menus to select all non-hydrogen atoms.
Click Apply , and then click Close .

The default values will calculate the RMSD using all atoms of the molecule.

To act on heavy atoms only, from the menu bar,
choose Edit | Select... to open the Select dialog.
Choose Add from the Selection Mode dropdown menu.
Choose Atom from the Scope dropdown menu.
Click the Property radio button.
Choose Element , does not equal and Hydrogen from the dropdown menus to select all non-hydrogen atoms.
Click Apply , and then click Close .

* Set Atom Group to Create New Group from Selection... . 
The RMSD calculation will be performed only on the selected (heavy) atoms.

* Note that the default values here will calculate the RMSD of 
the molecule without first aligning it. This is often termed the "Pose RMSD". 
To eliminate translational and rotational differences, you can set Atom Group to Fit to align the poses before calculating the RMSD. 

Choose the Group to choose the same set of atoms as the Atom Group . 
This ensures the minimum RMSD possible between two poses, also known as the "Conformation 
RMSD". Note that with this protocol, it is possible to align 
on one set of atoms and calculate the RMSD of another set.

* Run the protocol. When it has completed, open the report.

* In the Output Files section, there is an HTML file showing a table of the 
RMSD values. There is also a Perl file which runs a script to set up a 
dendrogram view of the results for clustering (if you have more than 2 
conformations). See Analyze Trajectory for more details.

# Calculate solvent accessibility

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_structure_calculate-solvent-accessibility.htm

## Calculate solvent accessibility

* Solvent accessibility is calculated by representing each atom as a 
collection of grid points distributed over a sphere whose radius is the 
sum of the atom's van der Waals radius and of a probe radius.
A grid point which is buried inside another atomic sphere 
contributes to the buried surface area.
A grid point which is not buried inside another atomic sphere 
contributes to the exposed surface area.

* The calculation is performed for all/selected amino acids in the 
context of all/selected atoms excluding solvent.

### How to calculate solvent accessibility

* Open the protein structure in a Molecule Window.

* Select Structure | Solvent Accessibility to open
the Solvent Accessibility dialog.

* Make changes as needed. If you wish to visualize the exposed and/or buried residues, check the Colored checkboxes to specify the color of the exposed and/or buried residues and their atoms.

The per-residue accessibility ( Residue Solvent Accessibility ), the per-residue accessibility restricted to side-chain atoms
( Sidechain Solvent Accessibility ), and the relative per-residue accessibility compared to the accessibility of only the residue
and the C, CA and N atoms of the previous and next residues ( Percent Solvent Accessibility ) are shown in the AminoAcid tab.

# Construction of molecular surfaces

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/tsk_structure_construction-molecular-surfaces.htm

## Construction of molecular surfaces

* Molecular surfaces are constructed by using a marching cubes algorithm creating an isosurface of a function which approximates the 
shape of a van der Waals surface, a soft surface, or of a solvent surface.

* The van der Waals surface is a surface enclosing the volume made up from the union of atom-centered spheres. The radius of a 
sphere is given by the van der Waals radius of the atom it is centered on.

* The soft surface is obtained as the isosurface f(r) = 0.6 where f(r) is defined as f(r) = sum(i) 
s i (1 - d i 2 /R i 2 ) 2 .
d i is the distance |r - r i | between point r and the position r i of atom i.
R i = 2.2*R(VDW) i is the scaled van der Waals radius R(VDW) of atom i.
s i is a scale factor which depends on the number of visible attachments N of atom i: s i = 1 if N ≤ 1, s i = 0.7 if N = 2, s i = 0.4 if N = 3, and s i = 0.2 if N > 4.
The sum over atoms i only includes atoms i for which d i < R i .

* The solvent surface is a surface enclosing the solvent excluded volume. It is the volume which can not be accessed by 
solvent modeled as a spherical probe. The default probe radius is 1.4 Å.

#### Further information

Tasks Structures

Some protocols and tools work with a generic set of molecules and some work

This is usually the case with automatically generated systems, but 
may not be the case if the molecules come from different sources
or were sketched manually.

* From the menu bar, choose File | Save As and save the contents of the Molecule Window as a .dsv file.

* Select all molecules except the first one. From the menu bar, choose Edit | Select All , 
and then hold the CTRL key and click the first molecule in the Hierarchy View to de-select it.

* Press the DELETE key.

* From the menu bar, select Structure | Animation | Load . Select the file you just
exported and click Open . This will check that the molecules are 
identical and insert the molecules in the file as conformations 
of the molecule in the Molecule Window.

* You started with the first conformation before loading 
all conformations, so there are two copies of the first conformation. 
In the Hierarchy View, select the second conformation in the list 
(this should be identical to the first). Delete it by pressing the DELETE key.

the selected molecule with respect to the non-selected molecule.

Switch to the Rotate tool.
In Track Surface mode, hold the SHIFT key while dragging with
the left mouse button.
In Track Ball mode, hold the SHIFT key while dragging outside the
green circle with the left mouse button. 
Again you can hold the CTRL key to only act on the selection.

* By using combinations of rotations and translations of the selection you 
can manipulate the selected molecule so that it is aligned to the 
other molecule.

# Working with sequence data

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/using_sequences.htm

## Working with sequence data

Two of the major classes of biological macromolecules are nucleic acids and 
proteins. These polymers are chains of well-defined monomeric subunits. In 
nucleic acids, the monomers are nucleotides. In proteins, the monomers are 
amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these subunits encodes critical 
information about their physical properties. The term "molecular sequence data" 
is commonly used to refer to this type of information.

Molecular sequence data is widely used in Life Sciences to study the basic 
biology of many types of systems. Sequence data has traditionally provided 
insights into the structural and functional characteristics of genes and 
proteins. More recently, it has been increasingly important in helping to 
understand genomic biology and gene and cell regulation. It also provides a 
starting point for engineering new variants of macromolecules that can 
subsequently be applied in diverse areas such as protein engineering and gene 
expression analysis.

In the Discovery Studio , three types of windows enable 
you to work with sequence data:

* Sequence Window - for working with primary sequence data and sequence alignments

* Sequence Annotation Window - for working with sequence annotation

* Sequence List Window - for 
working with lists or collections of non-homologous sequences

### Introduction to sequence data

In addition to the sequence windows, the application also provides functionality for
basic manipulation of sequence data. The Sequence Menu provides access to these commands. This section provides an overview of the
capabilities for working with sequence data in the Discovery Studio .

Sequences are represented using strings of letters that correspond with the primary 
structure of either nucleic acid or protein molecules. The two types of 
sequences are encoded using symbols that correspond with the standard molecular 
subunits of the different molecules. Nucleotide sequences have four standard 
subunit types: A,C,G,T (T in DNA being replaced by U in RNA). Protein sequences 
have 20 standard subunit types: A,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,K,L,M,N,P,Q,R,S,T,V,W,Y,Z. 
Nonstandard residues, for example selenocysteine, are usually represented 
using an ambiguity code (N in nucleotide sequences, X in protein sequences) or 
by using the code for an equivalent analog of a standard residue (e.g., cysteine 
for selenocysteine). The Discovery Studio uses the standard IUPAC codes for 
representing amino acids and nucleic acids .

Nucleotide sequences are routinely obtained by sequencing DNA or RNA directly. A 
variety of sequencing methodologies are in use for determining nucleotide 
sequences, most notably the Sanger dideoxy method. Protein sequences can also 
be determined directly from proteins using methods such as mass spectrometry 
and Edman degradation. However, protein sequences are more commonly inferred 
from the translation products of the nucleotide sequences of their 
corresponding genes.

### Types of sequence data

Although sequence data can be treated as strings of characters, other forms of
content, such as alignment data and annotation, are equally informative. In this
respect, sequence information in the Discovery Studio is commonly exposed at three
different levels: Primary Sequence Data, Sequence Alignment Data, and Sequence Annotation.

#### Primary sequence data

The fundamental information content in sequences is derived from the sequence of 
subunits. Primary sequence data is most commonly edited as an initial stage of 
curation after the raw data has been experimentally determined. Common reasons 
for editing primary sequence data are that during sequencing or translation 
individual residues may have been misinterpreted or multiple fragments of a 
sequence need to be merged. Alternatively, when engineering a sequence, it may 
be necessary to modify the primary sequence data directly.

Once the raw sequence has been accurately captured, a further stage of analysis 
is often basic characterization of the sequences to look at compositional and 
physicochemical properties. The latter is of particular interest in protein 
sequences where such properties may give clues about structure and function.

The Discovery Studio allows you to edit and visualize basic sequence data in the 
Sequence Window. You can open sequence data from most common file formats 
directly in the application, or you can type or paste 
data into an empty window. An example of the appearance of a sequence 
in the Sequence Window is shown in Figure 1. Once you have imported the 
sequence into a Sequence Window, you can inspect basic properties of the 
sequence by applying different display styles.

Figure 1: Primary sequence data for a protein molecule displayed in the Sequence Window

#### Sequence alignment data

Comparative analysis of different sequences is another method for extracting 
information. Sequences can be compared when they are descended from a common 
ancestral gene and thus contain regions of homology. Identification of 
homologous sequence regions can sometimes be achieved through manual inspection 
and editing of sequences, but is more commonly performed using automated 
methods.

Once an alignment is available, it is useful to be able to apply different 
visualizations to interpret patterns of sequence similarity and function. For 
example, applying particular color schemes to residues with similar 
physicochemical properties, or differentially coloring contrasting levels of 
sequence similarity at particular positions often provides guidance on the high 
level patterns in an alignment.

In the Discovery Studio , you can work with sequence alignments in the Sequence 
Window. The application provides comprehensive support for importing sequences 
from files or other windows in the application. You can manually align sets of sequences
in the Sequence Window or import from pre-aligned alignment 
files. Once created, a rich set of visualization options are available to apply 
to your data.

Figure 2: A protein sequence alignment and corresponding
secondary structure annotation displayed in the Sequence Window

#### Sequence annotation

A third level of sequence information representation is annotation. Both primary 
sequence and alignment analyses enable you to identify structural and 
functional features in sequences that correspond to specific locations in the 
primary sequence data. Features may be single contiguous regions or complex 
non-contiguous regions. Sequences are conveniently represented as textual or 
graphical sequence annotation.

The Sequence Annotation Window provides a rich graphical interface for 
displaying sequence features. In addition, the window provides different views 
that display information about basic compositional properties 
and other auxiliary data that may be contained in a sequence record such as 
literature citations. The Sequence Annotation Window also provides powerful 
capabilities for automatically computing and displaying basic sequence 
annotation.

Figure 3: An annotated nucleotide sequence displayed in the Sequence Annotation Window

#### Further reading

* [Brown, 1999]

* [Lewin, 2007]

* [Mount, 2001]

#### Further information

Sequence Window Sequence Annotation Window Sequence List Window Sequence Menu Supported file formats Amino Acid Symbols Nucleic Acid Symbols Sequence Window page - Preferences dialog Similarity subpage - Preferences dialog

# Working with the 2D Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_2d-view.htm

## Working with the 2D Window

The 2D Window displays high-quality 2D representations 
of molecular structures. You can launch the 2D Window to view a small molecule structure
as follows:

* If you are viewing a single small molecule, or have a single small molecule selected in
the Molecule Window, you can select Structure | Show 2D Structure from the menu bar.

* If you are working with a protein-ligand system in the Molecule Window, open the View Interactions tool
panel and click Show 2D Diagram . The receptor and
ligand are specified at the top of the tool
panel.

* The 2D Window is primarily a viewer, and only limited editing is possible.

* Stepping through ligands (from the View Interactions tool panel or the Data Table) does not update the ligand displayed in a linked 2D Diagram.
However, the 2D Diagram can be regenerated to show the current ligand by pressing the Show 2D Diagram button in the View Interactions tool panel.

Once you have displayed a molecule in the 2D Window, you can perform the following tasks:

* Change the display attributes of various types of objects

* Translate and zoom your view of a structure

* Edit the position of atoms and residues

* Select objects, which also selects them in other open windows

* Change the color of the background or objects in the view

* Print the 2D structure or save it to a graphics file.

### Style Key

The following details the various graphical elements in the 2D Window for a protein-ligand system when displayed using the default colors and styles:

| Display | Description |
| --- | --- |
| | Interactions are shown as dashed lines between receptor residues and ligand atoms. If multiple ligand atoms are involved in an interaction, the line ends at the geometric center of those atoms. Residues involved in interactions are colored by interaction. See Nonbond interactions for information about the interaction colors. Covalently bonded residues are represented by small discs. Neighboring residues are colored green. The solvent accessible surface of an interacting residue is represented by a halo around the residue. The diameter of the circle is proportional to the solvent accessible surface. The solvent accessible surface of an atom is represented by a blue halo around the atom. The diameter of the circle is proportional to the solvent accessible surface. |

When interacting residues are present, a legend of interaction types is displayed in the 2D window.
The visibility of the legend can be changed in the General tab of the display style dialog.

### Context menu

The following options are available by right-clicking in the 2D Window.

Copy: Copy the view to the clipboard for pasting.

Show All: Make all objects in the 2D Window visible.

Flip Vertical: Invert the X-axis coordinates of all visible objects in the 2D Window.

Flip Horizontal: Invert the Y-axis coordinates of all visible objects in the 2D Window.

Display Style...: Open the 2D Window Display Style dialog .

### Access methods

| Menu | Structure \| Show 2D Structure |
| --- | --- |
| Tools Explorer | View \| Tool Panels \| View Interactions \| Show 2D Diagram |

# Graphics View

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_3d-structure-view.htm

## Graphics View

The Graphics View displays graphical representations of 3D models created by, or
imported into the application. These graphical representations help you to understand molecular
structure, communicate chemical information, and produce effective reports and presentations.

It is important that you have a supported graphics card and driver when using the visualizer functionality. For details, see Configure your system and software for working with graphics .

Choose View | Graphics from the menu bar or press CTRL+G to toggle the display of the Graphics View
for a structure shown in the current Hierarchy View or Data Table View .

Many file formats display in the Graphics View when they are opened in a Molecule Window. For files with multiple molecules, the first molecule is typically displayed by default.However, if you insert a file, its contents are
not automatically visible. You can toggle the visibility of molecules from the Data Table View and Hierarchy View.

The Graphics View, Hierarchy View, and Data Table View act in parallel so that changes in one view are reflected in the other data views. For example, when you select objects in the Hierarchy View, the same objects are selected in the Graphics View.

You can use the tools available on the toolbars and the options and commands on the menus to build, edit, rotate, translate, scale , animate, and annotate the 3D graphical models of small molecules, macromolecules, crystals, and pharmacophores.

The most commonly used menu options and commands are also available on the Graphics
View context menu. To access the context menu, right-click in the Graphics view.

The Graphics View provides extensive control over model display type, surface representation, labeling, color scheme, lighting,
and other details of the representation and environment of the molecule. To change the display style, right-click the Graphics View and choose Display Style... to open the Graphics View Display Style dialog .
Note that you can also set the default display settings from the Display Styles subpage - Preferences dialog .

You can save your display settings that you made with the Display Style dialog by saving to the .dsv file format; your changes will not be affected by the preferences when you re-open the file.

# Working with the Molecule Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_3d-window.htm

## Working with the Molecule Window

The Molecule Window is a powerful tool for working with molecular structures and data. This topic covers the following:

* Supported data types

* Structure and property commands

* Opening Data in the Molecule Window

* Toolbars

The Molecule Window allows you to work with two broad categories of molecular data:

* 3D Structures: Molecular 3D structure data that can use to make inferences about 
functionality (e.g., protein structures and ligand-protein binding site complexes).

* Molecular Properties: Data you want to use for computing and analyzing properties (e.g., activity data and molecular descriptors of drug-like molecules).

Discovery Studio enables you to work seamlessly with either or both types of data in the same window,
the Molecule Window.

#### Molecule Window views

The Molecule Window provides different ways of viewing and manipulating molecular data:

* Graphics View : Displays the 3-dimensional structure of molecular objects

* Hierarchy View : Shows the hierarchical relationships between different 
objects (e.g., molecules and chains, cells and molecules)

* Data Table View : Displays molecular properties in a table.

Note that the views in a Molecule Window are linked, so that a selection in one view is reflected in the other open views.

##### View access methods

Multiple views can be open in the Molecule Window simultaneously. You can use the View menu or the following key combinations to display and hide the different views:

| Menu | View \| Graphics, Hierarchy, Data Table |
| --- | --- |
| Context menu | View \| Graphics, Hierarchy, Data Table |
| Keyboard shortcut | CTRL+G, CTRL+H, CTRL+T |
| Molecule Window | Arrow buttons on the sides of the open views |

Discovery Studio provides a wide range of commands for working with 3D structure data and molecular properties. These
commands are accessed through menus , toolbars , and tool panels . Commands are available based on the data displayed in the current view. For example, for commands that analyze structural properties, one or more structures must be displayed in the Molecule Window Graphics View. Similarly, to compute molecular 
properties, data must be accessible in the Data Table View.

Discovery Studio recognizes three broad classes of data that it can open in application:

* .dsv data The Discovery Studio file format, .dsv , which saves application-specific 
data such as layout of the views and objects 
such as surfaces and monitors. When you save data in this format, the data will reopen in the same state as when 
you closed the Molecule Window.

The Discovery Studio file format, .dsv , which saves application-specific 
data such as layout of the views and objects 
such as surfaces and monitors. When you save data in this format, the data will reopen in the same state as when 
you closed the Molecule Window.

* Structural data A number of file formats, such as .pdb , the primarily store structure data. These files open in the Graphics View by default. If the file contains multiple molecules, only the first is displayed initially, but you can control the visibility of other molecules using the Data Table 
and Hierarchy views.

A number of file formats, such as .pdb , the primarily store structure data. These files open in the Graphics View by default. If the file contains multiple molecules, only the first is displayed initially, but you can control the visibility of other molecules using the Data Table 
and Hierarchy views.

* Property data Many file formats contain molecular data that is primarily of interest for properties that can calculated from it (e.g., .sd , .smi , .mol and .mol2 formats). These types of files open in the Data Table View by default.

Many file formats contain molecular data that is primarily of interest for properties that can calculated from it (e.g., .sd , .smi , .mol and .mol2 formats). These types of files open in the Data Table View by default.

#### Working with Data in the Graphics View

When you visualize data in the Graphics view, commands that compute or analyze 3D structural information are 
enabled. The commands affect selected objects or all objects if nothing is 
selected, and have no effect on objects that are not visible.

Although the commands will not affect the objects that are not visible based on settings in the Data Table View and Hierarchy View, there are display style attributes that may cause some objects to be hidden from the view. The commands will affect these objects even though they are not visible.

#### Working with Data in the Hierarchy View

The Hierarchy View is useful for understanding the relationship between different objects in a 3D structure. For example, you may need to understand which chains belong to a particular molecule, or 
which atoms belong to a particular residue. The Hierarchy View enables you to visualize these relationships and in some cases modify them. You can also use this view to select and control the visibility of individual objects or sets of objects.

#### Working with Data in the Table View

If you work primarily with molecular properties, it is convenient to use the Data Table View exclusively. When working with properties it is unnecessary to visualize 3D structures, which reduces memory usage.

When you open a file, any properties stored in it are displayed in the Data Table View, which can be viewed, created, and modified. 
You can also choose to calculate basic molecular properties (e.g., Number of Atoms, Molecular Weight) for the molecule,
or calculate them automatically whenever you open a file. 

Additionally, the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol can
calculate advanced properties ranging from traditional molecular descriptors to user-built QSAR models.

The following features help with large numbers of molecules:

* Tags: You can tag individual molecules using the check boxes provided in the Data Table View. Tags make it easy to quickly retrieve or export a specific set of molecules.

* Lists: The following options allow you to restrict the current set of molecules in the Data Table View: List Only Visible Objects List Only Selected Objects List Only Tagged Molecules

* List Only Visible Objects

* List Only Selected Objects

* List Only Tagged Molecules

* Filters: The Data Table View provides advanced filtering to reduce the current view to a set of 
molecules that meet specific criteria (e.g., only display the top 5% of molecules with a particular score, or only show 
molecules with a specific name). Filtering is important because some calculations are only performed on molecules in the current view, regardless of whether they are selected.

The following toolbars are available for working with the Molecule Window. To view them, select View | Toolbars from the menu bar, and then choose from the following:

* Alignment

* Atom Colors

* Atom Display

* Protein Structure Display

* Nucleic Acid Structure Display

* View

# BLAST Results Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_blast-results-window.htm

## BLAST Results Window

The BLAST Results Window displays the results of the BLAST Search, BLAST Search (NCBI Server), and PSI-BLAST Search protocols. The 
results can be viewed in map, table, and text formats (Map View, Table View, and Text View). Open the <molecule>.xml output file 
to view the results.

#### Map View

Map View shows the coverages of the hits with sequences represented as bars that are color coded according to the bit score. The score color key 
and query sequence are displayed at the top of the map.

Zoom using View | Transform | Zoom In/Zoom Maximum/Zoom Out or the mouse wheel. At 
full size, the ruler displays the individual residue.

Hover over a hit to view the description of the database sequence, the sequence accession ID, the start and end position of the query sequence, 
the start and end of the database sequence of the hit, and the scores of the hit.

Left-click a bar to select it, or left-click and drag to select a group. Hold SHIFT or CTRL and left-click to select additional hits. Hits remain 
selected when you switch views.

When database sequence matches the query 
sequence and has hits in multiple regions, the matches are 
displayed as different bars in the same line (i.e., one line per sequence).

#### Table View

Table View is a sortable table that contains a row for each hit and the following columns:

* Title/Description - description of the database sequence

* Accession - accession ID of the database sequence

* Sequence Length - length of the database sequence

* Alignment Length - alignment length of the hit as reported in BLAST output, that is, the length used to calculate the Identity and Positive 
scores

* Bit Score - bit score of the hit

* E-value - e-value of the hit

* Identity - identity score of the hit as reported in BLAST output

* Positive - positive (similarity) score of the hit as reported in BLAST output

* Resolution - X-ray resolution of the hit as reported in the .pdb file and the resolution of NMR structure is assigned -1.0

* SCOP - SCOP ID of the hit. If a hit consists of multiple SCOP domains, multiple SCOP IDs are listed

* Ligand - names of the ligands in the hit as appear in the .pdb file. Each ligand is listed in the form [chainID]:[ligandName][ligandID]

Sort by clicking the column header. Left-click a row to select it. Hold SHIFT while clicking add a range of rows, or hold CTRL while clicking to 
add individual rows to your selection. Hits remain selected and sorted when you switch views.

You can open individual records in the Sequence Annotation Window by
double-clicking the record name.

When there are multiple hits to the same database sequence, the Table View only shows the hit of 
the highest bit score from that sequence. The selection of a row in the Table View selects all the hits of that sequence in the Map View.

#### Text Window

The Text Window shows the hits in the BLAST raw output format.

#### Context menu

Right-click the Map View or Table View for the following options:

* Copy (Map View) - copies the part of the Map View which are in display as a graphical object

* Copy (Table View) - copies the selected rows in the Table View as text

* Select All (both) - selects all the hits from Map View and Table View

* Display Style (Map View) - sets the display of the title, score color key, and ruler

* Get Structure Files (both) - retrieve the PDB files for selected hits and copy them to the protocol Output folder without loading them in the Molecule Window.

* Loading commands (both) - refer to the BLAST XML report Help 
topic

#### Further information

Search Sequences by Similarity tools BLAST XML report BLAST Search theory

# Data Table View

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_data-table.htm

## Data Table View

The Data Table View displays properties of objects in the Molecule Window in tabular form. The Data Table View groups properties into tabs by object. For example, click on the Atom tab to view the properties for all of the Atom objects. The properties are arranged in columns with the values in a row for each individual object. Note that when you import a .csv file, the rows are simply numbered since there are no objects.
Choose View | Data Table from the menu bar or press CTRL+T to toggle the display of the Data Table View
for a structure shown in the current Graphics View or Hierarchy View . Use the scroll bars and the arrow, Home, End, and Page keys to navigate the table.

The following is covered in this topic:

* Working with the Graphics View

* Molecule tab

* Working with rows

* Working with columns

* Tagging molecules

* Editing data

* Copying and pasting data

* Access methods

The Data Table View is useful for working with objects in the Graphics View.
You can toggle the Visible property checkbox (in the Visible column) to control the visibility of the object in the Graphics
View. Note that this property also affects all of the objects contained by that object. So if you hide a chain for example, all of the atoms within the chain will also be hidden.

The visibility checkbox behaves slightly
differently for molecules. If you have hidden atoms or residues within a molecule,
when you hide the molecule, all the objects within the molecule are hidden. However, when you return the molecule to view, the objects that were previously hidden remain hidden.This is useful for displaying a subset of
atoms such as a binding site because it allows you to quickly turn on and off
the visibility without changing which atoms are shown as part of the site.
If all objects belonging to a molecule are invisible, the checkbox will make
them all visible again.

The molecule tab displays the properties for all of the molecules loaded in the Molecule Window. It behaves slightly differently from other tabs, which
typically contain either data that is independent of molecules (such as
pharmacophore Queries) or data that is contained within molecules (such
as Chains, Residues, Atoms, and Bonds). Objects contained within molecules are only displayed if the parent molecule is visible. For example, if you load 1000 molecules,
and only the first one is visible, only the atoms in that molecule are listed
in the Atom tab. To show all the atoms in all of the molecules, you must make every
molecule visible, which may require a large amount of memory.

The molecule tab also has a number of additional features
not available in the other tabs:

* You can lock the visibility of a molecule and then toggle the visibility of other molecules (such as posed ligands) in turn using Navigation Controls .

* You can tag
molecules of interest.

* A standardized 2D chemistry depiction is available for small molecules in the Structure column
by right-clicking and choosing Show/Hide Chemistry , and as a tooltip when hovering over the row headers.

* Advanced filtering is available, which allows you to show only rows that
match specific criteria and then export them.

* You can color code rows by the activity (Activ) and uncertainty (Uncert)
properties.

* As discussed in the previous section, the visibility property of hidden children objects is retained when the visibility of the parent object is toggled.

When copying and pasting the Structure depiction into a different column, you can see the SMILES string.

#### Adding and removing rows

Each row in the table corresponds to an object of the type named in the tab
label, such as a Molecule, Atom or Bond. To add a new row, you must add a
new object. For example, in the Atom tab, there is no way to create a blank
row, but you can copy/paste another atom to create a new row, then modify
the new copy. Similarly, to remove a row you must delete the corresponding atom. Additionally, if you add or remove objects using the Graphics View or Hierarchy View, corresponding rows are added to the Data Table View.

#### Hiding and displaying rows

You can also hide or display rows based on visibility, or selection. In
the Molecule tab you can also hide or display rows that have been tagged .
Right-click and choose List Only Visible Objects , List Only Selected Objects , or List Only Tagged Molecules to toggle the listing of these objects. Note that hidden objects are not deleted.

The filters are continually updated. For
example, if you have List Selected Objects active,
and then deselect all molecules, no rows will be listed in the table.

Advanced filtering is available for the Molecule tab. Right-click and
choose Filter... to open the Filter dialog . Use Choice to set criteria for one
or more columns. Some of the criteria require you to specify a Value . To
return the rows to view, right-click and choose Remove
Filters .

#### Changing the row order

The order of the rows can be modified by sorting the data associated with any column. For example, to sort the atoms by name, double-click 
the Name column header in the Atom tab. The atoms will then be displayed in ascending 
alphanumeric order by name. Double-click again to display the rows in descending order. Note that for objects with the same value, the original order is preserved.

You can sort by more than one property by right-clicking and choosing Sort... to open the Sort dialog . The Sort dialog allows to choose up to three properties to sort by.

The sort order in the Hierarchy View can be synchronized to the Data Table View order with the Rearrange Molecules command.

#### Selecting rows

Click a row head or any cell in a row to select the row. Use CTRL+SHIFT to make contiguous selections of rows and CTRL+click to make non-contiguous selections. Select anywhere outside of the current selection to de-select the
other items.

When you select rows in the Data Table View, the corresponding objects are selected in the other views. Likewise, changes to selection in
the Graphics or Hierarchy views will change the selection in the Data Table View. However, if you select individual cells, selections are not reflected in the other views.

#### Adding, removing, and moving columns

Each column refers to an object property (attribute). You can add new
columns and remove columns by adding/removing attributes by right-clicking Add Attribute and Remove Attribute(s) . You can also rename columns that you added. Gray colored columns cannot be modified or removed.

To move a column, left-click and drag it to a new position.

#### Selecting columns

Click the header to select the column. Like rows, you
can select contiguous or non-contiguous collections of columns using
SHIFT+click and CTRL+click respectively.

You can quickly make charts by selecting columns of data and then select a chart option from the Chart menu.

#### Hidden columns

You can use the Show/Hide Columns dialog to hide columns by right-clicking and choosing Show/Hide Columns... . The list of which columns to hide is preserved in both DSV or MSV format files. The hidden data itself is always saved into any format that supports properties. You can update which columns are hidden by default in the Molecule tab from the Data Table subpage - Preferences dialog . However, saved settings will override default preferences when opening a DSV or MSV file.

Several columns are hidden by default in various tabs, including:

* __PDBRemarks__

* __PDBSeqres__

* 1-Letter

* 1-Letter & ID

* 1-Letter & ID & Insertion Code

* 3-Letter

* 3-Letter & ID

* Calculate Charges

* Color

* Default Ribbon Size

* ForcefieldFFML

* Fractional X

* Fractional Y

* Fractional Z

* Ribbon Size

* Ribbon Size Property

* Visibility Locked

In addition to the standard selection operations, the Molecule tab of
the Data Table View allows you to tag molecules. Tagging is more
persistent than selection, as selection can be modified inadvertently by
clicking in any one of the views. A molecule is tagged using the checkbox in the Tagged column. You can recall a tagged selection by right-clicking and choosing List Only Tagged Molecules . This results in only tagged molecules being listed in the Molecule tab, which makes it easy to select them or view
them in the Graphics View.

In the Atom tab, you can change the values of text and numeric properties such as Name , ID , and Partial Charge by clicking the cell, updating the value, and then 
pressing ENTER or by clicking outside the cell. If the value you have typed is not appropriate for the property, the cell will retain 
the original value. For example, typing a character string into the ID property (which is limited to integer numbers), 
or a character string into Partial Charge (which is a numerical value) is not allowed, and the value entered will be replaced with the 
original value. To cancel editing without making a change, press the ESC key.

Properties that have a light gray background cannot be edited.

For enumerated properties such as Hybridization , click the cell 
to display a down-arrow that you can use to choose a value from a list.

For properties such as Color and Element Type , click the cell to display a button that opens a dialog box for choosing an appropriate value.

#### Copying data

You can copy values from the Data Table to the clipboard and paste them as tab-separated values into other applications.

* Select the cells to be copied. Use SHIFT+click or CTRL+click to select contiguous or non-contiguous cells, rows, or columns.

* Right-click and choose Copy or press CTRL+C.

* It is not possible to copy a non-rectangular selection, one that includes different columns for different rows.

* By default, the column
headers are not copied with the data. However, you can change this behavior by deselecting Ignore column titles when copying to the clipboard in the Molecule Window page - Preferences dialog.

#### Pasting data

You can paste columnar data into existing columns in the Data Table. Columnar data can consist of a list of data strings from a variety of 
sources, such as Microsoft ® Word, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft WordPad, BIOVIA Materials Studio, etc. Any list of data separated 
by DOS or UNIX line endings can be pasted into the Data Table.

To paste data on the clipboard into one or more columns in the Data Table, select a range of cells or the entire column(s), and then press CTRL+V or right-click the selection and choose Paste .

Note that if you select a column and paste your data, all of the data on the clipboard is placed in the column. If there is more data in the column than the clipboard, the remaining values in the column will remain. If there is more data in the clipboard than in the column, the remaining values in the clipboard are not added.

## Dendrogram Window

The Dendrogram Window provides a view of the similarities
between discrete objects, with more closely related objects grouped closer together.
The objects are represented by the terminal nodes of the tree.

### Zooming

You can zoom in and out on the plot using the mouse wheel.

| To | Press |
| --- | --- |
| Zoom horizontally only | CTRL+mouse wheel |
| Zoom vertically only | SHIFT+mouse wheel |
| Zoom out horizontally | SHIFT+Left arrow |
| Zoom in horizontally | SHIFT+Right arrow |
| Zoom in vertically | SHIFT+Up arrow |
| Zoom out vertically | SHIFT+Down arrow |

### Repositioning

You can reposition the plot (e.g., to center a section of interest) by holding 
the mouse wheel down and dragging, or by using the UP, DOWN, LEFT, and RIGHT 
arrow keys.

Use the Center Structure and Fit to Screen tools in the View toolbar to recenter the view on the whole tree.

### Selecting

Click a node or branch on the plot to select it. Selecting 
a node or branch causes the selection of all of its children and all of the 
corresponding objects in related views (for example, 
the Data Table, the Graphics View, the Sequence View, and the Hierarchy View).

### Annotating

You can annotate the plot with text by opening the Sketching toolbar ,
selecting the Text tool, and then clicking the area of the plot
you wish to annotate.

### Context menu

Right-click the plot to display a context menu with the
following options:

Copy, Delete, Select All: See Edit menu for more information.

Recalculate: Recalculates the Dendrogram from its original source.

Show All, Show Only: Shows all nodes or selected nodes.

Display Style...: See Dendrogram Display Style dialog for more information.

# Hierarchy View

Source type: HTML

## Hierarchy View

The Hierarchy View displays the hierarchical organization of objects in
the active Molecule Window and can be used to select parts of the
structure that are difficult to select in the Graphics View, toggle the visibility of objects in the Graphics View, and modify the hierarchical
organization of some objects.

Choose View | Hierarchy from the menu bar or press CTRL+H to toggle the display of the Hierarchy View
for a structure shown in the current Graphics View or Data Table View .

The following is covered in this topic:

* Hierarchical relationships

* Selecting objects and toggling visibility

* Modifying the Hierarchy

* Group objects

* Access methods

Molecular data is represented in a hierarchical relationship that can be navigated by opening and closing nodes. For example, you can expand a small molecule node to reveal the atoms contained, or expand a protein to expose 
chains, which contain residues, which contain atoms. The following are examples of a small molecule and protein in the Hierarchy View:

Small Molecule

Protein

Each row in the Hierarchy View represents a separate and distinct molecule or part of a molecule, such as an atom, bond, label, amino acid, 
cell, or monitor. Each object in the hierarchy is represented by its name or, if no name has been assigned, its type in angle brackets 
(for example <Chain>), and a type-specific icon. The checkbox next to the object's name toggles its visibility. As in the above examples, each indentation represents a parent-child relationship.

A molecule might contain several chains, each of which contain several amino acids, each of which contain atoms. Bonds within the amino acid are contained by the amino acid, 
while bonds between amino acids are contained by the next higher level of organization, the amino acid chain. Objects at the same hierarchical level are connected by a vertical line.

In addition to molecular data, you can view other data types in the Hierarchy View. For example, each hydrogen bond monitor you create
contains a list of all hydrogen bonds present. Pharmacophore queries also
are represented as a set of hierarchically related logic operators (And, Or,
Exclude).

When you select an object in the Hierarchy View, the corresponding object is selected in the Graphics View. This is useful for identifying 
objects in the Graphics View that are more easily selected in the Hierarchy View, or objects that are hidden and therefore not shown in the Graphics View.

If an object contains a selected object, a small yellow selection marker appears in the corner of the object's icon. If you select a single atom in the Graphics View, you can identify the residue and the chain that the atom is contained 
in by looking for the markers in the Hierarchy View.

To make an object visible, check the checkbox next to the object's name, which also makes any objects contained in the
object visible. Conversely, to hide an object and the objects it contains, uncheck the checkbox.

The visibility checkbox behaves slightly
differently for molecules. If you have hidden atoms or residues within a molecule,
when you hide the molecule, all the objects within the molecule are hidden. However, when you return the molecule to view, the objects that were previously hidden remain hidden.This is useful for displaying a subset of
atoms such as a binding site because it allows you to quickly turn on and off
the visibility without changing which atoms are shown as part of the site.
If all objects belonging to a molecule are invisible, the checkbox will make
them all visible again. This is useful for displaying a subset of
atoms such as a binding site because it allows you to quickly turn on and off
the visibility without changing which atoms are shown as part of the site.
If all objects belonging to a molecule are invisible, the checkbox will make
them all visible again. To hide everything, click
the object to select it and its
children, then right-click and choose Hide or choose View | Visibility from the menu bar.

By default, bonds are not displayed in the Hierarchy View. To display bonds, right-click the Hierarchy View and choose Display Bonds .

You can change the organization of the data by dragging and dropping in the Hierarchy View according to the following rules:

The following rules apply:

* You can drag a molecule to or from a cell object.

* You can drag a molecule into another molecule to move it into a new chain of the target molecule.

* You can drag a chain (AminoAcidChain, NucleicAcidChain) to white space to remove it from the molecule and create a new molecule that contains the chain.

* You can drag an isosurface or density map to or from a cell object.

#### Renaming objects

You can rename any of the objects in the Hierarchy View by double-clicking it or selecting it and pressing F2, and then typing a new name. Note that the object will be renamed in all views.

You can create custom collections of objects called Groups, and then use the Hierarchy View to toggle the visibility or quickly recall the original selection.

* Select a group of objects using, for example, the select dialog or the Select tool .

* Right-click the Graphics View and choose Group... . You will be prompted for a name.

* Click OK . You can now click the group name in the Hierarchy View to reselect the grouped objects or use the checkbox to toggle the visibility.

* To remove a group in the Hierarchy View, select the group, and then right-click and choose Remove Group .

# Sequence Annotation Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_sequence-annotation-window.htm

## Sequence Annotation Window

The Sequence Annotation Window allows you to view and edit the annotations associated with an amino acid or nucleic acid sequence. Annotations are a 
useful way of attaching information about structural and functional properties of sequences.

There are several ways to open a Sequence Annotation Window :

* Open a sequence file that contains sequence annotation.

* Select one or more sequences in the Sequence Window , and the choose Sequence | Show Annotations from the menu bar.

* Select one or more proteins or nucleic acid structures in a Molecule Window , and choose Sequence | Show Annotations from the menu bar.

Alignment files and individual sequence files that do not contain sequence annotation will 
automatically open in the Sequence Window , you can still add annotations to these sequences by opening the Sequence Annotation Window from the Sequence Window .

In this application you can work with two types of sequence annotation:

* Sequence Features are used to store information associated with a particular region of a sequence. For example, in an 
amino acid sequence a feature may be associated with a specific binding site, while in a nucleic acid sequence, a feature may be associated 
with an individual gene.

* Sequence Annotations are used to store more general information about the sequence as a whole. Examples of sequence 
annotation are literature citations and taxonomic information.

When you open a sequence in the Sequence Annotation Window , annotations are displayed in three views:

* Graphics View - Displays an interactive graphical representation of the annotated sequence.

* Hierarchy View - Shows a hierarchical representation of the sequence features.

* Data Table View - Provides access to several tabular views of sequence features and sequence 
annotations.

The three views in the Sequence Annotation Window are fully interactive and any change you make in one view is automatically reflected in the other 
views.

If you are viewing the annotation for a sequence loaded in the Sequence Window , 
any changes made to that sequence, including selection updates, are reflected in the Sequence Annotation Window . It is not 
possible to modify the sequence directly in the Sequence Annotation Window and so only changes in selection update the 
Sequence Window.

The Sequence Annotation Window is able to calculate certain types of feature automatically when you open a sequence record. For nucleic acid 
sequences the following features are calculated:

* Open Reading Frames

* Restriction Enzyme Recognition Sites

* Nucleic Acid Subsequences

For amino acid sequences the following features can be automatically calculated:

* Proteolytic Enzyme Recognition Sites

* Amino Acid Subsequences

The settings for calculating Auto Features are accessed through the Auto Features subpage - Preferences 
dialog .

### Context menu

The Sequence Annotation Window context menu extends the Sequence Annotation Window capabilities as described below.

* Copy: This command is the same as 
the corresponding command under the Edit menu .

* Hide, Show, Show All, Show Only: These commands are the same as the corresponding commands under the Edit menu .

* Select All: Selects all sequence features in the current window.

* Features: These commands are the same as the corresponding commands under the Sequence 
menu .

* Translation...: Translates the current sequence to a protein. If a single feature is selected, the translation is 
performed automatically and the protein sequence is created in a new Sequence Window. If a single continuous range of sequence or 
nothing is selected, this invokes the Translation Dialog . This allows you to specify certain parameters for
the translation.

* Display Style: This command is the same as the corresponding command under View menu .

* Show Sequence: Opens the selected sequence or sequences in the Sequence Window . If the 
sequence is already open, the corresponding Sequence Window will become the
active window.

See Mouse and keyboard actions to learn how to work with the Sequence Annotation Window efficiently.

# Graphics View - Sequence Annotation Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_sequence-graphic-view.htm

## Graphics View - Sequence Annotation Window

The Graphics View of the Sequence Annotation Window provides a rich interactive viewer and editor 
for working with sequence annotation. The Linear Map View displays nucleotide and protein sequences on a single line. The cursor keys and horizontal scroll 
bar allow you to view those parts of the sequence that extend beyond the window.

By default, the map is drawn so that as much of the sequence as possible can be fit into the window. Therefore, successive lines are not necessarily 
evenly spaced. However, you may specify uniform line spacing in which case the line height will equal the height required for the line with the 
greatest number of features.

### Selecting features

Use the mouse to edit and select features in the Sequence Annotation Window. To select a feature use a single click. To 
select additional features press the CTRL key as you make additional mouse clicks. In addition, you can use drag selection to select a group of 
features.

### Editing Features

To edit a selected feature, right-click to open the context menu and invoke the Feature Editor dialog . 
Alternatively, execute the Sequence | Features | Edit... command from the main menu.

You can copy nucleic acid and protein features to the clipboard and paste them to the following destinations:

* Sequence Window - this will result in the corresponding sequence and any annotation being copied to the destination 
Sequence Window.

* Text File - a text copy of the sequence string will be copied to the text file.

* Graphics Editor - this will result in a graphic image of the current Sequence Annotation Window being copied to the destination 
graphics editor.

Pasting or cutting to the clipboard is not supported in the Sequence Annotation 
Window.

# Hierarchy View - Sequence Annotation Window

Source type: HTML

## Hierarchy View - Sequence Annotation Window

The Hierarchy View displays the hierarchical organization of sequence features in the active Sequence Annotation Window, which makes it easier 
to select features or sets of features that might otherwise be difficult to select in the Graphics View. The View | Hierarchy command toggles the display of the Hierarchy View for the sequence in the Graphics View or Data Table View.

The visibility of individual features or categories of features can be toggled by selecting the checkbox associated with those items. If you click a checkbox for a category where the visibility of individual items is mixed, on the first click all features are set to visible, and on a second click visibility of all features is turned off.

In addition to listing the sequence features, the Hierarchy View also lists entries for the Title, Ruler, and Sequence objects in the Graphics View. 
This provides an easy mechanism for toggling the visibility of those items.

Changes to feature data in the Hierarchy View, such as selection and deletion of any features, are immediately reflected in any other views 
currently open for that sequence.

Selecting the Title, Sequence, or Ruler items in the Hierarchy View does not result
in any corresponding selection in the Graphics View. These items correspond to display style options rather than sequence data.
