## Sequence List Window

The Sequence List Window allows you to view 
and open a collection of sequences. It 
opens by default when you open a file containing a set of non-aligned sequences. 
The sequences are considered not aligned if either of the following is true:

* The file contains a mix of protein and nucleic acid sequences in GenBank (.gb) or EMBL (.embl) format

* The file contains a list of annotated sequence records in GenBank, EMBL, or SWISSPROT format

The following columns are available for each record in the file:

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Name | The name of the sequence record |
| Type | The type of sequence |
| Description | The description line from the sequence record |
| Length | The number of residues in the sequence |

You can open individual records by
double-clicking the record name, or open selected records in either 
the Sequence Annotation Window or Sequence Window by right-clicking and choosing from the context menu.

### Context menu

Right-click the Sequence List Window to access the following options:

* Open in Annotation Window - Opens the selected sequence in the Sequence Annotation Window . This
menu item is only enabled when a single sequence is selected.

* Open in Sequence Window - Opens the selected sequence or sequences in the Sequence Window .

# Data Table View - Sequence Annotation Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_sequence-table-view.htm

## Data Table View - Sequence Annotation Window

The values of the properties of the features or annotations in a sequence can be
viewed in the Data Table View. In this window, properties of features 
or annotations of the same type are organized as a tabbed spreadsheet. The label on the tab indicates the object type. Clicking the tab displays the 
spreadsheet for features or annotations of that type.

### Editing data

Text and numeric properties such as Authors , Title , and Journal in the Literature Citation tab can be edited in the spreadsheet cell by clicking the cell. The property value is changed when 
pressing the ENTER key or by clicking outside the cell. If the value you have typed is not appropriate for the property, the cell will display the 
original value. To cancel editing, press the ESC key.

For enumerated properties such as Feature Type in the Feature tab, clicking the cell will display 
a down-pointing arrow at the right of the cell. Click the arrow to display a list of possible values for the property, and choose an entry from the list.

For properties such as Start , Stop and Comments in the Feature tab, click the cell to display a button that opens a dialog box that allows you to specify a new value.

### Data Table tabs

The Data Table View contains five different tabs:

#### Feature tab

The Feature tab lists information about each feature on a single row. You can edit the individual attributes of a feature by clicking in the cell 
corresponding to the data you wish to modify and clicking the corresponding control.

* Type - Indicates the feature type. To modify the type, select in the cell and choose a feature type from the drop down 
list.

* Start - Indicates the start coordinates of the feature segments. To modify values, click in the cell to launch the Location Editor dialog .

* Stop - Indicates the stop coordinates of the feature segments. To modify values, click in the cell to launch the Location Editor dialog .

* Strand - Indicates whether a feature on a nucleic acid strand is on the sense strand.

* Comment - Summarizes any comments for the feature. To modify values, click in the cell to launch the Feature Editor dialog .

#### Auto Feature tab

The Auto Feature tab lists information about automatically calculated features. The criteria for calculating Auto Features are exposed in the Auto Features subpage of the Preferences dialog. None of the data in the Auto Features tab is editable.

* Type - Indicates the type of Auto Feature.

* Start - Indicates the start coordinates of the feature segments.

* Stop - Indicates the stop coordinates of the feature segments.

* Name - Summarizes any information about the name of feature.

#### Literature Citation tab

The Literature Citation tab lists information about any references associated with sequence record.

* Authors - Indicates the authors of the article.

* Title - Indicates the title of the article.

* Journal - Indicates the journal in which the article was published.

* Pubmed - Indicates the PubMed ID.

* Comments - Summarizes any additional information about the citation.

#### Molecule tab

The Molecule tab lists information about basic molecular properties of the sequence.

* DNA/RNA - Indicates what type of nucleic acid the sequence is.

* Strand - Indicates if a nucleic acid sequence is single or double stranded.

* Genetic Code - Indicates the genetic code that should be used to translate or reverse translate a sequence.

* Composition - Provides information about the base composition of a nucleic acid sequence.

* Base Count - Indicates the number of bases in a nucleic acid sequence.

* Residue Count - Indicates the number of residues in an amino acid sequence.

#### Sequence tab

The Sequence tab lists information about miscellaneous properties of the sequence record.

* Locus - Appears for all sequences, and can be modified by the user.

* Title - Appears for all sequences.

* Definition - The textual definition or title of the sequence. It starts with the common name of the source organism, 
followed by the criteria that distinguish this sequence from the other parts of the source genome (gene name and what the gene codes for, the 
protein name and mRNA, or a description of the sequence's function if it is a noncoding region). The definition line of coding regions can end 
with a completeness qualifier such as complete sequence, complete genome, or CDS (complete coding sequence).

* Accession - The current accession number(s) that apply to the sequence entry. Accession numbers are assigned by 
GenBank and are normally changed only if there is an error in an existing number or if the sequence in question is new and you have just received 
an accession number from GenBank. Each accession number consists of an alphabetic character, followed by five digits. A semi-colon separates a list 
of accession numbers and a semi-colon also terminates the list. The first accession number listed is unique to this particular sequence entry. 
Each accession is shown as a link; if the accession has separate sequence data associated with it, clicking the link will download and open it. However, not all accession numbers have such data available and so clicking their link will generate an error.

* ID - This is the ID number assigned by the database from which the sequence was taken.

* GI - NCBI identifiers.The GI (GenBank Index) is a number assigned to the sequence by NCBI.

* Division - The GenBank division that the sequence is in, such as invertebrate or vertebrate.

* Comment - You can enter any additional text here.

* Keywords - Short phrases that provide information about the sequence entry. Use semicolons to separate the keyword 
phrases and insert a period after the last keyword phrase.

* REMARK - Accredited comments that have been added by database managers.

* Source - The source field contains taxonomic information about the origin of the sequence.

* Version - An identifier consisting of the primary accession number and a numeric version number associated with the 
current version of the sequence data in the record. This is followed by an integer key (a GI) assigned by the sequence by NCBI.

* DR/DB Source - Depending on the file format, a list of database cross references. Click to download the sequence with 
the corresponding reference number. DR=EMBL; DBSource = GenBank).

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Data Table |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard shortcut | CTRL+T |

# Sequence Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_sequence-window.htm

## Sequence Window

The Sequence Window allows you to view and edit molecular sequences and sequence alignments.
Note that protein and nucleotide sequences are displayed in separate Sequence Windows.

Use one of the following methods to open a Sequence Window:

* To open an existing sequence or sequence alignment file, choose File | Open... from the menu bar.

* To open an empty Protein Sequence Window or Nucleotide Sequence Window, choose File | New | Protein Sequence Window or File | New | Nucleotide Sequence Window from the menu bar.

* To view the sequence for a protein or nucleic acid structure in a Molecule Window , choose Sequence | Show Sequence from the menu bar. If a subset of the molecules is selected in the Data Table View, only the sequences of the selected molecules will appear in the Sequence Window.

* To open the sequence data for an annotated sequence, open the Sequence Annotation Window and choose Sequence | Show Sequence from the menu bar.

* To insert a new sequence above a specific sequence, place the cursor before the first residue of the sequence and press Enter .
Similarly, to insert a sequence below, place the cursor at any location other than the beginning of the sequence and press Enter .

You can open multiple Sequence Windows to view single sequences or sequence alignments.
A sequence can also appear in multiple Sequence windows, which are not related
to each other. See Sequence | Link Sequence and Structure... for more information.

### Sequence representation

The Sequence Window displays one or more sequences with the following information:

* Sequence name in the left pane

* Sequence in the right pane

* Ruler above the sequences

In protein sequences, residues are represented by 20 standard residue types (ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY), 2 ambiguous amino acids (B and Z for Asx and Glx), and "X" for unknown or nonstandard residues. In nucleotide sequences, residues are represented by the following letters: ABCDGHKMRSTUVWY and "N" for unknown or nonstandard residues. Known nonstandard residue data (identified by 3-letter abbreviations) is preserved. Gaps are represented by dashes, chain breaks by red flags, and domain boundaries by blue pipes. Domain boundaries are only displayed in the non-chain view layout after the chain view alignment has been established.

Hover over a specific residue to display the residue ID in the form of <chainID>:<residueID>. The residue ID consists of a 3-letter abbreviation, sequence number, and optional insertion code. If the sequence is linked to a 3D structure, the residue ID is the same as the ID shown in the Hierarchy View.

The text color and the background color of the sequence can be changed to reflect residue, alignment, or structural properties. You can customize the font of the residues, the sequence names, and the ruler using the Sequence Window Display Style dialog . 
The Font toolbar can be used to decorate residues, with customized colors (foreground, background, underline, overline, and carets) and style (italics and bold).

Use the Sequence Annotation Window to view a graphical representation of the feature annotations for an individual sequence. Select the sequence you want to view and choose Sequence | Show Annotations from the menu bar.

The Sequence Window may include an icon to the left of the sequence name:

| Icon | Description |
| --- | --- |
| | The sequence is linked to a 3D structure. |
| | The sequence-structure link is broken. For example, if you close the Graphics View, the link will break. Any change to a 3D structure or sequence that cannot be supported will also result in a broken link. In cases where the link has been broken because of a structural change, undo the operation that broke the link to re-establish it. |

Hover over the link icon to view a tooltip indicating the link status. 
When displayed in Chain View , the sequence name will also include the chain identifier specified from a linked molecule 
(if defined) and the number indicating the chain's sequential number in parentheses.
The chain identifier will persist after the molecule link is broken.

* Updates in the Sequence Window are reflected in the linked Graphics and Sequence Annotation Windows. Selections between these windows are mediated via the Sequence Window for sequences linked to structures. Most operations in these windows are synchronized. However, several operations, such as building and editing nucleic acids and capping proteins, will break the link. Building and edit amino acids is supported from either Molecule or Sequence Windows. When amino acid residues are deleted in the Molecule Window, they are replaced by gaps in the linked sequences.

* To avoid opening unwanted Sequence Annotation Windows, if the Sequence Window contains more than one sequence, the Sequence | Show Annotations menu command is disabled unless a single sequence is selected. Similarly, if the Graphics Window contains more than one molecule, Sequence | Show Annotations is disabled unless one or more molecules are selected.

### Context menu

The following options are available by right-clicking different parts of the Sequence Window. Note that the available options will vary depending on whether you click the sequence name, ruler, or sequence. Note that tools from the Sequence toolbar and Font toolbar are also available at the top of the context menu.

Cut: Remove the selected residues and store the sequence data on the clipboard for pasting.

Copy: Copy the selected sequence data to the clipboard for pasting.

Paste: Sequence data copied from the Sequence Window, Sequence Annotation Window can be pasted in the Sequence Window. 
Molecules copied from the Graphics View can also be pasted.

Delete: Remove the selected residues and gaps. If no residues are selected remove the residue after the cursor.

Erase: Replace the selected residues with gaps. If no residues are selected erase the residue after the cursor.

Hide: Hides selected sequences in the Sequence Window. Note that the sequences are hidden from view but not deleted.

Show All: Makes all sequences visible in Sequence Window.

Show Only: Shows only the selected sequences in Sequence Window.

Sort Sequences: Reorder sequences according to the alphabetic order of their names. Available when the cursor is in the sequence name panel.

Insert Sequence:

* New Sequence: Inserts a new sequence named Untitled1, Untitled2, etc. 
Sequences can also be inserted by pressing Enter in an active Sequence Window.

* From Windows: Opens the Insert Sequences From Windows dialog for inserting one or more sequences from another Sequence Window, Sequence Annotation Window, or Molecule Window. Note that sequences and molecules
can also be copied and pasted into the Sequence Window.

View:

* Wrapped View: Changes the Sequence Window to wrapped view.

* Extended View: Changes the Sequence Window to extended view.

* Chain View: Changes the Sequence Window to Chain View. This is only enabled when sequences have more than one chain. In this view, the chains are displayed in separate chain blocks and each block is referred to as a domain. When switching to this view, gaps are added as needed to maintain the alignment of the chains. Switching from this view back to the wrapped view or extended view will keep the domain boundary, which can be removed with Remove Domain Boundaries . After that, you can use Remove Gaps to remove the gaps.

* Show/Hide Ruler: Toggles the ruler display.

Chain and Domain: The same commands found in the Sequence | Chain and Domain menu.

Gaps: The same commands found in the Sequence | Gaps menu.

Display Style: The same commands found in the Sequence Window Display Style dialog .

Rename Sequence: The same commands found in the Sequence menu .

Extend Aligned Selection: Analyzes a sequence alignment for selected residues and gaps and extends the selection to include all residues and gaps aligned to the initial selection.

Residue Composition Table: Calculate the occurrence of each residue type in an alignment
and display the results in a Table View. Only alignment columns containing a selection
are reported or all columns if there are no selections. Consensus, trace, and hidden
sequences are excluded from the analysis. The following columns are shown in the table:

* Residue Type: Amino acid name and the corresponding single letter code.

* Total: Percent of each residue type for selected columns or all columns if there are no selections. 
Gaps are excluded from the calculation. For example, the total percentage of Alanine (A) is (total number of Alanine)/(total number of residues excluding gaps)

* Alignment columns: Percent of each residue type in the corresponding alignment column.
The alignment columns are labeled as follows: [Domain:] Column Number [(Ruler ID)], 
where [Domain:] is the domain index when the alignment is shown
in the chain view, Column Number is the alignment column position, and [(Ruler ID)] is the ruler label when it is
showing the first sequence or consensus residue identifiers. The percentages calculated include gaps. 
For example, the percent of Alanine (A) in alignment column 1 is (number of alanine residues in column 1)/(number of rows including gaps).

Fix Residue Block: Fixes the relative residue position for a set of selected residues from more than one sequence. When gaps are inserted into sequences, the fixed block moves together to retain the alignment.

Unfix Residue Block: Removes the fixed residue block set by Fix Residue Block command. This command is only enabled when the selection includes a fixed block.

Select Fixed Residue Blocks: Selects all residues in fixed residue blocks.

Show Annotations: Opens the selected sequence in the Sequence Annotation Window.

Alignment Index: Sets the ruler display style to show the ruler index (right-click over the ruler).

Residue ID: Sets the ruler display style to show the residue identifiers for the first visible sequence (right-click over the ruler).

Consensus ID: Sets the ruler display style to show the consensus ID. If any of the aligned residue identifiers
are different, an asterisk (*) character is displayed (right-click over the ruler).

BLAST Search...: Runs the BLAST Search protocol.

Align Sequences...: Runs the Align Sequences protocol.

See Mouse and keyboard actions to learn how to work with the Sequence Window efficiently.

### Printing

The content of the Sequence Window can be printed in any of the supported 
layout modes. Generally users will want to print in the default wrapped-view layout 
where the text is adjusted to fit the page. The printing characteristics in each of the 
layouts is as follows:

* Wrapped: The residue text width is adjusted to fit the printed page and wraps to new lines.

* Fit-to-width: Printing in this layout is similar to the wrapped view except that you can specify the number of residues per row. Use the print preview feature to check if the text wraps in one or more pages.

* Extended: Sequence names are printed only on the first page and the residue text continues on subsequent pages.

* Chain View: Similar to extended layout but only active chain domain content is printed.

The size of the text can be adjusted by changing the font. Use the print preview feature before printing.

# Working with windows

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_dvw_windows.htm

## Working with windows

Discovery Studio utilizes tabs to allow you to manage multiple views and windows while maximizing viewing space. The tab includes the title of the window, and the tab bar includes arrow buttons for navigating the tabs and an undock button that opens the views in a window separate from the client.

Although some windows open split views automatically, you can also split views by dragging the tab into the view. Depending on where you drop the tab, the view is split between the current window and the last active tab either side-by-side or top and bottom. You can split views in various combinations to achieve the optimal working environment for your task. Note that you can also drag tabs from one of the split views to another.

As mentioned previously, the tab bar has a button for undocking your windows from the client, which provides even more viewing area. You can open several at once by creating split views and undocking them individually. You can also drag tabs in separate windows back to the main client interface.

When you have multiple windows open in different split views, it may be difficult to locate a specific window. To return to a stacked view where all windows can be accessed from tabs across the top, choose Window | Arrange windows from the menu bar. To select a window from thumbnail views, choose Window | Choose .

You can also use the Expand , Maximize , and Minimize buttons to the right of the Undock button to change the view. When working with a split View, use Maximize and Expand to toggle between displaying the split view and a single tab. Use the Minimize button to hide a tab.

Use the Windows menu to manage and arrange your windows.

# Files Explorer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_mgd_files-explorer.htm

## Files Explorer

The Files Explorer provides a hierarchical view of the files and folders
that are accessible from within the software. This view allows you to navigate through 
the hierarchy and create, open, or modify files and folders. Having the Files Explorer
integrated into the main application greatly simplifies the process of importing data 
into the application.

When you first start the application, the Files Explorer is presented at the 
left side of the application window and displays a default set of root folders.

To view the Files Explorer

From the View menu, choose the Explorers | Files command.

To refresh the contents of the Files Explorer

Click the Files Explorer to ensure it is the active window and then press the F5 key.

To refresh a specific folder in the Files Explorer

* Collapse the folder by clicking the - symbol preceding the folder icon.

* Expand the folder by clicking the + symbol preceding the folder icon.The contents of the folder will be 
refreshed on expanding.

Refreshing the folder contents by collapsing and expanding
is supported only for folders that are on the local drive.

To hide the Files Explorer

Click the Close button at the right side of the Files Explorer title tab.

To reposition the Files Explorer

Click and drag the Files Explorer title tab to the desired location within 
the application workspace.

### Viewing contents

The contents of each folder is viewed in a tree that expands and contracts 
as defined by the user.

To expand a folder and view its contents

Do one of the following:

* Double-click a collapsed folder

* Click the + symbol preceding the folder icon

To collapse a folder and hide its contents

* Double-click an expanded folder

* Click the - symbol preceding the folder icon

### Setting the default folder

Once a default folder has been specified, it is used as the default location for saving protocol data files.

To set a folder as the default

* Navigate to the folder that you want to set as the default.

* Right-click the folder and choose Set Default . A blue triangle appears on the corner of the folder icon to 
indicate that this folder is now the default.

You can also set your default folder from the Preferences dialog on the Files Explorer page .

# Saving a file

Source type: HTML

## Saving a file

A variety of different file formats are supported to save data.

The most suitable format often depends on the type of data that is to be saved. For a full list of supported formats, including information 
about which ones that can be saved (exported), refer to Supported file formats .

| To | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Save data to a new file | Choose File \| Save As... from the menu bar. |
| Overwrite an existing file | Choose File \| Save As... from the menu bar and select the file you want to overwrite. |
| Update an existing file | Choose File \| Save from the menu bar, press CTRL+S, or click the Save button. |
| Export a storyboard as a movie | See Export movies . |
| Export an image | See Export images . |

### Saving multiple molecules in a .pdb file

The .pdb file format does not support saving more than one molecule. To
save multiple molecules in a .pdb file, it is necessary to
restructure the data so that it can be represented as a single molecule. This requires
that you modify the hierarchy so that the different molecules become chains of the same
molecule. You can do this by opening the Hierarchy View for the structure you are viewing, and dragging one molecule on to another so that they have the same
parent. See Hierarchy View for more information.

When saving a molecule with conformations to a .pdb file, only selected conformations will be saved as different models. If no conformation is selected, but there is a visible conformation, only the visible conformation is saved. If none of the conformations are selected or visible, only the molecule will be saved.

# Mouse and keyboard actions

Source type: HTML

## Mouse and keyboard actions

Certain mouse and keyboard actions are available regardless of the current selected tool mode. These are referred to as default actions in the
following table and can be used in any tool mode. Other mouse and keyboard actions are specific to particular tool modes and may behave differently
between modes. To customize keyboard actions, refer to Toolbar subpage - Preferences dialog for more information.

The following mouse and keyboard actions are covered here:

Default actions

* All tools

* Keyboard controls

Tool-specific actions

* Select tool

* Rotate tool

* Translate tool

* Zoom tool

* Torsion tool

* Sketching tool

* Sequence Window

* Annotation Window

* Charts

* Gestures

| To | Press |
| --- | --- |
| Select single object | Left-click the object |
| Select an object's parent in the Graphics View | Double-click the object to continue selecting the object's ancestry. For example, double-clicking a selected atom that has a residue as its parent will select the whole residue. If that residue has a chain as its parent, double-clicking the atom again will select the whole chain. By continuing this action, the molecule, cell, and root object (all objects) can be selected if the hierarchy exists. |
| Translate view in xy-plane | Middle-click and drag |
| Translate selected object in xy-plane | CTRL+middle-click and drag |
| Translate view along z-axis | SHIFT+middle-click and drag left or right (see Note 1 ) |

Track Surface is the default setting and allows rotation about some combination of the X and Y axes (or the Z axis if the SHIFT key is pressed as well) as the mouse is moved. The Track Ball setting uses the location of the cursor on the screen to determine the axis around which rotation occurs. # Working with protocols

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_ptc.htm

## Working with protocols

Protocols are tools that perform complex tasks on a Pipeline Pilot Server . Protocols are built from components that can read, write, filter, merge, and calculate data and can be customized if you have access to the Pipeline Pilot Client . For details about the Pipeline Pilot Client and Pipeline Pilot Server , see Using Pipeline Pilot .

The following topics are covered in this topic:

* Finding a protocol

* Running a protocol

* Stopping a protocol

* Downloading results

* Protocol options

* Viewing results

You can launch a protocol from a tool panel or directly from the Protocols Explorer . The tools are organized into the following tool sets:

| Tool set | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Macromolecules | Tools for constructing molecular structures and analyzing their behavior and exploring different types of data including primary sequence data and comparative sequence alignment data. |
| Small Molecules | Tools for developing mathematical relationships between biological activity and computed (or measured) properties, assessing the disposition and potential toxicity of a ligand within an organism, generating and analyzing conformations, and designing and analyzing small molecule libraries. |
| Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Tools for predicting and analyzing the interactions between protein receptors and ligands. |
| Pharmacophores | Tools for pharmacophore modeling. |
| Simulation | Tools for predicting and analyzing the electrostatic characteristics of molecules, making inferences about structural properties based on their electrostatics, and running energy calculations, solvation, energy minimization, and molecular dynamics simulations using CHARMm and other programs. |
| X-ray | Tools for building structural models of proteins and ligands from X-ray data. |

You can use the Feature Search box to quickly locate a protocol or other tool.

To run a protocol, you must have an active connection to a server. You can monitor your connection from the Active Server Bar . Click the active server bar to open the Change Server dialog to test and connect to a server.

To help with file management, output files that are not specifically set to be downloaded are removed when you restart the application. When you run jobs from the Protocols Explorer, the output files are set to be saved by default.

When run interactively (in the foreground) from a tool panel, the output files for only the ten most recent interactive jobs will be kept when the application is restarted. The output files for older jobs run interactively will be deleted from the disk. Jobs from a tool panel that are sent to the background will be kept by default.

To run from a tool panel

* From the Tools Explorer , open the tool panel that contains the protocol you want to run. If you know the name of the protocol, user the Feature Search tool in the upper left corner of the application to find it quickly.

* Click the protocol button to open the protocol dialog.

* Set the job parameters as desired.

* When using the dialog, you are not able to make changes in the Molecule Window. You can click the Toggle window docking icon on the Parameters Explorer and the Minimize icon on the Protocol dialog to switch between the two modes.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

* When you run directly from the dialog, the protocol is run in the foreground, which locks the application and then automatically opens the results when the job finishes. The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer . See Viewing results .

To run using the Protocols Explorer

* Choose a protocol from the list of available protocols in the Protocols Explorer .

* Use the Parameters Explorer to set the parameters to be used during the protocol run. You can right-click the Parameters Explorer and choose ...

You can right-click the Parameters Explorer and choose ...

* After setting the parameters, click the Run button in the Protocols toolbar. If the Run button is not visible, you can make the Protocols toolbar visible from the View | Toolbars submenu.

* While the job is running on the server, use the Jobs Explorer to monitor server location, current job status, and elapsed time.

* You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer . See Viewing results .

Temporary files created on the server are written to the temp folder in the job directory. 
To use the system temporary folder location, navigate to the Administration Portal of the server, 
and select Setup > Global Properties. In the Package dropdown list select BIOVIA/Discovery Studio Core and change the UseMDMJobTempDir global to False.

To stop a job running in the foreground

Click Stop

To stop a job running in the background

* Select the job in the Jobs Explorer . Use SHIFT+select or CTRL+select to choose multiple jobs to stop. You can also highlight the Jobs Explorer and choose Edit | Select All to choose all of the jobs in the window.

* Do one of the following: Click the Stop button in the Protocols toolbar . Right-click the job and select Stop

* Click the Stop button in the Protocols toolbar .

* Right-click the job and select Stop

A message dialog will prompt you to download the current output that has been generated. The following options are available:

* Yes: Stop the job and download the current output. The Intermediate folder will be retrieved regardless whether the Save intermediate files when running protocols preference is set in the Protocols page - Preferences dialog .

* No: Stop the job and delete the current output.

* Cancel: Continue the job.

* Help: Open this topic.

When you run a protocol, the results are created on the server. You have several options for downloading the files to the client after or during a job.

You can choose to save the output files for an interactive job by changing the status in the Saved column of the Jobs Explorer.

To automatically save results based on file size:

* Navigate to the Protocols page - Preferences dialog .

* Set the Maximum size for automatically downloading results to a size in MB below which the results will be downloaded when the job completes. Leave this field blank to automatically download all results regardless of size.

To save results that were not automatically saved:

* Click the Collect Result button in the Protocols toolbar .

To save results from a stopped job:

* Right-click the job and select Stop or click the Stop button on the Protocols toolbar.

* When prompted, choose to save the partial results when prompted. The Intermediate folder will be retrieved regardless whether the Save intermediate files when running protocols preference is set in the Protocols page - Preferences dialog . Note that most of the results retrieved are saved in this folder.

* Select the job in the Jobs Explorer . Use SHIFT+select or CTRL+select to choose multiple jobs. You can also highlight the Jobs Explorer and choose Edit | Select All to choose all of the jobs in the window.

For each download a folder with a time stamp is created in the Partial Output folder.

When setting up a protocol run, the following options are available by clicking the Options button in the Protocol Dialog or by right-clicking the Parameters Explorer . Note that you can also set preferences for protocols such as whether to save intermediate files or the maximum size for automatically downloading results in Protocols page - Preferences dialog .

You can switch between the protocol dialog and Parameters Explorer by using the Minimize and Maximize icons in the upper corner. Note that when using the dialog, you are not able to make changes in the Molecule Window unless you minimize the dialog.

| Action | Description | Dialog | Explorer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Run | Starts the job. | | + |
| Save Protocol As... | Creates a copy of the protocol that you can customize . | + | + |
| Save Protocol Settings | Sets the current parameter settings to be the defaults. Use the Restore Original Settings option to reset them. Modifying the default parameter values in Discovery Studio does not affect the settings of the protocol on the Pipeline Pilot Server . Other users, including those sharing the same machine, must update their own settings to customize their client. | + | + |
| Restore Original Settings | Resets the saved protocol settings to the original settings. | + | + |
| Maximize Protocol Dialog | Opens the protocol in the Protocol Dialog. | | + |
| Run in Foreground | The protocol will be run in the foreground, which locks the application and then automatically opens the results when the job finishes. If this is not selected, the job will run in the background. You can monitor the job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer . | + | |
| Debug Mode | Saves detailed debug messages generated during the run. Open the Output.log file in the Output folder to view the debug log. Additional progress messages may also display and the files are stored on the server for review. | + | + |
| Save Intermediate Directory | Saves the intermediate files generated during the run. These files may be useful when troubleshooting a run. The files can be found in the directory generated for the run in the default directory. | + | + |
| Use Default Path | Saves the files generated during the run in the default directory. You can change the default directory from the Files Explorer preferences . If this option is not selected, the Save Protocol Data dialog will open when you run the protocol that allows you choose the location for the generated files. | + | + |

When the job completes, you can double-click it in the Protocols Explorer to view the report, or expand the tree next to the protocol name to access links to the report and output files. You can also view the output files directly in the Output folder by using the Locate button in the Protocols toolbar .

# Parameter Help Explorer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_ptc_help-explorer.htm

## Parameter Help Explorer

If you are not connected to a Pipeline Pilot Server , the Parameter Help
Explorer is not available. To connect to a server, select File | Change Server... from the menu bar.

The Parameter Help Explorer provides context sensitive help information
related to the protocols and parameters launched from the Protocols
Explorer .

When a protocol is initiated from the Protocols Explorer, the Parameter
Help Explorer displays the overview text for the protocol. When an
individual parameter name or value is selected in the Parameters
Explorer , the Parameter Help Explorer shows help text that is specific
to the selected parameter. The help text for an individual parameter
includes the default value, guidelines for usage, and valid values
or ranges for the parameter.

The title of the parameter in the Parameter Help Explorer is displayed in color to help you differentiate between required and 
advanced parameters. Parameter titles for required parameters are displayed in red, while advanced parameters (not required to run 
the protocol) are displayed in purple.

When you first start the application and launch a protocol from the Protocols 
Explorer, the Parameter Help Explorer is presented at the bottom left hand corner 
of the application window and displays the overview text for the protocol.

# Jobs Explorer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_ptc_jobs-explorer.htm

## Jobs Explorer

The Jobs Explorer displays a list of jobs that have been initiated from the Protocols Explorer or that were launched from a tool panel and sent to the background. It allows you to monitor the progress of protocol jobs and display the results when the job is finished. When a new job is launched, it is automatically added to the top of the list in the Jobs Explorer. The number of recent jobs displayed in the Jobs Explorer is configured in the Protocols
page of the Preferences dialog.

The Jobs Explorer displays the following information in sortable columns for each job:

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Protocol Name | Name of the protocol. When the job completes, expand the tree next to the name to access links to the report and output files. |
| Saved | Indicates whether the files in the job folder are saved. Unsaved jobs will be deleted when the client is shut down. |
| Status | Current status of the job |
| Elapsed Time | Duration of the job |
| Details | Message indicating the current operation being performed by the server |
| Start Date | Starting date and time for the job |
| Output Location | Location of the job output files |
| Server Location | Name and port of the primary server where the job was submitted |

When the job completes, you can double-click it to view the report, or expand the tree next to the protocol name to access links to the report and output files.

To copy Jobs Explorer data to the clipboard, select the row(s) that you want to copy, and press CTRL+C.

### Jobs Backup File

The Jobs listed in the Jobs Explorer are saved in the Jobs.xml file in the %appdata%\BIOVIA\Discovery Studio Simulation\Experiment folder. 
A compressed backup of this file is created when opening and closing of the Discovery Studio client if the last backup file is older than 1 day. The maximum number of concurrent backup files is limited to three. 
The backup files are named Jobs.xml.x.gz (x=1, 2 or 3), where Jobs.xml.1.gz is the most recent backup.

To restore a backup file perform the following actions:

* Close the Discovery Studio client to ensure the file is unlocked.

* In the %appdata%\BIOVIA\Discovery Studio Simulation\Experiment folder uncompress the Jobs.xml.x.gz file containing the backup to be restored.

* Rename the uncompressed file to Jobs.xml .

| Menu | View \| Explorers \| Jobs |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard shortcut | CTRL+J |

## Parameters Explorer

The Parameters Explorer allows you to set up a protocol run by configuring the parameters that control the operation of protocol jobs. Parameters specify input structures or sequences, constraints, algorithms, and all other user-defined settings.

You can switch between the protocol dialog and Parameters Explorer by using the Minimize and Maximize icons in the upper corner. Note that when using the dialog, you are not able to make changes in the Molecule Window.

### Protocol options

Right-click the Parameters Explorer to access the following options:

| Option | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Run | Starts the job. |
| Save Protocol As... | Creates a copy of the protocol that you can customize . |
| Save Protocol Settings | Sets the current parameter settings to be the defaults. Use the Restore Original Settings option to reset them. Modifying the default parameter values in Discovery Studio does not affect the settings of the protocol on the Pipeline Pilot Server . Other users, including those sharing the same machine, must update their own settings to customize their client. |
| Restore Original Settings | Resets the saved protocol settings to the original settings. |
| Debug Mode | Saves detailed debug messages generated during the run. Open the Output.log file in the Output folder to view the debug log. Additional progress messages may also display and the files are stored on the server for review. |
| Save Intermediate Directory | Saves the intermediate files generated during the run. These files may be useful when troubleshooting a run. The files can be found in the directory generated for the run in the default directory. |
| Use Default Path | Saves the files generated during the run in the default directory. You can change the default directory from the Files Explorer preferences . If this option is not selected, the Save Protocol Data dialog will open when you run the protocol that allows you choose the location for the generated files. |

| Menu | View \| Explorers \| Parameters |
| --- | --- |

# Protocols Explorer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_ptc_protocols-explorer.htm

## Protocols Explorer

The Protocols Explorer provides access to the available protocols.
By default, it is located on the left side of the main application window.
However, you can change the default location as noted below.

The Protocols Explorer will not be visible if you are not
connected to a Pipeline Pilot Server .
To connect to a server, select File | Change Server... from the menu bar.

In addition to using the standard protocols that come with Discovery Studio ,
you can create custom protocols using Pipeline Pilot.
For details, see Customizing protocols .

Although you have access to all protocols in the Protocols Explorer,
you can also launch protocols from tool panels.
Tool panels are useful for grouping protocols and other tools according to 
functionality, which makes it easy to access all of the tools required
for specific tasks.
For details, see Working with tool panels .

##### Context menu

Right-click a protocol name to access the context menu.
The following options are always available:

Open: Opens the Parameter and Help Explorers for the protocol.

Refresh: Refreshes the view.

The following options are only available when connected to an on-prem server:

View Protocol: Opens the protocol in the Pipeline Pilot Client .
You must have a license for the Pipeline Pilot Client and
have it installed to use this feature.
Licenses are made available when the software is purchased. If you need further assistance relating to licenses you should initially contact your account manager. 
See the note in Installing Discovery Studio for information about installing the license.
Additionally, you must have a path set for the Pipeline Pilot Client Setting in the Protocols page - Preferences dialog for this feature to be enabled.

Rename: Rename a custom protocol.
You cannot rename protocols that are included with Discovery Studio .

Delete: Delete a custom protocol.
You cannot delete protocols that are included with Discovery Studio .

Export: Export the protocol XML file.
You can use the feature to share custom protocols with other users, or create a copy
of an existing Discovery Studio protocol to customize.

### Removing folders

This is only available when connected to an on-prem server.

To remove a folder

Right-click the folder and choose Remove Folder .

# Working with tool panels

Source type: HTML

## Working with tool panels

Tool panels provide access to tools that are grouped by general use. The tool panels are organized into tool sets grouped by the following major areas of discovery:

| Tool set | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Macromolecules | Tools for constructing molecular structures and analyzing their behavior and exploring different types of data including primary sequence data and comparative sequence alignment data. |
| Simulation | Tools for predicting and analyzing the electrostatic characteristics of molecules, making inferences about structural properties based on their electrostatics, and running energy calculations, solvation, energy minimization, and molecular dynamics simulations using CHARMm and other programs. Tools for adding constraints to molecular structures, and applying forcefields. |
| Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Tools for predicting and analyzing the interactions between protein receptors and ligands. |
| Pharmacophores | Tools for pharmacophore modeling. |
| Small Molecules | Tools for developing mathematical relationships between biological activity and computed (or measured) properties, assessing the disposition and potential toxicity of a ligand within an organism, generating and analyzing conformations, and designing and analyzing small molecule libraries. # Tools Explorer

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_tls_tools-explorer.htm

## Tools Explorer

The Tools Explorer displays the available tools grouped into tool panels by function. The panels that are available depend on the set of features you have chosen to license and install.

Each tool panel consists of one or more commands that are enabled or disabled based on the state of the active view and the current workflow. Some tools execute locally and may or may not allow input from dropdown menus.

Tool Panels are highly flexible. The default Tool Panels that are installed with Discovery Studio can be displayed or hidden, resized, and reordered. Additionally, you can create your own Custom Tool Panels that contain tools and explanatory text to walk users through an entire process. This topic covers the following:

* Customizing the view

* Heading options

* Creating custom tool panels

Only custom tool panels can be created, edited, deleted, exported, or imported. These actions are not available for the tool panels provided with Discovery Studio .

You can customize your view of the Tools Explorer, exposing just what you need to perform your tasks, and adjusting the views for efficient use.

Maximize or minimize a tool panel

* Click the tool panel header.

To reposition a tool panel

* Press CTRL and click and drag the tool panel header.

To view more than one tool panel at a time:

* Right-click on each tool panel header and choose Expand .

### Tool Panel Help

You can access help for a tool panel by clicking on "?" in the tool panel header. 
This option is not available for custom tool panels.

In addition to the diverse set of tool panels that group functionality by common tasks, you can create your own custom tool panels.

* Click the My Tools tool set. Note that you can also insert tool panels into existing tool sets.

* Right-click and choose Insert New Panel... .

* Add a Panel Name and click OK to open the Tool Panel Editor dialog.

* Drag tools and features from the list of Commands to the list of tools for the new panel. For headers and text, double click after dragging them to edit the text and style.

After adding a new panel, you can right-click and choose Edit... to make changes or Delete to remove it. You can share tool panels with colleagues by right-clicking and choosing Import... or Export... . You can also organize tool panels by dragging them and inserting separators by right-clicking and choosing Insert Separator .

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Explorers \| Tools |
| --- | --- |

## Discrimination of protein Secondary structure Class

Discrimination of protein Secondary structure Class (DSC) predicts protein
secondary structure from the primary sequence. The prediction can be based on
a single sequence or a sequence alignment. The overall per residue three-state
accuracy of the prediction is approximately 70%. A full scientific description
of DSC can be found in King and Sternberg, 1996 [King and Sternberg, 1996] .

#### Further information

# Solvent Accessible Surface

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/usng_vis_the_sas.htm

## Solvent Accessible Surface

Solvent Accessibility calculates the Solvent Accessible Surface (SAS) in Å 2 of 
protein and non-protein atoms and residues, other than water. The calculation is done for all/selected parts of the structure in the context of all/selected atoms excluding water. 
An enhanced grid-based numerical algorithm, similar to conventional methods,
is employed.
The following is a description of the method.

### Creating the neighbor atom list

First, a neighbor atom list is built for each atom, containing all atoms that 
potentially could eliminate any grid points on this atom.
The list is pre-sorted according to the distance from the atom.

The whole molecule is divided into cubic cells of 
length = 2*(R vdw +R s ), where R vdw is the 
largest van der Waals radius of any atom in the molecule and R s is the size of the solvent probe.
For any atom, only atoms in the neighboring cells (i.e., 3*3*3 - 1 = 26 cells)
and its own cell are checked when the neighbor lists are constructed. This
is the standard approach used by a number of applications 
( [Braun and Go, 1985] and [Grest, 1989] )
and has been used for calculating SAS numerically by the DCLM method [Eisenhaber, 1995] and analytically by the 
GETAREA method [Fraczkiewicz and Braun, 1998] .

Neighbor atom lists are sorted such that the nearby atoms are considered first.
Only 40% of the atoms in the neighbor list need to be considered before all grid 
points are eliminated for a totally buried atom. 
This significantly reduces computation time.

### Eliminating the grid points

A novel method is then used to construct grid points around each atom
and to count the grid points that are covered by neighboring atoms.
Those grid points will be eliminated.

A set of fullerene grid points on a unit sphere is sorted according
to descending z order.
Using simple calculus, if the grid points are evenly distributed on a spherical
surface, they are evenly distributed along the z-axis.
This is the most important property utilized in this algorithm.

For a given atom, A , the grid points of A are not
transformed to the molecular coordinate system; instead, the neighbor
atoms are rotated so that the nearest atom is on the +z-axis of the
grid coordinate system. The grid points of A are copied from
the pre-stored and pre-sorted grid point set. The memory usage is also
significantly reduced this way.

The next step is to find the grid points that will be eliminated by
the nearest atom. Suppose the nearest atom is atom B , and it
is placed on the +z-axis. Now atom A is positioned at the origin
(0,0,0) and its nearest atom, B , is positioned at (0,0,R AB ). If atom A has
a radius, R A , which is the sum of its van der Waals radius and
the solvent probe, and atom B has a radius, R B ,
a certain grid point on atom A , P(x,y,z) , will be eliminated
by atom B if:

Equation 1:

Since the grid points for atom A are pre-sorted according to
their z values and are evenly distributed along the z-axis, the elimination
procedure becomes simple: If the total number of grid points on
atom A is N , then the first NE points to be eliminated by atom B is approximately given by:

Equation 2:

Thus, only a few multiplication operations are needed to eliminate the first NE points even without any operation on the grid points. NE accounts for roughly 30% of N for SAS calculations.

This simple elimination is not only fast but also more accurate. Since no grid 
point coordinates are involved in the calculation, the process is exact to the accuracy
of the grid point; that is, the possible maximum relative error is 1/(2 N ). 
For any atom, the nearest neighbor always eliminates most of the grid points; hence, 
the largest possible error source is already minimized.

After the first elimination step, the distance comparison is applied to other 
neighbor atoms just as in other grid-based methods. Algorithms are also used to speed up the 
comparison.

If the total number of eliminated grid points on atom A with radius R A is NX , then the contribution of atom A to the exposed surface is given by:

Equation 3:

whereas the contribution of the atom to the buried surface is given by:

Equation 4:

### Residue solvent accessible surface

The Residue Solvent Accessibility is the sum of the surface of all atoms, including 
the backbone atoms, in each residue and the Side-chain Solvent Accessibility is the 
accessibility for just the side-chain atoms of amino acids.

The Percent Solvent Accessibility is 100 times the
Residue Solvent Accessibility divided by the residue solvent accessibility of the fully 
exposed amino acid residue calculated using the extended Ala-X-Ala tripeptide, where X is the
residue of interest. For standard amino acids, these fully exposed values are precalculated using the default probe radius (1.4Å) and highest grid resolution (960), with 
side-chains in an extended conformation so that consistent comparisons can be made.

This 
means that it is possible to obtain values in excess of 100%.

For nonstandard amino acids, the calculation 
is done for the conformation present in the structure, with neighbors replace by alanine residues.

Similarly, the Percent Sidechain Solvent Accessibility is the Sidechain Solvent Accessibility 
divided by the sidechain accessibility for the extended case times 100.

# Working with surfaces

Source type: HTML

Source section: client

Source file: client/working_with_surfaces.htm

## Working with surfaces

### Overview

There are two primary methods for generating surfaces:

* The View Interactions tools in the Receptor-Ligand Interactions tool set allows you to quickly generate surfaces with just a few clicks.

* The Create Surface dialog , which is available from the Structure | Surfaces menu, allows you to have complete control over surface generation, but requires additional effort.

### View Interactions tool panel

The View Interactions tool panel contains a section which provides a quick way to create surfaces on a
protein receptor, often in just one click. Surfaces are created on the
molecule that has been identified as the current receptor, which is indicated by the Define Receptor line of the tool panel. If a
current ligand is set, a receptor surface is created
within 5 Å of the ligand atoms. If a current ligand is not set, a
surface is generated for the entire protein excluding water residues and other ligands.

A variety of surface color types can be created. For details, see View Interactions . If you
do not have hydrogen atoms in your system, they will be included in
the surface calculation (though hidden). Water molecules are not included
in Receptor Surfaces .

### Create Surfaces dialog

Molecular surfaces created from the Structure menu
are based on the selected atoms, using the current
visible list of atoms as a context. This makes these surfaces more powerful
and easier to customize, but it typically requires additional setup
for all but the most trivial examples. Use this method if you want to create surfaces that
span multiple molecules that include hydrogen atoms or 
water residues. For details, see Display Style dialog .

You can adjust the display of surfaces from the surface tab of the display style dialog.

#### Further information

View Interactions Display Style dialog Surface tab - Graphics View Display Style dialog Receptor Surfaces: Theory

# Discovery Studio overview

Source type: HTML

Source section: dsvisualizer

Source file: dsvisualizer/about.htm

## Discovery Studio overview

Discovery Studio is a comprehensive software suite for Life Sciences research. It
consists of a set of products that enable researchers to capture, access, and analyze scientific data. By
using common underlying technologies and data models, the software allows the full range of
methodologies used in modern research to be seamlessly combined to solve diverse
computational problems.

This topic will help you become familiar with the basic architecture of Discovery Studio and the major features available in the client :

### Architecture

Discovery Studio is a software suite for performing computational analysis of data relevant to Life Sciences research. The product itself
comprises several distinct, but tightly integrated, functional layers. In addition, much of the science in Discovery Studio is deployed through
the Pipeline Pilot Server , which in turn provides other ways of accessing data and functionality. The following diagram illustrates how Discovery Studio Client interacts with Pipeline Pilot :

The following are the major parts of Discovery Studio :

* Clients

* Pipeline Pilot Server

* Protocols

* Standalone Applications

The clients are programs used to access the scientific functionality provided in Discovery Studio . The following clients are available:

* Discovery Studio Client: This client provides a rich set of viewers for working with molecular and sequence data. It also provides
significant functionality for analyzing scientific data. To learn more about the available features, see Discovery Studio Client .

* Pipeline Pilot Client : This client can be used to run and customize protocols , which in turn can be accessed from the other clients. To learn how to obtain a license for this client, see About Pipeline Pilot .

* Pipeline Pilot Webport: Pipeline Pilot supports the ability to run protocols from a web browser. All of the Discovery Studio protocols will run without modification through the Pipeline Pilot Webport.

Although Discovery Studio comes with a limited version of Pipeline Pilot Client to allow you to view the protocols, you need to purchase the full version separately in order to customize protocols, have access to additional component collections, or to use Pipeline Pilot Webport.

All protocol runs are performed and managed by the Pipeline Pilot Server . The server can be installed on a single machine with the clients, or can be installed on a separate server with one or more clients connected to it. For details, see Installing Discovery Studio .

The clients communicate with the server using the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP). You can develop against the SOAP services created within Pipeline Pilot to provide custom server access.

Protocols are collections of pipe-connected components (data processing building blocks) that execute scientific tasks. Individual protocols can be thought of as applications in their own right and often contain highly complex pipelines.

Protocols are launched from the clients and run as individual processes on the server. Individual protocols may in turn launch other processes to perform computations. Most commonly in Discovery Studio , Standalone Applications such as CHARMm and Catalyst perform many of the underlying computations.

For more information about the protocols available and how to use them, see Working with protocols .

The foundation of much of the advanced science delivered in Discovery Studio is a set of Standalone Applications that are developed as standalone products. The science underlying these applications
has been extensively validated and is referenced by hundreds of peer reviewed scientific articles. As
well as being accessible through the Visualizer, these applications can also be run from the
command line if desired.

Some of these applications have extensive command-line interfaces or command languages, and in a number of cases you can use them independently from Discovery Studio Client and Pipeline Pilot . Although Discovery Studio supports many Standalone Applications, the following four play the largest role:

* Catalyst : Analysis of pharmacophore data.

* CHARMm : Functionality for performing and analyzing molecular simulations of biological systems.

* CNX : Software for three-dimensional structure determination and analysis of macromolecules
using experimental crystallographic diffraction or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data.

* MODELER : Analysis of protein structures.

### Discovery Studio Client

The Discovery Studio has a rich and customizable interface that includes many tools for modifying 
and viewing data, running protocols, and analyzing the results.
The following illustrates the major features of the client:

To learn how to customize the client and use it more effectively, see Customizing the client .

#### Discovery Studio features

| Feature | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Feature Search Box | Use this to search and open functionality. For details, see Feature Search box . |
| Menu Bar | Select menu items to access commonly used tools, such as file access, editing, and viewing commands. For details, see Working with menu tools . |
| Toolbars | Click buttons to gain access to commonly used tools for viewing and editing data. For details, see Working with toolbars . |
| Tool Set Bar | Click buttons in the tool set bar to display different groups of related analysis tools in the Tools Explorer . |
| Windows | The Discovery Studio allows you to work with data in a variety of windows, including: Molecule Window : Edit and view molecular structures and property data. Sequence Window : Edit and view sequences and sequence alignments. Chart Windows : View and interact with charts such as point plots, histograms, and line plots. Script Window : Create, edit, and execute Perl scripts within the Visualizer. |
| Active Server Bar | Indicates the name and status of the active Pipeline Pilot Server for running protocols. To change the server, click and specify a different server name from the dialog that opens. For details, see Active server bar . |
| Status Bar | Displays information about the current application activity. For details, see Status bar . |
| Explorers | The Discovery Studio provides the following explorers for accessing tools and information: Files Explorer : Explore the file system to locate and open data files. Tools Explorer : Access tools for performing advanced analysis. Protocols Explorer : Access protocols that can be used to analyze data. Parameters Explorer : Change values of parameters to be used in a protocol run. Parameter Help Explorer : View help about the currently selected protocol or parameter. Jobs Explorer : Monitor the progress of protocols and display the results when done. |

* Molecule Window : Edit and view molecular structures and property data.

* Sequence Window : Edit and view sequences and sequence alignments.

* Chart Windows : View and interact with charts such as point plots, histograms, and line plots.

* Script Window : Create, edit, and execute Perl scripts within the Visualizer.

* Files Explorer : Explore the file system to locate and open data files.

* Tools Explorer : Access tools for performing advanced analysis.

* Protocols Explorer : Access protocols that can be used to
analyze data.

* Parameters Explorer : Change values of parameters to be used in a protocol run.

* Parameter Help Explorer : View help about the currently selected protocol or parameter.

* Jobs Explorer : Monitor the progress of protocols and display the results when done.

The Discovery Studio Visualizer is a powerful desktop application for viewing and editing
molecular structures, sequences, and other data relevant to Life Sciences research. It
provides a convenient interface for everyday data analysis tasks and enables you to share and view
data with other collaborators.

The Visualizer supports a wide variety of industry-standard formats. In addition, it reads and
writes the native formats used by the Discovery Studio product suite, making
it easy to view the results of colleagues who work with BIOVIA products. It also
integrates with your system's clipboard, making it possible to exchange data with
other applications.

A set of integrated analysis functions are provided that allows you to compute
basic properties of molecules and sequences. The Visualizer also provides access to
the Discovery Script Perl Application Programming Interface (API), which enables
you to create new analysis tools and to automate common tasks.

#### Further information

Getting started Working with the visualizer
