# catHypo Options

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_cathypo_options.htm

## catHypo Options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| -common | Instruct catHypo to run the HipHop algorithm. If not present in the command line, catHypo will use the HypoGen algorithm. |
| -excludedvolumes <n> | Add up to <n> excluded volumes to either HypoGen or HipHop models. The default is off. |
| -activ <title> | Use the <title> spreadsheet column instead of Activ to specify the activities of the compounds. The default is to use the Activ column. This parameter is only meaningful for HypoGen. |
| -uncert <title> | Use the <title> spreadsheet column instead of Uncert to specify the uncertainty values of the compounds. The default is to use the Uncert column. This parameter is only meaningful for HypoGen. |
| -min <n> | Any pharmacophore created must include at least <n> features. The default is 0. This parameter applies to both HypoGen and HipHop. |
| -max <n> | The pharmacophores created cannot have more than <n> features. The default is 10. The parameter applies to both HipHop and HypoGen. Note that HypoGen will not create pharmacophores with more than 5 features. |
| -dict <dict.ds_chm> | Use <dict.ds_chm> instead of system default dictionary. The default is /shares/Catalyst/conf/Dictionary.ds_chm. This parameter is used by both HypoGen and HipHop. |
| -sel <feat.lst> | Specify a selection of feature definitions from the dictionary. File <feat.lst> has one feature definition name per line, optionally followed by min and max number of instances to be added. If the -dict option is used and -sel is not, all feature definitions in <dict.ds_chm> will be used with any number of instances of each. This parameter applies to both HipHop and HypoGen. |
| -stat <file> | Use this option to specify statistical model for selectivity of pharmacophores instead of default [2]. The default file used is /shares/Catalyst/conf/default.hstat. This parameter is only applicable for HipHop. |
| -nochm | Do not export chm files for pharmacophores. |
| -align <type> | Alignments to HipHop pharmacophores will be computed and written to files <outhyponame>.*.<type>, where <type> is sd or mol2. This parameter only applies to HipHop. |
| -in <in.ds_chm> | Input pharmacophore for the refine command. See Adding Excluded Volumes to a Pharmacophore for details. |
| -HyposReported <n> | Use this option to control the number of pharmacophores <n> and compound alignments catHypo writes to the log files. Specifying a value as large as 100 for n might ensure that you do not miss potentially interesting output. The default for this parameter is 10. This parameter is used by HipHop and HypoGen. |
| -Spacing <n> | Specify the minimum distance between actual feature locations in training set molecules to identify candidate pharmacophores. Only configurations of features in the molecules with at least this distance between actual feature locations are considered when identifying candidate pharmacophores. The default value of this parameter is 297 picometers. The parameter is used by HipHop and HypoGen. The default of 297 picometers (2.97 angstroms) prevents both of the oxygens in a carboxyl group from simultaneously being assigned as hydrogen bond acceptors. The default value works well for most medium to large molecules, but may not be good for small molecules that do not have many features. If you are interested in pharmacophores where features are close together, you should set this parameter to a small number such as 50 picometers. |
| -MinPoints <n> | Sets <n> as the minimum number of feature points for a generated pharmacophore. For example, a pharmacophore with two hydrophobes and two negative ionizables has four points. A pharmacophore with two hydrophobes and one hydrogen bond acceptor also has four points since the hydrogen bond acceptor feature has both an atom and a projected point. The default for this parameter is 4, which is the minimum value for an enantio-selective pharmacophore. For very small rigid molecules that have few chemical features, you might need to set this value to a lower number. This parameter is used by HypoGen and HipHop. |
| -MinSubsetPoints <n> | To be considered, a pharmacophore must fit the most active molecules in the lead set at least partially. Only configurations of features in lead set molecules with at least the number of points specified by this parameter are considered when identifying a candidate pharmacophore. The default value of 4 works well for most training sets, but if the molecules are small, rigid, and have few features, you might need to set this value to a smaller value. This parameter is used by HypoGen and HipHop. |
| -SuperpositionError <S> | Adjusts the RMS fit of molecules to generated pharmacophores. Reducing the value of <n> from its default of 1 tightens the fit. This parameter is only used by HipHop. |
| -Misses <n> | Specify the number of molecules in your input set of lead compounds not required to map to all features in generated pharmacophores. That is, you can set the number of lead compounds that can "miss" mapping to generated pharmacophore features. Miss means that the compound does not map to all of the features in an output pharmacophore. Meaningful values of <n> are as low as 0, or as high as 1 less than the number of compounds designated with a 1 or a 2 in the Principal column in the input spreadsheet file. Compounds designated with a 0 in the MaxOmitFeat column of the input spreadsheet file are not allowed to miss mapping to generated pharmacophore features. The default value is 1. This parameter is only used by HipHop. |
| -FeatureMisses <n> | Specify the number of molecules in your input set of lead compounds that are allowed not to map to any one feature of a generated pharmacophore. The tables Sample pharmacophore generated with - FeatureMisses 3 and Sample pharmacophore generated with - FeatureMisses 1 below illustrate the usefulness of this option. Although three of the compounds in the table with -FeatureMisses set to 3 fail to map only one feature in a generated pharmacophore, it is the same feature. Lowering the setting for the -FeatureMisses option from 3 to 1 still allows compounds in the input set to miss a feature, but distributes the misses among features of a generated pharmacophore as shown in Sample pharmacophore generated with -FeatureMisses 1 below. Generally, the greater the value specified for the -FeatureMisses option, the less evidence there is that each individual feature of a generated pharmacophore is significant. Likewise, setting the -FeatureMisses option to a small value requires more input compounds to map to individual features, thus providing more evidence that the inclusion of any one feature in a pharmacophore is significant. A value for the -FeatureMisses option is meaningful only if it is less than the value specified for -Misses option. The default value is 1. This parameter is only used by HipHop. |
| -CompleteMisses <n> | Specify the number of molecules in your input set of compounds that do not have to map to more than one feature per generated pharmacophore. A value for n is meaningful only if it is less than the value you specify for the -Misses option. HipHop allows only compounds designated with a 2 in the MaxOmitFeat column in the input spreadsheet file to completely miss mapping to features in an output pharmacophore. The default value is 0. It is only used by HipHop. |
| -ToleranceFactor <n> | Specify the amount (floating point value) by which HipHop scales feature tolerance and depends on the following relationship: Tolerance = (ToleranceFactor)×(default tolerance for feature) The default value is 1. This parameter is only used by HipHop. |
| -CheckSuperposition <n> | Specify either an exact check on superposition or only a distance check when identifying configurations of features common to the set of input compounds. A configuration is a set of relative locations in 3D space, each of which is associated with a type of feature. A molecule matches a configuration if it possesses a set of features and a conformation such that the features can be superimposed with the corresponding conformation locations. A set of features is considered superimposed if each feature lies within a specified tolerance from the corresponding ideal location. A value of "1" turns the superposition check on and a value of "0" turns it off. The default value is 1. This parameter is only used by HipHop. |
| -WeightVariation <n> | Control how much feature weights are allowed to vary from the ideal value. Use a floating point value for <n>. Higher values of <n> favor pharmacophores with feature weights that differ widely from the ideal value, which is 2.0 for each feature weight. Lower values of n will favor pharmacophores with feature weights that differ little from the ideal value of 2.0. In effect, this parameter represents the penalty for a feature's weight deviating from the expected weight and restricts an "unreasonable" contribution to estimated activity by any particular feature. Feature weights represent the orders of magnitude of activity to which any pharmacophore feature contributes. The default of 0.302 represents the expected standard deviation of the feature weights for "good" pharmacophores. This parameter is only used by HypoGen. |
| -Mem <n> | Specify the maximum amount of physical memory <n> that HipHop can use. This value sets an upper limit in MB. When HipHop reaches this limit, it starts consuming virtual memory and switches to a slower but more compact algorithm and attempts to run to completion. If the memory limit is exceeded by a factor of 2, HipHop reports an early termination and partial results before the program halts. The default value is 60. This parameter is used by HipHop only. |
| -IdealHBondGeomOnly <n> | Constrains catHypo to consider only projected points at positions reflecting "ideal" hydrogen-bond geometry (e.g., three staggered positions on an -OH or two lone pair positions on a carbonyl oxygen). Normally Catalyst considers six positions on an -OH and three at a carbonyl oxygen. A value of 1 turns this option on and 0 turns it off. The default value is 0. This parameter is used by both HypoGen and HipHop. |
| -VariableWeight <n> | A value of 1 instructs HypoGen to try variable weights during the optimization to improve the models. The default value is 0. This parameter is only used by HypoGen. |
| -VariableTolerance <n> | A value of 1 instructs HypoGen to try to vary the tolerances during the optimization to improve the models. The default value is 0. This parameter is only used by HypoGen. |

Specify the minimum distance between
actual feature locations in training set molecules to identify candidate
pharmacophores. Only configurations of features in the molecules with at
least this distance between actual feature locations are considered when
identifying candidate pharmacophores. The default value of this parameter
is 297 picometers. The parameter is used by HipHop and HypoGen.

The default of 297 picometers (2.97 angstroms) prevents both of the
oxygens in a carboxyl group from simultaneously being assigned as

Specify the number of molecules in your input set
of lead compounds that are allowed not to map to any one feature of a

this option. Although three of the compounds in the table with -FeatureMisses

Generally, the greater the value specified

more input compounds to map to individual features, thus providing

Specify the amount (floating point value) by which

# Using catHypo

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_cathypo_usage.htm

## Using catHypo

To use catHypo

```text
catHypo <file.spst> <cmpdsdir> <cmpdstype> <outhyponame> <logname> <OPTIONS>
```

where:

* <file.spst> = 
a tab-delimited spreadsheet file that contains the compound Names, Activity values, and Uncertainty

* <cmpdsdir> = the directory that contains the conformer models

* <cmpdstype> = the compound format

* <outhyponame> = hypos output to <outhyponame>.<number>.ds_chm

* <logname> = catHypo log file

* <OPTIONS> = optional runtime arguments

# catSearch

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_catsearch.htm

## catSearch

The catSearch program allows you to search or browse a Catalyst database. The program creates datafiles ( .esp , .spst , .mol2 , or .sd ) that contain the compounds located by searching or browsing.

By default, the catSearch program uses the Fast searching
algorithm. To use the Best Flexible searching algorithm, specify the -bestFlexible argument in your catSearch command statement.

#### Further information

Using catSearch catSearch Options Catalyst Standalone Applications

Source type: HTML

## catSearch Options

| Option | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |

| -browse | Browses the database. See Using catSearch Command Line for details. | off |
| -bestFlexible | Search a database with the same algorithm employed by Catalyst's Best Flexible Search Databases/Spreadsheets menu item. When using -align without -bestMapping, the first mapping found will be exported aligned to the query. Note that using -bestMapping can increase search times. | off |
| -allMappings | Exports all mappings of all conformers aligned to the query. This option requires the options -sd, -align, and -allHitConfs. | off |
| -computeFits | Computes the fit values of the query and export them as a property in the exported .sd file. This option is valid for rigid fits only and requires the options -bestMapping and -align. | off |
| -align | Causes the compounds returned to align to the query for a .sd or .mol2 file. | off |
| -local | Runs search locally (i.e., does not use catDisk). Assumes database files are visible from the local host (NFS mounts are OK). This mode is limited to use on Windows. | off |

# Using catSearch

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_catsearch_usage.htm

## Using catSearch

#### General usage

From a command line, navigate to the directory in which you intend to use the files created by the catSearch program. Use the following form to run catSearch commands:

```text
catSearch DBname.bdb <commands> arguments [options] -local
```

Substitute -browse or -query (and optionally -bestFlexible) for <commands> and include the values required for the arguments and options. For details about available options, see catSearch Options , or type the following from the command prompt:

```text
> catSearch
```

#### Tasks

The following tasks can be performed with catSearch:

* Create an extended spreadsheet containing matching compounds

* Create a .mol2 file containing matching compounds

* Create a .sd file containing matching compounds

* Browse a database

* Search a database for a name or names

To create an extended spreadsheet containing matching compounds

```text
-esp filename.esp
-esp_withnames filename.esp
```

Use the -esp argument to create an extended spreadsheet file .esp containing
the compounds (and their related data) that match the Pharmacophore.
For filename.esp substitute the name of the .esp file to be created by
the catSearch program. You can import the extended spreadsheet file
into Catalyst if the database from which it was derived is installed with Catalyst. You can also use catSearch to search a .esp file
rather than a Database file ( .bdb ).

Use the "_withnames" extension to include compound names.

To create a .mol2 file containing matching compounds

```text
-mol2 filename.mol2
```

Use the -mol2 argument to create a .mol2 file containing compounds
(and all their related property data) that match the pharmacophore. For filename.mol2
substitute the name of the .mol2 file to be created by the catSearch
program. You can use the .mol2 file with other applications that
recognize the format.

To create a .sd file containing matching compounds

```text
-sd filename.sd
```

Use the -sd argument to create a .sd file containing compounds
(and all their related property data) that match the pharmacophore. For filename.sd,
substitute the name of the .sd file to be created by the catSearch
program. You can use the .sd file with other applications that recognize
the format, and you can use it for building a database with the
catDB program.

To browse a database

```text
catSearch DBname.bdb -browse -<filetype> filename.<filetype> [options] -local
```

The browse option places copies of all the compounds (up to the number specified by the -maxhits option) and all their related property (1D) data from the specified database or .esp file into the type of datafile you specify.

<filetype> are the types of output files ( .sd , .esp , etc.) For DBname.bdb, substitute the full pathname of the configuration
( .bdb ) file of the database you want to search. Alternatively you can
search a hit list in the form of a .esp file. For example:

```text
> catSearch output.esp -browse hypo.ds_chm -sd out.sd -local
```

The following options are appropriate for the browse command:

* -as2D

* -numhitsonly

* -maxhits n

* all output types (-sd, -esp, etc.)

For details see catSearch Options .

To search a database for a name or names

```text
catSearch DBname.bdb -name 'text' -<filetype> filename.<filetype> [options] -local
catSearch DBname.bdb -names <file> -<filetype> filename.<filetype> [options] -local
```

The -name option will search for compounds with names specified in text. The -names option will search the database for compounds with names specified in the <file>. <filetype> are the types of output files ( .sd , .esp , etc.) The % character can be used as a wild card. For example, %benz% will retrieve all names with benz or BENZ embedded within them.

For DBname.bdb substitute the full pathname of the configuration
( .bdb ) file of the database you want to search. Alternatively you can
search a hit list in the form of a .esp file.

For example:

```text
> catSearch output.esp -name 'text' -sd out.sd -local
```

The following options are appropriate for the -name and -names commands:

# citest

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_citest.htm

## citest

citest computes Compare/Fit operations between two objects geometrically and/or functionally by aligning features in one object with a similar set of features in another object. For example, you can determine how closely three atoms in one compound can be aligned with three atoms in a second compound, or determine how well atoms in a molecule match corresponding features in a pharmacophore, including whether the compound meets specified topology, angle, torsion, and chemical-function constraints.

One of two fitting algorithms can be used: fast fit (rigid) and best fit (flexible). Fast fit will find the best alignment between objects without changing the conformer models of a molecule. The best fit will allow conformers to change within a specified energy threshold in order to maximize the fit value.

# Using citest

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_citest_usage.htm

## Using citest

The following tasks can be performed with citest:

* Pharmacophore fittings to multiple ligands

* Compound-pharmacophore fitting

* Compound-compound fitting

* Pharmacophore-pharmacophore fitting

Pharmacophore fitting to multiple ligands

```text
citest -chm input.ds_chm -sd input.sd -outsd out.sd [OPTIONS]
```

where "input.ds_chm" is a Catalyst pharmacophore file ( .ds_chm ) and "input.sd" is a .sd file containing multiple ligands. The mapped 
ligands are exported to the .sd file out.sd. The mappings are aligned to the 
pharmacophore and contain properties such as Fit values, Activity Estimates, mapping information, etc.

To perform compound-pharmacophore fitting

```text
citest -chm input.ds_chm -cpd input.cpd [OPTIONS]
```

where "input.ds_chm" is a Catalyst pharmacophore file ( .ds_chm ) and "input.cpd" is a Catalyst molecule file ( .cpd ). Information about the fit results (e.g., Fit values, Activity Estimates, mapping information, etc.) are written to standard error and standard out.

To perform compound-compound fitting

```text
citest -cpd input1.cpd -cpd input2.cpd [OPTIONS]
```

When comparing two compounds, citest finds their optimum conformer fit. To compare molecules with different topology or atom orders, you may need to use the bungee option to indicate which atoms should be tethered together. These "tethered" atoms are the only parts of the two compounds that are matched in the Compare operation. You can associate many atom pairs using the bungee option. Typically you would specify at least three tethers. Only one mapping is possible when tethers are used.

To perform pharmacophore-pharmacophore fitting

```text
citest -chm input1.ds_chm -chm input2.ds_chm [OPTIONS]
```

By default, when comparing two pharmacophores, all combinations of features with location constraints on one pharmacophore are compared with the same features having location constraints on the other pharmacophore. All mapping combinations are presented for review. Unwanted mappings can be limited by attaching tethers between specified location constraints. Topology contained in a pharmacophore must have location constraints and tethers in order to be considered by citest.

Subsets of features with location constraints are considered. However, not every location constraint has to map to every other similar location constraint. The mappings are ranked primarily by the number of pairs of location constraints that match and then by the minimum rms displacement.

# BEST Method

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_best.htm

## BEST Method

The best-quality conformer generation method provides improved conformational coverage relative to the FAST method. It performs a more rigorous energy minimization in both torsional and Cartesian space, and uses the Poling algorithm . We suggest that BEST be used when conformational coverage is important (e.g., to build conformer models for automatic pharmacophore generation routines).

The following steps are performed:

* Conjugate-gradient minimization in torsion space.

* Conjugate-gradient minimization in Cartesian space.

* Perform Quasi-Newton minimization in Cartesian space.

You can set the maximum allowed number of cycles in Step 1 to be:

20 × <torsion_factor>

where <torsion_factor> is set by confAnalysis.best.torsion.factor .

The maximum allowed number of cycles in Step 2 is:

Max ( 1, ( 2 × <nCycles> × <Cartesian_CGfactor> / 9 ) )

where <nCycles> is the maximum number of minimization cycles and is automatically computed based on the number of atoms in the molecule, and <Cartesian_CGfactor> is set by confAnalysis.best.cg.factor .

The maximum allowed number of cycles in the third step is:

Max ( 0, ( <nCycles> × <Cartesian_QNfactor> - <nCGCycles>) )

where <nCycles> is the maximum number of minimization cycles, <Cartesian_QNfactor> is an integer set by confAnalysis.best.qn.factor , and <nCGCycles> is the number of cycles actually performed in the second step.

In addition, a shortcut is provided to obtain best/intermediate conformer models (which are between the fast and best models with regards to both time needed to generate them and quality of the conformers). The best/intermediate models are generated using only the second step with <Cartesian_QNfactor> set to 1. It can be turned on by setting confAnalysis.dbstd to true .

#### Further information

General Considerations for BEST Detailed Catalyst 
Parameters Catalyst Standalone Applications

# General Considerations for BEST

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_best_consider.htm

## General Considerations for BEST

##### Poling algorithm

The BEST conformation-generation routine in Catalyst uses a technique called poling (see References on poling ) to promote conformational variation. The function being minimized is modified to repel similar conformers. The addition of poling eliminates much of the redundancy in conformer generation and improves the coverage of conformational space. In general, the poling parameters do not need adjusting, and you would simply use the confAnalysis.best.no.poling parameter to turn off poling if this method is not producing desirable results. However, you may want to try changing poling parameters first.

The pole function is added to a regular molecular mechanics forcefield as an additional term:

Equation 1:

where the generalized functional form of the poling function is:

Equation 2:

and D i is defined by:

Equation 3:

D i = the root mean squared (rms) difference between the poling distances of the current conformation being poled and the corresponding distances in the j th previous conformations d ij that are within a specified rms (set by confAnalysis.best.min.rms.for.pole.confs ) computed over all N d poling distances. The weight W controls the amount of energy that the poling contributes to F total and is initially set by confAnalysis.best.pole.weight . After a defined number of conformations are generated, the weight is autoscaled so that the poling function contributes approximately the same energy to F total . D i is raised to a power of N , which controls the steepness of the poling function and can also be changed using the Catalyst.cfg parameter confAnalysis.best.pole.power .

Since choosing each interatomic distance as the poling distance ( N d in Equation 3 dramatically slows conformer generation [ 1 ], a distribution of chemically significant features (hydrogen-bond acceptors, hydrogen-bond-bond donors, and hydrophobic groups) is used. The most obvious set of poling distances would be all combinations of interfeature distances. However, this causes a quadratic increase in computation time as the number of features increases. To minimize the computational expense, Catalyst randomly selects up to a maximum of confAnalysis.best.max.poleDist.per.feature for each feature. The combined distances are the total poling distances, ND .

Poling distances between features that are in close topological proximity (fewer than 6 flexible bonds) are excluded. This significantly reduces distortion for small rigid molecules (previous versions used a value of 3) and can improve conformational coverage. The parameter confGen.minTopPolingLength controls the minimum number of flexible bonds required between poled features.

The weight is autoscaled throughout the BEST conformational analysis because the poling function must be appropriate for the other energy terms in the forcefield. If the poling energy is too high, the conformers repel each other to such an extent that it is impossible to find new low-energy conformers. If the poling energy is too low, similar conformers do not repel one another enough. The default weight is selected on the basis of scaling the poling energy to a known value ( F k ) at a known interconformer distance ( D k ). Equation 2 yields:

Equation 4:

The weight is initially set by confAnalysis.best.pole.weight . However, as the algorithm progresses, the weight is continually autoscaled to keep the pole contributions around F k (set by confAnalysis.best.conf.energy.for.pole.proximity ). D k in Equation 4 is the mean rms of the conformers being poled against, and N is the confAnalysis.best.pole.power . Autoscaling starts after confAnalysis.best.conf.count.for.pole.proximity conformers have been generated. The last confAnalysis.best.lookback.for.pole.proximity conformers are used to compute the average rms. At all times, the weight must be at least confAnalysis.best.pole.power . If the autoscaling causes the weight fall below this value, the weight is set at this minimum value.

During BEST analysis, a new conformer can be rejected for two reasons:

* The energy is above the threshold.

* The minimum rms to another conformation is less than confAnalysis.best.min.rms.for.conf.rejection .

The poling algorithm used for fast conformer analysis is similar to the algorithm used for BEST. However, for FAST, the parameters have been tuned for speed and diversity and cannot be adjusted.

##### References on poling

* [Smellie et al., 1995a]

* [Smellie et al., 1995b]

* [Smellie et al., 1995c]

##### Convergence

The BEST conformer search stops if any of three criteria are met:

* The desired maximum number of conformers is generated.

* The energy of any new conformer is too high according the predefined energy threshold, which is controlled by the -energy flag in catConf and by confAnalysis.catDB.maxEnergySpread in catDB .

* There are no possible new conformers after a certain number of trials (set by confAnalysis.best.max.successive.failures ).

##### Cis and trans configurations

Three Catalyst.cfg parameters affect the ratio of cis to trans conformers:

* confAnalysis.best.cisPeptideRatio

* confAnalysis.best.cisPeptideRatio.proline

* confAnalysis.best.cisPeptideRatio.nAlkylated

These parameters suggest the ratio of cis to trans conformers to be generated. The actual ratio may not match parameter values, since sampling is done before poling, which may remove some conformers.

##### Setting axial-equatorial ratios in rings

Axial-equatorial parameters only affect BEST conformer generation.

There are four Catalyst.cfg parameters that can be used to control the ratio of axial-equatorial centers in rings:

* confAnalysis.AxialEquatorialRatioNH

* confAnalysis.AxialEquatorialRatioNHeavy

* confAnalysis.AxialEquatorialRatioCHHeavy

* confAnalysis.AxialEquatorialRatioCHeavy2

If these values are set to a positive number, the number of axial and equatorial configurations will be affected. The values correspond to the target ratio of axial to equatorial centers that will be generated for the four groups listed: N-H, N-Heavy, C[H][Heavy], and C[Heavy][Heavy]. Setting these to a low number will result in a small number of axial centers. For example, a value of 0.1 will cause BEST conformer generation to attempt to create a conformer model that has 10% axial centers across all the conformers in the model. Setting these values to a negative number disables this control and the conformer models will be built without attempting to control the axial-equatorial ratio.

For the CHeavy2 parameter, the following logic is used to determine which ring substituent is larger. First, the bonds for atoms attached directly to the ring are counted. The atom with more bonds is larger. (e.g., -CH 3 has four bonds and -F has only one bond, thus the methyl group, -CH 3 , is larger than -F). If the number of bonds is the same, then the atomic numbers are compared. The atom with the larger atomic number is larger (e.g., -OH is smaller than -SH). If the number of bonds and the directly attached atoms are the same, both rings are considered to be of equal size. Trying to determine which group is larger beyond the above two criteria has little benefit. For example, if you want to use the molecular weights of the substituents, then you may have difficulty for a case such as this: -CH 2 -Cl and -CH(CH 3 ) 2 . The first group has a larger molecular weight than the second one, and the second group is bulkier than the first one.

# Chirality Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_chirality.htm

## Chirality Parameters

In a .mol file, chirality can be specified in the atom record, in the bond record, or via the 3D coordinates. Also, even if the chirality is set (R or S), Catalyst additionally decides if the chirality is considered to be known (absolute, e.g., R) or unknown for purposes of conformation generation (e.g., marked R? or S? ). If it is known or absolute, Catalyst assures that all conformers generated for that molecule preserve the input chirality. If it is unknown or considered unknown, Catalyst attempts to generate conformers for both chiralities. The flags import.keepMolFileChirality and import.useISISChirality control how the chirality is set and interpreted for molecules that are read from a .mol file.

Atom parity flags are used to assign chirality as known or unknown for 3D .mol files. If the flags are set to 1 or 2, the chirality is always marked as known. If the flags are set to 3, the chirality is set to unknown. If the atom parity flags are zero, the chiral centers are marked as unknown if import.keepMolFileChirality is false (default) and known if true . The actual chiral assignment (R or S) is obtained from the 3D coordinates in the file.

The parameter import.useISISChirality is used only for 2D molecules. If it is set to true (default) or if the string "-ISIS-" appears in the header section for that molecule, the bond records are preferentially used to assign absolute chiralities to the atoms. If there are no bond records, the atom parity settings are used to set chirality. If the parameter is false and there is no "-ISIS-" string in the header section, the atom parity flags are preferentially used to assign chirality. If only bond records exist, they are used to assign chirality. The following table summarizes the assignment of absolute or unknown chirality for all possible combinations (an asterisk ( * ) indicates all possibilities):

Table 1. Assignment of absolute or unknown chirality

| Value of import. KeepMolFile Chirality | Value of import. UseISISChirality parameter | Molecule dimensionality | Stereogenic atom | Atom parity | Bond parity | Resulting stereocenter assignment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| * | * | * | No | * | * | N/A |
| True | * | 3D | Yes | 0,1,2 | * | Assigned |
| False | * | 3D | Yes | 1,2 | * | Assigned |
| True | * | 3D | Yes | 3 | * | Unknown |
| * | True or ISIS | 2D | Yes | * | 1,6 | Assigned from bond |
| * | False | 2D | Yes | 1,2 | * | Assigned from atom |
| * | True or ISIS | 2D | Yes | * | 4 | Unknown |
| * | False | 2D | Yes | 3 | * | Unknown |
| * | * | 2D | Yes | 0 | 0 | Unknown |
| * | * | 2D | Yes | 1,2 | 0 | Assigned from atom |
| * | * | 2D | Yes | 0 | 1,6 | Assigned from bond |

When importing a .sd file, Catalyst evaluates each conformation to determine if it is a new molecule or a conformation of the previous molecule by comparing a canonical SMILES string. Since it is possible to have different configurations of stereo centers in the same molecule (e.g., if the chirality is marked as unknown), the default is to ignore chirality when doing the SMILES comparison. If the .sd file contains two stereoisomers, Catalyst (by default) interprets it as two conformations of the same molecule. Setting importMOL.treatStereoIsomersAsSameMol to false forces Catalyst to consider chirality in the SMILES strings. If the chirality is different, a new compound is created.

Catalyst assigns chirality in SMILES strings using bond-direction flags ( / \ ). The Catalyst SMILES convention for stereochemistry was developed before Daylight published their convention, which uses @ and @@ symbols for chirality and reserves bond-direction flags for interpreting cis and trans configurations.

By default, Catalyst attempts to read either set of symbols (bond-direction flags or @ and @@ ) to interpret chirality. However, some situations may confuse Catalyst. If the parameter importSMILES.explicitChirality is set to true , Catalyst considers only @ and @@ symbols for chirality and ignores bond-direction flags. To read Daylight SMILES strings, set this parameter to true and import the SMILES strings into Catalyst. Although this parameter can be used to read Daylight SMILES strings, Catalyst never writes standard Daylight SMILES strings. It is important that this parameter be used only for a single import, because Catalyst has difficulties assigning chirality to internally created SMILES strings when importSMILES.explicitChirality is true .

# General Considerations for FAST and BEST

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_fast-best_consider.htm

## General Considerations for FAST and BEST

##### Chirality

In Catalyst, a chiral center can be represented as absolute (the stereo center is known) or unknown (the correct configuration is unknown and marked with a "?"). This has a direct impact on the conformer-generation routines, because if a stereocenter is marked as unknown, it can be either R or S. The parameter confAnalysis.treatAcyclicNitrogenAsChiralCenter controls acyclic nitrogen configurations. If this parameter is set to true , each inversion of an acyclic nitrogen center is sampled during conformation generation.

Several other parameters control chirality (see Chirality parameters for details).

##### Removing similar conformers

You can control how the conformer-generation routines remove similar conformers to reduce redundancy in the models. If confGen.removeTopSymDuplicate is set to true , the conformers created by BEST or FAST are checked and all conformers that are separated by more than confGen.topSymRmsTol angstroms. If this parameter is set to 0.0, a more sophisticated algorithm is used (see discussion below). The algorithm checks all symmetrical mappings. If the number of possible mappings is greater than confGen.topSymMaxSymMappings , topological symmetry checking is not performed. Also, if confGen.topSymHeavyAtomOnly is set to true , only non-hydrogen atoms are considered in the rms checking.

If confGen.topSymRmsTol is 0.0 , similar conformers are identified using dual-level checking. First, the conformers are screened to determine if any two conformers are within the rms tolerance. The rms tolerance is computed as:

Equation 5:

where c is a scaling constant set by confGen.topSymRmsScalingConst , and N rot is the number of rotatable single bonds (allowing the tolerance to scale with molecular flexibility).

Any two conformers that are within this threshold are then submitted to a second level of checking, which is designed to identify conformers that have local diversity (i.e., differ greatly by one chemical group). These differences could be critical for database searching (pharmacophore identification, etc.), and should not be removed. The check is performed by computing the distances between atoms in each atom pair. If no distance is greater than a distance threshold, the higher-energy conformer is removed. The distance threshold is computed as:

Equation 6:

##### Systematic equatorial/axial ring flipping

Several parameters can be used to maximize conformational coverage for ring systems. If confAnalysis.systematicFlipAxialEquatorial is set to true , each ring conformer is submitted to the poling algorithm for minimization. The flipped version of the ring, if allowed (e.g., absolute chirality is not changed), is also submitted to the poling algorithm. To be flipped, the number of atoms in the ring must be at least confAnalysis.systematicFlipAxialEquatorialMinRingSize and not more than confAnalysis.systematicFlipAxialEquatorialMaxRingSize .

##### Separate conformer analysis for each isomer

The conformer generation algorithm 
generates conformer models for each isomer independently (controlled by confAnalysis.treatStereoIsomersSeparately ) and then combines the results. This improves the coverage of conformer models (especially for BEST), since the energy threshold, similarity measure, and poling violation are tested only within each isomer configuration. By default this technique is not used for molecules that have more than five unknown stereo centers. However, if confAnalysis.enumerateFirstFiveStereoCenters is set to true , separate isomers will be enumerated based on the first five unknown centers. The remaining combinations will not be enumerated.

The algorithm also uses a pre-filtering stage to remove redundancy before the conformer analysis is performed. Isomers that are topologically identical are removed. Also, since Catalyst implicitly considers mirror images of conformers that do not have absolute chiral centers, mirror image isomers are not explicitly generated unless confAnalysis.skipStereoIsomerMirrorImages is set to false .

# FAST Method

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_fast.htm

## FAST Method

The fast conformation-generation method uses one of three different algorithms depending on the size of the molecule. The conformational space of small molecules is generated using an efficient systematic search. Conformers for molecules that are neither too small nor too large , as measured by the flexibility of the molecule, are generated with a random search method that uses poling. If the molecule is too large , only one conformation is generated for each possible combination of stereocenters.

### Fast conformer generation for small molecules

Catalyst uses a quasi-exhaustive systematic search for small molecules. The conformational space is composed of discretized rotations about the rotatable bonds. These values are set using these parameters:

* sysSearch.sp3sp3SearchOffset

* sysSearch.sp3sp3SearchIncrement

* sysSearch.sp2sp2SearchIncrement

* sysSearch.sp2sp2SearchOffset

* sysSearch.sp3sp2SearchIncrement

* sysSearch.sp3sp2SearchOffset

The number of theoretical conformers is computed using a function that depends on the number of rotatable bonds, the number of possible torsion values for each rotatable bond, and the number of ring conformations. A systematic search is used if the number of theoretical conformations is less than confAnalysis.fast.systematic.upperbound .

Catalyst systematically searches the conformational space and removes conformations that have excessive van der Waals clashes. van der Waals scaling is controlled with the parameters sysSearch.sysSearch14VDWScale for 1-4 nonbond interactions and sysSearch.sysSearch1NVDWScale for other nonbond interactions. Catalyst checks for similarity between conformations by computing pairwise root mean squared (rms) errors and removes any that are within a certain threshold (for more information, see General Considerations for FAST and BEST ).

The selection of systematic or random sampling in fast conformer generation is controlled by confAnalysis.fast.systematic.upperbound .

Increasing this value may increase computation time.

### Fast conformer generation for medium-sized molecules

Catalyst uses a random search method with poling to generate conformers for medium-sized molecules. The molecule is split into pieces, a systematic search is performed on each piece, and then the pieces are randomly reconnected. Each new conformation is optimized using the poling algorithm. The poling parameters are preset for optimal performance and cannot be changed.

As in best-quality conformation generation, the conformations are generated until convergence is reached (for details, see General Considerations for FAST ). Conformer generation stops when no conformers within the energy threshold are found after N ( confAnalysis.fast.random.nAttempt ) consecutive attempts. If you want Catalyst to make more initial generation attempts before quitting, increase the confAnalysis.fast.random.nAttempt parameter.

### Fast conformer generation for large molecules

If the number of rotatable bonds is greater than confAnalysis.fast.maxRotatableBonds , Catalyst creates only one conformation for every possible combination of stereocenters.

# General Considerations for FAST

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_fast_consider.htm

## General Considerations for FAST

##### Ring fragments

To reduce the time needed to generate conformers, you can set Catalyst to not re-compute common structural motifs. If so, ring conformations are computed using distance geometry and the results are stored. When the same ring is found in a new molecule, previously generated ring conformations are reused. When Catalyst exits, the cached ring conformations are written to a file called fragments.data, which contains only ring fragments. On subsequent runs, this file is read to reuse the fragment conformations. This method makes the fast conformation-generation routine run faster. However, if you start with a different fragments.data file, the final conformations might be slightly different even though other initial conditions are the same.

Two Catalyst.cfg parameters control reading and writing the fragments.data file:

* confAnalysis.fast.readFragments

* confAnalysis.fast.writeFragments

Both are set to false by default, which means that the conformation-generation routine does not read a fragments.data file when it starts and does not write a file when it finishes.

The module for creating databases (catDB) also has two parameters that control reading and writing the fragments.data file:

* confAnalysis.catDB.fast.readFragments

* confAnalysis.catDB.fast.writeFragments

These are true by default. Therefore, if a fragments.data file exists in the run directory, catDB reads it and reuses the ring conformations by default and writes a new file when done.

The related parameter confAnalysis.fast.useFragments can be used to turn off the reuse of ring conformations for all fast conformation-generation routines including catDB. If this parameter is false , a new ring conformation is created whenever needed, with no regard to previous ring conformations.

##### Convergence

The random conformational search of FAST stops if any of the following conditions are met:

* The desired maximum number of conformers is generated

* The energy of any new conformer is too high according the predefined energy threshold confAnalysis.fast.maxEnergySpread (or confAnalysis.catDB.maxEnergySpread for catDB).

* When there are no possible new conformers after a certain number of trials, as set by confAnalysis.fast.random.nAttempt .

##### Algorithm information

Catalyst uses different conformer-generation algorithms depending on the size of the molecule. If confAnalysis.fast.printAlgorithmChange is true , a message is printed if poling (medium-sized molecules) is used or if only one conformer (large molecules) will be generated.

# Detailed Catalyst Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/catalyst_detailed_parameters.htm

## Detailed Catalyst Parameters

Many Catalyst parameters can be changed by using the Catalyst.cfg file, which is read when the Catalyst interface or a background job is started. Catalyst looks for the Catalyst.cfg file in the run directory first, and then in your home directory. Only one file is used per session. The Catalyst.cfg file is only read at startup, so you must change parameters before starting Catalyst.

Example :

```text
importMOL.realCompoundNameProperty=Name
```

Type: string Default: Name Description: For MOL/SD import, what 1D property overrides header compound name

If you want your component name to be replaced with the value in the <compound_id> property of the .sd file, replace Name with

```text
importMOL.realCompoundNameProperty="compound_id"
```

#### Default values

For parameters not defined in the Catalyst.cfg file, Catalyst uses the appropriate default values. All non-default Catalyst.cfg parameters used in the session are written to standard output.

The default parameter values produce the best results in most situations. However, you may occasionally need to change the values. This topic describes the parameters that can be adjusted to change the behavior of Catalyst.

### Parameters affecting conformation generation

Catalyst includes two types of conformer-generation routines: fast and best quality. Both methods generate conformers that provide broad coverage of the accessible conformational space. Fast generation takes less time, but best-quality generation provides more complete coverage of conformational space by optimizing the conformers in both torsional and Cartesian space, and by using poling. The fast method also uses poling, but only when necessary.

* FAST Method

* General Considerations for FAST

* BEST Method

* General Considerations for BEST

* General Considerations for FAST and BEST

* Chirality Parameters

## Catalyst Parameters

The Catalyst.cfg file is read from the run directory when a Catalyst 
command-line
executable is started. While these Catalyst configuration parameters allow
great flexibility and control in the use of Catalyst, the default
parameters are usually sufficient for most projects.

Carefully review each parameter before using it.

### Using a catalyst parameter file for defaults

If you find that there are a few parameters that you want to use for all your pharmacophore protocols, it
is possible to create a default Catalyst.cfg file that will be used for every run.

To use a catalyst parameter file for defaults

* Use a text editor to create a Catalyst.cfg file. This file contains the parameter name and the
parameter value. For example: // Comments are allowed
sysSearch.sp3sp3SearchOffset=120.0
confAnalysis.fast.printAlgorithmChange=TRUE

```text
// Comments are allowed
sysSearch.sp3sp3SearchOffset=120.0
confAnalysis.fast.printAlgorithmChange=TRUE
```

* Place this file in your user directory on the a Pipeline Pilot Server : <PP_INSTALL_DIR>/public/users/<user-name>/

A Catalyst.cfg file located in this directory will be used for all jobs unless a different file is specified using the
Catalyst Parameter File which will be used preferentially.

The following parameters affect conformation generation:

* Fast conformation generation

* Best-quality conformation generation

* Poling parameters

* Fast and best-quality conformation generation

* Chirality parameters

The following parameters affect hypotheses:

* HypoGen, HipHop, and HypoRefine

* Clustering and compare/fit

## Running Catalyst

Follow these instructions to run the standalone Catalyst executables on 
your local machine and
access advanced functionality from the command line.
For detailed information on how to run these applications from the
command line, see Using Catalyst .

The following runs a wrapper script (.bat or .sh depending on the platform) that invokes the specified Catalyst executable.

```text
<installation folder>\bin\<executable name>
```

where <installation folder> is your Discovery Studio installation folder.
This command displays help for the catalyst executable. To access functionality, you must include appropriate command
line arguments. More information can be found in Using Catalyst .

The following main Catalyst executables are available:

* catConf

* catDB

* catHypo

* catSearch

* citest

# Using Catalyst

Source type: HTML

## Using Catalyst

This section documents these executables and provides information about Catalyst configuration parameters
(previously known as .Catalyst parameters) that can be used to access advanced
functionality. Each of the executables have many command line 
arguments that can be used to access different algorithms. Details
of these parameters can be found in the following sections:

| Executable | Description |
| --- | --- |
| catConf | Take input files of compounds and produce output conformational models (sets of conformers) for each input compound. |
| catDB | Create, modify, move, delete and get summary information about a Catalyst database. |
| catHypo | Automatically generate hypothesis models. |
| catSearch | Search or browse a Catalyst database. |
| citest | Compute Compare/Fit operations between two objects geometrically and/or functionally by aligning features in one object with a similar set of features in another object. |

Most of the functionality can be accessed using these executables and the 
associated command line arguments. However, on occasion, you may find
it necessary to access advanced functionality that is only available 
using Catalyst configuration parameters. This is done by editing a text
file called Catalyst.cfg, adding the appropriate parameters and their values to 
the text file, and then placing it in the directory where you run 
the command line executable. The following topics cover the Catalyst 
configuration parameters in more detail:

* Catalyst Parameters

* Detailed Catalyst Parameters

# CHARMm

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

## CHARMm

Chemistry at HARvard Macromolecular Mechanics (CHARMm) is a versatile and widely 
used molecular simulation program.

CHARMm is installed by default as part of the Discovery Studio Collection within
an instance of a Pipeline Pilot Server . You can access it directly from
the Pipeline Pilot Client using the "Run CHARMm" and "Run CHARMm Script" components. 
Additionally, many of the protocols available from the Discovery Studio Client
make use of the CHARMm program.

Although many CHARMm functionalities are available through the components and protocols, more advanced functionality can be accessed by running CHARMm from the command line. The script to launch the CHARMm executable is available on the server in the bin folder of your Discovery Studio installation . For full details on how
to run the application from the command line, see Running CHARMm .

#### Further information

Running CHARMm Using CHARMm

# Running CHARMm

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/charmm_running.htm

## Running CHARMm

Follow these
instructions to run the full standalone version of CHARMm on your local machine and
access advanced functionality from the command line. For detailed information on how to use CHARMm from the
command line, see Using CHARMm .

CHARMm can be run on multiple processors using the message
passing interface (MPI). Discovery Studio automatically runs the correct
command for distributing CHARMm on the processors within a
machine. For more control, (e.g., to distribute CHARMm across
machines), you can modify the command to invoke mpirun
with the desired options. Additional information can be found in the Discovery Studio User
Guide.

### Command-line options

To run CHARMm from the command-line, use the charmm command available
in the bin folder of your server installation:

### LINUX

```text
<pps_install>
/apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin/charmm
```

where <pps_install> is the location of your Pipeline Pilot Server installation. 
This runs a wrapper script (.bat or .sh depending on the platform) which
then invokes one of the CHARMm executables.

```text
<pps_install>
```

Provide an input file and optionally capture the output using
standard input and output specifiers. For example, to read an input
file named energy.inp, use the following syntax:

```text
<pps_install>
/apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin/charmm < energy.inp
```

Use the following syntax to write the output to a file:

```text
<pps_install>
/apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin/charmm < energy.inp > energy.log
```

To run CHARMm on multiple processors, include the -np option. You must specify
the number of processors to be used:

```text
<pps_install>
/apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin/charmm -np <number>
```

Finally, you can view help for the available options by using the -h option:

```text
<pps_install>
/apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin/charmm -h
```

### Windows

On Windows, use the following syntax:

```text
"C:\Program Files\BIOVIA\PPS\apps\scitegic\dscore\server\bin\charmm.bat" < energy.inp
```

There is a limitation on the size of the input stream file on windows.
For larger stream files, we suggest creating a smaller script that just
streams the larger one.

# CNX

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/cnx.htm

## CNX

Crystallography and NMR eXplorer (CNX) is a software program suite for 
three-dimensional structure determination and analysis of macromolecules
using experimental crystallographic diffraction or nuclear magnetic resonance
(NMR) data.

CNX is based on the widely used programs X-PLOR and CNS. X-PLOR version 1.0 was
originally released in 1987 as a software package to combine single crystal
X-ray diffraction data and molecular dynamics for refinement [Brünger et al., 1987] .
Since then, X-PLOR has evolved into CNS and CNX.

The CNX application is installed by default as part of the Discovery Studio Collection
within an instance of a Pipeline Pilot Server . You can use the Pipeline Pilot Client or Discovery Studio Client to access the functionality via protocols supplied in the X-ray collection.

Although many CNX functionalities are available through the components and protocols, more advanced functionality can be accessed by running CNX from the command line. The script to launch the executable is 
available on the server in the bin folder of your Discovery Studio installation . For full details on how
to run the application from the command line, see Running CNX .

#### Further information

Running CNX Using CNX

==============================================================================================================
DOCUMENT 730
==============================================================================================================

# Running CNX

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/cnx_running.htm

## Running CNX

Follow these instructions to run the standalone version of CNX and the associated utility
programs on your local machine and access advanced functionality from the command line.
For detailed information on how to these applications from the command line, see Using CNX .

CNX includes the main CNX application and a number of utility programs that are run
from the apps/scitegic/dsxray/server/lib folder of a Linux server installation and
from the apps/scitegic/dsxray/server/bin folder of a Windows server installation.
The programs can also be invoked with the help of wrapper scripts located in the
apps/scitegic/dsxray/server/bin folder of a Linux or Windows server installation.
On the Windows platform, the wrapper scripts are Windows batch files named
<PROGRAM>.bat where <PROGRAM> is the name of the program, e.g.
cnx for the main CNX application.
On the Linux platform, the wrapper scripts are simply named after the program.
The wrapper scripts ensure that the environment required by all programs is set correctly.

However, to run CNX programs, some additional preparation may be necessary.

On the Windows platform, the PATH environment variable must include the location
of dynamic link libraries provided with the BIOVIA License Pack installation.
By default, this location is C:/Program Files (x86)/Common Files/BIOVIA/LicensePack.

On the Linux platform, the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable must include the
location of shared object libraries provided with the BIOVIA License Pack installation
as well as the location of shared object libraries provided with the scitegic/dsxray
package installation.
If <LP> is the BIOVIA License Pack installation directory, then
LD_LIBRARY_PATH needs to include the directory <LP>/linux/lib.
If <SERVER> is the server installation directory, then
LD_LIBRARY_PATH needs to also include the directory
<SERVER>/apps/scitegic/dsxray/server/lib.
In addition, the BIOVIA_LIC_PACK_DIR environment variable needs to be set to
the location of the BIOVIA License Pack installation directory.

Finally, on both the Windows and the Linux platform, the ACCELRYS_CNX environment
variable should be set to identify the location of CNX data files and scripts.
If <SERVER> is the server installation directory, then
the location is <SERVER>/apps/scitegic/dsxray/server/share/cnx/cnx.

Starting with Discovery Studio 2018, only 64-bit versions of the
CNX application and its associated utility programs are released.
However, the 64-bit versions can no longer take advantage of OpenMP shared memory
multiprocessing.
This limitation also requires that the environment variable OMP_NUM_THREADS is set to 1.

The following table describes the available programs and the
command used to run them:

| Program | Description |
| --- | --- |
| cnx | The cnx program is the main executable of the CNX Software Package. The program is most efficiently used via a set of CNX scripts that provide all the required input parameters for running the job. |
| genasf | The genasf program is a utility for creating a library file that contains the anomalous contribution to the atomic scattering factors at a user-specified wavelength. This library file can be used for running multiple anomalous dispersion (MAD) and single anomalous dispersion (SAD) phasing calculations. |
| PSmapx, PSmapy, and PSmapz | These programs are used in the generation of a Patterson Map and for visual analysis of the Harker sections. You can access these programs with the plot_patterson script. You can run the script after generating a CNX style map after the Patterson peak search to convert it to a postscript style map that can be visualized and printed. |
| to_cnx | The to_cnx program is a portable utility for converting scalepack or d*Trek style files to CNX format. |

### Command-line options

#### CNX

The input and output for the CNX program can be specified,
using standard input and output specifiers. For example, to read an input
file, map.inp, use the following from the command line:

```text
<installation folder>\bin\cnx < map.inp
```

Output is written to standard output, but can be saved to a file
as follows:

```text
<installation folder>\bin\cnx < map.inp > map.out
```

#### genasf

Only one parameter is required for running the genasf program. A value between 29.3 and 30,000 eV must be used.
The output file is named "anom.lib". For example, the following will create an anom.lib file for an anomalous contribution to atomic scattering factors
at a wavelength of 100 eV:

```text
<installation folder>\bin\genasf
```

```text
100
```

#### PSmapx, PSmapy, PSmapz

These executables are called internally by the plot_patterson script. After generating a Patterson map in CNX format
you can run the script and provide the appropriate content as follows:

In Linux please refer to this example of running the script:

```text
>./plot_patterson
```

```text
patterson map file -> patterson_map_x.map
```

```text
patterson plane (x/y/z) -> x
```

```text
postscript plot file [patterson.ps] -> patterson_x.ps
```

```text
minimum contour level [2.0] ->
```

```text
contour increment [0.5] ->
```

```text
plot scale factor [0.06] ->
```

```text
plot title -> Patterson Plot Axis X
```

Parameters left blank will use the values provided in the brackets "[ ]".

#### to_cnx

To execute the to_cnx program, provide input as follows:

```text
<installation folder>\bin\to_cnx file.sca file.cv
```

In this example, the output in CNX format is written to a file.cv. Additional options include:

```text
[-f hkl|dtrek] [-nomean]
```

These options allow for specification of the file format (i.e., scalepack [*.sca or *.hkl] or d*trek) and the option to not
include the mean intensities for anomalous d*trek files.

# MODELER

Source type: HTML

Source section: scientificapplications

Source file: scientificapplications/modeler.htm

## MODELER

MODELER is a program package that provides scientific algorithms used for building homology models including protein
sequence alignment, structure alignment, sequence similarity searching, model generation, and model refinements. Typically,
an alignment of a sequence to be modeled with known related structures is provided and MODELER automatically builds
one or more 3-dimensional structures for the model sequence.

The MODELER program is installed by default as part of the Discovery Studio Collection within
an instance of a Pipeline Pilot Server . You can access this functionality from the Pipeline Pilot Client via Protein Modeling components such as Align3D and Build Models.
Additionally, many of the Macromolecules protocols 
available through the Discovery Studio Client also make use of MODELER.

However, not all of the MODELER functionality is available through the components and protocols. More advanced functionality can be accessed by running MODELER from the command line. See the section on Running Modeler for details.

Running MODELER Using MODELER

## Abbreviation property

### Description

Abbreviation is the common three character representation of the Residue.
For example, the abbreviations for "Alanine" and "Adenosine" are "Ala" and "Ade".

| Abbreviation | Standard amino acids |
| --- | --- |
| Ala | Alanine |
| Arg | Arginine |
| Asn | Asparagine |
| Asp | Aspartic Acid |
| Cys | Cysteine |
| Gln | Glutamine |
| Glu | Glutamic Acid |
| Gly | Glycine |
| His | Histidine |
| Ile | Isoleucine |
| Leu | Leucine |
| Lys | Lysine |
| Met | Methionine |
| Phe | Phenylalanine |
| Pro | Proline |
| Ser | Serine |
| Thr | Threonine |
| Trp | Tryptophan |
| Tyr | Tyrosine |
| Val | Valine |

| Abbreviation | Non-standard amino acids |
| --- | --- |
| Aib | Methylalanine |
| Asx | Asparagine" or "Aspartic Acid |
| Cse | Selenocysteine |
| Glx | Glutamine" or "Glutamic Acid |
| Mse | Selenomethionine |
| Orn | Ornithine |
| Pca | Pyroglutamate |
| Ptr | Phosphotyrosine |
| Sep | Phosphoserine |
| Tpo | Phosphothreonine |
| Tys | Sulfotyrosine |

| Abbreviation | Standard nucleotides |
| --- | --- |
| Ade | Adenosine |
| Gua | Guanosine |
| Thy | Thymidine |
| Cyt | Cytosine |
| Urd | Uridine |

| Abbreviation | Non-standard nucleotides |
| --- | --- |
| 5MC | 5-methyl Cytosine |
| 2MG | 5-methyl Guanosine |
| 1MG | 1-methyl Guanosine |
| H2U | Dihydro Uridine |
| M2G | Dimethyl Guanosine |
| 5MU | 5-methyl Uridine |
| 1MA | 1-methyl Adenosine |
| OMC | O-methyl Cytosine |
| OMG | O-methyl Guanosine |
| OMU | O-methyl Uridine |
| PSU | Pseudo Uridine |
| 7MG | 7-methyl Guanosine |
| Ino | Inosine |

| Abbreviation | Other residues |
| --- | --- |
| Ace | Acetyl |
| Unk | Unknown |

### Applies to

The Abbreviation property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::AminoAcid , Mdm::NucleicAcid , Mdm::Nucleotide , Mdm::Residue , Sdm::Residue

### Using the Abbreviation property

#### Get

my $stringValue = $object->Abbreviation;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $stringValue | | | String |
| $object | | | Mdm::AminoAcid Mdm::NucleicAcid Mdm::Nucleotide Mdm::Residue Sdm::Residue |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript , SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate use of residue abbreviation property.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Mdm::Document::CreateFromPdbId('1crn');

my $index = 0;
my $residues = $document->Residues;
foreach my $residue (@$residues)
{
++$index;
print "Residue at $index is " . $residue->Abbreviation . "\n";
}
```

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate how to inset residue abbreviations.
use strict;
use SdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Sdm::Document::CreateProteinDocument();
my $sequence = $document->Sequences->Item(0);

# Inset standard and non-standard residues and gaps
$sequence->InsetAbbreviations( 0, "AlaGly---AlaGlxTpo" );
$document->UpdateViews();

# List residues
my $count = $sequence->ResidueCount;
for ( my $i = 0 ; $i < $count ; ++$i )
{
my $residue = $sequence->Residue($i);
print $residue->Abbreviation;
}

Mdm::PlanarPeptideViolationMonitor , Mdm::PlaneFeature , Mdm::PlaneMonitor , Mdm::PointFeature , Mdm::PointOffsetFeature , Mdm::Polydot , Mdm::PropertyLabel , Mdm::ProteinChiralityViolationMonitor , Mdm::ProteinNomenclatureViolationMonitor , Mdm::ProteinPose , Mdm::Query , Mdm::QueryAtom , Mdm::QueryBond , Mdm::QueryFeatureMap , Mdm::QueryOperator , Mdm::Residue , Mdm::Restraint , Mdm::RingAromaticFeature , Mdm::RotatableBondMonitor , Mdm::ScreenLabel , Mdm::Set , Mdm::ShapeFeature , Mdm::SideChainConformationViolationMonitor , Mdm::SlicingPlane , Mdm::Sphere , Mdm::Surface , ### Using the AcceptorFeatures filter

#### Get

my $arrayObject = $object->AcceptorFeatures;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $arrayObject | | | Mdm::Array |
| $object | | | Objects listed as Applies to |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
use strict;
use DSCommands;

# Create a query from a template molecules. Add HBAs to =O,
# HBD to N, and excluded volumes to all Halogens and
# projection points of HBAs and HBDs.

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();

$document->InsertFromSmiles(
'OC(=O)C1=CC=C(C=C1)CN/C2=C/C=C(C=C2)C=CC(=O)C[Cl]');
AddHydrogens($document);

my $atoms = $document->Molecules()->Item(0)->Atoms;
my $double_bond_oxygens = Mdm::Array::Create();
my $nitrogens = Mdm::Array::Create();
my $halogens = Mdm::Array::Create();

foreach my $atom (@$atoms)
{
if ( ( $atom->Element eq 'O' ) && ( $atom->BondCount == 1 ) )
{
$double_bond_oxygens->AddItem($atom);
}
$nitrogens->AddItem($atom) if ( $atom->Element eq 'N' );
$halogens->AddItem($atom) if ( $atom->Element =~ /(Cl|F|Br|I)\b/i );
}

# Create empty query
my $query1 = $document->CreateQuery();

# Create top level fit operator
my $fitOperator = $query1->CreateQueryOperator('queryFit');

# Features and location constraints
my $featureCount = 0;
foreach my $atom (@$double_bond_oxygens)
{
++$featureCount;
my $acceptorOperator = $fitOperator->CreateQueryOperator('queryInclude');
my $featureName = "HBA_" . $featureCount;
$acceptorOperator->Name($featureName);
my $newAcceptor = $acceptorOperator->CreateAcceptorFeature($atom);

# create the location constraints
my $locationfeatureHead =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newAcceptor->HeadFeature(), 2.2 );
my $locationfeatureTail =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newAcceptor->TailFeature(), 1.6 );
}

foreach my $atom (@$nitrogens)
{
++$featureCount;
my $featureName = "HBD_" . $featureCount;
my $donorOperator = $fitOperator->CreateQueryOperator('queryInclude');
$donorOperator->Name($featureName);
my $newDonor = $donorOperator->CreateDonorFeature($atom);

#create the location constraints
my $locationfeatureHead =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newDonor->HeadFeature(), 2.2 );
my $locationfeatureTail =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newDonor->TailFeature(), 1.6 );
}

# Add excluded volumes at the location of halogen atoms
foreach my $atom (@$halogens)
{
my $exclusionFeature = $fitOperator->CreateExclusionFeature( $atom, 1.2 );
}

# Add excluded volumes at the projection point of HBAs and HBDs
my $acceptorfeatures = $fitOperator->AcceptorFeatures;
foreach my $acceptor (@$acceptorfeatures)
{
my $molecule = $document->CreateMolecule();
my $atom = $molecule->CreateAtom("O");
$atom->XYZ = $acceptor->HeadXYZ();
$molecule->Select();

my $exclusionFeature = $fitOperator->CreateExclusionFeature( $atom, 1.2 );
}

my $donorfeatures = $fitOperator->DonorFeatures;
foreach my $donor (@$donorfeatures)
{
my $molecule = $document->CreateMolecule();
my $atom = $molecule->CreateAtom("O");
$atom->XYZ = $donor->HeadXYZ();
$molecule->Select();

my $exclusionFeature = $fitOperator->CreateExclusionFeature( $atom, 1.2 );
}

my $exclusionfeatures = $document->ExclusionFeatures();
my $exclusionfeatureCount = 0;
foreach my $exclusionfeature (@$exclusionfeatures)
{
++$exclusionfeatureCount;
my $name = "EV_" . $exclusionfeatureCount;
$exclusionfeature->Name($name);
}

# We will delete temporary atoms used to create EVs
# on projection points. Need to update objects before
# deleting so we preserve the X,Y,Z location.
$document->UpdateObjects();

# Delete temporary atoms
$document->DeleteObjects();
```

# ActivateFirstFrame function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/activatefirstframe_function.htm

## ActivateFirstFrame function

### Description

ActivateFirstFrame activates the first frame in an MDM animation. The active animation frame is the
only visible frame. When no animation frame is active, all animation frames are visible.

### Applies to

The ActivateFirstFrame function can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Animation

### Using the ActivateFirstFrame function

#### Instance

my $booleanValue = $object->ActivateFirstFrame();

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $booleanValue | | | Boolean |
| $object | | | Mdm::Animation |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
#
# NOTE: This script MUST be run from the DS client.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

sub Usage()
{
print "This example script is intended to run inside Discovery Studio.\n";
print "To run this script:\n";
print " 1 Start Discovery Studio.\n";
print " 2 Open a Molecule Window containing conformations.\n";
print " 3 Run this script within Discovery Studio.\n";
exit;
}

# Opens a molecule with conformations from the active Molecule Window.
my $document = DiscoveryScript::LastActiveDocument(MdmModelType);
Usage() unless ($document);
Usage() unless ( !DiscoveryScript::IsStandalone() );
Usage() unless ( $document->Conformations->Count > 0 );

print "Create an animation using conformation objects.\n";
my $animation = $document->CreateAnimation( $document->Conformations );
my $frameCount = $animation->FrameCount;
print "Number of animation frames: $frameCount frames.\n";

print "Saving the first frame to file.\n";
$animation->ActivateFirstFrame();
$document->Save( "FirstFrame.mol2", "mol2" );

# Illustrate how to activate the next and previous frames.
$animation->ActivateNextFrame();
$animation->ActivatePreviousFrame();

print "Saving the last frame to file.\n";
$animation->ActivateLastFrame();
$document->Save( "LastFrame.mol2", "mol2" );

print "Removing the first frame.\n";
my $firstFrame = $document->Conformations->Item(0);
$animation->RemoveFrame($firstFrame);

print "Adding the first frame back.\n";
$animation->AddFrame($firstFrame);
my $isTracked = $animation->IsFrameSelectionTracked();
if ($isTracked)
{
print "Frame selection is tracked.\n";
}
else
{
print "Frame selection is not tracked.\n";
}

print "Removing and de-activating all animation frames.\n";
$animation->RemoveAllFrames();
$animation->ResetFrame();

ActivateWindow sets the Discovery Studio client focus to

Chart::Document , DiscoveryScript::Document , Ffdm::Document , Mdm::Document , Protocol::Document , Sdm::Document

#### Instance

$object->ActivateWindow();

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $object | | | Objects listed as Applies to |

#### Defined by

DiscoveryStudioScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Illustrate how to invoke a Discovery Studio action (client only).
use strict;
use DiscoveryStudioScript;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document1crn = Mdm::Document::CreateFromPdbId('1crn');
my $document9ins = Mdm::Document::CreateFromPdbId('9ins');

print "Displaying hierarchy view...\n\n";
$document1crn->InvokeAction('ActionViewHierarchy');
$document9ins->InvokeAction('ActionViewHierarchy');

print "After opening PDB file 9ins, focus is on 9ins...\n\n";
sleep(3);

print "Set DiscoveryStudio focus on 1crn (client only)...\n\n";
$document1crn->ActivateWindow();
sleep(3);

print "Set DiscoveryStudio focus on 9ins (client only)...\n\n";

print "Activate 1crn window and select all 1crn objects...\n\n";

# NOTE: Since InvokeAction only applies if the script is run within\

# function SelectAll. For example:

#$document1crn->ActivateWindow() if (not DiscoveryScript::IsStandalone());
$document1crn->InvokeAction('ActionSelectAll');

print 'Is 1crn window active? ' . $document1crn->IsActiveWindow() . "\n";

Source type: HTML

## ActiveDocument property

### Description

ActiveDocument returns the currently active document, if any. If you are
running from the Script Window this will probably be the Script
document itself. You should check the document type via ClassName before
accessing document specific functionality. See also LastActiveDocument. Note:
When run outside of DS, this will always return a null object.

### Applies to

The ActiveDocument property can be used with the following objects:

DiscoveryScript

### Using the ActiveDocument property

#### Static Get

my $documentObject = DiscoveryScript::ActiveDocument();

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $documentObject | | | DiscoveryScript::Document |
| $object | | | DiscoveryScript |

#### Defined by

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# This script illustrates how connect to active documents.
# NOTE: This script MUST be run from the DS client.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

# Check that script is being run from within Discovery Studio
if ( DiscoveryScript::IsStandalone() )
{
print "This example script is intended to run inside Discovery Studio.\n";
print "Please load Discovery Studio and try again.\n";
exit;
}

# Get the current active Discovery Studio document.
# NOTE: This may produce a warning if there is no scripting
# interface the active document.
my $document = DiscoveryScript::ActiveDocument();
if ($document)
{
printf "The current active document is type: %s\n", $document->ClassName;
}

# Get the last active MDM document (Molecule Window) in Discovery Studio.
my $document2 = DiscoveryScript::LastActiveDocument(MdmModelType);
if ($document2)
{
printf "I have an Mdm document, type: %s\n", $document2->ClassName;
}
