```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# This script illustrates how to check if two perl references
# refer to the same molecular data model object.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();
$document->InsertFromSmiles('c1ccccc1');

my $atoms = $document->Atoms;
my $count = $atoms->Count;
my $random = int( rand($count) );

# Reference an random atom in the document.
my $randomAtom = $atoms->Item($random);

for ( my $i = 0 ; $i < $count ; ++$i )
{
print "Random atom is atom $i\n"
if ( $atoms->Item($i)->UniqueId == $randomAtom->UniqueId );
}
```

# UnlockVisibility function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

## UnlockVisibility function

### Description

UnlockVisibility unlocks the visibility state of selected objects.

### Applies to

The UnlockVisibility function can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Document

### Using the UnlockVisibility function

#### Command

$object->UnlockVisibility( [unlock] );

$object->UnlockVisibility( { Unlock => [unlock] } );

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [unlock] | Optional | True | Boolean |
| $object | | | Mdm::Document |

When used within the Discovery
Studio Client, this function will 
result in interactive updates.

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Illustrate the IsVisible and IsSelected properties.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Mdm::Document::CreateFromPdbId('1crn');

# lock the visibility of the first molecule
$document->Molecules()->Item(0)->Select;
$document->LockVisibility( );
$document->DeselectAll( );

my $object = $document->Atoms->Item(0);

my $visible = $object->IsVisible;
if ($visible) # Implicit check for non-zero (i.e. True) values.
{
print "Do something when the object is visible.\n";
}

my $selected = $object->IsSelected;
if ( !$selected ) # Implicit check for zero (i.e. False) values.
{
print "Do something when the object is not selected.\n";
}
```

```text
use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use strict;

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . "3fzm.pdb" );
die "Failed to create a valid MDM document!" unless $document;

my $ligandNonbondMonitor =
$document->CreateLigandNonbondMonitor(
{RequirePredefinedLigand=>False});

$document->FocusOnFirstLigand;
my $ligand = $document->LigandInFocus;
$ligandNonbondMonitor->IsNonbondTypeShown(Mdm::nonInteracting) = True;

for (my $index = 0; $index < 3; ++$index)
{
my $unsatisfiedNonbonds = $ligandNonbondMonitor->UnsatisfiedNonbonds;

printf "Shell: %d\n", $ligandNonbondMonitor->Shell;
foreach my $unsatisfied (@$unsatisfiedNonbonds)
{
printf "Unsatisfied interaction on atom %s of type(s) %s\n", 
$unsatisfied->Name, $unsatisfied->ChemistryName;
}

$ligandNonbondMonitor->ExpandShell();
$document->UpdateViews();
}
```

# UntileMolecules function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/untilemolecules_function.htm

## UntileMolecules function

### Description

UntileMolecules restores tiled molecules to their original positions.

### Applies to

The UntileMolecules function can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Document

### Using the UntileMolecules function

#### Instance

$object->UntileMolecules();

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $object | | | Mdm::Document |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate how to tile the Molecule Window.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();
$document->EnableUpdateViews(False);

# Create SMILES for several small molecules.
my %molecules = (
'benzene' => 'C1=CC=CC=C1',
'aspirin' => 'C(=O)(O)c1ccccc1OC(=O)C',
'acetaminophen' => 'O=C(O)Nc1ccc(O)cc1',
'dioxin' => 'ClC1=CC2=C(C=C1Cl)OC3=C(C=C(C(=C3)Cl)Cl)O2'
);
while ( my ( $name, $smiles ) = each(%molecules) )
{
$document->InsertFromSmiles($smiles);

my $index = $document->Molecules->Count - 1;
my $molecule = $document->Molecules->Item($index);
$molecule->Name = $name;
my $labelObject = $molecule->CreateLabel($name);
}

$document->AddHydrogenAtoms();
$document->EnableUpdateViews(True);

print "Displaying all molecules in the original layout...\n";
sleep(3);

print "Displaying all molecules after TileMolecules...\n";
$document->TileMolecules();
sleep(3);

print "Displaying all molecules after UntileMolecules...\n";
$document->UntileMolecules();
```

# UpdateAlignment function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/updatealignment_function.htm

## UpdateAlignment function

### Description

UpdateAlignment modifies the gapss positions based on data in an alignment file.
If a sequences with matching sequential residues and
matching Name is found in the supplied alignment file,
the gap positions are updated to match.

### Applies to

The UpdateAlignment function can be used with the following objects:

Sdm::Alignment

### Using the UpdateAlignment function

#### Instance

$object->UpdateAlignment( <path>, [formattype] );

$object->UpdateAlignment( { Path => <path>, FormatType => [formattype] } );

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <path> | Required | | String |
| [formattype] | Optional | "" | String |
| $object | | | Sdm::Alignment |

#### Defined by

SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate how to use UpdateAlignment function.
use strict;
use SdmDiscoveryScript;

my $samplesFolder = $ENV{ACCELRYS_ROOT} . '/share/Samples/';
my $filePath = $samplesFolder . 'GPCR Alignment.bsml';

my $document = DiscoveryScript::Open($filePath);
my $alignment = $document->Alignment;

# Remove all gaps.
$alignment->SelectAll();
$alignment->DeleteSelectedGaps();
$alignment->DeselectAll();
sleep(3);

# Load gaps from file.
$alignment->UpdateAlignment($filePath);
$document->UpdateViews();

printf "sequence count: %3d\n",$document->SequenceCount; 
my $index = 0;
while ( $index < $document->SequenceCount )
{
my $sequence = $document->Sequence($index);

print 'Sequence: ' . ++$index . "\t";
print 'Name: "' . $sequence->Name . "\"\n\t";
print 'Description: "' . $sequence->Description . "\"\n\t";
print 'Locus: "' . $sequence->Locus . "\"\n\t";
print 'Gene name: "' . $sequence->GeneName . "\"\n\t";
print 'Residues: ', $sequence->SequenceString . "\n";
}
```

# UpdateFeatures function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/updatefeatures_function.htm

## UpdateFeatures function

### Description

UpdateFeatures adds, replaces, or merges Sdm::Feature objects
from the specified sequence to the current sequence object.
The following parameters are available:

* FromSequence is the Sdm::Sequence with features to be
incorporated in to the current sequence object.

* ActionType is an enum Sdm::UpdateFeatureAction specifying
how to incorporate the features.

### Applies to

The UpdateFeatures function can be used with the following objects:

Sdm::AminoAcidSequence , Sdm::NucleicAcidSequence , Sdm::Sequence

### Using the UpdateFeatures function

#### Instance

$object->UpdateFeatures( <fromsequence>, <actiontype> );

$object->UpdateFeatures( { FromSequence => <fromsequence>, ActionType => <actiontype> } );

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <actiontype> | Required | | enum Sdm::UpdateFeatureAction |
| <fromsequence> | Required | | Sdm::Sequence |
| $object | | | Sdm::AminoAcidSequence Sdm::NucleicAcidSequence Sdm::Sequence |

#### Defined by

SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate how to merge features from one sequence to another.
use strict;
use SdmDiscoveryScript;

my $samplesFolder = $ENV{ACCELRYS_ROOT} . '/share/Samples/';
my $filePath = $samplesFolder . 'D.funebris ADH Gene.bsml';

my $document1 = DiscoveryScript::Open($filePath);
my $source = $document1->Sequence(0);

# Create a replicate sequence without features.
my $document2 = Sdm::Document::CreateProteinDocument();
my $target = $document2->Sequence(0);
$target->Name = '1crn copy';
$target->InsetSequenceString( 0, $source->SequenceString() );
$document2->UpdateViews();

# Merge features from source to target.
$target->UpdateFeatures( $source, Sdm::mergeFeatures );
$document2->ShowAnnotations(0);
$document2->UpdateViews();

my $index = 0;
my $count = $document2->SequenceCount;
printf "Found %d sequences\n", $count;
while ( $index < $count )
{
my $sequence = $document2->Sequence($index);

print 'Sequence: ' . ++$index . "\t";
print 'Name: "' . $sequence->Name . "\"\n\t";
print 'Description: "' . $sequence->Description . "\"\n\t";
print 'Locus: "' . $sequence->Locus . "\"\n\t";
print 'Gene name: "' . $sequence->GeneName . "\"\n\t";
print 'Residues: ', $sequence->SequenceString . "\n";
}
```

# UpdateFromBsmlAttributes function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/updatefrombsmlattributes_function.htm

## UpdateFromBsmlAttributes function

### Description

UpdateFromBsmlAttributes converts some attributes in an Sdm::AttributeMap to Sequence Data Model (SDM) objects.
Attributes are primarily used to persist non-standard data to BSML files.
Attributes are generally not updated until the SDM
is persisted to a BSML file and are used to define SDM objects on loading
a BSML file. This method forces an object's attributes to reset the object's
properties. The BuildBsmlAttributes can be used to update
the attributes to the current object state.

### Applies to

The UpdateFromBsmlAttributes function can be used with the following objects:

Sdm::Document

### Using the UpdateFromBsmlAttributes function

#### Instance

$object->UpdateFromBsmlAttributes();

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $object | | | Sdm::Document |

#### Defined by

SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# This script illustrates how to use the Sdm::AttributeMap.
use SdmDiscoveryScript;
use strict;

my $mdm = Mdm::Document::CreateFromPdbId('4phv');
my $document = Sdm::Document::CreateDocumentFromStructures($mdm);
my $alignment = $document->Alignment;

# Copy current document state to object attributes. Generally the 
# attribute data is not updated after loading a BSML file. To get 
# the current state as attributes call this function. 
$document->ClearBsmlAttributes();
$document->BuildBsmlAttributes();

# List the Alignment object attributes.
print "Alignment attributes...\n";
my $attributes = $alignment->AttributeMap;
my $key = $attributes->FirstKey;
while (!$key->IsEndKey)
{
print $key->Name . ":\t" . $attributes->Item($key) . "\n";
$key = $attributes->NextKey($key);
}
print "end\n\n";

# List the Sequence object attributes.
my $sequences = $document->Sequences;
my $i = 0;
foreach my $sequence (@$sequences)
{
print "Sequence $i attributes...\n";
my $attributes = $sequence->AttributeMap;
my $key = $attributes->FirstKey;
while (!$key->IsEndKey)
{
print $key->Name . ":\t" . $attributes->Item($key) . "\n";
$key = $attributes->NextKey($key);
}
print "end\n\n";

my $k = $attributes->FindItem('ResidueID');
print 'Find Name: ' . $k->Name . "\tValue: "
. $attributes->Item($k) . "\n\n";

# List the Feature object attributes.
my $features = $sequence->Features;
my $f = 0;
foreach my $feature (@$features)
{
print "Feature $f attributes...\n";
my $fattributes = $feature->AttributeMap;
my $fkey = $fattributes->FirstKey;
print $feature->Key . "\n";
while (!$fkey->IsEndKey)
{
print $fkey->Name . ":\t" . $fattributes->Item($fkey) . "\n";
$fkey = $fattributes->NextKey($fkey);
}

print "end\n\n";
++$f;
} 

++$i; 
}

# Update the current document to match attribute data.
$document->UpdateFromBsmlAttributes();
$document->UpdateViews();
```

# UpdateSequence function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/updatesequence_function.htm

## UpdateSequence function

### Description

UpdateSequence merges data from one sequence into another. Updated
data includes features, annotations, residue display style (when applied),
residue identifiers, selection, and taxonomy.
UpdateSequence requires sequences to have matching
name, residue types, and chain break positions.
It may be necessary to use Sdm::colorByCustomColor to see changes to the target alignment's foreground and background coloring.

### Applies to

The UpdateSequence function can be used with the following objects:

Sdm::AminoAcidSequence , Sdm::NucleicAcidSequence , Sdm::Sequence

### Using the UpdateSequence function

#### Instance

$object->UpdateSequence( <fromsequence> );

$object->UpdateSequence( { FromSequence => <fromsequence> } );

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <fromsequence> | Required | | Sdm::Sequence |
| $object | | | Sdm::AminoAcidSequence Sdm::NucleicAcidSequence Sdm::Sequence |

#### Defined by

SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# This script illustrates the use of UpdateSequence.
use strict;
use SdmDiscoveryScript;

# Load example data.
my $mdmDocument = Mdm::Document::CreateFromPdbId('4phv');
my $sdmDocument = Sdm::Document::CreateDocumentFromStructures($mdmDocument);
$mdmDocument->Close();
my $templateSequence = $sdmDocument->Sequences->Item(0);

# Create bare sequence with primary structure. Note the primary structure, 
# sequence name and chain break locations must match for UpdateSequence to 
# work.
my $document = Sdm::Document::CreateProteinDocument();
$document->DeleteAlignmentSequences();
my $alignment= $document->Alignment;
$alignment->InsertAlignmentString(
0, '4PHV', 
'PQITLWQRPLVTIKIGGQLKEALLDTGADDTVLEEMNLPGRWKPKMIGGIGGFIKVR'
.'QYDQILIEICGHKAIGTVLVGPTPVNIIGRNLLTQIGCTLNFPQITLWQRPLVTIK'
.'IGGQLKEALLDTGADDTVLEEMNLPGRWKPKMIGGIGGFIKVRQYDQILIEICGHK'
.'AIGTVLVGPTPVNIIGRNLLTQIGCTLNF');
my $sequence = $alignment->Sequences->Item(0);
$sequence->MarkStartOfChain(99);
$document->UpdateViews();

print 'Feature count of original template sequence: ' 
. $templateSequence->Features->Count . ".\n";

print 'Feature count of target sequence before update: ' 
. $sequence->Features->Count . ".\n";

# Update sequence copies features, selections, residue decorations
# and publication from the target sequence. 
$sequence->UpdateSequence($sdmDocument->Sequences->Item(0));
print 'Feature count of target sequence after update: ' 
. $sequence->Features->Count . ".\n";
```

# UpdateSequences function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/updatesequences_function.htm

## UpdateSequences function

### Description

UpdateSequences merges sequence data from one Sdm::Alignment object into another object.

For an Sdm::Sequence object, a matching sequence must be found in the passed alignment
object. For two sequences to match, they must have the same name, residue
order, and chain break positions. Additionally, each sequence should be uniquely identifiable.

Updated sequence data include features, annotations, residue display style (when applied),
residue identifiers, selection, and taxonomy.
It may be necessary to use Sdm::colorByCustomColor to see changes to the target alignment's foreground and background coloring.

### Applies to

The UpdateSequences function can be used with the following objects:

Sdm::Alignment

### Using the UpdateSequences function

#### Instance

$object->UpdateSequences( <fromalignment> );

$object->UpdateSequences( { FromAlignment => <fromalignment> } );

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <fromalignment> | Required | | Sdm::Alignment |
| $object | | | Sdm::Alignment |

#### Defined by

SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate how to use UpdateSequences function.
use strict;
use SdmDiscoveryScript;

my $samplesFolder = $ENV{ACCELRYS_ROOT} . '/share/Samples/';
my $filename = $samplesFolder . 'CDK2 Structures and Sequences.dsv';

# Load molecule and sequence data.
my $mdmDocument = DiscoveryScript::Open($filename);
my $sdmDocument = DiscoveryScript::LastActiveDocument(SdmModelType);
my $alignment = $sdmDocument->Alignment;

# Perform an action that returns a new sequence document, such as
# running a Pipeline Pilot protocol....

######################################################################
## Add your action here.
######################################################################

# Open the results file. Here we just open a second copy of the file.
my $mdmDoc2 = DiscoveryScript::Open($filename);
my $sdmDoc2 = DiscoveryScript::LastActiveDocument(SdmModelType);
$mdmDoc2->Close();

# Disable MDM client updates for better performance.
my $mdm = $sdmDocument->LinkedMdmDocument;
$mdm->EnableUpdateViews(0) if ($mdm);

$alignment->UpdateSequences($sdmDoc2->Alignment);

printf "sequence count: %3d\n",$sdmDoc2->SequenceCount; 
my $index = 0;
while ( $index < $sdmDoc2->SequenceCount )
{
my $sequence = $sdmDoc2->Sequence($index);

print 'Sequence: ' . ++$index . "\t";
print 'Name: "' . $sequence->Name . "\"\n\t";
print 'Description: "' . $sequence->Description . "\"\n\t";
print 'Locus: "' . $sequence->Locus . "\"\n\t";
print 'Gene name: "' . $sequence->GeneName . "\"\n\t";
print 'Residues: ', $sequence->SequenceString . "\n";
}

$sdmDoc2->Close();

# Re-enable MDM client updates.
$mdm->EnableUpdateViews(1) if ($mdm);
```

# Script Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/usng_dvw_script-window.htm

## Script Window

The Script Window provides an environment for writing, editing, debugging, and running scripts. 
It allows you to develop and test scripts until you are confident that they function correctly. In addition to 
standard text editing functions (cut, copy, paste, delete), you can control the font, line numbers, and script indentation.
For details, see the Script Window Display Style dialog help topic.

### Creating a script

To create a new script, choose File | New | Script Window from the menu bar.
This opens a new Script Window containing a template based on "Samples/Scripts/NewScript.pl". For details about creating scripts, see Writing scripts .

### Editing a script

You can open existing Perl scripts in several ways:

* Use the File | Open... command to open an existing Perl script.

* Drag and drop an existing Perl script file into the program main window.

* Select a Perl script file in the Files Explorer and select the Open With | Script Window context menu command.

By default, Perl scripts are executed when you open them. 
You can use the File Types subpage of the
Preferences dialog can to change the behavior so that the scripts open in a Script Window without executing.

#### Color code definitions

In the Script Window, the text of your script can be colored according to the syntax categories of the 
scripting language being used, making your script easier to read and errors easier to find. 
The colors represent the following categories in the script:

* Comments - blue on white, program documentation.

* Constants - magenta on white, numbers or strings.

* Identifiers - dark cyan on white, variable names.

* Statements - bold brown on white, functions.

* Preprocessor - purple on white, the #!/usr/bin/perl statements.

### Executing a script

To execute a script in the Script Window , click the Run button in the Scripting Toolbar .

### Debugging a script

The Script Window offers some basic capabilities for debugging scripts. 
Begin by clicking the Check Syntax button on the Scripting Toolbar to check the syntax of the script for basic errors.

After checking the syntax, run your script to check for errors. The Script Window displays errors in the Output View . 
Typically, the types of errors that debugging (as opposed to syntax checking) will highlight are:

* Attempting to use an invalid property or method (for example spelling the name incorrectly)

* Attempting to use a property or method that is not applicable to a given object (for example trying to create an atom in a sequence)

* Attempting to use a value that is invalid for a given property or method (for example
trying to open a document that does not exist)

To stop a script while it is running, click the button 
to the right of the progress indicator on the status bar. Documents will remain in whatever state they are in when the 
script stops running. However, note that it is not possible to resume execution of a script once it has been halted. 
Scripts are always run from the beginning.

You can undo the effects of running a script by clicking the Undo button on the 
Standard toolbar or by choosing Edit | Undo from the menu bar. As with other functions, 
using Undo will not delete any documents that were created by the script.

### Context menu

The Script Window context menu extends the Script Window capabilities as described below.

* Run - Executes the current script. This command is the same as the corresponding command on the Scripting Toolbar .

* Cut, Copy, and Paste - These commands are the same as the corresponding commands under the Edit menu .

* Select All - Selects all text in the current document.

* Find - Opens the Find panel, which allows you to search for text.

* Replace... - Opens the Find and Replace dialog, which allows you to search for, and replace text.

* Indent - Indents the currently selected text.

* Outdent - Removes the indent for the currently selected text.

* Output - Toggles the visibility of the Output View .

* Arguments - Toggles the visibility of the Arguments View .

* Display Style... - Opens the Script Window Display Style dialog .

#### Further information

# Valence property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/valence_property.htm

## Valence property

### Description

Valence specifies the current valence of an atom.

### Applies to

The Valence property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Valence

### Using the Valence property

#### Get

my $realValue = $object->Valence;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $realValue | | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::Valence |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate the use of ValenceMonitor objects.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use DSCommands;

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . "3ptb.pdb" );

# Creates a hydrogen-bond monitor between ligand and receptor atoms.
my $ligands = GetLigands($document);
my $ligandAtoms = $ligands->Item(0)->Atoms;
my $monitor = $document->CreateValenceMonitor($ligandAtoms);

$monitor->IsUnderValenceShown = True;

print "Found " . $monitor->OverValenceCount . " atoms over valence.\n";
print "Found " . $monitor->UnderValenceCount . " atoms under valence.\n";

my $valences = $monitor->Valences;

my $count = $valences->Count;
for ( my $index = 0 ; $index < $count ; ++$index )
{
my $valence = $valences->Item($index);
printf "Expected valence (for %s): %d \t Current valence: %d\n",
$valence->Name, $valence->ExpectedValence, $valence->Valence;
}
```

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate the use of various atom properties.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use DSCommands;

# Define atom properties to list.
# This may be specified on the command line.
my $residueAtomName = 'THR2:CA';
if ( @ARGV != 0 )
{
($residueAtomName) = @ARGV;
}

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . '1crn.pdb' );

# Get the specified atom.
my $atoms = FilterByString( $document, $residueAtomName );
die "Atom $residueAtomName not found. Aborting!\n\n"
if ( $atoms->Count == 0 );

my $atom = $atoms->[0];

# Print various atom properties. In the DiscoveryStudio client, the
# output will appear in the output pane of the scripting window.
print "List of properties for atom $residueAtomName:\n\n";
print 'Name: ' . $atom->Name . "\n";
print 'Element: ' . $atom->Element . "\n";
print 'Element Name: ' . $atom->ElementName . "\n";
print 'Element Symbol: ' . $atom->ElementSymbol . "\n";
print 'Mass: ' . $atom->Mass . "\n";
print 'Atomic number: ' . $atom->AtomicNumber . "\n";
print 'Charge: ' . $atom->Charge . "\n";
print 'Formal Charge: '
. $atom->FormalCharge->Numerator . "/"
. $atom->FormalCharge->Denominator . "\n";

print 'VDW Radius: ' . $atom->VdwRadius . "\n";
print 'Covalent Radius: ' . $atom->CovalentRadius . "\n";
print 'Chirality: ' . $atom->Chirality . "\n";
print 'Bond count: ' . $atom->BondCount . "\n";
print 'Bonding radius: ' . $atom->BondingRadius . "\n";
print 'Hybridization: ' . $atom->Hybridization . "\n";
print 'Hydrogen Count: ' . $atom->HydrogenCount . "\n";
print 'ImplicitHydrogen Count: ' . $atom->ImplicitHydrogenCount . "\n";
print 'Is Hydrogen Bond Acceptor: ' . $atom->IsHydrogenBondAcceptor . "\n";
print 'Is Hydrogen Bond Donor: ' . $atom->IsHydrogenBondDonor . "\n";
print 'Isotropic Displacement: ' . $atom->IsotropicDisplacement . "\n";
```

```text
use DSCommands;

my $monitor = $document->CreateValenceMonitor($ligandAtoms);

{

printf "Expected valence (for %s): %d \t Current valence: %d\n",
$valence->Name, $valence->ExpectedValence, $valence->Valence;
}
```

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate the use of various atom properties.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use DSCommands;

# Define atom properties to list.
# This may be specified on the command line.
my $residueAtomName = 'THR2:CA';
if ( @ARGV != 0 )
{
($residueAtomName) = @ARGV;
}

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . '1crn.pdb' );

# Get the specified atom.
my $atoms = FilterByString( $document, $residueAtomName );
die "Atom $residueAtomName not found. Aborting!\n\n"
if ( $atoms->Count == 0 );

my $atom = $atoms->[0];

# Print various atom properties. In the DiscoveryStudio client, the
# output will appear in the output pane of the scripting window.
print "List of properties for atom $residueAtomName:\n\n";
print 'Name: ' . $atom->Name . "\n";
print 'Element: ' . $atom->Element . "\n";
print 'Element Name: ' . $atom->ElementName . "\n";
print 'Element Symbol: ' . $atom->ElementSymbol . "\n";
print 'Mass: ' . $atom->Mass . "\n";
print 'Atomic number: ' . $atom->AtomicNumber . "\n";
print 'Charge: ' . $atom->Charge . "\n";
print 'Formal Charge: '
. $atom->FormalCharge->Numerator . "/"
. $atom->FormalCharge->Denominator . "\n";

print 'VDW Radius: ' . $atom->VdwRadius . "\n";
print 'Covalent Radius: ' . $atom->CovalentRadius . "\n";
print 'Chirality: ' . $atom->Chirality . "\n";
print 'Bond count: ' . $atom->BondCount . "\n";
print 'Bonding radius: ' . $atom->BondingRadius . "\n";
print 'Hybridization: ' . $atom->Hybridization . "\n";
print 'Hydrogen Count: ' . $atom->HydrogenCount . "\n";
print 'ImplicitHydrogen Count: ' . $atom->ImplicitHydrogenCount . "\n";
print 'Is Hydrogen Bond Acceptor: ' . $atom->IsHydrogenBondAcceptor . "\n";
print 'Is Hydrogen Bond Donor: ' . $atom->IsHydrogenBondDonor . "\n";
print 'Isotropic Displacement: ' . $atom->IsotropicDisplacement . "\n";
print 'Is Terminal Hydrogen: ' . $atom->IsTerminalHydrogen . "\n";
print 'Is Valence Satisfied: ' . $atom->IsValenceSatisfied . "\n";
print 'Lone Pair Count: ' . $atom->LonePairCount . "\n";
print 'Valence Count: ' . $atom->ValenceCount . "\n";
print 'Occupancy: ' . $atom->Occupancy . "\n";

printf "\n%s:\n", 'Display Properties';
print 'DisplayStyle: ' . $atom->DisplayStyle . "\n";
print 'Ball Size: ' . $atom->BallSize . "\n";
print 'Ball Size Default: ' . $atom->BallSizeDefault . "\n";
print 'CPK Scale: ' . $atom->CPKScale . "\n";
print 'CPK Scale Default: ' . $atom->CPKScaleDefault . "\n";
print 'Stick Radius: ' . $atom->StickRadius . "\n";
print 'Stick Radius Default: ' . $atom->StickRadiusDefault . "\n";
print 'Name: ' . $atom->Name . "\n";
```

# Vector property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/vector_property.htm

## Vector property

### Description

Vector indicates the dipole moment vector calculated by a
dipole moment monitor. The values of the X, Y and Z components of the
dipole moment vector are reported in Debye units.

The dipole moment is calculated as

D × Σ(i) |q i |(R i - C)

where the summation runs over all atoms,
q i is the partial charge of the i-th atom,
R i are the 3D coordinates of the i-th atom,
C is the 3D coordinates of the center of charge, and
D is a unit conversion factor.
D is given by D = Debye/(e Å); where the values used are 1 Debye = 3.335641 × 10 -30 Cm (coulomb-meters) 1 e = 1.602176 × 10 -19 C (coulomb) 1 Å = 10 -10 m (meters).

With these values, D equals approximately 4.8032.

### Applies to

The Vector property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::DipoleMomentMonitor

### Using the Vector property

#### Get

my $pointObject = $object->Vector;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $pointObject | | | Mdm::Point |
| $object | | | Mdm::DipoleMomentMonitor |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . "1crn.pdb" );

my $molecule = $document->Molecules->Item(0);

my $monitor = $molecule->CreateDipoleMomentMonitor();

my $center = $monitor->ChargeCenter();
my $vector = $monitor->Vector();
printf "Dipole moment center: %4.2f, %4.2f, %4.2f\n",
$center->X, $center->Y, $center->Z;
print "Dipole magnitude: " . $monitor->Magnitude . "\n";
printf "Dipole vector: (%4.2f, %4.2f, %4.2f)\n",
$vector->X, $vector->Y, $vector->Z;
```

# Version property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/version_property.htm

## Version property

### Description

Version specifies the version of a protocol.

### Applies to

The Version property can be used with the following objects:

Protocol::Document

### Using the Version property

#### Get

my $integerValue = $object->Version;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $integerValue | | | Integer |
| $object | | | Protocol::Document |

#### Defined by

ProtocolDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Describes how to launch a protocol.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use ProtocolDiscoveryScript;

my $samplesFolder = $ENV{ACCELRYS_ROOT} . '/share/Samples/Tutorials/Receptor-Ligand Interactions/';
my $infileName = '1EQG-ibuprofen.sd';
my $inputFile = $samplesFolder . $infileName;

# Protocol name and parameters
my $protocolName = 'Generate Conformations';
my %parameterHash = ( "Input Ligands" => $inputFile,
"Conformation Method" => "CAESAR", 
"Maximum Conformations" => 100,
);

print "Connecting to server...\n";
my $session = Protocol::Document::DefaultSession();
if ($session)
{
print "Connected to $session->{Server} as user $session->{User}.\n";
}
else
{
die "No Pipeline Pilot server found. Please connect to a valid server and try again.\n";
}

# Print default running folder, which can be changed
print "Running in $session->{RunFolder}...\n";

print "Open protocol document for $protocolName\n";
my $document = Protocol::Document::Create( $protocolName, $session );

my $guid = $document->Guid();
print "Protocol guid: $guid\n"; 
my $guid = $document->Guid();
print "Protocol guid: $guid\n";

my $version = $document->Version();
print "Protocol version: $version\n";
## Setup the protocol parameters

for my $key (keys %parameterHash) {
if ( $document->ItemExists($key) ) {
$document->ReplaceItem( $key, $parameterHash{$key} );
print "Set parameter '$key' : $parameterHash{$key}\n"; 
}
else{
print "\n<warning> not a valid parameter '$key'\n\n"; 
}
}

## Launch Pipeline Pilot protocol

my $saveIntermediateFiles = True;
my $maxFilesizeToDownload = 256;
my $showJobCompleteDialog = False;
my $task = $session->Launch(
$document, $maxFilesizeToDownload,
$saveIntermediateFiles, $showJobCompleteDialog
);

print "\nLaunch the protocol: $protocolName \n";
print "Task info\n";
print "Name: $task->{ProtocolName}\n";
print "Host: $task->{Host}\n";
print "RunPath: $task->{RunPath}\n";
print "TaskId: $task->{TaskId}\n";

## Track progress of task
print " $protocolName Task is running...\n";
my $times = 0;
while ( $task->IsRunnable() )
{
print "Status: $task->{State}\n";
sleep(5);
++$times;
if ( $times > 5 )
{
$task->KillTask();
}
}

$task->WaitForCompletion();

# get the log file
my $messages = $task->LogMessages;
print "$protocolName Log messages:\n";
map { print "$_\n"; } @$messages; 

my $finalStatus = $task->State;
my $finalMolecularData;
if ( $finalStatus eq Protocol::taskComplete )
{
print "$protocolName completed\n";
my $path = $task->RunPath;
my $outFile = "$path/Output/$infileName";
die "Output file was not found please check report!" if ( not -e $outFile );
# load the results 
DiscoveryScript::Open( { Path => $outFile, LoadAllObjects => True } ); 
}
else
{
print " $protocolName Task failed with status $finalStatus\n";
}
```

# VertexColors property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/vertexcolors_property.htm

## VertexColors property

### Description

Triangle mesh vertex colors of a surface object.
When setting the vertex colors, the number of colors must match the number of vertices.

### Applies to

The VertexColors property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Surface

### Using the VertexColors property

#### Get

my $colorarrayObject = $object->VertexColors;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $colorarrayObject | | | DiscoveryScript::ColorArray |
| $object | | | Mdm::Surface |

#### Set

$object->VertexColors = <colors>;

$object->VertexColors( <colors> );

$object->VertexColors( { colors => <colors> } );

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <colors> | Required | | DiscoveryScript::ColorArray |
| $object | | | Mdm::Surface |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w

# Surface VertexColors property

use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use strict;

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();
my $molecule = $document->CreateMolecule();
my $atom = $molecule->CreateAtom(Mdm::C);
my $atoms = $document->Atoms;
my $surface = $document->CreateSolidSurface($atoms, Mdm::surfaceStyleSoft, False, Mdm::surfaceColorByAtomCharge);
$document->DeselectAll();

my $colors = $surface->VertexColors;
my $colorCount = $colors->Count;
print "Number of colors = " . $colorCount . "\n";

foreach my $color (@$colors) {
print "Color = " . $color->Red . "," . $color->Green . "," . $color->Blue . "\n";
}

my $newColors = DiscoveryScript::ColorArray::Create();
for (my $index = 0; $index < $colorCount; ++$index) {
$newColors->AddItem(Mdm::Color::Create(
int(255 * rand()), 
int(255 * rand()), 
int(255 * rand())
));
}

$surface->VertexColors = $newColors;

$document->UpdateViews();
```

# VertexNormals property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/vertexnormals_property.htm

## VertexNormals property

### Description

Triangle mesh vertex normals of a surface object.
This is a read-only property. You cannot set the vertex normals.

### Applies to

The VertexNormals property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Surface

### Using the VertexNormals property

#### Get

my $pointarrayObject = $object->VertexNormals;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $pointarrayObject | | | Mdm::PointArray |
| $object | | | Mdm::Surface |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w

# Surface VertexNormals property

use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use strict;

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();
my $molecule = $document->CreateMolecule();
my $atom = $molecule->CreateAtom(Mdm::C);
my $atoms = $document->Atoms;
my $surface = $document->CreateSolidSurface($atoms, Mdm::surfaceStyleSoft, False, Mdm::surfaceColorByAtomCharge);
$document->DeselectAll();

my $normals = $surface->VertexNormals;
print "Number of normals = " . $normals->Count . "\n";

foreach my $normal (@$normals) {
print "Normal = " . $normal->X . "," . $normal->Y . "," . $normal->Z . "\n";
}
```

Mdm::Surface

MdmDiscoveryScript


# VisualizerCommands package

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/visualizercommands_package.htm

## VisualizerCommands package

### Description

VisualizerCommands provides high-level functions for accessing functionality
within other packages. You can use this file to include all the other
packages except for those not available in the free visualizer.

### Using the VisualizerCommands package

Access to the VisualizerCommands API is through the Perl use directive:

```text
use strict;
use VisualizerCommands;
```

The strict directive is optional, but strongly recommended as it restricts
the use of unsafe constructs. All available classes will be imported from the VisualizerCommands module.

#### Uses

MdmCommands , PharmacophoreCommands , SdmCommands

#### Used by

DSCommands

#### Module

VisualizerCommands.pm

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
use strict;
use VisualizerCommands;

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . "1kim.pdb" );

# From MdmDiscoveryScript
print "Document contains " . $document->Atoms->Count() . " atom(s)\n";

# From MdmCommands
my $ligands = GetLigands($document);

# From SdmDiscoveryScript
my $sequence = Sdm::Document::CreateProteinDocument();

# From SdmCommands
my $sequenceString = CreateSequenceFromMolecule($document);
```

# Volume property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/volume_property.htm

## Volume property

### Description

Volume indicates the volume of a surface.

### Applies to

The Volume property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Surface

### Using the Volume property

#### Get

my $realValue = $object->Volume;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $realValue | | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::Surface |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Demonstrate how to create a transparent surface.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . '101m.pdb' );

# Select heme atoms.
$document->SelectByProperty('Residue Name="HEM.*"; Atom label="*"');

# Create an array of all heme atoms.
my $hemeAtoms = $document->Filter( { Selected => 1 } )->Atoms;

# Create transparent surface around the heme group.
my $transparentSurface =
$document->CreateTransparentSurface( $hemeAtoms, Mdm::surfaceStyleSolvent,
False, Mdm::surfaceColorByElectrostaticPotential,
1.3, 0.6 );

$transparentSurface->IsBackSideColorEnabled(True);
$transparentSurface->IsBackSideTransparencyEnabled(True);

# Also create wiremesh surface around the heme group.
my $wiremeshSurface =
$document->CreateWiremeshSurface( $hemeAtoms, Mdm::surfaceStyleSolvent,
False, Mdm::surfaceColorByElectrostaticPotential, 2.0 );

print "Surface area: "
. $transparentSurface->Area . "\n"
. "Surface Volume: "
. $transparentSurface->Volume . "\n";
print "Surface probe radius: "
. $transparentSurface->ProbeRadius . "\n"
. "Transparency Level: "
. $transparentSurface->TransparencyLevel . "\n";

# Select all atoms within 6A of the heme and the surface.
$document->SelectByRadius( 6.0, 'Atom' );
$transparentSurface->Select();

# Show only the heme and neighboring atoms (other than water).
$document->FitView();
$document->InvertSelection();
$document->SelectByProperty('Residue name="HOH.*"; Atom label="*"');
$document->Hide();
$document->DeselectAll();

# Display the wiremesh surface with delay.
sleep(2);
$wiremeshSurface->SetVisible();
```

# WaitForCompletion function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/waitforcompletion_function.htm

## WaitForCompletion function

### Description

WaitForCompletion blocks until the launched protocol completes.

### Applies to

The WaitForCompletion function can be used with the following objects:

Protocol::Task

### Using the WaitForCompletion function

#### Instance

my $stateEnum = $object->WaitForCompletion();

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $stateEnum | | | enum Protocol::State |
| $object | | | Protocol::Task |

#### Defined by

ProtocolDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Describes how to launch a protocol.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use ProtocolDiscoveryScript;

my $samplesFolder = $ENV{ACCELRYS_ROOT} . '/share/Samples/Tutorials/Receptor-Ligand Interactions/';
my $infileName = '1EQG-ibuprofen.sd';
my $inputFile = $samplesFolder . $infileName;

# Protocol name and parameters
my $protocolName = 'Generate Conformations';
my %parameterHash = ( "Input Ligands" => $inputFile,
"Conformation Method" => "CAESAR", 
"Maximum Conformations" => 100,
);

print "Connecting to server...\n";
my $session = Protocol::Document::DefaultSession();
if ($session)
{
print "Connected to $session->{Server} as user $session->{User}.\n";
}
else
{
die "No Pipeline Pilot server found. Please connect to a valid server and try again.\n";
}

# Print default running folder, which can be changed
print "Running in $session->{RunFolder}...\n";

print "Open protocol document for $protocolName\n";
my $document = Protocol::Document::Create( $protocolName, $session );

my $guid = $document->Guid();
print "Protocol guid: $guid\n"; 
my $guid = $document->Guid();
print "Protocol guid: $guid\n";

my $version = $document->Version();
print "Protocol version: $version\n";
## Setup the protocol parameters

for my $key (keys %parameterHash) {
if ( $document->ItemExists($key) ) {
$document->ReplaceItem( $key, $parameterHash{$key} );
print "Set parameter '$key' : $parameterHash{$key}\n"; 
}
else{
print "\n<warning> not a valid parameter '$key'\n\n"; 
}
}

## Launch Pipeline Pilot protocol

my $saveIntermediateFiles = True;
my $maxFilesizeToDownload = 256;
my $showJobCompleteDialog = False;
my $task = $session->Launch(
$document, $maxFilesizeToDownload,
$saveIntermediateFiles, $showJobCompleteDialog
);

print "\nLaunch the protocol: $protocolName \n";
print "Task info\n";
print "Name: $task->{ProtocolName}\n";
print "Host: $task->{Host}\n";
print "RunPath: $task->{RunPath}\n";
print "TaskId: $task->{TaskId}\n";

## Track progress of task
print " $protocolName Task is running...\n";
my $times = 0;
while ( $task->IsRunnable() )
{
print "Status: $task->{State}\n";
sleep(5);
++$times;
if ( $times > 5 )
{
$task->KillTask();
}
}

$task->WaitForCompletion();

# get the log file
my $messages = $task->LogMessages;
print "$protocolName Log messages:\n";
map { print "$_\n"; } @$messages; 

my $finalStatus = $task->State;
my $finalMolecularData;
if ( $finalStatus eq Protocol::taskComplete )
{
print "$protocolName completed\n";
my $path = $task->RunPath;
my $outFile = "$path/Output/$infileName";
die "Output file was not found please check report!" if ( not -e $outFile );
# load the results 
DiscoveryScript::Open( { Path => $outFile, LoadAllObjects => True } ); 
}
else
{
print " $protocolName Task failed with status $finalStatus\n";
}
```

# WaitForUpdater function

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/waitforupdater_function.htm

## WaitForUpdater function

### Description

This function should be called to wait until updates of the
SQLITE database associated with a document have completed.
This eliminates database updates as a source of variability
in measuring the performance of individual operations in a
script.

### Applies to

The WaitForUpdater function can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Document

### Using the WaitForUpdater function

#### Instance

$object->WaitForUpdater();

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $object | | | Mdm::Document |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w

use strict;

use MdmDiscoveryScript;
use Time::HiRes qw(time);
use POSIX qw(strftime);

my $document = DiscoveryScript::OpenFromUrl( PdbUrlPrefix . '1tgn.pdb' );

my $molecules = $document->Molecules;
my $molecule = $molecules->Item(0);

for (my $i = 0; $i < 1000; ++$i) {
my $name = "Property #" . ($i + 1);
$molecule->SetProperty($name, "DATA");
}

my $t = time;
$document->WaitForUpdater();
$t = time - $t;
print "Time spent waiting = " . sprintf("%.3f seconds\n", $t) ;

$document->BeginBatch();
for (my $i = 0; $i < 1000; ++$i) {
my $name = "Property #" . ($i + 1);
$molecule->SetProperty($name, "MORE DATA");
}
$document->EndBatch();

$t = time;
$document->WaitForUpdater();
$t = time - $t;
print "Time spent waiting = " . sprintf("%.3f seconds\n", $t) ;

$t = time;
$document->Save("Output.dsv", "dsv");
$t = time - $t;
print "Time spent saving = " . sprintf("%.3f seconds\n", $t) ;

$document->Close();
```

# Weight property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/weight_property.htm

## Weight property

### Description

Weight specifies the feature weight to use for a query operator.

### Applies to

The Weight property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::QueryOperator

### Using the Weight property

#### Get

my $realValue = $object->Weight;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $realValue | | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::QueryOperator |

#### Set

$object->Weight = <weight>;

$object->Weight( <weight> );

$object->Weight( { Weight => <weight> } );

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <weight> | Required | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::QueryOperator |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
use strict;
use PharmacophoreDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();

# Create empty query
my $query1 = $document->CreateQuery();

# Create top level fit operator
my $fitOperator = $query1->CreateQueryOperator('queryFit');

# Create some features on the query
# Create a ring aromatic
$document->InsertFromSmiles('c1ccccc1');
$document->Molecules()->Item(0)->Name("benzene");
my $ringAromaticOperator = $fitOperator->CreateQueryOperator('queryInclude');
$ringAromaticOperator->Name('RA1');
my $ringAromaticFeatureObject =
$ringAromaticOperator->CreateRingAromaticFeature(
$document->Molecules()->Item(0)->Atoms );
$document->Molecules()->Item(0)->Select(); # delete later

# create the location constraints
my $locationFeatureHead =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature(
$ringAromaticFeatureObject->CentroidFeature(), 1.6 );
my $locationFeatureTail =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature(
$ringAromaticFeatureObject->NormalFeature(), 1.6 );

# Create a donor feature
my $molecule = $document->CreateMolecule();
my $atomObject = $molecule->CreateAtom("O");
$atomObject->XYZ = Mdm::Point::Create( -2, -4, 0 );

my $donorOperator = $fitOperator->CreateQueryOperator('queryInclude');
$donorOperator->Name('HBD1');
my $newDonor = $donorOperator->CreateDonorFeature($atomObject);

# Give the hydrogen bond donor a higher weight (2.0) than the default (1.0)
$donorOperator->Weight(2.0);

# create the location constraints
my $locationFeatureHead =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newDonor->HeadFeature(), 2.2 );
my $locationFeatureTail =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newDonor->TailFeature(), 1.6 );

# Create an acceptor feature at 0,6,2
my $atomObject1 = $molecule->CreateAtom("O");
$atomObject1->XYZ = Mdm::Point::Create( 0, 6, 2 );

my $acceptorOperator = $fitOperator->CreateQueryOperator('queryInclude');
$acceptorOperator->Name('HBA1');
my $newAcceptor = $acceptorOperator->CreateAcceptorFeature($atomObject1);

# create the location constraints
my $locationFeatureHead =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newAcceptor->HeadFeature(), 2.2 );

printf "%s Head: x: %.4f y: %.4f z: %.4f\n",
$locationFeatureHead->ClassName, 
$locationFeatureHead->XYZ->X, 
$locationFeatureHead->XYZ->Y,
$locationFeatureHead->XYZ->Z;

my $locationFeatureTail =
$fitOperator->CreateLocationFeature( $newAcceptor->TailFeature(), 1.6 );

printf "%s Tail: x: %.4f y: %.4f z: %.4f\n",
$locationFeatureHead->ClassName,
$locationFeatureTail->XYZ->X, 
$locationFeatureTail->XYZ->Y,
$locationFeatureTail->XYZ->Z;

$molecule->Select(); # Select this to delete at end

$document->UpdateObjects();
$document->DeleteObjects();
```

# X property

Source type: HTML

Source section: scripting

Source file: scripting/x_property.htm

## X property

### Description

X specifies the X coordinate of a position object.

### Applies to

The X property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Point2d , Mdm::Point , Sdm::FixedBlock

### Using the X property

#### Get

my $integerValue = $object->X;

my $realValue = $object->X;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $integerValue | | | Integer |
| $realValue | | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::Point2d Mdm::Point Sdm::FixedBlock |

#### Set

$object->X = <x>;

$object->X( <x> );

$object->X( { X => <x> } );

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <x> | Required | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::Point2d Mdm::Point Sdm::FixedBlock |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript , SdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Illustrate how to use the Mdm::Point objects.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

# Working with 2D points.
my $xy1 = Mdm::Point2d::Create( -1.0, -1.0 );
my $xy2 = Mdm::Point2d::Create( 1.0, 1.0 );

print "Point1 is: (" . $xy1->X . "," . $xy1->Y . ")\n";
print "Point2 is: (" . $xy2->X . "," . $xy2->Y . ")\n";
print "Sum of squares of Point1 is: " . $xy1->SumSquares . "\n";

my $distance = $xy1->CalculateDistance($xy2);
print "The distance between these points is: $distance\n";

print "The dot product between points is: "
. $xy1->CalculateDotProduct($xy2) . "\n";

$xy1->SetXY( 2.0, 2.0 );
print "Changing Point1 to: (" . $xy1->X . "," . $xy1->Y . ")\n\n";

# Working with 3D points.
my $xyz = Mdm::Point::Create( 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 );
print "Creating 3D point with value: ("
. $xyz->X . ","
. $xyz->Y . ","
. $xyz->Z . ")\n";

$xyz->SetXYZ( 0.0, 1.0, 2.0 );
print "Changing 3D point to: ("
. $xyz->X . ","
. $xyz->Y . ","
. $xyz->Z . ")\n";
```

```text
# Working with 2D points.
my $xy1 = Mdm::Point2d::Create( -1.0, -1.0 );
my $xy2 = Mdm::Point2d::Create( 1.0, 1.0 );

print "Point1 is: (" . $xy1->X . "," . $xy1->Y . ")\n";
print "Point2 is: (" . $xy2->X . "," . $xy2->Y . ")\n";
print "Sum of squares of Point1 is: " . $xy1->SumSquares . "\n";

my $distance = $xy1->CalculateDistance($xy2);
print "The distance between these points is: $distance\n";

print "The dot product between points is: "
. $xy1->CalculateDotProduct($xy2) . "\n";

$xy1->SetXY( 2.0, 2.0 );
print "Changing Point1 to: (" . $xy1->X . "," . $xy1->Y . ")\n\n";

# Working with 3D points.
my $xyz = Mdm::Point::Create( 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 );
print "Creating 3D point with value: ("
. $xyz->X . ","
. $xyz->Y . ","
. $xyz->Z . ")\n";

$xyz->SetXYZ( 0.0, 1.0, 2.0 );
print "Changing 3D point to: ("
. $xyz->X . ","
. $xyz->Y . ","
. $xyz->Z . ")\n";
```

## Zoom property

### Description

Zoom changes the view size using the specified view distance.

### Applies to

The Zoom property can be used with the following objects:

Mdm::Document

### Using the Zoom property

#### Get

my $realValue = $object->Zoom;

##### Parameters

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $realValue | | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::Document |

#### Set

$object->Zoom = <viewsize>;

$object->Zoom( <viewsize> );

$object->Zoom( { ViewSize => <viewsize> } );

| Name | Optional/Required | Default value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <viewsize> | Required | | Real |
| $object | | | Mdm::Document |

#### Defined by

MdmDiscoveryScript

### Examples

```text
#!/usr/bin/perl -w
# Illustrate the zoom function.
use strict;
use MdmDiscoveryScript;

my $document = Mdm::Document::Create();
$document->InsertFromSmiles('C1=CC=CC=C1');
$document->AddHydrogenAtoms();

# Zoom in from a distance of 60 angstroms.
my $z = 60; # set distance
for ( my $i = 0 ; $i < 50 ; ++$i )
{ 
$document->Zoom($z);
printf "%3d) %.3f\n ",$z,$document->Zoom(); 
$document->UpdateViews();
$z -= 1;
}
sleep(1);

# Zoom back out.
for ( my $i = 0 ; $i < 50 ; ++$i )
{
$document->Zoom($z);
$document->UpdateViews();
printf "%3d) %.3f\n ",$z,$document->Zoom(); 
$z += 1;
}
```

## Troubleshooting - Installation

If you experience problems installing or using the software, review the following topic for possible solutions for Windows or Linux installations.

You can view log files that detail errors, which are useful for troubleshooting in the following installation directories:

* Client : <Settings Folder>/Diagnostics

* Server : <pps_install> /logs

For details about default locations of folders in different operating systems, see Installation folders .

A complete set of instructions for installing Discovery Studio server and any additional components is provided in the Discovery Studio Installation Guide in the Discovery Studio Documentation ZIP file available with the installation artifacts.

### Windows systems

| Problem | Possible corrective action |
| --- | --- |
| You are prompted to install a redistributable during installation. | Cancel the installation and install the redistributable, which requires a reboot. For details, see Installing Discovery Studio . Try installing again after rebooting. |
| Files no longer open automatically with Discovery Studio , or Pipeline Pilot reports an error when launching Discovery Studio Visualizer or Discovery Studio . | Removing an older version of Discovery Studio or Discovery Studio Visualizer after installing this version may cause the file associations to be removed. To correct this problem, modify the file associations on the File Associations subpage - Preferences dialog . |
| The installed version of Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server specified is not compatible with this version of Discovery Studio or is a Pipeline Pilot Client -only installation. | To resolve this issue, choose one of the following solutions: Select an alternate location for Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server. If the current location contains a Pipeline Pilot Client installation, remove Pipeline Pilot Client before installing Discovery Studio with Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server. Install only the Discovery Studio Client and use the Active Server Bar to connect to a remote Pipeline Pilot server. |

* Select an alternate location for Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server.

* If the current location contains a Pipeline Pilot Client installation, remove Pipeline Pilot Client before installing Discovery Studio with Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server.

* Install only the Discovery Studio Client and use the Active Server Bar to connect to a remote Pipeline Pilot server.

### Linux systems

To increase the amount of data collected in the error log files, start the application with the -diagnostics flag.

| Problem | Possible corrective action |
| --- | --- |
| You have installed an upgrade of the Discovery Studio component collection and you can no longer run protocols. | License Pack needs to be configured to point to the updated directory: Navigate to <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin From the command prompt: > ./config_lp_location <LP_install> |
| Session management error. | If you log onto a Linux desktop as user_A, then log on to user_A's desktop as user_B via a terminal with the command su userB , you may get a session management error: Session management error: Authentication Rejected, reason : None of the authentication protocols specified are supported and host-based authentication failed Run the command su - userB to resolve this error. |
| Parallel Simulation protocols do not use the MPI_ROOT or MPI run environment variable even if it is set for the user | Discovery Studio uses a bundled version of Intel MPI to launch parallel simulation protocols for compatibility considerations. Other MPI implementations are not supported for parallel simulation protocols. |
| The default directory cannot be set in the Files Explorer. | You must have a valid home directory to store runtime files. The home directory is identified by the value of the HOME environment variable. If you do not have a valid home directory (that is, the directory does not exist, is not writable, or you do not have sufficient space available for the software to create runtime data files), you may encounter difficulties using the product. You can test whether your home directory is valid by launching a command shell and entering the following commands: > cd > pwd > touch <exampletestfile> where <exampletestfile> does not currently exist in your home directory. If these commands produce errors, you must create a home directory in order to run the product. Contact your system administrator. |
| The installed version of Pipeline Pilot Enterprise Server specified is not compatible with this version of Discovery Studio or is a Pipeline Pilot Client only installation. | To resolve this issue, choose one of the following solutions: Select an alternate location for Pipeline Pilot Server . Install only the Discovery Studio Client and use the Active Server Bar to use a remote Pipeline Pilot Server . |

# Troubleshooting - Licensing

Source type: HTML

Source section: troubleshooting

Source file: troubleshooting/ts_licensing.htm

## Troubleshooting - Licensing

Discovery Studio licensing is designed to help with license usage monitoring and to transparently manage usage compliance. However, to be successful, proper system setup and software installation maintenance are required.

The BIOVIA License Administration tool is provided to help you to configure your licensing setup, monitor usage, and diagnose any configuration problems you may encounter. It is also the way to access complete documentation, including error code tables, information about how the licensing system works, as well as configuration and maintenance instructions. Refer to Starting the License Administrator for information about running the License Administrator to configure and diagnose your licensing system.

Licenses are made available when the software is purchased. If you need further assistance relating to licenses you should initially contact your account manager.

Check the following list of solutions to common issues if you run into a licensing problem. If you are still encountering problems, contact Dassault Systèmes Customer Support .

* Is the license file installed and valid? When using an evaluation license, a license file is installed when you enter a password. If it is expired you will encounter an error and will need to enter a new password to extend the evaluation. If you are using your purchased license you must either connect to a license server or install a local license file if no license server is required for your license. To check your license status, start the License Administrator as noted above to review your current configuration.

* Is the license manager program running? If you are not using a local evaluation license or a local license file, then the license file is installed on the license server and the license manager program must be running for the license to be available to all client software installations. You can verify this by logging into the license server and running the License Administrator that is being used to manage the license manager program.

* Can this machine communicate with the license server machine? If you have verified that the license file is installed on the license server and the license manager program is running, the next step is to make sure that all software installations which are enabled by that license server are configured to communicate with it. To do this, start the License Administrator as described in the help topic mentioned above from the software installation you are configuring and set the server connection.

* Did you recently upgrade the component collection on a Linux machine? License Pack needs to be configured to point to the updated directory: Navigate to " <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin". From the command prompt: > ./config_lp_location <LP_install>

* Navigate to " <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/dscore/server/bin".

* From the command prompt: > ./config_lp_location <LP_install>

> ./config_lp_location <LP_install>

* Are the License Pack versions in my network compatible? Another problem which can happen when configuring a new version of the software is that the License Pack version being used on the license server is not compatible with the one being used by the client software installation. It is important that the license server is using the highest version of License Pack required by all the software it is supporting and that the server and client installations of BIOVIA software use the same License Pack version. The License Pack version information is displayed on the configuration summary screen when you run the License Administrator.

* License time out issues? Application fails to connect to the license server, in particular when you connect through a VPN. You can change the default timeout value from the server Administration Portal . Select the Setup > Global Properties page. In the Package dropdown select BIOVIA/Discovery Studio Core and change the FLEXLM_TIMEOUT global to a higher value. The value is specified in microseconds and has a default value of 4500000.

Select the Setup > Global Properties page. In the Package dropdown select BIOVIA/Discovery Studio Core and change the FLEXLM_TIMEOUT global to a higher value. The value is specified in microseconds and has a default value of 4500000.

* If you are still encountering problems, contact Dassault Systèmes Customer Support .

# Troubleshooting - Protocols

Source type: HTML

Source section: troubleshooting

Source file: troubleshooting/ts_protocol.htm

## Troubleshooting - Protocols

The table below covers basic problems encountered when trying to run a protocol. However, if you encounter difficulties with a specific run, you can use debug mode, which generates additional log messages and intermediate files that are useful for analyzing any problems during execution.

To run a protocol in debug mode, hold the SHIFT key and press F5. You do not need to click the Run button.

SHIFT+F5 works only when the Protocol tab is in focus (click it to bring it in focus).

The log and intermediate files are copied to the following locations:

* Log files (on server): <pps_install> /web/jobs/<user name>/<job id>/

* Intermediate files (on server): <pps_install> /web/jobs/<user name>/<job id>/Intermediate

### Common Problems

| Problem | Solution |
| --- | --- |
| There is a problem connecting to the server. | Use the Change Server dialog to connect to a server. Use the Test button to test the connection. The server name is how your client machine is able to address the server. To test a server's name and accessibility status, type "ping servername" in a command line window. In most cases, the server name is a simple machine name, such as "mainserver". If the server is configured to use a port number other than the default (9943), you need to specify the port number directly after the server name, separated by a colon. For example, mainserver:61143 . If the ping test fails or if your network service does not allow you to specify a server name, use the IP address instead. Examples of IP addresses include: 192.168.73.108 192.168.73.108:50043 . When using an IP address, ask your system administrator if the IP address will change at a later time. If it changes, you need to update the server's address in your Pipeline Pilot Client . A network name automatically maps to the current IP address, even if the address changes, so you do not need to worry about this when using machine names. To remove unwanted server names from the list, move the mouse over the item in the list and press DELETE. To see a complete list of the tests that were run and their results, click Details . If you are unable to make a successful server connection, you can send this information to your system administrator for further analysis. |
| The Protocols Explorer is not visible. | Discovery Studio Client is not connected to the server. You can point to a local (if installed) or remote server from the Active server bar , or choose File \| Change Server... from the menu bar. |
| When changing the server: "Could not connect to server hostname:port. Please select another server to connect to." | Either the server name or the port number are incorrect, and no server can be found at the address, or the server is not running. Check your settings and start the server if necessary. A common error is to specify the "http" port instead of the "https" port. If you omit the "http" or "https" from the server string, https is used to connect and so the port number must be the port number for the https port (for example, 9943). |
| "The server that you are attempting to connect to does not appear to have the Discovery Studio component collection installed." | The server does not have the Discovery Studio components installed, or the Discovery Studio installation failed. Check your most recent installation log file for errors: <pps_install> /logs/install/SciTegicInstall_Log_*.log. Search the log file for "dscore" to see if the package containing the component collection was installed. This message may also appear if the server is not able to run the protocol that performs this check (See Protocols Explorer is not visible ). If you are trying to connect to an older version of the server, you will need to upgrade it first. |
| "The version of the Discovery Studio component collection installed on server host:port is xxx, while the version of the client is x.x." | The server you are connecting to does not have a compatible version of the component collection installed. The component collection is normally upgraded during installation, so check the installation log files as discussed in the previous solution to make sure it was installed correctly. If you are trying to connect to an older version of the server, you will need to upgrade it first. |
| Protocols fail to run. There is a licensing error in the report's Error Messages section. | There was a licensing error on the server. See Troubleshooting- Licensing . |
| The run button is not active (gray) or the protocol will not start. | One or more parameter values are invalid or missing. Invalid or missing parameters are colored red in the parameters explorer. Hover over the parameter names for a tool tip that provides details (for example, "Parameter must be between 0 and 0.25"). Some parameters may become required when a related parameter is set. |
| The status in the Jobs Explorer indicates "Error" | Double-click the status to access the Output folder for the job. Many common errors are caught and added in to the Report.htm file. If that file exists, open it and look at the errors section. Some unexpected errors will result in the protocol failing. This may mean that no report file is generated. In such cases, you may have a file called Error.txt . This file contains a trace of what the server was doing when the error occurred. Double-click the file to view the details of the failure, though the messages here may be difficult to interpret. |
| Protocol fails with the message "Unable to Upload file" in the Details section of the Jobs Explorer and Error.txt includes "Permission denied by Admin to upload file." | The maximum upload file size should be increased to upload the input files. From the Pipeline Pilot Admin Portal, increase Security > Security Configuration > Upload > Maximum Upload File Size (mb) . |
| Protocol fails when writing files to the disk. | Ensure that the disk has sufficient space. Check the temporary folder usage and remove files if needed. |

# Verify Protein (MODELER)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/anly_vfpm_th.htm

## Verify Protein (MODELER)

The Verify Protein (MODELER) protocol evaluates a protein structure using the Discrete Optimized Protein Energy (DOPE) scoring function.

#### DOPE Scoring Function

Many statistical potentials, residue or atomic based, are used in 
evaluating the quality of protein structures and as potential energy functions 
in predicting protein structures.

DOPE [Shen and Sali, 2006] is an atomic based statistical potential in MODELER that is used for model evaluation 
and structure prediction. The DOPE score of a protein can be viewed as a 
conformational energy that measures the relative stability of a conformation 
with respect to other conformations of the same protein. It can assist in 
choosing the best model out of a set of predicted model structures of a protein 
sequence. Additionally, the statistical potential is also used as part of the 
energy function in predicting loop models or for optimizing the local structure 
of a mutated residue.

The pairwise statistical potential function of a protein with N atoms can be represented by the 
pairwise probability density function:

Equation 1:

where is the single body distribution 
function for atom i and is a constant for a given protein. The pairwise probability density 
function is proportional to and 
the (m,n) pair density, where m and n are the atom types of atom i and atom j respectively.

The probability of finding a pair of atom types m and n at distance r is defined as:

Equation 2:

where N mn (r) is the number of atom type pairs m and n found at a distance 
within [r, r + Δr]. The distance pdf is proportional to the number of (m,n) pairs 
in a spherical shell of volume 4πr 2 Δr, which in turn is proportional 
to the volume itself if a uniform distribution of the particles is assumed and the 
distance r is much smaller than the overall size of the molecular system. The density 
of (m,n) pairs at distance r is p mn (r)/(4πr 2 Δr).

For a finite system, such as a protein structure, the spherical shell can be partly 
outside of the protein boundary in many cases and the density should be more accurately 
represented by p mn (r)/n(r,a), where n(r,a) = 4πr 2 Δ(r). 
The normalization function depends on the size of the protein, which is represented by 
the radius of gyration, Rg, and the distance r. The bigger the r, the smaller the 
ξ(r)/Δr is, and the normalization function n(r,a) for a protein can be 
approximated by:

Equation 3:

where a = sqrt(5/3)Rg.

Therefore, the pairwise probability density function is:

Equation 4:

Based on Equation 1 through Equation 4, the pair potential at each distance interval 
can be derived from any known native protein structure. The scores used in 
MODELER are calculated as a weighted sum from a set of high resolution X-ray 
structures with low sequence homology:

Equation 5:

MODELER assigns 158 different atom types for all heavy atoms in the 
20 standard amino acid residue types. DOPE scores are calculated for each pair 
of heavy atoms, excluding the N-terminal nitrogen and C-terminal oxygen atoms, and 
tabulated for distances from 0 to 15 Å with an interval of 0.5 Å. The pair 
potential is derived for atom pairs between different residues, and the atom pairs 
involved in bond, angle, and torsion angle are excluded from the calculation.

Those scores are then fitted into the cubic spline function, which can be used 
to calculate the single point energy of a protein model as well as 
the first and second derivatives of the energy function in the molecular dynamics protocol.

Because the DOPE energy is not normalized based on the size of the protein, the absolute 
score for a protein is not meaningful. However, the relative energies of different 
conformations are useful in model evaluation.

Because the potential is derived from single chain protein structures, it is most reliable to use the score on single chain proteins.

DOPE scores can be calculated at high resolution using a bin size of 0.125 or at
regular resolution with a bin size of 0.5.

#### Normalized DOPE Score

The Normalized DOPE Score is a Z-score based on the statistics of raw DOPE. A Z-score 
measures the deviation of a raw score from a population mean in units of standard deviation.
It is defined as

Equation 6:

where x is the raw score, μ is the mean over a population, and σ is the standard deviation over the population.
For the Normalized DOPE score, the mean and standard deviations in Equation 6 are estimated based on the sequence of the protein, 
and statistical data collected from a database of 1,686,320 protein models. For details, see [Eramian et al., 2008]

# Add or Remove Capping Groups dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_capping_groups.htm

## Add or Remove Capping Groups dialog

The Add or Remove Capping Groups dialog allows capping groups to be added or removed from 
the N and C termini of protein chains. The capping groups can be added as separate residues or alternatively as part of the terminal amino acid. The latter is appropriate if the protein is to be subsequently modeled using the charmm36 forcefield.

### Adjust caps for all/selected termini

The Adjust caps for all/selected termini options allow you to 
choose whether to add caps to the N or C termini, or remove them.

Create caps as separate residues: Specifies whether the capping group should form a separate residue or be part of the terminal amino acid.

Add N terminus caps: The chosen capping group will be 
added to the selected N termini.

[dropdown list]: The N terminus capping group is 
chosen from this list. Available N cap groups are ACE (Acetyl) and CH3 (Methyl).

Add C terminus caps: The chosen capping group will 
be added to the selected C termini.

[dropdown list]: The C terminus capping group is 
chosen from this list. Available C cap groups are NH2 (Amine), NME (N-Methyl acetamide), 
OH (Hydroxyl), and CH3 (Methyl).

Remove caps: Any non-amino acid residues at the 
termini of protein chains will be removed. The resulting termini will be in the default charged form.

The CH3 capping group is provided for compatibility with some third-party software and 
is not recommended for simulations. Additionally, a separate OH capping group should generally be avoided, the same 
chemistry can be achieved by modifying the protonation state of the C-terminus or capping the C-terminus 
with OH by turning off the Create caps as separate residues option.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Build and Edit Protein \| Modify Structure \| Cap Termini... |

# Define Additional Restraints dialog

Source type: HTML
