## Define Additional Restraints dialog

The Define Additional Restraints dialog is used for the Build Homology Models,
Build Mutants, and Loop Refinement (MODELER) protocols and allows you to define the user distance restraints, secondary structure 
restraints,
and symmetry restraints.

### Build Homology Models protocol dialog commands

#### Distance tab

Residue 1 and Atom: Select the residue and atom from the list to specify the first atom in the distance 
restraints.

Residue 2 and Atom: Select the residue and atom from the list to specify the second atom in the distance 
restraints.

Distance (A): Specify the distance in Ångstroms.

Deviation (A): Specify the deviation of the distance
restraints. A larger value allows higher deviation from the specified distance.

#### Secondary Structure tab

Segment: Specify the segment in the form of chainID:[residueName][residueID]-[chainID]:[residueName][residueID] . 
Selected segments of the model sequence
in the Sequence Window are automatically filled into this dialog field.

Type: Select Helix or Strand secondary structure type from the parameter.

You can find the ID for a residue in the model sequence by hovering the mouse over it in the Sequence Window before opening the protocol. Note that the chain ID may be blank.

#### Symmetry tab

Note that symmetry restraints can only be applied if Cut Overhangs is False .

Segment 1 and Segment 2: Specify two segments in the model sequence to be related symmetrically to each other, in the form of chainID:[residueName][residueID]-[chainID]:[residueName][residueID] . For a
multiple chain sequence model, two chains that match sequentially are 
automatically filled in as symmetrical pairs by default. If two segments are specified as a symmetry
pair, the two segments in the model structure maintain symmetry for the specified
atoms.

Atom Type: Select C-alpha , Backbone , or All atoms from the
parameter list. Symmetry restraints using the C-alpha option have
the lowest computational cost.

#### Other commands

Add: Adds a new empty restraint entry to the table.

Remove: Removes selected restraints from the table.

### Loop Refinement (MODELER) protocol dialog commands

The restraints definition for this protocol works in the same way as the 
Build Homology Models protocol. However, the restraints
only apply to the loop region.

### Build Mutants protocol dialog commands

The restraints definition for this protocol works in the same way as the 
Build Homology Models protocol. However, the restraints
only apply to the residues that are mutated and their neighbors specified by the Cut Radius parameter. Each mutated residue segment will be
filled in the Secondary Structure tab as a separate line.

# Define Disulfide Bridges dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_define-disulfide-bridges.htm

## Define Disulfide Bridges dialog

The Define Disulfide Bridges dialog is used in Build Homology Models, 
Loop Refinement (MODELER) and Build Mutants protocols to 
allow you to specify which cysteine pairs to bond to create disulfide bridges.

### Build Homology Models

Cys1: Lists the cysteine residues in Model Sequence .

Cys2: Click a table cell to list the cysteine residues available 
for bridging with the selected residue in Cys1 .

### Loop Refinement (MODELER)

Cys1: Lists the cysteine residues in the Loops .

Cys2: Click a table cell to list the cysteine residues available 
for bridging with the selected residue in Cys1 . 
A cysteine residue is available for bridging if it is not forming a disulfide bridge with a cysteine residue 
outside the Loops (see Note) and is within 10 Å with Cys1 .

Distance: Reports the distance between the Cys1 and Cys2 .

### Build Mutants

Cys1: Lists the cysteine residues after mutation or the cysteine residues within the Cut Radius of the mutants. Residues mutated to cysteine and cysteine residues 
within the Cut Radius are shown in blue. Other cysteine residues currently forming 
disulfide bridge with the cysteine within the distance cutoff are shown in black.

Cys2: Click a table cell to list the cysteine residues after mutation available 
for bridging with the selected residue in Cys1 . 
A cysteine residue is available for bridging if it is not forming a disulfide bridge with a non-mutated cysteine residue (see Note) 
and is within 10 Å with Cys1 .

The Distance reported in the table is calculated with the C-alpha atom to C-alpha atom distance of the original amino acids (assuming both of them are not cysteines), 
However, if one of the original amino acids was a cysteine, the Distance reported would be from the atom SG in that residue to the other residue's C-alpha atom.

Two cysteine residues are assumed to form a disulfide bridge if 
the distance between their sulfur atoms is less than 2.5 Å.

Depending on the other constraints that are imposed by the inputs 
to the protocol, it is not always possible to successfully form disulfide bridges. If your final structure does not
contain the specified disulfide bridges, try adjusting some of the other parameters of the protocol.

### Access methods

# Edit Membrane dialog

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_edit-membrane.htm

## Edit Membrane dialog

The Edit Membrane dialog allows you to define the orientation and dimensions of a membrane.

### Molecule Orientation with Respect to Membrane

The membrane orientation is defined relative to the principal axes of a set of reference atoms. The set of reference atoms is either the set of currently selected atoms belonging to the protein to which the membrane is attached, or all atoms of the molecule if no atoms are selected. The first principal axis is specified in the Transmembrane Protein Preferences

Shift (Å): Specifies the distance along the membrane normal between the center of the membrane and the center of geometry of the reference atoms.

Tilt (degrees): Specifies the angle between the membrane normal and the first principal axes of the reference atoms.

Rotation (degrees): Specifies the rotation angle between the normal and the plane defined by the tilt angle and the second principal axis of the reference atoms.

### Dimensions

Thickness (Å): Specifies the thickness of the membrane in angstroms. The thickness used here refers to the thickness of the low dielectric region of the lipid bilayer occupied by the hydrocarbon chains of the lipids.

### Access methods

# Graft Loop dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_graft-loop.htm

## Graft Loop dialog

The Graft Loop dialog allows you to graft a loop from a template structure onto a target structure. This can either be used to build a loop in a gap in the target structure, or to alter the conformation of an existing loop to that of the template. You can retain the sequence of an existing loop or build the loop using polyalanine or the sequence of the template structure.

The loops are specified by entering their first and last residues in the form chain:residue (for example, B:ALA110). However, if you enter just a number, the first residue that matches this will be filled in. If appropriate selections have been made before opening the dialog, the loop residues will be filled in automatically.

### Target protein

The Target protein options allow you to specify the target protein and the loop to be modeled.

[list]: Sets the target protein (that is, the one undergoing modeling).

Loop start: Specifies the start of the loop. If the loop is missing, then the residue before the start of the gap should be entered.

Loop end: Specifies the end of the loop. If the loop is missing, the residue after the end of the gap should be entered.

### Template protein

The Template protein options allow you to specify the template protein and the loop to be modeled.

[list]: Sets the template protein.

Loop start: Specifies the start of the loop to be copied.

Loop end: Specifies the end of the loop.

### Other options

Loop sequence: Provides three choices: Original sequence of target , Use template sequence and Build as polyalanine . The first option is only available if an existing loop of the same length as the template loop is being modeled.

Stem length: Specifies how many residues either side of the loop are used in aligning the template loop onto the target structure.

If the target protein has an existing loop or there is a selection, then a command to remove the original loop or selection will be run before the actual loop graft is performed. Therefore, if you wish to return to the starting structure you will need to perform two Undo steps.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Prepare Protein \| Graft Loop |

# Modify Protonation State dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_modify-protonation.htm

## Modify Protonation State dialog

This dialog allows you to modify the protonation state of amino acid chain termini and ionizable amino acid side-chains. Select the residues to be modified before opening this dialog, otherwise all termini will be modified and all sidechains set by pH. Residues must be explicitly selected in order to modify them to the charged or neutral state.

To set the protonation using predicted residue pK values, use the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK command on the Prepare Protein tools panel before using this dialog.

### Modify termini group

Modify termini: Termini are modified according to the following options:

* Charged: Ensures selected N-termini have a formal charge of +1 on the nitrogen with three hydrogen atoms (unless the model is no-hydrogen). Selected C-termini will be a negatively charged carboxylate group.

* Neutral: Formal charges are removed from the selected termini and hydrogens adjusted accordingly.

* At pH: Adjusts the protonation of selected termini to be appropriate to the pH setting.

* Remove: Removes terminal characteristics from the selected residues.

### Modify side-chain protonation group

Modify side-chain protonation: Side-chains are modified according to the following options:

* Charged: Selected ionizable residues are modified to their charged form.

* Neutral: Selected ionizable residues are modified to their neutral form.

* At pH: Selected residues are modified to the protonation state appropriate to the desired pH.

### Protonation of Neutral Histidine

ND1: Neutral histidine residues are protonated at the ND1 position.

NE2: Neutral histidine residues are protonated at the NE2 position.

### Other controls

Desired pH: Sets the pH to be used with the At pH options for termini and side-chains.

Use predicted pK: Uses predicted pK values if they are available. Otherwise standard pKas will apply.

# Renumber Sequences dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_renumber_sequence.htm

## Renumber Sequences dialog

The Renumber Sequences dialog allows residues along a chain to be renumbered. 
It can be used when a Molecule Window or a Sequence Window is active. 
The options to renumber by ruler or reference are only available when it is launched from
a Sequence Window.

Renumber residue range from [residue] to [residue]: Renumbers the selected range of residues starting with the specified residue number. 
This option removes any insertion codes in the selected range. When invoked from
the Graphics View, residues must be selected from a single chain. When invoked from
the Sequence Window residues must be selected from a single sequence

Shift selected residue numbers: Renumbers the selected range of residues by incrementing or decrementing the 
residue number by the specified shift value while preserving insertion codes.
The selection requirements are the same as for renumbering a range.

Relabel selected residues with insertion codes: The first selected residue has the insertion code set as specified. Subsequent residues 
are labeled by incrementing the insertion code character up until Z. The residue 
number for all selected residues is set to the first selected residue. 
In addition to the selection requirements for renumbering a range, the selection
is limited to 26 or fewer residues.

Renumber selected sequences using ruler label: Residue identifiers of selected sequences are set to match the ruler labels in a Sequence Window. 
The new identifiers depend on the ruler display style in use. If the
ruler is not shown, residue identifiers are defined assuming the Alignment 
index display style is used and insertion codes are deleted. In the Chain View with the Alignment index ruler, 
ruler numbering restarts for each chain. When the ruler is set to show 1st sequence
residue ID or to Consensus ID , certain ruler positions may have
undefined values. The N-terminal residues that aligned to the undefined ruler positions are 
numbered decrementally from the first defined ruler position, and zero or negative integers are possible. 
The C-terminal residues that aligned to the undefined ruler positions are numbered incrementally starting from the last 
defined ruler position. For internal undefined positions, an insertion code is added.

Renumber selected sequences to match reference sequence below: Renumbers the currently selected sequences in 
the Sequence Window to match the reference sequence that can be specified using the dropdown list. 
Residues are renumbered according to the residue numbers in the reference protein sequence based on sequence alignment. For N-terminal residues 
that do not map to the reference sequence, the residues are numbered decrementally from the first aligned residue in the reference sequence, and zero or negative integers are possible. For C-terminal unaligned residues, the residues are numbered incrementally starting from the last aligned 
residue. For internal gaps, an insertion code is added.

#### To renumber a consecutive residue range

* Select the residues in a range.

* Click Renumber Sequences... to open the Renumber Sequences dialog.

* Do one of the following: Choose Renumber residue range and set starting from residue ID . Choose Shift selected residue numbers and set shift by . Choose Relabel selected residues with insertion codes and set starting from insertion code .

* Choose Renumber residue range and set starting from residue ID .

* Choose Shift selected residue numbers and set shift by .

* Choose Relabel selected residues with insertion codes and set starting from insertion code .

* Right-click the active Sequence Window and choose Display Style... to open the Display Style dialog, and then set the ruler to the desired option.

The Chain ID will not be modified by this command.

Chain ID will not be modified by this command.

# Enter Nucleotide Sequence dialog

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/dl_specify.htm

## Enter Nucleotide Sequence dialog

The Enter Nucleotide Sequence dialog allows you to specify the nucleotide sequence when you build a nucleic acid 
molecule using the commands Create/Grow at 3' or Prepend at 5' .

There are two ways to select nucleotides for creation or growth, or prepending:

* Use the list at the top of the dialog.

* Type the one-letter codes in the Sense text box.

In both cases, the only available residue codes are those that are appropriate for the selected 
nucleic acid type (RNA or DNA, single or multiple-stranded, A-, B-, or Z-helical). 
For example, a Z-helix only accepts alternating G and C residues.

You can only append or prepend standard 
nucleotides, but you can mutate a selected residue into any of the supported nucleotide types including Pseudouridine,
Dihydrouridine, Inosine, and user defined nucleotides. When the build action is set to Mutate, the Specify command opens the Choose one Nucleotide dialog instead of this dialog.

The length of a nucleotide sequence used to append or prepend residues is practically unlimited, except for the available resources.

[base]: This list can be used to select the bases to be inserted into the nucleotide sequences.

### Specify Nucleotide Sequence

Depending on the number of chains in the nascent nucleic acid molecule, the dialog displays one, two, or three sequences.

Sense: This strand is always shown. It is also the only text field that can be edited from the keyboard.
If the molecule contains a single strand, this is the only text box displayed. The text box values begin at the 5' end and end with 
the 3' terminus.

Antisense: This strand is always shown for double-stranded molecules. The text box values run from 
3' to 5' end and it is not editable. It is automatically updated to reflect the user-defined sequence of the Sense strand.

Hoogsteen: This strand is shown for the DNA triplex. Because the Hoogsteen pyrimidine chain
is parallel to the purine chain, the text box values begin at the 5' end and ends with the 3' terminus. This text box is not editable. 
It is automatically updated to reflect the user-defined sequence of the Sense strand.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Build and Edit Nucleic Acid \| Choose Nucleotide \| Specify... |

# Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/electrostatics_calculate_protein_ionization_and_residue_pk-para.htm

## Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK - Parameters

### Calculates the ionization and pH dependent properties of multiple protein molecules

Calculates the isoelectric point ( pI ), the titration curves and the pKs of the individual sites of titration of protein molecules. It also calculates the Net Charge of molecule and the electrostatic contribution to the protein stability, the Relative Folding Energy , as a function of pH.

For each input molecule, the protocol optionally performs the following:

* Protonates the structure and optimizes the hydrogen network at given pH.

* Creates a molecular model with all amino acid residues fully protonated and assigns average atomic charges corresponding to the fractional protonation of the acidic and basic residues at given pH. When the fully protonated model is created, the protocol also calculates the average Dipole Moment and the Net Charge Square , as a function of pH.

* Calculates the electrostatic contribution to the free energy, ddGsolv , of transferring the molecule from the solvent to a condensed (aggregated, crystalline) state as a function of pH.

The pH-dependent ddGsolv , Net Charge Square and the Dipole Moment can be used to determine the pH-range for optimal solubility. Larger values of ddGsolv and Net Charge Square correspond to increased solubility. A larger molecular dipole moment caused by larger asymmetry of protein charge distribution could decrease the solubility of the protein molecule and increase the viscosity of the solution, especially when solution pH is close to the isoelectric point where the electrostatic repulsion between solvated molecules is minimal.

Fully protonated structures can be further analyzed by the Electrostatics protocols, e.g., to study the changes of the electrostatic potential at different pH.

If an implicit membrane exists, the calculations will take into account the effect of the membrane. To add an implicit membrane to a protein:

* In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools.

* In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. A fast and accurate computational approach to protein ionization. Protein Science 2008 , 
17, 1955-1970.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include PDB, DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. Supported forcefields for the calculations are CHARMm, charmm36, and CHARMm Polar H. The input molecules that are not typed or typed with another forcefield will be typed or re-typed automatically. Use the Forcefield parameter to select one of the supported forcefields. Note : Each selected protein molecule should have at least one titratable amino acid residue. |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant of the protein and membrane interior. |
| Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant of the solvent. |
| Ionic Strength | Specifies the ionic strength of the solvent (M). |
| At pH | Specifies the pH value to protonate the molecule and to assign the average partial atomic charges in the fully protonated structure. Note : The At pH value must be inside the range defined by From pH and To pH parameters. |
| Protonate Molecule | If set to "True", protonates or deprotonates the acidic and basic groups at a pH defined by the value of At pH parameter and according to the Predicted pK values of ionizable residues. # Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/electrostatics_calculate_protein_ionization_and_residue_pk.htm

## Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Analyzing Results

The Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol performs the following for one or more protein systems:

* Predicts the pK 1/2 and titration curves for each titratable amino acid residues and N- and C-terminal groups.

* Calculates the total charge of the protein as a function of pH and predicts the isoelectric point (pI) of the protein.

* Calculates the electrostatic contribution to the free energy of folding as a function of pH. The free energy can be
used to estimate the protein stability at different solution pHs.

* Protonates the residues at a given pH according to predicted pK 1/2 . For HIS, ASP, and GLU residues the hydrogens are added
such that the system has lowest CHARMm energy. The nitrogen and oxygen atoms on the side-chain of ASN and GLN residues are also flipped if
necessary to obtain a conformation with lower energy.

* Creates a fully protonated model of the molecule by adding hydrogens to all titratible amino acid residues, including N- and C-terminal groups. 
Assigns mean atomic charges to protein atoms based on the fractional protonation of the acidic and basic residues at a given pH and ionic strength.
The fully protonated model, with mean atomic charges at a given pH can be used as input for the 
Electrostatic Potential
to study the change
in the 3-D distribution of the electrostatic potential with changing the acidicity and the ionic strength of the solution.

* Calculates the average dipole moment of the molecule as a function of pH.

* Calculates the electrostatic contribution to the solvation energy difference, ddGsolv, as a function of pH. 
The energy is defined as transferring a molecule from the solvent to a condensed (e.g. crystalline) phase and is 
calculated as the difference of the solvation energies between the molecule in a medium with a dielectric constant of the solvent
and in a medium with the dielectric constant of the condensed phase.

In the case of membrane proteins, an implicit membrane can be added to the molecular
model and the effect of the low-dielectric environment of the membrane will be taken into account in the
calculations.

This protocol calculates the ionization properties of one or more protein molecules.
The protocol can be run from the Tool Panel (recommended) or Protocols Explorer. 
The calculations require protein structures that are properly prepared and typed by the CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H
forcefield. The input structures that are not typed or typed with another forcefield, e.g. charmm22, charmm27 etc., will be 
automatically typed (or re-typed) with the forcefield specified by the Forcefield parameter.
For membrane proteins, an implicit membrane should be added.

* Load one or more protein molecules into a Molecule Window .

* Clean the protein structures. This can be done by running the Prepare Proteins protocol, which optionally includes the pK calculations and protonation. Alternatively, set the preferences in the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog dialog so that the Clean Protein tool will remove alternate conformations, add termini, and patch missing side-chain atoms, and then run the tool. Note that this tool does not refine the positions of any added atoms.

* To add an implicit membrane to the protein structure use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools panel or the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

* Apply the CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H forcefield to the protein structure. Use the Apply Forcefield command in the Change Forcefield tools panel.

* Make sure that all the prepared input protein molecules from steps above are loaded into one Molecule Window .

* Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK... to open the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the parameters as desired. For details, see Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

To view the predicted pK values and to observe the protonation of amino acid residues at a given pH

When the interactive job finishes, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer and click the Report link.
In the Report Summary Table, click the individual molecule link in ViewResults column
to open the output structure. Expand
the Data Table and open the AminoAcid tab.

The predicted pK values appear in three columns as Predicted C-term pK , Predicted N-term pK , and Predicted pK for the C-terminal, N-terminal, and
side-chain pK values respectively.

If the Protonate Molecule parameter was set to True , the protonation state of the protein in the output .mol2 file is reset at the given pH. The hydrogens of acidic and basic residues are added or removed, according to 
the predicted pK 1/2 , and the coordinates of the entire hydrogen network is optimized.
For each deprotonated histidine and protonated aspartic acid and glutamic acid, the hydrogen atom is positioned so that the tautomeric states of the residues are assgined to obtain the lowest CHARMm energy. Side-chain oxygen and nitrogen atoms of ASN and GLN residues are also flipped if necessary to obtain a lower energy conformation.

Alternatively, the protonation states of the residue side-chains and termini can be set using the Modify Termini and Change Sidechain Protonation State tools in the Build and Edit Protein tool panel according to the predicted pK 1/2 . However, the positions of the added protons
are not optimized according to energy criteria.

To investigate the pH dependent electrostatic properties

Click the individual molecule link in the Details column in the Summary Table. The detailed report of the protein is shown with the relative folding energy and the protein net charge (e.g., titration curve) plotted against solution pH.
The relative folding energy can be used to
compare the stability of two conformations as a function of pH. The protein net charge at the selcted pH
and the calculated isoelectric point are shown in the Summary table in the Report .

If Fully Protonated Model is set to True , net charge square and dipole moment
are also plotted against solution pH. If Calculate Solvation Energy is set to True ,
ddGsolv versus pH plot will also be shown in the detailed report of individial protein.

The transfer energy (ddGsolv), the net charge square and the dipole moment can be used to determine the pH-range for optimal solubility. 
The more positive values of ddGsolv and bigger values of net charge square correspond to increased solubility. 
A higher molecular dipole moment caused by larger asymmetry of protein charge 
distribution could decrease the solubility of the protein molecule and increase the viscosity of the solution, 
especially when solution pH is close to the isoelectric point where the charge-charge repulsion between solvated molecules is minimal.

To view the electrostatic potential of the molecule of mean charge at given pH

If Fully Protonated Model is set to True during the calculation,
a fully protonated molecule with atomic charges assigned according to the titration curve of each titratable site is created in the output.

* From the Report page, click individual molecule link in the ViewResults column in the Summary table.
The structure of the fully protonated model appears in the Molecule Window . 
From the menu bar click Structure|Monitor|Dipole Moment. The vector of molecular dipole moment calculated at the selected pH
appears in the structure, labeled with its value.

* In the Molecule Window , expand
the Data Table and open the Atom tab. The mean atomic charges calculated at the selected pH appear in the Partial Charge column, replacing the forcefield charges of the atoms of the titratable groups.

* To calculate and visualize the spatial and surface distribution of the average electrostatic potential at the selected pH, use the fully protonated structure as input to the Calculate Electrostatic Potential protocol in the same way as if typed with the standard forcefield parameters.

This fully protonated molecule is a model that represents the statistic average
of multiple protonation states of a protein in a given solution at a specific pH. It is not suitable as input to other
protocols, except the Calculate Electrostatic Potential protocol. In most cases, the total molecular charge of this model is not an integer.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

For each protein entry, the following files are created in the corresponding subfolder in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <protein>_OUT.mol2 | The molecular structure with the property values calculated by this protocol. |
| <protein>_FullyProtonated.mol2 | The molecular structure with all hydrogens added and with partial atomic charges adjusted to the fractional protonation of the titratable groups at the selected pH. This file is generated only when the Fully Protonated Model parameter is set to True . |
| <protein>.csv | Contains the raw data of the calculated pH dependent on the electrostatic energy and titration curve of the residues. |
| <protein>_pK.csv | Contains the predicted pK of the titratable residues. |
| <protein>_Charge_Dipole.csv | Contains the raw data of the pH dependency of the net charge, net charge square, dipole moment, the transfer energy ddGsolv and the solvation energies of the molecule in the condensed phase and in the solvent. This file is generated only when the Calculate Solvation Energy parameter is set to True . |

#### Further information

Theory - Protein Ionization and Residue pK Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK tutorial

## NCBI Entrez Sequence Search - Parameters

### Searches and retrieves protein and nucleotide sequences from NCBI

Uses the Entrez ESearch and EFetch utilities to search the Protein and Nucleotide databases at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). Enter search terms in the corresponding parameters and specify the type(s) of sequences you wish to retrieve. All search terms are combined using AND logic. Use the Advanced Parameter Text Query to perform more complex queries.

| Text Query | A word or phrase to search for, for example, stem cells . If this parameter is defined, all other search terms are ignored, except Sequence Type . Text Query accepts a combination of terms, fields, boolean operators to conduct advanced search. For example, use transporter[titl] AND ("Drosophila melanogaster"[orgn] OR "Mus musculus"[orgn]) and set the Sequence Type to Protein to find the transporter proteins in Drosophila melanogaster or Mus musculus. # NCBI Entrez Sequence Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/general_purpose_ncbi_entrez_sequence_search.htm

## NCBI Entrez Sequence Search

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

This protocol uses the Entrez ESearch and EFetch utilities to search the Protein and Nucleotide databases at 
the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) and retrieves protein or nucleotide 
sequences or both. You can search a sequence in the database 
by matching a word or phrase in any fields of a sequence record or in a specific field such 
as title, protein name, organism, etc. Enter search terms in the corresponding parameters and all 
search terms are combined using AND logic. Use the advanced parameter text query to perform more complex queries.

* Open the MacroMolecules | Query Online Databases tools and click NCBI Entrez Sequence Search to open the NCBI Entrez Sequence Search dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Enter a word or phrase in any of the search field or input a query string in the Text Query under
the Advanced parameter group. If Text Query is not empty, other search
fields will be ignored. For details about the search fields and other parameters, 
see NCBI Entrez Sequence Search - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, a Sequence List Window opens which contains the resulting sequences with the sequence name, the description, 
the sequence type, and the sequence length. A dialog also opens to report the number of hits. Click OK to close the dialog.

If the job ran in background, click on the job in Jobs Explorer to
open the experiment report. Review the information in the Summary and click on the View Result button to open the Sequence List Window.

From the Sequence List Window, select one or more proteins, right-click and choose Open in Annotation Window to open each selected sequence in a Sequence Annotation Window
or Open in Sequence Window to open all the selected sequences in one Sequence Window.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Protein Sequences.gb | Protein sequences retrieved by the query. |
| Nucleotide Sequences.gb | Nucleotide sequences retrieved by the query. |

# Prepare Proteins - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/general_purpose_prepare_protein-para.htm

## Prepare Proteins - Parameters

### Prepares imported protein structure(s) for further modeling

Addresses problems commonly found in protein structures obtained by experimental or third party modeling methods.

The following steps are performed:

* Standardize atom names, insert missing atoms in residues and remove alternate conformations. May also remove water and ligand molecules depending on the setting of Advanced|Keep Waters and Advanced|Keep Ligands .

* Insert missing loop regions based on SEQRES data from PDB files, _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme from mmCIF files, or user specified loop definitions (optional).

* Optimize short and medium size loop regions with the LOOPER algorithm (optional).

* Minimize the remaining loop regions (optional).

* Calculate the pK and protonate the structure (optional).

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Flook, P.K.; Yan, L. LOOPER: a molecular mechanics-based algorithm for protein loop prediction. Protein Engineering Design and Selection 2008 , 21(2), 91-100.

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. A fast and accurate computational approach to protein ionization. Protein Science 2008 , 17, 1955-1970.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. |
| Build Loops | Insert missing loops. Missing loops of lengths less than or equal to the Maximal Loop Length are inserted and initially refined using Modeler. Further refinement is optional using Looper and/or CHARMm minimization. Note: Only internal loop regions can be inserted. Missing residues at either the N- or C-terminal of a chain will not be added. Valid Values: True , False |
| Loop Definition | Source for missing loop definitions. The two options are: User : Loops are built as specified in the Loop List . SEQRES : All internal loops that are missing in the protein structure compared to the PDB SEQRES field or mmCIF _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme data will be inserted. If this option is used, the Input Protein needs to contain SEQRES or _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme data. Valid Values: User, SEQRES |
| Loop List | List of loops that will be inserted into the structure if User is selected for Loop Definition . The required format is: [loop1],[loop2],..,[loopN], where each item in the list specifies a loop. Define each loop as: [chainname]:[residue type][residue number]:[loop sequence], where chainname, residue type and residue number specify the residue after which the loop should be inserted, and loop sequence is the sequence of one-letter residue codes of the inserted loop. Example: "A:ASN5:DYA,A:GLY20:CDPAI". This parameter should only be used when running the protocol on a single protein molecule. |
| Maximal Loop Length | Maximal length of loops that will be inserted. Note: There is currently no known method to accurately predict the structure of long loop insertions (> 14 residues). Predictions for such loops should be subjected to further refinement and careful analysis. |
| Use Looper | Determines if short to medium size loops (as defined by the Maximal Loop Length parameter) are being refined using the Looper algorithm. Note: Depending on the number and length of loops, this step can require significant amount of computation time. See Also: Spassov, V.Z.; Flook, P.K.; Yan, L. LOOPER: a molecular mechanics-based algorithm for protein loop prediction. Protein Engineering Design and Selection 2008 , 21(2), 91-100. Valid Values: True, False |
| Use Looper Maximal Loop Length | Maximal length of loop regions for which the Looper method is used for prediction. Note: The method is most accurate for short to medium size loops (< 13 residues). |
| Use CHARMm Minimization | Determines if loops are further refined using a CHARMm minimization. Note : if Use Looper is True, minimization will only be performed for loops not already refined with the Looper algorithm (i.e. only loops longer than the Maximal Loop Length parameter in the Looper parameter group). Valid Values: True , False |
| Flexible Stem Residues | Number of stem residues at both ends of a loop region allowed to move in the optimization of an inserted loop. |
| Protonate | Protonates the final structure using the same method as used in the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol. This predicts the pK of the titratable residues and protonates as appropriate for the specified pH, then optimizes all of the hydrogen positions. See Also: Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. A fast and accurate computational approach to protein ionization. Protein Science 2008 , 17, 1955-1970. Valid Values: True , False |
| Protein Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant of the protein interior. |
| pH for Protonation | pH value to protonate the molecule. |
| Ionic Strength | Ionic Strength [M] of the solvent. |
| Energy Cutoff | Value of cutoff energy (kcal/mol) used to define the protonation sites included in the iterative mobile clusters. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Forcefield | Forcefield to be used for the calculations. Valid Values: CHARMm , CHARMPLR, charmm36 |
| Keep Ligands | Keep ligands other than water in the prepared structure. A ligand is defined as a chain in the Input Protein that does not contain any amino acids, nucleic acids or waters, but does contain at least one carbon atom. It can also be a molecule that does not contain chains but does contain at least one carbon atom. Valid Values: True , False |
| Keep Water | Set of water molecules to keep in the cleaned structure: None : Remove all water molecules. Selected : Keep only selected water molecules. All : Keep all water molecules. Valid Values: None , Selected, All |
| Disulfide Bridges | Comma-separated list of disulfide bridges to be imposed in inserted loop regions. A disulfide bridge consists of two Cysteine residues connected by '-', where a Cysteine residue is specified by [chain]:CYS[residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: "A:CYS32-A:CYS70,B:CYS15-B:CYS40A". This parameter should only be used when running the protocol on a single protein molecule. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

# Prepare Proteins

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/general_purpose_prepare_protein.htm

## Prepare Proteins

* Introduction

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

* Troubleshooting

### Description

The Prepare Proteins protocol prepares proteins for input into
other protocols, performing tasks such as inserting missing atoms in incomplete
residues, modeling missing loop regions, deleting alternate conformations (disorder), removing waters,
standardizing atom names, and protonating titratable residues using predicted pKs.

The protocol executes the following steps, some of which can be
controlled by parameters:

* Cleans the protein(s)

* Optimize side-chain conformation for residues with inserted atoms

* Remove water molecules (optional)

* Model missing loop regions based on PDB SEQRES or mmCIF _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme information or by user-definition (optional)

* Predict titration site pKs and protonate the structure at the specified pH (optional)

The protocol begins by standardizing atom names, removing alternate conformations (disorder), and inserting missing main and side-chain atoms using some of the techniques performed by the Clean Protein command on Prepare Protein tool panel. For additional information, see Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog .

If any residues have missing atoms, the atoms will be inserted by the protocol as discussed above and the conformation
of the side-chain atoms of those residues will be optimized using the ChiRotor algorithm (the same method as used in Side-Chain Refinement protocol). Other residues, including any completed prior to running the protocol, are fixed at their input position.

The protocol automatically detects if residues are missing in the input structure based on the SEQRES record
from a PDB file or _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme records in an mmCIF file, then optionally builds them and optimizes their conformation. Alternatively, you can
specify a segment by specifying a starting residue and the sequence to insert. The patched residue
segments are treated as loop regions and will be first optimized using the MODELER loop refinement algorithm 
(the same method as used in Loop Refinement (MODELER) protocol), which optimizes the added loops simultaneously and produces a single model structure. It is not intended
to provide the best conformation of all loops at this stage, but only to produce a structure having reasonable
loop conformations that do not clash with the rest of the structure. Then optionally, each loop is further
optimized sequentially using the Looper algorithm (the same method as used in Loop Refinement protocol).

In general, when loops are longer than 12 residues, their conformation cannot be accurately predicted and it is best not to patch those loops into the structure. There are two parameters control the length
of the loop: the first one controls the length of the loop to be patched, and the second one controls the length
of the loop to be optimized using the Looper refinement algorithm. If a loop is patched, but not
optimized with the Looper algorithm, its conformation is generated by the MODELER loop refinement algorithm and can be further minimized using the CHARMm minimization procedure. It is recommended that you use the
Looper refinement algorithm to optimize any patched loop shorter than 13 residues.

Often, the stem residues where the loop is inserted have missing atoms. In this case, the loop is extended
one residue on one or both of the N- or C-terminal side depending on which side has missing atoms. There is also
an option to specify how many stem residues you want to include in the loop optimization. Since you want to keep the coordinates of the atoms at their input
conformation, it is not recommended to
include stem residues in the loop refinement.

You can also specify disulfide bridges between the inserted loop Cys residues and any other Cys residues for loop refinement.

By default, water molecules are removed from the structure, but all or selected waters can be retained. Note that there is a limitation in the loop building method which may cause ligand bond orders to be corrupted if water molecules are retained and loops are built. Please check and correct ligand bond orders if necessary after preparing a structure under these conditions.
Any ligands in the protein structure are retained in the calculation by default, but you can specify to remove them. If the protein has any nucleic acid residues, they are retained in the calculation.

Finally, the protocol predicts the pK of the titratable residues and optimizes all of the hydrogen positions
using the same method as used in the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol.

* Load the input protein(s) in a new Molecule Window. Alternatively, the protocol can read the molecules directly from file using the Browse... option.

* Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Prepare Proteins... to open the Prepare Proteins dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Protein Molecules Set the Input Protein Molecules. You can select All, Selected, or Visible molecules from the active molecule window, or alternatively use the Browse option to select one or more structure files. The selected molecules should have unique names. If a name appears more than once, rename one of them. Build Loops Set this to True to model missing loop regions. Additional parameters under the Build Loops parameter group control the method by which missing loop regions are built
and optimized. If you want to use the Loop Refinement method to
optimize the inserted loops, set Use Looper to True . Protonate Calculates protein ionization and protonate the input protein structure. Parameters under the Protonate parameter group specify the pH value and dielectric constant used in the protein ionization calculation. For details about the remaining parameters, see Prepare Proteins - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | Set the Input Protein Molecules. You can select All, Selected, or Visible molecules from the active molecule window, or alternatively use the Browse option to select one or more structure files. The selected molecules should have unique names. If a name appears more than once, rename one of them. |
| Build Loops | Set this to True to model missing loop regions. Additional parameters under the Build Loops parameter group control the method by which missing loop regions are built and optimized. If you want to use the Loop Refinement method to optimize the inserted loops, set Use Looper to True . |
| Protonate | Calculates protein ionization and protonate the input protein structure. Parameters under the Protonate parameter group specify the pH value and dielectric constant used in the protein ionization calculation. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Prepare Proteins - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the prepared protein structure(s) are automatically opened in a new molecule window with the first one visible and the remainer initially hidden. If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the prepared structure.

Each prepared structure contains groups in its hierarchy that identify modifications made by the protocol.
The Added Loops assembly holds groups containing residues that were inserted by the protocol. 
The Fixed Side-chains assembly contains a group for each residue for which the side-chain was modeled by the protocol.

The Report contains tables with links to detailed sub-reports for each of the input protein structures, and also links to allow each prepared protein to be opened separately.

The Summary section of the sub-reports lists the segments that are missing in the input structure compared to its SEQRES or _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme records. The Details section of the sub-reports provides additional information on the steps executed by the protocol to prepare the input protein. These can include standardization of atom names, removal of alternate conformations, modification of termini and bond orders, patching and refinement of incomplete residues (backbone and side chains), and insertion and refinement of missing segments.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. Note that the results for each separate molecule are stored in subfolders; links to these files are present in the sub-reports. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <protein>/<protein>_prep.dsv | The molecule output after performing the preparation steps specified by the user. The Added Loops group in the hierarchy contains any residues that were inserted by the protocol. The Fixed Side Chains group contains any residue for which the side-chain was modeled by the protocol. |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <protein>/<protein>_RMSD.log | Log file containing RMSD and other information created during side-chain refinement. This file is only generated if there are side-chains to be refined. |
| <protein>/<protein>_charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine during side-chain refinement. This file is only generated if there are side-chains to be refined. |
| <protein>/<protein>.csv | Contains the raw data of the calculated pH dependent on the electrostatic energy and titration curve of the residues. This file is only generated if the Protonate option is enabled. |
| <protein>/<protein>.pK | Contains the predicted pK of the titratable residues. This file is only generated if the Protonate option is enabled. |

# RCSB Structure Search - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/general_purpose_rcsb_structure_search-para.htm

## RCSB Structure Search - Parameters

### Searches the RCSB structure database

Searches the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics (RCSB) Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure database.

You can perform advanced searches of the RCSB with a variety of criteria:

* ID : A number of different ID Type s are allowed, including PDB and PubMed.

* Keyword : Such as "P38 Map Kinase".

* Ligand : Search for ligands using fingerprint or qualitative graph matching criteria.

* Experimental Method : e.g. "X-RAY", "SOLUTION NMR".

* Resolution : To filter out low (or high) resolution structures.

* Release Date : The date the structures were released.

* Author Name : Find structures deposited by a particular author.

* SCOP Classification : Structural classification.

* Motif : Sequence motifs.

If searching for a ligand, the results can be aligned to the ligand query

The search results can be filtered using the Sequence Similarity Filter parameter, to return one representative structure for protein chain sequences clustered at various thresholds.

Alternatively, you can search using the RCSB JSON advanced parameter. The query needs to be written according to the documentation on the RCSB PDB website that provides this search, and must specify the return_type as "entry". See https://search.rcsb.org/ for details.

### Parameters

| Name | Description | | | | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ID | Search the PDB for known identifiers (IDs). You can do various different types of ID searches by changing the ID Type parameter. Four-letter PDB IDs are the default. For all ID types you can type in multiple space or comma separated IDs to search for several IDs at once. | | | | | | | | | | |
| ID Type | You can search for a number of different ID types: PDB : Four letter PDB ID, e.g. "1crn". PubMed : Numeric PubMed ID (PMID), e.g. "12929391" UniProt : Universal Protein Accession ID, combining Swiss-Prot, TrEMBL and PIR databases, e.g. "P80280". Chemical Component : PDB chemical component, e.g. "RSD", "RET", "ALA", "TYS" or "A1AC1" All types allow multiple IDs separated by space, comma or newline. Valid Values: PDB , PubMed, UniProt, Chemical Component | | | | | | | | | | |
| Keywords | Enter a keyword, phrase or series of keywords. Use the Search Scope to control what attributes to search and the Operator parameter to control whether to match the whole phrase or individual words. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Keywords Search Scope | Specify whether to search the full text or specific fields. The options are: Structure Attributes : searches the struct_keywords.text,struct.title and citation.title attributes. Full Text : searches the full text Valid Values: Structure Attributes , Full Text | | | | | | | | | | |
| Keywords Operator | contains_words : Any given word can match for a hit. contains_phrase : The whole given phrase must match for a hit. Valid Values: contains_words, contains_phrase | | | | | | | | | | |
| Ligand Query | Specify an MDL MOL/SD file that contains a substructure query. In Discovery Studio, select one of the visible molecules from a list. Query atoms are not currently supported and Hydrogen atoms are ignored. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Match Type | Exact or qualitative highly similar or substructure searches. Please note that the searches depend on the input ligand structure having bond orders and formal charges correctly assigned. In many cases different options will return the same results. The options cover all of the choices available from RCSB plus a simple exact match, including: Exact : Uses the InChIKey descriptor to find exact matches. graph-relaxed : Finds similar structures by Graph Matching comparison using element, formal charge and bond order. sub-struct-graph-relaxed : as above, but finds substructures. graph-relaxed-stereo : Finds similar structures by Graph Matching comparison using element, formal charge, bond order and atom/bond stereochemistry. sub-struct-graph-relaxed-stereo : as above but finds substructures. fingerprint-similarity : TREE and MACCS. See https://www.rcsb.org/docs/search-and-browse/advanced-search/chemical-search for details. Valid Values: Exact , graph-exact, graph-relaxed, graph-relaxed-stereo, graph-strict, fingerprint-similarity, sub-struct-graph-exact, sub-struct-graph-relaxed, sub-struct-graph-relaxed-stereo, sub-struct-graph-strict | | | | | | | | | | |
| Align to Query | Align the structures to the Ligand Query, if they contain a matching substructure. AlignmentRMS (Å) is added to each aligned structure. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | |
| Experimental Method | Method used to determine the structure. Most structures in the PDB have primary data associated with the experiment and therefore it sometimes useful to search based on this criteria. With the exception of NMR data where retrain coordinates are supplied, most associated data are in the form of structure factors. Valid options are: ELECTRON CRYSTALLOGRAPHY ELECTRON MICROSCOPY EPR FIBER DIFFRACTION FLUORESCENCE TRANSFER INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY NEUTRON DIFFRACTION POWDER DIFFRACTION SOLID-STATE NMR SOLUTION NMR SOLUTION SCATTERING THEORETICAL MODEL X-RAY DIFFRACTION Valid Values: , ELECTRON CRYSTALLOGRAPHY, ELECTRON MICROSCOPY, EPR, FIBER DIFFRACTION, FLUORESCENCE TRANSFER, INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY, NEUTRON DIFFRACTION, POWDER DIFFRACTION, SOLID-STATE NMR, SOLUTION NMR, SOLUTION SCATTERING, THEORETICAL MODEL, X-RAY DIFFRACTION | | | | | | | | | | |
| Has Experimental Data | Filter results based on whether experimental data is provided. This is most commonly used to find X-ray structures which have structure factors. If blank, no such filtering is performed. Note this can be used without specifying an experimental method. Valid Values: , True, False | | | | | | | | | | |
| Resolution | The X-ray resolution (Å). The smallest value for the interplanar spacings for the reflection data used in the refinement. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Resolution Lower Bound | Results will all have a resolution equal to or higher than this value. Setting this value will filter out higher quality structures. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Resolution Upper Bound | Results will all have a resolution equal to or lower than this value. Setting this value will filter out lower quality structures. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Release Date | Search on the date the structure was released to the public by the depositor. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Release Date Earliest | Search for structures deposited after this date. The date can be provided in many different formats. If the date is not fully specified, missing fields will be filled based on today's date. It is the user's responsibility to ensure there is no ambiguity; if a single number is entered then it will be interpreted as a month if it lies between 1-12, as a day if between 13-31 and otherwise as a year. For example, setting this parameter to Camelidae will only find structures that have been assigned as this family rather than as a specific species. To find all the hits for this family would require setting the parameter to list all of them i.e. Camelidae,Lama glama,Lama pacos,Camelus dromedarius etc. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Read Option | Options for reading structures: mmCIF: Reads all hits from mmCIF format files. PDB: Only reads hits which are available in the .pdb file format. Notes : mmCIF is now the standard archive format for RCSB Protein Data Bank structures, and therefore all hits should be available in this format. The legacy .pdb format cannot support all structures and therefore files may only be available for a subset of hits. Valid Values: mmCIF , PDB | | | | | | | | | | |
| Maximum | Maximum number of hits to return. Note that some RCSB files contain multiple models, which are returned as separate structures. Use the First Model Only parameter, which is in the Advanced group, to control whether all models for such hits should be returned or just the first. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. | | | | | | | | | | |
| Sequence Similarity Filter | Sequence similarity filter used to filter results from all other criteria. If no other criteria are defined this filter will not be applied. The RCSB protein polymer entities are clustered using MMseqs2 at 30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, 95%, and 100% sequence identity. For each cluster, a representative structure with the best resolution is read. If Keep Whole Structure is False , the structure is pruned to keep only the first instance of the relevant chain entity plus any non-protein moieties. Each downloaded structure will have properties detailing the Cluster Size, the Entities in Cluster, and the Cluster PDB IDs. To retrieve all structures for one cluster, copy the list of Cluster PDB IDs, open this protocol again, paste into the ID parameter and then run the search, with Maximum set to an appropriate value. Note: In the RCSB database, 'Entity' refers to a unique molecule, which may be a polymer chain, water molecule, or any other moiety such as a ligand or ion. In Discovery Studio, the Entity property is read for protein and nucleic acid chains from mmCIF format files. A multimeric structure can contain multiple instances of the same entity. For example, the 4INS insulin dimer contains four amino acid chains, consisting of two copies of two different protein sequences. The A and C amino acid chains have an Entity value 1, while amino acid chains B and D are Entity 2. Valid Values: , 100, 95, 90, 70, 50, 30 | | | | | | | | | | |
| Keep Whole Structure | If True, the entire structure containing each representative chain entity is kept. Otherwise, the structure is pruned to remove all protein chains except for the first instance of the entity; non-protein chains are all retained. Valid Values: True, False | | | | | | | | | | |
| SCOP Classification | Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) Classification Index. SCOP is a classification scheme for protein folds, useful in determining common structures where sequences may not be similar. Filtering by SCOP index allows you to retrieve hits in the same structural class as a protein of interest. Currently this requires the SCOP index number. You can find the number you need by searching http://scop.berkeley.edu/ . It is the number in square brackets. | | | | | | | | | | |

| Sequence Type | This parameter controls the target sequence type of the motif query. Either protein (pdb_protein_sequence), DNA (pdb_dna_sequence) or RNA (pdb_rna_sequence). Valid Values: pdb_protein_sequence , pdb_rna_sequence, pdb_dna_sequence | | | | | | | | | | |

Examples can be generated from the RCSB website by performing an advanced search and then clicking on the JSON button which appears in the QUERY section of the search panel. It is important to note that in order for the hits to be returned in the correct form for retrieval of the structures, you should include the term: "request_options" { "return_all_hits": true} and the return_type must be set to "entry" . Search the PDB for known identifiers (IDs). You can do various different types of ID searches by changing the ID Type parameter. Four-letter PDB IDs are the default.

For all ID types you can type in multiple space or comma separated IDs to search for several IDs at once.

You can search for a number of different ID types:

* PDB : Four letter PDB ID, e.g. "1crn".

* PubMed : Numeric PubMed ID (PMID), e.g. "12929391"

* UniProt : Universal Protein Accession ID, combining Swiss-Prot, TrEMBL and PIR databases, e.g. "P80280".

* Chemical Component : PDB chemical component, e.g. "RSD", "RET", "ALA", "TYS" or "A1AC1"

All types allow multiple IDs separated by space, comma or newline.

Valid Values: PDB , PubMed, UniProt, Chemical Component

Enter a keyword, phrase or series of keywords. Use the Search Scope to control what attributes to search and the Operator parameter to control whether to match the whole phrase or individual words.

Specify whether to search the full text or specific fields.

The options are:

* Structure Attributes : searches the struct_keywords.text,struct.title and citation.title attributes.

* Full Text : searches the full text

Valid Values: Structure Attributes , Full Text

* contains_words : Any given word can match for a hit.

* contains_phrase : The whole given phrase must match for a hit.

Valid Values: contains_words, contains_phrase

Specify an MDL MOL/SD file that contains a substructure query.

In Discovery Studio, select one of the visible molecules from a list.

Query atoms are not currently supported and Hydrogen atoms are ignored.

Exact or qualitative highly similar or substructure searches. Please note that the searches depend on the input ligand structure having bond orders and formal charges correctly assigned. In many cases different options will return the same results. The options cover all of the choices available from RCSB plus a simple exact match, including:

* Exact : Uses the InChIKey descriptor to find exact matches.

* graph-relaxed : Finds similar structures by Graph Matching comparison using element, formal charge and bond order.

* sub-struct-graph-relaxed : as above, but finds substructures.

* graph-relaxed-stereo : Finds similar structures by Graph Matching comparison using element, formal charge, bond order and atom/bond stereochemistry.

* sub-struct-graph-relaxed-stereo : as above but finds substructures.

* fingerprint-similarity : TREE and MACCS.

See https://www.rcsb.org/docs/search-and-browse/advanced-search/chemical-search for details.

Valid Values: Exact , graph-exact, graph-relaxed, graph-relaxed-stereo, graph-strict, fingerprint-similarity, sub-struct-graph-exact, sub-struct-graph-relaxed, sub-struct-graph-relaxed-stereo, sub-struct-graph-strict

Align the structures to the Ligand Query, if they contain a matching substructure. AlignmentRMS (Å) is added to each aligned structure.

Valid Values: True , False

Method used to determine the structure. Most structures in the PDB have primary data associated with the experiment and therefore it sometimes useful to search based on this criteria. With the exception of NMR data where retrain coordinates are supplied, most associated data are in the form of structure factors. Valid options are:

* ELECTRON CRYSTALLOGRAPHY

* ELECTRON MICROSCOPY

* EPR

* FIBER DIFFRACTION

* FLUORESCENCE TRANSFER

* INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY

* NEUTRON DIFFRACTION

* POWDER DIFFRACTION

* SOLID-STATE NMR

* SOLUTION NMR

* SOLUTION SCATTERING

* THEORETICAL MODEL

* X-RAY DIFFRACTION

Valid Values: , ELECTRON CRYSTALLOGRAPHY, ELECTRON MICROSCOPY, EPR, FIBER DIFFRACTION, FLUORESCENCE TRANSFER, INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY, NEUTRON DIFFRACTION, POWDER DIFFRACTION, SOLID-STATE NMR, SOLUTION NMR, SOLUTION SCATTERING, THEORETICAL MODEL, X-RAY DIFFRACTION

Filter results based on whether experimental data is provided. This is most commonly used to find X-ray structures which have structure factors. If blank, no such filtering is performed. Note this can be used without specifying an experimental method.

Valid Values: , True, False

The X-ray resolution (Å). The smallest value for the interplanar spacings for the reflection data used in the refinement.

Results will all have a resolution equal to or higher than this value. Setting this value will filter out higher quality structures.

Results will all have a resolution equal to or lower than this value. Setting this value will filter out lower quality structures.

Search on the date the structure was released to the public by the depositor.

Search for structures deposited after this date. The date can be provided in many different formats. If the date is not fully specified, missing fields will be filled based on today's date. It is the user's responsibility to ensure there is no ambiguity; if a single number is entered then it will be interpreted as a month if it lies between 1-12, as a day if between 13-31 and otherwise as a year.

The following table lists the meaning of several different dates if the search was performed on August 17, 2009.

| Date | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 2008/11/12 | November 12, 2008 |
| February | February 17, 2009 |
| 2007 | August 17, 2007 |
| 31st | August 31, 2009 |

# RCSB Structure Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/general_purpose_rcsb_structure_search.htm

## RCSB Structure Search

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output and input files

The RCSB Structure Search protocol allows you to search the Research
Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics ( RCSB ) Protein Data Bank ( PDB ). You can search via a number of
both simple and advanced criteria, including simple IDs, substructures
and sequence motifs.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open General Purpose | RCSB Structure Search .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set one or more search criteria parameters: Parameter Description ID A list of the IDs to retrieve. Numerous identifier types
can be used, specified by the "Type" parameter. The
default is to search by four letter PDB ID. Keywords Specify keywords to search for (e.g., a protein or organism name). Ligand Query Search for a given ligand for an exact match or for a substructure using graph matching methods or fingerprint similarity. The ligand structures are as specified in
the PDB, which may be a different protonation state or
isomer than expected. Try searching for uncharged ionizable
groups or using a different substructure option if you are unable to
find a known ligand. Read Option Choose whether to read the hits from mmCIF format files or the legacy .pdb format. The mmCIF format is now the standard archive format for RCSB Protein Data Bank structures, and all hits should be available in this format. The .pdb format cannot support all structures and therefore files may only be available for a subset of hits. For details about the remaining parameters, see RCSB Structure Search - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ID | A list of the IDs to retrieve. Numerous identifier types can be used, specified by the "Type" parameter. The default is to search by four letter PDB ID. |
| Keywords | Specify keywords to search for (e.g., a protein or organism name). |
| Ligand Query | Search for a given ligand for an exact match or for a substructure using graph matching methods or fingerprint similarity. The ligand structures are as specified in the PDB, which may be a different protonation state or isomer than expected. Try searching for uncharged ionizable groups or using a different substructure option if you are unable to find a known ligand. |
| Read Option | Choose whether to read the hits from mmCIF format files or the legacy .pdb format. The mmCIF format is now the standard archive format for RCSB Protein Data Bank structures, and all hits should be available in this format. The .pdb format cannot support all structures and therefore files may only be available for a subset of hits. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see RCSB Structure Search - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

When the job finishes, double-click it in the Jobs Explorer to open the Output folder in the Files Explorer. See Output and input files for details about the files generated by this protocol. If the job did not run successfully, the Jobs Explorer will report an error. See Troubleshooting - Protocols for details.

By default, intermediate files generated by this protocol are not saved. To save the intermediate files, select the Save intermediate files when running protocols option on the Protocols page of the Preferences dialog.

#### Output files

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| rcsb_results.mol2 | Downloaded molecules in .mol2 format. The results are aligned to the ligand if specified. Note that these structures may appear slightly differently according to the Read Option , and also compared to downloading them directly into Discovery Studio due to different defaults for PDB reading in Pipeline Pilot and Discovery Studio . For .pdb files, bond orders and charges for any nonstandard residues and small molecules are set using a residue database created from the PDB Ligand Expo database definitions. For mmCIF format, the Chemical Component definitions are embedded in the files. |
| HitIDs.txt | If the Read Option is mmCIF, contains a list of the four letter PDB ID codes retrieved and whether each is available in .pdb format. |
| PDBIDs.txt,mmCIF_IDs.txt | If the Read Option is PDB, these contain lists of the four letter PDB ID codes available in .pdb format and those only available in mmCIF format. |
| query.json | The search query. You can use these to repeat a search. See RCSB Search API for details of the search APIs. |
| ligandQuery.mol | An MDL MOL file query of the ligand or substructure used in the search. |
| SimilarityClusters.csv | Details of clusters found if Sequence Similarity Filter was used. |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

#### Input files

The following files are created in the Input directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| input_ligand.dsv | The ligand to use as a query, if Ligand Query is specified. |
| Protocol.pr_xml | The saved protocol and job parameters. You can load this file at any time to re-run this protocol with the same settings. You can also share it with other users. For details see Discovery Studio Parameters (PR_XML) . |
