# Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/inst_blast-databases.htm

## Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search

Discovery Studio includes the pdb_nr95 sequence database, which is generated from the sequences of PDB structures at 95% redundancy and is particularly suitable for homology modeling. Discovery Studio also includes the full PDB database, the Swiss-Prot database which is generated from the current uniprot_sprot.fasta sequences available from UniProt, and the antibody_variable database, which contains the variable domain sequences of various mammalian species

Historically, nr and UniRef90 databases were processed to include the taxonomic information and delivered with the Discovery Studio installer.
In the current version of Discovery Studio , the BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST search protocols have been updated to make use of the taxonomic information contained in the original databases without further processing.
As a result, those databases are no longer included with Discovery Studio .

To obtain the latest NCBI nr database, download nr (version 5 format) directly from NCBI. Other protein databases such as pdbaa may be downloaded if required and installed in a similar way. For UniRef90, you can download the sequences in FASTA format from the UniProt site and generate a database.
The previous version of the two databases are still available from the Dassault Systèmes Download Platform under the BIOVIA 2019 Golden level. See 3DS Support Resources for more information.

Some of these databases, particularly nr and UniRef90, are very large. In addition to requiring significant disk space to store, searching them can be excessively time consuming depending on the speed and memory of your server. A PSI-BLAST search may require several iterations, thus further increasing the time required. For these reasons, it may be preferable to use the BLAST Search (NCBI Server) protocol rather than performing the search locally.

The remainder of this topic discusses downloading and installing the current versions of the databases from the various sources.

### Disk Space Requirements

The size of databases from external sources is liable to change upwards, so these numbers should be taken as lower estimates. Make sure your target system has enough free disk space before downloading and extracting the database files.

* nr: The file https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/blast/db/nr-prot-metadata.json shows the current size of the nr database and lists the number of volumes to be downloaded.

* UniRef90: 125 GB for the installed database plus temporary use of >90 GB for the downloaded FASTA file.

### Download Files

* NCBI databases: You should be able to use any of the protein databases maintained by NCBI. 
You can download by using command line FTP or with an FTP client such as FileZilla, and connecting anonymously to ftp.ncbi.nih.gov . The version 5 databases are located in the blast/db folder, and the old version 4 databases are in blast/db/v4 . Download and review the README file first as it provides information about the available databases and detailed notes on methods for downloading and installing. The version 5 databases have reduced header record data, which makes them smaller and potentially faster to search than version 4. You can also download and review the blastdb-metadata-1-1.json file, which includes details such as file sizes, number of sequences and update dates for the various databases.
Smaller databases are contained in a single compressed archive <basename>.tar.gz while large databases are formatted in multiple archives, which are named
using the convention <basename>.<##>.tar.gz . All archives with the same base name are
required. Alternatively, you can download and extract these databases using the update_blastdb.pl script, which is available in <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/seqanal/bin/win64/BLASTPlus . This method may be preferable for downloading large multivolume databases, because if there is an error, you can re-run the command and it will recommence from the last successfully extracted file. > update_blastdb.pl --decompress <Database Name> Run with the argument --help to see options including choice of download location.

The version 5 databases are located in the blast/db folder, and the old version 4 databases are in blast/db/v4 . Download and review the README file first as it provides information about the available databases and detailed notes on methods for downloading and installing. The version 5 databases have reduced header record data, which makes them smaller and potentially faster to search than version 4. You can also download and review the blastdb-metadata-1-1.json file, which includes details such as file sizes, number of sequences and update dates for the various databases.
Smaller databases are contained in a single compressed archive <basename>.tar.gz while large databases are formatted in multiple archives, which are named
using the convention <basename>.<##>.tar.gz . All archives with the same base name are
required.

Alternatively, you can download and extract these databases using the update_blastdb.pl script, which is available in <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/seqanal/bin/win64/BLASTPlus . This method may be preferable for downloading large multivolume databases, because if there is an error, you can re-run the command and it will recommence from the last successfully extracted file.

```text
> update_blastdb.pl --decompress <Database Name>
```

Run with the argument --help to see options including choice of download location.

* UniRef90: You can download the uniref90.fasta.gz compressed sequence file from ftp.uniprot.org , in pub/databases/uniprot/current_release/uniref/uniref90 .

The details for basic installation and installing on a separate server are different for Windows and Linux operating systems. Note that the binary database files are cross platform and can be used on Windows and Linux platforms.

### Windows Installation

#### NCBI databases

Extract zipped tar files using WinZip or 7-Zip. Alternatively, you can use a Linux emulator such as cygwin and use gunzip and tar (described below).

#### UniRef90

Download and decompress the FASTA file, and then convert it into binary database files by running makeblastdb.exe . The binary files created can be used on Windows and Linux. makeblastdb.exe is available in <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/seqanal/bin/win64/BLASTPlus .

```text
> makeblastdb.exe –in "<FASTA file>" -dbtype prot –blastdb_version 5 -parse_seqids -hash_index -out <Database Name>
```

#### Installing on a Separate Server

You can install the databases outside of a Pipeline Pilot server installation, which allows them to be shared by multiple Pipeline Pilot servers or hosted on a file server with large amounts of disk space.

* Create a directory that can be accessed by 
the Pipeline Pilot server and put the database files there. Use the same procedure as in the basic Installation.

* Make sure the Pipeline Pilot service is started by a user with 
read access to the database files. On Windows, the Pipeline Pilot service will be 
running on the local system account by default. For more information, see How to stop and restart the Pipeline Pilot Server .

For more information, see How to stop and restart the Pipeline Pilot Server .

* In <pps_install> \public\DS\BLASTDB , create a text file for each
database named <database>.def . For example, nr.def , UniRef90.def , where <database> is the name of the database as it appears in the prefix of the formatted BLAST index files.

* Specify the full path of the database location (the directory you created) in each text file. On Windows, do not use mapped drive names in the path.

On Windows, do not use mapped drive names in the path.

### Linux Installation

#### Single file NCBI databases

Extract using the following command.

```text
tar -xvzf <basename>.tar.gz
```

#### Multiple file NCBI databases

```text
cat <basename>.*.tar.gz | tar -izxvf - -i
```

Download and decompress the FASTA file, and then convert it into binary database files by running makeblastdb . The binary files created can be used on Windows and Linux. makeblastdb is available in <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/seqanal/bin/linux64/BLASTPlus .

```text
> makeblastdb -in "<FASTA file>" -dbtype prot –blastdb_version 5 -parse_seqids -hash_index -out <Database Name>
```

#### Installing on a Separate Linux Server

* Create a directory that can be accessed by
the Pipeline Pilot server and put the downloaded NCBI or generated UniRef90 database files in it. Use the same procedure as in the basic Installation.

* Make sure that the Pipeline Pilot service is started by a user who has
read access to the database file. Typically the Pipeline Pilot Linux
server will run with the user account used to install the server.

* In <pps_install> /public/DS/BLASTDB , create a text file for each
database named <database>.def . For example, nr.def , UniRef90.def , where <database> is the name of the database as it appears
in the prefix of the formatted BLAST index files.

* Specify the full path of the database location (the directory you created) in each text file.

#### Further information

Creating and adding your own databases Installing the application

# Additional Macromolecules tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/macromolecules_additional_tools.htm

## Additional Macromolecules tools

The following tools are available from the Protocols Explorer :

| Tool | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Align Structures (MODELER) | This protocol aligns a set of protein sequences based on their structure similarity. It is available from the Protocols Explorer in the Macromolecules \| Align Structures folder. |
| Loop Refinement (MODELER) | This protocol optimizes one or more user-defined loop regions. A loop in this context is defined as a segment of consecutive residues. It is available from the Protocols Explorer in the Macromolecules \| Refinement folder. |
| Align Sequence Profiles (MODELER) | This protocol aligns two sets of pre-aligned sequences (that is, sequence profiles) using the SALIGN function in MODELER. It is similar to the Align Two Profiles mode in the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) protocol.It is available from the Protocols Explorer in the Macromolecules \| Sequence Analysis folder. |

# Nucleic acid structure

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/nabt_the_nucleic-acid-structure.htm

## Nucleic acid structure

#### Nucleic Acid Building Blocks

Nucleic acids are polymers consisting of nucleotide monomers. There are two basic types of nucleic acids: RNA and DNA. 
They differ in the types of their constituent nucleotide monomers. Five standard nucleobases are 
found in nucleic acids: Uracil, Thymine, Adenine, Cytosine, and Guanine. Nonstandard bases are 
also found in nucleic acid, such as in tRNA, including inosine, pseudouracil, 
dihydrouracil, and some methylated (ethylated) bases. The following abbreviations are 
used to designate the building blocks in nucleic acids:

* A or ADE (Adenine, appears in DNA or RNA, type: purine)

* G or GUA (Guanine, appears in DNA or RNA, type: purine)

* C or CYT (Cytosine, appears in DNA or RNA, type: pyrimidine)

* T or THY (Thymine, mainly appears in DNA, type: pyrimidine)

* U or URA (Uracil, mainly appears in RNA, type: pyrimidine)

* I or INO (Inosine, appears in tRNA, type: purine)

* P or PSU (Pseudouracil, type: pyrimidine)

* D or H2U (Dihydrouracil, type: pyrimidine)

The nucleobases (often referred to simply as bases) are attached to pentose 
sugars containing the characteristic furanose
ring: ribose (in RNA) or 2-dexyribose (in DNA). The C1' atom of the furanose sugar carries the base. 
The sugar and the base together
form a nucleoside. The O5' atom of the furanose sugar is attached to the phosphate group. 
The entire unit, consisting of a base,
furanose sugar, and phosphate, represents a nucleotide. A nucleotide contains a
nucleoside and a phosphate group.

Nucleotides join to form a nucleotide chain - a linear polymer with a defined
sequence and directionality.
The connection between two nucleotides is established by forming a bond between
the O3' atom of the previous nucleotide
and the phosphate group of the next nucleotide. The direction of the nucleotide
chain therefore points from the 5' end (beginning)
to the 3' end (the end of the chain).

Five standard bases are provided for the purpose of building nucleic acids: 
Uracil (mainly used for RNA),
Thymine (mainly used for DNA), Adenine, Cytosine, and Guanine (used both for
DNA and RNA).

Nonstandard bases supported by mutating (but not building) are: Inosine (INO), pseudouracil (PSU), and dihydrouracil (H2U).

#### The Number of Strands

Nucleic acids chains can form single-stranded molecules, antiparallel duplexes, or triplexes. Both DNA and RNA can
form single-stranded molecules. Duplexes can be formed by two DNA strands, two RNA strands, or by one DNA and one RNA
strand (hybrid duplex). Only DNA can form triplexes.

In a triple helix, one strand contains purines only. The other strand is antiparallel and contains the
complementary pyrimidines only. The third strand also consists exclusively of pyrimidines and is parallel to the purine strand.

#### Designation of Sense Strand

Each nucleotide chain has a uniquely defined directionality (or sense): from
the 5' end of the first nucleotide to the 3'
end of the last nucleotide. In a single-chained nucleic acid, the sense of the molecule is trivially defined as the sense of
the only chain present in the molecule.

In a duplex, the directionality of each strand is unambiguously defined, but
the directionality of the entire molecule is ambiguous.
The sense of a duplex is arbitrarily set by selecting one and only one strand in
the duplex. The sense of the entire duplex is then
set equal to the directionality of the selected strand. The remaining strand is
called the antisense strand.

The designation of the sense strand in a triple helix is not arbitrary. The
purine strand in a triple helix always defines the
sense. The antisense strand in a triplex is the pyrimidine strand that runs anti
parallel with respect to the sense strand.
The remaining pyrimidine strand that is parallel to the sense strand is termed 
Hoogsteen strand.

#### Base Pairing Rules

The bases facing one another in a duplex are paired most commonly according to 
Watson-Crick complementarity rules: A-T, A-U, and G-C.

In a triple helix, the bases in the purine strand are paired with the bases in the 
antiparallel pyrimidine strand
according to the Watson-Crick rules. The bases in the parallel pyrimidine strand
are paired with the purines in conformance
with the Hoogsteen complementarity rules.

#### Nucleic Acid Conformations

There are three major classes of nucleic acid conformations: A, B, and Z.
Not all types of nucleic acids can adopt any conformation. The following table
lists the conformations that are possible for any given type of nucleic acids.

#### Possible types of nucleic acid molecules

| Conf | SSR | DR | SSD | DD | DHDR | TD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| B | No | No | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Z | No | No | No | Yes | No | No |

Legend: SSR - Single Stranded RNA DR - Duplex RNA SSD - Single Stranded DNA DD - Duplex DNA DHDR - Duplex Hybrid DNA/RNA TD - Triplex DNA

The Z geometry only allows G-C and C-G alternating pairs (i.e., sense strand is GCGCGCGC, and the
complementary sequence of the antisense strand is CGCGCGCG).

Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tools

# Creating and adding your own databases

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_adding-your-own-databases.htm

## Creating and adding your own databases

This topic describes how to add your own sequence databases for the BLAST Search 
and the PSI-BLAST Search protocols.

Adding your own sequence databases for BLAST Search and 
the PSI-BLAST Search protocols

### 1. Prepare a sequence database in FASTA format.

Put all the sequences in the database into one FASTA file following the FASTA
file format. The header line of each sequence in the FASTA file may be a simple identifier or accession number, or it may also contain the database name e.g. sp for Swiss-Prot. 
This may be followed by a description.
The syntax can be found
from NCBI Web site . 
Note that gi numbers are no longer part of the usual NCBI format. Version 5 format has more stringent requirements; if it does not work for your headers then create the database as version 4. 

The following are example headers:

* >NF00489307

* >CAA29073.1 NF-M c-terminus, partial [Gallus gallus]

* >pdb|1qlo|A

* >2AAB_H Chain H, Structural Basis Of Antigen Mimicry In A Clinically Relevant Melanoma Antigen System

* >emb|CAA73704.1|

* >UniRef90_Q6GZX3 Uncharacterized protein 002L n=17 Tax=Iridoviridae TaxID=10486 RepID=002L_FRG3G

* >sp|Q6GZX4|001R_FRG3G Putative transcription factor 001R OS=Frog virus 3 (isolate Goorha) GN=FV3-001R PE=4 SV=1

### 2. Format the database into binary files.

Convert database into binary files by running makeblastdb executable against the FASTA file using the makeblastdb command.

Windows

You can find the makeblastdb executable at <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/seqanal/bin/win64/BLASTPlus

> makeblastdb.exe -in "<filename>" -dbtype prot -parse_seqids -blastdb_version <4|5> -hash_index -out <Database Name>

Linux

You can find the makeblastdb executable at <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/seqanal/bin/linux64/BLASTPlus

> makeblastdb -in "<filename>" -dbtype prot -parse_seqids -blastdb_version <4|5> -hash_index -out <Database Name>

Where <Database Name> is the name of the database. The binary files created are cross platform and
can be used on Windows and Linux platforms.

### 3. Add the database into the installation

There are two ways to add your own database into the Discovery Studio installation.

* Copy the files created above into the following location of your Pipeline Pilot server: <pps_install> /public/DS/BLASTDB

* Copy the files into a location where the Pipeline Pilot server can access and follow the instructions in Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search to configure the Pipeline Pilot server to recognize the location of your database.

Next, re-open the BLAST Search or the PSI-BLAST Search protocol in the application;
the value list for the Database parameter updates automatically.

Databases used by BLAST protocols BLAST Search PSI-BLAST Search

# Antibody Database

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_antibody-database.htm

## Antibody Database

Several antibody related protocols ( Identify Framework Templates , Model Antibody Loops and Antibody Modeling Cascade ) make use of a pre-compiled Antibody Database that is installed with Discovery Studio by default. The installed database consists of non-redundant antibody sequences and both non-redundant and redundant structures that are extracted from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB).

### Database Generation

The Antibody Database is generated as follows:

* Antibody structures in the RCSB Protein Data Bank are identified by scanning the corresponding sequences using Hidden Markov Models (HMM). The HMMs used in this step are the same as the ones used by the Annotate Antibody Sequences protocol.

* From these structures, the residue ranges for the identified antibody regions (Fab, Fv, VL, CL, etc.) are extracted. For Fab and Fv domains, the chain pairs in the 3D structures are identified by analyzing contacts. Ligands and water molecules are not extracted during this process since the regions extracted have to be part of an antibody amino acid chain. However, HETATMs that are part of amino acid chains (for example, MSE) are kept.

* The structures of the extracted regions are superimposed onto a reference structure for each domain type and stored.

* The sequences of the extracted regions are then clustered to identify redundant sequences (at 100% sequence identity). The sequence with best X-ray resolution in each cluster is kept as the non-redundant representative.

* Finally, the non-redundant sequences are aligned respectively based on four numbering schemes , and the loops are defined for all four 
schemes and saved in .bsml files.

### Alignment and Template Database

* The alignment files are located in $ <pps_install> /apps/scitegic/dsdata/data/Antibody , where $ <pps_install> is the location of your Pipeline Pilot server.

* The template database, including both the non-redundant and redundant antibody template structures, is stored in a compact binary format and the size is about 2.5 GB. To obtain the template structures in the database, use example protocol Retrieve Antibody Templates from Database

# Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_evtt.htm

## Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools

The Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools allow you to:

* Cluster protein sequences based on sequence identity

* Identify conserved residues (trace residues) based on sequence clustering

* Map trace residues to a 3D protein structure

* Cluster trace, exposed, or buried trace residues in 3D space according to residue side-chain distances

* Cluster any set of selected residues based on their side-chain distances

The following groups are available:

* Analyze Sequences

* Analyze Structures

These tools generate a sequence dendrogram from a set of aligned sequences using hierarchical clustering
method. Based on the sequence, the identity a cutoff set on the sequence dendrogram with
aligned sequences partitioned into subgroups. Residue conservation patterns represented by
the trace residues are analyzed based on
the sequence grouping at a specified distance cutoff. Those trace residues are considered
to be important for either biological function or protein folding.

For details about how the Trace Residues (Class Specific Residues and Conserved Residues) are created, see Theory - Calculating trace residues .

If any sequence has a linked structure in the Molecule Window, the Trace Residues are mapped to the 
structure by creating corresponding residue groups. Those residues can be further analyzed using the set 
of tools described in the Analyze Structure section below. The conserved surface residues
can be important for protein-protein, protein-DNA interactions, and protein-ligand binding.

Create Dendrogram and Trace Residues: Creates a sequence dendrogram using the
Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean (UPGMA) method, identifies trace residues, and creates consensus and trace sequences.
On the sequence dendrogram, a sliding bar changes the sequence grouping, which automatically re-calculates trace residues and consensus and trace sequences
based on the new sequence identity cutoff.

Show Consensus Sequences at Bottom: Toggles the display of the consensus sequence
at the bottom of the sequence alignment window.

Show Consensus Sequences Interspersed: Toggles the display of the consensus sequence
at the bottom of each sub-family of sequences from which the consensus sequence is created.

Show Trace Sequence: Toggles the display of the trace sequence.

These tools cluster trace residues (identified by the set of tools described in 
the Analyze Sequences section) and selected residues. A hierarchical method is used to cluster the residues based on pairwise
residue distances between specific side-chain atoms. For more detail, see Theory - Clustering residues .

Cluster Trace Residues: Creates a dendrogram for the trace residues of a selected protein structure.

Cluster Exposed Trace Residues: Creates a dendrogram for the exposed trace residues of a selected protein structure.

Cluster Buried Trace Residues: Creates a dendrogram for the buried trace residues of a selected protein structure.

Cluster Selected Residues: Creates a dendrogram for a set of selected protein residues.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Macromolecules \| Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern |

## Dendrogram Window (Residue)

The residue Dendrogram Window provides a view of the relative distances between residues. The residue names are listed along the y-axis, and the 
residue side-chain distances are listed along the x-axis. The actual value on the X-axis represents the branch length of the nodes and is half of the 
actual distance between two residues or groups of residues.

Changing the distances between residues may cause the Dendrogram to become out of sync with the 
Graphics View of the Molecule Window. Right-click and choose Recalculate to cluster based on the most current distances. Deleting residues from the Dendrogram Window causes an automatic recalculation of the dendrogram.

# Dendrogram Window (Sequence)

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_evtt_ar_op_sequence-dendrogram.htm

## Dendrogram Window (Sequence)

The sequence Dendrogram Window provides a view of the similarities 
between aligned sequences. More closely related sequences are grouped closer 
together. The sequences are represented by the terminal nodes of the tree. 
When using the Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools, the X axis shows 
the leaf length in units of percentage sequence difference, 
and the distance between two nodes is equal to (2 × leaf length). 
The pairwise percentage sequence identity of two groups of sequences 
represented by a cluster node is equal to [100 - (2 × leaf length)].

At a selected distance cutoff, the protein family can be divided into 
several subgroups. Drag the sliding bar along the X axis to set the cutoff. 
Alternatively, you can type in the desired distance cutoff and press ENTER .

Trace and consensus sequences are calculated from the subgroups based 
on the cutoff value. Whenever the cutoff value is changed (using the sliding 
bar), the trace and consensus sequences are recalculated. The trace and 
consensus sequences can be viewed in the corresponding Sequence View. 
Any coloring changes caused by changes in the trace and consensus sequences 
are also reflected in the corresponding Graphics View.

* The Dendrogram Window and Sequence View are closely related. 
Because they are synchronized, only one Dendrogram Window 
is allowed for each Sequence Window.

* Changes made to the
source Sequence Window's alignment will cause the Dendrogram Window to go out
of sync. This is indicated in the status bar of the Dendrogram Window.
Right-click and choose Recalculate to cluster 
based on the most current distances.

* Selecting a set of sequences in the Dendrogram Window will select the corresponding
sequences in the Sequence Window. However, deleting a set of sequences in the
Dendrogram Window will not delete the corresponding sequences in Sequence Window.

## How to Use Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern Tools

The Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern Tools allow you to use the evolutionary trace method to analyze the residue conservation pattern of a protein family using sequence alignment and 3D structures.
It can also cluster a selected set of residues based on side-chain distances. 
This topic discusses the following tasks:

* Analyze the residue conservation pattern in a protein family without protein structure

* Analyze the residue conservation pattern in a protein family with protein structure

* Cluster a set of selected residues

To analyze the residue conservation pattern in a protein family without protein structure

* Open a sequence of interest and use BLAST (NCBI Server) or BLAST to find homologous proteins and load the output alignment from the BLAST search. Alternatively, if 
you already have a protein sequence alignment file with four or more sequences, open it.

* Ensure that the desired preferences are set by choosing Edit | Preferences... | Evolutionary Trace from the menu bar. Note that Gap Treatment and Tie Breaking preferences are available in Edit | Preferences... | Phylogenetics and Edit | Preferences... | Dendrogram Window .

* With the Sequence Window active, open the Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tool 
panel and 
click Create Dendrogram and Trace Residues to create a Sequence Dendrogram
and trace residues for the sequences.

* Examine the trace sequence in the Sequence Window. All residue 
positions shown as non-gaps are trace residues.

* To view the trace residues mapped to each sequence, turn on trace residue coloring: Right-click the Sequence Window and choose Display Style . Click the Residue Color or Background Color tab and set Color by to Evolutionary Trace .

* Right-click the Sequence Window and choose Display Style .

* Click the Residue Color or Background Color tab and set Color by to Evolutionary Trace .

* The display of consensus and trace sequences can be toggled with the following tools: Show Consensus Sequences at Bottom: Shows the consensus sequences at the bottom of the Sequence Alignment. Show Consensus Sequences Interspersed: Sorts the consensus sequences according to
the order in the Dendrogram plot. Each consensus sequence appears
interspersed after each group of sequences for which the consensus sequence is
calculated. Show Trace Sequence: Shows or hides the trace sequence.

* Show Consensus Sequences at Bottom: Shows the consensus sequences at the bottom of the Sequence Alignment.

* Show Consensus Sequences Interspersed: Sorts the consensus sequences according to
the order in the Dendrogram plot. Each consensus sequence appears
interspersed after each group of sequences for which the consensus sequence is
calculated.

* Show Trace Sequence: Shows or hides the trace sequence.

* Adjust the sequence distance cutoff in the dendrogram view (trace residues are automatically recalculated). To adjust the distance cutoff: Drag the vertical bar on the dendrogram to the desired location. Enter the desired cutoff distance. Press ENTER to move the sliding bar.

* Drag the vertical bar on the dendrogram to the desired location.

* Enter the desired cutoff distance.

* Press ENTER to move the sliding bar.

Evolutionary trace analysis results depend heavily on the
input sequence alignment. Sequences selected
from the BLAST search should represent the function of the query protein or its close
relatives. In general, sequences that are more than 25% to 30% similar to the query sequence
are good candidates. Additionally, it is important to partition sequences into different
functional domains of interest before
the evolutionary trace analysis. Inclusion of unrelated domains in the sequence alignment
may result in misleading sequence clusters, which can lead to incorrect prediction of
trace residue.

To analyze the residue conservation pattern in a protein family with protein structure

* Open a sequence alignment file with at least four sequences in a Sequence Window.

* Open one or more 3D structures for those sequences in a Molecule Window.

* Follow the steps 3 through 7 in the first task topic.

* From the Molecule Window, press CTRL+H to open the Hierarchy View. Notice that three groups are
created for each protein and displayed under Protein Groups:
ET_Conserved_Residues, ET_ClassSpecific_Residues, and ET_Trace_Residues.

* Classify exposed and buried residues by choosing Structure | Solvent Accessibility... from the menu bar.

* From the Tools Explorer, cluster the trace residues using one of the following tools: Cluster Trace Residues: Clusters trace residues for each protein.
A residue dendrogram plot is created
for each protein with trace residues in the active Molecule Window. Cluster Exposed Trace Residues: Clusters the trace residues that are
exposed to solvent. Cluster Buried Trace Residues: Clusters the trace residues that are buried
in the protein core.

* Cluster Trace Residues: Clusters trace residues for each protein.
A residue dendrogram plot is created
for each protein with trace residues in the active Molecule Window.

* Cluster Exposed Trace Residues: Clusters the trace residues that are
exposed to solvent.

* Cluster Buried Trace Residues: Clusters the trace residues that are buried
in the protein core.

* You can highlight trace residues in the Graphics View as they appear in the Sequence Window by synchronizing the trace residue colors. Right-click the Sequence Window and choose Display Style... to open the Display Style dialog. Open the Residue Color or the Background Color tab and set Color structure by sequence and Protein display .

* Right-click the Sequence Window and choose Display Style... to open the Display Style dialog.

* Open the Residue Color or the Background Color tab and set Color structure by sequence and Protein display .

To cluster a set of selected residues

* Select
four or more residues to be clustered

* From the Tools Explorer, click Cluster Selected Residues .

At least four residues must be selected for clustering. If there are fewer than four trace
residues in a protein, no residue cluster window appears when any of the cluster trace residue commands are executed.

# Local databases

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_local-databases.htm

## Local databases

Several sequence databases used by BLAST and PSI-BLAST protocols 
are supported in the application. They are antibody_variable, PDB_nr95, PDB, and Swiss-Prot. 
These databases are provided with the software and can be used when you 
run BLAST or PSI-BLAST searches using the local server.

antibody_variable: This database consists of antibody variable domain sequences found in the NCBI non-redundant sequence database. It is mainly used by Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol.

PDB, PDB_nr95: These are derived from 
the PDB (Protein Data Bank) database maintained at the Research Collaboratory for
Structural Bioinformatics (RCSB) web site 
( https://www.rcsb.org/ ).

The majority of the protein structures in the PDB structure database are determined 
by X-ray, Electron Diffraction (ED), or NMR protocols, while a small subset of them are theoretical 
models. The sequences are extracted from the resolved residues as read from mmCIF format _atom.site records. 
Many PDB structures consist of multiple protein chains, for 
these each chain is a separate sequence entry in both the PDB 
and PDB_nr95 databases.
Nucleic acid sequences are excluded from these databases.

The PDB_nr95 database is created by taking one sequence from each cluster defined in the clusters-by-entity-95.txt file 
( https://www.rcsb.org/docs/programmatic-access/file-download-services#sequence-clusters-data ).
The sequence is chosen based on the resolution of the 
X-ray/ED structure, with X-ray/ED structures being selected over NMR structures. 
The final set of sequences is called PDB_nr95 because any two sequences 
in the database will have a sequence identity less than or equal to 95%.

Swiss-Prot: This is a database of protein sequences 
maintained by UniProt 
( https://www.uniprot.org/ ). 
It is a curated protein sequence database which provides a relatively 
high level of annotation. Our distribution does not include sequences 
in TrEMBL, which is a supplementary database to Swiss-Prot.

### Other databases which can be installed locally

In earlier releases, the following databases were created and available for download. 
However, although the last versions of these are still available they are no longer being updated. Instead, current equivalents can be obtained either as preformatted databases available for download from NCBI or by downloading the UniRef90 FASTA sequence file and creating a database from it.

nr: This is a database of sequences maintained 
by NCBI, the National Center for Biotechnology Information, 
( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov ). 
It contains non-redundant protein sequences from GenPept, Swissprot, PIR, PDF, PDB, and NCBI RefSeq.

UniRef90: This database is created using
CD-HIT [Li et al., 2001] by UniProt. 
It is a representative sequence set of UniProt at 90% pairwise sequence identity.

See Creating and adding your own databases for details on obtaining and installing these databases.

Additional protein databases are available from NCBI, which may be useful for specific purposes. 
It should be noted that the pdbaa database is prepared from the full sequence defined for each structure and may not exactly correspond to the residues resolved in the structure.
Therefore, while it may be appropriate to use in some contexts it is generally less suitable than ithe PDB_nr95 or PDB databases for applications such as homology modeling.

## NCBI databases

When you choose to run a BLAST Search (NCBI Server) protocol, the search is performed using
the remote server at the NCBI and the protein databases provided at the NCBI site. The databases supported
by NCBI are:

nr: Non-redundant protein sequences from GenPept,Swissprot, PIR, PRF, PDB, and NCBI RefSeq.

refseq_protein: NCBI protein reference sequences.

swissprot: Swiss-Prot sequence database (last major update).

pdb: Sequences derived from the 3D structure from the PDB database.

pat: Patented proteins from the STS division of GenBank, EMBL,
and DDBJ.

env_nr: Sequences from environmental samples, such as uncultured bacterial samples isolated from soil or marine samples. 
The largest single source is the Sargasso Sea project. This overlaps with nr.

Check the NCBI BLAST web site for more database information.

# Align Structures

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_3dma.htm

## Align Structures

Align Structures performs multiple structure alignment for a set of protein structures.

Optimal structure alignment of proteins provides a structural basis for protein 
similarity and is applicable in many areas of research. For example, protein
classifications based on protein structure similarity often give more valuable information about 
protein function than sequence similarity based analyses. Sometimes,
structure conservation can be found beyond detectable sequence homology. Structure 
alignment is often used to align a set of structural templates in homology modeling
when multiple templates are selected to build a homology model of a sequence.

Two main issues need to be addressed to obtain an optimal structure alignment. The first 
issue is the global optimization problem. That is, a large number of combinations of residue
equivalence in 3D space have to be searched to determine the optimal solution. For example, 
Proteins A and B are correctly aligned in the figure below (a), 
but misaligned in (b) in the figure where the two proteins are trapped in a local minimum.

Figure 1: 2D graphics representation of the protein alignment

The second issue is the determination of a target function. That is, whether 
the alignment is optimized to align either the largest number of residues, or 
for the lowest RMSD. There is no single correct solution to this and all the algorithms 
try to minimize the RMSD while maximizing the number of residues to
be aligned.

To fully explore all possible alignments is too time consuming and not
practical. Various heuristics are used by different programs to find the
optimal solution. Align Structures uses a fast algorithm to determine the initial
seed alignment based on a hash table. Align Structures then expands the seed alignment
into the full alignment. The similarity of a pair of proteins is calculated
based on the coordinates of their Cα atoms. 
Then, best-pairwise alignments for each pair of input structures are 
used to compute the final multiple structure alignment.

# Add Membrane and Orient Molecule

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_add-membrane-and-orient-molecule.htm

## Add Membrane and Orient Molecule

The orientation and the position of a molecule embedded in a lipid membrane is a result of a delicate balance between many different forces resulting from:

* The interactions of the molecule with the hydrophobic lipid tails and polar lipid heads

* The re-polarization of the solvent

* Changes in the surface tension around the exposed solvent atoms

* Changes in mobility of the surface groups etc.

When the molecule contains many polar or charged groups, as with most protein molecules, the polar effects of desolvation are very strong and constitute the major force responsible for the specific orientation of the protein relative to the membrane.

The Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol 
positions protein molecule in an implicit membrane which is represented by a planar low-dielectric slab to approximate
the non-polar part of the lipid bilayer. It uses either GBIM or GBSW CHARMm modules to calculate the polar contribution to the solvation energy in Generalized Born approximation with an implicit membrane. 
In addition, the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy are approximated with a solvent-accessible surface area dependent (SA) term, which is calculated with a uniform surface tension coefficient with the same value applied to all atoms. 
A detailed description of the GBIM and GBSW approaches can be found in [Spassov et al., 2002] and [Im, 2003] .

The protocol uses a stepwise search algorithm for the optimal orientation of the molecule relative to the membrane. The membrane 
is defined as a low-dielectric planar slab and the molecule is treated as a rigid body. The optimal orientation corresponds to the 
minimum solvation energy, calculated as a set of grid points in the space of the following three variables:

* Angle of molecule rotation around one of the principle axis of inertia, which is selected automatically

* Tilt angle of the selected axis relative to the membrane normal

* Distance from the molecular center of mass to the membrane mid-plane

The protocol has two possible starting positions for sampling the molecular orientation:

* If a membrane object is present in the input structure, the changes are referenced to the initial values of the tilt 
angle and the shift of the molecular center. The axis which has the smallest angle to the membrane normal is used
as the axis for calculating the tilt and rotation angle.

* If a membrane object is not present, a membrane is added to the model, at the origin of the coordinate system
with the normal parallel to the Z axis. It does three initial calculations to decide which principle axis of
the molecule will be used as the axis to define the tilt and rotation angle. Each calculation positions the
molecule so that the center of mass is on the membrane mid-plane and one of the principle axis is parallel with 
the membrane normal. The axis which resulted in the lowest solvation energy will be selected as the axis and
that particular orientation of the molecule will be used as the initial orientation for the sampling.

At the end of the search, the positive-inside rule [von Heijne, 1992] is applied and the membrane plane with more basic residues is defined as the cytoplasmic side, which is colored in blue.
If the predicted optimal orientation is not transmembrane or if the numbers of basic residues in both directions from membrane 
mid-plane are equal, then both planes of the membrane are colored green.

#### Further information

Add Membrane and Orient Molecule Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools

# Theory - Annotate Antibody Sequence

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_annotate-antibody.htm

## Theory - Annotate Antibody Sequence

### Antibody Structure

Antibodies are multidomain structures. They typically consist of four amino acid chains, two copies of the light (L) chain, and two copies of the heavy (H) chain. 
There are two types of light chains, kappa (κ) and lambda (λ), and five classes of heavy chains: alpha (α), gamma (γ), delta (δ), mu (μ) and epsilon (ε). Each of the light and heavy chains in turn consists of a variable domain (V L and V H ) and one or more constant domains (C L and C H ).

The variable domain consisting of a V L / V H pair is referred to as the F v region. The Fab (Fragment, antigen-binding) region contains a constant and a variable domain from each light-heavy chain pair. The remainder of the two heavy chains comprises the F c (Fragment, crystallizable) region.

Each of the antibody variable domains, V L and V H has three hypervariable loops, L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, and H3. These loops are often
referred to as Complementarity Determining Regions (CDRs). 
The CDR loops form the antigen binding site. They are the most variable part of the antibody structure and give the antibody its 
selectivity and specificity to antigen binding.

### Variable domain numbering schemes and CDR definitions

To allow easy comparison and modeling, several residue numbering schemes for the variable domains 
have been developed in the literature based on alignments of known antibody structures:

* IMGT [Lefranc, 1999]

* Chothia ( [Chothia and Lesk, 1987] and [Morea et al., 2000] )

* Kabat [Kabat et al., 1991]

* Honegger [Honegger and Plückthun, 2001]

The numbering schemes have a different definition for the CDR loops of the variable antibody domains.
In Discovery Studio , the IMGT scheme is the base of the CDR loop definition. The CDR loop regions of the other schemes are defined 
as shifts with respect to the CDR loops in the IMGT scheme. The following shifts are used:

| Domain | Scheme |
| --- | --- |
| Chothia | Kappa: -1,0;0,0;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,0;2,-1 Heavy: 0,-1;2,-2;3,-1 |
| Kabat | Kappa: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Lambda: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Heavy: 5,2;-1,8;2,0 |
| Honegger | Kappa: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Heavy: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 |

* Kappa: -1,0;0,0;2,-1

* Lambda: -2,0;0,0;2,-1

* Heavy: 0,-1;2,-2;3,-1

* Kappa: -3,2;0,4;0,0

* Lambda: -3,2;0,4;0,0

* Heavy: 5,2;-1,8;2,0

* Kappa: -2,0;0,9;2,-1

* Lambda: -2,0;0,9;2,-1

* Heavy: -2,0;0,9;2,-1

The three sets of number pairs for each variable domain specify the shifts for CDR1, CDR2, and CDR3 respectively. Each pair of numbers specifies the 
relative shift of the start and end of the CDR region with respect to the IMGT loop definition 
(i.e., -2,2 specifies a Kabat CDR loop region that is extended by two residues on both ends compared to the corresponding IMGT scheme).

Based on the work of Chothia (1987), five of the six CDR loops (L1, L2, L3, H1, and H2) can adopt a limited set of conformations (i.e., canonical 
conformations), while the conformation of loop H3 is highly variable. These canonical conformations are defined by Chothia according to the loop 
length and the conserved signature residue positions 
( [Morea et al., 2000] and [Chothia and Lesk, 1987] ). If the Chothia numbering is requested, the canonical type and the residues defining it can be identified. See Theory Model Antibody Loops (Canonical Structures) for more details on Canonical Structures.

### Germline Sequences

Each variable domain of an antibody is encoded in several gene segments. Both the light and the heavy variable domains consist of variable (V) and joining (J) genes. The V gene encodes the sequence from N-terminal to the beginning of the CDR3 loop, and J gene encodes part of the CDR3 to the end of the variable domain. A short diversity (D) gene is found between the V and J gene in heavy variable domain. As there are multiple copies of each type of gene, somatic recombination of the V(D)J gene segments give rise to the diversity of the antibody variable domains and their different antigen binding specificity.

In this protocol, germline V and J sequences are aligned to the input sequence based on the selected antibody numbering scheme. The best germlines match with the input according to sequence similarity are reported.

Details of the matching germline gene sequences can be obtained using the links in the protocol Report. These open a sequence alignment window for the matching region of the query sequence and the top hit(s), and also a table showing the identity, similarity and the range of residues matched. Similar details are available by displaying the annotated sequence in the Sequence Annotation Window.

# Bit score and the size of the search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_bit-score-and-size-of-search.htm

## Bit score and the size of the search

Each aligned segment pair has a normalized score (expressed in bits) that approximates the magnitude of the search space required to locate, by chance, a pair with an equally good or better HSP score. The score is calculated by normalizing the raw alignment score using statistical parameters K and lambda .

Equation 1:

Such scores are intuitively understandable as the significance of a segment pair score. To express such scores as a fraction, divide 1 by 2 to the number of
bits in the score. For example, if a segment pair has a bit-score of 16, the appropriate fraction 
(1/2 (16) =1/65,536) suggests that you will see a score this high by chance about once for every 65,000 independent segment pairs you examine.

The bit scores are absolute, but the expectation of finding any particular score depends on the size of the search space. The number of places where a segment pair
might originate is proportional to the product of the length of the query times the sum of the lengths of all the sequences searched. This product is multiplied by a
coefficient K to get the size of the search space. When searching protein databases with protein queries, K is approximately 0.13.

For a query sequence of length 300 aa searching a database of 12 million residues, the size of the search space is 300 x 12,000,000 x 0.13 or 468,000,000. For a
search this size, a score that only occurs once in every 65,000 potential segment pairs (that is, with a bit score of 16) is expected to occur about 7,200 times by
chance alone.

If the database being searched is highly redundant (as it might be if it contained 
several hundred homologous cytochromes), the size of the search space calculated 
by these methods will overestimate the size of the real search space.

# BLAST Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_blast.htm

## BLAST Search

BLAST, or Basic Local Alignment Search Tool, uses the method of Altschul et al. [Altschul et al., 1990] to search for similarities
between a query sequence and all the sequences in a database.

This release of BLAST Search implements version 2 of BLAST from the National
Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) described in Altschul et al., 1997 [Altschul et al., 1997] .

BLAST is a statistically driven search method that finds regions of similarity 
between a query sequence and database sequences and produces ungapped 
or gapped alignments of these regions. Within these aligned regions, the 
sum of the scoring matrix values of their constituent symbol pairs is 
higher than the level that you would expect to occur by chance alone. 
The application uses BLAST strictly to generate an ungapped alignment.

BLAST uses a substitution matrix (such as the BLOSUM or PAM matrices) 
to assign a score to the alignment of any pair of amino acids. An aggregate 
score for an alignment segment can be computed by summing the scores of 
each amino acid pair in that segment. When given two sequences to compare, 
the original (ungapped) BLAST algorithm searches for arbitrary but equal 
length segments within each sequence that have a maximal aggregate score 
that meets or exceeds some threshold or cutoff score. BLAST looks for 
locally optimal alignments between the two sequences whose scores cannot 
be improved either by extending or trimming. Such locally optimal alignments 
are called high-scoring segment pairs , or HSPs.

If we assume a simple protein model in which amino acids occur randomly at all positions and in proportion to the frequencies at which they are found within the database and query sequences, then we can compute a normalized score (expressed in units called bits) from the nominal score of an HSP. Such normalized scores allow direct statistical comparison of results regardless of the scoring system used (refer to Generating gapped extensions for a caveat to this).

Furthermore, the normalized score can be used to compute the expected value, or E-value, which is the number of distinct HSPs having at least that normalized score expected to occur by chance. This theory has not been proved for gapped local alignments and their associated scores, but there are indications that it remains valid [Altschul et al., 1997] .

# Build Homology Models

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_build-models.htm

## Build Homology Models

Protein and nucleic acid sequence determination has become routine in molecular biology 
laboratories, especially with the genomic sequencing efforts of recent years. 
As a result, the rate of publication of sequence information has increased 
dramatically. Several organizations have compiled databases to centralize the published 
information and to facilitate its use in research (for example emBL database, PIR/NbrF database, GenBank database). 
On the other hand, structural information from X-ray crystallographic or NMR results has 
accumulated more slowly. For instance, if a protein is not a close homologue of another protein
whose structure is already known, it can take months or years to perform a complete structural 
determination. Because of the disparate rates of sequence and structure determination, 
there are many proteins for which sequence information is known but the 3D structure is not.

It is advantageous to have a method whereby the conformation of a newly characterized 
protein can be predicted from its amino acid sequence. Homology modeling is the most reliable
method by which protein 3 dimensional structures can be predicted and is based on the 
assumption that the structure of the unknown protein is similar to known structures 
of some homologous reference proteins.

Early work dealing with building a protein by homology used only one known structure 
( [Browne et al, 1969] and [Shotton and Watson, 1970] ). Amino acid similarities between known 
and unknown proteins were used to determine where one protein would resemble the other. 
Following sequence alignment, the coordinates of the reference protein were then used to 
predict those of the unknown protein.

Further structural approaches have been suggested by Greer and Blundell:

* [Greer, 1980]

* [Greer, 1981]

* [Greer, 1985]

* [Blundell, 1987]

* [Blundell, 1988]

In their methods, multiple reference 
proteins are used, and a greater emphasis is placed on the conformational similarities 
between them. Less emphasis is placed on sequence alignment alone as a basis for generating the 
model. By determining which portions of the molecules do not vary from one member of a 
protein family to another, there is greater confidence that extrapolation to a new member 
will be accurate.

While several reference structures are used in the traditional homology model 
building process, only one set of coordinates can be used in any one peptide segment. 
MODELER [Sali and Blundell, 1993a] is able to simultaneously incorporate structural data from one or more 
reference proteins. Structural features in the reference proteins are used to derive 
spatial restraints which, in turn, are used to generate model protein structures using 
conjugate gradient and simulated annealing optimization procedures.

# Build Mutants

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_build-mutants.htm

## Build Mutants

When a residue is mutated to a different type, its conformation and the
conformation of the neighboring residues will change. Build Mutants 
automatically mutates the selected residues to the specific types and optimizes the
conformation of the mutated residues and their neighbors using MODELER .

Based on the testing results using different scoring functions and optimization protocols,
Feyfant et al. [Feyfant et al., 2007] found that the best protocol optimizes all the atoms of the mutated residues using
a scoring function, which includes molecular mechanics terms for the following:

* bond

* bond angle

* dihedral angle

* peptide bond planarity

* Lennard-Jones potential for non-bonded interaction

* homology
derived restraints for main-chain and side-chain dihedral angles

Protocol 5, based on work by Feyfant et al., performs similarly to protocol 6 to avoid possible 
partial unfolding of the structure when too many residues are selected for optimization.

Based on the observation in the paper, if a residue is mutated to another residue with
similar size, it is best to optimize only this residue without including any neighboring atoms.
If the size of the residue changes significantly, including atoms within 4.5 Å, this protocol is recommended.

# Building PSSM

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_building-pssm.htm

## Building PSSM

PSI-BLAST constructs a sequence profile [a position-specific, scoring 
matrix (PSSM)] from a multiple alignment of the highest scoring hits in an initial 
BLAST search. The PSSM is generated by calculating position-specific scores 
for each position in the alignment. Highly conserved positions receive high 
scores and weakly conserved positions receive scores near zero. The profile 
is used to perform further rounds of BLAST searches and the results of each 
"iteration" are used to refine the profile. This iterative searching 
strategy results in increased sensitivity.

PSI-BLAST constructs a sequence profile [i.e., a position specific scoring matrix (PSSM) from a multiple alignment 
of the highest scoring hits in an initial BLAST
search]. The PSSM is generated by calculating position-specific scores for each position in the alignment. Highly conserved positions receive high scores and weakly
conserved positions receive scores near zero. The profile is used to perform further rounds of BLAST searches and the results of each "iteration" are used to
refine the profile. This iterative searching strategy results in increased sensitivity.

When building the PSSMs, part of each score is based upon observed amino acid 
frequencies in the multiple alignment and part is based on prior knowledge 
of amino acid substitutability. The prior information, represented as "pseudocounts", 
is derived from a standard scoring matrix, such as BLOSUM62. Pseudocounts are 
particularly useful when the sequences included in the multiple alignments do 
not constitute an adequate sample of the protein family that they represent. 
A user-specified E-value cutoff is used to select the high-scoring sequences 
to be included in the PSSM calculation.

# Calculating trace residues

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_calculating-trace-residues.htm

## Calculating trace residues

From a multiple sequence alignment, residues conserved across the family of 
protein sequences are identified as conserved residues and are assumed to be 
essential for maintaining protein function. Based on the sequence dendrogram, 
sequences can be partitioned into subgroups at selected sequence distance 
cutoffs. The proteins in different subgroups may have similar functions, but 
different specificity. The residues responsible for the functional specificity 
are forced to mutate during evolution to make the distinction. Residues that are 
conserved within subgroups, but are different between subgroups, are identified as 
class-specific residues. The conserved residues and class-specific residues are 
called trace residues. When the evolutionary trace method is applied to different 
sequence identity cutoffs for the same sequence family, trace residues at 
different functional resolution can be identified.

Figure 1 shows a segment of DNA polymerase sequence for four subgroups in the
sequence family. Conserved residues are defined as residues conserved across the
sequence family and class-specific residues are defined as residues conserved
within each subgroup, but are different between subgroups.

Figure 1: Calculation of trace residues: conserved residues and 
class-specific residues from a sequence alignment

# Clustering and analysis of docked protein poses

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_clustering-and-analysis.htm

## Clustering and analysis of docked protein poses

The Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol generates a large number of docked poses for the input
receptor and ligand. The protocol provides a score, based on shape complementary,
to rank structures. The shape complementary score is based solely on
the properties of an individual pose. Recent work by Comeau et al. and Lorenzen and Zhang
( [Comeau et al., 2004] and [Lorenzen and Zhang, 2007] ) has shown 
that considering the properties of an ensemble of docked structures through 
clustering can help to filter the docked poses. A clustering analysis is provided by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol. 
It can also be generated as a post-processing step using the Process Poses (ZDOCK) protocol.

### Clustering

The clustering of the docked poses in the protocols is based on an all-against-all RMSD matrix. 
The RMSD between two docked poses is calculated based on the ligand residues within a user 
specified distance of the binding interface. A ligand residue is considered part of the 
binding interface, if at least one of its atoms is less than the user specified distance 
( Interface Cutoff protocol parameter) of any receptor atom. Only heavy atoms 
are considered in the RMSD calculation.

The RMSD matrix is not symmetric. 
For two poses, A and B, RMSD(AB) is calculated over the interface residues defined 
by pose A, and RMSD(BA) is calculated over the interface residues defined by pose B.

The clustering algorithm used by the protocols is similar to the one described 
by Comeau et al. [Comeau et al., 2004] and Lorenzen and Zhang [Lorenzen and Zhang, 2007] :

* Based on the RMSD matrix, the docked pose with the largest number of 
neighbors (i.e., poses with an RMSD below the user specified threshold 
defined by the RMSD Cutoff protocol parameter)
is selected as the first cluster center, its neighbors are assigned 
to the first cluster and removed from the RMSD matrix. The highest ranked pose in this clusted is assigned as the Top Cluster Pose.

* In the second step, the docked pose with the highest number of 
neighbors among the remaining poses is selected as the next cluster center.

* Its neighbors are assigned to the new cluster and removed from the RMSD matrix.

This process is repeated until the desired number of clusters is reached, 
or until no more poses remain that can serve as cluster centers.

### Distribution of binding interfaces

In addition to clustering information, the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) and Process Poses (ZDOCK) protocols also 
provide information about the distribution of docked poses 
on the surface of the receptor and ligand respectively in form of a color-coded surfaces. 
The information on pose distribution is calculated as follows:

* For each docked pose, the center of the binding interface is 
determined for the receptor and the ligand structure.

* All atoms in contact with the interface center are marked 
and the number of marks for a given atom is summed up over all docked poses.

* After all the docked poses have been processed, the value assigned to 
each atom counts for how many of the docked poses this atom was in contact with 
center of the binding interface.

* The atom-values are then averaged on the residue level and 
converted to a color scale, where red indicates the highest value, and blue 
corresponds to the lowest values.

Surface colors can be used to determine which parts of the 
receptor and ligand surfaces are most frequently part of the 
binding interfaces of the docked poses found by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol.

# Clustering residues

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_clustering-residues.htm

## Clustering residues

To define the functional interfaces of proteins, trace residues are mapped to 
the structure of one or more proteins in the sequence family and clustered in 3D 
space for each structure. Since protein structures are more conserved than 
sequences, especially at active sites, trace residue clusters identified from one 
protein structure can be applied to all the members in the sequence family.

Residues are clustered by means of hierarchical clustering algorithms [Hartigan, 1975] using average linkage methods and residue clusters represented by 
a dendrogram for visualization. Distances between side-chain atoms are used 
for clustering. The side-chain atoms of each residue are defined as follows:

Table 1. Side-chain atoms defined for naturally occurring protein residues

| Residue | Side-chain atom |
| --- | --- |
| Ala | CB |
| Arg | NH1, NH2 |
| Asn | OD1, ND2 |
| Asp | OD1, OD2 |
| Cys | SG |
| Gln | OE1, NE1 |
| Glu | OE1, OE2 |
| Gly | CA |
| His | ND1, CD2 |
| Ile | CD1 |
| Leu | CD1, CD2 |
| Lys | NZ |
| Met | CE |
| Phe | CH |
| Pro | CG |
| Ser | OG |
| Thr | OG1 |
| Trp | NE1 |
| Tyr | OZ |
| Val | CG1, CG2 |

When more than one atom is listed, the center of each atom is the side-chain 
atom position. For Phe, the side-chain atom position is the center of the phenyl 
ring.

# Composition-based statistics

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_composition-based-statistics.htm

## Composition-based statistics

PSI-BLAST differs from BLAST by taking the amino acid compositions of the query and database sequences into account when computing E-values. This is done because, for
gapped alignments, the pre-computed parameters K and lambda used by BLAST are based upon
comparisons of a large number of "random protein sequences" generated using standard amino acid frequencies. With this approach, it is possible for the lambda values to be greater than is warranted for a pair of sequences under consideration, especially when the sequences have a
similar, slightly biased amino acid composition. This can lead to a calculated E-value that is significantly smaller (i.e., better) than is justified. The same problem
can arise when using PSSM-based comparisons. In turn, it will yield run-away or divergent profiles for PSI-BLAST search.

To correct this problem, PSI-BLAST takes the sequence composition of the query
sequence and the database into account in calculating the statistical scores.
The specific method used to take composition into account is detailed in Schaffer, et al. [Schaffer et al., 2001] .

# Theory - Calculate Developability Indices

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_di.htm

## Theory - Calculate Developability Indices

Therapeutic proteins, especially antibodies, are used in the treatment of many medical conditions. Unfortunately, they tend to aggregate when stored at the high concentrations required for treatment, which decreases their activity and may cause immunological responses. Prediction of which proteins are least likely to aggregate can suggest suitable targets for development.

It has been shown that the predominant mechanism for aggregation is hydrophobic interactions on the surface of the protein ( [Bowerman et al.,2009] ). The Developability Index ( [Lauer et al., 2012] and [Chennamsetty et al., 2009a] ) combines the Protein Aggregation Score with the total molecular charge to obtain an overall measure of liability to aggregate.

### Calculation of Developability Index

The developability index of a protein is calculated as a weighted sum of the positive aggregation score and the square of the total molecular charge.

where APS is the positive aggregation score and is calculated as the summation of all positive atomic aggregation scores.

The weighting factor β is determined through data regression of long term stability data against APS and total charge. 
It allows for differences in the scaling of the APS and charge terms, and the relative importance of the two factors in determining the tendency to aggregate.
It is liable to be system dependent, as it can vary with formulation conditions such as pH, concentration of salts or other additives.

For antibodies, this score is calculated using the variable domains, which in turn are identified by the HMM method used
in Annotate Antibody Sequences protocol.

The total charge for the molecule at a given pH is calculated using the same method used by the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol. It is a representation of the equilibrium between multiple protonation states of the molecule in solution at a given pH and may not be an integer.

The molecules are ranked according to their DI values from low to high with highest value being most likely to aggregate and least favorable for development.

In addition, a net molecular aggregation score is calculated, for the variable domains and for the whole molecule, as the sum of all atomic aggregation scores.

# Pairwise alignment

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_distance-matrix-pairwise-alignments.htm

## Pairwise alignment

In the first stage of a multiple sequence alignment, the pairwise distances 
are calculated based on all pairwise sequence alignments. Two methods are offered 
to perform the pairwise alignments, the FASTA-type approach and the full dynamic 
programming approach, as specified by the Fast and Slow (default) options, respectively, for Pairwise 
Alignment Speed in the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) . Based on the pairwise alignment, 
the evolutionary 
distance between two sequences is defined as the mean number of differences 
per site in an alignment (ignoring sites with a gap when calculating the percent 
identity):

Equation 1:

Based on the pairwise distance, a guiding tree is created to decide the order 
for which sequences are added to the multiple sequence alignment. This is the 
most time-consuming part of the calculation. To align n sequences, n *( n - 1)/2 pairwise alignments are calculated to create the 
guiding tree. After that, only n - 1 calculations are needed to add each 
sequence progressively to the multiple sequence alignment. The FASTA approach is 
useful when large sets of protein sequences need to be aligned; it produces a 
fast pairwise alignment, but is less accurate than the full dynamic programming 
approach.

Source type: HTML

## Divergent sequences

The most divergent sequences (most different, on average, from all of the 
other sequences) are usually the most difficult to align correctly. It is 
sometimes better to delay the incorporation of these sequences until all of the 
more easily aligned sequences are merged first. This may give a better chance of 
correctly placing the gaps and matching weakly conserved positions against the 
rest of the sequences. A choice is offered to set a cutoff (the default setting 
is 40% identity or less with any other sequence) that will delay the alignment of 
the divergent sequences until all of the rest have been aligned.

# Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_dock-protein-rdock.htm

## Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK)

### RDOCK

RDOCK ( Li and Chen, 2003 ) is an algorithm 
for refinement of docked complexes and uses a CHARMm-based procedure for refinement and scoring. 
The predicted docked structures from ZDOCK are refined and re-ranked in order to 
pick out near-native structures.

RDOCK consists mainly of a two-stage energy minimization scheme that 
includes the evaluation of electrostatic and desolvation energies. 
During the two-stage energy minimization, RDOCK takes advantage of CHARMm 
( Brooks et al. 1983 ) 
to remove clashes and optimize polar and charge interactions. In the first 
stage of minimization, ionic amino acid side-chains are kept neutral, 
and then full charges are restored in the second stage. Without side-chain conformational 
search or filtering and clustering of resulting structures, RDOCK represents the simplest approach toward refining 
nonbound docking predictions. RDOCK makes the most powerful combination with 
ZDOCK with PSC only which is why we use this combination of ZDOCK and RDOCK in the 
ZDOCKpro software [Chen et al., 2003a] .

The RDOCK procedure removes any clashes resulting from ZDOCK conformations. Then, 
the electrostatics and desolvation energies are computed in RDOCK for all the optimized 
structures, and these structures are re-ranked according to the sum of these two energy terms. All structures 
that still have van der Waals (vdW) clashes after the first minimization are 
assigned a high RDOCK energy (1000 kcal/mol).

#### Energy minimization of ZDOCK complexes

During the RDOCK optimization, each ZDOCK prediction is run through 
130 steps of Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (ABNR) energy minimization 
with CHARMm, using the CHARMm Polar H forcefield 
in the following two stages [Chen et al., 2003a] :

* Minimization with ionic residues in neutral state Removing clashes: RDOCK first minimizes the vdW plus internal
(bond and angle) energies. All atoms are free to move. This scheme is
particularly suited to removing small clashes, leaving most structures
with favorable vdW energies after minimization [Li et al., 2003] . Optimizing polar interactions: RDOCK then minimizes the total
energy (which is the sum of Coulombic electrostatics, vdW, and internal
energies) of the complex. Non-hydrogen atoms are restrained harmonically
at their starting positions with a mass-weighted force constant of
20 kcal/(mol*Å). Ionic side-chains are kept at their neutral states during
this stage of minimization. A distance dependent dielectric constant
4r (r being the distance) is used here. Turning off charges prevents them
from dominating the total energy, thus allowing polar interactions to be
optimized first [Chen et al., 2003a] . The non-bond cutoff used in RDOCK is 17 Å.

* Removing clashes: RDOCK first minimizes the vdW plus internal
(bond and angle) energies. All atoms are free to move. This scheme is
particularly suited to removing small clashes, leaving most structures
with favorable vdW energies after minimization [Li et al., 2003] .

* Optimizing polar interactions: RDOCK then minimizes the total
energy (which is the sum of Coulombic electrostatics, vdW, and internal
energies) of the complex. Non-hydrogen atoms are restrained harmonically
at their starting positions with a mass-weighted force constant of
20 kcal/(mol*Å). Ionic side-chains are kept at their neutral states during
this stage of minimization. A distance dependent dielectric constant
4r (r being the distance) is used here. Turning off charges prevents them
from dominating the total energy, thus allowing polar interactions to be
optimized first [Chen et al., 2003a] .

The non-bond cutoff used in RDOCK is 17 Å.

* Minimization with ionic residues at charged state Optimizing charge interactions: Finally, the structures are subject to
energy minimization without any constraints. All ionic residues are in
their charged states during this minimization. This stage optimizes the
charge interactions [Chen et al., 2003a] .

* Optimizing charge interactions: Finally, the structures are subject to
energy minimization without any constraints. All ionic residues are in
their charged states during this minimization. This stage optimizes the
charge interactions [Chen et al., 2003a] .

RDOCK assumes "that if a complex structure still has clashes after the first step of energy minimization, 
it cannot be a hit". Therefore, re-rank penalizes all structures with vdW energies higher than 10 kcal/mol 
after the first minimization step by setting a clash flag for those hits. The desolvation 
energies of all the structures are computed based on the structures after both steps of minimization using the 
ACE algorithm [Chen et al., 2003a] .

#### Electrostatic and desolvation energy

During each minimization stage, the electrostatics energy (Elec) is calculated using CHARMm with a distance 
dependent dielectric constant, and for the second stage, all ionic side-chains are in their full charge 
states [Chen et al., 2003b] .

The Atomic Contact Energy (ACE) ( [Zhang et al., 1997] ) 
is used to estimate the contribution of the 
desolvation energy to the scoring function. The ACE score of a pair of protein atoms is defined 
as the free energy difference between two protein-atoms and water contacts and the sum of a 
protein-atom to protein-atom contact and a water to water contact.

The desolvation energy of forming a protein complex (DG ACE ) from 
individual receptor and ligand structures is the sum of the atomic ACE scores of 
all receptor-ligand atom pairs within a distance cutoff of 6 angstroms.

The scoring function of RDOCK is the sum of ACE desolvation energy and the CHARMm electrostatics energy [Chen et al., 2003b] :

Equation 1:

where b is a scaling factor, set by the user (default value = 0.9 ).
