# Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_dock-protein-zdock.htm

## Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)

### ZDOCK

A number of algorithms have been developed to address the initial stage 
of unbound protein-protein docking, such as FTDock, DOT, and GRAMM 
( [Gabb et al., 1997] , [Mandell et al., 2001] , [Vakser, 1997] , and [Chen et al., 2003b] ). 
ZDOCK is a rigid-body docking program that requires minimal 
information about the binding site and is 
targeted at initial-stage unbound docking. The program uses individual protein structures 
determined by experimental or computational methods as inputs and 
predicts the structure of a number of protein complexes (i.e., the top 2000 complexes). 
ZDOCK uses a simple shape complementarity method called Pairwise Shape Complementarity (PSC). 
The PSC method is optionally augmented with desolvation (DE) and 
electrostatic (ELEC) energy terms to rank the docked poses. [Chen and Weng, 2003] .

#### Pairwise Shape Complementarity

Shape complementarity is the fundamental component of protein-protein 
docking scoring functions. The shape complimentarity approach utilizes a 
geometric descriptor based on surface curvatures (Connolly) 
or surface areas [Chen and Weng, 2003] . 
Many soft-docking approaches use grid-based shape complimentarity (GSC) 
to score the predicted complexes. In the GSC approach, a layer of grid 
points surrounding the receptor is identified. 
The GSC score is equal to the total number of grid points overlapping any 
grid points corresponding to ligand atoms, minus a clash penalty [Chen et al., 2003a] . 
GSC-based approaches use a definition of the protein surface that does not account for surface curvature.

ZDOCK incorporates a simple and novel scoring function known as Pairwise Shape Complementarity (PSC) [Chen and Weng, 2003] . PSC is not based explicitly on protein surface curvature or surface 
area, but rather rewards all close atomic contacts between the protein receptor and the protein ligand within a specific cutoff distance [Chen and Weng, 2003] .

PSC has been shown to yield better results than the common grid-based 
shape complementarity (GSC) method. It rewards contiguous surface patches 
at the binding site and implicitly accounts for the curvature of the binding surface.

PSC is made up of two terms:

* Favorable term: Counts the total number of interface atom pairs within
a specified cutoff distance between receptor and ligand proteins.

* Penalty term: As in GSC, this is linearly proportional to the number of
overlapping grid points between receptor and ligand proteins.

To better calculate PSC with Fast Fourier Transform, [Chen and Weng, 2003] , 
use two complex functions, R PSC and L PSC to 
describe the geometrical characteristics of the 
receptor and ligand mapped on the grids. For further information, 
see the equations and figures in [Chen and Weng, 2003] .

#### Desolvation (DE) (optional term)

The use of a desolvation term has been shown to drastically improve 
docking performance [Chen and Weng, 2002] . 
ZDOCK estimates desolvation (DE) based on the Atom Contact Energy (ACE) [Zhang et al., 1997] . 
The ACE is defined as the free energy necessary to replace 
two protein atom-water contacts with the corresponding protein 
atom-protein atom and water-water contacts. Contrary to RDOCK which calculates 
the original ACE desolvation score based on the sum of the ACE scores 
of all ligand atom-receptor atom pairs in contact Zhang et al., 1997 , 
the ZDOCK scoring function uses non-pairwise ACE scores to speed 
up the calculations [Zhang et al., 1997] . 
In the ZDOCK score, the ACE terms represent the contact of a 
protein atom of a specific ACE type with a protein atom of a 
non-specific (averaged) type.

#### Electrostatics (ELEC) (optional term)

The electrostatic contribution to the docking score in ZDOCK 
is calculated based on the Coulombic formula and is expressed as 
the correlation between the partial charges of the ligand atoms 
with the electrostatic potential created by the receptor atoms 
( [Gabb et al., 1997] and [Chen et al., 2003b] ). 
Due to the noisy nature of the Coulombic energy term, the electrostatic 
contribution to the score is reduced by a scale factor b [Chen et al., 2003b] .

#### Search procedure

The ZDOCK search scheme exhaustively searches all rotational and translational 
space for the ligand protein relative to the receptor protein, which is 
fixed at its starting orientation. For the rotational search, evenly distributed 
Euler angles are used [Chen and Weng, 2002] . 
This angle set is equivalent to a uniformly distributed set of points 
on a projective sphere, which ensures that minimal orientations are required 
to cover the entire rotational space.

For each rotation, the algorithm rapidly scans translational 
space using FFT based on a 3D grid with step size of 1.2 angstroms. 
The top translational orientation is retained. Keeping only one orientation helps 
to keep the number of false positives low. The initial orientation 
of the ligand protein is defined by three Euler angles of rotational 
transformation in Cartesian space which can be randomized in a user-controlled 
way by providing a specific number for the seed of the random number generator [Chen and Weng, 2002] .

#### Blocking and filtering steps

If it is known from other sources (for example experimental evidence) 
that some residue(s) in the receptor and/or ligand should not be in the 
protein-protein binding interface, the atoms in the specified residue(s) 
are marked as a special type and only the penalty part of the PSC score 
is applied to them during the calculation. As a result, the complex conformation 
with the specified residue(s) in the interface get lower scores than other conformations. 
Blocking residues is an option of the ZDOCK calculation.

On the other hand, if it is known that some residue(s) should 
be part of the protein-protein binding interface, a procedure is 
used to filter out conformations that do not include the specified 
residue(s) in the interface. The residue is defined as inside the 
binding interface if any atom in that residue is within the 
distance cutoff to any atom from the other protein. Using available 
information to block out residues from the binding interface or to 
force residues to be inside the binding interface can reduce the 
number of hits for refinement stage and can also increase 
the confidence of the final prediction. Filtering residues can 
be performed after the ZDOCK calculation.

ZDOCK can tolerate conformational changes by allowing 
small clashes between the protein receptor and the protein ligand 
structures, and the clashes are removed during refinement by 
RDOCK (discussed in the following section).

#### System Size

Due to grid size restrictions in the Fast Fourier Transform calculations, the receptor and ligand structures must satisfy a system size condition.
If MaxR R is the maximum distance of any receptor atom to the receptor center, and MaxR L is the maximum distance of any ligand atom to the ligand center, the following must be satisfied:

MaxR R + MaxR L < 201 Å

Please note, if Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy is enabled, this limit is reduced to 197 Å.

#### Timing and Performance

It is very difficult to make general statements about the 
amount of time needed to perform a ZDOCK calculation. 
The reason for this is that the running time of a ZDOCK 
calculation not only depends to a large degree on the size of the 
input ligand and receptor structures but it also strongly depends 
on the shape of the molecules. In particular, since ZDOCK employs 
a cubic grid for the Fast Fourier Transformation, calculations 
require less time for structures that are close to spherical compared to 
elongated structures. In addition, it is clear that the machine on which 
the computation is run will also play a large role in the duration of the calculation. 
A general idea of the order of magnitude for the time required for a ZDOCK 
calculation can be obtained from the test system 1CGI. For this protein-protein complex, 
in which the ligand structure consists of 438 atoms, and the receptor structure has 1641 atom, 
a basic ZDOCK calculation requires about half an hour on a 3 GHz Intel Xeon machine. 
If the Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy option is selected, 
the computation time will roughly double. Also note that the memory requirements 
for the calculation also roughly doubles if electrostatic and desolvation energy 
terms are used for scoring compared to the basic version of ZDOCK based solely 
on shape complementarity (PSC).
In terms for performance, enabling the Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy option significantly improves the performance of ZDOCK as a stand-alone program as can be 
seen on the figure below. However, if ZDOCK calculation is combined with the ZRANK 
reranking method, the impact of the using the Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy terms is greatly reduced. And after reranking of the poses with ZRANK, and the 
overall performance between the two option is comparable as can be seen in the following figure:

# Rerank Docked Proteins (ZRANK)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_dock-protein-zrank.htm

## Rerank Docked Proteins (ZRANK)

### ZRANK

ZRANK Pierce and Weng, 2007 is a 
is a method for quickly and accurately reranking the docked protein complexes predicted by the ZDOCK rigid body docking program.

Compared to ZDOCK, the energy function used by ZRANK is more detailed. However, contrary to RDOCK, 
the method is fast enough to process the full set of ZDOCK predictions, even if detailed 6° sampling is used. Work by
Pierce and Weng [Pierce and Weng, 2007] shows that reranking ZDOCK predictions
with ZRANK significantly improves the success rate of protein-protein complex prediction. This makes
the method useful either for stand-alone reranking, or as a preprocessing step for refinement with RDOCK.

#### Scoring Function

The ZRANK scoring function is a linear combination of van der Waals attractive and repulsive energies, short and
long range repulsive and attractive energies, and desolvation [Pierce and Weng, 2007] . 
The van der Waals and short range electrostatics energies are calculated based on the parameters of the CHARMm 19 
polar hydrogen potential [Neria et al., 1996] . For long range interactions,
only fully charged side-chain atoms are used [Pierce and Weng, 2007] . The 
desolvation term is calculated using the Pairwise Atomic Contact Energy (ACE) [Zhang et al., 1997] .

# Dock Proteins

## Dock Proteins

Understanding the interactions that proteins make with other proteins in a cell is of critical 
importance to understanding processes such as signal transduction, cell regulation, and molecular 
recognition. However, experimental determination of the structures of such complexes is not 
trivial and recent efforts have focused on computational methods.

Protein-protein docking is the task of assembling separate protein components into protein-protein complexes 
or assemblies using computational methods. Typically such methods start with the three-dimensional (3D) structures 
of the individual components, often referred to as a protein receptor and a protein ligand. Such predictions 
can help researchers gain early insights into cellular function and aid rational approaches to disease 
treatment and drug design.

The protein-protein docking problem has interested biophysicists and computational biologists for decades, since 
it is important to the computational determination of 3D structure assemblies as well as drug design. Predictive 
information may also be provided in the absence of complete experimental data [Chen et al., 2003b] .

However, there are several issues when dealing with protein-protein docking - the large size of the system, the conformation 
changes of the proteins upon binding, and the availability of the individual 3D structures, or lack thereof. The large 
system size makes sampling conformational space prohibitively expensive, so to reduce the search space, Fast 
Fourier Transform (FFT) methods, geometric hashing, and bit mapping, are used to speed up 
calculations [Vajda and Camacho, 2004] .

Conformational changes upon complex formation greatly increase the complexity of the problem, despite structural 
flexibility being mostly restricted to surface amino acid side-chains. Specifically, near-native orientations 
may receive poor scores when individually determined (or unbound) protein structures are docked, as most 
docking algorithms cannot capture conformational changes effectively. Sometimes high-resolution 
structures of the proteins of interest, derived using X-ray crystallography or NMR, may not be available. 
Thus computational methods, such as homology modeling, may be necessary. Using incomplete (e.g. missing amino acid side-chains) 
experimental structures or erroneous models can lead to significant protein-protein docking inaccuracies. Recent efforts at 
predicting protein complexes have focused on better solutions to solve some of these problems [Chen et al., 2003b] .

The divide-and-conquer strategy is used widely in the docking field ( [Sternberg et al., 2000] and [Smith and Sternberg, 2002] ). 
This strategy starts with an initial-stage algorithm focused on retaining reasonably small number of near-native 
complexes (hits), followed by a refinement algorithm that is used to rank the hits. The best 
hit or complex structure is seen at the top of the list [Chen et al., 2003a] .

ZDOCKpro focuses on the unbound docking problem (where the structure of the complex is unknown) and adopts the 
divide-and-conquer approach, with two docking stages:

* ZDOCK , an initial stage algorithm [Chen et al., 2003a]

* RDOCK , a refinement stage algorithm [Li et al., 2003]

In the initial stage, the protein receptor and protein ligand are treated as rigid bodies and all six rotational 
and translational degrees of freedom are fully explored with scoring functions that are tolerant to conformational 
changes, also known as soft docking functions. In the refinement stage, a smaller number (tens to thousands) 
of near native structures obtained in the initial stage are refined and re-ranked using a 
more detailed energy function that takes into account conformational changes [Chen et al., 2003b] .

# Theory - Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_evolutionary-trace.htm

## Theory - Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern tools

To understand how proteins carry out certain biological functions - 
how they recognize ligands and form protein-protein or protein-ligand complexes - 
it is essential to be able to identify protein functional residues and 
interaction interfaces such as active sites or binding sites. Functional 
interfaces can serve as targets for structure-based drug design or to guide the 
site-directed mutagenesis in studying the protein structure-function 
relationship. X-ray crystallography is a powerful tool for studying protein 
function and structure. However, the number of protein sequences that have been 
determined is much greater than the number of proteins that have been structurally 
characterized. Even when structural information is available, it is still 
difficult to infer the roles of specific residues in protein function directly 
from the structure.

Exhaustive mutational analysis plays a major role in binding-site characterization. 
With the increasing size of sequence databases, a wealth of mutational data 
is already available, where sequences homologous to the protein of interest 
record mutation "experiments" that have passed the test of natural 
selection. The evolutionary trace method ( [Lichtarge et al., 1996] and [Lichtarge et al., 1997] ) is 
designed to extract the mutational data embedded in those sequences and infer 
which residues are likely to be important to protein function.

In general, functional residues undergo fewer mutations during evolution. On 
the other hand, certain functional residues are forced to mutate to achieve the 
selectivity of subgroups within the protein family. The evolutionary trace method 
makes a direct connection between residue conservation in aligned sequences and 
their functional importance. It also identifies functional specificity by 
partitioning the protein sequence alignment into subgroups according to the 
sequence similarity. Furthermore, if the 3D structure of the protein is known, 
exposed functional residues that are more likely to be responsible for binding or 
enzymatic activity can be distinguished from the buried residues that are more 
important for maintaining structural integrity. This method can be applied to 
proteins with experimentally determined structures as well as to theoretical 
models.

Evolutionary Trace analysis identifies the functional residues as follows:

* From a sequence alignment of a set of functionally related sequences, 
a sequence dendrogram is created using the hierarchical clustering method.

* From the sequence dendrogram, the sequence family is divided into sub groups
at different sequence distance cutoff.

* Based on the sequence alignment and the sub groups, the trace residues are 
identified and mapped to 3D structure if available.

* Exposed trace residues are clustered based on their residue side-chain 
distances using the hierarchical clustering method again to identify conserved
functional surface patches.

# Theory - Excipient Interaction

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_excipient.htm

## Theory - Excipient Interaction

The effect of excipients on the formulation properties of a protein is governed by their preferential interactions with sites on the protein surface. The ability to rapidly predict the likely interactions may assist in enabling formulation design early in the development of antibody therapeutics.

It is possible to calculate the preferential excipient coefficients for each residue in a protein using molecular dynamics (MD) techniques [Cloutier et al., 2019] , [Cloutier et al., 2020a] . 
However, these calculations are computationally expensive. A method has been developed in which a set of features describing local regions of an antibody surface is calculated. 
These are used to train a machine learning model for each of six commonly used formulation excipients, with the target per-residue preferential excipient coefficients being calculated using MD for a set of antibody structures. [Cloutier et al., 2020b] . 
The Predict Excipient Interactions protocol employs this approach.

### Feature Set

In all features for which they are required, the partial charges, vdW radii and Solvent Accessible Areas (SAA) values are calculated using CHARMm. As the charges depend on protonation state, the protein should be protonated with the appropriate conditions such as pH.

There are three general types of feature: One-hot vectors, single numeric values, and neighborhood features.

#### One-hot Vectors

This is a method of encoding categorical data in a numeric form appropriate for use in machine learning applications. Each one-hot vector is a set of properties with categorical names, only one of which should be set to 1 and all the others to 0.

* Residue Identity: A one-hot vector encoding the residue type, with histidine represented by HSD, HSE, or HSP depending on protonation.

* Secondary Structure: A one-hot vector indicating the secondary structure type (Helix, Sheet, or Loop)

#### Numeric Values

* Hydrophobicity: The normalized hydrophobicity according to the Black and Mould scale [Black and Mould, 1991] .

* Fractional Exposure: The ratio of the residue's SAA to the standard exposure in an extended Ala-X-Ala tripeptide.

* Aggregation Score: The aggregation score calculated at a radius of 5Å. See Theory - Protein Aggregation Scores for further details.

* Charge Map Score: The charge map score calculated at a radius of 10Å. See Theory - Surface Charge Maps and Viscosity Scores for further details.

#### Neighborhood Features

These features are calculated for each residue alone, and then for the residue plus all neighboring residues having an atom within a given cutoff distance. The cutoff distances used are 3, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 20, and 25Å. Various operations such as total or average are applied to obtain the feature values. The neighborhood features are:

* Protrusion Index (CX): A measure of protrusion from the surface of each atom [Pintar et al, 2002] : minimum: The lowest value of CX for any atom in the neighborhood. maximum: The highest value of CX for any atom in the neighborhood. average: The average value of CX over all atoms in the neighborhood.

* minimum: The lowest value of CX for any atom in the neighborhood.

* maximum: The highest value of CX for any atom in the neighborhood.

* average: The average value of CX over all atoms in the neighborhood.

* Depth Index (DPX): The distance of each atom to the closest atom on the surface [Pintar et al, 2003] : minimum: The lowest value of DPX for any atom in the neighborhood. maximum: The highest value of DPX for any atom in the neighborhood. average: The average value of DPX over all atoms in the neighborhood.

* minimum: The lowest value of DPX for any atom in the neighborhood.

* maximum: The highest value of DPX for any atom in the neighborhood.

* average: The average value of DPX over all atoms in the neighborhood.

* Electrostatic Potential: Electrostatic Potential is a simple Electrostatic Potential Property (EPOT). The method is adapted from that of Exner et al. [Exner et al, 2002] , and is a charge metric modified by the distance to the surface. It is dependent on the Depth Index calculation, which is performed regardless of the value of the Depth Index parameter, and it assumes that atomic charges have been set appropriately.

For each atom, q , is its partial charge. The distance to the surface d is the sum of the distance to the nearest surface atom, DPX , plus the vdW radius of that surface atom DPX_RAD —for hydrogen atoms the distance is taken as that of the attached heavy atom. A distance cutoff, dc , is set to 12Å. The electrostatic potential for each atom is calculated as: total: The total of EPOT values over all atoms in the neighborhood

* total: The total of EPOT values over all atoms in the neighborhood

* Solvent Accessible Surface Area: The SAA value calculated using CHARMm. Total: The total of SAA values for all atoms in the neighborhood. Hydrophobic: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Ala, Ile, Leu, Met, Phe, Trp, Tyr, and Val. Hydrophilic: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Arg, His, Lys, Asp, Glu, Ser, Thr, Asn and Gln. Positive: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Arg, Lys, and Hsp (positively charged Histidine). Negative: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Asp and Glu. Backbone: The sum of SAA values on all C, O, N, and attached H atoms in the neighborhood. Side-chain: The sum of SAA values on all side-chain atoms in the neighborhood.

* Total: The total of SAA values for all atoms in the neighborhood.

* Hydrophobic: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Ala, Ile, Leu, Met, Phe, Trp, Tyr, and Val.

* Hydrophilic: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Arg, His, Lys, Asp, Glu, Ser, Thr, Asn and Gln.

* Positive: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Arg, Lys, and Hsp (positively charged Histidine).

* Negative: The sum of SAA values on all atoms in neighborhood residues Asp and Glu.

* Backbone: The sum of SAA values on all C, O, N, and attached H atoms in the neighborhood.

* Side-chain: The sum of SAA values on all side-chain atoms in the neighborhood.

* Net Charge: Partial Charges. Total The net charge of all atoms in the neighborhood. Exposed The sum of partial charges on atoms with SAA > 0.

* Total The net charge of all atoms in the neighborhood.

* Exposed The sum of partial charges on atoms with SAA > 0.

### Machine learning models

##### Dataset preparation

The dataset of samples utilized for training and validating the models is a subset of the 
dataset described in Cloutier et al. [Cloutier et al., 2020b] . 
After excluding those derived from proprietary sequences, approximately ~18,600 residues were utilized
for feature generation. A slightly smaller feature set of 175 features were generated from the dataset—the shape index features were omitted as they are computationally demanding but did not appear to 
contribute significantly to the ML models. The features in the training data and the target excipient 
preferential interaction coefficient data were rescaled and normalized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

##### Implementation

The Elastic Net (EN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) models were implemented in the Python package 
Scikit-learn [Pedragosa et al, 2011] using the ElasticNet 
and SVR functions respectively. Prior to training the models, the dataset of samples were randomly split into
training, validation, and test data sets with the test data accounting for 10% of the total dataset. 
Hyperparameter tuning through 5-fold cross validation showed that the hyperparameters described in 
Cloutier et al. performed best, so those 
hyperparameters were chosen.

The EN hyperparameters outlined in Cloutier et al. 
were used to calculate the "alpha" and "l1_ratio" parameters of the ElasticNet function in Scikit-learn as follows:

All other parameters of the ElasticNet function used their default values. The SVM hyperparameters C and γ outlined in Cloutier et al. 
were used for their corresponding parameters in the SVR function in Scikit-learn and the cache parameters was set 
to 1024 MB. All other parameters of the SVR function used their default values.

##### Training and Evaluation

Training was carried out in Scikit-learn version 0.22.1. The performance of the models on the test data was validated 
through comparison of RMSEs (listed below) with the published results in Cloutier et al. 
Some minor deviations are expected due to the training set and test set differences.

| NaCl | 0.020559 | 0.019341 |

# Filtering out low complexity regions - BLAST Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_filtering-out-low-complexity-regions.htm

## Filtering out low complexity regions - BLAST Search

BLAST Search by default filters out regions of low complexity from query and database sequences using the SEG 
filter program 
( [Wootton and Federhen, 1993] and [Wootton and Federhen, 1996] ).
Altschul et al. [Altschul et al., 1994] offers a
general discussion of the role of filtering in search strategies.

Short repeats and low complexity sequences, such as glutamine-rich regions, confound most database searching methods. 
For BLAST Search, the random model against which the
significance of segment pair scores is evaluated assumes that at each position, each residue has a probability of occurring 
that is proportional to its composition in
the database as a whole. Low complexity or highly repetitive sequences are inconsistent with this assumption.

Certain types of low complexity sequences may not be detected by the filtering option in BLAST Search. 
For example, coiled-coil and transmembrane regions need to be detected
using the appropriate programs outside of BLAST. Amino acid characters in regions of low complexity are substituted 
with the letter X after
filtering.

## Filtering out low complexity regions - PSI-BLAST Search

PSI-BLAST Search can filter out regions of low complexity from query and database
sequences using the SEG filter program in the same way as BLAST Search. However, it
has been found [Schaffer et al., 2001] that when composite based scoring is used,
LC filtering does not improve the search results. By default, low complexity
filtering is turned off.

## Fuzzy bins

Sometimes the hash key described in Equation 1 misses the correct matches when the 
two pseudo-torsion angles are close together (for example 19° and 21°), but fall 
into two different hash bins (for example 0 and 1). A more relaxed matching criteria 
is devised using the "fuzzy" bin mechanism. In this case, four hash 
key values are defined for each 6-residue segment as follows:

Equation 1:

where Δ ij =1 when i = j and Δ ij =0 
otherwise, which leads to Tor (0) being the same as Tor in Equation 1 of Seed alignment analysis . 
The segment length, N , is set to 6.

The two segments from two proteins are considered to be a match if any of the Tor (j) in the first protein matches Tor (0) in the second protein, 
or if Tor (0) in the first protein matches any of the Tor (j) 
in the second protein. This allows one out of the three pseudo-torsion angles 
in the two segments to be mismatched by one bin size. For example, if the 6-residue 
segment from the first protein has the torsion hash value (that is, T i /P in Equation 1) to be (5,7,6), then the matching segment could have the torsion hash 
value of (5,7,6) with no mismatch, or (4,7,6), (6,7,6), (5,6,6), (5,8,6), (5,7,5), 
and (5,7,7) with one mismatch.

Using fuzzy bin logic requires slightly more computation time. However, 
in some cases it is necessary in order to identify the correct alignment. For 
example, without using the fuzzy bin option, proteins 1fna and 1ttg cannot 
be aligned by 3DMA, while with the fuzzy bin option, the two proteins are 
aligned over 70 residues (more than 70% of residues in the protein) with 
Cα RMSD of 1.95 Å.

# Generating gapped extensions

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_generating-gapped-extensions.htm

## Generating gapped extensions

Gapped extensions allow BLAST to maintain its sensitivity, while tolerating a much higher chance of missing any single moderately scoring HSP. However, gapped
extensions take about 500 times longer to execute than ungapped extensions. Therefore, BLAST triggers a gapped extension for an HSP only when its score exceeds a
moderate score Sg specifically chosen so that no more than about one gapped extension is invoked per 50 database sequences.

To generate the gapped local alignment, BLAST uses a standard dynamic programming algorithm for pairwise sequence alignment that traverses the cells of a path graph,
the dimensions of which are the lengths of the two sequences being compared, performing a fixed amount of computation per each cell. Starting from a single aligned pair
of residues called the seed, the dynamic programming proceeds both forward and backward through the path graph considering only those cells for which the optimal local
alignment score falls no more than X below the best alignment score yet found (this is a simple generalization of the BLAST
method for constructing HSPs). The region of the path graph explored adapts to the alignment produced.

The seed for the dynamic programming is the central residue pair of the length-11 segment of the HSP having the highest alignment score. If the HSP itself is shorter
than 11 residues in length, its central pair of residues is chosen.

The resulting gapped alignment is reported only if it has an E-value low enough to be of interest. For any alignment actually reported, BLAST performs a gapped
extension that records "traceback" information [Sankoff and Kruskal, 1983] using a substantially larger X parameter
than that employed during the search stage to increase the accuracy of the alignment.

Because BLAST produces gapped alignments only for those few database sequences 
likely to be related to the query, it cannot estimate the parameters necessary 
to compute normalized scores on the fly. Instead, BLAST must rely on estimates 
of these parameters generated beforehand by random simulation. For this reason, 
BLAST cannot use a scoring system for which no simulation has been performed 
and still produce accurate estimates of statistical significance.

## The guide tree

The trees used to guide the final multiple alignment process are calculated 
from the pairwise sequence distances generated by pairwise alignment using the 
neighbor joining method [Saitou and Nei, 1987] . 
This produces unrooted trees with branch lengths proportional to the estimated 
divergence along each branch, as in Figure 1(A). The root is placed by a mid-point 
method [Thompson et al., 1994b] at a position where 
the mean branch lengths on either side of the root are equal, as in Figure 1(B).

Figure 1: (A) An unrooted tree built using the neighbor-joining method. The numbers 
along the branches are the percentage divergence of the sequences. (B) The same tree rooted by profile weight. The weights assigned to each sequence are shown on the right-hand side. For example, the sequence indicated 
by an asterisk is (3.0/1 + 2.0/2 + 0.7/3) = 4.2

These trees are also used to derive a weight for each sequence [Thompson et al., 1994b] . 
The weights are dependent upon the distance from the root 
of the tree, with the result that sequences with common branch paths share the 
weight derived from the shared branch structure. As depicted in Figure 1(B), 
the weight for any sequence, S , that 
has a path consistency of n branches 
to the root can be calculated as:

Equation 1:

where, Δ i is the branch length and O i is 
the branch order defined as the number of sequences that own the branch.

The weights are normalized with the maximum weight equal to 1.0.

# Loop Optimization

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_loop-optimization.htm

## Loop Optimization

For the parts of the model sequence that are not aligned to any template structures, 
no homology restraints, such as Cα-Cα 
distance restraints, can be applied. During model generation, these parts of 
the model structure are optimized according to CHARMm-derived stereochemical 
and non-bonded restraints, as well as statistical preferences of the different 
residue types for the different regions of the Ramachandran Plot and for the 
different side-chain rotamers. Those parts of the structure generally have larger 
errors compared to the regions which are modeled based on a template structure.

The Build Homology Models protocol
allows further optimization of the loop regions, and the functional forms used are discussed 
in the Loop Refinement (MODELER) theory topic.

The loops are automatically defined based on the alignment between the model sequence
and the template(s). Any insertion in the model sequence (i.e., 
the residues in the model sequence not aligned to any of the template sequence(s)), plus 
2 residues on the N-terminal and 2 residues on the C-terminal side of the insertion 
are included in the loop. For deletions in the model sequence, the loop is formed
by two residues, one on each side of the deletion.

# Loop Refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_loop-refinement.htm

## Loop Refinement

Loop Refinement is a CHARMm based protocol that optimizes the conformation of a contiguous segment 
(i.e., a loop) of a protein structure. It is based on an improved version of LOOPER algorithm [Spassov et al., 2008] . It combines systematic conformational sampling of the loop backbone with CHARMm energy minimization.

You can use this approach to refine a loop structure from a homology model and
optimize a segment of the protein experimental structure where the structure is poorly defined.

You can run this protocol in Fast or Slow mode. Fast mode is considerably faster, 
but Slow mode predictions are statistically more accurate. Both modes consist of backbone conformation sampling, side-chain refinement and final scoring.

### Loop Prediction Stages

The algorithm predicts loops in four stages. Half loops are generated and minimized, full loops are constructed, and then loop side-chains are constructed and loops variants are optimized.

#### Stage 1 and 2: Generation of half loops and minimization

The initial two stages of loop prediction algorithm include a systematic search of 
loop structures by sampling the backbone dihedral angles φ and ψ. 
A set of up to five (φ, ψ) values for each residue are chosen based on the 
energy contour map [Ramachandran et al., 1963] ,

so that the individual residue conformation belongs to one of the low energy basins 
of local interactions and the combinations between them cover the principle changes 
in the direction of the peptide chain.

During the loop construction, the loop is divided into two halves: the N-terminal
half and the C-terminal half. Each half has N/2 residues for an even number of residue loops 
or the N-terminal half is one residue longer than the C-terminal half for an odd number
residue loops.

Each half is constructed independently from the end of the loop, and for each residue other than glycine, up to five initial conformational states are sampled in the slow mode: A (φ=-90°, ψ=180°), B (φ=-90°, ψ=120°), C (φ=-100°, ψ=10°), R (φ=-65°, ψ=-40°) and L (φ=60°, ψ=60°). The Fast mode samples only the states B , R and L . 
For glycine residues in both modes, four states are sampled: B (φ=-90°, ψ=90°), R (φ=-60°, ψ=-60°), L (φ=60°, ψ=60°) and P (φ=-90°, ψ=90°).

Energy minimization is then carried out on each half of the constructed loop backbone
with the rest of the protein fixed and in absence of the other half loop. 
Then, the N- and C- terminal half loops are ranked separately according to 
CHARMm energy and up to 150 conformations are retained for each half.

#### Stage 3: Construction of entire structure of loop backbone

A number of variants of loop backbone structure are constructed from all combinations of the
retained half loops by making the peptide bond between the two half loops
and energy minimized using the same CHARMm minimization protocol.

#### Stage 4: Construction of loop side-chains and optimization of loop variants

In the final stage, for each structure that resulted from the third stage, the side-chain atoms are positioned using
the same approach as with the Side-Chain Refinement protocol .
Then, resulting loops are fully minimized and a number
of top ranking loop conformations are retained.

### Filtering the ranked loop variants

At the end of each of the Looper stages, ranked structures are filtered based on the conformational similarity, which is defined as a difference in φ and ψ angles of no more than 30 degrees. Only the variant with the lowest energy is retained for further calculations.

### Scoring the conformations

CHARMm energy minimization in the first three stages is done without including the solvation 
energy term. In the final stage, each loop conformation is scored by adding the 
solvation energy term to other intramolecular energy terms. The solvation energy is 
calculated using the CHARMm GBIM Generalized Born module [Spassov et al., 2002] .

# Theory - Predict Humanizing Mutations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_machinehumanize.htm

## Theory - Predict Humanizing Mutations

Humanization of an antibody sequence aims to retain the antigen binding specificity of a non-human antibody while making it more similar to human antibodies to decrease immunogenicity. This topic covers the details of our implementation of a published machine learning (ML) method [Marks et al., 2021] that uses a large-scale antibody sequence database [Kovaltsuk et al., 2018] to build classifiers that can distinguish between human and murine sequences. This enables the suggestion of mutations to an input mouse sequence, which tend to increase its humanness and thus reduce its immunogenicity.

### Dataset Preparation

The dataset used for training and validating the models was a subset of the dataset used in the published method [Marks et al., 2021] . In particular, only human and native mouse sequences were retained. The availability of sequences for other organisms was limited—their inclusion could have impaired the correct classification of human versus mouse sequences. As a result, this implementation of the humanization algorithm is only suitable for humanizing mouse sequences.

For each V gene, a dataset was created consisting of human sequences of that V gene type and mouse sequences of the corresponding chain type. For example, one dataset consists of human heavy-chain V1 sequences and mouse heavy-chain sequences. The sizes of the different datasets were as follows:

### Feature Set

Each antibody sequence was numbered using the IMGT numbering scheme. For each standard IMGT position, a one-hot encoding was computed for the residue at that position. These one-hot encodings were then concatenated to form a binary vector.

### Random Forest Training and Validation

Random forest models were implemented in Python using the Scikit-learn package [Pedragosa et al, 2011] to classify human versus mouse sequences. For each model, the number of trees was set to 200, and the other parameters retained their default values. To validate model performance, a random train/test split was created for each dataset. In each case, all test set examples were classified correctly.

### Humanization Algorithm

The output scores produced by the random forest classifiers are used to guide a sequence-based humanization algorithm. These scores are numbers in the interval [0, 1]. A lower score indicates that a sequence is more likely to be a mouse sequence, while a higher score indicates that a sequence is more likely to be a human sequence.

To humanize a mouse sequence, residues in the IMGT framework region are repeatedly mutated until the score reaches a certain threshold value supplied by the user. This value is typically close to, but less than, 1. Mutations are chosen in a greedy manner—at each step, the mutation that leads to the greatest increase in the model score is selected.

## PDF for main-chain dihedral angles

The main chain conformation classes for a residue can be described by 
the main chain dihedral angles (φ,ψ). 
As previously discussed, the third main chain dihedral angle ω 
is separately described by a bimodal Gaussian PDF for Pro residues and 
a monomodal Gaussian PDF for all others. 
The distribution of φ,ψ 
pairs in the PDB database is approximated by six distinct Gaussian peaks [Sali and Blundell, 1993a] whose positions and widths are given in the table below.

Table 1. Parameters of the main chain conformation classes

| Conformation class | mean | mean | standard deviation | standard deviation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fi | yi | si(f) | si(y) | |
| A | -65 | -41 | 15 | 15 |
| B | -130 | 135 | 15 | 20 |
| P | -65 | 140 | 15 | 15 |
| G | 60 | 40 | 10 | 10 |
| L | 90 | -10 | 15 | 10 |
| E | 130 | 180 | 25 | 25 |

These peaks correspond to six main chain conformation classes:

* (A) alpha helix

* (B) idealized beta strand

* (P) polyproline conformation

* (G) positive φ region accessible to Gly residues

* (L) left-handed alpha helix

* (E) extended conformation

If the probability ω i that a restrained residue in the model is found in the main chain
conformation class i ( i =A,B,P,G,L,E) 
is known, then the PDF restraining the dihedral angles φ and ψ is given by a binomial 
function of the form:

Equation 1:

where . is the correlation coefficient between φ and ψ. 
Derivation of the probabilities ω i used in the above expression depends upon which other features of the 
protein structure were found to correlate with the main chain conformation 
class M. A careful study [Sali and Blundell, 1993a] using the local protein 
database revealed that PDFs were best suited for predicting 
ω i . The variables involved are:

* R Residue type of the restrained residue

* M' main chain conformation class for equivalent residue in
reference protein with known structure

* s Residue neighborhood difference

The residue neighborhood difference s is a value (typical range 0 to 2) that describes the dissimilarity between the residue-residue
neighborhoods of two equivalent residues in an alignment. It is computed using the following procedure:

* Find all neighbors of the residue in structure A (cutoff distance 6.0 Å is used).

* Find equivalent residues in the model (structure B) using the given sequence alignment.

* Find the sum of dissimilarity scores using a published matrix [Sali and Blundell, 1990] .

* Add a gap penalty if there is a deletion in structure B.

The residue neighborhood difference(s) is then the total score divided 
by the number of neighbors found in structure A. If no neighbors were 
found in A, then this implies a score of zero. MODELER then uses the 
conditional PDF to compute the probabilities ω i needed to restrain the main chain conformation class M via the equation above. Tests using 
known structures not involved in the fitting found this scheme to predict 
the main chain conformation class with a success rate of approximately 
73%. Allowing for swapping between the structurally similar B,P classes 
as well as between the L,G classes a prediction success of >87% was found [Sali and Blundell, 1993a] .

# Molecular PDF used for structure generation

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_molecular-pdf-used-for-structure-generation.htm

## Molecular PDF used for structure generation

The objective function used for structure generation in MODELER is referred to as a molecular PDF. This is a combination of all the feature PDFs, p F ( f i ) used to restrain particular geometric features ( f i ) of the protein model. We are 
searching for the 3D protein model that is consistent with the most probable values of the individual features. The feature PDFs measure the 
probability of occurrence for the values of a single feature. The molecular PDF then measures the probability of occurrence for values adopted by 
several features simultaneously.

If the feature PDFs are assumed to be independent, then the molecular PDF is simply a product of the feature PDFs:

Equation 1:

Finding a maximum for P leads to the most probable 3D model given the alignment of the sequence of the model with those of the known 
proteins. The assumption of the independence of the feature PDFs is equivalent to describing the system by a molecular energy function that is a sum 
of terms due to each feature PDF.

If a template structure has alternate locations (conformation), MODELER just takes 
one of the conformers - that with ' ', 'A', or '1' in column 17 in the .pdb file - and ignores any others.

# Align Multiple Sequences

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_multiple-sequence-alignment.htm

## Align Multiple Sequences

The Align Sequences protocol aligns multiple sequences using Align123, a method based on the CLUSTAL W
program [Thompson et al., 1994a] . 
CLUSTAL W aligns multiple sequences using a progressive pairwise alignment algorithm.
In the Align123 method the term for scoring a secondary structure match is added to the original CLUSTAL W multiple sequence alignment score.
This method is also used by the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) protocol to align multiple sequences to a sequence profile, or to align two sequence profiles.

The alignment consists of three main stages:

* All pairs of sequences are aligned separately to calculate a distance matrix giving a score for the divergence of each pair of sequences.

* A guide tree is calculated from the distance matrix.

* The sequences are progressively aligned according to the branching order in the guide tree.

Several unique features in this algorithm improve the sensitivity of the 
alignment of divergent protein sequences [Thompson et al., 1994a] .

* Individual weights are assigned to each sequence in a partial alignment to 
reduce the weight of near-duplicate sequences and increase the weight of the most 
divergent ones.

* Amino acid substitution matrices are varied at different alignment stages according to the divergence of the sequences to be aligned.

* Residue-specific gap penalties and locally reduced gap penalties in hydrophilic regions encourage new gaps in potential loop regions 
rather than regular secondary structure.

* Positions in early alignments where gaps have been opened receive locally reduced gap penalties to encourage the opening of new gaps at 
these positions.

#### Further information

# Multiple structure alignment

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_multiple-structure-alignment.htm

## Multiple structure alignment

After pairwise structure alignment, the next step of the described algorithm 
is to carry out multiple structure alignment. That is, given a set of proteins, 
determine subsets of them that form structural clusters with lower RMSD and 
longer alignment length than the user-defined target values. The basic principle 
of the algorithm is to construct a binary tree of structural similarity from 
the all-against-all pairwise alignments.

The multiple structure alignment and the binary tree are constructed by several 
cycles of analysis based on a hierarchical clustering method. One single cycle 
of analysis consists of calculating the pair-wise alignment matrix for the current 
list of nodes. Starting from each structure as the leaf node of the binary tree, 
the pair-wise alignment matrix is constructed and analyzed to determine the 
list of closest pairs of structures (a structure or node can only be in one closest 
pair in a cycle of analysis) above the alignment threshold. The alignment matrix 
is calculated based on the number of equivalent residues for each pair. For 
each closest pair of structures, a new node is created and the structure of 
the new node is calculated based on the weighted average coordinates of the 
matched Cα atoms from the pair of closest structures or nodes. 
If node k is constructed from node i and j , then the weighting factor of node i in node k is as follows:

Equation 1:

where Nleaf i and Nleaf j are the number of leaf nodes stemming from nodes i and j .

In the next round, the newly created nodes and the nodes that do not form a 
pair in this round are put into the node list and the same analysis repeated. 
The cycle represents an iterative merging process that ends when none of the 
structures at the current level of the binary tree can be aligned with any other. 
Those final nodes correspond to one or more clusters of the input protein structures, 
and the sequence alignments corresponding to those final nodes are saved and 
reported by the 3DMA protocol.

## Pairwise structure alignment

Pairwise structure alignment follows the steps listed below to progress 
from seed alignments to a pairwise structure alignment:

* Expansion of the seed alignments Because the six-residue segment is relatively short, many such segments 
can be categorized as similar between two proteins. Out of these large 
numbers of segments, many of them do not lead to the final correct alignment. 
The task in this step is to expand the seed alignment in the way that 
will lead to the optimal alignment solution. First, the residues in a seed alignment provide the basis for superimposing 
two proteins according to least-squares fitting. The equivalent residue 
pairs are removed or added to the seed alignment according to their Cα 
distances based on the current superimposed orientation. When the removal 
or addition of equivalent residues finishes, another superimposition is 
carried out based on the new set of aligned residues. Each cycle of expansion 
removes and adds equivalent residues to the alignment until there is no 
change in the number of residues, or until the maximum number of cycles 
(5) is reached. The algorithm also uses a continuity check to avoid inclusion 
of pairs of residues that are superimposed by chance.

* Residue rejection and addition Residue removal is carried out before addition, and the addition of new 
residues is performed with a lower tolerance than the removal. The residue 
removal checks for all the current residue equivalencies and rejects those 
where the separation is more than the user-defined distance limit. Residue

than 1.5 times that of the user-defined distance cutoff. All residues 
that satisfy this distance criterion are added at once. Added residues
do not have to be in sequential proximity to the previously built segments. This optimization algorithm has a limitation. User-defined distance limits 
larger than two-thirds of the separation between Cα

as an upper limit for the distance cutoff. A larger distance cutoff 
results in ambiguity when defining the residue equivalence array and the 
optimization might be trapped at a local optimum that is not ideal.

## Special gap penalties

In most dynamic programming applications, the initial gap opening and gap 
extension penalties are applied equally at every position in the sequence, 
regardless of the location of a gap. The exception is terminal gaps, which are 
usually allowed at no cost. In Multiple Sequence Alignment, before any pair of sequences or 
prealigned groups of sequences are aligned, a table of gap opening penalties for 
every position in the two (sets of) sequences are generated. Multiple Sequence Alignment treats the 
initial gap opening penalty (GOP) in a position-specific manner in order to make 
gaps more or less likely at different positions.

The local gap penalty modification rules are applied in a hierarchical manner. 
The exact details of each rule are given below:

* Lowered gap penalties at existing gaps If there is a gap at some position, 
the gap opening and gap extension penalties are lowered and the other rules do 
not apply. This makes gaps more likely at positions where there are already gaps.

stretch, which usually indicates a loop region in a protein structure. You may

# Theory - Predict Disulfide Bridges

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_predss.htm

## Theory - Predict Disulfide Bridges

Proteins may be stabilized by selective mutations to form disulfide bonds. However, identification of suitable sites requires more than spatial proximity. The resulting disulfide bond should have good stereochemistry 
( [Dombkowski, 2003] ), and other factors such as steric clashes and residue depth should be assessed ( [Dani et al., 2003] ).

The Predict Disulfide Bridges tool builds trial disulfide bridges between pairs of residues and retains those with the best geometry. The following properties that may influence the ability of the bridge to stabilize the protein are calculated for each resulting residue pair: steric clashes, solvent surface accessibility, residue depth, volume change, sequence separation, and thermal mobility.

### Prediction of Disulfide Bridge Sites

The following process is followed to predict disulfide bridge sites:

* Pairs of residues having a CB-CB distance between 3.0 and 5.0 Å and CA-CA distance between 3.6 and 7.0 Å are found.

* If there are any residues selected, only selected residues are considered. Cysteine residues that already form a disulfide bridge are excluded, although for validation purposes, the scripting API allows them to be included.

* For each residue in the pair, trial sulfur positions are generated with initial coordinates with a CB-SG distance of 1.81 Å, a CA-CB-SG angle of 114.6°, and with N-CA-CB-SG torsions of -60.0, 60.0 and 180.0°.

* Each of the resulting nine combinations is tested to see if it approximates to disulfide geometry, with an SG-SG distance between 1.0 and 3.0 Å and CB-SG-SG angles between 75.0 and 135.0°.

* A geometric clean is performed on each pair of sulfur atoms that meet the criteria.

* They are then checked for steric clashes with main-chain atoms within 2.0 Å.

* The energy of the resulting structures is calculated as follows: Where: and i and j are residue indices, χ 1 is the N-CA-CB-SG torsion (minima at ±60° and 180°), χ 3 is the CB i -SG i -SG j -CB j torsion (minima at -87° and +97°), θ is the CA-CB-SG angle with θ 0 = 114.6°, ø is the CB i -SG i -SG j angle with ø 0 = 104.15°, dss is the SG i -SG j distance with dss 0 = 2.04 Å and dcs is the CB-SG distance with dcs 0 = 1.81 Å.

Where:

and i and j are residue indices, χ 1 is the N-CA-CB-SG torsion (minima at ±60° and 180°), χ 3 is the CB i -SG i -SG j -CB j torsion (minima at -87° and +97°), θ is the CA-CB-SG angle with θ 0 = 114.6°, ø is the CB i -SG i -SG j angle with ø 0 = 104.15°, dss is the SG i -SG j distance with dss 0 = 2.04 Å and dcs is the CB-SG distance with dcs 0 = 1.81 Å.

* The sulfur pair with the lowest value of [energy + 10.0 × number of steric clashes] is retained.

* For cases where a residue could form a bridge to more than one other residue, the same test is applied so that each residue only participates in one disulfide bridge.

* For each of the final pairs of residues, a Predicted Disulfide Bridge Site object is created, which contains the information required for assessment and disulfide bridge creation.

* The sites are listed on the Hierarchy View under the Predicted Disulfide Bridge Sites assembly.

* The residue pairs are added to the Predicted Disulfide Bridge Residues assembly.

### Assessment of Disulfide Bridge Sites

For each pair of residues, the following properties are calculated:

* Score: Ranking calculated as 100 - 2*[energy + 10 × <number of steric clashes>].

* Energy: Quality of the S-S bond stereochemistry as described above.

* Bad Contacts: Number of steric clashes of the two sulfur atoms to main-chain atoms within 2.0 Å.

* Thermal Mobility: Sum of the average B-Factor for main-chain atoms in the residue pair.

* Sequence Separation: Sequence separation of the residue pair if they are in the same chain (inter-chain).

* Residue Depth: Average residue burial depth of the pair of residues. This is calculated by creating a solvent surface over the protein, with probe radius of 2.8 Å to smooth clefts in the structure. The depth is the distance from the centroid of the residue to the nearest surface point plus 1.4 Å (the radius of a water molecule).

* Volume Change: Calculated as 2 × <standard Voronoi volume of disulfide cysteine> - <sum of standard Voronoi volumes of the original residues>.

* Environment: Secondary structure environment of each of the residues. Disulfide bonds have been found to occur significantly more often between residues which are both in a coil, and less often for a helix-sheet pair compared to other environments.

* Solvent Accessibility: Average of the percent solvent accessibility for the pair of residues.

* Chi3: The CB-S-S-CB torsion angle.

These properties are reported in the Predicted Disulfide Bridge tab of the Molecular Data Table , which is automatically displayed sorted by Score .

A report is optionally displayed with the more significant properties tabulated and colored according to their favorability for disulfide stabilization, with green denoting more favorable characteristics, red unfavorable, and orange in between. This is intended to give guidance in selecting which mutations are more likely to produce stabilizing mutations. If this report is not required, you can disable it using the Predict Disulfide Bridges page - Preferences dialog .

You can browse the sites and zoom in on them using the site navigation tools on the tool panel.

### Creation of Disulfide Bridges

Once you have assessed the predicted sites, you can use the Create Disulfide Bridge tool to convert them into disulfide bridges. For each selected predicted site, this will mutate the pair of residues to cysteine with the SG atoms (and CB in the case of glycine) at the modeled coordinates, and bond the two SG atoms to form the bridge.

## Probability density functions

To predict a three-dimensional structure of a molecule, functional forms 
must be defined describing the geometric features of a molecule, such 
as bond lengths, bond angles, dihedral angles, and nonbond distances. 
In this topic the function forms used by MODELER are discussed and defined 
in terms of geometric restraints.

In many areas of molecular modeling, geometric features such as distances 
and dihedral angles may be restrained by setting lower and upper bounds 
on their allowed values. A pseudo-energy term and a restraining force 
are then applied if the geometric feature in a model molecule is found 
to be outside these bounds. MODELER describes restraints on such geometric 
features in terms of a probability density function (PDF) p (f) , for a feature f that is to be 
restrained. The area under the curve p(f) between f 1 and f 2 :

Equation 1:

is the probability of an event in which f is observed within 
this range. This must integrate to one over the range of all possible 
values for the feature f . This description is more complete than 
the use of mean values and/or lower and upper bounds as a description 
for restraints.

In addition, the concept of a conditional probability density function 
is important in comparative modeling. The PDF used to restrain a geometric 
feature f can be written as:

Equation 2:

This describes the probability density for f when the other 
features a,b,c .... are specified. As an example, p (χ 1 | 
residue_type, φ, ψ) 
could be used to describe the side-chain dihedral angle χ 1 for a known residue type and main-chain dihedral angles φ 
and ψ.

Specific types of PDFs are discussed in the following topics:

* PDF for bond lengths, bond angles, and dihedrals

* PDF for atom-atom repulsions

* Distance between two C-alpha atoms

* PDF for main-chain N-O distances

* PDF for side-chain - side-chain and side-chain - main-chain distances

* PDF for main-chain dihedral angles

* PDF for side-chain dihedral angles

# Derivation of probability density functions from known protein structures

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_probability-density-functions-observed-in-known-protein-structures.htm

## Derivation of probability density functions from known protein structures

The probability density functions (PDFs) used by MODELER are derived analytically 
using statistical mechanics and empirically using a database of known 
protein structures. Stereochemical restraints such as bond lengths, bond 
angles, dihedral angles, van der Waals repulsions, and disulfide bonds 
are derived from published parameters for a molecular mechanics forcefield [Brooks et al., 1983] . The disulfide bond 
is restrained by distances, angles, and the C-S-S-C dihedral angle. Restraints 
such as those applied to Cα-Cα 
distances, N-O distances for main-chain atoms, main-chain dihedral, and 
side-chain dihedral angle classes are derived empirically from a database 
of known homologous proteins and their structural alignments.

The method of deriving PDFs from the database of known proteins may be
found in Sali and Overington, 1994 [Sali and Overington, 1994] . The database 
and PDFs depending on it are regularly updated.

The database is considered a representative sample of globular proteins and is 
suitable for deriving the relationships between features of protein structures. These
relationships are expressed as PDFs. Features are derived at several levels. 
There are residue-residue relationships such as Cα-Cα distances, 
protein-protein relationships such as percentage sequence identity, residue
properties such as solvent accessibility, and protein properties such as resolution in X-ray diffraction.

Given the database of proteins, an analysis program is used to derive 
a table W f, a, b...c that approximates 
p(f |a, b, c...):

Equation 1:

This table contains the observed relative frequencies for a feature f given a, b...c . Nonlinear least squares regression is then used 
to derive an analytic function that fits the table W.

Equation 2:

where q represents a vector of nonlinear fitting parameters. The 
forms of the probability density function derived for various geometric 
features used by MODELER are described below.

## Align Sequence Profiles

One of the main problems in comparative and homology modeling is the accuracy of the
sequence alignment, which can be greatly improved by comparing the two sequence
profiles constructed from the homologues sequences.
The SALIGN function in the MODELER program [Marti-Renom et al., 2004] extends the sequence alignment 
algorithm to align two sequence profiles. A sequence profile can be generated from
a BLAST/PSI-BLAST search, a multiple sequence alignment, or a multiple structure
alignment.

The following topics are discussed below:

* Deriving the sequence profile from a multiple sequence alignment

* The alignment method and profile-to-profile substitution score

A sequence profile describes the probability of occurrence of each of the
twenty standard amino acids at a given alignment position. The probability is calculated
based on the multiple sequence alignment input.

A position-based weighting [Henikoff and Henikoff, 1994] is applied to each sequence for profile calculation,
assigning low weights to overrepresented sequences and high weights to unique 
sequences:

From equation 2, P i,a is calculated by two terms. The first term

alignment result is similar to the pairwise sequence alignment. Conversely, when 
the profile is represented by the alignment of many unique sequences, the first term 
dominates and P i,a will depend mainly on the occurrence of residue 
types found in the input sequence alignment.

### Alignment method and profile-to-profile substitution score

SALIGN aligns two sequence profiles using the dynamic programming method with an affine
gap penalty in the same way as pairwise sequence alignment. 
Replacing the residue substitution score in the pairwise
sequence alignment, the two profiles are compared using the profile substitution score
defined by the correlation coefficient between the two profiles. The substitution score S i,j between profile P at position i and profile Q at position j is calculated by:

# Progressive alignment

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_progressive-alignment.htm

## Progressive alignment

After the guide tree is created, the multiple sequence alignment proceeds to
a series of pairwise alignments to 
align larger and larger groups of sequences, following the branching order in the 
guide tree. The alignment proceeds from the tips of the rooted tree towards the 
root. At each stage, a full dynamic programming algorithm is used to align two 
existing alignments or sequences. The score at each alignment position is the 
average of all the pairwise substitution matrix scores from the amino acids in 
the two sets of sequences. If either set of sequences contains one or more gaps 
in one of the positions being considered, each gap versus a residue is scored as 
zero. The default amino acid substitution matrices in Multiple Sequence Alignment are rescored to 
have only positive values. Hence, this treatment of gaps treats the score of a 
residue versus a gap as having the worst possible score. When calculating the 
alignment score, each substitution matrix value is multiplied by the weights from 
the two sequences.

Sequence weights calculated from the guide tree are used as simple 
multiplication factors for scoring positions from different sequences or 
prealigned groups of sequences. Groups of closely related sequences receive 
reduced weights because they contain a great deal of duplicated information. 
Highly divergent sequences without any close relatives receive high weights.

The initial gap opening penalty (GOP) and gap extension penalty (GEP) can be 
set from the Multiple Sequence Alignment protocol user interface. 
Align123 then automatically attempts to adjust the gap 
penalties for each sequence alignment.

The GOP depends on the following factors:

* Substitution matrix - Varying the gap penalties used with different
substitution matrices can improve the accuracy of sequence alignments. Align123
uses the average score for two mismatched residues (i.e., off-diagonal values in
the matrix) as a scaling factor for the GOP.

* Similarity of the sequences - The percentage identity of the two (groups of)
sequences to be aligned is used to increase the GOP for closely related sequences
and to decrease the GOP for more divergent sequences on a linear scale.

* Lengths of the sequences - The scores for both true and false sequence
alignments increase with the lengths of the sequences. GOP is scaled by the
logarithm of the length of the shortest sequence.

Using these three modifications, the GOP is then calculated by:

Equation 1:

where, N and M are the lengths of the two sequences.

The GEP depends on the difference between the lengths of the two sequences to 
be aligned. If one sequence is much shorter than the other, the GEP is increased 
to inhibit the introduction of too many long gaps in the shorter sequence. The

# Protein Structure Abnormalities

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_protein-health.htm

## Protein Structure Abnormalities

The Validate Protein Structure tools check for abnormalities in the protein structure. The following
structural features are checked and reported:

* Bond length deviation from the standard values

* Bond angle deviation from the standard values

* Main-Chain φ,ψ angles not in the allowed Ramachandran region

* Side-Chain conformation not found in the selected rotamer library

* Nonplanar Peptide Bond

* Cis Peptide Bond

* Abnormal C-alpha to C-alpha distances

* Missing Main-Chain atoms

* Missing Side-Chain atoms

* Nonstandard atom names

* Chirality of the C-alpha atom

* Alternate Conformations

#### Bond length

The lengths of the following bonds are checked against the standard values provided
by Engh and Huber [Engh and Huber, 1991] . 
If a bond length outside the bond length tolerance (default 3-sigma) of the given standard value, it is
reported as a bond with error. Standard values are shown for specific residue 
types in some cases. For others, the values are listed in the All residue type row.

| Bond | Residue Type | Standard Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CA-C | All | 1.525 |
| CA-C | GLY | 1.516 |
| C-O | All | 1.231 |
| CA-CB | All | 1.530 |
| CA-CB | ALA | 1.521 |
| CA-CB | ILE, THR, VAL | 1.540 |
| CA-N | All | 1.458 |
| CA-N | PRO | 1.466 |
| CA-N | GLY | 1.451 |
| N-C | All | 1.329 |
| N-C | PRO | 1.341 |
| SG-SG | CYS | 2.00 |

#### Bond angle

Similar to bond length, bond angles are checked against the standard values provided
by Engh and Huber [Engh and Huber, 1991] . 
If a bond angle is outside the bond angle tolerance (default 3-sigma) of the given standard value, it is
reported as an angle with error. If an atom in an angle is specific to a particular
residue type, the residue type is specified in the parenthesis after the atom. Otherwise,
the angle is applicable to all residue types.

| Angle | Standard Value |
| --- | --- |
| C-N-CA | 121.7 |
| C-N(GLY)-CA(GLY) | 120.6 |
| C-N(PRO)-CA(PRO) | 122.6 |
| CA-C-N | 116.2 |
| CA(GLY)-C(GLY)-N | 116.4 |
| CA-C-N(PRO) | 116.9 |
| CA(GLY)-C(GLY)-N(PRO) | 118.2 |
| CA-C-O | 120.8 |
| CA-C-O | 120.8 |
| CB-CA-C | 110.1 |
| CB(ALA)-CA(ALA)-C(ALA) | 110.5 |
| CB(ILE)-CA(ILE)-C(ILE) CB(THR)-CA(THR)-C(THR) CB(VAL)-CA(VAL)-C(VAL) | 109.1 |
| N-CA-C | 111.2 |
| N-CA(GLY)-C(GLY) | 112.5 |
| N(PRO)-CA-C | 111.8 |
| N(PRO)-CA(GLY)-C(GLY) | 112.5 |
| N-CA-CB | 110.5 |
| N(ILE)-CA(ILE)-CB(ILE) N(THR)-CA(THR)-CB(THR) N(VAL)-CA(VAL)-CB(VAL) | 111.5 |
| N(ALA)-CA(ALA)-CB(ALA) | 110.4 |
| N(PRO)-CA(PRO)-CB(PRO) | 103.0 |
| O-C-N | 123.0 |
| O-C-N(PRO) | 122.0 |

#### Main-Chain conformation

The main-chain conformation (defined by the pair of φ=C-N-CA-C, ψ=N-CA-C-N angles) 
of each residue is checked against the Ramachandran map [Ramachandran et al., 1963] . A violation will be reported if it falls outside of an allowed region, with details as to whether it is disallowed, marginal or if it is a glycine or proline residue.

Statistics are reported detailing :

* Number of terminal residues

* Number of non-proline or glycine residues

* Number and percentage of these in allowed regions

* Number and percentage of these in marginal regions

* Number and percentage of these in disallowed regions

* Number of glycine residues

* Number of proline residues

* Total number of residues

As a guideline, a good protein structure would be expected to have at least 90% of its residues (excluding termini, glycine and proline) in allowed regions.

#### Side-Chain conformation

The side-chain conformation of each residue is checked against the selected rotamer libraries.
The supported rotamer libraries are:

* Ponder and Richards [Ponder and Richards, 1987]

* Sutcliffe [Sutcliffe et al., 1987]

* Oldfield

* Lovell, Word, and Richardson [Lovell et al., 2000]

* Dunbrack [Dunbrack and Cohen, 1997]

All of the rotamer libraries are backbone independent, except Dunbrack rotamer library.

For the backbone independent rotamer libraries, each residue has a few allowed conformations 
given by the values of the χ angles. If the side-chain torsion angles of a residue 
do not match any of the allowed conformations within a defined threshold, the residue 
will be reported as having a side-chain conformation violation.

For the backbone dependent rotamer library, the allowed-chain conformations are 
listed for different backbone conformations. If the conformation of a residue does not
fall into any of the combinations of the backbone and side-chain conformations listed in 
the database within a defined threshold, the residue will be reported as having a side-chain 
conformation violation.

#### Nonplanar peptide bond and cis-peptide

If the planarity of a peptide bond (the omega angle) deviates from 0° or 180° by
a defined threshold, the two residues forming the peptide bond will be reported.

Most peptide bonds are in trans conformation and if the planarity of a peptide bond (the omega angle) 
is close to 0°, within the defined cutoff, the two residues forming the peptide 
bond will be reported. It is common to have a cis peptide bond when one of the residues
forming the bond is a proline.

#### CA to CA distance

When the peptide bond between two consecutive residues is in the standard trans conformation,
the C-alpha distance between the two residues is around 3.8 Å. For a peptide bond in the cis conformation, this
distance is much shorter. The distances between consecutive C-alpha atoms are checked and deviations where distances are greater 
than 3.8 Å or smaller than 3.8 Å beyond the cutoff will be reported. An exception is made for cis-peptides, for which the distance is expected to be shorter, for which a mean value of 2.9 Å is used.

#### Missing atoms and nonstandard names

For each residue, the backbone and side-chain heavy atoms are checked against the standard
atom list based on the standard IUPAC atom names. The missing atoms will be reported

If a residue has atoms that are not found in the standard atom list, the atom is
listed under nonstandard atom names. This applies to any additional atoms in the residue
or atoms that are not comply to the standard name. For example, if a CD1 atom is named
as CD atom in isoleucine, the atom is reported as nonstandard atom name and at the same
time, CD1 atom is reported as missing from the residue under Missing Atom category.
This check applies to both heavy atoms and hydrogens.

#### Chirality

Checks for the chirality of the alpha carbon and report residues with nonstandard 
C-alpha chirality. In all naturally occurring amino acids, C-alpha atom has R chirality, 
except cystine or cysteine, which has S chirality at the C-alpha atom.

Checks for the presence of alternate conformations. While these are not actually a violation, they do represent areas where the structure is poorly defined and may need some correction before subsequent modeling operations are performed.
