# Theory - Protein Solubility Scores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_protein_solubility.htm

## Theory - Protein Solubility Scores

Therapeutic proteins, especially antibodies, are used in the treatment of many medical conditions. 
It is important that the designed antibodies have high solubility so that they can be stored and administered
at high concentrations. Predicted antibody solubility can be used to rank and filter antibody candidates
throughout the development cycle to reduce development risks.

### Calculation of Protein Solubility

Electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions are key factors that can affect the protein solubility and aggregation. 
It is known that the protein solubility is minimal at the isoelectric point [Tanford,1961] . 
This demonstrates the importance of the electrostatic interactions between protein molecules to protein solubility.
The electrostatic interactions between protein molecules are a combination of repulsive and attractive forces. 
In general the repulsive forces increase with the molecular net charge, Z, while the charge asymmetry could 
lead to attraction between protein parts with opposite, e.g. positive and negative, surface potential. 
As a first approximation the charge asymmetry can be evaluated by the molecular dipole moment, D. 
Another pH-dependent factor that influences the solubility is the solvation energy, ΔGsolv, 
as a part of the transfer energy of molecule from solution to condensed (crystalline or aggregated) phase [Tjong and Zhou,2008] . 
Based on validation with Ribonuclease SA mutants and Insulin on pH dependence of protein solubility, we propose 
the following empirical scoring function for electrostatic contribution to solubility, SpH(pH):

The net charge, Z, the dipole moment D, and ΔGsolv are calculated as a function of pH in the same way as in the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol, and α, β , and C are adjustable parameters.
The detail are discussed in Theory - Protein Ionization and pk Prediction .

Hydrophobic interaction between protein molecules is another attractive force to cause low solubility.
It can be approximated by the positive aggregation score (APS) as in Developability Indices (DI) :

where γ is a scaling parameter.

A more positive value of Solubility Score corresponds to a better solubility.

# PSI-BLAST Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_psi-blast.htm

## PSI-BLAST Search

PSI-BLAST, or Position-Specific Iterated BLAST, uses the methods described in Altschul et al. [Altschul et al. 1997] and Schaffer et al. [Schaffer et al. 2001] to search for similarities between protein query sequences and all the sequences in protein databases.

PSI-BLAST Search is a statistically driven search method that finds regions of similarity 
between a query sequence and database sequences and produces gapped alignments 
of those regions. Within these aligned regions, the calculated statistical score 
(E-value) should be better than the expected score of a random hit. For the 
most part, the description of the BLAST search algorithm given in the BLAST Search theory topic is applicable to PSI-BLAST Search. There are three main characteristics
that are unique to a PSI-BLAST Search: the use of PSSMs, iterative searching,
and composition-based statistics.

PSI-BLAST uses a profile [i.e., position-specific scoring matrices (PSSMs)] 
to score matches between query and database sequences, in contrast to BLAST, 
which uses pre-defined scoring matrices such as BLOSUM62. PSI-BLAST is more sensitive 
than BLAST in finding distantly related sequences.

PSI-BLAST can repeatedly search the target databases, using a multiple alignment 
of high scoring sequences found in each search round to generate a new PSSM 
for use in the next round of searching. PSI-BLAST iterates until no new 
hits are found, or a specified maximum number of iterations is reached, 
whichever comes first. Normally, the first round of searching uses a standard 
scoring matrix, effectively performing a blastp search.

PSI-BLAST takes the amino acid compositions of the query and database sequences into account when computing the 
statistical scores. It gives more sensitive search
results and reduces the chance of getting diverged PSSMs for low complexity sequences.

# Loop Refinement (MODELER)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_refine-loops.htm

## Loop Refinement (MODELER)

When a homology model is created, there are parts of the model sequence which 
are not aligned to any template structures. For these sections no homology restraints (such as 
Cα-Cα distance restraints) can be applied. These parts of the structure generally have greater errors 
compared to the regions which are modeled based on a template structure.

It is sometimes desirable to refine the loop conformation after model generation 
using a statistical pair potential by a more extensive molecular dynamics or simulated 
annealing procedure. This section discusses the energy function used by loop 
optimization in the MODELER program.

Loops can be defined automatically from the model to a template sequence alignment. Refer to Loop Optimization for the definition of loops.

Two types of energy functions are supported by the MODELER Loop Refinement - 
DOPE_Loop and (Fiser) Loop. Both include bonded terms (for example, bond length, bond angle, 
main-chain dihedral angle, side-chain dihedral angles and so forth) that correspond to 
terms in homology model building in MODELER. The two approaches differ mainly in the non-bonded terms. 
DOPE_Loop uses the DOPE potential [Shen and Sali, 2006] and (Fiser) Loop ( [Fiser et al., 2000] uses the Melo statistical potential [Melo and Feytmans, 1997] . 
In addition, DOPE_Loop includes solvation terms. Both Loop refinement approaches
apply the same optimization protocol, which was described by Fiser. In addition, DOPE_Loop has an option to use
a higher resolution grid (using a bin size of 0.125 vs 0.5).

DOPE_Loop generates more accurate models than the original (Fiser) Loop method, but at the expense of computation time.
The additional computation time is mainly spent on calculating the solvation energy term.

#### Non-Bonded terms in (Fiser) Loop Potential Function

The first part of the nonbonded potential is the Melo's potential, which
is a residue based, distance-dependent statistical potential of mean force. 
Each residue is represented by one or more atoms and atoms are classified into 40 types. 
This potential was obtained from atom pairs in known protein structures that 
were separated by 11 or more residues in sequence. The original potential in the 
histogram form [Melo and Feytmans, 1997] was converted into cubic splines in MODELER to allow the use of first derivatives in 
optimization. The second part of the nonbonded term is a harmonic lower bound on 
non-bonded atom-atom distances ( [Sali and Blundell, 1993a] - Equation 22).

#### Non-Bonded terms in DOPE_Loop Potential Function

DOPE_Loop nonbonded terms:

* Lennard-Jones

* DOPE statistical potential

* Charge-charge interaction

* Electrostatic contribution to the solvation energy

The charge model used in charge-charge interaction and solvation energy calculation
is point charge for ionizable amino acid residues.

The electrostatic contribution to the solvation energy is calculated using a Generalized Born 
implicit solvent model. The Born radii are calculated using a simplified version of the AGB method [Gallicchio and Levy, 2004] .
The original AGB method considers overlaps (Equations 2-3) that involve more than 2 spheres, 
so it is computationally expensive. MODELER implementation only uses two-sphere 
overlaps with exact overlap volumes (instead of the Gaussian approximation used by Gallicchio and Levy).

#### Further information

Loop Refinement (MODELER) Theory - Build Homology Models

## PDF for Chi1 dihedral angles

As shown in the table in PDF for side-chain dihedral angles ,
all residue types except Val and Ser have 
χ1 dihedral angles that most frequently fall into the 
"-" class. Val predominantly occupies the "t" class, while Ser is 
slightly more frequently found in the "+" class. A careful study of the effects 
of including various protein descriptors on the accuracy of predicting the 
χ1 side-chain dihedral conformation class c 1 has been performed [Sali and Blundell, 1993a] .
Using the alignments database, the optimum PDF for the prediction of the χ1 class probability ω1i, was found to be 
of the form p (χ1,| r , c' 1, r', s ), where r and c 1 are the residue type and 
χ1 class of the restrained residue in the model protein, r' and c' 1 
are the residue type and χ1 class of
an equivalent residue in a known reference protein, and s is the 
residue neighborhood difference. This scheme was found to be
most accurate in predicting the χ1 conformation class of 
large buried residues such as Trp, Cys, Leu, Val, and Tyr where a prediction success
of approximately 80% was found. It was least successful in predicting the 
χ1 conformation class of smaller exposed residues such as Asn, Met,
Arg, Glu, and Ser (approximately 50% successful).

# Theory - Calculate Aggregation Scores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_sap.htm

## Theory - Calculate Aggregation Scores

Therapeutic proteins, especially antibodies, are used in the treatment of many medical conditions. Unfortunately, they tend to aggregate when stored at the high concentrations required for treatment, which decreases their activity and may cause immunological responses. By predicting protein surface sites that are liable to aggregation, proteins with better stability can be engineered by selective mutation of the residues involved.

It has been shown that the predominant mechanism for aggregation is hydrophobic interactions on the surface of the protein. Therefore, a method is required that finds patches of exposed hydrophobic residues which are spatially close. The spatial aggregation propensity ( [Chennamsetty et al., 2009a] , [Chennamsetty et al., 2009b] , and [Chennamsetty et al., 2010] ) achieves this.

### Calculation of aggregation propensity scores

The method requires the calculation of the Solvent Accessible Area (SAA) for each atom.
The aggregation propensity score for each protein atom is defined as:

The following calculations are performed:

* The SAA of the fully exposed side-chain is precalculated by CHARMm for each standard amino acid from the central residue of an Ala-X-Ala tripeptide in the fully extended conformation.

* Black and Mould [1991] hydrophobicities are normalized such that glycine has a hydrophobicity value of zero. Thus amino acids more hydrophobic than glycine are positive, while hydrophilic residues are negative.

* The SAA values for each atom are calculated within CHARMm; this calculation includes all non-solvent residues in the structure.

* The per-atom aggregation propensity scores are calculated for spherical regions of radius R around every atom in the protein using the above equation.

* The aggregation propensity score for each residue is obtained as the average of its atomic aggregation scores. High aggregation scores indicate highly exposed hydrophobic regions.

* The molecular aggregation score is calculated as the sum of all atomic scores. For a given radius and size of molecule, this is an approximate indication of its overall tendency to aggregate. However, note that the Developability Index is likely to provide a better measure because it includes a net molecular charge term.

### Creation of aggregation site groups

After the aggregation propensity scores have been calculated, groups spanning aggregation sites are found by the following method:

* Only exposed residues (side-chain surface accessible area greater than 5Å 2 ) with an aggregation propensity score greater than zero are considered for inclusion in sites.

* Each site is seeded with the residue which has the highest aggregation propensity score and is not yet assigned to a site. The site center should have aggregation propensity score greater than 0.1.

* Neighboring residues with at least one atom within 3.5Å for all-atom structures, or 4.1Å for polar-hydrogen models, are recruited into the site group.

* Step 3 is repeated for the newly-recruited residues until there are no more within range that fulfill the site criteria.

Note that this procedure creates the groups Site1, Site2 etc in order of the highest individual residue score in each group, they are not ranked by any other criteria such as the total score.

## Scoring matrices and gap parameters

BLOSUM62 [Henikoff and Henikoff, 1992] has been empirically shown to be among the best 
for detecting weak protein similarities, and BLAST and PSI-BLAST use the BLOSUM62 scoring matrix 
by default. You can also select BLOSUM45, BLOSUM80, PAM70, and PAM30 scoring matrices. 
Each matrix is most sensitive for finding homologs at the corresponding evolutionary distance. 
For BLOSUM matrices, a smaller number corresponds to larger evolutionary distance; for PAM 
matrices, a larger number corresponds to larger evolutionary distance. The seminal paper on

# Theory Model Antibody Loops (Canonical Structures)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_search-antibody-loops-can-struct.htm

## Theory Model Antibody Loops (Canonical Structures)

Each of the variable domains of an antibody, VL and VH, has 3 hypervariable loops, L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, and H3, which form the antigen binding site. The antigen binding sites also referred to as complementarity determining regions (CDRs) have a very high degree of variability in their amino acid sequence between different antibodies, compared to the framework region, which is more conserved. However, work by Chothia and Lesk [Chothia and Lesk, 1987] found that despite sequence variability, five of the six CDR regions, L1, L2, L3, H1 and H2, can be clustered into sets with similar main-chain conformations. This small repertoire of main-chain conformations is referred to as "canonical structures" in the antibody literature [Morea et al., 2000] .

The work by Chothia and Lesk as well as later studies ( [Chothia and Lesk, 1987] , [Tramontano et al., 1990] , [Al-Lazikani et al, 1997] , [Morea et al., 2000] ) noted that the canonical structure type of a CDR loop region can often be identified by residue signatures (i.e., specific residue types at certain key positions in the amino acid sequence correlate with canonical types) for specific loop lengths. For modeling antibody loops this means that the canonical loop type can be determined from the amino acid sequence of the query. Once the canonical structure type is determined, templates with the same canonical type for the CDR loop can be selected, which are likely to have a structure that is similar to the loop in the target antibody structure, which can help in building more accurate models.

The information on canonical structure residue signatures available in the literature was summarized in [Morea et al., 2000] . Canonical Loop filtering in Discovery Studio largely follows the data presented in that paper. The definitions used in Discovery Studio are listed in the following tables. The Key Residues column in the tables contains the residue signatures that are characteristic of a canonical loop type. The residue signatures given in the tables list the residue types allowed at a given sequence number. Each item in the list consists of a number, corresponding to the residue number (according to the Chothia numbering scheme) of the specified position in the sequence, and a set of letters, which are the one letter codes of the allowed residue types for that position.

# Theory - Model Antibody Loops

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_search-antibody-loops.htm

## Theory - Model Antibody Loops

The selectivity of antibody binding with an antigen is determined by loop regions on the variable domains of the antibody. Each of the variable domains, V L and V H , have three hypervariable loops, L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, and H3, that form the antigen binding site. These loops are often referred to as Complimentarity Determining Regions (CDRs). See Theory - Annotate Antibody Sequence .

### Loop template Identification

The goal of the Discovery Studio method is to choose the best templates for modeling the conformation of each CDR loop region and rebuild the loops
for a given antibody structure. The first step is to identify the loop regions of the input protein. The following procedures are repeated for each chain of the input protein.

* For each chain, its variable domain type, residue numbers (according to one of the numbering schemes described above), and CDR regions are determined using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs).

* The residue numbering generated by the HMM search is used to align the input sequence chain with the prealigned antibody variable domains in the Antibody Database .

* Based on this alignment, sequences in the database are ranked according to sequence identity with the query sequence.

* If desired, the hits (most similar sequences) can be further filtered by Organism and Canonical Structure type. See Theory - Model Antibody Loops (Canonical Structures) .

* For each of the hits, each CDR region is evaluated separately. Based on the alignment, a CDR hit must have the same CDR length
between the query and the hit and must not have gaps between the hit and query at stem residues (four residues before and after the loop).

* The BLOSUM62 matrix is used to calculate a similarity score for the loop hit on the loop and stem residues between the hit and the query.

* For H3, the torso section (the first and last four loop residues) are considered more important than other loop residues. A 0.25 
scale is applied to the non-torso residues.

* For each loop, all of its hits are sorted according to the loop similarity score. You can specify how many top hits are used as modeling templates for 
each loop.

* For hits which have an identical score, further sorting is performed. Because the conformations of the three CDR loops in each chain are interdependent, the first criterion used is the sum of the scores for the other two loops. If there is still a tie, then crystallographic resolution followed by sequence identity are used.

* The report tabulates the hits in this order, with the score, resolution and the overall sequence identity and similarity being shown.

The second step creates an alignment between the input protein and the templates identified for modeling. The first two sequences in the alignment 
are taken from the input protein: one is used as the model sequence and the other is linked to the input antibody structure. The loops of these two 
sequences are fully unaligned to each other so that the input antibody structure is only used to build the core region of the model, and the loops 
will be modeled by the templates identified. The templates are aligned to the query sequence by the residue numbers based on the selected numbering scheme. 
The templates for each loop are aligned to the input sequence with the hit loop fully aligned and 
other loops fully shifted. One template can be used to model more than one
loop region, in which case it appears as one sequence entry in the alignment.

This alignment with the antibody templates can be used to build homology models .

# Seed alignment analysis

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_seed-alignment-analysis.htm

## Seed alignment analysis

A seed alignment is a pair of six-residue segments from two input structures 
that can be superimposed within 1 Å RMSD. A protein of length N has N -5 such segments defined by a sliding 
window of six residues. One way to find all the possible seed alignments 
is to do an all-against-all pairwise comparison by performing structural 
superimposition of all possible six residue segments. Given two proteins 
each having N residues, it computes ( N -5)×( N -6) 
superimpositions for all of the six residue segments. Alternatively, a Cα 
pseudo-torsion angle of four consecutive residues (see the Figure 2) can be used 
to compare a pair of residue segments. The advantage of using the pseudo-torsion 
angle is that the torsion angles can be put into a hash table. Using 
the hash table to look for similar segment pairs dramatically reduces 
the computation time. The best hash key found from various test cases 
is defined by the following equation:

Equation 1:

where T i is the Cα pseudo-torsion angle in degrees, P =20 is the torsion bin size, and N =6 
is the length of the residue segment. The square brackets represent rounding 
down to the closest integer.

Figure 2: Definition of the Cα pseudo-torsion angle

There is a problem with hashing protein conformations in this way, or with 
any other metric that defines relative conformation. That is, all helical structure in
proteins is essentially identical. This gives rise to a high population of 
hash entries for these conformations resulting in many false positive seed points. As a
result, more computation time is wasted comparing those seed points in the following 
alignment steps.

To solve this problem, an interesting statistical observation
was put into effect computationally. Optimal alignment of helical proteins invariably 
results in superposition of the end points of the secondary structure. Because of this, 
it is not necessary to use all the helical hash bin data. Instead, 
only the data from the helical end points are used and they often diverge slightly from
the ideal helical hash bins. This reduces the chance of false positive seed points. 
The only difference found when comparing results using and not using the helical hash
bins is in the computation time.

Beta strands are more variable so there is no issue with saturation of a single 
hash bin and no need for special treatment.

All six residue segments for all the proteins are sorted into one single 
hash table, grouping together the segments with similar torsion angles. 
The seed alignment is defined as any two segments from different proteins 
with the same hash value, Tor , and overlapping 
with a Cα RMSD less than or equal to the local RMSD 
cutoff of 1 Å.

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_sequence-dendrogram.htm

## Sequence dendrogram

A family of homologous sequences is aligned using a multiple sequence alignment 
program. Based on the alignment, the sequences are clustered, using Unweighted Pair 
Group Method with Arithmetic mean (UPGMA) [Sneath and Sokal, 1973] . The distance, D , between two nodes, a and b , in the sequence cluster 
is calculated as follows:

Equation 1:

where ID ij is the pairwise percentage sequence identity 
between sequence i in node a and sequence j in node b , and there are m and n sequences in nodes a and b , respectively.

The sequence cluster, or dendrogram, is a representation of the evolutionary 
or functional relationship of the sequences in the sequence family. Based on the 
dendrogram, sequences in a family can be divided into subfamilies at a given 
sequence identity cutoff. At different cutoffs, the subfamily represents 
different levels of functional resolution. At high sequence identity cutoffs, the 
subfamily consists of smaller groups of sequences and shows more functional 
specificity, while at low sequence identity cutoffs, the subfamilies are larger, 
with less specificity.

# Side-Chain Flexibility

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_side-chain-flex.htm

## Side-Chain Flexibility

The ChiFlex algorithm generates an ensemble of low protein conformations 
with varied side-chain conformations. It uses a modified version of the ChiRotor sampling algorithm [Spassov et al., 2007] .

The ChiFlex algorithm runs as follows:

* Remove side-chain atoms: - All side-chain atoms from specified residues are removed
for conformational sampling. However, backbone and side-chain atoms of the remaining residues are not modified.
This structure becomes the framework for the following steps.

* Sample side-chain conformations - The side-chain conformation of each
selected residue is sampled independently. During the sampling, each residue adopts 3 initial
conformations with χ1 = 60°, -60°, and 180° while all other χ angles are 
assigned the default CHARMm values. For each residue, the structures of the 3 
conformational states are optimized using CHARMm, and the atomic coordinates of the conformers are saved.
During the minimization, the framework (backbone), and the side-chain atoms 
of those residues which are not selected are fixed at their 
original position. The side-chain atoms of the residues selected for side-chain 
optimization are not present in this step. 
The optimal χ1 angles and the corresponding ChiFlex scores are saved for each conformation. 
The ChiFlex score is derived from the CHARMm energy of the χ1 conformer, 
normalized by the size of the residue.

* Generate ChiFlex conformers and perform final minimization - 
Multiple conformations of the complete structure are calculated by generating 
all possible combinations of the partial residue structures from the previous step.
During this process, residue conformations with an energy above a threshold value are excluded. 
Only the best scoring variant is used for structures with a degeneration of χ1 angles after the minimization.
Each structure is energy minimized, and then the final structures are ranked by the CHARMm energy.

#### Special Residues

Residues: Alanine, Glycine, Proline, and Cystine in disulfide bridges cannot be selected for conformational sampling.

# Side-Chain Refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_side-chain-refinement.htm

## Side-Chain Refinement

Side-Chain Refinement optimizes the protein side-chain conformation based on
systematic searching of side-chain conformation and CHARMm energy minimization 
using the ChiRotor algorithm [Spassov et al., 2007] .

ChiRotor has following steps:

* Removing side-chain atoms: This step removes all the side-chain atoms from the residues to 
be optimized. The side-chain atoms of those residues which are not chosen for optimization
remain on the structure. This structure becomes the framework for the following steps.

* Side-Chain conformation sampling: This step samples the side-chain conformation of each
residue to be optimized independently. During the sampling, each residue adopts 3 initial
conformations with χ = 60°, -60°, and 180° while other χ angles are at the
values as in the corresponding CHARMm forcefield .rtf files. For each residue, the 3 
conformational states are optimized using CHARMm and the two lowest energy conformers are saved.
During the minimization, the framework, i.e., the backbone as well as the side-chain atoms 
of those residues which are not chosen for optimization are present and fixed at their 
original position. The side-chain atoms of other residues chosen for side-chain 
optimization are not present. This step iterates through all the residues which are selected 
for optimization. At the end of this stage, if N residues are selected for side-chain 
refinement, 2N partial structures will be created each with the fixed part of the structure 
plus the residue to be optimized.

* Assemble and final minimization: The lowest energy conformation of each side-chain 
from step 2 are assembled into the structure framework and energy minimized using CHARMm.
From this minimized structure, starting from N-terminal, the first residue is replaced
by the second lowest energy side-chain conformer from step 2 and energy minimized. If 
the second side-chain conformer has lower energy after minimization, it will replace 
the first one. For some residues with non-symmetric planar end groups, such as Trp, His, Asn, and Gln 
the second cycle includes also an additional rotation corresponding to a change of 
180° of the terminal c angle.
This process enumerates through all the residues and when it completes,
one protein structure with optimized side-chain conformations is generated. All the
energy minimization in this step has flexible side-chains for those residues selected
for optimization, and all backbone atoms and all other side-chains are fixed.

#### Special Residues

Residues Alanine, Glycine, Cystine in disulfide bridges are not subject to side-chain 
refinement and will keep their input conformation.

In the second step of ChiRotor, proline residue is not sampled with 3 χ1 angles, instead, it
is built from the CHARMm template in the forcefield template definition and optimized.

# Statistical scores: E-value

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_statistical-scores-e-value.htm

## Statistical scores: E-value

To assess whether a given alignment between the query sequence and a 
database sequence constitutes evidence for homology, it helps to know 
how strong an alignment can be expected by chance alone. The statistic 
of a local gapless alignment is well understood. For a high scoring segment 
pair (HSP), that is, a gapless alignment segment whose score cannot be 
improved by extension or trimming, it is characterized by two statistical 
parameters, K and lambda . 
Most simply, the expected number of random HSPs (the E-value) with score 
at least S is given by the formula:

Equation 1.

where, m and n are the length of the query sequence and the sum of the lengths of the
database sequences. Score S is the alignment score calculated based on substitution matrix in case of BLAST or PSSM for
PSI-BLAST.

The statistics developed above have a solid theoretical foundation only for 
local alignments that are not permitted to have gaps and the statistical parameters 
can be calculated, using analytic formulas, from the substitution scores and 
the background residue frequencies of the sequences being compared. For gapped 
alignments, there is no analytical solution and these parameters must be estimated 
from a large-scale comparison of "random" sequences. PSI-BLAST uses 
estimates of K and lambda produced by random simulation [Altschul and Gish, 1996] .

# Align Structures (MODELER)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_structure-alignment.htm

## Align Structures (MODELER)

Multiple templates are often used in combination to model a sequence. The SALIGN 
command in MODELER aligns two or more template structures based on their structural 
similarity. This command is a general dynamic programming based alignment procedure 
for aligning sequences, structures or a combination of the two.

In the Align Structures (MODELER) protocol the weight matrix SALIGN uses for dynamic programing 
is a weighed sum of five protein structure and sequence features. The features used are:

* residue type : encoded in a residue type - residue type dissimilarity matrix.

* inter-molecular distance of residues pairs - The weight matrix for this feature is the Euclidean distance between the positions of two residues in the two compared sub-alignments that are already optimally aligned and superposed based on their coordinates alone. The optimal alignment is obtained by an iterative procedure. Distance is measured based on one specified fit_atom (e.g., Cα) per residue.

* fractional sidechain accessibility : The pair-wise residue-residue dissimilarity for this feature is based on classifying residues into the buried, semi-exposed, and exposed classes.

* secondary structure type : the pair-wise residue-residue dissimilarity for this feature is based on classifying residue secondary structure into helix, strand, and other.

* local conformation : the pair-wise residue-residue score is distance RMSD between the selected atoms (fit_atoms) from a window of residues centered on the two matched residues.

In the Align Structures (MODELER) protocol SALIGN is called multiple times. The first SALIGN call gives an initial alignment which is refined in the subsequent calls (this is optional and can be replaced by a user generated alignment). The inter-molecular distance feature (2) has non-zero weight only during the refinement stages as rigid body refinement is done using the alignment in memory.

If multiple structures are aligned a dendrogram of the N proteins in memory is calculated using the selected features. The multiple alignment is then a progression of N-1 pairwise alignments of the growing sub-alignments. A sub-alignment is an alignment of < N proteins.

# Generating models

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_structure-generation-using-modeler.htm

## Generating models

The previous topics give the definition of the PDFs and describe the procedures used to derive basis PDFs 
from a local protein database and to compute the feature PDFs and molecular PDF for a model
protein structure. The objective function ( F ) that is optimized 
by MODELER is the natural logarithm of the molecular PDF .

Equation 1:

Minimizing F corresponds to maximizing P but has advantages in terms of avoiding floating-point overflow issues. The
optimization takes place in two distinct stages. The first is a Cartesian space 
variable target function ( VTF ) conjugate gradient optimization. The
optimum of the MODELER PDF is sought by a series of target functions that eventually 
equals the full molecular PDF. The series starts only with sequentially local
restraints, adding longer range restraints as the calculation proceeds, until all 
restraints are being used and the full molecular PDF is calculated. The optional second
optimization stage consists of a restrained molecular dynamics (MD) simulated annealing 
scheme:

Figure 1: Optimization of the objective function for a linear starting model

Optimization of the objective function (curve) starts with a random or distorted template 
structure. The iteration number is indicated below each sample structure. The first ~2,000 iterations 
correspond to the variable target function method relying on the conjugate gradients technique. This 
approach first satisfies sequentially local restraints and slowly introduces longer range restraints 
until the complete objective function is optimized. In the last 4,750 iterations, molecular
dynamics with simulated annealing is used to refine the model.

The starting conformations used by MODELER are generated by the following scheme:

* First, superimpose all templates on the first 
template using the Cα atoms and the given
alignment. Each atom in the modeled protein, having an equivalent atom in at least one of the
templates, has coordinates that are the mean of the coordinates for the
template atoms. The remaining undefined atoms have their coordinates set by using internal 
coordinates derived from a CHARMm residue topology library.

* Next, a random coordinate shift 
(default between ± 4 Å) is added to each atomic position.
This scheme generates starting models similar to the templates for faster convergence.

# Substitution Matrices

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_substitution-matrices.htm

## Substitution Matrices

Three main series of substitution matrices are available for use with 
the Align123 program (Multiple Sequence Alignment):

* Dayhoff PAM series ( [Dayhoff et al., 1978] and [Jones et al., 1992] )
- based on observed substitution frequencies in a number of protein families. 
Higher PAM matrices are for more distantly related sequences.

* BLOSUM series [Henikoff and Henikoff, 1992] - derived from ungapped alignments with similar sequences clustered. 
Substitution frequencies are calculated for the clusters. 
Lower BLOSUM matrices are for more distantly related sequences.

* Gonnet series 
( [Gonnet et al., 1992] and [Benner et al., 1994] )
- similar to Dayhoff matrices and might be more sensitive to more distantly related sequences.

The default is the BLOSUM series. In each case, there is a choice of matrix, 
ranging from strict ones, useful for comparing closely related sequences to 
'soft' ones that are useful for comparing distantly related sequences. 
Depending on the distance measured from the guide tree between the two sequences 
or groups of sequences to be compared, different matrices from the selected 
series are used.

Table 1. Relationship between sequence distance and substitution matrix used by Align123

| Series class | Sequence identity | Series |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BLOSUM | 80-100 | BLOSUM80 |
| | 60-80 | BLOSUM62 |
| | 30-60 | BLOSUM45 |
| | 0-30 | BLOSUM30 |
| PAM | 80-100 | PAM20 |
| | 60-80 | PAM60 |
| | 40-60 | PAM120 |
| | 0-40 | PAM350 |
| Gonnet | 65-100 | Gonnet40 |
| | 45-65 | Gonnet80 |
| | 35-45 | Gonnet120 |
| | 25-35 | Gonnet160 |
| | 15-25 | Gonnet250 |
| | 0-15 | Gonnet300 |

# Theory - Surface Charge Maps and Viscosity Scores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_surface_charge_maps.htm

## Theory - Surface Charge Maps and Viscosity Scores

Therapeutic proteins, especially antibodies, are used in the treatment of many medical conditions. Highly concentrated solutions are often required in order to deliver a therapeutic dose in a small volume, but such solutions can be difficult to process and hard to inject. Prediction of proteins that are more likely to have lower viscosity can suggest suitable targets for development.

It has been shown that for highly concentrated antibody solutions, electrostatic interactions play an important role in viscosity. 
Negative charge-based descriptors have shown good correlation with viscosity, and a method quantifying these has been developed. See [Agarawal et al., 2016] and references therein. The method involves finding negatively charged surface patches, and summing these for the Fv region of the antibody.

### Calculation of Surface Charge Map scores

The surface charge map score (QMap) of each atom is calculated as:

where j is all the side-chain atoms that belong to an exposed residue and are within distance R= 10 Å of atom i. A residue is considered to be exposed if its solvent accessible surface area, calculated using CHARMm, is at least 10 Å 2 , and the partial charges are those assigned by the CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H forcefield at the formulation pH.

The total negative QMap score for the Fv domain is then calculated as:

where H is the Heaviside function and |.| is the absolute function.

The antibody variable domains are identified by the HMM method used
in the Annotate Antibody Sequences protocol.

Additionally, net molecular Negative QMAP and Positive QMAP scores are calculated for the whole molecule, where the Negative QMAP score is the sum of all negative atomic QMap scores, and the Positive QMap score is the sum of all positive atomic QMap scores.

### Verification against published method

In Discovery Studio , the QMap score calculated uses the same formula as the Surface Charge Map (SCM) 
score in the referenced paper, but with differences in implementation details:

* Discovery Studio method: The solvent surface accessible areas are calculated using CHARMm and atomic charges are assigned using the CHARMm Polar H or CHARMm forcefield.

* Published method: The solvent surface accessible areas are calculated using the VMD package and atomic charges are assigned using the CHARMM22 forcefield.

To verify that the scores obtained using Discovery Studio were consistent with the publication, the structures of a set of 87 IgG1 antibody Fv domains were predicted using the Antibody Modeling Cascade protocol. QMap scores were then calculated using the Calculate Protein Formulation Properties protocol, and SCM scores were calculated using the published method. These scores were found to correlate well; the correlation coefficient between the SCM score and the Negative QMap scores was 0.985.

# Transmembrane Prediction

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_transmembrane-prediction.htm

## Transmembrane Prediction

The Transmembrane Prediction tool scans one or more input protein sequences
for likely transmembrane helices. The approach is based on the approach by [Sonnhammer et al., 1998] .
It uses a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that has been trained on a set of membrane proteins with
helical membrane spanning regions.

The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) architecture used in Transmembrane Prediction 
is made up of 7 types of states corresponding to the core of the transmembrane helix, 
helix caps, cytoplasmic loops, short and long cytoplasmic loop states, and globular domains 
that are part of each loop.

The states have a close relationship with the biology of membrane proteins; loop 
states connect to other loops through a helix cap, helix core, and another helix
cap. These states correspond to one of three different labels, Inside (cytoplasmic), 
Helix (membrane spanning helix), and Outside (non-cytoplasmic).

The prediction of transmembrane helices is done by finding an optimal alignment 
of the sequence with the model using the N-Best algorithm. In the N-Best algorithm, 
the algorithm uses the model architecture to find the best labeling of the sequence 
given the model.

The calculation of the probabilities is based upon the forward-backward algorithm, in 
which the method finds the probability of each labeling (Inside, Outside, or Helix)
summed over all the possible alignments of the sequence to the model. Because these 
values are based on all possible alignments of the model instead of a single optimal 
alignment. Occasionally the raw probabilities will contradict the final labeling.

# Turning hits into HSPs

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prmo_the_turning-hits-into-hsps.htm

## Turning hits into HSPs

The central idea of the BLAST algorithm is that any statistically significant 
alignment between two sequences is likely to contain a high-scoring pair of 
aligned words. A word is a short sequence segment of specified length (usually 
three words for protein sequences). BLAST begins its comparison of a query sequence 
to a database by scanning the database for words that score at least the threshold 
score T when aligned with some word 
within the query sequence. Any word pair satisfying this condition is called 
a hit. The diagonal of a hit involving words starting at positions ( x, 
y ) of the database and query sequences is defined as x-y . 
The distance between two hits on the same diagonal is defined as the difference 
between their first coordinates.

Once a hit is identified, BLAST determines whether the hit lies within an 
alignment having an aggregate score high enough to be reported. It does this by extending the hit
in both directions until the running alignment score for that diagonal has dropped more than some 
quantity X below the maximum score so far 
attained. This extension step is quite costly, 
consuming around 90% of BLAST's execution 
time under most circumstances.

To reduce the number of extensions it has to perform, BLAST takes advantage 
of the fact that an interesting HSP is typically much longer than a single hit. 
In fact, it is likely to contain multiple hits on the same diagonal within a 
relatively short distance of one another. Therefore, BLAST chooses a length A and invokes an ungapped extension if (and only 
if) two non-overlapping hits are found on the same diagonal within distance A of one another (any hit that overlaps the most 
recent one is ignored).

#### Specifying the word size

BLAST and PSI-BLAST use a word size of 3 for proteins, which is appropriate 
for a wide range of searches. You can adjust the word size to 2 to increase sensitivity, at the price of speed.

BLAST theory

# Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_adpt.htm

## Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools

The Dock and Analyze Docked Protein Complexes tools allow you to display and analyze a
set of docked protein poses as generated by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol. It also allows the analysis of interactions at a protein-protein interface.
The tools are organized into Dock Proteins, Browse Poses, Calculate Ligand Interface RMSD, Refine Poses, and Analyze Interaction groups. For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools .

### Dock Proteins

Dock Proteins (ZDOCK): Opens the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol dialog. This protocol performs rigid body docking of two protein structures
using the ZDOCK algorithm [Chen and Weng, 2002] and clusters the poses according to the ligand position.

Process Poses (ZDOCK): Opens the Process Poses (ZDOCK) protocol dialog. This protocol allows selection of a subset from
a set of docked protein poses generated by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)
protocol, either according to pose rank or by specifying residues on the docking
interface.

### Browse Poses

The tools in the Browse Poses group allow you to display and navigate through the full ligand molecule of different docked poses.

Use Browse to choose the set of poses to be browsed with the Next and Previous buttons in the group.
The following options are available:

* Top Cluster Poses: Browse a set of Top Cluster Poses (best ranked pose of each cluster).

* Top Poses in Largest Clusters: Browse the top 100 poses belonging to the 10 largest clusters.

* Poses in a Cluster: Browse all poses belonging to a given cluster.

* All Poses: Browse all poses in the current window.

* Selected Poses: Browse selected poses. The browse set consists of the poses selected at the time the command is applied. The browse set is not dynamically updated to reflect changes in the selection during browsing. To change the browse set to a new selection, the command needs to be reapplied. If no poses are selected, this option defaults to all visible poses.

Top poses are determined by the scoring function used in the protocols. ZDock score is used by default, but you can set this to ZRank score when running the protocol.

Show/Hide Pose Dots: Toggles the display of the dot representations of the docked poses. The dot representing a docked pose is displayed as a sphere at the center of the binding interface between receptor and ligand.

Show Pose Dots on Receptor/Ligand: Toggles the view between receptor-centric (default) and ligand-centric view.

* The receptor centric view assumes that the docked complexes for all poses are superimposed such that the receptor structures overlap. The locations of the dots indicate the center of the binding interface on the receptor structure for each pose.

* The ligand-centric view assumes that the docked complexes for all poses are superimposed such that the ligand structures overlap. The locations of the dots indicate the center of the binding interface on the ligand structure for each pose.

Most commands in the tool panel can only be applied in the receptor centric view.

Show First Docked Complex: Displays the full ligand molecule of top ranked pose (according to ZRank or ZDock) in the current browse set, which is determined by the Browse list. The ligand structure for the pose will be labeled as Pose<N>_Cluster<M>_<ligand name> , where N is the pose number and M is the cluster number. The pose currently shown as full ligand molecule is considered the "Active Pose".

Show Previous Docked Complex: Iterates through the current browse set and displays them as full ligand molecules in order of decreasing pose rank (ZRank or ZDock). The pose ranked immediately ahead of the current Active Pose in the Browse Set will become the new Active Pose.

Show Next Docked Complex: Iterates through the current browse set and displays them as full ligand molecules in order of increasing pose rank (ZRank or ZDock). The pose ranked immediately after the current Active Pose in the Browse Set will become the new Active Pose.

Show Last Docked Complex: Jumps to the lowest ranked pose (according to ZRank or ZDock) in the current browse set and displays the corresponding full ligand molecule. This pose will become the new Active Pose.

Lock Visibility: Locks the visibility of the full ligand molecule for the Active Pose. After using this command, the full ligand molecule of the current Active Pose will remain visible along with the new Active Pose when Show Best , Next , or Previous is clicked.

Reset Visibility: Removes any full ligand structures generated by the other commands in the group.

### Calculate Ligand Interface RMSD

The tools in the RMSD group are used to calculate the RMSD between different 
docked poses or between docked poses and an experimental complex structure.

The RMSD calculation can only be applied to an experimental complex if it consists of receptor and ligand chains that have the exact same set of atoms as the receptor and ligand structures used in the ZDock calculation.

Before calculating the RMSD, follow these steps to superimpose the complex onto the receptor:

* Insert into the ZDOCK results window.

* Remove any moeties that are not present in the ZDOCK receptor and ligand structures.

* Select the complex and the receptor molecule.

* Show both of their sequences and ensure the receptor region is aligned.

* Use the Superimpose Proteins tools to superimpose by sequence alignment, ensuring the receptor molecule is set as the Reference Protein.

Define Ligand: Specifies the ligand to be used as reference for RMSD calculations.
By default, the ligand of the Active Pose is selected. 
To specify a pose that has been saved as a ligand structure using the Lock Visibility tool, select the ligand structure before using this command. To apply the
command to an experimental structure for which both receptor and ligand chains are part of the same molecule (e.g., an X-ray structure of a docked complex), select its ligand chains first.
The name of the specified pose (or molecule if using an experimental structure) is listed next to the button.

Select Binding Interface: Selects the residues 
at the binding interface between currently specified reference ligand and the corresponding receptor structure. 
The binding interface for the ligand is defined as any residue of the 
ligand that has any atom within a cutoff distance to a receptor atom. 
Similarly, the binding interface for the receptor is defined as any 
residue of the receptor that has any atom within a cutoff distance 
of a ligand atom. The cutoff distance can be defined on the Protein Docking page of the Edit | Preferences dialog. 
The tool can be used on the fully displayed structure of a 
docked protein pose and X-ray structures.

Calculate binding Site RMSD: Calculates 
the RMSD of the ligand binding site residues of the docked poses 
with respect to the specified reference ligand listed next to the Define Ligand button. The RMSD values are added as a property in the Protein Pose tab of the Data Table View.

There may be very slight differences in the atomic coordinates of a ligand pose when it is generated to display in the client, compared to the coordinates originally generated in the protocol. As the binding interface selection is per-residue and based on at least one atom of the residue being within the cutoff, this slight coordinate variation could cause an atom to fall either side of the cutoff and the binding interface may correspondingly change by a whole residue. This, in turn, can cause the binding site RMSDs for that pose to differ from those originally used to cluster the poses.

### Refine Poses

Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK): Opens the Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK) protocol dialog. This protocol optimizes and scores sets of docked protein poses generated by
the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol.

### Analyze Interaction

Analyze Protein Interface: Opens the Analyze Protein Interface protocol dialog. This protocol identifies the binding interface between two protein domains and calculates the interactions between them.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Analyze Docked Proteins |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Macromolecules \| Analyze Docked Proteins |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Analyze Docked Proteins |

Source type: HTML

## How to use the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools

The Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tool panel in the Macromolecules tool set allows you to dock proteins with the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol and display, further analyze, and refine the set of docked protein poses generated by the protocol. This topic covers the following tasks:

* Display and navigate through docked protein poses

* Select the binding interface of a protein pose

* Select the binding interface of an X-ray structure

* Calculate the RMSD of docked protein poses

* Analyze clustering information

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes .

Most of the tools in the Analyze Docked 
Proteins tool panel are designed to work with results generated by the protein 
docking protocols (the exception being the Dock 
Proteins (ZDOCK) , which will run the docking protocol). 
The tools are disabled unless a set of docked protein poses is present in 
the current window. Also note that 
in order for the tools to work, the parent ligand and receptor 
structures used to generate the docked poses must be present in the current 
window. The structures are automatically loaded in the result .dsv files 
and they should not be deleted from the window.

To display and navigate through docked protein poses

* Open the .dsv file containing a set of docked protein poses 
(e.g., from a Dock 
Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol run).

* In the Browse Poses group of the tools panel, specify the set of poses that you want to analyze
in more detail (Browse Set) using the Browse list.

* Click First in the Browse Poses to display the full structure of the best ranked pose among the selected set.
Poses are ranked by ranked by ZDock score unless you chose the option to order by ZRank score when running the docking protocol. 
The full receptor and ligand structures appear on the Hierarchy View , 
labeled Pose<N>_Cluster<M> followed by the molecule 
name, where N is the rank of the pose and M the number of the cluster to which the pose belongs.

* Use Next and Previous to cycle through 
the other poses in the Browse Set in order of decreasing or increasing 
pose rank.

To select the binding interface of a protein pose

The binding interface for the ligand is defined as any residue 
of the ligand that has any atom within a cutoff distance to a receptor atom. 
Similarly, the binding interface for the receptor is defined as any 
residue of the receptor that has any atom within a cutoff distance to a ligand 
atom. The cutoff distance is defined in the Protein Docking page of the Preferences dialog.

* If not already shown as a full structure, use the tool in the Browse Poses group as described in the previous section
to display the full structure pose for which you wish to select the binding interface.

* If not already listed as the reference ligand (next to the Define Ligand button in the Calculate Ligand 
Interface RMSD group), select the ligand molecule of the pose and click Define Ligand to specify it as 
reference ligand.

* Click Select Binding Interface to select the
residues in the binding interface for further analysis. The
selected residues are highlighted in yellow in the Molecule Window .

To select the binding interface of an X-ray structure

* Load the X-ray structure of the docked complex into the Molecule Window . Both the receptor and 
ligand must belong to a single molecule (i.e., separate chains of the same parent).

* Select the chains of the structure that correspond to the 
ligand portion of the complex from the Hierarchy View . 
The unselected parts of the molecule will be considered as 
the receptor. This also includes small molecule ligands or water molecules. 
It is recommended that you delete them from the structure first.

* Click Define Ligand to 
specify the selected chains as the ligand chains of the docked complex.

* Click Select Binding Interface to select the 
residues in the binding interface for further analysis.

To calculate the RMSD of docked protein poses

* Open the .dsv file containing a set of docked protein poses (e.g., from a Dock 
Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol run).

* If not already listed as the reference ligand (next to the Define Ligand button in the Calculate Ligand 
Interface RMSD group), select the ligand molecule of the pose and click Define Ligand to specify it as 
the reference ligand for the RMSD calculation.

* Click Calculate Binding Site RMSD . This adds a column named RMSD to <name of reference structure> POSE_RMSD_REFERENCE containing the RMSD values in the Data Table View under 
the ProteinPose tab.

In the case of an 
X-ray structure, there must be a one-to-one correspondence between the atoms in 
the X-ray structure and the atoms in the docked protein poses for the 
RMSD calculation to succeed. If this is not case, try cleaning the structures 
using the Prepare Protein tools using the same method used to prepare the structures for the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol.

To analyze clustering information

* The Hierarchy View contains clusters of docked protein poses under the group Clusters . Details of the clustering method can be found in Clustering 
and analysis of docked protein poses .

* Select Top Cluster Poses in the Browse drop down of the Browse Poses group to display only the dot representations of the best ranked pose of each cluster.

* Select Poses in a Cluster in the Browse list to display only the dot representations of poses belonging to the same cluster as the active pose.

* Select All Poses in the Browse list to display the dot representations for all poses.

* Click Show/Hide Pose Dots to show or hide the dot representations of poses in the selected Browse Set.

# Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_aggr.htm

## Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools

The Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools allow you to predict properties important to the formulation of protein therapeutics including solubility, viscosity and tendency to aggregate. They also allows you to view sites on the surface where proteins may aggregate, which may be targets for mutation studies.

Before running these tools, type the molecules using a forcefield from the Change Forcefield tool panel. 
In general, the CHARMm Polar H and charmm36 forcefields are suitable for standard protein systems,
and the former is preferred for calculation speed.
Choose CHARMm forcefield when nonstandard amino acids or ligands exist in the molecular system and cannot be typed by CHARMm Polar H or charmm36 forcefields. Refer to the help for the individual tools for more information about allowed forcefields. Also, see Supported forcefields .

Calculate Protein Formulation Properties: Opens the Calculate Protein Formulation Properties protocol dialog. 
This protocol calculates, for one or more protein molecules:

* Solubility Scores using a combination of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions.

* Viscosity Scores using the surface charge map method.

* Developability Indices (DI) based on the tendency to aggregate via hydrophobic interactions.

Predict Excipient Interactions: Opens the Predict Excipient Interactions protocol dialog. This protocol calculates predicts preferential antibody interactions with a range of common excipients using a machine learning method. Interactions with excipients can affect formulation properties including aggregation and viscosity.

Calculate Aggregation Scores: Opens the Calculate Aggregation Scores protocol dialog. This protocol calculates the Protein Aggregation Propensity on the input structure at one or more radii.

### View Aggregation Sites

After performing the calculation, the structure is updated with the calculated protein aggregation propensity scores for the specified radii, which are added as atom and residue properties to each amino acid. The properties are labeled Aggr R5 etc. for each radius value. Aggregation sites are defined as groups containing adjacent non-buried residues with positive residue aggregation propensity scores for each radius. Structures showing aggregation surfaces opened from the Calculate Protein Formulation Properties report can be used in the same way.

You can view these groups in the Hierarchy View under the Aggregation Sites node. A solvent accessible surface is created covering all non-solvent residues and colored according to the atom aggregation propensity score at the largest cutoff radius used. Residues with high aggregation propensity scores are colored red, through blue for lower scores. Additionally, a line plot of residue index versus aggregation (Aggr) propensity score and point plot of site ID versus aggregation (Aggr) propensity score are created. The latter allows visualization of the scores of the residues contributing to each site.

The tools in the View Aggregation Sites group allow you to display the surface and plots for any of the radii used in the calculation, and to view the aggregation sites. Please note that the specialized coloring requires the radius and site information and is therefore only supported by these tools. If the coloring of the atoms or surface is changed by other means, the Reset Display tool can be used to restore the aggregation coloring.

Define Protein: Defines the selected protein for which to display the aggregation propensity scores.
The first visible protein in the Molecule Window that has aggregation propensity score is used by default.

View at Cutoff Radius: Lists the cutoff radius values used in the protein aggregation calculation. Choosing a different radius will recolor the molecule and surface according to the aggregation propensity scores for that radius and update the plots. A large radius helps identify aggregation-prone regions, while a small radius allows the identification of residues that may be targeted for mutation to increase protein stability.

Show First Aggregation Site: Rotates the structure to the first defined aggregation site for the selected radius, selects and colors it, and leaves the remaining structure and surface colored light green.

Show Previous Aggregation Site: Displays the previous aggregation site as described for the first site.

Show Next Aggregation Site: Displays the next aggregation site as described for the first site.

Show Last Aggregation Site: Displays the last aggregation site as described for the first site.

Show/Hide Details of Site: Displays or hides the current site number, its total aggregation propensity score, and its constituent residues in descending score order. It also selects or deselects the currently viewed aggregation site.

Show/Hide Surface: Toggles the display of the surface for the defined protein. If the surface does not exist it will be recreated.

Reset Display: Recolors all of the structure and surface with the aggregation propensity scores for the current radius.

# Basics of protein structures

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_bldedit_th_basics-of-protein-structures.htm

## Basics of protein structures

Proteins are either linear polymers or aggregates of linear polymers. The building blocks of proteins are amino acids (or residues ). 
Of the 80 or so amino acids found in nature, 20 are the most commonly used in proteins.
Amino acids are generally specified by using a three-letter code or a single-letter code . In the following illustrations, the backbone atoms are colored green:

| Alanine (Ala, A) | Arginine (Arg, R) | Asparagine (Asn, N) | Aspartic Acid (Asp, D) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cysteine (Cys, C) | Glutamine (Gln, Q) | Glutamic Acid (Glu, E) | Glycine (Gly, G) |
| Histidine (His, H) | Isoleucine (Ile, I) | Leucine (Leu, L) | Lysine (Lys, K) |
| Methionine (Met, M) | Phenylalanine (Phe, F) | Proline (Pro, P) | Serine (Ser, S) |
| Threonine (Thr, T) | Tryptophan (Trp, W) | Tyrosine (Tyr, Y) | Valine (Val, V) |

The standard amino acids (with the exception of achiral Glycine) are all in the L isomeric configuration. For information on D-amino acids, see Theory - Build and Edit Protein tools .

In addition to the 20 standard amino acids, several nonstandard amino acids are supported including MethylAlanine[AminobutyricAcid] (Aib),
SelenoMethionine (Mse), SelenoCysteine (Cse), Ornithine (Orn), PhosphoTyrosine (Ptr), PhosphoSerine (Sep), PhosphoThreonine (Tpo), 
Pyroglutamate (Pca), and SulfoTyrosine (Tys). Additional nonstandard amino acids can also be defined.

In proteins and polypeptides, amino acid monomers are joined by peptide bonds, -CO-NH. The peptide bond is almost planar and, in most cases, assumes 
a trans conformation, with the sole exception of proline, which has a high probability of assuming a cis conformation.

The atoms -NH-C α -CO- that traverse the length of the polypeptide chain are referred to as backbone or main-chain atoms, while atoms 
attached to the backbone through the C α are known as side-chain atoms.

The backbone torsion angles around the N-C α and C α -C bonds are denoted φ and ψ respectively. These bonds are subject to 
relatively free rotation (with three major rotameric states), and are important descriptors of the local protein backbone conformation. The preferred 
φ and ψ angles of amino acids in a protein or peptide can be viewed on a Ramachandran plot .

# Hierarchy of protein structure

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_bldedit_th_hierarchy-of-protein-structure.htm

## Hierarchy of protein structure

The primary structure of the protein is the sequence of amino acids involved in protein chain formation. The secondary
structure of the protein refers to the conformation of the peptide chain.

There exist stable conformations of the polypeptide chain in which the backbone dihedral angles are locally repeating. Common examples are 
α -helices and β -strands . An α-helix is an element of secondary 
structure adopting a right-handed helical conformation with approximately 3.6 residues per turn. There is a repeating pattern of hydrogen 
bonds from the carbonyl oxygen of residue i to the amide hydrogen of residue i +4. Less common are 3 10 helices, slender versions of α-helices with three residues per turn. In a β-strand,
in turn, the amino acid backbone adopts an extended rather than helical conformation.

Several β-strands can align in either parallel or anti-parallel arrangements in which hydrogen bonds are formed between the CO oxygen of
one strand and the NH hydrogen of another strand. These sets of strands are then said to form a β -sheet .

Secondary structure elements classes have a lot of characteristic properties: for example, helices have certain preferences for amino acid location, especially
pronounced for helix capping residues. β-strands also have a set of preferential residues that favor β-sheet
formation. Perfect, text book helices and strands rarely occur in proteins; for example α-helices are often curved or bent and are more like
3 10 helices at termini. α-sheets exhibit right handed twists and may contain 
β-bulges. Altogether, secondary structures in proteins are closely packed and there are a number of secondary structure packing motifs called supersecondary structures.

The tertiary structure of a protein is synonymous with the 3D structure of a single peptide chain, where mutual orientation of all secondary
structure elements connected with loops is specified. A number of distinctive protein folds has been identified so far. They are generally classified as
α, β, α/β and α+β.

The quaternary structure describes the manner in which two or more polypeptide chains of the same or distinctive folds are combined together to form a larger system.

# Build and Edit Protein tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_bldt.htm

## Build and Edit Protein tools

The Build and Edit Protein tools allow you to quickly build and modify peptides and proteins. The following tasks are supported:

* Creating a new peptide chain or append to the end of a chain

* Inserting residues between two residues or after a selected residue in an existing structure

* Inserting a loop into a gap

* Mutating residues

* Changing the conformation of an existing chain

* Converting amino acids between L and D isomers

* Adding or removing capping groups

* Defining a nonstandard amino acid residue

* Creating a molecule from a protein sequence

For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Build and Edit Protein tools .

Build Action: Allows you to choose the method for building an amino acid chain:

* Create/Grow Chain: Create a new amino acid chain or add an amino acid to the C-terminus of an existing chain.

* Insert: Insert one or more amino acids into an amino acid chain. If the N-terminal residue is selected, the insertion will precede it. For other single selections, the insertion will be after the residue. If two adjacent bonded residues are selected, the new residues will be inserted between the selected residues. If they are not bonded, 
the loop is inserted to close the gap in the chain. The missing region is built by iteratively sampling closed loop conformations using the random tweak algorithm [Shenkin et al., 1987] to find a conformation with no bumps or minimum bumps with the rest of the protein.

* Mutate: Mutate one or more selected residues to a specific residue type.

Conformation: Allows you to select the geometry for the growing protein molecule, for non-rigid insertions, and for use with the Apply Conformation and Create Structure from Sequence tools. The following conformations are available:

* Right-hand Alpha Helix

* Left-hand Alpha Helix

* 3-10 Helix

* Pi Helix

* Beta Strand

* Extended

* Specify...

Apply Conformation: Applies the selected conformation to selected amino acids in the active peptide.

### Choose Amino Acid

There are buttons for adding 27 common amino acids to peptides. To specify a nonstandard amino acid, or a sequence of amino acids, click Specify... .

### Modify Structure

L/D Conversion: If specific amino acid residues or Cα atoms have been selected, these will be converted from L to D or vice versa. In most cases, the main-chain conformation will be unaffected, however note that in the case of cyclic peptides such as proline the main-chain conformation has to be altered to accommodate the other isomer. If a whole molecule that contains amino acid residues has been selected, the entire structure will be inverted thus converting all L amino acids to the D form or vice versa, and inverting the conformation so the handedness of helices switches. Any non-protein entities, such as ligands, which are included in the molecule will also be inverted. In either case the amino acid names and types will be adjusted as appropriate to the isomer. Refer to Theory - Build and Edit Protein tools for details.

Cap Termini: Opens the Add or Remove Capping Groups dialog , which allows you to cap all or selected termini.

### Advanced

Define Amino Acid: Opens the Define Amino Acid Template dialog , which allows you to define a template for a nonstandard amino acid.

Create Structure from Sequence: Generates a peptide molecule in the specified conformation in a new Molecule Window using a selected sequence in an active Sequence Window.

# How to use the Build and Edit Protein tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_bldt_hw.htm

## How to use the Build and Edit Protein tools

The Build and Edit Protein tools panel provides a suite of tools for building and modifying protein structures. This topic covers the following tasks:

* Build a peptide

* Append to the C terminus of an existing protein chain

* Insert amino acids before the N-terminus of an existing protein chain

* Insert amino acids into the middle of an existing protein chain

* Insert a loop into a gap in an existing protein chain

* Mutate a residue to a different type

* Alter the backbone conformation of part of a protein structure

* Convert specific amino acids between L and D isomer

* Switch handedness of an entire protein

* Add or removing capping groups on terminal residues

* Define a nonstandard amino acid template

* Build a protein molecule from a sequence

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Build and Edit Protein .

To build a peptide

* Choose Edit | Preferences... from the menu bar to open Preferences dialog and set the preferences on the Protein Utilities page preferences as desired.

* Choose File | New | Molecule Window from the menu bar to open a new Molecule Window.

* In the Tools Explorer, set Build Action to Create/Grow Chain .

* Set the desired backbone conformation in Conformation (the default is Extended ).

* From the Choose Amino Acid tool group, click single amino acids to begin adding them, or click Specify to open the Enter an Amino Acid Sequence dialog , which allows you to specify a sequence of standard or nonstandard amino acids.

To append to the C terminus of an existing protein chain

* Select an atom from the protein chain that you want to append.

* Open a Molecule Window with the protein into which you want to insert amino acids.

* Select the N-terminal residue.

* From the Tools Explorer, set Build Action to Insert .

* In the Choose Amino Acid tool group, click a single amino acid, or Specify to open the Enter an Amino Acid Sequence dialog , which allows you to specify a sequence of standard or nonstandard amino acids.

* Select the pair of bonded residues between which the insertion is to be made, or select a single residue other than the N-terminus.

* To show the gaps and find missing residue sequences, use the Protein Report command, which is available on both the Prepare Protein tools panel and the Protein Report and Analysis tools panel.

* Select the pair of residues before and after the gap.

* From the Choose Amino Acid tool group, click Specify... to open the Enter an Amino Acid Sequence dialog , which allows you to specify a sequence of standard or nonstandard amino acids. If the Gap Suggestion option appears in the dialog, click it to view the suggested sequence for insertion. This suggested sequence is obtained automatically from mmCIF files, or by comparing the ATOM record and SEQRES record in a PDB file by running Protein Report . It indicates the missing residues in the structure at the insertion point.

Insert Loop will not change the conformation of the existing part of the protein, and the loop conformation is created using the random tweak algorithm. Alternatively, you can insert a loop with a specific conformation using the Insert command with just the residue before the gap selected, but the conformation of the existing protein will be modified.

To mutate one or more residues to a different type

* From the Molecule Window, select one or more residues that you want to mutate.

* From the Tools Explorer, set Build Action to Mutate .

* In the Choose Amino Acid tool group, click a single amino acid, or Specify to open the Enter One Residue dialog , which allows you to specify a sequence of standard or nonstandard amino acids.

To alter the backbone conformation of part of a protein structure

* From the Molecule Window, select a contiguous range of residues for which you want to alter the backbone conformation.

* From the Tools Explorer, select a backbone conformation in Conformation (the default is Extended ).

* Click Apply Conformation .

To convert specific amino acids between L and D isomer

* Select the amino acids to be converted.

* Click on the L/D Conversion tool

To switch the handedness of an entire protein

* Select the protein molecule to be converted.

To add or remove capping groups on terminal residues

* From the Molecule Window, select at least one atom from each of the residues that you want to add capping groups to or remove them from. If nothing is selected, all residues are affected.

* From the Tools Explorer, click Caps... in the Modify Termini tool group to open the Add or Remove Capping Groups dialog .

* Choose whether to add caps to the N or C termini or remove them. If adding, select a capping group from the appropriate list. Note that if a terminus already has a capping group, it will be replaced with a new group.

* Click OK .

To define a nonstandard amino acid template

* Build the desired nonstandard amino acid. The easiest method is to create the most similar existing amino acid using Build and Edit Protein and then modify it using any of the chemistry editing and sketching tools.

* Check that nomenclature conforms as much as possible to normal conventions. Side-chain
atom names should employ the remoteness codes that are a transliteration of the Greek alphabet (ABGDEZHQIK).

* Ensure that bond orders and formal charges are correct.

* Click Define Amino Acid... to open the Define Amino Acid Template dialog.

* In the dialog, select an existing User template library , or type a name to add a new template library.

* Specify a Template name .

* Specify a unique Residue name , and then click OK .

The application will check that the residue name is not a duplicate of any standard or existing nonstandard amino acid name. The
template will then be created from the input structure and be available for use in Build and Edit Protein tools through
the Specify... tool.

To build a protein molecule from a sequence

* Open or create a sequence in a Protein Sequence Window.

* Click Create Structure from Sequence to build the peptide in a new Molecule Window.
