# Theory - Build and Edit Protein tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_bldt_th.htm

## Theory - Build and Edit Protein tools

The following topics describe the basics of protein chemistry. If you are familiar with proteins, their sequences, 
and their hierarchy of structures, then you can skip these topics.

* Basics of protein structures

* Hierarchy of protein structure

### Backbone conformations

Build and Edit Proteins supports a number of common backbone conformations, which are defined by the following pairs 
of phi and psi angles:

| Name | Phi | Psi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Right-hand Alpha Helix | -57 | -47 |
| Left-hand Alpha Helix | 57 | 47 |
| 3-10 Helix | -74 | -4 |
| Pi Helix | -53 | -70 |
| Beta Strand | -120 | 120 |
| Extended | -180 | -180 |

### D-Amino acid nomenclature

Build and Edit Proteins supports conversion between the L and D isomeric forms of amino acids. The D-amino acids are named according to PDB nomenclature:

| Name | PDB Name | Abbreviation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D-Alanine | DAL | Dal |
| D-Arginine | DAR | Dar |
| D-Asparagine | DSG | Dsg |
| D-AsparticAcid | DAS | Das |
| D-Cysteine | DCY | Dcy |
| D-Glutamine | DGN | Dgn |
| D-GlutamicAcid | DGL | Dgl |
| D-Histidine | DHI | Dhi |
| D-Isoleucine | DIL | Dil |
| D-Leucine | DLE | Dle |
| D-Lysine | DLY | Dly |
| D-Methionine | MED | Med |
| D-Phenylalanine | DPN | Dpn |
| D-Proline | DPR | Dpr |
| D-Serine | DSN | Dsn |
| D-Threonine | DTH | Dth |
| D-Tryptophan | DTR | Dtr |
| D-Tyrosine | DTY | Dty |
| D-Valine | DVA | Dva |

The single letter symbol is the same as for the L isomer.

Among the 20 standard amino acids, the C-beta atom of isoleucine and threonine is asymmetric. For isoleucine, 
L-isomer is (2S,3S) and D-isomer is (2R,3R). For threonine, L-isomer is (2S,3R) and D-isomer is (2R,3S).

# Create Homology Models tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_cmh.htm

## Create Homology Models tools

The Create Homology Models tool panel in the Macromolecules tool set enable you to create protein homology models from sequences of
interest.

### Searching for template structures

Before using these tools to creating a homology model from a protein sequence, you must identify homologous proteins with known 3-dimensional structures. You can use BLAST searching to identify homologous template structures and open them in Discovery Studio .

* From a Protein Sequence Window, select a protein sequence to search against.

* Use the Search Sequences by Similarity tools and click BLAST Search to open the BLAST Search protocol dialog. This protocol takes the selected sequence and searches against a 
PDB_nr95 database.

* In the Blast Result Window, select the hits you want to view, right-click and select Load Selected Structures to open them in a Molecule Window.

### Align Sequence Templates

Align Sequence to Templates: Align Sequence to Templates protocol dialog. This protocol aligns the query sequence with the template structures opened in the Molecule Window. It will prompt
you for several parameters:

* Input Model Sequence: Specifies the model sequence.

* Input Template Structures: Specifies one or more template structures.

* Create Sequence Profile: Controls whether additional homologous sequences
will be identified and used to assist the alignment between the model sequence and the template sequences. The
default value is True , which should be used in most cases. If the
model sequence is highly homologous to the template structures (i.e., sequence identity between the model and the
templates are larger than 60%), this parameter can be set to False to save computation time.

When the run finishes, the alignment of the model and template sequences open in a new Sequence Window and the
existing template structures are superimposed based on the sequence alignment.

### Build Model

Build Homology Models: Opens the Build Homology Models protocol dialog. This protocol will build 3D structures of the
model sequence based on sequence alignment created during the previous steps.

### Verify Models

This final step is optional.

Verify-Protein (MODELER): Opens the Verify-Protein (MODELER) protocol dialog. This protocol uses the MODELER Discrete Optimized Protein Energy (DOPE) method to calculate a DOPE score for each structure.

Verify-Protein (Profiles-3D): Opens the Verify-Protein (Profiles-3D) protocol dialog. This protocol evaluates the
quality of the model structures.

# Design Protein tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_dpm.htm

## Design Protein tools

The Design Protein tools allow you to:

* Predict sites for potential mutation of a pair of residues to form a disulfide bridge

* Predict model structures for a mutated protein from the original structure

* Calculate the energy effect of mutation for protein stability and protein binding affinity

* Calculate the pH dependent energy to predict the optimal solution pH for a protein

To calculate properties important to the formulation of biologics, and to predict and view sites on the surface where proteins may aggregate, which may be targets for mutation studies, see Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools .

### Predict and Create Disulfide Bridges

Predict Disulfide Bridges: Finds pairs of residues, which if mutated to cysteine, could form disulfide bridges with reasonable geometry. These sites are listed in tables together with data that allows you to assess whether the mutation is likely to be stabilizing. The residue pairs are listed in the Predicted Disulfide Bridge Residues assembly, and the predicted sites are listed in Predicted Disulfide Bridge Sites . Predict Disulfide Bridges acts on all or selected residues.

Define Protein: Defines the protein containing predicted disulfide sites to browse.

Show First Predicted Site: Selects the first predicted site and zooms in on it.

Show Previous Predicted Site: Displays the previous predicted site as described for the first site.

Show Next Predicted Site: Displays the next predicted site as described for the first site.

Show Last Predicted Site: Displays the last predicted site as described for the first site.

Create Disulfide Bridge: Creates a disulfide bridge for each selected predicted disulfide bridge site.

Clear Prediction: Clears groups and objects created by the prediction.

For more information, see Theory - Predict Disulfide Bridges .

The following tools, except Build Mutants , require a forcefield typed molecule. Before running these tools, choose the desired forcefield from Change Forcefield tool panel. In general, the CHARMm Polar H forcefield is suitable for standard protein systems or CHARMm if nonstandard amino acids or ligands are present. Refer to the help for the individual tools for more information about allowed forcefields.

### Mutate Protein

Build Mutants: Opens the Build Mutants protocol dialog. This protocol mutates a set of residues to the specified amino acid types. One or more model structures of the mutated protein will be created based on the original protein structure.

Side-Chain Refinement: Opens the Side-Chain Refinement protocol dialog. This protocol optimizes the side-chain conformation of selected or all residues in a protein structure using the ChiRotor algorithm. To create mutations manually, use the Build and Edit Protein tools to mutate the residue and then use this tool to optimize the side-chain conformation of those mutated residues. It is also possible to manually set the side-chain conformation of the mutated residues based on rotamer library using the Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools .

### Mutation Energy

Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding): Opens the Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) protocol dialog. This protocol calculates the free energy difference of the binding of two molecular partners due to a single point mutation of selected residues.

This method can scan each residue in a protein complex using any specified amino acid type. You can perform the commonly known virtual alanine scanning by mutating each residue in the protein to alanine. It can also mutate any selected residue to any of the 20 amino acid types for saturation mutagenesis. The free energy difference for each single point mutation is added to the amino acid of the input protein and the experimental report summarizes the mutation with the lowest and highest energies.

It is designed to predict binding energy changes for protein-protein binding, but can be used for protein-ligand binding as well. Additionally, this protocol can calculate the binding free energy differences as a function of solution pH.

Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability): Opens the Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) protocol dialog. This protocol evaluates the effect of single-point mutations on protein stability. It performs amino-acid scanning mutagenesis on a set of selected amino-acid residues by mutating each of them to one or more specified amino-acid types.

### pH Dependent Energy

Calculate pH Dependent Energy: Opens the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol dialog. This protocol predicts the protonation state of titratable residues in a protein structure and calculates the electrostatic contribution to the free energy of folding as a function of pH. The free energy can be used to estimate the protein stability in different solution pHs.

# Model Antibody tools

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_mam.htm

## Model Antibody tools

The Model Antibody tools allow you to annotate antibody sequences, create homology models for antibodies, and
refine CDR loops.

### Annotate Antibody

Annotate Antibody Sequence: Opens the Annotate Antibody Sequence protocol dialog. This protocol identifies antibody domains and complementary determining loop regions (CDR loops)in the amino acid sequence of an antibody and displays the annotation in a Sequence Annotation window.

Predict Antibody Paratopes: Opens the Predict Antibody Paratopes protocol dialog. This protocol predicts the antibody paratope in the antibody complementary determining regions (CDR) using Paragraph algorithm.

### Build Antibody Fab Regions

The tools in this group allow you to identify templates and build homology models of Fv or Fab domain of an antibody from the sequences of the light and heavy chain of an antibody, and to build and optimize the CDR loop regions of an antibody model.

Antibody Modeling Cascade: Opens the Antibody Modeling Cascade protocol dialog. This protocol automatically generates 3D model structures for one or more antibody Fab or Fv regions. It first identifies framework templates, builds framework models, and then models the antibody loops.

If you prefer to model individual antibody structures by manually selecting templates for each modeling step, use the individual protocols Identify Framework Templates , Model Antibody Framework and Model Antibody Loops in a stepwise manner.

Identify Framework Templates: Opens the Identify Framework Templates protocol dialog. This protocol identifies templates for the antigen-binding fragment (Fab fragment) or variable region (Fv) of an antibody sequence for homology modeling and reports them in a table.

You can also use BLAST Search or BLAST Search (NCBI Server) tool to find suitable templates for the light chain or heavy chain of an antibody.

Model Antibody Framework: Opens the Model Antibody Framework protocol dialog. This protocol builds a homology model of the Fv domain or the Fab domain of an antibody from the light chain and heavy chain sequences using a chimeric template structure. The chimeric template structure will be built automatically by superimposing light chain and heavy chain templates onto a framework template structure that determines the relative spatial orientation of the two chains.

Model Antibody Loops: Opens the Model Antibody Loops protocol dialog. This protocol automatically identifies the CDR loops of an antibody structure, finds the best templates for each loop region, and optionally, builds models based on the loop templates. The model structure remains the same as the input protein except the loop regions, which are built based on the loop templates using the MODELER homology modeling approach.

Graft Loop: Copies the loop conformation from a template structure onto the target antibody structure. For details, see Graft Loop dialog .

Loop Refinement: Opens the Loop Refinement protocol dialog. This protocol refines a selected loop of the antibody model using the Looper algorithm.

Predict Humanizing Mutations: Opens the Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol dialog.

### Build Full Length Antibody Model

Model Full Length Antibody: Opens the Model Full Length Antibody protocol dialog. This protocol builds models from full length sequences of Immunoglobulin gamma isotype (IgG) based on templates for IgG1 and IgG2.

### Humanization

Predict Humanizing Mutations: Opens the Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol dialog. This protocol predicts mutations which make a native antibody more human compatible.

Nucleic Acid Type: Allows 
you to select the number of chains in the nascent nucleic acid molecule 
and the type of the nucleic acid to be built. The following options are available:

* DNA - Single Strand

* DNA - Duplex (default)

* DNA - Triplex

* RNA - Single Strand

* RNA - Duplex

* DNA/RNA - Duplex

* RNA/DNA - Duplex

Conformation: Allows you to select
one of the three standard geometries (A, B, or Z) for the nascent nucleic acid 
molecule. The A helix is available to both RNA, DNA, and hybrid DNA/RNA duplex 
molecules. The B and Z conformations are only allowed for DNA molecules.

### Choose Nucleotide

These tools allow you to create a new nucleic acid molecule, grow the existing chain, or mutate a residue using the selected residue type. The supported residue types are:

* Ino (for the Mutate build action only)

* Psu (for the Mutate build action only)

* H2u (for the Mutate build action only)

Specify: Opens the Enter Nucleic Acid Sequence dialog , 
which enables textual, user-defined input specifying the sequence of nucleotides. 
You can paste a nucleotide sequence string into the text box. However, if the Build Action is set to Mutate , the Choose one Nucleotide dialog is opened, which allows you to select one standard or nonstandard nucleotide type.

### Modify Sugar

These tools allow you to modify the sugar moiety of the nucleic acid molecule. Only selected residues are altered, otherwise all residues in visible nucleic acid molecules are affected.

Deoxyribose: Transforms the sugar to the deoxyribose form, thus allowing conversion of RNA to DNA

Ribose: Transforms the sugar to ribose, allowing the conversion of DNA to RNA, or removal of other modifications.

Locked Ribose: Transforms the sugar to ribose with a methyl bridge between O2' and C4'. Note that this form is only appropriate for stabilizing 3'-endo ribose, as found in A-helices; if applied to other conformations a distorted structure is liable to be produced.

O2'Me-Ribose: Transforms the sugar to ribose with a methyl group added to the O2'.

### Other Modifications

These tools allow you to manipulate an existing nucleic acid molecule.

Cap/Prime: Toggles termini between capped and primed forms.

Ligate: Links two nucleic acid molecules.

Nomenclature: Applies standard names.

Renumber Sequence: Applies sequential residue numbers.

### Nucleic Acid Utilities

Nucleic Acid Report: Generates a textual report, which is particularly useful for structures from PDB files

Define Nucleic Acid: Opens the Define Nucleic Acid Template dialog , which allows you to define a template for a nonstandard nucleic acid that can then be used for mutation.

# How to use the Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_nabt_hw.htm

## How to use the Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tools

The Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tool panel allows you to generate and modify 
nucleic acids (DNA and RNA molecules) as single strands, duplexes, or triple helices. 
The tool panel allows you to:

* Create a nucleic acid molecule

* Append or prepend nucleotides to nucleic acid molecule

* Mutate a nucleotide residue

* Modify sugars

* Modify the termini of nucleic acid strands

* Ligate nucleic acids

* Reset the atom names according to the standard nomenclature

* Renumber the sequence

* Create a textual report

* Define a nonstandard nucleic acid template

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Build and Edit Nucleic Acid .

To Create a Nucleic Acid Molecule

* Make the Graphics View active
or open a new Molecule Window. If the Molecule Window already contains molecules, make sure that no atoms are selected. If this step is omitted, a new Molecule Window will be created automatically.

* From the Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tools, click Choose the Build Action and select either Create/Grow at 3' or Prepend at 5' . 
If you do not choose any option, the default is Create/Grow at 3' .

* Choose one of the following nucleic acid types: DNA - Single Strand DNA - Duplex (default) DNA - Triplex RNA - Single Strand RNA - Duplex DNA/RNA Duplex RNA/DNA Duplex

* DNA - Single Strand

* DNA - Duplex (default)

* DNA - Triplex

* RNA - Single Strand

* RNA - Duplex

* DNA/RNA Duplex

* RNA/DNA Duplex

* Choose one of the following conformations: A Helix (default) B Helix Z Helix Some combinations of nucleic acid types and conformations are not allowed.

* A Helix (default)

* B Helix

* Z Helix

Some combinations of nucleic acid types and conformations are not allowed.

* Create the molecule by either selecting one of the available nucleotides from the tool panel or by typing a sequence consisting of one 
or more nucleotides into the Enter Nucleotide Sequence dialog. Certain types of nucleotides are not allowed for
some nucleic acid types and/or conformations. For example, DNA - Triplex exclusively 
accepts purines, while Z Helix only accepts alternating C and G residues.

Either the 3' or the 5' terminal residue, corresponding to Create/Grow at 3' and Prepend at 5' , respectively,
of the sense strand in the newly created nucleic acid molecule is selected automatically to facilitate further 
growth of the molecule.

A duplex or triplex consists of two or three separate chains,
one for each strand, which form molecules. The following defaults are
used for chainIDs in a newly generated nucleic acid:

* S: Sense strand

* A: Antisense strand (if it exists)

* H: Hoogsteen strand (in a triplex)

The new molecule is named automatically according to the type of the nucleic acid
built (for example, DnaSingleStrand, DnaDuplex, DnaTriplex, RnaSingleStrand, and RnaDuplex, etc.).

To append or prepend nucleotides to nucleic acid molecule

* Select the chain of an existing nucleic acid molecule to which a new residue will be
appended or prepended. You may select any residue within the chain; it does
not need to be terminal.

* Set Build Action to Create/Grow at 3' or Prepend to 5' to append a new residue to the 3' or 5' of the selected chain.

* Set the conformation to either A Helix , B Helix , 
or Z Helix .

* Set the Nucleic Acid Type . 
To grow an existing molecule, the number of chains in the
selected nucleic acid type has to match the existing molecule. For example, you can only grow a DNA
double helix with one of the following choices: DNA Duplex , RNA Duplex , DNA/RNA Duplex , or RNA/DNA Duplex .

* Choose the nucleotide that will be appended or prepended to the chain. You can make the selection directly using the Choose Nucleotide tool group, 
or by using the Enter Nucleotide Sequence dialog. You can use Specify... to append or prepend multiple bases (or base pairs/triplets) to the selected chain.

When the molecule grows, the sense strand takes the residues specified from the tool panel and the 
other strand(s) grow following the pairing rules.

When the chain grows, the append point for the command Create/Grow at 3' automatically shifts to the 3' residue of the sense strand. Similarly, the prepend point for the 
command Prepend at 5' automatically moves to the 5' nucleotide in the growing strand. 
This is indicated by automatically shifting the selected residue to the growing end.

Whenever a residue is appended or prepended, all the residues in the growing chains 
(sense, antisense, and Hoogsteen if applicable) are renumbered. The 5' terminus is assigned 
the starting residue ID of 1.

To mutate a residue

* Select a single residue or any atoms within a residue.

* Click a nucleotide type from the tool panel to change the selected residue to the new type.

* Alternatively, click Specify to open the Choose one Nucleotide dialog , which allows the selection of the nucleotide type from a list that includes additional nonstandard types.

* Click Mutate .

The sugar and phosphate portions of the mutated nucleotide are left intact and the new base is superimposed on the existing base using the following criteria:

* Pyrimidine -> Purine: Superimposed atom pairs include C6-C8, N1-N9, and C2-C4.

* Purine -> Purine: Superimposed atom pairs include C8-C8, N9-N9, and C4-C4.

* Purine -> Pyrimidine: Superimposed atom pairs include C8-C6, N9-N1, and C4-C2.

* Pyrimidine -> Pyrimidine: Superimposed atom pairs include C6-C6, N1-N1, and C2-C2.

To modify sugars

* Select the residues to modify. Do not make a selection if all the residues should be converted.

* Click Deoxyribose , Ribose , Locked Ribose , or O2'Me-Ribose to convert the sugar of the selected residue(s) to that form.

To modify termini

* To modify all 3' and 5' termini of the nucleic acid molecules in the active Molecule Window, deselect any atoms 
that may have been selected, and then click Cap/Prime . 
This command converts all capped termini to primed or caps all the primed termini.

* To toggle the capping or priming state of a particular terminal residue (or a set of terminal residues), 
select the residues, and then click Cap/Prime .

Capping changes the phosphate group at 5' by a hydroxyl group and adds a hydrogen to the
O3' atom at the 3' end.

Priming reverts the action of capping; it converts the 5' terminal hydroxyl to a phosphate group and 
removes the hydrogen from the 3' terminal oxygen. The resulting 3' terminus contains a free 3' oxygen atom 
(not bound to hydrogen), and the resulting 5' terminus contains a free 5' phosphate group.

Cap/Prime also changes the residue inside a chain when there is a break (i.e., two consecutive
residues are not bonded to each other in the chain).

To ligate nucleic acid molecules

Ligation emulates the ligation reaction in cells, which is catalyzed by the
enzyme DNA ligase. Ligation forms a phosphodiester bond between the 5' phosphoryl and the 3'
hydroxyl groups of terminal residues in two nucleic acid molecules

* To link two molecules, select one 3' base and one 5' base from two different molecules. To link two chains from the same molecule, select one 3' base and one 5' base from the two strands. To make a cyclic molecule, select one 3' base and one 5' base from the same strand.

* Click Ligate .

To move the two ligated molecules so that the bonds formed between two molecules
have proper bond lengths, check the Move ligated fragment option on 
the Build and Edit Nucleic Acid page of the Preferences dialog. This only applies when two molecules are ligated and 
it is ignored for ligation within the same molecule.

The following steps occur during ligation:

* When two molecules are ligated, if there is a valid complementary base at the 
selected 3' and a valid complementary base at the selected 5' end, a bond is 
formed between the complementary bases (for duplex and triplex) provided that 
the distance between the bonded atoms is reasonably close to the expected bond length.

* Two ligated chains are merged into one and the bases are renumbered to 
have the 5' end starting with an ID of 1. If ligation creates a cyclic molecule, 
no renumbering of residue IDs takes place.

* Two ligated molecules are merged.

* If the Move ligated fragment option is checked, the mobile strand is 
positioned so that the first base is superimposed on the immobile part, 
as the immobile part grows by one base adopting the standard A form for both 
RNA and DNA. The complementary strand (antisense and/or Hoogsteen) also moves with the sense strand.

In a triplex, only selections belonging to 
the sense strand are acceptable. This limitation prevents inappropriate merging of chains 
(e.g., Hoogsteen and antisense).

To rename the atoms according to the standard nomenclature

* Select strands or at least one nucleoside within each strand. If no nucleosides are selected, all nucleosides in the active Molecule Window are renamed.

* Click Nomenclature .

To renumber a sequence

* Select strands or at least one nucleoside within each strand. If no nucleosides are selected, the command is applied to all nucleic acid strands in the active Molecule Window.

* Click Renumber Sequence to set the sequential index of the
bases in a strand running from 1 starting at the 5' end of the chain.

To generate a report

* Open a nucleic acid structure in a Molecule Window. This tool is particularly useful for examining structures imported from PDB files.

* Click Nucleic Acid Report . A report analogous to the protein report appears in a Text Window.

To define a nonstandard nucleic acid template

* Build the desired nonstandard nucleic acid. The easiest method is usually to create the most similar existing amino acid using Build and Edit Nucleic tools and then modify it using any of the chemistry editing and sketching tools.

* Check that nomenclature conforms as close as possible to normal conventions.

* Ensure that bond orders and any formal charges are correct

* Click Define Nucleic Acid... to open the Define Nucleic Acid Template dialog.

* Select an existing template library from User template
library or type in a name to add a new template library.

* Specify a Template name .

* Type a unique Residue name , and then click OK .

The application will check that the residue name is unique (not a duplicate of any standard or existing nonstandard nucleic acid name). The
template will then be created from the input structure and be available for use in Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tools via
the Specify... tool when the build action is set to Mutate .

#### Further information

Build and Edit Nucleic Acid tools Define Nucleic Acid Template Enter Nucleic Acid Sequence dialog Choose one Nucleotide dialog Nucleic acid structure Build and Edit Nucleic Acid page - Preferences dialog

# Prepare Protein tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_ppt.htm

## Prepare Protein tools

The Prepare Protein tools manipulate and interrogate protein structures. The following tasks are supported:

* Splitting structures into separate molecules

* Generating a report summarizing problems and information about the protein

* Cleaning protein molecules (add missing atoms, correct connectivity, correct names, etc.)

* Inserting missing loops

* Grafting loops from a template to a target protein

* Managing conformers (i.e., disordered residues)

* Renumbering sequences

* Calculate protein ionization and residue pKs

* Modifying protonation of termini and ionizable sidechains

* Preparing the protein automatically

For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use Prepare Protein tools .

### Split Chains

All: Splits out all chains and non-protein substructures into separate objects in the Hierarchy View and lists each 
amino acid sequence as a separate sequence in the Sequence View.

Protein: Splits out all protein chain substructures into separate objects in the Hierarchy View and lists each amino 
acid sequence as a separate sequence in the Sequence View.

Non-Protein: Splits out ligands and other non-protein substructures such as waters into separate objects in the 
Hierarchy View and lists any non-protein polypeptide sequences as separate sequences in the Sequence View.

### Manual Preparation

Protein Report: Generates a Protein Report for the molecules in the current Graphics View. An HTML 
formatted protein report is generated which summarizes information about the structure. 
In addition, this command generates phi/psi/omega angles and detects invalid residues and gaps in the protein chains.

Clean Protein: Performs the tasks specified in the Clean Protein subpage of the Preferences dialog. These actions can be used to correct problems due to nonstandard naming, structural disorder (structure with alternate conformations), protein residue connectivity and bond orders, and missing side-chain or backbone atoms. 
It can correct the enumeration of hydrogens according to the preferred hydrogen representation and protonation states of chain termini and side-chains (by standard pKa or by predicted pK ) to match the specified pH. If a predicted pK is not available, the standard pKa value is used. 
The Clean Protein command does not attempt to optimize bond angles, bond lengths, or the positions of added backbone atoms or side-chains to avoid steric clashes, so refinement may be necessary.

Show Clean Report: Displays an HTML report detailing the changes made by Clean Protein .

Insert Loop: Opens the Enter an Amino Acid Sequence dialog that you can use to specify a sequence of residues to close a gap in an amino acid chain. The missing region is built by iteratively sampling closed loop conformations using the random tweak algorithm [Shenkin et al., 1987] to find a conformation with no bumps or minimal bumps with the rest of the protein.

Graft Loop: Opens the Graft Loop dialog , which allows you to copy a loop conformation from a template structure onto the protein being modeled.

Manage Conformers: Opens the Manage Conformers dialog , which allow you to manipulate conformers in disordered protein structures.

Renumber Sequences: Opens the Renumber Sequences dialog , which allows you to apply a different sequence number range to the selected residues. This command is enabled when you have a range of residues selected in a Molecule window, or when Sequence window is active.

### Protonate Protein

Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK: Opens the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol dialog. This protocol calculates protein ionization and predicts the pK for each ionizable residue and optionally performs intelligent protonation.

Modify Protonation State: Opens the Modify Protonation State dialog , which allows you to modify the protonation of termini and ionizable sidechains.

### Automatic Preparation

Prepare Proteins: Opens the Prepare Proteins protocol dialog. This protocol prepares imported protein structures for further modeling operations. It performs many of the same functions as the Manual Preparation and Protonate Protein tools. Additionally, it refines the positions of any side-chains it has added to avoid steric clashes, and performs more sophisticated building of missing loops.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Prepare Protein |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Macromolecules \| Prepare Protein |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Prepare Protein |

# How to use the Prepare Protein tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_ppt_hw.htm

## How to use the Prepare Protein tools

The Prepare Protein tools can be used to interrogate and manipulate protein structures. These tools require at least one protein
structure in an active Graphics View. This topic covers the following tasks:

* Split the structure into separate molecules

* Clean imported protein structures

* Insert a loop

* Graft a loop

* Manage conformers

* Renumber a sequence

* Calculate protein ionization and residue pKs

* Modify protonation state of termini and ionizable sidechains

* Prepare a protein for modeling automatically

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Prepare Protein .

To split the structure into separate molecules

* Set the preferences you want to apply in the Split Structure subpage - Preferences dialog .

* To split both protein and non-protein moieties according to the current Split Structure preferences, click All in the Split tool group. Otherwise, click Protein or Non-Protein .

To clean imported protein structures

* Set preferences in the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog .

* Click Clean Protein .

To insert a loop

* To identify gaps in the structure, click Protein Report to color the residues adjacent to gaps and create groups that contain the residues.

* Select the residues adjacent to the gaps from the groups in the Hierarchy View.

* Click Insert Loop... to open the Enter an Amino Acid Sequence dialog , which allows you to specify missing residues. If the structure was imported from an mmCIF file or a PDB file containing SEQRES information, then a suggestion for the gap residues may be available.

To graft a loop

* Open the target structure to be modeled in a Molecule Window, and insert a second protein structure to serve as a template for the loops.

* Optionally, select the residues defining the loop in the target and template structures, which automatically completes the fields in the dialog box.

* Click Graft Loop... , which opens the Graft Loop dialog . Complete the fields as desired and click OK to graft the loop.

To manage conformers

* Click Manage Conformers... , which opens the Manage Conformers dialog . Note that this tool is only enabled if the structure contains disordered residues.

* Set the options as desired and click OK .

To renumber a sequence

* Select a contiguous range of residues to be renumbered in the Molecule Window or the Sequence Window.

* On the tool panel, click Renumber Sequences... , which opens the Renumber Sequences dialog . Note that the dialog differs depending on whether you launch it from a Molecule Window or Sequence Window.

To calculate protein ionization and residue pKs

* Click on the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK... command to open the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol dialog.

* Set the parameters as desired and click Run .

To modify protonation state of termini and ionizable sidechains

* To use predicted rather than standard pKa values, first calculate residue pKs as described above.

* To modify the protonation selectively, select the relevant termini and/or ionizable residues.

* Click Modify Protonation State to open the Modify Protonation State dialog .

To prepare one or more proteins for modeling automatically

* Click Prepare Proteins... to open the Prepare Proteins protocol dialog.

## Prepare Protein tools

The following topics describe the basics of protein chemistry. If you are familiar with proteins, their sequences, 
and their hierarchy of structures, then you can skip these topics.

* Basics of protein structures

* Hierarchy of protein structure

### Residue and terminus pK values

The Modify Termini tool on the Build and Edit Protein tools panel and Clean Protein tool on the Prepare Protein tool panel can adjust the protonation state of ionizable residues and terminal groups to be appropriate to a given pH. The following pK values are used [Creighton, 2002] :

| C-Terminus | 3.0 |
| --- | --- |
| Aspartic Acid | 3.9 |
| Glutamic Acid | 4.3 |
| Histidine | 6.0 |
| N-Terminus | 8.0 |
| Cysteine | 9.0 |
| Tyrosine | 10.0 |
| Lysine | 10.4 |
| Arginine | 12.0 |

## Protein Report and Analysis tools

The Protein Report and Analysis tools interrogate protein structures and summarize information in a Protein Report or quickly generate a protein-specific Hydrophobicity Plot or Ramachandran Plot . Analyze Crystal Contacts builds neighboring atoms based on crystal symmetry and analyzes contacts and interactions in crystal environment.

For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Protein Report and Analysis tools .

### Report on Structure

Protein Report: Generates a Protein Report for the proteins in the current Graphics View. An HTML 
formatted protein report is generated. Choose File | Save As... from the menu bar to save this report. This tool also generates phi/psi/omega angles and detects gaps in the protein chains.

### Analysis

Analyze Crystal Contacts: Opens the Analyze Crystal Contacts protocol dialog. This protocol builds a shell of symmetry related copies around the structure and analyzes contacts and interactions.

Hydrophobicity Plot: Generates a Hydrophobicity Plot for the 
proteins in the current Graphics View.

Ramachandran Plot: Generates a Ramachandran Plot for the proteins in the current Graphics View.

# How to use the Protein Report and Analysis tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_prt_hw.htm

## How to use the Protein Report and Analysis tools

You can use the Protein Report and Analysis tools to interrogate protein structures. Each of these tools requires a protein 
structure in an active Graphics View.

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Protein Report and Analysis .

To generate a protein report

* Click Protein Report . The Protein Report appears in a Text Window.

* Open the AminoAcids tab in the Data Table View to view the φ/ψ angles for the structure.

To analyze molecular contacts in a crystal environment

* Ensure that the active Graphics view contains one molecule that is in a Cell and has symmetry information. Typically this should be an unmodified crystal structure imported from the Protein Databank.

* Click Analyze Crystal Contacts... to open the Analyze Crystal Contacts protocol dialog.

* Set the parameters as desired and click Run .

* When the job completes, examine the resulting structure, which shows nonbonded interactions between the asymmetric unit and symmetry-related copies surrounding it. Groups are added containing residues that form contacts between the original structure and its copies.

* Open the Report for the job to view tabulated details of the contacts and interactions.

To generate a hydrophobicity plot

* Ensure that the running average window is appropriately set in the Hydrophobicity Plot preference page.

* If desired, select residues to limit the scope of the plot.

* Click Hydrophobicity Plot .

To generate a Ramachandran plot

* Ensure that the options are appropriately set in the Ramachandran Plot preference page.

* Click Ramachandran Plot .

# Superimpose Proteins tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_spt.htm

## Superimpose Proteins tools

The Superimpose Proteins tools allow you to superimpose protein structures based on the following matching residues:

* Sequence Alignment : The aligned residues from an existing sequence alignment in a Sequence Window.

* Protein Tethers : The residue ranges between the pairs of protein molecules defined by protein tethers.

* C-Alpha Pairs : The pairs of C-Alpha atoms that are already close, to improve the fit.

These tools can also be used to generate a transformation matrix to superimpose one molecule on another. In addition, you can use the Align and Superimpose Proteins tool to superimpose a large set of proteins (which may be from files), and the Align Structures tool to align a set of protein sequences based on their structural similarity and superimpose the protein structures.

### Manual Superimposition Tools

Superimpose by: Allows you to choose the superimposition method:

* Sequence Alignment: Superimposes one or more protein structures onto the reference protein. By default, this performs the superimpositions to the target independently for each sequence (pairwise). However, there is an option in Superimpose Proteins - preference page to perform the superimpositions using residues in the reference sequence for which there are aligned residues in all of the structures to be superimposed (common framework). If some residues from the reference protein are selected, only those residues that are selected and aligned will be used in the superimposition. To superimpose a subset of structures, make them visible and all others invisible.

By default, this performs the superimpositions to the target independently for each sequence (pairwise). However, there is an option in Superimpose Proteins - preference page to perform the superimpositions using residues in the reference sequence for which there are aligned residues in all of the structures to be superimposed (common framework).

If some residues from the reference protein are selected, only those residues that are selected and aligned will be used in the superimposition. To superimpose a subset of structures, make them visible and all others invisible.

* Tethers: Superimposes one or more protein structures onto the defined reference protein by matching the ranges of residues specified via protein tethers. Multiple tethers can be used, but they must specify ranges for the reference protein and one or more of the other structures visible in the Graphics View.

* C-Alpha Pairs: Superimposes one or more protein structures onto the reference protein by matching the residues having a Cα atom within a cutoff distance (default 2.5 Å) to a CÅ atom in the reference protein. If you create a C-Alpha monitor using the Show C-Alpha Monitor tool, the cutoff distance in the monitor will be used instead. This option is useful if you have structures that are approximately aligned and you can use it iteratively to improve the fit.

Reference Protein: Defines the currently selected protein molecule as the reference for the subsequent superimposition. The other visible molecules will be superimposed onto this structure. Proteins that are not visible in the Graphics View are not superimposed. The first protein in the Molecule Window is set as the reference by default.

Sequence Alignment: Opens the Align Sequences dialog, 
which allows sequences in the sequence window containing a link to the reference protein to be aligned. The alignment must contain sequences linked to the reference protein and at least one other protein visible in the Molecule window, and there must be an active server connection.

Create Protein Tether: Creates a tether object that defines a range of residues to be matched. You must select the first residue in the range from the reference molecule and the molecule to be fitted, and the end of the range for one or both of these molecules. If the length of ranges selected in each molecule differs, the longest range will be used. The range can span multiple chains.

Create/[sequence name]: Displays the name of the Sequence Window that contains a sequence linked to the reference protein and at least one other visible protein. 
If no such window exists, the tool indicates Create... , which opens a Sequence Window for the currently selected protein structures and opens the Align Sequences dialog. There must be at least two applicable protein structures, and there must be an active server connection to use this tool.

Superimpose: Superimposes one or more visible protein structures onto the reference protein using the currently specified method.

### View

Show C-Alpha Monitor: Creates a monitor object that connects pairs of C-Alpha atoms in different molecules within a specified cutoff distance (default 2.5 Å).

Show Report: Displays a report for the last superimposition. It contains RMSDs, number of residues used in the superimposition, and transformation matrices. Note that the RMSDs are also added as properties in the Molecule tab in the Data Table.

Align and Superimpose Proteins: Opens the Align and Superimpose Proteins protocol dialog.

Align Structures: Opens the Align Structures protocol dialog.

# How to use the Superimpose Proteins tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_spt_hw.htm

## How to use the Superimpose Proteins tools

The Superimpose Proteins tools allow you to superimpose one or more protein structures onto a reference structure. There are a variety of methods to define the residues to be used for the superimposition, within which corresponding pairs of atoms are matched to each other.

Alternatively, the tools can be used to generate transformation matrices. Such matrices can subsequently be applied to all, or selected parts of a structure and are useful for operations such as building crystal structures with non-crystallographic symmetry.

Additionally, you can run the Align and Superimpose Proteins protocol, 
which is useful for superimposing a large set of proteins (they can be from a file), and the Align Structures protocol, which you can use to align a set of protein sequences based on their structural similarity and superimpose the protein structures.

This topic discusses the following tasks:

* Superimpose proteins by sequence alignment

* Superimpose a pair of proteins using Protein Tethers

* Superimpose proteins by C-Alpha pairs

* Superimpose proteins by sequence alignment or by C-Alpha pairs using selected residues

* Generate a transformation matrix to superimpose one protein on another

* Align and superimpose a large set of proteins

* Align proteins using structural similarity and superimpose them

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Superimpose Proteins .

To superimpose proteins by sequence alignment

* Load one of the protein molecules into the Graphics View.

* Choose File | Insert From | File... or File | Insert From | URL... from the menu bar to insert the other molecule into the same view.

* Set Superimpose by to Sequence Alignment .

* Load an appropriate alignment from a file.

* Alternatively, click Create... to display the Sequence View if it is not already open, and to open the Align Sequences dialog to align the sequences.

* Select the reference molecule (i.e., the one onto which the other is to be
transformed) from the Molecule Window, and then click Reference Protein .

* Click Superimpose to perform the superimposition.

* You can view the RMSDs in the Molecule tab of the Data Table, or click Show Report .

To superimpose a pair of proteins using Protein Tethers

* Load one of the protein molecules into a Graphics View.

* Set Superimpose by to Tethers .

* Select the range to be matched from the reference molecule. Ensure that the first and the last residues in the range are selected. 
It does not matter whether the residues in the middle of the ranges are selected.

* Select the first residue in the range from the molecule to be superimposed.
Click Create Protein Tether to define the tether.

* If desired, repeat the two previous steps to define additional ranges for this molecule or for other molecules to be superimposed on the reference.

To superimpose proteins by C-Alpha pairs

The tool refines the existing superimposition of a set of approximately superimposed structures.

* Do one of the following: Perform a superimposition using other superimposition methods. Load a set of approximately superimposed structures. Manually translate and rotate one molecule onto another.

* Perform a superimposition using other superimposition methods.

* Load a set of approximately superimposed structures.

* Manually translate and rotate one molecule onto another.

* Set Superimpose by to C-Alpha Pairs .

* If you want to change the default cutoff distance of the C-Alpha pairs, click Show C-Alpha Monitor to create the monitor, and then edit the Distance Cutoff in the CAlphaMonitor tab of the Data Table View.

To superimpose proteins by sequence alignment or by C-Alpha pairs using selected residues

Sometimes you may want to superimpose proteins using a selected set of residues, such as the residues surrounding a ligand. You can achieve this by using the Superimpose by Sequence Alignment or C-Alpha Pairs method.

Follow the same steps in Superimpose by Sequence Alignment or Superimpose by C-Alpha Pairs , but select the residues in the Molecule Window to be used in superimposition from the reference protein before using the Superimpose tool.

Any residues aligned with the selected residues in the reference protein or the residues having C-Alpha atoms close enough to C-Alphas in the selected residues in the reference protein will be used to superimpose the proteins.

To generate a transformation matrix to superimpose one protein on another

* Follow any of the sets of instructions above, but check the Generate matrix checkbox in Superimpose Proteins page - Preferences dialog .

* You can edit the matrix by choosing Structure | Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix... from the menu bar, or apply it to all or part of the structure by choosing Structure | Superimpose | Apply Transformation Matrix... from the menu bar.

To align and superimpose a large set of proteins

* Open one or more protein structures.

* Click Align and Superimpose Proteins to open the Align and Superimpose Proteins protocol dialog.

* Set the parameters accordingly and click Run .

To align proteins using structural similarity and superimpose them

* Open two or more protein structures.

* Click Align Structures to open the Align Structures protocol dialog.

#### Further information

Superimpose Proteins tools Superimpose Proteins page - Preferences dialog Align and Superimpose Proteins Align Structures

## Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools

The Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools panel
contains controls for evaluating the suitability of different side-chain rotamers 
in a 3D protein structure.

For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools .

Rotamer Library: Sets the rotamer library of amino acid side-chain geometries to be searched. The available options are:

* Ponder and Richards (default): [Ponder and Richards, 1987]

* Sutcliffe: [Sutcliffe et al., 1987]

* Oldfield: [Oldfield, 2002]

* Lovell, Word, and Richardson: [Lovell et al., 2000]

Set Active Residue: Performs a search of the selected rotamer library
and lists the results in a table. The table displays the rotamers for the selected amino acid. The first entry contains the current conformation of the selected amino acid. For each entry, the following rotamer data are displayed:

* Probability [column]: Probability distribution of side-chain rotamer positions based on experimental observation of high resolution crystal structures (when available).

* Chi 1 [column]: First side-chain torsion angle (Chi_1) of the rotamer. Further chi angle columns are displayed as available for the particular amino acid in the chosen rotamer library.

Click the rows to replace the original amino acid with the corresponding rotamer.

### Show/Hide Rotamer Interactions

HBonds: Show or hide hydrogen bond monitors for the rotamer.

Bumps: Show or hide bump monitors for the rotamer.

Energy: Show or hide Dreiding energy monitors for the rotamer.

# How to use the Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_sscrt_hw.htm

## How to use the Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools

The following steps describe how to model side-chains in a structure by choosing from common conformations, known as rotamers. This is typically done during the building of X-Ray structures, after performing a mutation, or when inserting a missing section of a residue into an existing structure.

* Open a protein structure in a Molecule Window .

* Open the Macromolecules | Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools.

* Select the rotamer library from Rotamer Library .

* Toggle HBonds , Bumps , and Energy to monitor interactions between the selected side-chain and the rest of the structure as you explore the conformations.

* Select the complete residue you want to model.

* Click Set Active Residue to display the available rotamers for the selected amino acid.

* From the table displayed within the tool panel, select rows to view the available conformations. Choose the first row of the table to view the original conformation.

* Repeat the last three steps to model other residues.

Clicking on the Set Active Residue issues a command to set the rotamer and one to manage the rotamer monitors. Therefore to return to the previous state, it is necessary to Undo twice.

# Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_tmt.htm

## Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools

The Analyze Transmembrane Protein tool panel in the Macromolecules tool set allows you perform the following:

* Predict transmembrane protein regions of a protein from a protein sequence

* Add an implicit membrane to a protein structure

* Edit the properties of the membrane

For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools .

### Sequence

Predict Transmembrane Helices: Predicts transmembrane helices of a protein from its amino acid sequence using a Hidden Markov Model. The result of the prediction is displayed as a secondary structure cartoon in the Sequence Window.

### Create and Edit Membrane

Add: Adds an implicit membrane, represented by two parallel planes to the protein structure. The position of the membrane is determined by optimizing a simplified solvation energy. If there is a significant difference in the charges of protein residues that lie outside the membrane, the membrane plane on that side that has more positive protein residues is blue, whereas the other plane is green. If there is no significant charge difference between the sides, both planes are green.

Modify... Opens the Edit Membrane dialog to adjust the position and thickness of an implicit membrane. You can modify the position of the membrane by entering the desired values for the membrane center as well as the tilt and rotation angle. For a definition of the tilt and rotation angles, refer to the following section that describes the Membrane Orientation Monitor.

Add Orientation Monitor: Adds a monitor that tracks the position and relative orientation of the membrane with respect to the geometric center and principal axes of a protein. The tilt angle is defined as the angle between the first principal axis of the protein and the membrane normal (other principal axes can be specified in the preference dialog). The rotation angle is the angle between the second principal axis of the set of atoms and the normal to the plane defined by the first principal axis and the membrane normal. The arrows displayed by the monitor indicate the first (red tip) and second (green tip) principal axes of the protein.

### Optimize Membrane Orientation

Add Membrane and Orient Molecule: Opens the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol dialog. This protocol optimizes the position and orientation of a molecule relative to an implicit membrane
(see Solvent models in biomolecular simulations ).
If the input protein contains an implicit membrane created by the Add tool, the membrane is reoriented.

### Edit Protein

Select Membrane Region: Selects any residues of a protein that lies between the two planes of the implicit membrane and all residues of secondary structure elements containing at least one residue that lies between the two membrane planes.

Split Selected Segments: Separates each selected segment of a protein into separate chains and removes residues that are not selected. This command can be used in combination with Select Membrane Regions to split a transmembrane protein into individual transmembrane segments. This simplifies adjusting the relative orientation of the transmembrane segments.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Macromolecules \| Analyze Transmembrane Proteins |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Macromolecules \| Analyze Transmembrane Proteins |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Analyze Transmembrane Proteins |

# How to use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/prot_tmt_hw.htm

## How to use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools

The Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools can be used to predict transmembrane protein regions of a protein, add an implicit membrane to a protein structure, and edit the properties of the membrane.

This topic discusses the following tasks:

* Predict the transmembrane helices of a protein

* Add a membrane to a transmembrane protein structure

* Modify the position and thickness of a membrane

* Monitor the position of a membrane

* Split the transmembrane regions of a protein into separate chains

To access these tools, open Macromolecules | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins .

### Sequence

To predict the transmembrane helices of a protein

* Load the protein sequence into a Sequence Window .

* In the Sequence group, click Predict Transmembrane Helices to predict the transmembrane helices. The transmembrane helix prediction is displayed as a Secondary Structure Cartoon in the Sequence Window.

* Right-click the Sequence Window and choose Secondary Structure Cartoon to toggle the display of secondary structure cartoons.

### Membrane

To add a membrane to a transmembrane protein structure

* Load the protein structure into a Molecule Window .

* Select a protein molecule to which the implicit membrane should be added. If no molecule is selected, a membrane will be added to each molecule in the window.

* Click Add in the Membrane group to add an implicit membrane to the structure. A membrane with two parallel planes
is added in the Graphics View and a membrane object appears under the molecule in the Hierarchy View .

To modify the position and thickness of a membrane

* Select a membrane in the Molecule Window or select atoms from a molecule
which has a membrane object. Note that you do not need to select the membrane if only one is present.

* In the Membrane group, click Modify... to open the Edit Membrane Dialog.

* Enter the desired value in Shift text box to modify the distance of the membrane center from the center of geometry of the protein.

* Enter values for the following: Tilt : Modifies the tilt angle between the membrane normal an the reference principal axis of the protein Rotation : Modifies the rotation angle of the membrane with respect to the protein Thickness : Modifies the thickness of the membrane

* Tilt : Modifies the tilt angle between the membrane normal an the reference principal axis of the protein

* Rotation : Modifies the rotation angle of the membrane with respect to the protein

* Thickness : Modifies the thickness of the membrane

* Click OK to close the dialog and update the position of the membrane.

If a subset of the atoms from a molecule is selected, the membrane will be positioned according to the selected atoms, not the 
whole molecule.

To monitor the position of a membrane

* Select a membrane in the Molecule Window or select atoms from a molecule that has a membrane object. Note that you do not need to select the membrane if only one is present.

* In the Membrane group, click Add Orientation Monitor to add a Membrane Orientation Monitor to the Molecule Window . In the Hierarchy View the Membrane Orientation Monitor is parented by the protein structure.

If a subset of the atoms from a molecule is selected, 
the monitor will be set on the selected atoms, not the full molecule.

### Edit Protein

To split the transmembrane regions of a protein into separate chains

* Select a membrane in the Molecule Window . Note that if only one membrane is present, the command will apply to the protein containing that membrane.

* In the Membrane group, click Select Membrane Region to select residues that fall between the two membrane planes (as determined by the position of the C-alpha atom) and all residues of secondary structure elements containing at least one residue that lies between the two membrane planes.

* Click Split Selected Segments to split the selected segments into separate protein chains. The new segments will be labeled Seg1, Seg2, ...., SegN . All residues that do not fall inside the membrane are removed.

# Protein Report

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein-report.htm

## Protein Report

The Protein Report is a text document that summarizes key information about 
the protein structure(s) in the active Graphics View. If there is more than 
one molecule in the View, the report begins with a list of the molecules. The 
information for each molecule consists of the following sections, if they are 
relevant to that molecule:

* General information: Cell and Space Group, Crystallographic Resolution,
Molecular weight, amino acid chain names, total number of amino acid residues, experimental pH

* Sequence

* Comparison of the actual sequence with the PDB SEQRES records: this reports missing residues in the PDB atom
records in comparison with SEQRES records from PDB files

* Missing Residues from mmCIF data: if the structure has been read from an mmCIF file, this records missing residues based on the _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme data

* Residues with alternate conformations

* A list of incomplete or otherwise invalid residues

* Active site definitions

* Ligands, ions, etc.

* The number of solvent residues

* Biomolecule Generation: Supplies information about how to create biomolecular
complexes from the transformation matrix provided in the .pdb file. The transform
matrices are read in and can be edited or applied using the Structure | Superimpose | Edit Transformation Matrix... or Structure | Superimpose | Apply Transformation Matrix... commands.

* PDB header information

In addition to generating this text report, the phi, psi, and omega angles 
are calculated for each residue along the amino acid chains. These are stored 
as properties of the residues, and can be viewed in the Data Table 
(displayed via View | Data Table ) 
on the AminoAcid tab.

If the structure contains gaps in the chains, then in addition to the textual information, the structure is annotated with the addition of Gap Start and Gap End properties on the residues adjacent to the missing section. If SEQRES information is available then these properties show the residues missing at this point. These residues are also set up as Groups under the heading Gaps in Chain in the hierarchy view, to aid easy selection. Note that if the structure was read from an mmCIF file, these properties and groups will have been automatically created when it was opened.

If the structure contains incomplete or invalid residues, Groups are created for them under Invalid Residues in the hierarchy view.

# Add Membrane and Orient Molecule - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_add_membrane_and_orient_molecule-para.htm

## Add Membrane and Orient Molecule - Parameters

### Adds an implicit membrane to the molecular model and orients the protein relative to membrane

Uses a stepwise search algorithm for the optimal orientation of the molecule relative to an implicit membrane. The membrane is presented as a planar low-dielectric slab and the molecule is treated as a rigid structure. The optimal orientation corresponds to the minimum of the solvation energy calculated in Generalized Born / Solvent Accessible Surface Area approximation.

The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Solvent Model with Implicit Membrane | Specifies the implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using a pairwise approximation of volume integral extended with an analytical function to include the effect of the membrane. Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. Uses a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. See Also: Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S. Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility Continuum solvent models. J. Phys. Chem. B. 2002 106, 8726-8738. Feig, M; Brooks, C. Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations. Curr. Opin. Struct. Biol. 2004 14, 217-224. Valid Values: Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) , Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the interior of the solute molecule and the implicit membrane. The rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies the value of the dielectric constant of the solvent. |
| Salt Concentration | Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l) in GBSW. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these forcefields. Applies to GBIM. See Also: Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. If the selected Solvent Model with Implicit Membrane is "Generalized Born (GBIM)", it is recommended to be set to zero, to avoid large constant values added to the surface energy term. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol × Å 2 )) for calculating the non-polar contribution to solvation energy. The optimal values can vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields, or molecular systems. For transmembrane proteins and membrane peptides values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol × Å 2 ) are recommended. See Also: Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. |
| Membrane Thickness | Specifies the thickness (Å) of the low-dielectric planar slab in the implicit membrane model. Note: If the Solvent Model with Implicit Membrane is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM), the minimum allowed membrane thickness is 8.0 Å. |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Lower Cutoff Distance to Higher Cutoff Distance. |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. |
| Shift | Specifies the step (Å) and the range of shifting of the protein along the membrane normal. If a membrane is present in the input structure, the shift is related to the current position of the molecule. Without a membrane in the input structure, the shift is relative to membrane mid-plane. |
| Shift From | Specifies the initial displacement (Å) of molecular center from the membrane mid-plane. |
| Shift To | Specifies the final displacement (Å) of molecular center from the membrane mid-plane. |
| Shift Step Size | Specifies the step size (Å). |
| Tilt Angle | Specifies the step and the range of the changes of the tilt angle (in °). The tilt angle is the angle between one of the protein's axis of inertia and the membrane normal. If a membrane is present in the input structure, the tilt angle changes are related to the initial position of the molecule. Without a membrane in the input structure, the change of tilt angle is relative to the membrane normal (Z axis). |
| Tilt Angle Maximum Change | Specifies the maximum change of the tilt angle (°). The search of the optimal tilt angle is carried out in the interval from - value to + value of the parameter. |
| Tilt Angle Step Size | Specifies the tilt angle sampling step size (°). |
| Rotation Angle Step Size | Specifies the step size (°). |

Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures.

Specifies the implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are:

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using a pairwise approximation of volume integral extended with an analytical function to include the effect of the membrane.

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. Uses a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S. Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility Continuum solvent models. J. Phys. Chem. B. 2002 106, 8726-8738.

* Feig, M; Brooks, C. Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations. Curr. Opin. Struct. Biol. 2004 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) , Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW)

Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the interior of the solute molecule and the implicit membrane. The rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent.

When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons.

Specifies the value of the dielectric constant of the solvent.

Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l) in GBSW.

* Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773.

Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA.

Valid Values: True , False

Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy.
If the selected Solvent Model with Implicit Membrane is "Generalized Born (GBIM)", it is recommended to be set to zero, to avoid large constant values added to the surface energy term.

Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol × Å 2 )) for calculating the non-polar contribution to solvation energy. The optimal values can vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields, or molecular systems. # Add Membrane and Orient Molecule

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_add_membrane_and_orient_molecule.htm

## Add Membrane and Orient Molecule

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol optimizes the position and the orientation of a molecule relative
to an implicit membrane described in Solvent models in biomolecular simulations . The optimization algorithm uses a stepwise search for the minimum solvation energy of the molecule, calculated by CHARMm
modules GBIM and ASPENMB [Spassov et al., 2002] or GBSW [Im and Brooks,2003] .

The protocol re-orients the molecule to the membrane created by the Analyze Transmembrane Protein tools . If a membrane is not present in the input structure, the protocol adds a membrane object to the output structure according to the calculated optimal orientation and position.

# Align and Superimpose Proteins - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_align_and_superimpose_proteins-para.htm

## Align and Superimpose Proteins - Parameters

### Performs multiple sequence alignment and structure superimposition on two or more proteins

Uses Align123 to align protein sequences, then superimposes the protein structures by the alignment.

Align123 is a multiple sequence alignment method based on the ClustalW program. ClustalW aligns multiple sequences using a progressive pairwise alignment algorithm. It first generates all possible pairwise alignments for a list of sequences and then builds a guide tree based on pairwise 
sequence identity, aligning the sequences following the order of the guide tree. In Align123, the term for scoring a match of secondary structure can be added to the original ClustalW multiple sequence alignment score.

The protocol performs the following steps:

* Aligns protein sequences

* Superimposes protein structures

See Also:

* Thompson, J.; Higgins, D. G.; Gibson, T. J. Nucl. Acids Res. 1994 , 22(22), 4673-4680.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Reference Protein Molecule | Specifies the protein structure to be used as the reference for the superposition. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. Note: The name of the protein can only contain alpha-numerical, dot ".", underscore "_", and pipe "\|" characters. Other characters, such as spaces are not allowed. |
| Selected Residues | Specifies the list of residues from the reference protein to be used for superimposition. In Pipeline Pilot the selected residues are defined as a comma separated list of regions of one or more consecutive residues. Example: A:SER12-A:SER12,B:GLY114-B:PHE180. In Discovery Studio the residues are selected from the drop-down list. If this parameter is left empty, superimposition will be done on the whole protein. |
| Input Target Protein Molecules | Specifies protein structures to align and superimpose to the reference protein. In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. Note: Protein names can only contain alpha-numerical, dot ".", underscore "_", and pipe "\|" characters. Other characters, such as spaces are not allowed. |
| Using Atoms | Specifies whether to calculate the superimposition based only on C-Alpha Atoms or on all Main-chain Atoms . Valid Values: Main-chain Atoms , C-Alpha Atoms |
| Use Secondary Structures | Use secondary structure information of Input Protein Molecules in calculating alignment scores. In most cases, using secondary structure information will produce better alignments. Valid Values: True , False |
| Secondary Structure Weight | Specifies the weight of secondary structure information in calculating alignment scores. |

Specifies the protein structure to be used as the reference for the superposition. 
In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins.

Note:

In Discovery Studio the residues are selected from the drop-down list.
