## Align and Superimpose Proteins

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Align and Superimpose Proteins protocol uses the Align123 program to align protein sequences, and then superimposes the protein structures by the
alignment. Protein structures are selected from Molecule Window and files. The protocol is designed to superimpose a large number of homologous
proteins for comparing and analyzing their structures, such as comparing the binding site of large number of kinases. It can
handle many more structures than the structure alignment protocols, but only works well when the input proteins have
significant sequence similarity. It also has an option to superimpose based on selected residues, such as binding site
residues.

* Open one protein structure that will be used as the reference protein, or open the protein structures to be superimposed.

* Open Macromolecules | Superimpose Proteins tools and click Align and Superimpose Proteins... to open the Align and Superimpose Proteins dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select the opened protein molecule in the Input Reference Protein Molecule parameter.

* Use the Input Target Protein Molecules parameter to specify the proteins to be superimposed. Choose All , Selected , or Visible molecules from the active molecule window, or browse to select one or more protein structure files. 
Each file can contain one or more protein molecules and all of the proteins will be superimposed to the reference
protein specified by the Input Reference Protein Molecule parameter.

* Set Using Atoms to perform the superimposition based on Main-chain atoms or C-alpha atoms.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Align and Superimpose Proteins - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, a Sequence Window opens with the aligned protein sequences and
a Molecule Window opens with the superimposed protein structures. The sequences and the structures
are linked automatically. Open Report.htm by double clicking on the job from the Jobs Explorer to view the RMSD of each protein structure 
to the reference protein and the number of overlapping residues.
If the job ran in background, open the sequence alignment and superimposed
structures by clicking on the View Results from the experiment report.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

# Align Sequence to Templates - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_align_sequence_to_templates-para.htm

## Align Sequence to Templates - Parameters

### Aligns a protein sequence to a set of protein structures

Align the Input Model Sequence to a set of protein structures based on sequence similarity. This protocol is generally used to create input sequence alignment for building homology models. If there are more than one template structures specified, the sequences of the structures can be first aligned based on their structural similarity using the structure alignment method in MODELER program. Sequence profile can also be created for Input Model Sequence using BLAST and the resulting profile will be used to align the model sequence with the template sequences.

The following steps are performed:

* Create sequence profile (using BLAST Search)

* Align template structures (using MODELER)

* Align model sequence with templates (using Align123)

* Superimpose template structures

Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings and inputs.

The third step is carried out using different alignment options depending on whether steps 1 and 2 are executed or not:

* If sequence profile is created and template structures are aligned by structure alignment, the sequence profile will be aligned to structure profile using Align Two Profiles option in Align123 program.

* If sequence profile is not created, then Input Model Sequence will be added to the structure alignment using Align Sequences to a Profile option.

* If there is only one template or if the templates are not aligned based on structural similarity, Input Model Sequence or the sequence profile will be aligned to the templates using Align Sequences option.

### Parameters

| --- | --- |
| Input Model Sequence | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA, Genbank and SwissProt. In Discovery Studio, choose a sequence from all open Sequence Windows. |
| Input Template Structures | Specifies protein structures to be used as modeling templates. In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. Note: Protein names can only contain alpha-numerical, dot ".", underscore "_", and pipe "\|" characters. Other characters, such as spaces are not allowed. |
| Create Sequence Profile | If True, homologous sequences to the Input Model Sequence will be used to create sequence profile to assist the alignment between model sequence and template structures. The homologous sequences are identified from the Input Database using BLAST Search. When the sequence identity between the model sequence and templates is below 80%, this option is recommended. Valid Values: True, False |
| Server | Specifies to run BLAST search using NCBI server or local server. Depending on the server, the allowed Input Database will vary. Valid Values: Local , NCBI |
| Input Database | Specifies the name of the database for BLAST searching. Allowed databases for NCBI Server nr swissprot Allowed databases for Local server: UniRef90 Swiss-Prot Note: If you choose to create the profile by running BLAST on the local server using UniRef90 database, please download and install the database following the Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search topic in the Discovery Studio Help. |
| Scoring Matrix | Specifies the scoring matrix used in BLAST searching. The matrix assigns a score for aligning any possible pair of residues: BLOSUM45 : for particularly long and weak similarities. BLOSUM62 : for detecting most weak protein similarities. BLOSUM80 : for sequence length between 50 and 85 residues. PAM70 : for sequence length between 35 and 55 residues. PAM30 : for sequence length shorter than 35 residues. Valid Values: BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62 , BLOSUM80, PAM70, PAM30 |

## Align Sequence to Templates

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Align Sequence to Templates aligns a model sequence to sequences of the template structures and prepares the input sequence alignment
for building homology models in three main steps:

* Identify homologous sequences to model sequence (Optional): Including homologous sequences can improve the alignment between two distantly related sequences.
This protocol provides option to run BLAST on either the NCBI server or a local server to identify sequences 
homologous to the input model sequence. The sequence databases must be installed if a local server is selected.
See Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search for details.

Including homologous sequences can improve the alignment between two distantly related sequences.
This protocol provides option to run BLAST on either the NCBI server or a local server to identify sequences 
homologous to the input model sequence. The sequence databases must be installed if a local server is selected.
See Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search for details.

* Align template structures using structure alignment (Optional): If multiple template structures are selected as input, structure alignment is generally more reliable.
Therefore, templates are first aligned based on structural similarity using the MODELER structure alignment
algorithm (the same method as used in Align Structures (MODELER) ).
However, this option can be turned off and the template structures will be aligned with the model
sequence using the multiple sequence alignment algorithm.

If multiple template structures are selected as input, structure alignment is generally more reliable.
Therefore, templates are first aligned based on structural similarity using the MODELER structure alignment
algorithm (the same method as used in Align Structures (MODELER) ).
However, this option can be turned off and the template structures will be aligned with the model
sequence using the multiple sequence alignment algorithm.

* Align model sequence to templates: In this step, the protocol aligns the model sequence to the template sequences using the Align123 program. Depending on whether the first two steps are executed, the protocol automatically chooses one of
the alignment modes provided by the Align123 program (the
same as used in Align Sequences and Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) ).

In this step, the protocol aligns the model sequence to the template sequences using the Align123 program. Depending on whether the first two steps are executed, the protocol automatically chooses one of
the alignment modes provided by the Align123 program (the
same as used in Align Sequences and Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) ).

#### Scenarios

Depending on similarity of the model sequence to the templates and the number of template structures selected, you can choose whether to utilize the first two steps. The following table
summarizes the common use case scenario and suggested protocol settings.

| Scenario | Parameter values | Protocol actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The sequence is highly homologous (over 60% sequence identity) to the template and one template is selected. | Set the Create Sequence Profiles parameter to False . | The protocol will align the model and template sequences using the multiple sequence alignment method in Align123. |
| The sequence is highly homologous to the templates and more than one template is selected. | Set the Create Sequence Profiles parameter to False . | The protocol will first align the templates using the structure alignment algorithm. It then adds the sequence to the aligned structure profile using the sequence to profile alignment method in Align123. |
| The sequence is not highly homologous to templates and one template is selected. | Keep the Create Sequence Profiles parameter set to True . | The protocol will identify additional homologous sequences by searching against a sequence database using the model sequence as input. It then aligns the model sequence, hits from the search, and the template sequence using the multiple sequence alignment method in Align123. |
| The sequence is not highly homologous to the templates and more than one template is selected. | Keep the Create Sequence Profiles parameter set to True . | The protocol creates a sequence profile by searching a sequence database and aligns the hits with the input sequence. It then aligns the templates using the structure alignment method. Finally, it aligns the sequence profile to the structure profile using the profile to profile alignment method in Align123. |

# Align Structures - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_align_structures-para.htm

## Align Structures - Parameters

### Aligns and clusters a set of protein sequences based on 3D structural similarity

Uses the 3DMA program to align the sequences of two or more protein structures according to their 3D structural similarity.

The algorithm finds the matching segments of protein structure pairs by comparing the C-alpha pseudo-torsion angle within hash bins and then completes the alignment by discriminative extension of the matching segments. The multiple structure alignment is constructed through a progressive pairwise alignment based on an initial guide tree derived from all-against-all pairwise comparison.

Sequences are clustered into alignments according to their similarities, and more than one output alignment may be found.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. If you specify a single file, it must contain two or more molecules. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. Note: Molecule names can only contain alpha-numerical, dot ".", underscore "_", and pipe "\|" characters. Other characters, such as spaces are not allowed. |
| C-Alpha Distance Cutoff | C-alpha distance cutoff (Å) between aligned residues. Select a smaller C-Alpha Distance Cutoff to enforce smaller structural differences between aligned structures. |
| Length Cutoff | Minimum number of residues to be aligned. |
| Bin Size | Size (°) of the C-alpha pseudo-torsion angle bin used in initial pairwise structure comparison. A larger Bin Size increases the likelihood of generating fewer clusters with larger structural differences between the structures belonging to the same cluster. |
| Fuzzy Bins | Structure segments are divided into hash bins based on their C-alpha pseudo-torsion angles computed from four consecutive residues. Segments falling into the same hash bin are compared to find the matching segments between two proteins. When Fuzzy Bins is True, segments in adjacent hash bins are also compared. This requires slightly more computation time. However, in some cases it is necessary in order to identify the correct alignment. Valid Values: True, False |

In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. If you specify a single file, it must contain two or more molecules. 
In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files.

Note:

* Molecule names can only contain alpha-numerical, dot ".", underscore "_", and pipe "|" characters. Other characters, such as spaces are not allowed.

C-alpha distance cutoff (Å) between aligned residues.

Select a smaller C-Alpha Distance Cutoff to enforce smaller structural differences between aligned structures.

Minimum number of residues to be aligned.

Size (°) of the C-alpha pseudo-torsion angle bin used in initial pairwise structure comparison.

A larger Bin Size increases the likelihood of generating fewer clusters with larger structural differences between the structures belonging to the same cluster.

Structure segments are divided into hash bins based on their C-alpha pseudo-torsion angles computed from four consecutive residues. Segments falling into the same hash bin are compared to find the matching segments between two proteins. When Fuzzy Bins is True, segments in adjacent hash bins are also compared. This requires slightly more computation time. However, in some cases it is necessary in order to identify the correct alignment.

# Align Structures

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_align_structures.htm

## Align Structures

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Align Structures protocol aligns multiple protein sequences according to their structural similarity using the 3DMA program.
It reports the common alignment core of all the input proteins.
If input proteins are not all homologous, it automatically partitions them into different clusters
and reports each cluster alignment separately. Proteins that cannot be aligned to any other proteins are left out of the aligned clusters.

When aligning the proteins in each cluster, the protocol creates a guiding tree according to initial pairwise
structure alignment and progressively adds structures to the alignment. The number of aligned residues decreases as each
additional protein is added to the alignment because the protocol only reports residues that are aligned among all aligned
proteins.

* Optionally, open the structures to be aligned.

* Open the Macromolecules | Align Sequences and Structures tools and 
click Align Structures... to open the Align Structures dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Protein Structures . 
You can select All , Selected , or Visible molecules from the active molecule window, or alternatively 
use the Browse option to select one or more structure files.
The selected molecules must have unique names. If a name appears more than
once, rename one of them.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Structures - Parameters . The resulting alignment
depends slightly on the order of the input sequences. This is an intrinsic
limitation of the algorithm, a result of a trade-off made to avoid combinatorial
enumeration of all possible alignment paths. Typically, for pairwise alignments,
the results differ by 2-3 amino acids in the length of the alignment and
by 0.1 Å in RMSD. When aligning small proteins, especially proteins shorter then 50 residues, the Length Cutoff parameter should be set to a lower value.

The resulting alignment
depends slightly on the order of the input sequences. This is an intrinsic
limitation of the algorithm, a result of a trade-off made to avoid combinatorial
enumeration of all possible alignment paths. Typically, for pairwise alignments,
the results differ by 2-3 amino acids in the length of the alignment and
by 0.1 Å in RMSD.

When aligning small proteins, especially proteins shorter then 50 residues, the Length Cutoff parameter should be set to a lower value.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the aligned protein structures open in a Molecule Window and
the sequence alignment opens in a Sequence Window with the sequences linked to the structures. 
If there is more than one alignment cluster, each open in a separate window.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the structures and the sequence alignment.

The pairwise RMSD and the number of overlapping residues for each cluster are shown in the Summary section of the report.

The molecules of each cluster are superimposed according to their corresponding alignment to the first protein in the cluster. 
Main-chain atom RMSD for each pair of protein is shown in Report.htm.
Choose Structure | RMSD | by Sequence Alignment from the menu bar to calculate C-alpha or a different RMSD.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. Check the Summary and Error sections if protocol failed. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Cluster-*.bsml | Sequence alignment for each cluster. |
| Cluster-*.dsv | Superimposed protein molecules for each cluster. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opens the sequence alignment and molecule superimposition for every cluster. |

#### Further information

Choose an alignment protocol Theory - Align Structures

# Align Structures (MODELER) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_align_structures_modeler-para.htm

## Align Structures (MODELER) - Parameters

### Aligns a set of protein sequences based on 3D structural similarity

Uses the MODELER SALIGN function to either

* align multiple MacroMolecule data records or

* align one or more MacroMolecule data records to a reference alignment (a set of pre-aligned reference structures)

depending on the value of Alignment Type .

The MODELER SALIGN function aligns two or more protein sequences based on their structural similarity using a general dynamic programming based alignment algorithm. The weight matrix used for dynamic programming is a weighted sum of five protein structure and sequence features: residue type, intermolecular distance of residues pairs, fractional sidechain accessibility, secondary structure type and local conformation.

If Initialize Alignment is True, an initial sequence alignment is performed using only residue and secondary structure type. Otherwise, the input alignment is used as the initial alignment. Based on this initial alignment, SALIGN performs an iterative least-squares superposition of 3D structures to generate a multiple structure alignment.

See Also:

* MODELER SALIGN documentation at http://salilab.org/modeller/manual

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Alignment Type | Specifies the type of alignment to perform: Align Structures : align multiple structures. Extend Existing Alignment : align a set of multiple structures to a set of pre-aligned structures. Valid Values: Align Structures , Extend Existing Alignment |
| Input Sequence Alignment | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequence alignments in all open Sequence Windows. If Alignment Type is "Align Structures", at least two sequences in the selected alignment must have structure linking. If Alignment Type is "Extend Existing Alignment", at least one sequence in the selected alignment must have structure linking. |
| Input Protein Molecules | List of input protein structures which are linked to sequences in Input Sequence Alignment . In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose one or more protein structures from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Reference Sequence Alignment | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequence alignments in all open Sequence Windows. The alignment of structures in the reference sequence alignment will not be changed as new structures specified in the Input Sequence Alignment parameter group are added to the alignment. |
| Reference Sequence Alignment Input Protein Molecules | List of input protein structures which are linked to sequences in Reference Sequence Alignment . In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose one or more protein structures from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Gap Open Penalty | Penalty for creating a gap. Recommended value "0". |
| Gap Extension Penalty | Penalty for extending a gap. When the Gap Open Penalty is "0", pairs of residue positions are identified as equivalent when they have their selected atoms at most 2 times the value of the Gap Extension Penalty parameter (in Å) apart in the current superposition. |
| Overhang | Maximum number of unaligned residues at the termini that will not be penalized by any gap penalties (this makes it a pseudo local alignment) |
| Fast Alignment | Speed up the alignment calculation by considering fewer neighboring residues. Valid Values: True, False |
| Initialize Alignment | If True, perform an initial sequence alignment using the MODELER salign function with non-zero weights only for residue type and secondary structure data. If False, the input alignment is used as the initial alignment. Valid Values: True , False |

* Align Structures : align multiple structures.

* Extend Existing Alignment : align a set of multiple structures to a set of pre-aligned structures.

Valid Values: Align Structures , Extend Existing Alignment

In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequence alignments in all open Sequence Windows.

If Alignment Type is "Align Structures", at least two sequences in the selected alignment must have structure linking.

If Alignment Type is "Extend Existing Alignment", at least one sequence in the selected alignment must have structure linking.

In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose one or more protein structures from the list of all visible proteins.

The alignment of structures in the reference sequence alignment will not be changed as new structures specified in the Input Sequence Alignment parameter group are added to the alignment.

Maximum number of unaligned residues at the termini that will not be penalized by any gap penalties (this makes it a pseudo local alignment)

Speed up the alignment calculation by considering fewer neighboring residues.

## Align Structures (MODELER)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Align Structures (MODELER) protocol allows you to align a set of protein
sequences based on their structure similarity; the sequences of the protein
structures need to be collected in one Sequence
Window with or without initial alignment.

This protocol serves to prealign
protein structures to be used in the Build
Homology Models protocol to create the structures of a model sequence.

The protocol also allows you to align a set of protein structures to a set of prealigned protein structures.
If more than one proteins are to be added to the existing alignment, the new structures will be
aligned by structure alignment, and then the two sets of aligned structures will be merged together by
aligning two structure profiles.

The Align Structures (MODELER) protocol allows you to perform the following:

* Align a set of protein structures

* Align a set of protein structures to a preexisting structure alignment

* Open two or more protein structures into a single Molecule Window.

* Choose Sequence | Show Sequence from the menu bar to open the sequences
in a Sequence Window.

* In the Protocols Explorer , 
open Macromolecules | Align Structures | Align Structures (MODELER) .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Alignment Type Set to Align Structures . Input Sequence Alignment Select the corresponding Sequence Window name. Input Sequence Alignment | Input Protein Molecules Select two or more protein structures to align. For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Structures (MODELER) - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Alignment Type | Set to Align Structures . |
| Input Sequence Alignment | Select the corresponding Sequence Window name. |
| Input Sequence Alignment \| Input Protein Molecules | Select two or more protein structures to align. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Structures (MODELER) - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

* Open the structures of the preexisting alignment in a Molecule Window.

* Open the sequence alignment of the aligned structures in a Sequence Window.

* Open one or more protein structures to be added to the alignment in a new Molecule Window.

* Choose Sequence | Show Sequence from the menu bar to open the sequences
of the second set of molecules in a Sequence Window.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Macromolecules | Align Structures | Align Structures (MODELER) .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Alignment Type Set to Extend Existing Alignment . Input Sequence Alignment Select the second Sequence Window name. Input Sequence Alignment | Input Protein Molecules Select one or more protein structures to be added to the alignment. Reference Sequence Alignment Select the first Sequence Window name. Reference Sequence Alignment | Input Protein Molecules Select two or more
protein structures to which the previous selected
structures will be aligned. For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Structures (MODELER) - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Alignment Type | Set to Extend Existing Alignment . |
| Input Sequence Alignment | Select the second Sequence Window name. |
| Input Sequence Alignment \| Input Protein Molecules | Select one or more protein structures to be added to the alignment. |
| Reference Sequence Alignment | Select the first Sequence Window name. |
| Reference Sequence Alignment \| Input Protein Molecules | Select two or more protein structures to which the previous selected structures will be aligned. |

#### Viewing the report

Double-click on the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report. 
The summary section of the Report contains the main-chain RMSD and the number of overlapping residues between the superimposed input molecules.

If the run failed, check the Error section. Additionally, you
can open the MODELER log file to obtain detailed error information. First, check the MODELER log file for the error messages by searching for the
string "_E>". These messages are usually critical. Next, check for the warning messages by searching for the string "_W>".

#### Analyzing output alignment and superimposition

Click the View Results button in the report to open <alignment>.bsml and <alignment>.dsv to view the output alignment and superimposed protein structures.
All sequences in the Sequence Window are linked to corresponding protein structures automatically.

The input molecules are superimposed according to the output alignment to the first protein in the alignment. Main-chain atom RMSD for each pair of protein is also displayed in the report.
You can use the Structure | RMSD | by Sequence Alignment command to calculate C-alpha or other RMSD.

# Analyze Crystal Contacts - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_analyze_crystal_contacts-para.htm

## Analyze Crystal Contacts - Parameters

### Identifies contacts between symmetry-related molecules

Generates symmetry related molecules around the input structure. Contact surface areas and nonbond interactions between the original molecule and its symmetry mates are reported.

The display of the resulting structure in Discovery Studio can be centered on a region of interest specified as Focus Residues , otherwise on the original structure. The visibility of the surrounding copies can be limited to a shell of residues determined by the Display Cutoff .

The structure will have its carbon atoms colored to highlight the contact residues and to distinguish between the central molecule and symmetry copies:

* Contact residues in original molecule: light purple

* Contact residues in symmetry copies: light green.

* Other residues in original molecule: gray

* Other residues in symmetry copies: pale cyan

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Structure | The molecule file(s) or URL to read. In Discovery Studio, select a macromolecule which must be in a crystal cell. |
| Remove Alternate Conformers | If True, all alternate conformers will be removed. Valid Values: True , False |
| Symmetry Generation | Distance cutoff (Å) for symmetry neighbor generation. Copies of the Input Structure will be generated by applying symmetry transformations if the distance between any atom in the copy is within this distance of the original structure. |
| Residues Within Radius Only | Only generate residues that have at least one atom within the specified Symmetry Generation cutoff distance of the reference molecule. This can be useful for generating the environment around the central molecule if full molecule copies are not required. Valid Values: True, False |
| Exclude Special Positions | Specifies whether to filter atoms in the symmetry copies to exclude cases where a copy is very close to the original atom. This can occur if an atom lies on a crystallographic special position rather than a general position. Valid Values: True , False |
| Exclusion Tolerance | Specifies the minimum distance (Å) a symmetry generated atom can be from the original before it is filtered when Exclude Special Positions is True. |
| Check Occupancy | If True, then the suspected duplicate will only be excluded if its occupancy is less than 1. This allows for larger tolerances to be used in cases where occupancy is known. Valid Values: True , False |
| Display Cutoff | If this parameter is set, then the initial display will be limited to the central molecule and any residue in symmetry copies with at least one atom within this distance (Å) from it. If Focus Residues have been specified then these are used rather than the whole of the central molecule. |
| Focus Residues | Specifies a group of residues which are known to be of particular interest. If this parameter is set then the initial display of the structure will be centered on these residues, with only residues (whether from the central molecule or symmetry copies) which have an atom within the Display Cutoff being visible. This allows for easier visual assessment of the contacts and interactions in this region. In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace. You can also specify ranges of residues by specifying the first and last residue in the range. Example: "A:ASP64 A:GLY70 A:VAL80-A:GLU83". In Discovery Studio you specify the Focus Residues by selecting an existing group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the current selection by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu. This will be replaced in the output structure by a Focus Residues group which contains the full residues containing all atoms in the selection. |
| Contact Surface Definition | Parameters which control the definition of the contact surface areas. |
| Surface Area Probe Radius | Specifies the radius of the probing sphere (Å). The area is traced out by the center of the probe when the probe rolls over the protein surface, which in turn is defined by the van der Waals radii of the atoms. If a probe radius of 1.4 is used, the surface area reported by this protocol will be the differences in solvent accessible surface area when the ligand and receptor are in a complex and when they are isolated molecules. But if a value of 0.6 is used, the difference in areas will more closely represent the contact areas at the interface between the ligand and receptor. Valid Values: 1.4, 0.6 |
| Percent Contact Area Threshold | Specifies the percentage surface area change threshold between the complexed and isolated state for a residue to be classified as part of the interface. |
| Nonbond Interactions | Controls nonbond interaction calculations. The categories of nonbond interactions to be reported can be specified. The group contains parameters for adjusting the commoner interaction criteria. The nonbond monitor can be further adjusted when the crystal structure is displayed in Discovery Studio. Note that only direct interactions between the original structure and its symmetry copies are monitored. Indirect interactions between them (water mediated hydrogen bonds and other water hydrogen bond networks) can be examined using the Water Interactions option Valid Values: Hydrogen Bond , Electrostatic , Hydrophobic , Halogen , Miscellaneous , Unfavorable |
| Maximum Hydrogen Bond Distance | Maximum distance between a strong acceptor atom and a strong heavy atom hydrogen donor atom to be considered a hydrogen bond (Å). Oxygen and Nitrogen are strong donor/acceptor atoms. |
| Maximum Weak Hydrogen Bond Distance | Maximum distance (Å) between an acceptor atom and a heavy atom hydrogen donor atom to be considered a hydrogen bond if one or both are not strong (i.e. an element type other than Oxygen or Nitrogen.) |
| Maximum Salt Bridge Distance | Maximum distance between bridging atoms (Å). |
| Maximum Charge-charge Distance | Specifies the distance criterion for all favorable and unfavorable charge interactions. |
| Steric Bump VDW Fraction | Specifies the van der Waals (VDW)-based steric interaction parameter. |
| Water Interactions | Specifies whether to identify water interactions in the regions between the central molecule and symmetry copies. This allows water mediated (bridging) hydrogen bonds and water networks to be examined. The layer consists of all water molecules which lie within the Water Layer Cutoff distance of the non-water moieties of both the central molecule and of at least one symmetry copy. Valid Values: True , False |
| Water Mediated Only | Specifies whether to monitor all hydrogen bonds involving water or only those which form bridges. Valid Values: True , False |
| Water Layer Cutoff | Distance cutoff (Å) for the water layer. |

The molecule file(s) or URL to read.

If True, all alternate conformers will be removed.

Valid Values: True , False

# Analyze Crystal Contacts

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_analyze_crystal_contacts.htm

## Analyze Crystal Contacts

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Analyze Crystal Contacts protocol builds a shell of symmetry related copies around the asymmetric unit of a crystal structure and analyzes contacts and interactions. The contact residues are identified as the residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different in the isolated molecule compared to the crystal form.

* Load the structure into the Graphics View . This will typically be an unmodified crystal structure from the Protein Databank.

* If there is a region of the structure of particular interest that is not already defined as a Group, select the residues for that region; you can set the Focus Residues parameter to "Create New Group from Selection" later.

* Open the Macromolecules | Protein Report and Analysis tools and click Analyze Crystal Contacts... to open the Analyze Crystal Contacts dialog.

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Structure Select the structure to be analyzed. Focus Residues If required, select an existing group from the parameter menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the current selection by choosing the "Create New Group from Selection..." entry. Note that this will be replaced in the output structure by a Focus Residues group that contains the full residues containing all atoms in the selection. For details about the remaining parameters, see Analyze Crystal Contacts - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Structure | Select the structure to be analyzed. |
| Focus Residues | If required, select an existing group from the parameter menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the current selection by choosing the "Create New Group from Selection..." entry. Note that this will be replaced in the output structure by a Focus Residues group that contains the full residues containing all atoms in the selection. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Analyze Crystal Contacts - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, a new Molecule Window opens containing the structure surrounded by a shell of symmetry copies. 
If you ran the job in the background, double-click on the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report and click View Results to open the crystal contact structure, which is displayed as follows:

* The Graphics View is centered on the original structure, or the Focus Residues if specified.

* If Display Cutoff is set, the display of the surrounding region is limited to a shell of residues.

* Carbon atoms of the contact residues in the central molecule are colored light purple while those of the symmetry copies are light green.

* For non-contact residues, carbon atoms in the original molecule are gray while those of the copies are pale cyan.

* If specified, non-bond interactions and water interactions between the central molecule and the copies are shown.

Click the Molecule tab in the Data Table View to show the original molecule and symmetry copies. The Symmetry property details the symmetry operations and translations that generated each copy. There are also properties containing the contact surface areas between the central molecule and each copy.

The Hierarchy View contains the original molecule and the copies. The following assemblies containing groups of residues are present depending on the structure and protocol settings:

* Crystal Contact Residues: Residues that form the contact areas between the central molecule and each symmetry copy.

* Focus Contact Residues: Contact residues involving Focus Residues.

* Ligand Contact Residues: Contact residues involving Ligand group residues.

* Water Layer: Water residues in the Water Layer region between the central molecule and the symmetry copies.

Additionally, there is a Crystal Non-bond Interactions monitor and associated Monitored Atoms for Crystal Non-bond Interactions group. If the structure contains solvent, and water layer interactions were requested, a Water Layer Interactions monitor and its monitored atom group is created.

The Report tabulates the contact areas found between the central molecule and each symmetry copy. A second table provides a summary of the numbers of each category of non-bond interaction found between the central molecule and each copy. Each cell provides a link to a detailed table of interactions. Use the Back tool on the Report context menu to return to the main table.

Some structures in the Protein Databank have their symmetry transformations specified in a non-standard form, which cannot be correctly interpreted by the symmetry generator. Such cases are liable to yield anomalously high buried surface areas and/or an unusually high number of unfavorable interactions.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>_interactions.dsv | The output structure with symmetry copies, contact areas and nonbond interactions. |
| <molecule>_interactions.csv | A csv table with details of favorable nonbond interactions. |
| <molecule>_contact_areas.csv | A csv table with details of contact areas between the asymmetric unit and symmetry copies. |

# Analyze Protein Interface - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_analyze_protein_interface-para.htm

## Analyze Protein Interface - Parameters

### Analyzes interactions at a protein interface

Identifies the binding interface between two protein domains and calculates the interactions between them.

The interface residues can be identified as those within a specified cutoff distance of the neighboring chain or as the residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different depending on whether the protein chains are in a complex or are isolated.

The following properties and interactions between interface residues are calculated and annotated on the output molecule:

* Amino acid composition

* Hydrogen bonds

* Pi interactions

* Salt bridges

In addition, this information is reported in an xlsx file and a set of csv files.

Notes:

* The two protein domains must all be part of one molecule. One domain must be defined by the Ligand Chains parameter, which specifies one or more chains; the remainder of the structure forms the second domain.

* The calculation will be faster without explicit hydrogen atoms. However, results may vary in the absence of hydrogens due to the different hydrogen-bond perception.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Complex | Specifies the protein complex. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose the protein structures from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Ligand Chains | Specifies one or more chains to define the ligand in a molecular complex. The remaining chains in the molecular system are considered the receptor. A chain is defined as : [molecule name]:[chain name]_[chain number] Example: 1bxi:A_1,1bxi:B_2 |
| Maximum Hydrogen Bond Distance | Maximum distance between a strong acceptor atom and a strong heavy atom hydrogen donor atom to be considered a hydrogen bond (Å). Oxygen and Nitrogen are strong donor/acceptor atoms. |
| Maximum Weak Hydrogen Bond Distance | Maximum distance (Å) between an acceptor atom and a heavy atom hydrogen donor atom to be considered a hydrogen bond if one or both are not strong (i.e. an element type other than Oxygen or Nitrogen.) |
| Maximum Salt Bridge Distance | Maximum distance between bridging atoms (Å). |
| Neighbor Distance Cutoff | Cutoff (Å) used to determine whether 2 residues are neighboring. This information is reported in the 'Interface Interactions' table of the output. |
| Interface Definition | The interfacing residues can be defined by two methods: Distance Cutoff : Ligand residues that have at least one atom within the cutoff distance of the receptor or receptor residues that have at least one atom within the cutoff distance of the ligand. Contact Area : The residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different when the proteins are in a complex versus isolated. Valid Values: Distance Cutoff, Contact Area |
| Interface Distance Cutoff | Specifies the distance cutoff used to define interfacing residues (Å). |
| Surface Area Probe Radius | Specifies the radius of the probing sphere (Å). The area is traced out by the center of the probe when the probe rolls over the protein surface, which in turn is defined by the van der Waals radii of the atoms. If a probe radius of 1.4 is used, the surface area reported by this protocol will be the differences in solvent accessible surface area when the ligand and receptor are in a complex and when they are isolated molecules. But if a value of 0.6 is used, the difference in areas will more closely represent the contact areas at the interface between the ligand and receptor. Valid Values: 1.4, 0.6 |
| Percent Contact Area Threshold | Specifies the percentage surface area change threshold between the complexed and isolated state for a residue to be classified as part of the interface. |

Specifies the protein complex.
In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose the protein structures from the list of all visible proteins.

Specifies one or more chains to define the ligand in a molecular complex. The remaining chains in the molecular system are considered the receptor.

A chain is defined as :
[molecule name]:[chain name]_[chain number]

Example: 1bxi:A_1,1bxi:B_2

Maximum distance between a strong acceptor atom and a strong heavy atom hydrogen donor atom to be considered a hydrogen bond (Å). Oxygen and Nitrogen are strong donor/acceptor atoms.

Maximum distance (Å) between an acceptor atom and a heavy atom hydrogen donor atom to be considered a hydrogen bond if one or both are not strong (i.e. an element type other than Oxygen or Nitrogen.)

Maximum distance between bridging atoms (Å).

Cutoff (Å) used to determine whether 2 residues are neighboring. This information is reported in the 'Interface Interactions' table of the output.

The interfacing residues can be defined by two methods:

* Distance Cutoff : Ligand residues that have at least one atom within the cutoff distance of the receptor or receptor residues that have at least one atom within the cutoff distance of the ligand.

* Contact Area : The residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different when the proteins are in a complex versus isolated.

Valid Values: Distance Cutoff, Contact Area

Specifies the distance cutoff used to define interfacing residues (Å).

Specifies the radius of the probing sphere (Å). The area is traced out by the center of the probe when the probe rolls over the protein surface, which in turn is defined by the van der Waals radii of the atoms.

If a probe radius of 1.4 is used, the surface area reported by this protocol will be the differences in solvent accessible surface area when the ligand and receptor are in a complex and when they are isolated molecules. But if a value of 0.6 is used, the difference in areas will more closely represent the contact areas at the interface between the ligand and receptor.

Valid Values: 1.4, 0.6

Specifies the percentage surface area change threshold between the complexed and isolated state for a residue to be classified as part of the interface.

# Analyze Protein Interface

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_analyze_protein_interface.htm

## Analyze Protein Interface

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Analyze Protein Interface protocol provides methods for identifying the residues found at a protein-protein interface and analyzing the interactions that occur there. The interface residues can be identified as those within a specified cutoff distance of the neighboring chain or as the residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different depending on whether the protein chains are in a complex or are isolated.

The properties reported include:

* Amino acid composition for the entire complex

* Amino acid composition for the interface residues only

* Hydrogen bonds between the interface residues

* Pi interactions between the interface residues

* Salt bridges between the interface residues

If the interface residues are determined by a difference in the solvent accessible surface area (ΔSASA), the interface residues' ΔSASA and their polar and non-polar contributions are also reported.

* Load the protein structure consisting of a molecule containing two or more chains into a Graphics View.

* Delete water molecules, ions, and ligands that are not part of the binding interface. 
This will improve performance and make the protein-protein interactions easier to analyze. However, if there are water molecules that have been identified as significant for interaction, they can be retained.

* Clean the protein structure. 
Note that the calculation will be faster without explicit hydrogen atoms, but the hydrogen bonding could be different relative to a structure with hydrogen atoms.
For this application, alternate conformations can be kept as they may show interesting interactions. 
Any atoms or loops added near the binding interface are liable to make the results unreliable. These factors may influence your choice of preparation method. You can run the Prepare Proteins protocol to automatically prepare the structure, which adds hydrogens necessary for the chosen forcefield, completes residues with missing atoms, removes alternate conformations, and optionally builds missing loops. Alternatively, you can prepare the structure manually: Set the preferences on the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog so that termini will be added, set the hydrogen preference and other options as desired, and then use the Prepare Protein tools to clean the protein structures.

* You can run the Prepare Proteins protocol to automatically prepare the structure, which adds hydrogens necessary for the chosen forcefield, completes residues with missing atoms, removes alternate conformations, and optionally builds missing loops.

* Alternatively, you can prepare the structure manually: Set the preferences on the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog so that termini will be added, set the hydrogen preference and other options as desired, and then use the Prepare Protein tools to clean the protein structures.

* Open the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools and click Analyze Protein Interface... to open the Analyze Protein Interface dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Protein Complex Specify the protein structure to be analyzed. Ligand Chains Select one or more (but not all) chains from the list. Interface Definition Specify the method for determining the interface: Distance Cutoff: Residues in the ligand chains that have at least one atom within the distance cutoff of the receptor chains and residues in the receptor chains that have at least one atom within the distance cutoff of the ligand chains. Contact Area: The residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different when the ligand and receptor chains are in a complex versus isolated. For details about the remaining parameters, see Analyze Protein Interface - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Complex | Specify the protein structure to be analyzed. |
| Ligand Chains | Select one or more (but not all) chains from the list. |
| Interface Definition | Specify the method for determining the interface: Distance Cutoff: Residues in the ligand chains that have at least one atom within the distance cutoff of the receptor chains and residues in the receptor chains that have at least one atom within the distance cutoff of the ligand chains. Contact Area: The residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different when the ligand and receptor chains are in a complex versus isolated. |

* Distance Cutoff: Residues in the ligand chains that have at least one atom within the distance cutoff of the receptor chains and residues in the receptor chains that have at least one atom within the distance cutoff of the ligand chains.

* Contact Area: The residues whose solvent accessible surface area is different when the ligand and receptor chains are in a complex versus isolated.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Analyze Protein Interface - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, a Molecule Window opens that displays the annotated protein structure with hydrogen bond monitors, Pi interaction monitors, and salt bridge distance monitors for the interface.
Additionally, the carbon atoms of the interface residues from the ligand chains are colored green.

Two new groups are added, "Interface Ligand Residues" and "Interface Receptor Residues", which are groups of interface residues from the corresponding ligand and receptor chains.

Properties are added to the Molecule tab of the data table including the various types of contact surface area calculated and the number of hydrogen bond, Pi, and salt bridge interactions.

Most of the information produced by this protocol can be viewed in the output csv and xlsx files. These can be accessed from the Report, which can be displayed by double-clicking on the job in the Jobs Explorer .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. Check the Summary and Error sections if the protocol failed. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are indicated here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | Protein complex with interface residue groups and monitors. |
| AminoAcidComposition.csv | Percentages of each amino acid type for the entire complex and the interface residues. |
| HydrogenBonds.csv | Hydrogen bonds occurring at the interface of the complex. |
| InterfaceAnalysis.xlsx | Excel file containing data from each output csv file reported in separate sheets. |
| InterfaceInteractions.csv | A table of ligand interface residues along the top and receptor interface residues on the left. Each cell depicts the type of interaction occurring between the two interface residues. A "-" indicates no interaction, "N" indicates neighboring (i.e., the residues are within the cutoff distance), "H" indicates a hydrogen bond, "Pi" indicates a Pi interaction, and "SB" indicates a salt bridge. |
| ContactSurfaceArea.csv | Lists the surface area or contact area for each residue at the interface. The polar and non-polar contributions are also reported. |
| PiInteractions.csv | Pi interactions occurring at the interface of the complex. |
| SaltBridges.csv | Salt bridges occurring at the interface of the complex. |

# Build Homology Models - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_build_homology_models-para.htm

## Build Homology Models - Parameters

### Builds homology models of a protein sequence using one or more template structures

Uses MODELER automodel (and loopmodel if Refine Loops is True) to build homology models. An accurate sequence alignment between the model and the template proteins are essential to achieve high quality models.

Set Disulfide Bridges , Cis-Prolines , and Additional Restraints to add modeling restraints. Set Copy Ligands to copy ligands of the templates to the models as rigid bodies. If some sequence segments of the model sequence are not aligned with the templates, Refine Loops can be used to build additional refinement models for these segments.

The B-factors provided in homology models represent an average of the B-factors found in template structures from crystallographic origins. These B-factors may be useful for understanding the dynamics of the models, but should not be taken as accurate estimations of thermal motion.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence Alignment | Alignment of the model sequence to one or more template structures. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequence alignments in all open Sequence Windows. |
| Input Template Structures | Protein structures that have linked sequences in the Input Sequence Alignment to be used as modeling templates. In Pipeline Pilot, specify the template protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose the template structures from the list of all visible proteins. Note : In Discovery Studio, template structures have to be linked to the corresponding sequences in the Input Sequence Alignment and all template structures have to be in the same Molecule Window. Template structures have to have the exact same name as the corresponding sequences in the Input Sequence Alignment . For this reason, the only allowed characters for template and sequence names are alpha-numerical characters, dot "." and underscore "_". |
| Input Model Sequence | Name of the sequence for which to build models. |
| Copy From Templates | Group of parameters to specify parts of templates to be copied into the homology model. |
| Copy From Templates Ligands | Specifies a list of ligands (HETATM) to be copied from templates to model structures. Ligands are treated as 'block' residues (BLK residues). MODELER constrains BLK residues to their conformations in the templates from which they are copied and treats them as rigid bodies. No chemical information is used and all atoms in BLK residues are treated as type `undf'. MODELER ignores Lennard-Jones and Coulomb terms involving `undf' atoms. During optimization process, distance restraints are applied to preserve the relative position of the ligand atoms in the model compared to their position in the corresponding template as much as possible. In Pipeline Pilot, ligands are separated by commas and defined by [molecule]:[chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: "2cha::TOS51,3est::SO4290,3est::SO4295,3est::CA280". In Discovery Studio, select the ligands to copy in the drop-down list. Notes: Ligands listed here must NOT be included in the input alignment. NO DUPLICATES are allowed in the ligand list. If duplicate ligand identifiers should occur, please rename one of the ligands to make each ligand identifier in the list unique (e.g. either by changing the residue name or the chain id). See Also: MODELER documentation on BLK residues: http://salilab.org/modeller/manual/node101.html#SECTION001021200000000000000 |
| Copy From Templates Nucleic Acid Chains | Specifies a list of nucleic acid chains to be copied from templates to model structures. In Pipeline Pilot, the chains are separated by commas and defined by [molecule]:[chain]:[first residue]-[last residue]. Example: "3cro:A:DA1-DT20,3cro:B:DT1-DT20". In Discovery Studio, select the chains to copy in the drop-down list. Note: Chains listed here must NOT be included in the input alignment. |
| Copy From Templates Protein | Reference template used to copy coordinates for regions specified in Copy Regions . Copying coordinates from a template is generally only recommended if there is a high degree of sequence similarity between model and the template. |
| Copy From Templates Protein Copy Regions | Regions copied from the reference template. Coordinates for atoms in these regions are copied without further optimization. In Pipeline Pilot, list the regions as a comma separated list of residue ranges. A residue range consists of a starting residue and an ending residue connected by "-". A residue is specified by the index of the residue in the model sequence (starting with 1 for the first residue). Example: "18-22,35-41". In Discovery Studio, select the residues to be copied in the reference template, then check the corresponding check boxes in the drop down list of the parameter. Note: Reference template residues that are specified as part of the Copy Regions , but which are not aligned with a residue of the Input Model Sequence in the Input Sequence Alignment , are ignored. |
| Copy From Templates Protein Optimize Sidechains | Refine all side chains in Copy Regions . If False, only atoms that do not have corresponding template atoms are refined. Valid Values: True, False |
| Copy From Templates Waters | Specifies if water molecules are copied from the templates. If set to True, all water molecules in any of the template structures will be copied into the model. Quite often, waters from different templates will overlap and will create steric clashes. Therefore, the overlapping waters should be removed from the templates prior to model creation if this option is set to True. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number of Models | Number of models to be created. |
| Start Model Index | MODELER randomizes the initial structure before producing each final model. Use Start Model Index to change the randomization seed to build models from different initial structures. Start Model Index is also used in the output model names. For example, if you build two models for sequence xyz with Start Model Index = 3 , the output model names are xyz.M0003 and xyz.M0004 . |
| Optimization Level | Specifies the amount of molecular dynamics with simulated annealing to perform. High/Medium/Low: Different levels of sampling in simulated annealing step. None: No molecular dynamics with simulated annealing. Higher levels of sampling can produce more accurate models but also require more computation time. Valid Values: High , Medium, Low, None |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Cut Overhangs | Remove unaligned residues at the terminals in Input Model Sequence . Valid Values: True , False |
| Disulfide Bridges | List of disulfide bridges between cysteine residues. In Discovery Studio, use the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog to specify the list of disulfide bridges. In Pipeline Pilot, enter a comma separated list of disulfide bridges. A disulfide bridge consists of two cysteine residues connected by '-', where a cysteine residue is defined by :CYS[residue number]. The residue number is the sequential index of the residue, or if Input Sequence Alignment is read from a bsml file, residue numbers can be non-sequential (user specified) and may include insertion codes. Examples: ":CYS32-:CYS70,:CYS85-:CYS105" or ":CYS22-:CYS71A,:CYS45A-:CYS102". If the Input Model Sequence has multiple chains, the chain of the CYS residue needs to be specified as CH[chain index]. Example: "CH1:CYS32-CH1:CYS70,CH2:CYS15-CH2:CYS40A". |
| Cis-Prolines | List of proline residues in cis-conformation. In Discovery Studio, select cis-prolines in the drop-down list. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a comma-separated list of cis-proline residues. A proline residue is defined by :PRO[residue number]. The residue number is the sequential index of the residue, or if Input Sequence Alignment is read from a bsml file, residue numbers can be non-sequential (user specified) and may include insertion codes. Example: ":PRO12,:PRO23,:PRO33", or ":PRO11A,:PRO21,:PRO54A" If the Input Model Sequence has multiple chains, the chain of the PRO residue needs to be specified as CH[chain index]. Example: "CH1:PRO12,CH2:PRO15A,CH2:PRO53". |
| Additional Restraints | Adds distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and other MODELER restraints. MODELER provides a set of Python functions for generating and manipulating restraints. In Pipeline Pilot, the Python script entered here will be inserted into the MODELER special restraints function. An example Python script with explanatory comments is provided as the default value of the parameter. In Discovery Studio, use the Distance , Secondary Structure and Symmetry tabs of the Define Additional Restraints Dialog to specify the restraints. Discovery Studio will automatically generate a MODELER Python script from the data entered. The restraints should be specified using the residues from the model sequence. For example, to add a symmetry restraint, specify two segments from the model sequence which should be kept symmetrical during model generation. Notes : Symmetry Restraints can only be used if Cut Overhangs is False. |
| Refine Loops | Run refinement on detected loop regions which are defined as model sequence segments not aligned with any templates. Insertions up to 11 residues will be refined when this parameter is set to True. Valid Values: True, False |
| Refine Loops Number of Models | Specifies the number of models to be created by loop optimization. |
| Refine Loops Optimization Level | Specifies the amount of molecular dynamics with simulated annealing to perform for loop refinement. High/Medium/Low: Different levels of sampling in simulated annealing step. None: No molecular dynamics with simulated annealing. Higher levels of sampling can produce more accurate models but also require more computation time. Valid Values: High , Medium, Low, None |
| Refine Loops Use DOPE Method | Uses the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) method to refine loops. Select High Resolution to use the DOPE-HR method, a method very similar to the DOPE method but obtained at higher resolution. See Also: Shen, M.-Y.; Sali, A. Statistical potential for assessment and prediction of protein structures. Protein Science 2006 , 15, 2507-2524. Valid Values: True , False, High Resolution |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

* Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size.

* By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal.

Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing.

Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster).

Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers.

Preserve the initial order of the data records.
