# Build Homology Models

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_build_homology_models.htm

## Build Homology Models

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Build Homology Models protocol allows you to create protein
structures of a model sequence based on an alignment of the model sequence with
other related known protein structures.

The input alignment can be obtained from the Align Sequence to Templates protocol.

If there is any chain break in the model sequence in the Sequence Window, the model is built as multiple
chains. Chain breaks can be edited using the Sequence | Chain menu.

Ligands, nucleic acid chains, and waters in the template proteins can be copied into model structures, and are treated as rigid bodies in the model protein.

A domain or all structure of a template protein can be copied to the model protein. If this is specified,
then the part of the model structure that is aligned to the specified template will be directly copied from
the input template structure without further optimization.

If there are insertions or deletions in the model sequence with respect to the template(s)
according to the input sequence alignment, those regions are defined as loops and can
be further refined within this protocol.

The last step of the protocol calculates the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) score for each model and
the scores are reported in the output of the protocol for evaluating the quality of the models.

* Load one or more known protein structures into a Molecule Window. All templates must be loaded into a single Molecule Window.

All templates must be loaded into a single Molecule Window.

* Open an existing alignment of the template sequences and the model sequence into the Sequence Window. Note that the template sequences in the Sequence Window are automatically linked with the template structures in the Graphics View.

* Open the Macromolecules | Create Homology tools tools and click Build Homology Models... to open the Build Homology Models dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Sequence Alignment Select the loaded alignment Input Model Sequence Select the model sequence name. Input Template Structures Select all template structures. Cut Overhangs Set to True to cut terminal residues of the Input Model Sequence parameter that are not aligned with the templates. Disulfide Bridges Opens the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog to select pairs of Cysteine residues to connect by a disulfide bridge. Additional Restraints Opens the Define Additional Restraints dialog to define additional restraints including distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and symmetry restraints. Copy From Templates | Ligands Select any ligand to be copied from the template structures into the model structure. Copy From Templates | Nucleic Acid Chains Select any chain to be copied from the template structures into the model structure. Copy From Templates | Protein This parameter group specifies regions of the model for which the coordinates are copied from a specific template. The template from which the coordinates will be copied is specified in the Protein parameter. The Copy Regions parameter specifies a list of residues ranges for which to copy the coordinates and the Refine Sidechains parameter specifies if the side-chains in the copied regions will be refined. Number of Models Specify how many models to create, each from a different initial
structure. You can expand this group and set Start Model Index to use different initial structures. If there are insertions or deletions in the Input Model Sequence parameter with respect to the template(s) according to the Input Sequence Alignment parameter, those regions are defined as loops and you can set Refine Loops to True to build refinement models on these regions. Refer to Loop Optimization for the definition of loop. For details about the remaining parameters, see Build Homology Models - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence Alignment | Select the loaded alignment |
| Input Model Sequence | Select the model sequence name. |
| Input Template Structures | Select all template structures. |
| Cut Overhangs | Set to True to cut terminal residues of the Input Model Sequence parameter that are not aligned with the templates. |
| Disulfide Bridges | Opens the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog to select pairs of Cysteine residues to connect by a disulfide bridge. |
| Additional Restraints | Opens the Define Additional Restraints dialog to define additional restraints including distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and symmetry restraints. |
| Copy From Templates \| Ligands | Select any ligand to be copied from the template structures into the model structure. |
| Copy From Templates \| Nucleic Acid Chains | Select any chain to be copied from the template structures into the model structure. |
| Copy From Templates \| Protein | This parameter group specifies regions of the model for which the coordinates are copied from a specific template. The template from which the coordinates will be copied is specified in the Protein parameter. The Copy Regions parameter specifies a list of residues ranges for which to copy the coordinates and the Refine Sidechains parameter specifies if the side-chains in the copied regions will be refined. |
| Number of Models | Specify how many models to create, each from a different initial structure. You can expand this group and set Start Model Index to use different initial structures. |

If there are insertions or deletions in the Input Model Sequence parameter with respect to the template(s) according to the Input Sequence Alignment parameter, those regions are defined as loops and you can set Refine Loops to True to build refinement models on these regions. Refer to Loop Optimization for the definition of loop.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Build Homology Models - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* Analyzing output models

* PDF energy

* Troubleshooting

When the interactive job finishes, the model structures are opened into one Molecule Window together with all the templates. Models and templates 
are superimposed. The sequence alignment of the models and the templates is also opened and the sequences are linked to the corresponding structures.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the structures and the sequence alignment.

The number of output models is determined by the setting on the Number of Models parameter and the Refine Loops | Number of Loop Models parameter. For example, if the Number of Models parameter value is 3 and the Number of Loop Models parameter value is 2 , 9 models will be created with 3 initial models and 6 loop models built by further optimizing 
the loop regions of each of the corresponding initial models.

The MODELER PDF energy data and DOPE Scores are stored in each model structure.
Click the Molecule tab in the Data Table View to examine the PDF Total Energy , PDF Physical Energy , and DOPE Score for each model. 
Click the AminoAcid tab to examine the 40 PDF energy properties added
to each residue. All these property names are prefixed with PDF for clarity. PDF property names that contain N_ indicate
normalized PDF energies. You can select these properties and use the commands in the Chart menu to
create plots to aid in their analysis. Also, refer to the PDF Energy and PDF Energy Key sections below for more information.

Residue groups are created for each output model to indicate which parts of the model are highly homologous to the templates
and which parts are insertions (e.g., loops). If only one template was used in building the models, the following groups can be created:

* Identical: Residue types of the model and template are identical at these alignment positions.

* Strong Similarity: Residue types of the model and template are strongly similar at these alignment positions.

* Weak Similarity: Residue types of the model and template are weakly similar at these alignment positions.

* No match: Residue types of the model and template are not similar at these alignment positions.

* Insertion(i): Model residues at these positions are not aligned to any template residues (loops). A separate group is created for each loop segment, indexed by the number (i).

If the model is based on multiple templates, the following groups can be created:

* Identical: The Residue type of the model is identical to the residue type of at least one of the templates at these alignment positions.

* Non-Identical: The Residue type of the model does not match the residue type of any of the templates at these alignment positions.

* Insertion(i): Model residues at these positions are not aligned to any of the template residues (loops). A separate group is created for each loop segment, indexed by the number (i).

MODELER generates a large number of restraints to force a model towards the structure of the template(s) and to maintain good structure
geometry. At the end of a MODELER refinement, not all of the restraints are satisfied and the PDF energy (i.e., the value of the objective function)
associated with each residue can be summed to give an indication of the quality of the model in and around that residue. There is
no simple interpretation of the absolute value of the energy because parts of a model (for example residues adjacent to an insertion or deletion)
are almost certain to have higher restraint violations. The energies are useful in making comparisons between different models. Models with
lower energy in a given region are probably better in that region. If these models have been generated from different initial alignments of the
model sequence and the homologues, then lower energies are an indication of better alignment.

Molecular PDF energies for each model are observed in the Data Table View. PDF Total Energy is the total PDF energy,
that is the sum of the scoring function value of all homology-derived pseudo-energy terms and stereochemical pseudo-energy terms. PDF Physical Energy is the sum of energies of the stereochemical pseudo-energy terms which consist of valence
bonds, valence angles and torsion angles, improper torsion angles, and soft-sphere repulsion, as well as knowledge based non-bonded
potentials used only for loop and mutant modeling. Higher energy indicates a larger restraint violation in the model.

Molecular PDF energies for a model and a loop model are not directly comparable because the objective function for optimizing the loop is
different from the model building. PDF energy and DOPE scores are meaningful when comparing different basic models or comparing different 
loop models, but not for comparing basic models against loop models.

For each residue, PDF energy and normalized PDF energy are shown in the AminoAcid tab of Data Table View. The
PDF energy is the sum of PDF energies of a given restraint type involving a given residue, where the restraint type can be either a
homology derived restraint or stereochemical restraint. The normalized PDF energy is the PDF energy of a given residue divided by the number
of restraints of a given type associated with this residue.

Per-residue total PDF energy is stored in the molecule and can be used to create a variable-width ribbon or spectrum coloring on the
model using the Display Style... command on the Graphic View context menu (right-click in a blank area of the
Graphic View to display the context menu).

The quality of the model can be assessed using the Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) protocol. For structure regions that have a
low Verify Score and high PDF energies, it is necessary to re-evaluate the input alignment and regenerate the model with
refined alignment, or refine the structure using the Refine Loops protocol.

Build Homology Models produces slightly different results when the same calculation is executed on Windows and Linux. This is due to the
numerical differences in the floating point calculation. As a result, PDF energies or the atomic coordinates of the models calculated on
different hardware platforms are slightly different. The differences become larger with higher levels of optimization.

##### PDF Energies Key

The following table explains the meaning of the PDF energy types shown in the AminoAcid tab of the Data Table
View. The PDF energies are shown as PDF {Key} in the table and the normalized PDF energies are shown as PDF N_{Key} .

| Key | Energy type |
| --- | --- |
| Total | Residue PDF Energy |
| CACA | Distance restraints 1 (CA-CA) |
| NO | Distance restraints 2 (N-O) |
| PHPS | Phi/Psi pair of dihedral restraints |
| SSDS | Disulfide distance restraints |
| SSVA | Disulfide angle restraints |
| SSDA | Disulfide dihedral angle restraints |
| CHI1 | Side-chain Chi_1 dihedral restraints |
| CHI2 | Side-chain Chi_2 dihedral restraints |
| CHI3 | Side-chain Chi_3 dihedral restraints |
| CHI4 | Side-chain Chi_4 dihedral restraints |
| BLEN | Bond length potential |
| BANG | Bond angle potential |
| STOR | Stereochemical cosine torsion potential |
| SIMP | Stereochemical improper torsion potential |
| SFTS | Soft-sphere overlap restraints |
| OMGA | Main-chain Omega dihedral restraints |
| SDMN | Distance restraints 3 (SDCH-MNCH) |
| SDSD | Distance restraints 4 (SDCH-SDCH) |
| NONB | Non-bonded restraints |

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary that includes input and output files, the PDF Total Energy, the PDF Physical Energy, and the DOPE Score, and the parameters used. Check the Summary and Error sections if the protocol failed. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| *.dsv | The superimposed model and template structures. |
| *.bsml | Sequence alignment of models to templates. |

If you saved the Intermediate directory when running the protocol, you can open the MODELER log file to obtain
detailed error information. First, check the MODELER log file for error messages by searching for the string "_E>". These messages can only
rarely be ignored. Next, check for the warning messages by searching for the string "_W>".

# Build Mutants - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_build_mutants-para.htm

## Build Mutants - Parameters

### Mutates one or more residues of a protein and optimizes the local structure

Uses the MODELER program to mutate residues to specified types and optimize the conformation of both the mutated residues and any surrounding residues that lie within a specified Cut Radius . Mutants allows you to specify the residues you wish to mutate. Set Disulfide Bridges , Cis-Prolines , and Additional Restraints to add modeling restraints.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecule | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Mutants | List of residue mutations separated by comma. In Pipeline Pilot, a residue mutation is specified by a residue and its new residue name. A residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional) Examples: "A:ASN5GLN,B:THR28SER". In Discovery Studio, use the Define Mutants dialog to specify residue mutations. Select residues to be mutated from the Residue ID column and specify a new residue type in the Mutation column. Each selected residue can only be mutated into one new residue type. |
| Disulfide Bridges | List of disulfide bridges between Cysteine residues. In Pipeline Pilot, enter a comma separated list of disulfide bridges. A disulfide bridge consists of two Cysteine residues connected by '-', like B:CYS15-B:CYS40A, where a Cysteine residue is defined by [chain]:CYS[residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: "A:CYS32-A:CYS70,B:CYS15-B:CYS40A". In Discovery Studio, use the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog to specify the list of disulfide bridges. |
| Cis-Prolines | List of Proline residues in cis-conformation. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a comma-separated list of cis-Proline residues. A Proline residue is defined by [chain]:PRO[residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: "A:PRO12, A:PRO23, B:PRO12A". In Discovery Studio, select cis-Prolines in the drop-down list. |
| Additional Restraints | Adds distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and other MODELER restraints. MODELER provides a set of Python functions for generating and manipulating restraints. In Pipeline Pilot, the Python script entered here will be inserted into the MODELER special restraints function. An example Python script with explanatory comments is provided as default value of the parameter. In Discovery Studio, use the Distance , Secondary Structure and Symmetry tabs of the Define Additional Restraints dialog to specify the restraints. Discovery Studio will automatically generate a MODELER Python script from the data entered. The restraints should be specified using the residues from the model sequence. For example, to add a symmetry restraint, specify two segments from the model sequence which should be kept symmetrical during model generation. |
| Number of Models | Number of models to be created |
| Start Model Index | MODELER randomizes the initial structure before producing each final model. Use Start Model Index to change the randomization seed to build models from different initial structures. Start Model Index is also used in the output model names. For example, if you build two models for sequence "xyz" with Start Model Index ="3", the output model names are xyz.M0003 and xyz.M0004 . |
| Optimization Level | Specifies the amount of molecular dynamics with simulated annealing to perform. High/Medium/Low: Different levels of sampling in simulated annealing step. None: No molecular dynamics with simulated annealing. Higher levels of sampling can produce more accurate models but also require more computation time. Valid Values: High , Medium, Low, None |
| Cut Radius | Distance cutoff (Å) centered on the mutated residues for including neighboring residues in optimization. |

* Description

The Build Mutants protocol mutates selected residues to specified types and optimizes the conformation of both the mutated

The last step of the protocol calculates the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) score for each model and the scores are reported in the output of the protocol for evaluating the quality of the models.

# Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_calculate-mutation-energy-binding-para.htm

## Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) - Parameters

### Calculates the effect of mutations on the binding affinity

Performs combinatorial scanning mutagenesis in protein complexes. Depending on the selected in Mutation Sites mode generates all single, double or triple mutation sites from the set of selected residues, or use all of them to create mutants for all combinations of the specified amino-acid substitutions. For each single mutant the differences in the free energy of binding between the wild type and mutated structures is calculated.

Depending on the electrostatic model, specified by pH-dependent Electrostatics parameter, the calculations can be carried out either in a pH-independent or pH-dependent mode:

pH-independent mode : All electrostatic energy terms are calculated based on the protonation state of the input structure. Uses GBIM (Generalized Born with implicit membrane) approximation to account for the effect of the solvent. The electrostatic terms are approximated as a sum of Coulombic interactions and polar contributions to solvation energy. The energy function also contains the van der Waals interaction energy, a side-chain entropy term, and a non-polar surface dependent term.

pH-dependent mode : The mutation energy is calculated as a function of pH for the defined pH interval. The electrostatic terms are calculated by integration over the proton binding isotherms, derived from fractional protonations of acidic and basic residues which in turn are calculated using the same method as in the Calculate Protein Ionization component. The other terms are the same as in pH-independent mode.

The following residue properties are added to the data:

* MutationEnergy The total free energy difference between the wild type and mutated structures in pH-independent mode. It is calculated as a weighted sum of the VDW, Electrostatic, Entropy and Non-polar terms.

* MutationEnergy_pH The Mutation Energy calculated in pH-dependent mode at pH equal to the value of At pH parameter.

* ELEC : The electrostatic contribution to the mutation energy, calculated for the protonation state of input molecule.

* ELEC_pH : The electrostatic contribution to the mutation energy, calculated in pH-dependent mode at pH equal to the value of At pH parameter.

* VDW : The van der Waals contribution to mutation energy.

* ENTROPY : The side-chain entropy contribution to mutation energy.

* NonPolar : The non-polar (surface tension) contribution to mutation energy.

Notes:

* Only standard amino acid residues can be mutated.

* The input molecule can be typed with any one of the supported forcefields (except XPROLIG). However, the method supports only CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H. Therefore, the structures are internally re-typed accordingly to the Advanced/Forcefield parameter. In addition, all output molecules are typed by CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H, regardless of the forcefield type of the input molecule.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. pH-selective mutagenesis of protein-protein interfaces: In
silico design of therapeutic antibodies with prolonged half-life. PROTEINS: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics 2013 , 81, 704-714.

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S.Z. Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/solvent accessibility continuum solvent models J. Phys. Chem. B 2002 , 
106, 8726-8738.

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. A fast and accurate computational approach to protein ionization. Protein Science 2008 , 
17, 1955-1970.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. |
| Ligand Chain | Specifies one or more chains (ligands or/and subunits ) to define one of the binding partners in a molecular complex. A chain is defined as : [molecule name]:[chain name]_[chain number] Example: 1bxi:A_1,1bxi:B_2 |
| Mutation Sites | Specifies the number of residues to be mutated simultaneously. Available options are: Single Mutations : Generate single point mutations for the set of selected residues. For example, if 2 residues are selected to mutate to 2 different amino acid types in the Mutations parameter, 4 separate single mutations will be generated, e.g., if Mutations parameter is set to A:ALA5>HIS,ASP A:SER6>HIS,GLU then 4 single mutations: A:ALA5>HIS, A:ALA5>ASP, A:SER6>HIS, A:SER6>GLU will be generated. Double Mutations : Generates all combinations of double mutations for the set of selected residues. If N residues are selected to mutate to M amino acid types, the number of double mutations will be [N!/2(N-2)!]( M 2 ) . For example, if Mutations parameter is set to A:ALA5>HIS,ASP A:SER6>HIS,GLU then 4 double mutations: A:ALA5>HIS+A:SER6>HIS, A:ALA5>HIS+A:SER6>ASP, A:ALA5>ASP+A:SER6>HIS, A:ALA5>ASP+A:SER6>GLU will be generated. Triple Mutations : Similar to Double Mutations , but three residues will be mutated simultaneously. All Selected Residues : All of the selected residues will be mutated simultaneously to all combinations of defined amino acid types. For example, if 5 residues are selected each mutate to one amino acid type, except the last residue to be mutated to 2 different types, the number of mutations will be 2, e.g. A:HIS5>ALA A:SER6>ALA A:GLU7>ALA A:VAL8>ALA A:PHE9>ALA,HIS then the mutations will be: A:HIS5>ALA+A:SER6>ALA+A:GLU7>ALA+A:VAL8>ALA+A:PHE9>ALA and A:HIS5>ALA+A:SER6>ALA+A:GLU7>ALA+A:VAL8>ALA+A:PHE9>HIS. # Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_calculate-mutation-energy-binding.htm

## Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding)

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Output

* Analyzing Results

The Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) protocol evaluates the effect of mutations on the binding affinity of molecular partners in protein-protein and protein-ligand complexes. It performs combinatorial amino-acid scanning mutagenesis on a set of selected amino-acid residues by mutating them to one or more specified amino-acid types. The energy effect of each mutation on the binding affinity (mutation energy, ΔΔG mut ) is calculated as the difference between the binding free energy in the mutated structure and wild type protein:

ΔΔG mut = ΔΔG bind (mutant) - ΔΔG bind (wild type)

The binding free energy, ΔΔG bind , is defined as the difference between the free energy of the complex and unbound state. All energy terms are calculated by CHARMm and the electrostatics energy is calculated using a Generalized Born implicit solvent model. The total energy is calculated as an empirical weighted sum of van der Waals (E vdW ) interaction, electrostatic interactions (ΔG elec ), an entropy contribution (-TS sc ) related to the changes in side-chain mobility, and a non-polar, surface dependent, contribution to solvation energy (ΔG np ).

Depending on the selected electrostatic model, the calculations can be performed in pH-independent or pH-dependent mode.

#### pH-independent mode

The calculations are faster, but generally less accurate. The electrostatic calculations are based on the traditional approximation of fixed standard protonation states of all titratable residues. The total free energy, ΔGtot, of bound or unbound state are calculated as the following weighted sum of energy terms:

ΔG tot (T) = aE vdW + bΔG elec (T) - cTS sc + ΔG np

where a, b, and c are empirical scaling parameters. Initially the optimal values of scaling factors a = b ≈ 0.5 and c ≈ 0.8 were estimated from the best fit to experimental mutation energies of the results from the alanine scanning of the binding interface of 1a22 pdb structure. It has been found that the optimal values remain approximately the same for a large set of 380 mutations from 19 protein complexes.

Note that in this mode, the method allows for temperature-dependent calculations of mutation energy, in which case the temperature of the water solvent is taken into account and the dielectric constant of the solvent and the entropy terms are evaluated according to a user-specified temperature.

#### pH-dependent mode

The limitation of a fixed protonation state is overcome and the binding energy differences are reported as a function of pH instead of the single values returned by existing methods. Instead of fixed atomic charges, this mode uses a model with titratable acidic and basic residues. For this reason, the calculations of non-polar contributions to the free energy of binding are combined with calculations of protein ionization of the wild type and mutated structures in both the bound and unbound states. The electrostatic energy terms are obtained by integration over the proton binding isotherms, derived from the fractional protonation of the sites of titration. Note that this model also includes the effect of ionic strength, I, on the calculated free energy terms.

ΔG tot (pH) = aE vdW + ΔG elec (pH,I) - cTS sc + ΔG np

In this mode, the temperature changes are not taken into account and the results correspond to temperatures at or close to 20°C.

Note that empirical scaling is not applied to the electrostatic term. Tests on the same large set of 380 mutations have shown that in pH-dependent mode, the empirical scaling of the electrostatic term is no longer necessary (or even wrong) because of the more rigorous model of electrostatic interactions, while the optimal values of the other scaling factors remain the same.

A detailed description of this method can be found in [Spassov and Yan, 2013] .

Before running the protocol, prepare the protein taking into account of the following considerations:

* Remove the water molecules. The protocol uses an implicit solvent model GBIM.

* Remove the alternate conformations.

* Patch missing side-chain atoms if there are any incomplete residues and cap termini.

* If the protein has missing loop residues, it is desirable to model them in most cases, 
especially when the missing residues have acidic or basic titratable groups. However, if the loop is too long (e.g., longer than 12 residues)
the quality of the model is usually low. In this case, it is recommended that you not patch the missing loops.

* If you plan to use pH-independent mode, it is recommended that you predict the pK of the titratable residues and properly 
protonate the protein at the desired solution pH.
However, this is not necessary for pH-dependent mode where the effect of the changes in the protein ionization on
the electrostatic contribution to the free energy is derived from the fractional protonation of titratable residues. 
The latter is calculated internally for each pH step, similar to the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol, 
using a method described in detail in [Spassov and Yan, 2008] .

* Use Prepare Proteins protocol to prepare the input protein. 
All of the preparations listed above can be performed by the protocol.

* When working with high-resolution crystallographic structures, avoid additional minimization or other manipulation of atomic coordinates. Running the protocol with preliminary minimization or using input with previous energy minimization is risky
because applying additional minimization steps to the input structure only
could "over-stabilize" the wild type structure compared to the mutants. In cases where additional minimization is unavoidable, use a minimization protocol with the same GBIM solvation model and the same parameter values for Dielectric Constant and Solvent Dielectric Constant that you plan to use for this protocol.

Running the protocol with preliminary minimization or using input with previous energy minimization is risky
because applying additional minimization steps to the input structure only
could "over-stabilize" the wild type structure compared to the mutants. In cases where additional minimization is unavoidable, use a minimization protocol with the same GBIM solvation model and the same parameter values for Dielectric Constant and Solvent Dielectric Constant that you plan to use for this protocol.

To run the protocol:

* Load the protein structure into the Graphics View .

* Apply the CHARMm Polar H, CHARMm, or charmm36 forcefield to the protein structure. Use the Assign Forcefield command in the Change Forcefield tool panel. It is recommended that you use the CHARMm Polar H forcefield for all calculations whenever possible.
If the protein cannot be typed by CHARMm Polar H, you can use the charmm36 or CHARMm forcefield.

It is recommended that you use the CHARMm Polar H forcefield for all calculations whenever possible.
If the protein cannot be typed by CHARMm Polar H, you can use the charmm36 or CHARMm forcefield.

* Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Prepare Proteins... to open the Prepare Proteins dialog.
Set the Build Loops and Protonate options as desired. Set the Forcefield parameter in the Advanced group to match the forcefield used to type the protein in the previous step.

* To add an implicit membrane to the protein structure use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools panel or the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

* Select the residues to be mutated in the Molecule Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Design Protein tools and click Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding)... to open the Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select the structure as the Input Typed Molecule and set Ligand Chain to the chain IDs of one of the interaction partners.

* Set the Forcefield parameter in the Advanced group to match the forcefield used to type the protein in the previous step.

* Set Mutation Sites to the desired type of mutations. 
Click the Mutations parameter to open the Define Mutants dialog, which you can use to specify the amino acid types that each selected residue will be mutated into. If no residues are selected in the Molecule Window, all
amino acid residues will be listed for mutation and you can mutate all or a subset of them to specific types. Based on the settings of these two parameters, combinatorial mutations will be created by the protocol. For details of how the mutations are 
generated, see descriptions of the two corresponding parameters in Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) - Parameters . The protocol allows ligand and nonstandard residues in
the system as long as the ligand and residues can be typed by the selected forcefield. However, the residues
selected for mutation should be standard residues without missing atoms. If a residue has covalent bond with another residue via side-chain atoms (e.g., Cys residue in a disulfide bridge),
the mutation energy is not meaningful and the mutations that include this residue will be excluded from the calculation.

Based on the settings of these two parameters, combinatorial mutations will be created by the protocol. For details of how the mutations are 
generated, see descriptions of the two corresponding parameters in Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) - Parameters .

* The protocol allows ligand and nonstandard residues in
the system as long as the ligand and residues can be typed by the selected forcefield. However, the residues
selected for mutation should be standard residues without missing atoms.

* If a residue has covalent bond with another residue via side-chain atoms (e.g., Cys residue in a disulfide bridge),
the mutation energy is not meaningful and the mutations that include this residue will be excluded from the calculation.

* To select the pH dependent mode, set pH Dependent Electrostatics to True . If the mutations involve titratable acidic or basic residues, it is strongly recommended that you use pH-dependent mode, 
especially if the solution pH is well below or above pH 7-8, or the molecule has an abundance of histidines.

If the mutations involve titratable acidic or basic residues, it is strongly recommended that you use pH-dependent mode, 
especially if the solution pH is well below or above pH 7-8, or the molecule has an abundance of histidines.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| <molecule>.mol2 | Input structure with the Mutation Energy values and the effect of the mutation added as amino-acid residue properties. |
| --- | --- |
| MutationEnergy.csv | A csv table consisting of the full list of mutations with the mutation energy and the individual energy terms. |
| MutationEnergy_pH.csv (pH-dependent mode only) | A csv table with the mutation energy values reported as a function of pH for all mutations. |
| BindingEnergy_pH.csv (pH-dependent mode only) | A csv table with the values of the free energy of binding, ΔΔG bind (pH) of the wild type and mutants, reported as a function of pH. Note that the energy values for the wild type represent only the electrostatic contribution to the binding energy, while to compare the full effect of the mutations, the scaled contributions of all non-electrostatic terms are added to the electrostatic binding energy of mutants: ΔΔG bind (mutant) = ΔΔG elec ,bind(pH) + aΔΔE vdW ,mut + ... |
| Report.htm | Job summary including the input and output files, tables with up to five most favorable and five least favorable mutations, and the parameter settings used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm.log | File with log messages generated by the CHARMm program. Check for errors if protocol failed during the CHARMm calculation. |
| MutatedStructures | Directory with the mol2 files of saved mutated structures. |
| TitrationData (pH-dependent mode only) | Directory with subdirectories for the wild type and each of the mutant structures with titration data calculated for the bound and unbound state. It includes text files with calculated pK values and csv files with fractional protonation of individual residues. The TitrationData directory also contains an Elec_pH.csv file for each mutation that reports the electrostatic contributions to mutation energy as a function of pH. |

The TitrationData directory also contains an Elec_pH.csv file for each mutation that reports the electrostatic contributions
to mutation energy as a function of pH.

When the interactive job finishes, the structure in the active Molecule Window will be updated with the calculated Mutation Energy values for the lowest and highest energy mutations and the corresponding Effect of Mutation .
If you ran the protocol with single point amino acid scanning (i.e., with Mutation Sites set to Single Mutations ), the calculated Mutation Energy values
are added as residue properties to each mutated amino acid.

At the end of the run, a bar chart of mutation energy opens to allow you to visualize and compare 
the effect of different mutations. 
If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the updated structure and the bar chart.

The table in the Summary section of the report lists up to ten mutations with the five lowest energy mutations
and five highest energy mutations. The ranking of the mutations are sorted from
lowest to highest energy mutations. When the calculation is performed in pH-Dependent mode, a line plot of
mutation energy against pH is shown below the table for the corresponding mutations
listed in the table.

Additionally, the full list of mutations with calculated energy terms are provided in a csv file.
To view the full list of mutations, click Mutation Energy Terms in the Report or open MutationEnergy.csv from the Output folder. See Working with protocols for accessing the Output folder.

The values of mutation energy calculated as a sum of scaled van der Waals, electrostatic, non-polar, and entropy terms are shown
in the Mutation Energy column. The non-scaled values for each of these constituents are also
listed in separate columns.

The Effect of Mutation in the report and the Mutation Energy Terms tables are defined as follows:

| Property value | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Stabilizing | Mutation energy is less than -0.5 kcal/mol. |
| Neutral | Mutation energy is between -0.5 to 0.5 kcal/mol. |
| Destabilizing | Mutation energy is greater than 0.5 kcal/mol. |

If Maximum Structures to Save is greater than 0, the mutated structures with the lowest mutation energies are saved
in the Output/MutatedStructures directory.

# Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_calculate_mutation_energy_stability-para.htm

## Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) - Parameters

### Calculates the effect of mutations on the protein stability

Performs combinatorial scanning mutagenesis of protein molecules. Depending on the selected Mutation Sites mode this protocol generates all single, double or triple mutation sites from the set of selected residues or use all of them to create mutants for all combinations of specified amino-acid substitutions. For each mutant the protocol calculates the difference between the folding free energy of the wild type and mutated structure.

Depending on the electrostatic model, specified by the pH-dependent Electrostatics parameter, the calculations can be carried out either in a pH-independent or pH-dependent mode:

* pH-independent mode : All electrostatic energy terms are calculated based on the protonation state of input structure. This method uses GBIM (Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane) approximation to account for the effect of the solvent. The electrostatic terms are approximated as a sum of Coulombic interactions and polar contributions to solvation energy. The energy functional also contains van der Waals interaction energy, a side-chain entropy term and a non-polar surface dependent term.

* pH-dependent mode : The mutation energy is calculated as a function of pH for the defined pH interval. The pH-dependent electrostatic terms are calculated by integration over the proton binding isotherms, derived from fractional protonations of acidic and basic residues that are calculated according the model used by the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol. The remaining terms are the same as in pH-independent method.

The following residue properties are reported:

* Electrostatic Term: The electrostatic contribution to the folding energy difference between the wild type and mutated molecules.

* VDW Term: The van der Waals contribution to the binding energy differences.

* Entropy Term: The side-chain entropy contribution to the binding energy differences.

* Non-polar Term : The non-polar (surface tension) contribution to the binding energy differences.

* Mutation Energy The total free energy difference between the wild type and mutated structures. It is calculated as the weighted sum of the VDW, Electrostatic, Entropy and Non-polar terms.

Notes:

* Negative values of mutation energy correspond to a stabilizing effect of the mutation and vice versa.

* Only standard amino acid residues can be subject to mutation.

* The molecule must be typed with the CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H forcefield. If the molecule is typed with a forcefield different from the one specified in Forcefield parameter, the molecule will be re-typed internally.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L.; A pH-Dependent Computational Approach to the Effect of
Mutations on Protein Stability. Journal of Computational Chemistry 2016 , 37, 2573-2587.

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. pH-selective mutagenesis of protein-protein interfaces: In
silico design of therapeutic antibodies with prolonged half-life. PROTEINS: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics 2013 , 81, 704-714.

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S.Z. Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/solvent accessibility continuum solvent models J. Phys. Chem. B 2002 , 
1o6, 8726-8738.

| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Mutation Sites | Specifies the number of residues to be mutated simultaneously. Available options are: Single Mutations : Generate single point mutations for the set of selected residues. For example, if 2 residues are selected to mutate to 2 different amino acid types in the Mutations parameter, 4 separate single mutations will be generated, e.g., if Mutations parameter is set to A:ALA5>HIS,ASP A:SER6>HIS,GLU then 4 single mutations: A:ALA5>HIS, A:ALA5>ASP, A:SER6>HIS, A:SER6>GLU will be generated. Double Mutations : Generates all combinations of double mutations for the set of selected residues. If N residues are selected to mutate to M amino acid types, the number of double mutations will be [N!/2(N-2)!]( M 2 ) . For example, if Mutations parameter is set to A:ALA5>HIS,ASP A:SER6>HIS,GLU then 4 double mutations: A:ALA5>HIS+A:SER6>HIS, A:ALA5>HIS+A:SER6>ASP, A:ALA5>ASP+A:SER6>HIS, A:ALA5>ASP+A:SER6>GLU will be generated. Triple Mutations : Similar to Double Mutations , but three residues will be mutated simultaneously. All Selected Residues : All of the selected residues will be mutated simultaneously to all combinations of defined amino acid types. For example, if 5 residues are selected each mutate to one amino acid type, except the last residue to be mutated to 2 different types, the number of mutations will be 2, e.g. A:HIS5>ALA A:SER6>ALA A:GLU7>ALA A:VAL8>ALA A:PHE9>ALA,HIS then the mutations will be: A:HIS5>ALA+A:SER6>ALA+A:GLU7>ALA+A:VAL8>ALA+A:PHE9>ALA and A:HIS5>ALA+A:SER6>ALA+A:GLU7>ALA+A:VAL8>ALA+A:PHE9>HIS. Notes: The number of generated mutations rises quickly with the number of selected residues and the number of substitution types, especially with multiple mutations. # Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_calculate_mutation_energy_stability.htm

## Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability)

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Output

* Analyzing Results

The Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) protocol evaluates the effect of mutations on protein stability. 
It performs combinatorial amino-acid scanning mutagenesis on a set of selected amino-acid residues by mutating each of them to one or more specified amino-acid types. 
The energy effect of each mutation on the protein stability (mutation energy, ΔΔG mut ) is calculated as the difference of the free energy of folding between
the mutated structure and the wild type protein:

ΔΔG mut = ΔΔG folding (mutant) - ΔΔG folding (wild type)

The folding free energy, ΔΔGfolding, is defined as the free energy difference between the folded and unfolded states of the protein:

ΔΔG folding = ΔG fld - ΔG unf

and the ΔG fld and ΔG unf terms represent the free energies of folded and unfolded (denatured) states. Note that a
negative value of ΔΔG mut indicates the mutation has a stabilizing effect, and conversely, a positive value indicates the mutation has a destabilizing effect.

The energy of the folded state of the wild type is derived from the input structure. The structures of the mutants in the folded state are modeled by keeping the backbone rigid while optimizing the side-chains using the ChiRotor algorithm [Spassov et al., 2007] . Before evaluating the folding energy terms, the structures of the wild type and mutants are energy minimized using CHARMm.

The unfolded state is modeled as a relaxed penta-peptide in extended conformation with the mutated residue in the center. The peptide model is applied only to the short range interactions involving the mutated residues and it is extended with a Gaussian chain model to account for the long-range electrostatic interactions. 
This is based on the hypothesis that most of the contacts between amino acid residues in the unfolded protein are only sporadic if the residues are not immediate 
neighbors along the sequence. Considering that van der Waals interactions decline sharply with distance and contribute only at very close contacts, the method 
neglects the non-polar interactions between the residues that are separated by more than two peptide bonds in sequence.

All energy terms are calculated by CHARMm, and the electrostatics energy is calculated using a Generalized Born implicit solvent model. 
The total energy is calculated as an empirical weighted sum of van der Waals (E vdW ) interaction, electrostatic interaction (ΔG elec ), 
an entropy contribution (-TS sc ) related to side-chain mobility, and a non-polar, surface dependent, 
contribution to solvation energy (ΔG np ).

Depending on the electrostatic model selected, the calculations can be performed in pH-independent or pH-dependent mode.

#### pH-independent mode

The calculations are faster, but generally less accurate. The electrostatic calculations are based on the traditional approximation of 
fixed standard protonation states of all titratable residues. The total free energy, ΔGtot, of folded or unfolded state is calculated as the following weighted sum of energy terms:

ΔG tot (T) = aE vdW + bΔG elec (T) - cTS sc + ΔG np

where a, b, and c are empirical scaling parameters. It is recommended that you use the same values that have been found to be optimal for the Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) protocol (a = b = 0.5 and c = 0.8).

Note that in this mode, the method allows temperature-dependent calculations of mutation energy, in which case the temperature of the water solvent is taken into account and the dielectric constant of the solvent and the entropy terms are evaluated according to a user-specified temperature.

#### pH-dependent mode

The limitation of a fixed protonation state is overcome and the folding energy differences are reported as a function of pH instead of the single values returned by existing methods. Instead of fixed atomic charges, this mode uses a model with titratable acidic and basic residues. For this reason, the calculations of non-polar contributions to the free energy of folding are combined with calculations of protein ionization of the wild type and mutated structures in both the folded and unfolded states. The electrostatic energy terms are obtained by integration over the proton binding isotherms, derived from the fractional protonation of the sites of titration. Note that this model also includes the effect of ionic strength, I, on the calculated free energy terms.

ΔG tot (pH) = aE vdW + ΔG elec (pH,I) - cTS sc + ΔG np

Similar to the Calculate Mutation Energy (Binding) protocol, in pH-dependent mode the empirical scaling is not applied to the electrostatic term, while the recommended values of a = 0.5 and c = 0.8 remain the same as for pH-independent mode.

In this mode, the temperature changes are not taken into account and the results correspond to temperatures at or close to 20°C.

A detailed description of this method can be found in [Spassov and Yan, 2016] .

Before running the protocol, prepare the protein considering the following:

* Remove the water molecules. The protocol uses an implicit solvent model GBIM.

* Remove the alternate conformations.

* Patch missing side-chain atoms if there are any incomplete residues and cap termini.

* If the protein has missing loop residues, it is desirable to model them in most cases, 
especially when the missing residues have acidic or basic titratable groups. However, if the loop is too long (e.g., longer than 12 residues)
the quality of the model is usually low. In this case, it is recommended that you not patch the missing loops.

* If you plan to use pH-independent mode, it is recommended that you predict the pK of the titratable residues and properly 
protonate the protein at the desired solution pH.
However, this is not necessary for pH-dependent mode where the effect of the changes in the protein ionization on
the electrostatic contribution to the free energy is derived from the fractional protonation of titratable residues. 
The latter is calculated internally for each pH step, similar to the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol, 
using a method described in detail in [Spassov and Yan, 2008] .

* Use Prepare Proteins protocol to prepare the input protein. 
All of the preparations listed above can be performed by the protocol.

* When working with high-resolution crystallographic structures, avoid additional minimization or other manipulation of atomic coordinates. Running the protocol with preliminary minimization or using input with previous energy minimization is risky
because applying additional minimization steps to the input structure only
could "over-stabilize" the wild type structure compared to the mutants. In cases where additional minimization is unavoidable, use a minimization protocol with the same GBIM solvation model and the same parameter values for Dielectric Constant and Solvent Dielectric Constant that you plan to use for this protocol.

Running the protocol with preliminary minimization or using input with previous energy minimization is risky
because applying additional minimization steps to the input structure only
could "over-stabilize" the wild type structure compared to the mutants. In cases where additional minimization is unavoidable, use a minimization protocol with the same GBIM solvation model and the same parameter values for Dielectric Constant and Solvent Dielectric Constant that you plan to use for this protocol.

To run the protocol:

* Load the protein structure into the Graphics View .

* Apply the CHARMm Polar H, CHARMm, or charmm36 forcefield to the protein structure. Use the Assign Forcefield command in the Change Forcefield tool panel. It is recommended that you use the CHARMm Polar H forcefield for all calculations whenever possible. The protocol runs faster with the CHARMm Polar H forcefield, and there are negligible energy differences
between operating systems. If the protein cannot be typed by CHARMm Polar H, you can use the CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield. With the CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield, large differences of individual mutation energies may be observed between operating systems, 
but the overall accuracy of the predicted mutation energies across a large validation data set remains the same.

It is recommended that you use the CHARMm Polar H forcefield for all calculations whenever possible. The protocol runs faster with the CHARMm Polar H forcefield, and there are negligible energy differences
between operating systems. If the protein cannot be typed by CHARMm Polar H, you can use the CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield. With the CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield, large differences of individual mutation energies may be observed between operating systems, 
but the overall accuracy of the predicted mutation energies across a large validation data set remains the same.

* Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Prepare Proteins... to open the Prepare Proteins dialog.
Set the Build Loops and Protonate options as desired. Set the Forcefield parameter in the Advanced group to match the forcefield used to type the protein in the previous step.

* To add an implicit membrane to the protein structure, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools panel or the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

* Select the residues to be mutated in the Molecule Window.
Alternatively, open or create a sequence alignment in which the first sequence is that of the protein structure (or a unique section of it) and subsequent sequences contain the desired mutations.

* Open the Macromolecules | Design Protein tools and click Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability)... to open the Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select the structure as the Input Typed Molecule .

* Set the Forcefield parameter in the Advanced group to match the forcefield used to type the protein in the previous step.

* Set Mutation Sites to the desired type of mutations. 
If you have an alignment which specifies the mutations, click the Mutations from Alignment parameter and choose it. Otherwise, click the Mutations parameter to open the Define Mutants dialog, which you can use to specify the amino acid types that each selected residue will be mutated into. If no residues are selected in the Molecule Window, all
amino acid residues will be listed for mutation and you can mutate all or a subset of them to specific types. Based on the settings of these parameters, combinatorial mutations will be created by the protocol. For details about how the mutations are 
generated, see the descriptions of these parameters in Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) - Parameters . The protocol allows ligand and nonstandard residues in
the system as long as the ligand and residues can be typed by the selected forcefield. However, the residues
selected for mutation should be standard residues without missing atoms. If a residue has covalent bond with another residue via side-chain atoms (e.g., Cys residue in a disulfide bridge),
the mutation energy is not meaningful and the mutations that include this residue will be excluded from the calculation.

* If a residue has covalent bond with another residue via side-chain atoms (e.g., Cys residue in a disulfide bridge),
the mutation energy is not meaningful and the mutations that include this residue will be excluded from the calculation.

* To select the pH dependent mode, set pH Dependent Electrostatics to True . If the mutations involve titratable acidic or basic residues, it is strongly recommended that you use pH-dependent mode, 
especially if the solution pH is well below or above pH 7-8, or the molecule has an abundance of histidines.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| <molecule>.mol2 | Input structure with the Mutation Energy values and the effect of the mutation added as amino-acid residue properties. |
| --- | --- |
| MutationEnergy.csv | A csv table consisting of the full list of mutations with the mutation energy and the individual energy terms. |
| MutationEnergy_pH.csv (pH-dependent mode only) | A csv table with the mutation energy values reported as a function of pH for all mutations. |
| FoldingEnergy_pH.csv (pH-dependent mode only) | A table with the values of the free energy of folding, ΔΔG fold (pH) of the wild type and mutants, reported as a function of pH. Note that the energy values for the wild type represent only the electrostatic contribution to the folding energy. To compare the full effect of the mutations, the scaled contributions of all non-electrostatic terms are added to the electrostatic folding energy of mutants: ΔΔG fold (mutant) = ΔΔG elec ,fold(pH) + aΔΔE vdW ,mut + ... |
| Report.htm | Job summary including the input and output files, tables with up to five most favorable and five least favorable mutations, and the parameter settings used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm.log | File with log messages generated by the CHARMm program. Check for errors if protocol failed during the CHARMm calculation. |
| MutatedStructures | Directory with the mol2 files of saved mutated structures. |
| TitrationData (pH-dependent mode only) | Directory with subdirectories for the wild type and each of the mutant structures with titration data calculated for the folded and unfolded state. It includes text files with calculated pK values and csv files with fractional protonation of individual residues. The TitrationData directory also contains an Elec_pH.csv file for each mutation that reports the electrostatic contributions to mutation energy as a function of pH. |

The TitrationData directory also contains an Elec_pH.csv file for each mutation that reports the electrostatic contributions
to mutation energy as a function of pH.

When the interactive job finishes, the structure in the active Molecule Window will be updated with the calculated Mutation Energy values for the lowest and highest energy mutations and the corresponding Effect of Mutation .
If you ran the protocol with single point amino acid scanning (i.e., with Mutation Sites set to Single Mutations ), the calculated Mutation Energy values
are added as residue properties to each mutated amino acid.

At the end of the run, a bar chart of mutation energy opens to allow you to visualize and compare 
the effect of different mutations. 
If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the updated structure and the bar chart.

The table in the Summary section of the report lists up to ten mutations with the five lowest energy mutations
and five highest energy mutations. The ranking of the mutations are sorted from
lowest to highest energy mutations. When the calculation is performed in pH-Dependent mode, a line plot of
mutation energy against pH is shown below the table for the corresponding mutations
listed in the table.

Additionally, the full list of mutations with calculated energy terms are provided in a .csv file.
To view the full list of mutations, click Mutation Energy Terms in the Report or open MutationEnergy.csv from the Output folder. See Working with protocols for accessing the Output folder.

The values of mutation energy calculated as a sum of scaled van der Waals, electrostatic, non-polar, and entropy terms are shown
in the Mutation Energy column. The non-scaled values for each of these constituents are also
listed in separate columns.

The Effect of Mutation in the report and the Mutation Energy Terms tables are defined as follows:

| Property value | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Stabilizing | Mutation energy is less than -0.5 kcal/mol. |
| Neutral | Mutation energy is between -0.5 to 0.5 kcal/mol. |
| Destabilizing | Mutation energy is greater than 0.5 kcal/mol. |

The Effect of Mutation is a guideline and should be evaluated carefully. The most effective way to use the results of this protocol is to rank the mutations and identify hotspots of the most stablizing and destablizing mutations.

If Maximum Structures to Save is greater than 0, the mutated structures with the lowest mutation energies are saved
in the Output/MutatedStructures directory.

# Calculate Protein Formulation Properties - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_calculate_pfp-para.htm

## Calculate Protein Formulation Properties - Parameters

### Calculates biophysical properties important for protein formulation

Predicts properties including solubility, developability index (tendency to aggregate), and antibody viscosity.

For each input molecule, the protocol optionally performs the following:

* Protonates the structure at the specified pH.

* Calculates electrostatic properties, as described in the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol. These include the Isoelectric Point , pH of Maximum Stability , Net Charge , Dipole Moment ,and the pH-dependent electrostatic contribution to the protein solubility, SpH .

* Calculates aggregation scores.

* Calculates the Solubility Score . This is calculated using the pH-dependent relative solubility score ( SpH ) and the Positive Aggregation Score at radius 5Å as: Solubility Score = SpH - Aggregation Scaling * Aggregation Score A higher Solubility Score predicts higher solubility, which is usually desirable.

* Calculates the Developability Index for the whole molecule, and for the Fv region of antibodies as: DI = Aggregation Score - β x [ Net Charge ]² where β is the Weighting Factor A lower DI score predicts better developability.

* Calculates Charge Map scores. For antibody structures, viscosity has been found to correlate with the Negative Charge Map Score for the Fv region, so is reported as the Viscosity Score . A higher Viscosity Score predicts higher viscosity, which is undesirable. For other types of structure, the Charge Map (QMap) scores are calculated and available as properties on the atoms and molecule, but are not currently validated as having any correlation with viscosity so are not reported as such.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L. A fast and accurate computational approach to protein ionization. Protein Science 2008 , 
17, 1955-1970.

* Chennamsetty, N.; Voynov, V.; Kayser, V.;Helk, B.;Trout, B.L. Design of therapeutic proteins with enhanced stability. Proceedings of the National Academy of
Sciences , 2009 , 106(29), 11937-11942.

* Agrawal, N.J.; Helk, B.; Kumar, S.; Mody, N.; Sathish, H.A.; Samra, H.S.; Buck, P.M.; Li, L.; Trout, B.L., Computational tool for the early screening of monoclonal antibodies for their viscosities. mAbs. 2016 , 8(1)43-48.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include PDB, DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. Supported forcefields for the calculations are CHARMm, charmm36, and CHARMm Polar H. The input molecules that are not typed or typed with another forcefield will be typed or re-typed automatically. Use the Forcefield parameter to select one of the supported forcefields. Note : Each selected protein molecule should have at least one titratable amino acid residue. |
| At pH | Specifies the pH value at which to protonate the molecule and calculate the formulation properties. Note : The At pH value must be inside the range defined by From pH and To pH . |
| Ionic Strength | Specifies the ionic strength of the solvent (M). |
| Protonate Molecule | If set to "True", protonates or deprotonates the acidic and basic groups at a pH defined by the value of At pH parameter and according to the Predicted pK values of ionizable residues. Optimizes the positions of all hydrogen atoms, the configuration of proton binding sites of Asp, Glu and His residues and the orientation of Asn and Gln amide groups based on CHARMm energy. Valid Values: True , False |
| Fully Protonated Model | Generates a fully protonated structure with all hydrogens added to the acidic and basic groups of amino acid residues. At the given pH, assigns the average partial atomic charges to acidic and basic residues as well as terminal groups according to the calculated fractional protonation of the sites of titration. Calculates the molecular dipole moment and the net charge square as a function of pH. Notes : The fully protonated model is required for calculating Solubility Scores. If set "True", then for each input Macromolecule, two will be output. The fully protonated model can be distinguished from the 'normal' model by the property FullyProtonatedModel which is set to True or False as appropriate. Valid Values: True , False |
| Calculate Solubility Scores | Calculates the Solubility Score which combines the pH dependent contribution to the protein solubility, SpH , and the aggregation score of the molecule. The condensed state is defined by the Condensed State Dielectric Constant . The electrostatic free energy terms are calculated as a function of pH in the approximation of the Generalized Born model. The SpH values as a function of pH are calculated using the empirical scoring function: SpH (pH) = a Z 2 (pH) - b D 2 (pH) + c ΔΔGsolv(pH) + Const where Z is the protein Net Charge , D is the Dipole Moment , ΔΔGsolv is the transfer energy ddGsolv , and a , b , c , and Const are empirical parameters. The Solubility Score is calculated using SpH and the Positive Aggregation Score at radius 5Å as: Solubility Score = SpH - Aggregation Scaling * Aggregation Score Note : A more positive value of SpH corresponds to an increased solubility. | Dipole Scaling | Dipole moment scaling factor b in the empirical solubility scoring function SpH (pH). |
| Condensed State Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for the condensed (aggregated, crystalline) state, used in calculating the solvation energy. |
| Solvation Energy Scaling | ΔΔGsolv scaling factor c in the empirical solubility scoring function SpH (pH). |
| Non-electrostatic Term | The value of Const in the empirical solubility scoring function SpH (pH). |
| Aggregation Scaling | Scale factor applied to the aggregation term in the calculation of the Total Solubility Score . |
| Calculate DI Scores | Calculates Developability Index (DI) scores. The DI of a protein is a measure of its tendency to aggregate via hydrophobic interactions. The goal of the DI calculation is to analyze a series of homologous proteins and rank them based on their likelihood for aggregation. The DI is calculated from the aggregation propensity score ( APS ) and the weighted squared total charge, using the formula: DI = [ APS ] - β x [total charge]² If the protein is an antibody with one or more variable regions, then the APS will be calculated for these to generate DI(Fv) scores. A protein with a lower score is less likely to aggregate, which suggests an increased potential for development. Valid Values: True , False |

Developability Index: A Rapid in Silico tool for the Screening of Antibody Aggregation Propensity. J. Pharm. Sci., 2012, 101(1), 102-115. |

Valid Values: 5 , 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 |

Calculates the atomic charge map score, QMap[atom i ], as the summation of partial charges on side-chain atoms of an exposed residue (SAA > 10Å 2 ) which are within 10Å of atom i .
