# Calculate Protein Formulation Properties

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_calculate_pfp.htm

## Calculate Protein Formulation Properties

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Successful development of novel therapeutic proteins, especially monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), 
requires optimization of biophysical properties including solubility, viscosity, 
and tendency to aggregate. Highly concentrated solutions of mAbs are typically required to achieve a 
therapeutic dose in a small injection volume, and therefore high solubility is desirable. 
However, such solutions are often highly viscous, which makes them difficult to process and inject,
and are prone to aggregation.

The Calculate Protein Formulation Properties protocol calculates the Developability Index (DI), solubility, and viscosity for a homologous series of proteins to enable rapid 
assessment of their suitability before expressing, incubating, purifying, and storing the 
biologic.

#### Developability Index

Proteins, especially antibodies, tend to aggregate when stored at the high concentrations required for treatment, which decreases their activity and may cause an immunological response.

The DI is a measure used to rank the aggregation propensity of related proteins based on their hydrophobic and total charge properties. The DI is calculated from the Aggregation Propensity Score (APS) minus the weighted squared total of the charge as described by the following formula:

DI = [ APS ] - β x [total charge]²

where APS is the positive aggregation score and is calculated as the summation of all positive atomic aggregation scores. 
If the protein is an antibody with one or more variable regions, the APS will be calculated for these to generate DI(Fv) scores.

#### Solubility Scores

Solubility scores are calculated as a combination of the electrostatic contribution to 
the protein solubility at a given pH, and the hydrophobic interaction term characterized using the same positive 
aggregation score in the DI formula. For details, see Theory - Protein Solubility Scores .

#### Viscosity Scores

Relative viscosity scores for antibody structures are estimated using the surface charge 
map method [Agarawal et al., 2016] . 
This method quantifies electrostatic surface patches, and in the case of antibody structures 
it has been shown that negative electrostatic patches on the Fv region correlates well 
with experimentally determined viscosity.

* The DI and the viscosity score are parameterized and tested using antibody Fv domains. 
Further validation may be needed to apply the methods to other proteins or protein domains, and the scaling 
factor for DI may need to be retrained and adjusted.

* The solubility prediction is validated using various globular proteins, including ribonuclease SA, insulin, antibody Fab domains, etc. If only antibody Fv domains are
used for the prediction of the solubility of the full-length antibodies, you may need to retrain and adjust the Charge Scaling and Dipole Scaling parameters.

* Load one or more protein structures into the Graphics View .

* Clean the protein structures using the Prepare Protein tools ,
specifying the same forcefield as you want to use for the property prediction.
This step is optional, but is recommended to avoid issues when the protocol assigns forcefield types. You can do this automatically by running the Prepare Proteins protocol. Alternatively, set the preferences in the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog dialog so that the Clean Protein tool will remove alternate conformations, add termini, and patch missing side-chain atoms, and then run the tool. 
It is also recommended that you remove water molecules and all non-specific ligands and ions from the structure.

* Open the Macromolecules | Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools and click Calculate Formulation Properties... to open the Calculate Protein Formulation Properties dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Protein Molecules Choose the proteins for the calculation. pH Specify a pH value at which to calculate the properties, which should correspond to the formulation conditions. Ionic Strength Specify the ionic strength appropriate for the formulation conditions. Forcefield Choose a forcefield for the calculation.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | Choose the proteins for the calculation. |
| pH | Specify a pH value at which to calculate the properties, which should correspond to the formulation conditions. |
| Ionic Strength | Specify the ionic strength appropriate for the formulation conditions. |
| Forcefield | Choose a forcefield for the calculation. |

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* The electrostatic property calculations that contribute to the final property scores are performed using the same method used by the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol, which requires the CHARMm or CHARMm Polar H forcefield. Because of this, the protocol is limited to those forecfields.

* The default weighting factor for the DI calculation, β, was obtained using a cutoff radius of 5 Å. Changing the cutoff radius will potentially change the appropriate β value, which would require reparameterization against known stability data.

When the interactive job finishes, a Report window opens. Click View Results to open the result structures with calculated formulation properties in a single Molecule Window.

The report includes a sortable table of the calculated formulation properties, together with clickable links that show detailed results and individual structures. These structures have surfaces and Site groups added if the necessary properties have been calculated; if both aggregation and charge map properties are present, then two separate structures are opened to display them independently:

* Aggregation Propensity Surface: This surface is colored according to atomic aggregation scores. The regions predicted to be more susceptible to aggregation are red. You can perform a detailed analysis of the Aggregation Sites using the View Aggregation Sites viewing tools on the Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools panel.

* Charge Map Surface: This surface is colored according to residue surface charge map scores (Active QMap Score property on the AminoAcid tab of the Data Table). For antibody structures, negative electrostatic patches on the Fv region correlate with higher viscosity—these are red. 
Additionally, the Hierarchy View contains groups for Active QMap Score Sites and Negative Active QMap Score Sites. You can select and focus using standard Discovery Studio functionality. The surface is transparent and the atoms are also colored using the QMap property to facilitate analysis of the site groups.

If the Fully Protonated Model option was True , the table links will also display these in separate molecule windows.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link to open the Report, and then click View Results to open the result structures in one window, or click the table links to open individual structures with surfaces.

To further investigate aggregation sites and aggregation propensity scores at different radii or over a trajectory, 
refer to the Calculate Aggregation Scores section of the Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools panel.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including tabulated results, links to display detailed reports and individual structures, input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| ViewMolecules.ds_pl | Script that opens a Molecule Window in Discovery Studio containing all the structures for which the properties could be calculated. |
| SummaryResults.csv | A comma separated value file containing all of the calculated properties for each molecule. |
| Failed.txt | Text file containing the names of any structures for which properties could not be calculated, and an error message describing the problem encountered. A typical cause of failure is that a structure could not be typed with the chosen forcefield. |

The Output directory also contains a subfolder for each input molecule, containing the output structures and detailed properties.

#### Further information

Theory - Protein Solubility Scores Theory - Surface Charge Maps and Viscosity Scores Theory - Calculate Developability Indices Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools Calculate Protein Formulation Properties - Parameters

# Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_dock_proteins_zdock-para.htm

## Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) - Parameters

### Predicts the optimal docked poses for two protein structures

Uses ZDOCK to perform rigid body docking of two proteins. This method performs a systematic search of a uniform sample of docked protein poses and uses an internal scoring algorithm to predict the optimal interactions.

The following steps are performed:

* Calculate docked protein poses.

* Filter docked protein poses for poses with specific residues at the binding interface, as specified by Filter Poses|Receptor Binding Site Residues and Filter Poses|Ligand Binding Site Residues (optional).

* Rerank docked protein poses with ZRank (optional).

* Cluster docked protein poses and calculate density.

See Also:

* Chen, R.; Weng, Z. A novel shape complementarity scoring function for 
protein-protein docking. Proteins 2003 , 51, 397-408.

* Chen, R.; Li, L.; Weng, Z. P. ZDOCK: An initial-stage protein-docking 
algorithm. Proteins 2003 , 52(1), 80-87.

* Pierce B.; Weng Z. ZRANK: Reranking Protein Docking Predictions with an Optimized Energy Function. Proteins 2007 , 67(4): 1078-1086.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor Protein | Protein structure to use as the receptor. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Input Ligand Protein | Protein structure to use as the ligand. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Angular Step Size | Angular step size (°) for rotational sampling of ligand orientations. Allowed values for the Angular Step Size are 6 and 15. The default value 6, performs finer conformational sampling and thus typically results in more accurate predictions. Calculations with a 15 Angular Step Size are about 15 times faster since 3600 poses are sampled vs. 54000 poses for calculations with a 6 step. Valid Values: 6 , 15 |
| Receptor Blocked Residues | List of receptor residues which should not occur on binding site. In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace. You can also specify ranges of residues by specifying the first and last residue in the range. Example: "A:ASP64 A:GLY70 A:VAL80-A:GLU83". In Discovery Studio you specify the Receptor Blocked Residues by selecting an existing residue group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu. |
| Ligand Blocked Residues | List of ligand residues which should not occur on binding site. In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace. You can also specify ranges of residues by specifying the first and last residue in the range. Example: "A:ASP64 A:GLY70 A:VAL80-A:GLU83". In Discovery Studio you specify the Ligand Blocked Residues by selecting an existing residue group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu. |
| Platform | Platform to run on. The following options are available: CPU : Uses only CPUs (central processing unit). GPU : CPU (central processing unit) works together with a GPU (graphics processing unit) for faster computing. Note: A NVIDIA CUDA-capable video card and the appropriate driver are required to support a GPU calculation. Valid Values: CPU , GPU |
| GPU Device | Specifies the GPU device to use for the GPU platform. The GPU device index starts from 0. Notes: If this parameter is left blank, it will use the first GPU by default. If the GPU resources are managed by a queue management system, the value specified here will be ignored. When running in parallel on an unmanaged system with multiple GPUs, a comma separated list of device can be specified. Each process will be assigned the corresponding card. |
| Filter Poses | Parameters to select poses with a specified set of residues at the binding interface. The binding interface of the receptor is defined as the set of receptor residues which have atoms within the distance (Å) specified by the Distance Cutoff parameter of at least one ligand atom. Similarly the ligand binding interface is the set of ligand residues with at least one atom within the Distance Cutoff (Å) of any receptor atom. Only heavy atoms are considered. Note: A pose must have all residues listed as Receptor Binding Site Residues and Ligand Binding Site Residues in the binding site to pass filtering. If too many residues are selected it is likely that none of the poses will pass the filter. |
| Receptor Binding Site Residues | List of receptor residues which have to be on the binding site. In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace. You can also specify ranges of residues by specifying the first and last residue in the range. Example: "A:ASP64 A:GLY70 A:VAL80-A:GLU83". In Discovery Studio you specify the Receptor Binding Site Residues by selecting an existing residue group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu |
| Ligand Binding Site Residues | List of ligand residues which have to be on the binding site. In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace. You can also specify ranges of residues by specifying the first and last residue in the range. Example: "A:ASP64 A:GLY70 A:VAL80-A:GLU83". In Discovery Studio you specify the Ligand Binding Site Residues by selecting an existing residue group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu |
| Distance Cutoff | Distance cutoff (Å) to select binding site residues of a docked pose. A ligand (receptor) residue is part of the binding site if it has atoms within Distance Cutoff Å of at least one heavy atom of the receptor (ligand). Only heavy atoms are used in the calculation. Choosing a smaller value will in general reduce the number of poses that pass. |
| ZRank | Rerank initial-stage ZDOCK predictions with detailed electrostatics, van der Waals, and desolvation energy terms (ZRANK). See Also: Pierce B.; Weng Z. ZRANK: Reranking Protein Docking Predictions with an Optimized Energy Function. Proteins 2007 , 67(4): 1078-1086. Valid Values: True , False |
| ZRank Top Poses | Number of top scoring poses to be rescored with the ZRANK algorithm. Note that this parameter has to be greater than or equal to the Top Poses parameter specified for Clustering . In addition, filtering for binding site residues can reduce the number of poses below the value specified in this parameter. |
| ZRank Report Score Components | Report the solvation, electrostatic and van der Waals components of the ZRANK score in the results. Valid Values: True, False |
| Clustering | Parameters to control clustering of poses. |
| Clustering Top Poses | Number of top-scoring poses to cluster and report in the results. Notes: Filtering for binding site residues can reduce the number of poses below the value specified in this parameter. This parameter cannot be larger than 5000. If rescoring with ZRank is turned on, this parameter has to be smaller than or equal to the Top Poses parameter specified for ZRank ( ZRank is executed before clustering). |
| Clustering RMSD Cutoff | Maximal ligand interface RMSD (Å) from the cluster center for a pose to be included in a cluster. Using a smaller value will typically increase the number of clusters and reduce the average number of poses per cluster. |
| Clustering Interface Cutoff | Cutoff distance (Å) used to define the interface region between receptor and ligand. Only the ligand interface region is used to calculate the RMSD values for clustering. The ligand interface region is defined as all heavy atoms of any ligand residue with at least one atom within the Interface Cutoff distance of a receptor atom. |
| Clustering Maximum Number of Clusters | Maximum number of clusters that are reported. It must be smaller than the number of Top Poses specified. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy | If True, use shape complementarity, desolvation and electrostatic energy terms in the initial-stage ranking of the docked protein poses. If False, use only shape complementarity terms. The additional energy terms provide more accurate ranking at a greater computational cost (speed as well as memory usage). Valid Values: True, False |
| PreserveDisplayStyle | If True, preserve the original display style of the input structures, if False use ribbon style. Valid Values: True , False |
| Process Best Poses Only | Specifies whether to limit the clustering and output to only those poses that pass both the Filter Poses and ZRank criteria. Setting this to True can save time, if only these poses are of interest. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, the grid options, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Server Run On Grid | Run subprotocol on grid engine if available. Valid Values: True , False |
| Parallel Processing Server Run On Grid Queue Name | Queue name on the grid to submit jobs to. Leave blank to use default queue name. |
| Parallel Processing Server Run On Grid Grid Options | Grid engine specific command line parameters for the job submission. Leave blank to use defaults. Notes : Each of the ZDOCK process runs on 1 CPU process and 1 GPU if GPU option is selected. By default, the CPU and GPU are set to 1. If for any reason, there is a need to change the specification using different command line syntax, ensure only 1 CPU and 1 GPU is specified. In Pipeline Pilot, this is an array of command line options to send to the Grid engine submit command. In Discovery Studio, the options are comma separated. There are a number of parameters are translated to the correct command line options for whichever supported Grid Engine you are using. Example - Supported parameters Account=<Project/Account name> Maximum Execution Time=<DD:MM:SS> - LSF ignores seconds Number of Cores=<4> Number of GPUs=<1> Parallel Environment=<The Parallel Environment to use> - Only needed for SGE Other=<Additional Parameters sent directly to submit command line> If you just include one line, whatever you enter will be sent "as is" to the submission command. Example - sending GPU options directly to command line - PBS -l mem=2GB -l ncpus=1 -l ngpus=1 |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

# Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_dock_proteins_zdock.htm

## Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol provides rigid body docking of two
protein structures using the ZDOCK algorithm [Chen and Weng, 2002] as well as clustering
the poses according to the ligand position. Optionally, the docked poses can be filtered
for complexes that include a user specified set of residues at the binding interface.
In addition, the protocol provides the option of reranking the docked poses with
the ZRANK scoring function.

When preparing the input for this calculation, considering the following:

* If there are missing atoms or residues in the receptor or ligand protein, it is recommended that you model them before running this protocol. If the missing atoms or residues are on the protein surface, 
the predicted docked complexes could be wrong even if the missing part is not in the binding site. This is because the surface with missing atoms or residues could be incorrectly predicted as the binding site. If the missing atoms or residues are in the core of the protein, the effect on the prediction is decreased.

* If the missing atoms or residues are on the protein surface, 
the predicted docked complexes could be wrong even if the missing part is not in the binding site. This is because the surface with missing atoms or residues could be incorrectly predicted as the binding site.

* If the missing atoms or residues are in the core of the protein, the effect on the prediction is decreased.

* The atom types and allowed residue types are limited to standard amino acid residues. The atoms in the nonstandard residues are treated as carbons with zero charge.

* In general, water molecules should be removed before running the calculation. However, if water is included, the oxygen atom is treated the same as unknown atom (i.e., as carbon with zero charge).

* The calculation uses the first conformation if the input ligand or receptor have multiple conformations (e.g., structures from an NMR experiment). If a certain conformation other than the first 
should be used for running the calculation, delete all conformations except that one before running the protocol.

* Hydrogen atoms are not used in the calculations regardless of whether they exist in the input molecule.

To run the calculation:

* Load the first protein structure (referred to as receptor ) into a Graphics View .

* Insert the second protein structure (referred to as ligand ) into the same Graphics View .

* Use the Hierarchy View to delete the waters from the receptor and ligand molecules.

* If there are problems such as missing atoms or residues in the structures, correct them by running the Prepare Proteins protocol.
Alternatively, set the preferences in the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog dialog so that the Clean Protein tool will remove alternate conformations, add termini, and patch missing side-chain atoms, and then run the tool.

* Open the Macromolecules | Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools tools and click Dock Proteins (ZDOCK)... to open the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Structure Choose the receptor to be docked. Input Ligand Structure Choose the ligand for docking. For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) - Parameters . The structures selected as the Input Receptor Structure and Input Ligand Structure have to satisfy the following size constraint: MaxR R is the maximum distance of any receptor atom to the center of geometry of the receptor, and MaxR L is the maximum distance of any ligand atom to the center of geometry of the ligand.
The sum of MaxR R and MaxR L must be smaller than 201 Å. If Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy is enabled, this limit is reduced to 197 Å.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor Structure | Choose the receptor to be docked. |
| Input Ligand Structure | Choose the ligand for docking. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) - Parameters .

The structures selected as the Input Receptor Structure and Input Ligand Structure have to satisfy the following size constraint: MaxR R is the maximum distance of any receptor atom to the center of geometry of the receptor, and MaxR L is the maximum distance of any ligand atom to the center of geometry of the ligand.
The sum of MaxR R and MaxR L must be smaller than 201 Å. If Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy is enabled, this limit is reduced to 197 Å.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the run finishes, double-click the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report.htm . Review the Summary section of the report and click View Results to open the docking poses in a Molecule Window.

The top poses are reported with the poses clustered into groups according to their spatial proximity, which 
can be viewed in the Hierarchy View. You can use the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tools to browse and
analyze the poses. To help with the analysis,
colored surfaces are added to the input receptor and ligand structures to indicate how many of the top poses have their 
binding interface centered in a region of the molecular surface. The colors range from blue (few poses) to red (many poses). 
See Clustering and Analysis for details.

If any residues are selected in the Filter Poses parameters, the poses in the Molecule window
are the top poses that pass the filtering criteria.

Numerical results of the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) run are reported in the ProteinPose tab of the 
Data Table:

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ZDock Score | ZDock Score is the shape complementarity score calculated by the ZDOCK program. If the Use Electrostatic and Desolvation Energy advanced protocol parameter is set to True , the ZDOCK score also includes electrostatics and desolvation energy terms. Higher scores are better. |
| ZRank Score | ZRank Score is the energy of the docked posed calculated by the ZRANK rescoring method. This column is only present if the ZRank protocol parameter is set to True . Lower scores are better. |
| Rank | This displays rank of the docked protein poses. according to the ZDock Score. If the ZRank protocol parameter is set to True , the ZRank Score is used for ranking, otherwise the ZDock Score is used. |
| Density | Density is the number of docked protein poses that fall within the RMSD cutoff specified for clustering. This number represents the number of neighbors used in the first stage of clustering. |
| Cluster | This is the ID of the cluster the pose is assigned to. Clusters appear as groups in the Hierarchy View |
| Top Cluster Pose | Top Cluster Pose reports whether or not a docked protein pose is a the top ranked pose in its cluster. |
| Cluster Size | The size of the cluster that the docked protein pose belongs to. |

Use the Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes tool panel for further analysis of the docking results, 
including show or hide poses, browse poses so that a specific pose is displayed in full atomic detail, or to calculate the RMSD of the interface residues.

Additionally, use the Process Poses command on the tool panel to filter the poses 
if that was not included in the original calculation or to re-run the filtering or clustering using different criteria.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| ZDockResults.dsv | Protein poses produced by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol. Only the top poses, as specified by the corresponding parameter of the protocol, are reported. |
| ZDockResults.out | The top docked protein poses produced by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol in text format. Note that this file contains the same information as the ZDockResults.dsv file. It is included to facilitate further processing of the docked protein poses outside the Discovery Studio Client. |
| ZDockResults_all.dsv | The full set of docked protein poses produced by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol. No clustering or ZRank data is contained in this file. As in the ZDockResults.dsv file, the protocol adds colored surfaces to the input receptor and ligand structures that indicate how many poses have their binding interface centered in that region of the molecule. However, for the ZDockResults_all.dsv , the coloring is based on the full set of poses, whereas in the ZDockResults.dsv file only top poses are used. |
| zdock.out | The full set of docked protein poses produced by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol in text format. It is the output of the zdock standalone program. |
| AtomTypeWarnings.txt | Contains a list of atoms in the input structures that do not have parameters (ZDock or ZRank). If fewer than five unrecognized atoms are encountered, the list is reported directly in the warning section of the report. For the ZDOCK calculation, atoms of unrecognized type are treated as carbon atoms and are assigned the parameters for carbon. For the ZRANK calculation, atoms of unrecognized type are ignored. |

For the ZDOCK calculation, atoms of
unrecognized type are treated as carbon atoms and are assigned the parameters
for carbon. For the ZRANK calculation, atoms of unrecognized type are ignored.

#### Further information

# Identify Framework Templates - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_identify_framework_templates-para.htm

## Identify Framework Templates - Parameters

### Identifies framework templates for an input antibody sequence in a pre-compiled database

Identifies templates for the antigen-binding fragment (Fab fragment) of the Input Sequence . Depending on the parameter settings, templates are selected from a database based on sequence similarity or sequence identity of the framework regions of the light and heavy chain domains in the Fab region.

The following steps are performed:

* Identify antibody domains in the Input Sequence using Hidden Markov Models (HMM).

* Align the sequences of the identified VL, CL, VH or CH1 domains against a pre-compiled database consisting of non-redundant antibody domain sequences using the residue numbering assigned by the HMM.

* Based on this alignment, calculate the sequence similarity and identity of the input VL, CL, VH and CH1 domains to sequences in the alignment. Depending on the value of the Exclude CDR Regions parameter, the similarity and identity calculations are based only on residues in the framework region (i.e. exclude residues in the Complimentary Determining Regions (CDR)).

* Identify full length hits, antibody PDB sequences that contain all of the Fab domain types present in the input sequence.

* Calculate the overall similarity and identity for the full length hits and report the top hits.

* Create a sequence alignment for the full length hits.

* Copy the structures for the full length hits from the antibody database into the results folder.

In addition, the protocol also provides files with the top hits for each of the individual domains along with an alignment of the domain sequences, as well as the alignment and the structures of the top hits for the light and heavy chains (if present in the Input sequence ).

Note:

* If the input sequence contains multiple VL, CL, VH or CH1 domains, only the first domain of each type is used for the calculation.

* By default, templates are sorted by sequence similarity to the target sequence. To sort by sequence identity, change the value of the Template Ranking parameter in the Advanced parameter group.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Light Chain Sequence | Sequence of the Antibody Light Chain. The first VL and/or CL domains found in this sequence will be extracted. The sequence may also contain a heavy chain to be used instead of specifying a separate Heavy Chain Sequence . In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequences in any open Sequence Windows. |

# Identify Framework Templates

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_identify_framework_templates.htm

## Identify Framework Templates

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Identify Framework Templates protocol identifies template structures for the antigen-binding fragment (Fab fragment) or the variable region (Fv) of an antibody sequence.

Antibody domains of the input sequence are identified using Hidden Markov Models (HMM) defined using the Annotate Antibody Sequence protocol. 
Based on the HMM data, the protocol generates an alignment 
of the VH, CH1, VL, and CL domains of the input sequence and the corresponding domains in the antibody database. Templates that contain all 
of the domains in the input sequence are identified and the top hits are selected based on overall sequence similarity. The protocol generates 
a sequence alignment for the top hits and downloads the corresponding structures from the antibody database. Note that 
the sequence similarity is calculated based on all domains, but is limited to residues in the framework (non CDR) regions
if Exclude CDR Regions is set to True .

* Open the light and heavy chain sequences to be used to identify the framework templates in a Sequence Window. These can be specified separately or in one sequence, with the VL, CL, VH and CH1 domains being automatically extracted.

* Open the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tools and click Identify Framework Templates... to open the Identify Framework Templates dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Light Chain Sequence Select the light chain sequence to use as input, or a sequence containing both light and heavy domains. Heavy Chain Sequence Select the heavy chain sequence to use as input, if not present in the 'light chain sequence'. Maximum Templates Set the maximum number of protein templates to report. Resolution Threshold Set the threshold on the X-ray resolution of templates to report. For details about the remaining parameters, see Identify Framework Templates - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Light Chain Sequence | Select the light chain sequence to use as input, or a sequence containing both light and heavy domains. |
| Heavy Chain Sequence | Select the heavy chain sequence to use as input, if not present in the 'light chain sequence'. |
| Maximum Templates | Set the maximum number of protein templates to report. |
| Resolution Threshold | Set the threshold on the X-ray resolution of templates to report. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Identify Framework Templates - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, a dialog with a run summary is displayed. Click OK to open a table with the top overall template hits or click the Report button to open the protocol report in a new window.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the table with the top overall template hits.

The top template for the overall input sequence and the light and heavy chains are listed in a table at the beginning of the summary section of the report.
Note that the best hit for the overall sequence may not be the best hits for the individual chains. Therefore, the ranking of the individual chain hits are
shown for the overall hit in this table if the individual chain is among the top hits for its chain type (specified by the Maximum Templates parameter).

Additionally, separate tables are created for the top template hits for the overall sequence (i.e., covering all relevant input domains) and for the light and heavy chains, sorted by percentage sequence similarity. For hits with identical sequence similarity, the percentage sequence identity and then the resolution of the corresponding structure are used as secondary sorting criteria.
Click the column header in the table to sort it by a specific calculated property, such as similarity or identity.

Only sequences from structures with an X-ray resolution better than the specified Resolution Threshold are reported (the threshold does not apply to non X-ray structures). 
The sequence similarity is calculated using the SequenceSimilarityArray function, which is 
the same as used by Sequence Window to report the sequence similarity and identity in the status bar. 
The similarity is based on the length of the antibody domains identified in the input sequence, including gaps. 
For more detail about how the similarity and identity are calculated, see Similarity subpage - Preferences dialog .

#### Hit tables

Separate hit tables for overall, light chain, and heavy chain hits are saved in .csv format and can be opened by clicking on the link in the Results section in the Report.
The hit tables include the name of the hit (pdb id), chain id and residue index range of the domains with respect to the corresponding chain, sequence similarity and identity with or without the CDR regions,
resolution of the corresponding pdb structure, and a list of redundant hits (hits with identical sequence).

#### Sequence Alignments

The protocol generates separate sequence alignments for the hits listed in the tables in the report (i.e., for the overall hits, as well as for the light and heavy chain regions if applicable). You can load alignments into a Sequence Window by clicking the corresponding links in the Results section at the bottom of the report.

#### Template structures

The structures of the hits listed in the tables are automatically saved in the Templates directory in the Output folder. Only the residue ranges listed in the table are contained in the downloaded structures. You can load the structures into a Molecule Window by clicking the links in the Name columns in the hit tables of the report. Click a link in the Overall Templates table to open a new Molecule Window labeled Overall Framework Hits . Click other structure links in the same table to add the corresponding structures to the same Molecule Window. Links in the Light and Heavy Chain Templates tables open separate Molecule Windows labeled Light Chain Hits and Heavy Chain Hits . The structures in each window are presuperimposed.

If the input sequence contains multiple domains of the same type such as two variable heavy (VH) domains, only the first domain encountered of each type is used to search for templates. For sequences with multiple non-redundant Fab fragments, you must run the protocol separately on each Fab fragment sequence for which templates are to be identified.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| OverallHits.csv | Table listing properties of the top template hits that best match the overall input sequence (e.g., the Fab domain) in the input sequence. |
| OverallHits.bsml | Sequence alignment of the top template hits that best match the overall input sequence (e.g., the Fab domain) in the input sequence. |
| HeavyChainHits.csv | Table listing properties of the top template hits that best match the heavy chain in the input sequence. |
| HeavyChainHits.bsml | Sequence alignment of the top template hits that best match the heavy chain in the input sequence. |
| LightChainHits.csv | Table listing properties of the top template hits that best match the light chain in the input sequence. |
| LightChainHits.bsml | Sequence alignment of the top template hits that best match the light chain in the input sequence. |
| Templates (directory) | Directory containing the structures of the top hits. The hits for the overall input sequence (e.g. the Fab domains), and the light and heavy chains are located in separate sub-directories. |

#### Further information

Theory - Model Antibody Loops Theory - Model Antibody Loops (Canonical Structures)

# Loop Refinement - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_loop_refinement-para.htm

## Loop Refinement - Parameters

### Refines a loop region of a protein structure using energy optimization

Predicts the structure of a selected segment of a protein chain using a multi-step computational protocol. The calculations are based on an improved version of the ab initio loop prediction algorithm LOOPER. It combines systematic conformational sampling of the loop backbone with CHARMm energy minimization.

The computations can be carried out in a Fast or Slow mode, corresponding to the level of conformational sampling.
Initially a number of independent data records are created, corresponding to all combinations of sampled (φ,ψ) angles of the first and last residues of the loop. If Parallel Processing parameter is set to True, each data record is distributed to separate processor.

For each initial data records, the algorithm carries out four stage calculations to generate a number of low energy loop conformations:

* The first two stages create, a number of independently energy optimized variants of the left and right halves of the loop backbone (up to 50 prospective variants for the Fast mode and up to 150 for the Slow mode).

* The third stage combines all retained variants of the left and right halves and minimizes refines the loop backbone conformations. Up to Maximum Number of Models of lowest energy conformations are retained.

* The final stage constructs the loop side-chains and carries out a final minimization.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Flook, P.K.; Yan, L. LOOPER: a molecular mechanics-based algorithm for protein loop prediction. Protein Engineering Design and Selection , 2008 , 21(2), 91-100.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Protein Molecule | Specify a typed protein molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed protein structures. |
| Loop | Specifies the loop residues. The maximum loop length allowed is 14 residues. The selected loop region should not contain N- or C- terminal residues or chain gaps. In Pipeline Pilot a loop is defined by a starting residue and an ending residue connected by "-". A residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: A:LEU18-A:PRO22. In Discovery Studio select one or more consecutive residues to define the loop. |
| Fast Mode | Specifies the sampling of conformers at the different stages of the algorithm. When set to True, the sampling is less comprehensive and the results are statistically less accurate, but the execution is considerably faster. Valid Values: True , False |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Maximum Number of Models | Specifies the maximum number of models to be retained for further refinement after the third stage of calculations. |
| Maximum Number of Models to Save | Specifies the maximum number of protein structures to be generated and saved using the coordinates of top ranked loop models. |
| Parallel Processing | When set to True, this set of options allow the subprotocol to execute in parallel on one or more independent Pipeline Pilot servers, running local or remote. Additional parameters control the number of data records to send in each process batch, the list of Pipeline Pilot servers to use, the number of protocol processes that can be executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Note that not all parts of every protocol are run in parallel and that this method may not give perfect scaling. In general, it will yield improved performance when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. Note that by default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of 2 processes per protocol, this can be modified in the Pipeline Pilot administration page. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | The number of records to send to the remote server(s) for each subprotocol execution. In general, performance is optimized when the amount of time required to process each batch is at least 10 seconds (note that this can vary depending on the characteristics of the remote server's hardware) |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of Pipeline Pilot servers on which to execute the parallel subprotocol. The server names should be in the same format as the Pipeline Pilot Client's change server dialog (server-name:port-number). Specifying localhost as a server will cause the subprotocol to use its own Pipeline Pilot server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where 'localhost' requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of maximum number of batches that can be simultaneously executed on each remote server. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. If '*' is specified as the number of processes, then that server will only launch as many batches as the administrator of the remote server has permitted. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Whether to preserve the order of the data as it enters and leaves the remote subprotocol. Valid Values: True , False |

In Pipeline Pilot a loop is defined by a starting residue and an ending residue connected by "-". A residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: A:LEU18-A:PRO22.

# Loop Refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_loop_refinement.htm

## Loop Refinement

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

* Troubleshooting

The Loop Refinement protocol uses the Looper algorithm to optimize the structure of a selected non-terminal
loop region of a protein structure. It optimizes any loop region that contains up to 25 residues. For details, see Theory - Loop Refinement .

* Load the protein structure containing the loop of interest into the Molecule Window.

* Clean the protein structure using Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools.
You can do this automatically by running the Prepare Proteins protocol, which includes an option to refine any loops it adds using Looper. 
Alternatively, set the preferences in the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog dialog so that the Clean Protein tool will remove alternate conformations, add termini, and patch missing side-chain atoms, and then run the tool.

* Use the Assign Forcefield command in the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel to apply a CHARMm forcefield to the protein structure. The protocol cannot be used with XPROLIG or cff.

* From the Molecule Window, select a residue segment to be refined.

* Open the Macromolecules | Minimize and Refine Protein tools and click Loop Refinement... to open the Loop Refinement dialog.

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Protein Structure Set the input protein structure. Loop Choose the residue segment that you selected from the Molecule Window. Fast Mode Choose True for faster calculations or False for more accurate predictions. Parallel Processing Choose True to accelerate the calculations in case you are using a multiprocessor machine. For details about the remaining parameters, see Loop Refinement - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Protein Structure | Set the input protein structure. |
| Loop | Choose the residue segment that you selected from the Molecule Window. |
| Fast Mode | Choose True for faster calculations or False for more accurate predictions. |
| Parallel Processing | Choose True to accelerate the calculations in case you are using a multiprocessor machine. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Loop Refinement - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation. The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* The protocol allows ligand and non-standard residues in the system as long as the ligand and residues can be typed by the selected forcefield. However, the residues in the selected loop region should be standard residues.

* To set a disulfide bridge between a cysteine residue in the loop and another cysteine residue, create a bond between the two sulfur atoms of the two CYS residues in the Molecule Window.

* The recommended forcefield for this protocol is the CHARMm Polar H because it is better validated and much faster than "all atom" forcefields (e.g., CHARMm, charmm22, and charmm27). If you want to use an all atom forcefield, CHARMm is recommended.

* If you are using Parallel Processing, the protocol is designed to use a maximum of 24 processors in Fast mode and up to 120 processors in Slow mode. Therefore, the number of Parallel Processing Server Processes should not exceed these limits based on the mode you are using.

When the interactive job finishes, a Molecule Window opens with the loop models as well as the input protein. In addition, a Dendrogram shows the cluster of the loop models according the pairwise 
main-chain RMSD of the loop region. 
If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the windows with the results.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | Contains the conformations of all loop models, the corresponding energy of each loop model and the RMSD matrix of all the loop conformations. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opens the predicted structure in a Molecule Window and a dendrogram of the loop conformations based on the RMSD calculated using the main-chain atoms of the specified loop. |

#### Further information

Theory - Loop Refinement

# Loop Refinement (MODELER) - Parameters

## Loop Refinement (MODELER) - Parameters

### Refines one or more loop regions of a protein structure using MODELER

One or more selected loop regions will be refined using the MODELER energy function without homology constraints while other parts of the protein structure are held rigid. Set Disulfide Bridges , Cis-Prolines , and Additional Restraints to add modeling restraints.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecule | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose the protein structures from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Loops | Lists the loops separated by comma. In Pipeline Pilot a loop is defined by a starting residue and an ending residue connected by "-". A residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: A:LEU18-A:PRO22,B:ILE35-B:PRO41. In Discovery Studio select one or more consecutive residues to define each loop region. |
| Disulfide Bridges | List of disulfide bridges between Cysteine residues. In Pipeline Pilot, enter a comma separated list of disulfide bridges. A disulfide bridge consists of two Cysteine residues connected by '-', like B:CYS15-B:CYS40A, where a Cysteine residue is defined by [chain]:CYS[residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: "A:CYS32-A:CYS70,B:CYS15-B:CYS40A". In Discovery Studio, use the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog to specify the list of disulfide bridges. |
| Cis-Prolines | List of Proline residues in cis-conformation. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a comma-separated list of cis-Proline residues. A Proline residue is defined by [chain]:PRO[residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: "A:PRO12, A:PRO23, B:PRO12A". In Discovery Studio, select cis-Prolines in the drop-down list. |
| Additional Restraints | Adds distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and other MODELER restraints. MODELER provides a set of Python functions for generating and manipulating restraints. In Pipeline Pilot, the Python script entered here will be inserted into the MODELER special restraints function. An example Python script with explanatory comments is provided as the default value of the parameter. In Discovery Studio, use the Distance , Secondary Structure and Symmetry tabs of the Define Additional Restraints Dialog to specify the restraints. Discovery Studio will automatically generate a MODELER Python script from the data entered. The restraints should be specified using the residues from the model sequence. For example, to add a symmetry restraint, specify two segments from the model sequence which should be kept symmetrical during model generation. |
| Number of Models | Specifies the number of models to be created. |
| Start Model Index | MODELER randomizes the initial structure before producing each final model. Use Start Model Index to change the randomization seed to build models from different initial structures. Start Model Index is also used in the output model names. For example, if you build two models for protein structure xyz with Start Model Index = 3 , the output model names are xyz.L0003 and xyz.L0004 . |
| Optimization Level | Specifies the amount of molecular dynamics with simulated annealing to perform. High / Medium / Low : Different levels of sampling in simulated annealing step. None : No molecular dynamics with simulated annealing. Valid Values: High , Medium, Low, None |
| Use DOPE Method | Uses the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) method to refine loops. Select "High Resolution" to use the DOPE-HR method, a method very similar to the DOPE method but obtained at higher resolution. Valid Values: True , False, High Resolution |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |

# Loop Refinement (MODELER)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_loop_refinement_modeler.htm

## Loop Refinement (MODELER)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Loop Refinement (MODELER) protocol optimizes one or more user-defined loop regions. A loop in this context is defined as a segment of consecutive residues.

The final step of the protocol calculates the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) score for each model and
the scores are reported in the output of the protocol for evaluating the quality
of the models.

* Load a protein structure into a Molecule Window and select the residue segments to be optimized.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Macromolecules | Refinement | Loop Refinement (MODELER) .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Protein Molecule Select the protein in the Molecule Window. Loops Choose the residue segments from the Molecule Window. Disulfide Bridges Opens the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog . Select pairs of Cysteine residues to connect by a disulfide bridge. Cis-Prolines Builds the new proline
residues to cis conformation. Additional Restraints Set distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and symmetry restraints using the Define Additional Restraints dialog . Number of Models Specifies how many models to create, each from a different initial structure. Number of Models | Start Model Index MODELER randomizes the initial structure before producing each model. Use this to change the randomization seed used. Use DOPE Method Set to True or to High Resolution to use DOPE loop potential function . Otherwise, Fiser loop potential function will be used. For details about the remaining parameters, see Loop Refinement (MODELER) - Parameters . The protocol allows ligands and nonstandard residues in
the system. However, the residues
in the selected loop regions should be standard amino-acid residues.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecule | Select the protein in the Molecule Window. |
| Loops | Choose the residue segments from the Molecule Window. |
| Disulfide Bridges | Opens the Define Disulfide Bridges dialog . Select pairs of Cysteine residues to connect by a disulfide bridge. |
| Cis-Prolines | Builds the new proline residues to cis conformation. |
| Additional Restraints | Set distance restraints, secondary structure restraints, and symmetry restraints using the Define Additional Restraints dialog . |
| Number of Models | Specifies how many models to create, each from a different initial structure. |
| Number of Models \| Start Model Index | MODELER randomizes the initial structure before producing each model. Use this to change the randomization seed used. |
| Use DOPE Method | Set to True or to High Resolution to use DOPE loop potential function . Otherwise, Fiser loop potential function will be used. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Loop Refinement (MODELER) - Parameters .

The protocol allows ligands and nonstandard residues in
the system. However, the residues
in the selected loop regions should be standard amino-acid residues.

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the job finishes, double-click it in the Jobs Explorer to open the Report.htm . Review the Summary section of the report and click View Results to open a new Molecule Window with the loop models.

#### Viewing the report

* Check for errors in the Error section. If there are errors, open the modeler.log intermediate file and search for the string "_E>" for details. You can also check for warning messages by searching for the string "_W>" in the same file.

* View the Summary section to see the PDF Total Energy , PDF Physical Energy , and DOPE Score of
all output models.

#### Analyzing loop structures

The Molecule Window that opened contains the structures of predicted 
loop models and calculated properties of each model. 
The PDF Total Energy , PDF Physical Energy , and DOPE Score indicate the structure quality of each model. Additionally, the PDF Total Energy for each loop residue 
are displayed in the AminoAcid tab of the Data Table for each model structure.

#### Troubleshooting

If you saved the Intermediate directory when running the protocol, you can open the MODELER log file to obtain
detailed error information. First, check the MODELER log file for error messages by searching for the string "_E>", which usually indicate a serious issue. Then check for the warning messages by searching for the string "_W>".

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary that includes input and output files, the PDF Total Energy, the PDF Physical Energy, and the DOPE Score, and the parameters used. Check the Summary and the Error sections if protocol failed. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| *.dsv | Model structures. |

#### Further information

Theory - Loop Refinement (MODELER) Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Antibody Modeling Cascade - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_model_antibody_cascade-para.htm

## Antibody Modeling Cascade - Parameters

### Builds a model of an antibody Fab (Fragment, antigen binding) or Fv (variable) region

Builds homology models of an antibody Fab or Fv domain based on the sequence of the light and heavy chains.

The following steps are performed:

* Identify framework templates based on sequence similarity.

* Build a homology model for the framework regions. Models are built using a single, chimeric or a Top 5 template approach, depending on the setting of the Framework Template Type parameter.

* Identify CDR templates and use them to refine the CDR regions of the model.

* Optionally, if the predicted structure is a Fab region, it can be grafted onto a template full length structure.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequences | Sequences of antibody light and heavy chains. In Pipeline Pilot, specify an antibody sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose all or a selected subset of sequences in an open Sequence Window. Notes: The input sequences can consist of the following: Pairs of light and heavy antibody chains, which must have names which are either identical or differ only by a suffix _L, _H or _Lx, _Hx where x is any single character, or _VH/_VL/_VL_LAMBDA/_VL_KAPPA. Sequences containing both the light and the heavy chain with the chain break defined. Sequences containing both light and heavy domains in the same chain. Note that it is not always possible to automatically determine the correct chain break position in such cases, so the first two options are preferred. Sequences which are either all light antibody chains or all heavy antibody chains with no pairing. Any of the first three types may be used in the same input set. If Chain Permutation is True, then the input sequences can consist of at least one light and one heavy chain in any of the above forms with no restrictions on the names. Each possible Light/Heavy pairing will be modeled, the result being named by concatenation of the light and heavy chain names. |
| Chain Permutation | Create models for each light/heavy chain permutation. Valid Values: True, False |
| Maximum Permutations | Specifies the maximum number of permutations of light and heavy chains allowed. If no value is set then there is no upper limit. |
| Framework Template Type | Specifies the set of templates used to construct the framework regions Top 5 : Use the top 5 interface template hits. Chimeric : Use separate templates for the interface, light and heavy chain regions. Note: this option is only valid if the Input Sequences can form light and heavy chain pairs. Single : Use a single template. Valid Values: Top 5 , Chimeric, Single |
| Sequence Similarity Cutoff | Specifies the sequence similarity cutoff for templates to be considered for the Top5 framework template approach. Templates that do not fall within this range of percentage sequence similarity from the best hit are rejected. Note that this can lead to fewer than five templates being used if not all of the top five templates fall within the specified cutoff. |
| CDR Loop Definition | Specifies the numbering scheme used to define the Complementarity Determining Region (CDR). The following options are available: IMGT : Numbering scheme described in "The IMGT unique numbering for immunoglobulins, T cell Receptors and Ig-like domains". Lefranc, M.-P., The Immunologist , 1999 , 7 , 132-136 "IMGT unique numbering for immunoglobulin and T cell receptor variable domains and Ig superfamily V-like domains", LeFranc, et al. Dev. Comp. Immunol. , 2003 , 27 , 55-77. This scheme is used as a reference to define the CDR definitions for the other schemes. Chothia : Method described in the following papers: "Canonical Structures for the Hypervariable Regions of Immunoglobulins". Chothia, C. and Lesk, A.M., J. Mol. Biol. , 1987 , 196 , 901-917 "Standard Conformations for the Canonical Structures of Immunoglobulins". Al-Lazikani, et al. J. Mol. Biol. 1997 , 273 , 927-948. "Conformations of the Third Hypervariable Region in the VH Domain of Immunoglobulins". Morea, et al. J. Mol. Biol. 1998 , 275 , 269-294 "Antibody Modeling: Implications for Engineering and Design". Morea, et al. Methods , 2000 , 20(3) , 267-279. The CDR definitions for the Chothia scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -1,0;0,0;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,0;2,-1 Heavy: 0,-1;2,-2;3,-1 Kabat : Numbering scheme detailed in "Sequences of Proteins of Immunological Interest". Kabat, E. A., Wu, T. T., Perry, H. M., Gottesman, K. S., and Foeller, C., U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, NIH, Bethesda, MD., 1991 . The CDR definitions for the Kabat scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Lambda: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Heavy: 5,2;-1,8;2,0 Honegger : Numbering scheme described in "Yet Another Numbering Scheme for Immunoglobulin Variable Domains: An Automatic Modeling and Analysis Tool". Honegger, A. and Plückthun, A., J. Mol. Biol. , 2001 , 309 , 657-670. The CDR definitions for the Honegger scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Heavy: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Shifts are defined as three pairs of numbers separated by semicolons (e.g. -3,2;0,4;0,0) for each of the domain types Kappa, Lambda, and Heavy. Each pair of numbers specifies the relative shift of the start and end of the respective region (CDR1; CDR2; CDR3). The shifts are calculated with respect to the IMGT loop definition (i.e., -2,2 specifies a loop region that is extended by two residues on both ends compared to the corresponding loop based on the IMGT numbering scheme). |
| Loops to Model | Specifies the set of loop types to model. Valid Values: LIGHT_CDR1 , LIGHT_CDR2 , LIGHT_CDR3 , HEAVY_CDR1 , HEAVY_CDR2 , HEAVY_CDR3 |
| Filter By Canonical Structure | Specifies which of the loop types listed in Loops To Model should be filtered by canonical structure type. For the loop types selected, only antibody domains that match the canonical structure type of the corresponding CDR loop region of the query structure are considered as templates. See Also: Morea, V.; Lesk, A.M.; and Tramontano, A. Antibody Modeling: Implications for Engineering and Design. Methods 2000 , 20(3), 267-279. Valid Values: LIGHT_CDR1, LIGHT_CDR2, LIGHT_CDR3, HEAVY_CDR1, HEAVY_CDR2 |
| Full Length Graft Template | Specify a full length antibody structure to graft the predicted Fab structure onto. This option should not be used if the predicted structure is an Fv region or an unpaired light or heavy chain. The available options are: No template specified, just build the Fab or Fv region with no grafting. 1igy : crystal structure of an intact mouse monoclonal antibody, subclass IgG1. 1hzh : crystal structure of an intact human monoclonal antibody, subclass IgG1, with two loops, K:SER128-K:GLY136 and K:THR236-K:THR238 modeled. 1igt_model : model for an IgG2 antibody, based on the pdb crystal structure 1igt. 5dk3 : crystal structure of a full length antibody, subclass IgG4, with two loops, B:PRO230-B:PRO323 and G:PRO230-G:LEU235 modeled. User : use your own template file specified by the Input Template Structure parameter located under Template Source Valid Values: , User |
| Input Template Structure | Select a template structure. This parameter will be used only if the Full Length Graft Template parameter is set to User. |
| Advanced | |
| Exclude CDR Regions | Exclude antibody CDR regions from the sequence similarity and identity calculations used to rank framework templates. If this option is True, ranking of the templates will be performed using the following criteria in order to resolve tie-breaks: Similarity excluding the CDR regions Identity excluding the CDR regions Similarity for the full sequence Identity for the full sequence If this option is False then only the full sequence similarity and identity will be used for the ranking. Valid Values: True , False |
| Organism | Name or NCBI taxonomy id of the organisms to be selected from the framework and CDR template hits. If no organism is specified, all hits are reported. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported, as specified in the NCBI Taxonomy database. Examples: "human", "Homo sapiens", "house mouse", "Mus musculus" or "Caenorhabditis elegans" |
| Resolution Threshold | Only framework and CDR template structures with an X-ray resolution (Å) better than the Resolution Threshold are reported. Note: Only X-ray structures are affected. Structures for which the resolution is not defined, such as NMR structures, will not be filtered out, but they will be ranked lower than X-ray structures. The resolution for such structures will be reported as n/a. |
| Optimization Level | Specifies the amount of molecular dynamics with simulated annealing to perform. High/Medium/Low: Different levels of sampling in simulated annealing step. None: No molecular dynamics with simulated annealing. Higher levels of sampling can produce more accurate models but also require more computation time. Valid Values: High , Medium, Low, None |
| Number of Framework Models | Number of models to be created. |
| Number of CDR Models | Number of models to be created. |
| Maximum Templates Per Loop | Specifies the maximum number of protein templates for each loop. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True, False |
