Additionally, the Hierarchy View contains groups for QMap R10 Sites and Negative QMap R10 Sites. You can select and focus using standard Discovery Studio functionality. The surface is transparent and the atoms are also colored using the QMap R10 property to facilitate analysis of the site groups.

* Excipient Surface: The surface is colored according to the excipient coefficients, with areas of inclusion red and exclusion blue. Sites of high inclusion are created as groups on the Hierarchy View . If the All SVM/EN Predictions link is used, then a copy is created for each excipient type.

A second table contains links that generate different types of plots. They require that a molecule containing excipient, aggregation, and charge map properties is active in Discovery Studio . The plots are created only for the first visible molecule so that they do not repeat the same data when used with the windows containing tiled copies of the same molecule. Toggling the visibility of molecules updates the plot accordingly.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the result structures in one window, or click the table links to open individual structures with surfaces.

To further investigate aggregation sites and aggregation propensity scores, 
refer to the Calculate Aggregation Scores section of the Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools panel.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including tabulated results, links to display detailed reports and individual structures, input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| ViewMolecules.ds_pl | Script which opens a Molecule Window in Discovery Studio containing all the structures for which the excipient values could be predicted. |
| AllPredictedValues.csv | A comma separated value file containing all of the predicted excipient interaction coefficients for all molecules. |
| AllResidueFeatures.csv | A comma separated value file containing all of the residue feature values for all molecules. |

The Output directory also contains a subfolder for each input molecule, containing the output structures and detailed properties. The PlotScripts folder contains scripts which allow various plots to be created for molecules opened in Discovery Studio .

# Predict Humanizing Mutations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_predict_humanizing_mutations-para.htm

## Predict Humanizing Mutations - Parameters

### Suggests mutations for humanizing an antibody

Mutates residues in the framework regions of antibody variable light and heavy chains to make them more similar to human antibody sequences. By default, the native complementarity determining regions (CDR) are retained, as are the Vernier zone residues, which are framework residues important for stabilizing CDR conformation.

Each residue position in the variable domain of the query sequence is compared to the amino acid types found frequently in the human antibody sequences of the corresponding domain as well as to the type in the matching human germline sequences. Additionally, a prediction using a machine learning (ML) approach can be performed. The residue frequency data is derived from the large Observed Antibody Space (OAS) database, which is also used for training the ML models. Based on the analysis, each residue position can be mutated to one or more types of amino acids for humanization. The effects to protein stability of the suggested single mutation on those sites are evaluated. As a result, a number of mutated sequences are produced:

* Best_Single_Mutations sequence: the residue type found in the germline sequence or with frequency > 5% which produces the most stabilized structure.

* Germline_Substitutions sequence: residues mutated where appropriate to type found in best-matching human germline sequence.

* Frequent_Residue_Substitutions sequence: residues substituted where appropriate to the type found most frequently at that position in human antibodies.

* ML_Prediction_n sequence(s): sequence(s) mutated using the ML method.

Predicting the stabilities of the mutated sequences can be done in the context of a given antibody Fv or Fab structure which contains the query variable domain sequence. Alternatively, a starting structure can be automatically generated from the query sequence.

An interactive residue analysis report allows for detailed comparison of each residue in the sequence with the germline and species statistics, and also against the ML prediction(s) and an optional reference sequence.

See Also:

* Marks, C.; Hummer, A.M.; Chin, M.; Deane, C.M., Humanization of antibodies using a machine learning approach on large-scale repertoire data. Bioinformatics 2021 , 37(22) , 4041-4047

* Kovaltsuk A., Leem, J., Kelm, S., Snowden, J., Deane, C.M. and Krawczyk, K., Observed antibody space: a resource for data mining next-generation sequencing of antibody repertoires. The Journal of Immunology , 2018 , 201(8) ,2502-2509

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Query Sequence | The sequence to humanize. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose a sequence from an open Sequence Window. Note: The variable domain(s) will be extracted for analysis. If Query Structure is not specified and Calculate Mutation Energy is True, a model structure will be automatically generated based on the input query sequence. In this case, the input Query Sequence has to contain an Fv or Fab domain for model creation. Otherwise, the model structure will not be created and mutation energy will not be calculated. |
| Reference Sequence | Optional sequence which allows for comparison to other engineered leads. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose a sequence from an open Sequence Window. The light and heavy chains should be given in the same order as in the Query Sequence . |
| Query Structure | Specifies an optional protein structure on which to perform mutation energy calculations. The protein sequence of the structure must include the variable domains of the Query Sequence . If a protein structure is not specified and Calculate Mutation Energy is True, then a structure will be automatically modeled from the query sequence. Note: Generating model structure from the query sequence will take some time, so if the protocol is used repeatedly for the antibody it is recommended to save the model structure file for re-use. It will be in the results directory, named Predicted_Query_Structure.mol2 . |
| Germline Gene Sequence Options | Specifies how to obtain germline gene information. The options are: Identify Germline Sequences: Identifies V and J germline genes from the Germline Source which best match the Query Sequence . These genes should belong to the target organism, usually human. Provide Germline Sequences: Provide the required germline V and J gene sequences. These must be annotated with the IMGT residue numbering scheme so that they can be aligned correctly to the query sequence. This can be accomplished with the Prepare Germline Sources protocol. None: Do not use any germline gene sequences. In this case, no germline sequence information will be added to the residue reports or sequence substitutions. Instead, the gene name must be specified using the Heavy Chain V Gene and Light Chain V Gene parameters if the machine learning prediction or gene specific frequencies are required. Note that the example data files in the Discovery Studio distribution are a limited set of human genes as these are the only public, redistributable data available. It is recommended to obtain fuller sets of germline sequences, which can be prepared using the Prepare Germline Sources protocol. Valid Values: Identify Germline Sequences , Provide Germline Sequences, None |
| Identity Threshold | Percent threshold for matching germline sequences. If there is no sequence which has identity match at or above this value, no match will be returned. |
| IGH Germline Source | The default, IGH_GERMLINE_Example uses a small set of publicly available germline gene sequences. Alternatively, select User to browse to your own pre-aligned heavy chain V and J gene file. If the parameter is blank then no germline identification will be performed for the heavy chain. Valid Values: IGH_GERMLINE_Example , User, |
| User IGH Germline Source | Location of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the heavy chain V and J genes. This parameter will only be used if the IGH Germline Source parameter is set to User. |
| IGK Germline Source | The default, IGK_GERMLINE_Example uses a small set of publicly available germline gene sequences. Alternatively, select User to browse to your own pre-aligned heavy chain V and J gene file. The parameter can be set blank if the light chain is not a kappa domain, or if no germline identification is required for this domain. Valid Values: IGK_GERMLINE_Example , User, |
| User IGK Germline Source | Location of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the kappa light chain V and J genes. This parameter will only be used if the IGK Germline Source parameter is set to User. |
| IGL Germline Source | The default, IGL_GERMLINE_Example uses a small set of publicly available germline gene sequences. Alternatively, select User to browse to your own pre-aligned heavy chain V and J gene file. The parameter can be set blank if the light chain is not a lambda domain, or if no germline identification is required for this domain. Valid Values: IGL_GERMLINE_Example , User, |
| User IGL Germline Source | Location of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the lambda light chain V and J genes. This parameter will only be used if the IGL Germline Source parameter is set to User. |
| VH V Gene File | File containing sequence of germline V gene for the heavy chain. This should be in .bsml format and must be correctly annotated with IMGT residue IDs. Individual gene sequence files can be prepared with the Prepare Germline Sources protocol. |
| VH J Gene File | File containing sequence of germline J gene for the heavy chain. This should be in .bsml format and must be correctly annotated with IMGT residue IDs. Individual gene sequence files can be prepared with the Prepare Germline Sources protocol. |
| VL V Gene File | File containing sequence of germline V gene for the light chain. This should be in .bsml format and must be correctly annotated with IMGT residue IDs. Individual gene sequence files can be prepared with the Prepare Germline Sources protocol. |
| VL J Gene File | File containing sequence of germline J gene for the light chain. This should be in .bsml format and must be correctly annotated with IMGT residue IDs. Individual gene sequence files can be prepared with the Prepare Germline Sources protocol. |
| Heavy Chain V Gene | Set the V gene type for the heavy chain. This type will be used for the machine learning prediction and gene-specific frequencies if Germline Gene Sequence Options is set to None. Valid Values: IGHV1 , IGHV2, IGHV3, IGHV4, IGHV5, IGHV6, IGHV7 |
| Light Chain V Gene | Set the V gene type for the light chain. This type will be used for the machine learning prediction and gene-specific frequencies if Germline Gene Sequence Options is set to None. Valid Values: IGKV1, IGKV2 , IGKV3, IGKV4, IGKV5, IGKV6, IGLV1, IGLV2, IGLV3, IGLV4, IGLV5, IGLV6, IGLV7, IGLV8, IGLV10 |
| Residue Substitutions | This group of parameters controls the rules used to generate suggested mutations for humanizing the query sequence, using residues found with high frequency in human antibodies, and from the human germline sequence if this has been identified. Mutations are suggested using residue types frequently occurring at this position in the human antibody sequence alignment, to create the Frequent_Residue_Substitutions sequence. If a germline sequence has been identified or provided, then this will be compared to the query to produce a Germline_Substitutions sequence. In both cases, Vernier zone residues and those which are in CDR regions can be excluded from substitutions. |
| Frequent Residue Substitution Tolerance | For each sequence position, the residue type most frequently found in human sequences will be substituted if this frequency exceeds that of the residue type found in the query sequence by the specified percentage. |
| Germline Substitution Tolerance | For each sequence position, the residue type from the germline sequence will be substituted, if its frequency exceeds that of the residue type found in the query sequence by the specified percentage. |
| Exclude Substitutions | Specifies the conditions for which the query residue type should always be retained when creating the Frequent_Residues_Substitutions and the Germline_Substitutions sequences. Valid Values: Vernier Zone Residues , Kabat CDR Residues , IMGT CDR Residues , Query matches Germline |
| Use Gene-Specific Frequencies | If this parameter is True and the gene type for a chain has been identified then residue frequency data used will be for that gene only. Otherwise the full set of data for that chain type is used. Valid Values: True , False |
| Predict using Machine Learning | Predict humanizing mutations for murine sequences using a machine learning method. Valid Values: True , False |
| Target Scores | The target 'humanness' score(s) of the humanized sequence(s) using machine learning method. The IMGT framework regions of the input antibody sequence are mutated until the humanness score of the sequence calculated by the random forest model is greater than or equal to the given target score. One or more target scores can be specified and number of humanized sequences generated will correspond to the number of target scores. These values must be between 0 and 1 (inclusive) and separated by commas. |
| Calculate Mutation Energy | Specifies whether or not to assess mutation stability energies. If True, then single residue mutations will be performed using all residue types found in the germline and frequent (>5%) residue statistics for non-excluded positions, and any in the sequence predicted by machine learning. The best of the non-destabilizing mutations form the Best_Single_Mutations sequence. These best single mutations will then be performed simultaneously to assess how they interact. The combined mutation energies for the Germline_Substitutions , Frequent_Residue_Substitutions and Machine Learning Prediction sequences can also be calculated. | Local BLAST Search | Performs a local blast search of human mature antibody sequences, producing a sequence alignment BlastAlignment.bsml and additional information in the residue analysis report. This is a customized database created by searching the NRDB for antibody variable domain sequences, for organisms likely to be of interest in humanization studies (currently human, mouse, rat, horse, llama, rabbit and rhesus_macaque). Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. In this case, only the single mutations part is parallelizable, but as it is typically the most computationally intensive step the performance benefit can be worthwhile. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. This group of parameters controls the rules used to generate suggested mutations for humanizing the query sequence, using residues found with high frequency in human antibodies, and from the human germline sequence if this has been identified.
Mutations are suggested using residue types frequently occurring at this position in the human antibody sequence alignment, to create the Frequent_Residue_Substitutions sequence. If a germline sequence has been identified or provided, then this will be compared to the query to produce a Germline_Substitutions sequence. In both cases, Vernier zone residues and those which are in CDR regions can be excluded from substitutions.

For each sequence position, the residue type most frequently found in human sequences will be substituted if this frequency exceeds that of the residue type found in the query sequence by the specified percentage.

For each sequence position, the residue type from the germline sequence will be substituted, if its frequency exceeds that of the residue type found in the query sequence by the specified percentage.

Specifies the conditions for which the query residue type should always be retained when creating the Frequent_Residues_Substitutions and the Germline_Substitutions sequences.

Valid Values: Vernier Zone Residues , Kabat CDR Residues , IMGT CDR Residues , Query matches Germline

If this parameter is True and the gene type for a chain has been identified then residue frequency data used will be for that gene only. Otherwise the full set of data for that chain type is used.

Valid Values: True , False

Predict humanizing mutations for murine sequences using a machine learning method.

The target 'humanness' score(s) of the humanized sequence(s) using machine learning method.

The IMGT framework regions of the input antibody sequence are mutated until the humanness score of the sequence calculated by the random forest model is greater than or equal to the given target score.

One or more target scores can be specified and number of humanized sequences generated will correspond to the number of target scores. These values must be between 0 and 1 (inclusive) and separated by commas.

If True, then single residue mutations will be performed using all residue types found in the germline and frequent (>5%) residue statistics for non-excluded positions, and any in the sequence predicted by machine learning. The best of the non-destabilizing mutations form the Best_Single_Mutations sequence. These best single mutations will then be performed simultaneously to assess how they interact.

The combined mutation energies for the Germline_Substitutions , Frequent_Residue_Substitutions and Machine Learning Prediction sequences can also be calculated.

If no Query Structure is specified, then a structure will be automatically generated from the query sequence. Note that this step will take some time, so if the protocol is used repeatedly for the same query sequence it is sensible to save the structure file for re-use. It will be in the results directory, named Predicted_Query_Structure.mol2

Mutations with an energy greater than this cutoff will be considered to be destabilizing. Single mutations will only be included in the Best Single Mutations sequence if they are below this cutoff.

If True, the simultaneous mutation energy for the Frequent Residue Substitutions and the Germline Substitutions sequences will be calculated.

Valid Values: True, False

If True, the simultaneous mutation energy for the ML Prediction sequence(s) will be calculated.

The antibody_variable blast database is used for this search. This is a customized database created by searching the NRDB for antibody variable domain sequences, for organisms likely to be of interest in humanization studies (currently human, mouse, rat, horse, llama, rabbit and rhesus_macaque). Because the organism classification available for the NRDB is not always reliable, in particular for non-native sequences, those which contain descriptions including terms such as engineered, humanized, chimeric or mutated are excluded. This database is installed in shortcut:/Discovery Studio BLAST BLASTDB .

Specifies the maximum number of hits, filtered by organism, to return from the BLAST search. If left blank then all filtered hits are returned.

Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records.

Notes :

* Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. In this case, only the single mutations part is parallelizable, but as it is typically the most computationally intensive step the performance benefit can be worthwhile.

* By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal.

Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing.

Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster).

Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers.

# Predict Humanizing Mutations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_predict_humanizing_mutations.htm

## Predict Humanizing Mutations

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Output

* Analyzing Results

The Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol takes a query antibody sequence and suggests mutations for engineering it to be more human-like.

The goal is to engineer an antibody variable domain such that the resulting antibody retains the antigen binding specificity and affinity of the original non-human antibody, but with low human immunogenicity and without compromising stability.
This entails mutating residues in the framework regions to make them more similar to the types found in human antibodies.
By default, the native CDR regions that confer the desired binding affinity and specificity are retained, along with the Vernier residues, which are framework residues important for stabilizing CDR conformation [Almagro and Fransson, 2008] . You can then assess the mutations for impact on antibody stability.

There are two sources of data for residue types found at each sequence position in human antibodies. 
One is to use a closely matching human germline gene sequence.
The other is a set of frequency statistics compiled by extracting all human antibody variable domain sequences from the Observed Antibody Space database (OAS) [Kovaltsuk et al., 2018] . The VH, VL_Kappa, and VL_Lambda domain sequences are then numbered using the IMGT scheme, and the frequency of each residue type found at each sequence position is counted for individual domain type. 
The sequences in the OAS database are further clustered by matching the V gene types, such as IGHV1, IGHV2, etc. Then gene-specific statistics are collected for each residue from the corresponding cluster, including the D and J encoding regions.

The Predict Humanizing Mutations protocol creates multiple sequences depending on the options selected. These can include one containing mutations suggested by the frequency statistics, and another containing mutations based on comparison to germline gene sequence. Additionally, a machine learning (ML) method can predict humanizing mutations for a range of target "humanness" scores [Marks et al., 2021] .
The protocol can also generate a sequence that contains mutations produced by screening the different residue types found for each position by the ML method, from the germline, and those with frequency above 5%, for structural stability. If mutation energy calculations have been performed, then structures with these mutations are created. Additionally, an interactive residue analysis report is displayed for each variable domain in the query sequence, which allows detailed examination of the residues and possible substitutions at each sequence position.

For more information, see Theory - Predict Humanizing Mutations .

* Load a query antibody sequence into a Sequence Window. The query antibody sequence should include a light and/or heavy variable domain.

* Optionally, load a reference antibody sequence with the same variable domain type or types as the query for comparison.

* Optionally, load the corresponding Fv or Fab region antibody structure, which ideally should be prepared and typed with the CHARMm Polar H forcefield.

* Open the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tools and click Predict Humanizing Mutations... to open the Predict Humanizing Mutations dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Query Sequence Select the non-human sequence to be used as input. Query Structure Select an antibody structure containing the Query Sequence to use for mutation energy calculations. Germline Gene Sequence Options Specify how to select a germline gene sequence for comparison. Calculate Mutation Energy Specify whether to calculate mutation energies for the suggested mutations.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Query Sequence | Select the non-human sequence to be used as input. |
| Query Structure | Select an antibody structure containing the Query Sequence to use for mutation energy calculations. |
| Germline Gene Sequence Options | Specify how to select a germline gene sequence for comparison. |
| Calculate Mutation Energy | Specify whether to calculate mutation energies for the suggested mutations. |

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Predict Humanizing Mutations - Parameters

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to the background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary that includes input and output files, the PDF Total Energy, the PDF Physical Energy, and the DOPE Score, and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| *.mol2 | Models with mutations. |
| *.bsml | Sequence alignment with substitutions. |

* Examining interactive residue analysis reports

* Analyzing residue substitution alignment

* Analyzing mutated models

When the interactive job finishes, the interactive residue analysis reports, residue substitution sequence alignment, and any multiple mutation models are opened. 
For a background job, double-click it in the Jobs Explorer to open the experiment report and click the View Results button in the Results section in the report.

These reports contain a wealth of data for each residue in the query sequence and their possible substitutions. Examine details using the links in query cells. Pay particular attention to hotspots, which are framework positions for which the residue type does not match the germline gene and has a low occurrence (<5%) in the human frequency statistics.

For each residue position in the query domain, the main table shows:

* Kabat and IMGT residue number and CDR regions

* Residue type found in the query

* Reference and germline (if used)

* ML predictions (if used)

* Up to three residue types found with frequency above 5% in the human statistics database

Hover over residues to display additional information, including the Chothia and Honegger numbering, and all residue types found above 3% frequency in the database. It will also be indicated if the position has a dominant type (frequency >75%) and the query sequence has a different type.
If a BLAST search of the antibody_variable database has been performed, the residue types found for the top ten hits are displayed.
The positions of the VL and VH interface residues and Vernier residues are indicated in the main table and the residue details. Additionally, the positions of interface residues in the framework region are provided, showing whether they are of a conserved type [McCafferty et al., 1996]

This alignment consists of two copies of the query sequence, or of the full sequence of the input structure if it was provided:

* Sequence annotated with the usual antibody features and coloring for the IMGT scheme.

* Sequence showing the hotspots, Vernier residues and the combined Kabat and IMGT CDR regions. The hotspots are displayed in bold font and underlined in orange. Those not excluded from substitution by any of the criteria specified by the Exclude Substitutions parameter are displayed in orange. The combined Kabat and IMGT CDR regions are displayed in bold font and the conventional CDR colors. Vernier residues are indicated by blue carets. Double-click the sequence to open the Sequence Annotation window, which contains features for Vernier residues, CDR regions, and hotspots. Hover over the features for detailed information.

* The hotspots are displayed in bold font and underlined in orange.

* Those not excluded from substitution by any of the criteria specified by the Exclude Substitutions parameter are displayed in orange.

* The combined Kabat and IMGT CDR regions are displayed in bold font and the conventional CDR colors.

* Vernier residues are indicated by blue carets.

Double-click the sequence to open the Sequence Annotation window, which contains features for Vernier residues, CDR regions, and hotspots. Hover over the features for detailed information.

These sequences are followed by the Frequent_Residue_Substitutions sequence, the Germline_Substitutions sequence, sequences predicted for each target score by the ML method, and, if mutations have been performed, the Best_Single_Mutations sequence.

If mutation energy calculations have been performed, the structures arising from combining the mutations are displayed. These can be further assessed using other Discovery Studio tools, in particular Calculate Protein Formulation Properties .

#### Further information

Antibody Modeling Cascade Calculate Mutation Energy (Stability) Theory - Predict Humanizing Mutations

# Process Poses (ZDOCK) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_process_poses_zdock-para.htm

## Process Poses (ZDOCK) - Parameters

### Reranks, clusters and filters docked protein poses from ZDOCK

Filters docked protein poses generated by ZDOCK to give a new pose list containing only the poses with the specified residues at the docking interface between the two proteins.

It can also be used to rerank docked poses from a previous experiment using a more detailed energy function (ZRank) as well as to cluster any set of docked protein poses using different criteria.

The following steps are performed:

* Filter docked protein poses for poses with specific residues at the binding interface, as specified by Filter Poses|Receptor Binding Site Residues and Filter Poses|Ligand Binding Site Residues (optional).

* Rerank docked protein poses with ZRank (optional).

* Cluster docked protein poses and calculate density.

See Also:

* Pierce B.; Weng Z. ZRANK: Reranking Protein Docking Predictions with an Optimized Energy Function. Proteins 2007 , 67(4): 1078-1086.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor Protein | Protein structure to use as the receptor. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Input Ligand Protein | Protein structure to use as the ligand. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Input Poses | Set of docked protein poses to be processed. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file with docked protein poses in ZDock output format. In Discovery Studio you specify the Input Poses by selecting an existing group of protein poses in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected poses by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." entry in the parameter drop down menu. |
| Filter Poses | Parameters to select poses with a specified set of residues at the binding interface. The binding interface of the receptor is defined as the set of receptor residues which have atoms within the distance specified by the Distance Cutoff parameter of at least one ligand atom. Similarly the ligand binding interface is the set of ligand residues with at least one atom within the Distance Cutoff of any receptor atom. Only heavy atoms are considered. Note: A pose must have all residues listed as Receptor Binding Site Residues and Ligand Binding Site Residues in the binding site to pass filtering. |
| Receptor Binding Site Residues | List of receptor residues which have to be on the binding site. A residue is specified by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by comma. Example: "A:LEU18,A:PRO22". In Discovery Studio you specify the Receptor Binding Site Residues by selecting an existing residue group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu |
| Ligand Binding Site Residues | List of ligand residues which have to be on the binding site. A residue is specified by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by comma. Example: "A:LEU18,A:PRO22". In Discovery Studio you specify the Ligand Binding Site Residues by selecting an existing residue group in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." in the parameter drop down menu |
| Distance Cutoff | Distance cutoff (Å) to select binding site residues of a docked pose. A ligand(receptor) residue is part of the binding site if it has atoms within Distance Cutoff Å of at least one heavy atom of the receptor(ligand). Only heavy atoms are used in the calculation. Choosing a smaller value will in general reduce the number of poses that pass. |
| ZRank | Rerank initial-stage ZDOCK predictions with detailed electrostatics, van der Waals, and desolvation energy terms (ZRANK). See Also: Pierce B.; Weng Z. ZRANK: Reranking Protein Docking Predictions with an Optimized Energy Function. Proteins 2007 , 67(4): 1078-1086. Valid Values: True , False |
| ZRank Top Poses | Number of top scoring poses to be rescored with the ZRANK algorithm. Note that this parameter has to be greater than or equal to the Top Poses parameter specified for Clustering . In addition filtering for binding site residues can reduce the number of poses below the value specified in this parameter. |
| Clustering | Parameters to control clustering of poses. |
| Clustering Top Poses | Number of top-scoring poses to cluster and report in the results. Notes: Filtering for binding site residues can reduce the number of poses below the value specified in this parameter. This parameter cannot be larger than 5000. If rescoring with ZRank is turned on, this parameter has to be smaller than or equal to the Top Poses parameter specified for ZRank ( ZRank is executed before clustering). |
| Clustering RMSD Cutoff | Maximal ligand interface RMSD (Å) from the cluster center for a pose to be included in a cluster. Using a smaller value will typically increase the number of clusters and reduce the average number of poses per cluster. |
| Clustering Interface Cutoff | Cutoff distance (Å) used to define the interface region between receptor and ligand. Only the ligand interface region is used to calculate the RMSD values for clustering. The ligand interface region is defined as all heavy atoms of any ligand residue with at least one atom within the Interface Cutoff distance of a receptor atom. |
| Clustering Maximum Number of Clusters | Maximum number of clusters that are reported. It must be smaller than the number of Top Poses specified. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| PreserveDisplayStyle | If True, preserve the original display style of the input structures, if False use ribbon style. Valid Values: True , False |

Protein structure to use as the ligand. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins.

The Process Poses (ZDOCK) protocol allows selection of a subset from

either according to pose rank or by specifying residues on the docking interface.
It can also be used to cluster the same set of poses using different clustering criteria.
In addition, the protocol provides the option of reranking the docked poses with the ZRANK scoring function.

used as input for

The structures selected as the Input Receptor Structure and Input Ligand Structure parameter values have to correspond to the receptor and ligand structures
used as input for
the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. ## Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK) - Parameters

### Refines docked protein poses from ZDOCK using CHARMm energy minimization

Uses CHARMm to energy optimize a set of docked protein poses generated by the ZDOCK rigid-body docking method. The molecules must be typed with the CHARMm Polar H forcefield.

See Also:

* Li, L.; Chen, R.; Weng, Z. P. RDOCK: Refinement of rigid-body protein docking predictions. Proteins 2003 , 53, 693-707.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor Protein | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Input Ligand Protein | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein structure file. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose a protein structure from the list of all visible proteins. |
| Input Poses | Set of docked protein poses to be refined. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file with docked protein poses in ZDock output format. In Discovery Studio you specify the Input Poses by selecting an existing group of protein poses in the parameter drop down menu. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected poses by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ..." entry in the parameter drop down menu. |
| Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant used in the refinement. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Beta | Scaling factor that weighs the contribution of the desolvation energy compared to the electrostatic energy in the total RDock energy: E_RDock=E_sol+ Beta *E_elec2 Published results were obtained with a value of 0.9. See Also: Li, L.; Chen, R.; Weng, Z. P. RDOCK: Refinement of rigid-body protein docking predictions. Proteins 2003 , 53, 693-707. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. * Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK) provides optimization and scoring of a set of docked protein poses generated by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol - a rigid docking method, using a CHARMm minimization.
For more details, refer to Theory - Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK) .

* From the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol output, load the results .dsv file containing a set of docked poses into the Graphics View .

* The atom types and allowed residue types are limited to standard amino acid residues, and most of the small molecule ligands and metal ions are not allowed. 
Remove any non-amino acid groups from the ligand and receptor structures. Make sure that the C-termini is in standard charged form (i.e., as COO- group).

For details about the remaining parameters, see Refine Docked Proteins (RDOCK) - Parameters . optimized. The analysis of the results should focus on complexes that are unlikely to have clashes. To make it

with E_vdw2 < 10 kcal/mol have a clash value of 0. To display

# Calculate Aggregation Scores - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_sap-para.htm

## Calculate Aggregation Scores - Parameters

### Calculates protein aggregation propensity scores using CHARMm

Calculates regions on the protein surface that have a tendency to aggregate and thus lower the stability of the protein. Residues in these sites may be targets for mutations to reduce the likelihood of aggregation.

The following calculations are performed:

* The Solvent Accessible Surface area ( SAA ) is calculated for the side-chain of each residue using CHARMm.

* Per atom aggregation propensity score is calculated as the ratio of the actual side-chain SAA to the SAA of side-chain atoms in a fully exposed residue of the same type, multiplied by the residue hydrophobicity, for all residues within the Cutoff Radius of each atom.

* The per-residue value is then the average of the per-atom aggregation propensity scores for that residue.

* If there are multiple conformations, the SAA values and aggregation scores are averaged before reporting results. Conformations can either be present in the Input Typed Protein or read from a Trajectory File .

Notes:

* The protein must be typed with one of the supported forcefields: CHARMm, CHARMm Polar H, charmm19, charmm22, charmm27 or charmm36

* The calculation may be performed on multiple conformations contained in a dsv or Trajectory File .

See Also:

* Chennamsetty, N.; Voynov, V.; Kayser, V.; Helk, B.; Trout, B.L. Design of therapeutic proteins with enhanced stability. Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci., 2009, 106(29), 11937-11942.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Protein | Specify a typed protein. If the file contains multiple conformations, these are read and the SAA values and aggregation scores are averaged before reporting results. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed protein, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Cutoff Radius | Distance cutoff (Å) for calculating the aggregation propensity score. A small radius will create sites focused on a few residues whereas a larger radius will show broader regions liable to aggregate. Allowed values for the Cutoff Radius are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 15. Any combination of these values can be used within the same calculation to provide a set of scores at the various radii. Valid Values: 5 , 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 , 15 |
| Trajectory File | Conformations from a DCD file to be appended to the Input Typed Protein . Note that this option should only be used if the Input Typed Protein does not already contain these conformations. Notes: A DCD file is generated by a CHARMm dynamics simulation and contains coordinates of each trajectory frame. The molecules in the files must have the same number of atoms. |
| Frame Start | Specify the frame number in the DCD file to begin trajectory loading. |
| Frame Stop | Specify the frame number in the DCD file to end trajectory loading. If unspecified, the last frame in the DCD file will be used. |
| Frame Increment | Specify the increment in the frame number in the DCD file for trajectory loading. |

Specify a typed protein. If the file contains multiple conformations, these are read and the SAA values and aggregation scores are averaged before reporting results.

In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed protein, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures.

Allowed values for the Cutoff Radius are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 15. Any combination of these values can be used within the same calculation to provide a set of scores at the various radii.

# Calculate Aggregation Scores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_sap.htm

## Calculate Aggregation Scores

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Therapeutic proteins, such as antibodies, have a tendency to aggregate in high concentrations. This can lead to a decrease in activity as well as elicit immunological responses. This protocol calculates the protein aggregation propensity, which is a measure of the tendency of surface residues to aggregate. Sites with a high aggregation propensity score on a protein surface specify regions that are prone to aggregation. Identifying these areas allows you to use targeted mutation to engineer therapeutic proteins with higher stability.

This is licensed separately and not part of maintenance updates.

* Load a protein structure into the Graphics View .

* Clean the protein structure using the Prepare Protein tools . You can do this automatically using the Prepare Proteins protocol. Alternatively,
set the preferences on the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog and click the Clean Protein tool
so that the alternate conformations are removed, termini are added, and missing
side-chain atoms are patched.

* Use the Apply Forcefield command in the Change Forcefield tools to apply a CHARMm forcefield to the protein structure.

* Open the Macromolecules | Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools and click Calculate Aggregation Scores... to open the Calculate Aggregation Scores dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule Choose the protein for the calculation. Cutoff Radius Choose one or more radius values for the calculation. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Aggregation Scores - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Choose the protein for the calculation. |
| Cutoff Radius | Choose one or more radius values for the calculation. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Aggregation Scores - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the structure in the active Molecule Window is updated with the calculated protein aggregation propensity scores for the specified radii and the scores are added as atom and residue properties to each amino acid. The aggregation propensity score properties are labeled Aggr R5 etc. for each radius value used in the calculation. Molecular scores for each radius are calculated as the sum of atomic scores and are displayed in the data table and in the Report.

Aggregation sites are defined as groups containing adjacent exposed residues with high aggregation propensity scores. These groups are created in the Hierarchy View in a node named Aggregation Sites.

A solvent surface is created covering all non-solvent residues, colored according to the atom aggregation propensity score at the largest cutoff radius used. Atoms with high aggregation propensity scores are colored red, through blue for lower scores. Atoms in residues for which a score could not be calculated are pale green.

Additionally, two plots are created from the results: a line plot of residue index versus aggregation propensity score, and a point plot of site ID versus aggregation propensity score (residues that are not part of any site are shown as Site 0).
If no sites are identified for the largest radius used, the point plot will not be created.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the Jobs Explorer and click the Report link to open the Report, and click View Results to open the updated structure.

To examine the aggregation sites and aggregation propensity scores at the various radii used for a calculation, 
refer to the View Protein Aggregation Sites section of the Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools panel.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| {molecule name}.mol2 | Structure file containing the aggregation propensity scores |

#### Further information

Predict Protein Formulation Properties tools Theory - Calculate Aggregation Scores Calculate Aggregation Scores - Parameters

# Side-Chain Refinement - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_side-chain_refinement-para.htm

## Side-Chain Refinement - Parameters

### Refines protein side-chain conformations

Optimizes the conformation of the selected aminoacid side-chains using the ChiRotor algorithm. ChiRotor is based on systematic searching of side-chain conformation and CHARMm energy minimization.

The following data properties are added to the output molecule:

* ChiRotor RMSD : Side-chain RMSD of all refined residues.

* ChiRotor E-elec : Electrostatic energy after side-chain refinement.

* ChiRotor E-total : Total energy after side-chain refinement.

* ChiRotor E-vdw : Van der Waals energy after side-chain refinement.

* Residue RMSD : Side-chain RMSD of the individual residues.

Note :

* All RMSD values are calculated relative to Input Typed Protein Molecule .

* The protein needs to be typed with a supported forcefield.

See Also:

* Spassov, V.Z.; Yan, L.; Flook, P.K. The Dominant Role of Side-Chain Backbone Interactions in Structural Realization of Amino Acid-Code. ChiRotor: A Side-Chain Prediction Algorithm Based on Side-Chain Backbone Interactions. Protein Science , 2007b 16, 494-506.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Protein Molecule | Specify a typed protein. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed protein, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed proteins. Supported forcefields : CHARMm :The CHARMm forcefield is a general purpose, all-atom, class I forcefield. CHARMm Polar H : The CHARMm polar hydrogen forcefield uses a polar hydrogen model that is similar to the CHARMm forcefield. charmm19 : The charmm19 forcefield is a polar hydrogen forcefield parameterized for proteins and peptides. charmm22 : The charmm22 forcefield is an all-atom, class I forcefield. charmm27 : The charmm27 forcefield is a superset of charmm22 forcefield, with the additional coverage for nucleic acids. charmm36 : The charmm36 forcefield has improvement on protein side chain conformations and includes lipids, carbohydrates, and many small molecules. |
| Selected Residues | Amino acid residues that should be refined (minimized). The residues are defined by: [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Example: A:TYR33,A:LEU44 Notes : The residues selected should be standard amino acids and should conform with the forcefield. The following residues are excluded from refinement: ALA, GLY, and N-terminus PRO. Any amino acids or residues selected which cannot be rotated will also be ignored. |

Specify a typed protein. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed protein, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed proteins.

Supported forcefields :

* CHARMm :The CHARMm forcefield is a general purpose, all-atom, class I forcefield.

* CHARMm Polar H : The CHARMm polar hydrogen forcefield uses a polar hydrogen model that is similar to the CHARMm forcefield.

* charmm19 : The charmm19 forcefield is a polar hydrogen forcefield parameterized for proteins and peptides.

* charmm22 : The charmm22 forcefield is an all-atom, class I forcefield.

* charmm27 : The charmm27 forcefield is a superset of charmm22 forcefield, with the additional coverage for nucleic acids.

* charmm36 : The charmm36 forcefield has improvement on protein side chain conformations and includes lipids, carbohydrates, and many small molecules.

Amino acid residues that should be refined (minimized).

The residues are defined by:
[chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional).

Example: A:TYR33,A:LEU44

Notes :

* The residues selected should be standard amino acids and should conform with the forcefield.

* The following residues are excluded from refinement: ALA, GLY, and N-terminus PRO.

* Any amino acids or residues selected which cannot be rotated will also be ignored.

# Side-Chain Refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_side-chain_refinement.htm

## Side-Chain Refinement

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Side-Chain Refinement protocol optimizes the protein side-chain conformation based on
systematic searching of side-chain conformation and CHARMm energy minimization
using ChiRotor algorithm.

* Load a protein structure into the Graphics View .

* Clean the protein structure using Prepare Protein tools . You can do this automatically by using the Prepare Proteins protocol; note that this refines any sidechains it completes using the ChiRotor method. Alternatively,
set the preferences on the Clean Protein subpage - Preferences dialog and click the Clean Protein tool and
so that the alternate conformations are removed, termini are added, and missing
side-chain atoms are patched.

* Apply a forcefield to the protein structure. Use the Apply Forcefield command in the Change Forcefield tools panel.
Only forcefields of the CHARMm family can be used. The protocol cannot be used with XPROLIG or cff.

* Select the residues to be refined in the Molecule Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Minimize and Refine Protein tools tools and click Side-Chain Refinement... to open the Side-Chain Refinement dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Protein Molecule Select the open protein structure. Selected Residues If only a subset of residues should be refined, select the relevant residues in the Molecule Window and then set this parameter to select the side-chains to include for optimization For details about the parameters, see Side-Chain Refinement - Parameters . The protocol allows ligand and nonstandard residues in
the system as long as the ligand and residues can be typed by the selected forcefield. However, only the
side-chains of the standard residues can be refined by this protocol. The recommended forcefield for this protocol is the
CHARMm Polar H forcefield because it is better validated and faster in comparison to all atom forcefields (for example,
CHARMm, charmm22, and charmm27). If an all atom forcefield is desired, the CHARMm forcefield is recommended.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Protein Molecule | Select the open protein structure. |
| Selected Residues | If only a subset of residues should be refined, select the relevant residues in the Molecule Window and then set this parameter to select the side-chains to include for optimization |

For details about the parameters, see Side-Chain Refinement - Parameters .

* The protocol allows ligand and nonstandard residues in
the system as long as the ligand and residues can be typed by the selected forcefield. However, only the
side-chains of the standard residues can be refined by this protocol.

* The recommended forcefield for this protocol is the
CHARMm Polar H forcefield because it is better validated and faster in comparison to all atom forcefields (for example,
CHARMm, charmm22, and charmm27). If an all atom forcefield is desired, the CHARMm forcefield is recommended.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the atomic coordinates of the structure in the active Molecule Window will be updated with 
the refined side-chain coordinates of selected residues.
If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then click View Results to open the updated structure.

The <protein>_RMSD.log file contains information about the energy and RMSD for the refined structure.
The energies for the input structure and the refined structure are listed at the top of the file.

* EINIT - total energy of the initial input structure

* EOUTPUT - total energy of the refined structure

* INI-ELEC and OUT-ELEC - electrostatic energies of the initial structure and the refined structure

* INI-VDW and OUT-VDW - van der Waals energies of the initial structure and the refined structure

The file also lists information for each refined residue. The rows have the following format:

```text
<i> :<NAM><N> RMS = <RMSD> SA = <SA> <A>
```

where

* <i> is the index of the residue

* <NAM><N> are the three-letter residue code and number from the input file

* <RMSD> is the side-chain heavy-atom RMSD of the residue with respect to the input structure

* <SA> is the fraction of the residue surface that is solvent accessible

* <A> indicates if the residue is buried ( B ) or exposed ( S ).

The total side-chain RMSD data are shown at the bottom of the file. CORE is the RMSD of the buried residues
(residues with fractional accessibility less than 0.1), SURFACE is the RMSD of the exposed residues, and ALL is the 
RMSD of all residues.

Alanines, Glycines, and Cystines involved in
predefined disulfide bridges are not refined. They are also excluded from the RMSD calculation.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |

| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <protein>.mol2 | Protein structure with refined side-chains. |
| <protein>_RMSD.log | Log file containing RMSD and other information for the refined side-chains. A more detailed description is given below. |
| <protein>_charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_verify_protein_modeler-para.htm

## Verify Protein (MODELER) - Parameters

### Assesses the quality of a set of protein structures

Uses discrete optimized protein energy (DOPE) in MODELER to determine the quality of one or more protein structures.

DOPE scores are reported for each input protein structure, which can be used to compare different conformations of a protein. A lower score indicates smaller model errors. The DOPE Score is not normalized on protein size, so DOPE scores of proteins with different sequences should not be compared directly.

To compare proteins with different sequences, use the Normalized DOPE Score which is also reported by the protocol. The Normalized DOPE Score is a Z-score derived from the statistics of raw DOPE Scores on a database of models. Positive scores are likely to be poor models, while scores lower than -1 are likely to be native-like.

The protocol also adds a DOPE Profile property to each residue in the protein, which is the adjusted DOPE energy of each residue based on the observed average energy of the corresponding residue type. DOPE profile energies below zero tend to point to higher local model quality, whereas values above zero indicate lower quality.

Note:

* DOPE is only defined for the standard 20 amino acids, so the DOPE Profile values are only meaningful for standard amino acids. Values for other residue types should be ignored. They do not contribute to the overall DOPE scores.

See Also:

* Shen, M.-Y.; Sali, A. Statistical potential for assessment and prediction of protein structures. Protein Science 2006 , 15, 2507-2524.

* Eramian D.;Eswar, N.;Shen, M.-Y.;Sali, A. How well can the accuracy of comparative protein structure models be predicted? Protein Science 2008 , 17, 1881-1893.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. |
| Use DOPE-HR | Uses the DOPE-HR method, which is very similar to the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) method but is obtained at higher resolution. Valid Values: True, False |
| Smooth Window Size | Specifies the window size for smoothing per-residue scores (no smoothing when the size is 1). |

In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files.

Uses the DOPE-HR method, which is very similar to the DOPE (Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) method but is obtained at higher resolution.

# Verify Protein (MODELER)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_verify_protein_modeler.htm

## Verify Protein (MODELER)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Verify Protein (MODELER) allows you to select the best structure from a collection
of protein molecules with the same protein sequence. This protocol uses the MODELER DOPE
(Discrete Optimized Protein Energy) method to calculate a DOPE score for each structure.
A lower score indicates a statistically better model.

* Load the protein molecules you want to verify into the Graphics View .

* Open the Macromolecules | Create Homology Models tools and click Verify Protein (MODELER)... to open the Verify Protein (MODELER) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select the protein molecules that you wish to verify in the Input Protein Molecules parameter; you can choose All, Selected or Visible proteins from the active molecule window or alternatively browse for files containing one or more structures.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Verify Protein (MODELER) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, model scores will be added to the protein in the active Molecule Window.
Open the Data Table View and click on Molecule tab to view the scores.

If the job was run in the background, expand the results in the
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link to view the Report, and click View Results to open the protein and view the calculated scores.

Report.htm Contains a Summary section that lists the DOPE Score and the Normalized DOPE Score for each protein.

The raw DOPE Score is a statistical energy score that you can use to compare different conformations of a protein. A lower score indicates smaller model errors. However, the DOPE score has an arbitrary scale and it is not normalized on protein size, so you should not compare DOPE scores of proteins with different sequences.

The Normalized Dope Score is a Z-score derived from the statistics of raw DOPE Scores from a database of models. Since it is normalized for protein size, you can use it to compare models of proteins with different sequence. Positive scores are likely to be poor models, while scores lower than -1 are likely to be native-like.

In addition to the DOPE scores for the whole structure reported in the Summary of the report, the protocol also adds a DOPE Profile property to each residue in the protein. The values reported represent the set of contributions to the DOPE energy of each residue. The DOPE Profile can be used to evaluate the local quality of the model. DOPE profile energies below zero tend to indicate higher local model quality, whereas values above zero indicate lower local model quality.

DOPE is only defined for the standard 20 amino acids, so the DOPE Profile values are only meaningful for standard amino acids. Values for other residue types should be ignored. They do not contribute to the overall DOPE scores.

#### Creating a line plot of the DOPE profile

* In the Data Table, click the AminoAcid tab.

* Choose Chart | Line Plot from the menu bar to create a Line Plot of the
Verify score.

* Set X and Y to FullName and DOPE Profile .

* Set Color by Data Series to Molecule , and then click OK to create the line plot. If there are multiple proteins visible, the line plot will show each molecule as a separate colored line.

* Selections on the line plot are reflected in the Molecule Window. Hover the mouse over points on the line plot to see the residue ID and the DOPE Profile
value. When the Smooth Window Size parameter is larger than zero, the curve is smoothed using a running window
averaging technique. Smoothing the curve in this way tends to average out spurious noise. The Window Size parameter
specifies the size of the window (number of residues) used for the smoothing process. Smaller values produce higher resolution (but possibly
noisier) curves.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| *.mol2 | Output protein structure with DOPE Score . |

# Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/protein_modeling_verify_protein_profiles-3d-para.htm

## Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) - Parameters

### Validates protein structures

Uses Profiles-3D Verify to check the validity of a protein structure (e.g. a homology model) by measuring the compatibility score of each residue in the given 3D environment. Score for each residue and whole protein are reported and the expected high and low score for a protein of the same size is given as reference point.

The following scores are added to the data:

* Verify Score : Calculated Profile-3D score of the protein structure.

* Verify Expected High Score : The higher value of statistically expected score for proteins with same amino-acid composition.

* Verify Expected Low Score : The lower value of statistically expected score.

If the value of Verify Score is less than Verify Expected Low Score , the structure has the properties of a misfolded protein.

If an implicit membrane exists for the input protein, the low dielectric environment of the membrane will be taken into account when calculating the scores. The amino acids embedded in the membrane slab will be considered as fully buried and the interaction between an amino acid residue and membrane is non-polar. Use Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools in Discovery Studio or Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol to add an implicit membrane to the protein molecule.

See Also:

* Bowie, J. U.; Lüthy, R; Eisenberg, D. A method to identify protein sequences that fold into a known three-dimensional structure. Science 1991 , 253, 164-170.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecules | In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files. |
| Smooth Window Size | Specifies the window size for smoothing per-residue scores (no smoothing when the size is 1). |
| Secondary Structure Method | Specifies the secondary structure definition method. Valid Values: Kabsch-Sander , PDB |

In Pipeline Pilot, specify one or more protein structure files. Supported file formats include DSV, MSV, PDB, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose All, Selected or Visible protein molecules in the active window or Browse for protein structure files.

Specifies the window size for smoothing per-residue scores (no smoothing when the size is 1).

Specifies the secondary structure definition method.

Source type: HTML

## Verify Protein (Profiles-3D)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) allows you to evaluate the fitness of a protein sequence in its current 3D environment.
It can be applied to assess the quality of a theoretical model or to examine the characteristics of an experimental structure.
For example, it can be used to find hydrophobic patches on the surface of a structure. In the case of membrane proteins, an implicit membrane can be added to the molecular 
model and the non-polar environment of the membrane will be taken into account when calculating the scores.

* Load the protein molecules you want to verify in a Molecule Window.

* To add an implicit membrane to a protein structure use Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools panel or Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

* If you want to run the protocol on a set of residues in a single protein molecule, select the residues.

* Open the Macromolecules | Create Homology Models tools and click Verify Protein (Profiles-3D)... to open the Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select the protein molecules that you want to verify in the Input Protein Molecules parameter; you can choose All, Selected or Visible proteins from the active molecule window or alternatively browse for files containing one or more structures.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* Viewing the results

* Analyzing the Verify score of the protein

* Analyzing the Verify score of the amino acid residue

* Creating a Line Plot of the residue score

* Troubleshooting

When the interactive job finishes, a message displays the score for the input protein. Click the Report button to open the Report.htm file and click View Results to open the annotated structure.
The protein molecule in the active Molecule Window is updated with the Verify score and per-residue Verify scores,
which are shown in the Data Table View .

Groups are created for valid (residue Verify score >=0) and invalid (residue Verify score <0) residues. You can view the groups with the Hierarchy View .

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link and then click View Results to open the Report and the annotated structure.

The Verify score of the protein is the sum of the scores of all residues in the protein. This is a useful measure of the overall quality of the
structure.

The Verify score is shown in the Molecule tab of the Data Table along with the expected high and low Verify scores for
proteins of similar size. The expected high scores are based on a statistical analysis of high-resolution structures in the Protein Data Bank. The
expected low score is 45 percent of the high score and is typical of grossly misfolded structures having this sequence length.

If the model structure has a Verify score higher than the expected high score, the structure is likely to be correct. If the overall quality score
is between the reference values, then some or all of the structure may be incorrect, and it requires closer scrutiny. If the overall quality is lower
than the expected low score, the structure is almost certainly misfolded.

The Verify score of an amino acid residue indicates whether a residue is in the desired 3D environment. For example, a low score is given to a
hydrophobic residue on a protein's surface and a polar residue in the protein's core. Regions of the protein over which the score approaches zero
or becomes negative are likely to be misfolded. In homology modeling, a model region with a low score should be carefully examined. You may be able to improve the quality by adjusting low-scoring sequence alignments and rebuilding the model. On the other hand, if a surface patch of a protein
shows a low Verify score, it may indicate that it is interacting with other proteins and should be buried internally.

* In the Data Table, click the AminoAcid tab.

* Choose Chart | Line Plot from the menu bar to create a Line Plot of the
Verify score.

* Set X and Y to FullName and Verify Score respectively.

* Set Color by Data Series to Molecule , and then click OK to create the line plot. If there are multiple proteins visible, the line plot will show each molecule as a separate colored line.

* Selections on the line plot are reflected in the Molecule Window. Hover the mouse over points on the line plot to see the residue ID and the Verify
score value. When the Smooth Window Size parameter is larger than zero, the curve is smoothed using a running window
averaging technique. Smoothing the curve in this way tends to average out spurious noise. The Window Size parameter
specifies the size of the window (number of residues) used for the smoothing process. Smaller values produce higher resolution (but possibly
noisier) curves. Smooth Window Size values from 5 to 25 typically produce good results.
