# Align Sequences and Structures tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/seqanly_ast.htm

## Align Sequences and Structures tools

The Align Sequences tools align a set of protein sequences based on the sequence or structure similarity.

### Align By Sequence Similarity

These tools allow you to align sequences by sequence similarity. You can align a set of protein sequences, add a set of sequences to an existing alignment, or combine two alignments. Optionally, you can add secondary structure to score the alignment. Several types of secondary structures can be used in scoring the alignment.

* For a sequence linked to a 3D structure in the Molecule Window, the PDB secondary structure is used. If the PDB secondary structure is not available, the Kabsch-Sander definition is used. For a sequence without known structure, you can predict the secondary structure using the DSC method.

* For transmembrane proteins, predict the transmembrane helix regions using the Predict Transmembrane Helices tool on Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel.

To see the secondary structure cartoon in the Sequence Window , right-click the Sequence Window and choose Layout | Secondary Structure Cartoon .

When aligning sequences, you can specify additional options or constraints including fixing well-aligned regions and aligning sequences by their chains. To fix an alignment region, select a region in the Sequence Window, then click the fix link near the top of the tool panel. To align sequences by their chains, switch to chain view . For details, see Sequence Window .

Align Sequences: Opens the Align Sequences protocol dialog. This protocol aligns all or selected sequences in the current Sequence Window. Gaps are inserted or removed to update the alignment.

Align Sequence Profiles: Opens the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) protocol dialog. This protocol aligns a set of sequences to an existing alignment or aligns two alignments. A new Sequence Window displays the aligned sequences.

### Align By Structure Similarity

These tools allow you to create a sequence alignment based on the similarity of the corresponding 3D structure.

Align Structures: Opens the Align Structures protocol dialog. This protocol uses a set of protein structures to find the best superimposition of the proteins and then extracts the sequence alignment based on the matching C-Alpha positions. If the input proteins are not all similar, the similar structures are clustered and more than one sequence alignment are potentially returned.

When the protocol completes, one or more sequence alignments are opened in Sequence Windows. Corresponding structures are superimposed based on the sequence alignment.

Alternatively, you can manually superimpose two or more protein structures in the current Molecule Window using the Superimpose by Tether or Superimpose by C-Alpha Pairs tool on the Superimpose Proteins tool panel. You can extract a sequence alignment by identifying matching C-Alpha from the superimposed protein structures in the Molecule Window by clicking the create sequence alignment link below the Align Structures tool.

### Access methods

## Analyze Sequences tools

The Analyze Sequences tools allow you to calculate biophysical properties for sequences, predict sequence features, create hydropathy plots and perform phylogenetic analysis.

### Predict Sequence Properties

Predict Sequence Properties: Opens the Predict Sequence Properties protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to calculate a range of biophysical properties, predict sequence features such as post-translational modification sites, and create hydropathy plots.

### Phylogenetics

In the application, phylogenies are reconstructed from sequence alignments using distance matrix methods. 
A number of different methods are available for calculating distances between sequences. The suitability of each method depends 
on factors such as the type of sequence, degree of sequence divergence, and sequence composition.

The following phylogenetic analysis tools are available on the Analyze Sequences tool panel:

Tree Building Method: Choose the method for reconstructing the 
phylogenetic relationships. Available methods are:

* UPGMA

* Neighbor Joining

Distance Method: Choose the estimation method for measuring the
distance between sequences. Different methods are 
available depending on whether protein or nucleotide sequences are being analyzed.

Available methods for protein sequences:

* Absolute (# differences)

* Uncorrected ('p')

* Poisson Correction

Available methods for nucleotide sequences:

* Jukes-Cantor

* Tajima-Nei

* Kimura 2-Parameter

* Tamura-Nei

* LogDet/Paralinear

Mode: Allows you to choose the mode for reconstructing the phylogenetic relationships. 
Available modes:

* Best Tree

* Bootstrap

Number of Replications: Choose the number of bootstrap replications to be generated. 
The following sample sizes can be used:

* 10

* 100

* 1,000

* 10,000

Create Phylogenetic Tree: Invokes the phylogenetic estimation.

At least four sequences are required to calculate a phylogenetic tree.

of sync. This is indicated in the status bar of the Dendrogram Window.

based on the most current distances.

in the Dendrogram Window will select the corresponding sequences in Sequence Window. However,
deleting a set of sequences in the Dendrogram Window will not delete the corresponding sequences in Sequence Window.

# How to use the Analyze Sequences tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

## How to use the Analyze Sequences tools

The Analyze Sequences tools allow you to calculate biophysical properties for sequences, predict sequence features, create hydropathy plots and perform phylogenetic analysis
of nucleic acid or amino acid sequences using a sequence alignment as input.

To calculate biophysical properties for one or more sequences

* Activate a sequence window containing one or more protein sequences.

* From the Analyze Sequences tool panel, select Predict Sequence Properties... to open the Predict Sequence Properties dialog.

* Ensure that the Calculate Biophysical Properties parameter is set to True.

* If you do not wish to predict any sequence features, deselect the Annotation Types.

* Run the protocol. When it finishes, go to the Jobs Explorer and open Report.htm . The summary table shows the calculated biophysical properties for each sequence.

To predict sequence features for one or more sequences

* Activate a sequence window containing one or more protein sequences. Optionally, the sequences may be linked to protein structures if filtering by solvent accessible area or isotropic displacement is required.

* Select the desired features to be predicted from the Annotation Types parameter, and specify any User-defined Motifs.

* Set the parameters in the Filters group to specify the desired filtering by antibody domain, solvent accessible area and isotropic displacement.

* Run the protocol. When it finishes, the sequence window will be updated to show the predicted features and antibody sequences will be aligned according to the numbering scheme.

* If the prediction was performed for one sequence, the Sequence Annotation window will be automatically opened to allow further examination of the predicted features; otherwise it may be opened manually for individual sequences using the context menu.

* For further details, go to the Jobs Explorer and open Report.htm , and click on the Features links in the summary table.

To display hydropathy plots

* In the Advanced parameter group, set the Hydropathy Window Size to a value appropriate for the size of feature you wish to highlight.

* Run the protocol. When it finishes, go to the Jobs Explorer and open Report.htm . The summary table includes links to open Kyte-Doolittle and Free Energy hydropathy plots.

* Click on each of these links to display the table containing the plot data and create each plot.

The calculations detailed above are performed simultaneously using the default settings in the Predict Sequence Properties protocol; the examination of the results requires different methods.

To perform a phylogenetic analysis of a sequence alignment

* Open a sequence alignment file with at least four sequences in a Sequence Window.

* From the Analyze Sequences tool panel, select Tree Building Method and Distance Method . Specify any application defaults 
you want to change using the Phylogenetics page of the Preferences dialog.

* Choose the estimation Mode . To 
calculate the single optimal tree, choose Best Tree . To perform 
a bootstrap analysis of the data set choose Bootstrap .

* If desired, use the Dendrogram page of the Preferences dialog to control whether to display negative branch lengths as dashed lines.

* Click Create Phylogenetic Tree . When the computation is complete, the phylogenetic tree is displayed in a 
new Dendrogram Window.

* Analyze and change the appearance of the Dendrogram using the Dendrogram toolbar .

# Phylogenetics

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/seqanly_the_phylogenetics.htm

## Phylogenetics

Comparative sequence analysis is a well established methodology for predicting structural 
and functional similarities between macromolecular data. Many common methods, such as BLAST [Altschul et al., 1997] or 
profile analysis, are statistically based approaches that quantify sequence similarity regardless
of the origins of the data being analyzed. Phylogenetic methods differ from these approaches
in that they make explicit assumptions about the underlying evolutionary processes that result in 
changes at the sequence level.

Phylogenetic relationships are most commonly expressed in the form of networks (or trees) that 
summarize the divergence events that have occurred among sequences over time. Individual internal 
nodes (or branching points) correspond to distinct historical divergence events. Terminal nodes (or tips)
correspond to the actual sampled sequences. In addition, the phylogenetic distances between data can also be represented 
on these networks, typically by scaling the lengths of the branches that connect different nodes together. An illustration 
of the basic terminology is presented in Figure 1.

Figure 1: Basic terminology for describing phylogenetic trees

Three categories of methods are commonly used to generate phylogenies from molecular sequence data:

* Distance Matrix methods

* Parsimony methods

* Maximum Likelihood methods

The application provides two methods, UPGMA [Sneath and Sokal, 1973] and Neighbor Joining [Saitou and Nei, 1987] , for reconstructing 
evolutionary relationships using Distance Matrix methods.

Reconstructing a phylogeny using Distance Matrix methods is a two step process:

* The calculation of a pairwise distance matrix: Distances are calculated for all pairwise sequences using the chosen distance. A variety of distances are supported for nucleic acid and amino acid sequences in the application. More details about individual distances are provided in the Sequence distance metrics section in this Help topic.

* The reconstruction of the phylogenetic tree from the distance matrix: Two methods are provided 
in the application; Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic mean (UPGMA) and Neighbor 
Joining. The former method generates ultrametric trees in which all terminal nodes are 
equidistant from the ancestral internal node. This is effectively equivalent to assuming a 
constant rate of molecular evolution in all lineages, something which is generally uncommon. The 
most common scenario in which evolutionary rates are constant is when sequences that have 
evolved over a short period of time are being analyzed. The alternative method, Neighbor 
Joining, does not make the assumption of constant evolutionary rates and is generally preferred.

Both UPGMA and Neighbor Joining are guaranteed to generate a single best tree. In many
situations, particularly when there is reason to believe that there is limited phylogenetic
signal in the data set being analyzed, it is valuable to have some additional method for 
estimating the confidence that can be attached to a particular tree. A widely used method is 
bootstrap analysis [Felsenstein, 1985] ,
which works in the following manner:

* N randomized data sets are generated from the original sequence alignment by
sampling alignment positions with replacement. For a single random sample, an alignment equal
in length to the original data set is generated by repeatedly adding a randomly sampled
position from the starting alignment. This process is illustrated in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Simplified representation of bootstrap resampling procedure

* A phylogenetic tree is reconstructed from each random bootstrap sample.

* The single best tree for the original tree is estimated. Each internal node in the tree
has a unique set of nodes beneath it and the occurrence of this node is counted in the bootstrap
tree sample. If the node is present above the bootstrap threshold level, the node is shown resolved
in the final consensus tree. If the occurrence falls below the threshold, the node is collapsed and is
not shown in the final consensus tree. Figure 3 illustrates the procedure for constructing a consensus
tree.

Figure 3: Procedure for constructing a strict consensus tree. In this example, only
nodes that are recovered in 100% of trees are resolved in the final consensus tree.

In a data set with a strong phylogenetic signal, most nodes should appear resolved in the bootstrap
tree. In data sets with poor phylogenetic signal, the resulting bootstrap trees have little structure.

### Sequence distance metrics

A variety of sequence distance metrics are provided for phylogenetic analysis. Different distances should be applied 
depending on the characteristics of the sequence alignment for which a phylogeny is being reconstructed.

For amino acid sequences, the available distances are as follows:

* Absolute (# differences): Reports the distance as the 
absolute number of residue positions at which the sequences differ.

* Uncorrected ('p'): Reports the distance as the 
percentage number of residue positions at which the sequences differ.

* Poisson Correction: Estimates the number of 
substitutions per residue position under the assumption that the number of 
amino acid substitutions at each position follows a Poisson distribution. 
This distance may be useful when analyzing large amino acid sequence 
alignments.

For nucleic acid sequences, the available distances are as follows:

* Absolute (# differences): Reports the distance as the
absolute number of residue positions at which the sequences differ.

* Uncorrected ('p'): Reports the distance as the
percentage number of residue positions at which the sequences differ.

* Jukes-Cantor: This distance assumes an explicit
model of nucleotide substitution in which the rate of substitution is the same
between all four nucleotides.

* Tajima-Nei: The Tajima-Nei distance [Tajima and Nei, 1984] does not assume
that the substitution rates of different nucleotides are equal and is usually a fairly
robust estimator of evolutionary distance.

* Kimura 2-Parameter: The Kimura 2-parameter distance [Kimura, 1980] allows
for differences between transitional and transversional substitution rate.

* Tamura-Nei: The Tamura-Nei distance [Tamura and Nei, 1993] assumes a model
which considers differences in the rate of AG versus CT substitutions. This model is
useful for analyzing mitochondrial DNA sequences.

* LogDet/Paralinear: The LogDet method [Lockhart et al., 1994] is useful when
comparing sequences that have very different base composition biases.

# Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_align_sequence_profiles_align123-para.htm

## Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) - Parameters

### Aligns sequences or sequence profiles

Aligns a set of sequences to a sequence profile or aligns two sequence profiles using Align123, a multiple sequence alignment method based on the ClustalW program. ClustalW aligns multiple sequences using a progressive pairwise alignment algorithm. It first generates all possible pairwise alignments for a list of sequences and then builds a guide tree based on pairwise sequence identity, aligning the sequences following the order of the guide tree.

In Align123, the term for scoring a match of secondary structure can be added to the original ClustalW multiple sequence alignment score.

There are two alignment types:

* Align Sequences to a Profile : align a set of multiple sequences to a set of pre-aligned sequences (a profile)

* Align Two Profiles : align two sets of pre-aligned sequences (two profiles).

See Also:

* Thompson, J.; Higgins, D. G.; Gibson, T. J. Nucl. Acids Res. 1994 , 22(22), 4673-4680.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Alignment Type | Type of alignment to perform: Align Sequences to a Profile : align a set of multiple sequences to a set of pre-aligned sequences (a profile) Align Two Profiles : align two sets of pre-aligned sequences (two profiles). Valid Values: Align Sequences to a Profile , Align Two Profiles |
| Input Sequence Alignment | Select a sequence window with the Discovery Studio client or an alignment file with the Pipeline Pilot client. If Alignment Type is Align Sequences to a Profile , select an alignment that holds pre-aligned sequences (the profile). If Alignment Type is Align Two Profiles , select an alignment as the first profile. |
| Input Sequence Set | Select a sequence window with the Discovery Studio client or an alignment file with the Pipeline Pilot client. If Alignment Type is Align Sequences to a Profile , selects an alignment that holds the sequences to be aligned to the profile. If Alignment Type is Align Two Profiles , selects an alignment as the second profile. |
| Use Secondary Structures | Use secondary structure information when calculating alignment scores. Aligned residues with the same secondary structure type will have a favorable alignment score. In the Discovery Studio client, the possible values are: DSC : Use the secondary structure predictions obtained through the DSC method. TRANSMEM : Use the secondary structure predictions obtained through the TRANSMEM method (applicable to transmembrane proteins). Note that only helical secondary structure elements are considered if this option is selected. None : Do not use secondary structure. Note: For input sequences that have linked protein structures, the PDB secondary structure definition will be used if the parameter is either DSC or TRANSMEM. If the PDB definition is not available, secondary structure calculated by Kabsch-Sander method will be used. For sequences without linked structure, the secondary structure must be predicted before running the protocol using the DSC or TRANSMEM method as appropriate. In the Pipeline Pilot client, specify the input file containing secondary structure information or leave blank if you do not want to use secondary structure information. The file format for the secondary structure information is as follows: #SEQID 1abc #num id predsec predrel 1 P _ 9 2 L _ 9 3 P _ 9 4 Q H 5 5 S H 9 6 F H 9 7 L H 9 . . . The first line (a # in the first column is necessary) specifies the sequence name. Consecutive rows contain tab separated entries. The (#num...) line defines the order and composition of information carried in the file. The following keywords are required: num: residue number (e.g., from the PDB file). id: residue type. predsec: the predicted secondary structure (H : helix, E : sheet, - : Coil). predrel: the relative significance of the predicted secondary structure. (value between 0 and 9, where 9 is a very confident prediction). |
| Secondary Structure Weight | Specifies the weight of secondary structure information in calculating alignment scores. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Pairwise Alignment | Specifies the method for initial pairwise alignment. The available options are: Fast : Use the method of Wilbur and Lipman, which is extremely fast but approximate. Slow : Use dynamic programming, which is slow but accurate. This option is appropriate for short sequences but can be very slow when aligning many (e.g. >20) long (e.g. >1000 residue) sequences. See Also: Wilbur WJ and Lipman DJ, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 1983;80(3):726 Valid Values: Slow, Fast |
| Pairwise Alignment Scoring Matrix | Scoring Matrix for pairwise alignment (Used only when the Pairwise Alignment is Slow ). The matrix assigns a score for aligning any possible pair of residues: BLOSUM 30 : for detecting most weak protein similarities. PAM 350 : for shorter sequences. Gonnet 250 : for initial comparisons of sequences. Identity : a residue is considered similar to itself, but not other residues. Valid Values: BLOSUM 30 , PAM 350, Gonnet 250, Identity |
| Pairwise Alignment Gap Open Penalty | Gap open penalty for pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Slow ). Use a larger number to decrease the likelihood of a gap being opened. |
| Pairwise Alignment Gap Extension Penalty | Gap extension penalty for pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Slow ). Use a larger number to reduce the likelihood of gaps being extended. |
| Pairwise Alignment K-Tuple | Size of the exact matching fragment for initial pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ). Increase this parameter for better speed, decrease it for better sensitivity. For longer sequences (e.g. >1000 residues) you may need to increase the default value. The maximum allowed value is 2. |
| Pairwise Alignment Gap Penalty | Gap penalty for initial pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ). A lower value will increase the likelihood of gaps in the alignment. Except for extreme values, this parameter has little affect on the speed or sensitivity. |
| Pairwise Alignment Top Diagonals | Minimum K-tuple (exact) matches on each diagonal (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ). Increase the parameter value for higher speed, decrease it for better sensitivity. |
| Pairwise Alignment Window Size | Number of diagonals that are used around each of the "best" diagonals (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ). Increase the parameter value for higher speed, decrease it for better sensitivity. |
| Multiple Alignment | Set of parameters for multiple sequence alignment step after the initial pairwise alignment. |
| Multiple Alignment Scoring Matrix | Scoring matrix for final alignment. The matrix assigns a score for aligning any possible pair of residues: BLOSUM : for detecting most weak protein similarities. PAM : for shorter sequences. Gonnet : for initial comparisons of sequences. Identity : a residue is considered similar to itself, but not other residues. Valid Values: BLOSUM , PAM, Gonnet, Identity |
| Multiple Alignment Gap Open Penalty | Gap open penalty for final alignment. Use a larger number to decrease the likelihood of a gap being opened. |
| Multiple Alignment Gap Extension Penalty | Gap extension penalty for final alignment. Use a larger number to decrease the likelihood of a gap being opened. |
| Delay Divergent | Percent sequence identity level required to delay the addition of a sequence to the alignment. Sequences that are less identical than this level to any other sequences will be aligned later. Used only if Alignment Type is Align Sequences or Align Sequences to a Profile . |
| Special Gap Penalties | Set of parameters to fine-tune gap penalties. |
| Residue Specific Penalties | Use gap penalties that reduce or increase the gap opening penalties based on amino-acid type. E.g. positions that are rich in glycine are more likely to have an adjacent gap than positions that are rich in valine. Valid Values: True , False |
| Hydrophilic Penalties | Reduce gap penalty for stretches of hydrophilic residues (five or more residues). You can define the set of hydrophilic residues in the Hydrophilic Residues parameter. Valid Values: True , False |
| Hydrophilic Residues | Set of hydrophilic residue types used in Hydrophilic Penalties . |
| Gap Separation Distance | Gaps that are less than the specified number of residues apart are penalized more than other gaps. This decreases the chance of gaps being too close to each other. Note that this does not prevent gaps in close proximity, but it makes them less frequent, promoting a block-like appearance of the alignment. |
| Turn off End Gap Separation | Ignore gaps at both sequence ends in the Gap Separation Distance calculation. This is useful when you wish to align fragments where the end gaps are not biologically meaningful. Valid Values: True, False |
| Remove Existing Gaps | Remove all gaps from input alignment. Only set this parameter to False if you are confident about the positions of the gaps in the input alignment. Used only if Alignment Type is Align Sequences or Align Sequences to a Profile . Valid Values: True , False |

Valid Values: Align Sequences to a Profile , Align Two Profiles

# Align Sequence Profiles (Align123)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_align_sequence_profiles_align123.htm

## Align Sequence Profiles (Align123)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Align Sequence Profiles protocol aligns a set of sequences to an existing alignment or
aligns two existing alignments, e.g., two profiles using the Align123 algorithm, a progressive pairwise alignment algorithm
modified from the CLUSTAL W program. The two supported alignment modes are:

* Align a set of sequences to an existing alignment (sequence to profile)

* Align two existing alignments (profile to profile)

* Load a prealigned set of sequences from a sequence alignment file into a Sequence Window.

* Load one or more sequences to be aligned into another Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Align Sequences by Structure tools and click Align Sequence Profiles... to open the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set Alignment Type to Align Sequences to a Profile .

* Select a Sequence Window name from the Input Sequence Alignment parameter.
Sequences in this Sequence Window are pre-aligned (i.e., the sequence profile).

* Select a Sequence Window name from the Input Sequence Set parameter.
This set of sequences will be aligned to the profile.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* Load another prealigned set of sequences from a sequence alignment file into a new Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Align Sequences by Structure tools and click Align Sequences... to open the Align Sequences dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set Alignment Type to Align Two Profiles

* Select a Sequence Window name from the Input Sequence Alignment parameter.
This is the set of sequences in the first profile.

* Select a Sequence Window name from the Input Sequence Set parameter.
This is the set of sequences in the second profile.

When the interactive job finishes, a new Sequence Window will be opened with the aligned sequences. A dialog 
shows sequence similarity and identity of those sequences.

If the job ran in background, double-click the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the report. Review the results in the Summary section.
Check the Error section if the protocol run failed.
Open the output sequence alignment in a new Sequence Window by clicking View Results in the report.

If any of the sequences has a corresponding 3D structure in a Molecule Window, the sequences can be linked to 
the structures automatically depending if the structures are not already linked to other open sequences.
To force the link of the structures and the output sequences, 
choose Sequence | Link Sequence and Structure... from the menu bar.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <alignment>.bsml | The output sequence alignment. |

# Align Sequence Profiles (MODELER) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

## Align Sequence Profiles (MODELER) - Parameters

### Aligns two protein sequence profiles

Uses MODELER SALIGN to align two sets of pre-aligned protein sequences (profiles). The algorithm combines sequence information and prior information to calculate the matching score at each position in the resulting alignment.

The accuracy of an alignment between two protein sequences can be improved by including profile information. Profiles can be obtained from BLAST searches, multiple sequences alignments, or other resources.

See Also:

* MODELER SALIGN documentation at http://salilab.org/modeller/manual/node294.html#CMD:alignment.salign

* Marti-Renom, M.A.; Madhusudhan, M.S.; Sali, A. Alignment of protein sequences 
by their profiles. Protein Science 2004 , 13, 1071-1087.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence Alignment 1 | Alignment that holds the first pre-aligned sequence profile. In Pipeline Pilot Client, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose a sequence alignment from the list of opened Sequence windows. |
| Input Sequence Alignment 2 | Alignment that holds the second pre-aligned sequence profile. In Pipeline Pilot Client, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose a sequence alignment from the list of opened Sequence windows. |
| Scoring Matrix | Specifies the scoring matrix for assigning a score for aligning any possible pair of residues: as1 : for pairwise alignments of sequences that share from 30% to 45% sequence identity. 120pam : for shorter sequences. blosum62 : for detecting most weak protein similarities. gonnet : for initial comparison of sequences. Valid Values: as1, 120pam, blosum62 , gonnet |
| Gap Open Penalty | Penalty to open a gap. Use a larger negative number to decrease the likelihood of a gap being opened. |
| Gap Extension Penalty | Penalty to extend a gap. Use a larger negative number to decrease the likelihood of gap being extended. |
| Smooth Profile Weight | Weighting factor applied to the profile term computed from prior information, i.e. scoring matrix, when calculating the input sequence profile. See Also: Modeler documentation at http://salilab.org/modeller/manual/node288.html Marti-Renom, M.A.; Madhusudhan, M.S.; Sali, A. Alignment of protein sequences by their profiles. Protein Science 2004 , 13, 1071-1087. |
| Unpenalized Overhang | The maximum number of unaligned residues allowed at the terminals before a penalty is applied. If one input profile is much longer than the other profile, increase this number to avoid penalties for terminal gaps. |

Alignment that holds the first pre-aligned sequence profile.

In Pipeline Pilot Client, specify a sequence alignment file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, and FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose a sequence alignment from the list of opened Sequence windows.

Alignment that holds the second pre-aligned sequence profile.

* as1 : for pairwise alignments of sequences that share from 30% to 45% sequence identity.

* 120pam : for shorter sequences.

* blosum62 : for detecting most weak protein similarities.

* gonnet : for initial comparison of sequences.

## Align Sequence Profiles (MODELER)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Align Sequence Profiles protocol aligns two sets of prealigned sequences
(i.e., sequence profiles) using the SALIGN function in MODELER. It is
similar to the Align Two Profiles mode in the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) protocol.

A profile can contain one sequence or a set of aligned sequences. Input profiles
can be created using the following protocols in the application:

* BLAST or PSI-BLAST search

* Align Sequences

* Align Structures

* Align Structures (MODELER)

* Load two existing sequence alignments into two different Sequence Windows.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Sequence Analysis | Align Sequence Profiles .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Sequence Alignment 1 Select a Sequence Window name. Input Sequence Alignment 2 Select the other Sequence Window name. For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Sequence Profiles - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence Alignment 1 | Select a Sequence Window name. |
| Input Sequence Alignment 2 | Select the other Sequence Window name. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Sequence Profiles - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

When the job finishes, right-click it in the Jobs Explorer and select Locate to open the Output folder in the Files Explorer. See Output and input files for details about the files generated by this protocol. If the job did not run successfully, the Jobs Explorer will report an error. See Troubleshooting - Protocols for details.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. Check the Summary and the Error sections if protocol failed. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <alignment 1>-<alignment 2>.bsml | The profile alignment file. |

rarely be ignored. Next, check for the warning messages by searching for the string "_W>".

| Multiple Alignment Gap Extension Penalty | Gap extension penalty for final alignment. Use a larger number to decrease the likelihood of a gap being opened. |
| Delay Divergent | Percent sequence identity level required to delay the addition of a sequence to the alignment. Sequences that are less identical than this level to any other sequences will be aligned later. |
| Special Gap Penalties | Set of parameters to fine-tune gap penalties. |
| Residue Specific Penalties | Use gap penalties that reduce or increase the gap opening penalties based on amino-acid type. E.g. positions that are rich in glycine are more likely to have an adjacent gap than positions that are rich in valine. Valid Values: True , False |
| Hydrophilic Penalties | Reduce gap penalty for stretches of hydrophilic residues (five or more residues). You can define the set of hydrophilic residues in the Hydrophilic Residues parameter. Valid Values: True , False |
| Hydrophilic Residues | Set of hydrophilic residue types used in Hydrophilic Penalties . |
| Gap Separation Distance | Gaps that are less than the specified number of residues apart are penalized more than other gaps. This decreases the chance of gaps being too close to each other. Note that this does not prevent gaps in close proximity, but it makes them less frequent, promoting a block-like appearance of the alignment. |
| Turn off End Gap Separation | Ignore gaps at both sequence ends in the Gap Separation Distance calculation. This is useful when you wish to align fragments where the end gaps are not biologically meaningful. Valid Values: True, False |
| Remove Existing Gaps | Remove all gaps from input alignment. Valid Values: True , False |

Select a sequence window with the Discovery Studio client or an alignment file with the Pipeline Pilot client.

Use secondary structure information when calculating alignment scores. Aligned residues with the same secondary structure type will have a favorable alignment score.

In the Discovery Studio client, the possible values are:

* DSC : Use the secondary structure predictions obtained through the DSC method.

* TRANSMEM : Use the secondary structure predictions obtained through the TRANSMEM method (applicable to transmembrane proteins). Note that only helical secondary structure elements are considered if this option is selected.

* None : Do not use secondary structure.

Note: For input sequences that have linked protein structures, the PDB secondary structure definition will be used if the parameter is either DSC or TRANSMEM. If the PDB definition is not available, secondary structure calculated by Kabsch-Sander method will be used. For sequences without linked structure, the secondary structure must be predicted before running the protocol using the DSC or TRANSMEM method as appropriate.

In the Pipeline Pilot client, specify the input file containing secondary structure information or leave blank if you do not want to use secondary structure information.

The file format for the secondary structure information is as follows:

The first line (a # in the first column is necessary) specifies the sequence name. Consecutive rows contain tab separated entries.
The (#num...) line defines the order and composition of information carried in the file. The following keywords are required:

* num: residue number (e.g., from the PDB file).

* id: residue type.

* predsec: the predicted secondary structure (H : helix, E : sheet, - : Coil).

* predrel: the relative significance of the predicted secondary structure. (value between 0 and 9, where 9 is a very confident prediction).

Specifies the weight of secondary structure information in calculating alignment scores.

If running from Discovery Studio, set this parameter to True to use the fixed residue blocks of the input sequence window to fix those alignment positions.

To fix a residue block in sequence window, you can highlight a block of residues in the sequence window, right-click and use Fix Residue Block .

If running from Pipeline Pilot, use a text file to assign alignment positions to be fixed between sequences. Blocks of fixed residues should be specified in the following format:

The sequence names used in the text file must correspond to the names in the input alignment. The order of the sequences must correspond to the order of the sequences in the input alignment. The ranges specified correspond to the residue ranges of the block in each sequence (based on a sequential indexing of the residues starting at 1. Note that any gaps are disregarded in the indexing). If a sequence in the alignment is not part of a block, it should be listed with range 0-0 .

Note:

* Blocks of fixed residues that span domain boundaries are ignored.

Specify whether to align individual chains separately.

Valid Values: True, False

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Specifies the method for initial pairwise alignment.

The available options are:

* Fast : Use the method of Wilbur and Lipman, which is extremely fast but approximate.

* Slow : Use dynamic programming, which is slow but accurate. This option is appropriate for short sequences but can be very slow when aligning many (e.g. >20) long (e.g. >1000 residue) sequences.

* Wilbur WJ and Lipman DJ, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 1983;80(3):726

Valid Values: Slow, Fast

* BLOSUM 30 : for detecting most weak protein similarities.

* PAM 350 : for shorter sequences.

* Gonnet 250 : for initial comparisons of sequences.

* Identity : a residue is considered similar to itself, but not other residues.

Valid Values: BLOSUM 30 , PAM 350, Gonnet 250, Identity

Gap open penalty for pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Slow ).

Use a larger number to decrease the likelihood of a gap being opened.

Gap extension penalty for pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Slow ).

Use a larger number to reduce the likelihood of gaps being extended.

Size of the exact matching fragment for initial pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ).

Increase this parameter for better speed, decrease it for better sensitivity. For longer sequences (e.g. >1000 residues) you may need to increase the default value. The maximum allowed value is 2.

Gap penalty for initial pairwise alignment (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ).

A lower value will increase the likelihood of gaps in the alignment. Except for extreme values, this parameter has little affect on the speed or sensitivity.

Minimum K-tuple (exact) matches on each diagonal (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ).

Number of diagonals that are used around each of the "best" diagonals (used only when Pairwise Alignment is Fast ).

# Align Sequences

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_align_sequences.htm

## Align Sequences

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

Align Sequences aligns two or more protein
sequences using the Align123 algorithm, a progressive pairwise alignment algorithm
modified from the CLUSTAL W program.

* Load two or more protein sequences into a Sequence Window.

* To fix a block of residues to their input alignment position, select the residue block in
the Sequence Window and then right-click and choose Fix Residue Block .

* When sequences have more than one chain and each chain should be aligned independently, switch
to chain view by right-clicking the Sequence Window and choosing Layout | Chain View .
Each chain block can be aligned separately and you can prepare the input by
shifting a chain up or down to the previous or the next chain block by right-clicking and choosing Chain | Shift Domain Up or Chain | Shift Domain Down , or by swapping the order of two adjacent chains from a sequence by choosing Chain | Swap Domains .

* Open the Macromolecules | Align Sequences and Structures tools and click Align Sequences to open the Align Sequences dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select a Sequence Window name for the Input Sequence Set parameter.

* To fix a block of residues to their input alignment position, make sure there is at least one
fixed residue block defined and set the Fix Alignment Positions parameter to True .

* To align sequences by chain, make sure there is more than one chain in the input sequences
and the sequence window is in chain view.
Set the Align by Chain parameter to True .

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Align Sequences - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. 
Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the 
results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the sequences in the current Sequence Window will be updated with gap positions
from the output alignment. A dialog reports the sequence similarity and identity of the aligned sequences.

If the job ran in background, expand the results in the Jobs Explorer and click the Report link. Review the results in the Summary section of the report or
check the Error section if the protocol run failed.
Open the output sequence alignment in a new Sequence Window by clicking View Results button on the report.
Alternatively, you can apply the output alignment to the sequences that are already in the Sequence
Window:

* Select the Sequence Window.

* On the Sequence menu, choose Update Alignment .

* Choose the .bsml file that contains the output alignment.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <alignment>.bsml | The output sequence alignment. |

#### Further information

Align Multiple Sequences theory

# Annotate Antibody Sequence - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_annotate_antibody_sequence-para.htm

## Annotate Antibody Sequence - Parameters

### Annotates an antibody amino acid sequence

Identifies and annotates domains and Complementarity Determining Regions (CDR) in the amino acid sequence of an antibody.

The following steps are performed:

* Identify antibody domains and CDR loop regions using a Hidden Markov Model (HMM).

* Renumber residues in antibody domains according to the specified Annotation Scheme and align sequences by residue identifiers if specified in the Align Residue Identifiers parameter.

* Identifies germline sequences according to the Identify Germline Sequences settings.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequences | In Pipeline Pilot, specify an antibody sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose all or a selected subset of sequences in an open Sequence Window. |
| Annotation Scheme | Specifies the numbering scheme used to renumber antibody variable domains and to define the Complementarity Determining Region (CDR) in the Input Sequences . The following options are available: IMGT : Numbering scheme described in "The IMGT unique numbering for immunoglobulins, T cell Receptors and Ig-like domains". Lefranc, M.-P., The Immunologist , 1999 , 7 , 132-136 "IMGT unique numbering for immunoglobulin and T cell receptor variable domains and Ig superfamily V-like domains", LeFranc, et al. Dev. Comp. Immunol. , 2003 , 27 , 55-77. This scheme is used as a reference to define the CDR definitions for the other schemes. Chothia : Method described in the following papers: "Canonical Structures for the Hypervariable Regions of Immunoglobulins". Chothia, C. and Lesk, A.M., J. Mol. Biol. , 1987 , 196 , 901-917 "Standard Conformations for the Canonical Structures of Immunoglobulins". Al-Lazikani, et al. J. Mol. Biol. 1997 , 273 , 927-948. "Conformations of the Third Hypervariable Region in the VH Domain of Immunoglobulins". Morea, et al. J. Mol. Biol. 1998 , 275 , 269-294 "Antibody Modeling: Implications for Engineering and Design". Morea, et al. Methods , 2000 , 20(3) , 267-279. The CDR definitions for the Chothia scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -1,0;0,0;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,0;2,-1 Heavy: 0,-1;2,-2;3,-1 Kabat : Numbering scheme detailed in "Sequences of Proteins of Immunological Interest". Kabat, E. A., Wu, T. T., Perry, H. M., Gottesman, K. S., and Foeller, C., U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, NIH, Bethesda, MD., 1991 . The CDR definitions for the Kabat scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Lambda: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Heavy: 5,2;-1,8;2,0 Honegger : Numbering scheme described in "Yet Another Numbering Scheme for Immunoglobulin Variable Domains: An Automatic Modeling and Analysis Tool". Honegger, A. and Plückthun, A., J. Mol. Biol. , 2001 , 309 , 657-670. The CDR definitions for the Honegger scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Heavy: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Shifts are defined as three pairs of numbers separated by semicolons (e.g. -3,2;0,4;0,0) for each of the domain types Kappa, Lambda, and Heavy. Each pair of numbers specifies the relative shift of the start and end of the respective region (CDR1; CDR2; CDR3). The shifts are calculated with respect to the IMGT loop definition (i.e., -2,2 specifies a loop region that is extended by two residues on both ends compared to the corresponding loop based on the IMGT numbering scheme). |
| Align Residue Identifiers | Align Input Sequences by inserting gaps to align residues with matching residue identifiers. Residue identifiers are added by the protocol based on the specified antibody Numbering Scheme . Valid Values: True, False |
| Renumber Sequences | Renumber the residues in the Input Sequences according to the selected Annotation Scheme (Chothia, IMGT, Kabat, Honegger). If False, keep residue numbers in Input Sequences . Note: If an amino acid chain in the input sequences contains multiple antibody domains, an offset of 200 will be added to the residue ids of each additional domain (i.e. +200 for the second domain, +400 for the third domain, etc.). The reason for this is to avoid duplicate residue ids within the same amino acid chain. Valid Values: True , False |
| Identify Germline Sequences | Identifies germline genes which best match the Input Sequences . Valid Values: True , False |
| Identity Threshold | Percent threshold for matching germline sequences. If there is no sequence which has identity match at or above this value, no match will be returned. |
| Best Only | If True, finds only the germlines with the highest identity and similarity. If False, finds all germlines with identity above the Identity Threshold. Valid Values: True , False |
| IGH Germline Source | Base name of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the heavy chain V and J genes. The file must be located in shortcut:/Discovery Studio AntibodyDB/Germlines . Alternatively, select User to browse to your own pre-aligned heavy chain V and J gene file. Valid Values: IGH_GERMLINE_Example , User, |
| User IGH Germline Source | Location of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the heavy chain V and J genes. This parameter will only be used if the IGH Germline Source parameter is set to User. |
| IGK Germline Source | Base name of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the kappa light chain V and J genes. The file must be located in shortcut:/Discovery Studio AntibodyDB/Germlines . Alternatively, select User to browse to your own pre-aligned kappa light chain V and J gene file. Valid Values: IGK_GERMLINE_Example , User, |
| User IGK Germline Source | Location of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the kappa light chain V and J genes. This parameter will only be used if the IGK Germline Source parameter is set to User. |
| IGL Germline Source | Base name of .bsml file containing pre-aligned germline sequences for the lambda light chain V and J genes. The file must be located in shortcut:/Discovery Studio AntibodyDB/Germlines . Alternatively, select User to browse to your own pre-aligned lambda light chain V and J gene file. Valid Values: IGL_GERMLINE_Example , User, |

| Advanced | Set of less commonly used parameters. |
| User CDR Loop Definition | Add user defined CDR Loop Definitions based on shifts with respect to the IMGT numbering scheme. Each pair of numbers specifies the relative shift of the start and end of the region with respect to the IMGT loop definition (i.e., -2,2 loop region that is extended by two residues on both ends compared to the corresponding loop based on the IMGT numbering scheme). Valid Values: True, False |
| User CDR Loop Definition Kappa | Specifies the user loop definition for kappa variable domain using the shifts with respect to IMGT definition. |
| User CDR Loop Definition Lambda | Specifies the user loop definition for lambda variable domain using the shifts with respect to IMGT definition. |
| User CDR Loop Definition Heavy | Specifies the user loop definition for heavy variable domain using the shifts with respect to IMGT definition. |
| Annotate Canonical Types | Annotate CDR loops in the Input Sequences with the Chothia canonical type. Valid Values: True , False |
| E-Value Cutoff | Specifies the upper bound on the E-value for HMM hits to be considered as antibody domains. The E-value is a criterion of statistical significance. It measures the expectation of observing a hit for a random sequence. Therefore a lower E-value indicates a more significant hit. Full antibody domain sequences generally have e-values below 1e-40. Partial antibody sequences will have higher values. While the default value of 1e-20 should allow these to be detected, it may also pass similar sequences which are not true antibodies, such as T-cell receptor sequences. So if this distinction is important, a lower value such as 1e-30 is recommended. |

# Annotate Antibody Sequence

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_annotate_antibody_sequence.htm

## Annotate Antibody Sequence

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Analyzing Results

The Annotate Antibody Sequence protocol identifies and annotates domains and Complementarity 
Determining Regions (CDR) of antibody sequences. See Theory - Annotate Antibody Sequence .

Several Hidden Markov Models (HMM) are precomputed for the protocol and used to scan the input
protein sequence to identify the antibody domains. The following domains can be identified by the HMM model:

| Domain Name | Domain Type |
| --- | --- |
| VL_Kappa | variable light chain, kappa |
| VL_Lambda | variable light chain, lambda |
| VH | variable heavy chain |
| CL_Kappa | constant light chain, kappa |
| CL_Lambda | constant light chain, lambda |
| CH1_ALPHA | constant heavy chain CH1, alpha |
| CH1_GAMMA | constant heavy chain CH1, gamma |
| CH1_MU | constant heavy chain CH1, mu |
| CH2_ALPHA | constant heavy chain CH2, alpha |
| CH2_EPSILON | constant heavy chain CH2, epsilon |
| CH2_GAMMA | constant heavy chain CH2, gamma |
| CH3_ALPHA | constant heavy chain CH3, alpha |
| CH3_EPSILON | constant heavy chain CH3, epsilon |
| CH3_GAMMA | constant heavy chain CH3, gamma |
| CH4_EPSILON | constant heavy chain CH4, epsilon |

Residues in variable domains are renumbered according to one of the following commonly used annotation schemes from the antibody literature:

* IMGT: [LeFranc et al., 2003] and [LeFranc, 1999]

* Chothia: [Al-Lazikani et al, 1997] , [Morea et al., 2000] , and [Chothia and Lesk, 1987]

* Kabat: [Kabat et al., 1991]

* Honegger: [Honegger and Plückthun, 2001]

If an amino acid chain of the input sequence contains multiple antibody domains, an offset of 200 will be added to the residue IDs of each additional domain (i.e., +200 for the second domain, +400 for the third domain, etc.) This prevents duplicate residue IDs within the same amino acid chain. You may see some domains start at residue IDs smaller than the offset (e.g., 197 for the second domain) since some of the domains start with negative residue IDs without the offset.

The protocol also identifies the CDR loop regions consistent with the selected annotation scheme as defined in the above cited literature. The CDR regions are determined based on the alignment of the input sequence to the precomputed Hidden Markov Models for which the range of the CDR loop regions is known. If the Chothia scheme is used, then the canonical type of the CDRs and the canonical residues pertaining to it can be identified.

Additionally, the germline V and J genes that best match the sequence can be identified and aligned to the input sequence.

The example germline sequences provided with Discovery Studio are limited to publicly available human germline V and J genes. Incomplete germline data may cause false matching. To avoid this, obtain a more extensive set of germline sequences and use the Prepare Germline Source example protocol to format them for use by this protocol.

* Load the sequences to annotate in a Sequence Window.

* If you want to annotate only a subset of sequences, select these sequences in the Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Model Antibody tools and click Annotate Antibody Sequence... to open the Annotate Antibody Sequence dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Sequences parameter and then set the remaining parameters as needed. For details, see Annotate Antibody Sequence - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the input sequences in the active Sequence Window are updated with the antibody annotations. Antibody domains are indicated with colored carets according to the color map below. Additionally, CDR loops are highlighted with bold pink colored font for light chain variable domains and bold red colored font for heavy chain variable domains. The coloring of the CDR loops is based on the CDR loop definition consistent with the specified annotation scheme. If canonical residues have been identified when using the Chothia numbering, these will be indicated by bold font and red underlining.

To display the residue numbers according to the selected annotation scheme, right-click the Sequence Window and choose Display Style... ) to open the display style dialog. Change the ruler style in the General tab of the dialog to 1st sequence residue ID or Consensus ID .

If only one sequence was annotated, the Sequence Annotation Window automatically opens with the domains and loop regions showing in the Graphics View. Domains are colored according to the color map below. If germline genes were identified, these will be shown in orange, while canonical residues are displayed below the sequence line colored red, green or blue depending on which CDR they pertain to. They are grouped together in the annotation hierarchy view to allow them to be selected together.

If more than one sequence was annotated, you can open the Sequence Annotation view for any given sequence by selecting it, right-clicking, and choosing Show Annotations .

From the Jobs Explorer , open Report.htm .
Review the Antibody Domains and CDR Loop Regions in the summary table. If germline genes have been identified then the report will summarize these and provide links to alignment and csv files containing details.

If the job ran in background, open Report.htm from the Jobs Explorer .
Review the Antibody Domains and CDR Loop Regions in the summary table
and click View Results button to open the annotated sequences.

# BLAST Search - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_blast_search_ds_server-para.htm

## BLAST Search - Parameters

### Searches local protein databases with a query sequence using BLAST+

Identifies regions of similarity between a query sequence and database sequences and produces gapped or ungapped alignments of these regions using BLAST+ BLASTp algorithm.

Note:

* The PDB_nr95, PDB, Swiss-Prot and antibody_variable databases are installed by default. Other databases are available. Please refer to Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search topic in the Discovery Studio Help for further details of how to obtain and install these if required.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA, Genbank, and SwissProt. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequences in all open Sequence Windows. |
| Input Database | Name of the database to be searched. Discovery Studio provides the following databases: PDB_nr95 : non-redundant protein chains from Protein Data Bank. Chains are clustered with a 95% sequence identity threshold, and only representative chains are used to create this database. PDB : protein chains from Protein Data Bank. antibody_variable : antibody variable domain sequences for a subset of mammalian organisms extracted from NCBI nr database. Swiss-Prot : the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (fully annotated curated entries). Notes: The PDB_nr95 and PDB databases have sequences which are extracted from PDB structures. These are therefore the most appropriate choice for use in workflows such as homology modeling where linked structures and sequences are required. The PDB_nr95, PDB, Swiss-Prot and antibody_variable databases are installed with the product. In addition to these databases, preformatted protein databases including nr can be downloaded directly from NCBI. The UniRef90 database can be generated by downloading the UniRef90 FASTA file and running the makeblastdb command. For details for downloading and installing preformatted NCBI protein databases and UniRef90 database, please refer to the Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search topic in the Discovery Studio Help. |
| Organism | Name or of the organisms to be selected from the BLAST hits. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported, as specified in the NCBI Taxonomy database. Examples: "human", "Homo sapiens", "house mouse", "Mus musculus", "Caenorhabditis elegans" Notes: Organism filtering depends on the database containing taxonomy information for each sequence. This is included in the databases provided by BIOVIA, in the form of "NCBI_tax_id=<tax_id>" fields in the description. Preformatted databases which can be downloaded directly from NCBI now contain taxonomy data, which can be extracted for each hit. The protocol then edits this into the search results in our NCBI_tax_id format so that filtering can be applied. The UniRef FASTA format files contain TaxID= fields. If a search is performed using a database prepared from such data, this protocol will transform it into our NCBI_tax_id format so that filtering works as usual. If a BLAST hit has multiple entries, it is selected if one or more of the descriptions match the Organism parameter. |
| E-value Cutoff | Sets the threshold expectation value for keeping hits. It describes the probability that a hit is observed by chance. A lower E-value Cutoff will typically result in fewer, but more significant hits. See Also: Karlin, S. and Altschul, S.F. Methods for assessing the statistical significance of molecular sequence features by using general scoring schemes. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA (1990), 87:2264-2268. |
| Maximum Hits | Number of sequences to be reported. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Scoring Matrix | Scoring matrix used in searching. The matrix assigns a score for aligning any possible pair of residues: BLOSUM45 : for particularly long and weak similarities. BLOSUM62 : for detecting most weak protein similarities. BLOSUM80 : for sequence length between 50 and 85 residues. PAM70 : for sequence length between 35 and 55 residues. PAM30 : for sequence length shorter than 35 residues. Valid Values: BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62 , BLOSUM80, PAM70, PAM30 |
| Gap Penalties | Value pair for the gap open and gap extension penalties. Increase the Existence to prevent a gap from being opened. Increase the Extension to prevent a gap from being extended. The recommended value for each Scoring Matrix is: Existence: 15 Extension: 2 for BLOSUM45 Existence: 11 Extension: 1 for BLOSUM62 Existence: 10 Extension: 1 for BLOSUM80 Existence: 10 Extension: 1 for PAM70 Existence: 9 Extension: 1 for PAM30 Valid Values: Existence: 9 Extension: 2, Existence: 8 Extension: 2, Existence: 7 Extension: 2, Existence: 12 Extension: 1, Existence: 11 Extension: 1 , Existence: 10 Extension: 1 |
| Gapped Alignment | Specifies whether to generate gapped alignment or ungapped alignment. See Also: Karlin, S. and Altschul, S.F. Methods for assessing the statistical significance of molecular sequence features by using general scoring schemes. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA (1990), 87:2264-2268. Valid Values: True , False |
| Filter Low Complexity | Specifies whether to mask off segments of the query sequence that have low compositional complexity. Filtering can remove hits that are statistically significant but biologically uninteresting (e.g., hits against common acidic-, basic- or proline-rich regions). Valid Values: True , False |
| Word Size | Specifies the length (either 2 or 3) of the initial matching segment. A larger value tends to yield more accurate results, but takes more computation time. Valid Values: 2, 3 |
| Other Options | Specifies any additional options. BLAST provides several advanced options that are not explicitly supported by this protocol. Any additional options specified here will be included in the blast command line, for example -s T . See the NCBI BLAST documentation for details of the available options. Note that these additional options will not be tested for validity. |

In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA, Genbank, and SwissProt. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequences in all open Sequence Windows.

Name of the database to be searched.

Discovery Studio provides the following databases:

* PDB_nr95 : non-redundant protein chains from Protein Data Bank. Chains are clustered with a 95% sequence identity threshold, and only representative chains are used to create this database.

* PDB : protein chains from Protein Data Bank.

* antibody_variable : antibody variable domain sequences for a subset of mammalian organisms extracted from NCBI nr database.

* Swiss-Prot : the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (fully annotated curated entries).

Notes:

* The PDB_nr95 and PDB databases have sequences which are extracted from PDB structures. These are therefore the most appropriate choice for use in workflows such as homology modeling where linked structures and sequences are required.

* The PDB_nr95, PDB, Swiss-Prot and antibody_variable databases are installed with the product.

* In addition to these databases, preformatted protein databases including nr can be downloaded directly from NCBI.

* The UniRef90 database can be generated by downloading the UniRef90 FASTA file and running the makeblastdb command.

* For details for downloading and installing preformatted NCBI protein databases and UniRef90 database, please refer to the Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search topic in the Discovery Studio Help.

Name or of the organisms to be selected from the BLAST hits.

Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported, as specified in the NCBI Taxonomy database.

Examples: "human", "Homo sapiens", "house mouse", "Mus musculus", "Caenorhabditis elegans"

* Organism filtering depends on the database containing taxonomy information for each sequence.

* This is included in the databases provided by BIOVIA, in the form of "NCBI_tax_id=<tax_id>" fields in the description.

* Preformatted databases which can be downloaded directly from NCBI now contain taxonomy data, which can be extracted for each hit. The protocol then edits this into the search results in our NCBI_tax_id format so that filtering can be applied.

* The UniRef FASTA format files contain TaxID= fields. If a search is performed using a database prepared from such data, this protocol will transform it into our NCBI_tax_id format so that filtering works as usual.

* If a BLAST hit has multiple entries, it is selected if one or more of the descriptions match the Organism parameter.

Sets the threshold expectation value for keeping hits.

It describes the probability that a hit is observed by chance. A lower E-value Cutoff will typically result in fewer, but more significant hits.

See Also:

* Karlin, S. and Altschul, S.F. Methods for assessing the statistical significance of molecular sequence features by using general scoring schemes. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA (1990), 87:2264-2268.

Number of sequences to be reported.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Scoring matrix used in searching.

The matrix assigns a score for aligning any possible pair of residues:

* BLOSUM45 : for particularly long and weak similarities.

* BLOSUM62 : for detecting most weak protein similarities.

* BLOSUM80 : for sequence length between 50 and 85 residues.

* PAM70 : for sequence length between 35 and 55 residues.

* PAM30 : for sequence length shorter than 35 residues.

Valid Values: BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62 , BLOSUM80, PAM70, PAM30

* Existence: 15 Extension: 2 for BLOSUM45

* Existence: 11 Extension: 1 for BLOSUM62

* Existence: 10 Extension: 1 for BLOSUM80

* Existence: 10 Extension: 1 for PAM70

* Existence: 9 Extension: 1 for PAM30

Valid Values: Existence: 9 Extension: 2, Existence: 8 Extension: 2, Existence: 7 Extension: 2, Existence: 12 Extension: 1, Existence: 11 Extension: 1 , Existence: 10 Extension: 1

Specifies whether to generate gapped alignment or ungapped alignment.

Valid Values: True , False

Specifies whether to mask off segments of the query sequence that have low compositional complexity. Filtering can remove hits that are statistically significant but biologically uninteresting (e.g., hits against common acidic-, basic- or proline-rich regions).

Specifies the length (either 2 or 3) of the initial matching segment. A larger value tends to yield more accurate results, but takes more computation time.

Valid Values: 2, 3

Specifies any additional options.

BLAST provides several advanced options that are not explicitly supported by this protocol. Any additional options specified here will be included in the blast command line, for example -s T . See the NCBI BLAST documentation for details of the available options. Note that these additional options will not be tested for validity.

# BLAST Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_blast_search_ds_server.htm

## BLAST Search

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The BLAST Search protocol identifies homologous relationships between a protein query
sequence and sequences in a database. It is a statistically driven search
method that finds regions of similarity between a query sequence and database
sequences, producing ungapped or gapped alignments of these regions. It is
based on the blastall program from [Altschul et al., 1990] .

#### Databases

Several sequence databases are provided with each Discovery Studio release to
be used by this protocol and you can also add your own databases .

#### Identifying homologs with 3D structure

Although the PDB and PDB_nr95 sequence databases are much smaller databases
compared to nr, UniRef90, or Swiss-Prot, they are quite important and
useful because the sequences in the former two databases have known 3D structures.
By searching against PDB or PDB_nr95, you can obtain template structures
for homology modeling. In addition, finding homologous sequences in these
databases can provide a more detailed annotation to the query sequence
compared to other sequence matches. For example, you can study the active
site of the sequence based on the template structure, etc. To increase
the remote homology matches, PSSMs (position-specific, scoring matrix)
created from searching UniRef90 can be used to search PDB or PDB_nr95 [Kitson, 2002] using PSI-BLAST Search
(refer to PSI-BLAST Search for more information).

* Load a protein sequence into the Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Search Sequences by Similarity tools and click BLAST Search... to open the BLAST Search dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Sequence Specify the name to be analyzed. Input Database Select an installed database from the list. For details about the databases and how to install them, see Local databases and Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search . Input Database | Organism Set the Organism parameter under the Input Database parameter group if the BLAST hits should be filtered by organism. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported. For details about the remaining parameters, see BLAST Search - Parameters and the Advanced BLAST and PSI-BLAST parameters Help topics.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence | Specify the name to be analyzed. |
| Input Database | Select an installed database from the list. For details about the databases and how to install them, see Local databases and Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search . |
| Input Database \| Organism | Set the Organism parameter under the Input Database parameter group if the BLAST hits should be filtered by organism. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see BLAST Search - Parameters and the Advanced BLAST and PSI-BLAST parameters Help topics.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the hits will be shown in the BLAST Results Window . Use the following information in the Table View of the BLAST Results Window to evaluate hits:

* Bit score: The bit score is calculated from the raw score by normalizing with the statistical variables that define a given scoring
system. Therefore, bit scores from different searches, even those employing different scoring matrices, can be compared. The higher the
score the better the alignment.

* E-value: The E-value is a statistical score which estimates the chance of finding such a hit in a given sequence
database. For the same hit, this score can change when the database changes since it is calculated depending on the constitution of the
database sequences. The lower the E-value, the better the alignment. A hit with lower sequence identity but longer alignment may have
E-value better than a hit with higher sequence identity and shorter alignment.

* Alignment Length

* Identity: Pairwise sequence identity between the query and the hit.

* Similarity: Pairwise sequence similarity between the query and the hit.

* Resolution: X-ray resolution for the PDB hit.

* SCOP codes: SCOP codes for the PDB hit.

* Ligand: Ligands near the PDB hit.

* Organism: Scientific organism name of the hit.

The profile file, <sequence>_profile.pir can be used in the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) protocol or the Align Sequence Profiles (MODELER) protocol for further
profile alignment calculation.

In the output profile, there are no gaps in the input sequence (i.e., the residues in the hits that are not aligned to the input sequence are deleted). 
This provides a clean view of the statistics of the residues that could occur at each position of the input sequence.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the
Jobs Explorer and click View Results to open the BLAST Results Window .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <sequence>.xml | Opens the BLAST Results Window. |
| <sequence>_profile.pir | Contains the alignment of the query sequence to all hit sequences. |
| blastseqs.fasta | A FASTA sequence file, containing the results nucleic acid or amino acid sequences. |
| PDBresolution.txt | A text file describing the X-ray resolution of each PDB hit. |
| HspSCOPs.txt | A text file describing the SCOP code of each PDB hit. |
| HspLigands.txt | A text file describing the ligands near each PDB hit. |
| Organism.txt | A text file describing the organism of each hit. |
| <sequence>_filtered.xml,<sequence>_profile_filtered.pir,blastseqs_filtered.fasta, PDBResolution_filtered.txt, HspLigands_filtered.txt, HspSCOPs_filtered.txt | Contain the same results as previously described files, but filtered by organism (present if the Organism parameter was set). |

#### Further information
