## BLAST Search (NCBI Server) - Parameters

### Searches protein databases at the NCBI with a query sequence using BLAST

Uses the BLAST server at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). BLAST is a statistically driven search method that finds regions of similarity between a query sequence and database sequences and produces gapped or ungapped alignments of these regions.

The NCBI maintains up-to-date protein databases that enable you to perform sequence similarity searches over the internet against all publicly available sequence data.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA, Genbank, and SwissProt. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequences in all open Sequence Windows. |
| Input Database | Name of a NCBI database for searching: nr : non-redundant protein sequences. refseq_protein : reference proteins. swissprot : Swissprot protein sequences. pataa : patented protein sequences. pdb : Protein Data Bank proteins. env_nr : environmental samples. See Also: Check the NCBI BLAST web site for more database information. Valid Values: nr, refseq_protein, swissprot, pataa, pdb , env_nr, User |
| User Specified Database | Allows the specification of a database other than those known of at the time of the protocol release. Requires that Custom is chosen as the Input Database. It is the user's responsibility to specify a valid database name. |
| Organism | An organism name to limit search. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported, as specified in the NCBI Taxonomy database. Examples: "human", "Homo sapiens", "house mouse", "Mus musculus" or "Caenorhabditis elegans" |
| E-value Cutoff | Threshold expectation value for hits to be reported. This is the E-value from the Karlin-Altschul equation. A value of 10 means that 10 such matches are expected to be found merely by chance. If the statistical significance ascribed to a match is greater than this threshold, the match will not be reported. A lower E-value Cutoff will typically result in fewer, but more significant hits. See Also: Karlin, S. and Altschul, S.F. Methods for assessing the statistical significance of molecular sequence features by using general scoring schemes. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA (1990), 87:2264-2268. |
| Maximum Hits | Number of sequences to be reported. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Time Out | Specifies the time out in minutes. If empty, the program will wait until the results come back. |
| Scoring Matrix | Scoring matrix used in searching. The matrix assigns a score for aligning any possible pair of residues: BLOSUM45 : for particularly long and weak similarities. BLOSUM62 : for detecting most weak protein similarities. BLOSUM80 : for sequence length between 50 and 85 residues. PAM70 : for sequence length between 35 and 55 residues. PAM30 : for sequence length shorter than 35 residues. Valid Values: BLOSUM45, BLOSUM62 , BLOSUM80, PAM70, PAM30 |
| Gap Penalties | Value pair for the gap open and gap extension penalties. Increase the Existence to prevent a gap from being opened. Increase the Extension to prevent a gap from being extended. The recommended value for each Scoring Matrix is: Existence: 15 Extension: 2 for BLOSUM45 Existence: 11 Extension: 1 for BLOSUM62 Existence: 10 Extension: 1 for BLOSUM80 Existence: 10 Extension: 1 for PAM70 Existence: 9 Extension: 1 for PAM30 Valid Values: Existence: 9 Extension: 2, Existence: 8 Extension: 2, Existence: 7 Extension: 2, Existence: 12 Extension: 1, Existence: 11 Extension: 1 , Existence: 10 Extension: 1 |
| Gapped Alignment | Specifies whether to use gapped BLAST or ungapped BLAST algorithm. The ungapped BLAST algorithm invokes the older, ungapped style of alignment, according to the Karlin-Altschul statistics. See Also: Karlin, S. and Altschul, S.F. Methods for assessing the statistical significance of molecular sequence features by using general scoring schemes. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA (1990), 87:2264-2268. Valid Values: True , False |
| Use Composition Based Statistics | Use the amino acid composition of the individual database sequences involved in reported alignments when calculating the E-values. This improves the accuracy of E-values and thus reduces the number of false positives. The options are: False : Do not adjust the scores. This option must be chosen if you wish to turn off the Gapped Alignment setting to perform an ungapped alignment. True : Basic Composition score adjustment as in earlier versions. Conditional Compositional Score Matrix Adjustment : This is the recommended option. Universal Compositional Score Matrix Adjustment See Also: Altschul SF, Wootton JC, Gertz EM, et al. Protein database searches using compositionally adjusted substitution matrices. FEBS J. 2005 ;272(20):5101-5109. Valid Values: False, True, Conditional Compositional Score Matrix Adjustment , Universal Compositional Score Matrix Adjustment |
| Filter Low Complexity | Specifies whether to mask off segments of the query sequence that have low compositional complexity. Filtering can remove hits that are statistically significant but biologically uninteresting (e.g., hits against common acidic-, basic- or proline-rich regions). Valid Values: True , False |
| Word Size | Specifies the length (either 2 or 3) of the initial matching segment. A larger value tends to yield more accurate results, but takes more computation time. Valid Values: 2, 3 |
| URL | URL for online BLAST server |

In Pipeline Pilot, specify a sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA, Genbank, and SwissProt. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of sequences in all open Sequence Windows.

# BLAST Search (NCBI server)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_blast_search_ncbi_server.htm

## BLAST Search (NCBI server)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

BLAST Search (NCBI server) identifies homologous relationships between a protein query
sequence and sequences in databases using the BLAST algorithm. The computation
is performed using the BLAST server on the NCBI site and searches against
the databases from the NCBI site. The BLAST Search and BLAST Search (NCBI server) protocols are
distinguished by the databases employed for searching. When you use the
BLAST Search (NCBI server) protocol, you search against the most up-to-date sequence databases maintained by NCBI.

* Load a protein sequence into the Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Search Sequences by Similarity tools and click BLAST Search (NCBI Server)... to open the BLAST Search (NCBI Server) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Sequence Specify the name to be analyzed. Input Database Select an installed database from the list. For details about the databases, see NCBI databases . For details about the remaining parameters, see BLAST Search (NCBI server) - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence | Specify the name to be analyzed. |
| Input Database | Select an installed database from the list. For details about the databases, see NCBI databases . |

For details about the remaining parameters, see BLAST Search (NCBI server) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the hits are shown in the BLAST Results Window . Use the following information in the Table View of the BLAST Results Window to evaluate hits:

* Bit score: The bit score is calculated from the raw score by normalizing with the statistical variables that define a given scoring
system. Therefore, bit scores from different searches, even those employing different scoring matrices, can be compared. The higher the
score the better the alignment.

* E-value: The E-value is a statistical score which estimates the chance of finding such a hit in a given sequence
database. For the same hit, this score can change when the database changes since it is calculated depending on the constitution of the
database sequences. The lower the E-value, the better the alignment. A hit with lower sequence identity but longer alignment may have
E-value better than a hit with higher sequence identity and shorter alignment.

* Alignment Length

* Identity: Pairwise sequence identity between the query and the hit.

* Similarity: Pairwise sequence similarity between the query and the hit.

* Resolution: X-ray resolution for the PDB hit.

* SCOP codes: SCOP codes for the PDB hit.

* Ligand: Ligands near the PDB hit.

The profile file, <sequence>_profile.pir can be used in the Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) protocol or the Align Sequence Profiles (MODELER) protocol for further
profile alignment calculation.

In the output profile, there are no gaps in the input sequence (i.e., the residues in the hits that are not aligned to the input sequence are deleted). 
This provides a clean view of the statistics of the residues that could occur at each position of the input sequence.

If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the
Jobs Explorer and click View Results to open the BLAST Results Window .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <sequence>.xml | Opens the BLAST Results Window. |
| <sequence>_profile.pir | Contains the alignment of the query sequence to all hit sequences. |
| blastseqs.fasta | A FASTA sequence file, containing the results nucleic acid or amino acid sequences. |
| PDBresolution.txt | A text file describing the X-ray resolution of each PDB hit. |
| HspSCOPs.txt | A text file describing the SCOP code of each PDB hit. |
| HspLigands.txt | A text file describing the ligands near each PDB hit. |

#### Further information

BLAST Search PSI-BLAST Search BLAST Results Window BLAST XML report BLAST Search theory

# Predict Sequence Properties - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_predict_sequence_properties-para.htm

## Predict Sequence Properties - Parameters

### Predict sequence properties

Predicts one or more of the following sequence properties:

* Sequence Motif: Find sequence motif based on PROSITE motif syntax. For antibody sequences, the results can be filtered by domain. If a structure is provided, the results can also be filtered by solvent surface accessibility and thermal mobility.

* Conserved amino acids in antibody structures.

* Antigenic sites: Identified by EMBOSS's antigenic tool using the method of Kolaskar and Tongaonkar.

* Structural properties: If a structure is provided, then bridging and free cysteine residues can be identified.

* Molecular properties predicted by the EMBOSS pepstats tool: Molecular weight Isoelectric Point Charge Molar Extinction Coefficient at A280 for reduced and disulfide bridge forms Extinction Coefficient (1mg/ml) at A280 for reduced and disulfide bridge forms Improbability of expression in inclusion bodies Probability of expression in inclusion bodies

* Molecular weight

* Isoelectric Point

* Charge

* Molar Extinction Coefficient at A280 for reduced and disulfide bridge forms

* Extinction Coefficient (1mg/ml) at A280 for reduced and disulfide bridge forms

* Improbability of expression in inclusion bodies

* Probability of expression in inclusion bodies

* Kyte-Doolittle Hydropathy: Calculates Kyte-Doolittle hydropathy values of the amino acids in the protein sequence within a window of specified length as the window is moved along the sequence.

* Hydropathy Free Energy: Calculates free energy values of the amino acids in the protein sequence within a window of specified length as the window is moved along the sequence in two lipid environments. The first energy value is calculated in octanol (equivalent to inside a lipid bilayer) environment and the second energy value is calculated in the interface of a synthetic lipid bilayer. The energy difference is the best indicator of the location of probable transmembrane regions.

Note that for antibody sequences, the antibody domains and complementarity determining regions (CDRs) are determined according to the selected numbering scheme. If more than one sequence is selected as input, they will be aligned based on the numbering scheme.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequences | In Pipeline Pilot, specify a protein sequence file. Supported file formats include BSML, PIR, FASTA. In Discovery Studio, choose all or a selected subset of sequences in an open Sequence Window. |
| Input Protein Structures | Specifies protein structures from which data such as residue solvent accessibility or isotropic displacements can be extracted. The protein sequences from the structures must match those in the Input Sequences . The names of the structures and sequences must match and be unique. The structure data are optional, allowing for structure-based filtering and for structure-based properties such as free/disulfide cysteines to be found. |
| Calculate Biophysical Properties | Specifies whether to calculate biophysical properties for each sequence and tabulate the results in the Report file. These include: Molecular weight Isoelectric point Charge Molar extinction coefficients Probability/improbability of expression in inclusion bodies These calculations are performed using EMBOSS pepstats. Valid Values: True , False |
| Annotation Types | Specify the set of predicted features to annotate: Sequence motifs: Search the sequence for defined PROSITE-style motifs. Conserved amino acids: Find conserved amino acids in antibodies. Antigenic regions: Predict potentially antigenic regions of a protein sequence. Structure-based sites: Search for sites defined by the 3-dimensional structure (e.g., free/disulfide cysteine residues.). This option is only available if Input Protein Structures has been specified. Valid Values: Sequence motifs , Conserved amino acids , Antigenic regions |
| Motifs | Sequence motifs, in particular those that identify post-translational modifications. Default motifs are defined in files here: shortcut:/Discovery Studio Data/SequenceMotifs . Additionally, you can specify motifs using the User-defined Motifs parameter. Each motif definition consists of a name , a motif and optionally a filter which specifies which antibody domains to include. The name is a unique identifying string consisting of alphanumeric characters and underscores. The PROSITE-style motif syntax is: The standard IUPAC one-letter codes for the amino acids are used The symbol x is used for a position where any amino acid is accepted Ambiguities are indicated by listing the acceptable amino acids for a given position between square parentheses [ ] and the unacceptable amino acids for a given position between curly brackets { } Repetition of an element of the pattern can be indicated by following that element with a numerical value or a numerical range between parenthesis For example: [DE](2)HS {P} X(2)PX(2,4)C The filter can be any of: VL, VH for the variable domains CL, CH1, CH2, CH3 for the constant domains L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, H3 for the CDR regions. The filters can be combined e.g. L1,H3 means find the motif in L1 and H3 CDR loops. There are also predefined combinations V (all variable), CDR (all CDRs), H (all heavy chain), L (all light chain) and CH (all heavy chain constant) domains. |
| User-defined Motifs | Specifies user-defined motifs to search for. Each motif definition should be entered on one line and consist of a name , a motif and optionally a filter which specifies which antibody domains to include. The name, motif and filter must be separated by spaces. The name is a unique identifying string consisting of alphanumeric characters and underscores. The PROSITE-style motif syntax is: The standard IUPAC one-letter codes for the amino acids are used The symbol x is used for a position where any amino acid is accepted Ambiguities are indicated by listing the acceptable amino acids for a given position between square parentheses [ ] and the unacceptable amino acids for a given position between curly brackets { } Repetition of an element of the pattern can be indicated by following that element with a numerical value or a numerical range between parenthesis For example: [DE](2)HS {P} X(2)PX(2,4)C The filter can be any of: VL, VH for the variable domains CL, CH1, CH2, CH3 for the constant domains L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, H3 for the CDR regions. The filters can be combined e.g. L1,H3 means find the motif in L1 and H3 CDR loops. There are also predefined combinations V (all variable), CDR (all CDRs), H (all heavy chain), L (all light chain) and CH (all heavy chain constant) domains. So a motif named Cysteine_In_Fv specifying cysteine residues within the variable domains could be defined as: Cysteine_In_Fv C VL,VH or as Cysteine_In_Fv C V |
| Filters | Specifies the filters to be applied to the sequence features. |
| Solvent Accessibility Threshold | Specifies the percent solvent accessibility threshold for filtering sequence features. If the feature contains one or more residues of at least this accessibility, it will be retained. All features except for disulfide bridges are filtered. If the threshold is set to zero, no filtering will be performed. |
| Isotropic Displacement Threshold | Specifies the average isotropic displacement threshold. If a feature contains one or more residues of at least this value, it will be retained. All features are filtered. If the threshold is set to zero, or if the input protein does not contain isotropic displacements, no filtering will be performed. |
| Antibody Domain Filtering | Specifies whether, in the case of antibody structures, to restrict certain features to specific domains. The following options are available: Default filters: Filters defined in the motif definition files will be applied. User-defined: Filtering will be performed for all motifs, antigenic sites and structural features using the specified user-defined filter. None: No domain filtering will be performed. Valid Values: Default filters , User-defined, None |
| User-defined Filter | Specifies an antibody domain filter to be applied to all sequence features if Antibody Domain Filtering is set to User-defined. The filters can be any of the following VL, VH for the variable domains CL, CH1, CH2, CH3 for the constant domains L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, H3 for the CDR regions These can be combined (e.g., "L1, H3" means find the motif in L1 and H3 CDR loops.) Valid Values: VL, VH, CL, CH1, CH2, CH3, L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, H3 |
| Annotation Scheme | Specifies the numbering scheme used to renumber antibody variable domains and to define the Complementarity Determining Region (CDR) in the Input Sequences . The following options are available: IMGT: Numbering scheme described in: "The IMGT unique numbering for immunoglobulins, T cell Receptors and Ig-like domains". Lefranc, M.-P., The Immunologist , 1999 , 7 , 132-136 "IMGT unique numbering for immunoglobulin and T cell receptor variable domains and Ig superfamily V-like domains", LeFranc, et al. Dev. Comp. Immunol. , 2003 , 27 , 55-77. This scheme is used as a reference to define the CDR definitions for the other schemes. Chothia: Method described in the following papers: "Canonical Structures for the Hypervariable Regions of Immunoglobulins". J. Mol. Biol. , 1987 , 196 , 901-917 "Standard Conformations for the Canonical Structures of Immunoglobulins". Al-Lazikani, et al. J. Mol. Biol. 1997 , 273 , 927-948. "Conformations of the Third Hypervariable Region in the VH Domain of Immunoglobulins". Morea, et al. J. Mol. Biol. 1998 , 275 , 269-294 "Antibody Modeling: Implications for Engineering and Design". Morea, et al. Methods , 2000 , 20(3) , 267-279. The CDR definitions for the Chothia scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -1,0;0,0;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,0;2,-1 Heavy: 0,-1;2,-2;3,-1 Kabat : Numbering scheme detailed in "Sequences of Proteins of Immunological Interest". Kabat, E. A., Wu, T. T., Perry, H. M., Gottesman, K. S., and Foeller, C., U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, NIH, Bethesda, MD., 1991 . The CDR definitions for the Kabat scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Lambda: -3,2;0,4;0,0 Heavy: 5,2;-1,8;2,0 Honegger : Numbering scheme described in "Yet Another Numbering Scheme for Immunoglobulin Variable Domains: An Automatic Modeling and Analysis Tool". Honegger, A. and Plückthun, A., J. Mol. Biol. , 2001 , 309 , 657-670. The CDR definitions for the Honegger scheme correspond to the following shifts with respect to the IMGT CDR definitions: Kappa: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Lambda: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Heavy: -2,0;0,9;2,-1 Shifts are defined as three pairs of numbers separated by semicolons (e.g. -3,2;0,4;0,0) for each of the domain types Kappa, Lambda, and Heavy. Each pair of numbers specifies the relative shift of the start and end of the respective region (CDR1; CDR2; CDR3). The shifts are calculated with respect to the IMGT loop definition (i.e., -2,2 specifies a loop region that is extended by two residues on both ends compared to the corresponding loop based on the IMGT numbering scheme). Valid Values: Chothia, Kabat, Honegger, IMGT |
| Advanced | Advanced options |
| Minimum Antigenic Region Length | Minimum length of antigenic region. Must be an integer from 1 to 50. The EMBOSS default is 6. |
| Hydropathy Window Size | Specifies the window size to be used for the moving average for the Kyte-Doolittle and Free Energy hydropathy plots. This can be adjusted according to the size of feature of interest. For instance, 19 residues would be about the size of a membrane spanning alpha-helix. If the window size is set to zero, the plot data will not be calculated. If the plot data have been calculated, the Report will contain links that display the plots in Discovery Studio. |

# Predict Sequence Properties

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_predict_sequence_properties.htm

## Predict Sequence Properties

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

* Further Information

The Predict Sequence Properties protocol performs a range of feature predictions and biophysical property calculations for one or more protein sequences. The following features can be predicted:

* Sequence motifs based on PROSITE [Bairoch and Bucher, 1997] motif syntax. The protocol provides a set of motifs that predict various post-translational modification (PTM) sites. User-defined motifs can also be specified.

* Conserved amino acid residues in antibody structures, according to the specified numbering scheme (for example, IMGT ).

* Antigenic sites, which are predicted using the EMBOSS [Rice et al.,2000] antigenic tool [Kolaskar and Tongaonkar, 1990] .

* Structural properties (bridging and free cysteine residues can be identified if a structure is provided).

#### Feature Filtering

The above mentioned sequence features can be filtered by one or more of the following criteria:

* Antibody domain: The features can be filtered to retain only those that are within the specified antibody domain or complementarity determining regions (CDRs). The PTM motif definitions include default antibody filter definitions; the Structural Properties are by default filtered to include only those in the variable domain. You can also specify user-defined filters for user-defined motifs, or to be applied to all features.

* Solvent Accessibility: If a structure with the same sequence is supplied, the features can be filtered to retain only those with at least one residue with percent accessibility greater than a specified threshold (i.e., those at the surface of the molecule).

* Isotropic displacement: If a structure with the same sequence is supplied and the structure data includes isotropic displacement information, the features can be filtered to retain only those with thermal mobility above a specified threshold.

For antibody sequences, the domains and CDRs are determined according to the specified numbering scheme, and if there is more than one antibody sequence in the input they will be aligned using this numbering.

#### Calculated Biophysical Properties

The following biophysical properties are calculated for each sequence using the EMBOSS pepstats tool:

* Molecular weight

* Isoelectric point: Solution pH at which the protein net charge is 0. This is predicted using EMBOSS pepstat. When the input sequence has multiple chains, the charges at the N and C terminii of each chain will be included in the prediction.

* Charge: Net molecular charge calculated based on standard protonation of titratable residues.

* Extinction coefficient (1 mg/ml) at A280 for reduced and disulfide bridge forms: Predicts how much light a protein of 1mg/ml concentration absorbs
at a wavelength of 280nm for two forms: one with all cysteine residues as free cysteines (reduced form) and another one with all cysteines forming disulfide bridges (disulfide bridge form).

* Molar extinction coefficient at A280 for reduced and disulfide bridge forms: Molar extinction (or absorption) coefficients
is proportional to the number of tryptophan (W), tyrosine (Y), and cysteine (C) residues in the protein. At a wavelength of 280nm, it is equal to nW*5500 + nY*1490 + nC*125. The molar extinction coefficient can be used to estimate the molar concentration of a 
protein when measured absorbance of the protein solution is available.

* Improbability of Expression in Inclusion Bodies (IEIB) [Harrison, 2000] : 
IEIB is a measure of the solubility of a protein or vice versa the likelihood of forming dense, insoluble protein aggregates (inclusion body)
when the protein is over-expressed in Escherichia coli . A number closer to 1 indicates high solubility, and a number closer to 0 indicates
low solubility and high chance to form aggregates with a 0.5 cutoff.

#### Hydropathy Plots

You can generate two types of Hydropathy plots for the protein sequence using a moving window. The plot shows
which region of the protein sequence is more hydrophobic and which is more hydrophilic.

* Kyte-Doolittle: Generated via the EMBOSS pepwindow tool [Kyte and Doolittle, 1982] .

* Hydropathy Free Energy: Calculates the free energy values of the amino acids in the sequence in two lipid environments using the EMBOSS octanol tool [White and Wimley, 1999] . These are octanol (equivalent to inside a lipid bilayer) and the interface of a synthetic lipid bilayer. The energy difference is also calculated, as it indicates the location of probable transmembrane regions.

* Load a protein sequence into the Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Sequences tools and click Predict Sequence Properties... to open the Predict Sequence Properties dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Sequences Sequences to be analyzed Input Protein Structures Structures to be used for filtering. This is optional and you can leave it blank if you do not have an input structure. Calculate Biophysical Properties Whether to report properties for the whole sequence Annotation Types Set of features used to annotate the sequences Motifs Set of sequence motifs to annotate the sequences Filters Antibody and structural filters to apply For details about the remaining parameters, see Predict Sequence Properties - Parameters . It is possible to add your own motif definition to the library. Default motifs are defined in files in the following folder: $ <pps_install> \apps\scitegic\dsdata\public\data\SequenceMotifs . You can edit them to change the existing definition, or add additional files for new motifs. The changes will be automatically available in the Motifs parameter.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequences | Sequences to be analyzed |
| Input Protein Structures | Structures to be used for filtering. This is optional and you can leave it blank if you do not have an input structure. |
| Calculate Biophysical Properties | Whether to report properties for the whole sequence |
| Annotation Types | Set of features used to annotate the sequences |
| Motifs | Set of sequence motifs to annotate the sequences |
| Filters | Antibody and structural filters to apply |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Predict Sequence Properties - Parameters .

It is possible to add your own motif definition to the library. Default motifs are defined in files in the following folder: $ <pps_install> \apps\scitegic\dsdata\public\data\SequenceMotifs . You can edit them to change the existing definition, or add additional files for new motifs. The changes will be automatically available in the Motifs parameter.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, the input sequences in the active Sequence Window are updated with the feature annotations. For antibody sequences, the CDR regions are also annotated and the sequences aligned according to the specified numbering scheme.

If only one sequence was annotated, the Sequence Annotation Window automatically opens with the feature and antibody domains and CDRs showing in the Graphics View. If more than one sequence was annotated, you can open the Sequence Annotation Window for any sequence by selecting it, right-clicking, and choosing Show Annotations .

#### Style and Color of Features in Sequence Window

| Feature Type | Sequence Window Style | Color |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sequence motif | Caret | Purple |
| conserved amino acids | Overline | Cyan |
| antigenic regions | Underline | Pink |
| free cysteines | none | Lime |
| disulfide cysteines | none | Gold |
| light chain CDR | Bold | Magenta |
| heavy chain CDR | Bold | Red |

#### Viewing the Report

From the Jobs Explorer , open Report.htm . The summary table reports the calculated biophysical properties for each sequence, and also contains links that open the hydropathy plots and tables of information about the features. The feature table lists the full set of features including those that are being filtered.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated during the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| *.bsml | Annotated sequence alignment |
| Report.htm | Job summary including biophysical properties table, links to display feature tables and hydrophobicity plots, input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol (errors are listed here) |
| Features/*.csv | Table of features |
| Plots/*.csv | Hydrophobicity plot data |

#### Motif Syntax

User-defined motifs are specified using PROSITE-style syntax:

* The standard IUPAC one-letter codes for the amino acids are used

* The symbol x is used for a position where any amino acid is accepted

* Ambiguities are indicated by listing the acceptable amino acids for a given position between square parentheses [ ] and the unacceptable amino acids for a given position between curly brackets { }

* Repetition of an element of the pattern can be indicated by following that element with a numerical value or a numerical range between parenthesis

For example: [DE](2)HS{P}X(2)PX(2,4)C

#### Antibody Filtering

Antibody filters can be any of the following:

* VL, VH for the variable domains

* CL, CH1, CH2, CH3 for the constant domains

* L1, L2, L3, H1, H2, H3 for the CDR regions

These can be combined e.g. L1,H3 means find the motif in L1 and H3 CDR loops. There are also predefined combinations V (all variable), CDR (all CDRs), H (all heavy chain), L (all light chain) and CH (all heavy chain constant)
domains.

## PSI-BLAST Search - Parameters

### Searches local protein databases with a query sequence using BLAST+ PSI-BLAST

PSI-BLAST is a statistically driven search method that finds regions of similarity between a query sequence and database sequences and produces gapped alignments of these regions. PSI-BLAST is an iterative search method that uses position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM) to score matches between query and database sequences.

Note:

* The PDB_nr95,PDB, Swiss-Prot and antibody_variable databases are installed by default. Other databases are available. Please refer to Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search topic in the Discovery Studio Help for further details of how to obtain and install these if required.

Note : If a PSSM file for restart is specified, then the sequence will be read from it rather than from this input sequence. |
| Input Database | Name of the database to be searched. Discovery Studio provides the following databases: PDB_nr95 : non-redundant protein chains from Protein Data Bank. Chains are clustered with a 95% sequence identity threshold, and only representative chains are used to create this database. PDB : protein chains from Protein Data Bank. antibody_variable : antibody variable domain sequences for a subset of mammalian organisms extracted from NCBI nr database. Swiss-Prot : the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (fully annotated curated entries). Notes: The PDB_nr95 and PDB databases have sequences which are extracted from PDB structures. These are therefore the most appropriate choice for use in workflows such as homology modeling where linked structures and sequences are required. The PDB_nr95, PDB, Swiss-Prot and antibody_variable databases are installed with the product. In addition to these databases, preformatted protein databases including nr can be downloaded directly from NCBI. The UniRef90 database can be generated by downloading the UniRef90 FASTA file and running the makeblastdb command. # PSI-BLAST Search

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sequence_analysis_psi-blast_search.htm

## PSI-BLAST Search

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

PSI-BLAST Search is a profile-based method for remote homology identification. PSI-BLAST Search uses the methods described by
Altschul et al. [Altschul et al., 1997] and Schaffer et al. [Schaffer et al., 2001] to
search for similarities between a protein query sequence and all the sequences in a protein sequence database.
PSI-BLAST stands for Position-Specific Iterated BLAST.

#### Databases

Several sequence databases are provided with each Discovery Studio release for use with this protocol. Additionally, you can add your own databases .

#### Specifying the number of rounds to iterate

When run with the default settings, PSI-BLAST performs five search rounds as suggested by Schaffer et al. [Schaffer et al., 2001] .
The first round is a BLASTP-style search. However, if after any round of searching no new matches are found, no more
iterations are performed (a condition known as convergence). The chances of finding false positive matches increase with
the number of search rounds because the profile can diverge. Considering that each search round takes as long as a single
equivalent run of BLAST, you should consider breaking the job into a series of low-round searches, saving the PSSM
in a checkpoint file at each step. Upon examination of the output, you can decide whether to restore the PSSM and
continue searching. An indication for profile divergence is that the sequences found in the first round as high confidence
hits become low confidence hits or even disappear from the hit list in the later rounds.

#### Choosing a database for creating PSSMs

Using a sequence profile, you can identify remote homology more sensitively,
comparing to pairwise sequence comparison methods based on substitution
matrices. To maximize the sensitivity as well as the selectivity of the
search, it is important to optimize the protocol for calculating the sequence
profiles. Search the largest sequence database so that the chances of
finding close homologs in the initial step by BLASTP-style search are
maximized. These homologs in turn are used to create PSSMs for following
iterations. In contrast, if the database being searched is highly
redundant, redundant sequences recruited in the initial step can give
wrong statistics for the PSSM, which could lead to sequence profile divergence
and increase the chance of getting false positive matches. Based on the
highly redundant database, the size of the search space used in calculating
the E-value of the matches is also overestimated. Studies [Park et al., 1998] have found that a sequence database at 90% pairwise sequence
identity is well-suited for PSI-BLAST search. Discovery Studio provides the UniRef90 database
specifically based on this consideration. It is a non-redundant protein
sequence database in which any pairwise sequence identity is less than
90%.

* Load a protein sequence into the Sequence Window.

* Open the Macromolecules | Search Sequences by Similarity tools and click PSI-BLAST Search... to open the PSI-BLAST Search dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Sequence Specify the name to be analyzed. Input Database Select an installed database from the list. For details about the databases and how to install them, see Local databases and Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search . Organism Set the this parameter if the PSI-BLAST hits should be filtered by organism. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported. For details about the remaining parameters, see PSI-BLAST Search - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Sequence | Specify the name to be analyzed. |
| Input Database | Select an installed database from the list. For details about the databases and how to install them, see Local databases and Installing databases for BLAST Search and PSI-BLAST Search . |
| Organism | Set the this parameter if the PSI-BLAST hits should be filtered by organism. Organism names should preferably be the scientific name of the organism. However, a number of common synonyms are supported. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see PSI-BLAST Search - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Viewing and analyzing the results are similar to the BLAST Search protocol.

The BLAST Results Window only shows the last iteration of the PSI-BLAST Search
results. Only the sequence, alignment, and structure of the hits
in the last iteration can be loaded.

#### E-values change when PSSMs are used

The E-value reflects the possibility of finding a match with score S by chance from the database, and it is dependent on
the size of the database and the scoring system in use. Matches with lower E-values are more significant.
For a PSI-BLAST search, E-values for a given
database sequence change between search rounds. This is most conspicuous between the first and second
search rounds. In the first search round, matches
between query and database sequences are scored using a static scoring matrix. In contrast, successive
search rounds determine scores by comparing
database sequences to the PSSM. In addition, if more sequences are added to the set used to make PSSMs
as the search iterates, the scores for matching
sequences may change. It is not possible to predict whether the score for an individual sequence will
increase or decrease between search rounds.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <sequence>.xml | Opens the BLAST Results Window. |
| <sequence>_profile.pir | Contains the alignment of the query sequence to all hit sequences. |
| blastseqs.fasta | A FASTA sequence file, containing the results nucleic acid or amino acid sequences. |
| <sequence>.pssm | Checkpoint file. Note this cannot be opened directly in the DS Client. |
| PDBresolution.txt | A text file describing the X-ray resolution of each PDB hit. |
| HspSCOPs.txt | A text file describing the SCOP code of each PDB hit. |
| HspLigands.txt | A text file describing the ligands near each PDB hit. |
| <sequence>_filtered.xml,<sequence>_profile_filtered.pir,blastseqs_filtered.fasta, PDBResolution_filtered.txt, HspLigands_filtered.txt, HspSCOPs_filtered.txt | Contain the same results as previously described files, but filtered by organism (present if the Organism parameter was set). |

# Verify Protein (Profiles-3D)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sima_prof3d_th.htm

## Verify Protein (Profiles-3D)

The Verify Protein (Profiles-3D) protocol measures the compatibility of an amino acid
sequence with a 3D protein structure. It is based largely on algorithms
developed in the laboratory of Dr. David Eisenberg at the University of
California, Los Angeles. This method reduces the 3D structure to a simplified
1D representation called an environment string , which is then
compared with the 1D amino acid sequence. The method can be used to check
the validity of a hypothetical protein structure by measuring the compatibility
of that structure with the sequence of the protein.
In the case of integral membrane proteins the effect of a lipid membrane is included in the calculation of Profile-3D scores.
For this purpose the membrane is modeled as a planar slab and a zero solvent accessibility is assigned to the atoms inside the membrane interior.

The method involves two basic operations:

* Reducing the 3D structure to a 1D string
of residue environments. These environments are categorized according to: The area of the side-chain that is buried, either in the protein or in the membrane The fraction of the side-chain area that is exposed to polar environment, either to polar 
atoms in a protein or to the solvent. If an atom is inside a membrane,
only the area exposed to polar protein atoms is added to the polar area. The local secondary structure

* The area of the side-chain that is buried, either in the protein or in the membrane

* The fraction of the side-chain area that is exposed to polar environment, either to polar 
atoms in a protein or to the solvent. If an atom is inside a membrane,
only the area exposed to polar protein atoms is added to the polar area.

* The local secondary structure

* Calculating the profile score for a model
structure. This is calculated from the string of residue environments
and a precalculated scoring matrix. The scoring matrix is calculated
from the probabilities of finding each of the twenty amino acids in
each of the environment classes as observed in a database of known structures
and related sequences.

## The 3D-1D scoring matrix

Although the environment string is one-dimensional, like an amino acid 
sequence, it cannot be compared to or aligned with a sequence without some 
measure of the compatibility of each of the twenty naturally occurring amino 
acids with each of the eighteen environment classes. The 3D-1D scoring matrix is 
a 20 x 18 matrix that contains exactly this information. Each element, s i,j , in the matrix is a score that indicates the 
compatibility of residue i with environment j . The greater the 
value, the greater the compatibility; negative values indicate poor 
compatibility.

The individual matrix elements are information values [Fano, 1961] and are calculated as:

Equation 1.

where P ( i : j ) is the probability of finding residue i in environment j , and P i is the overall 
probability of finding residue i in any environment. For the 3D-1D 
scoring matrix, these probabilities were estimated from a database of 16 known 
protein structures and sets of homologous sequences aligned to the sequences of 
the 16 structures. The structures chosen and the methods for selecting and 
aligning the related sequences are described by Lüthy et al. [Lüthy et al., 1991] . For 
each residue position in each of the 16 sets of aligned sequences, the 
environment class was determined from the known structure.

The probability, P ( i : j ), was then estimated as:

Equation 2.

where N i,j is the number of positions in the 16 alignments 
at which one or more residues of type i were found to align with 
environment j . The denominator is the total number of residue 
replacements found for all environments of type j .

The probability, P i , was estimated as:

Equation 3.

where N i is the number of positions in the 16 alignments 
at which one or more residues of type i occurred. The denominator is the 
total number of residue replacements in the database of alignments (8273 for the 
16 alignments used to generate the 3D-1D scoring matrix).

The boundaries of the environment classes (Figure 1 in Determining the 
residue environment ) were then adjusted iteratively, the matrix being 
recalculated each time so as to maximize S t , the total 3D-1D 
score summed over all residue types and environment classes in the 16 
alignments:

Equation 4.

# Calculation of area buried and polar fraction

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sima_prof3d_th_calculation-of-area-buried-and-fraction-polar.htm

## Calculation of area buried and polar fraction

The solvent-accessible area of each atom in a side-chain is measured by first 
placing an imaginary solvent sphere around the atom, with a radius equal to the 
sum of the van der Waals radius of the atom [Richmond and Richards, 1978] and the 
radius of a water molecule. Sample points are placed on this sphere every 0.75 Å. 
If a sample point is not within the solvent sphere of any other protein 
atom, then that point is considered accessible to the solvent; otherwise, it is 
considered buried. The solvent-accessible surface area of the atom, denoted A a , is then calculated as:

Equation 1.

where n a is the number of sample points accessible to the 
solvent, n t is the total number of sample points on the 
solvent sphere, and A t is the total surface area of the 
solvent sphere. The solvent-accessible area of the side-chain is then calculated 
as the sum of the solvent-accessible areas of its constituent atoms, including 
the alpha carbon. The area of the side-chain that is buried in the protein is 
defined as the difference between the solvent-accessible area of the side-chain 
in the protein and in a Gly-X-Gly tripeptide. The latter value has been tabulated 
for each of the 20 amino acids by Eisenberg et al. [Eisenberg et al., 1989] .

The fraction of the side-chain area covered by polar atoms is calculated as:

Equation 2.

where N p is the number of sample points covered by polar 
atoms (nitrogen, oxygen, or solvent) for all atoms in the side-chain and N t is the total number of sample points for all atoms in the 
side-chain. Sample points covered by atoms of the side-chain itself are excluded 
from both of the counts N p and N t . If a 
sample point lies within the solvent spheres of both a polar and a nonpolar atom, 
then that point is counted in N p if, and only if, the polar 
atom is the closer of the two.

# Determining the residue environment

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sima_prof3d_th_determining-residue-environment.htm

## Determining the residue environment

The environment of each residue in the 3D structure of a protein is first 
classified according to the area of the side-chain that is buried in the protein. 
A residue is considered to be exposed to solvent (environment class E) if the area 
buried is less than 40 Å 2 , partially buried (class P) if the 
area buried is between 40 and 114 Å 2 , and buried (class B) if 
the area buried is greater than 114 Å 2 . The buried and partially 
buried classes are further subdivided according to the fraction of the side-chain 
area that is exposed to polar atoms ("polar fraction", denoted as f ). 
For this purpose, polar atoms are defined as the atoms in the solvent molecule 
and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms of the protein. The buried class is subdivided 
into classes B 1 ( f < 0.45), B 2 (0.45 ≤ f < 0.58), and B 3 ( f > 0.58). The partially 
buried class is subdivided into classes P 1 ( f < 0.67) and 
P 2 ( f > 0.67). The properties of these six basic 
environment classes (E, P 1 , P 2 , B 1 , 
B 2 , and B 3 ) are summarized in Figure 1. The determination 
of the boundaries between them is explained in The 3D-1D scoring 
matrix .

Figure 1: The six basic protein residue environment classes and their
properties (after figure 4 of Bowie et al., 1991 [Bowie et al., 1991] ).

Protein residues in each of the six basic environment classes in Figure 1 can 
be subdivided into three further categories according to the local secondary 
structure: alpha helix, beta sheet, or other. The result is a total of eighteen 
distinct environment classes.

#### Further information

# Interpreting the 3D-1D score in structure verification

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sima_prof3d_th_interpreting-3d-1d-score-in-structure-verification.htm

## Interpreting the 3D-1D score in structure verification

When the 3D profile method is used to verify a structure, the raw
compatibility score alone is difficult to interpret. In this case, it is
necessary not only to compensate for length effects, but also to compare the
score to those obtained using structures known to be correct.
Lüthy et al. [Lüthy et al., 1992] dealt with this problem by calculating the 3D-1D self-compatibility scores 
for all structures in the Protein Data Bank determined at resolutions less 
than or equal to 2 Å and with R-factors less than 20%. They constructed a 
log-log scatter plot of these scores against sequence length and found that they 
fell approximately on a straight line. A linear least-squares fit to these data, 
transformed from the logarithmic coordinates, yielded the following relation:

Equation 1.

where S calc is the score expected for a correct structure 
having sequence length L . This equation is plotted as the solid curve in
figure 2 of Lüthy et al. [Lüthy et al., 1992] . In the same figure, these authors plotted 
the self-compatibility scores of several structures known to be incorrect. They 
found that severely misfolded structures typically had scores less than 
0.45 S calc . The self-compatibility scores of most structures 
in the protein data bank fall between S calc and 
0.45 S calc . This score range provides a useful rule-of-thumb 
for interpreting the 3D-1D self-compatibility score of a hypothetical protein 
structure. A score outside the lower limit of this range indicates a structure 
that is almost certainly incorrect. A score within the range, but at the lower 
end of it, indicates a structure that may be correct, but that is of questionable 
quality. A score near or above the high end of the range indicates a reliable 
structure.

Lüthy et al. [Lüthy et al., 1992] also provide several caveats that must be considered 
when interpreting a self-compatibility score:

* Correctly folded oligomeric proteins may have unusually low scores if the 
score is calculated for the individual protomers, rather than for the complete 
oligomer. This effect results from the incompatibility of the protein interface 
regions with exposed environments. The effect is negligible for large proteins, 
but can be significant for small ones.

* A model protein with only a few incorrect regions may have an overall 
self-compatibility score above 0.45 S calc . Local errors of 
this kind can often be found, however, by analyzing a graph of the local 3D-1D 
score (calculated in a fixed-length sliding window) versus position in the 
sequence. The results of the sliding window analysis are sensitive to the window 
length. A smaller window gives greater resolution, but may introduce spurious 
noise. A larger window tends to average out the insignificant noise, but at the 
cost of lower spatial resolution. Lüthy et al. [Lüthy et al., 1992] found that a window 
length of 21 was useful for analyzing grossly misfolded structures.

* If a portion of a hypothetical structure is essentially unfolded (i.e., all 
side-chains in that region are completely accessible to solvent), the local 3D-1D 
score may not detect the abnormal structure if most of the residues in that 
region are compatible with exposed environments.

# Test the validity of a preliminary or model structure

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/sima_prof3d_th_test-validity-of-preliminary-or-model-structure.htm

## Test the validity of a preliminary or model structure

The Verify Protein protocol is generally employed in the final phase of a 
homology modeling project or for testing a preliminary protein structure based on 
experimental data. It depends on the principle that a protein's structure must be 
compatible with its own sequence. The strategy used by Verify Protein involves 
constructing the 3D profile of a protein and measuring its compatibility with the 
sequence of the same protein. It is also possible to use Verify Protein to 
calculate local 3D-1D scores in a fixed-length sliding window (typically about 5 
to 20 residues long). These can be plotted against residue position to reveal 
local regions of relatively high or low 3D-1D compatibility [Lüthy et al., 1992] . 
Regions having unusually low scores are likely to be places where the 
backbone has been incorrectly threaded through the electron density data (if the 
structure is experimental) or where additional energy minimization or other 
structural refinements are necessary (if the structure is a model).

# General macromolecule tasks

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/tsk_macromolecules-general.htm

## General macromolecule tasks

The tasks below are basic tasks for working with macromolecules. For a comprehensive 
list of macromolecule tasks that includes basic tasks and tasks that involve working 
with the Macromolecules tool set, see Tasks - Macromolecules .

The general tasks for working with macromolecules are organized as follows:

* Protein Modeling tasks

* Sequence tasks

* Automatically prepare an imported protein structure

* Add hydrogen atoms to a protein structure

* Display a protein structure as a solid ribbon

* Graft a template loop structure onto a model

* Identify and patch residues with missing atoms in a protein structure

* Identify missing residues in a protein structure and insert them

* Keep the first set of alternate conformations from an experimental structure and delete the others

* Remove disulfide bonds from a protein structure

* Remove HetAtoms from a protein structure

* Select all C-Alpha atoms in a protein structure

* Create homology models for a homo-multimer

* Prepare a membrane protein for modeling and simulation

* Set the distance cutoff for the interface definition in the Analyze Docked Protein tools

This is an automatic alternative to using the Manual Preparation tools such as Clean Protein and Insert Loop on the Prepare Protein toolpanel.

* Open a structure in a Molecule Window.

* On the Prepare Protein toolpanel, click Prepare Proteins... to open the Prepare Proteins protocol dialog.

* Set the parameters as desired and click Run .

To add hydrogen atoms to a protein structure

If you are sure the structure does not have defects, such as incomplete side-chains, you can use the
standard Add hydrogens method. Otherwise, it is advisable
to add hydrogens at the same time as cleaning the defects.

* Select Edit | Preferences... from the menu bar to open the Preferences dialog.

* From the tree View, select Protein Utilities | Clean Protein .

* Check the Modify Hydrogens checkbox, and choose either All or Polar .

* Ensure all other preferences are set to perform the desired clean actions, and then click OK .

* On the Prepare Protein tool panel, click Clean Protein .

* The requested clean operations will be performed, including hydrogen addition.

To display a protein structure as a solid ribbon

* If you want to change the display for only part of the structure, make an appropriate selection.
Otherwise ensure selections are cleared by left clicking in an empty part of the Molecule Window.

* Right-click the Molecule Window containing the protein structure and choose Display style... from the context menu. This opens the Display Style dialog.

* Select the Protein tab on the Display Style dialog.

* Click on the Solid ribbon radio button.

* If the display of individual atoms is not desired, select the Atom tab and choose the None radio button.

* Click OK .

To graft a template loop structure onto a model

There are three different scenarios when grafting a loop onto a model from a template structure:

* The loop in the model structure has the same sequence length as the template

* The loop in the model structure has different sequence length from the template

* The loop in the model structure is missing

#### Loop has same sequence length

If the loop length is the same between the model and the template, take the following steps:

* Optionally, select the corresponding loop from the model and the template structures in the 3D or Hierarchy view. Make sure that only the loop residues are selected and no stem residues are included.

* Open the Prepare Protein tools and click Graft Loop... .
The Target protein (the model), Template protein and corresponding Loop start and Loop end parameters 
are automatically filled with the correct values if the loop was preselected.

* If you opened the dialog without prior selection of the loop, select the Target protein and the Template protein and manually enter the Loop start and Loop end parameters for the Target protein and the Template protein . They
are specified in the form <chainID>:<ResidueName><ResidueNumber> .
You can also enter the residue number in the Loop start and Loop end parameters and then press the tab key. The
full residue name will be filled. However, this only works for single chain proteins or the first chain
in a multi-chain protein.

* Choose one of the options in Loop sequence to specify what sequence
to use when grafting the loop: model sequence, template sequence, or polyalanine.

* Decide how many residues on each side of the loop you want to use to superimpose to the template
and the model and set the Stem length accordingly.

#### Loop has different sequence length

If the loop length is the different between the model and the template, follow the previous instructions. However, Loop sequence can only be set to template structure or be polyalanine.

#### Loop is missing

If the loop is missing in the starting model structure, follow the instructions
as above. However, in this case, the Loop start and Loop end parameters
of the Target protein will be specified using the N- and C-terminal stem residues of the 
missing loop. The N- and C-terminal stem residues of the missing loop of the Target protein and 
the loop residues of the Template protein can be optionally selected prior to opening the Graft Loop 
dialog. Alternatively the residues can be specified manually in the dialog as described above. The Loop sequence can only be set to the template sequence or polyalanine.

To identify and patch residues with missing atoms in a protein structure

Quite often, the coordinates of some of the atoms in a PDB structure cannot be determined experimentally
due to poor structural resolution. The following steps show you how to identify and complete partial residues.

* Open a protein structure in the Molecule Window .

* Open the Macromolecules | Protein Report and Analysis tools.

* Click Protein Report , to open an HTML report.

* Residues with missing atoms are listed in the "Incomplete or Invalid Residues" section.

* Choose Edit | Preferences... from the menu bar.

* In the Preferences dialog tree view choose Protein Utilities | Clean Protein .

* In the Correct problems section check the Incomplete residues checkbox.

* Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Clean Protein .

If Display Report on the Protein Utilities | Clean Protein preferences page is turned on, a report will be shown listing what atoms are added to which residues.

To identify missing residues in a protein structure and insert them

Often, the coordinates of some residues cannot be
determined experimentally due to poor structural resolution.
Those residues are missing from the PDB structure, but are usually
listed in the SEQRES record in a .pdb file, or in _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme records in a macromolecular .cif file. The following steps
illustrate how to insert the missing residues into the structure.

To identify missing residues:

* Open the Protein Report and Analysis tools and click Protein Report .

* In the protein report, first check if there are any incomplete or invalid residues. If there are any, use Clean Protein to patch in the missing atoms.

* Then in the protein report, look for the "Comparison of actual sequence versus
PDB SEQRES records" or "Missing Residues from mmCIF data" section: If residues are missing at the start of a chain,
it is reported as "Start of chain <chain Identifier> appears to be missing
- residues: X ... Y", where X ... Y is the list of names of the missing residues. If residues are missing at the end of a chain, it is reported as
"End of chain <chain identifier> appears to be missing - residues: X ... Y". If residues are missing from the interior of a chain, it is reported as
"Gap found between residues: A and B", where A and B include the chain
identifier, residue name, and residue sequence number.
This is followed by the sequence of missing residues.

* If residues are missing at the start of a chain,
it is reported as "Start of chain <chain Identifier> appears to be missing
- residues: X ... Y", where X ... Y is the list of names of the missing residues.

* If residues are missing at the end of a chain, it is reported as
"End of chain <chain identifier> appears to be missing - residues: X ... Y".

* If residues are missing from the interior of a chain, it is reported as
"Gap found between residues: A and B", where A and B include the chain
identifier, residue name, and residue sequence number.
This is followed by the sequence of missing residues.

* Expand the tree in the Hierarchy View to see the
residue names and select residue A as listed in the report. The groups listed under Gaps in Chain can help in locating the desired residue.

* Choose Edit | Preferences | Protein Utilities from the menu bar.

* Check the Insertion without moving existing structure checkbox, and
then click OK .

* Open the Build and Edit Protein tool panel.

* In the Choose Build Action section,
choose Insert .

* In the Choose Amino Acid section,
click Specify... to open the Enter an Amino Acid Sequence dialog.

* Click on Gap Suggestion to automatically fill in the one letter sequence code of the missing residues from the report to the Specify Sequence textbox.

If there are no SEQRES or _pdbx_poly_seq_scheme records available for the protein structure, gaps within a chain are determined from connectivity. In this case, the above steps may still be performed, but it will be necessary to enter the sequence of the missing section manually.

To optimize the coordinates of the residues:

The above procedure adds missing residues to the structure. However the coordinates of
the residues are not optimized. They can be optimized using the Loop Refinement tool as follows:

* Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools.

* Choose either the CHARMm Polar H or the CHARMm forcefield, and then click Apply Forcefield .

* Check the Status to make sure the molecule is properly typed.

* In the Molecule Window, select the loop residues from the Hierarchy View .

* Open the Macromolecules | Minimize and Refine Protein tools and click Loop Refinement... to open the Loop Refinement dialog.

* Select the protein structure to refine in the Input Typed Protein Molecule parameter. The Loop parameter is automatically filled with
the residues selected in the Hierarchy View .

* Run the calculation. This will take from several minutes up to an hour depending
on the length of the loop, the forcefield used, and the speed of the machine.

* When the job is finished, the results with the loops sorted by the energy and
the input structure are displayed.

* Click different rows in the Data Table View to see the corresponding
loop conformation.

To keep the first set of alternate conformations from an experimental structure and delete the others

Some crystallographic structures are disordered and the .pdb file contains alternate conformations. Some
modeling operations (e.g., forcefield typing) cannot operate on disordered structures. The following steps
illustrate how to remove the alternate conformations:

* Open a protein structure with alternate conformations in the Molecule Window .

* In the Preferences dialog, open Protein Utilities | Clean Protein .

* In the Correct problems section, check the Alternate conformations (retain one
set) checkbox.

If Display Report on the Protein Utilities | Clean Protein preferences page is turned on, a report will be displayed that details the affected residues.

If you want to delete conformations selectively, or keep conformers other than the first set, use the Manage Conformers tool.

To remove disulfide bonds from a protein structure

* Open the structure in a Molecule Window.

* Open the Hierarchy View for the structure and expand the molecule to be modified.

* Right-click in the Hierarchy View and select Display Bonds from the context menu (unless there
already is a checkmark next to Display Bonds ).

* Expand any protein chains with disulfide bonds so that residues and
bonds are visible. These bonds will include intrachain disulfide bridges in addition to peptide links.

* Inter-chain disulfide bonds are shown under the molecule level of the Hierarchy View .

* Select the disulfide bonds that are to be removed.

* Press the Delete key to remove the selected bonds.

To remove HetAtoms from a protein structure

If a structure has been read from a .pdb file, atoms from HETATM records will have been added
to a group named Hetatm. Removing the contents of this group will leave just the protein structure.

* Open the Hierarchy View for the structure and
expand the molecule to be modified.

* Click on the Hetatm group in the located in the hierarchy tree under the molecule to select all atoms belonging to the Hetatm group in the structure.

* Press the Delete key to remove the selected atoms.

To select all C-Alpha atoms in a protein structure

* Choose Edit | Select from the menu bar or press CTRL+E to open the Select dialog .

* Set the Selection Mode to Add or Replace as appropriate.

* Set the Scope to Atom .

* Set the Property to Name , and 
select CA from the dropdown list.

* Click Apply .

* To ensure that other atoms such as Calcium, which might
also be labeled CA, are not included in the selection,
set the Selection Mode to Intersection , set the Property to Element and
choose Carbon from the dropdown list before clicking Apply .

To create homology models for a homo-multimer

While building homology models for a homo-multimer, it is desirable to maintain the symmetry between the monomers. 
Modeler provides a method for achieving this by setting symmetry restraints. This approach is slightly
different from building a monomer by homology modeling and then using a symmetry matrix to add 
other subunits since during model building, the atoms on the interface of the subunits are 
optimized in the presence of the symmetry mates and are better positioned. This is performed as follows using a homo-dimer and the Macromolecules tools.

* Open the monomer sequence you want to model in a Sequence Window.

* From the Search Sequences by Similarity tool panel, open BLAST Search... .
Select the query sequence as input and run the protocol to identify a suitable template.

* When the BLAST search finishes, review the hits from the BLAST Result window to identify a
suitable template, which should also be a homo-dimer.

* Choose File | open URL... from the menu and open the dimeric template structure, press CTRL-Q to show its sequence in the Sequence Window, and then copy the query sequence into the template Sequence Window.

* Right-click the Sequence Window and choose View | Chain View .

* Double click the query sequence in the first chain view to select the chain
and then CTRL-C to copy it. Position the cursor
in the second chain view at the beginning of the query sequence and
paste the copied chain into it..

* Align the sequences using the Align Sequences... protocol and set the Align By Chain parameter to True . This will ensure that the 
two chains of the homo-dimer will be aligned independently and each chain will be aligned
in the same way to the corresponding template chains.

* Open Build Homology Models... and
set Input Sequence Alignment to the output alignment from the previous step. Set the Input Template Structures and Input Model Sequence parameters accordingly.

* Open the Advanced parameters and click Additional Restraints to open the Define Additional Restraints dialog.
Open the Symmetry tab. The Segment 1 and Segment 2 parameters are completed automatically.
Use Atom Type to set the symmetry restraints as desired, and then click OK . Symmetry restraints cannot be used if Cutoff Overhangs is True, so set that parameter False.

* Symmetry restraints cannot be used if Cutoff Overhangs is True, so set that parameter False.

* Run the calculation to generate the models, which should maintain symmetry between the two monomers.

To prepare a membrane protein for modeling and simulation

A number of tools including Calculate Protein Ionization and 
Residue pK and Add Membrane and Orient 
Molecule use the Generalized Born (GB) approximation which supports the inclusion of an implicit membrane in the solvation model.
In these tools the effect of the membrane is automatically included in the calculations of GB energy terms
if a membrane object is added prior to the molecular structure being analyzed.

Discovery Studio provides two methods for adding a membrane object and to set the
molecular structure in an optimal orientation to the membrane. The faster method is to use the Add and Modify commands on the Macromolecules | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools.
Additionally, you can use Add Membrane and Orient Molecule from the tool panel. 
The latter offers additional parameters and can be used as a refinement to the initial orientation provided by the Add command.

* Use the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools to type the molecule
with a forcefield (it is best to use CHARMm, charmm36, or CHARMm Polar H since Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK supports these three forcefields).

* Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools and click Add in the Create and Edit Membrane group.

* Click Add Membrane and Orient Molecule .

* From the dialog, reduce the search range so that the Shift is from -5 to 5 and the Tilt Angle Maximum Change is set to 30 degrees.

* Run the calculation. When it finishes, the coordinates of the input molecule will be updated with the optimized orientation to the membrane.

* Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK .

* Select the structure from the previous step as the Input Typed Protein Molecule and run the protocol. When the job finishes,
the input molecule will be updated with the correct protonation states for those titratable residues.

To set the distance cutoff for the interface definition in the Analyze Docked Protein tools

* Open the Protein Docking page.

* Set the Distance cutoff value to the desired number in angstroms.

* Show the sequence of a 3D protein structure

* Color protein structures by sequence similarity
