To show the sequence of a 3D protein structure

* Open the protein structure in a Molecule Window.

* Select Sequence | Show Sequence from the menu bar. The Sequence Window is displayed below the Molecule Window by default. Alternatively, press CTRL-Q .

To color protein structures by sequence similarity

* Open the protein structures you wish to color in a Molecule Window. If
the structures are not already in the same file, choose File | Insert from the menu bar to combine the contents of the various files, or drag the structure files into the
Molecule Window from the Files Explorer.

* Choose Sequence | Show Sequence from the menu bar to open the protein
sequences in a new Sequence Window.

* If desired, manually align the sequences to highlight regions of homology.

* Right-click the Sequence Window and choose Display Style .

* Select the Color Scheme tab and choose the Background or Foreground option
depending on whether you want to customize the background or residue text colors
in the alignment.

* Select the Aligned Sequence similarity color scheme from the list.

* Select the Color molecule objects checkbox.

* If you want to color the protein structure atoms by similarity, click the Atoms radio button.

* If you want to color the protein structure (e.g,. schematic or ribbon display)
by similarity, click the Protein display radio button.

* Click OK . The appearance of the protein structures is updated.

To create an annotated sequence from a protein structure

* Open a Molecule Window containing your protein structure.

* Click Menu | Sequence | Show Annotations . A new window will appear displaying a graphical
representation of the corresponding sequence. The sequence may already be annotated
with automatically generated annotations depending on your application preferences.

* Switch back to the Molecule Window. Select a region of interest in your
structure. For example, if you are working with a protein sequence and the Protein Groups node is available in the Hierarchy view , expand the Protein Groups node and select the Hydrophobic group.

* Switch back to the Sequence Annotation Window.

* Right-click and select Features | Add... from the context menu to open the Feature Editor dialog. The domain Start and Stop positions will be filled in to correspond to the residue range selected from the structure.

* Use the Keyword dropdown list to specify the feature type. If an appropriate keyword is not available, you can add a new keyword by typing in the drop down list.

* Click the OK button to close the Feature Editor dialog.

To display a secondary structure cartoon on the sequence

* To show the available secondary structures as a cartoon, right-click the Sequence Window and choose on the Sequence toolbar. To display only a specific secondary structure (e.g., Kabsch and Sander), choose Sequence | Secondary Structure | Visibility... from the menu bar.

* From the Secondary Structure Visibility dialog, click the desired secondary structure (e.g., Kabsch and Sander).
To display more than one secondary structure, CTRL+click the two parameter boxes.

* Repeat the first step to toggle the selected secondary structure cartoon display.

To link a sequence to a structure

In general, when you open a structure and corresponding sequence in the application,
they are automatically linked so that selections and edits in one window update
the same data in the other. However, sometimes it
is necessary to explicitly link a structure and sequence. For example, if the sequence
differs from the structure, they cannot be linked. In this case it
is necessary to first edit the sequence or structure so that they match before linking them.

* Switch to the Sequence Window that contains the sequence to be linked. Ensure that the sequences and names are identical to those in the structure.

* Choose Sequence | Link Sequence and Structure... from the menu bar.

* Either click Link all matching structures or Specify , select the sequence you want to link from the Sequence: list, and then select the structure you want to link to from the Molecule: list.

* The Status pane of the dialog will report any issues that would prevent linking.

* Click Link . The sequence and structure are now linked.

To freeze part of an alignment

Gaps can be inserted into more than one sequence simultaneously.

* Ensure that the sequences you want to realign together are adjacent.
Do this by dragging and dropping the sequence labels.

* Select a block of sequences by left-clicking the
top left residue, and then dragging down to the bottom right.

* Right-click and choose Fix Residue Block . The fixed block is shown with a gray background.

* Once a block is created, inserting gaps inside the block is not allowed, but adding a gap to one of the sequences before the block
will automatically insert gaps to all the sequences involved in the fixed block. To remove gaps before the fixed block,
the gaps have to be aligned between all the sequences and have to be selected before they can be deleted.

* Reselect the block, then right-click and choose Unfix Residue Block to unfreeze.

To copy a sequence from a text file or email message directly into a sequence window

* Open the document that contains the sequence.

* Select the region you want to import and copy it to the clipboard. There is no need
to remove numbers, spaces or other characters from the sequence.

* Click on a Sequence Window to active it or open a new Sequence Window.

* To insert a new sequence after the current sequence, click in the sequence panel and press Enter . To insert a sequence before the current sequence, place the 
cursor at the first position before pressing Enter .

* Right-click the sequence panel and choose Paste . Note that only valid residues from the copied
sequence are inserted.

See also:

Tasks - Macromolecules Sequence menu

To insert or remove a sequence chain break

To insert a chain break into a sequence

* Select a pair of adjacent residues in the Sequence Window or place
the cursor between them.

* Right-click and choose Chain | Insert Chain Break .

To remove a chain break from a sequence

* Select one residue before and after the chain break in the Sequence Window.

* Right-click and choose Chain and Domain | Remove Chain Break .

To save a sequence or sequence alignment as an image

You can use one of the following two methods to save a sequence or sequence alignment as an image:

* From the menu bar, choose File | Save as... and set Set type to to Image Files.
This saves only the portion of the sequence displayed in the Sequence Window.

* Select everything in the sequence window and copy and paste it into another application as an image. This displays
the full sequence alignment as one image.

To calculate bootstrap values for a phylogenetic tree

* Open a sequence alignment in the Sequence Window. Ensure that the alignment contains
at least four sequences.

* Open the Analyze Sequences tool panel and set the Tree Building Method .
Unless the sequences being analyzed are closely related (e.g., < 5% average divergence),
it is recommended that you choose the Neighbor Joining method.

* Set Mode to Bootstrap .

* Set Number of Replications to specify the bootstrap sample size.
This number determines the number of random bootstrap samples of the data that will be
generated and from which phylogenies they will be reconstructed. For large data sets,
this analysis may take significant time.

* Click Create Phylogenetic Tree to calculate the tree.
When the computation completes, the phylogenetic tree is displayed in a new Dendrogram Window.

Analyze Sequences tools Phylogenetics theory Generate a tree from an amino acid multiple sequence alignment Generate a tree from a nucleic acid multiple sequence alignment

To change the appearance of a bootstrap tree

The appearance of a bootstrap tree can be modified
using the Dendrogram toolbar and the Dendrogram Window Display Style dialog.
You can modify the general appearance of the tree using the Dendrogram toolbar.

* Click View | Toolbars | Dendrogram to display the toolbar if necessary.

* Click Slanted View on this toolbar.
Viewing in this mode may be useful when you want to distinguish
high-level branching patterns among a set of sequences.

* Click Radial View to display
the dendrogram as a radial tree. This mode is useful when you have
many nodes and you wish to discern high level branching patterns.

* Select a node by clicking it in the Dendrogram window, 
then click Root on the toolbar to root the tree on this node.
This action is particularly valuable when there is a clear
ancestral sequence (usually the sequence with the longest branch
length) from which other sequences are descended. Rooting
the tree on the ancestral node often provides insight into the
order of branching events among the other descendant sequences.

From the menu bar, choose View | Display Style... to open the
Dendrogram Window Display Style dialog. You can modify the appearance of the label font using the controls
in the Branch label font group.

* Open the General tab. Check the Visibility | Show branch labels checkbox and then click Apply . Repeat to toggle the label display on again.

* Open the Bootstrap tab. Check the Display percentages in
the Bootstrap Labels group.

* In the Bootstrap Filter group,
change the Collapse Nodes value to 75 %. This causes any internal nodes
that are in 75% or more of the bootstrap sample trees to be
shown resolved. In sequence alignments with a weak phylogenetic signal,
it may be useful to reduce this value to distinguish any branching
patterns that are supported at all. Conversely, in data sets with
strong phylogenetic signals, it may be valuable to increase
the value to closer to 100 % to emphasize
only well-supported branching points.

* In the Bootstrap Filter group,
change the Label Nodes value to specify which nodes
should be labeled. This value must be greater than the Collapse Nodes value.

To generate a tree from an amino acid multiple sequence alignment

* Open an amino acid sequence alignment in the Sequence Window. Ensure that the alignment contains
at least four sequences.

* Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Sequences tools and set the Tree Building Method .
Unless the sequences being analyzed are closely related (e.g., < 5% average divergence) it is recommended that you choose
the Neighbor Joining method.

* Set the Distance Method . In general, the Uncorrected ('p') distance is a good
choice for amino acid sequences.

* Use Mode to set the mode of estimation.
To calculate the single optimal tree, choose
the Best Tree option.
To perform a bootstrap analysis of the data set,
choose the Bootstrap option.

* Click Create Phylogenetic Tree to calculate the tree.
When the computation completes the phylogenetic tree is displayed in a new
Dendrogram Window.

Analyze Sequences tools Phylogenetics theory Calculate bootstrap values for a phylogenetic tree Generate a tree from a nucleic acid multiple sequence alignment

To generate a tree from a nucleic acid multiple sequence alignment

* Open a nucleic acid sequence alignment in the Sequence Window. Ensure that the alignment contains
at least four sequences.

* Open the Macromolecules | Analyze Sequences tools and set the Tree Building Method .
Unless the sequences being analyzed are closely related (e.g., < 5% average divergence), it is
recommended that you choose the Neighbor Joining method.

* Set Distance Method . In general, the Tamura-Nei option is a good choice for nucleic acid sequences. In cases where sequences show extreme base composition biases, the LogDet/Paralinear method may be a better alternative.

* Choose the Mode of estimation. To calculate the single optimal tree, choose Best Tree option. To perform a bootstrap analysis of the data set,
choose the Bootstrap option.

* Click Create Phylogenetic Tree to calculate the tree. When the computation completes, the
phylogenetic tree is displayed in a new Dendrogram Window.

Analyze Sequences tools Phylogenetics theory Generate a tree from an amino acid multiple sequence alignment

To save a dendrogram

* Make the Dendrogram Window the active window.

* Choose File | Save As... from the menu bar.

* Enter a file name and the location where you want to save the Dendrogram. The application can only
save Dendrograms as NEXUS formatted files [Maddison et al., 1997] .

To import phylogenetic tree data

* From the menu bar, choose File | Open... to launch the Open dialog.

* On the dialog, click the Files of Type dropdown arrow and select Dendrogram . Discovery Studio can only read Dendrograms from NEXUS formatted files [Maddison et al., 1997] .

* Select the file containing the tree you wish to display,
and then click Open to view it in the Dendrogram Window.

# Choose an alignment protocol

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsmacromolecules

Source file: tsmacromolecules/tsk_pm_choose-alignment-protocol.htm

## Choose an alignment protocol

Discovery Studio has a variety of alignment protocols to suit your needs. This topic discusses how to choose the most
appropriate alignment protocol for different tasks. Alignment protocols are divided into three basic categories:

* Sequence alignment protocols: Aligns sequences based on sequence similarity. No structures are involved. Align Sequences Align Sequence Profiles

* Align Sequences

* Align Sequence Profiles

* Structure alignment protocols: Aligns protein sequences based on their 3D structure similarity. Align Structures Align Structures (MODELER)

* Align Structures

* Align Structures (MODELER)

* Sequence and Structure alignment protocols: Protocols that involve structure and sequence comparisons. Align and Superimpose Proteins Align Sequence to Templates

* Align and Superimpose Proteins

* Align Sequence to Templates

This protocol aligns two or more protein sequences based on sequence similarity and is recommended for most cases.
It allows you to add a secondary structure matching score to the alignment and also allows you to maintain the input
alignment of some regions while aligning other parts of the sequences. It can also align sequences by individual
chains for sequences with multiple chains.

For details, see Align Sequences .

This protocol aligns a set of sequences to prealigned sequences (sequence profile), or aligns two sets of prealigned sequences (two profiles).

For details, see Align Sequence Profiles (Align123) .

This protocol aligns two or more protein structures.
If the input proteins are not all homologous, it automatically partitions them into different clusters 
and reports each cluster alignment separately. Proteins that cannot be aligned to any other proteins will
be left out of the aligned clusters. This protocol is most useful when you want to align a
set of structures and identify their commonly aligned cores, especially for distantly related proteins. The 
reported alignment will display significant structure similarity between the aligned proteins.

For details, see Align Structures .

This protocol is an alternative to Align Structures protocol that aligns two or more protein structures. 
It differs from the Align Structures protocol in that it will report alignment even when the input structures are not homologous. 
It produces suitable structure alignment for homology modeling. A weakness of this protocol is that
it cannot align proteins that are drastically different in size (e.g., single-domain with a multidomain protein).

For details, see Align Structures (MODELER) .

This protocol takes a set of protein structures as input, aligns their sequences using the multiple sequence alignment
method from the Align Sequences protocol and superimposes the protein structures
based on the aligned residues provided by the sequence alignment. It is designed to superimpose a large number of homologous 
proteins for comparing and analyzing their structures, such as comparing the binding site of large number of kinases. It can 
handle many more structures than the other structure alignment protocols, but only works well when the input proteins have 
significant sequence similarity. It also has an option to superimpose based on selected residues, such as binding site
residues.

For details, see Align and Superimpose Proteins .

This protocol combines structure alignment (for aligning templates) and sequence alignment (for aligning the model 
sequence with the templates) into one protocol. It uses some of the methods used in other structure and sequence
alignment protocols discussed in the previous sections. It is the recommended protocol to use for preparing input
alignment for building homology models. It combines multiple steps into one to make the workflow easier and provides 
options that allow you to add homologous sequences from a sequence database to assist the alignment between the model 
and templates.

For details, see Align Sequence to Templates .

Source type: HTML

## Macromolecules tools

The Macromolecules tools provide rich functionalities that allow you to work with protein sequences and structures 
as well as nucleotide sequences and structures. The following is a summary of the main functions of these tools.

* Search online protein or nucleic acid sequence databases using keywords or phrases, 
search sequence databases based on sequence similarity, and align protein sequences based on their
sequence or structure similarity

* Create protein model structures using the homology modeling method and refine the structures using the CHARMm based ab-initio approach

* Build and edit protein and nucleic acid structures

* Prepare protein structures for other simulation calculations or docking experiments

* Create model structures for protein mutations and predict mutation energy for protein stability or 
binding affinity for use in protein engineering

* Predict docked protein complexes from individual protein structures

To get started, see the following:

## Macromolecules tool panels

The following tool panels are available in the Macromolecules tool set :

| Tool Panel | Tasks |
| --- | --- |
| Build and Edit Nucleic Acid | Generate, modify, and characterize nucleic acids as single strands, duplexes, or triple helices. |
| Build and Edit Protein | Build and modify peptides and proteins. |
| Query Online Databases | Search and retrieve protein structures from RCSB or search and retrieve sequences from NCBI database. |
| Protein Report and Analysis | Create a report detailing the properties of a protein. Build a shell of symmetry related copies around the structure and analyzes contacts and interactions. |
| Prepare Protein | Prepare proteins for further analysis. Actions include chain splitting, protonation, and manual or automatic preparation (clean, insert or graft loop, manage conformers, modify protonation state, and renumber sequences.) |
| Search Sequences by Similarity | Search sequence databases using BLAST methods. |
| Align Sequences and Structures | Align sequences based on their sequence or structure similarities. |
| Analyze Sequences | Perform phylogenetic analysis to a set of aligned protein or nucleotide sequences. |
| Analyze Protein Conservation Pattern | Identify functionally significant trace residues and exposed sites. |
| Superimpose Proteins | Superimpose protein structures based on the matching tether, alignment, or C-Alpha pairs. Additional tools are available to view C-Alpha Trace or Monitor, transform coordinates, and align and superimpose proteins. |
| Create Homology Models | Identify templates and align model sequence to templates. Build homology models based on the sequence alignment and the templates and verify model structures. |
| Search Side-Chain Rotamers | Evaluate the suitability of different side-chain rotamers of a residue in a 3D protein structure and replace the side-chain conformation with a rotamer state from a rotamer library. |
| Minimize and Refine Protein | Minimize portions or all of a protein structure or systematically search and refine the conformation of a loop or side-chains of a protein structure. |
| Model Antibody | Annotate the sequence, build a model, refine antibody loops, model a full length antibody, and predict humanizing mutations. |
| Dock and Analyze Protein Complexes | Display and analyze a set of docked protein poses as generated by the Dock Proteins (ZDOCK) protocol |
| Design Protein | Predict and create disulfide bridges. Build mutants and calculate mutation energy. |
| Predict Protein Formulation Properties | Calculate properties important to the formulation of biologics, and examines protein aggregation sites. |
| Analyze Transmembrane Proteins | Predict transmembrane helix regions of a protein from a sequence, add an implicit membrane to a protein structure, and edit the properties of the membrane. |

# Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog

## Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog

The Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog allows you to specify a query atom. The
specification includes the possible element types, charges, valences, hydrogen
counts, and lone pair counts.

Aromatic: This checkbox allows you to define the selected atom is part of an aromatic 
system.

Aliphatic: This checkbox allows you to define the selected atom is part of an aliphatic 
system.

Exocyclic: This check box allows you to specify whether the selected atom is exocyclic.

Endocyclic: This check box allows you to specify whether the selected atom is endocyclic.

Bridgehead: This check box allows you to specify whether the selected atom is a bridgehead.

Use atom stereochemistry: If the stereochemistry of the selected atom should be accounted for in the 
query, check this box.

[atom type]: These options allow you to define the type assigned to the selected atom; Any , Halogen , Any non-carbon , and Elements are the available choices. The Elements option allows you to manually specify a series of elements possible for the selected atom. Click button to elements them from a periodic table.

Charges: These options allow you to specify a range of charges on the selected atom. 
Values between -7 and +7 can be selected by clicking the corresponding buttons. The entire range of 
positive or negative charges can be selected using the Positive and Negative checkboxes.

Hydrogen counts: This option allows you to define the number of hydrogens specified on the 
selected atom. The values between 0 and 8 are available by clicking the corresponding buttons. Any combination of these 
values can be selected.

Lone pair counts: This option allows you to define the number of lone pairs specified on the 
selected atom. The values between 0 and 4 are available by clicking the corresponding buttons. Any combination of these 
values can be selected.

Coordination numbers: This option allows you to define the coordination numbers specified on the 
selected query atom. Values between 0 and 8 are available by clicking the corresponding buttons. Any combination of these 
values can be selected. This option may be particularly useful when defining 
the coordination numbers to be queried for metal centers.

Valences: This option allows you to define the valences specified on the selected atom. 
Values between 0 and 8 are available by clicking on the corresponding buttons. Any combination of 
these values can be selected.

The buttons used to select the values of Charges , Hydrogen counts , Lone pair counts , Coordination numbers , and Valences are grayed out when they are not selected, and become prominent upon selection.

Reset: Clicking this button will reset the options in this dialog to the status 
specified when the dialog was opened - not to the default settings of the 
chosen query atom.

### Access methods

| Tools Explorer | Customize Pharmacophore Features \| Query Atom Specification... |

# 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_3d_qsar_pharmacophore_generation-para.htm

## 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters

### Generates predictive pharmacophore models from a set of ligands

Uses HypoGen to derive Structure Activity Relationship (SAR) pharmacophore models from a set of molecules for which activity values are known.

Optionally, generates excluded volume features using inactive compounds.

Input ligand data should contain the following properties:

* Activ : the compound's tested activity. Data such as IC50 values should be used and all values should be greater than 0.0. Ideally the data should span 4 orders of magnitude. If logarithmic data is used, Logarithmic Activity must be set to "True".

* Uncert : the uncertainty in the activity value, a ratio of the reported value to the minimum and maximum values,
must be greater than 1.0. 3.0 is used if the property is missing.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. The input ligands should contain the following properties: Activ: the compound's tested activity. Data such as IC50 values should be used and all values should be greater than 0.0. Ideally the data should span 4 orders of magnitude. If logarithmic data is used, Logarithmic Activity must be set to True. Uncert: the uncertainty in the activity value, a ratio of the reported value to the minimum and maximum values, must be greater than 1.0, set to 3.0 if the property is missing. |
| Activity Property | The name of the property containing molecular activity data. By default, Activ is used, if blank then Activ is used. Note: Internally this property is converted to Activ , so any messages will refer to that name. |
| Uncertainty Property | The name of the property containing molecular uncertainty data. By default, Uncert is used, if blank then Uncert is used. Note: Internally this property is converted to Uncert , so any messages will refer to that name. |
| Logarithmic Activity | The activity property contains logarithmic values. The values will be converted to linear values using the formula: activity = 10 ** ( -logarithmic_activity ). Note: Significant figures are not considered during the conversion. Slight differences in the activity values can lead to different final pharmacophores. It is recommended to convert the activity values to a linear scale manually, so that the proper number of significant figures can be used. Valid Values: True, False |

Valid Values: NONE, FAST , BEST, CAESAR |

Molecules that contain rings also found in the file will only use these ring conformations. Conformations for rings not found in the file are generated from scratch. Note: Only FAST and CAESAR will use this file. It have no effect on other methods. By default this parameter is blank and all ring conformations are generated from scratch. |

Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. # 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_3d_qsar_pharmacophore_generation.htm

## 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The 3D Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship (QSAR) Pharmacophore Generation protocol
can be used to generate predictive pharmacophores. It uses the Catalyst HypoGen
algorithm, [Li et al., 2000] , to derive SAR hypothesis
models (pharmacophores) from a set of ligands with known activity values on a given biological target.

3D QSARs differ from typical QSAR methods in that descriptors are derived
from ligand alignments or by how well ligands fit a pharmacophore,
rather than molecular features. Often, the descriptors are
concerned with the overall molecule rather than a single
substituent.

There are several methods for generating 3D QSAR models.
One example computes steric and electrostatic fields and
correlates this with activity. This approach requires a prealignment
step prior to the analysis. The Create 3D QSAR Model protocol in the QSAR 
folder uses this approach.

The 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation protocol generates 3D QSAR
models that are based on how well a series of ligands fit a
pharmacophore. The better a ligand fits a pharmacophore
(i.e., the more features that map and the closer they are to the
feature centroids), the more active it is predicted to be.

For this protocol, the input ligands should contain Activ and Uncert properties:

* Activ is the ligand's tested activity. Data such as IC50 values should be used, and all values should be greater than 0.0 . Ideally the data should span 4 orders of magnitude. If the data is logarithmic, set Input Properties/Logarithmic Activity to True .

* Uncert is the uncertainty in the activity value. A ratio of the reported value to the minimum and maximum values must be greater than 1.0 . 3.0 is used if the property is missing. For example, if Activ is 0.001 and the Uncert is set to 3.0 , the Activ is considered to be between 0.001/3.0 = 0.00033 and 0.001*3.0 = 0.003 .

Molecular properties such as these can be added using Add Attribute .

If you have activity data with a different property name, set Input Properties/Activity Property to the property name. Likewise for uncertainty data.

To ensure proper exploration of the ligand conformational and pharmacophoric space,
run the Generate Conformations protocol before running this protocol. You can also generate the conformations on the fly using Conformation Generation and associated parameters.

* Ensure that the input ligands have the following molecular properties: Activ (representing the ligand's tested activity)
and Uncert (representing the ratio range of uncertainty in the activity value). You can add
molecular properties using the Add Attribute dialog. If these properties are not included, they will be assigned a default value of 0.0 and 3.0 , respectively.

* Open the Pharmacophores | Create a Pharmacophore Automatically tools and click 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation to open the 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Features Comma separated list of pharmacophore features to be used in pharmacophore hypothesis generation. You can
select the desired pharmacophore features and the minimum and maximum values for the final pharmacophores. For details about the remaining parameters, see 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters . If using
the Maximum Excluded Volumes parameter, we recommend using a value of 5 . When generating SAR pharmacophores, which include
excluded volumes, the algorithm looks for differences in the steric
bulk between the most active compound and the inactive
compounds. However, it is possible to explicitly specify
which compounds to use for this analysis. This is done by
adding a Principal property to the input ligands. For normal
SAR hypothesis model generation, this property is ignored.
However, when using the HypoRefine algorithm to add excluded volumes, these values can be used to determine which
molecules are used when placing the excluded volumes. The following values
are available: 0,NULL : Ignore compound in excluded volume addition 1 : Treat compound as Inactive 2 : Treat compound as Active

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Features | Comma separated list of pharmacophore features to be used in pharmacophore hypothesis generation. You can select the desired pharmacophore features and the minimum and maximum values for the final pharmacophores. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters .

* If using
the Maximum Excluded Volumes parameter, we recommend using a value of 5 .

* When generating SAR pharmacophores, which include
excluded volumes, the algorithm looks for differences in the steric
bulk between the most active compound and the inactive
compounds. However, it is possible to explicitly specify
which compounds to use for this analysis. This is done by
adding a Principal property to the input ligands. For normal
SAR hypothesis model generation, this property is ignored.
However, when using the HypoRefine algorithm to add excluded volumes, these values can be used to determine which
molecules are used when placing the excluded volumes. The following values
are available: 0,NULL : Ignore compound in excluded volume addition 1 : Treat compound as Inactive 2 : Treat compound as Active

* 0,NULL : Ignore compound in excluded volume addition

* 1 : Treat compound as Inactive

* 2 : Treat compound as Active

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

For details about interpreting the log file generated by this protocol, see Analyzing 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Log Files and Cost Analysis in HypoGen .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. See the Detail section for information about each of the pharmacophores generated, including the feature definitions, the tolerances, the total cost, the correlation in the training set, etc. If you see the NULL Hypothesis in this list, it may indicate that the results are not significant. For a description of how to interpret the cost information, see Cost Analysis in HypoGen . |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Query_N.ds_chm | Contains pharmacophore models generated by the algorithm, where N is the corresponding model ranked by the cost values. |
| Ligands_N.sd | Contains training set ligands aligned to each pharmacophore, where N is the corresponding model ranked by the cost values. |
| Validation/Ligands_N.sd | Contains the test set ligands aligned to each pharmacophore, where N is the corresponding model ranked by the cost values. |
| ViewResults_N.ds_pl | Allows you to view the ligands aligned to the pharmacophore. A ViewResults_N.ds_pl file is created for each pharmacophore generated, where N is the corresponding model ranked by the cost values. |
| Query.log | A log file generated during the run. For details about interpreting the log file, see Analyzing 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Log Files and Cost Analysis in HypoGen . |
| Query_full.log | A more extensive log file that is generated during the run. |
| Detailed Analysis Report | A graphical cost analysis of the run. |
| mols.spst | A tab delimited molecular spreadsheet file used by the HypoGen algorithm. The file provides molecular properties required by the algorithm such as Activity ( Activ ) and Uncertainty ( Uncert ) values. |

#### Further reading

* [Guner et al., 2001]

* [Guner et al., 2004]

# Add to Ligand Profiler Database - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_add_to_ligand_profiler_database-para.htm

## Add to Ligand Profiler Database - Parameters

### Adds a pharmacophore to the Ligand Profiler Pharmacophore Database

The Ligand Profiler database can be searched using Ligand Profiler.

Pharmacophores in the database can be classified into a hierarchy of categories. You can control which categories the pharmacophore will be added to.

The Input Pharmacophore is classified by several parameters. Some of these take a single value such as:

* Target Class

* Target Subclass

* Target Family

* Target Acronym

For each, choose one of the predefined values, or select CUSTOM (the last value) and fill in the associated custom text value.

There are also parameters that take multiple values such as:

* Target

* Drug Classification

* Therapeutic Classification

* Action Mode

For each, choose one or more of the predefined values or enter comma separated text values in the associated custom text field.

There are several extended text descriptor parameters:

* Notes

* Bibliography

* Actives

Each require a text entry.

Notes:

* The Ligand Profiler Pharmacophore database can be searched using Ligand Profiler. When accessing the Input LigandProfilerDB Pharmacophores parameter in the Ligand Profiler protocol, the Ligand Profiler Pharmacophore database is displayed in a searchable, hierarchical list. The hierarchy is as follows: Target Class Target Subclass Target Family Target Acronym Using this parameter it is easy to search for and select all the pharmacophores derived from a particular target class, subclass, or family and use them to screen a set of ligands.

Using this parameter it is easy to search for and select all the pharmacophores derived from a particular target class, subclass, or family and use them to screen a set of ligands.

* The Ligand Profiler Pharmacophore Database is located at: PP/public/DS/LigandProfilerDB/Standard

The Ligand Profiler Pharmacophore Database is located at:

* Use Remove From Ligand Profiler Database to remove pharmacophores.

# Auto Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_auto_pharmacophore_generation-para.htm

## Auto Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters

### Generates a set of selective pharmacophore models from a single ligand

The models are generated from the features of the ligand. The following feature types are considered:

* HB_ACCEPTOR

* HB_DONOR

* HYDROPHOBIC

* NEG_IONIZABLE

* POS_IONIZABLE

* RING_AROMATIC

A set of candidate pharmacophore models are enumerated from the features. The pharmacophores with the highest selectivity as predicted by a Genetic Function Approximation (GFA) model are selected.

The GFA model for the selectivity of a pharmacophore is built from a training set of 500 pharmacophore models. This set is used for searching the MiniMaybridge database in Discovery Studio. The logarithmic values of the number of database search hits are used as the targets (a value of -1.0 is used if no hit from DB search), and the number of total features in pharmacophore models and the feature-feature distance bin values are used as the descriptors for training the GFA model.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligand | Specify the MDL MOL/SD file that contains the ligand to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify a ligand in an active Molecule Window. Notes: It is recommended to perform bond localization for the molecule if it has partial formal charges or partial double bonds, otherwise, the input ligand will be rejected. Only the first ligand will be used for Auto Pharmacophore Generation if more than one ligand exists in the input source. |
| Maximum Features | Maximum number of features to consider in the output pharmacophore. |
| Minimum Feature Distance | Minimum distance in Å between features in the generated pharmacophore. |
| Maximum Pharmacophores | Number of pharmacophores to generate. The "best" pharmacophores are output first, using an internal scoring function. In actual usage, the first pharmacophore may not be the best. |

Specify the MDL MOL/SD file that contains the ligand to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify a ligand in an active Molecule Window.

Notes:

* It is recommended to perform bond localization for the molecule if it has partial formal charges or partial double bonds, otherwise, the input ligand will be rejected.

* Only the first ligand will be used for Auto Pharmacophore Generation if more than one ligand exists in the input source.

Maximum number of features to consider in the output pharmacophore.

Minimum distance in Å between features in the generated pharmacophore.

The "best" pharmacophores are output first, using an internal scoring function. In actual usage, the first pharmacophore may not be the best.

# Auto Pharmacophore Generation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_auto_pharmacophore_generation.htm

## Auto Pharmacophore Generation

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Analyzing Results

The Auto Pharmacophore Generation protocol considers the following feature types to generate a selective pharmacophore model from a single ligand:

* Hydrogen bond acceptor (HB_ACCEPTOR)

* Hydrogen bond donor (HB_DONOR)

* Hydrophobic feature (HYDROPHOBIC)

* Negative ionizable feature (NEG_IONIZABLE)

* Positive ionizable feature (POS_IONIZABLE)

* Aromatic ring (RING_AROMATIC)

A set of candidate pharmacophore models are enumerated from the features. The protocol chooses the pharmacophore with the highest selectivity as predicted by a Genetic Function Approximation (GFA) model.

This protocol requires a ligand structure as input.

* Load the ligand structure into the Graphics View .

* If the ligand has partial double bonds or partial formal charges, you should perform bond localization for the ligand by choosing Chemistry | Bond | Localize Bonds from the menu bar.

* Open the Pharmacophores | Create a Pharmacophore Automatically tools and click Auto Pharmacophore Generation to open the Auto Pharmacophore Generation dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the parameters as desired. For details, see Auto Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the job is done, a pharmacophore model will be displayed in the 3D Window of the input ligand. The pharmacophore model should be aligned well with the ligand.

If the job ran in background mode, open Report.htm. To display the result, click the View Results button.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

## Build 3D Database - Parameters

### Builds a multi-conformation ligand database

Uses Catalyst to generate a ligand database. The database is automatically indexed with sub-structure, pharmacophore feature, and shape information to allow fast database searching.

Use Search 3D Database to browse or search the database.

Note:

* By default, databases are visible to all users on the server. Use the Visibility parameter in the Advanced group to create a database only visible to you.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Name Property | The name of the property containing unique ligand name data. By default, Name is used, if blank then Name is used. Note: Internally this property is converted to Name , so any messages will refer to that name. |
| Database Name | The output database name. Databases that are visible to all users (the default) are stored in a subfolder in PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/DS/CatalystDB/ on the server. Databases that are visible to only the user are stored in a subfolder in PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/users/ USERNAME /CatalystDB/ on the server. The database name is used as the subfolder name. By default all database data files are created in this directory. Included in the standard files are a .info file, which contains database statistics, and a .spst file, which contains an entry for each molecule in the database. On on-prem installations large database data files can be stored in a different location using the Database Files Directory parameter. Note: The database name must be unique and must contain alphanumeric characters. |
| Number of Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. |
| Conformation Method | Algorithm for generating conformations: FAST: quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations. BEST: ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR: very quickly provides conformations by sampling torsions. Valid Values: FAST , BEST, CAESAR |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Discard Existing Conformations | If True, discard existing input conformations, otherwise use all existing input conformations. Valid Values: True , False |
| Database Files Directory | By default all database data files are created in PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/DS/CatalystDB/ DBName on the server. Optionally, the user can specify the directory in which to create the database files DBName .0.bdb, DBName .2.bdb, DBName .3.bdb, etc.. These database files may be large. The DBName .bdb and DBName .spst files are always created in PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/DS/CatalystDB/ DBName on the server If you are accessing a remote server, you must have permissions to access the specified directory. If the client is unable to browse to the directory, you can manually enter the path on the server as a value for the Database File Directory parameter. Notes: On a cloud installation this option is not supported. On Windows, mapped drives may not be accessible to the server. When using the Database Files Directory, it is imperative that the directory on their machine has the correct permissions = 2775 or 2777. One can use the chmod command on a linux machine to set the correct permissions: chmod -R 2775 DatabaseFileDirectory where DatabaseFileDirectory is the directory selected for database files. |

The files are stored in PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/DS/CatalystDB Users Only: Accessible to user only. # Cluster Pharmacophores - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_cluster_pharmacophores-para.htm

## Cluster Pharmacophores - Parameters

### Clusters pharmacophores based on distance

Computes distance between each pair of pharmacophores. The distance is a function of the number of common pharmacophore features and the root-mean-squared displacement between the matching features.

First, pair-wise root-mean-square fits are performed on all pharmacophore pairs and the value for the following function:

F ij = pairs + 1/(rms + 1.01)

is computed. Here pairs is the number of spheres common to both pharmacophores in a particular mapping, and rms is the minimum root-mean-square displacement between the matching pharmacophore features. All possible mappings between two pharmacophores are performed, and the F ij function is evaluated. The largest functional value is used for a particular pair of pharmacophores. A similarity function is defined as:

S ij =F ij /sqrt(F ii *F jj )

and a distance function as:

D ij = 1 - S ij .

In Discovery Studio, the distance matrix can be displayed using an interactive dendrogram.

Four files are created:

* pharmacophores_clus.html: Contains the distance matrix in HTML format.

* pharmacophores_clus.dsv: Contains all the input pharmacophores.

* pharmacophores_clus.pl: A script used to view the results as a dendrogram in Discovery Studio.

* mappings.log: Detailed information about the pharmacophore feature mappings between the pharmacophores.

Note:

* A feature based pharmacophore must be used. For example, a pharmacophore created using Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation or 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation.

This parameter is typically only changed by experts. A default .Catalyst parameter settings file can be created in the users directory on the server: $PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/users/ username /Catalyst.cfg If it exists, it is used when this parameter is left blank. |

# Cluster Pharmacophores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_cluster_pharmacophores.htm

## Cluster Pharmacophores

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Cluster Pharmacophores protocol computes a distance between each pair of pharmacophores. This distance is a function of the number of common
pharmacophore features and the root-mean-squared displacement between the matching features. The distance matrix is clustered and presented as a
dendrogram upon completion.

* Open the Pharmacophores | Compare Pharmacophores tools and click Cluster Pharmacophores to open the Cluster Pharmacophores dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Use the Input Pharmacophores parameter to navigate to a queries file. For details about the remaining parameters, see Cluster Pharmacophores - Parameters .

For details about the remaining parameters, see Cluster Pharmacophores - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Perl script used to view results in graphics. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| pharmacophores_clus.dsv | Contains all of the input pharmacophores. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| pharmacophores_clus.html | Contains the distance matrix in HTML format: 2hbd1hba 3funcs 4FeatShape 2hbd1hba 0.00000 0.57224 0.57225 3funcs 0.57224 0.00000 0.57226 4FeatShape 0.57225 0.57226 0.00000 | | 2hbd1hba | 3funcs | 4FeatShape | 2hbd1hba | 0.00000 | 0.57224 | 0.57225 | 3funcs | 0.57224 | 0.00000 | 0.57226 | 4FeatShape | 0.57225 | 0.57226 | 0.00000 |

# Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/pharmacophore_common_feature_pharmacophore_generation-para.htm

## Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation - Parameters

### Generates common feature pharmacophore models from a set of ligands

Uses HipHop to generate common feature pharmacophores among a set of up to 32 active Input Ligands .
The algorithm can also optionally use information from inactive ligands to place excluded volume features.

The input ligands should contain the following properties:

* Principal : Indicates whether the ligand is active (2), moderately active (1) or inactive (0). A value of 2 is used if the property is missing.

* MaxOmitFeat : Indicates how many features are allowed to miss for each
molecule. A value of 0 is used if the property is missing.

See Also:

* Barnum, D.; Greene, J.; Smellie, A.; Sprague, P. Identification of common functional configurations among molecules. J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. 1996 , 36, 563-571.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. There is an upper limit of 32 active compounds. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. The input ligands should contain the following properties: Principal: indicates activity level of the molecule. Set to 2 if the property is missing. 2: Active, consider conformations of this molecule as a reference molecule. Highly important in placing pharmacophore features. Each input data set must contain at least one reference molecule. 1: Moderately active, consider conformations of this molecule when placing pharmacophore features. 0: Inactive, not considered when placing pharmacophore features, used in placing excluded volumes. MaxOmitFeat: indicates how many features are allowed to miss for each molecule. Set to 0 if the property is missing. 0: All features in the generated pharmacophore must map to this compound. 1: All but one of the features in the generated pharmacophore must map to this compound. 2: No features in the generated pharmacophore need to map to this compound. |
| Input Ligands Preprocessing | Options for ligand standardization. ClearStereo: Sets all atoms and bonds to NoStereo. ClearUnknownStereo: Sets all atoms and bonds that are marked UnknownStereo to NoStereo. KeepSmallestFragment: In the case of multi-fragment ligands, retain the fragment with the fewest atoms. KeepLargestFragment: In the case of multi-fragment ligands, retain the fragment with the most atoms. RemoveLargestFragment: In the case of multi-fragment ligands, remove the fragment with most atoms. Valid Values: ClearStereo, ClearUnknownStereo, KeepSmallestFragment, KeepLargestFragment, RemoveLargestFragment |
| Conformation Generation | Each molecule in Input Ligands must have a good set of conformations. If they are not present in the input data, they can be added using one of the following algorithms: FAST: quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations. BEST: ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR: very quickly provides conformations by sampling torsions. NONE: uses existing conformations. Valid Values: NONE, FAST , BEST, CAESAR |
| Maximum Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. |
| Discard Existing Conformations | If True, discard existing input conformations, otherwise use all existing input conformations. Valid Values: True , False |
| Energy Threshold | Conformations are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol). For a molecule with stereo isomers, this threshold applies to conformations for each individual isomer. |
| Ring Fragments File | File (fragments.data) that contains the ring conformations to use. The Catalyst Ring Fragment Writer component can be used to generate the file. Molecules that contain rings also found in the file will only use these ring conformations. Conformations for rings not found in the file are generated from scratch. Note: Only FAST and CAESAR will use this file. It have no effect on other methods. By default this parameter is blank and all ring conformations are generated from scratch. |
| Save Conformations | Save the generated conformations in a MDL MOL/SD file. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |
| Features | A comma separated list of pharmacophore features to be used in pharmacophore generation. Both predefined and customized pharmacophore features are available. Up to 10 different features may be chosen. Each feature is followed by the desired minimum and maximum count of that feature that can occur in the generated pharmacophores. The predefined features with default minimum and maximum values are: HB_ACCEPTOR 0 5 HB_ACCEPTOR_lipid 0 5 HB_DONOR 0 5 HYDROPHOBIC 0 5 HYDROPHOBIC_aromatic 0 5 HYDROPHOBIC_aliphatic 0 5 NEG_CHARGE 0 5 NEG_IONIZABLE 0 5 POS_CHARGE 0 5 POS_IONIZABLE 0 5 RING_AROMATIC 0 5 HBA_HEAVY 0 5 HBA_PROJECTION 0 5 POS_IONIZABLE_1 0 5 ZN_BINDER 0 5 iHBA 0 5 iHBD 0 5 iHBA_SB 0 5 iHBD_SB 0 5 iRINGAROMATIC 0 5 iSulfur_INT 0 5 iNOS 0 5 iHBD_carbon 0 5 iHalogen_INT 0 5 iFluorine_INT 0 5 iAmide 0 5 Use the name of the feature stored in the dictionary when using customized features. In Discovery Studio, a dialog lists the predefined features as well as any customized features. Customized features can be built using the Customize Pharmacophore Features tool. Features created by this tool are written to a dictionary file located at: [Settings Folder]/Catalyst/conf/Dictionary.ds_chm In Pipeline Pilot, when using customized features you must also set the location of the Dictionary.ds_chm that contains the definition of the customized feature using the CustomDictionary implementation parameter. |
| Maximum Pharmacophores | Number of pharmacophores to generate. The "best" pharmacophores are output first, using an internal scoring function. In actual usage, the first pharmacophore may not be the best. |
| Minimum Interfeature Distance | The minimum spacing in Å between feature points. The default value of 2.97 Å works well for most medium to large molecules, but may be too great for small molecules that do not have many features. For a pharmacophore where the features are close together, try a smaller value, such as 0.5 Å. |
| Maximum Excluded Volumes | Maximum number of excluded volume features allowed. The algorithm will optimize and attempt to return the minimum number of excluded volumes until the maximum limit is reached. The algorithm will attempt to add excluded volumes in regions that are occupied by an inactive molecule but not the active molecules. By default, the selection of the active and inactive molecules is done automatically. You can optionally designate which molecules will be used to place the excluded volumes by adding the molecular property Principal . When placing an excluded volume, the Principal values have the following meaning: 0: The ligand is inactive. 1: The ligand is moderately active. 2: The ligand is active. |
| Validation | Validation of the generated pharmacophore models using active/inactive ligands. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves as well as an optimal cutoff values are reported. Evaluate the pharmacophore model by reviewing the area of the ROC curve (AUC). A value closer to 1 indicates good selectivity, whereas a value closer to 0.5 indicates random selection. The cutoff value indicates a good pharmacophore fit value to separate actives from inactives. The cutoff displayed on the plot is the pharmacophore fit value that gives the highest accuracy calculated as: (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN) where TP = number of true positives TN = number of true negatives FP = number of false positives FN = number of false negatives Valid Values: True, False |
| Active Ligands | Input data set of active ligands for validation. |
| Inactive Ligands | Input data set of inactive ligands for validation. |
| Validation Conformation Generation | Each molecule in Input Ligands must have a good set of conformations. If they are not present in the input data, they can be added using one of the following algorithms: FAST: quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations. BEST: ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR: very quickly provides conformations by sampling torsions. NONE: uses existing conformations. Valid Values: NONE, FAST , BEST, CAESAR |
| Validation Conformation Generation Maximum Conformations | Maximum conformations for validation. |
| Validation Conformation Generation Discard Existing Conformations | Discard existing conformations for conformation generation in validation. Valid Values: True , False |
| Validation Conformation Generation Ring Fragments File | File (fragments.data) that contains the ring conformations to use. The Catalyst Ring Fragment Writer component can be used to generate the file. Molecules that contain rings also found in the file will only use these ring conformations. Conformations for rings not found in the file are generated from scratch. Note: Only FAST and CAESAR will use this file. It have no effect on other methods. By default this parameter is blank and all ring conformations are generated from scratch. |
| Validation Conformation Generation Energy Threshold | Conformations are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol). For a molecule with stereo isomers, this threshold applies to conformations for each individual isomer. |
| Validation Fitting Method | Choose the type of fitting to use in validation: Rigid: performs rigid fit between ligand and pharmacophore. Flexible: Each conformation of the ligand may be slightly modified to better fit the pharmacophore. Valid Values: Rigid , Flexible |
| Validation Maximum Omitted Features | The maximum number of features that are allowed to miss when mapping the ligand to the pharmacophore. A value of -1 has special meaning: It instructs the server to consider all feature subsets of the pharmacophore. It is equivalent to n-1 , where n is the total number of features in the pharmacophore. For a pharmacophore with 5 features, -1 allows up to 4 features to miss. The number of subsets grows very quickly as the total number of features in the pharmacophore increases. To avoid excessive memory use and calculation time, Maximum Omitted Features is limited in the fitting calculation (not the client): Total Features = 1-6: Maximum Omitted Features limited to (Total Features - 1) or less Total Features = 7-9: Maximum Omitted Features limited to 4 or less Total Features = 10: Maximum Omitted Features limited to 3 or less Total Features = 11-19: Maximum Omitted Features limited to 2 or less Total Features = 20+: Maximum Omitted Features limited to 1 or less |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Minimum Features | Minimum number of features required in each pharmacophore. |
| Maximum Features | Maximum number of features permitted in each pharmacophore. |
| Number of Leads That May Miss | Number of active molecules in the input set that do not have to map to all features in a generated pharmacophore. |
| Minimum Feature Points | Minimum number of feature points for a generated pharmacophore. For example, a pharmacophore with two hydrophobes and two negative ionizables has four points. A pharmacophore with two hydrophobes and one hydrogen bond acceptor also has four points since the hydrogen bond acceptor has both an atom and a projected point. The default for this parameter is 4, which is the minimum value for an enantio-selective pharmacophore. For very small rigid molecules that have few chemical features, you might need to set this value to a lower number. |
| Minimum Features in Moderately Active | Minimum number of features required to be found in the moderately active molecules. For small or rigid molecules, try setting this to a lower value than the default (4). |
| Feature Misses | This option lets you specify the number of molecules in your input set of lead compounds that are allowed not to map to any one feature of a generated pharmacophore. Lowering the setting for the Feature Misses option from 3 to 1 still allows compounds in the input set to miss a feature, but distributes the misses among features of a generated pharmacophore. Generally speaking, the greater the value you specify for the Feature Misses option, the less evidence there is that each individual feature of a generated pharmacophore is significant. Stating it another way, setting the Feature Misses option to a small value requires more input compounds to map to individual features, thus providing more evidence that the inclusion of any one feature in a pharmacophore is significant. A value for the Feature Misses option is meaningful only if it is less than or equal to the value you specify for Number of Leads That May Miss option. The default for this value is 1. |
| Complete Misses | The Complete Misses option lets you specify the number of molecules in your input set of compounds that do not have to map to more than one feature per generated pharmacophore. A value for Complete Misses is meaningful only if it is less than the value you specify for the Number of Leads That May Miss option. Remember, HipHop allows only compounds designated with a 2 for the MaxOmitFeat property to completely miss mapping to features in an output pharmacophore. The default for this parameter is 0. |
| Stereoisomers As Different Molecules | If True, each stereoisomer is treated as a different molecule. Note : Because known stereo centers are treated as separate molecules, use the ClearStereo or ClearUnknownStereo option in the Input Ligands Preprocessing parameter to clear the chirality. Valid Values: True, False |
| Align Ligands to Hypothesis | If True, the input ligands will be aligned to the generated pharmacophore and exported to the Output directory. If False, the input ligands are not exported. Valid Values: True , False |
| Best Mapping Only | If True, only the best mapping for each ligand will be returned. Otherwise all mappings will be returned for each ligand. Valid Values: True , False |
| Check Superposition | Use an exact check on superposition, alternative is to use distance check. Valid Values: True , False |
| Superposition Error | Adjusts the RMS fit of molecules to generated pharmacophore, after alignment. Value can be reduced from default of 1.0 to tighten the fit. Value must be greater than 0.0 and less than or equal to 1.0. |
| Scale Feature Blob Size | Scales feature tolerance by the following equation: Tolerance = (Tolerance Factor) * (default tolerance for feature) The default tolerance for all features is 1.6 Å, except for projection points, which have a default value of 2.2 Å |
| Maximum Mappings | Ignore mappings beyond this many top mappings. After the active ligands are optimally aligned to the pharmacophore, each inactive ligand is mapped to the pharmacophore using up to Maximum Mappings mappings and Maximum Confs Per Mapping conformations. Excluded volumes are then placed in an attempt to remove all the inactive ligand poses. Considering more mappings and conformations could increase computation time. Considering too few could result in pharmacophores that still map to the inactive ligands. Only applicable if Maximum Excluded Volumes > 0. |
| Maximum Confs Per Mapping | Ignore conformations beyond this many top conformations per mapping. Only applicable if Maximum Excluded Volumes > 0. |
| Memory | The amount of physical memory (MB) used in the HipHop algorithm. When memory reaches this limit, it starts consuming virtual memory and switches to a slower but more compact algorithm and attempts to run to completion. If the memory limit is exceeded by a factor of 2, HipHop will report an early termination and partial results. |
| Explore Exhaustive HBond Geometry | Explore exhaustive hydrogen bond geometries. The alternative is to explore only 'ideal' hydrogen bond geometries. Valid Values: True , False |
| Catalyst Parameter File | File containing .Catalyst parameter settings to define the default behavior of Catalyst programs. The file can be created using the Catalyst Parameter Settings component. This parameter is typically only changed by experts. A default .Catalyst parameter settings file can be created in the users directory on the server: $PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/users/ username /Catalyst.cfg If it exists, it is used when this parameter is left blank. |

* Total Features = 20+: Maximum Omitted Features limited to 1 or less

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Minimum number of features required in each pharmacophore.

Maximum number of features permitted in each pharmacophore.

Number of active molecules in the input set that do not have to map to all features in a generated pharmacophore.

Minimum number of feature points for a generated pharmacophore.

For example, a pharmacophore with two hydrophobes and two negative ionizables has four points.

A pharmacophore with two hydrophobes and one hydrogen bond acceptor also has four points since the hydrogen bond acceptor has both an atom and a projected point.

The default for this parameter is 4, which is the minimum value for an enantio-selective pharmacophore. For very small rigid molecules that have few chemical features, you might need to set this value to a lower number.

Minimum number of features required to be found in the moderately active molecules.

For small or rigid molecules, try setting this to a lower value than the default (4).

This option lets you specify the number of molecules in your input set of lead compounds that are allowed not to map to any one feature of a generated pharmacophore. Lowering the setting for the Feature Misses option from 3 to 1 still allows compounds in the input set to miss a feature, but distributes the misses among features of a generated pharmacophore.

Generally speaking, the greater the value you specify for the Feature Misses option, the less evidence there is that each individual feature of a generated pharmacophore is significant. Stating it another way, setting the Feature Misses option to a small value requires more input compounds to map to individual features, thus providing more evidence that the inclusion of any one feature in a pharmacophore is significant. A value for the Feature Misses option is meaningful only if it is less than or equal to the value you specify for Number of Leads That May Miss option. The default for this value is 1.

The Complete Misses option lets you specify the number of molecules in your input set of compounds that do not have to map to more than one feature per generated pharmacophore. A value for Complete Misses is meaningful only if it is less than the value you specify for the Number of Leads That May Miss option.

Remember, HipHop allows only compounds designated with a 2 for the MaxOmitFeat property to completely miss mapping to features in an output pharmacophore. The default for this parameter is 0.

If True, each stereoisomer is treated as a different molecule.

Note :

* Because known stereo centers are treated as separate molecules, use the ClearStereo or ClearUnknownStereo option in the Input Ligands Preprocessing parameter to clear the chirality.

If True, the input ligands will be aligned to the generated pharmacophore and exported to the Output directory. If False, the input ligands are not exported.

If True, only the best mapping for each ligand will be returned. Otherwise all mappings will be returned for each ligand.

Use an exact check on superposition, alternative is to use distance check.

Adjusts the RMS fit of molecules to generated pharmacophore, after alignment. Value can be reduced from default of 1.0 to tighten the fit. Value must be greater than 0.0 and less than or equal to 1.0.

Scales feature tolerance by the following equation:

Tolerance = (Tolerance Factor) * (default tolerance for feature)

The default tolerance for all features is 1.6 Å, except for projection points, which have a default value of 2.2 Å

Ignore mappings beyond this many top mappings.

After the active ligands are optimally aligned to the pharmacophore, each inactive ligand is mapped to the pharmacophore using up to Maximum Mappings mappings and Maximum Confs Per Mapping conformations. Excluded volumes are then placed in an attempt to remove all the inactive ligand poses. Considering more mappings and conformations could increase computation time. Considering too few could result in pharmacophores that still map to the inactive ligands.

Only applicable if Maximum Excluded Volumes > 0.

Ignore conformations beyond this many top conformations per mapping. Only applicable if Maximum Excluded Volumes > 0.

The amount of physical memory (MB) used in the HipHop algorithm. When memory reaches this limit, it starts consuming virtual memory and switches to a slower but more compact algorithm and attempts to run to completion. If the memory limit is exceeded by a factor of 2, HipHop will report an early termination and partial results.

Explore exhaustive hydrogen bond geometries. The alternative is to explore only 'ideal' hydrogen bond geometries.

File containing .Catalyst parameter settings to define the default behavior of Catalyst programs. The file can be created using the Catalyst Parameter Settings component. This parameter is typically only changed by experts.

A default .Catalyst parameter settings file can be created in the users directory on the server: $PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/users/ username /Catalyst.cfg

If it exists, it is used when this parameter is left blank.
