# Create Pharmacophore Manually tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_cpmt.htm

## Create Pharmacophore Manually tools

The Create Pharmacophore Manually tools can be used to manually create a pharmacophore model from a template molecule.

### Vector Features

Acceptor Feature: The Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature is a vector pointing
toward an atom that can serve as a hydrogen bond acceptor (e.g., a carbonyl oxygen). By default the Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature is oriented along
the vector that is the average of the lone pair vectors, which is called the
Projection Orientation.

To create a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature, select an atom or atoms that can serve as hydrogen
bond acceptors and click the Acceptor button.

To change the length of the Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature, make sure the AcceptorFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible, and
edit the Length property.

Change the orientation from the default Projection orientation to any of the lone pair
orientations. The lone pair orientations are designated First Lone Pair , Second Lone Pair , and Third Lone Pair .
You can edit the Orientation property in the Acceptor Feature Properties
dialog box by selecting First Lone Pair , Second
Lone Pair , Third Lone Pair , or Projection .
The default setting is Projection , so if you select Third
Lone Pair for a carbonyl oxygen (which only has two lone pairs), the Orientation property is reset to Projection .

Donor Feature: The Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature is a vector pointing
toward an atom that can serve as a hydrogen bond donor (e.g., the hydrogen on a
hydroxyl group).

To create a Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature, select an atom that can serve as hydrogen bond donors, and click Donor .

To change the length of the Hydrogen Bond Donor, make sure the DonorFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and edit the Length property.

Aromatic Ring Feature: The Aromatic Ring Feature represents an aromatic
ring.

To create a Aromatic Ring Feature, select at least three atoms in an aromatic ring and click Aromatic Ring
Feature .

### Point Feature

Point Feature: The Point Feature is placed at the
geometrical center of the objects you specify.

To create a Point Feature, select a set of objects and click Point Feature .

To change the type of the Point Feature, and thus the nature of the query, make sure the PointFeature tab in the Data Table View is
visible, and choose one of the following Types :

* Hydrophobe

* Hydrophobe_Aromatic

* Hydrophobe_Aliphatic

* Ionizable_Negative

* Ionizable_Positive

* Charged_Negative

* Charged_Positive

The position of the point feature is linked to the position of the atom or the group of atoms which were used to define it. As a result, the point feature cannot be moved independently. In order to move the point feature, either move the atom or group of atoms or cut and paste the ligand containing the atom or group of atoms. Cutting the ligand breaks the link between point feature and atom or atoms and allows the point feature to be moved independently.

### Constraints

Location Constraint: A Location Constraint Feature is an object
that represents a location in space within a given radius.

To create a Location Constraint Feature, select one of the following:

* An atom

* A Point Feature

* A Hydrogen Bond Acceptor Feature

* A Hydrogen Bond Donor Feature

* A Centroid Feature

* A Point Offset Feature

* An Aromatic Ring Feature

To change the radius, select the Location Constraint Feature, make sure the LocationFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and
edit the Radius cell.

Exclusion Constraint: (Catalyst & Isentris type query) The Exclusion Constraint Feature
is an object that represents an excluded volume in space, within a given radius.

To create an Exclusion Constraint Feature, select an atom and click Exclusion
Constraint .

To change the Exclusion Constraint Feature's radius, select the Exclusion Constraint Feature,
make sure the ExclusionFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and edit the Radius property.

Shape Feature: The Shape Feature represents atoms
contained within a surface. The Shape Feature uses a surface to represent the
shape of the molecule.

To create a Shape Feature, select an entire molecule and click Shape Feature .

To change the similarity tolerance, select the Shape Feature, make sure the ShapeFeature tab in the Data Table View is visible and
edit the Tolerance property.

# Compare Pharmacophores tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_cpt.htm

## Compare Pharmacophores tools

The Compare Pharmacophores tools allow you to compare two pharmacophores or cluster a set of pharmacophores.

### Compare Two Pharmacophores

Pharmacophore Comparison: Opens the Pharmacophore Comparison protocol dialog. This protocol uses Catalyst to map and align two pharmacophores. A root-mean-squared error is reported for the matching pharmacophore features. The Best Mapping Only parameter can be changed to return multiple mappings.

### Cluster Several Pharmacophores

Cluster Pharmacophores: Opens the Cluster Pharmacophores protocol dialog.
The distance is a function of the number of common pharmacophore features and the root-mean-squared displacement between the matching features.

Pair-wise root-mean-square fits are performed on all pharmacophore pairs and the following function is computed:

F ij = pairs + 1/(rms + 1.01)

where pairs is the number of spheres common to both pharmacophores in a particular mapping, and rms is the minimum root-mean-square displacement between the matching pharmacophore features. All possible mappings between two pharmacophores are performed, and the F ij function is evaluated. The largest functional value is used for a particular pair of pharmacophores. A similarity function is defined as:

S ij =F ij /sqrt(F ii *F jj )

A distance function as:

D ij = 1 - S ij .

The distance matrix is displayed using an interactive dendrogram.

A feature based pharmacophore must be used. For example, a pharmacophore created using Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation or 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation.

## Edit and Cluster Features tools

The Edit and Cluster Features tool panel provides a quick way to selectively display, cluster, and edit a set of pharmacophore query
features.

### Find Features

Feature Mapping: Opens the Feature Mapping protocol dialog. This protocol identifies all possible locations 
of pharmacophore features on the input molecules.

Interaction Generation: Opens the Interaction Generation protocol dialog. This protocol creates a pharmacophore query from a Ludi interaction map.
The interaction map is created in a receptor active site sphere and consists of hydrogen bond acceptor, hydrogen bond donor, and hydrophobic features.

### Select Feature Category

Current Feature: Choose a feature to display. For example, to hide all the Hydrophobe pharmacophore features in the Molecule Window, choose Hydrophobe as the current feature, and then click Show/Hide Hydrophobe in the Show/Hide group.

### Show/Hide

Show/Hide <Current Feature>: Shows or hides the current feature (selected above).

Show/Hide Location Spheres: Toggles the display of the location spheres on the current feature. For example, to
turn off the display of the location constraints for all pharmacophore features, choose Select Feature Category | Current Feature | All Features , and then click Show/Hide Location Spheres .

Show/Hide All Non-Features: Toggles the display of all non-feature objects. This is a useful option if you have a collection of pharmacophore features displayed in a protein and you want to hide the protein to improve the visualization of the features.

### Cluster

Cluster Current Feature: Performs a hierarchical clustering of the current feature and opens a Dendrogram Window. Move the slider in the Dendrogram Window to highlight the cluster centers of the feature groups in the Molecule Window.

If no members of the current feature are selected, clustering is performed using all the members of the current feature.

If some members of the current feature are selected, clustering is performed using only the selected members.

The calculation is not performed if there are less than two members of the current feature.

Show Only Cluster Centers: Displays only the cluster centers of the current feature based on the
position of the Dendrogram Window slider. Change the
position of the slider and click this button to display the other centers. The Dendrogram Window must be current to enable this feature.

Keep Only Cluster Centers: Deletes all the non-center clusters of the current feature based on the
position of the Dendrogram Window slider. To undo your
changes, click Undo on the Standard toolbar. The Dendrogram Window must be current to enable this feature.

### Edit

Keep Only Current Feature Selections: Allows you to keep selected members of the current feature. The
Molecule Window must be current to enable this feature.

You can also use this in conjunction with the cluster centers feature described in the clustering section. To include other members of the current feature in addition to the cluster centers, select the tab of the Molecule Window, press SHIFT and select the additional members, and then click this button. This action retains the cluster centers based on the position of the Dendrogram Window slider, as well as the manually selected members of the current feature.

Merge Hypotheses: Allows you to perform a simple merge of two or more hypotheses.

Average Pharmacophore Features: Converts a collection of selected pharmacophore features of the same type to a single feature.
You can also use it for excluded volumes. The new feature is placed at the center of the selected features. The tolerance of the new feature is the larger of the following:

* A default value of 1.6 Å for all feature points except projection points (2.2 Å) and excluded volumes (1.2 Å)

* The average distance between each feature in the original collection and the new feature

Merge Hypotheses can be used to:

* Merge two or more pharmacophores to a single pharmacophore by selecting the collection of features you want to combine (e.g., Hydrophobic groups) one group at a time

* Reduce the number of excluded volumes by selecting groups you want to combine

The Customize Pharmacophore Features tools allow you to create customized pharmacophore features.

### Feature Mapping

Map ALL Selected: Creates a pharmacophore feature definition that requires a matching ligand to have all of the selected
pharmacophore features.

Map ANY Selected: Creates a pharmacophore feature definition that requires a matching ligand to have at least one of
the selected features.

For example, if you select two molecules that are not contained in any query, Map ANY Selected and Map ALL Selected will create a new query that contains a top-level query operator representing the "Map ANY" or "Map ALL" criterion. The top-level
query operator in turn contains two query operators, one for each of the molecules.

Map ALL Selected and Map ANY Selected will move selected molecules that are not part of a query into an existing or new query. This process entails breaking existing links to sequence information.

Exclude Selection from Mapping: Excludes the selected feature from the mapping definition. In the query hierarchy, this introduces one query operator representing the combination of the general rule and specific exceptions. Expanding this
operator, the general rule is represented as the first query operator, with the specific exceptions following.

Create Mapping: Creates a mapping of all the selected features. This is needed to specify a single feature representing
features matched with Map ANY , or when features are to be excluded. The mapping point, which can be created using the Query toolbar, can be a query atom, atom, query bond, bond, point feature,
etc. For example, to create a pharmacophore definition that requires one of several hetero-aromatic groups
to match, you could add a centroid feature to each of the aromatic groups using the Query toolbar. To create the Map ANY feature for these groups,
select each centroid, and click Create Mapping . The created centroid feature will be the mapping point.

Show Mappings: Toggles the display of the feature mappings.

Show Only: Shows only the selected features while hiding the details of the underlying topologies. This is useful if
you want to see only the selected pharmacophores from a larger set in a Molecule Window. The Show Only functionality in the Molecule Window will show all selected objects, which includes the underlying topology that defines the feature. Show Only shows only the top level objects.

Simplify Customized Feature View: Improves the visualization of pharmacophore features. The display style is set to Ball and Stick, query atoms and bonds are hidden allowing
you to see the underlying chemistry, and atoms and bonds that have multiple definitions (e.g., a query atom defined as [C N O S]) are colored mauve.

### Add Vector

Hydrogen Bond Acceptor: Adds a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor feature to the selected atom. This can be used when adding another substructure to the Hydrogen Bond Acceptor definition or when creating a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor feature from scratch. Each 
substructure requires a Hydrogen Bond Acceptor vector feature to be associated with it. 
Use Create Mapping to associate all the vectors to a single definition.

Hydrogen Bond Donor: Similar to Hydrogen Bond Acceptor, 
but adds a Hydrogen Bond Donor feature.

Query Atom Specification: Launches the Edit Query Atom Attributes dialog .

collection of elements [C,N,S])

* Allowed charges

* Hydrogen counts

* Lone pair counts

## Search, Screen, and Profile

The Search, Screen, and Profile tools allows you inspect the mappings of a pharmacophore to several ligands, screen ligand libraries with several pharmacophore feature combinations, use multiple pharmacophores to map multiple ligands, and search or browse a ligand database.

### Mapping

Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping: Opens the Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping protocol dialog. This protocol identifies ligands that map to a pharmacophore and aligns them to that pharmacophore. The pharmacophore can contain combinations of substructures, 3D constraints, features, shapes, excluded volumes, etc. Depending on the pharmacophore, additional properties may be added, these include:

* FitValue: A measure of how well the ligand fits the pharmacophore. The higher the fit score, the better the match.

* ShapeSimilarity: A value between zero and one that measures the overlap of the mapped conformation and the shape constraint.

* MappedAtoms: An array of atoms that map the pharmacophore in the format AtomIndex, X, Y, Z, Tolerance, Location feature name.

### Screening

Screen Library: Opens the Screen Library protocol dialog. This protocol enumerates many possible subset pharmacophores from a query and screens the input ligands against each pharmacophore. The pharmacophores are created based on the parameters
of the protocol.

For example, if there are a total of 8 pharmacophore features in the input query,
the Minimum Features parameter is set to 4 ,
the Maximum Features parameter is set to 6 , and the Maximum Subset of Pharmacophores parameter is set to 100 ,
then a 100 pharmacophore subset of all possible 4, 5, and 6 feature pharmacophores from the 8 features
will be used in the analysis.

The protocol analyzes large collections of pharmacophore features to extract the most relevant pharmacophore models. It is intended to support the structure based pharmacophore tools (e.g., analyzing output from Interaction Generation), but can be used to analyze any set of pharmacophore features.

It is possible to specify combinations of Minimum Features, Maximum Features, Selected Features, and Feature Groups such that there are no legal candidate pharmacophores to test.

### Profile Ligands using Pharmacophore DB

Ligand Profiler: Opens the Ligand Profiler protocol dialog. This protocol maps a set of input ligands to a set of input pharmacophores.

PharmaDB Filter: Opens the PharmaDB Filter protocol dialog. This protocol filters PharmaDB entries based on selected properties. The ouput can be used as input to the PharmaDB Profiler protocol.

PharmaDB Profiler: Opens the PharmaDB Profiler protocol dialog. This protocol maps a set of ligands against a PharmaDB hit list, which can be generated using the PharmaDB Filter protocol.

### Search DB - Indexed for Speed

This protocol uses Catalyst to identify ligands in a database that map to a pharmacophore, and optionally aligns the ligands to the query. # Theory - Pharmacophores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the.htm

## Theory - Pharmacophores

A pharmacophore model, according to IUPAC definition, is "an ensemble of steric 
and electronic features that is necessary to ensure the optimal intermolecular interactions 
with a specific biological target and to trigger (or block) its biological response". 
In Discovery Studio , a pharmacophore is defined as the essential features or chemical 
substructures and their corresponding 3D locations that are responsible for the similar 
biological activities of a set of compounds. Typically, pharmacophore features include 
hydrophobic, aromatic, hydrogen bond acceptor, hydrogen bond donor, positive ionizable 
and negative ionizable.

The following picture shows a typical pharmacophore model 
with three types of chemical features and their 3D location constraints:

The pharmacophore model consists of one Hydrogen Bond Acceptor (HBA, in green), 
three Hydrophobic centers (in light blue), and one Negative Ionizable center 
(in dark blue). Since a hydrogen bond is directional, each HBA feature is 
specified with two points: one is the location of the associated heavy atom, 
and the other is the projection point, which defines the direction for forming a 
hydrogen bond with a target. Each sphere defines the location tolerance of a 
particular feature point.

The Pharmacophore protocols allow you to generate pharmacophores, perform ligand-pharmacophore comparisons and fitting, etc. The following Help topics discuss the theory behind the protocols and tools:

* Pharmacophore generation

* Hypothesis clustering

* Pharmacophore scoring

# Generating predictive pharmacophores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_3dqsar.htm

## Generating predictive pharmacophores

In the application, predictive pharmacophores are generated using the
HypoGen algorithm. The HypoGen algorithm uses the data selected by you (that is the training set, conformational models, pharmacophore features, parameters and so on) to generate the top scoring predictive pharmacophores.

### Three phases

Predictive pharmacophores are generated in three phases - a constructive, a subtractive, and an optimization phase.

#### Constructive phase

Conceptually speaking, the
constructive phase is similar to the HipHop algorithm. The idea is to
generate pharmacophores that are common among the active molecules in the
training set. This is done in several steps:

* The active molecules are identified.

* All pharmacophores (maximum five features) among the two most
active molecules are identified and stored.

* Those pharmacophores that fit the remaining active molecules are kept.

The algorithm first identifies the lead compounds, which include the most
active compound and compounds whose activities satisfy the following
condition:

Equation 1:

where, MA is the activity of the most active compound, Unc is
the uncertainty of the compounds, and A is the activity of the compound in 
question. If there are more than eight lead compounds, only the top eight are used.

HypoGen identifies all allowable pharmacophores consisting of up to five features
among the two most active compounds. This is done using a pruned exhaustive
search of all the conformations similar to the HipHop algorithm.

Finally, HypoGen investigates the remaining active compounds in the list. 
Only the pharmacophores that fit a minimum subset of features of the 
remaining active compounds are kept.

#### Subtractive phase

In this phase, the program removes
pharmacophores from the data structure that are not likely to be useful. The
pharmacophores that were created in the constructive phase are inspected. If
they are common to most of the inactive compounds, they are removed from
consideration.

First, the inactive compounds are identified. A compound is considered inactive
if the activity is 3.5 orders of magnitude, by default, greater than the most
active compound:

Equation 2.

where, A is the activity of the compound in question and MA is 
the activity of the most active compound. Any pharmacophore that matches more
than half of the compounds identified as inactive is removed.

#### Optimization phase

The optimization is done using the well-known algorithm simulated annealing.
The algorithm applies small perturbations to the pharmacophores created in
the constructive and subtractive phases in an attempt to improve the score.
The steps include selecting a new pharmacophore from the list of
possibilities, rotating a vectored feature, translating a randomly selected
feature in the pharmacophore, adding a new features, and removing a feature.
Acceptance of each step is determined based on a score that measures the
errors in the activity estimates from regression and the complexity of the
pharmacophore. The algorithm accepts all improvements and some
detrimental steps based on a probability function. The highest scoring,
unique pharmacophores are exported.

### Adding excluded volumes

Optionally, excluded volumes can be added to the pharmacophores 
during the optimization using the HypoGenRefine algorithm.

# Generating common feature pharmacophores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_cfgen.htm

## Generating common feature pharmacophores

In the application, common feature pharmacophores are generated using the HipHop algorithm. HipHop identifies configurations or three-dimensional
spatial arrangements of chemical features that are common to molecules in
a training set. The configurations are identified by a pruned exhaustive
search, starting with small sets of features and extending them until no
larger common configuration is found. Training set members are evaluated
on the basis of the types of chemical features they contain, along with the
ability to adopt a conformation that allows those features to be
superimposed on a particular configurations. You can define how many
molecules must map completely or partially to the pharmacophore. This
option allows broader and more diverse pharmacophores to be
generated.

The resultant pharmacophores are ranked as they are built.
The ranking is a measure of how well the molecules map onto the proposed
pharmacophores, as well as the rarity of the pharmacophore model. If a 
pharmacophore model is less likely to map to an inactive compound, it will
be given a higher rank; the reverse is also true. A summary of the
ranking formula is given below.

Let us define the fit of a molecule to a given configuration of K features as ( K + 1) if the molecule 
matches all K features of the configuration, i if the molecule matches the i th least 
selective subset of ( K - 1) of the K features (1 <= i <= K ), and 0 if otherwise.

Let M be number of molecules given and q ( x ) be the fraction of these molecules 
whose fit to the configuration is x . Let p ( x ) be the probability that an arbitrary 
molecule (perhaps randomly chosen from some large database of N molecules, N >> M ) has a fit x to the configuration.

The rank assigned to the configuration is:

Equation 1:

The higher the rank, the less likely it is that the M molecules fit the configuration as well as they 
do because of a chance correlation.

The value p ( x ) is estimated using the following regression model:

Equation 2:

Where:

K i = Number of instances of feature definition i in the configuration and

disp = Measure of the dispersion of the locations in the configuration, calculated
from Equation 3;

Equation 3:

L j is the position of the j th location in the 
configuration and is 
the centroid of the locations (projected hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor points and normal points are ignored 
for this purpose). The default C values provided with HipHop were empirically determined by multiple 
least-squares regression on the number of hits found when 1500 randomly chosen configurations were used to search the 
BioByteMasterFile database. 1

Values for the C constants are specified in the Install Directory/share/Catalyst/conf/default.hstat file.

```text
-6.6 !constant term, C0

HB_ACCEPTOR 2.5

HYDROPHOBIC 1.9
```

# Cost analysis in HypoGen

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_costanalys_hypogen.htm

## Cost analysis in HypoGen

HypoGen selects the best hypotheses from many possibilities by applying 
a cost analysis. The overall cost of each hypothesis is calculated by summing 
three cost factors - a weight cost, an error cost, and a configuration cost. 
HypoGen also calculates two theoretical costs, the null and fixed costs, that 
can be used to determine the significance of the selected hypotheses. 
The cost values of the optimized hypotheses should lie somewhere between these 
two costs. The closer it is to the fixed cost and the further away it is from 
the null cost, the more statistically significant the hypothesis is believed 
to be.

### Cost components

As stated previously, there are three components of the hypothesis cost - 
the weight, error and configuration component. The weight component is a 
value that increases in a Gaussian form as the feature weight deviates from 
an ideal value (2.0). The error component increases as the root mean squared 
difference between the estimated and measured activities for the training set 
molecules increases. The configuration component is a constant cost, which 
depends on the complexity of the hypothesis space being optimized. It is 
equal to the entropy of the hypothesis space.

#### Error and weight

The error and the weight components are estimated using the probability distribution shown here:

Equation 1:

The error and weight components of the hypothesis cost are estimated by 
taking -ln P of Equation 1 as shown here:

Equation 2:

where, σ and Δ 
are constant parameters derived from expected values of weights and errors, 
and x is the deviation from the expected values for each. The σ 
values are log(uncertainty) and 0.302 for the error and weight components, respectively. 
The Δ values are log (1.1) and 0.2 for the error and weight components. 
The deviation for the errors is the actual minus the predicted scaled 
activity values for the training set members, and the deviation for the 
weights is the difference between the average of the feature weights and 
the ideal weight (2.0). The error component of the cost is computed by 
summing Equation 2 across all leads and the weight component is computed by 
summing across all features.

#### Configuration

The configuration is log 2 P , where P is the 
number of initial hypotheses created in the constructive phase and that 
survived the subtractive phase. In standard HypoGen mode, the configuration 
should not be greater than 17.0.

### Cost values

As stated previously, there are three costs reported by HypoGen - 
the hypothesis cost, the fixed cost, and the null cost. In terms of 
hypothesis significance, what really matters is the magnitude of the 
difference between the cost of any returned hypothesis and the cost of the 
null hypothesis. In general, if this difference is greater than 60, there 
is an excellent chance the model represents a true correlation. Because most 
returned hypotheses are higher in cost than the fixed-cost model, a 
difference between the fixed cost and the null cost of 70 or more is 
necessary in order to achieve the difference of 60. If a returned hypotheses
has a cost that differs from the Null hypothesis by 40-60, there is a high 
probability (75%-90%) that it represents a true correlation to the data. As
the difference becomes less than 40, the likelihood of the hypothesis 
representing a true correlation in the data rapidly drops 
below 50%. Under these conditions, it may be difficult to find a predictive 
model.

#### Hypothesis cost

The cost for each hypothesis is the summation of the three cost 
components multiplied by a coefficient (default coefficient is 1.0 for 
each) as shown below:

Equation 3:

where, e , w , and c are the coefficients 
associated with the error ( E ), weight ( W ), and 
configuration ( C ) components, respectively. By default these 
coefficients are set to 1.0.

#### Fixed cost

The fixed cost, shown in Equation 4, represents the simplest model that fits 
the data perfectly. If such a hypothesis existed, the x terms in 
Equation 2 would be zero for both the error and weight components. Therefore, the 
fixed cost is a
combination of the first three terms of Equation 2 and the configuration cost.

Equation 4:

#### Null cost

The null cost, shown in Equation 5, represents the cost of a hypothesis with 
no features that estimates every activity to be the average activity. Since 
the null hypothesis has no features, there is no contribution from the weight or configuration component.

Equation 5:

### How variable weights and tolerances affect calculation of the cost

The configuration cost accounts for all the possible hypotheses plus all 
the possible combinations of relative weights or tolerances for each. The 
tolerance component of the cost is calculated using Equation 2. The σ and 
δ values are derived from the discrete choices of possible tolerance 
values. The optimization prefers to use a smaller tolerance unless there is 
an improvement in correlation when increased. The hypothesis cost, with 
variable weights and tolerances, is shown in Equation 6:

Equation 6:

The fixed cost under these conditions is shown here:

And the null cost is exactly the same as above.

# Excluded volumes effect on Fit scores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_excluded_volumes_fit.htm

## Excluded volumes effect on Fit scores

You can add an excluded-volume constraint to a pharmacophore to specify one 
or more spherical spaces in a pharmacophore that must not contain any atoms 
or bonds. For example, you might want to represent a region of a query that 
cannot contain any topology because it might impinge sterically on a 
receptor.

A pharmacophore with an excluded volume only matches if no atoms 
penetrate the excluded area. Penetration is defined differently in 
Rigid (FAST searching) and Flexible (BEST searching) fitting modes.

### Rigid fitting

In Rigid fitting, the distance between an atom and an excluded volume ( d ) must be 
greater than the tolerance of the excluded volume plus the approximate VDW radius of 
the atom (Hydrogen atoms are excluded) ( t ) times the ExcludedVolumeXFactor parameter ( x ). If d < t , then the Fit score is
modulated, thus:

| Condition | Modulator |
| --- | --- |
| d < xt | 0 |
| xt ≤ d ≤ t | |
| d > t | 1 (Fit is unchanged) |

### Flexible fitting

In Flexible fitting, each excluded volume is treated as a pseudo atom 
with VDW radius 
equal to its tolerance. The VDW interaction energy between the atoms of the 
molecule and the resulting excluded volume pseudo atoms is calculated. If 
the excess energy is below a small threshold (40,000 joules/mol) 
then the excluded volumes are considered 
to be satisfied. During the optimization, the position of the atoms of the molecule 
are optimized such that the best geometry, according to the FIT score, where 
the excluded volume VDW energy is below this threshold is returned as the hit.

### Comparing the fittings

Due to the differences between Rigid (FAST searching) and 
Flexible (BEST searching) fitting, a geometry that is a BEST hit is not necessarily also a FAST 
hit. The BEST algorithm allows for some overlap of atoms and excluded volumes, and also uses a VDW energy penalty as described above.

# HipHopRefine algorithm to add excluded volumes

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_hiphoprefine.htm

## HipHopRefine algorithm to add excluded volumes

The HipHopRefine algorithm is accessible through the Common Feature 
Pharmacophore Generation protocol and the Steric Refinement with Excluded
Volumes protocol. If inactive ligand data is included in the Common Feature
Pharmacophore Generation protocol and Maximum Excluded volumes is greater than 0 , the algorithm will use a refinement step of adding excluded volumes as a 
post-processing step to the HipHop algorithm.

By using the Steric Refinement with Excluded Volumes protocol, the 
HipHopRefine algorithm can be used to add excluded volumes to any 
feature-based pharmacophore with location constraints, whether it is created 
by HipHop, HypoGen, or from a template molecule. The term HipHopRefine is 
relevant in the following way: as HipHop refers to the algorithm for searching
for common pharmacophores among molecules, HipHopRefine refers to the 
algorithm that searches for common steric hindrances in molecules.

The input into the HipHopRefine algorithm is:

* A set (1 or more) of compounds which are known to be active.

* A pharmacophore capable of mapping the active compounds and 
producing alignments.

* A set of compounds which are inactive. Inactive compounds that 
do not map the pharmacophore are ignored. At least one inactive that 
maps the pharmacophore is required for determining excluded volume 
candidate locations.

The algorithm identifies excluded volume locations by a four-step process. 
The first step is to align the active molecules to the pharmacophore and 
choose one mapping from each compound to generate a volume that is accessible 
(AS). The second step is to align the inactive molecules to the pharmacophore. 
The sum of all mappings of all conformations of all inactive compounds is 
termed the Inactive Space (IS). In the third step, the Candidate Space (CS) 
is computed. CS is the volume that is occupied by the inactives but is not 
part of the AS. In the fourth and final step, regions of the CS are ranked 
according to how many inactive mappings occupy the space. Excluded volume 
locations are then determined by recursively partitioning this space to add 
as few excluded volumes as possible to remove each mapping. All volumes are 
calculated on a cubic grid. The grid spacing is set to the product of the 
excluded volume size (default = 1.2 Å and the so-called ExcludedVolumeXFactor 
(default = 0.85 Å), and represents the hard cutoff radius at which the excluded 
volume becomes an impenetrable sphere.

* Create AS: The Active Space (AS) is our best attempt to mimic the binding
site configuration of the active compounds. The intention is to make the AS
as small as possible, allowing the maximum remaining CS to add excluded
volumes. Conceptually, only a single active configuration is required to
instill activity, so a single mapping to the pharmacophore of each active
compound is used to determine the AS. Starting from the first active compound
in the list, the shape similarity of each mapping of this active to all the
mapping of all other compounds is determined. The set of individual compound
mappings with the highest overall similarity is then chosen to represent
the AS. In addition, one grid size spacing is added to the atom radius of all
heavy atoms in each compound mapping in the AS to allow for gridding effects.

* Create IS: The Inactive Space (IS) is generated by enumerating over all
mappings of the inactive compounds including mirror images if necessary. Any
inactive compounds that do not map the pharmacophore are ignored at this stage,
assuming that missing the pharmacophore is the reason for their inactivity.
Parameters for the compare operation can be modified to ensure a nearly
exhaustive set of mappings is used, namely the compare.maxMappings parameter
(default 100 ), which controls the number of unique atom-query mappings
enumerated, and the compare.maxConfsPerMapping parameter (default 12 ), which
controls the number of conformations of each atom-query mapping to enumerate and
can be set to a high number (e.g., 1000 ).

* Create CS: The Candidate Space (CS) is then derived as
the simple combination of the bit strings representing the volumes of the AS
and IS; CS = IS^AS.

* Rank elements of CS: In effect, for each inactive mapping
we have a bit string representing the volume that the mapping protrudes from
the AS. The best location for adding a single excluded volume is determined
by ranking each bit position by the number of inactive mappings that occupy
the corresponding grid position. The scoring mechanism attempts to more
heavily weight the possibility of removing more molecules rather than more
mappings. Each mapping is inversely weighted by the number of mappings in a
particular compound [i.e., weight = 1/(total compound mappings]. In other
words, a mapping from a compound that maps only once (weight = 1/1) carries
100 times the weight of a mapping of another compound that has 100 distinct
mappings (weight = 1/100).

An excluded volume added at a particular grid location will eliminate any 
mapping which occupies that grid position. In bit string terms, selecting bit n as a candidate location will remove all bit strings which bit n is set. You can then select from these remaining bit positions in the same way, 
recursively, in a greedy-algorithm recursive partitioning approach. The 
output of the algorithm is a ranked set of bit positions, which is converted 
back to true coordinates. Excluded volumes are added to the pharmacophores 
at these points in rank order.

# HypoGenRefine algorithm to add excluded volumes

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_hypogenrefine.htm

## HypoGenRefine algorithm to add excluded volumes

The HypoGenRefine algorithm enhances the HypoGen algorithm to place
excluded volumes in key locations in an attempt to model unfavorable steric
interactions.

The HypoGenRefine algorithm makes two modifications to the HypoGen
algorithm:

* The subtractive phase is eliminated. In HypoGen, the subtractive
phase is used to identify and remove pharmacophores that exist in 
both the active and inactive molecules, since these pharmacophores 
cannot discriminate between active and inactive compounds. When 
attempting to incorporate steric effects, however, these are the 
potentially interesting pharmacophores. An inactive compound may 
contain the active pharmacophore, but be inactive due to unfavorable 
steric effects. Therefore, these pharmacophores remain as potential 
candidates in HypoGenRefine.

* New move types are added to the optimization phase. As a 
possible move type during the optimization, an excluded volume can 
be added or removed from the candidate pharmacophore.

When placing an excluded volume, HypoGenRefine inspects the volume space 
of the active and inactive molecules to locate reasonable positions for 
adding an excluded volume. Excluded volumes are placed using the following 
steps:

* Align the active molecules to the candidate pharmacophore.

* Align the inactive molecule that has the best fit to the candidate pharmacophore.

* Find atoms in the inactive molecules that are at least a minimum 
distance from any atoms in the active molecules. These are the 
candidate points to add an excluded volume.

* Select one of the points at random and place an excluded volume.

In the application, it is possible to estimate the activity of a ligand
using a predictive pharmacophore. Predictive pharmacophores are
created using the HypoGen algorithm that is accessible in the 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation protocol. If a predictive
pharmacophore is submitted to the Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping protocol, an Estimated Activity value is computed 
for each mapping and conformation in addition to a Fit score.

# Hydrophobe identification algorithm

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_pharm-features_hydrophobe-id-algorithm.htm

## Hydrophobe identification algorithm

Given a conformation, we want to identify its hydrophobic 
surface regions and to mark the effective center of each region with a point. 
Before describing the algorithm, we need a few definitions.

The accessible surface s of an atom is the portion of the 
surface that can be touched by a probe sphere that 
does not collide with any other atom of the molecule. 
The following FAST, approximate method for calculating s suffices in practice. 
A set of points is distributed uniformly on the surface of the atom in question. 
A probe sphere is placed tangent to the atom at each point, and then its is checked for a collision with the van der Waals radius of any other 
atom of the molecule. The fraction f of the grid points that are accessible is determined and then set where r is the van der Waals 
radius of the atom.

The topology-dependent term t for an atom depends on the type 
of the atom and its neighbors. Because our goal is to assign hydrophobicity 
to small groups of atoms, our typing system works different than 
that of Ghose and Crippen, where the goal is to reproduce a partition 
coefficient for the entire molecule. In particular, we reduce the 
hydrophobicity of an atom if there are nearby hydrophilic atoms rather 
than simply add an opposing contribution for the hydrophilic atoms.

Our t values are determined according to a set of simple rules 
that were chosen to reflect the judgment of medicinal chemists on a set 
of test molecules as succinctly as possible. Hydrogens are ignored - their contributions are 
reflected in the value for the adjacent atom. The t value for a nonhydrogen atom 
is one times the appropriate factors for all categories into which 
the atom falls, as defined in the table below.

For example, all three atoms in CC=O fall in Category 6 ("less than or equal 
to 2 bonds away from O with double bond") 
and so are assigned t = 0. A negatively charged O falls in 
Category 3 and so is assigned t = 0. C in nitrile falls in 
Category 13 and so is assigned t = 0.25. Finally, 
Cl in CH 3 Cl falls in no special category, and so 
is assigned a full t = 1.

Many of the parameters can be changed using the Catalyst 
parameters listed below. The hydrophobic regions are calculated once and 
then stored for future use, so the Catalyst parameters have no effect on database 
compounds that have already been created.

Hydrophobic
regions are calculated once and stored in Catalyst
databases. Hydrophobic definitions should be set during
Database construction. During database search and/or
further processing of database hits you should ensure that
the same hydrophobic definitions are used so that the same
fit values are reported.

| Category | Default value of t | Description | Catalyst parameter that controls default value for: t | Catalyst parameter that controls default value for: Number of bonds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | N, O, or H | | |
| 2 | 0 | S in SH | | |
| 3 | 0 | <2 bonds away from charged atom | | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromChargedAtom |
| 4 | 0 | <2 bonds away from OH or NH, no delocalized electrons | | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromOHNH |
| 5 | 0 | <1 bond away from SH, no delocalized electrons | | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromSH |
| 6 | 0 | <2 bonds away from O with double bond | | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromOWithDoubleBond |
| 7 | 0 | <1 bond away from S with valence > 2 | | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromSWithValLargerThanTwo |
| 8 | 0 | S with double bond | | |
| 9 | 0.6 | 3 bonds away from O with double bond | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Atom.factorNNeighborsAwayFromOSS | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromOWithDoubleBond + 1 |
| 10 | 0.6 | 2 bonds away from S with valence >2 | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Atom.factorNNeighborsAwayFromOSS | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Neighbor.numBondLessEqualFromSWithValLargerThanTwo + 1 |
| 11 | 0.6 | 1 bond away from S with double bond | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Atom.factorNNeighborsAwayFromOSS | |
| 12 | 0 | ≥2 instances of any of previous 3 conditions | | |
| 13 | 0.25 | 1 neighboring O or N, no delocalized electrons | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Atom.factorOneNeighboringOOrN | |
| 14 | 0 | >1 neighboring O or N, no delocalized electrons | FunctionMapping.Hydrophobe.Atom.factorTwoOrMoreNeighboringOOrN | |

The hydrophobicity ( h ) of an atom is ts .

Let h min be one half the h value of an exposed methyl carbon terminating a carbon chain. 
We require that each identified hydrophobic group include at least this much hydrophobicity.

Once we have determined h for each atom, we proceed to identify groups of atoms that form a hydrophobic region as follows:

* Define groups for rings of size 7 or less. A group is defined for 
each such ring satisfying the following conditions: The sum of h values for the atoms in 
the ring is at least h min and Either of: All substituents are on one side of the plane of the ring or At least two neighboring (bonded) ring atoms 
must have h > 0. The two neighboring ring atoms must 
not have substituents with more than two heavy atoms attached 
(including the attached ring atom). Therefore, para-methyl cyclohexanol 
has a hydrophobic region on the ring, but para-ethyl cyclohexanol 
does not. Also, ring atoms that have substituents with short 
branches (less than two heavy atoms) are only considered as 
one of the neighboring ring atoms if the substituent atom has 
a hydrophobic value greater than 5. The intent of conditions b.i and b.ii is to ensure that the ring presents 
one large surface rather than two or more small ones. Each group is 
marked by the centroid of the ring's atoms, weighting each atom by its h value. Then all atoms in rings of size 7 and smaller are removed 
from further consideration.

* The sum of h values for the atoms in 
the ring is at least h min and

* Either of: All substituents are on one side of the plane of the ring or At least two neighboring (bonded) ring atoms 
must have h > 0. The two neighboring ring atoms must 
not have substituents with more than two heavy atoms attached 
(including the attached ring atom). Therefore, para-methyl cyclohexanol 
has a hydrophobic region on the ring, but para-ethyl cyclohexanol 
does not. Also, ring atoms that have substituents with short 
branches (less than two heavy atoms) are only considered as 
one of the neighboring ring atoms if the substituent atom has 
a hydrophobic value greater than 5.

* All substituents are on one side of the plane of the ring or

* At least two neighboring (bonded) ring atoms 
must have h > 0. The two neighboring ring atoms must 
not have substituents with more than two heavy atoms attached 
(including the attached ring atom). Therefore, para-methyl cyclohexanol 
has a hydrophobic region on the ring, but para-ethyl cyclohexanol 
does not. Also, ring atoms that have substituents with short 
branches (less than two heavy atoms) are only considered as 
one of the neighboring ring atoms if the substituent atom has 
a hydrophobic value greater than 5.

* Define groups for atoms with three or more bonds. A group is defined 
for each atom with three or more bonds and those of its neighbors that 
are not bonded to any other atom, provided that the sum of the h values for the atoms in 
the group is at least h min . Each group is marked 
by the centroid of the atoms, weighting each atom by its h value. 
Then all atoms with three or more bonds and all their neighbors having 
only one bond are removed from further consideration.

* Divide the remaining atoms into chains. First, all atoms with h = 0 are removed. Any rings that are left can be treated like chains 
by arbitrarily choosing one ring atom to be the start of a chain.

* Define zero or more groups for each chain. Chains are divided into 
contiguous groups such that the sum of h values for the atoms 
in each chain-group is at least h min and less than twice h min . If exactly one atom in the chain-group has 
only one bond, the group is marked by that atom's position. Otherwise 
the group is marked by the weighted centroid of the atoms.

# Pharmacophore generation

Source type: HTML

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_pharm-generation.htm

## Pharmacophore generation

There are several ways to generate pharmacophores in the application
You can:

* Generate a pharmacophore from a set of active ligands using 
the Common Feature Pharmacophore Generation protocol. Optionally,
the algorithm can add excluded volumes to the pharmacophore models 
using information from inactive ligands.

* Generate a predictive pharmacophore from a set of ligands for which
the activity values on a biological target have been measured 
using the 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation protocol. Again, the
algorithm can add excluded volumes to these models based on information
from the inactive ligands in the training set.

* Generate a pharmacophore from a template ligand or ligands using 
the Feature Mapping protocol and the Pharmacophores tools tool.

* Generate a receptor-ligand pharmacophores using the Interaction Pharmacophore Generation protocol.

* Sketch a pharmacophore using the Query toolbar .

The following Help topics discuss theory of these algorithms:

* Pharmacophore features

* Generating common feature pharmacophores

* Generating predictive pharmacophores

* Generating structure-based pharmacophores

* Generating non-bond interaction pharmacophores

# Ligand-Pharmacophore scoring

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_pharm-ligand-scoring.htm

## Ligand-Pharmacophore scoring

A ligand-pharmacophore mapping is done using the following steps:

* A set of mappings between the pharmacophore features
and matching features in the conformations of the molecule is 
calculated. You
can require that all features must map to a corresponding
feature on the ligand or you can consider mappings of a 
subset number of features (controlled by the Maximum Omitted Features parameter. For
example, if this parameter is set to 1 , 
the application considers
mappings of the ligands with N features of the pharmacophore
and N-1 features of an N feature pharmacophore. A value of -1 for this parameter instructs the application to use
all combinations of feature subsets.

* The pharmacophore-ligand mappings are then fitted to
minimize the distance between the pharmacophore features
and the mapped atoms on the ligand. The fitting is done
using the algorithm published by Kabsch [Kabsch, 1978] . There
are three types of fitting methods used in the application - 
Rigid, Flexible, and None. In rigid fitting, the
conformations are held rigid and the best fit is computed
using the Kabsch algorithm. In Flexible fitting, the 
conformations are manipulated within a specified energy 
threshold to minimize the distances between pharmacophore
features and mapped atoms on the molecule. In None, no 
manipulation of the conformation is done and no Kabsch 
fitting is done either. Instead, the fit value between
the pharmacophore and ligand is computed in the current
pose.

* The best fitting mappings with multiple conformations
are optionally returned.

#### Fit value

In comparing a ligand and a pharmacophore, the quality of the mapping is 
indicated by the fit value. A higher fit value represents a better fit; a 
perfect mapping of features would result in a fit value equivalent to the 
sum of the weights of the features in the pharmacophore.

The computed fit value depends on two parameters, the weights W assigned to the 
pharmacophore features φ , and how close the features in the molecule are to the 
centers of the corresponding location constraints in the pharmacophore.

Weights on features indicate the importance of the feature relative to other
features.

The fit value F is computed from the sum of all mapped features as:

where the sum of the square errors SSE for all location constraints c is defined by:

where D is the displacement of the feature from the center of the location constraint, and T is the radius of the location constraint sphere for the feature (tolerance).

The hypothesis and conformation are aligned in such a way that the fit is
maximized (minimize the weighted sum of square displacements).

# Pharmacophore scoring

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_pharm-scoring.htm

## Pharmacophore scoring

In the application, many protocols rely on comparing a set
of ligands to a pharmacophore and determining if there is a match
and how well the pharmacophore fits. The pharmacophore may be
a collection of pharmacophore features , a shape query, a shape and
pharmacophore feature combination query, or a substructure query.
In addition, the pharmacophore may contain excluded volumes that
represent regions of space where the ligand being fitted cannot
occupy. The protocols that compute a ligand-pharmacophore mapping
and fit or a pharmacophore-pharmacophore mapping and fit are:

* Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping

* Pharmacophore Comparison

* Screen Library

* Search 3D Database

# Generating non-bond interaction pharmacophores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_rl-interaction-pharm-gen.htm

## Generating non-bond interaction pharmacophores

The Interaction Pharmacophore Generation protocol generates selective pharmacophore models based on non-bond receptor-ligand interactions. 
The procedure is summarized as follows:

* Enumerate non-bond interactions between the receptor and ligand

* Place a corresponding pharmacophore feature on the ligand for each non-bond interaction

* All possible pharmacophore combinations are enumerated

* Use a GFA model to select candidates

* Add Excluded volumes or shape constraints

All selected non-bond interactions are enumerated between the receptor and the ligand. There are many possible interactions that can be enumerated. The high level categories include:

* Hydrogen Bonds

* Electrostatic

* Hydrophobic

* Halogen

* Miscellaneous

The following pharmacophore features corresponding to the non-bond interaction are placed on the appropriate position of the ligand.

| Non-bond Type | Pharmacophore Feature Type |
| --- | --- |
| Conventional Hydrogen Bond | iHBD, iHBA |
| Carbon Hydrogen Bond | iHBD_carbon |
| Pi Donor Hydrogen Bond | iHBD, HYDROPHOBE_aromatic |
| Salt Bridge | iHBD_SB, iHBA_SB |
| Attractive Charges | POS_IONIZABLE, NEG_IONIZABLE |
| Pi-Cation | HYDROPHOBE_aromatic, POS_IONIZABLE |
| Pi-Anion | HYDROPHOBE_aromatic, NEG_IONIZABLE |
| Pi-Pi Stacked | iRINGAROMATIC |
| Pi-Pi T-Shaped | HYDROPHOBE_aromatic |
| Amide Pi Stacked | HYDROPHOBE_aromatic, iAmide |
| Alkyl | HYDROPHOBE |
| Pi-Sigma | iSigma_C_INT,iRINGAROMATIC |
| Pi-Alkyl | iRINGAROMATIC,HYDROPHOBE |
| Halogen (Fluorine) | iFluorine_INT |
| Halogen (Cl, Br, I) | iHalogen_INT |
| Metal-Acceptor | iHBA |
| Sulfur-X | iSulfur_INT, iNOS |
| Pi-Sulfur | iSulfur_INT, HYDROPHOBE_Aromatic |
| Pi-Lone Pair | iHBA, HYDROPHOBE_Aromatic |

The basic goal of building a pharmacophore model is to search for multiple ligands that can bind to the same receptor. Therefore, the model should be sensitive enough to find potential novel 
ligands that can bind to the protein. However, it needs to be selective so that the false positive candidates are avoided.

These two factors usually conflict, so a trade-off is made. The first control for such a trade-off is to constrain the number of features in the pharmacophores. 
A good starting point for the number of pharmacophore features is four to six. If the total of matching features for a protein complex is much greater than the minimum number specified, then there may be too many candidates. 
The most selected candidates from the large pool should be used, which is done by using a well trained GFA model .

The GFA model for predicting the selectivity of a pharmacophore is built from a training set of 1544 pharmacophore models, each with two to eight features. This set is used for searching a database of 5384 diverse, druglike molecules. 
The logarithmic values of the number of database search hits are used as the targets. The following log values are used for zero hits based on the number of features:

* Two to five features: log(0.3)

* Six features: log(0.1)

* Seven Features: log(0.03)

* Eight features: log(0.01)

The number of total features in the pharmacophore models and the feature-feature distance bin values are used as the descriptors for training the GFA model.

The GFA model has excellent prediction for selectivity.

By default, residue atoms 4.1 to 5.0 Å from the ligand are used to place excluded volumes. Only the heavy atoms are used. 
The excluded volumes are placed at the centroid of the atoms and the size are proportional to the number of atoms. 
Optionally, shape constraints of the ligand is added to the pharmacophores instead of excluded volumes.

# Generating structure-based pharmacophores

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_sbpharm.htm

## Generating structure-based pharmacophores

In the application, structure-based pharmacophores are generated using the
following steps:

* Define a binding or active site in a protein.

* Generate an Interaction Map and represent it using Hydrogen Bond Donors
and Acceptors and Hydrophobic pharmacophore features .

* Optionally, add excluded volumes using the locations of protein atoms
near the binding or active site.

* Optionally, cluster the pharmacophore and excluded volume features.
The hierarchical clustering method [Hartigan, 1975] used is the UPGMA algorithm
(Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic mean), a variation of
the Average Linkage method. The distances are computed between each
feature to calculate the clusters. In the case of the Hydrogen Bond
Donors and Acceptors, the heavy atom location of the feature is used
when computing the distances.

* Screen a set of ligands using the pharmacophore information. The
Screen Library protocol randomly selects a subset of pharmacophores
(set by the Maximum Subset of Pharmacophores parameter) from all
possible combinations of pharmacophores with a minimum number of
features set by the Minimum Features parameter and a maximum
number of features set by the Maximum Features parameter. The ligands
are screened against this subset of pharmacophores.

Pharmacophores tools Theory - Pharmacophore

# Shape scoring

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/phcp_the_shape-ligand-scoring.htm

## Shape scoring

In this application, a shape query is defined by a set of 3D coordinates, each
with a corresponding radius. Typically, these points are the centers of atoms
in a template molecule, and the radius associated with each point depends on 
the atom type. Shapes can be constructed automatically from a single conformation
of a molecule, or from a set of aligned molecules using the Query toolbar .

Shape matching is performed by shape similarity, where a shape query defines a volume in space that is the union of a set of spheres.
During a search, each candidate conformation is converted to a similar volume. By default, conformations that have 0.7 to 1.3 times the length of the shape query on the x-axis, y-axis, z-axis, and 0.7 to 1.3 of the total volume are considered for the more computationally expensive mapping phase. During the mapping, the two volumes are aligned, and their intersection and union are approximated. The similarity of the shape query to the molecule is computed as the volume
of the intersection divided by the volume of the union of the aligned shapes.

Depending on the similarity tolerance, a hit may have more or less
volume that protrudes from the shape. Use the Minimum Similarity Tolerance and Maximum Similarity Tolerance attributes to control which values of the shape similarity returns a hit. The Minimum and Maximum Extents Ratio attributes for X, Y, Z, and Volume determine which conformation candidates are considered for mapping. The Extents attributes are used to quickly find reasonable initial candidates, and not perform the more expensive mapping process to shapes that are furthest out of bounds. You can view and edit these attributes in the ShapeFeature tab of the Data Table, or in the Attributes dialog .

A shape in a mixed pharmacophore that contains pharmacophore features and
a shape component is processed differently from a shape-only query.
In a shape-only query, the shape is aligned to each candidate
compound, the similarity is computed, and if the similarity tolerance is
satisfied, the candidate is considered a hit. The shape in a mixed
query is also aligned to the candidate compound, and the tolerance is tested.
Furthermore, the transformation used to align the location constraints
to the molecule is applied to the shape. Then, the similarity of
the shape to the molecule is computed without further alignment.
If this similarity value satisfies the tolerance, the candidate is considered a hit.

A hit from a mixed query search can be interpreted as a molecule
that:

* Satisfies the feature-only query.

* Has similarity to the shape greater than the specified tolerance.

* Satisfies the shape similarity tolerance when the orientation of the shape is fixed relative to the location constraints.

Pharmacophores tools Theory - Pharmacophore

# Work with 3D fingerprints

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/tsk_3d-fingerprints.htm

## Work with 3D fingerprints

This topic covers the following aspects of 3D fingerprints created using the Create 3D Fingerprints protocol:

* Advantages of 3D fingerprints

* Adjust parameters in 3D Fingerprint protocol

* Considering space and time when generating 3D fingerprints

* Select pharmacophore features in 3D fingerprint generation

* Set the bin size tolerance

* Supported bin schemes for the 3D Fingerprint protocol

* Use and apply generated 3D fingerprints

To achieve optimal intermolecular interactions with a specific biological target
and change its biological process, a drug molecule must have a set of steric and electronic features
in a specific 3D configuration. 3D fingerprints analyze 3D pharmacophore features and their relative 3D locations,
and code this information into bins. The bin values can be used to significantly speed up pharmacophore
searches (this information is automatically stored in databases created by the Build 3D Database
protocol), to perform similarity comparisons, or to measure pharmacophore diversity.

### Adjust parameters in the Create 3D Fingerprints protocol

When creating 3D pharmacophore fingerprints, all three point pharmacophore
features are enumerated, placed in a grid in a canonical manner,
then an integer value is computed that represents the three point pharmacophore.
This value is known as the "on bit" for that pharmacophore.
A fingerprint is all the "on bits" for that molecule.
A similar method is used for the four point pharmacophores as well.

It is possible to control how the grid is generated by modifying the bins.
You can change the bin size, the bin tolerance, and the bin scheme in the Create 3D Fingerprints protocol.
Here are some general suggestions when changing these value:

* If the bin size is increased for a single conformer molecule, try increasing the tolerance .

* For a molecule with multiple conformers (~100 conformers for example),
set tolerance to zero in order to reduce the size of the 3D fingerprints.

* Use the exact same parameters for all molecules in a study.

Two parameters have significant impact on the fingerprint size and the
computation time for generating it. Using a small bin size for flexible
molecules with a large number of conformations will significantly increase
the number of unique fingerprints. You can increase the bin size to reduce
the number of fingerprints. However, using a bin size that is too large can reduce the
information in the fingerprints. Increasing the bin size tolerance can also increase
the number of fingerprints. For example, if you set the bin size tolerance
equal to the bin size, there could be up to eight times more fingerprints than when not using a tolerance.

Use the following rule of thumb when selecting features: Only select features that are relevant to the problem under
investigation. Unrelated features add considerable noise to the QSAR study.
Vector features such as hydrogen bond donors have two points, a head and a tail. By default, the heads
are selected in 3D fingerprint generation. You can optionally use the projection points.

The bin size tolerance is used to reduce the "edge" effects in 3D
fingerprint generation. Edge effects occur when two very close distances
fall into different bins. This can lead to two different fingerprints for
two very similar 3D configurations. Increasing the Tolerance improves the overlap.
However, increasing bin size tolerance can significantly increase the size of fingerprints,
which does not necessarily add useful information. The general guideline is:
for small or rigid molecules, set a bin size tolerance close to the bin size.
For molecules with conformation models, especially when a molecule has a large number
of conformations, set bin size tolerance to zero. An obvious reason is that the conformations
already include the variation of feature locations.

There are two bin schemes that can be used when creating fingerprints, Uniform and User Specified . User Specified provides full flexibility
for bin specification. The size of each bin can be separately adjusted.

Fingerprints can be used in pharmacophore similarity search. For instance,
you can convert a 3D pharmacophore into a set of fingerprints as a
reference, and then use the same 3D fingerprint coding setting to generate
the fingerprints for a set of ligands. After that, you can perform a similarity search
for the ligand set using the pharmacophore fingerprints as the reference.
You can also use the fingerprints of one molecule as a reference, and search
for the molecules with similar pharmacophore configurations using the Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints protocol.

Create 3D Fingerprints

# Work with the Catalyst database

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/tsk_catalyst-database.htm

## Work with the Catalyst database

Catalyst databases are located in the /public/DS/CatalystDB directory of the Pipeline Pilot installation. The 
databases can be accessed using the following protocols:

* Search 3D Database

* Browse 3D Database

* Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping

* Create 3D Fingerprints

* Ligand Profiler

* Screen Library

All databases stored in this location are available by protocols containing
the Input Database parameter. Click the dropdown arrow on the Input Database parameter to display the list. Four databases are provided with Discovery Studio - DruglikeDiverse , MiniMaybridge , Sample , and scPDB . Additionally, any databases created by the Build 3D Database protocol are automatically copied to this location.

To install an existing database

* Create a directory in the /public/DS/CatalystDB area of the Pipeline Pilot installation with the same 
base name as the .bdb file for this database (e.g., create a Sample directory for Sample.bdb ).

* Place the .bdb file in this directory (for example., copy Sample.bdb to this directory).

* In the .bdb file, change the host to localhost , and change the paths to the correct locations 
of the 0bdb , 2bdb , 3bdb , and 4bdb files.

The files must be on a disk that is accessible by the host running Pipeline Pilot . Make
sure that the Pipeline Pilot service is started by a user who is logged in with read access to the database files. Typically, the Pipeline Pilot Server Linux
server will run as the user account that installed the Pipeline Pilot Server . For a Windows server, Pipeline Pilot is running as the
local system account by default.

To change the user account

* On the Windows machine where the Pipeline Pilot Server is installed, open the Control Panel , select Administrative Tools , and select Component Services .

* Open Services (Local) .

* Right-click Pipeline Pilot Service 26.1.0 and choose Stop .

* Right-click again and choose Properties .

* Open the Log On tab and select This Account .

* Enter the user name and password.

* Click OK to close the dialog.

* Right-click the service and choose Start .

See How to stop and restart the Pipeline Pilot Server for more information.

### SPST files

Optionally, create an .spst file that contains the 1D data. The .spst file can be split into several .spst files. These files can be compressed with gzip or winzip to save disk space. They are required to be in the same directory 
of the database or a subdirectory called spst_files . No change is required for the .spst files shipped with the commercial 
databases. Copy the spst_files directory to the database location. Searches through the application join the 1D data from the .spst file(s) with the exported hit lists.

# Create custom features from SMARTS

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/tsk_create_features_from_smarts.htm

## Create custom features from SMARTS

To create a custom pharmacophore feature from SMARTS:

* In a text editor, create a tab-delimited file representing the SMARTS pattern and name that defines the groups of the pharmacophore feature. Each row in the file represents a separate group of the pharmacpohore feature.

* Open the Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features tools and click Create Features from SMARTS... to open the protocol.

* Copy the contents of the file and paste to the SMARTS parameter.

* Click Run .
The protocol creates a substructure query for each group in the tab-delimited file.

* Inspect the charges, atoms types, and bond types of each substructure query to ensure that the SMARTS definition produced the desired substructure. Make needed modifications using the Query Atom Specification... or the Query Bond Specification... commands in the Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features tools.

* To combine the substructure queries into a single pharmacophore feature, open the Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features tools and select all the queries and click Map ANY Selected . This combines them to a single query using an OR operator.

* For each substructure in turn, use the hierarchy view to select one or more atoms that will define the mapping point of the pharmacophore feature. With the appropriate atoms selected, use the Pharmacophores | Create Pharmacophore Manually | Query Features... command to create a centroid for each group.

* Select all the centroids and click Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features | Create Mapping... command to create a pharmacophoric point (Feature Map) to which all the centroids are connected by the OR operator.

* Save the pharmacophoric point in the dictionary using Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features | Add Feature To Dictionary .

# Customize features

Source type: HTML

Source section: tspharmacophores

Source file: tspharmacophores/tsk_customizing-features.htm

## Customize features

Customized pharmacophore features are represented by objects organized in a hierarchy. The basic structure of this hierarchy is the same for 
isolated custom features and queries assembled from several custom features. A top-level query object represents the custom feature or query. The 
query object contains a hierarchy of query operator objects that represent the query logic. A valid query contains a single top-level ("root") 
query operator. The query operator objects in turn contain objects that represent the query features, such as atoms, point features, or location 
features.

The following is covered in this topic:

* Query Logic

* Substructure Queries

* Query attributes for atoms and bonds

* 3D Queries

Each query operator has a Query Logic attribute that reports the role of the operator within the query. The following are possible values of this attribute:

* And: Indicates that all features that follow will match.

* Or: Indicates that one of the features 
that follows will match.

* Exclude: Either defines a feature that should not be matched, or a general feature
that should be matched, but with special features that should not be matched. For example, if the general feature to be matched is a six-membered
ring, the special feature could be a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring. You will need to exclude all possible mappings.

You will need to exclude all possible mappings.

* Fit: Used with queries that employ location and/or exclusion features to specify spatial constraints
that matching structures have to satisfy. In general, fit operators are top-level operators (i.e., they are not part of another query operator).

* Shape: Used with shape features. If a query includes a shape feature, the shape feature is contained in a Shape operator.

* Include: Provides a simplified representation of a standard feature defined in the Catalyst
feature dictionary, such as a hydrogen bond acceptor, hydrogen bond donor, positive ionizable, or negative ionizable feature.

A simple substructure query that requires matching a single fragment is represented as follows:

A substructure query that requires matching two fragments ("match all") is represented as follows:

A substructure query that requires at least one of two fragments to match ("match any") is represented as follows:

A substructure query that requires one fragment to be matched and a second fragment to not be matched without dependencies between the two fragments, is represented as follows:

A substructure query that requires one fragment to be matched, requires a second fragment to not be matched, and requires the second
fragment to share a common substructure with the first fragment is represented as follows:

In this case, it is necessary to define associations or mappings between atoms and bonds of the two fragments in order to specify the common 
substructure between the two fragments. Otherwise, the query is not valid.

To create the mapping, select the atoms that should correspond to each other, open the Pharmacophores | Customize Pharmacophore Features tools, and then click Create Mapping . The mapping is stored in a Feature Map object attached to the Exclude query 
operator.

For substructure queries, it is possible to specify query attributes for atoms and bonds. Atom query attributes are specified in a QueryAtom object attached to the atom. Bond query attributes are specified in a QueryBond object 
attached to the bond. The object hierarchy for a simple single substructure query has the general form:

The complete query hierarchy is shown in the Hierarchy View of the Molecule Window. Query operators have no 3D representation in the Graphics View.

3D queries require the specification of 3D objects and their association with the underlying chemical structure. A 3D query contains one or more 
3D query features as subqueries. A 3D query feature contains specifications of 2D substructures and the mapping of that substructure to 3D objects 
such as points, vectors, and planes. These generic 3D objects are represented by PointFeature , VectorFeature , and PlaneFeature objects.

You can create the mapping by selecting the objects that should be mapped, and clicking Create Mapping in the Customize Pharmacophore Features tool panel. A 3D object is created if it doesn't exist. The mapping between the objects is stored in a Feature Map object attached to the 3D object.

For example, the Catalyst feature dictionary contains a standard hydrogen bond acceptor feature, HB_ACCEPTOR, and a standard hydrogen bond donor feature, HB_DONOR. Importing both features into a new Molecule Window by clicking Add Feature From Dictionary in the Customize Pharmacophore Feature tool panel will result in the following hierarchy displayed in the Hierarchy View:

The hydrogen bond acceptor feature (under Query HB_ACCEPTOR) defines three 3D objects to be mapped: an atom (the acceptor atom which defines the position of the tail of the 3D vector), a point that defines the position of the head of the 3D vector, and a 3D vector. Each of the three objects contains a Feature Map object that stores the mapping information.

Similarly, the hydrogen bond donor feature (under Query HB_DONOR) defines three 3D objects to be mapped: the donor atom, the head point of a 3D 
vector, and the 3D vector.

To combine these two features into a single feature that maps to either the acceptor or the donor feature, perform the following steps:

* Select the HBA query operator under the HB_ACCEPTOR query.

* Select the HBD query operator under the HB_DONOR query.

* Click Map ANY Selected in the Customize Pharmacophore Feature tool panel. This moves the HBA and HBD query operators under an "OR" query
operator.

* Select the vector named AcceptorVector from the hydrogen bond acceptor feature and the vector named DonorVector from the hydrogen bond donor feature.

* Click Create Mapping . This creates a mapped vector under the top-level query operator, and 
relates it to the hydrogen bond acceptor and donor vectors. It also maps the heads and tails of the vectors.

The end result of these steps is a single custom feature that exposes an atom, a point, and a vector as 3D objects for mapping in 3D queries.
