# Define and Edit Binding Site tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/anly_bdst.htm

## Define and Edit Binding Site tools

The Binding Site tools allow you to identify,
edit, and display binding sites of a receptor.

Define Receptor: The current receptor is displayed at the top of the panel. If no
receptor has been defined, the first visible molecule will be used as
the receptor. You can change the current receptor by clicking this
with the receptor molecule visible and selected.

For later calculations, receptors should have hydrogens and complete valence shells so that they
can be atom typed .
They also cannot have alternate conformations . The Data Table functionality depends on the
receptor being defined, including receptor-ligand hydrogen bonds.
For further information, see Define a receptor .

### Define Site

These tools allow you to identify sites within the
receptor by several methods.

From Receptor Cavities: Derives binding sites from cavities in the structure of the receptor. The first binding site found is displayed as a set of points and a transparent red sphere. If there is a ligand chain within the receptor molecule, the binding site cavity will likely not be detected. For further information, see Site finding and Reparenting .

This method will create binding sites as well as spheres. The volume is calculated as one of the attributes of a binding site. You can view the volume in the BindingSite tab of the table, or in the Attributes dialog . The volume is defined as the product of number of site points and the cube of the
grid spacing. The grid spacing and the minimum site volume can
be adjusted in the Define and Edit Binding Site page - Preferences dialog .

From PDB Site Records: PDB files often have active sites defined using SITE records. When
a PDB file is imported, groups are created for each SITE. This tool
highlights each site with a transparent red sphere.

From Current Selection: Creates a sphere around the centroid of selected objects (e.g., atoms or binding site points) with the radius
adjusted to include them. If a receptor is not defined,
the selected molecule is used. Note that the minimum radius is 5 Å.

### Change Site Size

+ Expand: Increase the sphere radius by 1 Å.

- Contract: Decrease the sphere radius by 1 Å.

For binding sites created from the cavity search method, Expand and Contract have a different
function.
These tools are applied to selected site
points, or to the entire site if no site points are selected.
Contract will remove the outermost layer of site points if they do not neighbor the receptor. Expand adds a layer of site points
to the points not neighboring the receptor.

### Display

These navigation tools allow you to step through the sites in the
current window.

Show First Site: Displays the first site of the first
molecule.

Show Previous Site: Display the previous site in
the hierarchy.

Show Next Site: Display the next site in the
hierarchy.

Show/Hide Site Spheres: Displays or hides selected site spheres. This action applies to all spheres if none are selected.

Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres: Displays or hides residues of the receptor that do not fall within
selected spheres. This action applies to all spheres if none are selected.

Discovery Studio uses the following criteria to determine if a group of atoms is a ligand when 
a molecule is imported. A ligand group contains atoms that:

* are not in an amino or nucleic acid chain

* are not in a water chain

* are in a chain or residues

* are bonded to each other

* satisfy the criteria defined by the ligand definition preferences

# Dock Ligands tools

Source type: HTML

## Dock Ligands tools

The Dock Ligands tools allow you to simulate the docking of ligands into a protein receptor binding site. In addition, several scoring functions are available for evaluating docked poses.

### High-Throughput Screening

Dock Ligands (LibDock): Opens the Dock Ligands (LibDock) protocol dialog. This protocol performs a high-throughput docking by aligning ligand conformations to polar and apolar receptor interaction sites (hotspots). Conformations can be pre-calculated or generated on the fly using Catalyst.
Since some of the output poses may have hydrogen atoms in close proximity to the receptor, a CHARMm minimization step can be enabled to optimize the docked poses further (increases CPU time).

Dock Ligands (GOLD): Opens the Dock Ligands (GOLD) protocol dialog. This protocol docks ligand using the GOLD (Genetic Optimization for Ligand Docking) program, which uses a genetic algorithm for docking flexible ligands into receptor binding sites.

### Docking Optimization

Dock Ligands (CDOCKER): Opens the Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) protocol dialog. This protocol performs the following steps to dock and refine ligands:

* Ligands are docked into an active site using a CHARMm-based molecular dynamics (MD) scheme.

* Random ligand conformations are generated using high-temperature MD.

* The conformations are translated into the binding site.

* Candidate poses are created using random rigid-body rotations followed by simulated annealing.

* Minimization is performed to refine the docked ligand poses.

In Situ Ligand Minimization: Opens the In Situ Ligand Minimization protocol dialog. This protocol minimizes ligands in the presence of a rigid or flexible receptor using CHARMm.

### Scoring

Score Ligand Poses: Opens the Score Ligand Poses protocol dialog. This protocol scores ligand poses using a series of scoring functions. The range of scoring functions includes:

* CDOCKER Scores

* LigScore1 and LigScore2

* PLP1 and PLP2

* Jain

* PMF and PMF04

* Ludi scores (1,2,3)

* Goldscore *

* Chemscore *

* ASP *

* CHEMPLP *

Scoring functions with a * require a valid GOLD installation and license .

Calculate Binding Energies: Opens the Calculate Binding Energies protocol dialog. This protocol estimates the binding energy between a receptor and a ligand. Optionally, you can calculate the average binding energy across a set of related poses. In addition, you can calculate the loss of conformational entropy and energy of a bound ligand.

### Interaction Filters

Define Interaction Site: Defines interaction sites from selected atoms. The sites are represented as colored spheres. See General receptor-ligand interactions tasks | Define an interaction site .

# Specify control ligands

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_fsd_hw_specify_control_ligands.htm

## Specify control ligands

Some protocols allow you to specify a set of ligands that are known to be active, and 
therefore can be used as controls. You can remove this control information if it is already present.

In virtual screening protocols, including a set of potent inhibitors, if known, 
as control ligands can be useful for the following reasons:

* The correct docking and scoring of candidate control ligands helps to confirm 
that the docking and scoring methodologies and parameters are appropriate for the target receptor.

* The identification of hit ligands among the (random) input ligands is aided by 
the ranking of suitable control ligands. Including control ligands allows you to visualize 
enrichment rates using tools such as Hit Rate Plots and ROC plots .

You can modify the behavior of the control ligands from the Parameter Explorer as follows:

* In addition to the Input Ligands , you can specify a set of Input Control Ligands . These
ligands will have a new property added with the name specified by the Input Control Ligand Property parameter. This
property is set to 1 for the control ligands to distinguish them from the non-control ligands in the data set. The
control ligands will then be merged into the regular input ligands so that the total number of ligands to run through the job is the sum of the
number in the two input data sets. You specify the control ligands in the same way as specifying the input ligands, using Specify Ligands .

* By setting the Input Preserve Controls In Input parameter to False , all ligands in the Input Ligands set will have the property specified by the Input Control Ligand Property parameter removed.

* The Input Control Ligand Property parameter specifies the name of the property to use for the control ligands. A 
property by this name is added to the control ligands and may be removed from the regular input ligands if you do not wish to preserve controls.

The De Novo Link protocol suggests modifications to a ligand scaffold 
to increase binding by placing fragments into the binding site. Upon completion, 
the protocol does not actually create the ligand-fragment bond(s). It simply positions 
the fragment in such a way as to take advantage of nearby interaction 
sites (that is, sites for hydrogen bond formation and hydrophobic interaction) while 
simultaneously aligning the fragment to a ligand link site.

To fuse the ligand scaffold and fragments, delete the extraneous atoms and use commands 
in the Sketching toolbar to create 
the necessary bonds.

# CDOCKER

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_cdocker.htm

## CDOCKER

CDOCKER is an implementation of a CHARMm based docking tool using a rigid receptor ( Wu et al. 2003 ). 
The following steps are included in the CDOCKER protocol:

* A set of ligand conformations are generated using high-temperature molecular dynamics with different random seeds. This step can be skipped to
dock the input conformation(s) only.

* Random orientations of the conformations are produced by translating the center of the ligand to a specified location within the receptor active
site, and performing a series of random rotations. A softened energy is calculated and the orientation is kept if the energy is less than a 
specified threshold. This process continues until either the desired number of low-energy orientations is found, or the maximum number of bad
orientations have been tried. This step can be skipped to use the input orientation only.

* Each orientation is subjected to simulated annealing molecular dynamics. The temperature is heated up to a high temperature then cooled to the 
target temperature.

* A final minimization of the ligand in the rigid receptor using non-softened potential is performed.

* For each final pose, the CHARMm energy (interaction energy plus ligand strain) and the interaction energy alone are calculated. The poses are
sorted by CHARMm energy and the top scoring (most negative, thus favorable to binding) poses are retained.

For performance, many of these steps use a nonbond energy grid, rather than the full potential energy terms usually used by CHARMm. This provides a 
significant time saving at the cost of some accuracy. You can specify whether to use a grid or full potential for the simulation and minimization steps.

Although the CHARMm forcefield is usually used, cff may also be used. However that forcefield was not used in any validation studies.

#### Further information

Theory - Receptor-Ligand Interactions

DOCUMENT 2773
==============================================================================================================

# Docking

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_docking.htm

## Docking

Docking small molecules (ligands) into larger protein molecules (receptors) is a complex and difficult task. This application contains several protocols to help with docking. The docking algorithms include CDOCKER, LibDock, and MCSS.

Docking is often approximated to a Lock and Key process where the conformation of a ligand and receptor do not change during binding. This is the simplest to simulate, but is generally thought to be unreasonable. Ligands are often flexible and occupy multiple conformations in solution. Furthermore, although the conformations of receptors are more well defined, they too can change, particularly on ligand binding in the so called Induced Fit model.

Most Docking routines can be run in a completely rigid mode, where a single conformation of the receptor and the ligand is used. This mode is of little use other than validating docking approaches. The most common approximation for docking is to hold the protein in a rigid conformation and dock a series of ligand conformations into the active site. The majority of the docking protocols work in this way.

You can also perform Flexible Docking, which allows for the optimization of a selected set of side-chains during flexible ligand docking. You may also specify pregenerated receptor conformations that include side-chain and backbone flexibility. Although this is a more realistic approach, flexible docking generally takes more CPU time and generates more data than rigid docking protocols.

### Docking Theory

The following docking theory topics are available:

* CDOCKER - Uses a random initial ligand placement and full CHARMm forcefield based docking

* LibDock - Fast docking based on binding site features ("hotspots")

* MCSS - Uses CHARMm to dock fragments using a unique computationally efficient Multiple Copy Simultaneous Search algorithm

#### Further information

Theory - Receptor-Ligand Interactions

# Fragment fitting

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_fragment-fitting.htm

## Fragment fitting

After generating interaction sites, the next step is to fit fragments
onto the interaction sites. Ludi searches the list of interaction sites
by distance criteria for suitable sets containing 2 to 6 sites to match
the fragments. The distance criterion used for selecting suitable interaction
sites is based upon the distances between the interaction sites i and j , R ij .
If these values fall within a specified range, a fit of the fragment
is performed.

The default range is calculated from the optimum value R opt using the following expressions:

Equation 1:

and

Equation 2:

The typical value of (Δ R ) max is 0.2 Å- 0.6 Å.

For example, if three aromatic interaction sites i , j , and k are found with suitable values for R ij , R ik , and R jk , 
then three atoms of a lipophilic fragment (e.g., atoms 1, 3, and 5 of a phenyl group) are fitted onto these three points.

Required interactions may be specified using target atoms of the receptor. Any fragment fit that does not interact with the entire set 
of specified target atoms is rejected.

To fit the fragment, Ludi performs a root mean square (RMS) superposition using the algorithm published by Kabsch [Kabsch, 1978] . A fragment fit is accepted if the RMS value is less than a user-defined threshold 
(typically 0.2 Å to 0.6 Å, but for fitting of large fragments, the RMS is allowed to exceed the value of the threshold), and 
there is no van der Waals overlap of the fitted fragment with the protein, and, optionally, no unacceptable electrostatic repulsions are 
found. When the receptor structure is not known, a fragment fit is accepted only if the fragment remains inside the union volume defined 
by the set of active analogs. When run in link mode, no van der Waals overlap of the fitted fragments with the scaffold ligand is allowed 
except at the link site.

Searching of fragment conformations may be performed by suitable choice of the parameter controlling bond rotation. Conformational 
searching may be done either one rotatable bond at a time, with all other torsion angles remaining at the starting reference value, or 
two rotatable bonds at a time, depending on the setting of the parameter.

The increment used for rotating torsions depends on the ideal periodicity of the dihedral angle, which is determined from the hybridization 
of the two central atoms. For example, for a rotatable bond between 2 sp 3 carbons, the periodicity is 3, and 
the rotation is done in 120° increments. For a rotatable bond between 2 sp 2 carbons, the periodicity is 2, 
and the rotation is done in 180° increments.

# Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_grow-scaffold.htm

## Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration

The goal of lead optimization in drug discovery is to take promising compounds and scaffolds and make chemical modifications to improve biological potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters, bioavailability, and decrease toxicity. Computational tools for lead optimization can propose synthetically feasible candidates from a reagent library representing accessible chemistry, focused on the protein target.

The Grow Scaffold protocol uses a reaction-based in situ enumeration approach to identify and prioritize which reagents are most likely to produce potential active compounds for the receptor binding site. Reaction-based enumerations are derived from a reaction scheme (e.g., Figure 1) and the corresponding reagent libraries.

Figure 1: A reaction scheme for an amide formation.

In Grow Scaffold, the implementation of the reaction scheme to the scaffold is made by considering the reaction in two halves: the scaffold reacts with an amine reagent (Figure 2), and the scaffold reacts with an acid reagent (Figure 3). The advantage of this implementation is that a generic scaffold can be used with both types of reagents in a single enumeration. You can specify one or more single-bonded atoms as grow points on the scaffold, which serve as reaction points for the enumeration.

Figure 2: The reaction of the scaffold with an amine reagent.

Figure 3: The reaction of the scaffold with an acid reagent:

Grow Scaffold identifies the reagent fragments that can be enumerated with the scaffold within the receptor binding site. 
Reagents fragments are linked to the scaffold site by sampling the torsion angle of the link bond between the fragment and the scaffold to identify positions that are most compatible with the binding site. In addition, you can specify residues on the protein that are required to form interactions with the linked fragments. The sampling space can be explored further by enabling reagent-fragment conformations. Optionally, each ligand can be minimized in the presence of the receptor, with optional protein flexibility and implicit solvation. An outline of the algorithm is shown in Figure 4.

Figure 4: Workflow of the Grow Scaffold protocol.

The enumerated ligands are ranked using a Pareto analysis where the number of interactions formed with the protein and fragment "novelty" are maximized and Lipinski violations and receptor bumps are minimized. In addition, ligand-protein interactions are calculated, including protein residues, interaction types, and interaction distances.

Using the residue interaction filter during the enumeration, with a post in situ ligands minimization step, may result in residue-interaction changes.

### Reactions and Reagents

Discovery Studio includes several common reaction schemes and corresponding example reagent libraries. The example reagent libraries were created using a diverse sampling of the DiscoveryGate chemical database. Reagents are filtered by physico-chemical profiles and undesirable functional groups. In addition, the reagents must be available from at least two vendors. In general, each library contains around 1000 diverse entries.

| Default Reaction | Corresponding Reagent Libraries |
| --- | --- |
| Amide Synthesis | Amines, Acids |
| Esterification | Alcohols, Acids |
| Kumada Coupling | Halides, Organosilanes |
| Kumada Coupling | Halides, Grignard Reagents |
| Negishi Coupling | Halides, Organozinc Halides |
| Stille Coupling | Halides, Organotins |
| Suzuki Coupling | Halides, Boronic Acids |
| Williamson Ether Synthesis | Halides, Alcohols |

Reaction schemes represent single reactions. Multiple cascading reactions are not supported.

You can use your own custom reagent libraries instead of the example reagent libraries. They may include mixed reagents (for example, a library containing both amine and acid reagents) as the reaction scheme identifies only those reagents which can be used for a particular enumeration. Appropriate reagents are identified by having the common substructure defined in the reaction scheme. Please note that some reagents may contain more than one instance of this substructure. For example, the reagent may have two amine substituents and thus two enumerated products may be possible from this single reagent.

You can also specify your own custom reaction schemes, but they must be used with custom reagent libraries. Custom reaction schemes can be defined using the RXN or SMIRKS formats, and need to be written as half-reactions, with one reactant and product. For RXN files, atom-atom mapping is required as this specifies which reactant atom becomes which product atom through the reaction. An example of two half-reactions with atom-atom mapping is shown in Figure 5.

Figure 5: The two half reactions that define the complete amide synthesis reaction scheme.

The first half-reaction shows a reaction of carboxylic acid reagents to fragments that can form an amide bond to the scaffold grow point. The single bonded oxygen of the carboxylic acid is transformed to an amide bond with an X-atom to indicate the link with the scaffold. X and Z symbols are used for RXN and SMIRKS files, respectively, to represent the scaffold. The two reactions in Figure 5 can be used to define the complete amide synthesis reaction scheme in Figure 1.

An advantage of half-reactions is that they can be used individually, or together to define the complete reaction scheme. If you are using a mixed reagent library (e.g., a library containing both amine and acid reagents) the use of only the amine half-reaction of the amide synthesis would allow you to extract solely those reagents with amine substituents for the enumeration.

You can have your own reactions and SD files to appear as parameter options by copying them to the installation folder. For information see Grow Scaffold - Parameters .

When creating a custom RXN file, ensure that the reaction drawn consists of a single reaction, not multiple cascade reactions.

# Hydrophobic contacts rules

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_hydrophobic-contacts-rules.htm

## Hydrophobic contacts rules

Ludi is capable of distinguishing between aliphatic and aromatic interaction
sites to allow for some flexibility in the subsequent fragment fitting.

It has been argued by
Burley and Petsko [Burley and Petsko, 1986] that interactions between aromatic systems play a significant role in
the packing of a protein. As benzene has a large quadrupole moment, 2.9×10 -10 C
m 2 [Battaglia et al., 1981] ,
one might anticipate that quadrupole-quadrupole interactions contribute
significantly to the binding of a ligand to its protein. It is clear,
however, that aliphatic and aromatic side-chains pack closely together
to form the hydrophobic core of proteins. Thus, to account for hydrophobic
pockets, it may be advisable not to distinguish between aliphatic and
aromatic interactions sites. Ludi allows you to proceed in both ways.

When considering aliphatic and aromatic interaction sites, the following rules apply. If the ligand atom is an aliphatic carbon, then 
aliphatic interaction sites L ali are generated with R C..L = 4 Å. A user-defined number of interaction sites are 
positioned roughly equally spaced on a sphere around each aliphatic carbon atom.

If the ligand atom is an aromatic carbon, then aromatic binding sites L aro are generated with 
R C..L = 4 Å using the same algorithm as for aliphatic carbons. Additional binding sites are 
generated with R C..L = 6 Å above and below the plane of the aromatic rings.
(This was found to be necessary to allow for perpendicular arrangements of aromatic rings.)

The aromatic interaction sites L aro in amide groups are positioned 4 Å above and below the plane 
of the planar amide group. The aromatic interaction sites L aro of sulfur are generated with 
R S..L = 4.8 Å using the same algorithm as for the rules for aliphatic and aromatic carbons. The rules for amide groups and 
sulfur are based on examinations of protein structures present in the Protein Data Bank [Bernstein et al., 1977] . They may be rationalized by electrostatic interactions and/or interactions between π electron systems 
( [Reid et al., 1985] and [Stoddard et al., 1990] ).

#### Further information

De Novo Link Rules governing the generation of interaction sites theory Prioritizing fitted fragments theory Fragment fitting theory Interaction site generation theory Link sites: aligning fragments with partially built ligands theory Theory - De Novo

# Influence of forcefield, partial, and formal charges on scoring functions

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_influence-of-forcefield-partial-formal-charges-on-scoring-functions.htm

## Influence of forcefield, partial, and formal charges on scoring functions

Several of the available scoring functions depend on the values of atom 
charges (both partial and formal) and also the choice of forcefield. Atom 
partial charges are automatically recalculated when performing a scoring 
calculation, and these partial charges depend on the forcefield choice. 
Any previously calculated partial charges are ignored in scoring calculations. 
Two forcefields are available when calculating ligand-protein scores, 
CFF and DREIDING. If CFF is chosen, then partial charges will be assigned 
to all atoms of the ligand and protein based on the CFF charging rules. 
If DREIDING ( [Mayo et al., 1990] is selected, then the Gasteiger charging method will be employed 
to calculate the partial charges of ligands and proteins. The forcefield 
selected will also affect the van der Waals energy term used in both LigScore1 
and LigScore2.

LigScore1 uses the partial charges on the atoms of both ligand 
and receptor to determine whether an atom is polar or nonpolar based on 
a cutoff threshold. This influences the computation of C+Pol and TotPol2.

LigScore2 types atoms of ligands and proteins as polar or nonpolar 
based on rules that employ only formal charges, ignoring partial charges.

PLP1 and PLP2 do not use any charge information, so 
partial charges, formal charges, and forcefield have no effect on the 
computed scores.

The Jain scoring function depends explicitly on the formal 
charge values in the polar attractive and repulsive interaction terms. 
The function is independent of both partial charges or forcefield.

The PMF and Ludi scoring functions depend implicitly 
on formal charges in their atom typing assignment rules, but are independent 
of partial charges or forcefield.

# Interaction site generation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_interaction-site-generation.htm

## Interaction site generation

Interactions leading to reversible binding between a protein and a ligand are usually formed through favorable non-covalent contacts such 
as hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic interactions. For each nonbonded contact, an atom or functional group of the protein interacts with an atom 
or functional group of the ligand.

Ludi models protein-ligand interactions through the use of interaction sites .
For each atom or functional group of the protein that is capable of
participating in a nonbonded contact, a set of interaction sites is
generated. This set of interaction sites encompasses the range of suitable
positions for a ligand atom or functional group involved in the putative
interaction. The density of interaction sites within the set is adjustable
by the user.

When the structure of the receptor is not known, Ludi generates an interaction site for each functional group in the set of active analogs 
(a set of ligands known to bind to the protein following a particular biophore).

Ludi distinguishes four types of interaction sites:

* H-donor

* H-acceptor

* lipophilic-aliphatic

* lipophilic-aromatic

The aromatic and aliphatic interaction sites are suitable for hydrophobic interactions. The H-donor and H-acceptor interaction sites are 
suitable for hydrogen bond formation. Ludi also generates metal interactions sites of the following metal ions: Fe, Ca, Zn, and Mg. The sites 
are hydrogen-bond acceptor sites that are distributed on a sphere centering around the metal ion.

Ludi models the H-donor and H-acceptor interaction sites with vectors (atom pairs) to account for the strong directionality of hydrogen bonds. 
H-donor sites are represented by D-X vectors R D-X = 1 Å and H-acceptor sites are 
represented by A-Y vectors R A-Y = 1.23 Å.

These vector lengths were chosen to simplify the subsequent fitting of fragments containing N-H
or O-H groups (which are fitted onto the donor interaction site D-X) or carbonyl groups C=O (which are fitted onto the acceptor interaction site A-Y).

The use of atom pairs for H-donor and H-acceptor interaction sites makes subsequent fragment fitting straightforward although some fragments 
will not use both positions (e.g., if a fragment containing an ether moiety is fitted onto an H-acceptor site, the ether oxygen is fitted onto 
the position A and the adjacent position Y is not used).

A statistical analysis of hydrogen bond geometries in crystal packings of small molecules reveals a rather broad distribution (see Table 1 in Rules governing the generation of interaction sites for
more information). Ludi takes this distribution into account by generating
an ensemble of interaction sites distributed over the region of acceptable
geometries. This approach has the advantage that it is purely geometrical
and therefore avoids costly calculations of potential energy functions.

# Jain scoring function

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_jain.htm

## Jain scoring function

A. N. Jain developed an empirical scoring function through an evaluation of the structures and binding affinities of a series of 
protein-ligand complexes. The Jain score is a sum of five interaction terms [Jain, 1996] . 
These terms describe:

* Lipophilic interactions

* Polar attractive interactions

* Polar repulsive interactions

* Solvation of the protein and ligand

* An entropy term for the ligand

Only proximate protein-ligand atoms are considered for the pairwise 
interaction terms. The lipophilic and polar interaction terms are each 
represented by a weighted sum of a Gaussian and a sigmoidal function. 
This functional form is short-ranged with a pronounced maximum that 
occurs at close surface contacts. It also incurs a significant penalty 
for short contacts between protein and ligand atoms.

Options are provided to ignore non-polar hydrogens of the receptor or ignore water molecules when calculating the Jain score.

## Lead Optimization

Lead optimization is a stage in drug discovery in which the lead compound is modified to improve potency, selectivity, or pharmacokinetic properties. The lead compounds, often found in high-throughput screening as hits, usually lack druglike properties. However, they can be used as starting points or scaffolds to explore more chemical space. There are various ways to perform lead optimization. In Discovery Studio , in situ enumeration and fragment replacement are two ways to grow a scaffold and perform scaffold hopping.

* Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration

* Scaffold hopping by fragment replacement

# LibDock

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_libdock.htm

## LibDock

The LibDock docking program ( [Diller and Merz, 2001] , [Diller and Li, 2003] , and [Rao et al., 2007] )
performs the following steps using a set of pre-generated ligand conformations and a receptor with a specified binding site:

* Remove hydrogen atoms.

* Rank ligand conformations and prune by Solvent Accessible Solvent Area (SASA).

* Find hotspots using a grid placed into the binding site and using polar and apolar probes.
The number of hotspots are pruned by clustering to a user defined value.

* Dock ligand poses by aligning to the hotspots. This is performed by using triplets (i.e., three ligand atoms 
are aligned to three receptor hotspots). Poses which result in protein clashes are removed.

* A final Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) pose optimization stage is performed using a simple pair-wise score (similar to Piecewise Linear Potential ). The top scoring ligand poses are retained.

* Hydrogen atoms are added.

Hydrogen atoms added in the final step may result in small bumps with the protein. Therefore, minimization should be performed prior to using scoring functions that are sensitive to such bumps.

# Scoring

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_ligand-scoring.htm

## Scoring

Ligand scoring is a method to rapidly estimate the binding affinity of a ligand, based on a candidate ligand pose geometry 
docked into a target receptor structure.

Scoring methods typically use empirical functions developed by fitting
various functional forms, which characterize various aspects of the receptor-ligand
interactions against binding affinity data. An alternative approach
makes use of statistical analysis of known ligand-receptor
structures and the frequency of occurrence of specific receptor-ligand
interactions without requiring any information about binding affinities.
This approach is generally referred to as a knowledge-based approach.
Both types of scoring function method are available in the application
which includes:

* Jain

* LigScore1

* LigScore2

* Ludi

* Piecewise Linear Potential (PLP)

* Potential of Mean Force (PMF)

The first four of the above methods were developed using the empirical
fitting approach. The PMF function was developed using the knowledge-based
statistical approach. The PLP function was originally developed as a
docking function, but has been shown to correlate well with binding affinities.

# LigScore1 scoring function

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_ligscore1.htm

## LigScore1 scoring function

LigScore1 is a fast scoring function for predicting receptor-ligand binding affinities.

Three descriptors are used to calculate LigScore1 (cfg. Equation 1), which is computed in units of pK i (-log K i ), where K i has units of mol/L. These descriptors are:

* vdW: This is a softened Lennard-Jones 6-9 potential, and 〈 〉 describes the summation of all interactions between the ligand and protein atoms. The vdW descriptor is expressed in units of kcal/mol.

* Cpos_tot: This is a count of the buried polar surface area between a receptor and ligand which involves attractive 
receptor-ligand interactions. The descriptor is expressed in units of Å 2 .

* TotPol 2 This is the squared sum of the total polar surface area of the receptor and the ligand molecule expressed in Å 2 .

When scoring ligands, the individual contributions of these descriptors may also be provided along with the overall LigScore1 value.

The coefficients for the LigScore1 depend on the forcefield (CFF or DREIDING) [Mayo et al., 1990] employed for the calculation of the vdW descriptor and the corresponding charge model (Gasteiger or CFF) used to assign atoms as polar or nonpolar.

Equation 1:

The coefficients of Equation 1 were obtained through regression analysis of the binding affinities of a series of protein-ligand complexes [Krammer et al., 2005] and are shown in the table below.

| Name | Forcefield | C | β 1 | β 2 | β 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pK i LigScore1_CFF | CFF | 0.4896 | 0.04551 | 0.1439 | 0.00101 |
| pK i LigScore1_Dreiding | Dreiding | -0.3498 | 0.04673 | 0.1653 | 0.001132 |

There is a typographical error in the constant term for LigScore1_Dreiding in [Krammer et al., 2005] ; it is missing the minus in table for C .

# LigScore2 scoring function

Source type: HTML

## LigScore2 scoring function

LigScore2 is a fast scoring function for predicting receptor-ligand binding affinities.

Three descriptors are used to calculate LigScore2 (cfg. Equation 1), which is computed in units of pK i (-log K i ), where K i has units of mol/L. These descriptors are:

* vdW: This is a softened Lennard-Jones 6-9 potential, and 〈 〉 describes the summation of all interactions between the ligand and protein atoms. The vdW descriptor is expressed in units of kcal/mol.

* Cpos_tot: This is a count of the buried polar surface area between a receptor and ligand which involves attractive 
receptor-ligand interactions. The descriptor is expressed in units of Å 2 .

* BuryPol 2 : This is the squared sum of the buried polar surface area of the receptor and the ligand molecule expressed in 
Å 2 . This term accounts for the desolvation penalty incurred by desolvating water molecules from the ligand and receptor cavity so that the ligand can form binding interactions with the receptor.

When scoring ligands, the individual contributions of these descriptors may also be provided along with the overall LigScore2 value.

The coefficients used in the calculation of LigScore2 depend on the forcefield (CFF or DREIDING [Mayo et al., 1990] ) employed for the calculation of the vdW descriptor.

Equation 1:

The coefficients of Equation 1 were obtained through regression analysis of the binding affinities of a series of protein-ligand complexes [Krammer et al., 2005] and are shown in the table below.

| Name | Forcefield | C | β 1 | β 2 | β 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pK i LigScore2_CFF | CFF | 1.900 | 0.0730 | 0.06246 | 0.00007324 |
| pK i LigScore2_Dreiding | Dreiding | 1.539 | 0.07622 | 0.6501 | 0.00007821 |

# Link sites: aligning fragments with partially built ligands

Source type: HTML

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_link-sites-aligning-fragments-with-partially-built-ligands.htm

## Link sites: aligning fragments with partially built ligands

Ludi is capable of fitting fragments onto interaction sites and simultaneously
aligning (i.e., linking) them with an existing ligand. For this purpose,
link sites are defined on the ligand.

A link site is a hydrogen atom that can be replaced by a suggested
fragment. You can either specify these link sites, or allow Ludi to
assume that all of the hydrogen atoms of the positioned ligand (within
a user-specified cutoff radius) are link sites.

Ludi does not actually create the ligand-fragment bond(s). It simply positions the 
fragment in such a way as to take advantage of nearby interaction sites (i.e., sites for hydrogen bond formation and hydrophobic interactions) 
while simultaneously aligning the fragment to a ligand link site.

Ludi may suggest one, two, or three links to an existing ligand. For multiple links, Ludi aligns the fragment to multiple link sites on the 
existing ligand. If the partially built ligand is composed of multiple pieces, Ludi may suggest fragments to connect the pieces (i.e., bridges). 
Figure 1(a) shows a partially built ligand and a fragment aligned at one link site. The two examples in Figure 1(b) are two-link alignments; the
second demonstrates the use of a bridge fragment. A three-link example is given in Figure 1(c). The result after merging and bonding the fragments and 
ligands is also shown in the figure.

Figure 1: One, two, and three link examples in Ludi

# Ludi fragment libraries

Source type: HTML

## Ludi fragment libraries

There are two types of Ludi fragment libraries:

* receptor library (standard library)

* link library

The receptor or standard library is used for De Novo Receptor, and the link library is used for De Novo Link and De Novo Evolution. 
Both library types consist of two files, one specifying fragment topologies and the other specifying the interaction types of fragment 
functional groups.

The link library is similar to the standard library. The main difference between the two is that the link library contains
definitions of link sites for the fragments. These are atoms that can be removed to bond the fragment to the scaffold.

There are several receptor and link libraries included in the standard installation which are listed in Table 1 and Table 2 . There is additional information provided for the original Ludi Standard libraries developed by
Böhm [Böhm, 1992b] in Table 3 .

During the fragment fitting process, fragments may be kept rigid, or bonds may be rotated one or two at a time to 
generate new fragment conformations, depending on the setting of the appropriate bond rotation parameter.

Alternatively, conformational flexibility can be taken into account by including several conformers for a 
fragment in the library. For example, multiple conformers are stored for several dipeptides, corresponding to 
highly populated regions in the Ramachandran Plot. Another example occurs for hydroxy compounds (for example, naphthol) 
where two rotamers of the hydroxy group are stored in the fragment library.

Optionally, enantiomers of each fragment may also be considered in the fitting process.

For each of the fragments in the standard library, between three and eight atoms are defined to be fitted onto

# Ludi scoring function

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_ludi-score.htm

## Ludi scoring function

Ligand-receptor complexes may be evaluated using the empirical scoring functions available from the Ludi algorithm. The Ludi score is a sum 
of five contributions [Böhm 1994a] :

* Contributions from ideal hydrogen bonds.

* Contributions from perturbed ionic interactions (ionic interaction
is the interaction of donor and acceptor in the receptor [e.g. COO-, or -NH3+]).

* Contributions from lipophilic interactions.

* Contributions due to the freezing of internal degrees of freedom of the ligand.

* Contributions due to the loss of translational and rotational entropy of the ligand.

This scoring function, termed Energy_Estimate_1 , was derived by empirically fitting a set of protein-ligand complexes with 
experimentally measured binding affinities. A second scoring function, Energy_Estimate_2 , was subsequently determined by including 
additional complexes and refitting the weights associated with the above terms. A final scoring function, Energy_Estimate_3 , was 
determined with the same set of complexes used for Energy_Estimate_2 and including an additional contribution in the function to 
account for aromatic-aromatic interactions [Böhm, 1998] .

# De Novo

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_ludi.htm

## De Novo

De Novo ligand design identifies potential novel ligands by screening a
library of small molecules to find those that are complementary to a
target receptor. Complementarity is defined as an appropriate spatial
orientation of hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic functional groups. Molecules
that cannot be fitted without incurring van der Waals clashes or electrostatic
repulsions are screened out during the search process. De Novo methods use the 
Ludi algorithm which works in three steps.

* Interaction sites within a defined search sphere inside the target receptor are calculated. Typically, the search sphere 
definition is based on the location of a set of known ligands which bind within the receptor cavity.

* Ludi-formatted libraries are searched for fragments that can fit inside the sphere while forming favorable interactions with 
the interaction sites.

* An alignment or linking for the fragments is proposed.

To generate the interaction sites, Ludi uses a set of rules that are
intended to cover the complete range of energetically favorable orientations
for hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts. These rules are based on
a statistical analysis of nonbonded contacts found in the following literature:

* [Baker and Hubbard, 1984]

* [Görbitz, 1989]

* [Görbitz and Etter, 1992]

* [Klebe, 1991]

* [Kroon et al., 1975]

* [Murray-Rust and Glusker, 1984]

* [Taylor and Kennard, 1984]

* [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985]

They are also described in the rules
governing the generation of interaction sites topic.

Fitting fragments to the interaction sites, and the subsequent alignment (that is., linking) of fragments to a partially 
built ligand is controlled by several options. After fitting and aligning, the coordinates of the suggested fragments are written 
out in .pdb or .mol format, depending on the input library format.

# Dock Fragments (MCSS)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_mcss.htm

## Dock Fragments (MCSS)

The Dock Fragments (MCSS) fragment docking program performs an exhaustive search of a specified protein site for low energy poses using a unique computationally efficient approach [Evensen et al., 1997] , [Miranker and Karplus, 1991] . In this approach, fragment copies are initially randomly distributed in the specified protein search sphere. In the following iteration cycles, energy minimizations are performed on all fragments. During the energy minimization the fragments are flexible and can sample different conformations.

Each functional group feels the average field of the fixed target protein and the interactions between the group 
replicas are omitted using the time-dependent Hartree approximation [Elber and Karplus, 1990] .
After each fragment minimization step, fragments replicas approaching the same minimum are removed before a 
new energy minimization step is performed. Identical minima are determined by calculating the RMS differences 
of the fragments.

The major steps in the procedure are as follows:

* Distribute fragment replicas in the protein search sphere

* Perform a CHARMm energy minimization

* Prune replicas to remove fragments that converged to the same minima

Steps 2 and 3 are repeated until convergence.

The energy minimization includes the protein-fragment and the fragment energy. The MCSS_Score property is the negative value of the final fragment energy.

# Non-bond interaction strength

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_nonbond-strength.htm

## Non-bond interaction strength

Molecular recognition in biological systems is driven by specific interactions between two partner molecules. The optimization of these interactions underpins all structure-based drug design, and requires knowledge about interaction geometries and approximate affinity contributions of all types of interactions [Bissantz et al., 2010] . Non-bond interactions encompass a multiplicity of different types of chemistry and geometries. The very weakest hydrogen bonds (in energy terms) are barely distinguishable from van der Waals interactions, while the strongest ones (in energy terms) are stronger than weak covalent bonds [Panigrahi et al., 2007a] . The characteristics of non-bond interactions have been studied extensively in numerous ways, from experimental calorimetric and spectroscopic studies, to statistical analyses of structural data such as the Cambridge Structural Database ( https://www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/solutions/csd-system/components/csd/ ) and Protein Data Bank ( http://www.rcsb.org/ ), to theoretical quantum mechanical calculations.

While it is desirable to associate non-bond interactions with energy terms, there are limitations:

* It is generally acknowledged that molecular interactions do not behave in an additive fashion. Consequently, it is impossible to separate out the large number of attractive and repulsive interactions in a single protein-ligand complex, while also taking into consideration such aspects as solvation processes, and long-range interactions.

* A single protein-ligand complex or crystal structure, with its inherent experimental uncertainty and errors, gives a misleadingly static view of interactions. A macromolecular complex is actually an ensemble of conformations with varying degrees of freedom in both the ligand and the protein.

* Extensive computer simulations, which are required to attempt to quantify the role and strength of specific interactions, are not generally feasible when working with high throughput virtual screening data. Thus the non-bond interactions in Discovery Studio are determined by geometry rather than more expensive energy calculations, and the energy or strength of specific interactions is not calculated.

Nevertheless there are a number of considerations that can provide indirect insights into the significance and influence of specific interactions:

* Interaction types

* Geometry of interactions

* Participating functional groups

The categorization of interaction types helps to rapidly reveal the different interactions and forces influencing the binding of a protein-ligand complex. These categories can also help to characterize the nature of a particular binding pocket, and types, such as water hydrogen bonds, can aid in identifying structural waters.

Some interactions types are, by their very nature, more significant and energetically favorable than others such as charged interactions and hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bonds are by far the most well-studied interactions in biological recognition processes, but the last thirty years have seen the emerging recognition of many more types of specific interactions. For example, the introduction of fluorine to improve metabolic stability and modulate physicochemical properties has emerged as a particularly useful type of interaction to exploit in lead optimization [Böhm et al., 2004] . Fluorine and halogen interactions are becoming accepted as semidirectional weak to medium strength interactions, depending on the experimental system, and can compete or act synergistically with weak to moderately strong hydrogen bonds [Wilcken et al., 2013] . Some interactions are less well-studied and less common, such as sulfur interactions, which are generally considered to be similar in nature to weak hydrogen bonds [Zhou et al., 2009] . Nevertheless, they can be useful when optimizing particular chemical systems and understanding stabilizing interactions of protein structure.

The geometric limits defining the perception of interactions were derived from numerous studies of the distribution and frequency of interactions from structural sources such as the Cambridge Structural Database and Protein Data Bank. Most of the interactions include both distance and angle criteria, which can be modified to customize the interaction perception, as well as the option to omit the angle criteria completely. A simple (but limited) inference is that as the interaction distance approaches the maximum criteria value, the strength of the interaction decreases. Shorter distances (above the steric bump van der Waals criteria) are likely to indicate a stronger relative interaction. Angles formed by interactions are less useful in surmising interaction strength, and should only be considered in terms of perceiving the presence of the interaction. Gauging interaction strength beyond this becomes difficult, even without considering such effects as desolvation, cooperative binding, and the extended network of interactions that stabilize the protein.

The nature and environment of the functional groups in partner molecules influence interaction strengths. Hydrogen bonds formed by good donors (O–H, N–H) and good acceptors (N, O, halide) are considered strong interactions, while interactions involving a poor donor (C–H, S–H) or a poor acceptor (π-cloud, multiple bonds), or where both the donor and acceptor are poor (C–H…π), are considered weak interactions [Panigrahi et al., 2007a] . Within the strong hydrogen bonds, interactions between amide C=O and OH are known to have shorter median distances than those involving NH donors. Charged hydrogen bonds (salt bridges) are shorter and stronger than comparable uncharged ones. However this does not necessarily translate into more favorable binding free energies [Bissantz et al., 2010] , which is a reminder of the complexity of understanding interactions and translating these to optimized protein-ligand complexes.

Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents on aromatic rings affect the strength of hydrophobic interactions, as do the substituent positions ( [Meyer et al., 2013] , [Salonen et al., 2011] ). Neighboring functional groups can also cause furcation of interactions such as hydrogen bonds, which affects the strength of the interactions and complicates the analysis of the significance of a structural feature [Panigrahi et al., 2007b] .

# Non-bond Interactions

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_nonbondinteractions.htm

## Non-bond Interactions

Non-bond interactions are interactions between two molecules or close contacts within macromolecules. Identifying and optimizing these interactions between a ligand and a protein is often a goal in structure-based drug design. You can use the non-bond interactions tools to identify many different types of attractive interactions, including traditional interactions that have been well understood for decades (for example, classic hydrogen bonds) as well as more recently discovered interactions such as weak hydrogen bonds with carbon donors [Bissantz et al., 2010] . The different types of interaction vary in strength, but the cumulative effect of even the weaker types can be significant.

In addition to attractive forces, another important consideration is repulsive interactions. These unfavorable interactions can occur due to incorrect structure determination, incorrect bond order determination or ionization state, or when modifying functional groups, during the process of lead optimization. You can use the non-bond interaction tools to identify these types of unfavorable interactions (for example, steric interactions, mismatched hydrogen bond pairs, and repulsive charge interactions).

Displayed non-bond interactions are dynamically recalculated if the positions or chemistry of the monitored atoms are changed.

The interactions only occur between certain atom types and must be within a certain distance, angle constraints, and other criteria. For example, for a hydrogen bond to occur between two molecules, a hydrogen bond donor atom must be within a certain distance (typically 3-4 Å) of a hydrogen bond acceptor atom on the other molecule. Also the angles formed between the associated groups of atoms must be within a specific range. This topic describes the default criteria used in Discovery Studio for all types. The criteria used for determining the various interactions can be set via the following methods:

* Interaction Criteria dialog on the View Interactions tool panel

* Attributes dialog for the monitor

* Non-bond Monitor tab of the Data Table

Many parameters for the interactions are hidden in the Data Table View, which can be exposed by right-clicking and choosing Select Columns .

There are several types of interactions that can be monitored (details are listed below). The categories of interactions are:

* Hydrogen Bonds

* Electrostatic

* Hydrophobic

* Halogen

* Miscellaneous

* Unfavorable

Many interactions are between single atom pairs. However, some interactions are based on groups of atoms, (for example, Pi-Pi, Pi-alkyl, and so on). In these cases, a sphere is displayed at the center of the atoms contributing to the interaction, with a radius proportional to the cube root of the number of atoms involved.

| Category | Sub-Category | Type | Color | References | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Classical | Conventional Hydrogen Bond | | [Baker and Hubbard, 1984] , [Bissantz et al., 2010] | 1KIM |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Non Classical | Carbon Hydrogen Bond | | [Pierce, et al.,2002] | 1KIM |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Non Classical | Pi Donor Hydrogen Bond | | [Bissantz et al., 2010] | 1KIM |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Water | Water Mediated Hydrogen Bond | | [Bissantz et al., 2010] | 1KIM |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Water | Water Hydrogen Bond | | | 1KIM |
| Hydrogen Bonds | Salt Bridge | Salt Bridge | | [Bissantz et al., 2010] | 1KIM |

#### Classical

Conventional Hydrogen Bond interactions can exist between a hydrogen bond donor atom and an acceptor atom. Atoms of element types N, O, P, and S are considered as classical hydrogen bond donor atoms, and hydrogen atoms are considered as hydrogen bond donors if connected to such atoms. In this case, the heavy atom is no longer considered as a hydrogen bond donor. Atoms of element types N, O, P, and S are also hydrogen bond acceptor atoms if at least one electron lone pair is present (for example, NH 3 but not NH 4 + ).

However, an sp 2 -hybridized N atom with at least one electron lone pair is not considered a hydrogen bond acceptor atom if it is connected by a single bond to another sp 2 -hybridized atom. Additionally, atoms of element type F, Cl, Br, and I are also considered hydrogen bond acceptor atoms.

Hydrogen bonds are shown whether or not explicit hydrogen atoms are displayed. If a molecule contains no explicit hydrogen atoms, the identification of hydrogen bonding pairs may be less accurate.

If both atoms are N or O, the distance criterion d between the heavy donor and acceptor atoms is 3.4 Å by default ( Strong H-bond D(H)...A (max dist) ). 
Otherwise the distance criterion is 3.8 Å ( Weak H-bond D(H)...A (max dist) ). If there is an explicit hydrogen atom, the distance dh between the hydrogen atom and the acceptor atom must be less than the specified distance criterion -0.7 Å (that is, 2.7 Å or 3.1 Å). See Figure 1 and Figure 2 .

By default, angle constraints are checked to determine whether a hydrogen bond is present. For a general hydrogen bond X-D-H...A-Y, where D is the hydrogen bond donor heavy atom, H is the explicit donor hydrogen if present, A is the hydrogen bond acceptor atom, X is any non-hydrogen atom attached to the donor atom, and Y is any atom attached to the acceptor atom. The angles that can be constrained are X-D-A, D-H-A, D-A-Y, and H-A-Y. These must all lie within the minimum (90° by default) and maximum (180° by default) values of the following angle parameters: Hydrogen-bond X-D-A angle , Hydrogen-bond D-H-A angle , Hydrogen-bond D-A-Y angle , and Hydrogen-bond H-A-Y angle .

In the case of an sp hybridized donor atom, its hydrogen atom will be colinear with the D-X bond, so any interaction should lie closer to this vector. Therefore, a stricter minimum angle constraint Hydrogen Bond with Sp donor X-D-A (135° by default) is applied.

Figure 1. Hydrogen bond when an explicit hydrogen exists. The angles and distances used to determine if an interaction exists are shown.

Figure 2. Hydrogen bond when an explicit hydrogen does not exist. The angles and distances used to determine if an interaction exists are shown.

#### Non Classical

Carbon Hydrogen Bond interactions are considered weaker hydrogen bonds where the donor is a polarized carbon atom. A carbon atom is considered to be a donor if it is either in an acetylene group or if it is adjacent to an oxygen or nitrogen atom.

These interactions are determined using the same geometric criteria used for classical hydrogen bonds with the exception of the default distance criterion being 3.8 Å ( Weak H-bond D(H)...A (max dist) ).

Pi-Donor Hydrogen Bond interactions are hydrogen bonds that occur between hydrogen bond donor atoms and a Pi ring that functions as a hydrogen bond acceptor. The following tests are performed to find these interactions:

* Hydrogen bond donor atoms are found.

* C-H donors are excluded because they form Pi-Sigma interactions.

* The distance between each donor heavy atom and the centroid of each Pi ring is tested to find those within the Pi-Donor (max dist) cutoff (4.2 Å by default).

* The angle between the donor heavy atom-centroid vector and the normal to the ring plane should be less than the Pi-Donor angle (40° by default).

* The positions of each of the donor's explicit or implicit hydrogen atoms are found. A heavy-H-centroid angle must exist that deviates from linearity by no more than the Pi-Donor deviation angle (40.0° by default).

#### Water

The Water monitor is useful for identifying bridging water molecules (that is, when a water molecule is hydrogen bonded to two different molecules such as a protein and a ligand or two domains of a protein) and to visualize water networks. After all hydrogen bonds have been determined, the bonds that bridge chains are classified as Water Mediated Hydrogen Bonds and colored mid blue. Other hydrogen bonds involving at least one water molecule are classified as Water Hydrogen Bonds and colored light blue.

#### Salt Bridge

Salt Bridge interactions are relatively strong non-bonded interactions between pairs of oppositely charged groups where hydrogen bonding also occurs, which can be observed at longer range than uncharged hydrogen bonds. Interactions are classified as salt bridges for pairs of atoms closer than 4.0 Å ( Salt bridge D(H)...A (max dist) ), where one atom is positively charged, one is negatively charged, and there is a hydrogen bond between them.

| Category | Sub-Category | Type | Color | References | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Electrostatic | Charge | Attractive Charges | | [Wolber and Langer, 2005] | 1KIM |
| Electrostatic | Charge | Salt Bridge | | [Bissantz et al., 2010] | 1KIM |
| Electrostatic | Pi-Charge | Pi-Cation | | [Gallivan and Dougherty, 1999_A] [Biot et al., 2002] | 1KIM |
| Electrostatic | Pi-Charge | Pi-Anion | | [Frontera et al., 2011] | 1KIM |

#### Charge

Attractive Charge interactions exist between atoms bearing opposite whole or fractional formal charges that are within the Charge-charge (max dist) cutoff (5.6 Å by default).

Salt Bridge interactions are also listed in the Electrostatic category as well as in the Hydrogen Bonds category since they can be considered members of both.

#### Pi-Charge

Pi-Cation interactions can exist between a positively charged atom and the electrons of a delocalized Pi system. The following tests are performed to find them:

* Cations are considered to be atoms that have a formal charge of at least +0.5. This allows the inclusion of delocalized cationic species such as lysine and arginine side chains.

* The distance between a cation and the centroid of a Pi ring should be less than the Pi-Cation (max dist) cutoff (5.0 Å by default, see R in Figure 3. )

* The angle between the cation-centroid vector and the normal to the ring plane should be less than the Pi-Cation maximum angle (40° by default, see θ in Figure 3. )

Pi-Anion interactions are calculated in the same manner as Pi-Cation interactions, but only atoms with charges of -0.5 or less are considered.

Figure 3. Example of a Pi-atom interaction (for example, Pi-cation, Pi-anion, and so on). The important measurements are the angle θ and the distance R.

| Category | Sub-Category | Type | Color | References | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrophobic | Pi-Hydrophobic | Pi-Pi Stacked | | [McGaughey, et al.,1998] | 1KIM |
| Hydrophobic | Pi-Hydrophobic | Pi-Pi T-Shaped | | [McGaughey, et al.,1998] | 1KIM |
| Hydrophobic | Pi-Hydrophobic | Amide-Pi Stacked | | [Mitchell, et al 1994] | 1KIM |
| Hydrophobic | Alkyl Hydrophobic | Alkyl | | [Wolber and Langer, 2005] | 1KIM |
| Hydrophobic | Mixed Pi/Alkyl Hydrophobic | Pi-Sigma | | [Ozawa et al., 2008] | 1KIM |
| Hydrophobic | Mixed Pi/Alkyl Hydrophobic | Pi-Alkyl | | | 1KIM |

#### Pi-Hydrophobic

Pi rings are defined as planar ring systems composed of sp 2 hybridized atoms. They include (but are not confined to) aromatic rings.

Pi-Pi stacked interactions are determined following the methodology of McGaughey et al. [McGaughey, et al.,1998] . Stacked and staggered Pi-Pi interactions are determined by the following tests:

* The distance between the centroid of each Pi ring pair is determined to find those which fall within the cutoff distance ( Pi-Pi centroid (max dist) , 6 Å by default, see R cen , Figure 4. )

* For these interactions, an atom from each ring must be within the ( Pi-Pi closest atom (max dist)) cutoff, 4.5 Å by default, see R clo , Figure 4. )

* The angle θ between the normal of one or both rings and the centroid-centroid vector must be between 0° and ± the Stacked Pi-Pi theta angle cutoff (50° by default), and the angle γ between the normal to each ring must be between 0° and ± the Stacked Pi-Pi gamma cutoff angle (35° by default).

Figure 4. Example of a Pi-Pi interaction. The distances and angles needed for an interaction are labeled.

Pi-Pi T-shaped interactions occur if the following conditions are met:

* The distance between the centroid of each pair of Pi rings is determined to find those which fall within the Pi-Pi centroid (max dist) cutoff distance (6 Å by default).

* An atom from each ring should be within the Pi-Pi closest atom (max dist) cutoff (4.5 Å by default).

The angle ω between the normal of one or both rings and the centroid-centroid vector must be between 0° and ± the T-Shaped Pi-Pi theta angle cutoff (30° by default), and the angle γ between the normal to each ring must be within the T-Shaped Pi-Pi gamma angle cutoff (55° by default) or greater.

Amide-Pi Stacked interactions occur between an amide group and a Pi ring if the following criteria are met:

* The distance between the centroid of the amide group and the Pi rings falls within the Pi-Pi centroid (max dist) (6 Å by default).

* An atom from each group should be within the Pi-Pi closest atom (max dist) (4.5 Å by default).

The angle ω between the normal of one or both groups and the centroid-centroid
vector must be between 0° and ± the Stacked Pi-Amide theta angle cutoff distance (40° by default), and the angle γ between the normal to each must be between 0° and ± the Stacked Pi-Amide gamma angle cutoff (20° by default).

#### Alkyl Hydrophobic

Alkyl groups are defined as the following non-polarized, non-Pi systems:

Predominantly aliphatic amino acid side-chains: These include Alanine, Valine, Leucine, Isoleucine, Methionine, Selenomethionine, Cysteine, Proline, atoms CB, CG, and CD of Lysine, and atoms CB and CG of Arginine.

Hydrophobic groups on ligands are contiguous sets of atoms that are not adjacent to concentrations of charge (charged atoms or electronegative atoms). A group of atoms is considered hydrophobic if their surface area is equal or greater than the area of a methyl group multiplied by the Surface area scale factor (default 0.65), which corresponds to the surface area of a chlorine atom.

The criteria for this type of interaction are met when if the groups' centroids are within the Alkyl centroid (max dist) cutoff (5.5 Å by default) and they have at least one pair of atoms within the same Pi-Pi closest atom (max dist) cutoff used for Pi-Pi interactions.

#### Mixed Pi/Alkyl Hydrophobic

Pi-Sigma interactions (sometimes referred to as CH-π interactions) are weak interactions between a hydrogen and a Pi ring system. An interaction of this type must meet the following conditions:

* The hydrogens acting as the donor can be implicit or explicit hydrogens. They must be connected to a non-aromatic carbon atom.

* The distances between the hydrogen and the center of the Pi ring must be within the Pi-Sigma (max dist) cutoff (4.1 Å by default, see R in Figure 5. )

* The C-H-centroid angle cannot deviate from linearity by more than the Pi-Sigma deviation angle (20° by default, see δ in Figure 5 ) and the angle between the C-centroid vector and the normal to the ring plane is not more than the Pi-Sigma angle (45° by default, see θ in Figure 5 ).

Figure 5. Illustration of a Pi-Sigma interaction.

Pi-Alkyl interactions exist where the centroids of a Pi ring and an alkyl group are within the Alkyl centroid (max dist) cutoff (5.5 Å by default) and they have at least one pair of atoms within the same Pi-Pi closest atom (max dist) cutoff as used for Pi-Pi interactions.

| Category | Sub-Category | Type | Color | References | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Halogen | Fluorine | Halogen (Fluorine) | | [Müller, et al. 2007] , [Bissantz, et al., 2010] , [Auffinger, et al., 2004] | 1BL6 |
| Halogen | Cl, Br, I | Halogen (Cl, Br, I) | | [Bissantz, et al., 2010] , [Auffinger, et al., 2004] | 1P5E |

#### Fluorine

Halogen (Fluorine) interactions are carbon-bound halogen interactions (C-X...B-Y) that have similar structural significance to weak hydrogen bonds. Interactions with carbon-bound fluorine are monitored and identified separately from the interactions involving Cl, Br, and I. Additionally, halogen interactions (including F) with hydrogen donors are identified separately.

Fluorine interactions (C-F...B-Y) are identified and monitored with all hydrogen donors and the specific case where B is carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. In all cases, a maximum distance criterion ( Fluorine non-bond (max dist) is 3.7 Å by default) is used. When the interaction is with a hydrogen donor, the hydrogen bond angle criteria are used and the interaction is identified as both a fluorine and a hydrogen bond interaction.

Fluorine interactions with carbon and oxygen are limited to C=O moieties. Nitrogen interactions are limited to nucleophilic nitrogen. These interactions are also limited by the same maximum distance criterion (3.7 Å by default). However, no angle constraints are applied.

#### Cl, Br, I

Halogen (Cl, Br, I) interactions have distance criteria defined as a fraction of the sum of the atoms' van der Waals radii (controlled by Halogen (Cl, Br, I) VDW fraction (max) ). The default fraction is 1, using the full van der Waals distance as the cutoff. As with fluorine interactions with a hydrogen donor, halogen interactions with hydrogen donors use the hydrogen bond angle criteria to identify interactions.

Non-fluorine halogen interactions to carbon and oxygen are also limited to C=O moieties. Additionally, interactions with (B-Y) N-C, N-S, N-P, S-C, S-S and S-P are considered. A separate set of angle criteria are used in these cases ( Halogen (Cl, Br, I) bond X-B-Y angle with a default between 75° and 180° and Halogen (Cl, Br, I) bond C-X-B angle with a default between 120° and 180°).

| Category | Sub-Category | Type | Color | References | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Miscellaneous | Metal | Metal-Acceptor | | | 3EST |
| Miscellaneous | Sulfur | Pi-Sulfur | | [Ringer, et al., 2007] | 1ALO, 1KIM, 1J4H |
| Miscellaneous | Sulfur | Sulfur-X | | [Pal and Chakrabarti, 2001] | 1ALO |
| Miscellaneous | Lone Pair | Pi-Lone Pair | | [Egli and Sarkhel, 2007] , [Gallivan and Dougherty, 1999] | 1B4V, 2MHR |

#### Metal

Metal-Acceptor interactions are analogous to hydrogen bonds and can exist between metal cations and hydrogen bond acceptors. The geometric parameters are the same as for hydrogen bonds, with the metal in place of the heavy atom hydrogen donor.

The standard Discovery Studio definition of what is considered to be metal is used (that is, everything except H-He, B-Ne, Si-Ar, As-Kr, Te-Xe, At-Rn, and Uuo). Because formal charges cannot be automatically assigned to all metals on input (it is often not possible to accurately deduce the oxidation state) all metal atoms are assumed to be cationic.

#### Sulfur

In addition to hydrogen bonds, sulfur can participate in the interactions described below.

Pi-Sulfur interactions can adopt two distinct configurations: face on and edge on. The following tests
are used to determine Pi-Sulfur interactions:

* Sulfur atoms that have not already been found to be participating in a Pi-Donor interaction are considered.

* The distance between each such sulfur atom and the centroid of each Pi ring and the angle between the sulfur-centroid and the normal to the ring plane are tested. Either the distance must be within the Pi-Sulfur face-on (max dist) (4.5 Å by default) and the angle less than the Pi-Sulfur face-on angle (25.0° by default), or the distance must be within the Pi-Sulfur edge-on (max dist) cutoff (6.0 Å by default) and the angle greater than the Pi-Sulfur edge-on cutoff (70° by default).

Sulfur-X interactions are found between divalent sulfur and N, O, or S atoms. For a system Y 1 -S-Y 2 interacting with X, where X=N, O, or S the following tests are performed:

* The distance between S and X must be within a fraction of the sum of their VDW 
radii, the fraction being the Maximum Sulfur-X VDW fraction (1.0 by default - R in Figure 6.)

* One of the angles Y-S-X must be close to 180°.
The deviation from 180° is measured by testing the acute angle of intersection between the lines Y-S and S-X - see δ in Figure 6 .
The maximum allowed deviation is given by the Sulfur-X deviation angle , and is 30° by default. The Sulfur-X deviation angle can be set to any value from 0° to 180°.

* In cases where X is an sp 2 hybridized atom (for example, a carbonyl oxygen), the acute angle θ formed by the intersection between the line Y-S and a line normal to the plane of X and its attached atoms is tested - see θ in Figure 6 .
The maximum allowed value of this angle is given by the Sulfur-X theta angle , and is 90° by default. Since an acute angle cannot exceed a value of 90°, this effectively imposes no constraint, but you can adjust this. The Sulfur-X theta angle can be set to any value from 0° to 90°.

Figure 6. Illustration of a Sulfur-X interaction.

#### Lone Pair

A lone pair can form a favorable interaction with positively polarized Pi rings. The following tests are performed:

* Hydrogen bond acceptor atoms are considered provided they do not already participate in other atom-Pi ring interactions.

* The distance between the acceptor and the ring centroid is within the Pi-Lone Pair (max dist) cutoff (3.0 Å by default).

* The angle between the acceptor-centroid vector and the normal to the ring plane is less than the Pi-Lone Pair angle (45° by default).

By default, all unfavorable interactions are displayed as red dashed lines. In some cases, an unfavorable interaction will have both an unfavorable and a favorable interaction type associated with it. This is indicative that a small adjustment of the structure could produce a favorable interaction at this position.

#### Steric Bumps

Unfavorable steric interactions between atom pairs are identified as close contacts relative to the van der Waals distance between atoms. A steric bump occurs when the atom-atom distance is less than or equal to a threshold expressed as a fraction of the sum of the atoms' van der Waals radii. The default VDW fraction is 70% of the sum of the van der Waals radii.

When bound hydrogen atoms are implicit, united atom radii are used.

#### Charge Repulsion

Repulsive charge interactions are monitored between atoms bearing the same-signed whole or fractional formal charge. These interactions are pruned to account for compensating neighboring charges to show genuinely unfavorable interactions ( Charge-charge (max dist) is 5.6 Å by default).

#### Acceptor-Acceptor Clashes

If two acceptor atoms are within the Acceptor-acceptor (max dist) cutoff distance (3.0 Å by default), and if the estimated lone pair positions are such that the angles A-Lp-A ( Acceptor-acceptor A-Lp-A ) are greater than 90.0°, and the torsion A-Lp-Lp-A ( Acceptor-acceptor A-Lp-Lp-A torsion ) is less than 15.0°, it is considered to be an acceptor-acceptor clash. 
See Figure 7 .

Figure 7. Illustration of the important measurements in an acceptor-acceptor clash.

#### Donor-Donor Clashes

Two donor atoms within hydrogen bonding distance constitute an unfavorable interaction. In the case where there are explicit hydrogens, there is an
additional check to make sure they are pointing towards each other such that the angles H-H-D are greater than 120° by default.

Figure 8. H-H-D angles are measured to determine if a donor-donor clash exists.

#### Metal Repulsion

By analogy with hydrogen bonds, a close interaction between a metal ion and a donor is considered to be a repulsive interaction.

#### Unsatisfied

Hydrogen bond donor, hydrogen bond acceptor, and charged atoms that are not participating in a non-bond interaction are identified as unsatisfied. By default, atoms identified as unsatisfied are not displayed. To display them, open the Non-bond Monitor Display dialog on the View Interactions menu and check the Unsatisfied box. Only atoms that are monitored can be identified as unsatisfied. When the monitor is created, a group called Monitored Atoms is added. Select this group to highlight the monitored atoms.

Additionally, unsatisfied interactions are not monitored for certain scopes. If the Molecular Scope is intermolecular or if the monitored pair scope is interactionsExternalToMonitoredScope , it is not possible to distinguish between a non-bond outside of the search scope and a truly unsatisfied interaction. The same argument applies when the monitored pair scope is interactionsWithinMonitoredScope . However in that case, the unsatisfied non-bond atoms near the surface identify atoms that are available to form interactions.

#### Further information

Non-bond interaction strength Interaction Options dialog Interaction Criteria dialog
