# Piecewise Linear Potential (PLP)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_piecewise-linear-potential.htm

## Piecewise Linear Potential (PLP)

Piecewise Linear Potential is a fast, simple, docking function that
has been shown to correlate well with protein-ligand binding affinities.
PLP scores are measured in arbitrary units, with negative PLP scores
reported in order to make them suitable for subsequent use in consensus
score calculations. Higher PLP scores indicate stronger receptor-ligand
binding (larger pK i values).

Two versions of the PLP function are available: 
PLP1 [Gehlhaar et al., 1995] and 
PLP2 [Gehlhaar et al., 1999] .

### PLP1

In the PLP1 function, each non-hydrogen ligand or non-hydrogen receptor atom is assigned a PLP atom type. Hydrogens are excluded from 
consideration. There are four PLP atom types:

* Hydrogen bond (H-bond) donor only.

* H-bond acceptor only.

* Both H-bond donor and acceptor.

* Non-polar.

When PLP1 is the docking function, the internal energy is calculated for each new ligand conformation. This energy is used only to avoid van der 
Waals clashes and is not used for the PLP score. The forcefield that provides the atomic parameters in this case is the generally robust DREIDING [Mayo et al., 1990] .

There are two types of pairwise interactions in PLP1 as shown in Table 1, namely H-bond and steric. The two interactions are described by the 
same functional form, but with different parameters (Figure 1 and Table 2). The PLP1 score is the sum of the function values of all pairwise 
interactions in a receptor-ligand complex.

Table 1: Interaction types of PLP1

| Ligand PLP type: | Receptor PLP type: | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Donor | Acceptor | Both | Non-polar | |
| Donor | Steric | H-bond | H-bond | Steric |
| Acceptor | H-bond | Steric | H-bond | Steric |
| Both | H-bond | H-bond | H-bond | Steric |
| Non-polar | Steric | Steric | Steric | Steric |

Figure 1: Functional form of PLP1

The values of A-F are given in Table 2.

Table 2: Parameters for PLP1 functional form

| Interaction type | A | B | C | D | E | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H-bond | 2.3 | 2.6 | 3.1 | 3.4 | -2.0 | 20.0 |
| Steric | 3.4 | 3.6 | 4.5 | 5.5 | -0.4 | 20.0 |

### PLP2

In the PLP2 function, PLP atom typing remains the same as in PLP1. In addition, an atomic radius is assigned to each atom except for 
hydrogen. There are three different radii:

* Small: a value of 1.4 for F and metal ions (including Zn, Mn, Mg, and Fe).

* Medium: a value of 1.8 for C, O, and N.

* Large: a value of 2.2 for S, P, Cl, and Br.

There are three types of pairwise interactions in PLP2 as shown in Table 3, namely H-bond, dispersion, and repulsion. There are two types 
of functional forms. The H-bond and dispersion interactions have the same functional form, but different parameters (Figure 2 and Table 4). 
A scaling factor is used for H-bond and repulsion terms based on the angle formed by the corresponding receptor-ligand atoms. The PLP2 score 
is the sum of the function values of all pairwise interactions in a receptor-ligand complex.

Table 3: Interaction types of PLP2

| Ligand PLP type: | Receptor PLP type: | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Donor | Acceptor | Both | Non-polar | |
| Donor | Repulsion | H-bond | H-bond | Dispersion |
| Acceptor | H-bond | Repulsion | H-bond | Dispersion |
| Both | H-bond | H-bond | H-bond | Dispersion |
| Non-polar | Dispersion | Dispersion | Dispersion | Dispersion |

Figure 2: Functional forms of PLP2

* Pairwise potential for H-bond and dispersion terms.

* Pairwise potential for repulsion terms.

* Scaling factor for H-bond and repulsion terms based on the angle formed by the receptor and ligand atoms.

The values of A-F are given in Table 4, where σ is the sum of the PLP atomic radii of receptor and ligand atoms.

Table 4 - Parameters for PLP2 functional form

| Interaction type | A | B | C | D | E | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H-bond | 2.3 | 2.6 | 3.1 | 3.4 | -4.1 | 15.0 |
| Dispersion | 0.93σ | 1.0σ | 1.25σ | 1.5σ | -0.4 | 15.0 |
| Repulsion | 3.2 | 6.0 | | | 1.5 | 15.0 |

# Potential of Mean Force (PMF)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_potential-mean-force.htm

## Potential of Mean Force (PMF)

The PMF [Muegge and Martin, 1999] and PMF04 [Muegge, 2006] scoring functions were developed based on statistical analysis of the 3D structures of protein-ligand complexes. They were found to 
correlate well with protein-ligand binding free energies while being fast and simple to calculate. The scores are calculated by summing pairwise 
interaction terms over all interatomic pairs of the receptor-ligand complex. The PMF04 score is an updated version of the original PMF score. A 
larger data set was used for parameterization and, additionally, metal ion and halogen
potentials are included. The PMF scores are reported in 
arbitrary units with the sign reversed to allow for subsequent use in consensus score calculations. A higher score indicates a stronger 
receptor-ligand binding affinity.

The receptor and ligand structures must have explicit hydrogen atoms and correct bond order information to ensure correct atom typing for the 
PMF calculation.

While the hydrogen atom type was included in the parameterization scheme for PMF, it can be optionally ignored, as suggested by the authors, in
the score calculation. Options are also available for setting distance cutoffs for the calculation of carbon-carbon interactions and other interactions
as discussed by Muegge and Martin [Muegge and Martin, 1999] .

# Prioritizing fitted fragments

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_prioritizing-fitted-fragments.htm

## Prioritizing fitted fragments

An important aspect of searching through large numbers of structures is prioritizing the hits. Ludi approaches the problem as follows:

Initially, Ludi rejects any hit in which:

* The fragment overlaps with the receptor.

* In link mode, the fragment overlaps the ligand except at the link site atoms.

* You have specified that electrostatic repulsion be checked, and the fragment does not pass the check.

* You have specified that a check be made for unpaired polar groups, and the fragment fit buries an unpaired polar group on either the 
fragment or the receptor.

* The fragment does not pass any of the specified filters.

A fragment does not 
pass the electrostatic check if a fragment polar atom is closer than 
a user-defined threshold distance (typically 3.5 Å for O––O 
contacts) to a receptor atom of the same polarity. Receptor atoms that 
hydrogen bond with the fragment are excluded from this check.

The hits are the prioritized using an empirical scoring function. Whenever a fragment can fit in multiple orientations, only the 
highest scoring pose is retained.

#### Further information

De Novo Link Theory - Fragment fitting Theory - De Novo

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_receptor-mode-scoring-functions.htm

## Receptor mode scoring functions

In receptor mode, Ludi offers four empirical scoring functions. The original receptor mode scoring
function (Eq. 1) is a two-term scoring function in which the first term measures the number and
quality of receptor-fragment hydrogen bonds, and the second term measures the receptor-fragment hydrophobic contact area. 
The second term is weighted such that 60 Å 2 of
hydrophobic contact surface is equivalent to an unperturbed hydrogen bond.

| (1) | |
| --- | --- |

In Eq. 1 the summation is over fragment-receptor hydrogen bonds; Δ R is the deviation of the H ––– O/N 
hydrogen bond length from the ideal value (1.9 Å); Δα is the deviation of the hydrogen bond angle 
(N/O-H ––– O/N) from its ideal value (180°); and A lipo is the area (Å 2 ) of hydrophobic 
contact between the receptor and fragment. Where f (Δ R ) and f (Δα) are defined as follows:

| (2) | f (Δ R ) =1 | for Δ R ≤ 0.2 Å |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (3) | f (Δ R ) = 1 - (Δ R - 0.2)/0.4 | for 0.2 Å < Δ R < 0.6 Å |
| (4) | f (Δ R ) = 0 | for Δ R ≥ 0.6 Å |
| (5) | f (Δα) = 1 | for Δα ≤ 30° |
| (6) | f (Δα) = 1 - (Δα - 30)/50 | for 30° < Δα < 80° |
| (7) | f (Δα) = 0 | for Δα ≥ 80° |

The second scoring function (Eq. 8), termed Energy_Estimate_1, gives a score that is correlated with the dissociation constant, K i , for the ligand-receptor complex [Böhm, 1994a] as shown in Table 1.

| (8) | Score | = -100 log( K i ) |
| --- | --- | --- |

Table 1. Correlation between the Ludi score and dissociation constant, K i , for Ligand-receptor complexes

| Score | K i |
| --- | --- |
| 100 | 100 mM |
| 200 | 10 mM |
| 300 | 1 mM |
| 600 | 1 μM |
| 900 | 1 nM |

The relationship between the dissociation constant and the free energy of binding, Δ G , at equilibrium is expressed in Eq. 9, where R is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature. By substituting Eq. 9 into Eq. 8 the score is shown to be proportional to the free energy of binding at 25°C: (Eq. 10)

| (9) | Δ G = - R T ln ( K i ) = -2.303 R T log ( K i ) |
| --- | --- |
| (10) | Score = -73.33 Δ G (T = 298 K) |

The Ludi score is calculated from Eq. 10, with Δ G expressed by an empirical function (Eq. 1 through Eq. 10) [Böhm, 1994] .

| (11) | |
| --- | --- |

The values of the adjustable parameters, listed in Table 2, were obtained by fitting
experimental binding constants of 45 protein-ligand complexes.

Table 2: Values for adjustable parameters of Eq. 11

| Parameter | Value (kcal/mol) |
| --- | --- |
| Δ G 0 | 1.23 |
| Δ G hb | -1.07 |
| Δ G ion | -1.88 |
| Δ G lipo | -0.038 |
| Δ G rot | 0.33 |

In Eq. 11, Δ G 0 represents the contribution to the binding energy that does not directly depend on any specific interactions with the receptor (e.g., the contribution to binding energy due to loss of translational and rotational entropy of the fragment). 
Δ G hb and Δ G ion represent the contributions from an ideal hydrogen bond and an unperturbed ionic interaction, 
respectively. The Δ G lipo term represents the contribution from lipophilic interactions. The lipophilic contribution is assumed 
to be proportional to the lipophilic contact surface, A lipo , between the receptor and the fragment. The Δ G rot term 
represents the contribution due to the freezing of internal degrees of freedom in the fragment. NR is the number of acyclic 
sp 3 -sp 3 and sp 3 -sp 2 bonds. Rotations of terminal methyl or amino groups and flexibility of cyclic 
portions of the fragment are not taken into account. f (Δ R ) and f (Δα) are given in the Eqs. above.

The third scoring function (Eq. 12), termed Energy_Estimate_3, [Böhm, 1998] adds a term to Eq. 11 to account for aromatic-aromatic interactions:

| (12) | |
| --- | --- |

In the new term, the angular dependence of aromatic-aromatic interactions is ignored and a simple distance cutoff is used:

| (13) | f ( R ) = 1.0 | for R < 4.5 Å |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (14) | f ( R ) = 0 | for R ≥ 4.5 Å |

The values of the adjustable parameters, listed in Table 3, for the third scoring function
were obtained by fitting the experimental binding constants of 82 protein-ligand complexes.

Table 3: Values for adjustable parameters of Eq. 12

| Parameter | Value (kcal/mol) |
| --- | --- |
| Δ G 0 | -0.65 |
| Δ G hb | -0.72 |
| Δ G ion | -1.38 |
| Δ G lipo | -0.027 |
| Δ G rot | 0.21 |
| Δ G aro | -0.71 |

The scoring function, Energy_Estimate_2, is equivalent to Energy_Estimate_3 (Eq. 12) with Δ G aro-aro = 0.

# Rules governing the generation of interaction sites

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_rules-governing-generation-of-interaction-sites.htm

## Rules governing the generation of interaction sites

Interaction site generation is based on the rules used by the Ludi
algorithm. The position of an interaction site is described by the
distance R , the angle α, and the dihedral angle ω as defined in the following
figure:

Figure 1: Geometric parameters used for interaction site generation

The structures on the left are groups on the protein. The interaction sites are represented by the N-H groups on the right [Böhm, 1992b] .

The available experimental data for nonbonded contact geometries in
crystal packings of small organic molecules are used to define the
allowed values for R, α, and ω.
The region in space defined by these values is then populated by
discrete interaction sites. The error introduced into the subsequent
fitting of fragments by this description of the binding region
is of the order of the distance between the interaction sites.
However, since the accuracy of the atomic positions in a crystallographic
protein structure is within approximately 0.2 Å - 0.5
Å, this simplification appears to be justified. The rules
are summarized in the following table and described in more detail
in the following sections.

Table 1. Geometric parameters describing the allowed range of nonbonded contact geometries 
used by Ludi .

| Enzyme functional group | Interaction site | Geometric parameters | Reference(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C=O | D-X | R O../D = 1.9 Å α = 110 - 180° ω = 0 - 360° | [Murray-Rust and Glusker, 1984] , [Taylor and Kennard, 1984] , and [Klebe, 1991] |
| N-H O-H | A-Y | R H..A = 1.9 Å α = 150 - 180° ω = 0 - 360° | [Taylor and Kennard, 1984] , [Görbitz, 1989] , and [Klebe, 1991] |
| N-H (charged) | A-Y | R H..A = 1.8 Å α = 150 - 180° ω = 0 - 360° | [Taylor and Kennard, 1984] , [Görbitz, 1989] , and [Klebe, 1991] |
| COO- | D-X | R O../D = 1.8 Å α = 100 - 140° ω = -50 - 50°, 130 - 230° | [Görbitz and Etter, 1992] |
| =N- | D-X | R N../D = 1.9 Å α = 150 - 180° ω = 0 - 360° | [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] and [Klebe, 1991] |
| R-O-R (sp 2 ) | D-X | R O../D = 1.9 Å α = 100 - 140° ω = -50 - 50° | [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] , [Klebe, 1991] , and [Baker and Hubbard, 1984] |
| R-O-R (sp 3 ) | D-X | R O../D = 1.9 Å α = 90 - 130° ω = -70 - 70° | [Taylor and Kennard, 1984] , [Klebe, 1991] , and [Kroon et al., 1975] |

### H-donor and H-acceptor rules

The hydrogen bond geometry of carbonyl groups in the solid state has been investigated extensively 
( [Murray-Rust and Glusker, 1984] , [Taylor and Kennard, 1984] , and [Klebe, 1991] ). The available data 
show a distribution of α from 100° to 180° with a preference for the lone pair direction (α = 120°, ω = 180°). 
However, as this preference is not particularly pronounced, and the other regions are also significantly populated, so an even distribution of 
interaction sites was chosen with:

R O../D = 1.9 Å α = 110 - 180° ω = 0 - 360°

The optimal O../D-X hydrogen bond is assumed to be linear (Å O../D-X = 180°). This distribution 
is used for the backbone carbonyl groups and those in the side-chains of the amino acids Asn and Gln.

The distribution of H-acceptor atoms around a N-H group is tighter than that around a carbonyl group. The statistical analyses that have been 
published ( [Taylor and Kennard, 1984] , [Görbitz, 1989] , and [Klebe, 1991] ) all show a strong preference 
for a linear hydrogen bond with Å N-H..O/N = 150° - 180°. A similar distribution was also found around 
N-H groups in aromatic rings 
( [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] and [Klebe, 1991] ). The available data indicate 
similar distributions for N-H and O-H. Therefore, identical rules were chosen for both groups and interaction sites are generated with:

R H..A = 1.9 Å α = 150 - 180° ω = 0 - 360°

This distribution is used for the backbone N-H groups and the H-donor groups in the side-chains of the amino acids His, Gln, Asn, Ser, Thr, and 
Tyr. For charged amino groups, a slightly shorter hydrogen bond length R H..A = 1.8 Å is used. This shorter hydrogen 
bond length for charged groups was also observed experimentally [Görbitz, 1989] .

A problem arises with the generation of the position of the second atom Y adjacent to the H-acceptor position A. The optimal position of this 
second atom is difficult to obtain from the available experimental data. The position of the site Y was generated assuming 
Å N-H..A-Y = 0°, Å H..A-Y = 120°, and 
R A-Y = 1.23 Å, although the particular choice of the angle and the dihedral is admittedly somewhat arbitrary.

The hydrogen bond contact patterns around carboxylic acids have been studied by Görbitz and Etter [Görbitz and Etter, 1992] . The data indicate a preference for Å C=O..H = 120° 
and Å O-C-O..H = 0, 180°. They find no indication that syn hydrogen bonds are inherently more favorable than anti . Their data has been translated into the
following rules to generate the interaction sites around a carboxylic acid:

R O../D = 1.8 Å α = 100 - 140° ω = -50 - 50°, 130 - 230°

The distribution of H-donors around an unprotonated nitrogen in aromatic rings has been investigated by Vedani and Dunitz [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] . The distribution of hydrogen donors is narrower than that around a carbonyl group. The 
following rule (which applies to the unprotonated nitrogen in the side-chain of His) is derived from the results of
Vedani and Dunitz [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] :

R N../D = 1.9 Å α = 150 - 180° ω = 0 - 360°

Hydroxyl groups can act both as hydrogen donors and hydrogen acceptors. Although a detailed analysis of high resolution protein structures [Baker and Hubbard, 1984] shows that hydroxyl groups act more often as donors than acceptors, 
the possibility to act as an acceptor has to be taken into account.

For sp 2 oxygens, as found in the side-chain of Tyr, there is a clear preference for the hydrogen donor groups to lie in the plane of 
the aromatic ring. The data of 
Vedani and Dunitz [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] ,
Klebe [Klebe, 1991] , and 
Baker and Hubbard [Baker and Hubbard, 1984] are used to 
derive the following rule:

R O../D = 1.9 Å α = 100 - 140° ω = -50 - 50°

For sp 3 oxygen the data by Kroon et al. [Kroon et al., 1975] indicate a preference for the donor 
group to lie in the plane of the lone pairs (Å C-O..H = 109 ± 20°). However, no evidence 
is obtained for any preference of the lone pair direction within that plane. This contrasts with data obtained by Vedani and Dunitz [Vedani and Dunitz, 1985] and Klebe [Klebe, 1991] , who report a preferred 
orientation of hydrogen donor groups in the direction of the lone pairs. Since the experimental data is used merely to establish the allowed 
values for hydrogen bond patterns, an allowance is made for hydrogen bonds not pointing in the direction of the lone pair:

R O../D = 1.9 Å α = 90 - 130° ω = -70 - 70°

# Scaffold hopping by fragment replacement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_scaffold-hopping.htm

## Scaffold hopping by fragment replacement

Compounds derived from the same scaffold sometimes contain the same undesired property. In these cases, a different scaffold is needed to overcome the bad property. The process of identifying isofunctional molecular structures with significantly different scaffolds is called scaffold hopping (also known as, lead hopping). It is often used to replace an undesirable or patented core scaffold with a different chemotype.

The Replace Fragment protocol performs scaffold hopping by replacing part of the scaffold structure while maintaining the favorable binding between the receptor and the ligand. It first searches the fragment libraries to identify isosteric fragments, and then uses the isosteric fragments to replace the original fragment.

The fragment libraries are organized according to the number of attachment points and whether the fragment contains rings:

Figure 1: Organization of the fragment libraries

The fragment libraries can be prepared from a large ligand library using the Generate Fragment Libraries example protocol in Discovery Studio . The default libraries are generated using BIOVIA SCD and scPDB database. They are installed in < Pipeline Pilot Server directory>/apps/scitegic/dsdata/public/data/ReplaceFragment/Fragments . The statistics of the fragments are as follows:

| Number of R | Total Fragments | Unique Rings | Hetero Rings | Heteroaromatic Rings | Monocyclic Rings | Bicyclic Rings | Tricyclic Rings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1R-linear | 139201 | | | | | | |
| 1R-cyclic | 477749 | 9414 | 8879 | 4880 | 754 | 4251 | 4326 |
| 2R-linear | 183713 | | | | | | |
| 2R-cyclic | 400399 | 10852 | 10261 | 5678 | 782 | 4771 | 5223 |
| 3R-linear | 124621 | | | | | | |
| 3R-cyclic | 169795 | 8179 | 7680 | 4194 | 651 | 3536 | 3935 |

By default, the protocol uses the Num_Rings, Num_AromaticRings, and Molecular_SurfaceArea properties to calculate the similarity. These properties have been shown to give the best balance between chemotype diversity and isofunctional similarity with the original lead compound. The number of similar fragments is controlled by the maximum distance and the maximum number of fragments.

## Selecting the library to search

For the De Novo protocols, a fragment library must be specified using 
the Files Explorer . Several receptor and link 
libraries are provided with the installation of Discovery Studio .

A fragment library consist of two files:

* A structure file ( .str or .struct extensions).

* A targets file containing the specification of the ligand atoms for fragment matching ( .trg or .inp extensions).

Any one of these file types can be specified as the fragment library. 
When the job is run, a file with the same root name and appropriate extension corresponding to the other file type within the same 
folder is automatically identified.

# Surfaces theory

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_the_surfaces.htm

## Surfaces theory

### Receptor Surface

Receptor surfaces are on a receptor, covering atoms that are close to the current ligand. 
Atoms belonging to ligands and water residues are not included.

Ligands are identified as members of the Ligand Groups assembly.
The current ligand is identified either by the Current Ligand group, or, if such a group does not exist, is taken as the first ligand.
You can change the current receptor or ligand using Define Receptor and Define Ligand s in the View Interactions tool bar.

A receptor and ligand residue are considered to be in close contact if the distance between any pair of atoms does not exceed 5 Å.
You can adjust the radius in 1 Å increments using the Expand and Contract buttons.

To ensure consistent surfaces, Hydrogen atoms are automatically added if needed, but hidden.
Since water residues are not included in the surface construction, hydrogen atoms are not added to water residues.

The color of the surface vertices is obtained according to procedures outlined in the following sections.

### Receptor Surface Colored By Hydrogen Bond Donor/Acceptor

The color of the surface vertices is derived from the classification of the atoms covered by the surface
as either hydrogen bond donors or hydrogen bond acceptors.

If an atom is a hydrogen bond donor, the atom is assigned a fictitious charge of +1.
If an atom is a hydrogen bond acceptor, the atom is assigned a fictitious charge of -1.
All other atoms are ignored.
Since hydrogen atoms have been added, none of the atoms are classified as both a hydrogen bond donor
and hydrogen bond acceptor, as only the hydrogen atoms themselves are considered donors.

The charges are used to calculate a single-valued "potential" function at the location of each surface vertex.
The potential is obtained as the weighted average ∑ q w(q)*q of all charges q, with the weight w(q) for an individual charge q
set to the ratio s(q)/S, where s(q) is the inverse of the square distance between the position of the surface vertex and the position of the atom
carrying the charge, and S = ∑ q s(q) is the sum of the contributions s(q) from all charges.

This potential is then mapped using a numerically mapped color spectrum.

The default color spectrum used is Green-White-Magenta with RGB values of (0, 255, 0) for Green, (255, 255, 255) for White, and (255, 0, 255) for Magenta.
The full color map range of values is -1.0 to +1.0. However, it is narrowed to -0.1 to +0.1 by default for improved color contrast.
Negative values (Green) correspond to hydrogen bond acceptors, whereas positive values (Magenta) correspond to hydrogen bond donors.
The color map does not clip values that lie outside the (narrowed) range so values less than -0.1 are mapped to green and values larger 
than +0.1 are mapped to magenta.
The color map contains 256 individual colors obtained from interpolating between the three original spectrum colors.

### Receptor Surface Colored By Interpolated Charge

The procedure to arrive at the color of the surface vertices is analogous to the procedure described for the hydrogen bond donor/acceptor surface. 
In this case, the charges q used are the partial charges assigned to each atom covered by the surface. If no partial charges are available, the Gasteiger charge is calculated.

The default color spectrum used is Red-White-Blue with RGB values of (255, 0, 0) for Red, (255, 255, 255) for White, and (0, 0, 255) for Blue.
The full color map range of values is -1.0 to +1.0. However, it is narrowed to -0.1 to +0.1 by default for improved color contrast.
The color map does not clip values that lie outside the (narrowed) range, so that values less than -0.1 are mapped to the color Red and values larger than +0.1 are mapped to the color Blue.
The color map contains 99 individual colors obtained from interpolating between the three original spectrum colors.

### Receptor Surface Colored By Hydrophobicity

The procedure to arrive at the color of the surface vertices is analogous to the procedure described for the hydrogen bond donor/acceptor surface.
For each atom covered by the surface which is part of an amino acid residue, the hydrophobicity of the residue according to the Kyte-Doolittle scale is used as the fictitious charge on the atom.

The default color spectrum used is Blue-White-Brown with RGB values of (0, 0, 255) for Blue, (255, 255, 255) for White, and (139, 69, 19) for Brown.
The full color map range of values is -4.5 to +4.5. However, it is narrowed to -3.0 to +3.0 by default for improved color contrast.
Negative values (Blue) correspond to hydrophilic residues, whereas positive values (Brown) correspond to hydrophobic residues.
The color map does not clip values that lie outside the (narrowed) range, so that values less than -3.0 are mapped to the color Blue and values larger than +3.0 are mapped to the color Brown.
The color map contains 13 individual colors obtained from interpolating between the three original spectrum colors.

### Receptor Surface Colored By Ionizability

The procedure to arrive at the color of the surface vertices is analogous to the procedure described for the hydrogen bond donor/acceptor surface.
Fictitious charges are assigned to heavy atoms covered by the surface which are also part of an amino acid residue.
The charge value depends on the residue type.
For arginine residues, the atoms NE, NH1 and NH2 are assigned a charge of +1/3.
For histidine residues, the atoms ND1 and NE2 are assigned a charge of +1/2.
For lysine residues, the atom NZ is assigned a charge of +1.
For aspartic acid residues, the atoms OD1 and OD2 are assigned a charge of -1/2.
For glutamic acid residues, the atoms OE1 and OE2 are assigned a charge of -1/2.

The default color spectrum used is Red-White-Blue with RGB values of (255, 0, 0) for Blue, (255, 255, 255) for White, and (0, 0, 255) for Blue.
The full color map range of values is -1.0 to +1.0. However, it is narrowed to -0.1 to +0.1 by default for improved color contrast.
Negative values (Red) correspond to acidic residues, whereas positive values (Blue) correspond to basic residues.
The color map does not clip values that lie outside the (narrowed) range, so that values less than -0.1 are mapped to the color Red and values larger than +0.1 are mapped to the color Blue.
The color map contains 64 individual colors obtained from interpolating between the three original spectrum colors.

### Receptor Surface Colored By SAS (Solvent Accessibility Surface)

For each atom covered by the surface which is part of a residue for which the value V of the relative residue solvent accessibility ("Percent Solvent Accessibility") has been calculated, the value V is assigned to the atom. The final color of a surface vertex is then obtained by mapping the value V of the atom closest to the surface vertex. Atoms with a distance of more than 4 Å from the surface vertex are ignored. If there is no close enough atom, the surface vertex is colored white.

The default color spectrum used is Green-White-Blue with RGB values of (0, 255, 0) for Green, (255, 255, 255) for White, and (0, 0, 255) for Blue.
The full color map range of values is 0.0 to 100.0. However, it is narrowed to 10.0 to 25.0 by default for improved color contrast.
Small values (Green) correspond to buried residues, whereas large values (Blue) correspond to exposed residues.
The color map does not clip values that lie outside the (narrowed) range, so that values less than 10.0 are mapped to the color Red and values larger than 25.0 are mapped to the color Blue.
The color map contains 64 individual colors obtained from interpolating between the three original spectrum colors.

### Receptor Surface Colored By Aromatic Edge/Face

To arrive at a value q to be mapped to a color, the atoms covered by the surface which are part of amino acid residues are first attributed to aromatic rings depending on the residue type.
For each aromatic ring, the ring center and ring normal are calculated.
For histidine residues, the atoms CG, ND1, CD2, CE1 and NE2 are considered to be part of an aromatic ring.
For phenylalanine and tyrosine residues, the atoms CG, CD1, CD2, CE1, CE2 and CZ are considered to be part of an aromatic ring.
For tryptophan residues, the atoms CG, CD1, CD2, NE1, CE2 are considered to be part of a five-membered aromatic ring, and the atoms CD2, CE2, CE3, CZ2, CZ3 and CH2 are considered to be part of a six-membered aromatic ring.
The dot product dp between surface vertex normal and ring normal is calculated.
Since the relative orientation of the normals does not matter and to disambiguate between edges (dot product is 0) and faces (dot product is either +1 or -1), the dot product is then further transformed to arrive at the final value q = 2 * dp 2 - 1.
As a result, edges will map to the value -1, and faces will map to the value +1.
The value q is centered at the ring center, and the distance between surface vertex position and ring center is used in the calculation of the weighting factor w(q).
The remainder of the mapping procedure is then analogous to that described for the hydrogen bond donor/acceptor surface.

The default color spectrum used is Blue-White-Orange with RGB values of (0, 0, 255) for Blue, (255, 255, 255) for White, and (255, 127, 0) for Orange.
The full color map range of values is -1.0 to +1.0. However, it is narrowed to -0.1 to +0.1 by default for improved color contrast.
Negative values (Blue) correspond to the edges of aromatic rings, whereas positive values (Orange) correspond to the faces of aromatic rings.
The color map does not clip values that lie outside the (narrowed) range, so that values less than -0.1 are mapped to the color Blue and values larger than +0.1 are mapped to the color Orange.
The color map contains 64 individual colors obtained from interpolating between the three original spectrum colors.

#### Further information

Color Mapping dialog

# View Interactions tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/rcli_vit.htm

## View Interactions tools

A common task in Discovery Studio is to view a binding site and ligand in the Graphics View to understand the interactions between them. 
The View Interactions tools allow you to characterize and visualize ligand binding sites within receptors and to analyze the interactions between receptor residues and bound ligands. 
For an in-depth discussion of non-bond interactions, see Non-bond Interactions .

This set of tools analyzes the interactions between a receptor and a ligand. It can be used to view the interactions in a receptor-ligand complex determined by experiment or obtained from a set of ligands docked with a receptor.

### Define the receptor and ligand

Define Receptor: Defines the receptor to be used. By default, the first molecule in the active Molecule Window is set to be the receptor. You can change this by selecting a receptor and clicking this.

Define Ligand: Defines the selected molecule or ligand group as the current ligand. A current ligand is used to determine the starting position of the navigation tools. It is also used by the other tools that require a ligand.

The following navigation tools allow you to step through the ligands and change the current ligand definition.

Show First Ligand: Hides the current ligand and displays only the first ligand.

Show Previous Ligand: Hides the current ligand and displays only the previous ligand.

Show Next Ligand: Hides the current ligand and displays only the next ligand.

Show Last Ligand: Hides the current ligand and displays only the last ligand.

When navigating the ligands, only the visibility of the ligands will change. Receptors and other objects will maintain their current visibility.

### Display receptor-ligand interactions

Ligand Interactions: Creates a ligand monitor for analyzing interactions between the defined ligand and receptor. It shows the first interaction shell of the ligand with the receptor. The monitor is automatically updated based on changes to the chemistry. In addition, changes to the current defined ligand and receptor are also updated as you use the navigation buttons to browse the ligands or change the defined receptor. See Non-bond Interactions .

For details about visualizing non-bonded interactions with or without modifying the protein display, see General receptor-ligand interactions tasks | Visualize non-bonded interactions and General receptor-ligand interactions tasks | Visualize non-bonded interactions (without modifying protein display) .

Interaction Options: Controls the display of interactions while editing the complex. See Interaction Options dialog .

Expand: Displays additional shells of the non-bond monitor.

Expanding the shells of interactions for the non-bond monitor can be useful for understanding the supporting interactions of the residues that interact with the ligand.

Contract: Displays fewer shells of the non-bond monitor.

Show Distances: Displays labels of the interaction distances.

Show Types: Displays labels for the different interaction types.

### Display receptor surfaces

Receptor surfaces provide unique insight into the inner workings of a receptor. A surface is created on a receptor close to the current ligand, and Hydrogens are added automatically. The surface can be colored by a number of receptor atom properties. See Surfaces theory .

Non-bond interactions can also be visualized to better understand the interactions
responsible for binding. See Non-bond Interactions .

These tools create surfaces with a single click. For more control and customization of surfaces, use the Create Surface dialog , which is available from the Structure | Surfaces menu.

Aromatic: Creates a surface colored blue for aromatic ring edges and orange for aromatic ring faces.

H-Bond: Creates a surface colored by hydrogen bond type, with receptor donors colored in magenta and receptor acceptors in green.

Charge: Creates a surface colored by the interpolated
atomic charge of the receptor atoms.

Hydrophobic: Creates a surface colored by the hydrophobicity
of the receptor residues, from blue for hydrophilic to brown for hydrophobic.

Ionizability: Creates a surface colored by the ionizability
of the receptor residues, from blue for basic to red for acidic.

SAS: Creates a surface colored by the solvent accessibility
of the receptor residues from blue for exposed to green for buried.

When creating receptor surfaces, new groups are
created for the receptor atoms, pocket atoms (receptor atoms within a given radius
of the ligand), and ligand atoms.

Expand: Increases the radius from the ligand used to define the surface.

Contract: Decreases the radius from the ligand used
to define the surface.

### Change the visibility of the receptor and ligand.

Receptor: Controls the visibility of receptor atoms.

Ligand: Controls the visibility of the ligand.

Interacting Atoms: Controls the visibility of receptor 
atoms and residues that have non-bond interactions.

Pocket Atoms: Controls the visibility of pocket
atoms.

### Show receptor-ligand interactions on a 2D diagram.

Show 2D Diagram: Generates a 2D depiction of the defined ligand and the binding site residues of the
defined receptor, including amino acid residues, waters, and metal atoms. You can
use the diagram to select objects in the corresponding binding site displayed in
the Molecule Window. Interactions, such as hydrogen bond, charge-charge,
and Pi interactions
between the surrounding residues and the ligand are also displayed. Solvent accessibility
of the ligand atom and the amino acid residues are shown in light blue shading surrounding
the atom or residue. Heavier shading indicates more exposure to solvent.

### Analyze receptor-ligand interactions for a set of ligands.

Analyze Ligand Poses: Opens the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol dialog. This protocol calculates favorable and unfavorable interactions between a receptor and ligand poses. Additionally, the ligands can be filtered based on receptor interactions.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Receptor-Ligand Interactions \| View Interactions |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Receptor-Ligand Interactions \| View Interactions |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| View Interactions |

## Analyze Ligand Poses - Parameters

### Calculates receptor-ligand interactions

Calculates nonbonded interactions between a receptor and ligand poses. A table with statistical analysis of the interactions is provided. A histogram or heat map can be created to easily identify receptor interactions. The solvent accessible surface area SASA of the free and docked ligand can be calculated by using the Calculate Solvent Accessibility option.

In addition, ligands can be filtered by receptor interactions specified in Interacting Residues .

The following interaction categories are included:

* Favorable

* Unfavorable

* Charge

* Halogen

* Hydrophobic

* HydrogenBond

* Other

Depending on the Scope settings, properties many be added. For example, Unfavorable Total , Unfavorable A:GLU225 , etc.

Note:

* The frequency data from the histogram plots are also available in CSV file format for further analysis.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor when Hydrogen Bonds and/or Contacts properties are calculated. Ensure receptors have hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. By specifying Interacting Residues ligands can be filtered. |
| Interacting Residues | Ligands that do not have favorable interactions with the specified protein residues are filtered. Disabled when empty. Notes : The Interacting Residues Required parameter controls the filter logic (AND/OR logic). In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace e.g., "A:TYR132 A:HIS58". In Discovery Studio you specify the Interacting Residues by selecting an existing residue group. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ...". |
| Interacting Residues Required | Required Interacting Residues for a ligand to pass the filter. The following filter options are available: Any : Any of the specified residues should form an interaction with a ligand (OR logic). All : All of the specified residues should form an interaction with a ligand (AND logic). Valid Values: Any , All |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Rotated Atoms Property | Name of a property which contains the flexible receptor atom coordinates. Note : The flexible atom property will no longer be valid after changing the receptor atom order (such as after typing). |

Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. # Analyze Ligand Poses

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_analyze_ligand_poses.htm

## Analyze Ligand Poses

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

This protocol allows you to calculate non-bond receptor-ligand interactions on a set of ligand poses (e.g., the results of a docking run). Depending on the selected scope (i.e., molecule, chain, residue or atom), properties are added to easily identify the interacting protein region. Ligands can be filtered based on a specified residue selection. 
Optionally, one can determine the solvent accessible surface area (SASA) of the free and the bound ligand.
Tables summarizing the calculated interactions as well as histograms are available from the report and provide important information for further analysis. Additionally, heat map scripts are available to interactively visualize the receptor-ligand interactions.

The following interaction types are included in the calculation:

* Favorable

* Unfavorable

* Charge

* Halogen

* Hydrophobic

* HydrogenBond

* Other

This protocol takes into account the receptor's atom flexibility for each ligand by reading a property (created by protocols such as Dock Ligands (GOLD) , In Situ Ligand Minimization , and Flexible Docking ) that contains indices and coordinates of the rotated protein atoms. Therefore, changing the receptor atom order, for example by typing, may cause these properties to be out of sync, leading to erroneous results. To avoid this, use the Change Forcefield tool panel in the Simulation tool set to type the receptor with the CHARMm forcefield before running these protocols to ensure the receptor atom order is maintained.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools and click Analyze Ligand Poses to open the Analyze Ligand Poses dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Select the receptor from the list of molecules. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . For details about the remaining parameters, see Analyze Ligand Poses - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Select the receptor from the list of molecules. |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Analyze Ligand Poses - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

For details about visualizing non-bonded interactions with or without modifying the protein display, see "To visualize non-bonded interactions" and "To visualize non-bonded interactions (without changing the display of protein)" in General receptor-ligand interactions tasks .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Ligand poses with non-bond interaction properties. |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | The output file containing the ligands that failed, or were filtered. |
| <Frequencies_(Atoms\|Residues).csv | A CSV file formatted file containing residue or atom interaction frequency (depending on the protocol setting). |
| <ligands>_Residue.html | A file containing residue-interaction histograms. |
| <ligands>_stats.html | A file containing a statistical analysis of the interacting residues. |
| ViewHeatMap_<Type>.ds_pl | Open this file to view a heat map of the specified interaction type. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the output fragments with the input target receptor in a Molecule Window with the view centered on the binding site. Use the View Interactions tools to identify fragment hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View . |

#### Further information

Non-bond Interactions Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Calculate Binding Energies - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_calculate_binding_energies-para.htm

## Calculate Binding Energies - Parameters

### Estimates binding free energy using CHARMm implicit solvation models

The binding free energy is estimated between each ligand and the receptor. The free energy of binding for a receptor-ligand complex can be calculated from the free energies of the complex, the receptor, and the ligand. Using CHARMm based energies and implicit solvation methods it is possible to estimate these free energies and thus calculate an estimate for the overall binding free energy.

The following steps are performed:

* In Situ Ligand Minimization

* Calculate Ligand Conformational Entropy

* Binding Energy

Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings.

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* Binding Energy : Binding energy(kcal/mol)

* Ligand Energy : Ligand energy (kcal/mol)

* Protein Energy : Protein energy (kcal/mol)

* Complex Energy : Complex energy (kcal/mol)

* Entropic Energy : Entropic energy (kcal/mol)

The following properties are only added if Ligand Conformational Entropy is enabled:

* Ligand Conformational Energy : Energy difference (kcal/mol) of the ligand to the lowest-energy conformation

* Ligand Conformational Entropy : Uses a partition function to estimate ligand conformational entropy (kcal/mol-K)

* Total Binding Energy : Total binding energy (kcal/mol) which is the sum of Binding Energy + Ligand Conformational Energy

Notes:

* The receptor must be typed with the CHARMm forcefield.

* Receptor typing may change the atom order and therefore can result in incorrect Flexible Receptor Atom Property values being used. The Correct Rotated Atom Properties protocol in the examples folder will type the receptor and correct the Flexible Receptor Atom Property values in the ligand file accordingly. Ligand flexible receptor atom properties are created by protocol such as Dock Ligands (GOLD), or In Situ Ligand Minimization.

* An in situ ligand minimization step can be performed prior to the binding energy calculation to optimize the ligand in the binding pocket.

* The ligand free-energy change for "conformer focusing" can be estimated (Tirado-Rives, et al. , 2006). A bond ligand is typically not in the lowest-energy conformation for the unbound ligand and there is a loss of conformational degrees of freedom. This calculation does not include the receptor.

See Also:

* Tirado-Rives, J.; Jorgensen W. L. Contribution of conformer focusing to the uncertainty in predicting free energies for protein-ligand binding. J. Med. Chem. 2006 , 49, 5880-5884.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Receptor typed with CHARMm forcefield. |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Group by Property | Group the ligands by this property and calculate the average binding energies for each group. For example, an input SD file contains several ligands. Some ligands have more than one pose. In the SD file, different ligand poses of the same ligand share the same ligand name. If "Name" is chosen, then the binding energy averaged over all the poses for the same ligand will be reported for each ligand. |
| Flexible Receptor Atom Property | Name of a property which contains the flexible receptor atom coordinates. For example, after running ligand minimization with flexible receptor atoms or residues, a property named "Receptor.Positions" will be created for each of the flexible receptor atoms with the 3D coordinate in the following format: X1 Y1 Z1 atno AtomIndex1 X2 Y2 Z2 atno AtomIndex2 ... If this property is not found in the input ligands, it will be ignored. Note: Changing the order or number of atoms in the system, for example by typing, may make these properties out of date, giving erroneous results. A workaround is to type the receptor with CHARMm force field prior to docking so that the receptor atom order will not be changed. |
| In Situ Ligand Minimization | Perform a ligand minimization in the presence of the receptor prior to the binding energy calculation. Valid Values: True, False |
| Sphere of Flexible Atoms | Defines a Sphere within which the receptor atoms are free to move during the minimization. In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6). In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list. |
| Flexible Residues | Selects a group of receptor residues which will be flexible during minimization. |
| In Situ Ligand Minimization Minimization | Parameters for in situ ligand minimization. |
| In Situ Ligand Minimization Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not possible. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer |
| In Situ Ligand Minimization Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| In Situ Ligand Minimization Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization (kcal/mol-Å). If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| In Situ Ligand Minimization Minimization Energy Change | A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase. |
| Ligand Conformational Entropy | Calculate the ligand conformational entropy and energy. Note: Depending on the ligand flexibility the run time may increase significantly. Valid Values: True, False |
| Maximum Alignment RMSD | Maximum RMSD (Å) value for considering two poses as identical. |
| Conformation Generation | Conformation Generation |
| Conformation Method | Algorithm for generating conformations: FAST: quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations. BEST: ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR: very quickly provides conformations by sampling torsions. Valid Values: FAST , BEST, CAESAR |
| Maximum Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. |
| Ligand Conformational Entropy Minimization | Parameters for minimization. |
| Ligand Conformational Entropy Minimization Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not possible. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer |
| Ligand Conformational Entropy Minimization Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of minimization cycles. |
| Ligand Conformational Entropy Minimization Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance (kcal/(mol x Å)) applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Ligand Conformational Entropy Minimization Minimization Energy Change | A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : A modification of the Generalized Born model that allows for an implicit membrane in the calculations of the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. Not available if in-situ ligand minimization is on. Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) : The most rigorous yet slowest solvent approximation method based on continuum electrostatics. Not available if in-situ ligand minimization is on. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM), Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV) or PBSA is selected , this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. For GB and GBMV, this parameter is set to 1.0 internally and cannot be changed. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to GBIM or GBSW, the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is recommended to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for bulk solvent used in various implicit solvent models, including GB, GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Minimum hydrogen radius (Å) when Implicit Solvent Model is GB or GBIM. Note: Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address instabilities during the calculation, as the Generalized Born implicit solvent model has not been well validated for these forcefields. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). See Also: Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481. Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments: Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13. Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. |
| Salt Concentration | Salt concentration (mol/l) used in GBSW or PBSA. |
| Input Atomic Radii | Specify source of input atomic radii used in various implicit solvent models, including GBSW, GBMV or PBSA. van der Waals radii is the default. For charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, radii set derived by Nina et al. is recommended. See Also: Nina M.; Beglov D.; Roux B. Atomic Born radii for continuum electrostatic calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations. J. Phys. Chem. B 1997 , 101 , 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. |
| Use Molecular Surface | Whether to approximate Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) results with molecular surface. Applicable to GBSW only. Valid Values: True , False |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance . When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA)", an infinite cutoff will be used. |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Electrostatics | Treatment of long range electrostatics. Valid Values: Spherical Cutoff , Particle Mesh Ewald |
| Kappa | Specifies the width of the Gaussian function in the Particle-Mesh-Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/(Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance) and 6/(Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance). |
| Order | Specifies the order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle-Mesh-Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Estimate Entropy | Include translational and rotational entropy terms in the calculation. Only vacuum or distance-dependent implicit solvent model is supported. Valid Values: True , False |
| Entropy Temperature | Temperature at which to estimate entropy (K). |
| Partial Charge Estimation | Choose a method to assign partial charges. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,

For example, an input SD file contains several ligands. Some ligands have more than one pose. In the SD file, different ligand poses of the same ligand share the same ligand name. If "Name" is chosen, then the binding energy averaged over all the poses for the same ligand will be reported for each ligand.

Name of a property which contains the flexible receptor atom coordinates. X1 Y1 Z1 atno AtomIndex1

X2 Y2 Z2 atno AtomIndex2

If this property is not found in the input ligands, it will be ignored.

Note:

* Changing the order or number of atoms in the system, for example by typing, may
make these properties out of date, giving erroneous results. A workaround is to type the receptor with CHARMm force field prior to docking so that the receptor atom order will not be changed.

Perform a ligand minimization in the presence of the receptor prior to the binding energy calculation.

Defines a Sphere within which the receptor atoms are free to move during the minimization.

In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6).

In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list.

Selects a group of receptor residues which will be flexible during minimization.

Parameters for in situ ligand minimization.

Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are:

* Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate
vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions.

* Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation.

* Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations.

* Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not possible.

* Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation.

* Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) : The most rigorous yet slowest solvent approximation method based on continuum electrostatics. Not available if in-situ ligand minimization is on.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

# Calculate Binding Energies

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_calculate_binding_energies.htm

## Calculate Binding Energies

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Binding Energies protocol allows you to estimate the binding energy between a receptor and a ligand. You can optionally calculate the average binding energy across a set of related poses. Additionally, you can calculate the loss of conformational entropy and energy of a bound ligand [Tirado-Rives and Jorgensen, 2006] .

To calculate the binding energy and conformational entropy, you must specify a single receptor structure and a set of ligand poses. To calculate the average, you must group the ligands by a property such that each group has more than one member.

The binding energy is calculated using the following equation:

Energy Binding = Energy Complex - Energy Ligand - Energy Receptor

You can perform an optional In Situ Ligand Minimization step 
to remove any ligand van der Waals clashes prior to
calculating the binding energy and conformational entropy.
Without the minimization step, the binding energy values may have unreasonable values. You can minimize the ligands via either the In Situ Ligand Minimization step in this protocol, or the In Situ Ligand Minimization protocol. Note that these two approaches have different default parameter values and you may get slightly different minimized poses. To obtain the same minimized ligand poses, set Distance-Dependent Dielectrics to False in the In Situ Ligand Minimization protocol, and set Nonbond List Radius and Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to 13 and 9 respectively in this protocol.

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Ensure that the receptor is typed with the CHARMm forcefield.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools and click Calculate Binding Energies to open the Calculate Binding Energies dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Receptor typed with the CHARMm forcefield. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Receptor typed with the CHARMm forcefield. |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Binding Energies - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

This protocol uses special properties on the ligand specified by Flexible Receptor Atom Property , which indicates the location of flexible receptor atoms. Such properties, such as those created by the Dock Ligands (GOLD) and In Situ Ligand Minimization and Flexible Docking protocols,
use the atom indices. Changing the order or number of atoms in the system, for
example by typing, may leave these properties out of date, giving erroneous
results. A workaround is to type the receptor with CHARMm forcefield
before docking so the receptor atom order will not be changed.

By default the Estimate Entropy is enabled and the translational and rotational entropy 
properties are added:

* Protein Entropic Energy: Rotational and translational entropy of the protein (kcal/mol).

* Ligand Entropic Energy>: Rotational and translational entropy of the ligand (kcal/mol).

* Complex Entropic Energy: Rotational and translational entropy of the complex (kcal/mol).

* Entropic Energy: Difference between entropic energies of the complex, protein and ligand (kcal/mol).

* Rotational entropy: Rotational entropy calculated from the principal moments of inertia for the ligand (kcal/mol).

* Translational entropy: Corrected translational entropy for the ligand (kcal/mol).

* Rotational and translational entropy: Entropy Sum of the rotational and corrected translational entropies for the ligand (kcal/mol).

* The entropy is reported in energy terms (i.e., T * ΔS)

* These terms are not included in the binding energy but can be added to obtain the total binding energy. This is not done by default due to the accuracy of the entropy calculation.

* The entropy values are calculated using a CHARMm command that first calculates the principal moments of inertia for the complex, protein, and ligands. Using statistical mechanics, the principal moments are converted into rotational and translational entropies using the default Entropy Temperature of 298.15 K and a Σ value of 1 (for non-symmetric molecules). See Gaussian for details.

Enabling Ligand Conformational Entropy a set of ligand conformations is created and CHARMm minimized to calculate the relative energy with respect to the lowest energy pose. Using a modified partition function, the ligand conformational entropy is estimated. Detailed information can be found at Tirado-Rives and Jorgensen, 2006 .

The Ligand Conformational Energy is calculated with the following equation:

The following properties are added:

* Ligand Conformational Energy: Energy difference of the ligand to the lowest-energy conformation (kcal/mol).

* Ligand Conformational Entropy: Ligand conformational entropy (kcal/mol-K).

* Ligand Relative Energy: Energy difference to the low energy pose (kcal/mol).

* Ligand Degeneracy: Degeneracy of this ligand (states that have the same energy).

* Ligand RMSD to Reference: RMSD to low energy pose.

* Number of Ligand Conformations: Number of distinct conformation poses.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Contains the ligands molecules with the associated calculated Binding Energy values. Each molecule has the Protein Energy, Ligand Energy, Complex Energy, Binding Energy properties, and optionally Entropic Energy property, if Estimates Entropy is selected when running the protocol. For each unique value of the Input Group by Property in the input file, the Average Binding Energy is also reported. |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | Contains ligands that failed the protocol. |
| charmm.log | CHARMm log file. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open ViewResults.ds_pl to view the ligands in the Molecule Window . The Input Receptor is also shown, with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify ligand hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View . |

#### Further information

Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing
