If this percentage is less than the specified value, the fragment is discarded. For example, a value of 70 means that only those fragments whose surfaces are 70% in contact with the receptor are suggested by Ludi. A value of zero for this parameter means that the surface area contact criterion is not used. Increasing the value of the Minimum Surface parameter will reduce the number of hits. The algorithm that Ludi uses to calculate the surface area yields only approximate values, so the Minimum Surface parameter should be viewed as a rough paring method. |
| Hit Criteria Minimum Score | Minimum score for a fragment fit. Note : If you modify this parameter, you may get different results, even if you do not adjust the other parameters. This is because the algorithm will pursue more iterations to satisfy the score threshold. |
| Hit Criteria Maximum Unfilled Cavity | Maximum size for buried cavities produced by a fragment fit (Å 3 ). If the specified value is larger than 0, Ludi searches for buried cavities after fitting a fragment, and, if the cavity is larger than the value specified, the fit is rejected. The size of the cavity is determined by the number of unoccupied cubes between the protein and the ligand with no connection to bulk solvent. |
| Hit Criteria Limit Number of Hits | Limit the number of hits returned. The value can be set in Hit Criteria Maximum Number of Hits . Valid Values: True, False |
| Hit Criteria Maximum Number of Hits | Maximum number of fragments Ludi suggests. When the number of accepted fragments equals the specified value, Ludi discontinues searching the fragment library. |
| Hit Criteria Search Method | Determines the fragment search method. The following options are available: FAST : as soon as a hit has been found with a matching set of interaction sites, no further attempts are made to fit this set of fragment target sites to any of the matched interaction sites. The fragment position with the highest score is saved. BEST : fitting is exhaustive, allowing all combinations of interaction sites to be matched against a specific set of target sites on the fragment, and the fragment position with the best score is saved. Note : The combinations of target sites that Ludi considers for a specific fragment is specified in the target library file. Valid Values: FAST , BEST |
| Hit Criteria Reject Bifurcated Hydrogen Bonds | Reject bifurcated hydrogen bonds. A bifurcated hydrogen bond is one in which an acceptor is symmetrically paired with two donors or vice versa. Valid Values: True, False |
| Hit Criteria Reject Unpaired Buried Polar Groups | Reject hits that bury unpaired polar groups on either the fitted fragment or the receptor. Valid Values: True , False |
| Hit Criteria Minimum Electrostatic Repulsion Distance | Reject electrostatic repulsions of the specified minimum distance or less (Å). Leave blank to consider all interactions. For example, if fragments are being fit at a metal ion coordination sites. The distance separating polar oxygen pairs or oxygen/nitrogen pairs is compared to the value of the parameter plus 0.8 Å. A default value of 2.5 Å is recommended. |
| Interaction Site | Parameters that control the interaction site generation. |
| Interaction Site Density of Lipophilic Sites | Density of lipophilic sites. When Ludi finds an interaction site, it populates the site with points or vectors that represent the geometry of the site. This parameter specifies how dense Ludi should make the population of points in interaction sites for lipophilic atoms. Too large a value here slows down the Ludi program though it increases the chances of finding suitable fragments. A value between 10 and 25 is recommended. |
| Interaction Site Density of Polar Sites | Density of polar sites. When Ludi finds an interaction site, it populates the site with points or vectors that represent the geometry of the site. This parameter specifies how dense Ludi should make the population of vectors in interaction sites for hydrogen bonds. Too large a value here slows down the Ludi program though it increases the chances of finding suitable fragments. A value between 15 and 25 is recommended. |
| Interaction Site Preselection Factor | Preselection factor controls the Ludi algorithm for selecting the combination of interaction sites onto which a fragment is fit. Ludi searches the list of interaction sites by distance criteria for suitable pairs, triplets, and quadruplets to match the fragments. For each set of interaction sites, the distances between interaction sites are compared to the fragment's corresponding intramolecular distances. For any corresponding pair of interaction site distance and fragment intramolecular distance, if the difference between the two is greater than the product of the values of the Preselection Factor parameter and the Maximum RMSD (see Fitting ), then the fragment is not fit to that set of interaction sites. Recommended values are between 1.5 and 2.5. Values larger than this tend to increase the time it takes for Ludi to fit fragments but can increase the number of fragments that Ludi is able to suggest. Values smaller than this speed up the Ludi program at the expense of sometimes missing a potentially useful fragment. |
| Interaction Site Differentiate Lipophilic Interactions | Match aliphatic fragment atoms with aliphatic receptor atoms, or aromatic fragment atoms to aromatic receptor atoms. Valid Values: True, False |

Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure receptors have hydrogens and complete valence shells.

In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules.

* The receptor should not contain alternate conformations.

* You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor.

Only fragments which interact with all specified receptor atoms are selected. 
Specified atoms should be in the site sphere.

In Discovery Studio, select a group containing the desired receptor atoms.

Defines a sphere in the receptor where receptor-ligands interactions are permitted.

In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6).

In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list.

Select a link fragment library file. Fragment libraries consist of two files that need to be in the same directory, however, only one needs to be selected.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Parameter that control the fragment fitting.

Ludi scoring function to use to prioritize the fragment hits for receptor-based runs.

Three different algorithms are available, each estimates the change in free energy upon binding the fragment to the receptor. Each fragment is evaluated as a function of the potential number of hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic and ionic contacts it can make and an estimate is made of the penalty due to freezing the internal degrees of freedom of the ligand.

The following scoring functions are available:

* Energy estimate 1

* Energy estimate 2

* Energy estimate 3

Valid Values: Energy estimate 1, Energy estimate 2, Energy estimate 3

Relative weight for aligning a fragment with lipophilic interaction sites.
A factor of 10 can be effective.

Relative weight for aligning a fragment with the hydrogen bond interaction sites.
A factor of 10 can be effective.

Specifies the maximum number of attempts to fit a fragment to a set of interaction sites (maximum 1000000).

Maximum root mean square deviation (RMSD) from maximal receptor ligand interaction (Å). At each receptor interaction site there is some range of interaction geometry between the ligand and receptor that maximizes the interaction. Deviation from this maximum, therefore, constitutes a measure of the quality of fit. Poor fits have high deviations and good fits have low deviations. As Ludi fits each fragment to the interaction sites, the RMSD is computed. For most fragments, if the RMSD exceeds the value of Maximum RMSD, the fragment is discarded. If Ludi is trying to fit a large fragment, it may allow the RMSD to exceed the value of the Maximum RMSD parameter.

* None : only existing library conformations are used.

* One at a Time : conformations are generated by rotating each rotatable bond without changing the angle of other rotatable bonds in the fragment.

* Two at a Time : rotatable bonds are altered in pairs to generate new fragment conformations.

Note :

* The degree of rotation depends on the periodicity of the dihedral angle. For bonds connecting two sp3 carbons, the rotation is done in 120° increments. For bonds connecting two sp2 carbons, the rotation is done in 180° increments. For fragments with multiple rotatable bonds, only one bond is modified at a time.

Valid Values: None, One at a time, Two at a time

Generate and fit both the fragments in the library and their mirror image.

Valid Values: True, False

Parameters for filtering fragments.

A fragment is only accepted if all specified groups are found.

A fragment is rejected if any of the specified groups is found.

A fragment is accepted if all of the specified elements are found.

A fragment is rejected if any of the specified elements is found.

Minimum number of atoms in the fragments.

Maximum number of atoms in the fragments (for libraries with larger fragments a value of 150 is suggested).

Require fragments to contain charged functional groups.

* No formal charge requirement : no fragment charge required

* Positive (ammonium, amidino, guanidino) : positive fragment charge required

* Negative (carboxylate) : negative fragment charge required

Valid Values: No formal charge requirement , Positive (ammonium, amidino, guanidino), Negative (carboxylate)

Comma separated range of fragments in the library to search. The first fragment in the library is indicated by 1. The last fragment is indicated by END.

Parameters for controlling the criteria for a hit.

Minimum distance (Å) that must separate intermolecular pairs of carbon atoms. As Ludi considers each library fragment, it fits the fragment onto the interaction sites, then checks that the fragment's carbon atoms do not overlap receptor carbon atoms. Pairs of carbon atoms whose centers are separated by a distance less than or equal this value are considered to have undesirable overlap.
Although the value for the Minimum Separation parameter only pertains to pairs of carbons, Ludi derives threshold distances for other atom pairs from it and checks all intermolecular pairs for overlap. The threshold distances for non-carbon atoms are obtained by scaling the specified value in a manner consistent with the relative sizes of the carbon and non-carbon van der Waals radii.
A value between 3.0 and 3.5 is recommended.

Minimum percentage of surface area contact between the fragment and receptor. When Ludi considers whether it is appropriate to suggest a particular fragment, one of the criteria it considers is the percentage of the fragment surface area that is in contact with the receptor. If this percentage is less than the specified value, the fragment is discarded. For example, a value of 70 means that only those fragments whose surfaces are 70% in contact with the receptor are suggested by Ludi. A value of zero for this parameter means that the surface area contact criterion is not used. Increasing the value of the Minimum Surface parameter will reduce the number of hits. The algorithm that Ludi uses to calculate the surface area yields only approximate values, so the Minimum Surface parameter should be viewed as a rough paring method.

Minimum score for a fragment fit.

* If you modify this parameter, you may get different results, even if you do not adjust the other parameters.
This is because the algorithm will pursue more iterations to satisfy the score threshold.

The size of the cavity is determined by the number of unoccupied cubes between the protein and the ligand with no connection to bulk solvent.

Limit the number of hits returned. The value can be set in Hit Criteria Maximum Number of Hits .

Maximum number of fragments Ludi suggests. When the number of accepted fragments equals the specified value, Ludi discontinues searching the fragment library.

Determines the fragment search method. 
The following options are available:

* FAST : as soon as a hit has been found with a matching set of interaction sites, no further attempts are made to fit this set of fragment target sites to any of the matched interaction sites. The fragment position with the highest score is saved.

* BEST : fitting is exhaustive, allowing all combinations of interaction sites to be matched against a specific set of target sites on the fragment, and the fragment position with the best score is saved.

Valid Values: FAST , BEST

Reject bifurcated hydrogen bonds. A bifurcated hydrogen bond is one in which an acceptor is symmetrically paired with two donors or vice versa.

Reject hits that bury unpaired polar groups on either the fitted fragment or the receptor.

Valid Values: True , False

The distance separating polar oxygen pairs or oxygen/nitrogen pairs is compared to the value of the parameter plus 0.8 Å. A default value of 2.5 Å is recommended.

# De Novo Receptor

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_de_novo_receptor.htm

## De Novo Receptor

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The De Novo Receptor protocol identifies potential fragments that fit
well within a user-specified binding site of a receptor. The De Novo method
is advantageous as it is fast and the variety of molecules that can
be generated is extremely large.

The protocol uses a library of fragments and suggests how suitable fragments can be positioned into clefts of protein
structures (for example an active site of an enzyme) in such a way that hydrogen bonds can be formed with the enzyme and
hydrophobic pockets are filled with hydrophobic groups.
An advantage to this approach is that it is fast and a large number of fragments can be screened quickly.
The protocol uses pregenerated libraries of these fragments, which can be generated using the De Novo Library Generation protocol.

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Ensure that the receptor has hydrogens added and atom valencies are satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed.

* From the Graphics View, select the receptor.

* Open the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel and
click Define Receptor .

* Use the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel to define a receptor sphere.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Fragment Based Design tools and click De Novo Receptor to open the De Novo Receptor dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Choose the selected receptor. Input Site Sphere Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Input Fragment Libraries Specify a receptor fragment library . For details about the remaining parameters, see De Novo Receptor - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Choose the selected receptor. |
| Input Site Sphere | Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. |
| Input Fragment Libraries | Specify a receptor fragment library . |

For details about the remaining parameters, see De Novo Receptor - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| DeNovo.log | Contains the output from the Ludi inhibitor program. |
| <ludilibrary>.sd | Contains all the fragments identified by Ludi as a hit. |
| Ludi.interactionmap.mol2 | Contains the Ludi interaction map (see Interaction site generation ). Ludi models the H-donor and H-acceptor interaction sites with vectors (atom pairs) to account for the strong directionality of hydrogen bonds. H-donor vectors are represented by N-H , and H-acceptor vectors are represented by C=0 . Lone carbon atoms indicate Ludi aliphatic and aromatic sites. |
| Ludi.targetsites.txt | Contains the Ludi target sites. During a Ludi run up, to 6 fragment atoms, or groups of fragment atoms, are fit to the receptor. This file lists the fragment target atoms selected from the fragment library file during the fitting procedure. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the output fragments with the input target receptor in a Molecule Window with the view centered on the binding site. Use the View Interactions tools to identify fragment hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View . |

#### Further information

# Dock Fragments (MCSS) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_dock_fragments_mcss-para.htm

## Dock Fragments (MCSS) - Parameters

### Places fragments in a receptor active site using MCSS (Multiple Copy Simultaneous Search)

MCSS (Multiple Copy Simultaneous Search) is used for ligand design. MCSS generates a collection of positioned and oriented chemical functional groups that interact in some way with the binding-site region of a molecule.

The MCSS protocol consists of several steps:

* Generate fragment conformations.

* Distribute fragment copies randomly in the receptor search sphere cavity.

* CHARMm fragment minimization.

* Cluster and remove fragments that converge to similar positions.

Notes:

* Steps 3 and 4 are repeated until convergence.

* Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings.

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* MCSS_Score : fragment score (negative energy value)

* MOL_NUMBER : molecule number

* POSE_NUMBER : pose number

* RMSD_Cluster : root mean square deviation (RMSD) to the cluster center

* Cluster : cluster number

See Also:

* Miranker, A.; Karplus, M. Functionality maps of binding sites: a multiple copy simultaneous search method. Proteins: Struct., Funct., Bioinf. 1991 , 11, 29-34

* Caflisch, A.; Miranker, A.; Karplus, M. Multiple copy simultaneous search and construction of ligands in binding sites: application to inhibitors of HIV-1 aspartic proteinase, J. Med. Chem. 1993 , 36, 2142-2167.

* Evensen, E.; Joseph-McCarthy, D.; Karplus, M. MCSS version 2.1, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA USA, 1997.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure receptors have hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Input Fragments | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. Notes: Fragments with more than 70 atoms are rejected. |
| Generate Conformations | Generate conformations for each incoming fragment. This will increase the conformational space explored during MCSS docking. Each conformation will go through the MCSS docking cycle and the final output will only contain the top scoring fragments. Notes: This option is only available, if the fragments are not grouped. Depending on the number of rotatable bonds this will increase the computational time significantly. Valid Values: True, False |
| Conformation Method | Algorithm for generating conformations: FAST: quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations. BEST: ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR: very quickly provides conformations by sampling torsions. Valid Values: FAST, BEST , CAESAR |
| Maximum Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. |
| Discard Existing Conformations | Discard existing input conformations. Valid Values: True , False |
| Use Template Fragments | Dock predefined fragments specified in the Fragments parameter. Valid Values: True, False |
| Fragments | A list of predefined fragments. These fragments are defined under Advanced in the Fragment SMILES Templates parameter. Valid Values: 2-butene, 2-butyne, 5-methylene-dihydropyridine, N-methyl acetamide , N-methyl-acetamide with one water, N-methylmethylaminomethylketone, acetate, acetate ion (aspartate side chain), acetonitrile, acetylene, arginine side chain (propylguanidinium ion), asparagine side chain (acetamide), benzene, cyclohexane, cysteine side chain (methanethiol), dimethyl acetamide, dimethyl ether, glutamate side chain (butanoic acid), glutamine side chain (propanamide), histidine side chain (5-methyl imidazole), isoleucine side chain (butane), leucine side chain (isobutane), lysine side chain (1-amino pentane ion), methane, methanol, methionine side chain (ethanethiol), methyl ammonium, methyl cyclohexane, phenol, proline side chain (dimethylpyrolidine), propane, propyne, protonated piperidine, thiazole, threonine side chain (ethanol), trifluoromethane, trimethylamine ion, tryptophan side chain (3-methylindole), tyrosine, vinylogous peptide subunit (N-2-butyl-acetamide), water |
| Input Site Sphere | Defines a sphere in the receptor where receptor-ligands interactions are permitted. In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6). In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list. |
| Number of Replicas | The number of random fragment replicas which are initially placed into the receptor sphere cavity. Note: Disabled when fragments are grouped. |

Percentage : The percent of the incoming data to keep (e.g., "15" would keep exactly 15% of the incoming data). | Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Iteration Profile | Iteration profile for the MCSS minimization. The following options are available: Default : 500 steps of steepest descent followed by 300 steps of additional steepest descent and then 20x500 steps of Powell minimization. Fast : 200 steps of steepest descent followed by 100 steps of additional steepest descent and then 5x200 steps of Powell minimization. Conjugate : 500 steps of steepest descent followed by 300 steps of additional steepest descent and then 20x500 steps of conjugate gradient. Descent : 2000 steps of steepest descent followed by another 2000 steps of additional steepest descent and then 20x500 steps of Powell minimization. Determines how Number of Replicas Number to Keep is applied:

* Number of Records : 
The number is the exact number of incoming records to keep.

* Proportion : 
The number is the proportion of the entire incoming data set to keep (e.g., 0.15 would keep exactly 15% of the incoming data).

* Percentage : 
The percent of the incoming data to keep (e.g., "15" would keep exactly 15% of the incoming data). (This is just the proportion times 100, but it's sometimes easier to think in percentages rather than proportions).

Valid Values: Number of Records , Proportion, Percentage

Cluster information is added to data stream.

In addition, a second output file is created containing only the best scoring fragment pose for each cluster.

Root mean square deviation (RMSD) threshold for pose clustering (Å).

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Iteration profile for the MCSS minimization. The following options are available:

* Default :
500 steps of steepest descent followed by 300 steps of additional steepest descent and then 20x500 steps of Powell minimization.

* Fast :
200 steps of steepest descent followed by 100 steps of additional steepest descent and then 5x200 steps of Powell minimization.

* Conjugate :
500 steps of steepest descent followed by 300 steps of additional steepest descent and then 20x500 steps of conjugate gradient.

* Descent :
2000 steps of steepest descent followed by another 2000 steps of additional steepest descent and then 20x500 steps of Powell minimization.

* User Defined :
External file which contains the CHARMm minimization script (please ensure the format is correct).

Valid Values: Default , Fast, Conjugate, Descent, User Defined

User Defined Minimization file (IPF). Please ensure that this file is in the correct format.

Method for assigning partial charges to the fragment during forcefield assignment.

Valid Values: MMFF, CHARMm , cff

Fragments with a larger root mean square deviation (RMSD) value (Å) are considered duplicates during the minimization cycle and are removed. A large value will reduce the number of poses returned.

Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation.

Available options are:

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics

Dielectric constant for the solvent model.

The initial energy cutoff for deleting groups with unfavorable interaction energies after the second set of minimization steps (kcal/mol). The value is the negative of the MCSS_Score.

The final cutoff for deleting groups with unfavorable interaction energies (kcal/mol).
The value is the negative of the MCSS_Score.

Nonbonded atom cutoff (Å).

Generates a random distribution of functional groups in a given sphere such that no group is closer than a user-specified distance cutoff to any portion of the binding region.

If set to False, it is assumed that the fragments are already distributed in the search sphere.

* If this option is set to False, the fragment templates are disabled.

* This option is available if Conformation Generation is set to False.

Controls the canonical SMILES calculation for grouping fragments which are
already distributed together.

* If multiple actions are selected, they are performed in the given order.

Valid Values: Kekulize , StandardizeStereo, StandardizeCharges, MakeAllAtomsCarbon, MakeAllBondsSingle, ClearStereo, ClearUnknownStereo , ClearCisTransBondStereo , ClearCharges, SetStereoFromCoordinates, RepositionStereoBonds, ClearQueryInfo , NeutralizeBondedZwitterions

Distance threshold for generating random fragments (Å).
A fragment is rejected if the fragment-protein distance is smaller than the specified value.

Seed for the random number generator to distribute the fragments in the search sphere.

* Valid SMILES pattern

* Name for the filter

Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records.

Notes :

* Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size.

Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster).

# Dock Fragments (MCSS)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_dock_fragments_mcss.htm

## Dock Fragments (MCSS)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dock Fragments (MCSS) protocol is a fully automated fragment docking implementation which is based on Harvard MCSS version 2.1, developed in collaboration with M. Karplus ([Evensen et al., 1997] and [Miranker and Karplus, 1991]) . MCSS searches for low energy fragment binding positions in a protein receptor.

Functional groups can then be linked together to construct ligands that are complementary to the binding site of the target, or these fragments can be used to modify ligands to improve their binding affinity.

MCSS is limited to 70 fragment atoms and a low number of rotational bonds.

For a description and details about the strengths and weaknesses of the available docking protocols, see Choose a docking protocol .

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Ensure that the receptor has hydrogens added and all atom valencies are satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed.

* From the Graphics View, select the receptor.

* Open the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel and
click Define Receptor .

* Click From Current Selection .

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Fragment Based Design tools and click Dock Fragments (MCSS) to open the Dock Fragments (MCSS) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Select the receptor from the list of molecules.
The receptor must have hydrogens added and all atom valencies satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed. Input Ligands Specify the fragments to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Site Sphere Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Number of Replicas Determines how many initial fragment replicas are generated in the cavity of the receptor sphere. The number should be increased for smaller fragments or a large sphere. A higher number of replicas increases the calculation time. For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Fragments (MCSS) - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Select the receptor from the list of molecules. The receptor must have hydrogens added and all atom valencies satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed. |
| Input Ligands | Specify the fragments to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Site Sphere | Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. |
| Number of Replicas | Determines how many initial fragment replicas are generated in the cavity of the receptor sphere. The number should be increased for smaller fragments or a large sphere. A higher number of replicas increases the calculation time. |

A higher number of replicas increases the calculation time.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Fragments (MCSS) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

View the docked in the Molecule Window .
The Input Receptor is also 
shown, with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the fragments and view the 3D structure, a 2D 
depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify, fragment hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

Docked fragments are sorted by the MCSS_Score. The MCSS_Score is the negative sum of the fragment-protein interaction energy and the fragment energy.
When comparing MCSS_Scores for different fragments, it is recommended that you add the fragment vacuum energy, which can be calculated with the Calculate Energy protocol.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <fragment>.sd | Contains the docked fragments with the MCSS_Score. |
| <fragment>_clustered.sd | If Cluster Results is enabled, this file is generated. It contains the top scoring poses for the set clustering Radius . Each cluster contains statistical information about the center: Cluster: Cluster center number MCSS_Score_Mean: The mean MCSS_Score score of the cluster MCSS_Score_StdDev: The MCSS_Score Standard deviation of the cluster MCSS_Score_N: The number of fragments that are in the cluster (including the top scoring cluster center) |
| <fragment>_fail.sd | Contains any fragments that failed. It is not created if there are no failures. |
| RMol.log | Log file containing information on random fragment placement, if that calculation was performed. |
| MCSS.log | Log file containing information on the CHARMm iterations. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the docked fragments with the input receptor in a Molecule Window with the view centered on the binding site. |

* Cluster: Cluster center number

* MCSS_Score_Mean: The mean MCSS_Score score of the cluster

* MCSS_Score_StdDev: The MCSS_Score Standard deviation of the cluster

* MCSS_Score_N: The number of fragments that are in the cluster (including the top scoring cluster center)

# Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_dock_ligands_cdocker-para.htm

## Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) - Parameters

### Docks ligands into an active site using CHARMm

Uses a CHARMm-based molecular dynamics (MD) scheme to dock ligands into a receptor binding site. Random ligand conformations are generated using high-temperature MD. The conformations are then translated into the binding site. Candidate poses are then created using random rigid-body rotations followed by simulated annealing. A final minimization is then used to refine the ligand poses.

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* TopHits : Number of hits per ligand.

* -CDOCKER_ENERGY : Negative of the CDOCKER energy.

* -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY : Negative of the CDOCKER interaction energy.

* POSE_NUMBER : Pose number.

See Also:

* Wu, G.; Robertson, D. H.; Brooks, C. L. III; Vieth, M. Detailed Analysis of Grid-Based Molecular Docking: A Case Study of CDOCKER - A CHARMm-Based MD Docking Algorithm. J. Comp. Chem. 2003, 24, 1549.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure the receptor has hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Site Sphere | Defines a sphere in the receptor for initial ligand placement. In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6). In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list. Notes: If the ligand is already placed in the active site, a sphere definition is not required. In this case the sphere coordinates and radius are calculated from the ligand center and the radius of gyration, respectively. The radius of the sphere may affect the docking results due to the location of the energy grid. |
| Top Hits | Number of diverse top poses saved. The diversity can be controlled by Pose Cluster Radius . |
| Pose Cluster Radius | Radius for pose clustering to increase the diversity of the docked poses (Å). If no value is specified, the clustering is disabled. |
| Random Conformations | Number of starting random conformations generated from equilibration and minimization of the starting ligand structure. If set to 0, the original input structure is used and no conformers are generated. |
| Random Conformations Dynamics Steps | Number of steps of high temperature MD used to generate random starting conformations. |
| Random Conformations Dynamics Target Temperature | Target temperature in the high temperature MD used to generate random starting conformations (K). |
| Include Electrostatic Interactions | Include electrostatics in random structure generation. Valid Values: True , False |
| Orientations to Refine | Number of rotated ligand orientations to refine for each of the conformations from dynamics. If set to 0, no rotations are performed. |
| Maximum Bad Orientations | Maximum number of ligand orientations to evaluate per dynamics conformation for generating the starting ligand poses. |
| Orientation vdW Energy Threshold | Maximum van der Waals energy when evaluating different ligand orientations. Conformations exceeding this threshold will be discarded. |
| Simulated Annealing | Perform simulated annealing refinement. Valid Values: True , False |
| Heating Steps | Number of heating phase steps during simulated annealing. |
| Heating Target Temperature | Heating stage target temperature during simulated annealing (K). |
| Cooling Steps | Number of cooling phase steps during simulated annealing. |
| Cooling Target Temperature | Cooling stage target temperature during simulated annealing (K). |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Forcefield | Forcefield for atom typing: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. Note : The cff forcefield uses the full potential and hence requires more CPU time (i.e., not grid-based). Valid Values: CHARMm , cff |
| Use Full Potential | Use full potential for CDOCKER, or a faster grid-based method. Valid Values: True, False |
| Ligand Partial Charge Method | Choose a method to assign partial charges. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone : Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF : Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF : Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF |
| Final Minimization | Refined pose minimization method: Off : No minimization. Grid-based : Fast, but less accurate. Full potential : Slow, but most accurate. Note : A full potential minimization is always performed when cff is selected. Valid Values: Off, Grid-based, Full Potential |
| Final Minimization Gradient Tolerance | Average gradient tolerance during the final minimization (kcal/mol-Å). The minimization routine will exit if the average gradient is less than or equal to this value. |
| Prepare Input Receptor | Prepares and verifies the Input Receptor for docking by: Adding hydrogen to satisfy any unsatisfied valencies Removing alternate aminoacid conformations Valid Values: True , False |
| Grid Extension | Grid extension beyond ligand bounds (Å). The algorithm first calculates the smallest containing box around the ligand. Each side of the box is then extended by half this value. |
| Random Number Seed | Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock. The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers. See Also: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/ |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

# Dock Ligands (CDOCKER)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_dock_ligands_cdocker.htm

## Dock Ligands (CDOCKER)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) protocol is an implementation of the CDOCKER algorithm [Wu et al., 2003] .
It allows you to run a refinement docking of any number of ligands with a single protein receptor.

CDOCKER is a grid-based molecular docking method that employs CHARMm. The receptor is held rigid while the ligands are allowed to flex during the
refinement. For predocked ligands, prior knowledge of the binding site is not required. It is possible, however, to specify the ligand placement in the active site using a binding site sphere.

Random ligand conformations are generated from the initial ligand structure through high temperature molecular dynamics, followed by random
rotations. The random conformations are refined by grid-based (GRID 1) simulated annealing and a final grid-based or full forcefield
minimization.

The high temperature molecular dynamics step can change the ligand stereochemistry.
For example, a cis double bond can be reorganized to form a trans bond.

The output of this protocol is a set of refined ligand poses that can be loaded into the Molecule Window.

For a description and details about the functionality of the available docking protocols, see Choose a docking protocol .

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Ensure that the receptor has hydrogens added and atom valencies are satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed.

* Optionally, open the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel and 
click Define Site from Receptor Cavities to find and define binding site spheres.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools and click Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) to open the Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Choose the selected receptor. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . The ligands should be approximately located in the receptor cavity if no Input Site Sphere is specified. Ligands must have hydrogens and complete valence shells so they can be atom typed. Input Site Sphere If the ligands are not already placed in proximity of the binding site, choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Choose the selected receptor. |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . The ligands should be approximately located in the receptor cavity if no Input Site Sphere is specified. Ligands must have hydrogens and complete valence shells so they can be atom typed. |
| Input Site Sphere | If the ligands are not already placed in proximity of the binding site, choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. |

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) - Parameters . Note that the protocol performs several steps , which can be controlled by the
protocol parameters. For example, to simply run a simulated annealing
and minimization on the ligand in the active site, without generating
new ligand conformations or trying different orientations, you can
set the parameters Random Conformations and Orientations to Refine to zero.

Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Dock Ligands (CDOCKER) - Parameters .

Note that the protocol performs several steps , which can be controlled by the
protocol parameters. For example, to simply run a simulated annealing
and minimization on the ligand in the active site, without generating
new ligand conformations or trying different orientations, you can
set the parameters Random Conformations and Orientations to Refine to zero.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

View the docked ligands in the Molecule Window .
The Input Receptor is also 
shown, with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D 
depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify ligand hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm_logs.zip | Contains the CHARMm log files for each input ligand (i.e., charmm_<ligand name>.log ). |
| <ligands>.sd | Contains the docked ligand poses. In addition to the structural information, each record includes the CDOCKER score reported as the negative value (i.e., -CDOCKER_ENERGY), where a higher value indicates a more favorable binding. This enables the energy to be used like a score. This score includes internal ligand strain energy and receptor-ligand interaction energy, and is used to sort the poses of each input ligand. The negative of the interaction energy is also reported as -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY . The energy values can be viewed from within the Molecule Window . |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | Contains any ligands which failed the docking process. If no failures occurred, the file will not be present. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the docked ligands with the input receptor in a Molecule Window with the view centered on the binding site. |
