| Max Hits to Save | Maximum number of poses for each ligand that will be saved. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Max Number of Hits | Specifies the maximum number of hits saved for each ligand during hotspots matching before entering the final pose minimization. This number does not determine how many hits are written to the final results file. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimum LibDockScore | If a value is specified, poses below this score are not reported. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Final Score Cutoff | Fraction of the top scoring poses reported. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Max BFGS Steps | Maximum number of minimization steps during the final pose optimization. A BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) method is used to optimize the score after hotspot matching. The optimization can be turned off by setting this parameter to 0. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Rigid Optimization | If set to True, the pose is treated as rigid and the conformation is not changed. Only translational and rotational movement is applied to optimize the LibDock score. Valid Values: True, False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Keep Hydrogens | If set to True hydrogen atoms are not removed from the input conformations during the docking process. This option is only available when BFGS optimization is disabled. Valid Values: True, False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Max Conformation Hits | Maximum number of poses to be kept per conformation | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Max Start Conformations | Maximum number of conformations for each ligand. The ligands are selected by solvent accessible surface area. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Steric Fraction | Maximum number of steric clashes allowed before the pose-hotspot alignment is terminated. Specified as a fraction of the heavy atom count (allowed values 0 to 1). | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Final Cluster Radius | Radius for the final clustering (Å). After the docking, the poses are minimized and clustered using the specified cut-off value. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Apolar SASA Cutoff | Maximum value for the apolar solvent accessible surface area (Å 2 ). Poses with SASA below this value will be rejected. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Polar SASA Cutoff | Maximum value for the polar solvent accessible surface area (Å 2 ). Poses below this value will be rejected. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Surface Grid Steps | Number of grid points used for calculating the solvent accessible surface area. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Conformation Method | Algorithm for generating conformations: FAST quickly provides a set of diverse low-energy conformations. BEST ensures the best coverage of the compound's conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR is a very fast conformation generation program. NONE No conformations are generated. Valid Values: FAST , BEST, CAESAR, NONE | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Maximum Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Discard Existing Conformations | Discard (or use) existing input conformations. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Energy Threshold | Conformations of separate isomers are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol). | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| DSReport Summary | Print summary of conformation generation to the Discovery Studio report. Valid Values: True, False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Separate Conformations | If True, each record is treated separately (including enantiomers) and a set of conformations is generated for each record. If False, consecutive structures, which only differ in stereo-chemistry (e.g., enantiomers) are enumerated. Note : Set this option to True if you want to ensure that all ligands are enumerated, regardless of stereo-chemistry. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing an in situ minimization after docking. An in situ minimization will remove an receptor-hydrogen bond clashes which can occur with LibDock, and hence increase the quality of the results. However, it increase the docking time significantly. Available options are: Do not minimize : Do not perform an in situ ligand minimization. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Adopted Basis NR : Uses an adopted basis Newton-Raphson (NR) algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever Adopted Basis NR is not possible. Valid Values: Do not minimize , Smart Minimizer, Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| RMSD Cutoff | Poses with an RMSD less than this value (Å) will be considered duplicates. A higher specified RMSD value will reduce the number of ligand poses returned. Note : Filtering can be disabled by setting the value to 0 or leaving it blank. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Flexible Residues | Selects a group of receptor residues which will be flexible during minimization. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimization Max Steps | Max number of cycles for the minimization. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Å). For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimization Energy Change | A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimization Forcefield | Forcefield for atom typing: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimization Sphere of Flexible Atoms | Defines a sphere. Residues of the receptor are free to move during the minimization if any atom of the residue is within the sphere. The format of the sphere is x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the center 3D coordinate and r specifies the radius of the sphere. In Discovery Studio, the sphere must be defined using the Binding Site Tools. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : A modification of the Generalized Born model that allows for an implicit membrane in the calculations of the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None, Distance-Dependent Dielectrics , Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. For GB and GBMV, this parameter is set to 1.0 internally and cannot be changed. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to GBIM or GBSW, the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is recommended to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for bulk solvent when Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW or GBIM. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Van der Waals radius scaling factor used for the Born radius calculation in the Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Specifies the minimum hydrogen radius (in Å) when Solvent Model is Generalized Born for charmm22, charmm27 or charmm36 forcefields. Note that using Generalized Born with these forcefields has not been well validated and may lead to instabilities. Applies to GB and GBIM. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). See Also: Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481. Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments: Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13. Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Salt Concentration | Salt concentration (mol/l) in GBSW. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Input Atomic Radii | Atomic radii used in GBSW and GBMV: van der Waals radii : Default. radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields. See Also : Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Use Molecular Surface | Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs (Å). Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Lower Cutoff Distance to Higher Cutoff Distance. For PBSA implicit solvent model, an infinite cutoff will be used. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching (Å). | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching (Å). | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Verbose | Amount of information in the LibDock log file. A higher value creates a larger amount of information. Valid Values: 0 , 1, 2, 3 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| sp2-sp2 rotation | Include ligand sp2-sp2 bond rotations during docking. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Grid Scoring | Perform scoring using a grid approximation. Using a grid is generally faster. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Hotspots File | Hotspots file in pdb format. This file should be created by LibDock. If not specified, a hotspots file is calculated by LibDock. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |

Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure the receptor has hydrogens and complete valence shells.

In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules.

Notes:

* The receptor should not contain alternate conformations.

* You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor.

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

Defines a sphere in the receptor where receptor-ligands interactions are permitted.

In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6).

In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list.

Note:

* If an existing hotspot file is specified, the number will be determined automatically.

LibDock employs a hotspots matching algorithm to dock ligands. This matching algorithm employs an RMSD tolerance (Å) to accept or reject any given match. Increasing the tolerance will generally result in more docked poses.

LibDock can perform docking in four different modes:

* High Quality

* Fast Search

* Fast Search for SASA (Solvent Accessible Surface Area)

* User Specified

Fast Search is most appropriate for docking a very large dataset. In the User Specified mode all advanced parameters are accessible.

| Parameter | High Quality | Fast Search | Fast Search for SASA |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Max Hits to Save | 100 | 30 | 20 |
| Max BFGS Steps | 50 | 25 | 20 |
| Max Conformation Hits | 30 | 20 | 10 |
| Max Start Conformations | 1000 | 100 | 35 |
| Steric Fraction | 0.1 | 0.2 | 0.13 |
| Final Cluster Radius | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| Final Score Cutoff | 0.5 | 0.1 | 0.05 |
| Apolar SASA Cutoff | 15.0 | 25.0 | 25.0 |
| Polar SASA Cutoff | 5.0 | 15.0 | 15.0 |

Valid Values: High Quality , Fast Search, Fast Search for SASA, User Specified

Maximum number of poses for each ligand that will be saved.

Specifies the maximum number of hits saved for each ligand during hotspots matching before entering the final pose minimization. 
This number does not determine how many hits are written to the final results file.

If a value is specified, poses below this score are not reported.

Fraction of the top scoring poses reported.

Maximum number of minimization steps during the final pose optimization. A BFGS (Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno) method is used to optimize the score after hotspot matching. The optimization can be turned off by setting this parameter to 0.

If set to True, the pose is treated as rigid and the conformation is not changed.
Only translational and rotational movement is applied to optimize the LibDock score.

Valid Values: True, False

If set to True hydrogen atoms are not removed from the input conformations during the docking process. This option is only available when BFGS optimization is disabled.

Maximum number of poses to be kept per conformation

Maximum number of conformations for each ligand. 
The ligands are selected by solvent accessible surface area.

Maximum number of steric clashes allowed before the pose-hotspot alignment is terminated.
Specified as a fraction of the heavy atom count (allowed values 0 to 1).

Radius for the final clustering (Å). After the docking, the poses are minimized and clustered using the specified cut-off value.

Maximum value for the apolar solvent accessible surface area (Å 2 ). Poses with SASA below this value will be rejected.

Maximum value for the polar solvent accessible surface area (Å 2 ). Poses below this value will be rejected.

Number of grid points used for calculating the solvent accessible surface area.

* FAST quickly provides a set of diverse low-energy conformations.

* BEST ensures the best coverage of the compound's conformational space (requires more CPU time).

* CAESAR is a very fast conformation generation program.

* NONE No conformations are generated.

Valid Values: FAST , BEST, CAESAR, NONE

Maximum number of conformations to be generated.

Discard (or use) existing input conformations.

Valid Values: True , False

Conformations of separate isomers are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol).

Print summary of conformation generation to the Discovery Studio report.

If True, each record is treated separately (including enantiomers) and a set of conformations is generated for each record. If False, consecutive structures, which only differ in stereo-chemistry (e.g., enantiomers) are enumerated.

Note :

* Set this option to True if you want to ensure that all ligands are enumerated, regardless of stereo-chemistry.

Algorithm to use for performing an in situ minimization after docking.

Available options are:

* Do not minimize : Do not perform an in situ ligand minimization.

* Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation.

* Adopted Basis NR : Uses an adopted basis Newton-Raphson (NR) algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions.

* Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation.

* Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations.

* Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever Adopted Basis NR is not possible.

Valid Values: Do not minimize , Smart Minimizer, Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell

Poses with an RMSD less than this value (Å) will be considered duplicates.
A higher specified RMSD value will reduce the number of ligand poses returned.

* Filtering can be disabled by setting the value to 0 or leaving it blank.

Selects a group of receptor residues which will be flexible during minimization.

Max number of cycles for the minimization.

A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Å).

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined.

A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit.

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase.

Forcefield for atom typing:

* CHARMm : 
General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules.

* cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules.

* MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions.

Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF

Defines a sphere. Residues of the receptor are free to move during the minimization if any atom of the residue is within the sphere. The format of the sphere is x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the center 3D coordinate and r specifies the radius of the sphere.

In Discovery Studio, the sphere must be defined using the Binding Site Tools.

Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation.

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

* Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV .

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : A modification of the Generalized Born model that allows for an
implicit membrane in the calculations of the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy.

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None, Distance-Dependent Dielectrics , Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)

Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system.

If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present.

If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. 
For GB and GBMV, this parameter is set to 1.0 internally and cannot be changed.

Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to GBIM or GBSW, the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is recommended to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons.

Dielectric constant for bulk solvent when Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW or GBIM.

Van der Waals radius scaling factor used for the Born radius calculation in the Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield.

Specifies the minimum hydrogen radius (in Å) when Solvent Model is Generalized Born for charmm22, charmm27 or charmm36 forcefields. Note that using Generalized Born with these forcefields has not been well validated and may lead to instabilities. Applies to GB and GBIM.

Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA.

Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy.

Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ).

* Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and
conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481.

* Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments:
Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13.

* Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738.

* Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study
of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918.

Salt concentration (mol/l) in GBSW.

Atomic radii used in GBSW and GBMV:

* van der Waals radii : Default.

* radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields.

See Also :

* Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248.

Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al.

Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW.

Distance cutoff value to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs (Å).

Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored.

Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Lower Cutoff Distance to Higher Cutoff Distance.

For PBSA implicit solvent model, an infinite cutoff will be used.

Higher cutoff distance to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching (Å).

Lower cutoff distance to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching (Å).

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Amount of information in the LibDock log file. A higher value creates a larger amount of information.

Valid Values: 0 , 1, 2, 3

Include ligand sp2-sp2 bond rotations during docking.

Perform scoring using a grid approximation. Using a grid is generally faster.

Hotspots file in pdb format. This file should be created by LibDock. If not specified, a hotspots file is calculated by LibDock.

Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records.

Notes :

* Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size.

* By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal.

Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing.

Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster).

Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers.

Preserve the initial order of the data records.

# Dock Ligands (LibDock)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_dock_ligands_libdock.htm

## Dock Ligands (LibDock)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dock Ligands (LibDock) protocol is an interface to the LibDock program developed by Diller and Merz [Diller and Merz, 2001] .

LibDock uses protein site features referred to as HotSpots. HotSpots consist of two types: polar and apolar.
A polar Hotspot is preferred by a polar ligand atom (for example a hydrogen bond donor or acceptor) and an apolar HotSpot is preferred by an apolar atom (for example a carbon atom).
The receptor HotSpot file is calculated prior to the docking procedure. However, if desired, a predefined or user adjusted HotSpot file can be used.
The protocol allows the user to specify several modes for generating ligand conformations for docking. If an input ligand file consists of ligand conformations, the conformer generation can be turned off.

The rigid ligand poses are placed into the active site and HotSpots are matched as triplets. The poses are pruned and a final optimization step is
performed before the poses are scored. Ligand hydrogens, which are removed during the docking process, are added to the ligand poses. These hydrogens
are not optimized, so they may require further optimization to ensure that receptor-ligand hydrogen bonds are formed correctly.

For a description and details about the strengths and weaknesses of the available docking protocols, see Choose a docking protocol .

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Ensure that the receptor has hydrogens added and atom valencies are satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed.

* From the Graphics View, select the receptor.

* Open the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel and
click Define Receptor .

* Click From Current Selection . Ensure the
sphere is selected in the Parameters Explorer.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools and click Dock Ligands (LibDock) to open the Dock Ligands (LibDock) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Choose the selected receptor. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Site Sphere Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Number of Hotspots Determines how many hotspots are generated. A greater number of hotspots will result in more pose alignments with a tradeoff in increased calculation time. Conformation Method This protocol allows you to generate conformations of the ligands or to use precalculated ligand conformations. If the selected ligands already
have 3D conformations, you may turn the conformation generation off by setting this parameter to None . Other settings of this parameter will generate conformations using a component from the Generate Conformations protocol. For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Ligands (LibDock) - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Choose the selected receptor. |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Site Sphere | Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. |
| Number of Hotspots | Determines how many hotspots are generated. A greater number of hotspots will result in more pose alignments with a tradeoff in increased calculation time. |
| Conformation Method | This protocol allows you to generate conformations of the ligands or to use precalculated ligand conformations. If the selected ligands already have 3D conformations, you may turn the conformation generation off by setting this parameter to None . Other settings of this parameter will generate conformations using a component from the Generate Conformations protocol. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Ligands (LibDock) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

View the docked ligands in the Molecule Window .
The Input Receptor is also 
shown, with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D 
depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify ligand hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table
View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligand>.sd | Contains the docked ligands. The file contains information of the Hotspots used during the alignment algorithm. Each ligand contains pose contains three atoms which can be labeled with the DSCommand CreateHotSpotsLabels. |
| <ligand>_fail.sd | Contains any ligands that failed. |
| <ligand>_conformers_fail.sd | Contains any ligands that failed the ligand conformer generation. It is not created if none of the ligands failed the ligand conformer. |
| Hotspots-<receptor>.pdb | Displays the polar (red) and apolar (gray) Hotspots locations in the active site. |
| Hotspots-<receptor>-docked.pdb | Shows only Hotspots which were used for docking (i.e., pose alignment). |
| Hotspots.log | Hotspots log file, if a Hotspots calculation was required. |
| LibDock.log | Log file containing information on each ligand docked. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opens the docked ligands in a Molecule Window. |

#### Further information

Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

## Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) - Parameters

### Docks ligands into an active site using 3D restraints and optimize with CHARMm

Uses 3D restraints specified via a pharmacophore to perform an initial ligand docking. The pharmacophore can be substructure or feature-based, but restraints are only generated if location features are present. We suggest using shape or excluded volume features to restrict the pharmacophore mappings from clashing with the receptor. Predefined ligand conformations can be used or generated on the fly using Catalyst. CHARMm is then used to perform a simulated annealing optimization followed by a minimization. Distance restraints are applied between the mapped atoms and the location features during the CHARMm simulation.

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* TopHits : Number of hits per ligand.

* -CDOCKER_ENERGY : Negative of the CDOCKER energy.

* -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY : Negative of the CDOCKER interaction energy.

* POSE_NUMBER : Pose number.

The following steps are performed:

* Creates ligand conformations

* Maps ligands to the pharmacophore

* Refines mappings using CDOCKER

Note :

* Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure the receptor has hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Conformation Generation | Algorithm for generating conformations: FAST: quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations. BEST: ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). CAESAR: very quickly provides conformations by sampling torsions. NONE: uses existing conformations. Valid Values: NONE, FAST , BEST, CAESAR |
| Maximum Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. |
| Discard Existing Conformations | Discard (or use) existing input conformations. Valid Values: True , False |
| Energy Threshold | Conformations of separate isomers are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol). |
| Input Pharmacophore | Specify a pharmacophore model to be used as restraints in the simulation. This may be identified either from a Molecule Window, or from a file in DS_CHM format. |
| Fitting Method | Choose the type of fitting: Rigid : Rigid fit between ligand and pharmacophore. Flexible : Flexible fit between ligand and pharmacophore. Valid Values: Rigid , Flexible |
| Best Mapping Only | If true, only the best mapping for each ligand will be returned. Otherwise all mappings will be returned for each ligand. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number to Keep | The number of mappings to keep for each molecule. The top scoring mappings are kept. |
| Cluster Pharmacophores | Cluster results to get a more diverse set of pharmacophore mappings. Valid Values: True , False |
| Cluster Pharmacophores RMSD Threshold | The RMSD threshold for the cluster (A). |
| Maximum Omitted Features | The maximum number of features that are allowed to miss when mapping the ligand to the pharmacophore. A value of -1 has special meaning: It instructs the server to consider all feature subsets of the pharmacophore. |
| Simulated Annealing | Perform simulated annealing refinement. Valid Values: True , False |
| Heating Steps | Number of heating phase steps during simulated annealing. |
| Heating Target Temperature | Heating stage target temperature during simulated annealing (K). |
| Cooling Steps | Number of cooling phase steps during simulated annealing. |
| Cooling Target Temperature | Cooling stage target temperature during simulated annealing (K). |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Score Threshold | Poses with a lower score (negative of the CDOCKER energy, i.e. , -CDOCKER_ENERGY ) will be discarded. |
| Forcefield | Forcefield for atom typing. The following options are available: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff |
| Use Full Potential | Use full potential for CDOCKER, or a faster grid-based method. Valid Values: True, False |

By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF |
| Final Minimization | Refined pose minimization method: Off : No minimization. Grid-based : Fast, but less accurate. Full potential : Slow, but most accurate. Note : A full potential minimization is always performed when cff is selected. Valid Values: Off, Grid-based, Full Potential |
| Grid Extension | Grid extension beyond ligand bounds (Å). The algorithm first calculates the smallest containing box around the ligand. Each side of the box is then extended by half this value. |
| Random Number Seed | Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock. The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers. See Also: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/ |
| Pharmacophore Restraint Force | Harmonic restraint force applied during pharmacophore docking [kcal/mol]. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |

This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |

| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

# Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_dock_ligands_pharmacophore_restraints_and_charmm.htm

## Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output and input files

* Analyzing results

The Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) protocol
allows you to use experimental data in a docking protocol. Often experimental
data can be used to remove undesired poses. For example,
by specifying Interaction Filters during post-processing docking results using a pharmacophore.
This protocol uses this information to perform the initial docking and to restrain the ligand during optimization.

Experimental data can be used to design a 3D pharmacophore.
This can be from direct evidence, for example by including
a restrained substructure of a common core. You can also use
less stringent pharmacophores, for example the presence of a
hydrogen bond donor or acceptor in a particular location.
Any 3D pharmacophore that contains location constraints can
be used in the initial docking of the ligand. Harmonic
restraints are then created between the location constraints and the mapped atoms.

Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) performs the following steps:

* (Optional) Ligand conformations are generated for the ligands using Generate Conformations .
Alternatively, pre-generated conformations may be provided.

* The conformations are then mapped to the pharmacophore using Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping .
You can optimize each output mapping or just the best mapping.
You can add excluded volume or shape constraints to prevent the
mappings from clashing with the protein, reducing the number of
mappings that would otherwise be attempted.

* Restraints are set up between the location constraints in the
pharmacophore and the mapped atoms in the ligand.

* Simulated annealing and minimization steps from the CDOCKER protocol are
then used to optimize the ligand pose in the active site.

* An energy filter is applied to remove poses that still clash with the protein

For a description and details about the strengths and weaknesses of the available docking protocols, see Choose a docking protocol .

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View . Ensure that the receptor has hydrogens added and all atom valencies are satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Select the receptor from the dropdown list of molecules. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Conformation Generation By default, conformations for each ligand are generated by the protocol. You may change
the conformation generation method or choose None to use the existing ligand conformations. Refer to Generate Conformations for more details. Input Pharmacophore Specify the input source.
You may
select the pharmacophore from a Molecule Window or a file. Any pharmacophore containing Location Constraints
can be used. The protocol uses Ligand Pharmacophore Mapping to perform an initial docking of the ligands. Any pharmacophore containing location constraints can be used by this protocol.
A harmonic restraint is created to tether the closest mapped atom to
the location of the location constraint. For example, to dock to
a restrained core, you can use the Query Toolbar (choose View | Toolbars | Query from the menu bar)
to add location constraints to a core substructure (not including
hydrogen atoms). You may also use more abstract pharmacophores using standard
or customized pharmacophore features. We suggest using excluded volume or
shape features to prevent bad initial mappings where the ligands clash with the protein. For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) - Parameters .

A harmonic restraint is created to tether the closest mapped atom to
the location of the location constraint. For example, to dock to
a restrained core, you can use the Query Toolbar (choose View | Toolbars | Query from the menu bar)
to add location constraints to a core substructure (not including
hydrogen atoms). You may also use more abstract pharmacophores using standard
or customized pharmacophore features. We suggest using excluded volume or
shape features to prevent bad initial mappings where the ligands clash with the protein.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

When the job finishes, double-click it in the Jobs Explorer to open the Output folder in the Files Explorer. See Output and input files for details about the files generated by this protocol. If the job did not run successfully, the Jobs Explorer will report an error. See Troubleshooting - Protocols for details.

By default, intermediate files generated by this protocol are not saved. To save the intermediate files, select the Save intermediate files when running protocols option on the Protocols page of the Preferences dialog.

#### Output files

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm_<ligand name>.log | Complete CHARMm log file for each input ligand. |
| <ligands>.sd | The refined ligands. In addition to the structural information, each record includes the system energy reported as the negative value of the energy (i.e., -CDOCKER_ENERGY), where a higher value indicates a more favorable binding. This enables the energy to be used like a score. Additional properties from CHARMm and the Pharmacophore Mapping will also be present. The properties can be viewed from within the Molecule Window . |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | Contains ligands that failed to dock. The property ErrorText will give details of why the ligand failed to dock, for example, No Map Found indicates that the ligand did not map to the Input Pharmacophore. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the docked ligands with the input receptor in a Molecule Window with the view centered on the binding site. For details, see Analyzing results . |

#### Input files

The following files are created in the Input directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <receptor>.dsv | The input receptor. |
| <ligands>.sd | The ligands used in the calculation. |
| query.ds_chm | The pharmacophore to use for the initial docking and restraints. |
| Protocol.pr_xml | The saved protocol and job parameters. You can load this file at any time to re-run this protocol with the same settings. You can also share it with other users. For details see Discovery Studio Parameters (PR_XML) . |

Open ViewResults.ds_pl to view the docked ligands in the Molecule Window .
The Input Receptor is also 
shown, with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D 
depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify ligand hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

# Flexible Docking - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_flexible_docking-para.htm

## Flexible Docking - Parameters

### Simulates protein flexibility and docks ligands with an induced fit receptor optimization

Docks ligands into a receptor with flexible amino acid side-chains.

The following steps are performed:

* Calculates receptor conformations using ChiFlex

* Creates ligand conformations

* Performs ligand docking into each active protein conformation site using LibDock

* Clustering to remove similar ligand poses (pose are clustered regardless of the protein conformation since the protein conformations are rebuild during the next step)

* Refines selected protein side-chains in the presence of the rigid ligand using ChiRotor

* Performs a final ligand refinement using CDOCKER

Notes:

* Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings.

* The receptor must be typed with a supported forcefield.

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* ChiFlex Energy : Energy of the selected residues after creating side-chain conformations.

* Residues Side-Chain Conformations : Residues selected for creating side-chain conformations.

* ChiRotor E-total : Total energy after side-chain refinement.

* ChiRotor E-vdw : Van der Waals energy after side-chain refinement.

* ChiRotor E-elec : Electrostatic energy after side-chain refinement.

* Protein Conformation : Index of protein conformation.

* LibDock Pose : LibDock pose number.

* LibDock Score : LibDock score.

* -CDOCKER_ENERGY : CDOCKER energy score.

* -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY : CDOCKER interaction energy score.

* Rotated Residues : List of rotated residues.

* Receptor Positions : The coordinates of the flexible receptor atoms.

See Also:

* Koska, J.; Spassov, V.Z.; Maynard, A.J.; Yan, L.; Austin, N.; Flook, P.K.; Venkatachalam, C.M.
Fully automated molecular mechanics based induced fit protein-ligand docking method, J. Chem. Inf. Model. , 2008 , 48(10), 1965-1973.

### Parameters

| Grid Extension | Grid extension beyond ligand bounds (Å). The algorithm first calculates the smallest containing box around the ligand. Each side of the box is then extended by half this value. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Random Number Seed | Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock. The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers. | Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. Please note the following amino acids are ignored: ALA, GLY, and PRO.
If no value is specified, the residues specified in Selected Residues are used for creating the conformations.

When set to True, only protein side-chain conformations are generated, no docking is performed. The generated protein conformations are saved. This is a useful way to run ChiFlex (i.e., side-chain conformation generation) without performing docking.

Torsion angle cutoff (degrees) to determine if two side-chain chi1 angles are the same or not.

Only conformations where torsion angles differ by more than this specified value will be considered distinct.

Increasing this limit will exponentially increase the CPU time and the number of protein conformations created.

Generate conformations of each ligand. This is can be turned off if the ligands already have conformations.

Algorithm for generating conformations:

* FAST : Quickly provides a set of diverse low-energy conformations.

* BEST : Ensures the best coverage of the compound's conformational space (requires more CPU time).

* CAESAR : Very fast conformation generation program.

Valid Values: FAST , BEST, CAESAR

Maximum number of conformations to be generated.

Discard (or use) existing input conformations.

Conformations of separate isomers are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol).

Parameters for LibDock ligand docking.

Number of polar or apolar receptor hotspots for conformer matching. A larger number will increase the computational time.

Note:

* If an existing Hotspot file is specified, the number will be determined automatically.

Maximum number of poses for each ligand that will be saved.

LibDock employs a hotspots matching algorithm to dock ligands. This matching algorithm employs an RMSD tolerance (Å) to accept or reject any given match. Increasing the tolerance will generally result in more docked poses.

LibDock can perform docking in four different modes:

* High Quality

* Fast Search

* Fast Search for SASA (Solvent Accessible Surface Area)

* User Specified

Notes :

* Fast Search is most appropriate for docking a very large dataset. In the User Specified mode all advanced parameters are accessible.

* It is not recommended to use High Quality when working with a very flexible protein and flexible ligands.

* Please refer to the Discovery Studio help on Flexible Docking for more information.

The RMSD to the best pose is calculated and poses less than the specified value but with lower docking scores are removed. This procedure is repeated for the next best scoring pose and so on.

A higher specified RMSD value will reduce the number of ligand poses and shorten the docking time. The filtering can be disabled by setting the value to 0 or leaving it blank.

# Flexible Docking

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_flexible_docking.htm

## Flexible Docking

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output and input files

* Analyzing results

This protocol allows for some receptor flexibility during docking of
flexible ligands [Koska et al., 2008] .
The side-chains of specified amino acids are allowed to
move during docking. This allows the receptor to adapt to different ligands
in an induced-fit model. The protocol uses a combination of components from
other protocols to perform the docking, and is based on methods within
CHARMm to sample side-chain and ligand conformations.

The Flexible Docking protocol performs the following steps:

* Calculate receptor side-chain conformations: Initially,
the protocol creates protein side-chain conformations using the ChiFlex algorithm.

* Create ligand conformations: Low energy ligand conformations are
created for the docking process using Generate Conformations .

* Perform initial placement of the ligand conformations: The ligand conformations are
docked into the active site of each receptor side-chain conformation using LibDock .

* Clustering to remove similar ligand poses: Poses are clustered regardless of the protein conformation
since the protein conformations are rebuilt during the next step.

* Refine side-chains: In the presence of the ligand, the
specified receptor side-chain residues are
refined using the ChiRotor algorithm.

* Refine docking: A final simulated annealing and energy minimization of each ligand pose is performed
using CDOCKER .

Steps 1, 2, and 4 may be skipped depending on settings. If you have an existing protein conformation file, you can disable the calculation of the receptor side-chain conformations to perform an ensemble docking with side-chain optimization. Additionally, if you wish to only generate protein side-chain conformations, you can disable the docking and refinement processes.

* Due to the combinatorial nature of the steps in this protocol, the conformational space to be searched can expand quickly depending on the input and parameter settings. A large number of flexible residues and ligand conformations may require significant CPU time, and memory. For example, 8 flexible protein residues may generate 200 or more conformations. 
A fairly rigid ligand with 4 rotatable bonds may generate 25 ligand conformations. 
Docking the ligand conformations into the protein conformations (25x200) can be a time-consuming step. Also, the number of poses saved per protein conformation depends on the Docking Preference > Max Hits to Save parameter. 
Assuming 100 hits are saved for each protein conformation, 20,000 (100x200) poses could be created. 
Next, those 20,000 poses are compared to each other by calculating their pair-wise RMSD to remove similar poses using a clustering algorithm. This step can be very time consuming and memory intensive. 
Therefore, you should estimate the number of ligand poses to be processed in the docking and clustering steps before running this protocol.

For example, 8 flexible protein residues may generate 200 or more conformations. 
A fairly rigid ligand with 4 rotatable bonds may generate 25 ligand conformations. 
Docking the ligand conformations into the protein conformations (25x200) can be a time-consuming step.

Also, the number of poses saved per protein conformation depends on the Docking Preference > Max Hits to Save parameter. 
Assuming 100 hits are saved for each protein conformation, 20,000 (100x200) poses could be created. 
Next, those 20,000 poses are compared to each other by calculating their pair-wise RMSD to remove similar poses using a clustering algorithm. This step can be very time consuming and memory intensive. 
Therefore, you should estimate the number of ligand poses to be processed in the docking and clustering steps before running this protocol.

* For a description and details about the strengths and weaknesses of the available docking protocols, see Choose a docking protocol .

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Open the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel and
click Define Receptor .

* Ensure that the structure you want to define as the receptor is open in a Molecule Window. The receptor must be typed with the CHARMm forcefield.

* Use the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel to define a sphere in the protein active site.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Flexible Docking .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Protein Molecule Select a typed receptor from the list of molecules. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . If the selected ligands already have 3D conformations, you can turn the conformation generation off by setting the Generate Ligand Conformations parameter to False . Make sure that the ligands have all
valencies satisfied. Input Site Sphere Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted. Note that the sphere can be defined using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Selected Residues Select the receptor residues which should be considered flexible during the docking process. The residues should be amino acids and should not include ALA, GLY, or PRO (these residues will be rejected).
Note that the computational effort increases significantly with the number of residues selected. Generate Protein Conformations The initial protein conformation generation step can be skipped if desired,
and pre-generated receptor conformations supplied. 
You can also specify a different residue subset for the receptor
conformation generation. This is typically used to restrict the protein
generation step using a smaller selection, while using the full set for the
side-chain optimization step. If the Generate Protein
Conformations Selected Residues is not specified, the
value of Selected Residues is used. For details about the remaining parameters, see Flexible Docking - Parameters .

By default, intermediate files generated by this protocol are not saved. To save the intermediate files, select the Save intermediate files when running protocols option on the Protocols page of the Preferences dialog.

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

Open ViewResults.ds_pl to view the docked ligands in the Molecule Window .
The Input Receptor is also 
shown, with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D 
depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify ligand hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .
