# Generate Analog Conformations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_generate_analog_conformations-para.htm

## Generate Analog Conformations - Parameters

### Generates analog conformations given a 3D conformation of the lead ligand and the target protein

Generates geometries of compounds in a congeneric series as typically required in lead optimization.

Required inputs are:

* Lead ligand(s), which should have a well-defined 3D geometry in the frame of reference of the protein binding pocket.

* Analog ligands, which do not need to have geometries in the protein frame of reference.

If more than one input lead ligand is present, the one with the highest similarity with each analog is chosen as the template for structure generation.

The protocol works by first detecting the common and different atoms between each analog and the lead compound by the maximum common substructure (MCS) method. It assigns the coordinates of the common atoms of the analog directly from the corresponding lead atom, and generates new coordinates for the atoms that differ. Since there can be more than one way in which an analog compound can match the lead compound topology, and the fact that multiple conformations are generated for the atoms that differ, the output typically results in more than one conformation per analog.

If an Input Receptor is specified, the binding energy for each conformation is obtained by performing a single point CHARMm energy calculation on the complex, free protein, and ligand. The results are sorted with the most favorable energy conformation appearing first. However, this energy is unlikely to reliably predict binding affinity because it does not involve structure optimization. For ranking ligands in accordance with affinity, it is recommended that the In-situ Minimization parameter is enabled. In this case, the geometries are optimized and binding energies are re-evaluated using the MM-GBSA method as a default scoring option. The in-situ minimization can be performed with a rigid protein or with flexible local residues, and optional ligand core restraints. See the corresponding parameter help for details.

The top scoring geometry and the associated top MM-GBSA binding energy score is saved in the Top Scoring Conformations file. These geometries can be used for additional calculations including alternative scoring methods or free energy calculations.

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* Binding Energy : Binding energy calculated using the MM-GBSA or other methods.

* AnalogIndex : Automatically assigned numeric ID to the analog.

* ChosenLeadIndex : The index of the input lead ligand used as the template, if multiple input lead ligands are supplied.

* FractionCommonAtoms : Fraction of the analog ligand atoms that are common with the lead.

Note :

* Geometries will not be generated for analogs that do not meet the minimum similarity threshold with respect to the lead. For such cases, alternative methods should be used.

See Also:

* Template-Based Method for Conformation Generation and Scoring for Congeneric Series of Ligands, E. Prabhu Raman J. Chem. Inf. Model 2019 , 59 , 2690.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Lead Ligands | Specify one SD file that contains the ligands to be used as the lead for the calculation. There can be more than one lead compound. In that case, for each analog compound, the best matching lead is chosen as the template for structure generation. The lead compounds should have well defined 3D geometries in the binding site frame of reference. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. |
| Input Analog Ligands | Specify the analog ligands for which 3D geometries need to be determined. These compounds do not need to be positioned in the binding site frame of reference. Molecules should have a unique Name , as multiple conformations may be generated per analog ligand. |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. The receptor must be typed with the CHARMm forcefield and is used to calculate the binding energy of the generated conformations. If a receptor is not supplied, the analog conformations are generated without any information about the protein. If the user chooses, the ligand can be minimized in the binding pocket with or without local protein flexibility and with or without ligand core restraints. Note : A receptor is optional, but recommended. |
| In-situ Minimization | Minimize the ligands in the presence of the receptor. Since the minimization is performed in-vacuo , a distance-dependent dielectric is used to avoid overestimating electrostatic interactions. Following the minimization, a single point energy is calculated using the chosen implicit solvent model. The in-situ minimization can be performed with a rigid protein or flexible local residues. The residues are chosen based on proximity to the lead compound(s). The core atoms of the ligand, or equivalently a subset of the common atoms can also be optionally constrained during the minimization. Valid Values: True , False |
| Radius of Flexible Residues | Protein residues that are located within this distance from the lead compound will be selected to be flexible during in-situ protein-ligand minimization. For this option to be meaningful, only a single lead compound should be supplied. For efficiency, only values greater than 0 and less than or equal to 5 Å are allowed. If left empty, the protein will be held rigid. |
| Ligand Core Constraint | A restraint can be applied to restrict ligand-atom movement during minimization. This is only applied to the atoms that are designated as the common core by the MCS method. The following constraints are available: None : No constraint applied. Harmonic Absolute : Require the atoms to stay near the initial position. Valid Values: None , Harmonic Absolute |
| Maximum Conformations per Analog | Maximum number of conformations generated for each analog ligand. This number is used prior to entering the in-situ minimization stage. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| RMSD Cutoff for Pose Selection | Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) value (Å) used to filter similar conformations. |
| Minimum Similarity | Minimum fraction of common atoms between the lead ligand and the analog. Analog ligands which have a lesser fraction of common atoms will be rejected. This is done as there should be reasonable overlap between the two to ensure reliable analog geometry generation |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the final scoring. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : A modification of the Generalized Born model that allows for an implicit membrane in the calculations of the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) : The most rigorous yet slowest solvent approximation method based on continuum electrostatics. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None, Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) , Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM), Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) |
| Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant used in various implicit solvent models, including GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA. Note: When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Generalized Born", this value is fixed at 1.0. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for bulk solvent used in various implicit solvent models, including Generalized Born, GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Minimum hydrogen radius (Å) when Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born". Note: Used only for charmm22 and charmm27 forcefields to address instabilities during the calculation, as the Generalized Born implicit solvent model has not been well validated for these forcefields. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | The constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | The surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Salt Concentration | Salt concentration (mol/liter) used in various implicit solvent models, including GBSW, GBMV or PBSA. |
| Input Atomic Radii | Specify source of input atomic radii used in various implicit solvent models, including GBSW, GBMV or PBSA. van der Waals radii are the default. For charmm22 and charmm27 force fields, radii set derived by Nina et al. is recommended. See Also: Nina M.; Beglov D.; Roux B. Atomic Born radii for continuum electrostatic calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations. J. Phys. Chem. B 1997 , 101 , 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. |
| Use Molecular Surface | Whether to approximate Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) results with molecular surface. Used only when Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW)". Valid Values: True , False |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. Minimum fraction of common atoms between the lead ligand and the analog. Analog ligands which have a lesser fraction of common atoms will be rejected. This is done as there should be reasonable overlap between the two to ensure reliable analog geometry generation

Implicit solvent model to use in the final scoring.

Available options are:

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

* Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV .

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : A modification of the Generalized Born model that allows for an
implicit membrane in the calculations of the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy.

* Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) : The most rigorous yet slowest solvent approximation method based on continuum electrostatics.

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None, Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) , Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM), Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA)

Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields.

Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield.

Minimum hydrogen radius (Å) when Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born".

* Used only for charmm22 and charmm27 forcefields to address instabilities during the calculation, as the Generalized Born implicit solvent model has not been well validated for these forcefields.

Whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA.

The constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy.

The surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy.

Salt concentration (mol/liter) used in various implicit solvent models, including GBSW, GBMV or PBSA.

Specify source of input atomic radii used in various implicit solvent models, including GBSW, GBMV or PBSA. van der Waals radii are the default. For charmm22 and charmm27 force fields, radii set derived by Nina et al. is recommended.

Nina M.; Beglov D.; Roux B. Atomic Born radii for continuum electrostatic calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations. J. Phys. Chem. B 1997 , 101 , 5239-5248.

Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al.

Whether to approximate Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) results with molecular surface. Used only when Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW)".

# Generate Analog Conformations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_generate_analog_conformations.htm

## Generate Analog Conformations

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Generate Analog Conformations protocol allows you to obtain 3D geometries of ligands in a congeneric analog series of compounds, given the 3D geometry of one or more lead compounds in a series and the corresponding target protein structure [Raman, 2019] . Required inputs are one or more lead ligands with well defined 3D geometry in the frame of reference of the protein binding pocket, and analog ligands that do not need to have geometries in the frame of reference. If more than one input lead ligand is present, the protocol will choose the lead that is most similar to each analog when generating that structure.

The protocol works by first detecting the common and different atoms between each analog and the lead compound by way of the maximum common substructure (MCS) method. It assigns the coordinates of the common atoms of the analog directly from the corresponding lead atom, and generates coordinates of the atoms that differ. Since there can be more than one way in which an analog compound can match the lead compound topology, and because multiple conformations are generated for the atoms that differ, the output typically results in more than one conformation per analog.

If a protein is supplied, for each conformation, binding energy is obtained by performing a single point CHARMm energy calculation on the complex and free protein and ligand, and the results are sorted with the most favorable energy conformation appearing first. However, this energy is unlikely to reliably predict binding affinity because it does not involve structure optimization.

For ranking ligands in accordance with affinity, choose the in-situ minimization option. In this case, the geometries are optimized and binding energy is re-evaluated using the MM-GBSA method as a default scoring option. You can perform the in-situ minimization with a rigid protein or with flexible local residues. The residues are chosen based on proximity to the lead compound, so you should only use this option when there is a single lead compound. You can optionally constrain the core atoms of the ligand, or a subset of the common atoms during the minimization. The top scoring geometry and the associated top MM-GBSA binding energy score is saved in the Top Scoring Conformations file. You can then use these geometries for additional calculations including alternate scoring methods or free energy calculations.

* Geometries will not be generated for analogs that do not meet the minimum similarity threshold with respect to the lead. Use an alternate method for such cases.

* The Input Receptor must be pretyped with the CHARMm forcefield.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tools and click Generate Analog Conformations... .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Lead Ligands Specify the ligand to be used as lead or template for structure generation. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Analog Ligands Specify the ligands to be used as analogs for which 3D geometries are desired. For details, see Specifying Ligands . It is helpful to have a unique Name attribute for each ligand to help with analysis after the run. Input Receptor Select the receptor from the list of molecules. Maximum Conformations per Analog Choose the maximum number of geometries for each analog ligand For details about the remaining parameters, see Generate Analog Conformations - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Lead Ligands | Specify the ligand to be used as lead or template for structure generation. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Analog Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used as analogs for which 3D geometries are desired. For details, see Specifying Ligands . It is helpful to have a unique Name attribute for each ligand to help with analysis after the run. |
| Input Receptor | Select the receptor from the list of molecules. |
| Maximum Conformations per Analog | Choose the maximum number of geometries for each analog ligand |

Specify the ligands to be used as analogs for which 3D geometries are desired. For details, see Specifying Ligands .

It is helpful to have a unique Name attribute for each ligand to help with analysis after the run.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Generate Analog Conformations - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Load the results from the report page by clicking the View Results icon to open the following files:

* Analog_Conformations : All conformations generated for the analogs that were successfully processed by the protocol.

* Top_Scoring_analog_Conformation : Only the top scoring conformation for each processed analog.

A method for distinguishing analogs in the Analog_Conformations file is via the AnalogIndex attribute. If multiple lead compounds were present, the ChosenLeadIndex attribute identifies which lead was used as template for a given analog.

A method for analyzing the Top_Scoring_analog_Conformation file is to select the Name and Binding Energy columns and plot them using Chart > Bar Chart . You can then identify ligands for additional scoring for which the top scoring geometries can be used.

#### Further information

# Grow Scaffold - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_grow_scaffold-para.htm

## Grow Scaffold - Parameters

### Grows a scaffold in a binding site

Grows the Input Ligand Scaffold at the Scaffold Grow Points based on the selected Reactions and Reagents . The enumerated ligands fit the binding site of the Input Receptor . Optionally, it is possible to specify Interacting Residues at the Input Receptor to filter non-interacting leads, and to perform an in-situ minimization using CHARMm. You can specify a custom library using the Reactions Custom and Reagents Custom parameters.

The following steps are performed:

* Create a reagent library

* Calculate a protein grid

* Enumerate scaffold link points

* Filter ligands by residue interactions

* Minimize ligands

* Prioritize ligands (Pareto sort)

In the Pareto sort, ligands are prioritized to optimize receptor-interactions, minimize receptor-bumps, minimize Lipinski's rule of five violations, and optimize ligand novelty.

This protocol adds many properties to the ligands including:

* Fragment Name R n : Fragments added to the scaffold at link site n .

* Reaction Name R n : Reaction at link site n .

* Fragment Library File Name R n : Fragment library at link site n .

* Ligand Novelty Index : Index of the novelty ranking (see Notes for more information).

Notes:

* Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings.

* Ligand novelty is calculated by ranking and sorting the ligands by, number of chain assemblies, number of double and aromatic bonds, and N,S,O atom count.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Note: You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Interacting Residues | List of protein residues to have nonbond interactions with the added fragments. Notes : A fragment passes if it interacts with any of the specified residues (OR logic). In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace e.g., "B:ILE82 B:MET156". In Discovery Studio you specify the Interacting Residues by selecting an existing residue group. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ...". |
| Input Ligand Scaffold | Ligand scaffold for linking Reagents at the specified Scaffold Grow Points . Note: In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. |
| Scaffold Grow Points | A list of terminal scaffold-atom numbers to use as link points for the Reagents . Notes : Link points should be terminal atoms. In Discovery Studio select atoms from the Input Ligand Scaffold . In Pipeline Pilot enter a comma or space separated list e.g., 22,24. |
| Reactions | Reactions between the Input Ligand Scaffold and the Reagents at the Scaffold Grow Points . The list of reactions is generated from a file that can be modified to suit your needs (see Notes). Additionally, files specified in Reactions Custom can be selected but will only be applied to custom reagents selected in Reagents . Notes : The Reactions and Reagents are generated from the ReactionFile.txt located in the dsdata/public/data/GrowScaffold/Library directory. For extending the default reagents and reaction library please refer to ReadMe.txt and ReactionFile.txt in the dsdata/public/data/GrowScaffold/Library directory. |

Reaction files must specify an atom to link the fragment. Use an X and Z symbol for RXN and SMIRKS files, respectively. Custom reactions need to be written as half-reactions, with one reactant and the product. The two half-reactions can be used at the same time to represent the complete reaction. Custom RXN files need to have atom-atom mappings defined to specify which reactant atom becomes which product atom through the reaction. * Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV .

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW)

Dielectric constant used in various implicit solvent models, including GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA.

* When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Generalized Born", this value is fixed at 1.0.

Dielectric constant for bulk solvent used in various implicit solvent models, including Generalized Born, GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA.

Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs.

Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored.

Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance .

When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA)", an infinite cutoff will be used.

Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching.

When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance .

When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically.

Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Torsion step for rotating the scaffold-fragment link [°] to eliminate fragment-ligand and fragment-protein clashes. A value of 0 will disable sampling.

* Torsion sampling will decreases performance.

Allow exhaustive torsion sampling. When set to False, the sampling is aborted when the first fragment position that fits is found. When set to True, sampling is exhaustive and all fragment torsional positions that fit are saved.

* For sites with multiple links, this parameter can increase the run time significantly.

Generate conformation from the reagents. The conformational sampling increases the number of ligands by creating a larger number of reagent poses to fit into the protein binding pocket.

* Increased conformation decreases performance.

* Performance can be improved by enabling Parallel Processing .

Maximum number of conformations to generate.

Maximum number of conformations to save for each ligand. Each generated conformation is fitted into the protein binding pocket and torsion sampling is performed; however only one pose is saved after the torsion sampling. Therefore the maximum number of conformations to save should be less than or equal to the maximum conformations to be generated.

The scaffold enumeration is terminated after a specified number of ligands are created (disabled when empty).

Disable prioritization step 5. This might be useful for large data sets where the Pareto sorting can result in large memory allocation, or run times.

Valid Values: True , False

If set to True, fragment properties appended to the output ligand files.

Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records.

* Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size.

* By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal.

Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing.

Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster).

Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers.

Preserve the initial order of the data records.

# Grow Scaffold

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_grow_scaffold.htm

## Grow Scaffold

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Grow Scaffold protocol allows you to perform reaction-based ligand enumeration within a protein active site for lead optimization. Beginning with a scaffold positioned in the binding site of the receptor, you can select positions to act as reaction vectors for the enumeration, and then the reactions and reagents to be used. Enumerated ligands may optionally be minimized and are returned Pareto sorted by interactions formed with the protein (maximized), Lipinski violations (minimized), receptor bumps (minimized) and ligand "novelty" (maximized). Ligand "novelty" is calculated by ranking and sorting the ligands by, number of chain assemblies, number of double and aromatic bonds, and N,S,O atom count.

For further details, see Lead optimization and Optimizing lead compounds from a scaffold in a protein active site .

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tools and click Grow Scaffold to open the Grow Scaffold dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Select the receptor from the list of molecules. Input Ligand Scaffold Specify the scaffold to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Scaffold Grow Points Group containing terminal scaffold-atom numbers to use as link points. Reactions Reactions between the Input Ligand Scaffold and the Reagents at the Scaffold Grow Points . 
A table with the predefined reactions can be reviewed here Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration . Reagents Reagents to react with the Input Ligand Scaffold at the Scaffold Grow Points .
A table with the predefined reagents can be reviewed here Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration . For details about the remaining parameters, see Grow Scaffold - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Select the receptor from the list of molecules. |
| Input Ligand Scaffold | Specify the scaffold to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Scaffold Grow Points | Group containing terminal scaffold-atom numbers to use as link points. |
| Reactions | Reactions between the Input Ligand Scaffold and the Reagents at the Scaffold Grow Points . A table with the predefined reactions can be reviewed here Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration . |
| Reagents | Reagents to react with the Input Ligand Scaffold at the Scaffold Grow Points . A table with the predefined reagents can be reviewed here Scaffold optimization by in situ enumeration . |

Group containing terminal scaffold-atom numbers to use as link points.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Grow Scaffold - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Load the results from the report page by clicking the View Results icon. This view allows you to browse through the ligands in the receptor site. Use the View Interactions tools to identify fragment hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

The enumerated ligands have been Pareto sorted by interactions formed with the protein, Lipinski violations, receptor bumps, and fragment "novelty". Numerous properties are reported for the ligands generated. For each R-group position (grow point) ligands will include properties with the details of the fragment attached, the reaction used, and the library the fragment came from:

* Fragment Name Rn: Fragments added to the scaffold at link site n.

* Reaction Name Rn: Reaction at link site n.

* Fragment Library File Name Rn: Fragment library at link site n.

The protein-ligands interactions formed by enumerated ligands are also reported as properties such as the interaction type, protein residues, and interaction distance:

* Aromatic Ring Atoms, Aromatic Ring Residues, Aromatic Ring Distance

* Hydrogen Bond Atoms, Hydrogen Bond Residues, Hydrogen Bond Distance

* Hydrophobic Atoms, Hydrophobic Residues, Hydrophobic Distance

* Negative Charge Atoms, Negative Charge Residues, Negative Charge Distance

* Positive Charge Atoms, Positive Charge Residues, Positive Charge Distance

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Ligands poses with hydrogen bond, and contact properties added. For hydrogen bonds and contacts, the columns are added in order to facilitate the creation of a Heat Map (e.g., the number of hydrogen bonds to each residue). |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | The output file containing the ligands that failed. |

# In Situ Ligand Minimization - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_ligand_minimization-para.htm

## In Situ Ligand Minimization - Parameters

### Minimizes a series of ligand poses using CHARMm

Uses CHARMm to minimize ligands in the presence or absence of a rigid or flexible receptor.

This protocol adds several properties to the data stream including:

* -In-Situ Start Energy : The negative of the ligand energy (kcal/mol) before minimization.

* -In-Situ Final Energy : The negative of the final ligand energy (kcal/mol) after minimization.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Flexible Receptor Atom Property | Name of a property which contains the flexible receptor atom coordinates. For example, after running ligand minimization with flexible receptor atoms or residues, a property named "Receptor.Positions" will be created for each of the flexible receptor atoms with the 3D coordinate in the following format: X1 Y1 Z1 atno AtomIndex1 X2 Y2 Z2 atno AtomIndex2 ... If this property is not found in the input ligands, it will be ignored. Note: Changing the order or number of atoms in the system, for example by typing, may make these properties out of date, giving erroneous results. A workaround is to type the receptor with CHARMm force field prior to docking so that the receptor atom order will not be changed. |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure the receptor has hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Minimization Sphere of Flexible Atoms | Defines a sphere in the receptor where residues are free to move. In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6). In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list. |
| Flexible Residues | Group of receptor residues which will be flexible during minimization. Note : Limited to 200 residues. |
| Input Forcefield | Forcefield for atom typing: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF |
| Minimization | Parameters that control the minimization. |
| Substructure Constraints | Apply a substructure constraint during minimization to limit ligand movement. Valid Values: True, False |
| Substructure Constraints Input Substructure | Constraint substructure. The file can be in DSV or SD file format. Ligands without a substructure match will not be constrained. In Discovery Studio, select a set of atoms as the target substructure. Notes: Hydrogen atoms are ignored. The file should only contain a single molecule. A property Constrained Ligand Atoms is added to indicate the atoms IDs of the constrained atoms. |
| Substructure Constraints Input Substructure Selection | When multiple substructures are found for a ligand, the following options are available: Nearest : Constrain only the substructure match with the lowest RMSD. All : Constrain all matched substructures. Valid Values: Nearest , All |

For example, this can be useful when the core of a ligand should not move, or should do so only slightly. The following constraints are available: Fixed : Apply fixed constraint. Harmonic Absolute : Require the atom(s) to stay near the initial position. Harmonic BestFit : Similar to Harmonic Absolute , but rotation and translation are allowed to minimize the restraints energy. This makes it useful for holding inter-atom geometry intact while allowing for block motion. Valid Values: Fixed , Harmonic Absolute, Harmonic BestFit |
| Substructure Constraints Force | The force applied for the harmonic constraint. |
| Hydrogen Flexibility | Allow for receptor hydrogens atoms in the vicinity of the ligand to be flexible. Valid Values: True, False |
| Hydrogen Flexibility Radius | Search radius of the hydrogen flexibility from the initial ligand atom position (Å). |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. The Smart Minimizer option is custom for In-Situ Ligand Minimization and consists of some pre-defined minimization steps that have been pre-determined to work well for receptor ligand data. Valid Values: Smart Minimizer , Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell |
| Minimization Steps | Max number of minimization steps to perform. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization (kcal/(mol-Å). If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |

If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |

# In Situ Ligand Minimization

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_ligand_minimization.htm

## In Situ Ligand Minimization

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

This protocol minimizes a series of ligands. If a receptor molecule is specified,
minimization is performed in the presence of the receptor ( in situ ).
Otherwise, ligands are minimized in a vacuum. For in situ minimization, the receptor is held rigid. However,
residues with atoms inside the specified sphere, or in a list of
flexible residues are allowed to move.

The CHARMm, cff, or MMFF forcefield may be specified. The
ligands and receptor are typed on the server.

* To minimize in the presence of a receptor, load the structure you want to define as the receptor into the Graphics View .

* Open the Small Molecules | Minimize Ligands tools and click In Situ Ligand Minimization to open the In Situ Ligand Minimization dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be minimized. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Receptor If desired, select the structure you want to define as the receptor. Receptors must have hydrogens
added and complete valencies so they can be atom typed. If you do not specify a receptor, the ligands will be minimized in vacuum. For details about the remaining parameters, see In Situ Ligand Minimization .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be minimized. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Receptor | If desired, select the structure you want to define as the receptor. Receptors must have hydrogens added and complete valencies so they can be atom typed. If you do not specify a receptor, the ligands will be minimized in vacuum. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see In Situ Ligand Minimization .

* Optionally, you can define a sphere that excludes residues that contain atoms that lie within it from being held rigid. Select the receptor, and then from the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel, click From Current Selection . Set the Minimization Sphere of Flexible Atoms to the newly defined coordinates of the sphere. Alternatively, you can create a group of residues and use that to define the
flexible residues. Select the residues you want to exclude from being held rigid. Right-click and choose Group to open the Edit Group dialog and create a group from the selection. Choose the new group in the Flexible Residues parameter.

Alternatively, you can create a group of residues and use that to define the
flexible residues. Select the residues you want to exclude from being held rigid. Right-click and choose Group to open the Edit Group dialog and create a group from the selection. Choose the new group in the Flexible Residues parameter.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

This protocol will make use of special properties on the ligand specified by Flexible Receptor Atom Property indicating the location of flexible receptor atoms.
These properties, such as those produced by the Dock Ligands (GOLD) and Flexible Docking protocols
use the atom indices. Changing the order or number of atoms in the system, for
example by typing, may make these properties out of date, giving erroneous
results. A workaround is to type the receptor with CHARMm force field
prior to docking so that the receptor atom order will not be changed.

If you specified a receptor, the ligands are minimized in situ ,
so that the receptor is included and interactions between the ligand 
poses and the receptor will affect the calculation.

The output ligand file contains details of the initial and final energy of the minimized structures. 
The negatives of these energies are included as -In-Situ Starting Energy and -In-Situ Final Energy properties. The final gradient is also included as the In-Situ Gradient property.

If you chose to run the protocol with receptor flexibility, the output file will contain a property 
called Receptor.Positions that contains the coordinates of the updated receptor atoms. 
You can view the updated receptor conformations using the ViewResults.ds_pl output 
file. You can also use files with this property in the Score Ligand Poses and Calculate Binding Energies protocols.

For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm_<ligand name>.log | A complete CHARMm log file for each input ligand. |
| <ligands>.sd | The minimized ligands. Each .sd file is annotated with the initial and final energies of the system and the selected forcefield. These values can be seen by reading the .sd file into a Molecule Window . |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | Contains the ligands that failed the minimization. It is not created if none of the ligands failed the minimization. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the minimized ligands with the input receptor in a Molecule Window . If a Minimization Sphere of Flexible Atoms was specified, changes to the receptor structure may be seen while stepping through the ligands. |

#### Further information

Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Replace Fragment - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_replace_fragment-para.htm

## Replace Fragment - Parameters

### Replaces ligand fragments with bioisosteres

Replaces ligand fragments of the Input Ligand to generate novel ligands. The replacement fragments are bioisosteres from default libraries or custom libraries designated by the parameters in the Fragment Libraries group.

You can optionally specify an Input Receptor , and the generated ligands will fit in the binding site. Additionally, it is possible to specify Interacting Residues to filter non-interacting ligands and to perform an in-situ ligand minimization. As a final step, the ligands are prioritized using a Pareto sort.

This approach can be useful for performing scaffold hopping of an active molecule with the aim of discovering structurally novel ligands with modified central core structures that can still bind to a receptor.

The following steps are performed:

* Library Search: finds suitable fragments

* Fragment Placement: places/fits the fragment to the new location

* Fragment Matching: finds suitable fragments that fit the receptor cavity

* Ligand Minimization : in-situ ligand/fragment minimization

* Pareto Sort: ranks and sorts the novel ligands

This protocol adds many properties to the data stream including:

* Fragment Selected : SMILES string of the selected ligand fragment.

* Fragment Replaced : SMILES string of the replaced fragment.

* Fragment Similarity : Similarity value of the fragment with values between 0 to 1.

* RigidGroups : IDs of the atoms held rigid during fragment placement.

* Ligand Novelty Index : Index of the novelty ranking (see Notes for more information).

Notes:

* Steps in italics may be skipped depending on settings.

* When using more than one attachment, the fused fragments may have some residual strain due to the restricted space.

* For fragments with one attachments the number for fragment conformations saved can be set by Number of 1R Fragment Conformations .

* In the Pareto sort, ligands are prioritized to optimize receptor-interactions, minimize receptor-bumps, minimize Lipinski's rule of five violations, and optimize ligand novelty.

* Ligand novelty is calculated by ranking and sorting the ligands by, number of chain assemblies, number of double and aromatic bonds, and N,S,O atom count.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure receptors have hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Interacting Residues | List of protein residues to have nonbond interactions with the added fragments. Notes : A fragment passes if it interacts with any of the specified residues (OR logic). In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace e.g., "B:ILE82 B:MET156". In Discovery Studio you specify the Interacting Residues by selecting an existing residue group. Alternatively, you can define a new group based on the currently selected residues by choosing "Create New Group from Selection ...". |
| Input Ligand | Ligand to be used for fragment replacement. In Discovery Studio, choose a visible ligand. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a ligand. |
| Fragment to Replace | Select the fragment to replace. In Discovery Studio, you can select a predefined group or create a group from currently selected atoms. In Pipeline Pilot, it should be entered as the indices of the atoms in the fragment, for example, "1 2 4 16 17 18" or "1,3,5-7" or "1-20" are legal. |
| Fragment Libraries | Specify the fragment libraries to search: One Attachment (Linear) One Attachment (Cyclic) Two Attachments (Linear) Two Attachments (Cyclic) Three Attachments (Linear) Three Attachments (Cyclic) Notes: The default fragment libraries are located in [PP_Install_Directory]/apps/scitegic/dsdata/public/data/ReplaceFragment/Fragments You can use your own fragment libraries by selecting SMILES files in Fragment Libraries Custom , the fragments will override the appropriate default library type. The example protocol Generate Fragment Libraries can be used to prepare such libraries. When selecting Two/Three Attachments fragment libraries, one or more of the R groups may be replaced with hydrogens, therefore creating hits with a single or double attachment. Valid Values: One Attachment (Linear) , One Attachment (Cyclic) , Two Attachments (Linear) , Two Attachments (Cyclic) , Three Attachments (Linear) , Three Attachments (Cyclic) |
| Fragment Libraries Custom | SMILES fragment file(s) with one/two or three attachment points. If left blank, the default library will be used. Notes: The example protocol Generate Fragment Libraries can be used to create a custom library. The fragments are analyzed and assigned to the selected Fragment Libraries type, overriding the default library. |
| Generate Fragment Conformations | Generate fragment conformation. The conformational sampling increases the number of ligands by creating a larger number of fragment poses to fit the site. Notes : Increased conformation decreases performance. Performance can be improved by enabling Parallel Processing . Valid Values: True, False |
| Generate Fragment Conformations Maximum | Maximum number of fragment conformations to generate. |
| Generate Fragment Conformations Conformations to Keep | Maximum number of conformations to save for each ligand. Each generated conformation is fitted into the protein binding pocket and torsion sampling is performed; however only one pose is saved after the torsion sampling. Therefore the maximum number of conformations to save should be less than or equal to the maximum conformations to be generated. |
| Minimization | Minimize the ligands in the presence/absence of the receptor. During the minimization all atoms are allowed to move freely. However, depending on the Ligand Constraint setting, the scaffold movement can be restricted. In addition, a property RMSD Scaffold is calculated for each ligand to indicate the shift from the initial scaffold location (the portion of the ligand that was not replaced with a new fragment) after the minimization. The minimization adds several properties such as, -In-Situ Starting Energy , -In-Situ Final Energy . Valid Values: True, False |
| Ligand Constraint | You can apply a constraint to restrict scaffold-atom movement during minimization. The following constraints are available: None : No constraint is applied and all ligand atoms are allowed to move. Fixed : Scaffold is fixed and fragments can move. Harmonic Absolute : Scaffold atoms to stay near the initial position. Harmonic BestFit : Similar to Harmonic Absolute , but rotation and translation are allowed to minimize the restraints energy of the scaffold. This makes it useful for holding inter-atom geometry intact while allowing for block motion. Valid Values: None , Fixed, Harmonic Absolute, Harmonic BestFit |
| Input Forcefield | Forcefield to use for typing. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF |
| Ligand Partial Charge Method | Choose a method to assign partial charges. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF |
| Flexible Residues | A group of receptor residues which will be flexible during minimization. In Discovery Studio, a residue group can be defined in advance or created on the fly. In Pipeline Pilot, uses standard CHARMm selection syntax. For example, specify "sele ires 1:10 end" to select the first 10 residues. Note that no more than 200 residues can be selected. See Also: CHARMm selection syntax: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/select/ |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer |
| Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Angstrom). For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Specifies an implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent, about the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) |
| Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant used in various implicit solvent models, including GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA. Note: When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Generalized Born", this value is fixed at 1.0. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for bulk solvent used in various implicit solvent models, including Generalized Born, GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA. |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance . When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA)", an infinite cutoff will be used. |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Fragment Breaking | If the selected fragment contains more than 14 heavy atoms, it will be broken into smaller fragments in order to search the fragment library. There is also an option to break fragments with 14 heavy atoms or less to increase the number of hits returned. |
| Break Small Fragments | Break selected fragments with 14 or less heavy atoms. If the selected fragment has more than 14 heavy atoms, it is always broken into smaller fragments. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number of Attachments | Generate fragments with one, two, and/or three attachment points (R atoms) Valid Values: One , Two , Three |
| Maximum Number of Fragments | Maximum number of smaller fragments to generate for each input fragment. Leave it blank if you want all fragments. |
| Maximum Number of Atoms | Maximum number of atoms in each generated fragment. |
| Skip Terminal Bonds | Specify whether or not to skip bonds to terminal atoms when selecting bonds to break in order to generate fragments. Valid Values: True, False |
| Fragment Search | Parameters for searching the fragment library. |
| Properties for Similarity | Properties to use in searching similar fragments. Valid Values: FCFP_2, FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6, PHFP_2, PHFP_3, PHFC_2, PHFC_3, MDLPublicKeys, AlogP, Molecular_Weight, Num_Atoms, Num_Bonds, Num_H_Donors, Num_H_Acceptors, Num_Rings , Num_AromaticRings , Molecular_SurfaceArea , Molecular_PolarSurfaceArea, C_Count, N_Count, O_Count, P_Count, S_Count |
| Number of Similar Fragments | Specify the number of top-scoring (more similar) fragments to keep for each input fragment. |
| Maximum Distance | Maximum value allowed for the distance between the original fragment and the similar ones calculated based on the specified molecular properties. Only similar fragments within this distance are considered, even if this results in fewer than Number of Similar Fragments being considered. Note: Leave blank to allow any distance. |
| Prioritize Ligands | Ligands are prioritized using a Pareto sort to optimize receptor-interactions, minimize receptor-bumps, minimize Lipinski's rule of five violations, and optimize ligand novelty. Ligand novelty is calculated by ranking and sorting the ligands by, number of chain assemblies, number of double and aromatic bonds, and N,S,O atom count. A Ligand Novelty Index is added to indicate the ranking (most novel ligand has a value of 1). Note : For large dataset this can require a significant amount of memory and can result in long runtimes. Valid Values: True , False |
| Maximum Enumerations | The scaffold enumeration is terminated after a specified number of ligands are created (disabled when empty). |
| Maximum Out of Plane Angle | Maximum deviation for out-of-plane angles for aromatic ring systems (°). Disabled if set to 0. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True, False |

# Replace Fragment

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_replace_fragment.htm

## Replace Fragment

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

This protocol allows you to generate novel compounds with different scaffolds by replacing one or more fragments in a lead structure. The diverse structures often offer different choices in terms of chemical accessibility and prospect for lead optimization (e.g., lowering the chance of drug development attrition due to undesirable ADMET properties).

Optionally enumerated ligands can be minimized and returned Pareto sorted by interactions formed with the protein (maximized), Lipinski violations (minimized), receptor bumps (minimized), and fragment "novelty" (maximized). In the absence of a protein, ligands are Pareto sorted by Lipinski violations and fragment "novelty".
Ligand "novelty" is calculated by ranking and sorting the ligands by, number of chain assemblies, number of double and aromatic bonds, and N,S,O atom count.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Lead Optimization tools and click Replace Fragment to open the Replace Fragment dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Select the receptor from the list of molecules. This parameter is optional. If no receptor is specified, the steps involving the receptor will be skipped. Input Ligand Specify the ligand to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Fragment to Replace Group containing the atoms or fragments to replace. See Edit Group dialog . For details about the remaining parameters, see Replace Fragment - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Select the receptor from the list of molecules. This parameter is optional. If no receptor is specified, the steps involving the receptor will be skipped. |
| Input Ligand | Specify the ligand to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Fragment to Replace | Group containing the atoms or fragments to replace. See Edit Group dialog . |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Replace Fragment - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

View the ligands in the Molecule Window .
The Input Receptor is shown if it was specified. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D 
depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify, fragment hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Ligands poses with hydrogen bond, and contact properties added. For hydrogen bonds and contacts, the columns are added in order to facilitate the creation of a Heat Map (e.g., the number of hydrogen bonds to each residue). |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | The output file containing the ligands that failed. |
