# Score Ligand Poses - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_score_ligand_poses-para.htm

## Score Ligand Poses - Parameters

### Scores ligand poses using a series of scoring functions

Calculates ligand binding in an active receptor site using a wide selection of scoring functions. The score can be used to assess ligand binding. The scores calculated are always reported as positive values to ensure that a higher score indicates more favorable binding.

The range of scoring functions includes:

* CDOCKER Scores †

* LigScore1 and LigScore2

* PLP1 and PLP2

* Jain

* PMF and PMF04

* Ludi scores (1,2,3)

* CDOCKER Score

* Goldscore *

* Chemscore *

* ASP *

* CHEMPLP *

Depending on the settings this protocol adds many properties to the data stream.

Notes:

* † The CDOCKER scoring function requires a receptor that can be typed (i.e., no unfilled valencies).

* Receptor flexibility can be included if the ligands are the result of a Ligand Minimization, Flexible Docking or Dock Ligands (GOLD) protocol.

* * A valid GOLD license must be obtained from CCDC before using any of the GOLD scoring functions.
Free evaluations of GOLD can be obtained by contacting: admin@ccdc.cam.ac.uk 
phone: +44 1223 336394

* When using a GOLD scoring function ensure that the GOLD installation folder is correctly specified in the <Pipeline Pilot Install Folder>/apps/scitegic/dscore/server/share/SBD/GOLD_location file.

* When using a version lower than GOLD 4.1 not all functionality might be available.

See Also :

* Wu, G.; Robertson, D. H.; Brooks, C. L. III; Vieth, M. Detailed Analysis of Grid-Based Molecular Docking: A Case Study of CDOCKER - A CHARMm-Based MD Docking Algorithm. J. Comp. Chem. 2003, 24, 1549.

* Krammer, A.; Kirchhoff, P. D.; Jiang, X.; Venkatachalam, C. M.; Waldman, M.
"LigScore: a novel scoring function for predicting binding affinities", J. Mol. Graph. Model. , 2005 , 23, 395-407.

* Muegge, I. "PMF Scoring Revisited" J. Med. Chem. 2006 , 49(20), 5895-5902.

* Muegge, I.; Martin, Y. C. A "General and Fast Scoring Function for 
Protein-Ligand Interactions: A Simplified Potential Approach" J. Med. Chem. 1999 , 42(5), 791.

* Hartshorn, M.J.; Verdonk, M.L.; Chessari, G.; Brewerton, S.C.; Mooij, W.T.M.; Mortenson, P.N.; Murray, C.W. "Diverse High-Quality Test Set for the Validation of Protein-Ligand Docking Performance", J. Med. Chem. , 2007 , 50 , 726-741.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Structure to use as the receptor. Ensure the receptor has hydrogens and complete valence shells. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all visible molecules. Notes: The receptor should not contain alternate conformations. You can use the protein tools in Discovery Studio to prepare a receptor. |
| Input Site Sphere | Defines a sphere in the receptor where receptor-ligands interactions are permitted. In Pipeline Pilot, define the sphere as x,y,z,r where x,y,z specifies the coordinates of the center and r is the radius of the sphere ( e.g. , 83.2,-43.3,42.24,6). In Discovery Studio, define the sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tools and then select the coordinates from the list. Note : A Binding Site or Site Sphere is required for: LigScore1, LigScore2, GOLD scores. |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Rotated Atoms Property | A comma separated list with ligand property names for rotatable receptor atoms (e.g., Receptor.Positions). If the property is found the ligand is scored with the updated receptor atoms. Note : To enable this feature for the GOLD scoring functions, please set the GOLD Retrieve Rotatable H Positions to True. |
| Input Control Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the control ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands will be tagged with the Control property to distinguish them from unknowns. A hit rate graph or ROC plot can later be generated from this to compare how highly different scoring functions were able to rank the known actives. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Preserve Controls In Input | Preserves the control ligand property, if control ligands are included in the input ligands. Otherwise the control ligand property will be removed from all input ligands. Valid Values: True , False |
| Input Control Ligand Property | Name of the property to use for identifying control ligands. A non-zero value for this property indicates the ligand is a control. |
| Scoring Functions | Select one or more scoring functions to be calculated for each ligand. CDOCKER Scores LigScore1 and LigScore2 PLP1 and PLP2 Jain PMF and PMF04 Ludi 1, Ludi 2, and Ludi 3 CDOCKER Score Goldscore* Chemscore* ASP* CHEMPLP* Chemscore Kinase* Chemscore P450 CSD* Chemscore P450 PDB* Goldscore P450 CSD* Goldscore P450 PDB* Note: * A valid GOLD license must be obtained from CCDC before using any of the GOLD scoring functions. The score value returned may be the negative of the selected score to provide a consistent interpretation of that data, i.e. ,a more positive value indicates a better score. Valid Values: CDOCKER Scores, LigScore1 , LigScore2 , PLP1 , PLP2 , Jain , PMF , PMF04 , Ludi Energy Estimate 1, Ludi Energy Estimate 2, Ludi Energy Estimate 3, Goldscore, Chemscore, ASP, CHEMPLP, Chemscore Kinase, Chemscore P450 CSD, Chemscore P450 PDB, Goldscore P450 CSD, Goldscore P450 PDB |
| CDOCKER Scores | Calculate CDOCKER scoring functions. The scores are reported as the negative of the energy values. See Also: Wu, G.; Robertson, D. H.; Brooks, C. L. III; Vieth, M. Detailed Analysis of Grid-Based Molecular Docking: A Case Study of CDOCKER - A CHARMm-Based MD Docking Algorithm. J. Comp. Chem. 2003, 24, 1549. |
| Scores | Scores to calculate: -CDOCKER_ENERGY : CDOCKER energy score (negative of the energy) -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY : CDOCKER interaction score (negative of the energy) Valid Values: -CDOCKER_ENERGY , -CDOCKER_INTERACTION_ENERGY |
| Ligand Partial Charge Method | Choose a method to assign partial charges. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF |
| LigScore | Parameters for LigScore scoring functions. |
| Scoring LigScore Forcefield | Forcefield to use for LigScore1 and LigScore2 Dreiding : DREIDING forcefield with Gasteiger charges CFF : Consistent Force Field Valid Values: Dreiding , CFF |
| Scoring LigScore Energy Grid Extension | Extension of the binding-site (Å). A site extension is used to calculate the energy and surface grids for ligand scoring. The ligand volume must be contained within the grid dimension. |
| Scoring LigScore1 Label | The base name for the property that will contain LigScore1 values in the results. The property name for the score will have the forcefield name appended Dreiding or cff, for example "LigScore1_Dreiding". |
| Scoring LigScore1 Minimum Score | Minimum LigScore1 score. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Scoring LigScore1 Report Individual Contributions | Output the individual descriptors that contribute to the score. Valid Values: True, False |
| Scoring LigScore2 Label | The base name for the property that will contain LigScore2 values in the results. The property name for the score will have the forcefield name appended Dreiding or cff, for example "LigScore1_Dreiding". |
| Scoring LigScore2 Minimum Score | Minimum score for LigScore2. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Scoring LigScore2 Report Individual Contributions | Output the individual descriptors that contribute to the score. Valid Values: True, False |
| PLP | Parameters for PLP scoring functions. |
| Scoring PLP1 Label | The property name that will contain the negative of PLP1 values in the results. |
| Scoring PLP1 Minimum Negative Score | Minimum score for the negative of the PLP1 value. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Scoring PLP2 Label | The property name that will contain the negative of PLP2 values in the results. |
| Scoring PLP2 Minimum Negative Score | Minimum score for the negative of the PLP2 value. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Jain | Parameters for the Jain scoring function. |
| Scoring Jain Label | The property name that will contain Jain values in the results. |
| Scoring Jain Minimum Score | Minimum score for Jain. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Scoring Jain Ignore Non-Polar Hydrogens | Ignore non-polar hydrogen atoms when computing the score. Valid Values: True, False |
| Scoring Jain Ignore Water | Ignore water molecules when computing the score. Valid Values: True, False |
| PMF | Parameters for PMF scoring function. |
| Scoring PMF Label | The property name that will contain the negative of PMF values in the results. |
| Scoring PMF Minimum Negative Score | Minimum score for the negative of the PMF values. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Scoring PMF Ignore Hydrogens | Ignore hydrogen atom contributions. Valid Values: True , False |
| Scoring PMF Carbon-Carbon Cutoff | Cutoff distance for carbon-carbon interactions (Å). Please note, the default value of 12 showed an improved score-activity correlation (Krammer et al ., 2005) than the originally published value of 6 (Muegge and Martin, 1999). |
| Scoring PMF Other Interactions Cutoff | Cutoff distance for other atom interactions (Å). Note: The default value of 12 showed an improved score-activity correlation (Krammer et al ., 2005) than the originally published value of 9 (Muegge and Martin, 1999). |
| PMF04 | Parameters for PMF04 scoring function. |
| Scoring PMF04 Label | The property name that will contain the negative of PMF04 values in the results. |
| Scoring PMF04 Minimum Negative Score | Minimum score for the negative of the PMF04 value. Ligand poses that score below this threshold will be removed from the result set. |
| Scoring PMF04 Ignore Hydrogens | Ignore hydrogen atom contributions. Valid Values: True , False |
| Scoring PMF04 Carbon-Carbon Cutoff | Cutoff distance for carbon-carbon interactions (Å). |
| Scoring PMF04 Other Interactions Cutoff | Cutoff distance for other atom interactions (Å). |
| Ludi | Parameters for Ludi scoring functions. |
| Scoring Ludi Score Label | The base name for the calculated Ludi score properties. For example, the default Ludi name will create the property names: Ludi_1, Ludi_2, and Ludi_3. |
| Scoring Ludi 1 Minimum Score | Molecules with a Ludi 1 score below this value will be filtered from the results, if specified. |
| Scoring Ludi 2 Minimum Score | Molecules with a Ludi 2 score below this value will be filtered from the results, if specified. |
| Scoring Ludi 3 Minimum Score | Molecules with a Ludi 3 score below this value will be filtered from the results, if specified. |
| Scoring Ludi Report Individual Contributions | Output the individual descriptors that contribute to the score. Valid Values: True, False |
| GOLD | GOLD Scoring function parameters. |
| Output Level | GOLD output file level: 0 : No GOLD log files are created. Recommended for high-throughput virtual screening. 1 : Minimal information is returned with warnings log and GOLD main log file. 2 : All GOLD log files are returned. This option may create a large amount of data and depending on the number of input ligands, may affect speed. Valid Values: 0, 1 , 2 |
| Perform Local Optimization | Perform local optimization (simplexing) to minimize the docked ligand pose before rescoring. Simplexing is important if you are to obtain meaningful scores. Due to the nature of scoring functions, one finds that small changes in location or conformation of the pose can have large effects on the calculated score. Note : Simplexing can also affect rotatable protein hydrogen atoms. Valid Values: True , False |
| Retrieve Rotatable H Positions | Retrieve rotatable hydrogen position properties, if available. Properties specified in Rotated Atoms Property will be used to update the receptor coordinates as each score is calculated. When rescoring a GOLD solution file it is possible to use the optimized positions of the polar protein hydrogen atoms that were generated during the original docking. If this option is not switched on (or no rotatable H positions are available) then the default hydrogen atoms positions specified in the protein input file will be used. The rotatable atom positions should be in the following format: X1 Y1 Z1 # atno AtomIndex1 X2 Y2 Z2 # atno AtomIndex2 For example: 49.9664 85.0298 58.7180 # atno 777 44.0652 86.6980 50.6555 # atno 1152 Valid Values: True, False |
| Receptor Depth Scaling | Hydrogen bonds deep in the pocket are rewarded with an increased score, while the scores of those closer to the solvent-exposed surface are decreased. Simultaneously, the scores attributed to lipophilic interactions are reduced (only available for Chemscore functions). This procedure has been shown to increase the relative scores of active molecules compared to inactive molecules across a diverse range of proteins. Note : See the GOLD documentation for further information. Valid Values: True, False |
| Report Individual Contributions | Add individual score contribution properties. Valid Values: True, False |
| Fix All Receptor Rotatable Bonds | During all dockings receptor serine, threonine, and tyrosine hydroxyl groups are optimized i.e. rotated during docking, as are lysine NH3+ groups. If this is undesirable this rotation can be disabled by setting the value to True. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parameter Files | Override the scoring parameter file for the selected scoring function. It contains all the parameters used by the GOLD for the selected scoring function selected. A full description of the meaning of the various parameters is given elsewhere. If blank, GOLD default settings will be used Warning The format of the parameter file is strict: incorrect syntax may cause GOLD to behave in unexpected ways or even to crash. Because of the large number of parameters, no guarantee can be given that the program will behave reliably with anything other than the default parameterization. |
| Parameter Files Goldscore | Override the scoring parameter file. This file contains all the parameters used for Goldscore. A full description of the meaning of the various parameters is given in the GOLD manual. If no file is specified the GOLD default settings will be used. Note: The format of the parameter file is strict. Incorrect syntax may cause GOLD to behave unexpectedly. |
| Parameter Files Chemscore | Override the scoring parameter file. This file contains all the parameters used for Chemscore. A full description of the meaning of the various parameters is given in the GOLD manual. If no file is specified the GOLD default settings will be used. Note: The format of the parameter file is strict. Incorrect syntax may cause GOLD to behave unexpectedly. |
| Parameter Files ASP | Override the scoring parameter file. This file contains all the parameters used for ASP. A full description of the meaning of the various parameters is given in the GOLD manual. If no file is specified the GOLD default settings will be used. Note: The format of the parameter file is strict. Incorrect syntax may cause GOLD to behave unexpectedly. |
| Parameter Files CHEMPLP | Override the scoring parameter file. This file contains all the parameters used for CHEMPLP. A full description of the meaning of the various parameters is given in the GOLD manual. If no file is specified the GOLD default settings will be used. Note: The format of the parameter file is strict. Incorrect syntax may cause GOLD to behave unexpectedly. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Use Input Binding Site | Use a binding site for defining the shape of the receptor binding pocket. Valid Values: True, False |
| Input Binding Site | Receptor binding site defines a volume where receptor-ligand interactions can occur. In Discovery Studio, select a binding site on the receptor. The binding site can be defined using the Defined and Edit Binding Site tools. In Pipeline Pilot, select a Binding Site file. The Binding Site file can be created using Discovery Studio or the Site Detection component. Note : A Binding Site or Site Sphere is required for: LigScore1, LigScore2, GOLD scores. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

Perform local optimization (simplexing) to minimize the docked ligand pose before rescoring. Simplexing is important if you are to obtain meaningful scores. Due to the nature of scoring functions, one finds that small changes in location or conformation of the pose can have large effects on the calculated score.

Retrieve rotatable hydrogen position properties, if available.

Properties specified in Rotated Atoms Property will be used to update the receptor coordinates as each score is calculated.

When rescoring a GOLD solution file it is possible to use the optimized positions of the polar protein hydrogen atoms that were generated during the original docking. If this option is not switched on (or no rotatable H positions are available) then the default hydrogen atoms positions specified in the protein input file will be used.

The rotatable atom positions should be in the following format:

X1 Y1 Z1 # atno AtomIndex1

X2 Y2 Z2 # atno AtomIndex2

For example:

49.9664 85.0298 58.7180 # atno 777

44.0652 86.6980 50.6555 # atno 1152

This procedure has been shown to increase the relative scores of active molecules compared to inactive molecules across a diverse range of proteins.

* See the GOLD documentation for further information.

# Score Ligand Poses

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/receptor-ligand_interactions_score_ligand_poses.htm

## Score Ligand Poses

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Score Ligand Poses protocol offers a selection of scoring functions to evaluate ligand binding in a receptor cavity.

| Scoring Function | Comments |
| --- | --- |
| CDOCKER Scores | CHARMm forcefield-based scoring functions used in the CDOCKER docking algorithm. [Wu et al., 2003] |
| LigScore1 | Empirical scoring function developed by Krammer et al., 2005 |
| LigScore2 | Empirical scoring function developed by Krammer et al., 2005 |
| PLP1 | Empirical scoring function developed by Gehlhaar et al., 1995 |
| PLP2 | Empirical scoring function developed by Gehlhaar et al., 1999 |
| Jain | Empirical scoring function developed by Jain, 1996 |
| PMF | Knowledge based scoring function developed by Muegge and Martin, 1999 |
| PMF04 | Knowledge based scoring function developed by Muegge, 2006 |
| Ludi Energy Estimate 1 | Empirical scoring function developed by Böhm 1994a |
| Ludi Energy Estimate 2 | Empirical scoring function developed by Böhm 1998 |
| Ludi Energy Estimate 3 | Empirical scoring function developed by Böhm 1998 |
| Goldscore * | Empirical scoring function. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| Chemscore * | Empirical scoring function. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| ASP * | Knowledge based scoring function. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| CHEMPLP * | Empirical scoring function. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| Chemscore Kinase * | Empirical scoring function optimized for kinases. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| Chemscore P450 CSD * | Empirical scoring function optimized for heme-containing proteins. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| Chemscore P450 PDB * | Empirical scoring function optimized for heme-containing proteins. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| Goldscore P450 CSD * | Empirical scoring function optimized for heme-containing proteins. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |
| Goldscore P450 PDB * | Empirical scoring function optimized for heme-containing proteins. For more information, see GOLD documentation at CCDC . |

Scoring functions with a * require a valid GOLD installation and license .

Typically, the ligands will have been docked into the receptor before running this protocol. The output of protocols that modify the receptor
conformation, for example Flexible Docking, can be used here and the flexibility is taken into account by the scoring functions.

* Load the structure you want to define as the receptor
into the Graphics View .

* Depending on the scoring functions selected, you may need to specify a binding site or sphere. Use the Binding Site tools to define the
binding site.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools and click Score Ligand Poses to open the Score Ligand Poses dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Receptor Select the receptor from the list of molecules.
The receptor must have hydrogens added and all atom valencies satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed. Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Site Sphere Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted (not required for Ludi scores). You can define a sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Optionally, you can specify an Input Binding Site . Rotated Atoms Property If the ligands contain a property with information on the conformation of the protein, this can be used to
calculate the scores of the protein ligand complex, incorporating receptor flexibility. This parameter 
is set by default to handle the output of the Docking protocols available within Discovery Studio . Scoring Scores Set the scoring functions you want to evaluate. For details about the remaining parameters, see Score Ligand Poses - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Receptor | Select the receptor from the list of molecules. The receptor must have hydrogens added and all atom valencies satisfied so that atoms can be properly typed. |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Site Sphere | Choose the coordinates of the sphere where receptor-ligand interactions are permitted (not required for Ludi scores). You can define a sphere using the Define and Edit Binding Site tool panel. Optionally, you can specify an Input Binding Site . |
| Rotated Atoms Property | If the ligands contain a property with information on the conformation of the protein, this can be used to calculate the scores of the protein ligand complex, incorporating receptor flexibility. This parameter is set by default to handle the output of the Docking protocols available within Discovery Studio . |
| Scoring Scores | Set the scoring functions you want to evaluate. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Score Ligand Poses - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the run finishes, view the scored ligands in the Molecule Window . The Input Receptor is displayed with the view centered on the binding site. This view allows you to browse through the ligands and view the 3D structure, a 2D depiction, and property data simultaneously. Use the View Interactions tools to identify ligand hydrogen bonds, bumps, and Pi interactions. For details about viewing, sorting, and filtering the results in the Data Table View, see Analyzing results with the Data Table View .

If you have specified control ligands , you can create hit rate plots to analyze the results further.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| LigScore-<receptor>.log | Log file from calculating the non-Ludi scoring functions. The file is only present if one or more of the non-Ludi scoring functions have been calculated. If parallel processing was enabled, the log file from each chunk is concatenated. |
| LudiScore-<receptor>.log | Log file from the Ludi Score calculation. The file is only present if one or more Ludi scoring functions have been calculated. If parallel processing was enabled, the log file from each chunk is concatenated, prefixed by the chunk number. |
| <ligands>.sd | Contains all the ligands successfully processed by the scoring calculations. |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | Contains ligands that were filtered or failed the scoring calculation. It is not created if ligands were not filtered or did not fail. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Open this file to view the scored ligands with the input receptor in a Molecule Window with the view centered on the binding site. |

# General receptor-ligand interactions tasks

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/tsk_rcli-general.htm

## General receptor-ligand interactions tasks

The following are basic tasks for working with receptor-ligand interactions.
For a comprehensive list that includes more advanced tasks, see Tasks - Receptor-Ligand Interactions .

* Apply receptor flexibility in binding energy and scoring

* Calculate RMSD of a docked ligand pose

* Change the radius of the binding sphere

* Choose a binding sphere versus binding site

* Prepare the protein

* Define a receptor

* Define a binding site from cavity detection

* Define a receptor binding sphere

* Define an interaction site

* Display only residues in the vicinity of the binding sphere

* Find a binding cavity based on ligand shape

* Find receptor binding sites

* Generate a hit rate plot or an enrichment curve

* Visualize non-bonded interactions

* Visualize non-bonded interactions (without modifying protein display)

* Visualize residues inside an active binding site

* Visualize the surface inside a buried binding site using transparent sides

To apply receptor flexibility in binding energy, scoring, or pose analysis calculations

Some protocols (e.g., Dock Ligands (GOLD) ) add flexible receptor atom properties to the ligands (usually named Receptor.Positions or Gold.Protein.RotatedAtoms). These can be used to visualize the flexible (i.e., rotated) receptor atoms when stepping through the ligands in the Molecule Window, 
or as input for the Calculate Binding Energies , Score Ligand Poses , and Analyze Ligand Poses protocols.

Make sure that the name in the file that stores the flexible atoms property is specified in the Read protein flexibility from parameter in the Molecule Window preferences .

If the ligand poses have a property with a name that matches one in either the Flexible Receptor Atom Property or Rotated Atoms Property parameter, then the receptor coordinates will be updated before the energy or score is calculated. The default values for these parameters should work in most cases. However, if the properties are from a different receptor, or the receptor has been modified (typed, for example), then you may want to either remove the properties or unset the parameter in the protocol.

When the protocol finishes, the output file is loaded with the receptor molecule defined as the receptor. You can check that the properties are correct by stepping through the ligand poses and viewing the updated flexible atoms in the Graphics View.

To calculate the RMSD of a docked ligand pose

* Load the ligand pose into a Molecule Window.

* Load the x-ray pose into the same Molecule Window. This should be in a
molecule by itself, you may need to cut out the residue or chains from a
protein structure.

* Select the reference structure. From the menu bar, choose Structure | RMSD | Set Reference .
This defines the selected structure as the reference for the RMSD
calculation.

* From the menu bar, choose Structure | RMSD | All Atoms or Heavy Atoms (the latter will exclude hydrogen atoms).

* A report page opens with the results of the RMSD calculation. RMSD properties are also added to each molecule.

You can also perform this task on a series of ligands using the Calculate RMSD protocol. Make sure that the x-ray poses are
the first pose of each ligand in the input.

See also:

Tasks - Receptor-Ligand Interactions

To change the radius of the binding sphere

* Select the sphere from the 3D, Hierarchy, or Table views.

* From the menu bar, choose Edit | Attributes... .

* Change the Radius , and then click OK .

You can also use the +Expand and -Contract buttons in the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools panel to adjust the sphere size.

To choose a binding sphere versus a binding site

A Binding Sphere is used in several protocols
(e.g., Dock Ligands (LibDock) , Dock Fragments (MCSS) ) to define a protein binding region.
The sphere encloses an active region's residues in the protein binding site where receptor-ligand interactions are allowed to occur.
You can create a binding site sphere with the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools.

A Binding Site consists of grid points that represent the continuous volume of a protein binding cavity.

To prepare the protein

Proteins downloaded from the PDB may have problems that should be corrected before defining a receptor. Use the Prepare Protein tools to correct the following common problems:

* Remove alternate conformations

* Remove HetAtoms from a protein structure (optionally)

* Add hydrogens

* Correct missing or incorrectly specified residues

* Detect valency violations and correct them by changing the bond type or changing the formal charge

* Optimize the protonation state and hydrogen positions with the Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol

To define a receptor

Successful docking or scoring of ligands requires accurate representation of the receptor structure.

* Correct any problems with the protein. See Prepare the protein .

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools.

* If the receptor is not already defined, click Define Receptor .

To define a binding site from cavity detection

* In the Molecule Window, select the protein of interest

* Click From Receptor Cavities to detect binding site cavities.
A red sphere is automatically displayed centered at this site cavity.

* You can step through the binding sites in the Graphics View by clicking Next in the Display group.

To define a receptor binding sphere

* If the receptor is not already defined click Define Receptor .

* Select receptor atoms or residues in the vicinity of the binding site.

* Click From Current Selection .

* A red binding site sphere will be displayed in the center of the
selection.

To define an interaction site

* In the Molecule Window, select the receptor of interest and select an atom or a
collection of atoms that should interact with the ligand.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Dock Ligands tools.

* Click Define Interaction Site .

* A colored sphere will be displayed around the atoms that indicate the interaction type.
Based on the selected atom-type different receptor-ligand interactions are possible: Hydrophobic: Requires the ligand to form an non-polar interaction (e.g., carbon). Hydrogen bond acceptor: Requires the ligand to be a hydrogen bond donor (e.g., oxygen). Hydrogen bond donor: Requires the ligand to be a hydrogen bond acceptor (e.g., polar hydrogen). Metal ion interaction: Requires the ligand to have an oxygen or nitrogen with a lone pair (e.g., Zn).

* Hydrophobic: Requires the ligand to form an non-polar interaction (e.g., carbon).

* Hydrogen bond acceptor: Requires the ligand to be a hydrogen bond donor (e.g., oxygen).

* Hydrogen bond donor: Requires the ligand to be a hydrogen bond acceptor (e.g., polar hydrogen).

* Metal ion interaction: Requires the ligand to have an oxygen or nitrogen with a lone pair (e.g., Zn).

The interactions sites can be specified in the following protocol:

* Dock Ligands (GOLD)

The Dock Ligands (Pharmacophore Restraints and CHARMm) protocol requires a pharmacophore to restrain ligands.

To display only residues in the vicinity of the binding sphere

* If the receptor is not already defined click Define Receptor

* Define the sphere by clicking From Current Selection .

* A red binding site sphere will be displayed in the center of the selection.

* Change the sphere radius to ensure that the desired residues are enclosed in the sphere.

* Click on the Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres and Show/Hide Site Spheres to hide the sphere.
Now only residues close to the binding site are visible.

To find a binding cavity based on ligand shape

* In the Molecule Window, select the protein of interest.

* Click Define Receptor .

* Find the ligand of interest in the Molecule Window. If the ligand is
part of the receptor, it should be moved out for the site-detection algorithm
to work correctly. This can be done by either selecting the ligand in the Molecule Window Hierarchy View and dragging it out of the
Cell, or by cutting and pasting.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site (Advanced) tools.

* With the ligand still selected, click Find Site as Volume of Selected Ligand .

* The Binding Site will be displayed in the Molecule Window.

To find receptor binding sites

* Click From Receptor Cavities . Each found cavity will be filled with green jacks that are engulfed by red binding site spheres.

* You can step through the Binding Sites in the Graphics View by using the arrows in the Step through Binding Sites group.

To generate a hit rate plot or an enrichment curve

* Open the docking results that contains the docked ligands and the control ligands in a Molecule Window.

* The control ligands should have an attribute associated with each entry. If they do not, add them using the Add Attribute dialog.

You can generate enrichment or ROC curve from the input molecules by using the Calculate ROC Curve protocol. You can also generate a hit rate plot from the menu bar as follows:

* Choose Chart | Hit Rate Plot from the menu bar to open the Hit Rate Plot Options dialog .

* Select the attributes that should used for the analysis (e.g., docking score).

* Select an attribute that identifies the control ligands. The control attribute can be specified by a specific value
or by selecting ligands with control values that are not empty.

* Click OK to generate the Hit Rate plot . You can set the color of the lines from the Advanced tab on the Hit Rate Plot Display Style .

To visualize non-bonded interactions

* Open a protein ligand complex in a Molecule Window.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tools to define the receptor and the ligand

* From the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | View Interactions tool panel, click Ligand Interaction . By default, the view automatically zooms in on the ligand and the non-bonded interactions are displayed.
The view is automatically simplified by hiding any non-participating residues. If multiple ligands exist (e.g., from a docking analysis), use the Show First, Next, Previous, and Last Ligand buttons in the tool panel to display interactions the other ligands.

If multiple ligands exist (e.g., from a docking analysis), use the Show First, Next, Previous, and Last Ligand buttons in the tool panel to display interactions the other ligands.

* Alternatively, you can quickly analyze a set of docked poses using the Analyze Ligand Poses protocol.

To visualize non-bonded interactions (without changing the display of protein)

At times it may be desirable to view non-bond interactions between a protein and a ligand without changing the display of the protein (e.g., if the display of the binding site residues have been purposely altered for illustration purposes).

* Open a protein ligand complex in a Molecule Window and modify the display of the specific residues of interest.

* Select the ligand and open Structure | Monitor | Non-bond Interactions... from the menu bar.

* Select the Interaction Types of interest (e.g., Hydrogen Bond, Electrostatic, etc.) and set Molecular Scope to Any interaction with selection . This shows intermolecular interactions between the ligand and the protein, and intramolecular interactions in the ligand.

When considering multiple ligands the steps above are different. Since the ligands change, as you browse through them, it is not possible to use Selection when defining the interactions. Instead, create an interaction monitor on everything, turn off the view of the interacting regions that are of no interest, and browse through the ligands:

* With only the protein visible (no ligands) use choose Structure | Monitor | Non-bond Interactions from the menu bar. Select the desired interactions and set the Molecular Scope to Any interaction with selection .

* In the Hierarchy View, uncheck the Non-bond monitor to turn off the display of the interactions.

* Lock the visibility of the protein and use the Small Molecules | Molecule Browser to step through the ligands. Only the new interactions (those between the protein-ligand and ligand-ligand atoms) are visible. The protein-protein interactions remain hidden.

To visualize residues inside an active binding site

* Open the protein in a new Molecule Window and select the molecule or any atom.

* Click Define Receptor . This creates a SBD_Receptor group of the protein and enables you to find receptor cavities.

* Click From Receptor Cavities .

* By default only the largest binding site is displayed. However, you can step through the remaining
binding sites by using the arrows in the Step through Binding Sites group.

* Select a site and click From Current Selection .

* Click Center and Fit to Screen to center and zoom in on the selection.

* From the menu bar, choose View | Visibility | Hide to make the binding site points invisible.

* From the tool panel, click Show/Hide Residues Outside Spheres to hide all residues that are not part of the sphere.

* Only residues with atoms inside the sphere are now visible.

To visualize the surface inside a buried binding site using transparent sides

Analyzing a binding site buried within a protein can be a challenging task. However, by using the two-sided surface transparency functionality makes the process easier.

* Load a protein-ligand complex of interest in a new Molecule Window.

* Select the molecule in the Hierarchy View.

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools, and then click Define Receptor .

* Click From Receptor Cavities to identify binding sites
from cavities in the structure. The first site identified will be used in this example.

* In the Hierarchy View, select Site 1 . Expand the cell and
molecule objects to reveal it.

* From the menu bar, choose Edit | Select to open the Select dialog.

* Change the Scope to Atom and set the Radius to 3 . Check the Replace Selection checkbox, and then Select . This selects all atoms within three angstroms of the site. Close the dialog.

* Choose Structure | Surface | Add from the menu bar, and then
click OK to accept the defaults to create a surface on this
selection.

* Select the surface in the Hierarchy View.

* Choose View | Visibility | Show Only , and then choose View | Fit to view from the menu bar to hide the rest of the system and focus on the surface.

* Rotate the surface to view the binding site. However, as it
is enclosed, you cannot see the "inside" of the surface.

* Choose View | Display Style from the menu bar to open the Display
Style dialog. Check the Reverse Side checkbox to color both sides of
the surface differently. Ensure the reverse side transparency slider is all the
way to the left to make it completely transparent. Click OK .

* Now, as you rotate the surface, the receptor-facing side has been made
transparent, so you can see through to the ligand-facing side of the surface.
This is a useful technique for visualizing an enclosed binding site.

If you have a ligand present in an active site, choose Scripts | Ligand Interactions | Create Surface Around Ligand from the menu bar to perform similar steps.

# Site Finding and Reparenting

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsrlinteractions

Source file: tsrlinteractions/tsk_site-finding_reparenting.htm

## Site Finding and Reparenting

### Site Finding

You can determine receptor binding sites from the PDB Site Records , or use one of 
the site finding tools to automatically locate binding sites.
One option identifies cavities within the receptor, while the other builds a binding site based on a ligand molecule in a known location. 
The algorithm for both is based on a grid search and "eraser" algorithm.

* For both methods, the receptor and ligand must be separate molecules. The calculation will fail if the ligand is a chain within the receptor
molecule. You can correct this by reparenting the ligand.

* Make sure hydrogen atoms are added to both protein and ligand molecules before running the tools.

To find the binding sites using the eraser algorithm

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site tools.

* Define the receptor .

* Click From Receptor Cavities .

Binding Sites are derived from cavities within the structure of the receptor. The first binding site found is displayed.

To find a binding site based on the volume of a ligand

* Open the Receptor-Ligand Interactions | Define and Edit Binding Site (Advanced) tools.

* Click Find Sites as Volume of Selected Ligand .

To change the default site finding options

Set the desired parameters in the Binding Site page of the
Preferences dialog.

### Reparenting

Sometimes there is no hierarchical distinction between ligand and receptor molecules. For example, the ligand
may be defined as one chain of the receptor molecule. In these cases, you must change the hierarchy so that the receptor
and ligand are in separate molecules.

For example, if you use Define Receptor , Find Sites as Volume of Selected Ligand may not work because the ligand(s) are considered part of the receptor.
You can correct this by reparenting them in the hierarchy.

To reparent ligands

* Open the Hierarchy View .

* Select the ligand chain.

* Drag and drop, or cut and paste to change the hierarchy such that the ligand is part of a separate molecule.

The ligand is now recognized as separate from the receptor, and the site finding tools will work correctly. 
Open the Molecules tab in the Data Table View , and click the rows to visualize the molecules
in the Molecule Window .

# Analyze Trajectory tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_att.htm

## Analyze Trajectory tools

The Analyze Trajectory tool panel contains tools that allow you to analyze a trajectory or any set of molecular conformations of a molecular system
loaded into the Graphics View .

To check if the molecular system has conformations, open the Data Table View . If a Conformation tab is present in the table, the molecular system contains conformations that can be analyzed by these tools.

The following commands are available:

### View and Manipulate

Sample Conformations: Opens the Choose Trajectory Frames dialog , which allows you to keep a subset of the conformations from the molecule for analysis.

Export Conformations: Opens a dialog for exporting the conformations of the molecule in .pdb or .mol2 format, one file for each conformation.

Process Trajectory Files: Opens the Process Trajectory Files protocol dialog. This protocol can combine trajectory files from
multiple dynamics simulations into one and can also save a subset of the frames or atoms from one or more trajectories. In addition, it
converts energy file from the CHARMm simulation into tabular form (CSV format).

Export Conformations as Trajectory: Opens the Export Conformations as Trajectory protocol dialog. This protocol exports a typed molecule and writes conformations into a DCD file.

### Analyze

Create Plot: Opens the Choose Plot Axes dialog , 
which allows you to create a plot using the different aspects of a trajectory.

Analyze Trajectory: Opens the Analyze Trajectory protocol dialog. This protocol analyzes structural properties of a molecular dynamics trajectory.

Cluster Conformations: Opens the Cluster Conformations , protocol dialog. This protocol clusters conformations from molecular dynamics trajectories into a user-defined number of conformational states.

Estimate Free Energy Landscape: Opens the Estimate Free Energy Landscape , protocol dialog. This protocol analyzes an input dataset or simulation trajectory and estimates a free energy landscape. This protocol can perform statistical reweighting to correct for energetic biases applied during Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics.

Measure Trajectory Features: Opens the Measure Trajectory Features , protocol dialog. This protocol analyzes a molecular dynamics trajectory and returns time-series data for further analysis.

Analyze Trajectory Features: Opens the Analyze Trajectory Features , protocol dialog. This protocol computes time-lagged cross-covariance and cross-correlation within or between trajectory features, providing interactive plots and cross-feature data matrices.

Detect and Analyze Pockets: Opens the Detect and Analyze Pockets , protocol dialog. This protocol identifies pockets from molecular dynamics trajectories and characterizes them for further analysis.

Calculate Interaction Energy: Opens the Calculate Interaction Energy protocol dialog. This protocol calculates the nonbonded interactions (i.e., the van der Waals term and the electrostatic term) between two sets of atoms in a specified structure or trajectory.

### Advanced

Trajectory Principal Component Analysis: Opens the Trajectory Principal Component Analysis protocol dialog. This protocol performs a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on a set of molecular conformations (e.g., from a molecular dynamics trajectory).

Radial Distribution Function: Opens the Radial Distribution Function protocol dialog. This protocol uses the radial distribution function (RDF) to describe the structural correlation between atoms in a condensed phase. RDF, which is also called the pair correlation function, is commonly used in the study of the liquid state.

Calculate Radius of Gyration: Calculates the radius of gyration of applicable molecules and their children for each trajectory frame, or for a selected trajectory frame. When the calculation finishes, each frame has a new property, Radius of Gyration.

# Electrostatic Potential - PBEQ

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_electrostatic_potential_the.htm

## Electrostatic Potential - PBEQ

The Discovery Studio protocol Calculate Electrostatic 
Potential is based on the CHARMm program module PBEQ [Im et al., 1998] .

To understand the applications and parameters for which PBEQ is appropriate, 
it is useful to have a basic knowledge of the method used in the calculation. 
A brief description of the theory and algorithm is presented here and in the 
following topics:

* Models

* Poisson-Boltzmann equation

* Finite difference approximation

* Electrostatic Potential

* Total electrostatic energy and solvation energy

* PBEQ implementation

* Limitations of the PBEQ model

PBEQ is a program that calculates electrostatic properties for charged molecules.
Some of the properties of interest are:

* Electrostatic potential at any point in space: Φ(r)

* Electrostatic energy of a charge q: q Φ ( r )

* Total electrostatic energy

From these basic properties, other quantities can be calculated, such as:

* Solvation energy (electrostatic contribution)

* Binding energy (electrostatic contribution)

All of these quantities are derived from the electrostatic potential Φ(r).

Figure 1. Spatial distribution of the electrostatic potential of the Antibody 17b (2NXY.pdb). The shown isopotential surfaces are: -1.0 kcal/mol.e (red) +1.0 kcal/mol.e (blue) 0 kcal/mol.e (green)

# PBEQ implementation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_ds-pbeq-implementation.htm

## PBEQ implementation

The finite difference solution of the Poisson-Boltzmann equation implemented 
in PBEQ can be divided into five basic steps.

* Map molecule onto grid PBEQ defines automatically the size and location of the 
grid with respect to the molecule, based on the chosen size of grid spacing h and the minimum distance of protein atoms from the box walls D . 
Initially the molecule is oriented with the long axis of inertia along the X axis and the molecular center of mass at the origin of coordinate system. 
The center of the grid box is also set at the center of coordinate system and the number of the grid points in X, Y and Z directions is defined in a manner to warranty that the distance from the center of each one atom from boundary is no less than D.

grid with respect to the molecule, based on the chosen size of grid spacing h and the minimum distance of protein atoms from the box walls D . 
Initially the molecule is oriented with the long axis of inertia along the X axis and the molecular center of mass at the origin of coordinate system. 
The center of the grid box is also set at the center of coordinate system and the number of the grid points in X, Y and Z directions is defined in a manner to warranty that the distance from the center of each one atom from boundary is no less than D.

* Distribute point charges onto grid The finite difference formulas include the charge at each 
grid point. Because the atomic charges do not, in general, fall on grid 
points, each charge must be distributed to the surrounding grid 
points. This is done using a 3rd-order 
B-splines interpolation over nearest 27 grid points.

* Define dielectric map and ion exclusion map This is accomplished by creating the dielectric boundary between 
molecule and solvent using the atomic radii and a probe radius which you 
define. The dielectric boundary is the molecular surface, defined 
by the van der Waals contact and reentrant surfaces [Lee and Richards, 1971] . The midpoint of each grid line is then assigned either the
interior or exterior dielectric constant, depending on whether it is inside
or outside the molecular surface. This yields three times as
many dielectric points as grid points, which allows a more detailed representation
of the solvent-accessible surface. A grid line is the line connecting
two adjacent grid points. You can also specify an ion exclusion radius, which should
be equal to the average radius of the solvent ions. Because PBEQ uses
point charges that reside at the center of atoms, no charge due to solvent
ions should be allowed to approach closer to the molecular surface than
the radius of the ions. This creates a Stern layer around the molecular
surface, which has the exterior dielectric constant but an ionic strength
of 0.0.

* Set boundary conditions The grid points at the boundary of the grid represent a special 
case, because they have no outside neighbors. 
These points are assigned values at the beginning of the calculation and

# Electrostatic Potential

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_electrostatic-potential.htm

## Electrostatic Potential

The basic electrostatic property calculated by PBEQ is the electrostatic potential. To examine the factors that contribute to the electrostatic potential of a charged molecule in solvent, consider a simple example. Figure 1 shows two charges in a low dielectric medium, ε s , surrounded by a solvent with a high dielectric, ε 0 .

Figure 1: Contributions to electrostatic potential

The solvent molecules and ions respond to the field 
generated by each charge in the solute. This response, which consists 
of both dipolar reorientation and electronic polarization, in turn, sets 
up a field at the position of the original charges which is called their 
reaction field [Bottcher, 1973] . The strength 
of this field is determined by the magnitude of the charge, its distance 
from the dielectric boundary, the shape of that boundary, and the interior 
and exterior dielectric constants. The reaction field is felt by all charges 
in the system, including the source charge itself. Therefore, the external 
( ext ) electrostatic potential at a charge location is the sum of the interaction 
of each charge with its self -reaction field, the reaction fields of the 
other charges ( cross ), and direct Coulomb ( coul ) interaction with the 
other charges.

Equation 1:

Each point charge in addition generates its own 
Coulomb potential that acquires an infinite value in its location according 
to Equation 2, ( Models ). Then the total 
electrostatic potential equals:

Equation 2:

The solution to the Poisson-Boltzmann equation is Φ total . The finite difference technique 
leads to the charge smeared onto the grid (see Equation 2 in Finite 
difference approximation , for the value of charge density), which eliminates 
infinities but provides computational artifacts which depend on the grid 
resolution and molecule mapping.

# Finite difference approximation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_finite-difference-approximation.htm

## Finite difference approximation

PBEQ uses the finite difference method [Klapper et al., 1986] , [Im et al, 1998] , 
which involves mapping a molecule onto a 3D orthorhombic grid box, 
with spacing between grid points of size h (as shown 
in Figure 1 in two dimensions). In the DS implementation the numbers of the grid points in X, Y and Z directions are defined by the grid spacing h and the minimum distance of protein atoms to boundary D .

The interior of the solvent-accessible 
surface is assigned one dielectric, and the exterior is assigned another.

Figure 1: Two-dimensional mapping of a solvated molecule on PBEQ grid

The DS PBEQ implementation allows also to model proteins or other molecules integrated in lipid membranes [Im et al., 1998] . For this purpose the hydrophobic region occupied by the lipid tails can be defined as a planar slab with a low dielectric constant, e.g., ε = 2, that is different from the dielectric constant of the protein interior.
For a more adequate modeling of lipid bilayers, PBEQ allows also to define two additional planar slabs with a third dielectric constant corresponding to the regions occupied by the mobile polar lipid headgroups ( see Fig. 2).

Figure 2: Two-dimensional mapping of a molecule in membrane on PBEQ grid

The Poisson-Boltzmann equation must be satisfied everywhere 
in the grid, and, in particular, at each grid point. If the cube of side h surrounding a grid point is considered, as shown in Figure 1 above, the derivatives 
in the equation can be replaced by finite differences over this cube, and the 
continuous functions φ, ρ , and ε can be replaced by their values at the grid points [Klapper et al., 1986] .

Using this strategy, a finite difference formula can be obtained in which the potential at any grid point depends on the charge at the grid point, 
the value at the grid point, the grid spacing h , and the potential and dielectric values of the six neighboring grid points [Klapper et al., 1986] .

Figure 3: Cube of side h surrounding grid point

The black circles are the six surrounding grid points. Note that, associated with 
each grid point i , is a charge q i , a Debye-Huckel inverse length and a potential φ i . The dielectric values, however, are associated with the midpoints of the 
lines between the grid points.

Equation 1:

where:

N = 1 for linear equation (Equation 7, Poisson-Boltzmann equation )

N = (1 + φ 0 2 /3! + φ 0 4 /5! +...) for nonlinear 
equation (Equation 8, Poisson-Boltzmann equation )

Equation 1, above, is equivalent to the model with charge 
density ρ 0 obtained by the uniform 
smearing of the charge q 0 within the cube:

Equation 2:

The potential at each grid point can therefore be calculated and changes as its neighbors' potentials change. If this calculation is 
repeated iteratively, the potentials become more accurate with each iteration, until they meet the convergence criteria.

# Limitations of the PBEQ model

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_limitations-of-the-ds-model.htm

## Limitations of the PBEQ model

Although the Finite difference approximation yields accurate results in most cases [Klapper et al., 1986] , [Im et al., 1998] , [Jo et al., 2008] .
This is a numerical method which approximates the analytical 
solution. Consequently, there are conditions in which the approximation 
breaks down. In particular, errors are largest close to charges (within 
1 Å), and close to the dielectric boundary [Gilson and Honig, 1987] . The accuracy at these points can be improved by using
focusing, but you should be aware of the limitations.

# Models

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_models.htm

## Models

In classical electrostatics theory, materials are considered to be homogeneous dielectric media, 
which can be polarized by electrical charges. So a dielectric constant can
be used as a bulk measure of
the polarizability of the media, rather than explicitly accounting for the polarization of each atom. 
This is therefore a continuum model.

The simplest model is described by Coulomb's law, where the electrostatic energy G between two charges i and j is given by:

Equation 1:

and the potential at atom i due to a charge at atom j is:

Equation 2:

Where:

q j = charge on atom j ε = dielectric constant r ij = distance between atoms i and j

Although Coulomb's law is valid only for an infinite medium 
of a uniform dielectric, this model is often used in modeling 
software because of the computational simplicity. However, most biological 
molecules are functional in water, a solvent with considerably higher 
dielectric constant than the molecular interior. Therefore, if the solvent 
molecules are not treated explicitly, Coulomb's law is a poor approximation 
of electrostatic interactions.

Widely used in macromolecular electrostatics 
are implicit solvent models that treat the water environment as a high-dielectric 
continuum, interacting with the atomic charges embedded in the low-dielectric 
macromolecular interior. The most popular are based on the Finite Difference approximation to solve the Poisson-Boltzmann equation , such as used in PBEQ [Im et al., 1998] and [Jo et al., 2008] or in other similar programs [Klapper et al., 1986] , [Nicholls and Honig, 1991] , [Rocchia et al., 2002] , and in alternative approaches based on the Generalized Born 
approximation [Still et al., 1990] ) as used in
CHARMm.

# Poisson-Boltzmann equation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_posson-boltzmann-equation.htm

## Poisson-Boltzmann equation

A molecule such as a protein has a low dielectric constant as its dipolar groups are 
frozen into a hydrogen bonded lattice and cannot reorient in an external electrostatic field. 
A value near 2 measures its electronic polarization response while a value near 4 includes 
some contributions from dipole reorientation. Water, on the other hand, has a very high 
dielectric constant (80) since its dipoles reorient freely. Therefore, a molecule in aqueous 
solution yields a system with two very different dielectric media. The effects of this large 
difference can be considerable and should be accounted for by the electrostatic model. 
The Poisson-Boltzmann model assigns a distinct dielectric constant to the solute and the solvent. 
This makes it a good representation of the solvated molecules.

The electrostatic field ( E ) and electrostatic displacement ( D ) as 
functions of r are defined as:

Equation 1:

where:

* Φ(r) = electrostatic potential

* ε(r) = dielectric "constant"

* r = position vector (x, y, z)

* ▽ = vector differential operator

In a system with charges and inhomogeneous dielectric media, Poisson's equation relates the electric displacement to the charge density ρ(r):

Equation 2:

Substituting for D(r) from above,

Equation 3:

The charge density ρ(r) can be separated into two components:

Equation 4:

* ρ int is an interior charge distribution of the fixed positions of all charges in the molecule.

* ρ ext is an exterior charge density, which accounts for the redistribution of ions in solution in response to the electric potential in solution.

This charge density can be modeled by a Boltzmann distribution, giving:

Equation 5:

* ε = dielectric constant of the solvent

* Φ = electrostatic potential (in units of k T /e)

* e = electronic charge

* N A = Avogadro's number

* I = ionic strength (mol/L)

* k = Boltzmann constant

* T = temperature

* κ = Debye-Huckel inverse length

If the charge density of the molecule and the ionic strength of the solution are low, 
this term can be approximated by the linear term:

Equation 6:

Substituting these expressions for the charge density into the Poisson 
equation (Equation 3, above) gives the linear and nonlinear forms of the Poisson-Boltzmann 
equation:

Equation 7:

Equation 8:

where equals 
0 inside the molecule and equals in the solvent.

The Poisson-Boltzmann equation appears to be a good model, because it accounts for both 
the effect of dielectrics and ionic strength. Unfortunately, this equation can be solved 
analytically only for systems with simple dielectric boundary shapes, such as 
spheres and planes. In particular, the linear Poisson-Boltzmann solution for a single 
point charge, q i , placed at the origin of the coordinate 
system has the Debye-Huckel form:

Equation 9:

Most molecules of interest have complex shapes, and their conformations may have
a significant effect on the resulting electrostatic properties. The alternative to 
analytical solutions is to use numerical techniques to find an approximate solution.

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/anly_pbeq_the_total-electrostatic-energy.htm

## Total electrostatic energy and solvation energy

An important property that can be calculated from the potential is the total electrostatic energy of the system:

Equation 1:

Since the finite difference Poisson-Boltzmann solution 
yields φ total , it is 
difficult to obtain a value of G E using Equation 
1, above. However, the closely related quantity, the total grid energy (Grid Energy) is easily calculated:

Equation 2:

The superscript t+g refers to 
"total plus own grid energy", which is a reminder that φ own i has not been subtracted to yield G E as per 
Equation 1, above.

The value of G E can easily be 
determined for the processes where the "grid energy" is canceled out. 
In particular, the electrostatic component to the solvation energy can 
be computed using two calculations with identical grid mappings and the 
same interior dielectric. In the first calculation, the exterior dielectric 
is set to the value of the solvent (for example, 80.0 for water). In the second 
calculation the dielectric constant of the reference solvent is set to 1.0 (vacuum). The difference in the total electrostatic 
energies for these two calculations is the change in the electrostatic 
energy of transfer from vacuum to solvent which is the electrostatic component 
of the solvation energy.

Equation 3:

where G ε (ε s ,ε) is the electrostatic energy of a solute with a 
dielectric constant ε s in a solvent with constant ε.

Since the same grid mapping is used, and all the charged grid points are in the same (interior) dielectric region, 
Φ own i is the same for both calculations and is therefore canceled out as desired. Hence:

Equation 4:

In addition to canceling out the Φ own i , 
the technique described above also cancels out the direct Coulombic potentials 
between the charges in the molecule. However, if you are interested in the 
total energy of a system (for example, to compare conformations in a 
solution) you must add the Coulombic energy and the other forcefield terms. For this purpose you can use the Calculate 
Energy protocol with the Implicit Solvent parameter set to Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) .

# Forcefield Window

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/dl_missing-parameters.htm

## Forcefield Window

The Forcefield Window displays missing or estimated atom types and parameters of
a molecular system after a forcefield has been applied to it or when a user defined forcefield file ( .ffml file) is opened.
It also contains very useful information on the way each residue in the molecule is typed. Depending
on the molecular
system and forcefield, some of the following tabs may not be available.

Residues: This tab lists residues that cannot be typed by standard residue templates (for example standard amino acids, DNA etc.) defined in the standard forcefield files.

For a residue to be typed successfully by a forcefield template, the following conditions need to be satisfied:

* The residue name and atom names in the residue need to match those in the corresponding forcefield residue templates.

* For chain molecules, forcefield templates also specify out-of-residue atoms for bonds across the residue boundary, 
(i.e., atoms belonging to the preceding and following residues in the sequence). During the atom typing process, 
the typing algorithm looks for out-of-residue atoms, and if they are missing in the preceding and following residues, 
then the current residue is considered to have failed the standard template matching, and typing rules will be applied.

For residues that cannot be typed successfully by a forcefield template, typing rules will be applied to type the residues and the result will be listed in this tab.

The five columns on this tab display the name of the residue, the status of typing for the residue, 
the name of the chain which contains the residue, and the sum of formal and partial charges of the residue.

The status of typing for the residue may be:

* No matching template - The residue does not match any templates in the forcefield.

* Matches custom template - The residue matches a custom template added earlier using Add Residue Template .

You can click on each row to inspect the corresponding residues in the Molecule Window and determine whether the residue should be modified to match an existing standard residue template, or if the assigned atom types in the residue are expected.

Atoms: Shows the atom types. The status of the atom type can be Missing , indicating that atom type is not found in the current forcefield, or Generated , 
when a new atom type has been created using automated parameter estimation, or Modify Atom Type... .

If an appropriate ForcefieldType cannot be
found for an atom, its ForcefieldType cell will contain a question mark (?). You can use Modify Atom Type... to either 
assign it to an existing atom type, or create a new atom type for it.

For the remaining tabs the status of the parameter may be:

* Missing - The parameter is missing from the forcefield.

* Estimated - The parameter was created using automated parameter estimation

* User Defined - The parameter was entered by the user or read from a user-defined forcefield ( .ffml file).

Bonds: Shows the bond parameters with force constants and reference bond lengths.

Angles: Shows the angle parameters with force constants and reference bond angles.

Torsions: Shows the torsion parameters with barrier heights and phase.

Impropers: Shows the improper parameters with force constants and equilibrium values.

Nonbonds: Shows the van der Waals nonbond parameters, with minimum distances and minimum energies.

If the Forcefield Window
is associated with a Molecule Window, clicking on the row number in any of the tabs
will select the corresponding residue, atom, or atoms for the missing parameter in the Molecule Window.

# Calculate Electrostatic Potential - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/electrostatics_calculate_electrostatic_potential-para.htm

## Calculate Electrostatic Potential - Parameters

### Calculates the electrostatic potential of a molecule

Calculates the spatial distribution of the electrostatic potential (kcal/mol.e) and the potential at the atoms of the solute molecule using the CHARMm PBEQ module. The PBEQ calculations are based on a two-dielectric implicit solvent model and use a finite difference method to solve the Poisson-Boltzmann equation using an orthorhombic grid box.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constants for the solute and the solvent. |
| Solute | Specifies the dielectric constant of the solute. |
| Solvent | Specifies the dielectric constant of the bulk solvent. |
| Ionic Strength | Specifies the ionic strength of the solvent. The ionic strength is equal to the salt concentration (M) for monovalent salt. |
| Grid Spacing | Specifies the distance between the grid points (Å) of the finite-difference grid box used in first step of the PBEQ calculations. The Grid Spacing value should be less than the Minimum Distance To Boundary. |
| Minimum Distance To Boundary | Specifies the minimum distance of protein atoms from the walls of the grid box (Å). This parameter defines the dimension of the orthorhombic grid box. Should be greater than 3.0 Å, the thickness of a water layer. |
| Focusing | Specifies whether to run a second calculation with a smaller and finer grid. If True , the focusing grid is defined by the Focusing parameters. The focusing calculations use the potential from the previous, coarse grid calculations to set up the boundary potential. Valid Values: True, False |
| Focusing Grid Spacing | Specifies the distance between the grid points (Å) of the grid box used in the focusing step of the calculations. Note : The value of the Focusing Grid Spacing parameter has to be less than the Grid Spacing value used in the first, coarse grid step. |
| Focusing Minimum Distance To Boundary | Specifies the minimum distance of protein atoms from the walls of the grid box in the focusing calculations (Å). |
| Focusing Group Of Atoms | Specifies a group of atoms for the focusing calculation.
