# Calculate Electrostatic Potential

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/electrostatics_calculate_electrostatic_potential.htm

## Calculate Electrostatic Potential

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

This protocol calculates the spatial distribution of the electrostatic potential of a molecule by solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation using CHARMm PBEQ module. The potential values are calculated on a discretized grid inside an orthorhombic grid box. For membrane proteins, an implicit membrane can be added to the molecular model; the effect of the dielectric environments of the hydrophobic part of membrane and the membrane head group regions will be taken into account. The results can be visualized and used in the following ways:

* The electrostatic potential on the grid can be visualized in the context of the molecular structure in the Graphics View .

* The electrostatic energy terms can be used to calculate the electrostatic contributions to solvation energy, as discussed in the Total electrostatic energy and solvation energy theory section.

* The average atomic or residue potentials can be used to evaluate the electrostatic interaction energy between any groups of atoms, such as protein and a 
ligand, or to study the effect of mutations or conformational changes, as explained in the Analyzing results section.

Electrostatic potential calculations require the assignment of atomic charges and radii. Use the Change Forcefield tools
to assign forcefield type and atomic partial charge before running the protocol.

* Load or create a molecular structure in the Molecule Window .

* Open the Change Forcefield tools and choose the desired forcefield to type the molecule. The forcefield atomic charges represent a standard state of protonation of the acidic and basic groups, which is approximately correct at normal pH. For a more accurate model, you can use the fully protonated structure generated by Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol.
In this model the atomic charges are replaced by the mean atomic charges calculated according to the fractional protonation of the sites of titration at the chosen pH .

The forcefield atomic charges represent a standard state of protonation of the acidic and basic groups, which is approximately correct at normal pH. For a more accurate model, you can use the fully protonated structure generated by Calculate Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol.
In this model the atomic charges are replaced by the mean atomic charges calculated according to the fractional protonation of the sites of titration at the chosen pH .

* To add an implicit membrane to the protein structure use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools panel or the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. Additionally you can use the Membrane parameter to define the thickness and the dielectric constant of the regions occupied by the polar lipid heads.

* Open the Run Simulations tools and click Calculate Electrostatic Potential... to open the Calculate Electrostatic Potential dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the parameters as desired. For details, see Calculate Electrostatic Potential - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the interactive job finishes, a molecular surface colored by the electrostatic potential from the grid is added to the output molecule.
A grid object is also added to the molecule. 
If you ran the job in the background, expand the results in the 
Jobs Explorer, click the Report link, and then
click View Results in the report.

There are several methods for analyzing the data:

* By default, the first opened grid object represent the -1.0 kcal/mol isopotential surface. To create new isopotential surface, select the grid object from the Hierarchy View and choose Structure | Isosurface | New Contour from the menu bar. The common practice is to color the negative potential in red and the positive in blue. In many cases it is useful to add the zero potential surface to discriminate the regions of negative and positive potential for the investigation of the possible paths of docking ions or charged ligands, as well as identifying prospective sites for protein-protein interactions.

To create new isopotential surface, select the grid object from the Hierarchy View and choose Structure | Isosurface | New Contour from the menu bar. The common practice is to color the negative potential in red and the positive in blue.

In many cases it is useful to add the zero potential surface to discriminate the regions of negative and positive potential for the investigation of the possible paths of docking ions or charged ligands, as well as identifying prospective sites for protein-protein interactions.

* The average atomic potential in kcal/e, defined as the electrostatic potential averaged on the closest grid points to the center of an atom, can be found in the Average Potential column in the Atom tab of the Data Table when the Atomic Potential parameter is set to True . Also, when the Atomic Potential parameter is set to True , the average potential for each residue is calculated as the average of the corresponding atomic potentials and added as Average Potential column to the AminoAcid and Residue tabs. You can select all or part of the Average Potential column and choose Chart | Line Plot from the menu bar to create a plot of the electrostatic potential against the residue index. Besides the sign, the numerical values of the average potential obtained at atoms with non-zero formal charges are meaningless, because of the "numerical singularity" at the atomic centers of the charged atoms. However, you can use effectively the average atomic potential to evaluate the electrostatics interaction from the rest of the molecule with a specific group of atoms, such as a ligand, a specific protein residue or an ion. For this purpose, select the atoms of interest, e.g. the ligand or the residue, and use the Clear Charges parameter from Advanced parameter to group the atoms and run the protocol. The charges on the selected atoms will be set to zero during the calculation and the average potential values at these atoms are now meaningful and represent the potential from the rest of molecular system at the centers of these atoms. If you calculate the sum of the products of Average Potential and the atomic Partial Charges in the Atom tab you can evaluate the interaction energy of the selected group with the rest of molecule. To evaluate the effect of a mutation or conformational change, for example on a ligand or substrate, repeat the calculations with the new structure and compare the differences in the atomic potentials.

The average atomic potential in kcal/e, defined as the electrostatic potential averaged on the closest grid points to the center of an atom, can be found in the Average Potential column in the Atom tab of the Data Table when the Atomic Potential parameter is set to True .

Also, when the Atomic Potential parameter is set to True , the average potential for each residue is calculated as the average of the corresponding atomic potentials and added as Average Potential column to the AminoAcid and Residue tabs.

You can select all or part of the Average Potential column and choose Chart | Line Plot from the menu bar to create a plot of the electrostatic potential against the residue index.

Besides the sign, the numerical values of the average potential obtained at atoms with non-zero formal charges are meaningless, because of the "numerical singularity" at the atomic centers of the charged atoms.

However, you can use effectively the average atomic potential to evaluate the electrostatics interaction from the rest of the molecule with a specific group of atoms, such as a ligand, a specific protein residue or an ion. For this purpose, select the atoms of interest, e.g. the ligand or the residue, and use the Clear Charges parameter from Advanced parameter to group the atoms and run the protocol. The charges on the selected atoms will be set to zero during the calculation and the average potential values at these atoms are now meaningful and represent the potential from the rest of molecular system at the centers of these atoms. If you calculate the sum of the products of Average Potential and the atomic Partial Charges in the Atom tab you can evaluate the interaction energy of the selected group with the rest of molecule.

To evaluate the effect of a mutation or conformational change, for example on a ligand or substrate, repeat the calculations with the new structure and compare the differences in the atomic potentials.

| Term | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Grid Energy | The sum of the product of electrostatic potential and the grid charge at each grid point. Only differences in total grid energies from two calculations using exactly the same grid definition are meaningful. The absolute value of the total grid energy of a single calculation is not meaningful. |

# Work with forcefields

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/forcefields.htm

## Work with forcefields

The use of forcefields is central to using molecular mechanics for molecular simulation. 
Forcefields define the parameters, which coupled with the simulation
equations, allow for simulation of molecules. In molecular mechanics, simple
equations of motion are used to describe the motions of atoms within a molecule.
For example, bond stretches are often simulated by a simple harmonic description
such as "balls on a spring". The set force constants to use for bonds between
all combinations of atom types make up the bond parameters. Typically
forcefields contain bond, angle, and torsion parameters, along with atom
charges, radii, and van der Waals energy minima to represent non-bonded
interactions.

Applying a forcefield to a molecule involves several steps. First, atom
types and atomic charges are assigned to each atom, and a residue type to
each residue. Next, a consistency check is performed to ensure that each
combination of atom types has a parameter in the forcefield. For example,
that all pairs of bonded atom types have corresponding bond parameters.
These first steps can occur interactively in the Discovery Studio client,
or automatically as a part of a protocol. When running interactively, any
missing parameters are reported to the user who can then enter
user-supplied values or enable parameter estimation. The typed molecule
(containing atom types, residue information, and atomic charges) and the
forcefield are then combined to produce the various input files for a
simulation. This last step occurs inside the various simulation components on
the server.

In Discovery Studio , you typically work with forcefields using the functionality provided 
in the Change Forcefield tools. You cannot view the 
forcefields per se, but after typing a system, you are able to view and edit any estimated or 
missing parameters using the Forcefield Window.

### Introduction to forcefields

Discovery Studio supports several different forcefields. Some, like the
charmm27 forcefield, are only parameterized for molecules built from known
biological subunits, i.e., proteins and nucleic acids. Others, such as
CHARMm, are more general, and in addition to biopolymers, also allow
simulation of a wide range of drug-like molecules.

The forcefield tool contains a drop-down list of forcefields. It also
contains a Browse... option that allows you to select a file containing
user-values for estimated or missing parameters.

#### Typing a molecule

Typing is done either by using a set of rules based on the names of the
atoms and residues (typically used for biological monomers), or by
connectivity. For example, in the CHARMm forcefield, the first step is to
identify any residues which are already "known", typically biopolymer
subunits such as amino acids and nucleotides. This is done by checking
that the residue name and atom names match those in the residue template
file (RTF). Each residue that matches a template entry is given a property
"ForceFieldTemplate" that indicates which residue it matched.

New residue templates are created for the remainder of the atoms that fail this
residue template check. And for these residues, the property
ForceFieldTemplate is set to None . 
For CHARMm, CHARMm Polar H, charmm19, charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, a series of 
connectivity tests are then run on the atoms in the unknown residues to
determine the atom types. This follows a set of predefined rules
and can type many biologically
relevant molecules. Occasionally an atom type cannot be identified, 
and manual customization is required.

In the user interface, typing is performed by clicking Apply Forcefield in the Change Forcefield tools. 
If the residue types successfully, a message appears in the status area
(e.g., "1crn typed with CHARMm"). If more information is available 
on typing then the More... button becomes active. 
Clicking this button will open the Forcefield Window. If you select a row in this window, a
corresponding selection in the Molecule Window will be made, enabling you to
quickly identify the following:

* Residues that did not match the forcefield templates

* Atoms that could not be typed, or were assigned newly created
types

* Parameters that were estimated or missing - see next
section

An alternate method is to use the structure matching typing tool by clicking Assign Forcefield... in the charmm36 forcefield tools. This method matches each residue with its template in the forcefield 
by structure matching. It also has the advantage to be able to recognize the applicable patches automatically. It only supports 
charmm22, charmm27, and charmm36 forcefields. It accepts user defined templates and uses them in the typing.

#### Modifying estimated parameters

The next stage in typing is to check that for the atom types and
connectivity within the molecule, all the required parameters are
present in the forcefield.

For example, are there bond parameters for
every pair of connected atom types and angle parameters for every
angle?

Some forcefields will fail to type at this point if there are
any missing parameters. However, the default for forcefields other than cff and MMFF is
to then estimate missing parameters. In parameter estimation, any missing
parameters (due to newly created atom types or unusual
connectivity for example) are estimated. The estimation is based on similar systems
that are in the parameter list. For example, if an sp 2 carbon
is attached to an sp 3 nitrogen, the average value for all other parameters of
this type is taken to create the parameters for this new combination.
However, this estimation is primitive, and you are encouraged to
obtain high quality parameters from other sources,
such as high-level quantum mechanical calculations, in order to obtain
high quality simulation results. If the automatic parameter estimation is turned off
on the forcefield preference page, or for forcefields that do not support parameter estimation,
missing parameters are left unknown.

When typing interactively in the client, the Forcefield Window lists
these missing or estimated parameters. You can modify these parameters 
and save it as a .ffml file
that contains the missing and estimated parameters. You can also 
modify the missing and estimated parameters by editing the file with a text editor.
You can then use the .ffml file when you type a molecule to include these changes
during the typing process. To do this, use the Browse... option in the
Forcefield dropdown list. The .ffml file is a set of extensions to an
existing forcefield and can be used in combination to store customized
parameter sets for a molecule.

#### Creating the simulation files

The last phase of typing is to create the input files for simulation. These
files vary according to which forcefield engine you are using. Typically
this stage is done automatically inside the simulation components on the
server. If you save the intermediate files when running a protocol, expert
users may inspect these files.

#### Further information

Forcefield Window Change Forcefield tools Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Supported file formats Supported forcefields CHARMm forcefields

# Protein Ionization and Residue pK

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/prmo_the_piapp.htm

## Protein Ionization and Residue pK

The side-chain of a set of protein residues, including Asp, Glu, Arg, Lys, His, Tyr, Cys, and the N-termini and C-termini of each chain, are 
titratable. For each of those residues, the pK 1/2 of the side-chains in the model compounds are determined experimentally [Thurlkill et al., 2006] . The model compounds are pentapeptides with the titratable residue in the 
middle and two alanines on each side.

Using the theory developed by Bashford and Karplus [Bashford and Karplus, 1991] , 
the pKs of titratable residues and the other ionization properties of a protein structure are derived from the fractional protonation of the acidic and basic groups,
calculated as a function of pH and the ionic strength. The fractional protonation of the sites of titration is evaluated from the pKs of the model compounds and 
the electrostatic interactions of each residue with the rest of 
molecule and with the solvent, treating the system as a statistical ensemble of all possible protonation states of the sites of titration. For a protein of N titratable sites, there 
are 2 N titration states to consider. To reduce the cost of calculation, a method was developed that considers the interaction of the 
titratable sites in a local cluster based on an energy cutoff. The interaction with the rest of the titratable sites are approximated by a mean-field 
potential [Spassov and Bashford, 1999] .

Electrostatic interaction energies are calculated using an implementation of Generalized Born solvation model in CHARMm and the atomic parameters 
are taken from either CHARMm or CHARMm polar hydrogen forcefields.

The following ionization properties and energy terms are calculated for a protein molecule:

* The fractional protonation as a function of pH and the pK of each titratable amino acid residue.

* The net charge of the molecule as a function of pH.

* Electrostatic energy of the fully deprotonated states, including the solvation term and the Coulomb term. This energy is not pH dependent.

* Energy of protonation at given pH (i.e., the energy to protonate a protein from fully deprotonated states to the protonation state of a given 
pH). The sum of the pH independent electrostatic energy term with this one is the electrostatic energy of the system at a given pH.

* Relative folding energy (the electrostatic contribution) is calculated using the zero state model approximation. Assuming the free energy of 
folding can be calculated by the energy difference of the folded and unfolded states, which individually can be decomposed into 
pH independent and protonation energy terms. The pH independent energy term of the unfolded state is a constant and the protonation energy
term is modeled by the free energy of protonation of the 
model compounds (i.e., assuming there is no electrostatic interaction between the titratable sites in the unfolded states). This approximation 
assumes that the effect of the interactions between the titratable sites cancels out from the ensemble of the unfolded structures. With this 
approximation, the relative free energy of folding is the protonation energy of the protein minus the protonation energy of the 
model compounds.

* A protein model with pH-dependent mean atomic charges, where the partial charges of the atoms forming the acidic and basic groups are adjusted according to the fractional protonation of the 
corresponding sites. In combination with CHARMm PBEQ calculations, this model can be used to calculate and visualize the spatial distribution of the mean electrostatic potential at different pH.

* The pH-dependence of the net charge square, the electrostatic contribution to the transfer energy of the molecule from a condensed state to the solvent and the average dipole moment. 
The electrostatic repulsion between the protein molecules [Tanford, 1961] is approximately proportional to the net charge square of the molecule. 
The transfer energy from a medium with a lower dielectric constant (e.g., the condensed or crystalline state) to the solvent [Tjong and Zhou, 2008] , 
the total molecular charge, and the asymmetry of the molecular charge distribution [Chari et al., 2012] are
related to the protein solubility and the viscosity of the protein solutions.

Existing protein ionization methods either treat the protein system as a single conformer or an ensemble of conformations. In the latter case the side-chain conformational relaxation and 
other phenomena, such as ion-binding to the protein surface, are not taken into account. This model leads to the use of a relatively high 
dielectric constant for the protein interior to improve pK prediction accuracy. Similar approaches have been made by others. For example in the study 
by Antosiewicz et al. [Antosiewicz et al., 1994] it was shown that the best results are achieved with 
dielectric constant of 20, using a similar electrostatic model based on the Poisson-Boltzmann approach.

Our current implementation 
treats the protein as a single conformer embedded in a two-dielectric medium, the test results for this method show that 
a lower dielectric constant of 10-11 gives the lowest RMSD compared to the experimentally obtained pK data.

In the case of integral membrane proteins the method allows to account for the effect of a lipid membrane on the ionization characteristics of 
the titratable groups. For this purpose the membrane is modeled as a planar low-dielectric slab and a Generalized Born solvation model
with implicit membrane (GBIM) [Spassov et al., 2002] is used to calculate the effective Born radii.

A detailed description of the method can be found in [Spassov and Yan, 2008]

# Cutting QM-MM bonds

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_cut.htm

## Cutting QM-MM bonds

The QM region usually contains the most significant part of molecular systems 
in a study. For instance, the entire ligand in a protein-ligand complex is contained by the 
QM region so that the charge distribution and its polarization due to the protein 
environment can be more accurately described in a QM treatment. In certain cases, 
it is also necessary to include part of the protein fragments in the QM region 
so that the interaction between protein and ligand can be better described. 
In such a case, there is inevitably a bond cut between QM and MM regions. 
The following figure shows QM-MM calculation of protein complex 1g49. 
To study the pi-pi interaction between the ligand and residue His701, 
both ligand and the side-chain of His701 are included in QM region:

Figure 1: Treating the pi-pi interaction
in 1g49 by QM-MM. The QM atoms are shown in "ball and stick"

A rule of thumb for a QM-MM bond cut is to minimize the perturbation on both 
QM and MM sides. For instance, the bonds that are intersected by the 
boundary between the quantum and molecular mechanics regions are 
(and should always be) single carbon-carbon bonds of low polarity. 
Where the QM-MM boundary intersects bonds, the quantum region is capped by 
hydrogen atoms at the cleavage sites (see Handling of the QM-MM boundary ). 
It is recommended that bond cuts on the protein backbone should also be avoided.

### Specific requirements for Discovery Studio

In addition to the above guidelines for a QM-MM bond cut, there are additional requirements for Discovery Studio . For standard amino acids
( forcefield template property is not None ), the side-chain linked by C-alpha and C-beta bond, is considered a forcefield charge group, and can be included or excluded from the QM region. This allows you to cut the C-alpha-C-beta bond between QM and MM regions.

However, no standard residues must be included in or excluded from the QM region as a whole. You can divide a nonstandard residue into QM and MM parts by breaking the nonstandard residue into two nonstandard smaller residues:

* Select the QM atoms in the residue and cut them from the protein.

* Paste back into the same Graphics View. The QM atoms are back to the original position, 
but they belong to a different small molecule named "Molecule" in the Hierarchy View.

* Merge the small molecule back to the protein by dragging it
into the root of the protein in the Hierarchy View. Now, the small molecule
is a chain of the protein complex.

* Restore the cut bond and apply forcefield typing to the merged protein complex. 
The newly created chain can now be selected as the QM atoms.

#### Further information

Setting up QM-MM calculations

# DMol3 settings in QM-MM calculations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_dmol3-settings.htm

## DMol3 settings in QM-MM calculations

The QM-MM DMol 3 settings allow you to set up and display the parameters for a DMol 3 calculation on the QM region for a 
QM-MM protocol run.

### Basic DMol3 Settings

#### Quality

A description of the DMol 3 basis sets can be found in the paper by Delley [Delley, 1990] .

The following options control the parameters that govern the accuracy of the DMol 3 step:

| Quality | DMol 3 Basis Set | Integration Grid | DMol 3 Cutoff | SCF Density Convergence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultra coarse | minimal | xcoarse | 3.0 Å | 5.0–10 -4 |
| Coarse | DN | coarse | 3.4 Å | 1.0–10 -4 |
| Medium (default) | DND | medium | 3.9 Å | 1.0–10 -5 |
| Fine | DNP | fine | 4.4 Å | 1.0–10 -6 |
| Ultra fine | extended | xfine | 4.9 Å | 1.0–10 -7 |

#### Functionals

A discussion on the performance of various DFT functionals on atomic and molecular properties is given by Riley et al. [Riley et al., 2007] .

| Type | Name | Description | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LDA | PWC | Parameterization of Ceperley and Alder data | [Perdew and Wang, 1992] |
| VWN | Vosko-Wilk-Nusair LDA functional | [Vosko, Wilk, and Nusair, 1980] | |
| GGA | PW91 | Perdew-Wang generalized-gradient approximation | [Perdew and Wang, 1992] |
| BP | Becke exchange plus Perdew correlation | [Becke, 1988] and [Perdew and Wang, 1992] | |
| PBE | Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof correlation (default) | [Perdew et al., 1996] | |
| RPBE | Revised PBE functional by Hammer et al. | [Hammer et al., 1999] | |
| HCTH | Hamprecht, Cohen, Tozer, and Handy functional | [Boese and Handy, 2001] | |
| BLYP | Becke exchange plus Lee-Yang-Parr correlation | [Becke, 1988] and [Lee et al., 1988] | |
| BOP | Becke One Parameter functional | [Tsuneda et al., 1999] | |
| VWN-BP | BP functional with the local correlation replaced by the VWN functional. | [Vosko et al., 1980] , [Becke, 1988] , and [Perdew and Wang, 1992] | |

### Advanced DMol3 Settings

These settings are located in the Advanced parameter group.

#### Multiplicity

This parameter determines the electronic spin state to be imposed in the calculation, and may be further enforced if the calculation is performed as 
spin restricted or spin unrestricted.

The following options are available:

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Smart | If the QM system has an even number of electrons, a spin-restricted calculation is performed that yields a singlet spin state (default). |
| Auto | Used for QM systems with odd numbers of electrons. Makes DMol 3 converge to the lowest spin state by performing an unrestricted calculation. |
| Spin restricted | Enforces a spin-restricted calculation regardless of whether the number of electrons is even or odd. In the latter case, this may result in DMol 3 not converging to the ground state. |
| Singlet | It is not possible to force DMol 3 to perform an unrestricted singlet calculation, otherwise a spin unrestricted calculation, as for Auto , is used. |
| Doublet | Forces DMol 3 to a doublet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |
| Triplet | Forces DMol 3 to a triplet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |
| Quartet | Forces DMol 3 to a quartet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |
| Quintet | Forces DMol 3 to a quintet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |
| Sextet | Forces DMol 3 to a sextet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |
| Septet | Forces DMol 3 to a septet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |
| Octet | Forces DMol 3 to an octet spin state as a spin-unrestricted calculation. |

The DMol 3 server determines the number of electrons in the calculation by adding the
number of electrons for each atom in the Quantum Atoms parameter group and the link atoms, minus the Charge value (see below).

In order to decide which number of electrons to expect in cases where the Quantum Atoms parameter group is 
set so that it induces bond breaks between the QM and MM regions, you should consider the actual QM system used during the run (i.e., the one 
where the broken bonds are saturated by hydrogen atoms).

#### Charge

This sets the charge to be used in the quantum calculation. If it is not set, the sum of formal charges on the atoms in the QM region is used. If Charge is not set, the QM atoms' net charge is the sum of formal charges of the Quantum Atoms parameters group.

If Expand QUANTUMm Atoms is set to True , Charge must be not set because the QUANTUMm server may expand the quantum region , possibly changing the charge for the QM region. If Charge is set, Expand QUANTUMm Atoms must be set False .

#### Occupancy

This DMol 3 parameter defines how the molecular orbitals are filled.

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Thermal | Smears electrons over several orbitals using finite-temperature Fermi function using a range parameter of 0.005 Hartree (default). |
| Fermi | Fills up orbitals with an integer number of electrons. |

Thermal smearing alleviates problems in SCF convergence, especially in the presence of point 
charges, which are usually present in QM-MM calculations.

Setting up QM-MM calculations

# Setting up QM-MM calculations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_setting-up.htm

## Setting up QM-MM calculations

The main input to a QM-MM protocol is a molecule containing a non-periodic system of interest (periodic systems are not currently supported).

Once a suitable non-periodic input system has been specified, the electronically important area of the structure that will be examined using 
the quantum mechanical (QM) treatment must be defined. In QM-MM calculations, this is achieved by creating a group of QuantumAtoms that contain all the atoms in the QM zone. The remaining atoms, not defined in this set, are treated using molecular mechanics (MM).

Setting up a QM-MM calculation involves the following steps:

* Select the QM-MM protocol you want to run: Minimization (QM-MM) or Calculate Energy (QM-MM) .

* Specify the structure for the calculation.

* Define the quantum atom region.

* Select an electronic embedding method.

### Preparation of the structure

The following prerequisites apply:

* The whole simulation system must be in a single molecule within the Hierarchy View . Multiple chains can be used for systems containing disconnected fragments, such as a receptor ligand complex.

* The simulation system must be 0D periodic (i.e., 3D periodicity is not supported.)

* The whole simulation system must be typed using the CHARMm forcefields . The reason for the QM region to be included in typing is 
that parameters are needed to evaluate the van der Waals interaction between the QM and MM regions , which is handled at the 
classical level. Also, in cases where covalent bonds between the QM and MM regions are cut, certain cross-border boundary terms must be retained, and therefore QM atoms at the border need 
forcefield types.

The fixed atom constraints , harmonic atom restraints , harmonic 
distance restraints , and harmonic dihedral restraints present in the structure are 
compatible with the QM-MM protocols. They may be activated or de-activated in the advanced parameters settings. However, SHAKE constraints are not currently available in QM-MM minimizations.

### The quantum atom region

The active chemical groups should enter the QM zone. For example, these groups may be reactive species (in the case of enzyme catalysis), or a ligand 
inside the binding pocket of a receptor.
It is not necessary for the QM region to be a complete residue or chain; the molecular entities making up the 
region may be disconnected. However, the latter situation may cause the convergence of the QM calculation to become difficult.

For more detailed information about dividing bonded atoms, see Cutting covalent QM-MM bonds .

In essence, apart from the addition of link atoms (if bonds between the QM and MM regions are broken)
and the presence of an external potential arising from the point charges of the MM atoms, the QM calculation performed at each boundary between the two regions is a plain DMol 3 calculation.

To define the quantum atoms

* Ensure that the file containing the input structure is the active window.

* Select the atoms to be contained in the QM region.

* In the Parameters Explorer, do one of the following: Choose Create New Group from selection... from the dropdown list for the Quantum Atoms parameter value. The selected atoms are assigned to the QM region and named Group by default. Create a group from the menu by selecting Edit | Group... , and then enter a name for the group on the Edit Group dialog .

* Choose Create New Group from selection... from the dropdown list for the Quantum Atoms parameter value. The selected atoms are assigned to the QM region and named Group by default.

* Create a group from the menu by selecting Edit | Group... , and then enter a name for the group on the Edit Group dialog .

* Choose the group in the Quantum Atoms parameter.

Refer to DMol 3 settings in the QM-MM protocols for specific 
parameter descriptions.

#### Automatic adjustment of the quantum region

The QUANTUMm server will use the atoms from the specified group and check that it contains only complete charge groups. If this is not the case, Expand QUANTUMm Atoms (in Advanced parameters) is set to True by default. This shifts further MM atoms into the QM region to comply with this criterion, and it will determine the QM region charge accordingly . However, if Expand QUANTUMm Atoms is set to False , the protocol will potentially fail at an early stage. Since in some situations it is hard to predict which charge groups the force field server will construct at run-time, it is recommended to allow the expansion of the quantum region.

The quantum region actually used by the QUANTUMm server and the QM charge will be reported after the run.

* The reported QM-MM non-covalent interaction energy terms refer to the QM fragment as a whole, so they are not broken down to the interactions of the individual fragments comprising the QM region.

* By default, thermal smearing of the orbital occupancy is applied.

* No electrostatic cutoffs are applied in the QM calculation. Currently, all MM point charges enter the QM external potential (apart from modifications in the link atom region ).

### The forcefield (MM) region

This region is simply the complement to the QM region that you have chosen. As in the case of the Calculate Energy (QM-MM) or Minimization (QM-MM) protocols, the cutoff 
radii for non-bonded interactions may be specified. They apply to the MM-MM electrostatic and van der Waals interactions handled by the 
CHARMm server at each step of the QM-MM calculation.

### The QM-MM embedding method

You have the choice between two electronic embedding schemes: neglect boundary charge and disperse boundary charge. In all cases where no bonds between the QM and MM regions are broken, both schemes will give the same results. For more information, refer to Handling of the QM-MM boundary .

### Characteristics of the QM-MM minimizer

QM-MM minimizations are performed using the QM-MM simulation server's HDLC optimizer [Billeter et al., 2000] . It employes the "maximum force" criterion for convergence.

Apart from the normal operating mode where QM and MM energies and gradients are evaluated at each step of the QM-MM calculation, the minimizer also provides the 
micro-iterative optimization scheme [Kästner et al., 2007] . In this mode, the MM 
region is minimized while keeping the QM region fixed in the micro iterations. Once these achieve convergence, the QM zone is allowed to relax in 
the next step (macro iteration), and this scheme is repeated until overall convergence is achieved.

If you use this mode, it is recommended that you greatly increase the Max Steps .

#### Further information

Minimization (QM-MM) Calculate Energy (QM-MM)

# DMol3 functionals

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_th_dmol3-functionals.htm

## DMol3 functionals

Density functional theory begins with a theorem by 
Hohenberg and Kohn [Hohenberg and Kohn, 1964] , later
generalized by Levy [Levy, 1979] , 
which states that all ground-state properties are functionals of 
the charge density ρ. Specifically, the total energy E t may be written as:

Equation 1:

The final term in Equation 1 requires some approximation for this method to be computationally tractable. A simple and 
surprisingly good approximation is the local density approximation, which is based on the known exchange-correlation energy of the uniform electron 
gas. The local density approximation assumes that the charge density varies slowly on an atomic scale (i.e., each region of a molecule actually looks 
like a uniform electron gas). The total exchange-correlation energy can be obtained by integrating the uniform electron gas result:

Equation 2:

where ε xc [ ρ ] is the exchange-correlation energy per particle in a uniform electron gas and here ρ is the number of particles.

### Local functionals

The exchange-correlation energy is given by Equation 2. The specific local functionals provided in DMol 3 are the 
VWN functional [Vosko et al., 1980] and PWC [Perdew and Wang, 1992] . 
The default is PWC.

### Nonlocal functionals

The so-called nonlocal or gradient-corrected functionals depend on dρ/dr as well as on ρ. This provides a considerable increase in the accuracy of predicted energies and structures, but with an additional cost.

DMol 3 functionals are described further in DMol 3 Settings in QM-MM protocols .

# QM-MM embedding

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_th_embedding.htm

## QM-MM embedding

An important characteristic of QM-MM methods is the way in which interactions between the QM region and the MM regions are treated.

### Electrostatic QM-MM interactions

As far as the Coulomb interaction between the electronic density of the QM region and the forcefield point charges is concerned, QM-MM methods in this application
always employ electronic embedding. This means that the forcefield atoms' partial charges enter the QM calculation as an external potential, thereby polarizing the QM electronic 
density relative to a QM calculation in vacuo , and giving rise to an electrostatic interaction energy between the QM density and the point 
charges. Currently, these QM-MM protocols
do not use cutoffs (see also cutoffs in CHARMm ) 
in order to restrict the QM region's electrostatic interaction.

For those cases where covalent bonds cross the QM-MM border, the QM-MM server offers two variants of electronic embedding, each of them 
modifying the set of point charges at the cross-border region: the neglect or disperse boundary charge options.

The QM energy reported in the Report.htm output file contains the electrostatic QM-MM interaction energy, the forces reported by 
the QM server also contain QM-MM
contributions.

The QM-MM electrostatic interaction energy is the Coulombic energy between the QM density (distorted by the forcefield) and the
MM point charges. This means that the energy to deform the QM density from its value
in a vacuum is not included. A QM 
calculation in a vacuum would be needed to retrieve the full QM-MM electrostatic interaction energy.

The alternative "mechanical" embedding (where forcefield-like point charges are assigned to the 
QM atoms before the calculation begins, so that they interact with the MM region's point charges) is not available.

In electronic embedding, terminating link atoms (if present) are also polarized by the forcefield 
point charges in the QM step.

### Van der Waals type QM-MM interactions

Contrary to the handling of the electrostatic interactions in QM-MM methods, the van der Waals interactions are treated entirely at the classical level. 
This means that appropriate forcefield parameters must be determined for all atoms in the simulation. The van der Waals QM-MM interaction energy (and forces) are part of the CHARMm simulation server energy and is listed as a separate term in the Report.htm output file.

This interaction is computed by applying group -based cutoffs in CHARMm, in 
contrast to the settings used in the Calculate Interaction Energy protocol which uses atom based cutoffs. As a consequence there may be
small deviations in the results for the interaction energies calculated by these two protocols.

### Bonding QM-MM interactions

Covalent bonds between the QM and MM region represent another kind of QM-MM interaction. Details of how such bonding interactions are handled can be 
found in Handling of the QM-MM boundary .

# Handling of the QM-MM boundary

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_th_handling-boundary.htm

## Handling of the QM-MM boundary

Special attention must be paid to the QM-MM boundary whenever it contains regions where covalent bonds cross the I and O regions.
Several issues may arise from such situations, and are discussed below.

At this point that in the prevalent part of the QM-MM boundary with no intersected covalent
bonds, the QM-MM van der Waals interaction helps to prevent clashes of the two regions through its 
short-range repulsive part; in this application QM-MM methods do not make special provisions there.

### Covalent QM-MM bonds

The occurrence of covalent bonds between the quantum mechanical (QM) and molecular mechanics (MM) regions in the input structure makes 
modifications of the QM and MM calculations necessary. A typical situation is depicted in Figure 1a, where A denotes one QM atom of the QM 
region (labeled I ) and B is its bonded MM atom in the MM region (labeled O ).

Figure 1: (a) Covalent bond between QM atom C A (region I ) and MM atom C B . (b) 
Saturation of the dangling bond by a hydrogen "link" atom forming region L .

### Bonded interactions at the boundary

#### Modifications to the QM calculation

As shown in Figure 1b, the bond crossing the QM-MM boundary is broken and its parent
atoms are saturated by introducing a hydrogen "link" atom (labeled L , also called "capping" or 
"terminating" atom) to the QM system which is placed between the unsaturated QM atom ("QM host") and its MM bonding partner ("MM host"). The 
QM-MM server makes this modification internally; the presence of link atoms can be confirmed by inspecting the input and output files 
produced by the QM calculation. The QM-MM calculation assume that you have set up the QM region such that no conjugate or multiple bonds are bisected and 
that no isolated hydrogens remain in the MM region. The protocol performs a check for broken bonds before the calculation begins.

##### Link atom positioning

In order to minimize the impact of link atoms on the geometry in the boundary region, their position commonly is restrained. In the spirit 
of Sauer's QM-Pot method 
( [Eichler et al., 1997] , [Sierka and Sauer, 1997] , and [Sierka and Sauer, 2000] ), 
QM-MM always places each link atom onto the line connecting its QM- and MM-host atom, respectively, and maintains the length of the bond to the QM host atom
at a standard value.

##### Avoiding overpolarization

With each link atom closely approaching their respective MM host atoms, the QM calculation may be impaired through the proximity of the 
point charges of these MM atoms (see figure 2a). QM-MM offers two methods to modify the set of point charges which enter the QM calculation 
( [Bakowies and Thiel, 1996] and [Antes and Thiel, 1998] ):

* "disperse boundary charge" (figure 2b) : the charge of the MM host atom is set to
zero. In order to restore the point dipoles formed by 
the MM host and its bonding neighbors, corrective charges are added along each of the MM host's bonds into the MM region.

* "neglect boundary charge" (figure 2c): all charges belonging to the charge group nearest to L are set to zero.

Figure 2: Black circles represent Forcefield charges. Dashed ellipses represent charge groups. (a) Initial situation at the L region. The red arrow depicts the proximity of L to the charge q B (b) Disperse boundary charge: 
q B is zeroed, and two additional point charges (green) placed close to the bonding neighbors of C B , respectively. (c) Neglect boundary charge: all forcefield charges in the charge group related to L are set to zero.

#### Modifications to the MM calculation

In order to preserve the QM-MM bond between C A and C B in additive QM-MM embedding, various bonding forcefield terms 
are extended from the MM atoms into the QM region, see figure 3.

Figure 3 Schematic representation of some cross-border forcefield terms retained in QM-MM
calculations: (a) two-body bonding term (b) three-body angular term (c) dihedral term

As a guideline, all cross-border covalent terms which cannot be sufficiently described by having the link atom in the QM calculation in 
place of the MM host atom are retained. These comprise:

* the QM host-MM host atom two-body bond terms.

* all angle bonding terms where one atom is in the MM region.

* dihedral terms where one atom is in the MM region.

* improper terms where one atom is in the MM region.

Because all atoms must be typed in a QM-MM calculation, it is guaranteed that
the QM atoms carrying cross-border forcefield terms have the appropriate forcefield types.

* [Das et al., 2002]

* [Sherwood et al., 2003]

# Overview of QM-MM

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_th_overview.htm

## Overview of QM-MM

Applying QM-MM protocols to a simulation system involves dividing the input system into two regions:

* The central region ( I ), to be treated by a quantum mechanical (QM) calculation

* The outer region (O), to be treated by molecular mechanics (MM) methods

Quantum mechanical treatment brings a higher level of theory, enabling you to model additional phenomena to traditional forcefield techniques, for example, where a chemical reaction occurs or polarization effects in I play an important role. The remaining 
bulk of the structure is described using a forcefield. The way in which the two regions are allowed to interact and how the total QM-MM energy is 
evaluated define the specific QM-MM protocol employed. Special care must be taken in handling the interactions at the boundary zone when covalent 
bonds between QM and MM bonds are intersected.

QM-MM calculations offer a number of advantages over pure QM or MM calculations:

* Limiting the computationally expensive QM calculation to the region of interest allows high-precision calculations to be carried out over 
relatively short time spans. Over the same time period, a QM treatment of the whole system could only yield low accuracy results, or a high 
precision calculation on the whole system would require an unreasonably long calculation time.

* Most classical forcefields are not appropriate for situations where electronic rearrangements take place (e.g., chemical reactions or 
for excited molecular states). Here, QM is mandatory.

* QM treatment may improve the accuracy of modeling intricate interactions, such as chelate coordination or hydrogen bonding.

* In cases where polarization effects play an important role, a QM approach is often required. Although polarizable forcefields are available, 
they have not yet reached the stage of general applicability.

* QM-MM protocols can be invaluable in situations where forcefield parameters for the functional groups in the core region of a system are not known or estimated (e.g., organometallic complexes). Such regions can be treated quantum mechanically instead of deriving and 
validating new forcefield parameters. However, the van der Waals interactions 
between I and O still need to be handled classically.

* The QM-MM protocols used in this approach make it easy to select particular molecular orbitals (MO) in the QM region for post-SCF treatment (e.g.,
configuration interaction), a step which usually proves difficult to achieve from a pure QM calculation on all atoms where delocalized 
valence MOs are produced.

* A QM treatment of the important core atoms makes it possible to calculate properties of those atoms that are not amenable to or accurate 
enough with MM. Examples include dipole moments, vibrational frequencies, NMR shieldings, circular dichroism spectra, and UV-Vis absorption 
and fluorescence energies.

* An estimate of the interaction energies between the QM and MM atoms is easily accessible though QM-MM calculation if they do not share covalent bonds. However, it requires special techniques to derive this value from a pure QM treatment.

As an illustration of a system that could be analyzed by QM-MM, consider a ligand molecule inside the binding pocket of a receptor protein (Figure 1). A natural division would define the ligand as the QM region ( I ) and the remainder of the system as the MM zone ( O ).

Figure 1: Schematic representation of the calculation regions defined for a QM-MM treatment. The ligand in ball-and-stick
representation is chosen as the I region. The remaining receptor protein constitutes the O region.

#### Physical quantities from QM-MM

Although schemes for QM-MM calculations may differ considerably with respect to how the interaction between subsystems and the atoms in the boundary region are 
handled, the expression of the QM-MM total potential energy, E tot , usually contains the total QM (post-)SCF energy, E QM , from 
some calculation on the I region, the potential energy of the O region, E MM , and a QM-MM interaction energy, 
E QMMM . These are combined to yield a continuous function of all coordinates. The general formal expression for E tot is:

Equation 1:

This makes it possible to compare energies of different conformers, perform geometry optimizations, and so forth, as long as the atomic 
composition of both subsystems remains unchanged.

In some schemes used in QM-MM calculations, Equation 1 may be recast. Refer to the section 
on QM-MM potential energy expressions for more details.

#### Characterization of QM-MM

Generally, QM-MM can be classified according to how:

* The interaction between the QM and MM atoms is described

* The bonds crossing the I to O region are handled

* The QM-MM total energy is composed

# QM-MM potential energy expression

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/qmmm_th_potential-energy-expressions.htm

## QM-MM potential energy expression

QM-MM methods differ in the way the total potential energy, E tot is composed from the energies of the quantum and forcefield 
calculations. In this application, an additive scheme is employed. This means that at each step of a QM-MM calculation, two separate calculations are 
carried out:

* the QM calculation on the I region, including terminating hydrogens if applicable as the link atoms, L. This gives E QM ( I+L ) 
which is the total (post-) SCF QM energy. Since QM-MM methods employ electronic embedding , the QM-MM
electrostatic interaction energy is contained in E QM . This energy is denoted as E QM (I+L ↔ O ele ).

* the MM calculation on the O region, including cross QM-MM boundary bonding forcefield terms ( cb ) if covalent bonds crossing the QM-MM boundary need to be cut. The energy E MM ( O+cb ) also 
contains the QM-MM van der Waals interaction energy. This term is denoted E MM ( O+cb ↔ I vdW ).

Putting the two energy terms together gives the final expression for the total QM-MM potential energy (see Eq-1 ):

# Supported forcefields

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/select_forcefield_hw.htm

## Supported forcefields

This application provides a rich collection of forcefields, which differ in the parameter coverage, accuracy and computational efficiency. One of 
the first essential tasks in a molecular modeling project is to choose a suitable forcefield to describe the energy function of the molecular system 
of interest.

This topic covers the strengths and weaknesses of the following supported forcefields, and provides general guidelines for choosing one:

* CHARMm

* CHARMm Polar H

* charmm19

* charmm22

* charmm27

* charmm36

* cff

* MMFF

The XPROLIG forcefield is designed for structure refinement in X-ray crystallography. It cannot be used for simulation in this application.

The CHARMm forcefield is a general purpose, all-atom, class I forcefield. It has the broadest coverage for organic molecules amongst all the 
forcefields available in this application [Brooks et al., 1983] .

The CHARMm forcefield has optimized parameters for proteins and nucleic acids, and a large collection of general parameters for majority of 
organic molecules, including nonstandard amino acids, nonstandard nucleic acid bases, and cofactors. It also has parameter coverage for all the 
physiologically relevant metal ions, and is able to estimate missing parameters based on the local chemical environment of the atom.

#### Pros and Cons

* The CHARMm forcefield can be used for simulations with different solvent models, including explicit solvents and various types of 
generalized Born implicit solvent models.

* With a broad coverage for organic molecules and an adequate accuracy for proteins, the CHARMm forcefield is widely used for studying 
protein-ligand, protein-protein interactions.

The CHARMm polar hydrogen forcefield uses a polar hydrogen model that is similar to the 
CHARMm forcefield. Hydrogens bonded to polar heavy atoms (for example nitrogen, oxygen) are modeled explicitly, and those attached to non-polar 
heavy atoms (for example carbon) are "combined" with the bound heavy atom to form "extended" atoms. Some of the parameters of such extended atoms 
are adjusted in order to approximate the results of an all-atom representation.

The CHARMm Polar H forcefield was originally developed to increase the computational efficiency. In the past, this feature has been useful 
for "in vacuum" simulations, where nonpolar hydrogen atoms account for half of the total number of particles. The computational advantage is now 
becoming less important, due to the improvement in computer hardware and the increased usage of explicit solvent simulation where a polar hydrogen 
model makes little difference in speed.

* CHARMm Polar H improves the speed of the calculation.

* The results are not as accurate.

The charmm19 forcefield is a polar hydrogen forcefield parameterized for proteins and peptides [Neria et al., 1996] .

* Several popular implicit solvent models in the CHARMm program, such as generalized Born (GenBorn), have been developed based on this forcefield.
Therefore, charmm19 gives the best simulation accuracy in these solvents.

* It does not have significant coverage for other organic molecules and is therefore limited to protein simulation.

The charmm19 forcefield is parameterized using a specific set of nonbond cutoff distances which 
should be applied in simulations that use this forcefield.

The charmm22 forcefield is an all-atom, class I forcefield [MacKerell et al., 1998] . It is 
highly optimized for reproducing conformational properties and energetics of proteins and peptides in explicit solvent environments.

* The charmm22 forcefield provides the highest accuracy for protein simulation in the condensed phase.

* The charmm22 forcefield also performs well for many of the implicit solvent models supported in this application, such as generalized Born 
models GBSW and GBMV.

* Like charmm19, charmm22 has limited coverage for general organic molecules and is limited to modeling proteins and peptides.

The charmm27 forcefield is a superset of charmm22 forcefield, with the additional coverage for nucleic acids [Foloppe and MacKerell, 2000] and [MacKerell and Banavali, 2000] . The 
high quality of its nucleic acid parameters have been demonstrated in many applications.

* With a highly accurate parameter set for both proteins and nucleic acids, charmm27 is the best choice for studying protein-nucleic acids binding,
in explicit solvent, or in generalized Born solvent models.

* CMAP correction accurately reproduces peptide backbone dihedral distributions.

* The charmm27 forcefield does not currently have wide coverage for other general types of organic molecules.

The charmm36 forcefield is a revised version of charmm22 and charmm27 forcefield, with improved backbone CMAP and side-chain torsion parameters for proteins and peptides [Best et al., 2012] .

* The protein backbone CMAP parameters in charmm36 have been optimized to correct a bias toward alpha helix formation in charmm22 and CMAP. It is suitable for both 
simulations of unfolded or intrinsically disordered proteins and for investigating protein-folding mechanisms.

The cff forcefield is a general purpose, class II forcefield, with a good parameter coverage for many organics molecules. As a class II 
forcefield, it has additional cross terms in its potential energy function [Maple et al., 1994] , 
compared to the class I forcefields discussed above.

* Derived from high level quantum mechanical calculations in the gas phase, cff gives the highest accuracy for studying properties that do not 
depend heavily on a condensed phase environment. For example, its ability to reproduce vibrational spectral is better than many other 
forcefields.

* Because of its good coverage, the cff forcefield has been used to studying energetics and dynamics of many biomolecules.

* It has not been widely tested to work with many implicit solvent models in this application.

* It cannot be run with simulations in parallel mode.

Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield 
for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions [Halgren, 1996] .

* MMFF has a wide coverage for all organic molecules, which allows for a large number of compounds to be treated, as required for database
screening in drug design.

* While it is highly successful with general organic molecules, MMFF is considered to be less accurate for protein simulations in explicit 
solvent when compared with charmm27. To remedy this deficiency, structural restraints may be applied on protein molecules when simulating 
protein-ligand complexes using MMFF forcefield.

* MMFF has not been adequately tested or validated for working with implicit solvent models in this application.

* Like cff, MMFF currently cannot be run with simulations in parallel mode.

# Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_allostery_th.htm

## Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance

Allosteric communication is a fundamental mechanism by which proteins transmit signals from one site to another, often resulting in functional conformational changes that modulate activity. Discovery Studio includes the Analyze Trajectory Features protocol to compute time-lagged cross-covariance and cross-correlation from input files containing measured trajectory features. It identifies correlated motions and detects feature dependencies that may indicate allosteric communication pathways.

Cross-covariance and cross-correlation are metrics for examining how fluctuations between feature pairs 
are dynamically coupled over time. While they are related, they provide slightly different insights.

### Cross-Covariance

Cross-covariance measures how fluctuations in two features co-vary relative to their mean values. 
It considers both the magnitude and direction of fluctuations, making it useful for detecting coordinated movements:

where:

* and are feature values at time

* and are mean values

* is the time lag

* is the total number of frames

Cross-covariance retains information about absolute fluctuation magnitudes, making it sensitive to 
structural rearrangements. Positive values indicate coordinated fluctuations, while negative values 
indicate anticorrelated dynamics.

### Cross-Correlation

Cross-correlation normalizes the covariance by the standard deviations of each feature, 
resulting in a value between -1 and 1:

and are the standard deviations of features and , respectively.

Cross-correlation highlights the relative strength of dynamic coupling without accounting for 
absolute fluctuation magnitudes. This normalization makes it easier to compare coupling strength 
across features with different scales.

### Angular Data Handling

Dihedral angles and other angular measurements exhibit cyclical behavior that requires special handling. 
The Convert Angular Data parameter converts angles from radians to complex 
exponential representation:

This transformation accounts for the wrap-around nature of angular data, preventing artificial 
discontinuities at the ±π boundary.

### Data Normalization

The Normalize parameter scales features to comparable ranges using:

* is the original feature value

* is the mean of the feature

* is the standard deviation of the feature

Normalization is recommended when features have very different scales or when a few measurements 
have much larger values that might overshadow smaller but important changes. For example, if some 
distance measurements are consistently much larger than others, normalization ensures all features 
contribute equally to the analysis rather than allowing large values to dominate.
Normalization may not be necessary when the system is relatively small and conformational 
changes are stable, or when absolute magnitudes are important for interpretation.

#### Further information

Analyze Trajectory Features

# Change Forcefield tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_cft.htm

## Change Forcefield tools

Molecules are
automatically typed by the current forcefield when a simulation is run. If you are not familiar with the forcefield selection, you do not need to use this tool.

The Change Forcefield tools allow you to prepare structures for and to run molecular simulations. A molecular system is prepared for simulation when it meets the following
criteria:

* Forcefield was applied

* No missing forcefield types

* No missing forcefield parameters

For a description of these tools, see below. For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Change Forcefield tools .

### All Forcefields

For details about selecting an appropriate forcefield, see Supported forcefields . The following forcefields are supported:

| Forcefield | Description | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CHARMm | General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. | [Momany and Rone, 1992] |
| CHARMm Polar H | The polar hydrogen version of the CHARMm forcefield. | [Neria et al., 1996] |
| charmm19 | Academic polar hydrogen atom forcefield for proteins. | [Neria et al., 1996] |
| charmm22 | Academic all-atom forcefield used for simulating protein systems. | [MacKerell et al., 1998] |
| charmm27 | Academic all-atom forcefield used for simulating nucleic acids and protein systems. | [Foloppe and MacKerell, 2000] and [MacKerell and Banavali, 2000] |
| charmm36 | Academic all-atom forcefield used for simulating proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, carbohydrates, and small molecules. | [Best et al., 2012] |
| cff | Consistent Force Field (cff). Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids, and general organic molecules. | [Maple et al., 1994] |
| MMFF | Merck Molecular Force Field (MMFF). Class II forcefield for small organic molecules (pharmaceutical compounds) (MMFF94S). | [Halgren, 1996] |
| XPROLIG | Used for typing molecules involved in x-ray applications. A molecule typed by XPROLIG cannot be used in CHARMm-based calculations. | |

A molecule that has alternative conformers can only be typed by XPROLIG, and not by any of 
the simulation forcefields. Before you type a molecule with a non-XPROLIG forcefield, make sure that alternative conformer atoms are 
removed from the molecule. To do this, open the Data Table, select all the rows in the Conformer category, and remove the selected items by 
pressing DELETE, or use the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein | Clean Protein tool to remove alternate conformers from the molecule.

By default, when the forcefield is applied, attempts are made to ensure that the molecule simulates correctly by performing the following steps:

* Add hydrogens appropriate for the selected forcefield.

* Estimate and assign partial charges to the system.

* Determine forcefield atom types by using residue templates or by applying forcefield-specific typing rules.

* Identify missing forcefield types and allow you to assign them to known types for that forcefield.

* Identify missing forcefield parameters, estimating their values (CHARMm forcefield only), or allow you to save to a file and then 
specify values for them.

For example, the following is the procedure to assign atom types and partial charges in the CHARMm forcefields (CHARMm, CHARMm polar hydrogen, charmm19/22/27/36):

* The typing algorithm attempts to match residues in the molecule with those defined by the forcefield residue templates.

* When a match is found, the forcefield types and partial charges from the template are assigned to those atoms in the molecule.

The forcefield residue templates typically only cover common biopolymers such as proteins and nucleic acids. For the large number of small 
molecules that are not recognized by the forcefield residue templates, a set of SMILES rules is invoked to determine the forcefield atom types, 
and a set of bond charge increment rules are used to assign partial charges.

The typing using CFF and MMFF forcefield is different from that in the CHARMm forcefields; atom typing and charging using these two forcefields are
based entirely on internal typing rules, rather than using residue templates matching.

Forcefield: Select from standard forcefields or choose Browse to access user-defined forcefields ( .ffml files). If you select a 
forcefield from a file, the file name is displayed as the forcefield.

Partial Charge: Select the partial charge estimation method used when typing with CHARMm forcefield. The following options are available:

| Partial Charges | Comment |
| --- | --- |
| Momany Rone | Default for CHARMm, use the original Momany Rone charges. |
| CFF | Use the charges from the CFF forcefield for residues without matching templates. |
| MMFF94 | Use the charges from the MMFF94 forcefield for residues without matching templates. |
| Existing | Use the existing partial charges for all atoms. |

Apply Forcefield: Applies the selected forcefield to the structure in the current Molecule Window.

Apply Forcefield is a client command and can only type a small number of lipid molecules with the charmm36 forcefield. 
Therefore, for explicit membrane simulations, use the Assign Forcefield protocol to type the system with the charmm36 forcefield.

### charmm36 Forcefield

Assign Forcefield: Opens the Assign Forcefield protocol dialog. This tool is
recommended when assigning the charmm36 forcefield because it assigns forcefield types by structural matching
to the templates and follows the CHARMm patching mechanism exactly.

For charmm36 forcefield, the MATCH typing engine [Yesselman et al., 2012] will be used to generate forcefield templates for unmatched small molecules. However, this protocol does not estimate atom types
for unknown biopolymer residues and missing parameters for those residues. In this case, you can still use the Apply Forcefield tool, which will attempt
to estimate atom types and parameters if any of them are missing in the forcefield. However, it will treat patched 
residues as unknown residues and create new residue types for them, which could lead to slight deviation 
from the original design of the forcefield parameters, such as CMAP terms.

This protocol runs on the server and the custom residue templates added by the Add Residue Template tool will not be picked up automatically. 
However, you can supply them to the protocol using the Custom RTF File and Custom Parameter File parameters.

Type Ligands with MATCH: Opens the Type Ligands with MATCH protocol dialog. This tool is 
recommended when assigning the charmm36 forcefield to a set of ligands for FEP calculations so that the ligands will be typed consistently.

### Forcefield Status

Status: Displays the status after typing with a selected forcefield.

Ensure that the intended Molecule Window is in focus. Otherwise, the status will indicate that the molecular system is not active.

More: Displays the missing types and parameters if there was a typing failure. If the use automatic parameter estimation is enabled for CHARMm forcefields, this also displays the automatically assigned types
or parameters. You can also save the forcefield to a text file ( .ffml file) and then open the modified forcefield using the Forcefield Browse... option.

Clear Forcefield: Clears the existing forcefield from the structure in the current Molecule Window.

A typed molecule will have a ForcefieldFFML property, which contains any estimated parameters during the typing process.

### Forcefield Customization

Add Residue Template: Adds the typing information of a selected residue to your forcefield library. This will create an RTF (Residue Topology File) and a PRM (Parameter File) file in your forcefield folder, which can be used later to type the same residue. The RTF file will be used to assign atom types and partial charges to the residue, and the PRM file will provide parameters needed to type the residue.

Modify Atom Type: Allows you to choose from a list of existing atom types or enter a new atom type for the selected atoms. Forcefield parameters will be recalculated automatically after a different atom type is chosen for selected atoms.

For details about performing specific tasks using these tools, see How to use the Change Forcefield tools .

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Simulation \| Change Forcefield |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Simulation \| Change Forcefield |
| View | View \| Tool Panels \| Change Forcefield |
