# How to use the Change Forcefield tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_cft_hw.htm

## How to use the Change Forcefield tools

The Change Forcefield tool panel allows you to apply a selected forcefield, check for missing atom types, clear atom types, and save forcefields for editing. It provides access to detailed typing information (such as which residues do not have associated force field templates), and are typed using typing rules. In addition, you can customize forcefields by adding new residue templates and defining new atom types.

Atom typing is an essential step required before performing any energy calculation, minimization, and MD simulations, because correct parameterization means a reasonable potential function for the molecular system, which is a key prerequisite for obtaining scientifically meaningful results.

You can use the CHARMm forcefield with automatic parameter estimation to
quickly prepare a structure for minimization. You may want to edit the
parameters, partial charges, and missing types for further simulation protocols.

To access these tools, open Simulation | Change Forcefield .

To prepare a structure for simulation

* Select a Forcefield . To import a user-defined forcefield (FFML file) choose Browse... and navigate to the file.

* Click Apply Forcefield . The specified 
forcefield is loaded in order to assign forcefield types
and identify missing forcefield parameters. This forcefield remains loaded
and associated with the system, and is continually updated with the number of
missing types and parameters. To better prepare the system for simulation,
you can adjust the hydrogens of the system before assigning
forcefield types. In addition, following the assignment of the forcefield type,
the atoms of the system are assigned partial charges according to rules in the
forcefield.

* The Status indicates when the system is typed and ready for simulation.

* For more information about the status of the system, click More... to display estimated, missing, or
user defined types or parameters, or residues typed by typing rules 
but not a standard force field template.

Only up to 100 residues per structure can have nonstandard force field templates. Simulation will fail when there are more than 100 nonstandard residues.

To choose a partial charge method for CHARMm forcefield

CHARMm forcefield supports several different partial charge estimation methods for residues that do not match forcefield templates. When the CHARMm forcefield is selected, the partial charge method used in typing can be selected from the Partial Charge list. This is provided as a convenient access to the Partial charge estimation method option in Forcefield preferences .

To re-apply a forcefield

To re-apply a forcefield, click Apply Forcefield . This is only necessary if you have modified the chemistry.

If all the atoms in a system already have forcefield types, clicking Apply Forcefield will not change them.
Partial charges are preserved unless you click Clear Forcefield first.

For the XPROLIG forcefield, you can enable automatic re-typing when there are changes to the history by checking Automatically re-type molecule when chemistry changes on the Forcefield page of the preferences dialog.

Re-typing is usually successful because the most likely
chemistry changes are the addition of waters and other
easily handled occurrences. You can determine whether
automatic assignment has been successful by checking the Status .

To type a molecule using structure match method

Traditionally forcefield typing uses name match for residue and atoms. The Assign Forcefield... tool does the assignment by structure match between a residue and its template in the forcefield. 
This is a new method that only supports charmm22, charmm27, and charmm36 forcefields.

To clear an existing forcefield

To clear the existing forcefield information from the current system, click Clear Forcefield . This is only necessary if you want to discard all existing forcefield typing information, including atom types, residue templates, and partial charges so they can be regenerated with a new forcefield.

To add customized residue templates

The residue templates provided by the forcefield only cover 
standard amino acid residues, nucleic acid residues, and a few common ligands.
In some situations, you may need customized residue templates 
that can be reused in typing. This can be done as follows:

* Select a residue in the Hierarchy View, or from the Data Table.

* Click Add Residue Template .

The typing information, including atom types, partial charges, topology, and parameters of this residue is saved in the Forcefield folder. In the future, if a residue with the same name and topology is typed, it will be assigned the saved typing information.

To modify the residue template, you can modify the residue in the Molecule Window, select the residue, and click Add Residue Template again to update the typing information.

If you are an expert user familiar with CHARMm file formats, you can add and modify the RTF (Residue Topology File) and PRM (Parameter File) files for the customized residues directly. These files are saved in the Forcefield folder: <Settings Folder>/Forcefield where each forcefield has its own subfolder that contains RTF and PRM files.

For details about locations of folders in different operating systems, see Installation folders .

If a customized residue template is no longer needed, remove the corresponding RTF and PRM files from the forcefield folder and restart the application.

To modify atom types

In some situations, you may want to manually assign or create new atom types:

* Select the atom you want to modify from the Hierarchy View.

* Click Modifies Atom Type .

* Choose a new atom type from a list of existing atom types, or define a new atom type at the bottom of the Choose a Forcefield Type dialog .

After a new atom type is selected, forcefield parameters for the system will be recalculated automatically.

To edit atom partial charges

You can edit the partial charges on atoms by changing the Partial Charge property of selected atoms in the Atom tab in the Data Table .

To add missing parameters or modify existing parameters

Systems containing missing forcefield parameters are not prepared
for simulation and must have these parameters set before they can
be used. This procedure can also be used to modify existing estimated parameters or parameters that have an equivalent value.
Proceed with appropriate caution, as further extensive research may be
required to define reliable forcefield parameters.

* Use established investigation or research techniques to determine the
values for the missing parameters.

* Click More... to view the missing parameters.

* Open the tab containing the parameters you want to modify.
Parameters that can be modified appear with a white background.

* Change the parameters in the table, there is no need to re-type the
system.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Simulation \| Change Forcefield |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Simulation \| Change Forcefield |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Change Forcefield |

## CHARMm forcefields

CHARMm uses a flexible and comprehensive empirical energy function that is a summation of many individual energy terms. The energy function 
is based on separable internal coordinate terms and pairwise nonbond interaction terms [Brooks et al., 1983] . 
The total energy is expressed by the following equation:

A more specific statement of the function is [Brooks et al., 1983] :

The electrostatic energy:

can be calculated using ε = 1 (or any other specified value), or ε = c R , where c is a constant and R is the distance between two atoms. The former model is called CDIE (constant dielectric model) and the latter is called RDIE (distance dependent dielectric model), which mimics increased dielectric screening in the condensed phase. This model is considered to be a rough approximation of the solvent effect and should not be combined with explicit solvent in simulations.

# Energy Minimization

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_energy_th_charmm-minimization.htm

## Energy Minimization

All dynamics simulations begin with
an initial structure that may be derived from experimental data or from theoretical model buildings. Energy minimization
is performed on structures prior to dynamics to relax the conformation and remove
steric overlap that produces bad contacts. In the absence of an experimental
structure, a minimized ideal geometry can be used as a starting point.

Each of the minimization methods available in CHARMm, together with implementation considerations, is listed below:

* Adopted Basis-set Newton-Raphson (ABNR) : The ABNR method performs an energy minimization using a 
Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement
coordinates of the last positions. The second derivative matrix is constructed numerically from the change in the gradient vectors, and is inverted by an eigenvector
analysis that allows the routine to recognize and avoid saddle points in the energy surface. At each step, the residual gradient vector is calculated and used to add a
steepest descent step, incorporating the new direction into the basis set. This algorithm is the method of choice for most applications, where the ligand is in a reasonable starting point. Because it avoids the large storage requirements of the full NRAP second derivative method,
larger systems can be minimized more efficiently. ABNR is not compatible with the SHAKE constraints. Results from using the ABNR method with SHAKE constraints are
invalid.

This algorithm is the method of choice for most applications, where the ligand is in a reasonable starting point. Because it avoids the large storage requirements of the full NRAP second derivative method,
larger systems can be minimized more efficiently.

ABNR is not compatible with the SHAKE constraints. Results from using the ABNR method with SHAKE constraints are
invalid.

* Steepest Descent (SD) : A simple, first
derivative method. Uses only first derivative information and saves only the
current location of the coordinates from iteration to iteration. In general, .sd converges slowly to a local minimum in a complex potential energy
surface. This method is useful for small changes, such as the removal
of unfavorable steric contacts

* Conjugate Gradient (CONJ) : Exhibits better
convergence than the steepest descent method. The method is iterative and
makes use of the previous history of minimization steps and the current gradient
to determine the next step

* Powell (POWE) : A variation of the conjugate
gradient method with improved efficiency. Use whenever the ABNR method (described
below) is not possible

* Smart Minimizer : The Smart Minimizer method begins
with the Steepest Descent method, followed by the Conjugate Gradient method for faster
convergence towards a local minimum. Use this method when the initial structure is far away from
the minimized structure. Due to its robustness, this is the default for
most protocols.

For a general discussion of minimization methods, see the following:

* [Fletcher, 1969]

* [Press et al., 1987]

For specific discussion of the conjugate gradient method, see the following:

* [Fletcher and Reeves, 1964]

For specific discussion of the Powell method, see one of the following:

* [Gunsteren and Karplus, 1980]

* [Powell, 1977]

# Parameter estimation for CHARMm forcefields

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_energy_th_charmm-parameter-est.htm

## Parameter estimation for CHARMm forcefields

The CHARMm forcefield can optionally estimate forcefield parameters for terms not in the forcefield itself. Values for missing parameters
are estimated using existing parameters for similar atom types. Typically, the average of a set of pre-existing parameters for similar atoms is used to estimate parameters for new atom types. This Help topic gives some details about the estimation process.

### Rules for estimating parameters

The first stage of parameter estimation is typing. If the atom typing process fails to type an atom and estimation is desired, then you can create a
new atom type and follow the estimation rules below.

At this point, there is a typed molecule and an atom type (including
generated atom types) for each atom. The forcefield
parameters can be searched for any exact matches and those parameters can be included directly
from the forcefield. Next, for each missing parameter, 
forcefield parameters can be estimated.

Assuming there is not an exact match in the forcefield, 
various increasingly generic rules are tried. For the first rule for which parameters
are found, the forcefield parameters are averaged for each match.
In decreasing degrees of similarity, the following rules are applied:

* Exact: An exact match of an atom type

* Equivalent: An equivalent atom type match from the equivalent atom
table ( Table 1 )

* Hybridization: Matches the atom's element and hybridization state

* Element: Matches the atom's element

The following rules are used to estimate the missing parameters for each
of the parameter types:

* Bond parameters: A bond with missing parameters is
analyzed and classified into six different levels
of similarity to an existing bond parameter. The
classification is based on the level of chemical
similarity of the two bonded atoms.
These categories and their similarity levels
are explained in Table 2 .
The set of bonds with the highest similarity are
then used to estimate the bond parameters. For
example, if a given bond between two atoms is not
found, the atom parameters are identified for a
bond between these atoms equivalent types. If there are no
matches found at that level, then any matches
where one atom has an exact match and the other
matches the element and hybridization state are
identified and averaged to calculate the estimated
parameters. If there are still no matches found, then the 
search is continued to the next level of similarity
until (at the worst case) bond parameters for the
bond length are estimated as the sum of the
covalent radius of the two atoms, with a force
constant of 300 kcal/mol Å 2 .

* Angle parameters: Missing angle parameters are
estimated in a similar way, according to the
average of the most similar entries in the
forcefield. Similarity levels are defined in Table 3 . When no matches are found,
an estimate is made based on the hybridization of
the center atom. For example 180° is used for sp hybridized atoms, 120° for sp2 and 109.5° for sp3 atoms.

* Torsion parameters: Missing torsion parameters are estimated by determining the atom types of the middle two atoms.
The atom types are then assigned to one of the following categories: Aromatic, Planar Non-Aromatic, Non-Planar Non-Aromatic, or sp atom.
Based on the combination of the atom types of the two center atoms, Table 4 is used to estimate the torsion parameters.

* Improper (out-of-plane) dihedral parameters:
Missing improper dihedrals are estimated based on
the element types of the sp2 center and the
atom double bonded to it. All Improper parameters
for matching elements are then averaged to estimate
the missing terms.

### Tables

Table 1 Equivalent atom types

| Atom Type | Bond | Angle | Torsion | Improper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HO | H | H | H | H |
| HT | H | H | H | H |
| HC | H | H | H | H |
| CT3 | CT | CT | CT | CT |
| CT4 | CT | CT | CT | CT |
| CP3 | CT | CT | CT | CT |
| CUA2 | CUA1 | CUA1 | CUA1 | CUA1 |
| CUA3 | CUA1 | CUA1 | CUA1 | CUA1 |
| C3 | C | C | C | C |
| C4 | C | C | C | C |
| CM | C | CM | CM | CM |
| CQ66 | C6R | C6R | C6R | C6R |
| CR66 | C6R | C6R | C6R | C6R |
| CS66 | C6R | C6R | C6R | C6R |
| CPH1 | C5R | C5R | C5R | C5R |
| CPH2 | C5R | C5R | C5R | C5R |
| CR55 | C5R | C5R | C5R | C5R |
| CR56 | C5R | C5R | C5R | C5R |
| CUY1 | CM | CM | CM | CM |
| CUY2 | CM | CM | CM | CM |
| NX | NP | NP | NP | NP |
| N3 | NT | NT | NT | NT |
| NR1 | N5R | N5R | N5R | N5R |
| NR2 | N5R | N5R | N5R | N5R |
| NR3 | N5R | N5R | N5R | N5R |
| NR55 | N5R | N5R | N5R | N5R |
| NR56 | N5R | N5R | N5R | N5R |
| NR66 | N6R | N6R | N6R | N6R |
| NC | NP | NC | NP | NP |
| NC2 | NC | NC | NC | NC |
| OA | O | O | O | O |
| OAC | O | O | O | O |
| OE | OT | OT | OT | OT |
| OS | OT | OT | OT | OT |
| OC | O | OC | OC | O |
| OH2 | OW | OW | OW | OW |
| OT | O | OT | OT | OT |
| SE | ST | ST | ST | ST |
| SO1 | SK | SK | SK | SK |
| SO2 | SK | SK | SK | SK |
| SO3 | SK | SK | SK | SK |
| SO4 | SK | SK | SK | SK |
| P6R | PT | PT | PT | PT |
| PO3 | PT | PT | PT | PT |
| PO4 | PT | PT | PT | PT |
| PUA1 | PT | PT | PT | PT |
| PUY1 | PT | PT | PT | PT |

Table 2 Criteria for finding similar bonds

| Similarity level | Name | Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | exact, equivalent | one atom matches by atom type, the other matches by equivalent atom type |
| 4 | exact, hybridization | one atom matches by atom type, the other matches by element and hybridization |
| 3 | hybridization, hybridization | one atom matches by atom type, the other matches by element and hybridization |
| 2 | exact, element | one atom matches by atom type,the other matches by element |
| 1 | element, element | both atoms match by element |

Table 3 Criteria for finding similar angle parameter

| Similarity level | Name | Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | exact, exact, element | center atom and one end atom match by atom type, the other end atom matches by element |
| 3 | exact, equivalent, element | center atom matches by equivalent type, one end atoms matches by type, and the other matches by element |
| 2 | element, exact, element | center atom matches by type, two end atoms by element |
| 1 | element, equivalent, element | center atom matches by equivalent type, two end atoms by element |

Table 4 Torsion parameter estimation [barrier height (kcal/mol), periodicity and reference angle value (degrees)]

| | Aromatic Barrier height | Aromatic Period | Aromatic Angle | Planar Non-Aromatic Barrier height | Planar Non-Aromatic Period | Planar Non-Aromatic Angle | Non-Planar Non-Aromatic Barrier height | Non-Planar Non-Aromatic Period | Non-Planar Non-Aromatic Angle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aromatic | 2.5 | 2 | 180 | 0.5 | 2 | 180 | 0.01 | 6 | 0 |
| Planar Non-Aromatic | 0.5 | 2 | 180 | 2.5 | 2 | 180 | 0.1 | 3 | 0 |
| Non-Planar Non-Aromatic | 0.01 | 6 | 0 | 0.1 | 3 | 0 | 0.2 | 3 | 0 |

# Run Enhanced Sampling Simulations tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_es.htm

## Run Enhanced Sampling Simulations tools

The Run Enhanced Sampling Simulations tool panel contains tools that allow you to setup and run enhanced sampling simulations.

### Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (GaMD)

GaMD Equilibration: With a typed molecule open, this button opens the GaMD Equilibration dialog. This protocol prepares a previously solvated and equilibrated system for GaMD.

GaMD Production: With the molecule generated by GaMD Equilibration open, this button opens the GaMD Production dialog. This protocol runs a production simulation using GaMD.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Simulation \| Run Enhanced Sampling Simulations |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Simulation \| Run Enhanced Sampling Simulations |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Run Enhanced Sampling Simulations |

# Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_gamd_th.htm

## Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics

Discovery Studio includes protocols, GaMD Equilibration and GaMD Production , that support Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD). GaMD is an enhanced sampling technique that flattens free energy landscapes to lower energy barriers for conformational transitions without the need to define a collective variable or reaction coordinate. In addition, harmonic boost potentials from GaMD follow a Gaussian distribution, which facilitates accurate reweighting of free energy landscapes [Pang et al., 2017] .

Flattening of the free energy landscape is accomplished by applying a boost potential, , to the system potential, , resulting in a new, biased system potential, . The boost potential , is calculated according to:

where represents a threshold energy and is a harmonic scaling constant. During GaMD Equilibration, the values of and are automatically determined based on constraints described in [Pang et al., 2017] .

### GaMD Parameters

Although GaMD requires no predefined collective variable to accelerate sampling, some parameters must be configured to enable the enhanced sampling technique:

* Boost Potential: Determines how the boost potential is applied. Boost potentials are energies that can be applied to different kinds of potentials, biasing and flattening the free energy landscape. The parameter selects exactly which potentials are boosted. Options include the following: Dual Boost: Boost potential is applied to the dihedral potential and the remainder of the total potential ( total - dihedral ). Total Potential: Boost potential is applied only to the total potential. Dihedral Potential: Boost potential is applied only to the dihedral potential.

* Dual Boost: Boost potential is applied to the dihedral potential and the remainder of the total potential ( total - dihedral ).

* Total Potential: Boost potential is applied only to the total potential.

* Dihedral Potential: Boost potential is applied only to the dihedral potential.

* Boost Potential Threshold: Configures when a boost potential is applied. Although you do not manually configure the exact value of the energy threshold, the choice of Vmax or Vmin determines how the threshold is calculated. The equations for how the thresholds are calculated are described in [Pang et al., 2017] . During GaMD Equilibration, Vmin, Vmax, and energy thresholds are calculated from simulation data and updated at set intervals. During GaMD Production, Vmin, Vmax, and energy thresholds are fixed and the Boost Potential Threshold does not vary with time.

* During GaMD Equilibration, Vmin, Vmax, and energy thresholds are calculated from simulation data and updated at set intervals.

* During GaMD Production, Vmin, Vmax, and energy thresholds are fixed and the Boost Potential Threshold does not vary with time.

* Boost Potential Standard Deviation: When set to value n , this parameter prevents the boost potential from taking a value greater than n standard deviations away from the mean boost potential energy. This constraint ensures that the distribution of boost potentials is narrow enough for accurate reweighting.

### Statistical Reweighting

Once one or more production simulations from GaMD Production are complete, you can perform a reweighting analysis using the Estimate Free Energy Landscape protocol. In Discovery Studio , reweighting is performed as follows:

* Estimate the probability density for some observables using a kernel density approach.

* Within each density window, use cumulant expansion to the second order to correct for boost potentials applied to each observation within the window.

This approach is similar to other established methods in the field, but has the benefit of requiring less parameters to determine histogram bins. See [Wang et al., 2021] for more information about GaMD and reweighting.

# Dynamics time step

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_heat_th_dynamics-time-step.htm

## Dynamics time step

Molecular dynamics simulation involves the numerical integration
of the equation of motion governed by Newton's second law. The
integration time step should be chosen to achieve high accuracy at
a reasonable computational cost. The time step should be chosen to
be smaller than the length of the time corresponding to the fastest
motion in a molecule. Typically, this motion is the vibration of a
bond containing a hydrogen (with a period less than 0.001 ps) that
would require a time step of 0.0005 ps.

The simulation length necessary to perform dynamics simulations should
also be considered. This time can range from nanoseconds to microseconds.
The characteristic times for common molecular events are listed in
the following table:

| Event | Time |
| --- | --- |
| Bond stretch | ~1 to 20 fs |
| Elastic domain modes | 100 fs to several ps |
| Water reorientation | 4 ps |
| Interdomain bending | 10 ps to 100 ns |
| Globular protein tumbling | 1 to 10 ns |
| Aromatic ring flipping | 100 ms to several sec |
| Allosteric shifts | 2 ms to several sec |
| Local denaturation | 1 ms to several sec |

To allow larger time steps and shorter real-time dynamics simulations,
the energy and force of certain high-frequency motions, such as bond
stretching, may be removed by constraining them to their initial or
equilibrium values. This is a reasonable approximation because it
is assumed that the harmonic stretching of bonds is restricted by a
large force constant and, particularly for bonds containing hydrogens,
is not significantly coupled to other motions of the system.

The method used in CHARMm to constrain these motions is the SHAKE algorithm. SHAKE is available in the Equilibration,
Heating, Minimization, and Production protocols,
as well as the Standard Dynamics Cascade. The SHAKE option can be applied to all covalent bonds involving hydrogen atoms.
A two-fold increase in the time step (to 0.002
ps) is then suggested. Note that bonds are constrained to their respective distances listed in the parameter table 
of the current
forcefield. SHAKE is also used as a
minimization parameter option.

The SHAKE parameter is an advanced protocol parameter that is set to False by default.
To enable the SHAKE algorithm constraint, set the parameter value to True under the Advanced group in the 
Parameters Explorer.

Equilibration : Equilibration is achieved by allowing
the system to evolve spontaneously for a period of time and integrating the
equations of motion until the average temperature and structure remain stable.
This is facilitated by periodically reassigning velocities appropriate to the
desired temperature. Generally, the procedure is continued until various statistical
properties of the system become independent of time.

Production : In the final molecular dynamics
simulation, CHARMm takes the equilibrated structure as its starting
point. In a typical simulation, the trajectory traces the motions
of the molecule through a period of at least several hundred picoseconds.
Just as with energy minimization, provision is made to update the
list of nonbonded interactions periodically. Additional options for
handling
nonbonded interactions and the environment are available, which makes the
dynamics facility quite flexible.

# Molecular dynamics

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_heat_th_molecular-dynamics.htm

## Molecular dynamics

One of the most important computational techniques in CHARMm is molecular
dynamics simulation. In CHARMm, molecular dynamics simulations are
performed using a classical mechanics approach in which Newton's equations
of motion are integrated for all atoms in the system.

Molecular dynamics can be used to generate a realistic model of a
structure's motion, perform conformational searching, produce a time
series analysis of structural and energetic properties, explore energy
decay, and analyze solvent effects. Molecular dynamics simulations
may help in understanding critical aspects of protein function that
involve both small-scale and large-scale atomic movements.

The essence of the molecular dynamics technique is in the numerical integration of Newton's equations of motion relating the 
mass and acceleration of an atom in
the system to the gradient of the potential energy field (the force on the atom). Given acceleration, an approximate 
velocity for the atom can be computed for a given
period of time and changes in atomic coordinates can be determined.

Several methods are available for numerical integration in CHARMm, such as Leap frog and two velocity Verlet variants.
For detailed discussion of these methods and other numerical methods for integrating differential equations, see one of the following:

* [Allen and Tildesley, 1987]

* [Haile, 1992]

# Dihedral restraint

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_minim_th_dihedral-constraint.htm

## Dihedral restraint

Restraining a dihedral angle formed by four atoms near a selected value is essential for some studies. CHARMm and NAMD use a harmonic 
potential to restrict the motion of a
dihedral angle usually to a value close to a reference position. For example, if you are investigating the adiabatic energy 
barrier to rotation about a bond, one approach is to
restrain the value of that particular dihedral angle and minimize the rest of the structure subject to the restraint. 
When the procedure is repeated for a set of values of
the angle in the range 0 to 360 degrees, a complete energy profile for rotation about the bond emerges. A similar 
process is used to generate
φ/ψ maps and other multi-dimensional energy surfaces for the study of molecular conformations.

In the DihedralRestraint tab of the Data Table View , you can edit the force constant, periodicity, and reference angle
used in the calculation.

## Distance restraint

A distance restraint in CHARMm places a potential between two or more
atoms to restrain the distance between these atoms to a reference value.
The restraining potential used in CHARMm is defined:

where, r is the distance between two atoms, r min is the minimum distance (threshold minimum), r max is the maximum distance (threshold maximum), k min is the force constant for the lower limit (force constant minimum), k max is the force constant for the higher limit (force constant maximum), f max is the maximum force to apply before using a linear relationship, and r lim is the value of r where the force equals f max .

The distance restraint described here is actually the NOE restraint in CHARMm and
is primarily used for the incorporation of NOE inter-proton distance information into a molecular dynamics simulation.

A simple harmonic distance restraint can be constructed by setting 
r min = r max , k min = k max and f max to infinity.
When Discovery Studio creates a distance restraint, it sets it as a harmonic distant restraint by default except f max is set at 10.
In the DistanceRestraint tab of the Data Table View , you can edit those parameter values.
NAMD only supports simple harmonic distance restraint and if r min and r max or k min and k max have 
different values, the average of them will be used in NAMD simulation.

NOE (or distance) restraints can be used, for example, to force an extended conformation into a helical conformation. 
Following a final minimization, the structure can be examined to measure the deviations from an idealized geometry.

# Fixed atom constraint

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_minim_th_fixed-atom-constraints.htm

## Fixed atom constraint

The simplest type of constraint is to fix atoms to fixed points in space so that they do not move during a minimization or dynamics 
simulation. Both CHARMm and NAMD avoid calculating most interactions in which all affected atoms are fixed 
except when fixedAtomsForces is turned on in NAMD simulation.
You can then save
computation time by calculating only those energy terms that involve at least one atom that is free to move. Energy terms between 
fixed atoms remain the same between
energy evaluation steps. Because some energy terms are omitted, the total energy calculated with fixed atoms will be different from the total energy of the 
same system with all atoms free. The forces on the
movable atoms will, however, be identical.

Fixed atom constraints are not compatible with constant pressure simulations in CHARMm. NAMD does not have this limitation. Consider using harmonic restraints with NPT in CHARMm.

#### Further information

Change Forcefield tools Dihedral restraint theory Distance restraint theory Harmonic restraint theory

## Nonbonded energy terms

In molecular modeling, electrostatic (Coulombic) and van der Waals
interactions are referred to collectively as nonbonded
interactions .

Calculating nonbonded interactions can be computationally expensive.
To avoid significant increases in calculation times, approximation
schemes are often employed. Choosing the best method for your particular
structure can save computational time without sacrificing accuracy.

### Computing the electrostatic potential

The electrostatic potential is computed using the partial charges
assigned to the atoms in the system. Several different
approaches are included in CHARMm for calculating the electrostatic
interactions:

* Option one - applies regular Coulombic electrostatic interaction
terms and is applied if there is no periodic boundary defined for
the system and the Implicit Solvent Model parameter
is set to None in the Parameters Explorer.

* Option two - introduces an approximate solvent screening term in
the dielectric constant by setting the dielectric constant proportional
to r, that is, Equation 1: resulting in the electrostatic interaction of the form Equation 2: This option is intended as an approximate way to deal with solvent
affects without explicitly including solvent atoms and is employed
if there is no periodic boundary defined for the system and the Implicit
Solvent Model parameter is set to Implicit
Distance-Dependent Dielectrics in the Parameters Explorer.

Equation 1:

resulting in the electrostatic interaction of the form

Equation 2:

This option is intended as an approximate way to deal with solvent
affects without explicitly including solvent atoms and is employed
if there is no periodic boundary defined for the system and the Implicit
Solvent Model parameter is set to Implicit
Distance-Dependent Dielectrics in the Parameters Explorer.

* Option three (extended electrostatics) - uses a multipole approximation
to permit efficient (i.e., time-saving) evaluation of all of the
electrostatic interactions in the system. The approach treats short-range
interactions in the usual way, but expresses long-range, group-group
interactions in terms of multipoles. Multipole expansion is truncated
after quadrupole moments. A constant dielectric is used. This approach is designed particularly for simulations where the details
of solvation and solvent polarization are of interest and a solvent
is being included explicitly, usually as a result of a Solvation protocol
using explicit periodic boundaries. In this case the Implicit
Solvent Model parameter is set to None in
the Parameters Explorer.

This approach is designed particularly for simulations where the details
of solvation and solvent polarization are of interest and a solvent
is being included explicitly, usually as a result of a Solvation protocol
using explicit periodic boundaries. In this case the Implicit
Solvent Model parameter is set to None in
the Parameters Explorer.

* Option four: Uses the Generalized Born model to approximate solvent
effect and is employed if there is no periodic boundary defined for the system
and the Implicit Solvent Model parameter
is set to Implicit Generalized Born in
the Parameters Explorer. In this option, the calculation of the Generalized Born solvation energy and forces is
achieved following a formulation similar to that of Still and co-workers and as described
by Dominy and Brooks [Dominy and Brooks, 1999] . It should be noted that when using this model for minimization or
molecular dynamics simulation, care should be taken to ensure that
the atomic radius assigned to hydrogen atoms is reasonably large to
avoid stability problems during simulations. This is especially true
for the charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, since in these forcefields
the van der Waals radius for polar hydrogens is small enough to cause
instabilities for many protein systems. For this reason, Discovery
Studio automatically scales up the polar hydrogen radius in the Generalized
Born scripts for the charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields. The optimal value for the Lambda parameter in Generalized Born method
is dependent on the forcefield type and the nature of the molecular
system: see the Dominy and Brooks reference for details. Reasonable
values that should be suitable for general cases are defined
by default in the application. However, for some systems, you may
find it necessary to vary the Generalized Born Lambda Constant advanced
parameter in the Parameters Explorer to make the simulation stable.

In this option, the calculation of the Generalized Born solvation energy and forces is
achieved following a formulation similar to that of Still and co-workers and as described
by Dominy and Brooks [Dominy and Brooks, 1999] .

It should be noted that when using this model for minimization or
molecular dynamics simulation, care should be taken to ensure that
the atomic radius assigned to hydrogen atoms is reasonably large to
avoid stability problems during simulations. This is especially true
for the charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, since in these forcefields
the van der Waals radius for polar hydrogens is small enough to cause
instabilities for many protein systems. For this reason, Discovery
Studio automatically scales up the polar hydrogen radius in the Generalized
Born scripts for the charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields.

The optimal value for the Lambda parameter in Generalized Born method
is dependent on the forcefield type and the nature of the molecular
system: see the Dominy and Brooks reference for details. Reasonable
values that should be suitable for general cases are defined
by default in the application. However, for some systems, you may
find it necessary to vary the Generalized Born Lambda Constant advanced
parameter in the Parameters Explorer to make the simulation stable.

### Computing van der Waals energy

The van der Waals energy is approximated in the CHARMm empirical energy function by the Lennard-Jones potential energy function. This function is often referred to as
a 6-12 potential because the attractive force is proportional to R -6 , while the repulsive force is modeled by R -12 .

### Nonbonded list

Nonbonded interactions refer to van der Waals terms and electrostatic interactions between atom pairs which are not covalently bonded with each other.

To maximize the efficiency of the nonbonded calculations, a list is created that contains all pair interactions to be considered. Atom pairs are not included in the
list if they are too far apart (beyond the long-range cutoffs), or if they are directly connected (either through a bond or a bond angle). In the latter case, the atoms
will be present in the excluded list.

The list generation approach available in CHARMm was chosen
over other alternatives (such as a pairwise search over all atoms)
for two reasons:

* During minimization or molecular dynamics simulation, the relative
positions between atoms do not change radically between one step
and the next

* A pairwise search through the list of atoms is relatively costly in computational terms

The list of atoms is updated periodically during energy minimization
or molecular dynamics simulation to account for changes in atomic positions.
If electrostatic groups are used, the list is stored in terms of group
pairs. This leads to improved efficiency and a smaller list, as well
as the ability to handle long-range group interactions.

* Nonbonded terms are defined on atom pairs and, for a first approximation,
would require N 2 calculations, where N is the total number
of atoms. To avoid this computational burden, various truncation
and approximation schemes can be employed in constructing the nonbonded lists

The nonbonded calculation encompasses two steps: list generation and energy computation. The same nonbonded specification should be used for all energy calculations
within a given project. Should it be necessary to use separate nonbonded specifications, the implications of these changes must be carefully evaluated.

The nonbonded list is primarily generated or modified automatically
by the scripts used to drive CHARMm.

### Updating nonbonded lists

During an energy minimization or molecular dynamics simulation, the
nonbonded list is updated according to a heuristic test, based on
the defined Nonbond List Radius (CUTNB) and Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance (CTOFNB) parameter values, that is performed at each step of the minimization
or dynamics simulation process.

The heuristic test for determining whether the nonbonded list requires
updating follows this procedure:

* Every time energy is called, displacement is computed for each atom since the list update.

* If any atom has moved by a distance greater than (CUTNB-CTOFNB)/2.0,
it is possible that some atom pairs in which the two atoms are now
separated by less than CTOFNB, are not in the atom pairs list. Therefore,
a list update is done.

* If all atoms have moved by less than the value defined by (CUTNB-CTOFNB)/2.0,
then all atom pairs within the CTOFNB distance are already accounted
for in the nonbonded list and no update is necessary.

The Nonbond List Radius (CUTNB), Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance (CTOFNB), Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance (CTONNB) parameters are defined by default as 14 , 12 , and 10 , respectively.
These values can be changed by editing the appropriate parameters in the Parameters Explorer.

### Nonbonded cutoffs

For a typical macromolecule, nonbonded interactions represent the bulk of the energy evaluation time. The efficiency of the nonbonded calculation is increased by
including only atom pairs that are closer than the cutoff distance in a nonbonded list. The cutoff distance criterion, while computationally efficient, has some
disadvantages. The possibility always exists that the overall nonbonded interactions at long range are not negligible because such interactions are numerous.
However, the slope of the van der Waals and electrostatic potentials in this region is small.

A more significant disadvantage is that a discontinuity in the energy function results at the cutoff distance. For energy minimization of molecular dynamics
calculations, this discontinuity can significantly distort computational results. For example, the total energy of the molecular system may not be conserved under such
circumstances.

To resolve these difficulties, both the van der Waals and electrostatic energy terms can be modified by techniques that smooth the function around the cutoff
distance, as described in the following paragraphs:

* Switching function : The size of the nonbonded lists can be made smaller by indicating a distance to
be applied to a switching function beyond which no interaction is computed

Two variables corresponding to the start and finish of the switching regions (r on and r off , respectively)
are required to define the switching function. Depending on the value of r ij , the following values are used to multiply individual electrostatic
or van der Waals energy terms:

* If r ij < r on , then use 1.0

* If r on < r ij < r off , then use:

Equation 3:

* If r ij > r off , then use 0.0

However, energy can still be significant at the cutoff distance and this can result in artificially large forces at long range. This is especially true
for relatively short (that is, less than 12 Å) cutoff distances and small buffer regions (that is, when r off - r on < 3
Å).

### Dielectric constant

The dielectric constant is an experimentally derived property of the bulk solvent that reflects the polarizability of the solvent molecules. A polarizable solvent
such as water has a greater dielectric constant than less polar liquids. Electrostatic interactions in such high dielectric polarizable solvents are greatly
attenuated.

A dielectric constant of 1.0 is suitable for simulating solvated systems which include solvent molecules explicitly. For simulations that do not explicitly include solvent molecules
, a number of models have been used to approximate the dielectric effect of solvents.

A relatively large dielectric constant can be used for simulating the aqueous environment of small systems. However, most calculations on molecular systems use a
smaller dielectric constant. For example, a dielectric constant between 2.0 and 10.0 has been employed for simulations in the interior of a protein.

For electrostatic interactions in closely packed molecules, the number of solvent molecules between two interacting charges is usually less than that which would be
experienced in the bulk solvent. Thus, the dielectric constant for the micro solvent environment is often not as great as for the bulk solvent. To simulate this effect,
a distance-dependent dielectric constant can be used. This constant also acts as an approximate solvent screening term in which the electrostatic interaction experiences
a greater and greater attenuation as the two charges are separated. The RDIE keyword is used to specify the use of this distance-dependent dielectric constant in energy
calculations.

# Solvent models in biomolecular simulations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_minim_th_solvent_model.htm

## Solvent models in biomolecular simulations

Most biomolecules are functional in an aqueous environment.
The importance of solvent effect on the structure, energetics and dynamics of biomolecules has long been recognized.

Ideally, including solvent molecules explicitly in a simulation provides the most accurate description of the molecular system.
In a typical solvated system, solvent molecules occupy more than 85 percent of the total volume, making the
explicit solvent simulations expensive in terms of computational cost.

A popular alternative to explicit solvent simulation is the use of
implicit solvent model. In an implicit solvent simulation, the polar and non-polar effects of the solvent are accounted
for in an averaged way, without explicitly including each solvent molecule in the calculation.

The CHARMm module in the application provides a number of implicit solvent models, which
vary in computational complexity and accuracy, and can be used in different scenarios.

### Explicit Solvation

With explicit solvation, the energy of the system is the total molecular mechanics forcefield energy
of solute, solvent and their images. The following explicit solvation methods are available in the application:

* Explicit Solvation in Periodic Boundary Condition (PBC): Choose to 
solvate the solute system in one of the
cubic, orthorhombic, or truncated octahedron water box, based on the shape of the solute molecule.
You can also choose to add counterions to neutralize the system, and to explicitly add salt according to a desired
concentration.

* Explicit Solvation in Spherical Boundary: Choose to solvate 
part of or the entire solute in a water sphere. This type of explicit solvation
is particularly useful for studying ligand-receptor complex, where only part of the solute system, the ligand binding site, is of
interest.

The Explicit Solvation in Periodic Boundary Condition (PBC) is the
only solvent model with which the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) option to compute long range electrostatic interactions can be applied.

### Implicit Solvent Model

In most implicit solvent models, the free energy of a structure is decomposed into additive components: gas-phase forcefield energy E(gas) and
solvation free energy G(solv):

Equation 1:

The solvation free energy is further decomposed into electrostatic and non-polar contributions, and is written as:

Equation 2:

The electrostatic solvation energy G(elec) accounts for the electrostatic interaction between the solute and the polarizable solvent.
The latter is usually treated as a continuum dielectric medium, described by the Poisson-Boltzmann equation, or one of the Generalized 
Born model.
The non-polar term G(np) includes the unfavorable hydrophobic contribution and the favorable van der Waals interaction between the solute and
the solvent. This term is often assumed to be proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA):

Equation 3:

where, a is the surface area coefficient and b is a constant term.

Some of the implicit solvent models based on Generalized Born approximation, such as GBIM and GBSW implemented in CHARMm, 
support the modeling of membrane proteins. These methods model the non-polar region of the lipid membrane as a low dielectric slab,
represented by the region between the two planes shown here, and treat the polar head groups of the lipid molecules 
as part of the bulk polar solvent:

Figure 1: Dielectric model of a protein embedded in membrane

The thickness of the non-polar region of a typical biological membrane is ~ 30 Å. 
As with many other implicit models, the dielectric properties of the system are defined by 
two dielectric constants. The dielectric constant of the membrane slab, ε m , is assumed to have
the same value as the solute molecule. The polar head group and bulk solvent is approximated by ε w .

When modeling transmembrane proteins, it is appropriate to set ε w = 80 for the water solvent and 
ε m = 1 or 2 for the membrane non-polar region.

### Methods for estimating the electrostatic solvation energy G(elec)

* Distance dependent dielectrics: The use of distance dependent dielectrics is not a well
founded implicit solvent model, but a crude way
to approximate some of the screening effect of the solvent by empirically
making the dielectric constant increase linearly with distance between two solute atoms.
The physical validity of such approximation is difficult to establish.

The use of distance dependent dielectrics is not a well
founded implicit solvent model, but a crude way
to approximate some of the screening effect of the solvent by empirically
making the dielectric constant increase linearly with distance between two solute atoms.
The physical validity of such approximation is difficult to establish.

* Generalized Born with pairwise summation (GenBorn): In this option, the calculation of the Generalized Born solvation energy and forces is achieved following a formulation
similar to that of Still et al. [Still et al., 1990] and as described by Dominy and Brooks [Dominy and Brooks, 1999] .
Briefly, a pairwise sum of atomic volumes is used to calculate the effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation. It should be noted that when using this model for minimization or
molecular dynamics simulation, care should be taken to ensure that
the atomic radius assigned to hydrogen atoms is reasonably large to
avoid stability problems during simulations. This is especially true
for the charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, because in these forcefields
the van der Waals radius for polar hydrogens is small enough to cause
instabilities for many protein systems. For this reason, Discovery
Studio automatically scales up the polar hydrogen radius in the Generalized
Born scripts for the charmm22, charmm27, and charmm36 forcefields. The optimal value for the Lambda parameter in Generalized Born method
is dependent on the forcefield type and the nature of the molecular
system: see the Dominy and Brooks reference for details. Reasonable
values that should be suitable for general cases are defined
by default in the application. However, for some systems, you may
find it necessary to vary the Generalized Born Lambda Constant advanced
parameter in the Parameters Explorer to make the simulation stable.

In this option, the calculation of the Generalized Born solvation energy and forces is achieved following a formulation
similar to that of Still et al. [Still et al., 1990] and as described by Dominy and Brooks [Dominy and Brooks, 1999] .
Briefly, a pairwise sum of atomic volumes is used to calculate the effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation.

It should be noted that when using this model for minimization or
molecular dynamics simulation, care should be taken to ensure that
the atomic radius assigned to hydrogen atoms is reasonably large to
avoid stability problems during simulations. This is especially true
for the charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, because in these forcefields
the van der Waals radius for polar hydrogens is small enough to cause
instabilities for many protein systems. For this reason, Discovery
Studio automatically scales up the polar hydrogen radius in the Generalized
Born scripts for the charmm22, charmm27, and charmm36 forcefields.

The optimal value for the Lambda parameter in Generalized Born method
is dependent on the forcefield type and the nature of the molecular
system: see the Dominy and Brooks reference for details. Reasonable
values that should be suitable for general cases are defined
by default in the application. However, for some systems, you may
find it necessary to vary the Generalized Born Lambda Constant advanced
parameter in the Parameters Explorer to make the simulation stable.

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM): In this method, the Generalized Born approximation is extended by including an implicit membrane (IM) in the calculation
of the electrostatic contribution to the solvation free energy [Spassov et al., 2002] .
Additionally, the non-polar solvation energy terms, including the effect of membrane, can be calculated by the solvent-accessible surface 
approximation using CHARMm ASPENRMB method. The GBIM model is applicable for energy calculations, minimization, and molecular dynamics simulations of protein and peptides 
in the environment of biological membranes.
The GBIM model is used also as the basic solvation model in other computational methods such as prediction of ionization properties of proteins
in the Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol, or refinement of loop structures in the Loop Refinement protocol.

In this method, the Generalized Born approximation is extended by including an implicit membrane (IM) in the calculation
of the electrostatic contribution to the solvation free energy [Spassov et al., 2002] .
Additionally, the non-polar solvation energy terms, including the effect of membrane, can be calculated by the solvent-accessible surface 
approximation using CHARMm ASPENRMB method.

The GBIM model is applicable for energy calculations, minimization, and molecular dynamics simulations of protein and peptides 
in the environment of biological membranes.
The GBIM model is used also as the basic solvation model in other computational methods such as prediction of ionization properties of proteins
in the Protein Ionization and Residue pK protocol, or refinement of loop structures in the Loop Refinement protocol.

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume integration (GBMV): In this newly developed Generalized Born method, the effective
Born radii is calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. A higher-order correction
term to the Coulomb field approximation is included to improve agreement with the radii calculated from solving
Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) equation [Lee, 2002] . Tests conducted since 2002 indicate that the electrostatic solvation energy calculated from GBMV method is
highly accurate, achieving errors of 1% for relative solvation energies between different proteins
and 0.4% between different conformations of the same protein, when the results from PB calculations are used as reference.

In this newly developed Generalized Born method, the effective
Born radii is calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. A higher-order correction
term to the Coulomb field approximation is included to improve agreement with the radii calculated from solving
Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) equation [Lee, 2002] .

Tests conducted since 2002 indicate that the electrostatic solvation energy calculated from GBMV method is
highly accurate, achieving errors of 1% for relative solvation energies between different proteins
and 0.4% between different conformations of the same protein, when the results from PB calculations are used as reference.

* Generalized Born with a simple switching (GBSW): The methodology of the GBSW model is similar to that of GBMV, but replacing its computationally expensive molecular
surface approximation with a van der Waals-based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary [Im, 2003] . The GBSW method is slightly less accurate than the GBMV in calculating of electrostatic solvation energies.
However, because of its use of the smoothed dielectric boundary instead of a sharp molecular surface, the change in the
polarization forces vary more smoothly, compared those obtained from GBMV. Tests show that the GBSW method tends to produce stable
molecular dynamics trajectories, while the GBMV method sometimes causes the energy of the system to drift significantly. The GBSW method is about 2-3 times faster than the GBMV method.
Similar to GBIM, the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane.

surface approximation with a van der Waals-based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary [Im, 2003] .

The GBSW method is slightly less accurate than the GBMV in calculating of electrostatic solvation energies.
However, because of its use of the smoothed dielectric boundary instead of a sharp molecular surface, the change in the
polarization forces vary more smoothly, compared those obtained from GBMV. Tests show that the GBSW method tends to produce stable

The GBSW method is about 2-3 times faster than the GBMV method.
Similar to GBIM, the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane.

* Poisson-Boltzmann equation with non-polar surface area (PBSA): The PBSA method may be considered as the gold standard for implicit solvent models based on continuum electrostatics [Feig et al., 2004]. In this approach, the Poisson-Boltzmann equation is solved numerically on a 3D grid, and the calculated electrostatic potentials is used
to estimate the electrostatic solvation free energy. Although the PB calculation is more accurate than other implicit solvent methods deployed in the application, it is computationally expensive.
In the application, the PBSA method is only available for evaluate single point energy, and cannot be used in minimization or dynamics simulation.

The PBSA method may be considered as the gold standard for implicit solvent models based on continuum electrostatics [Feig et al., 2004]. In this approach, the Poisson-Boltzmann equation is solved numerically on a 3D grid, and the calculated electrostatic potentials is used
to estimate the electrostatic solvation free energy.

Although the PB calculation is more accurate than other implicit solvent methods deployed in the application, it is computationally expensive.
In the application, the PBSA method is only available for evaluate single point energy, and cannot be used in minimization or dynamics simulation.

In this version of the CHARMm in the application,
the GBMV and GBSW methods are not compatible and should not be used with the CFF or MMFF force fields.
Also, large cutoff values (e.g., 18 Å) are recommended when one of the GB/PB methods is used to
describe the effect of solvation.

# Run Free Energy Simulations tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_rfest.htm

## Run Free Energy Simulations tools

The Run Free Energy Simulations tool panel contains tools that allow you to setup and run free energy simulations.

### Free Energy Perturbation

Pair Ligands for FEP: With two 
ligands selected, this button pairs the ligands into an assembly. The ligands have to be typed by either CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield. This 
button can be used to manually pair ligands for use in Set Up Relative FEP Calculations protocol.

Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP: Opens the Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP protocol dialog. Given a set of ligands, this protocol generates a set 
of optimal pairs based on chemical and topological similarity in order 
to plan a set of relative FEP calculations that spans the entire set.

Set Up Relative FEP Calculations: Opens the Set Up Relative FEP Calculations protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to prepare simulation systems
of free ligand and protein-ligand complexes prior to running free 
energy molecular dynamics simulations.

Free Energy Perturbation (FEP): Opens the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to perform free energy perturbation molecular dynamics simulations using the NAMD parallel molecular dynamics program designed for high-performance simulation of large biomolecular systems.

Collate FEP Simulation Results: Opens the Collate FEP Simulation Results protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to calculate the relative free energy of binding for multiple pairs of ligands to a specific receptor. It takes the combined results from Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) simulation runs for free ligand pairs and the corresponding protein-ligand complexes. Optionally, it derives the absolute free energies for the full set of ligands from the relative free energies.

CHARMm Relative FEP Calculations (GPU): Opens the CHARMm Relative FEP Calculations (GPU) protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to run alchemical free energy simulations in the NPT thermodynamic ensemble. The protocol uses the CHARMm molecular dynamics program's DOMDEC GPU platform.

### Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (Prototype)

Enumerate Ligands for MSLD: Opens the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to generate R-group enumerations around a lead compound to be used in multi-site lambda dynamics (MSLD) calculations.

Set Up MSLD Calculations: Opens the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to prepare simulation systems of free ligand and protein-ligand complex prior to running MSLD simulations..

MSLD Bias Optimization and Production: Opens the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to optimize biasing potential functions that are added to the simulation energy to facilitate transitions between substituents during a Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) simulation and subsequent production simulations.

Collate MSLD Simulation Results: Opens the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to calculate the relative free energy of binding for a combinatorial library of ligands modeled by MSLD. It takes the combined results from MSLD Optimization and Production protocol runs for free ligand and the corresponding protein-ligand complex.

### Access methods

| Menu | Tools \| Simulation \| Run Free Energy Simulations |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Run Free Energy Simulations |

# Run Simulations tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_rst.htm

## Run Simulations tools

The Run Simulations tool panel contains tools that allow you to run molecular simulations on a structure 
loaded in the Graphics View .

### Tools

Calculate Energy: Opens the Calculate Energy protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to evaluate the potential energy of a specified structure. You can also use several methods to estimate the entropy of the system.

Clean Geometry: Uses a fast, Dreiding-like forcefield to optimize the geometry of the selection in a Molecule Window. If nothing is selected all visible molecules are cleaned.

Minimization: Opens the Minimization protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to minimize the energy of a structure
through geometry optimization. If there is a selection of atoms within the
structure, only those atoms will be allowed to moved, a fixed atom
constraint is created for all the other atoms.

### Dynamics

Standard Dynamics Cascade: Opens the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol dialog. This protocol applies a set of defined simulation procedures to the input structure. Minimization, equilibration, and production dynamics stages are performed.

Dynamics (Production): Opens the Dynamics (Production) protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to perform molecular dynamics simulations in a chosen thermodynamic ensemble.

The progress of a
minimization or production dynamics stage can be followed when running interactively by setting the Save Results Frequency to the number of steps you want between each update.

Dynamics (NAMD): Opens the Dynamics (NAMD) protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to perform molecular dynamics simulations using the NAMD parallel molecular dynamics program designed for high-performance simulation of large biomolecular systems.

### Advanced

Dynamics (Heating or Cooling): Opens the Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to control the temperature of a system when performing a molecular dynamics simulation.

Dynamics (Equilibration): Opens the Dynamics (Equilibration) protocol dialog. This protocol establishes the target temperature for a system using molecular dynamics simulation.

Solvation: Opens the Solvation protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to create an explicitly solvated system using CHARMm.

Solvate with Explicit Membrane: Opens the Solvate with Explicit Membrane protocol dialog. This protocol adds explicit membrane and water to a transmembrane protein.

Solvation and Solvate with Explicit Membrane protocols add a BoxShape attribute to the molecule. If you remove the added water, you must remove the BoxShape attribute using Remove Attribute dialog before running any subsequent simulation protocols.

### Steered Molecular Dynamics

Create Pulling Atom Pair: Creates a pulling atom pair from a pair of selected atoms. See Create Pulling Atom Pair .

Steered Molecular Dynamics: Opens the Steered Molecular Dynamics protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to run molecular dynamics simulation while applying 
a steering force to a pair of selected atoms.

Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces: Opens the Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to analyze a collection of Steered Molecular Dynamics (SMD) runs and calculate the free energy as a function of the reaction coordinate or pulling distance.

### Electrostatic Potential

Calculate Electrostatic Potential: Opens the Calculate Electrostatic Potential protocol dialog. This protocol calculates the electrostatic potential of a solute molecule based on implicit solvent model by solving Poisson-Boltzmann equation using the CHARMm PBEQ module.

### QM

Calculate Energy (QM-MM): Opens the Calculate Energy (QM-MM) protocol dialog. This protocol allows you to evaluate the QM-MM potential energy of a specified structure. A chosen region of atoms is treated quantum mechanically and the remainder of the system is handled with molecular mechanics.

Calculate Energy (DFT): Opens the Calculate Energy (DFT) protocol dialog. This protocol calculates the energy or optimizes the geometry of a small molecule using density functional theory quantum mechanics method in DMol 3 . Additionally, you can visualize the HOMO/LUMO molecular orbitals, electron density, and electrostatic potential.

Minimization (QM-MM): Opens the Minimization (QM-MM) protocol dialog. This protocol minimizes the energy of a structure through geometry optimization with QM-MM potential. The QM region of atoms is treated by a quantum calculation using the DMol 3 server and the rest, MM, is handled by the CHARMm forcefield.

### Access methods

| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Simulation \| Run Simulations |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Run Simulations |

# Setup Constraints tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_sct.htm

## Setup Constraints tools

Use the Setup Constraints tools to put constraints on atoms in your structure before running CHARMm and Dynamics (NAMD) simulation protocols. To create a constraint,
select the atoms to be constrained and click one of the constraint tools described below. The constraint will be visible in the Graphics View and an entry is created on the corresponding tab in the Data Table View with editable parameters. The following options are available:

* Create Fixed Atom Constraint

* Create Dihedral Restraint

* Create Harmonic Restraint

* Create Distance Restraint

Although you set up constraints before you launch a simulation protocol, you must also specify which constraints are to be applied when setting the run options. Also, when running the Minimization tool , you can minimize a subset of atoms by selecting them. A fixed atom constraint will be created on the remaining atoms automatically.

Create Fixed Atom Constraint: Fixes selected atoms in space so they do not move during a minimization or dynamics simulation.
This potentially reduces computation time by omitting any interactions that include only fixed atoms from the nonbonded lists. 
For more information on the theory see Fixed atom constraint .

Create Dihedral Restraint: Restraining a dihedral angle formed by four atoms near a selected value using a force constant ( k cal/mol). This is essential for some studies.

For example, if you are investigating the adiabatic energy barrier to rotation about a bond, you must fix the value of that particular dihedral
angle and minimize the rest of the structure subject to the constraint. When the procedure is repeated for a set of values of the angle in the
range 0 to 360 degrees, a complete energy profile for rotation about the bond emerges. A similar process is used to generate φ/ψ maps and
other multidimensional energy surfaces for the study of molecular conformations. 
For more information on the theory see Dihedral restraint .

Create Harmonic Restraint: Similar to a fixed atom constraint, but allows some freedom while restraining them near a particular position in space with a force constant ( k cal/mol/A 2 ).

The basic difference between a constraint and a restraint is that a constraint completely removes the given degrees of freedom from the system while a restraint retains them but applies a penalty function to the energy if the atoms involved move away from the desired configuration. Historically these two terms have been used interchangeably in some software packages such as NAMD.

For CHARMm, you can specify two additional parameters for a harmonic restraint in the Data Table View :

* Use Mass Weighting

* Harmonic Restraint Type

Mass weighting is recommended for most operations involving harmonic restraints for the following reasons:

* The results obtained will be similar regardless of which atom representation is used (extended vs. explicit) for hydrogen atoms.

* Hydrogen atoms are allowed greater relative freedom if present.

* The character of the normal modes of a molecule are unperturbed with mass weighting (essential if normal modes or low frequency motions are of interest).

You can set the harmonic restraint type to Absolute or Best Fit . Absolute restraints specify a location in a Cartesian space where an atom must remain proximal. The best fit restraint is similar to the absolute restraints except that the reference coordinates are implicitly rotated and translated so as to best fit the selected atoms to minimize the restraint energy. This makes it useful for holding inter-atom geometry intact while allowing for block or rigid body motion. Due to the nature of the best fit, this restraint term does not add any net force or torque to the system (unlike the absolute restraint type). 
For more information on the theory see Harmonic restraint .

It is possible to
combine multiple restraints in one energy calculation, but no atom may
participate in more than one harmonic restraint set.

Create Distance Restraint: Restricts the distance between two atoms or two centroids to a reference value. This restraint is primarily used for the incorporation of NOE inter-proton distance information into a molecular dynamics simulation with a force constant ( k cal/mol/A 2 ). For example, distance restraints can be used to force an extended conformation into a helical conformation.
For more information on the theory see Distance restraint .

Constraints and restraints are objects in the Molecule Window that can be selected, edited, and deleted from the Data Table View , Hierarchy View , or Graphics View . You can also undo a recently applied constraint by pressing CTRL+Z or by choosing Edit | Undo from the menu bar.

| Menu | Tools \| Simulation \| Setup Constraints |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Setup Constraints |

# Placement of counter ions using the Solvation protocol

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_solvent_th_counter-ions.htm

## Placement of counter ions using the Solvation protocol

In explicit solvent simulations, counter ions are often needed 
to ensure that the total system is charge-neutral and 
that the simulation is conducted at a desired experimental 
ionic concentration. The charge-neutrality is particularly 
important for simulations using the Particle-Mesh-Ewald 
(PME) method in calculating long range electrostatics.

In the Solvation protocol, the number 
of counter ions added to the system is determined 
by the desired ionic concentration and the total 
net charge of molecular system prior to
solvation. First, appropriate anions or cations are 
added to neutralize the charge on the solute
molecule. Then, additional anions and cations are 
added to keep the system neutral and to raise the
ionic concentration to the desired level.

Take, for example, a protein with a net charge of -4e where you want use the sodium chloride counter ions with the ionic concentration set to 1 M. The Solvation protocol will first add four sodium cations to neutralize the protein charges. This number of counter ions is only used to neutralize the system. Additional counter ions are then needed to set the ionic concentration at desired value of 1 M. The number of additional sodium and chloride ions are calculated by multiplying the total number of water molecules by the ratio of the desired ionic concentration of 1 M, and the standard water concentration of 55 M.

All counter ions are randomly placed in the solvent box, within three angstroms of the closest solute atoms.

# Theory - Simulation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/sima_th.htm

## Theory - Simulation

### CHARMm

CHARMm is a highly flexible molecular mechanics and dynamics program. It derives from the program CHARMM (Chemistry at HARvard Molecular 
Mechanics), which was originally developed in the laboratory of Professor Martin Karplus at Harvard University, and has been continuously 
improved by many of the researchers around the world under the leadership of Professor Karplus.

CHARMm performs well over a broad range of calculations and simulations, including calculation of geometries, interaction and conformation 
energies, local minima, barriers to rotation, time-dependent dynamic behavior, and free energy [Momany and Rone, 1992] . 
CHARMm is designed to give good results for a wide variety of modeled systems, from isolated small molecules to solvated 
complexes of large biological macromolecules. However, it does not have adequate coverage for organometallic complexes.

The following topics provide specific details about CHARMm theory:

* CHARMm forcefields

* Nonbonded energy terms

* Fixed atom constraint

* Harmonic restraint

* Dihedral restraint

* Distance restraint

* Molecular dynamics

* Dynamics time step

* Solvent models in biomolecular simulations

* Placement of counter ions using the Solvation protocol

* Energy Minimization

### Electrostatics

The Electrostatics protocols calculate the electrostatic potential, using the CHARMm program PBEQ, and the protein
ionization and pK of titratable residues.

The following topics provide specific details about Electrostatics theory:

* Protein Ionization and Residue pK

* Electrostatic Potential

### QM-MM

QM-MM protocols allow you to perform combined quantum mechanics (QM) and molecular mechanics (MM) forcefield calculations. It derives
from the ChemShell program
suite [Sherwood et al., 2003] , which is developed by the groups of Paul Sherwood (STFC at Daresbury, UK),
Walter Thiel (Max-Planck Institut für Kohlenforschung, Mülheim), and Richard Catlow (The Royal Institution of Great Britain).

The QM-MM program allows the calculation of QM-MM single point energies and geometry optimization minimizations using DMol 3 as the quantum server and the CHARMm
forcefield [Momany and Rone, 1992] .

The following topics provide specific details about QM-MM theory:

* Overview of QM-MM methodology

* QM-MM embedding

* QM-MM energy expressions

* Handling of the QM-MM boundary

### GaMD

Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) is a robust computational method for simultaneous unconstrained enhanced sampling and free energy calculations of biomolecules. It works by adding a harmonic boost potential to smooth the biomolecular potential energy surface and reduce energy barriers. GaMD greatly accelerates biomolecular simulations by orders of magnitude. It provides unconstrained enhanced sampling without the need to set predefined reaction coordinates or collective variables.

For details, see Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulations and analysis .

### Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance

Allosteric communication is a fundamental mechanism by which proteins transmit signals from one site to another, often resulting in functional conformational changes that modulate activity. Time-lagged cross-covariance and cross-correlation of measured trajectory features can identify correlated motions and detect feature dependencies that may indicate allosteric communication pathways.

For details, see Cross-Correlation and Cross-Covariance .
