## Analyze Trajectory - Parameters

### Calculates RMSD and geometries of dynamics trajectories

Performs the following property calculations and manipulations over all conformations of a molecule, including:

* Root mean square deviation (RMSD) to any frame in the trajectory, with or without superimposition.

* RMSD to a specified structure.

* RMSD to all frames, allowing clustering of the results.

* Atomic RMS fluctuation (RMSF) from the average structure in the trajectory and the residue RMSF as the average of the atomic RMSF.

* Superimpose frames using a selection.

* Distance, angle, torsion, and non-bond interaction measurements.

* Protein torsion analysis.

* Sampling of a large trajectory file (DCD) into smaller pieces for analysis.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Molecule | Select a structure with conformations for trajectory analysis. If the input structure does not have any conformation, one or more trajectory files corresponding to this structure should be provided. |
| Input Molecule Frame Start | Specify the frame number in the input molecule to begin trajectory analyzing. |
| Input Molecule Frame Stop | Specify the frame number in the input molecule to end trajectory analyzing. If unspecified, the last frame in the input molecule will be used. |
| Input Molecule Frame Increment | Specify the increment in the frame number in the input molecule for trajectory analyzing. |
| Trajectory File | Select a trajectory (DCD) file to be processed. DCD file is generated by CHARMm during dynamics simulations and contains coordinates of each trajectory frame. Conformations from the DCD file will be appended to the input molecule. It must match the molecule specified by Input Molecule File with the same number of atoms. |
| Frame Start | Specify the frame number in the DCD file to begin trajectory loading. |
| Frame Stop | Specify the frame number in the DCD file to end trajectory loading. If unspecified, the last frame in the DCD file will be used. |
| Frame Increment | Specify the increment in the frame number in the DCD file for trajectory loading. |

# Analyze Trajectory

## Analyze Trajectory

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Analyze Trajectory protocol allows you to analyze structural properties of a molecular dynamics trajectory. You can perform one or more of the
following analyses:

* Calculate geometric properties such as distance, angle and torsion, or non-bond interactions (such as hydrogen bonds and bumps, etc.) for each simulation frame.

* Calculate protein main- and side-chain torsion angles for each frame.

* Calculate the RMSD between different conformations or against a specified molecule for a group of atoms or all atoms, 
and optionally create a new superimposed trajectory.

* Calculate RMSD between all frames to allow clustering of the frames.

* Calculate the atomic RMS fluctuation (RMSF) from the average structure in the trajectory and report the residue RMSF as average of the atomic RMSF.

* Sample a trajectory by specifying frame start, frame stop, and frame increment parameters for either frames in the input molecule or 
in an additional trajectory file. Sampling with latter method uses memory efficiently and can be used for very large trajectories.

To calculate distance, angle, torsion angles, or non-bond interactions along a trajectory, select the appropriate atoms and choose Structure | Monitor from the menu bar to define the desired geometrical properties before running
the protocol. The main chain and side-chain torsional angles for proteins and peptides are automatically recognized by the protocol and do not
need to be defined.

To analyze results from multiple DCD files generated by consecutive simulation runs, 
use the Process Trajectory Files protocol to merge the frames first.
You can also use Process Trajectory Files protocol to create a subset
of atoms to be analyzed before running this protocol.

* Do one of the following: Load a molecular structure in the Graphics View that contains trajectory
information. Such a structure is created when you run one of the simulation dynamics protocols such as Dynamics (Production). The
loaded structure should have one conformation for each frame in the trajectory, which you can see in the Conformations tab in the Data Table View . Load a molecular structure in the Graphics View and add
a trajectory into it using the Choose an Animation File dialog. Load a molecular structure in the Graphics View and 
choose a trajectory file and the frames to be analyzed from the protocol interface in step 4. This method uses the least amount of memory and is the preferred method for very large trajectory files.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

To analyze the results, open Report.htm. Depending on the type of analysis requested, the report will include a line plot 
(e.g., RMSF line plot) or heat map to show the summary of the analysis. Additionally, the analyzed properties are stored either in 
the Molecule.dsv or corresponding csv files. You can open these files and create plots for more detailed information.

An additional column is added to the Conformation tab in the Data Table for each of the properties that were selected for
analysis. Additionally, RMSD or torsional angle values are added to the Conformation tab in the Data Table if RMSD or Torsion
Angles calculations were requested for analysis. RMSF values are added to the Atom and Residue tabs 
in the data table if an RMSF calculation was requested.

Non-bond interaction monitors can potentially have thousands of entries, exceeding the limit of columns the data table handles.
Therefore, they are saved in <Monitors>.csv , and the first 1000 interactions are saved according to the frequency appearing in all frames. The RMSD and RMSF data are also written to RMSD.csv and RMSF.csv .

If RMSD is calculated for all frames and the scope is set to Molecule , you can view the cluster of the frames by clicking RMSD Dendrogram in the Results section of the protocol report.

The cluster center is defined as the frame with the smallest RMSD from all other frames in the same cluster. Selecting a cluster node in the dendrogram makes the cluster center conformation in the linked Molecule Window visible.

Insights into the atomic structure, dynamics, and energetics of a molecular process can be obtained from analyzing molecular dynamics trajectories.

Two major groups of trajectory properties can be analyzed in Discovery Studio : global energetic properties and structural properties.

* Global energetic properties: These include temperature, total energy, total potential energy, and various energy
components of the potential energy function of the system. Analyzing these properties as a function of simulation time provides important
information regarding the overall stability of a trajectory and the validity of simulation protocols. For example, a plot of temperature as a
function of time for the heating phase should indicate whether the heating protocol is applied as expected. Similarly, a plot of energy versus time provides critical information regarding energy conservation in the NVE ensemble. Analyzing the global 
energetics is usually the first step in the entire trajectory analysis process because the most obvious artifacts or simple errors may be 
revealed during these analyses.

* Structural properties: These include distance, angle, torsion, as well as the protein backbone and side-chain
torsion angles. RMSD between different conformations can also be computed. Analyzing the temporal history of these properties is useful in
identifying structural transitions in simulated systems. Generating a cross correlation plot of two structural properties may be helpful in
discovering or confirming trends in the dynamics.

The Create Plot... button in the Analyze Trajectory tools provides access to the Choose Plot Axes dialog , which allows you to plot global and structural properties. You can also select columns in the Conformation tab in the Data Table and create a plot using various plotting tools in
the Chart menu .

Given a long MD trajectory, it is often useful to focus on the frames that show interesting structural and dynamic behavior. The Sample Trajectory... button in the Analyze Trajectory tools can be used for this purpose. It
provides access to the Choose Trajectory Frames dialog , which allows you to choose the start
frame, end frame, and interval size to create a new trajectory from the original.

When RMSD Reference is set to Specify a Molecule , the reference
molecule will be added as the last conformation in the output molecule. If you do not want this conformation in your subsequent simulation
or analysis (e.g., when planning to continue the dynamics production from this run), delete this conformation from the Hierarchy View.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv: | The molecular system file with new properties added by the Analyze Trajectory protocol, or new conformations added from the Trajectory File . |
| [RMSD \| RMSF \| <Monitors>].csv | The table of RMSD, RMSF, or non-bond interaction values calculated by the Analyze Trajectory protocol. |
| Cluster_Conformations*.pl | Perl scripts that show dendrograms of RMSD values. This file is only generated when RMSD Reference is set to All Frames and the Scope is Molecule . Opening the file will display a Dendrogram Window in which the conformations are clustered according to the similarity of calculated RMSD values. Similar conformations are grouped closer together. Click a node to select the corresponding conformations in the Molecule Window. The conformation representing the cluster center is made visible. |

# Analyze Trajectory Features - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_analyze_trajectory_features-para.htm

## Analyze Trajectory Features - Parameters

### Analyze features from molecular dynamics trajectories

Analyze Trajectory Features computes time-lagged cross-covariance and cross-correlation for one or two CSV files. The protocol requires a measured dataset, which you can generate using Measure Trajectory Features or Detect and Analyze Pockets . The input must correspond to a unique feature. You can compare two features by using two input files. Use this protocol to identify correlated motions and detect feature dependencies, which could indicate allosteric motion.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Comparative Analysis Type | Types of comparative analysis to perform: Cross-covariance measures how two features change together over time, accounting for both their co-movement and scale. Cross-correlation is a normalized version of covariance that focuses on co-movement only, independent of scale. Select one or both. The analysis will compare features within the input file or, if additional input data is provided, between the Input Data and the Additional Input Data . Valid Values: Cross-covariance, Cross-correlation |
| Input Data | Specify the input data as a CSV file for comparative feature analysis. The dataset must be generated by the Measure Trajectory Features protocol or the Detect and Analyze Pockets protocol, specifically the "feature_data" output. All input features are expected to be of the same category/type. Custom CSV files may be used, provided they follow the same structure: a consistent set of feature columns followed by the final three columns named "Time", "Source Index", and "Source File", in that order. |
| Input Data Convert Angular Data | If set to "True", Complex Exponential Representation applies a transformation to represent angular features as exp(iθ). This ensures continuity across angle boundaries (e.g., between -π and π ), making it suitable for features such as dihedral angles. Only accepts angles in radians. If set to "False", the data remains untransformed. Valid Values: True, False |
| Input Data Normalize | If set to "True", each feature is normalized to have zero mean and unit variance prior to computing cross-covariance or cross-correlation. Recommended if Additional Data is provided. If set to "False", the original (unscaled) data is used for analysis. Valid Values: True , False |
| Additional Data | Specify the additional data as a CSV file for comparative feature analysis with the Input Data . This dataset is optional and should be generated by the Measure Trajectory Features protocol or the Detect and Analyze Pockets protocol, specifically the "feature_data" output. All features within the file are expected to be of the same category/type, but can be different than the Input Data . Custom CSV files may be used, provided they follow the same structure: a consistent set of feature columns followed by the final three columns named "Time", "Source Index", and "Source File", in that order. |
| Additional Data Convert Angular Data | If set to "True", Complex Exponential Representation applies a transformation to represent angular features as exp(iθ). This ensures continuity across angle boundaries (e.g., between -π and π ), making it suitable for features such as dihedral angles. Only accepts angles in radians. If set to "False", the data remains untransformed. Valid Values: True, False |
| Additional Data Normalize | If set to "True", each feature is normalized to have zero mean and unit variance prior to computing cross-covariance or cross-correlation. Recommended if Additional Data is provided. If set to "False", the original (unscaled) data is used for analysis. Valid Values: True , False |
| Minimum Time Lag | The analysis will include all time lag values starting from this minimum. Time lag represents the number of frames by which data is shifted when computing cross-covariance or cross-correlation. |
| Maximum Time Lag | Defines the upper limit of time shift applied during the analysis. Time lag values between the minimum and maximum (inclusive) will be evaluated. The Maximum Time Lag can be set to (number of frames - 5) to cover all possible time delay comparisons. This limit ensures the Pearson correlation calculation has a minimum of 5 samples for statistical validity. |
| Time Lag Stride | Controls how many frames the time lag increases by between calculations (e.g., a stride of 1 computes at every step, a stride of 2 skips every other frame). |

bottom-right.

# Assign Forcefield

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_assign_forcefield.htm

## Assign Forcefield

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

In a forcefield-based simulation, each of the atoms in the structure need to be assigned with a proper forcefield type. 
CHARMM uses residue templates to describe the topology of a residue. Each template contains the composition of atoms, 
bonds, angles, etc. The matching between a residue and its template has traditionally been accomplished by name 
matching (i.e., both the names of the residue and each atom in the residue have to match those defined in the template.) 
The assignment will fail if the names do not match. This has proved to be a challenge because there are different 
conventions for naming residues and their atoms.

However, in this protocol, the match between a residue and its template is accomplished via structure matching. 
If a residue and a template are equivalent in chemistry, a match is made and forcefield types are assigned based on one-to-one
atom matching. Another important feature is that it can apply the patches defined in the forcefield to generate patched residues.
If a residue is patched, a Patch property is added to the residue and the simulation protocols will be 
able to use this information to set up the patching commands directly. In addition, it also allows custom topology and parameter 
files to be specified when it is necessary to extend the forcefield.

The completeness of the input structure, especially the terminal residues, affects the correctness of the 
assignment. Before running the protocol, run Clean Protein using the following preferences:

* Turn on Correct problems for Alternate conformations and Incomplete residues . These options allow Clean Protein to remove alternate conformations and patch missing atoms for any amino acid residues.

* Turn on Modify termini and Merge capping group options.

If a terminal residue needs to be capped by a capping fragment, 
use Cap Termini... and turn off Create caps as separate residues option.

Currently, only the following versions of the academic CHARMM force fields are supported:

* charmm22

* charmm27

* charmm36

For charmm36 forcefield, the MATCH typing engine [Yesselman et al., 2012] will be used to generate forcefield templates for unmatched small molecules.

* Load the structure you want to type into the Molecule Window.

* Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools and click Assign Forcefield... to open the Assign Forcefield dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Molecule Choose the molecule to be analyzed. Forcefield Name Choose the desired forcefield. For details about the remaining parameters, see Assign Forcefield - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Molecule | Choose the molecule to be analyzed. |
| Forcefield Name | Choose the desired forcefield. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Assign Forcefield - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If the run is successful, all residues will be matched correctly to a template and assigned proper forcefield types.
Open the output molecule file to find all the forcefield assignment information in its data table. This includes the forcefield name and 
custom forcefield FFML in the molecule tab, forcefield template and patch in the residue tab, and forcefield types and partial charges in the atom tab.
You can then use the typed molecule in subsequent simulation tasks.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with assigning some residues with proper templates, the status of the run will be set as error. The list of such residues
will be shown in the error section of the report. You can open the molecule output file (with partial assignments) to inspect these residues. The ForcefieldType column of the
Residue tab will have a value of "?" in the data table. If it is an incomplete residue, you can add the missing atoms and rerun the assignment.
If the template is missing in the forcefield RTF file, you can make your own RTF file and use it as a custom RTF file when you rerun the protocol.

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule containing assigned forcefield types. If a template is not found for a residue, the ForceFieldTemplate property of the residue and the ForcefieldType properties of its atoms will be shown as "?". |

#### Further information

Change Forcefield tools

# Calculate Energy - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_energy-para.htm

## Calculate Energy - Parameters

### Calculates single point energy and estimates entropy using CHARMm

Optionally, the entropy of the system can be estimated based on rotation, translation, and vibrational components.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane. Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant. Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) : The most rigorous yet slowest solvent approximation method based on continuum electrostatics. Only available for Energy calculations. Notes: To add an implicit membrane to a molecule: In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools. In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM), Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. For GB and GBMV, this parameter is set to 1.0 internally and cannot be changed. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to GBIM or GBSW, the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is recommended to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for bulk solvent used in various implicit solvent models, including Generalized Born, GBMV, GBSW, GBIM, or PBSA. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these forcefields. Applies to GB and GBIM. See Also: Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | The constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol × Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol × Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol × Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol × Å 2 ). See Also: Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481. Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments: Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13. Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. |
| Salt Concentration | Salt concentration (mol/liter) used in GBSW and PBSA. |
| Input Atomic Radii | Specify source of input atomic radii used in various implicit solvent models, including GBSW, GBMV or PBSA. van der Waals radii are the default. For charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields, radii set derived by Nina et al. is recommended. See Also: Nina M.; Beglov D.; Roux B. Atomic Born radii for continuum electrostatic calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations. J. Phys. Chem. B 1997 , 101 , 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. |
| Use Molecular Surface | Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW. Valid Values: True , False |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance . When Implicit Solvent Model is set to "Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA)", an infinite cutoff will be used. |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Electrostatics | Specifies how to treat long range electrostatics. Three options are available: Automatic : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used if the information for periodic boundary condition (i.e. the BoxShape property of the input molecule) is available, otherwise, the Spherical Cutoff method is used. Spherical Cutoff : the spherical cutoff is used for the electrostatic interactions. Particle Mesh Ewald : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used. Note : When Spherical Cutoff option is selected, all non-bonded energy will be calculated without using periodic boundary condition. If the periodic boundary condition is not set up for the input molecule (e.g., the BoxShape property is not defined), the PME option will not work properly. Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald |
| Kappa | The width of the Gaussian function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ) and 6/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ). |
| Order | The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4. |
| Estimate Entropy | Specifies whether to include entropy terms in the energy. Only vacuum or distance-dependent implicit solvent model is supported. Valid Values: True, False |
| Entropy Temperature | Temperature at which to estimate entropy (K). |
| Entropy Mode | Choose how the entropy should be calculated. Available options are: Normal Mode : Uses more memory and only applies to smaller systems. Translational and Rotational Only : Do not calculate vibrational entropy. Uses less memory and can be used to larger systems. Quasiharmonic Mode : Requires a dynamics trajectory for the system. Valid Values: Normal Mode , Quasiharmonic Mode, Translational and Rotational Only |
| Entropy Trajectory File | The CHARMm trajectory (DCD) file used in quasiharmonic mode calculation. |

Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures.

Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation.

Available options are:

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

* Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane.

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant.

* Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA) : The most rigorous yet slowest solvent approximation method based on continuum electrostatics. Only available for Energy calculations.

* To add an implicit membrane to a molecule:

* In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools.

* In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM), Poisson Boltzmann with non-polar Surface Area (PBSA)

Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to GBIM or GBSW, the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is recommended to use a dielectric constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons.

# Calculate Energy

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_energy.htm

## Calculate Energy

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Energy protocol allows you to evaluate the potential energy of a specified structure. You can also use several methods to
estimate the entropy of the system.

The Calculate Energy protocol can be used to confirm that a given system does not exhibit serious distortion from typical equilibrium
molecular geometries or possess substantial atomic overlap. Alternatively, the Calculate Energy protocol can be used to compare the relative stability of
different configurations of the same structure; or as a prelude to lengthy simulations to confirm the availability of appropriate forcefield
parameters.

* Load the structure whose energy you wish to calculate into the Molecule Window.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Calculate Energy... to open the Calculate Energy dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule . For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Energy - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

In the Molecule tab of the Data Table View, several energy
properties are added, including the total energy (CHARMm Energy) and
energies for the various terms of the CHARMm energy equation .
If an entropy calculation was requested the entropy terms will also be
displayed.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule with energy properties added to the molecule. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language (FFML) file used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog

# Calculate Energy (DFT) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_energy_dft-para.htm

## Calculate Energy (DFT) - Parameters

### Performs density functional QM calculation using DMol3

Calculates a variety of molecular and atomic properties using density functional theory (DFT) implemented in DMol 3 .

DMol 3 has long been one of the fastest methods for molecular DFT calculations and can quickly perform structure optimizations of molecular systems using delocalized internal coordinates.

The following molecular and atomic properties can be calculated:

* Total_Energy_DMol3: The total energy of the molecule.

* Binding_Energy_DMol3: The interaction energy between all the atoms in the molecule. Also known as cohesive energy.

* HOMO_Energy_DMol3: The energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO).

* LUMO_Energy_DMol3: The energy of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO).

* Band_Gap_Energy_DMol3: The energy difference between LUMO and HOMO.

* Dipole_Mag_DMol3: The magnitude of the dipole moment.

* Dipole_Components_DMol3: The components of the dipole moment along each of the axes. Three separate properties will be added: Dipole_X_DMol3 , Dipole_Y_DMol3 and Dipole_Z_DMol3 .

* Dielectric_Energy_DMol3: The energy stored in the dielectric in a solvated system. It is always equal to the solvation energy of the molecule.

* Solvation_Energy_DMol3: The solvation energy calculated as the difference of the total energy of the molecule in solvation and the total energy of the molecule in vacuum.

* Surface_Area_DMol3: The solvent accessible surface area of the molecule.

* Cavity_Volume_DMol3: The volume of cavities in the solvation calculation.

* ESP_Charges_DMol3: The atomic charges calculated from the electrostatic potential.

* Mulliken_Charges_DMol3: The atomic charges calculated using the Mulliken method.

* Hirshfeld_Charges_DMol3: The atomic charges calculated using the Hirshfeld method.

In addition, the HOMO/LUMO molecular orbitals, the electron density and electrostatic potential can be visualized in the Discovery Studio Client.

Notes:

* The input ligands are required to have 3D coordinates.

* Geometry optimization calculations take significantly longer than a single point energy calculation.

* The COSMO continuum solvation model is used when a solvent is selected.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| DMol3 Properties | Specifies which properties to calculate by DMol 3 . The following properties are available only when the Solvent parameter in DMol3 Settings is not set to None: Dielectric_Energy_DMol3 Solvation_Energy_DMol3 Surface_Area_DMol3 Cavity_Volume_DMol3 Valid Values: Total_Energy_DMol3 , Binding_Energy_DMol3 , HOMO_Energy_DMol3 , LUMO_Energy_DMol3 , Band_Gap_Energy_DMol3, Dipole_Mag_DMol3 , Dipole_Components_DMol3, ESP_Charges_DMol3 , Mulliken_Charges_DMol3, Hirshfeld_Charges_DMol3 |
| DMol3 Settings | The DMol3 Settings group allows you to select the type of calculation to be performed, and specify calculation-specific settings. In addition to the user-defined input parameters, the following DMol 3 keywords are specified: Opt_iterations: 50 Opt_max_displacement: 0.3000 (Å) Pseudopotential: none Aux_density: octupole Occupation: thermal 0.0050 Scf_charge_mixing: 0.2000 Scf_iterations: 50 Scf_diis: 6 pulay Kpoints: on |
| Task | Specifies the type of calculation to be performed: Energy: Performs a single-point energy calculation. Geometry Optimization: Searches for a minimum energy structure. Valid Values: Energy , Geometry Optimization |
| Functional | The exchange-correlation functional to be used in the quantum calculation. Local Density Approximation (LDA) functionals: PWC VWN Gradient corrected Generalized Gradient Approximations (GGA) functionals: PW91 BP PBE BLYP BOP VWN-BP RPBE HCTH Hybrid functional: B3LYP Notes : GGA provides a better overall description of the electronic subsystem than the LDA functionals. The LDA description tends to overbind atoms, so that the bond lengths and the cell volume are usually underestimated by a few percent and the bulk modulus is correspondingly overestimated. GGA corrects this error but may underbind instead, leading to slightly long bond lengths. B3LYP includes a portion of exact exchange from Hartree-Fock theory along with exchange and correlation contributions from other functionals with carefully chosen weights. The weights are obtained by fitting to experimental data. B3LYP gives better results but requires significantly more CPU time. Valid Values: PWC , VWN, PW91, BP, PBE, BLYP, BOP, RPBE, HCTH, VWN-BP, B3LYP |
| Add Dispersion Correction | Specify whether to add a dispersion correction to the DFT energy. This option is available when Functional is: "PBE", "PW91" "VWN", "PWC". Notes : The TS scheme is used when the Functional is "PBE". The OBS scheme is used when the Functional is "PWC", "VWN", "PW91". Valid Values: True, False |
| Quality | Specifies the overall quality for the DMol 3 calculation. This quality affects the basis set, k-point, and SCF convergence criteria. Available options are Coarse, Medium and Fine. These three levels offer progressively more accuracy at the expense of longer calculation times: Coarse : Uses DN basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-4. Medium : Uses DND basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-5. Fine : Uses DNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-6. Valid Values: Coarse , Medium, Fine |
| Multiplicity | Specifies the spin state to use in the calculation. Available options are: Auto: Determines the ground spin state using a spin-unrestricted calculation. Singlet: Determines the ground spin state using a spin-unrestricted calculation. Doublet: Set the ground spin state to doublet. Triplet: Set the ground spin state to triplet. Quartet: Set the ground spin state to quartet. Quintet: Set the ground spin state to quintet. Sextet: Set the ground spin state to sextet. Septet: Set the ground spin state to septet. Octet: Set the ground spin state to octet. Spin restricted: Set the ground spin state to spin restricted. Valid Values: Auto , Singlet , Doublet , Triplet , Quartet , Quintet , Sextet , Septet , Octet , Spin restricted |
| Solvent | DMol3 allows you to simulate a solvent environment using the COSMO continuum solvation model. Valid Values: Acetone, Acetonitrile, Benzene, Carbon tetrachloride, Chloroform, Diethyl ether, Dimethyl sulfoxide, Ethanol, Methanol, Methylene chloride, n-Hexane, n-Hexadecane, Nitrobenzene, Pyridine, Water, None |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Visualization | What to visualize in the Discovery Studio Client. Molecular Orbitals: Visualize the HOMO and LUMO molecular orbitals. Potential: Visualize the potential on the electron density isosurface. Valid Values: Molecular Orbitals , Potential |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

* Solvation_Energy_DMol3

Specifies the type of calculation to be performed:

* Geometry Optimization: Searches for a minimum energy structure.

Valid Values: Energy , Geometry Optimization

The exchange-correlation functional to be used in the quantum calculation.

* PWC

* PW91

* BP

Notes :

* GGA provides a better overall description of the electronic subsystem than the LDA functionals. The LDA description tends to overbind atoms, so that the bond lengths and the cell volume are usually underestimated by a few percent and the bulk modulus is correspondingly overestimated. GGA corrects this error but may underbind instead, leading to slightly long bond lengths.

* B3LYP includes a portion of exact exchange from Hartree-Fock theory along with exchange and correlation contributions from other functionals with carefully chosen weights. The weights are obtained by fitting to experimental data.

* B3LYP gives better results but requires significantly more CPU time.

Valid Values: PWC , VWN, PW91, BP, PBE, BLYP, BOP, RPBE, HCTH, VWN-BP, B3LYP

Specify whether to add a dispersion correction to the DFT energy. This option is available when Functional is: "PBE", "PW91" "VWN", "PWC".

* The TS scheme is used when the Functional is "PBE".

* The OBS scheme is used when the Functional is "PWC", "VWN", "PW91".

Valid Values: True, False

Specifies the overall quality for the DMol 3 calculation. This quality affects the basis set, k-point, and SCF convergence criteria. Available options are Coarse, Medium and Fine. These three levels offer progressively more accuracy at the expense of longer calculation times:

* Coarse : Uses DN basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-4.

* Medium : Uses DND basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-5.

* Fine : Uses DNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-6.

Valid Values: Coarse , Medium, Fine

Specifies the spin state to use in the calculation. Available options are:

* Auto: Determines the ground spin state using a spin-unrestricted calculation.

* Singlet: Determines the ground spin state using a spin-unrestricted calculation.

* Doublet: Set the ground spin state to doublet.

* Quartet: Set the ground spin state to quartet.

* Quintet: Set the ground spin state to quintet.

* Sextet: Set the ground spin state to sextet.

* Septet: Set the ground spin state to septet.

* Octet: Set the ground spin state to octet.

* Spin restricted: Set the ground spin state to spin restricted.

Valid Values: Auto , Singlet , Doublet , Triplet , Quartet , Quintet , Sextet , Septet , Octet , Spin restricted

DMol3 allows you to simulate a solvent environment using the COSMO continuum solvation model.

Valid Values: Acetone, Acetonitrile, Benzene, Carbon tetrachloride, Chloroform, Diethyl ether, Dimethyl sulfoxide, Ethanol, Methanol, Methylene chloride, n-Hexane, n-Hexadecane, Nitrobenzene, Pyridine, Water, None

What to visualize in the Discovery Studio Client.

# Calculate Energy (DFT)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_energy_dft.htm

## Calculate Energy (DFT)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Energy (DFT) protocol allows you to calculate the energy or optimize the geometry of a set of small molecules using the density functional quantum mechanics method in DMol 3 . Properties such as the total energy, HOMO energy, LUMO energy, dipole, atomic charges, etc. can be returned.

* Load the structure(s) into the Molecule Window. 3D coordinates are required.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Calculate Energy (DFT)... to 
open the Calculate Energy (DFT) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Ligands . For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Energy (DFT) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

A new Molecule Window will be opened when the job is finished. The calculated molecular properties can be found in the Molecule tab of the Data Table View. If there are atomic properties such as 
fitted atomic charges, they can be found in the Atom tab of the Data Table View. The isosurface of the electron density colored by the electrostatic potential
is added for up to the first 100 molecules. By default, the isovalue of the electron density is 0.03, and the coloring scheme is spectrumRainbow1 with a range from -0.05 to 0.1. 
The HOMO and LUMO can be visualized using scripts accessible from the report. The positive phase of the molecular orbitals uses an isovalue of 0.01 and is colored blue, 
while the negative phase uses an isovalue of -0.01 and is colored red.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <Input Ligands>.mol2 | The output ligands with calculated properties added. |
| ViewHOMO.ds_pl | Script to visualize the HOMO molecular orbitals. |
| ViewLUMO.ds_pl | Script to visualize the LUMO molecular orbitals. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Script to open or update the ligands in the Molecule Window and visualize the electrostatic potential mapped on the isosurface of the electron density. |

#### Further information

Quantum mechanical theory related to descriptors

## Calculate Energy (QM-MM) - Parameters

### Calculates single point energy using QUANTUMm

Uses a hybrid of quantum and classical molecular mechanics (QM-MM). In this approach, some atoms are treated by classical molecular mechanics (CHARMm) and some are treated by quantum mechanics (DMol3).

In addition to the total energy, the QM, MM, and interaction energies are also reported.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with the CHARMm forcefield.

| Quantum Atoms | Allows selection of atoms to be used as the quantum region. In Discovery Studio, a group of atoms can be selected. In Pipeline Pilot, standard CHARMm selection syntax can be used. Note : The speed of the calculation depends on this parameter. There is a limit of 1000 atoms but a job of this size may take a long time to finish. |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. |
| DMol3 Settings | Specify settings for the quantum calculation. |

Coarse: Uses DN basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-4. Medium: Uses DND basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-5. Fine: Uses DNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-6. Ultra fine: Uses TNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-7. Valid Values: Ultra coarse, Coarse, Medium , Fine, Ultra fine |

# Calculate Energy (QM-MM)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_energy_qm-mm.htm

## Calculate Energy (QM-MM)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Energy (QM-MM) protocol allows you to evaluate the QM-MM potential energy of a specified structure. A chosen region of atoms is
treated quantum mechanically and the remainder of the system is handled
with molecular mechanics.

This protocol can be used to compare the relative stability of different configurations of the same structure.
The Calculate Energy (QM-MM) protocol also gives an estimate of the non-covalent QM-MM interaction energy and updates the partial charges in the quantum region with the ESP charges from the quantum calculation.

Note: The QM-MM simulation protocols require the following:

* The complete system is contained in one molecule. To merge several molecules into a single Molecule Window, use the Hierarchy View .

* The complete system (i.e., QM and MM atoms) is typed with the CHARMm forcefield. To type the system, use the Apply Forcefield command from the Change Forcefield tools.

* Open a structure in the Graphics View.

* Make sure that the simulation system consists of one molecule. To do this, open the Hierarchy View and
drag all required molecules under a single
molecule in the hierarchy. You can only select a single molecule
to run this calculation. However, the molecule can contain
multiple disconnected fragments.

* Apply a forcefield to the molecule using the Apply Forcefield tool in the Change Forcefield tools. The atoms that will be treated quantum mechanically must be included in the force field typing. Please note that only CHARMm force field is supported in the current release of QM-MM protocols.

* Select the atoms that you wish to use as the QM region and create a group by choosing Edit | Group... from the menu bar. The QM region must span whole charge groups. Otherwise, the calculation will stop at an
early stage with the following error in the report: "QM region specified is not valid". Refer to Cutting covalent QM-MM bonds for help on providing a compliant QM region.

The QM region must span whole charge groups. Otherwise, the calculation will stop at an
early stage with the following error in the report: "QM region specified is not valid". Refer to Cutting covalent QM-MM bonds for help on providing a compliant QM region.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Calculate Energy (QM-MM)... to open the Calculate Energy (QM-MM) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule The molecule to be used in the calculation. Quantum Atoms Choose the group of atoms you created. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Energy (QM-MM) - Parameters . For more information, refer to the guidelines in Setting up QM-MM calculations and DMol 3 settings in the QM-MM protocols .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | The molecule to be used in the calculation. |
| Quantum Atoms | Choose the group of atoms you created. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Energy (QM-MM) - Parameters . For more information, refer to the guidelines in Setting up QM-MM calculations and DMol 3 settings in the QM-MM protocols .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Report.htm contains a summary of key energy terms, including:

* QUANTUMm Energy : The total QM-MM potential energy (i.e. the sum of the QM Energy and the MM Energy below).

* QM Energy : The potential energy of the QM subsystem (i.e., the expectation value of the QM hamiltonian, including the
classical Coulomb repulsion energy between the atomic nuclei in the QM system). It contains the energetic effects from the QM
atoms' Coulomb interaction with the MM point charges, and also contributions from the terminating link atoms (if bonds had to be broken
between the QM and MM fragment).

* MM energy : The potential energy of the MM subsystem. It contains the van der Waals interaction energy between the QM and MM atoms and bonding
energy contributions from the QM-MM border in case bonds stretch from the MM into the QM region.

* QM-MM Electrostatic Interaction Energy : The Coulomb interaction energy between the electron density of the QM atoms 
and the point charges of the MM atoms. This energy is an approximation to the full QM-MM electrostatic interaction energy because 
the energy to polarize the QM density from its vacuum state is not included.

* QM/MM van der Waals Interaction Energy : This is calculated by the CHARMm simulation engine by applying the van der Waals interaction
forcefield parameters defined for the complete system.

* QM-MM Interaction Energy : The sum of QM-MM Electrostatic Interaction Energy and QM-MM van der Waals Interaction Energy .

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The molecule with the partial charges of the atoms in the quantum region updated from the ESP charges of the QM calculation. |
| dmol3.log | Contains a report of the DMol 3 phase of the job. This report lists the atomic coordinates of the input QM region (possibly containing terminating hydrogen atoms), the settings used, and the results obtained. |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine for the MM and QM/MM cross-border regions. |
| quantumm.log | Contains a report of the QM-MM calculation progress. |

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Overview of QM-MM Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_free_energy_from_steering_forces-para.htm

## Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces - Parameters

### Calculates Free Energy using Jarzynski Equality

Calculates the free energy profile from a series of steering force profiles obtained from Steered Molecular Dynamics protocol using Jarzynski equality. Each individual force profile is integrated to give the work distribution and then the Jarzynski Equality is applied to compute the free energy. Block average and two extrapolation methods (linear extrapolation and cumulative integral extrapolation) are also employed to improve the accuracy.

See Also:

* F. M. Ytreberg and D. M. Zuckerman, J. Comput. Chem. 2004 , 25, 1749-1759.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Steering Force Profile Files | The files containing the distance and steering force data in CSV file format. In Discovery Studio, choose a list of folders containing these CSV files. |
| Random Number Seed | The seed for the random number generator when block average is computed. A system generated seed will be used if it is left blank. |

The files containing the distance and steering force data in CSV file format.
In Discovery Studio, choose a list of folders containing these CSV files.

The seed for the random number generator when block average is computed. A system generated seed will be used if it is left blank.

# Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_free_energy_from_steering_forces.htm

## Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces protocol allows you to analyze a collection of Steered Molecular Dynamics (SMD) runs and calculate the free energy as a function of the reaction coordinate or pulling distance. The free energy profile is calculated by applying three different methods, which involve variations of applying the Jarzynski's equality. The first method calculates F jarz , which is obtained by a straightforward application of the equality. In addition, two other improved estimates F lin and F ci are reported, which involve extrapolation of block averaged results, as described below.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulation tools and click Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces . You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Steering Force Profile Files Choose the parent job folder that contains .csv format files having the distance and steering force data from previous Steered Molecular Dynamics runs. See Steering Force Profile Files dialog . Random Number Seed Choose a seed for the random number generator when block average is calculated. A system generated seed will be used if it is left blank. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Steering Force Profile Files | Choose the parent job folder that contains .csv format files having the distance and steering force data from previous Steered Molecular Dynamics runs. See Steering Force Profile Files dialog . |
| Random Number Seed | Choose a seed for the random number generator when block average is calculated. A system generated seed will be used if it is left blank. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The first plot in the Summary tab shows the individual force-profiles for each run in a different color, which is plotted as the Work (kcal/mol) as a function of distance (Å). The protocol considers the first distance as zero. Therefore it is important that all runs start from the same distance between the two atoms involved in pulling.

The second plot shows the calculated free energy as a function of pulling distance computed using three methods. F jarz is obtained through a straightforward application of the Jarzynski equality. For each value of the reaction coordinate F jarz is computed as an average over N trajectories, and is given by:

F lin and F ci result from two different ways of better estimating the free energy by applying extrapolation methods. Common to both methods, the Jarzynski equality is applied to compute the F jarz values for randomly chosen subsets or samples of the data. Further, an F jarz trend is obtained as a function of the sample size. F lin is obtained by the linear extrapolation of the tail of this average F jarz trend in the limit of infinite sample size. F ci uses the same sample data generated above, but adopts a cumulative integral extrapolation, where not just the tail of the curve, but the entire F jarz curve is used for estimation. For details, please see [Ytreberg and Zuckerman, 2004]

The second plot can be used to calculate free energy difference between two states. If the SMD simulation involved a ligand unbinding from a protein, a difference can be computed between the F-value of the distance that corresponds to the bound and unbound states. It is important to verify that the F-values of the states of interest are stable and converged.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| PMF.csv | The output free energy profile. The three profiles F jarz , F lin , and F ci are reported as a function of the pulling distance. This file can be used to calculate Free energy between two chosen states provided the values of the chosen states are stable and plateaued. |

# Calculate Interaction Energy - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_interaction_energy-para.htm

## Calculate Interaction Energy - Parameters

### Calculates the interaction energy between sets of atoms across all conformations using CHARMm

Uses CHARMm. The interaction energy is defined as the sum of the van der Waals and electrostatic energy.

The interaction energy is broken down per-residue if Residue Selection 2 is specified.

The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |

See Also: CHARMm select syntax: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/select/ |

Interaction energy between the first group of atoms and each residue in this selection will be calculated. In Discovery Studio, a residue group can be defined in advance or created on the fly. In Pipeline Pilot, uses CHARMm selection syntax " sele ires index1 : index2 " to select residues based on their indexes. For example, specify "sele ires 1:10 end" to select the first 10 residues. Note that no more than 200 residues can be selected. See Also: CHARMm select syntax: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/select/ |

| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to use when Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent Dielectrics. |

| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |

# Calculate Interaction Energy

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_calculate_interaction_energy.htm

## Calculate Interaction Energy

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output and input files

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Interaction Energy protocol allows you to calculate
the nonbonded interactions (i.e., the van der Waals term and the electrostatic term)
between two sets of atoms in a specified structure or
trajectory.

* Load the molecular structure you wish to analyze into a
Molecule Window. For meaningful
results, use the output molecule from a dynamics simulation or an energy minimized structure. The
interaction energy is calculated for each conformation of the molecule if conformations are present.

* Apply a forcefield to the molecule using the Apply Forcefield tool in the Change Forcefield tools.

* Create two groups of atoms. The interaction energy between one group and the other will be calculated. For each group, select the atoms or residues, then choose Edit | Group... from the menu bar.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Simulation | Calculate Interaction Energy .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule Choose the molecule to use in the calculation. Atom Selection 1 Choose the first group of atoms you created. Atom Selection 2 or Residue Selection 2 The interaction energy will be calculated between the atoms in Atom Selection 1, and the atoms in Atom Selection 2, or each residue in Residue Selection 2, depending on which parameter is set. You will get a "Group is ambiguous" error if two or more groups have the same name. Resolve this by renaming the groups so that they are unique. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Interaction Energy - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Choose the molecule to use in the calculation. |
| Atom Selection 1 | Choose the first group of atoms you created. |
| Atom Selection 2 or Residue Selection 2 | The interaction energy will be calculated between the atoms in Atom Selection 1, and the atoms in Atom Selection 2, or each residue in Residue Selection 2, depending on which parameter is set. |

You will get a "Group is ambiguous" error if two or more groups have the same name. Resolve this by renaming the groups so that they are unique.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Interaction Energy - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

When the job finishes, the computed
energy value is displayed in the Details column of the Jobs Explorer. In the case of a trajectory, the interaction
energy of the last frame is reported. See Output and input files for details about the files generated by this protocol. If the job did not run successfully, the Jobs Explorer will report an error. See Troubleshooting - Protocols for details.

By default, intermediate files generated by this protocol are not saved. To save the intermediate files, select the Save intermediate files when running protocols option on the Protocols page of the Preferences dialog.

#### Output files

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule. If the input molecule contains multiple conformations (i.e., a trajectory) then each conformation is updated with a value for the total interaction energy, along with the van der Waals and electrostatic components of the interaction energy. If the molecule has only one conformation, these energy values are added as properties of the molecule. The trajectory can be sampled and analyzed using the Analyze Trajectory tool panel . |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

#### Input files

The following files are created in the Input directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <molecule>.dsv | The input molecule that was selected from the application for the Calculate Interaction Energy protocol. |
| Protocol.pr_xml | The saved protocol and job parameters. You can load this file at any time to re-run this protocol with the same settings. You can also share it with other users. For details see Discovery Studio Parameters (PR_XML) . |

The interaction energy and its components (Van der Waals and
electrostatics) between the two specified groups is available in the Report.htm file as well as in the Molecule tab of the Data
Table View for the resulting Molecule.dsv file.

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Analyze Trajectory tool panel
