# Cluster Conformations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_cluster_conformations-para.htm

## Cluster Conformations - Parameters

### Cluster conformations from simulation trajectories into discretized states

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Data | Cluster conformations according to features of this specified dataset in CSV format. This dataset must have been generated by the Measure Trajectory Features protocol. If desired, additional features may be manually added to the columns of the Measure Trajectory Features dataset for every corresponding trajectory frame so long as there is no conflict in column names. |
| Features | If provided, specifies the features to cluster. Multiple features should be separated by a comma; therefore, feature names should not contain any commas. All features (other than the reserved features specified below) will be processed by removing invariant features and feature normalization. If more than two features are specified and the Minimum Explained Variance Ratio is greater than zero, then principal component analysis will also be performed to reduce the dimensionality of the input dataset. The following feature names (non-case-sensitive) are reserved for internal use: index source source index time time (ps) step boost potential average boost potential total energy bond energy angle energy torsion energy improper torsion energy electrostatic energy van der waals energy boundary energy misc energy kinetic energy temperature potential energy average temperature pressure group pressure volume |
| Distance Metric | Specifies the distance metric to use for input data. An angular distance metric should be used for angular data such as dihedral angles (unless these angles have already been projected into Euclidean space). Valid Values: Euclidean , Angular |
| Simulation Data | Cluster simulation conformations according to features measured from a set of molecular dynamics trajectories. |
| Feature Type | Specifies what type of feature to measure from the Input Trajectory . RMSD : measures root-mean-square deviation of all Input Atoms from Reference Atoms . If no Reference Molecule is specified, then the first frame of the Input Trajectory serves as the Reference Molecule . SASA : measures the solvent accessible surface area of each residue from the Input Trajectory . Dihedral : measures dihedrals (phi, psi, chi1, chi2, chi3, chi4) for each residue of the Input Trajectory . Distance : measures distances between contacts according to Distance Type and Distance Cutoff . If no Input Data is provided and the Feature Type is left blank, then atomic coordinates for each frame of the simulation trajectories will be used as the input dataset. Valid Values: RMSD, SASA, Dihedral, Distance, |
| Distance Type | Distance Type specifies how to calculate distances between residues. Options include: All Contacts : measures distances for intermolecular and intramolecular contacts. Intermolecular Contacts : measures distances for all residue contacts between separate molecules. Intramolecular Contacts : measures distances between residues on the same molecule that are separated by 6 or more other residues. Valid Values: All Contacts , Intermolecular Contacts, Intramolecular Contacts |
| Distance Cutoff | Distance Cutoff specifies the minimum distance threshold between nearest atoms in two different residues for a contact to be observed. |
| Input Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to each trajectory file in Input Trajectory . This file is used as the topology for reading DCD files; thus, each DCD file should share a common topology. |
| Input Trajectory | One or more simulations in DCD format. These trajectories will be measured according to the method specified by Feature Type . |
| Input Atoms | In Discovery Studio, Input Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. In Pipeline Pilot, Input Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Input Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be measured. No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning onto a reference conformation. |
| Input Bias Potentials | Input Bias Potentials is an optional parameter that provides an energy table in CSV format. This table must contain values of the biasing potentials in column named "Boost Potentials", and there should be as many rows as there are frames in the corresponding trajectory. Certain simulations such as Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (GaMD) apply biasing potentials that flatten the free energy landscape and accelerate conformational sampling. Thus, when analyzing distributions of features from biased simulations, it is useful to know the exact biasing potential for each frame. For this reason GaMD simulations will return a CSV file ("*_energy.csv") containing the values of the boost potentials. For each DCD file that you specify in Input Trajectory , you may specify the corresponding CSV file containing boost potentials. When specifying more than one CSV, files should be separated by a comma. Note also that the order in which the CSV files are specified is important, as the first CSV file will correspond to the first DCD file, the second CSV file will correspond to the second DCD file, and so on. |
| Reference Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to a reference molecule. The Input Trajectory will be compared to this reference molecule for calculating certain features (i.e. RMSD) or for superposing atomic coordinates from the Input Trajectory onto the atomic coordinates of the Reference Molecule . If a Reference Molecule is required for measuring a feature type and if the molecule is not specified, then the first frame of the first Input Trajectory will be used as the reference. |
| Reference Atoms | In Discovery Studio, Reference Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. In Pipeline Pilot, Reference Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Reference Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be yielded while iterating through the Input Trajectory for measuring certain features. No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning the Input Trajectory onto a Reference Molecule . Note that if Reference Atoms does not contain the same amount of atoms as Input Atoms , then featurization methods will attempt to match reference and input atoms using a basic, local alignment if required. |
| Superpose Frames on Reference | If set to "True", Superpose Frames on Reference specifies to superpose atoms from the Input Trajectory onto the Reference Molecule . If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are not specified or the number of atoms in the mobile and fixed set are not equal, then the superpositioning method performs a basic, local alignment to match residues of Input Trajectory to the Reference Molecule . Matched residues are then superposed. If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are specified and contain the same number of atoms, then Mobile Atoms from the Input Trajectory will be superposed onto Fixed Atoms from the Reference Molecule . Valid Values: True , False |
| Mobile Atoms | Specifies the mobile set of atoms from the Input Molecule that will be superposed onto the set of Fixed Atoms . |
| Fixed Atoms | Specifies the fixed set of atoms from the Reference Molecule that the Mobile Atoms from the Input Molecule will be superposed onto. |
| Trajectory Iteration | Specifies the parameters that control iteration through the Input Trajectory and intermediate datasets. |
| Batch | Specifies how many frames from the Input Trajectory to load during each iteration. Smaller values of Batch will use less memory but require more time to complete. Larger values of Batch will use more memory but require less time to complete. |
| Stride | Specifies how to sample frames from an Input Trajectory . A Stride of "1" means to take every frame, and a Stride of "n" means to take every nth frame after the first frame. |
| Skip | Specifies how many frames to skip from the beginning of each Input Trajectory . |
| Clustering | Specifies a group of parameters that control K-means clustering. |
| Number of Clusters | Number of Clusters controls the discretization of simulation frames into N number of states. |
| Number of Epochs | Number of Epochs controls the maximum number of times that the K-means clustering algorithm iterates through the full dataset. |
| Maximum Iterations without Improvement | Maximum Iterations without Improvement specifies the maximum number of times that the K-means clustering algorithm may iterate through the entire dataset when there is no improvement in inertia (a clustering metric). |
| Cluster Center Tolerance | Cluster Center Tolerance specifies the minimum L2-normalized change in cluster center position required for clustering to be considered converged. Once this criterion is met, clustering will terminate early due to convergence. |
| Minimum Explained Variance Ratio | Clustering will perform dimensionality reduction on input datasets when more than two features exist in the input dataset. After performing principal component analysis (PCA), the number of principal components (PC) used for clustering will be selected according to the fraction of variance accounted for by each PC. PCs are numbered incrementally starting from 1, and lower PC numbers will explain more variance than higher PCs numbers. The Minimum Explained Variance Ratio determines the number of components used for clustering by summing the explained variance ratio from each PC (starting from PC1) until the value specified by the Minimum Explained Variance Ratio is achieved. Alternatively, if the Minimum Explained Variance Ratio is set to zero, no dimensionality reduction will be performed, and clustering will be attempted for all input features directly. |
| Save All Conformations | When Save All Conformations is True, a trajectory file in DCD format will be output for each clustered state containing all conformations from the input trajectories belonging to the corresponding state. Valid Values: True, False |

Cluster conformations according to features of this specified dataset in CSV format. This dataset must have been generated by the Measure Trajectory Features protocol. If desired, additional features may be manually added to the columns of the Measure Trajectory Features dataset for every corresponding trajectory frame so long as there is no conflict in column names.

If provided, specifies the features to cluster. Multiple features should be separated by a comma; therefore, feature names should not contain any commas. All features (other than the reserved features specified below) will be processed by removing invariant features and feature normalization. If more than two features are specified and the Minimum Explained Variance Ratio is greater than zero, then principal component analysis will also be performed to reduce the dimensionality of the input dataset.

# Cluster Conformations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_cluster_conformations.htm

## Cluster Conformations

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

* Analyzing results

Cluster Conformations removes solvent atoms and discretizes molecular dynamics trajectories into a user-defined number of conformational states. Discretization may be based on features including root-mean-square distance from a reference conformation (RMSD), solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), dihedral angles (Dihedral), intermolecular or intramolecule residue contacts, or Cartesian coordinates of molecule atoms.

* Load the molecule whose trajectory you want to analyze into the Molecule Window. Ensure that the molecule opened in the Molecule Window corresponds to the set of trajectories that will be analyzed. All simulation trajectories must derive from a shared structure from which the structure and forcefield have not been edited. If you are unsure if several simulations share a common forcefield and topology, then analyze trajectories one at a time with the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

If you are unsure if several simulations share a common forcefield and topology, then analyze trajectories one at a time with the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

* Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Cluster Conformations... to open the Cluster Conformations dialog.

* Set parameters for the simulation: Select the Feature Type to measure. If blank, Cartesian coordinates of non-solvent atoms are used as input features. In general, contact-based features (intermolecular or intramolecular residue distance) are a good starting point for clustering. Set the Input Molecule and Input Trajectory . If you want to measure features from an Input Molecule when the Input Molecule and Reference Molecule are in separate Molecule Windows, make sure that the Measure Trajectory Features protocol is docked into the Discovery Studio window by minimizing the protocol window. Features are restricted to atoms specified in Input Atoms and Reference Atoms . Define these atoms by creating groups in the Molecule Window. When measuring features that depend on a frame of reference, you can use the Superpose Frames on Reference parameters to control superpositioning of frames. If no Reference Molecule is specified, the frame of reference defaults to the first frame of the first Input Trajectory . You can use Mobile Atoms to specify exact atoms to superpose from the Input Molecule , or Fixed Atoms to specify the exact atoms to superpose onto from the Reference Molecule . In the case that either the mobile and fixed atoms are not specified, or the number of mobile and fixed atoms are unequal, superpositioning is attempted by aligning the amino acid sequence of the Input Molecule to the Reference Molecule based on the atoms specified by Input Atoms and Reference Atoms . For details about the parameters, see Cluster Conformations - Parameters .

* Select the Feature Type to measure. If blank, Cartesian coordinates of non-solvent atoms are used as input features. In general, contact-based features (intermolecular or intramolecular residue distance) are a good starting point for clustering.

* Set the Input Molecule and Input Trajectory . If you want to measure features from an Input Molecule when the Input Molecule and Reference Molecule are in separate Molecule Windows, make sure that the Measure Trajectory Features protocol is docked into the Discovery Studio window by minimizing the protocol window.

If you want to measure features from an Input Molecule when the Input Molecule and Reference Molecule are in separate Molecule Windows, make sure that the Measure Trajectory Features protocol is docked into the Discovery Studio window by minimizing the protocol window.

* Features are restricted to atoms specified in Input Atoms and Reference Atoms . Define these atoms by creating groups in the Molecule Window.

* When measuring features that depend on a frame of reference, you can use the Superpose Frames on Reference parameters to control superpositioning of frames. If no Reference Molecule is specified, the frame of reference defaults to the first frame of the first Input Trajectory .

* You can use Mobile Atoms to specify exact atoms to superpose from the Input Molecule , or Fixed Atoms to specify the exact atoms to superpose onto from the Reference Molecule . In the case that either the mobile and fixed atoms are not specified, or the number of mobile and fixed atoms are unequal, superpositioning is attempted by aligning the amino acid sequence of the Input Molecule to the Reference Molecule based on the atoms specified by Input Atoms and Reference Atoms .

For details about the parameters, see Cluster Conformations - Parameters .

* Click Run . The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | Output molecule containing all atoms from the input trajectories and representative conformational states. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | Output molecule containing non-solvent atoms from the input trajectories and representative conformational states |
| <molecule>.dcd | Coordinates for each representative conformational state stored into a simulation trajectory. Trajectory frame corresponds to simulation state. If multiple trajectory files are provided with filenames of the form <molecule>_<integer>.dcd , each file contains all frames assigned to the conformational state indicated by <integer> . |
| clustered_data.csv | The output dataset clustered from the input trajectories. |
| pca_factors.csv | Loading factors that describe contributions of each feature to each principal component. Only generated when the dataset is subject to principal component analysis. |
| pca_projections.csv | Projections of input features from each trajectory frame onto principal components. Only generated when the dataset is subject to principal component analysis. |
| scatter.png | If more than two features or principal components (PCs) are used for clustering, this image contains a pairplot showing distributions of each feature or PC along the diagonal subplots, and scatterplots of clustered observations along off-diagonal subplots (using pairs of features/PCs). |

When the protocol is complete, the report displays a summary table displaying the number of conformations in each state, the mean value of each feature for each state, and the standard deviation of each feature for each state. This information can be useful to describe differences in features between different conformational states. The report also include a time-series plot for each input trajectory displaying the conformational state in each frame of the trajectory.

Additionally, an output molecule (with or without solvent) contains representative conformations for each conformational state for visualizing and comparing structures from different states.

#### Troubleshooting

All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it is automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools. If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not complete. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Measure Trajectory Features

# Collate FEP Simulation Results - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_collate_fep_simulation_results-para.htm

## Collate FEP Simulation Results - Parameters

### Collects and analyzes results from FEP calculations

Collects the results from multiple relative FEP calculations performed using the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol and calculates the absolute free energies for the ligands in a congeneric set, given the experimental absolute free energy value of one ligand in the set.

The protocol requires the specification of two directories, one for the FEP simulation data pertaining to the simulation involving the ligands in solution, and the other for the protein-ligand complexes in solution. Each of these directories should contain sub-folders, each of which should contain a simulationinfo.xml file and a free energy data file(fepdata.fepout). The simulationinfo.xml file specifies the names of ligands involved in each perturbation and whether the simulation involves the free ligand or the complex. The .fepout file is produced during the NAMD FEP production and contains the raw free energy data. These files are automatically created by the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol.

If a Reference Ligand Name is specified, in addition to reporting the relative binding free energy for each pair, the protocol will calculate the absolute free energy for all the ligands by traversing the connected graph created by linking the relative free energy calculations. For this step, the absolute experimental binding free energy of the reference ligand is required. If this value is unknown, it could be set to zero; in that scenario the computed free energies will be relative to that of the reference ligand and not true absolute values.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| FEP Data Directory Ligand | Parent directory that contains subdirectories with the results of the pairwise relative FEP simulations with the free ligand. |
| FEP Data Directory Complex | Parent directory that contains subdirectories with the results of the pairwise relative FEP simulations with the protein-ligand complex. |
| Extreme Value Threshold | Relative free energy threshold in kcal/mol used to flag potentially unreliable relative free energy, and resulting absolute free energy values. Based on empirical observations, the magnitude of relative free energy values within a congeneric series is rarely larger than 4 kcal/mol. Accordingly, values larger than the threshold are likely to be a result of inaccuracy in the simulation, possibly due to non-convergence. This threshold is used to mark the predictions as likely unreliable. |
| Absolute Free Energy | Information required to calculate absolute free energies. |
| Lead Ligand Name | Name of the ligand which should be used as reference to calculate the absolute binding free energy of the entire set of congeneric ligands. |
| Lead Ligand Free Energy | Experimental absolute binding free energy of the lead ligand in kcal/mol. Note: This value can be set to 0 if the actual value is unknown. The binding free energies calculated for the remaining ligands are relative to this ligand and hence are not absolute values. |
| Input Ligands | Specify one Mol2 or DSV file that contains the ligands to be used for computing free energy values. This should be the same file that was used as input to the Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP protocol. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Input Relative FEP Values File | A .csv file containing relative free energy values. This file can be supplied if you want to manually collate the relative free energy values from a set of FEP calculations and supply it to this protocol for computing absolute free energies of the input ligand set. If this file is specified, then FEP Data Files Directory parameter is disabled and the relative free energy values are obtained exclusively from this file. Each record in the file must contain the following three properties: Lig1Name , Lig2Name , and calc_ddg . Example of a .csv file Lig1Name,Lig2Name,calc_ddg 2j,2i,-1.11645 2l,2m,-1.836 2n,2l,1.37985 .... |
| Temperature | Temperature (K) at which to compute the free energy. Should be the same as set in the simulation. |

# Collate FEP Simulation Results

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_collate_fep_simulation_results.htm

## Collate FEP Simulation Results

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Collate FEP Simulation Results protocol allows you calculate the relative binding free energy of a pair of ligands from
the two corresponding solvated ligand pair and solvated protein-ligand complex FEP simulations, e.g. the relative Free Energy Pertubation (FEP) calculations. It can also integrate a set of relative FEP calculations 
spanning a congeneric ligand dataset. It represents the sixth in a 
series of protocols comprising the FEP workflow:

* Generate Analog Conformations

* Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) , or alternatively, use Change Forcefield tools to type ligands with CHARMm forcefield.

* Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP

* Set Up Relative FEP Calculations

* Free Energy Perturbation (FEP)

In this protocol, results from two sets of FEP calculations are 
required which comprise the solvated free ligand pair and the solvated ligand pair in complex with 
the protein. Each of these sets contain one or more FEP 
calculations that are initially planned using the FEP workflow indicated above. When a reference ligand is identified and its experimentally 
known absolute free energy (ΔG) is provided, the absolute free energies 
of the entire set are calculated by traversing the network formed by the 
set of ΔΔG calculations.

The FEP data is provided by specifying two directories, one for the FEP calculations of the free ligand pair, and the other for the corresponding protein-ligand complex. Each of these directories must contain subdirectories with the FEP simulation results of each pair, e.g., a .fepout file and a simulationinfo.xml file which are generated by the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol. The simulationinfo.xml files are read by the protocol to determine the identities of the ligands involved in each FEP simulation, whether the simulation involves the free ligand pair or the protein-ligand complex. The .fepout file produced by FEP simulation is used to calculate the relative free energy between each pair. See the Analyzing Results section in Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) for details of this calculation. All of this information is collected for the free ligand pair and protein-ligand complex simulations and aggregated.

The Extreme Value Threshold parameter is provided to flag ΔΔG 
calculations that result in unusually high values in magnitude. Such 
values are rarely observed experimentally, and therefore, simulations that 
result in these values are likely not converged fully or may be 
problematic for other reasons. This parameter does not alter the results
numerically, but simply serves as a means to mark the resulting ΔΔG and
ΔG values as likely unreliable . You can change this value in the 3-5 kcal/mol range to monitor the sensitivity of the results to the threshold.

If a Reference Ligand Name is specified, in addition to reporting the
relative binding free energy for each pair, the protocol will calculate
the absolute free energy for all the ligands by traversing the 
connected graph created by linking the relative free energy 
calculations. For this step, the absolute experimental binding free 
energy of the reference ligand is required. If this value is unknown, it
could be set to zero; in that scenario the computed free energies will 
be relative to that of the reference ligand and not true absolute 
values.

* Open the Simulations | Run Free Energy Simulations tools and click Collate FEP Simulation Results... .

* For FEP Data Directory Ligand parameter, specify the Output directory containing the results of the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol run on free ligand pair systems.

* For FEP Data Directory Complex parameter, specify the Output directory containing the results of the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol run on protein-ligand complex systems.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Collate FEP Simulation Results - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to
send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the 
status dialog and allows you to continue using while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Optionally, you could provide a .csv file for the Input Relative FEP Values File parameter containing the ΔΔG values corresponding to each ligand pair. For example, the Pairwise ddGs .csv file that is automatically generated by this protocol can be provided as input if you wish to re-run the calculation with a different value for Extreme Value Threshold . When the Input Relative FEP Values File is specified, the protocol runs faster.

Upon the completion of the run, the relative FEP values ΔΔG are tabulated in the Results section. Each relative FEP entry specifies the name of the ligands involved in the perturbation (Lig1Name, Lig2Name). The ΔΔG values are also graphically depicted in a bar plot. If the Lead Ligand Name parameter was specified, the absolute free energies ΔG are computed for the entire set, which are tabulated and graphed as with the ΔΔG values.

When absolute free energies ΔG are computed, a graph showing the connectivity network of the ligands and their pairwise ΔΔG values is created and can be opened by ViewResults in the protocol Report .

From a typical run two files are produced.

* Absolute dGs: Contains ΔG values of ligands.

* Pairwise ddGs: Contains ΔΔG values obtained from the FEP calculations.

#### Further information

Lead Optimization Tools Run Free Energy Simulations tool

# Create Pulling Atom Pair

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_create_pulling_atom_pair.htm

## Create Pulling Atom Pair

* Description

* Setting up and running

The Create Pulling Atom Pair command allows you to specify a pair of atoms on which the external Steered Molecular Dynamics (SMD) force will act. The applied velocity via a spring is identical in magnitude and is applied to the two atoms during SMD. The vector joining the two atoms therefore serves as an "axis" for the SMD pulling experiment. This is a necessary step before initiating the Steered Molecular Dynamics protocol. Typically, this would involve one atom from the ligand and one from the protein. The two atoms could also belong to the same molecule (e.g., an application involving the unraveling of a protein by pulling the N and C-termini).

To create a pulling atom pair:

* Select two atoms in the Graphics View. Click the first atom, and then SHIFT+click the second atom.

* Click Create Pulling Atom Pair to create the pair.

A two-headed arrow indicates the vector joining the two atoms. The size of the arrow is proportional to the mass of molecule containing the atom. Since the magnitude of velocity applied on the two atoms via a spring are identical, typically the ligand would show a larger arrow due to its smaller size. Thus the arrow is a measure of displacement that will be imparted to each molecule due to the application of an external force during the SMD pulling.

# Detect and Analyze Pockets - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_detect_analyze_pockets-para.htm

## Detect and Analyze Pockets - Parameters

### Detect and analyze pockets from molecular dynamics trajectories

Note:

* This protocol is only supported on Linux servers.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to each trajectory file in Input Trajectory . This file is used as the topology for reading DCD files. Each DCD file should share a common topology. |
| Input Trajectory | One or more simulations in DCD format. |
| Pocket Analysis Type | Pocket Analysis Type specifies the type of analysis used for characterizing pocket dynamics throughout a molecular dynamics trajectory. Choosing the appropriate analysis type affects how pockets are characterized and what properties are emphasized in the resulting data. Occurrence Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on how frequently they appear at each location throughout the trajectory. This analysis is particularly useful for identifying transient pockets and understanding how often specific pocket regions are accessible during the simulation. It provides insights into the temporal stability and persistence of pocket features. Default isovalue for Occurrence Analysis is 0.5 . Spatial Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on the density or count of alpha spheres (Voronoi vertices) at each location across all snapshots. This type provides a more structural view of the pocket's geometry, highlighting areas with consistently high densities of interaction points and revealing the most prominent pocket regions. The analysis is also influenced by pocket size, with larger pockets typically generating higher density values. Default isovalue for Spatial Analysis is 8 . Druggability Analysis : Detects and analyzes only druggable pockets that are suitable for small molecule drug binding. This analysis incorporates geometric and physicochemical properties to predict which pocket areas are most likely to bind drug-like molecules effectively, based on methods described by Schmidtke et al. Specifying a Custom Isovalue is not an option for this selection. Note: This protocol is only supported on Linux servers. References: Schmidtke, Peter, and Xavier Barril. "Understanding and Predicting Druggability. A High-Throughput Method for Detection of Drug Binding Sites." Journal of Medicinal Chemistry 53.15 (2010). Valid Values: Occurrence Analysis , Spatial Analysis, Druggability Analysis |
| Custom Isovalue | Enter Custom Isovalue here. Accepted isovalues for Spatial Analysis is a positive float, and for Occurrence Analysis is a float between 0 and 1. Leave blank to use default values. Custom Isovalue sets a threshold that determines which regions are included in the analysis and visualization of pockets. This parameter is crucial for distinguishing pocket regions of interest in Spatial and Occurrence Analysis. Higher Isovalues: In both Occurrence and Spatial Analysis, setting a higher isovalue focuses the analysis on the most pronounced features. In Occurrence Analysis, a high isovalue selects regions that frequently appear as pockets, emphasizing critical functional sites that are regularly accessible throughout the trajectory. For Spatial Analysis, a high isovalue focuses on deeper and larger cavities, highlighting the most prominent structural features of the pocket. Lower Isovalues: Lowering the isovalue includes more regions, capturing broader pocket features. This setting is beneficial for identifying transient pockets that may appear less frequently but could be critical for processes like allosteric regulation or transient protein-protein interactions. In Spatial Analysis, a lower isovalue can help visualize shallower pockets and smaller cavities that may still be functionally relevant. Choosing Isovalues for Different Biological Systems: Enzymes and Receptors: For systems where stable and frequently utilized binding sites are of interest (e.g., in drug design or substrate binding studies), higher isovalues might be more appropriate to focus on highly relevant, consistently present pockets. Transient Protein Complexes: In studies of transient interactions, such as those in signaling pathways or temporary enzyme complexes, lower isovalues can be useful to capture fleeting pockets that may be critical for short-lived interactions. Membrane Proteins: For membrane proteins, where the distinction between internal pockets and the membrane interface is crucial, isovalues might need fine-tuning to differentiate between surface-exposed and buried pockets effectively. Note : Setting the isovalue too high or too low for your specific system might result in no pockets being detected. A very high isovalue could overlook smaller yet significant pockets, while a very low isovalue might clutter the analysis with too many insignificant features, obscuring relevant pockets. |
| Trajectory Iteration | Specifies the parameters that control iteration through the Input Trajectory . |
| Batch | Specifies how many frames from the Input Trajectory to load during each iteration. Smaller values of Batch will use less memory but require more time to complete. Larger values of Batch will use more memory but require less time to complete. |
| Stride | Specifies how to sample frames from an Input Trajectory . A Stride of "1" means to take every frame, and a Stride of "n" means to take every nth frame after the first frame. |
| Skip | Specifies how many frames to skip from the beginning of each Input Trajectory . |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to each trajectory file in Input Trajectory . 
This file is used as the topology for reading DCD files. Each DCD file should share a common topology.

One or more simulations in DCD format.

* Occurrence Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on how frequently they appear at each location throughout the trajectory. This analysis is particularly useful for identifying transient pockets and understanding how often specific pocket regions are accessible during the simulation. It provides insights into the temporal stability and persistence of pocket features. Default isovalue for Occurrence Analysis is 0.5 .

* Spatial Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on the density or count of alpha spheres (Voronoi vertices) at each location across all snapshots. This type provides a more structural view of the pocket's geometry, highlighting areas with consistently high densities of interaction points and revealing the most prominent pocket regions. The analysis is also influenced by pocket size, with larger pockets typically generating higher density values. Default isovalue for Spatial Analysis is 8 .

* Druggability Analysis : Detects and analyzes only druggable pockets that are suitable for small molecule drug binding. This analysis incorporates geometric and physicochemical properties to predict which pocket areas are most likely to bind drug-like molecules effectively, based on methods described by Schmidtke et al. Specifying a Custom Isovalue is not an option for this selection.

References:

* Schmidtke, Peter, and Xavier Barril. "Understanding and Predicting Druggability. A High-Throughput Method for Detection of Drug Binding Sites." Journal of Medicinal Chemistry 53.15 (2010).

Valid Values: Occurrence Analysis , Spatial Analysis, Druggability Analysis

* Higher Isovalues: In both Occurrence and Spatial Analysis, setting a higher isovalue focuses the analysis on the most pronounced features. In Occurrence Analysis, a high isovalue selects regions that frequently appear as pockets, emphasizing critical functional sites that are regularly accessible throughout the trajectory. For Spatial Analysis, a high isovalue focuses on deeper and larger cavities, highlighting the most prominent structural features of the pocket.

* Lower Isovalues: Lowering the isovalue includes more regions, capturing broader pocket features. This setting is beneficial for identifying transient pockets that may appear less frequently but could be critical for processes like allosteric regulation or transient protein-protein interactions. In Spatial Analysis, a lower isovalue can help visualize shallower pockets and smaller cavities that may still be functionally relevant.

* Membrane Proteins: For membrane proteins, where the distinction between internal pockets and the membrane interface is crucial, isovalues might need fine-tuning to differentiate between surface-exposed and buried pockets effectively.

# Detect and Analyze Pockets

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_detect_analyze_pockets.htm

## Detect and Analyze Pockets

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

* Analyzing results

Detect and Analyze Pockets removes solvent atoms and detects pockets in molecular dynamics trajectories using mdpocket [Schmidtke et al., 2011] . Pockets can be identified based on frequency, density, and isovalue threshold. Measurements are restricted to atoms specified in Input Molecule .

* Load the molecule in a Molecule Window. Ensure that the molecule corresponds to the set of trajectories that will be analyzed. All simulation trajectories must derive from a common topology and forcefield (i.e., the structure and forcefield have not been edited.) If you are unsure if several simulation results share a common forcefield and topology, analyze the trajectories for each, one at a time, with the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

If you are unsure if several simulation results share a common forcefield and topology, analyze the trajectories for each, one at a time, with the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

* Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Detect and Analyze Pockets... to open the Detect and Analyze Pockets dialog.

* Set parameters for the simulation: Set the Input Molecule and Input Trajectory . Select the Pocket Analysis Type that you want to use for analyzing pocket dynamics. You can choose to set a Custom Isovalue to fine tune how the pocket detection is performed. You can use Trajectory Iteration to control how the trajectory is iterated so that only a subset of frames is analyzed. For details about all of the parameters, including Pocket Analysis Type and Custom Isovalue , see Detect and Analyze Pockets - Parameters .

* Set the Input Molecule and Input Trajectory .

* Select the Pocket Analysis Type that you want to use for analyzing pocket dynamics.

* You can choose to set a Custom Isovalue to fine tune how the pocket detection is performed.

* You can use Trajectory Iteration to control how the trajectory is iterated so that only a subset of frames is analyzed.

For details about all of the parameters, including Pocket Analysis Type and Custom Isovalue , see Detect and Analyze Pockets - Parameters .

* Click Run . The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule. In this output molecule file, identified pockets are stored as a collection of isosurfaces. Protein atoms that participate in the pocket are stored as Atom Groups and can be seen in the Hierarchy window. |
| pocket_data | Directory containing detailed analysis data of each pocket in CSV format. |
| feature_data | Directory containing detailed analysis data of each feature for all pockets in CSV format. |
| mean_local_hydrophobic_density.csv | Only available when Druggability Analysis is chosen under Pocket Analysis Type . Among the available features, mean local hydrophobic density of the binding site is one of the most prominent descriptors in terms of druggability prediction, combining size and spatial distribution of hydrophobic subpockets. This CSV allows you to track and compare this numerical descriptor of druggability across individual pockets and time steps. |

Visualizing the output molecule provides insights into pocket distributions and their interactions with amino acids. Through the Hierarchy window's Pockets group, you can select specific Atom Groups that highlight protein atoms that contribute to each pocket. Furthermore, you can explore pocket geometries through interactive isosurfaces, with the ability to dynamically adjust isovalues to examine how they affect pocket shapes and volumes. The following detailed results are provided in CSV format: per-pocket results are stored in the pocket_data folder, and per-feature results aggregated across all pockets are available in the feature_data folder.

| Result | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Pocket Volume | Estimation of the total volume of the binding pocket using a Monte-Carlo algorithm. |
| Pocket Surface Area | Total surface area of the pocket measured using a standard 1.4Å probe, representing the total accessible surface on the receptor side. |
| Pocket Polar Surface Area | Surface area of the pocket that consists of polar atoms, measured using a 1.4Å probe, indicating regions favorable for polar interactions. |
| Pocket Apolar Surface Area | Surface area of the pocket that consists of apolar atoms, measured using a 1.4Å probe, indicating regions favorable for hydrophobic interactions. |
| Pocket Surface Area (2.2Å Probe) | Similar to the standard surface area, but measured using a larger 2.2Å probe, which can reveal different accessibility characteristics. |
| Pocket Polar Surface Area (2.2Å Probe) | Polar surface area measured with a 2.2Å probe, providing an alternative view of polar accessibility. |
| Pocket Apolar Surface Area (2.2Å Probe) | Apolar surface area measured with a 2.2Å probe, providing an alternative view of hydrophobic accessibility. |
| Mean Local Hydrophobic Density | A measure of the clustering of hydrophobic regions within the pocket, and a prominent descriptor of druggability of the pocket. |
| Hydrophobicity Score | Measure of the pocket's overall hydrophobic character based on the average hydrophobicity of all residues involved in the binding site (using [Monera et al., 1995] scale). |
| Volume Score | Average relative volume score of all amino acids that contact the pocket, providing insight into the spatial characteristics of the binding site. |
| Polarity Score | Averaged polarity scores of all residues in the pocket, which quantifies the its hydrophilic character. |
| Charge Score | Average electrical charge of all amino acids in contact with the pocket, indicating the pocket's overall electrical characteristics. |
| Polar Atoms Proportion | Percentage of polar atoms among all atoms defining the pocket, providing a measure of the pocket's polar/apolar balance. |

#### Troubleshooting

All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it is automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools. If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not complete. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog

# Dynamics (Equilibration) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_dynamics_equilibration-para.htm

## Dynamics (Equilibration) - Parameters

### Equilibrates a molecule with molecular dynamics using CHARMm

Initializes the atom velocities using Target Temperature and performs equilibration molecular dynamics. The final velocities are stored in a restart (.rst) file that should be used as the input to a production dynamics step.

The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

Note:

* This protocol can be run as part of the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol, which performs minimization and dynamics calculations.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Simulation Time (ps) | Time length (ps) of dynamics simulation. |
| Save Results Interval (ps) | The time interval in picosecond (ps) to save coordinates, energies, and restart file during the simulation. Notes For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval (ps) . At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved. Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time (ps)/Save Results Interval (ps). |
| Restart File | Specifies which restart file (*.rst) to use for this simulation. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane. Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant. Notes: To add an implicit membrane to a molecule: In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools. In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. For GB and GBMV, the dielectric constant is fixed as 1.0 internally and can not be changed. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) or to Generalized Born with Simple SWitching (GBSW), the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a Dielectric Constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW, or GBIM. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Specifies scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these forcefields. Applies to GB and GBIM. See Also: Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). | Input Atomic Radii | Atomic radii used for GBSW and GBMV: van der Waals radii : Default. radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields. | Use Molecular Surface | Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW. Valid Values: True , False |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Equilibration | Equilibration Parameters |
| Equilibration Time Step (fs) | Time step (fs) to use for the dynamics simulation. |
| Apply SHAKE Constraint | Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation. Valid Values: True , False |
| Equilibration Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation. |
| Equilibration Adjust Velocity Frequency | Specifies the frequency of velocity adjustments during the simulation, in number of steps. |

By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock. The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers. See Also: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/ |

| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |

Spherical Cutoff : the spherical cutoff is used for the electrostatic interactions. Particle Mesh Ewald : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used. | PMass | Specifies the mass of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. Units in Atomic Mass Unit (AMU). |

Velocity Verlet (VVER): the velocities and positions are calculated at the same time points. In Discovery Studio, the VVER integrator and Nose dynamics are always used together. | Number of Processors | Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server. Note : The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel. The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel. |

# Dynamics (Equilibration)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_dynamics_equilibration.htm

## Dynamics (Equilibration)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dynamics (Equilibration) protocol establishes the
target temperature for a system using molecular dynamics simulation.

Equilibration is performed after the initial Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) phase in a
molecular dynamics simulation in order to stabilize the molecular system
near the target temperature, and usually precedes the production phase.

The purpose of the equilibration phase is to ensure that the
system is in equilibrium, where thermal energy is distributed
among various degrees of freedom governed by the laws of thermodynamics.

Equilibration is achieved by allowing the system to evolve for a period of
time and integrating the equations of motion until the average temperature
and structure remain stable. This is facilitated by periodically reassigning
velocities appropriate to the desired temperature. Generally, the procedure
is continued until various statistical properties of the system become independent of time.

For molecular systems solvated in a periodic boundary condition (PBC)
with explicit solvent, the equilibration protocol can be run with the Constant Pressure option to better mimic experimental conditions.

* Load a structure you wish to equilibrate into the Graphics View. This is usually the result of a Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) protocol used to bring the structure to the desired temperature.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Dynamics (Equilibration)... to open the Dynamics (Equilibration) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Select the structure as the Input Typed Molecule parameter
value.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Dynamics (Equilibration) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

You can validate an equilibration run by monitoring drifts and fluctuations in temperature and energy. Systematic drifts in the temperature or energy towards 
the end of a trajectory usually indicate insufficient equilibration. You can visually check the temperature and energy changes versus the simulation time in the 
plots in the summary section of the report. A warning message is reported in the summary if the final temperature is off target by 10% or more. Thermal fluctuations
in these properties are normal and their magnitude varies markedly with the size of the simulated systems. The general rule is that the ratio of energy fluctuation
to average energy should be proportional to the reciprocal of the square root of the number of particles in the system.

In addition to checking for energetic fluctuations, you can verify the stability of the equilibrated system by running an animation with various structural monitors turned on to look for any signs of steric clash or violations of certain structural constraints. See Structure | Animation .

You can also check the output CVS energy table for information about various energy terms and their changes with simulation time.

* By default, the SHAKE constraints are applied to all bonds involving hydrogens, and the default time step is 2fs. 
In general, dynamics simulations may fail if the input structure has bad van der Waals clashes. Failures are typically more frequent when the SHAKE option is
enabled. The problem is not with the SHAKE option, but is an indication that the input structure is not properly minimized. 
If the simulation fails, check that the initial structure does not have bad clashes. You can extend the minimization steps in this protocol
to ensure the input structure is fully minimized before dynamics simulation starts.

* Running long dynamics simulation with large solvated molecular system requires a lot of memory. If the server does not have enough memory, the
protocol may fail in the post processing stage, but the main simulation results are available. When the report shows an error, first
check the charmm.log file to make sure that CHARMm run finished successfully. Then check that output DSV files exist. If the post processing step
failed to generate the output DSV files, do one of the following: Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory: From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_eq.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_eq.ene to each conformation. Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

* Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory: From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_eq.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_eq.ene to each conformation.

* From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder.

* Open Input/<molecule>.dsv .

* Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder.

* Select <molecule>_eq.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_eq.ene to each conformation.

* Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule with trajectory frames stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order (i.e., the first conformation corresponds to the first trajectory frame saved by CHARMm). The time-dependent energy properties from the simulation are also stored with each conformation in this .dsv file. The trajectory can be sampled and analyzed using the Analyze Trajectory tool panel , or the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>_noconfs.dsv | The output molecule without conformations. In this file, the molecule has the final coordinate of the dynamics simulation. This can be used together with the <molecule>.dcd file for trajectory analysis. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule without solvent. This file has all of the conformations and solvent molecules removed for easy visualization. |
| <molecule>.dcd | The trajectory file generated by CHARMm. It saves the coordinates of each step for this dynamics simulation. You can import the trajectory frames to the molecule using Structure \| Animation \| Load... , or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>.ene | The energy file generated by CHARMm. It saves the time-dependent energy properties for this dynamics simulation. Its values will be loaded into the molecule when a corresponding dcd file is imported ( Structure \| Animation \| Load... from the menu bar). |
| <molecule>_energy.csv | Contains the same information as <molecule>.ene, but in CSV format. |
| <molecule>_eq.rst | The restart file generated by CHARMm when the Equilibration Save Restart File parameter is set to True . A restart file can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language (FFML) file, used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Analyze Trajectory tool panel Analyze Trajectory Structure | Animation Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing
