# Dynamics (NAMD)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_dynamics_namd.htm

## Dynamics (NAMD)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dynamics (NAMD) protocol allows you to perform molecular dynamics simulations in a chosen thermodynamic ensemble. The protocol uses the NAMD parallel molecular dynamics program designed for high-performance simulation of large biomolecular systems [Phillips et al., 2005] . 
For more information see http://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/namd/ .

The Discovery Studio The server installation includes the following NAMD versions:

| Platform | Version |
| --- | --- |
| CPU Windows | NAMD 2.13 for Win64 |
| CPU Linux | NAMD 3.0.1 for Linux x86 64 multi-core |
| GPU Windows | NAMD 2.13 Win64-CUDA (NVIDIA CUDA acceleration) |
| GPU Linux | NAMD 3.0.1 Linux-x86_64-multicore-CUDA-12.6 (NVIDIA CUDA acceleration) |

The protocol is typically run using an equilibrated input structure. A structure can be minimized and equilibrated using the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol.

You can choose one of the following thermodynamic ensembles to run the Dynamics (NAMD) protocol:

* NPT: Constant-temperature, constant-pressure ensemble (NPT), which mimics experimental conditions, is obtained by controlling the temperature and pressure during the dynamics simulation. The NPT dynamics can only be used for molecular systems that are solvated in a solvent box with periodic boundary conditions.

* NVT: Constant-temperature, constant-volume ensemble (NVT), also referred to as the canonical ensemble , is obtained by controlling the temperature during the simulation.

* NVE: Constant-energy, constant-volume ensemble (NVE), also referred to as the microcanonical ensemble , is obtained by solving the standard Newton equations of motion without temperature and pressure control.

* Load a structure into the Graphics View. Typically this will be the results of a Dynamics (Equilibration) protocol run at the desired temperature.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Dynamics (NAMD)... to open the Dynamics (NAMD) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule .

* If you continue the simulation from a previous run of a CHARMm or NAMD dynamics protocol, set the parameters in the Restart Files group. See Dynamics (NAMD) - Parameters .

* By default, the simulation time is set to be 10ps, which is short for most dynamics simulations. 
Depending on the purpose of your simulation, you may want to increase this using the Simulation Time (ps) parameter.

* If you increase the simulation time, be sure to evaluate and reset
the Save Results Interval (ps) parameter accordingly so that no more than several hundred frames are saved. Saving a lot of frames requires heavy system resources at the end of the run, especially for large solvated molecular systems.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Dynamics (NAMD) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be typed automatically using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not run. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

Several energy terms, including total energy fluctuation are shown in the summary section of the report. 
The temperature and the total energy versus simulation time are plotted in the summary for an easy visual check. 
The energy terms and plots provide a good indication whether the production run was stable.
A warning message appears in the report if the final temperature is off target by 10% or more.

You can also check the output CVS energy table for information about various energy terms and their changes with simulation time.

Additionally, you can use tools in the application to analyze the trajectories in various ways to gain more information about the molecular system. For example:

* Create a trajectory animation for a qualitative visualization of the molecular structure. See Structure | Animation | Create/Remove .

* Calculate RMS movement from a reference conformation to understand the extent of a conformational transition. See Analyze Trajectory .

* Apply hydrogen bond monitors to trajectory frames for information on specific interactions within the molecular system during the course of the simulation. See Structure | Monitor .

* Calculate structural properties such as torsion, distance, and angle to study changes in certain regions of the molecule. See Analyze Trajectory .

* Calculate electrostatics solvation energies for specific trajectory frames to study the interaction between solute and solvent. See Solvation Energy.

* By default, the SHAKE constraints are applied to all bonds involving hydrogens, and the default time step is 2fs. Dynamics simulations may fail if the input structure has bad van der Waals clashes and the failure is seen more often with the SHAKE option enabled. The problem is not with the SHAKE option itself, but is an indication that the input structure is not properly minimized. If the simulation fails, check that the initial structure is properly minimized. Use Standard Dynamics Cascade to minimize and equilibrate the structure before running this protocol.

* Running long dynamics simulation with large solvated molecular system will require large memory. If the server does not have enough memory, the
protocol may fail in the post processing stage, but the main simulation results are available. When the report shows error for the run, first
check the namd.log file to make sure that NAMD run finished successfully. Then check if the output DSV files exist. If the post processing step
failed to generate the output DSV files, do one of the following: Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory. From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_output.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the trajectory as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_output.ene to each conformation. Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

* Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory. From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_output.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the trajectory as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_output.ene to each conformation.

* From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder.

* Open Input/<molecule>.dsv .

* Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder.

* Select <molecule>_output.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the trajectory as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_output.ene to each conformation.

* Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

* NAMD treats nonbond cutoff slightly different from CHARMm. If a dynamics run is started in CHARMm and continued in NAMD, you might see a spike in total energy, which should go back to normal quickly. In addition, if Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method is used in the electrostatic energy calculation, there is a difference between NAMD and CHARMm: NAMD includes the PME energy in its electrostatic energy term, while CHARMm does not.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule. In this output molecule file, trajectory frames are stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order. The time-dependent energy properties from the simulation are also stored with each conformation in this file. You can sample and analyze the trajectory using the Analyze Trajectory tool panel , or the Analyze Trajectory protocol. |
| <molecule>_noconfs.dsv | The output molecule without conformations. In this file, the molecule has the final coordinate of the dynamics simulation. This can be used together with the <molecule>.dcd file for trajectory analysis. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule without solvent. This file has all of the conformations and solvent molecules removed for easy visualization. |
| <molecule>.dcd | The trajectory file generated by NAMD. It saves the coordinates of each step for this dynamics simulation. You can import the trajectory frames to the molecule using Structure \| Animation \| Load... , or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>.ene | The energy file generated by NAMD. It saves the time-dependent energy properties for this dynamics simulation. Its values will be loaded into the molecule when a corresponding dcd file is imported ( Structure \| Animation \| Load... from the menu bar). |
| <molecule>_energy.csv | Contains the same information as <molecule>.ene, but in CSV format. |
| <molecule>_restart.pdb | Restart file with the atomic coordinates of the final structure in pdb format that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_restart.vel | Restart file with atomic velocities that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_restart.xsc | Restart file with periodic cell parameters and periodic system data that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| namd.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the NAMD simulation engine. |

#### Further information

NAMD Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Analyze Trajectory tool panel Analyze Trajectory Structure | Animation Run a parallel calculation

# Dynamics (Production) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_dynamics_production-para.htm

## Dynamics (Production) - Parameters

### Performs molecular dynamics on a pre-equilibrated molecule using CHARMm

Dynamics provides insights into the motions of a molecule with time and can be used to sample the conformations available at a given temperature.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

* When setting Platform to OpenMM GPU , only the CHARMm, CHARMm Polar H and academic charmm forcefields are supported.

* The molecular system should be well equilibrated.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Simulation Time (ps) | Time length (ps) to perform the dynamics simulation. |
| Save Results Interval (ps) | The time interval in picosecond (ps) to save coordinates, energies, and restart file during the simulation. Notes For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval (ps) . At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved. Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time (ps)/Save Results Interval (ps). |
| Restart File | Specifies the name of the restart file (*.rst) to use when starting the production stage. |
| Platform | Choose to run CHARMm on CPU or OpenMM GPU. Notes: Currently OpenMM GPU is only available on Linux. OpenMM GPU only supports CHARMm, CHARMm Polar H and academic charmm forcefields. OpenMM GPU does not support the truncated octahedron cell shape. Valid Values: CPU , OpenMM GPU |
| GPU Device | Specifies the GPU device(s) to use for the OpenMM GPU platform. The GPU device index starts from 0. For multiple GPUs, use comma to delimit the indices. For example, "0,1" will allow both GPU 0 and 1 to be used. Note: If the GPU resources are managed by a queue management system, the value specified here will be ignored. If this parameter is left blank, it will use the first GPU by default. |
| Production Type | Specifies type of production to run: NPT: Constant pressure and temperature dynamics NVT: Constant temperature dynamics NVE: Dynamics without temperature/pressure control. Note: On CPU platform, NVT uses Berendsen weak coupling method to control temperature; but NPT uses Nosé-Hoover thermostat for temperature control and Langevin piston for pressure control. On OpenMM GPU platform, both NVT and NPT use Langevin thermostat for temperature control. NPT uses Monte-Carlo barostat sampling method for temperature control. Valid Values: NPT , NVT, NVE |
| TMass | Specifies the mass (in (kcal/mol)ps^2) of the thermal piston in the Hoover constant temperature method. Only applicable to NPT simulation on CPU platform. |
| TGamma | The friction coefficient (in ps -1 ) used to control temperature in Langevin thermostat. Only applicable to NVT/NPT simulation on OpenMM GPU platform. |
| PMass | Specifies the mass (in Atomic Mass Unit (AMU) ) of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. Applicable to NPT on CPU platform only. |
| PGamma | Specifies the collision frequency (in ps -1 ) of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. In OpenMM, this refers to the Monte-Carlo barostat sampling frequency. Applicable to NPT simulation. |
| Reference Pressure | Specifies the pressure (in atmospheres) at which the simulation is performed. Applicable to NPT simulation only. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane. Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant. Note: To add an implicit membrane to a molecule: In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools. In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. In OpenMM GPU platform, implicit solvent models are not available and this parameter can only be set to None. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. For GB and GBMV, the dielectric constant is fixed as 1.0 internally and can not be changed. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) or to Generalized Born with Simple SWitching (GBSW), the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a Dielectric Constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW or GBIM. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Specifies scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these forcefields. Applies to GB and GBIM. See Also: Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). See Also: Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481. Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments: Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13. Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. |
| Salt Concentration | Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l). Only applicable to GBSW. |
| Input Atomic Radii | Atomic radii used for GBSW and GBMV: van der Waals radii : Default. radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields. See Also : Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. |
| Use Molecular Surface | Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW. Valid Values: True , False |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Production | Production Parameters |
| Production Time Step (fs) | Time step (fs) to use for dynamics simulation. |
| Apply SHAKE Constraint | Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation. Valid Values: True , False |
| Production Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation. |
| Production Temperature Coupling Decay Time | Specifies the temperature coupling decay time (ps) for the Berendsen thermal coupling method. |
| Production Random Number Seed | Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock. The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers. See Also: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/ |
| Production Save Restart File | When set to True, save a restart file in the Output Directory for use by later dynamics stages. Note: Restart files can be very large, so you should exercise care when setting this parameter to True. Valid Values: True , False |
| Production Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance . |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Dynamics Integrator | Chooses a dynamics integrator to perform numerical integration of the equation of motion. Two choices are supported: Leapfrog Verlet Integrator (LEAP): the atom velocities and positions are calculated at time points that differ by a half time step. Velocity Verlet (VVER): the velocities and positions are calculated at the same time points. In Discovery Studio, the VVER integrator and Nose dynamics are always used together. It is not available in heating dynamics simulation or in constant pressure simulation. Valid Values: Leapfrog Verlet |
| Number of Processors | Specifies the number of processes a CHARMm calculation will be running on. Note : The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel. The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel. OpenMM GPU platform can only run on one CPU process. |
| Electrostatics | Specifies how to treat long range electrostatics. Note : The Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) option can only be applied to explicit solvation in Periodic Boundary Condition (PBC) model. Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald |
| Kappa | The width of the Gaussian function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ) and 6/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ). |
| Order | The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4. |
| Run On Grid | Run the protocol on the grid engine. Valid Values: True , False |
| Queue Name | Specify the name of the queue on the grid engine to submit the job to. Leave blank to specify the default queue. |
| Grid Options | Grid engine specific command line options for the job submission. Leave blank to use defaults. Notes : Ensure that the Number of Processors is specified to be the same as Number of Cores here. The former parameter controls the number of processes CHARMm will be running on and the latter parameter controls reserving the cores with the queuing system. In Pipeline Pilot, this is an array of command line options to send to the Grid engine submit command. In Discovery Studio, the options are comma separated. There are a number of parameters translated to the correct command line options for whichever supported Grid Engine you are using. Example - Supported parameters Account=<Project/Account name> Maximum Execution Time=<DD:MM:SS> - LSF ignores seconds Number of Cores=<4> - Get 1 CPU core if left blank Number of GPUs=<1> - Leave this blank for CPU calculation Parallel Environment=<The Parallel Environment to use> - Only needed for SGE Other=<Additional Parameters sent directly to submit command line> If you just include one line, whatever you enter will be sent "as is" to the submission command. Example - sending GPU options directly to command line - PBS -l mem=2GB -l ncpus=4 -l ngpus=1 |

Notes

* For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval (ps) .

* At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved.

* Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time (ps)/Save Results Interval (ps).

Specifies the name of the restart file (*.rst) to use when starting the production stage.

Choose to run CHARMm on CPU or OpenMM GPU.

* OpenMM GPU does not support the truncated octahedron cell shape.

Valid Values: CPU , OpenMM GPU

Specifies the GPU device(s) to use for the OpenMM GPU platform. The GPU device index starts from 0. For multiple GPUs, use comma to delimit the indices. For example, "0,1" will allow both GPU 0 and 1 to be used.

Note:

* If the GPU resources are managed by a queue management system, the value specified here will be ignored.

* If this parameter is left blank, it will use the first GPU by default.

Specifies type of production to run:

* NPT: Constant pressure and temperature dynamics

* NVT: Constant temperature dynamics

* NVE: Dynamics without temperature/pressure control.

* On CPU platform, NVT uses Berendsen weak coupling method to control temperature; but NPT uses Nosé-Hoover thermostat for temperature control and Langevin piston for pressure control.

* On OpenMM GPU platform, both NVT and NPT use Langevin thermostat for temperature control. NPT uses Monte-Carlo barostat sampling method for temperature control.

Valid Values: NPT , NVT, NVE

Specifies the mass (in (kcal/mol)ps^2) of the thermal piston in the Hoover constant temperature method. Only applicable to NPT simulation on CPU platform.

The friction coefficient (in ps -1 ) used to control temperature in Langevin thermostat. Only applicable to NVT/NPT simulation on OpenMM GPU platform.

Specifies the mass (in Atomic Mass Unit (AMU) ) of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. Applicable to NPT on CPU platform only.

Specifies the collision frequency (in ps -1 ) of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. In OpenMM, this refers to the Monte-Carlo barostat sampling frequency. Applicable to NPT simulation.

Specifies the pressure (in atmospheres) at which the simulation is performed. Applicable to NPT simulation only.

Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation.

Available options are:

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

* Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane.

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant.

* To add an implicit membrane to a molecule:

* In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools.

* In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

* In OpenMM GPU platform, implicit solvent models are not available and this parameter can only be set to None.

See Also:

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)

Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system.

If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present.

If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. 
For GB and GBMV, the dielectric constant is fixed as 1.0 internally and can not be changed.

Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) or to Generalized Born with Simple SWitching (GBSW), the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a Dielectric Constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons.

Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW or GBIM.

Specifies scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model.
Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields.
Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield.

* Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773.

Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA.

Valid Values: True , False

Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy.

Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ).

* Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and
conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481.

* Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments:
Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13.

* Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738.

* Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study
of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918.

Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l). Only applicable to GBSW.

Atomic radii used for GBSW and GBMV:

* van der Waals radii : Default.

* radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields.

See Also :

* Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248.

Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al.

Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Production Parameters

Time step (fs) to use for dynamics simulation.

Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation.

Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation.

Specifies the temperature coupling decay time (ps) for the Berendsen thermal coupling method.

Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock.

The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers.

* https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/

When set to True, save a restart file in the Output Directory for use by later dynamics stages.

Note: Restart files can be very large, so you should exercise care when setting this parameter to True.

Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step.

In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax.

In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax.

Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored.

Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance .

When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance .

When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically.

Two choices are supported:

* Leapfrog Verlet Integrator (LEAP): the atom velocities and positions are calculated at time points that differ by a half time step.

* Velocity Verlet (VVER): the velocities and positions are calculated at the same time points. In Discovery Studio, the VVER integrator and Nose dynamics are always used together. It is not available in heating dynamics simulation or in constant pressure simulation.

Valid Values: Leapfrog Verlet

Specifies the number of processes a CHARMm calculation will be running on.

Specifies how to treat long range electrostatics.

Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald

The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4.

Run the protocol on the grid engine.

Specify the name of the queue on the grid engine to submit the job to. Leave blank to specify the default queue.

# Dynamics (Production)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_dynamics_production.htm

## Dynamics (Production)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Dynamics (Production) protocol allows you to perform molecular dynamics simulations
in a chosen thermodynamic ensemble.

Typically, a Dynamics (Production) protocol takes an equilibrated structure input
as its starting point. Use Standard Dynamics Cascade to minimize and equilibrate the structure before running.

You may choose one of the following thermodynamic ensembles to run
the Dynamics (Production) protocol:

* NPT : The constant-temperature, constant-pressure
ensemble (NPT), which mimics experimental conditions, is
obtained by controlling the temperature and pressure during the dynamics simulation.
The NPT dynamics can only be used for molecular systems solvated in a solvent box with periodic boundary conditions.

* NVT : The constant-temperature, constant-volume
ensemble (NVT), also referred to as the canonical ensemble , is
obtained by controlling the temperature during the simulation.

* NVE : The constant-energy, constant-volume ensemble (NVE), also referred to as the microcanonical ensemble , is obtained by
solving the standard Newton equations of motion without temperature and
pressure control.

* Load a structure into the Graphics View. Typically this will be
the results of a Dynamics (Equilibration) or a Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol run at the desired temperature.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Dynamics (Production)... to open the Dynamics (Production) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule .

* If starting from an equilibrated structure or a previous production run, you should set the Restart File parameter to the restart (rst) file produced by
the previous run.

* By default, the simulation time is set to be 10ps, which is short for most dynamics simulations. 
Depending on the purpose of your simulation, you may want to increase the time by setting the Simulation Time (ps) .

* If you increase the simulation time, be sure to evaluate and reset
the Save Results Interval (ps) parameter accordingly so that no more than several hundred frames are saved. Saving a lot of frames requires heavy system resources at the end of the run, especially for large solvated molecular systems.

* For details about the remaining
parameters, see Dynamics
(Production) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

Several energy terms, including total energy fluctuation are shown in the summary section of the report. 
Additionally, the temperature and the total energy versus simulation time are plotted in the summary for an easy visual check. 
The energy terms and plots provide a good indication whether the production run was stable.
A warning message is given in the report if the final temperature is off target by 10% or more.

You can also check the output CVS energy table for information about various energy terms and their changes with simulation time.

Additionally, you can analyze the trajectories produced by a Dynamics (Production) run in various ways using the tools in the application to gain atomistic
information about the molecular system. For example:

* Create a trajectory animation for a qualitative visualization of the molecular structure. See Structure | Animation | Create/Remove .

* Calculate RMS movement from a reference conformation to understand the extent of a conformational transition. See Analyze Trajectory .

* Apply non-bond monitors to trajectory frames for information on specific interactions within the molecular system during the course of the simulation. See Structure | Monitor .

* Calculate structural properties such as torsion, distance, and angle to study changes in certain regions of the molecule. See Analyze Trajectory .

* Calculate electrostatics solvation energies for specific trajectory frames to study the interaction between solute and solvent. See Solvation Energy.

* By default, the SHAKE constraints are applied to all bonds involving hydrogens, and the default time step is 2fs. 
In general, dynamics simulations may fail if the input structure has bad van der Waals clashes. Failures are typically more frequent when the SHAKE option is
enabled. The problem is not with the SHAKE option, but is an indication that the input structure is not properly minimized. 
If the simulation fails, check that the initial structure does not have bad clashes. You can extend the minimization steps in this protocol
to ensure the input structure is fully minimized before dynamics simulation starts.

* Running long dynamics simulation with large solvated molecular system requires a lot of memory. If the server does not have enough memory, the
protocol may fail in the post processing stage, but the main simulation results are available. When the report shows an error, first
check the charmm.log file to make sure that CHARMm run finished successfully. Then check that output DSV files exist. If the post processing step
failed to generate the output DSV files, do one of the following: Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory: From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_prod.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_prod.ene to each conformation. Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

* Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory: From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_prod.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_prod.ene to each conformation.

* From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder.

* Open Input/<molecule>.dsv .

* Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder.

* Select <molecule>_prod.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_prod.ene to each conformation.

* Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule. In this output molecule file, trajectory frames are stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order (i.e., the first conformation corresponds to the first trajectory frame saved by CHARMm). The time-dependent energy properties from the simulation are also stored with each conformation in this .dsv file. The trajectory can be sampled and analyzed using the Analyze Trajectory tool panel , or the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>_noconfs.dsv | The output molecule without conformations. In this file, the molecule has the final coordinate of the dynamics simulation. This can be used together with the <molecule>.dcd file for trajectory analysis. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule without solvent. This file has all of the conformations and solvent molecules removed for easy visualization. |
| <molecule>.dcd | The trajectory file generated by CHARMm. It saves the coordinates of each step for this dynamics simulation. You can import the trajectory frames to the molecule using Structure \| Animation \| Load... , or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>.ene | The energy file generated by CHARMm. It saves the time-dependent energy properties for this dynamics simulation. Its values will be loaded into the molecule when a corresponding dcd file is imported ( Structure \| Animation \| Load... from the menu bar). |
| <molecule>_energy.csv | Contains the same information as <molecule>.ene, but in CSV format. |
| <molecule>_prod.rst | The restart file generated by CHARMm when the Production Save Restart File parameter is set to True . A restart file can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language (FFML) file, used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

If you get the following error in the report: "CHARMm Simulation has failed. Unable to use OpenMM GPU.", please check the graphics card and drivers to ensure that the required card and libraries are installed properly. For more information, see the System Requirements document included with the installation files.

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Analyze Trajectory tool panel Analyze Trajectory Structure | Animation Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Estimate Free Energy Landscape - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_estimate_free_energy_landscape-para.htm

## Estimate Free Energy Landscape - Parameters

### Estimate a free energy landscape from a dataset or set of simulations

Estimation of a free energy landscape can provide insight into the configurational space of a molecular system. To achieve this, a dataset must be provided or calculated from a set of molecular dynamics trajectories. In either case, data should span timescales relevant to the molecular behavior of interest and should derive from multiple, independent molecular dynamics trajectories in order to avoid bias. Any bias from the sampling strategy will be propagated to the estimated free energy landscape.

In order to estimate the energy landscape, either provide a dataset previously generated by Measure Trajectory Features to the Input Data parameter or configure the Simulation Data parameter group to correctly measure features from a set of molecular dynamics trajectories.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Data | Estimate a free energy landscape from features of this specified dataset in CSV format. This dataset must have been generated by the Measure Trajectory Features protocol. If desired, additional features may be manually added to the columns of the Measure Trajectory Features dataset for every corresponding trajectory frame so long as there is no conflict in column names. |
| Features | If provided, specifies the features to use as axes of the free energy landscape plot. Multiple features should be separated by a comma; therefore, feature names should not contain any commas. If more than two features are specified, the first two features will be used as axes and subsequent features will be sampled but not displayed. Thus, a position in the XY-plane represents the mean potential of mean force across all features beyond the second position. If not provided, all features (other than the reserved features specified below) will be processed by removing invariant features, feature normalization, and dimensionality reduction with principal component analysis. The first two principal components will be selected as axes for the free energy landscape. The following feature names (non-case-sensitive) are reserved for internal use: index source source index time time (ps) step boost potential average boost potential total energy bond energy angle energy torsion energy improper torsion energy electrostatic energy van der waals energy boundary energy misc energy kinetic energy temperature potential energy average temperature pressure group pressure volume |
| Simulation Data | Estimate a free energy landscape from features measured from a set of molecular dynamics trajectories. |
| Feature Type | Specifies what type of feature to measure from the Input Trajectory . RMSD : measures root-mean-square deviation of all Input Atoms from Reference Atoms . If no Reference Molecule is specified, then the first frame of the Input Trajectory serves as the Reference Molecule . SASA : measures the solvent accessible surface area of each residue from the Input Trajectory . Dihedral : measures dihedrals (phi, psi, chi1, chi2, chi3, chi4) for each residue of the Input Trajectory . Distance : measures distances between contacts according to Distance Type and Distance Cutoff . Valid Values: RMSD, SASA, Dihedral , Distance |
| Distance Type | Distance Type specifies how to calculate distances between residues. Options include: All Contacts : measures distances for intermolecular and intramolecular contacts. Intermolecular Contacts : measures distances for all residue contacts between separate molecules. Intramolecular Contacts : measures distances between residues on the same molecule that are separated by 6 or more other residues. Valid Values: All Contacts , Intermolecular Contacts, Intramolecular Contacts |
| Distance Cutoff | Distance Cutoff specifies the minimum distance threshold between nearest atoms in two different residues for a contact to be observed. |
| Input Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to each trajectory file in Input Trajectory . This file is used as the topology for reading DCD files; thus, each DCD file should share a common topology. |
| Input Trajectory | One or more simulations in DCD format. These trajectories will be measured according to the method specified by Feature Type . |
| Input Atoms | In Discovery Studio, Input Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. In Pipeline Pilot, Input Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Input Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be measured. No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning onto a reference conformation. |
| Input Bias Potentials | Input Bias Potentials is an optional parameter that provides an energy table in CSV format. This table must contain values of the biasing potentials in column named "Boost Potentials", and there should be as many rows as there are frames in the corresponding trajectory. Certain simulations such as Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (GaMD) apply biasing potentials that flatten the free energy landscape and accelerate conformational sampling. Thus, when analyzing distributions of features from biased simulations, it is useful to know the exact biasing potential for each frame. For this reason GaMD simulations will return a CSV file ("*_energy.csv") containing the values of the boost potentials. For each DCD file that you specify in Input Trajectory , you may specify the corresponding CSV file containing boost potentials. When specifying more than one CSV, files should be separated by a comma. Note also that the order in which the CSV files are specified is important, as the first CSV file will correspond to the first DCD file, the second CSV file will correspond to the second DCD file, and so on. |
| Reference Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to a reference molecule. The Input Trajectory will be compared to this reference molecule for calculating certain features (i.e. RMSD) or for superposing atomic coordinates from the Input Trajectory onto the atomic coordinates of the Reference Molecule . If a Reference Molecule is required for measuring a feature type and if the molecule is not specified, then the first frame of the first Input Trajectory will be used as the reference. |
| Reference Atoms | In Discovery Studio, Reference Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. In Pipeline Pilot, Reference Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Reference Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be yielded while iterating through the Input Trajectory for measuring certain features. No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning the Input Trajectory onto a Reference Molecule . Note that if Reference Atoms does not contain the same amount of atoms as Input Atoms , then featurization methods will attempt to match reference and input atoms using a basic, local alignment if required. |
| Superpose Frames on Reference | If set to "True", Superpose Frames on Reference specifies to superpose atoms from the Input Trajectory onto the Reference Molecule . If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are not specified or the number of atoms in the mobile and fixed set are not equal, then the superpositioning method performs a basic, local alignment to match residues of Input Trajectory to the Reference Molecule . Matched residues are then superposed. If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are specified and contain the same number of atoms, then Mobile Atoms from the Input Trajectory will be superposed onto Fixed Atoms from the Reference Molecule . Valid Values: True, False |
| Mobile Atoms | Specifies the mobile set of atoms from the Input Molecule that will be superposed onto the set of Fixed Atoms . |
| Fixed Atoms | Specifies the fixed set of atoms from the Reference Molecule that the Mobile Atoms from the Input Molecule will be superposed onto. |
| Trajectory Iteration | Specifies the parameters that control iteration through the Input Trajectory . |
| Batch | Specifies how many frames from the Input Trajectory to load during each iteration. Smaller values of Batch will use less memory but require more time to complete. Larger values of Batch will use more memory but require less time to complete. |
| Stride | Specifies how to sample frames from an Input Trajectory . A Stride of "1" means to take every frame, and a Stride of "n" means to take every nth frame after the first frame. |
| Skip | Specifies how many frames to skip from the beginning of each Input Trajectory . |
| Estimator Parameters | This group of parameters controls how the free energy landscape is estimated. |
| Bandwidth | Specifies the bandwidth for kernel density estimation. The same bandwidth is used for all dimensions, so feature normalization is recommended if features occur across different scales. If bandwidth is not provided, cross-validation will be used to select a bandwidth value that maximizes the likelihood. |
| Distance Metric | Specifies the distance metric to use for input data. An angular distance metric should be used for angular data such as dihedral angles. Valid Values: Euclidean , Angular |
| Number of Vertices per Dimension | Specifies how many datapoints to sample along each feature dimension. Note that the total number of vertices must be less than or equal to 1,000,000. Thus, as more features are specified, the number of vertices per dimension must decrease. |
| Minimum Count per Bin | Specifies the minimum number of observations for each kernel density window in order to estimate the energy density. If a window is excluded, the corresponding potential of mean force is set to the maximum value observed. |

* RMSD : measures root-mean-square deviation of all Input Atoms from Reference Atoms . If no Reference Molecule is specified, then the first frame of the Input Trajectory serves as the Reference Molecule .

* SASA : measures the solvent accessible surface area of each residue from the Input Trajectory .

* Dihedral : measures dihedrals (phi, psi, chi1, chi2, chi3, chi4) for each residue of the Input Trajectory .

* Distance : measures distances between contacts according to Distance Type and Distance Cutoff .

Valid Values: RMSD, SASA, Dihedral , Distance

Distance Type specifies how to calculate distances between residues. Options include:

* All Contacts : measures distances for intermolecular and intramolecular contacts.

* Intermolecular Contacts : measures distances for all residue contacts between separate molecules.

* Intramolecular Contacts : measures distances between residues on the same molecule that are separated by 6 or more other residues.

Valid Values: All Contacts , Intermolecular Contacts, Intramolecular Contacts

Distance Cutoff specifies the minimum distance threshold between nearest atoms in two different residues for a contact to be observed.

Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to each trajectory file in Input Trajectory . 
This file is used as the topology for reading DCD files; thus, each DCD file should share a common topology.

One or more simulations in DCD format. 
These trajectories will be measured according to the method specified by Feature Type .

In Discovery Studio, Input Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. 
In Pipeline Pilot, Input Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Input Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be measured. 
No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning onto a reference conformation.

Input Bias Potentials is an optional parameter that provides an energy table in CSV format. This table must contain values of the biasing potentials in column named "Boost Potentials", and there should be as many rows as there are frames in the corresponding trajectory.

Certain simulations such as Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (GaMD) apply biasing potentials that flatten the free energy landscape and accelerate conformational sampling. Thus, when analyzing distributions of features from biased simulations, it is useful to know the exact biasing potential for each frame. For this reason GaMD simulations will return a CSV file ("*_energy.csv") containing the values of the boost potentials.

For each DCD file that you specify in Input Trajectory , you may specify the corresponding CSV file containing boost potentials. When specifying more than one CSV, files should be separated by a comma. Note also that the order in which the CSV files are specified is important, as the first CSV file will correspond to the first DCD file, the second CSV file will correspond to the second DCD file, and so on.

Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to a reference molecule. The Input Trajectory will be compared to this reference molecule for calculating certain features (i.e. RMSD) or for superposing atomic coordinates from the Input Trajectory onto the atomic coordinates of the Reference Molecule . If a Reference Molecule is required for measuring a feature type and if the molecule is not specified, then the first frame of the first Input Trajectory will be used as the reference.

In Discovery Studio, Reference Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. 
In Pipeline Pilot, Reference Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Reference Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be yielded while iterating through the Input Trajectory for measuring certain features. 
No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning the Input Trajectory onto a Reference Molecule .
Note that if Reference Atoms does not contain the same amount of atoms as Input Atoms , then featurization methods will attempt to match reference and input atoms using a basic, local alignment if required.

If set to "True", Superpose Frames on Reference specifies to superpose atoms from the Input Trajectory onto the Reference Molecule . If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are not specified or the number of atoms in the mobile and fixed set are not equal, then the superpositioning method performs a basic, local alignment to match residues of Input Trajectory to the Reference Molecule . Matched residues are then superposed. If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are specified and contain the same number of atoms, then Mobile Atoms from the Input Trajectory will be superposed onto Fixed Atoms from the Reference Molecule .

Valid Values: True, False

Specifies the mobile set of atoms from the Input Molecule that will be superposed onto the set of Fixed Atoms .

Specifies the fixed set of atoms from the Reference Molecule that the Mobile Atoms from the Input Molecule will be superposed onto.

Specifies the parameters that control iteration through the Input Trajectory .

Specifies how many frames from the Input Trajectory to load during each iteration. Smaller values of Batch will use less memory but require more time to complete. Larger values of Batch will use more memory but require less time to complete.

Specifies how to sample frames from an Input Trajectory . A Stride of "1" means to take every frame, and a Stride of "n" means to take every nth frame after the first frame.

Specifies how many frames to skip from the beginning of each Input Trajectory .

This group of parameters controls how the free energy landscape is estimated.

Specifies the bandwidth for kernel density estimation. The same bandwidth is used for all dimensions, so feature normalization is recommended if features occur across different scales. If bandwidth is not provided, cross-validation will be used to select a bandwidth value that maximizes the likelihood.

Specifies the distance metric to use for input data. An angular distance metric should be used for angular data such as dihedral angles.

Valid Values: Euclidean , Angular

Specifies how many datapoints to sample along each feature dimension. Note that the total number of vertices must be less than or equal to 1,000,000. Thus, as more features are specified, the number of vertices per dimension must decrease.

Specifies the minimum number of observations for each kernel density window in order to estimate the energy density. If a window is excluded, the corresponding potential of mean force is set to the maximum value observed.

# Estimate Free Energy Landscape

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_estimate_free_energy_landscape.htm

## Estimate Free Energy Landscape

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

* Analyzing results

Estimation of a free energy landscape can provide insight into the configurational space of a molecular system. To achieve this, a dataset must be provided or calculated from a set of molecular dynamics trajectories. When a dataset is measured from one or more trajectories, specify parameters from the Simulation Data group in the same manner as in Measure Trajectory Features . Regardless if a dataset is provided or measured from a set of trajectories, data should span timescales relevant to the molecular behavior of interest and should derive from multiple, independent molecular dynamics trajectories to avoid bias. Any bias from the sampling strategy is propagated to the estimated free energy landscape.

Estimate Free Energy Landscape supports reweighting of simulation data from Gaussian accelerated Molecular Dynamics. To perform reweighting, provide Input Bias Potentials when measuring simulation features. The resulting dataset will include the boost potentials required for statistical reweighting.

* If you provide Simulation Data , load the molecule that has the trajectory you want to analyze into the Molecule Window. When providing Simulation Data , ensure that the molecule opened in the Molecule Window corresponds to the set of trajectories that will be analyzed. This means that all simulation trajectories must all derive from a shared structure from which the structure and forcefield have not been edited. When in doubt, use the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

* Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Estimate Free Energy Landscape... to open the Estimate Free Energy Landscape dialog.

* If you provide an existing dataset, then set Input Data to the data file in CSV format. You can optionally set Features to a comma-separated list of column names that will be used as axes in the energy landscape. Otherwise, all non-reserved features will be subject to dimensionality reduction with principal component analysis. For additional information regarding this parameter, see Estimate Free Energy Landscape - Parameters .

* If you provide Simulation Data , set Feature Type , Input Molecule , and Input Trajectory according to the documentation for Measure Trajectory Features . For more information regarding these parameters, refer to Estimate Free Energy Landscape - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation. The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

To measure features from an Input Molecule when the Input Molecule and Reference Molecule are in separate Molecule Windows, ensure the Estimate Free Energy Landscape protocol is docked into the Discovery Studio window by minimizing the protocol window.

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| simulation_data.csv | The output dataset measured from the input trajectories. |
| pca_loadings.csv | Loading factors that describe contributions of each feature to each principal component. Only generated when the dataset is subject to principal component analysis. |
| pmf.csv | Values of all grid points with the corresponding estimated potential of mean force. This dataset is used to plot the energy landscape. |
| pmf.png | Plotted estimate of the free energy landscape. The same figure is included in the job report. |

Estimate Free Energy Landscape will provide a plot of the estimated landscape in the generated report. In this image, a low potential of mean force corresponds to a more probable configuration from the input data. Note that the lowest potential of mean force observed is set to zero, and regions with an insufficent number of observations will be set to the maximum potential of mean force observed. If features from an input dataset are unselected, the first two principal components will be labeled, and a table containing loading factors from principal component analysis can be viewed. If features are calculated from simulation data, a copy of the simulation data will be provided. In addition, if more than two features are measured, then principal component analysis will be performed and the loading factor table will be provided.

#### Troubleshooting

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it is automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is not successful, the protocol will not run. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Theory - GaMD

# Solvate with Explicit Membrane - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_explicit-para.htm

## Solvate with Explicit Membrane - Parameters

### Solvate with explicit membrane

Solvates a membrane protein with an explicit membrane. The protocols adds the following entities to the protein surroundings:

* Explicit bilayer of lipids

* Water

* Counterions (optionally)

Notes:

* The input protein molecule should be typed with charmm36 forcefield and well minimized.

* The input protein should be pre-positioned with the normal of the membrane aligned to the z-axis and the origin located at the center of the membrane. Use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol to accomplish this task.

* When Equilibration is enabled, it is recommended to use multiple processors to reduce the running time, and if possible set Platform to GPU . When selecting GPU, a NVIDIA CUDA-capable video card and the appropriate driver are required to support a GPU calculation.

* The View Results script will open the protein and hide the hydrogens for better viewing.

### Parameters

| Name | Description | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. Note: The input protein molecule should be typed with charmm36 forcefield and well minimized and cannot contain chains with chain name L. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Lipid Type | Type of lipid bilayer in the membrane. The following lipid types are supported: Name Full Name POPC 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine POPE 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine DPPC 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine DMPC 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine DLPC 1,2-dilauroyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine Custom User-supplied lipid file Note: Custom lipid type should be supplied as a pre-equilibrated box in crd format. Only lipids contained in charmm36 forcefield are supported. Custom lipid chain names should be predefined as L. The equilibration will start with a 1000-step minimization followed by three stages of NVT or NPT dynamics. Restart files from a previous stage, when available, are used as the starting configuration for the next stage. The grid-steered molecular dynamics approach developed by Wells et al. is utilized to prevent solvent molecules from artificially infiltrating the core of the membrane during the initial stages of equilibration. Water and ions are repelled from membrane core with grid force constant of k = 0.05 kcal mol -1 /Å -2 . # Solvate with Explicit Membrane

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_explicit.htm

## Solvate with Explicit Membrane

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Solvate with Explicit Membrane protocol embeds a transmembrane protein into
a pre-equilibrated lipid bilayer and then adds water and optionally ions to each side of the 
bilayer to fully solvate the protein-lipid system. Several types of pre-equilibrated lipid bilayers 
with homogenous lipid types are provided. You can provide customized lipid boxes 
with a variety of lipid types, including homogenous and heterogenous lipids, and 
assymetrical lipid bilayers with different lipid compositions in the two layers. This protocol supports more than 400 lipid types included in the charmm36 forcefield.

The initial system created will have clashes between the protein and lipid molecules, water, and ions. The protocol includes optional steps to remove the clashes and to equilibrate the system using NAMD. After the equilibration steps, the system
is typically ready as input for running dynamics production using the Dynamics (NAMD) or Dynamics (Production) protocol.

* If a customized membrane box is provided, it should contain water on each side of the lipid and be pre-equilibrated.
The membrane should be positioned so that it is centered at [0,0,0] and the z-axis is
perpendicular to the membrane plane.

* If the system is not well equilibrated after running the protocol with Equilibration enabled, take the output coordinates and use the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol to fully prepare the system.

* Open the protein in a Graphics view and use the Prepare Protein tools to clean the protein.

* Type the protein using the charmm36 forcefield.

* Position the protein using the Add command on the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel. 
It adds an implicit membrane object and positions the protein so that the transmembrane segment is embedded in the implicit membrane slab. The z-axis of the protein is perpendicular to the
added implicit membrane plane, and the center of x and y is at the origin of the membrane (for example, [0,0]). If the protein is not positioned correctly relative to the implicit membrane, manually adjust its position using Modify... on the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel.

If the protein is not positioned correctly relative to the implicit membrane, manually adjust its position using Modify... on the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tool panel.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Solvate with Explicit Membrane... to open the Solvate with Explicit Membrane dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule parameter
to the structure.

* Set the Lipid Type parameter as desired.

* If you choose Equilibration , the protocol will perform a three-stage equilibration on the prepared system. Without equilibration, the protocol typically finishes in a couple of minutes. However, the equilibration step runs several NAMD dynamics simulations and can take many hours depending on the size of the molecular system and the available computing power. The equilibration can be run in MPI mode with multiple CPU cores.

Without equilibration, the protocol typically finishes in a couple of minutes.
