# GaMD Production - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_gamd_production-para.htm

## GaMD Production - Parameters

### Run a Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics Simulation

Runs a Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulation using NAMD. In this protocol, a boost potential will be applied to the system potential in order to flatten the energy landscape and accelerate conformational sampling.

Notes:

* Before running this protocol, the input system should be equilibrated using the GaMD Equilibration protocol.

* The simulation parameters (other than Simulation Time) and advanced parameters should be consistent between GaMD Equilibration and GaMD Production protocols.

* For accurate statistical reweighting, ensure that the Average Boost Potential (kcal/mol) time-series is stable and the Boost Potential (kcal/mol) histogram is approximately Gaussian. Both of these plots may be found in the simulation report.

* More information on NAMD can be found at http://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/namd

See Also:

* James C. Phillips, Rosemary Braun, Wei Wang, James Gumbart, Emad Tajkhorshid, Elizabeth Villa, Christophe Chipot, Robert D. Skeel, Laxmikant Kale, and Klaus Schulten,
Scalable molecular dynamics with NAMD. Journal of Computational Chemistry , 26:1781-1802, 2005 .

* Yi Wang, Christopher B. Harrison, Klaus Schulten, J. Andrew McCammon,
Implementation of Accelerated Molecular Dynamics in NAMD. Computational Science & Discovery , 4(1):015002, 2011 .

* Yui Tik Pang, Yinglong Miao, Yi Wang, and J. Andrew McCammon,
Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics in NAMD. Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation , 13(1):9-19, 2017 .

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | The molecular system on which to perform the GaMD simulation in DSV format. The molecule must have a forcefield applied and should have previously been equilibrated with "GaMD Equilibration." Boost potential parameters are extracted from the DSV. |
| Simulation | Simulation type: NPT : Isothermal-isobaric ensemble dynamics simulation, in which both pressure and temperature are conserved. Both temperature and pressure control methods are needed. It corresponds most closely to laboratory conditions with the system open to ambient temperature and pressure. Valid Values: NPT |
| Simulation Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation. |
| Simulation Time (ps) | Total time of the dynamics simulation in picoseconds. Simulation starts at time zero and ends at the specified value. |
| Simulation Time Step (fs) | Integration time step of the dynamics simulation in units of femtoseconds. |
| Report Interval (ps) | Time interval for reporting simulation data in units of picoseconds. |
| Advanced | Advanced parameters. |
| Multiple Timestep | To further reduce the cost of computing full electrostatics, NAMD uses a multiple timestepping integration scheme. In this scheme, the total force acting on each atom is broken into two pieces, a quickly varying local component and a slower long range component. The local force component is defined in terms of a splitting function. The local force component consists of all bonded and van der Waals interactions as well as that portion of electrostatic interactions for pairs that are separated by less than the local interaction distance determined by the splitting function. The long range component consists only of electrostatic interactions outside of the local interaction distance. Since the long range forces are slowly varying, they are not evaluated every timestep. Instead, they are evaluated every timesteps, specified by the NAMD parameter fullElectFrequency. An impulse of times the long range force is applied to the system every timesteps (i.e., the r-RESPA integrator is used). For appropriate values of , it is believed that the error introduced by this infrequent evaluation is modest compared to the error already incurred by the use of the numerical (Verlet) integrator. Improved methods for incorporating these long range forces are currently being investigated, with the intention of improving accuracy as well as reducing the frequency of long range force evaluations. In the scheme described above, the van der Waals forces are still truncated at the local interaction distance. Thus, the van der Waals cutoff distance forms a lower limit to the local interaction distance. While this is believed to be sufficient, there are investigations underway to remove this limitation and provide full van der Waals calculations in O(N) time as well. One of the areas of current research being studied using NAMD is the exploration of better methods for performing multiple timestep integration. Currently the only available method is the impulse-based Verlet-I or r-RESPA method which is stable for timesteps up to 4 fs for long-range electrostatic forces, 2 fs for short-range nonbonded forces, and 1 fs for bonded forces Setting rigid all (i.e., using SHAKE) increases these timesteps to 6 fs, 2 fs, and 2 fs respectively but eliminates bond motion for hydrogen. The mollified impulse method (MOLLY) reduces the resonance which limits the timesteps and thus increases these timesteps to 6 fs, 2 fs, and 1 fs while retaining all bond motion. |
| Full Electrostatic Frequency | Specifies the number of timesteps between each full electrostatics evaluation. It is recommended that Full Electrostatic Frequency be chosen so that the product of Full Electrostatic Frequency and Timestep does not exceed 4.0 unless Rigid Bonds is set to all or MOLLY is specified, in which case the upper limit is perhaps doubled. |
| Nonbonded Frequency | Specifies how often short-range nonbonded interactions should be calculated. Setting Nonbonded Frequency between 1 and Full Electrostatic Frequency allows triple timestepping where, for example, one could evaluate bonded forces every 1 fs, short-range nonbonded forces every 2 fs, and long-range electrostatics every 4 fs. |
| MTS Algorithm | Specifies the multiple timestep algorithm used to integrate the long and short range forces. impulse/verletI is the same as r-RESPA. constant/naive is the stale force extrapolation method. Valid Values: impulse , constant |
| Long Splitting | Specifies the method used to split electrostatic forces between long and short range potentials. The c1 option uses a cubic polynomial splitting function: S 3 (r) = 1 - 3 / 2 * (r / r cut ) + 1 / 2 * (r / r cut ) ^ 3, to affect C 1 continuity in the splitting of the electrostatic potential The c2 option uses a quintic polynomial splitting function, S 5 (r) = 1 - 10 * (r / r cut )^3 + 15 * (r / r cut ) ^ 4 - 6 * ( r / r cut ) ^ 5, to affect C 2 continuity in the splitting of the electrostatic potential. The S 5 splitting function, contributed by Bruce Berne, Ruhong Zhou, and Joe Morrone, produces demonstrably better long time stability than S 3 without requiring any additional computational cost during simulation, since the nonbonded forces are calculated via a lookup table. Note that earlier options xplor and sharp are no longer supported. Valid Values: c1 , c2 |
| Use MOLLY | Specify whether to use mollified impulse method (MOLLY). This method eliminates the components of the long range electrostatic forces which contribute to resonance along bonds to hydrogen atoms, allowing a Full Electrostatic Frequency of 6 (vs. 4) with a 1 fs timestep without using Rigid Bonds set to all. You may use Rigid Bonds set to water but using Rigid Bonds set to all with MOLLY makes no sense since the degrees of freedom which MOLLY protects from resonance are already frozen. Valid Values: True, False |
| MOLLY Tolerance | Convergence criterion for MOLLY algorithm. |
| MOLLY Iterations | Maximum number of iterations for MOLLY algorithm. |
| Pressure Control | Constant pressure simulation (and pressure calculation) require periodic boundary conditions. Pressure is controlled by dynamically adjusting the size of the unit cell and rescaling all atomic coordinates (other than those of fixed atoms) during the simulation. Pressure values in NAMD output are in bar. PRESSURE is the pressure calculated based on individual atoms, while GPRESSURE incorporates hydrogen atoms into the heavier atoms to which they are bonded, producing smaller fluctuations. The TEMPAVG, PRESSAVG, and GPRESSAVG are the average of temperature and pressure values since the previous ENERGY output; for the first step in the simulation they will be identical to TEMP, PRESSURE, and GPRESSURE. The phenomenological pressure of bulk matter reflects averaging in both space and time of the sum of a large positive term (the kinetic pressure, nRT/V ), and a large canceling negative term (the static pressure). The instantaneous pressure of a simulation cell as simulated by NAMD will have mean square fluctuations (according to David Case quoting Section 114 of Statistical Physics by Landau and Lifshitz) of kT/(Vβ) , where β is the compressibility, which is RMS of roughly 100 bar for a 10,000 atom biomolecular system. Much larger fluctuations are regularly observed in practice. The instantaneous pressure for a biomolecular system is well defined for "internal" forces that are based on particular periodic images of the interacting atoms, conserve momentum, and are translationally invariant. When dealing with externally applied forces such as harmonic constraints, fixed atoms, and various steering forces, NAMD bases its pressure calculation on the relative positions of the affected atoms in the input coordinates and assumes that the net force will average to zero over time. For time periods during with the net force is non-zero, the calculated pressure fluctuations will include a term proportional to the distance to the affected from the user-defined cell origin. A good way to observe these effects and to confirm that pressure for external forces is handled reasonably is to run a constant volume cutoff simulation in a cell that is larger than the molecular system by at least the cutoff distance; the pressure for this isolated system should average to zero over time. Because NAMD's impulse-based multiple timestepping system alters the balance between bonded and non-bonded forces from every timestep to an average balance over two steps, the calculated pressure on even and odd steps will be different. The PRESSAVG and GPRESSAVG fields provide the average over the non-printed intermediate steps. If you print energies on every timestep you will see the effect clearly in the PRESSURE field. Valid Values: Langevin Piston |
| Langevin Piston | Langevin piston pressure control method. The parameters LangevinPistonTarget, LangevinPistonPeriod, LangevinPistonDecay and LangevinPistonTemp must be set. NAMD provides constant pressure simulation using a modified Nosé-Hoover method in which Langevin dynamics is used to control fluctuations in the barostat. This method should be combined with a method of temperature control, such as Langevin dynamics, in order to simulate the NPT ensemble. The Langevin piston Nose-Hoover method in NAMD is a combination of the Nosé-Hoover constant pressure method as described in GJ Martyna, DJ Tobias and ML Klein, "Constant pressure molecular dynamics algorithms", J. Chem. Phys 101(5), 1994, with piston fluctuation control implemented using Langevin dynamics as in SE Feller, Y Zhang, RW Pastor and BR Brooks, "Constant pressure molecular dynamics simulation: The Langevin piston method", J. Chem. Phys. 103(11), 1995. |
| Langevin Piston Target | Specifies target pressure in bar for Langevin piston method. A typical value would be 1.01325 bar, atmospheric pressure at sea level. |
| Langevin Piston Period | Specifies barostat oscillation time scale in fs for Langevin piston method. If the instantaneous pressure did not fluctuate randomly during a simulation and the decay time was infinite (no friction) then the cell volume would oscillate with this angular period. Having a longer period results in more averaging over pressure measurements and hence slower fluctuations in the cell volume. A reasonable choice for the piston period would be 200 fs. |
| Langevin Piston Decay | Specifies barostat damping time scale in fs for Langevin piston method. A value larger than the piston period would result in underdamped dynamics (decaying ringing in the cell volume) while a smaller value approaches exponential decay as in Berendsen's method above. A smaller value also corresponds to larger random forces with increased coupling to the Langevin temperature bath. Typically this would be chosen equal to or smaller than the piston period, such as 100 fs. |
| Surface Tension Target | Specifies surface tension target (dyn/cm). Must be used with Use Flexible Cell and periodic boundary conditions. The pressure specified in Langevin Piston Target becomes the pressure along the z axis, and surface tension is applied in the x-y plane. |
| Use Group Pressure | Whether to use group or atomic pressure. Pressure can be calculated using either the atomic virial and kinetic energy (the default) or a hydrogen-group based pseudo-molecular virial and kinetic energy. The latter fluctuates less and is required in conjunction with rigidBonds (SHAKE). Valid Values: True , False |
| Use Flexible Cell | Whether to allow anisotropic cell fluctuations. NAMD allows the three orthogonal dimensions of the periodic cell to fluctuate independently when this option is enabled. Valid Values: True, False |
| Use Constant Ratio | When enabled, NAMD keeps the ratio of the unit cell in the x-y plane constant while allowing fluctuations along all axes. Notes : The Use Flexible Cell option is required for this option. Use Constant Area and Use Constant Ratio are mutually exclusive. Valid Values: True, False |
| Use Constant Area | When enabled, NAMD keeps the dimension of the unit cell in the x-y plane constant while allowing fluctuations along the z axis. Notes : This is not currently implemented in Berendsen's method. Use Constant Area and Use Constant Ratio are mutually exclusive. Valid Values: True, False |
| Temperature Control | Temperature control method. The following options are available: Langevin Dynamics Valid Values: Langevin Dynamics |
| Langevin Dynamics | Temperature control by Langevin dynamics. The Langevin temperature is set to be the same as the target temperature of the simulation. Other parameters can optionally be set to control the behavior of this feature. |
| Langevin Damping | Damping coefficient for Langevin dynamics (1/ps). This is applied to all atoms (unless Langevin Hydrogen is off, in which case only non-hydrogen atoms are affected). If not given, a PDB file is used to obtain coefficients for each atom (see Langevin File and Langevin Column below). |
| Langevin Hydrogen | If Langevin Damping is set then setting Langevin Hydrogen to off will turn off Langevin dynamics for hydrogen atoms. This parameter has no effect if Langevin coupling coefficients are read from a PDB file. Valid Values: True , False |
| Langevin File | PDB file to use for the Langevin coupling coefficients for each atom. If this parameter is not specified, then the PDB file specified by coordinates is used. |
| Langevin Column | Column of the PDB file to use for the Langevin coupling coefficients for each atom. The coefficients can be read from any floating point column of the PDB file. A value of 0 indicates that the atom will remain unaffected. Valid Values: X, Y, Z, O , B |
| Nonbonded Interactions | Options to control the way that non-bonded interactions are calculated. |
| Cutoff | Cutoff in local interaction distance (Å). This is common to both electrostatic and van der Waals calculations. Please refer to NAMD user manual for detailed information how this is combined with other parameters. |
| Pairlist Distance | Distance between pairs for inclusion in pair lists (Å). A pair list is generated Pairlists per Cycle times each cycle, containing pairs of atoms for which electrostatics and van der Waals interactions will be calculated. This parameter is used when switching is set to on to specify the allowable distance between atoms for inclusion in the pair list. This parameter is equivalent to the X-PLOR parameter CUTNb. If no atom moves more than pairlistdistcutoff during one cycle, then there will be no jump in electrostatic or van der Waals energies when the next pair list is built. Since such a jump is unavoidable when truncation is used, this parameter may only be specified when switching is set to on. If this parameter is not specified and switching is set to on, the value of cutoff is used. A value of at least one greater than cutoff is recommended. |
| Switching | Whether to use switching function. If switching is specified to be off, then a truncated cutoff is performed. If switching is turned on, then smoothing functions are applied to both the electrostatics and van der Waals forces. Valid Values: True , False |
| Switching Distance | Distance at which to activate switching/splitting function for electrostatic and van der Waals calculations (Å). The value of switchdist must be less than or equal to the value of cutoff, since the switching function is only applied on the range from switchdist to cutoff. |
| Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant for the system. A value of 1.0 implies no modification of the electrostatic interactions. Any larger value will lessen the electrostatic forces acting in the system. |
| Nonbonded Scaling | Scaling factor for electrostatic and van der Waals forces. A value of 1.0 implies no modification of the interactions. Any smaller value will lessen the nonbonded forces acting in the system. |
| PME | Whether to use particle mesh Ewald (PME) for electrostatics. PME is an efficient full electrostatics method for use with periodic boundary conditions. None of the parameters should affect energy conservation, although they may affect the accuracy of the results and momentum conservation. Note that periodic boundary condition is required. Valid Values: Automatic , True, False |
| PME Tolerance | PME direct space tolerance. It affects the value of the Ewald coefficient and the overall accuracy of the results. |
| PME Interpolation Order | Charges are interpolated onto the grid and forces are interpolated off using this many points, equal to the order of the interpolation function plus one. |
| PME Grid Spacing | Maximum space between grid points (Å). The grid spacing partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. If any of the grid sizes below are not set, then PME Grid Spacing must be set (recommended value is 1.0 Å) and will be used to calculate them. If a grid size is set, then the grid spacing must be at least PME Grid Spacing (if set, or a very large default of 1.5). |
| PME Grid Size X | Number of grid points in x dimension. The grid size partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. For speed, this number should have only small integer factors (2, 3 and 5). |
| PME Grid Size Y | Number of grid points in y dimension. The grid size partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. For speed, this number should have only small integer factors (2, 3 and 5). |
| PME Grid Size Z | Number of grid points in z dimension. The grid size partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. For speed, this number should have only small integer factors (2, 3 and 5). |
| Pairlist | To reduce the cost of performing the non-bonded interactions, NAMD uses a non-bonded pair list which contained all pairs of atoms for which non-bonded interactions should be calculated. Performing the search for pairs of atoms that should have their interactions calculated is an expensive operation. Thus, the pair list is only calculated periodically, at least once per cycle. Unfortunately, pairs of atoms move relative to each other during the steps between preparation of the pair list. Because of this, if the pair list were built to include only those pairs of atoms that are within the cutoff distance when the list is generated, it would be possible for atoms to drift closer together than the cutoff distance during subsequent timesteps and yet not have their non-bonded interactions calculated. |
| Steps per Cycle | Number of timesteps in each cycle. Each cycle represents the number of timesteps between atom reassignments. |
| Split Patch | Specifies how to assign atoms to patches. When set to hydrogen, hydrogen atoms are kept on the same patch as their parents, allowing faster distance checking and rigid bonds. Valid Values: hydrogen |
| Hgroup Cutoff | Used for group-based distance testing. It should be set to twice the largest distance which will ever occur between a hydrogen atom and its mother. Warnings will be printed if this is not the case. This value is also added to the margin. The unit is in %Aring; |
| Margin | Extra length in patch dimension (Å). It is used in determining the size of the cubes of space with which NAMD uses to partition the system. The value of this parameter will not change the physical results of the simulation. Unless you are very motivated to get the very best possible performance, just leave this value at the default. |
| Pairlist Minimum Processors | Pairlists may consume a large amount of memory as atom counts, densities, and cutoff distances increase. Since this data is distributed across processors it is normally only problematic for small processor counts. Set Pairlist Minimum Processors to the smallest number of processors on which the simulation can fit into memory when pairlists are used. |
| Pairlists per Cycle | Rather than only regenerating the pairlist at the beginning of a cycle, regenerate multiple times in order to better balance the costs of atom migration, pairlist generation, and larger pairlists. |
| Output Pairlists Frequency | Specify how often to print warnings. If an atom moves further than the pairlist tolerance during a simulation (initially (pairlistdist - cutoff)/2 but refined during the run) any pairlists covering that atom are invalidated and temporary pairlists are used until the next full pairlist regeneration. All interactions are calculated correctly, but efficiency may be degraded. Enabling outputPairlists will summarize these pairlist violation warnings periodically during the run. |
| Pairlist Shrink | In order to maintain validity for the pairlist for an entire cycle, the pairlist tolerance (the distance an atom can move without causing the pairlist to be invalidated) is adjusted during the simulation. Every time pairlists are regenerated the tolerance is reduced by this fraction. The unit is Å. |
| Pairlist Grow | In order to maintain validity for the pairlist for an entire cycle, the pairlist tolerance (the distance an atom can move without causing the pairlist to be invalidated) is adjusted during the simulation. Every time an atom exceeds a trigger criterion that is some fraction of the tolerance distance, the tolerance is increased by this fraction. The unit is in Å. |
| Pairlist Trigger | The goal of pairlist tolerance adjustment is to make pairlist invalidations rare while keeping the tolerance as small as possible for best performance. Rather than monitoring the (very rare) case where atoms actually move more than the tolerance distance, we reduce the trigger tolerance by this fraction. The tolerance is increased whenever the trigger tolerance is exceeded, as specified by pairlistGrow. Unit is in Å. |
| Rigid Bonds | Controls if and how SHAKE is applied. Valid choices are none, water or all. When water is selected, the hydrogen-oxygen and hydrogen-hydrogen distances in waters are constrained to the nominal length or angle given in the parameter file, making the molecules completely rigid. When rigidBonds is all, waters are made rigid as described above and the bond between each hydrogen and the (one) atom to which it is bonded is similarly constrained. For the default case none, no lengths are constrained. Valid Values: none, water, all |
| Rigid Iterations | The maximum number of iterations SHAKE will perform before giving up on constraining the bond lengths. If the bond lengths do not converge, a warning message is printed, and the atoms are left at the final value achieved by SHAKE. The default value is 100, however, convergence is usually reached after fewer than 10 iterations. |
| Rigid Tolerance | Allowable bond-length error for SHAKE (Å). The SHAKE algorithm is assumed to have converged when all constrained bonds differ from the nominal bond length by less than this amount. |
| Rigid Die on Error | Exit and report an error if rigidTolerance is not achieved after rigidIterations. Valid Values: True, False |
| Use SETTLE | Whether to use the non-iterative SETTLE algorithm to keep waters rigid rather than the slower SHAKE algorithm. Rigid Bonds should be enabled for this to take effect. Valid Values: True , False |
| Random Number Seed | Number used to seed the random number generator if temperature or langevin is selected. This can be used so that consecutive simulations produce the same results. If no value is specified, NAMD will choose a pseudo-random value based on the current UNIX clock time. The random number seed will be output during the simulation startup so that its value is known and can be reused for subsequent simulations. Note that if Langevin dynamics are used in a parallel simulation (i.e., a simulation using more than one processor) even using the same seed will not guarantee reproducible results. |
| Allow COM Motion | Specifies whether or not motion of the center of mass of the entire system is allowed. If this option is set to no, the initial velocities of the system will be adjusted to remove center of mass motion of the system. Note that this does not preclude later center-of-mass motion due to external forces such as random noise in Langevin dynamics, boundary potentials, and harmonic restraints. Valid Values: True, False |
| Zero Momentum | If enabled, the net momentum of the simulation and any resultant drift is removed before every full electrostatics step. This correction should conserve energy and have minimal impact on parallel scaling. This feature should only be used for simulations that would conserve momentum except for the slight errors in PME. (Features such as fixed atoms, harmonic restraints, steering forces, and Langevin dynamics do not conserve momentum; use in combination with these features should be considered experimental.) Valid Values: True, False |

When dealing with externally applied forces such as harmonic constraints, fixed atoms, and various steering forces, NAMD bases its pressure calculation on the relative positions of the affected atoms in the input coordinates and assumes that the net force will average to zero over time. For time periods during with the net force is non-zero, the calculated pressure fluctuations will include a term proportional to the distance to the affected from the user-defined cell origin. A good way to observe these effects and to confirm that pressure for external forces is handled reasonably is to run a constant volume cutoff simulation in a cell that is larger than the molecular system by at least the cutoff distance; the pressure for this isolated system should average to zero over time.

Because NAMD's impulse-based multiple timestepping system alters the balance between bonded and non-bonded forces from every timestep to an average balance over two steps, the calculated pressure on even and odd steps will be different. The PRESSAVG and GPRESSAVG fields provide the average over the non-printed intermediate steps. If you print energies on every timestep you will see the effect clearly in the PRESSURE field.

Valid Values: Langevin Piston

Langevin piston pressure control method. The parameters LangevinPistonTarget, LangevinPistonPeriod, LangevinPistonDecay and LangevinPistonTemp must be set.

NAMD provides constant pressure simulation using a modified Nosé-Hoover method in which Langevin dynamics is used to control fluctuations in the barostat. This method should be combined with a method of temperature control, such as Langevin dynamics, in order to simulate the NPT ensemble.

The Langevin piston Nose-Hoover method in NAMD is a combination of the Nosé-Hoover constant pressure method as described in GJ Martyna, DJ Tobias and ML Klein, "Constant pressure molecular dynamics algorithms", J. Chem. Phys 101(5), 1994, with piston fluctuation control implemented using Langevin dynamics as in SE Feller, Y Zhang, RW Pastor and BR Brooks, "Constant pressure molecular dynamics simulation: The Langevin piston method", J. Chem. Phys. 103(11), 1995.

Specifies target pressure in bar for Langevin piston method. A typical value would be 1.01325 bar, atmospheric pressure at sea level.

Specifies barostat oscillation time scale in fs for Langevin piston method. If the instantaneous pressure did not fluctuate randomly during a simulation and the decay time was infinite (no friction) then the cell volume would oscillate with this angular period. Having a longer period results in more averaging over pressure measurements and hence slower fluctuations in the cell volume. A reasonable choice for the piston period would be 200 fs.

Specifies barostat damping time scale in fs for Langevin piston method. A value larger than the piston period would result in underdamped dynamics (decaying ringing in the cell volume) while a smaller value approaches exponential decay as in Berendsen's method above. A smaller value also corresponds to larger random forces with increased coupling to the Langevin temperature bath. Typically this would be chosen equal to or smaller than the piston period, such as 100 fs.

Specifies surface tension target (dyn/cm). Must be used with Use Flexible Cell and periodic boundary conditions. The pressure specified in Langevin Piston Target becomes the pressure along the z axis, and surface tension is applied in the x-y plane.

Whether to use group or atomic pressure. Pressure can be calculated using either the atomic virial and kinetic energy (the default) or a hydrogen-group based pseudo-molecular virial and kinetic energy. The latter fluctuates less and is required in conjunction with rigidBonds (SHAKE).

Valid Values: True , False

Whether to allow anisotropic cell fluctuations. NAMD allows the three orthogonal dimensions of the periodic cell to fluctuate independently when this option is enabled.

When enabled, NAMD keeps the ratio of the unit cell in the x-y plane constant while allowing fluctuations along all axes.

Notes :

* The Use Flexible Cell option is required for this option.

* Use Constant Area and Use Constant Ratio are mutually exclusive.

When enabled, NAMD keeps the dimension of the unit cell in the x-y plane constant while allowing fluctuations along the z axis.

* This is not currently implemented in Berendsen's method.

Temperature control method. The following options are available:

* Langevin Dynamics

Valid Values: Langevin Dynamics

Temperature control by Langevin dynamics. The Langevin temperature is set to be the same as the target temperature of the simulation. Other parameters can optionally be set to control the behavior of this feature.

Damping coefficient for Langevin dynamics (1/ps). This is applied to all atoms (unless Langevin Hydrogen is off, in which case only non-hydrogen atoms are affected). If not given, a PDB file is used to obtain coefficients for each atom (see Langevin File and Langevin Column below).

If Langevin Damping is set then setting Langevin Hydrogen to off will turn off Langevin dynamics for hydrogen atoms. This parameter has no effect if Langevin coupling coefficients are read from a PDB file.

PDB file to use for the Langevin coupling coefficients for each atom. If this parameter is not specified, then the PDB file specified by coordinates is used.

Column of the PDB file to use for the Langevin coupling coefficients for each atom. The coefficients can be read from any floating point column of the PDB file. A value of 0 indicates that the atom will remain unaffected.

Valid Values: X, Y, Z, O , B

Options to control the way that non-bonded interactions are calculated.

Cutoff in local interaction distance (Å). This is common to both electrostatic and van der Waals calculations. Please refer to NAMD user manual for detailed information how this is combined with other parameters.

Distance between pairs for inclusion in pair lists (Å).

A pair list is generated Pairlists per Cycle times each cycle, containing pairs of atoms for which electrostatics and van der Waals interactions will be calculated. This parameter is used when switching is set to on to specify the allowable distance between atoms for inclusion in the pair list. This parameter is equivalent to the X-PLOR parameter CUTNb. If no atom moves more than pairlistdistcutoff during one cycle, then there will be no jump in electrostatic or van der Waals energies when the next pair list is built. Since such a jump is unavoidable when truncation is used, this parameter may only be specified when switching is set to on. If this parameter is not specified and switching is set to on, the value of cutoff is used. A value of at least one greater than cutoff is recommended.

Whether to use switching function. If switching is specified to be off, then a truncated cutoff is performed. If switching is turned on, then smoothing functions are applied to both the electrostatics and van der Waals forces.

Distance at which to activate switching/splitting function for electrostatic and van der Waals calculations (Å). The value of switchdist must be less than or equal to the value of cutoff, since the switching function is only applied on the range from switchdist to cutoff.

Dielectric constant for the system. A value of 1.0 implies no modification of the electrostatic interactions. Any larger value will lessen the electrostatic forces acting in the system.

Scaling factor for electrostatic and van der Waals forces. A value of 1.0 implies no modification of the interactions. Any smaller value will lessen the nonbonded forces acting in the system.

Whether to use particle mesh Ewald (PME) for electrostatics. PME is an efficient full electrostatics method for use with periodic boundary conditions. None of the parameters should affect energy conservation, although they may affect the accuracy of the results and momentum conservation. Note that periodic boundary condition is required.

Valid Values: Automatic , True, False

PME direct space tolerance. It affects the value of the Ewald coefficient and the overall accuracy of the results.

Charges are interpolated onto the grid and forces are interpolated off using this many points, equal to the order of the interpolation function plus one.

Maximum space between grid points (Å). The grid spacing partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. If any of the grid sizes below are not set, then PME Grid Spacing must be set (recommended value is 1.0 Å) and will be used to calculate them. If a grid size is set, then the grid spacing must be at least PME Grid Spacing (if set, or a very large default of 1.5).

Number of grid points in x dimension. The grid size partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. For speed, this number should have only small integer factors (2, 3 and 5).

Number of grid points in y dimension. The grid size partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. For speed, this number should have only small integer factors (2, 3 and 5).

Number of grid points in z dimension. The grid size partially determines the accuracy and efficiency of PME. For speed, this number should have only small integer factors (2, 3 and 5).

To reduce the cost of performing the non-bonded interactions, NAMD uses a non-bonded pair list which contained all pairs of atoms for which non-bonded interactions should be calculated. Performing the search for pairs of atoms that should have their interactions calculated is an expensive operation. Thus, the pair list is only calculated periodically, at least once per cycle. Unfortunately, pairs of atoms move relative to each other during the steps between preparation of the pair list. Because of this, if the pair list were built to include only those pairs of atoms that are within the cutoff distance when the list is generated, it would be possible for atoms to drift closer together than the cutoff distance during subsequent timesteps and yet not have their non-bonded interactions calculated.

Number of timesteps in each cycle. Each cycle represents the number of timesteps between atom reassignments.

Specifies how to assign atoms to patches. When set to hydrogen, hydrogen atoms are kept on the same patch as their parents, allowing faster distance checking and rigid bonds.

Valid Values: hydrogen

Used for group-based distance testing. It should be set to twice the largest distance which will ever occur between a hydrogen atom and its mother. Warnings will be printed if this is not the case. This value is also added to the margin. The unit is in %Aring;

Extra length in patch dimension (Å). It is used in determining the size of the cubes of space with which NAMD uses to partition the system. The value of this parameter will not change the physical results of the simulation. Unless you are very motivated to get the very best possible performance, just leave this value at the default.

Pairlists may consume a large amount of memory as atom counts, densities, and cutoff distances increase. Since this data is distributed across processors it is normally only problematic for small processor counts. Set Pairlist Minimum Processors to the smallest number of processors on which the simulation can fit into memory when pairlists are used.

Rather than only regenerating the pairlist at the beginning of a cycle, regenerate multiple times in order to better balance the costs of atom migration, pairlist generation, and larger pairlists.

Specify how often to print warnings. If an atom moves further than the pairlist tolerance during a simulation (initially (pairlistdist - cutoff)/2 but refined during the run) any pairlists covering that atom are invalidated and temporary pairlists are used until the next full pairlist regeneration. All interactions are calculated correctly, but efficiency may be degraded. Enabling outputPairlists will summarize these pairlist violation warnings periodically during the run.

In order to maintain validity for the pairlist for an entire cycle, the pairlist tolerance (the distance an atom can move without causing the pairlist to be invalidated) is adjusted during the simulation. Every time pairlists are regenerated the tolerance is reduced by this fraction. The unit is Å.

In order to maintain validity for the pairlist for an entire cycle, the pairlist tolerance (the distance an atom can move without causing the pairlist to be invalidated) is adjusted during the simulation. Every time an atom exceeds a trigger criterion that is some fraction of the tolerance distance, the tolerance is increased by this fraction. The unit is in Å.

The goal of pairlist tolerance adjustment is to make pairlist invalidations rare while keeping the tolerance as small as possible for best performance. Rather than monitoring the (very rare) case where atoms actually move more than the tolerance distance, we reduce the trigger tolerance by this fraction. The tolerance is increased whenever the trigger tolerance is exceeded, as specified by pairlistGrow. Unit is in Å.

Controls if and how SHAKE is applied. Valid choices are none, water or all.

When water is selected, the hydrogen-oxygen and hydrogen-hydrogen distances in waters are constrained to the nominal length or angle given in the parameter file, making the molecules completely rigid. When rigidBonds is all, waters are made rigid as described above and the bond between each hydrogen and the (one) atom to which it is bonded is similarly constrained. For the default case none, no lengths are constrained.

Valid Values: none, water, all

The maximum number of iterations SHAKE will perform before giving up on constraining the bond lengths. If the bond lengths do not converge, a warning message is printed, and the atoms are left at the final value achieved by SHAKE. The default value is 100, however, convergence is usually reached after fewer than 10 iterations.

Allowable bond-length error for SHAKE (Å). The SHAKE algorithm is assumed to have converged when all constrained bonds differ from the nominal bond length by less than this amount.

Exit and report an error if rigidTolerance is not achieved after rigidIterations.

Whether to use the non-iterative SETTLE algorithm to keep waters rigid rather than the slower SHAKE algorithm. Rigid Bonds should be enabled for this to take effect.

Number used to seed the random number generator if temperature or langevin is selected. This can be used so that consecutive simulations produce the same results. If no value is specified, NAMD will choose a pseudo-random value based on the current UNIX clock time. The random number seed will be output during the simulation startup so that its value is known and can be reused for subsequent simulations. Note that if Langevin dynamics are used in a parallel simulation (i.e., a simulation using more than one processor) even using the same seed will not guarantee reproducible results.

Specifies whether or not motion of the center of mass of the entire system is allowed. If this option is set to no, the initial velocities of the system will be adjusted to remove center of mass motion of the system. Note that this does not preclude later center-of-mass motion due to external forces such as random noise in Langevin dynamics, boundary potentials, and harmonic restraints.

If enabled, the net momentum of the simulation and any resultant drift is removed before every full electrostatics step. This correction should conserve energy and have minimal impact on parallel scaling. This feature should only be used for simulations that would conserve momentum except for the slight errors in PME. (Features such as fixed atoms, harmonic restraints, steering forces, and Langevin dynamics do not conserve momentum; use in combination with these features should be considered experimental.)

# GaMD Production

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_gamd_production.htm

## GaMD Production

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

* Analyzing results

The GaMD Production protocol facilitates Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulations of solvated input systems that were equilibrated by GaMD Equilibration .

Currently, GaMD only supports a constant temperature and constant pressure ensemble (NPT) that mimics experimental conditions by controlling the temperature and pressure during the dynamics simulation. NPT dynamics can only be used for molecular systems that are solvated in a solvent box with periodic boundary conditions.

GaMD is run using the NAMD parallel molecular dynamics program, which is designed for high-performance simulation of large biomolecular systems [Phillips et al., 2005] . For more information see http://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/namd/ .

* Load a structure into the Graphics View. Typically this will be the results of a GaMD Equilibration or GaMD Production protocol run at the desired temperature. Note that simulation parameter values should be constant between equilibration and production protocols.

* Open the Simulation | Enhanced Sampling tools and click GaMD Production... to open the GaMD Production dialog.

* Set the Input Typed Molecule .

* By default, Simulation Time (ps) is set to be 1000ps , which is short for most dynamics simulations. Depending on the purpose of your simulation, you may want to increase this value. If you increase the simulation time, be sure to evaluate and reset the Report Interval (ps) parameter accordingly so that no more than a couple thousand frames are saved. Saving too many frames requires heavy system resources at the end of the run, especially for large solvated molecular systems.

* For details about the parameters, see GaMD Production - Parameters . The forcefield parameters must be identical to the parameters used in the prior GaMD Equilibration . If forcefield parameters must be changed, another run of GaMD Equilibration should be performed.

The forcefield parameters must be identical to the parameters used in the prior GaMD Equilibration . If forcefield parameters must be changed, another run of GaMD Equilibration should be performed.

* Click Run to start the calculation. The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule. In this output molecule file, restart files and GaMD parameters from the simulation end state are stored into the output molecule. No conformations are provided by default. If you wish to view the full trajectory, then you can load the trajectory file into the output molecule with Structure \| Animation \| Load... or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol . You can sample and analyze the trajectory using the Analyze Trajectory tool panel. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule without solvent. This file has all solvent molecules removed, but retains all conformations for easy visualization. |
| <molecule>.dcd | The trajectory file generated by NAMD. It saves the coordinates of each step for this dynamics simulation. You can import the trajectory frames to the molecule using Structure \| Animation \| Load... , or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>.ene | The energy file generated by NAMD. It saves the time-dependent energy properties for this dynamics simulation. Its values will be loaded into the molecule when a corresponding dcd file is imported ( Structure \| Animation \| Load... from the menu bar). |
| <molecule>_energy.csv | Per-frame energy values and GaMD parameters in CSV format. Includes information from <molecule>.ene. |
| <molecule>_restart.pdb | Restart file with the atomic coordinates of the final structure in pdb format that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_restart.vel | Restart file with atomic velocities that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_restart.xsc | Restart file with periodic cell parameters and periodic system data that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_restart.xst | Restart file with periodic cell parameters and periodic system data for each frame of the simulation trajectory that can be used to continue the current dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_xplor.psf | Topology containing information about atoms, bonded interactions, and nonbonded interactions in XPLOR format. |
| namd.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the NAMD simulation engine. |

You can analyze results in the same manner as other molecular simulation such as Dynamics (NAMD) . In addition, you should inspect the GaMD Production report to evaluate boost potentials applied during the GaMD simulation:

* Average boost potential: Throughout the simulation, the average boost potential should fluctuate around some mean value. When inspecting the histogram of boost potentials, you should observe an approximately Gaussian distribution.

* Distribution of boost potentials: How well the distribution reflects normality depends on how many total frames are output during the simulation. Thus, when you adjust simulation time, take care in adjusting the report interval. It is recommended that you save at least 1000 frames. The total number of frames can be calculated by dividing Simulation Time (ps) by the Report Interval (ps) .

When interpreting results, keep in mind that GaMD sampling is biased to accelerate sampling. To recover the original free energy landscape, use the Estimate Free Energy Landscape protocol when the per-frame boost potentials are provided in the energy table.

#### Troubleshooting

* If the simulation fails, check that the initial structure was properly minimized and equilibrated. Use Standard Dynamics Cascade to minimize and equilibrate the structure before running GaMD Equilibration, and ensure that GaMD parameters have converged during GaMD Equilibration before running GaMD Production.

* NAMD treats nonbond cutoff slightly different from CHARMm. If a dynamics run is started in CHARMm and continued in NAMD, you might see a spike in total energy, which should go back to normal quickly. In addition, if Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method is used in the electrostatic energy calculation, there is a difference between NAMD and CHARMm: NAMD includes the PME energy in its electrostatic energy term, while CHARMm does not.

#### Further information

NAMD Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog GaMD Theory Analyze Trajectory tool panel Analyze Trajectory Estimate Free Energy Landscape Structure | Animation

# Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_generate_ligand_pairs_for_fep-para.htm

## Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP - Parameters

### Generates ligand pairs based on similarity

Given a set of input typed ligands, generates a set of optimal pairs based on chemical and topological similarity in order to maximize the total similarity of a network spanning the entire set. The set of pairs is intended to be used to run relative FEP calculations and should be used as an input for Set Up Relative FEP Calculations protocol.

The protocol works by first computing a similarity matrix comprising a Maximal Common Substructure (MCS) based metric for each unique pair. From this matrix connections are chosen between ligands such that most similar ligands are connected to the best extent possible, which is accomplished using a maximum similarity algorithm. For a dataset with N ligands, the result is a set of N-1 pairs.

The similarity between any two ligands L1 and L2 is computed as exp[-Beta*(nL1+nL2-2*nMCS)], where nL1, and nL2 are the number of heavy atoms in the two ligands. nMCS is the number of heavy atoms in the MCS and Beta is a user-defined parameter.

Notes:

* Supported forcefields are CHARMm and charmm36

* Chirality differences are perceived based on positions of the substituents attached to chiral centers. Thus, input molecules involving transformations in chirality must be well aligned to each other.

* Similarity between pairs of ligands that have chirality differences in ring atoms is set to 0 to avoid pairing them. This is done because the FEP workflow currently does not support such transformations.

See Also:

* Liu et al. Lead Optimization mapper: automating free energy calculations for lead optimization. J. Comput. Aided. Mol. Des. 2013 , 27 , 755.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Ligands | Specify a MOL2 or DSV file that contains a set of typed ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. Note: Ligands must be typed with CHARMm or charmm36 forcefields. |
| Lead Ligand Name | Optional name of the lead ligand. The set of pairs generated will be ordered by decreasing similarity with respect to the lead. The specified name must be a valid name of a ligand in the Input Typed Ligands . If not provided, the first ligand is considered as the lead. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| MCS Similarity Parameters | Parameters pertaining to the MCS similarity calculation. |
| Score Type | Options available for the similarity score: SimScore = 2*nMCS/(nL1 + nL2) ExpSimScore = exp[-Beta*(nL1+nL2-2*nMCS)] Both measures make use of nL1 and nL2, the number of heavy atoms in each ligand, respectively. In addition, the number of atoms in the Maximal Common Substructure nMCS is also used. Valid Values: SimScore, ExpSimScore |
| Beta | Prefactor in the exponential formula for the calculation of exponential similarity score (ExpSimScore). ExpSimScore = exp[-Beta*(nL1+nL2-2*nMCS)] |
| Proceed After MCSS Timeout | If the two ligands are large (> 600 Da), then the MCS algorithm may not exhaustively detect the entire common region shared by them. This parameter by default is set to False, which would reject ligand pairs if the MCS algorithm times out. However, in many cases the MCS algorithm is able to map a substantial portion of the common region. In this case, the user has the option to set this parameter to True, running the risk of an inaccurate similarity metric for those pairs. Valid Values: True, False |

Specify a MOL2 or DSV file that contains a set of typed ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window.

Note:

* Ligands must be typed with CHARMm or charmm36 forcefields.

Optional name of the lead ligand. The set of pairs generated will be ordered by decreasing similarity with respect to the lead. The specified name must be a valid name of a ligand in the Input Typed Ligands . If not provided, the first ligand is considered as the lead.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Parameters pertaining to the MCS similarity calculation.

Options available for the similarity score:

* SimScore = 2*nMCS/(nL1 + nL2)

* ExpSimScore = exp[-Beta*(nL1+nL2-2*nMCS)]

Both measures make use of nL1 and nL2, the number of heavy atoms in each ligand, respectively. In addition, the number of atoms in the Maximal Common Substructure nMCS is also used.

Valid Values: SimScore, ExpSimScore

Prefactor in the exponential formula for the calculation of exponential similarity score (ExpSimScore).

If the two ligands are large (> 600 Da), then the MCS algorithm may not exhaustively detect the entire common region shared by them. This parameter by default is set to False, which would reject ligand pairs if the MCS algorithm times out. However, in many cases the MCS algorithm is able to map a substantial portion of the common region. In this case, the user has the option to set this parameter to True, running the risk of an inaccurate similarity metric for those pairs.

Valid Values: True, False

# Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_generate_ligand_pairs_for_fep.htm

## Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP protocol allows you to create a set of ligand pairs given a set of congeneric ligands as input. The pairs thus generated constitute a spanning tree which includes each input ligand as a node, and each pair as an edge. The algorithm used to obtain the pairs maximizes chemical similarity and thus the spanning tree is an optimal traversal solution from any ligand in the set to others. This protocol represents the third in the series of steps comprising the FEP workflow:

* Generate Analog Conformations

* Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) , or alternatively, use Change Forcefield tools to type ligands with CHARMm forcefield.

* Set Up Relative FEP Calculations

* Free Energy Perturbation (FEP)

* Collate FEP Simulation Results

The pairs generated here can be used as input for the subsequent protocols in the workflow to obtain the relative free energy difference for each pair and collated to obtain the absolute free energies of the entire set of congeneric ligands.

You can use input ligands that are either manually created or generated using the Generate Analog Conformations protocol. It is important that the ligand geometries are in the frame of reference of the receptor binding site as these geometries will be used as the initial conformation in subsequent FEP calculations.

The protocol first generates a similarity matrix from the Maximal Common Substructure (MCS) between each ligand pair. From this matrix, connections are chosen between ligands such that most similar ligands are connected to the best extent possible, which is accomplished using a similarity maximizing spanning tree generation algorithm. For a dataset with N ligands, the result is a set of N-1 pairs. The similarity between any two ligands L1 and L2 is computed as exp[-Beta*(nL1+nL2-2*nMCS)], where nL1, and nL2 are the number of heavy atoms in the two ligands. nMCS is the number of heavy atoms in the MCS and Beta is a user-defined parameter, set to 0.1 by default. See [Liu at al., 2013]

The successful execution of the protocol results in a PairsForFEP file that contains molecular assemblies, each of which contain two ligands. This file can be used as input for the Set Up Relative FEP Calculations protocol in combination with a typed protein to generate solvated systems for conducting the FEP calculations.

It is recommended that the optional Lead Ligand Name parameter be specified to be the Name of one of the Input Typed Ligands . Specifying this orders the generated pairs in decreasing similarity from the lead ligand. This also sets the direction of perturbation between the pair of ligands systematically from the ligand that is more similar to the lead to the one that is less.

* In the Graphics View, open a set of ligands that have the conformations in the frame of reference of the receptor binding site.

* Open the Simulations | Change Forcefield tools to type the ligands with either the CHARMm or charmm36 forcefields. It is recommended that you type ligands with the charmm36 forcefield using Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype)... .

* Open the Simulations | Run Free Energy Simulations tools and click Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP... .

* Choose a set of ligands for the Input Ligands parameter.

* Set the Lead Ligand Name to that of the lead compound.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* The input ligands must have an assigned forcefield or the protocol will fail. The allowed forcefields are charmm36 and CHARMm.

* The subsequent protocols in the FEP workflow will require the use of a typed protein. Please ensure that you can type the protein with the same forcefield as the ligands before proceeding. The recommended forcefield is charmm36. However, if not all the ligands and the protein can be typed by this forcefield, you should choose CHARMm forcefield to type all molecules.

* Chirality differences are perceived based on positions of the substituents attached to chiral centers. Thus, input molecules involving transformations in chirality must be well aligned to each other.

From a typical run, the following output are produced.

* PairsforFEP.dsv: Contains pairs of ligands, each under a molecular assembly. Use this file as input for Set Up Relative FEP Calculations .

* MCS_Matrix.txt: A text file containing all unique pairs of ligands and their associated MCS similarity.

* Open the Report of the job and click on ViewResults to open the network graph that shows the connectivity network of the ligands and their pairwise similarities. Nodes in this graph represent ligands and edges represent the planned relative FEP calculations to be performed. The display positions of nodes can be modified by selecting a node and moving it by holding down Ctrl and dragging the cursor. Use the middle mouse button to zoom in and out the graph. The size of the nodes can also be modified using the Display Style dialog, for example you can change the Ball size to a different value on the Atom tab.

Nodes in this graph represent ligands and edges represent the planned relative FEP calculations to be performed. The display positions of nodes can be modified by selecting a node and moving it by holding down Ctrl and dragging the cursor. Use the middle mouse button to zoom in and out the graph.

The size of the nodes can also be modified using the Display Style dialog, for example you can change the Ball size to a different value on the Atom tab.

#### Further information

Lead Optimization Tools Run Free Energy Simulations tool

# Measure Trajectory Features - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_measure_trajectory_features-para.htm

## Measure Trajectory Features - Parameters

### Measure features from molecular dynamics trajectories

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Feature Type | Specifies what type of feature to measure from the Input Trajectory . RMSD : measures root-mean-square deviation of all Input Atoms from Reference Atoms . If no Reference Molecule is specified, then the first frame of the Input Trajectory serves as the Reference Molecule . SASA : measures the solvent accessible surface area of each residue from the Input Trajectory . Dihedral : measures dihedrals (phi, psi, chi1, chi2, chi3, chi4) for each residue of the Input Trajectory . Distance : measures distances between contacts according to Distance Type and Distance Cutoff . Pocket Detection : analyzes and identifies transient and static pockets within the protein structure across the Input Trajectory to assess changes in pocket volume according to Pocket Analysis Type and optional Custom Isovalue . Valid Values: RMSD, SASA, Dihedral , Distance |
| Distance Type | Distance Type specifies how to calculate distances between residues. Options include: All Contacts : measures distances for intermolecular and intramolecular contacts. Intermolecular Contacts : measures distances for all residue contacts between separate molecules. Intramolecular Contacts : measures distances between residues on the same molecule that are separated by 6 or more other residues. Valid Values: All Contacts , Intermolecular Contacts, Intramolecular Contacts |
| Distance Cutoff | Distance Cutoff specifies the minimum distance threshold between nearest atoms in two different residues for a contact to be observed. |
| Pocket Analysis Type | Pocket Analysis Type specifies the type of analysis used for characterizing pocket dynamics throughout a molecular dynamics trajectory. Choosing the appropriate analysis type affects how pockets are characterized and what properties are emphasized in the resulting data. Occurrence Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on how frequently they appear at each location throughout the trajectory. This analysis is particularly useful for identifying transient pockets and understanding how often specific pocket regions are accessible during the simulation. It provides insights into the temporal stability and persistence of pocket features. Default isovalue for Occurrence Analysis is 0.5 . Spatial Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on the density or count of alpha spheres (Voronoi vertices) at each location across all snapshots. This type provides a more structural view of the pocket's geometry, highlighting areas with consistently high densities of interaction points and revealing the most prominent pocket regions. The analysis is also influenced by pocket size, with larger pockets typically generating higher density values. Default isovalue for Spatial Analysis is 8 . Valid Values: Occurrence Analysis , Spatial Analysis |
| Custom Isovalue | Enter Custom Isovalue here. Accepted isovalues for Spatial Analysis is a positive float, and for Occurrence Analysis is a float between 0 and 1. Leave blank to use default values. Custom Isovalue sets a threshold that determines which regions are included in the analysis and visualization of pockets. This parameter is crucial for distinguishing pocket regions of interest in Spatial and Occurrence Analysis. Higher Isovalues: In both Occurrence and Spatial Analysis, setting a higher isovalue focuses the analysis on the most pronounced features. In Occurrence Analysis, a high isovalue selects regions that frequently appear as pockets, emphasizing critical functional sites that are regularly accessible throughout the trajectory. For Spatial Analysis, a high isovalue focuses on deeper and larger cavities, highlighting the most prominent structural features of the pocket. Lower Isovalues: Lowering the isovalue includes more regions, capturing broader pocket features. This setting is beneficial for identifying transient pockets that may appear less frequently but could be critical for processes like allosteric regulation or transient protein-protein interactions. In Spatial Analysis, a lower isovalue can help visualize shallower pockets and smaller cavities that may still be functionally relevant. Choosing Isovalues for Different Biological Systems: Enzymes and Receptors: For systems where stable and frequently utilized binding sites are of interest (e.g., in drug design or substrate binding studies), higher isovalues might be more appropriate to focus on highly relevant, consistently present pockets. Transient Protein Complexes: In studies of transient interactions, such as those in signaling pathways or temporary enzyme complexes, lower isovalues can be useful to capture fleeting pockets that may be critical for short-lived interactions. Membrane Proteins: For membrane proteins, where the distinction between internal pockets and the membrane interface is crucial, isovalues might need fine-tuning to differentiate between surface-exposed and buried pockets effectively. Note : Setting the isovalue too high or too low for your specific system might result in no pockets being detected. A very high isovalue could overlook smaller yet significant pockets, while a very low isovalue might clutter the analysis with too many insignificant features, obscuring relevant pockets. |
| Input Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to each trajectory file in Input Trajectory . This file is used as the topology for reading DCD files; thus, each DCD file should share a common topology. |
| Input Atoms | In Discovery Studio, Input Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. In Pipeline Pilot, Input Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Input Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be measured. No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning onto a reference conformation. |
| Input Trajectory | One or more simulations in DCD format. These trajectories will be measured according to the method specified by Feature Type . |
| Input Bias Potentials | Input Bias Potentials is an optional parameter that provides an energy table in CSV format. This table must contain values of the biasing potentials in column named "Boost Potentials", and there should be as many rows as there are frames in the corresponding trajectory. Certain simulations such as Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (GaMD) apply biasing potentials that flatten the free energy landscape and accelerate conformational sampling. Thus, when analyzing distributions of features from biased simulations, it is useful to know the exact biasing potential for each frame. For this reason GaMD simulations will return a CSV file ("*_energy.csv") containing the values of the boost potentials. For each DCD file that you specify in Input Trajectory , you may specify the corresponding CSV file containing boost potentials. When specifying more than one CSV, files should be separated by a comma. Note also that the order in which the CSV files are specified is important, as the first CSV file will correspond to the first DCD file, the second CSV file will correspond to the second DCD file, and so on. |
| Reference Molecule | Typed structure in DSV format corresponding to a reference molecule. The Input Trajectory will be compared to this reference molecule for calculating certain features (i.e. RMSD) or for superposing atomic coordinates from the Input Trajectory onto the atomic coordinates of the Reference Molecule . If a Reference Molecule is required for measuring a feature type and if the molecule is not specified, then the first frame of the first Input Trajectory will be used as the reference. |
| Reference Atoms | In Discovery Studio, Reference Atoms may be specified with an Atom Group. In Pipeline Pilot, Reference Atoms may be specified with a string of atom numbers separated by spaces. Reference Atoms represents the set of atoms that will be yielded while iterating through the Input Trajectory for measuring certain features. No atoms outside of this group can be analyzed; however, atoms outside of this group can be used for superpositioning the Input Trajectory onto a Reference Molecule . Note that if Reference Atoms does not contain the same amount of atoms as Input Atoms , then featurization methods will attempt to match reference and input atoms using a basic, local alignment if required. |
| Superpose Frames on Reference | If set to "True", Superpose Frames on Reference specifies to superpose atoms from the Input Trajectory onto the Reference Molecule . If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are not specified or the number of atoms in the mobile and fixed set are not equal, then the superpositioning method performs a basic, local alignment to match residues of Input Trajectory to the Reference Molecule . Matched residues are then superposed. If Mobile Atoms and Fixed Atoms are specified and contain the same number of atoms, then Mobile Atoms from the Input Trajectory will be superposed onto Fixed Atoms from the Reference Molecule . Valid Values: True, False |
| Mobile Atoms | Specifies the mobile set of atoms from the Input Molecule that will be superposed onto the set of Fixed Atoms . |
| Fixed Atoms | Specifies the fixed set of atoms from the Reference Molecule that the Mobile Atoms from the Input Molecule will be superposed onto. |
| Trajectory Iteration | Specifies the parameters that control iteration through the Input Trajectory . |
| Batch | Specifies how many frames from the Input Trajectory to load during each iteration. Smaller values of Batch will use less memory but require more time to complete. Larger values of Batch will use more memory but require less time to complete. |
| Stride | Specifies how to sample frames from an Input Trajectory . A Stride of "1" means to take every frame, and a Stride of "n" means to take every nth frame after the first frame. |
| Skip | Specifies how many frames to skip from the beginning of each Input Trajectory . |

Specifies what type of feature to measure from the Input Trajectory .

* RMSD : measures root-mean-square deviation of all Input Atoms from Reference Atoms . If no Reference Molecule is specified, then the first frame of the Input Trajectory serves as the Reference Molecule .

* SASA : measures the solvent accessible surface area of each residue from the Input Trajectory .

* Dihedral : measures dihedrals (phi, psi, chi1, chi2, chi3, chi4) for each residue of the Input Trajectory .

* Distance : measures distances between contacts according to Distance Type and Distance Cutoff .

* Pocket Detection : analyzes and identifies transient and static pockets within the protein structure across the Input Trajectory to assess changes in pocket volume according to Pocket Analysis Type and optional Custom Isovalue .

Valid Values: RMSD, SASA, Dihedral , Distance

Distance Type specifies how to calculate distances between residues. Options include:

* All Contacts : measures distances for intermolecular and intramolecular contacts.

* Intermolecular Contacts : measures distances for all residue contacts between separate molecules.

* Intramolecular Contacts : measures distances between residues on the same molecule that are separated by 6 or more other residues.

Valid Values: All Contacts , Intermolecular Contacts, Intramolecular Contacts

Distance Cutoff specifies the minimum distance threshold between nearest atoms in two different residues for a contact to be observed.

* Occurrence Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on how frequently they appear at each location throughout the trajectory. This analysis is particularly useful for identifying transient pockets and understanding how often specific pocket regions are accessible during the simulation. It provides insights into the temporal stability and persistence of pocket features. Default isovalue for Occurrence Analysis is 0.5 .

* Spatial Analysis : Detects and analyzes pockets based on the density or count of alpha spheres (Voronoi vertices) at each location across all snapshots. This type provides a more structural view of the pocket's geometry, highlighting areas with consistently high densities of interaction points and revealing the most prominent pocket regions. The analysis is also influenced by pocket size, with larger pockets typically generating higher density values. Default isovalue for Spatial Analysis is 8 .

Valid Values: Occurrence Analysis , Spatial Analysis

* Higher Isovalues: In both Occurrence and Spatial Analysis, setting a higher isovalue focuses the analysis on the most pronounced features. In Occurrence Analysis, a high isovalue selects regions that frequently appear as pockets, emphasizing critical functional sites that are regularly accessible throughout the trajectory. For Spatial Analysis, a high isovalue focuses on deeper and larger cavities, highlighting the most prominent structural features of the pocket.

* Lower Isovalues: Lowering the isovalue includes more regions, capturing broader pocket features. This setting is beneficial for identifying transient pockets that may appear less frequently but could be critical for processes like allosteric regulation or transient protein-protein interactions. In Spatial Analysis, a lower isovalue can help visualize shallower pockets and smaller cavities that may still be functionally relevant.

* Enzymes and Receptors: For systems where stable and frequently utilized binding sites are of interest (e.g., in drug design or substrate binding studies), higher isovalues might be more appropriate to focus on highly relevant, consistently present pockets.

* Transient Protein Complexes: In studies of transient interactions, such as those in signaling pathways or temporary enzyme complexes, lower isovalues can be useful to capture fleeting pockets that may be critical for short-lived interactions.

* Membrane Proteins: For membrane proteins, where the distinction between internal pockets and the membrane interface is crucial, isovalues might need fine-tuning to differentiate between surface-exposed and buried pockets effectively.
