# Measure Trajectory Features

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_measure_trajectory_features.htm

## Measure Trajectory Features

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

* Analyzing results

Measure Trajectory Features measures time-series features from molecular dynamics trajectories. Supported features include root-mean-square distance from a reference conformation (RMSD), solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), dihedral angles (Dihedral), and intermolecular or intramolecular distances between nearest atoms of residues (Distance), and volume of available binding pockets at each time frame (Pocket Detection). Measurements are restricted to atoms specified in Input Atoms and Reference Atoms .

Measure Trajectory Features removes all solvent atoms (water, anions, and cations) defined in Solvation before measuring time-series features from molecular dynamics trajectories. When a system has been solvated in Discovery Studio , the protocol automatically discards common ion types (SOD, POT, MG, CAL, CLA, SO4, H2PO4, HPO4, NO3) unless they are explicitly included in Input Atoms , preventing these ions from biasing distance calculations or trajectory alignment. If you need to retain a particular ion for analysis (e.g., a metal-binding site), ensure the corresponding atoms are included in the Input Atoms selection, though be aware that retaining highly mobile ions may interfere with proper superimposing of the trajectory.

You can use the dataset generated by Measure Trajectory Features in other analysis methods such as Estimate Free Energy Landscape .

* Load the molecule whose trajectory you want to analyze in a Molecule Window. Ensure that the molecule corresponds to the set of trajectories that will be analyzed. This means that all simulation trajectories must derive from a shared structure from which the structure and forcefield have not been edited. If you are unsure if several simulations share a common forcefield and topology, then analyze trajectories one at a time with the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

If you are unsure if several simulations share a common forcefield and topology, then analyze trajectories one at a time with the output molecule from the same run of the simulation protocol that produced the output trajectory.

* Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Measure Trajectory Features... to open the Measure Trajectory Features dialog.

* Set parameters for the simulation: Select the Feature Type that you want to measure. Set the Input Molecule and Input Trajectory . When measuring features that depend on a frame of reference, you can use the Superpose Frames on Reference parameters to control superpositioning of frames. If no Reference Molecule is specified, the frame of reference defaults to the first frame of the first Input Trajectory . In Discovery Studio , Input Atoms and Reference Atoms are defined with groups created in the Molecule Window. Atoms specified in Input Atoms and Reference Atoms can prevent certain features from being measured. For example, dihedrals require a set of four linked atoms to calculate a single dihedral angle. If only side chain atoms are selected, then Chi1 and Chi2 dihedrals can not be calculated as N and CA atoms will be missing from the atom selections. You can use Mobile Atoms to specify exact atoms to superpose from the Input Molecule , or Fixed Atoms to specify the exact atoms to superpose onto from the Reference Molecule . In the case that either the mobile and fixed atoms are not specified, or the number of mobile and fixed atoms are unequal, superpositioning is attempted by aligning the amino acid sequence of the Input Molecule to the Reference Molecule based on the atoms specified by Input Atoms and Reference Atoms . For details about the parameters, including Input Atoms and Reference Atoms , see Measure Trajectory Features - Parameters .

* Select the Feature Type that you want to measure.

* Set the Input Molecule and Input Trajectory .

* When measuring features that depend on a frame of reference, you can use the Superpose Frames on Reference parameters to control superpositioning of frames. If no Reference Molecule is specified, the frame of reference defaults to the first frame of the first Input Trajectory .

* In Discovery Studio , Input Atoms and Reference Atoms are defined with groups created in the Molecule Window. Atoms specified in Input Atoms and Reference Atoms can prevent certain features from being measured. For example, dihedrals require a set of four linked atoms to calculate a single dihedral angle. If only side chain atoms are selected, then Chi1 and Chi2 dihedrals can not be calculated as N and CA atoms will be missing from the atom selections.

* You can use Mobile Atoms to specify exact atoms to superpose from the Input Molecule , or Fixed Atoms to specify the exact atoms to superpose onto from the Reference Molecule . In the case that either the mobile and fixed atoms are not specified, or the number of mobile and fixed atoms are unequal, superpositioning is attempted by aligning the amino acid sequence of the Input Molecule to the Reference Molecule based on the atoms specified by Input Atoms and Reference Atoms .

For details about the parameters, including Input Atoms and Reference Atoms , see Measure Trajectory Features - Parameters .

* Click Run . The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If you want to measure features from an Input Molecule when the Input Molecule and Reference Molecule are in separate Molecule Windows, make sure that the Measure Trajectory Features protocol is docked into the Discovery Studio window by minimizing the protocol window.

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| simulation_data.csv | The output dataset measured from the input trajectories. |

Results are provided in a table, and units of the measured features are as follows: RMSD in angstroms SASA in squared angstroms Dihedral in radians Distance in angstroms Pocket Detection in cubed angstroms

* RMSD in angstroms

* SASA in squared angstroms

* Dihedral in radians

* Distance in angstroms

* Pocket Detection in cubed angstroms

You can analyze the resulting dataset with Estimate Free Energy Landscape .

#### Troubleshooting

All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it is automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools. If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not complete. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Estimate Free Energy Landscape

# Minimization - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_minimization-para.htm

## Minimization - Parameters

### Performs an energy minimization on a molecule using CHARMm

Updates the coordinates of the molecule and adds energy properties.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

* If part of the molecule is selected, only the selected part will be minimized.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Minimization | Minimization parameters. |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer |
| Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Å). For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Minimization Energy Change | A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase. |
| Minimization Save Results Frequency | When set to a number other than zero, the intermediate results are saved into a file every this number of steps. This will also enables reporting of intermediate progress. Setting to zero means do not save these intermediate results, speeding up the calculation, reducing the required disk space, and turning off progress reporting. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane. Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant. Notes: To add an implicit membrane to a molecule: In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools. In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) or to Generalized Born with Simple SWitching (GBSW), the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a Dielectric Constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. Notes: For GB and GBMV, the dielectric constant is fixed as 1.0 internally and can not be changed. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW or GBIM. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Specifies scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these forcefields. See Also: Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). See Also: Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481. Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments: Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13. Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. |
| Salt Concentration | Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l). Only applicable to GBSW. |
| Input Atomic Radii | Atomic radii used for GBSW and GBMV: van der Waals radii : Default. radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields. See Also : Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. |
| Use Molecular Surface | Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW. Valid Values: True , False |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance . |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Electrostatics | Specifies how to treat long range electrostatics. Three options are available: Automatic : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used if the information for periodic boundary condition (i.e. the BoxShape property of the input molecule) is available, otherwise, the Spherical Cutoff method is used. Spherical Cutoff : the spherical cutoff is used for the electrostatic interactions. Particle Mesh Ewald : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used. Note : When Spherical Cutoff option is selected, all non-bonded energy will be calculated without using periodic boundary condition. If the periodic boundary condition is not set up for the input molecule (e.g., the BoxShape property is not defined), the PME option will not work properly. Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald |
| Kappa | The width of the Gaussian function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ) and 6/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ). |
| Order | The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Minimization Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Apply SHAKE Constraint | Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number of Processors | Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server. Note : The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel. The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel. |
| Run On Grid | Run the protocol on the grid engine. Valid Values: True , False |
| Queue Name | Specify the name of the queue on the grid engine to submit the job to. Leave blank to specify the default queue. |
| Grid Options | An array of command line options to include in the grid engine submit command. The list below shows supported parameters which will be translated into command line options for the supported grid engines. Account=<Project/Account name> Maximum Execution Time=<DD:MM:SS> - LSF does not use seconds Number of Cores=<16> Parallel Environment=<The Parallel Environment to use> - Only needed for SGE Other=<Additional Parameters sent directly to submit command line> Note: If you just want to send a single line "as is" to the submission command, you can omit the "Other=" part. The format will be grid engine specific. For example, you can use the following for a PBS grid engine: -l procs=16 -l walltime=08:00:00 -A PROJECTID If you request multiple cores, you also need to manually set the Number of Processors parameter to the same number as the number of cores. |

Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures.

Minimization parameters.

Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are:

* Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate
vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions.

* Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation.

* Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations.

* Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails.

* Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation.

Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer

Maximum number of cycles for the minimization.

A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Å).

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined.

A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit.

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase.

When set to a number other than zero, the intermediate results are saved into a file every this number of steps. This will also enables reporting of intermediate progress.

Setting to zero means do not save these intermediate results, speeding up the calculation, reducing the required disk space, and turning off progress reporting.

Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation.

Available options are:

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

* Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None .

* Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane.

* Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant.

* To add an implicit membrane to a molecule:

* In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools.

* In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol.

See Also:

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)

Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system.

If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present.

If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent.

Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) or to Generalized Born with Simple SWitching (GBSW), the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a Dielectric Constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons.

* For GB and GBMV, the dielectric constant is fixed as 1.0 internally and can not be changed.

Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW or GBIM.

Specifies scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model.
Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields.
Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield.

Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these forcefields.

* Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773.

Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA.

Valid Values: True , False

Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy.

Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ).

* Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and
conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481.

* Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments:
Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13.

* Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738.

* Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study
of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918.

Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l). Only applicable to GBSW.

Atomic radii used for GBSW and GBMV:

* van der Waals radii : Default.

* radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields.

See Also :

* Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248.

Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al.

Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW.

Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs.

Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored.

Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance .

Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching.

When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance .

When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically.

Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching.

Specifies how to treat long range electrostatics. Three options are available:

* Automatic : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used if the information for periodic boundary condition (i.e. the BoxShape property of the input molecule) is available, otherwise, the Spherical Cutoff method is used.

* Spherical Cutoff : the spherical cutoff is used for the electrostatic interactions.

* Particle Mesh Ewald : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used.

Note :

* When Spherical Cutoff option is selected, all non-bonded energy will be calculated without using periodic boundary condition.

* If the periodic boundary condition is not set up for the input molecule (e.g., the BoxShape property is not defined), the PME option will not work properly.

Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald

The width of the Gaussian function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ) and 6/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ).

The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax.

Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation.

Valid Values: True, False

Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server.

* The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel.

* The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel.

Run the protocol on the grid engine.

# Minimization

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_minimization.htm

## Minimization

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Minimization protocol minimizes the energy of a structure through geometry
optimization.

For example, you can use the Minimization protocol to prepare a crystallographic
protein structure (which might possess some inaccuracies in local molecular
geometries) for molecular dynamics simulation.

To minimize multiple small molecules at once, use the Ligand Minimization (Receptor-Ligand Interactions) protocol.

* Load the structure you wish to minimize into the Graphics View.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Minimization... to open the Minimization dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule . For details about the remaining parameters, see Minimization - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

All dynamics simulations begin with an initial structure that may be derived from experimental data or from other sources. Energy minimization
is performed on structures prior to dynamics to relax the conformation and remove steric overlap that produces bad contacts.

The results of a minimization may be assessed by comparing the energies and energy gradients of the final structure with those of the initial
structure. These values are presented in the report file, and as
properties in the output file. The "Minimization Criteria" property
details whether the minimization converged to within convergence
criteria. If the minimization failed to converged you will get a
message such as: Minimization exiting with number of steps
limit (200) exceeded . If the minimization failed to converge,
check the convergence criteria (Minimization RMS Gradient and
Minimization Energy Change) or try running with a larger number of
steps.
You should also check the RMS movement between the final and initial structures.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The molecule output after energy minimization with energy properties added to the molecule. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language (FFML) file used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the charmm simulation engine. |

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Calculate Energy Dynamics (Equilibration) Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) Dynamics (Production) Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# Minimization (QM-MM) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_minimization_qm-mm-para.htm

## Minimization (QM-MM) - Parameters

### Performs an energy minimization on a molecule using QUANTUMm

Minimizes the energy of a molecule using a hybrid of quantum and classical molecular mechanics (QM-MM). In this approach, some atoms are treated by classical molecular mechanics (CHARMm) and some are treated by quantum mechanics (DMol3).

In addition to minimizing the atom coordinates, the QM, MM, total, and interaction energy for both the initial and final structures are also reported.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with the CHARMm forcefield.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a CHARMm typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Quantum Atoms | Allows selection of atoms to be used as the quantum region. In Discovery Studio, a group of atoms can be selected. In Pipeline Pilot, standard CHARMm selection syntax can be used. Note : The speed of the calculation depends on this parameter. There is a limit of 1000 atoms but a job of this size may take a long time to finish. |
| Minimization | The Minimization group contains settings that control the geometry optimization. |
| Max Gradient | The maximum magnitude of any gradient component (in kcal/mol/Å) used to determine convergence of geometry optimization. |
| Max Steps | The maximum number of steps to be used in geometry optimization. |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. |
| DMol3 Settings | Specify settings for the quantum calculation. |
| Quality | The accuracy of the quantum calculation. Available options are: Ultra coarse: Uses minimal basis set with SCF density convergence of 5.0e-4. Coarse: Uses DN basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-4. Medium: Uses DND basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-5. Fine: Uses DNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-6. Ultra fine: Uses TNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-7. Valid Values: Ultra coarse, Coarse, Medium , Fine, Ultra fine |
| Functional | The exchange-correlation functional to be used in the quantum calculation. Local Density Approximation (LDA) functionals: PWC VWN Gradient corrected Generalized Gradient Approximations (GGA) functionals: PW91 BP PBE BLYP BOP VWN-BP RPBE HCTH Hybrid functional: B3LYP Notes : GGA provides a better overall description of the electronic subsystem than the LDA functionals. The LDA description tends to overbind atoms, so that the bond lengths and the cell volume are usually underestimated by a few percent and the bulk modulus is correspondingly overestimated. GGA corrects this error but may underbind instead, leading to slightly long bond lengths. B3LYP includes a portion of exact exchange from Hartree-Fock theory along with exchange and correlation contributions from other functionals with carefully chosen weights. The weights are obtained by fitting to experimental data. B3LYP gives better results but requires significantly more CPU time. Valid Values: PWC, VWN, PW91, BP, PBE , BLYP, BOP, VWN-BP, RPBE, HCTH, B3LYP |
| Add Dispersion Correction | Specify whether to add a dispersion correction to the DFT energy. This option is available when Functional is: "PBE", "PW91" "VWN", "PWC". Notes : The TS scheme is used when the Functional is "PBE" The OBS scheme is used when the Functional is "PWC", "VWN", "PW91". Valid Values: True, False |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Advanced Minimization | Allows you specify additional settings for controlling the geometry optimization. |
| Minimization Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied during minimization. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Constraints tool panel. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm selection syntax. |
| Use Micro-iterative Scheme | Use the micro-iterative optimization scheme. This aims to reduce the number of quantum calculations by optimizing the MM region with fixed ESP charges for each geometry of the QM atoms. Valid Values: True, False |
| Advanced DMol3 Settings | Allows you specify additional settings for the quantum calculation. |
| Multiplicity | The spin multiplicity for the quantum calculation. Available options are: Smart - use Spin Restricted if the number of electrons is even, otherwise use Auto. Spin Restricted Auto - perform a spin unrestricted calculation to determine the optimal spin state. Singlet Doublet Triplet Quartet Quintet Sextet Septet Octet Valid Values: Smart , Spin Restricted, Auto, Singlet, Doublet, Triplet, Quartet, Quintet, Sextet, Septet, Octet |
| Charge | The charge on the QM region to be used in the quantum calculation. If unspecified, the sum of formal charges on the atoms in the QM region is used. Note : When "Expand Quantum Atoms" from the Advanced parameters is set, the only allowed option is to leave the QM region charge unspecified. |
| Occupancy | The occupancy of electronic levels in the quantum calculation. Available options are: Thermal : use thermal smearing of electronic occupancy. Fermi : fill the lowest available electronic levels. Valid Values: Thermal , Fermi |
| Maximum SCF cycles | Maximum SCF iterations the QM server is allowed at each geometry. |
| Expand Quantum Atoms | If requested, allows the QUANTUMm server to assign MM atom atoms to the quantum region in order to make sure that the Quantum Atoms group consists of complete MM charge groups. In this case, the quantum region net charge is always determined by the sum of its atoms' formal charges. Valid Values: True , False |
| Electronic Embedding Method | Specifies the treatment of atomic charges in the QM-MM boundary region. Available options are: Neglect boundary charges - charges on MM atoms in a charge group connected to the QM region are neglected. Disperse boundary charges - charges on MM atoms connected to the QM region are distributed over the MM atoms connected to those boundary MM atoms. Valid Values: Neglect boundary charges , Disperse boundary charges |
| Creates Molecular Orbitals | Whether to create Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO) and Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital (LUMO) in the output. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number of Processors | When set to a value greater than 1, each DMol3 step of the calculation is performed as a parallel calculation using the specified number of parallel processes. When set to 1, a serial calculation is performed. |
| Run On Grid | Run the protocol on the grid engine. Valid Values: True , False |
| Queue Name | Specify the name of the queue on the grid engine to submit the job to. Leave blank to specify the default queue. |
| Grid Options | An array of command line options to include in the grid engine submit command. The list below shows supported parameters which will be translated into command line options for the supported grid engines. * If you request multiple cores, you also need to manually set the Number of Processors parameter to the same number as the number of cores.

# Minimization (QM-MM)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_minimization_qm-mm.htm

## Minimization (QM-MM)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Minimization (QM-MM) protocol minimizes the energy of a structure through geometry optimization using the hybrid delocalized internal coordinate (HDLC) optimizer developed by
Billeter et al. [Billeter et al., 2000] . The QM region of atoms is treated by a quantum
calculation using the DMol 3 server and the rest, MM, is handled by the CHARMm forcefield.

The protocol also gives an estimate of the non-covalent QM-MM interaction energy at the final geometry and updates the partial charges in the quantum region with the ESP charges from the last quantum calculation.

Note: The QM-MM simulation protocols require the following:

* The complete system is contained in one molecule. To merge several molecules into a single Molecule Window, drag and drop them in the Hierarchy View .

* The complete system (i.e., QM and MM atoms) is typed with the CHARMm forcefield. To type the system, use the Apply Forcefield command from the Change Forcefield tools.

* Open the structure you wish to minimize into the Graphics View.

* Make sure that the simulation system consists of one molecule. To do this, open the Hierarchy View and
drag all required molecules under a single
molecule in the hierarchy. You can only select a single molecule
to run this calculation. However, the molecule can contain
multiple disconnected fragments.

* Make sure that the CHARMm forcefield has been applied to the molecule. Use the Apply Forcefield command in the Change Forcefield tool panel to assign a forcefield to the simulation system. The
atoms that will be treated quantum mechanically must be included in the
typing.

* Select the atoms that you wish to use as the QM region and create a group by choosing Edit | Group... from the menu bar. The QM region must span whole charge groups; otherwise, the calculation will stop at an early stage with the Report.htm output file stating "QM region specified is not valid". Refer to Cutting covalent QM-MM bonds how to provide a compliant QM region.

The QM region must span whole charge groups; otherwise, the calculation will stop at an early stage with the Report.htm output file stating "QM region specified is not valid". Refer to Cutting covalent QM-MM bonds how to provide a compliant QM region.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Minimization (QM-MM).... to open the Minimization (QM-MM) dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule Choose the loaded molecule. Quantum Atoms Choose the group of atoms you created to define the QM region. For details about the remaining parameters, see Minimization (QM-MM) - Parameters . For more information, refer to the guidelines in Setting up QM-MM calculations and DMol 3 settings in the QM-MM protocols .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Choose the loaded molecule. |
| Quantum Atoms | Choose the group of atoms you created to define the QM region. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Minimization (QM-MM) - Parameters . For more information, refer to the guidelines in Setting up QM-MM calculations and DMol 3 settings in the QM-MM protocols .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Report.htm includes a summary of key energy terms, reported at the initial and final structures:

* QUANTUMm Energy : This is the total QM-MM potential energy (i.e. the sum of the "QM energy" and the "MM energy" below).

* QM Energy : This is the potential energy of the QM subsystem, i.e. the expectation value of the QM hamiltonian, including the
classical Coulomb repulsion energy between the atomic nuclei in the QM system. Note that it contains the energetic effects from the QM
atoms' Coulomb interaction with the MM point charges, and also contributions from the terminating link atoms (if bonds had to be broken
between the QM and MM fragment).

* MM Energy : This is the potential energy of the MM subsystem. It contains the van der Waals interaction energy between the QM and the MM atoms and bonding
energy contributions from the boundary in cases where bonds stretch from the MM into the QM region.

* Additional MM Energy Terms : In present simulations, these will always be zero.

* QM/MM Electrostatic Interaction Energy : This is the Coulomb interaction energy between the electron density of the QM atoms and the point charges of the
MM atoms. Note that this energy is an approximation to the "full" QM-MM electrostatic energy since the energy to polarize the QM density from its vacuum state is not included.

* QM/MM van der Waals Interaction Energy : This is calculated by the charmm simulation engine by applying the van der Waals interaction
forcefield parameters defined for the complete system.

* QM/MM Interaction Energy : The sum of "QM/MM Electrostatic Interaction Energy" and "QM/MM van der Waals Interaction Energy".

Energy contributions from harmonic constraints are omitted from any of the reported energy terms -
this is contrast to the Minimization Protocol , where these are part of the CHARMm total potential energy.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The minimized molecule with the partial charges of the atoms in the quantum region updated from the ESP charges of the last QM calculation. |
| dmol3.log | The output of the final DMol 3 phase of the calculation including the final coordinates of the QM region, a summary of the DMol 3 settings used, and the results for each SCF iteration. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The minimized molecule. |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |
| quantumm.log | Contains a progress report of the QM-MM calculation. |

The QM-MM simulation server does not currently produce restart or trajectory files that can be used
in Discovery Studio .

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing

# MSLD Bias Optimization and Production - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_msld_biasopt_and_production-para.htm

## MSLD Bias Optimization and Production - Parameters

### MSLD Bias Optimization and Production

Runs MSLD bias optimization and production simulations on input Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) systems. The input systems are prepared using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol. A multi-phase MSLD bias optimization calculation is performed, which is followed by multiple trajectories of production simulations for each system.

Biasing potentials are necessary to allow for efficient transitions between multiple substituents during production MSLD simulations and need to be optimized for each system. Bias optimization can involve up to three phases. Each phase involves iterative optimization of four types of biasing potentials employed in MSLD simulations, in which short simulations are run. At the end of each iteration, the free energy profile for each substituent as a function of lambda is calculated, and the biasing potentials are adjusted to enhance the flatness of the profiles. Multiple iterations of bias optimization allow for obtaining flattened landscapes leading to efficient exchange of substituents and therefore enhanced sampling in MSLD simulations. The free energy profiles corresponding to pairwise exchanges between substituents on a site are also calculated, and targeted for flattening. Convergence is determined by the flatness of the computed free energy landscapes at the end of each iteration and is quantified by root mean squared deviation (RMSD) with respect to a fully flat, zero free energy profile. Averages computed over single and pairwise lambda profiles are used to determine flatness.

Iterations are performed until the free energy landscape flatness criteria are met up to the Maximum Number of Iterations . By default, the three phases involve 100, 10, and 5 iterations of 100ps, 1ns, and 2ns, for phases 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Each phase begins with the initial conformation, but with the biases optimized from the prior phase.

Following bias optimization, multiple trajectories of production MSLD production simulations are run to calculate relative free energies of the different ligands present in the system. Multiple simulations can be run using this protocol in order to obtain error estimates from averaging results. The simulations can be optionally equilibrated for a time set by Equilibration Time (ps) , prior to running production which is set by Simulation Time (ps) .

Upon completion of the simulations, results are post-processed and a statistical analysis is performed.

In addition to multi-site free energy values, single-site values are also calculated. These values are relative free energies local to each site and do not take cooperative effects from other sites into account and at best are an approximate estimate. They can be used to understand individual site preferences for different substituents when sampling is not adequate enough to allow for simultaneous population of substituents on all sites.

For binding free energy calculations, the solvated free ligand, and the solvated protein-ligand complex are the required input systems.

Notes:

* Use BLaDE is enabled by default when using DOMDEC GPU to leverage the BLaDE platform for a significant speed increase.

* BLaDE requires PME electrostatics and restraints are not fully supported in BLaDE.

* This protocol is only supported on Linux servers.

See Also:

* Hayes et al. Adaptive Landscape Flattening Accelerates Sampling of Alchemical Space in Multisite Lambda Dynamics. J. Phys. Chem. B 2017 , 121 , 3626.

* Hayes et al. Approaching Protein Design with Multisite Lambda Dynamics: Accurate and Scalable Mutational Folding Free
Energies in T4 Lysozyme. Prot. Sci. 2018 , 27 , 1910.

* Raman et al. Automated, Accurate, and Scalable Relative Protein-Ligand Binding Free Energy Calculations using Lambda Dynamics. ChemRxiv 2020 .

# MSLD Bias Optimization and Production

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_msld_biasopt_and_production.htm

## MSLD Bias Optimization and Production

* Description

* Considerations for running

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol allows you to optimize biasing potential functions that are added to the simulation energy to facilitate transitions between substituents during a Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) simulation and subsequent production simulations. For a background on lamda dynamics, see [Kong and Brooks, 1996] , [Knight and Brooks, 2011] , and [Raman et al., 2020] .

Bias optimization is accomplished by running a series of short MSLD simulations iteratively, learning the free energy landscape of transformations between the different substituents on each site, and 
adjusting the potentials to allow for the flattening of the free energy 
landscape. The biasing potentials must be optimized for each molecular system in a custom manner, and thus this step is necessary prior to running the production stage. The MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol
performs the following:

* Optimize bias in three phases, with each phase progressively 
increasing iteration length to allow for increasingly refined bias 
estimates.

* Initiate multiple production 
simulations. The 
substituents on each site in the MSLD system are sampled 
simultaneously and the statistical occurrences of each ligand with the 
multi-site combinatorial substitutions are collected to 
calculate the relative free energies of the corresponding ligands.

* Collate results obtained for the protein-ligand complex and free ligand 
systems to calculate binding free energies.

The MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol MSLD systems prepared using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol as input. 
For calculating binding free energies, solvated protein-ligand complex 
and solvated ligand systems are required as input. The MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol represents the fourth step of the MSLD workflow:

* Type the ligands with charmm36 forcefield using the Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) protocol or with CHARMm using Apply Forcefield command on the Change Forcefield tool panel.

* Generate input ligands for the calculation using the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD for MSLD protocol.

* Generate simulation systems using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol.

* Optimize biasing potential functions and run production simulations using the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol.

* Calculate the relative binding free energies by analyzing the results using the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol.

In this protocol, four biasing potential functions are optimized and 
used in production simulations. Each site in the ligand is considered independent for the purpose of bias optimization. 
By default, the first, second, and third phases of bias optimization are 
100 x 100 ps, 10 x 1 ns, and 5 x 2 ns simulations. Later 
phases run fewer iterations with longer simulations, which supports 
increasingly refined adjustments to biases. You can reduce the run time by disabling 
later phases of bias optimization. However, that may affect accuracy for 
systems involving a large number of ligands, or large differences in 
substituent size. See [Raman et al., 2020] and [Hayes at al., 2017] for details.

* For each site, the free energy landscape as a function of lambda is evaluated and flattened by adding the biasing potentials.

* Free energy landscapes are calculated for each unique pair of substituents at each site to facilitate pairwise transitions.

* At the end of each iteration, the protocol calculates composite flatness parameters corresponding to single ( Average RMSD ) and pairwise ( Average Pairwise RMSD ) free energy. Values close to zero imply highly flattened landscapes, which are desirable for enhanced transitions between substituents, and improve efficiency in subsequent production calculations.

Following bias optimization, multiple independent 
simulations are run for each input system to allow for the calculation of the standard 
deviation as an estimate of the uncertainties of the predictions. Three 20 
ns simulations are run by default. Upon completion of the simulations, 
the lambda trajectory data is post-processed and a statistical analysis 
is performed. The relative free energy values for the combinatorial 
library are calculated as the difference of the average free energy in 
the complex state and the same in free ligand state. The relative free 
energies are normalized with respect to the first ligand in the 
combinatorial library, which has the core substituent on all sites. As a 
result, the first ligand will have zero free energy.

For challenging 
multi-site systems with a large number of combinatorial ligands, all ligands may not be sampled during the production simulations. For such cases, the additive free 
energy table can provide approximate estimates. The additive free 
energies reported for the combinatorial library neglect cooperativity 
between different sites, but may provide better sampling statistics than the 
multi-site estimates since they are calculated based on single site probabilities alone. While the estimates reported in the free energy table are more rigorous in nature as
they account for inter-site cooperativity, published results on many protein-ligand test systems have shown the additive estimates to be useful when the former are unavailable.
Additionally, single-site free energy estimates are presented, from which the additive free energies are calculated. 
These values are relative free energies local to each site. They allow 
assessment of the affinities of substituents on each site independent of 
other sites. For more information, see [Raman et al., 2020] .

In addition to relative binding free energies, the protocol also supports the calculation of relative hydration free energies. Hydration free energy calculations require the ligand system in solvent and vacuum. Owing to the smaller size of these systems compared to solvated complex system, hydration free energy calculations require significantly less time to complete.

* The protocol is not supported on Windows servers.

* It is recommended that the protocol be run on the DOMDEC GPU 
platform for speed. The DOMDEC GPU platform only supports a single 
GPU.

* When running on a GPU platform, increasing the Number of Cores per Simulation from 1 to 2, 4, or 8 will typically result in better performance.

* Binding, 
Hydration, and Single free energy calculations are supported Binding requires the 
solvated complex and solvated ligand as inputs. Hydration requires the solvated ligand and vacuum ligand as 
inputs. Single allows you to run one of the three possible 
systems. This may be useful if you want to re-run either the complex or the ligand system, but not both. After running two single calculations, use the Collate 
MSLD Simulation Results protocol to combine the 
results.

* Binding requires the 
solvated complex and solvated ligand as inputs.

* Hydration requires the solvated ligand and vacuum ligand as 
inputs.

* Single allows you to run one of the three possible 
systems. This may be useful if you want to re-run either the complex or the ligand system, but not both. After running two single calculations, use the Collate 
MSLD Simulation Results protocol to combine the 
results.

* To run the protocol on a server with a grid engine: Enable Parallel Processing and Run on Grid , and specify Grid Options to request one GPU and the appropriate number of CPUs. The Number of Cores per Simulation and Grid Options parameters should specify the same number of CPU cores. The Number of Cores per Simulation and Grid Options values pertain to a single simulation. The protocol automatically requests the specified resource for each independent simulation separately. For example, when running 3 independent simulations, if you set Number of Cores per Simulation to 4 CPUs and Grid Options to 1 GPU, 
the protocol will request 1 GPU and 4 CPUs for each simulation.

* Enable Parallel Processing and Run on Grid , and specify Grid Options to request one GPU and the appropriate number of CPUs.

* The Number of Cores per Simulation and Grid Options parameters should specify the same number of CPU cores.

* The Number of Cores per Simulation and Grid Options values pertain to a single simulation. The protocol automatically requests the specified resource for each independent simulation separately. For example, when running 3 independent simulations, if you set Number of Cores per Simulation to 4 CPUs and Grid Options to 1 GPU, 
the protocol will request 1 GPU and 4 CPUs for each simulation.

* To run the protocol on a non-grid server, set GPU Device to a specific GPU index and the Number of Cores per Simulation to the appropriate number of CPUs. 
If multiple GPUs are available, the GPU indices can be specified separated by comma (for example, 0,1). On non-grid systems, use the Parallel Processing Server Processes parameter to control the number of simulations being run on each GPU (see MSLD Bias Optimization and Production - Parameters .)

On non-grid systems, use the Parallel Processing Server Processes parameter to control the number of simulations being run on each GPU (see MSLD Bias Optimization and Production - Parameters .)

* For large combinatorial libraries or systems that involve chemically and structurally diverse substituents, enabling Phase 3 of bias optimization may result in improved accuracy. For such systems, increasing the Number of Simulations parameter to 6 and Number of Simulations to Combine parameter to 2 would 
combine the six 20 ns simulations into three 40 ns segments resulting in better sampling and therefore more accurate predictions.

* The analysis at the end of the simulations may require high memory. If a long running task fails due to insufficient memory, you can still analyze the results using the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol if the simulations finished successfully ( prod.lmd files are available in the simulation directories in the Output folder.)

* In the Graphics View, open MSLD molecules prepared using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol.

* Open the Simulations | Run Free Energy Simulations tools and click MSLD Bias Optimization 
and Production... .

* For a binding free energy calculation, under Input MSLD Systems, 
set Solvated Complex to the solvated 
protein-ligand complex molecule. Set Solvated Ligand to the solvated 
MSLD ligand molecule.

* Set Platform to DOMDEC GPU .

* For details about the remaining parameters, see MSLD Bias Optimization and Production - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

#### Restarting

You can restart the bias optimization stage by providing input 
molecules that were subject to prior bias optimization. To restart bias 
optimization, set Bias Optimization to Restart and change the 
number of iterations accordingly. You can also subject a set of bias 
optimized systems to production by setting Bias Optimization to None , and Production to True .

The report from the protocol displays the calculated relative free energy values for each ligand in the combinatorial library. A table lists the average free energy in the ligand and complex states, and a difference of these free energies as the average relative binding free energy, which are normalized with respect to the free energy of the first ligand that models the core substituents on all sites. Additionally, additive and single-site free energy tables are displayed for multi-site systems.

#### Output

The following files are created in the Output directory. If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| BiasOpt_Phase<N>.mol2 | The output molecules containing the optimized bias information from phase N. |
| Phase<N>_Bias_Estimates.htm | Estimates of free energy differences obtained from optimized fixed biases from phase N. |
| Results/Plots.html | A report that plots the single and pairwise lambda free energy landscapes from the final iteration. |
| Ligands with calculated free energies | Combinatorial ligand library along with the calculated ΔΔG values. |
| Free energy table | CSV file with the combinatorial ligand library along with the calculated ΔΔG values. |
| Single site free energy table | CSV file with the single site ΔΔG values also shown in the single-site tables in the Report . |
| <System>/<Index>/prod.dcd | Contains the simulation trajectory, where <System> refers to Complex/Ligand/Vaccum system. |
| <System>/<Index>/charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |
| <System>/<Index>/prod.lmd | Contains lambda trajectory output from the simulation. This file for each trajectory can be re-processed by the Collate MSLD Simulation Results . |

#### Next step

The protocol provides the calculated free energies needed to 
prioritize ligands in accordance with binding affinity. You can 
optionally re-analyze the results using Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol to calculate the free energies with a different lambda threshold 
value.

# Collate MSLD Simulation Results - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_msld_collate-para.htm

## Collate MSLD Simulation Results - Parameters

### Collects and analyzes results from MSLD simulations

Collects the results from multiple MSLD calculations performed using the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol and re-calculates the free energies for the ligands of the combinatorial library.

As one of the inputs, the protocol requires the MSLD multi-topology molecule, which could be either the ligand system or the protein-ligand complex system. In addition, the protocol requires the specification of two sets of Lambda trajectory files generated by MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol. One set of the files MSLD pertains to the ligands in solution, and the other for the protein-ligand complexes in solution. Multiple .lmd files (prod.lmd) corresponding to each independent simulation can be specified.

The protocol analyzes each simulation trajectory and calculates averaged free energy values over the independent simulations and the corresponding standard deviation. The relative free energy values for the combinatorial library is calculated as the difference of the average free energy in the complex state and the same in free ligand state. The relative free energies are normalized with respect to the the first ligand in the combinatorial library which has the core substituent on all sites, as a result of which the first ligand will have zero free energy.

The Lambda Threshold parameter determines the value of Lambda above which any substituent is considered to be in its end-state or active. It should be set to a value very close to 1. For certain challenging systems which exhibit a lack of sampling for a large number of ligands, setting it to lower values may improve the population statistics and allow for obtaining approximate free energy estimates. However, it should be noted that reducing the threshold from the default value of 0.99 deviates the free energy values from the exact estimate.

Another way to obtain an approximate estimate for ligands that are not sampled, is to sum up the single site estimates corresponding to the substituents. However, it should be noted that this estimate neglects the cooperativity between the sites.

Notes:

* For ligands that are not sampled in either the free ligand or the complex state simulations, the free energy cannot be calculated, which is indicated by 'NA'.

* If the first ligand is not sampled at all in the simulations, then the free energies are not normalized.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify any one of the molecular structures containing the multi-topology molecule. This can the input structure used for the ligand system in the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing the MSLD system, the supported file formats are DSV and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Lambda Trajectory Files Ligand | The files containing the Lambda trajectory output of MSLD simulation for the ligand system. In Discovery Studio, choose a list of folders containing these files. |
| Lambda Trajectory Files Complex | The files containing the Lambda trajectory output of MSLD simulation for the protein-ligand complex system. In Discovery Studio, choose a list of folders containing these files. |
| Lambda Threshold | The value of Lambda that should be exceeded for a substituent to be considered in its end state. This should be a value very close to unity. |
| Number of Simulations to Combine | Number of Simulations to combine. By setting this to a number greater than one, data from multiple simulations can be combined into one. |
