# Collate MSLD Simulation Results

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_msld_collate.htm

## Collate MSLD Simulation Results

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol allows you to re-calculate the relative binding free energies by analyzing the results of the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol. The relative binding free energies of a combinatorial library of ligands modeled in the MSLD systems are calculated with respect to the free energy of the core ligand. The Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol represents the fifth optional step of the MSLD workflow:

* Type the ligands with charmm36 forcefield using the Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) protocol or with CHARMm using Apply Forcefield command on the Change Forcefield tool panel.

* Generate input ligands for the calculation using the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD for MSLD protocol.

* Generate simulation systems using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol.

* Optimize biasing potential functions and run production simulations using the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol.

* Calculate the relative binding free energies by analyzing the results using the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol.

The Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol uses the lambda trajectory files ( prod.lmd ) generated for two systems from the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol to calculate free energies. The lambda files represent the solvated free ligand MSLD system and the complex with the protein. Each of the two runs may involve multiple trajectories.

Each lambda trajectory file is processed to calculate averaged free energy values for the independent ligand and protein-ligand complex simulations and corresponding standard deviation for both systems. The relative free energy values for the combinatorial library is calculated as the difference of the average free energy in the complex state and the same in free ligand state. The relative free energies are normalized with respect to the first ligand in the combinatorial library, which has the core substituent on all sites. As a result, the first ligand will have zero free energy.

In addition to multi-site free energy values, single-site values are also calculated. These values are relative free energies local to each site and do not take cooperative effects from other sites into account and at best are a rough estimate.

This protocol may require high memory. For analyzing trajectories longer than 20ns, you can rerun the protocol on a server with higher memory (16GB) in the case of a failure.

* In the Graphics View, open one of the molecules from the input of the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol for the free ligand system.

* Open the Simulations | Run Free Energy Simulations tools and click Collate MSLD Simulation Results... .

* Set Input Typed Molecule to one of the MSLD molecules from the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol run.

* Set Lambda Trajectory Files Ligand and Lambda Trajectory Files Complex to the appropriate subdirectory in the Output directory of the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol run.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Collate MSLD Simulation Results - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The results are reported as follows:

* The Multi-Site Free Energy table in the Report lists the averaged free energies computed for each combinatorial ligand, along with a standard deviation.

* The Calc ΔΔG column contains the relative binding free energy for each combinatorial ligand, which can be used to select ligands that bind favorably to the protein. More negative values indicate more favorable binding.

* The StDev column reports the standard deviation of the calculated ΔΔG values arising from averaging results from multiple production runs for both the ligand and protein-ligand complex states.

* Average free energies are reported for the free ligand and the protein-ligand complex states. Cases where a substituent is not sampled are indicated by NA. Single-Site Free Energy tables list the free energy values for each site calculated independent of other sites.

* Occasionally, depending on the number of combinatorial ligands in the MSLD system, not all ligands may be sampled, which leads to NA values for free energy estimates. A workaround for obtaining an approximate estimate for ligands that are not sampled is to calculate the sum the single site estimates corresponding to the substituents. Note that this estimate neglects the cooperativity between the sites.

* The Lambda Threshold parameter determines the value of lambda above which any substituent is considered to be in its end-state or active. It should be set to a value very close to 1. For certain challenging systems that exhibit a lack of sampling for a large number of ligands, setting it to a lower value may improve the population statistics and allow for obtaining approximate free energy estimates. Note that reducing the threshold from the default value of 0.99 deviates the free energy values from the exact estimate.

#### Output

The following files are produced for a typical run.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Ligands with calculated free energies | Combinatorial ligand library along with the calculated ΔΔG values. |
| Free energy table | CSV file with the combinatorial ligand library along with the calculated ΔΔG values. |
| Single site free energy table | CSV file with the single site ΔΔG values also shown in the single-site tables in the Report . |

#### Further information

Lead Optimization Tools Run Free Energy Simulations tool

## Enumerate Ligands for MSLD

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol allows you to generate input ligands for setting up Multi-Site Lambda dynamics (MSLD) calculations. For a background on lamda dynamics, see [Kong and Brooks, 1996] , [Knight and Brooks, 2011] , and [Raman et al., 2020] .

The inputs include a core ligand, one or more sites of modification specified, and choice of R-groups or substituents at each site. The protocol will generate a list of ligands that will serve as input for the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol. The Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol represents the second step of the MSLD workflow:

* Generate input ligands for the calculation using the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD for MSLD protocol.

* Generate simulation systems using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol.

* Optimize biasing potential functions and run production simulations using the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol.

* Calculate the relative binding free energies by analyzing the results using the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol.

The core ligand must be in the same frame of reference as the receptor binding site. If the core ligand is typed, the generated ligands are typed with the same forcefield. Two forcefields are supported: charmm36 and CHARMm. The output ligands contain an MSLD Site property which indicates whether it is the core ligand (MSLD Site=0) or represents a substituent (MSLD Site=1,2,..).

* Select one or more Hydrogen atoms in the core ligand to be defined as substitution sites. Only Hydrogens can be selected to designate sites. It is recommended that the parent atoms of selected hydrogens 
are separated by 4 bonds or more to ensure consistent atom type assignment
to the core of all enumerated variants.

* Set Core Structure to the desired ligand.

* Set MSLD Sites to Create New Group From Selection... .

* Set R Groups for each site from the available options for groups. You can add new groups by modifying the Advanced | Custom Substituents parameter.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

One file containing the enumerated ligands is produced for a typical run. It contains the input core molecule, and the enumerated ligands. Each enumerated ligand models one modification at a single site.

file containing the enumerated ligands as input for the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol.

# Set Up MSLD Calculations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_msld_setup-para.htm

## Set Up MSLD Calculations - Parameters

### Generates simulation systems for MSLD

Prepares structures to run Multi Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) calculations, given multiple typed ligands, and a typed protein. The input ligands must have the "MSLD Site" property which encodes whether it is the core ligand (MSLD Site=0) or represents a substituent (MSLD Site=1,2,..). Only one core ligand is allowed. Each non-core ligand serves to indicate a substituent at a specific site and its chemical structure should differ from the core ligand at only a single site.

A MSLD simulation of a protein-ligand system represents a competitive binding process where the multiple substituents on each site in the ligand compete for interactions with the protein and surrounding environment. Multiple substituents competing at multiple sites results in sampling of a large number of combinations or physical ligands in a single simulation. The first substituent in each site is the one represented by the core ligand, whereas the remaining ones are assigned based on the non-core ligands supplied as input to the protocol.

The protocol uses the maximum common substructure (MCS) method to detect the common and different parts between the core ligand and non-core ligands designated for each site separately. This results in as many MCS structures as the number of sites. The MCS is further shrunk based on differences in partial charges or atom types. An intersection of atoms from the multiple calculated MCS structures is performed to identify the atoms that belong to a common core, and those that needed to be modeled to represent the different substituents on each site.

A solvated ligand system and a solvated protein-ligand complex are generated which are used for the MSLD Bias Optimization protocol.

The input ligands for this protocol may be prepared using the following steps:

* The Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol can be used to generate the ligand set in the frame of reference of the binding site.

* The Forcefield tool panel from the Discovery Studio client can be used to assign either CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield to the ligands and to the protein.

Notes:

* Hydrogens must be present in the ligands.

Note: Ligands must be typed with CHARMm or charmm36 forcefields. |

# Set Up MSLD Calculations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_msld_setup.htm

## Set Up MSLD Calculations

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol generates simulation systems for performing Multi-Site Lambda Dynamics (MSLD) calculations to determine relative binding free energies. For a background on lamda dynamics, see [Kong and Brooks, 1996] , [Knight and Brooks, 2011] , and [Raman et al., 2020] .

The inputs include a set of ligands and a protein typed with the same forcefield. The output systems are prepared for calculation of the relative binding free energies of a combinatorial library of ligands. The Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol represents the third step of the MSLD workflow:

* Type the ligands with charmm36 forcefield using the Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) protocol or with CHARMm using Apply Forcefield command on the Change Forcefield tool panel.

* Generate input ligands for the calculation using the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD for MSLD protocol.

* Generate simulation systems using the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol.

* Optimize biasing potential functions and run production simulations using the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol.

* Calculate the relative binding free energies by analyzing the results using the Collate MSLD Simulation Results protocol.

The following conditions must be met before running the protocol, which will be satisfied if you use the Enumerate Ligands for MSLD protocol to prepare the ligands per the MSLD workflow.

* The input ligands must be in the same frame of reference as the receptor binding site.

* The input ligands must have the MSLD Site property defined. The MSLD Site property indicates whether the ligand is the core ligand (MSLD Site=0) or represents a substituent (MSLD Site=1,2,...). Only one ligand should be defined as the core.

* The MSLD Site property indicates whether the ligand is the core ligand (MSLD Site=0) or represents a substituent (MSLD Site=1,2,...).

* Only one ligand should be defined as the core.

* Each non-core ligand represents a substituent at a specific site and its chemical structure differs from the core ligand at only a single site.

The protocol performs the following steps:

* Ligands belonging to each site are grouped and the maximum common substructure (MCS) method detects the atoms that are chemically equivalent between the ligands and the core ligand.

* The set of common atoms is further reduced based on differences in partial charges and/or atom types. This action is performed separately for sets of ligands belonging to the distinct sites and the information is merged to generate a multi-topology ligand.

* A solvated ligand system is created by solvating the multi-topology ligand.

* A solvated protein-ligand complex system is created by merging the multi-topology ligand with the input receptor and solvating it. This system is used as input for the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol.

* The input ligands for this protocol can also be generated manually by manually creating copies of the core ligand and modifying the copied molecules using the Small Molecules tool panel. If the ligands are created manually, ensure that each ligand has molecular property MSLD Site and is typed by either CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield.

* The input ligands must have consecutive MSLD site numbers. Skipping a site is not allowed. For example, an input system with MSLD sites 2, 4, and then 5 is not allowed because site 1 and 3 are missing.

* In the Graphics View, open a pregenerated list of ligands that have the conformations in the frame of reference of the receptor binding site.

* Open the protein receptor in another window and use the Change Forcefield tools panel to type it using either CHARMm or charmm36, whichever is used for the ligands.

* Open the Simulations | Run Free Energy Simulations tools and click Set Up MSLD Calculations... .

* Set Input Typed Ligands to Visible or All .

* Set Input Receptor to the typed protein.

* Set the Solvation parameters. These are used to solvate the ligand and protein-ligand complex systems for subsequent MSLD simulations. If the MSLD simulations will be run on the CPU platform, you need to increase the Minimum Distance From Boundary for ligand to 15.0 or more. See the Solvation protocol help for more information on solvation parameters.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Set Up MSLD Calculations - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

#### Output

The MSLD Systems file is produced for a typical run which contains the following molecules.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| MSLD ligand in Vacuum | Merged multi-topology ligand generated from the corresponding ligands from the input. Multiple groups are created under the molecule and are named "MSLD" followed by indices for the site and the substituent. Select these to highlight the groups that belong to different sites and substitutions. |
| MSLD solvated ligand | Single solvated multi-topology ligand system to be used in the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol. |
| MSLD solvated complex | Single solvated protein-ligand complex, including the multi-topology ligand, to be used in the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol. |

#### Next step

After the Set Up MSLD Calculations protocol completes, you can use the
MSLD solvated ligand and MSLD solvated complex as input for the MSLD Bias Optimization and Production protocol.

#### Further information

Lead Optimization tools Run Free Energy Simulations tools

### Processes Trajectory Files

Samples a subset of frames from trajectory files or merges multiple trajectory files into a single file. The following tasks can be done:

* Save a subset of frames from large trajectory files (DCD) for analysis

* Concatenate multiple trajectory files into a single DSV and DCD file

* Save a subset of residues molecule for analysis

* Concatenate multiple CHARMm energy files into a CSV file

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Molecule | Select a structure with conformations for trajectory analysis. If the input structure does not have conformations, provide one or more trajectory files corresponding to this. |
| Trajectory Files | Select one or more trajectory (DCD) files to be processed. DCD files, which are generated by CHARMm during dynamics simulations, contain coordinates of each trajectory frame. Conformations from the DCD files will be appended to the input molecule. The conformations should have the same number of atoms as the Input Molecule . When multiple trajectory files are merged together, make sure that the trajectory files are generated with the same saving frequency and time step, otherwise, the merged frames in the trajectory file may not be consistent with the header of the file and may have missing frames. |
| Frame Start | The frame number in the DCD file to begin trajectory loading. |
| Frame Stop | The frame number in the DCD file to end trajectory loading. If not specified, the last frame in the DCD file will be used. |
| Frame Increment | The frame number increment to be used for trajectory loading. |
| Energy Files | Select optional CHARMm energy (ENE) files to be processed. ENE files are generated by CHARMm during dynamics simulations and contain time-dependent energy properties. The ENE files should contain the same number of frames as the trajectory files. If no trajectory file is selected, the CHARMm energy files will be concatenated and saved into a CSV file. |
| Residues to Save | Select a subset of residues to be saved in output files (DSV and DCD file). If this is empty, the whole molecule be saved. Notes : In Discovery Studio, specify the Residues to Save by choosing an existing residue group. Alternatively, you can specify Residues to Save by choosing Create New Group from Selection ... . In Pipeline Pilot, a residue is defined by [chain]:[residue name][residue sequence number][insertion code] (insertion code is optional). Multiple residues are separated by a whitespace (e.g., "B:ILE82 B:MET156"). Alternatively, the name of a predefined group or assembly can be used. The basic unit to save is residue. Even if a residue is partially selected, the whole residue will be saved. |
| Add Trajectory to Input Molecule | Whether to add the trajectory to the Input Molecule. This can slow down the protocol significantly if the trajectory is large. Valid Values: True, False |

## Radial Distribution Function - Parameters

### Calculates a radial distribution function for two sets of atoms in a trajectory using CHARMm

The radial distribution is the probability of finding an atom from one set at a given distance from an atom of a second set, calculated from all such interactions in a set of conformations. It is particularly useful to study the solvent density at certain distances from one or more solute atoms.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

In Discovery Studio, an atom group can be defined in advance or created on the fly. When the group name is Water-O, Water-H, or Water, all water oxygen atoms, water hydrogen atoms, or water residues will be used in the calculation. In Pipeline Pilot, use standard CHARMm selection syntax. For example, specify "select type H* end" to select all hydrogen atoms. See Also: CHARMm select syntax: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/select/ |

# Radial Distribution Function

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_radial_distribution_function.htm

## Radial Distribution Function

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Radial Distribution Function (RDF) protocol uses the RDF
to describe the structural correlation between atoms in a condensed phase. RDF, which
is also called the pair correlation function, is commonly used in the study of the
liquid state.

Suppose that a liquid mixture contains two types of atoms A and B, the RDF of
(A,B) is the number density of atom B (normalized with respect to bulk density)
that will be found at a given distance from any atom of type A.
Analyzing the profile of the
RDF is very useful for understanding the nature
of solute-solvent, solvent-solvent interactions. It has been shown to be
directly related to the Potential of Mean Force (PMF) between the two types
of atoms, mediated by the surrounding atoms.

* Load a molecule that contains a set of conformations into the Molecule Window. For example, the output molecule from a dynamics simulation may be
used. The radial distribution function is calculated as the average of all the trajectory frames. The original MD trajectory may be obtained
in non-periodic or periodic boundary condition (PBC). If the MD trajectory is obtained using periodic boundary condition (PBC), only
orthorhombic boxes are supported for computing RDF. This means that in the current release, the RDF for a trajectory obtained using truncated
octahedral box will be calculated incorrectly.

* Create two groups of atoms for which the radial distribution function will be computed. Select the atoms for each group and choose Edit | Groups... . Note that the two sets of atom selections do not have to define different
atom groups. If two identical groups are specified, the protocol calculates the self radial distribution. Otherwise, a mutual pair correlation
function between two different sets of atoms is computed. It is important to note that in calculating RDF, correlation peaks due to covalent bonds between atoms are excluded, as they do
not provide useful structural information and only make the results confusing. As a result,
for liquid water, when you select the hydrogen atoms as
solvent and oxygen atoms as solute to calculate RDF,
the peak that reflects the oxygen-hydrogen covalent bonds will not show up in the results curve.

* Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Radial Distribution Function... to open the Radial Distribution Function dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule Choose the loaded structure. Atom Selection 1 and Atom Selection 2 Choose the groups of atoms you created. For details about the remaining parameters, see Radial Distribution Function - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Choose the loaded structure. |
| Atom Selection 1 and Atom Selection 2 | Choose the groups of atoms you created. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Radial Distribution Function - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

The radial distribution function
is used extensively in structural and computational biochemistry because it provides detailed information regarding the modifications of the solvent
structure induced by the presence of a solute.
For example, analysis of the RDF of water oxygen and specific residues at a protein
surface has been used to gain better understanding of the nature of hydrophobic interactions
in the context of protein folding [Kovacs et al., 1997] .
RDFs have also been used to analyze the interactions between charges on amino
acids and explicit water molecules, which has led to the development of
a suitable set of atomic radii to be used in continuum electrostatics
calculations of solvation free energy [Nina et al., 1997] .

On a simplistic level, peaks in the of RDF versus
distance indicate areas of high frequency of occurrence at those
distances. This is often reflective of a preferred geometry such as a
hydrogen bond.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm.log | Detailed log messages produced during the CHARMm calculation of RDF. |
| RDF.png | The calculated RDF curve displayed in Report.htm. |
| rdf.csv | Contains the raw data of the calculated radial distribution function. This can be used to recreate the plot within Discovery Studio . |

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations

# Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_set_up_rel_fep_calculations_openfe-para.htm

## Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) - Parameters

### Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE)

Prepares structures to run relative FEP calculations in OpenFE, given a set of ligands. Atom mapping is performed on the ligands provided followed by the construction of an FEP network outlining transformations. The resulting output graph files are used for the Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol.

The input ligands for this protocol should be prepared using the Generate Analog Conformations protocol so that the ligands are all set in the frame of reference of the binding site.

Notes:

* Provided ligands must be prepared with hydrogens present. The Generate Analog Conformations protocol can be used for this preparation.

* Transformations that involve breaking bonds (e.g., ring opening or ring closing transformations) are not supported.

* It is recommended to provide input ligands with unique names and avoid spaces in ligand names.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify two or more ligands that are aligned and positioned correctly within the context of the protein. Provided ligands must be prepared and have hydrogens present, the Generate Analog Conformations protocol can be used for this. |
| Refine Alignment | When set to True, performs an additional shape-based alignment step to optimize the pre-aligned input ligands. Notes: It is still expected that the input ligands are aligned and positioned correctly within the context of the protein using the Generate Analog Conformations protocol. Valid Values: True , False |
| Atom Mapper | Specifies which atom mapper(s) to use for creating atom mappings that define which atoms are mutated during the alchemical transformation. LOMAP : Uses LOMAP, a maximal common substructure (MCS) based approach. This approach is less sensitive to the alignment of the input ligands. Kartograf : Uses Kartograf, an approach that considers the 3D geometries of the ligands. This approach is more sensitive to the alignment of the input ligands but can be a better choice for certain stereoisomers or when handling molecular symmetry. Valid Values: LOMAP , Kartograf |
| Ligand Network | Specifies the type(s) of networks to construct using the generated atom mappings. Minimal spanning tree : Constructs a network with as few edges as possible while maximizing total score (score here reflects the difficulty of each ligand transformation). Maximal network : Constructs a network containing all possible proposed mappings. Minimal redundant network : Constructs a network with as few edges as possible while maximizing total score (score here reflects the difficulty of each ligand transformation), ensuring that every node has at least two edges for statistical redundancy. Radial network : Constructs a radial network (also known as hub-and-spoke or star map) where all ligands connect to a central ligand. Valid Values: Minimial spanning tree , Maximal network, Minimal redundant network , Radial network |
| Central Ligand | Specifies the ligand to use as the central ligand for the radial network. |
| Custom Edges | This file is for specifying custom edges in the protocol. The format of this file is a series of *TAB-delimited* columns, where each row represents an edge (connection) between two ligands in the network. Each edge is specified as follows: <LIGAND1> <LIGAND2> In the above example, each field denoted by the characters "<>" should be replaced by the actual ligand names. The fields represent: LIGAND1 : The name of the first ligand in the pair LIGAND2 : The name of the second ligand in the pair View the examples below: Example - Create an edge between ligand_A and ligand_B: ligand_A ligand_B Example - Create multiple edges: ligand_A ligand_B ligand_B ligand_C ligand_A ligand_C Notes: Spaces will be ignored. Blank lines are skipped. Lines beginning with "#" are skipped. If a proposed edge is scored to be too difficult of a transformation for a particular network then it will not be included. This can vary depending on the chosen atom mapping. |

When set to True, performs an additional shape-based alignment step to optimize the pre-aligned input ligands.

* Radial network : Constructs a radial network (also known as hub-and-spoke or star map) where all ligands connect to a central ligand.

Valid Values: Minimial spanning tree , Maximal network, Minimal redundant network , Radial network

Specifies the ligand to use as the central ligand for the radial network.

This file is for specifying custom edges in the protocol. The format of this file is a series of *TAB-delimited* columns, where each row represents an edge (connection) between two ligands in the network. Each edge is specified as follows:

In the above example, each field denoted by the characters "<>" should be replaced by the actual ligand names. The fields represent:

# Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_set_up_rel_fep_calculations_openfe.htm

## Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

* Analyzing results

The Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol allows you to prepare structures to run relative FEP calculations in OpenFE, given a set of ligands that are aligned and set in the frame of reference of the binding site. Atom mapping is performed on the provided ligands followed by the construction of an FEP network that outlines transformations. The resulting output graph files are used for the Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol.

* You can prepare input Ligands for this protocol using the Generate Analog Conformations protocol.Hydrogens must be present in the ligands.

* It is recommended to provide input ligands with unique names and avoid spaces in ligand names.

* Transformations that involve breaking bonds (for example, ring opening or ring closing transformations) are not supported.

* In the Graphics View, open a prepared set of ligands that are aligned and have conformations in the frame of reference of the binding site.

* Set Input Ligands to the file containing the prepared ligands.

* Choose the Atom Mappers to use for generating the atom mapping for the construction of the FEP ligand perturbation network. It is recommended to choose both LOMAP [Liu et al., 2013] and Kartograf [Ries et al., 2024] in most cases.

* Choose the Ligand Networks to construct using the generated atom mappings. Minimal redundant network is recommended in most cases.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Set Up Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to the background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| aligned_ligands.sdf | Contains ligands after refined alignment. This is only generated when Refine Alignment is True. |
| network_visualization.html | An interactive report for visualizing the constructed networks. Choose a combination of network type and atom mapping to display the corresponding network as an interactive graph. Nodes on the graph can be dragged around to reposition for clarity if needed. Clicking on an edge will display the atom mapping of the corresponding ligands taking part in the edge and the score of the mapping. Atoms created or destroyed over the course of the transformation are highlighted in red, while atoms that are transformed are highlighted in blue in the mapping image. A score greater than 0.65 is generally good but it is recommended to take into account both the score and the mapping itself. |
| network_<atom mapping>_<network type>.graphml | A GraphML file containing the ligand perturbation network. The file contains coordinates of the ligands, the transformations, and all relevant information on the ligands required to move forward to the Relative FEP Calculations (OpenFE) protocol. |
| network_<atom mapping>_<network type>.png | An image depicting the topology of the corresponding network. |
| mapping_images | A directory containing image depictions of all ligand to ligand atom mappings. |

You can perform most of the analysis using the Ligand Networks interactive report. It is recommended to view the networks of interest in both atom mappings and visually inspect the edges to find a balance of a good score and appropriate mapping. In some cases, it is possible to encounter high score but poor mapping (for example, an atom being destroyed instead of being mapped), which can occur with the Kartograf atom map if the input ligands' alignment is not ideal. When Refine Alignment is True, it is recommended to visualize the aligned ligands to ensure that the new conformations are still in the frame of reference of the binding site.

#### Further information

Lead Optimization Tools Run Free Energy Simulations tool Calculating relative binding free energies with OpenFE alchemical free energy perturbation

# Set Up Relative FEP Calculations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_set_up_relative_fep_calculations-para.htm

## Set Up Relative FEP Calculations - Parameters

### Generates simulation systems for relative FEP calculations

Prepares structures to run relative FEP calculations, given one or more pairs (assembly) of typed ligands, and a typed protein. The calculation is set up to transform the first ligand in each pair into the second. For each pair, a merged dual topology molecule is generated based on the identified common and different set of atoms in the topologies and nonbonded parameters. For each pair, a solvated ligand system and a solvated protein-ligand complex is then generated. These structures are used for the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol.

The dual topology generation works by first detecting the common and different atoms between the ligands by a maximum common substructure (MCS) method. After assigning topology and parameters to the ligands, the common set of atoms are further checked for any difference in atom-types or partial charges, based on which additional atoms are moved from the common to the different set.

The input ligand pairs for this protocol may be prepared using the following steps:

* The Generate Analog Conformations protocol can be used to generate the conformations of the ligand set in the frame of reference of the binding site.

* The Forcefield tool panel from the Discovery Studio client can be used to assign either CHARMm or charmm36 forcefield to the ligands and to the protein.

* The Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP protocol should then be used to pair ligands based on similarity.

Notes:

* Hydrogens must be present in the ligands.

* Chirality differences are perceived based on positions of the substituents attached to chiral centers. Thus, input molecules involving transformations in chirality must be well aligned to each other.

* Transformation involving pairs of ligands that have chirality differences in ring atoms is not supported.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligand Pairs | Typed pairs of ligands coupled in a molecular assembly. The recommended way of generating pairs is by using the Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP protocol. In the Discovery Studio client any two typed ligands can be manually coupled to form a molecular assembly by using the Pair Ligands for FEP button. |
| Input Receptor | Specify a typed protein. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. Notes: Supported forcefield types are charmm36 and CHARMm. |
| Solvation | Adds water molecules, and optionally counterions, to the FEP ligand and protein-ligand complex. Solvent molecules may be added in either a cubic or orthorhombic shaped box for the complex and cubic for the ligand. Applies periodic boundary conditions to the solvated molecule to use in the simulation. |
| Ligand | Solvation parameters for the ligand. The shape of the solvation box is set to Cubic. |
| Ligand Minimum Distance From Boundary | Specify the minimum distance (Å) from periodic boundary. |
| Protein-ligand Complex | Solvation parameters for the Protein-ligand complex. |
| Protein-ligand Complex Cell Shape | Specify the cell shape used in the explicit periodic boundary solvation model. Valid Values: Cubic , Orthorhombic |
| Protein-ligand Complex Minimum Distance From Boundary | Specify the minimum distance (Å) from periodic boundary. |
| Add Counterion | Specify whether counterions should be added to the explicitly solvated system. Counterions keep the system neutral and set the ionic concentration of the system to a desirable value. Valid Values: True , False |
| Salt Concentration | Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l) of the explicitly solvated system. |
| Cation Type | Specify the type of cations for counterion placement. Valid Values: Sodium , Potassium, Magnesium, Calcium |
| Anion Type | Specify the type of anions for counterion placement. Valid Values: Sulfate, Chloride , H2PO4, HPO4 |
| Random Seed | A user-specified positive integer to initialize the random number generation. Leave this blank if you would like to get a different random series each time you run the protocol. This is used to place the ions randomly in the solvent. |
| Advanced | Advanced Parameters |
| Minimum Similarity | Minimum similarity between ligands in each pair. Similarity is calculated as 2*nMCS/(nL1+nL2), where nMCS is the number of atoms in the maximal common substructure; nL1 and nL2 are the number of atoms for ligands 1, and 2, in each ligand pair, respectively. This threshold is set to ensure reasonable overlap between the ligands to facilitate convergence in the subsequent FEP calculation. |
| Maximum Core RMSD | Maximum RMSD between the common core atoms allowed between the ligands in each pair. |
| Proceed After MCSS Timeout | If the two ligands are large (MW > 600), then the MCSS algorithm may not exhaustively detect the entire common region shared by them. However, in many cases the MCSS algorithm is able to map a substantial portion of the common region. If set to True the dual topology is generated despite of MCSS timeout. In this scenario, the topology should be carefully inspected before running an FEP calculation. Valid Values: True, False |
| Protein-Ligand Complex Minimization | Minimize the unsolvated protein-ligand complex. Valid Values: True , False |
| Partial Charge Tolerance | Partial charge difference threshold for duplicating atoms. |

Typed pairs of ligands coupled in a molecular assembly. The recommended way of generating pairs is by using the Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP protocol. In the Discovery Studio client any two typed ligands can be manually coupled to form a molecular assembly by using the Pair Ligands for FEP button.

Specify a typed protein. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures.

* Supported forcefield types are charmm36 and CHARMm.

Adds water molecules, and optionally counterions, to the FEP ligand and protein-ligand complex. Solvent molecules may be added in either a cubic or orthorhombic shaped box for the complex and cubic for the ligand. Applies periodic boundary conditions to the solvated molecule to use in the simulation.

Solvation parameters for the ligand. The shape of the solvation box is set to Cubic.

Specify the minimum distance (Å) from periodic boundary.

Solvation parameters for the Protein-ligand complex.

Specify the cell shape used in the explicit periodic boundary solvation model.

Valid Values: Cubic , Orthorhombic

Specify whether counterions should be added to the explicitly solvated system.

Counterions keep the system neutral and set the ionic concentration of the system to a desirable value.

Valid Values: True , False

Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l) of the explicitly solvated system.

Specify the type of cations for counterion placement.

Valid Values: Sodium , Potassium, Magnesium, Calcium

Specify the type of anions for counterion placement.

Valid Values: Sulfate, Chloride , H2PO4, HPO4

A user-specified positive integer to initialize the random number generation. Leave this blank if you would like to get a different random series each time you run the protocol. This is used to place the ions randomly in the solvent.

Advanced Parameters

Minimum similarity between ligands in each pair. Similarity is calculated as 2*nMCS/(nL1+nL2), where nMCS is the number of atoms in the maximal common substructure; nL1 and nL2 are the number of atoms for ligands 1, and 2, in each ligand pair, respectively. This threshold is set to ensure reasonable overlap between the ligands to facilitate convergence in the subsequent FEP calculation.

Maximum RMSD between the common core atoms allowed between the ligands in each pair.

If the two ligands are large (MW > 600), then the MCSS algorithm may not exhaustively detect the entire common region shared by them. However, in many cases the MCSS algorithm is able to map a substantial portion of the common region. If set to True the dual topology is generated despite of MCSS timeout. In this scenario, the topology should be carefully inspected before running an FEP calculation.

Valid Values: True, False

Partial charge difference threshold for duplicating atoms.

# Set Up Relative FEP Calculations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_set_up_relative_fep_calculations.htm

## Set Up Relative FEP Calculations

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Set Up Relative FEP Calculations protocol allows you to generate simulation systems for performing multiple FEP calculations to determine relative binding free energies. The inputs include one or more pairs (assemblies) of ligands and a typed protein. These systems are set up to calculate the alchemical free energy change of transforming the first ligand in each pair to the second one. This protocol represents the fourth in the series of steps comprising the FEP workflow:

* Generate Analog Conformations

* Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) , or alternatively, use Change Forcefield tools to type ligands with CHARMm forcefield.

* Generate Ligand Pairs for FEP

* Free Energy Perturbation (FEP)

* Collate FEP Simulation Results

For each ligand pair, a merged dual topology molecule is generated based on the identified similarity and differences in the topologies, non-bond parameters, and partial charges. The dual topology molecules are then solvated to generate solvated ligand systems. Secondly, the dual toplogy molecules are merged with the Input Receptor and solvated to generate solvated protein-ligand complex systems. These structures can be used in the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol.

The input paired ligands must be in the same frame of reference as the receptor binding site for the FEP calculations. Ligands must be typed with either the CHARMm or charmm36 forcefields. To ensure this, please follow the steps of the FEP workflow detailed above in sequence.

The protocol requires an Input Receptor typed with the same forcefield as the ligands. Use the Change Forcefield tools panel for this task.

* Input Ligand pairs for this protocol can also be generated manually using the Pair Ligands for FEP button.

* Hydrogens must be present in the ligands.

* Ligands in each pair must have at least 20% of the atoms in common or the corresponding pair will fail. This can be modified by the Advanced | Minimum Similarity parameter.

* Chirality differences are perceived based on positions of the substituents attached to chiral centers. Thus, input molecules involving transformations in chirality must be well aligned to each other.

* In the Graphics View, open a pregenerated list of paired ligands that have the conformations in the frame of reference of the binding site.

* Open the protein receptor in another window and type it using either CHARMm or charmm36. Use the same forcefield that are used for the ligands.

* Open the Simulations | Run Free Energy Simulations tools and click Set Up Relative FEP Calculations... .

* Set Input Ligand Pairs to the file containing ligand pairs.

* Set Input Receptor to the typed protein.

* Set the solvation parameters. These are used to solvate the ligand and protein-ligand complex systems in later FEP simulations. See the Solvation protocol help for more information on solvation parameters.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Set Up Relative FEP Calculations - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

From a typical run, three files are produced.

* Dual Topology Ligands: It contains one or more molecules generated from the corresponding ligand pairs from the input. Each molecule contains a ligand pair with merged dual topology, which in addition to the different parts, contains a single copy of the common groups between the two ligands. Two groups are created under the molecule, that are named "FEP 0" and "FEP 1". Select these to highlight the groups that are different between the two ligands. "FEP 0" contains atoms that will disappear during the FEP calculation, and "FEP 1" contains atoms that will appear.

* Solvated Ligands: One or more solvated dual topology ligand systems to be used in alchemical calculations using the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol to obtain the alchemical free energy of transformation in solution.

* Solvated Complexes: One or more solvated protein-ligand complexes, with each ligand pair defined in dual topology, to be used in alchemical calculations using the Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) protocol to obtain the alchemical free energy of transformation in the solvated protein environment.

#### Further information

Lead Optimization Tools Run Free Energy Simulations tool

# Solvation - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_solvation-para.htm

## Solvation - Parameters

### Solvates a system by adding water molecules

Adds water molecules and optionally counterions to a molecule. Solvent molecules may be added in several arrangements, including a sphere or a box. Adds either explicit periodic boundary or harmonic restraints to the molecule to allow simulation of the solvent. The solvated system can be optionally minimized so that the VDW clashes can be cleaned up.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Solvation Model | Choose an explicit solvation model. Available options are: Explicit Periodic Boundary : Solvates the molecule with periodic boundary conditions (PBC). Explicit Spherical Boundary with Harmonic Restraint : Solvates the molecule with spherical boundary conditions. Valid Values: Explicit Periodic Boundary , Explicit Spherical Boundary with Harmonic Restraint |
| Cell Shape | Specify the cell shape used in the explicit periodic boundary solvation model. Note: The Truncated Octahedron cell shape is not supported by OpenMM GPU . Valid Values: Cubic, Orthorhombic , Truncated Octahedron |
| Minimum Distance From Boundary | Specify the minimum distance (Å) from periodic boundary. |
| Center of Mass | Specify the center-of-mass of the explicit solvents for the spherical boundary solvation. In Discovery Studio, select a molecule, a chain in the molecule, or a site sphere (which you can create using the Binding Site Tool). In Pipeline Pilot, specify the coordinates of the sphere in the format: x,y,z |
| Radius of Sphere | Specify the radius of explicit solvents (Å) for spherical boundary solvation model. The value should be between 10 and 200. |
| Add Counterion | Specify whether counterions should be added to the explicitly solvated system. Counterions keep the system neutral and set the ionic concentration of the system to a desirable value. If the molecule is typed with cff, CHARMm, charmm27 or charmm36 forcefield, the counterions will also be typed. Counterions will be added but will not be typed if another forcefield is used. Valid Values: True , False |
| Salt Concentration | Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l) of the explicitly solvated system. |
| Cation Type | Specify the type of cations for counterion placement. Valid Values: Sodium , Potassium, Magnesium, Calcium |
| Anion Type | Specify the type of anions for counterion placement. Valid Values: Sulfate, Chloride , H2PO4, HPO4, NO3 |
| Random Seed | A user-specified positive integer to initialize the random number generation. Leave this blank if you would like to get a different random series each time you run the protocol. This is used to place the ions randomly in the solvent. |
| Minimization | Minimization for solvated system. Valid Values: True, False |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR , Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer |
| Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Angstrom). For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Number of Processors | Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server. Note : The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel. The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel. |

Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures.

Choose an explicit solvation model. Available options are:

* Explicit Periodic Boundary : Solvates the molecule with periodic boundary conditions (PBC).

* Explicit Spherical Boundary with Harmonic Restraint : Solvates the molecule with spherical boundary conditions.

Valid Values: Explicit Periodic Boundary , Explicit Spherical Boundary with Harmonic Restraint

Note:

* The Truncated Octahedron cell shape is not supported by OpenMM GPU .

Valid Values: Cubic, Orthorhombic , Truncated Octahedron

Specify the minimum distance (Å) from periodic boundary.

Specify the center-of-mass of the explicit solvents for the spherical boundary solvation.

In Pipeline Pilot, specify the coordinates of the sphere in the format: x,y,z

Counterions keep the system neutral and set the ionic concentration of the system to a desirable value. If the molecule is typed with cff, CHARMm, charmm27 or charmm36 forcefield, the counterions will also be typed. Counterions will be added but will not be typed if another forcefield is used.

Valid Values: True , False

Valid Values: True, False

Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are:

* Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions.

* Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation.

* Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails.

* Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation.

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined.

Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server.

# Solvation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_solvation.htm

## Solvation

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Solvation protocol allows you to create an explicitly solvated system.
Water molecules, and optionally counterions, can be added 
with a variety of boundary conditions, including spherical or periodic cell.
With periodic boundary conditions, you can choose a cubic, orthorhombic, or a truncated
octahedral cell shape. Optionally, you can minimize the solvated system using CHARMm to resolve
van der Waals clashes and bad geometry in the input structure.

Typically, the solvated model generated by this protocol is used as input for
other simulation protocols, such as the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol.

* Load a structure you wish to solvate into the Graphics View.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Solvation... to open the Solvation dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule . For details about the remaining parameters, see Solvation - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield.

* If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

While the solvent added comes from a well minimized source, the
created interface between the solute and solvent is crude.
For this reason, it is important to minimize and equilibrate the solvated system 
before running production dynamics (e.g., by using the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol).

Solvation often adds a large number of solvent molecules to the system, which
significantly increases the number of atoms. Further simulations on
solvated systems usually require increased system resources, particularly
memory, than simulations using implicit solvation methods.

The input molecule is reoriented during solvation. This is required for running subsequent simulation of the
solvated system using the particle mesh Ewald method.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule after explicit solvation, which includes water molecules added by the protocol. Opens in the Graphics View. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language ( FFML ) file used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Calculate Energy Minimization Heating Dynamics (Equilibration) Dynamics (Production) Forcefield page - Preferences dialog
