# Standard Dynamics Cascade - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_standard_dynamics_cascade-para.htm

## Standard Dynamics Cascade - Parameters

### Performs a set of minimization and equilibration steps followed by molecular dynamics using CHARMm

Combines common simulation steps to create a standard dynamics cascade.

The following steps are performed:

* Minimization with steepest descent

* Minimization with conjugate gradient

* Dynamics with heating

* Equilibration dynamics

* Production dynamics

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Specify a typed molecule. In Pipeline Pilot, specify a file containing a typed molecule, the supported file formats are DSV, MSV, and MOL2. In Discovery Studio, choose from the list of all the visible typed structures. |
| Minimization | Minimization Parameters |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent , Conjugate Gradient, Powell |
| Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Å). |
| Minimization Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Minimization2 | Second Minimization Parameters. |
| Minimization2 Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR , Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell |
| Minimization2 Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the second minimization stage. |
| Minimization2 RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. |
| Minimization2 Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Heating | Heating Parameters |
| Heating Simulation Time (ps) | Time length (ps) to perform the dynamics simulation. |
| Heating Time Step (fs) | Time step (fs) to use for dynamics simulation. |
| Heating Initial Temperature | Specifies starting temperature (K) for heating simulation. |
| Heating Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for heating stage. |
| Heating Adjust Velocity Frequency | Specifies the frequency of velocity adjustments during the simulation, in number of steps. |
| Heating Save Results Interval (ps) | The time interval in picosecond (ps) to save coordinates, energies, and restart file during the simulation. Notes For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval . At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved. Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time/Save Results Interval. |
| Heating Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Equilibration | Equilibration Parameters |
| Equilibration Simulation Time (ps) | Time length (ps) to perform the dynamics simulation. |
| Equilibration Time Step (fs) | Time step (fs) to use for the dynamics simulation. |
| Equilibration Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation. |
| Equilibration Adjust Velocity Frequency | Specifies the frequency of velocity adjustments during the simulation, in number of steps. |
| Equilibration Save Results Interval (ps) | The time interval in picosecond (ps) to save coordinates, energies, and restart file during the simulation. Notes For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval (ps) . At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved. Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time (ps)/Save Results Interval (ps). |
| Equilibration Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Production | Production Parameters |
| Production Simulation Time (ps) | Time length (ps) to perform the dynamics simulation. |
| Production Time Step (fs) | Time step (fs) to use for dynamics simulation. |
| Production Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation. |
| Production Temperature Coupling Decay Time | Specifies the temperature coupling decay time (ps) for the Berendsen thermal coupling method. |
| Production Save Results Interval (ps) | The time interval in picosecond (ps) to save coordinates, energies, and restart file during the simulation. Notes For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval (ps) . At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved. Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time (ps)/Save Results Interval (ps). |
| Production Save Restart File | Specifies whether this stage should save a restart file for use by later dynamics stages. Note: Restart files can be very large, so the user should exercise care when setting this parameter to True. Valid Values: True , False |
| Production Constraints | Allows selection of which restraints/constraints shall be applied for this simulation step. In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. You can also select a stream file which contains restraints/constraints specified in standard CHARMm syntax. In Pipeline Pilot, restraints/constraints can be specified using standard CHARMm syntax. |
| Production Type | Specifies type of production to run: NPT: Constant pressure and temperature dynamics. NVT: Constant temperature dynamics using Berendsen weak coupling method. NVE: dynamics without temperature/pressure control. Valid Values: NPT , NVT, NVE |
| TMass | Specifies the thermal mass in the Hoover constant temperature method. |
| PMass | Specifies the mass of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. Units in Atomic Mass Unit (AMU). |
| PGamma | Specifies the collision frequency of the Langevin piston for constant pressure control. |
| Reference Pressure | Specifies the pressure at which the simulation is performed. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. Can also be used for molecules with membranes. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . Similar to GBIM , the GBSW method also allows to extend the solvation model with an implicit membrane. Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) : An extension of the Generalized Born model that will take account of an implicit membrane defined in the input molecule when calculating the electrostatic contribution to solvation energy. If there is no implicit membrane then the method is similar to Generalized Born, but allows user defined intra-molecular dielectric constant. Notes: To add an implicit membrane to a molecule: In Discovery Studio, use the Analyze Transmembrane Proteins tools. In Pipeline Pilot, use the Add Membrane and Orient Molecule protocol. See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW), Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) |
| Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to be used to model the molecular system. If the Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent, this parameter is applied to the entire space of the molecular system, including explicit solvent molecules if present. If one of the Generalized Born implicit solvent models is selected (GB, GBIM, GBSW, or GBMV), this parameter applies to the interior of the solute molecule while the rest of the space has the dielectric properties of the solvent. For GB and GBMV, the dielectric constant is fixed as 1.0 internally and can not be changed. Additionally, if there is an implicit membrane present and the Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) or to Generalized Born with Simple SWitching (GBSW), the membrane and the interior of the solutes are assumed to have the same dielectric permittivity as defined by this parameter. When modeling a membrane system, it is appropriate to use a Dielectric Constant of 2, corresponding to the dielectric properties of saturated hydrocarbons. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is GB, GBMV, GBSW, or GBIM. |
| Generalized Born Lambda Constant | Specifies scaling factor for the Van der Waals radius in the calculation of Born radius in Generalized Born solvation model. Values between 0.69 to 0.92 are used for different forcefields. Leave it empty to use a recommended value suitable for the current forcefield. |
| Minimum Hydrogen Radius | Used only for charmm22, charmm27 and charmm36 forcefields to address the loss of accuracy in the calculation of GB solvation energy, because of the very small VDW radii of some hydrogens in these force fields. Applies to GB and GBIM. See Also: Dominy,B.N; Brooks C.L.III, Development of a Generalized Born Model Parameterization for Proteins and Nucleic Acids, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1999 , 103, 3765-3773. |
| Use Non-polar Surface Area | Specifies whether the non-polar surface area should be used to approximate the non-polar component of the solvation energy, which is assumed to be linearly proportional to the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). Expressed as the sum of a constant term and a term proportional to the changes to SASA. Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-polar Surface Constant | Specifies the constant term (kcal/mol) used in calculating the non-polar surface contribution to the solvation energy. |
| Non-polar Surface Coefficient | Specifies the surface tension coefficient (kcal/(mol x Å 2 )) used in calculating the non-polar contribution to the solvation energy. The optimal values could vary depending on the implicit solvent models, force fields and molecular systems. For globular proteins the commonly used values are typically set to 0.005 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ), but can go up to 0.02-0.03 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). For membrane proteins and peptides we recommend some elevated values from 0.015 to 0.04 kcal/(mol x Å 2 ). See Also: Chen, J.; Brooks C.L.III, Implicit modeling of nonpolar solvation for simulating protein folding and conformational transitions, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. , 2008 , 10, 471-481. Tanizaki, S.; Feig, M., A generalized Born formalism for heterogeneous dielectric environments: Application to the implicit modeling of biological membranes, J. Chem. Phys., 2005 , 122, 124706-13. Spassov, V.; Yan, L.; Szalma, S., Introducing an implicit membrane in Generalized Born/Solvent Accessibility continuum solvent models, J. Phys. Chem. B, 2002 , 106, 8726-8738. Im, W.; Feig, M.; Brooks C.L.III, An implicit membrane Generalized Born Theory for the study of structure, stability, and interactions of membrane proteins, Biophys. J. , 2003 , 85, 2900-2918. |
| Salt Concentration | Specifies the salt concentration (mol/l). Only applicable to GBSW. |
| Input Atomic Radii | Atomic radii used for GBSW and GBMV: van der Waals radii : Default. radii from Nina et al. : Recommended for charmm22/27/36 forcefields. See Also : Nina, M.; Beglov, D.; Roux, B. Atomic radii for continuum electrostatics calculations based on molecular dynamics free energy simulations, J. Phys. Chem. B , 1997 , 101 (26), 5239-5248. Valid Values: van der Waals radii , radii from Nina et al. |
| Use Molecular Surface | Specifies whether to use molecular surface in GBSW. Valid Values: True , False |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. Within this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are scaled smoothly using either a shifting or switching function (depending on the forcefield) from Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance to Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance . |
| Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance | Higher cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the end point of switching. When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance | Lower cutoff distance (Å) to use for non-bonded interactions. It defines the starting point of switching. When empty, this parameter will be set to a default value by CHARMm automatically. |
| Electrostatics | Specifies how to treat long range electrostatics. Three options are available: Automatic : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used if the information for periodic boundary condition (i.e. the BoxShape property of the input molecule) is available, otherwise, the Spherical Cutoff method is used. Spherical Cutoff : the spherical cutoff is used for the electrostatic interactions. Particle Mesh Ewald : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used. Note : When Spherical Cutoff option is selected, all non-bonded energy will be calculated without using periodic boundary condition. If the periodic boundary condition is not set up for the input molecule (e.g., the BoxShape property is not defined), the PME option will not work properly. Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald |
| Kappa | The width of the Gaussian function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ) and 6/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ). |
| Order | The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Dynamics Integrator | Chooses a dynamics integrator to perform numerical integration of the equation of motion. Two choices are supported: Leapfrog Verlet Integrator (LEAP): the atom velocities and positions are calculated at time points that differ by a half time step. Velocity Verlet (VVER): the velocities and positions are calculated at the same time points. In Discovery Studio, the VVER integrator and Nose dynamics are always used together. It is not available in heating dynamics simulation or in constant pressure simulation. Valid Values: Leapfrog Verlet |
| Apply SHAKE Constraint | Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation. If SHAKE causes a failure in any of the minimization steps, the protocol will try to rerun the minimization without SHAKE automatically. Valid Values: True , False |
| Random Number Seed | Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock. The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers. See Also: https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/ |
| Number of Processors | Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server. Notes : The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel. The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel. |
| Run On Grid | Run protocol on grid engine if available. Note: If no grid engine is configured, this parameter has no effect. Valid Values: True , False |
| Queue Name | Specify the name of the queue on the grid engine to submit the job to. Leave blank to specify the default queue. |
| Grid Options | An array of command line options to include in the grid engine submit command. The list below shows supported parameters which will be translated into command line options for the supported grid engines. Account=<Project/Account name> Maximum Execution Time=<DD:MM:SS> - LSF does not use seconds Number of Cores=<16> Parallel Environment=<The Parallel Environment to use> - Only needed for SGE Other=<Additional Parameters sent directly to submit command line> Note: If you just want to send a single line "as is" to the submission command, you can omit the "Other=" part. The format will be grid engine specific. For example, you can use the following for a PBS grid engine: -l procs=16 -l walltime=08:00:00 -A PROJECTID If you request multiple cores, you also need to manually set the Number of Processors parameter to the same number as the number of cores. |

Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are:

* Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate

* Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations.

* Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails.

Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent , Conjugate Gradient, Powell

* Spherical Cutoff : the spherical cutoff is used for the electrostatic interactions.

* Particle Mesh Ewald : the Particle Mesh Ewald method is used.

Note :

* When Spherical Cutoff option is selected, all non-bonded energy will be calculated without using periodic boundary condition.

* If the periodic boundary condition is not set up for the input molecule (e.g., the BoxShape property is not defined), the PME option will not work properly.

Valid Values: Automatic , Spherical Cutoff, Particle Mesh Ewald

The width of the Gaussian function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. The value should be between 3/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ) and 6/( Nonbond Higher Cutoff Distance ).

The order of the B-spline charge interpolation function in the Particle Mesh Ewald calculation. It must be an even number and at least 4.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

* Leapfrog Verlet Integrator (LEAP): the atom velocities and positions are calculated at time points that differ by a half time step.

* Velocity Verlet (VVER): the velocities and positions are calculated at the same time points. In Discovery Studio, the VVER integrator and Nose dynamics are always used together. It is not available in heating dynamics simulation or in constant pressure simulation.

Valid Values: Leapfrog Verlet

Specifies whether to apply SHAKE constraint which fixes all bonds involving hydrogens in the simulation. If SHAKE causes a failure in any of the minimization steps, the protocol will try to rerun the minimization without SHAKE automatically.

Random number seed for CHARMm. By default a seed is supplied to achieve consistent results with the same input on the same system with the same number of processes. However, for a purely random run, do not specify a value, in which case, the seed is generated using the system clock.

The seed format is one to four positive integers, separated by spaces. To ensure a random run, clear the default value and leave this parameter blank. To ensure a reproducible run, provide four positive integers.

* https://academiccharmm.org/documentation/version/c44b2/random/

Allows for the use of multiple processors on a server.

Notes :

* The CFF and MMFF forcefields are not supported to run in parallel.

* The Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM) implicit solvent model is not supported to run in parallel.

Run protocol on grid engine if available.

Note:

* If no grid engine is configured, this parameter has no effect.

Specify the name of the queue on the grid engine to submit the job to. Leave blank to specify the default queue.

An array of command line options to include in the grid engine submit command.

The list below shows supported parameters which will be translated into command line options for the supported grid engines.

* Account=<Project/Account name>

* Maximum Execution Time=<DD:MM:SS> - LSF does not use seconds

* Number of Cores=<16>

* Parallel Environment=<The Parallel Environment to use> - Only needed for SGE

* Other=<Additional Parameters sent directly to submit command line>

* If you just want to send a single line "as is" to the submission command, you can omit the "Other=" part. The format will be grid engine specific. For example, you can use the following for a PBS grid engine: -l procs=16 -l walltime=08:00:00 -A PROJECTID

If you just want to send a single line "as is" to the submission command, you can omit the "Other=" part. The format will be grid engine specific. For example, you can use the following for a PBS grid engine:

-l procs=16 -l walltime=08:00:00 -A PROJECTID

* If you request multiple cores, you also need to manually set the Number of Processors parameter to the same number as the number of cores.

# Standard Dynamics Cascade

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_standard_dynamics_cascade.htm

## Standard Dynamics Cascade

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol applies a set of 
simulation procedures to the input structure. You can modify the
parameters of each step to achieve diverse simulation objectives. 
Typically, it is used to minimize and equilibrate the molecular system
and prepare for input to production dynamics using either CHARMm or NAMD.
The Standard Dynamics Cascade consists of the following steps:

* Minimization: An initial minimization stage,
typically using the robust Steepest Descent algorithm to resolve any
initial poor contacts within the system without creating large distortions
in the overall structure. Optionally, you can add constraints to restrict the movement
of certain part of the structure, such as the protein backbone, solvent molecules, etc.

* Minimization2: A second minimization stage,
typically using the Conjugate Gradient method. This is
used once initial poor contacts are relieved to ensure that a low
energy starting point is supplied to subsequent dynamics stages.
You can remove the constraints used in the first minimization step or change to different types of constraints to achieve
different goals of the minimization.

* Heating: A molecular dynamics simulation stage to heat the system to reach
a target temperature. Proper and careful minimization is always required prior to performing the heating stage.

* Equilibration: A molecular dynamics
simulation stage to equilibrate the system at a target temperature. The purpose of the equilibration
stage is to ensure that the energy in the
system is distributed appropriately among all degrees of freedom. This allows
the system to achieve thermal equilibration at the target temperature.

* Production: A molecular dynamics production run in a suitable thermodynamic ensemble
(NVT, NPT or NVE ensembles) at a given temperature based on the equilibrated
system from the previous step. The results of the production
stage are stored in the simulation trajectory, from which structural and
energetics properties can be calculated and subsequently analyzed.

* Load the structure you wish to run through the dynamics cascade into the
Graphics View.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Standard Dynamics Cascade... to open the Standard Dynamics Cascade dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Typed Molecule .

* By default, the simulation time for the equilibration stage and production stage are set to be 10ps, which is short for most 
input systems. Depending on the purpose of your simulation, you may want to increase the equilibration and production time by setting the Simulation Time under the two corresponding parameter groups. Typically, this protocol is used as the 
initial equilibration stage before production dynamics using CHARMm or NAMD. Therefore, it is recommended to set the production stage relatively
short and evaluate at the end of the run to make sure that the system is properly equilibrated based on the energy and temperature of the
output system before initiating a long production run.

* If you increase the simulation time for the Production stage, be sure to evaluate and reset
the Save Results Interval (ps) parameter accordingly so that no more than several hundred frames are saved. Saving a lot of frames requires heavy system resources at the end of the run, especially for large solvated molecular systems.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Standard Dynamics Cascade - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

For any dynamics simulation, it is important to monitor the temperature and energy of the system during the simulation
to ensure a stable trajectory. For each stage of the dynamics simulation, the following information is given in the report:

* Heating: A warning is reported if the final temperature is off target by 10% or more, and the temperature and energy versus simulation time plots will be shown in the summary for easy visual check.

* Equilibration: As with the heating phase, a warning is reported if the final temperature is off target by 10% or more, and the temperature and energy versus simulation time plots will be shown in the summary.

* Production: The temperature and the total energy versus simulation time are plotted in the final summary. 
A warning message is reported if the final temperature is off target temperature by more than 10%. 
If the system is not fully equilibrated in the equilibration stage, the energy will not show convergence in the production stage. However,
typically, there is no need to rerun the equilibration stage. Continue running the production stage to effectively bring the system to equilibration. 
Review the Energy plot in the report to identify the frame in which the system has reached equilibration (e.g., when
the energy vs. simulation time converges in the plot.

<molecule>.dsv, which contains the time-dependent energetic properties and trajectory frames from the production phase, is saved at the end of the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol.
You can sample and analyze the energies and trajectory conformations using the tools in the Analyze Trajectory tool panel, especially the Analyze Trajectory... tool. 
You can also plot the energetic properties using various charting tools .
Note that if the CHARMm executable is terminated during the production step, partial results are shown in the report.

Another smaller output file, <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv, is also created for convenience. 
If you are not interested in the dynamics properties of the solvent, use this file for analysis to save resources.

Alternatively, if you only want to analyze the energetic properties in the production phase without loading all the conformations into the client, 
you can open the energy table in the <molecule>_energy.csv file and plot different energy terms (e.g., potential energy, kinetic energy, etc.) against simulation time
using charting tools .

The results for each of these stages can also be analyzed individually if intermediate files are saved. 
Each stage of the standard dynamics cascade protocol is saved in a separate folder under the Intermediate folder. 
For example, the Heating stage is saved under the Intermediate/3_Heating folder.
You can analyze the energetic and structural properties of each stage using the trajectory ( .dcd ) and energy ( .ene ) files under these folders. 
Careful analysis should be carried out on the two connecting regions of the trajectory: the region linking heating and equilibration, 
and that linking equilibration and production. 
For a successful dynamics run, discontinuities in energetic and structural properties should be minimal in these connecting regions.

* By default, the SHAKE constraints are applied to all bonds involving hydrogens, and the default time step is 2fs. 
In general, dynamics simulations may fail if the input structure has bad van der Waals clashes and the failure occurs more often with the SHAKE option
enabled. The problem is not with the SHAKE option, but is an indication that the input structure is not properly minimized. 
If the simulation fails, check that the initial structure does not have bad clashes. You can extend the minimization steps in this protocol
to ensure the input structure is fully minimized before dynamics simulation starts.

* Running long dynamics simulation with large solvated molecular system requires a lot of memory. If the server does not have enough memory, the
protocol may fail in the post processing stage, but the main simulation results are available. If the report shows an error, first
check the charmm.log file to make sure that CHARMm run finished successfully. Then check that output DSV files exist. If the post processing step
failed to generate the output DSV files, do one of the following: Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory. From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate | 5_Production folder. Select <molecule>_prod.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_prod.ene to each conformation. Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

* Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory. From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate | 5_Production folder. Select <molecule>_prod.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_prod.ene to each conformation.

* From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder.

* Open Input/<molecule>.dsv .

* Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate | 5_Production folder.

* Select <molecule>_prod.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_prod.ene to each conformation.

* Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule with trajectory frames from the production phase in the simulation cascade stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order (i.e., the first conformation corresponds to the first trajectory frame in the production phase saved by CHARMm). The time-dependent energy properties from the production phase are also stored with each conformation in this .dsv file. |
| <molecule>_noconfs.dsv | The output molecule without conformations. In this file, the molecule has the final coordinate of the dynamics simulation. This can be used together with the <molecule>.dcd file for trajectory analysis or input to restart another dynamics simulation using either CHARMm or NAMD. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule with the conformations, but with the solvent molecules removed for easy visualization. |
| <molecule>.dcd | The trajectory file generated by CHARMm. It saves the coordinates of the specified frames in the production stage. You can import the trajectory frames to the input molecule using Structure \| Animation \| Load... , or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol. |
| <molecule>.ene | The energy file generated by CHARMm. It saves the time-dependent energy properties for the production stage. Its values will be loaded into the molecule when a corresponding dcd file is imported ( Structure \| Animation \| Load... from the menu bar). |
| <molecule>_energy.csv | Contains the same information as <molecule>.ene, but in CSV format. |
| <molecule>_*.rst | Several restart file, for each major step of the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol. A restart file can be used to continue a dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language (FFML) file, used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

The .dsv file created
by this protocol shows an animation when loaded back into the application.
When showing an animation, the View | Display Style... command is disabled. 
To enable this command, open the Hierarchy View and select the top-most node of the structure hierarchy.

#### Further information

Considerations for running simulations Calculate Energy Minimization Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) Dynamics (Equilibration) Dynamics (Production) Forcefield page - Preferences dialog Change Forcefield tools Analyze Trajectory tool panel Analyze Trajectory... Structure | Animation

The following steps are performed:

* Minimization

* Dynamics with heating

* Equilibration dynamics

* Production dynamics

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield (charmm36 or CHARMm-MomanyRone.)

* Particle Mesh Ewald electrostatics are used.

In Discovery Studio, restraints/constraints can be specified using the Setup Constraints tool panel. # Standard Dynamics Cascade (OpenMM)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_std_dyn_casc_openmm.htm

## Standard Dynamics Cascade (OpenMM)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output

The Standard Dynamics Cascade (OpenMM) protocol applies a set of 
simulation procedures to the input structure. You can modify the
parameters of each step to achieve diverse simulation objectives. 
This protocol is typically used to minimize and equilibrate the molecular system
and prepare it for input to production dynamics. It is also possible to carry out production dynamics.

The Standard Dynamics Cascade consists of the following steps:

* Minimization: An initial energy minimization stage resolves unfavorable atomic contacts and optimizes the system geometry. The minimization continues until the root-mean-square value of all force components reaches a tolerance of 10 kJ/mol/nm (default), ensuring the system reaches a stable energy minimum. By default, the number of iterations is unlimited, allowing the minimization to run until convergence is achieved. This process carefully relaxes the structure without creating large distortions. Optionally, you can apply harmonic restraints to restrict the movement of specific atoms during minimization, such as keeping the protein backbone fixed while allowing side chains and solvent molecules to optimize their positions.

* Heating: A molecular dynamics simulation stage 
heats ( Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) ) the system to reach
a target temperature. Proper and careful minimization is always required prior to performing the heating stage.

* Equilibration: A molecular dynamics simulation stage equilibrates ( Dynamics (Equilibration) ) the system to achieve proper energy distribution across all degrees of freedom at the target temperature. This stage supports both NVT (constant volume) and NPT (constant pressure) ensemble simulations. Temperature is maintained using a Langevin thermostat with a configurable friction coefficient (default: 1.0 ps^-1), which couples the system to a heat bath at the target temperature. For NPT simulations, pressure is regulated using a Monte Carlo barostat at the specified reference pressure (default: 1.0 bar), with pressure moves attempted at regular intervals defined by the pressure frequency parameter. The equilibration runs for a configurable duration and time step (default: 2 fs), allowing the system density, box dimensions, and atomic velocities to stabilize before production sampling. You can apply harmonic position restraints if needed to allow gradual relaxation of specific structural elements, such as maintaining protein backbone geometry while equilibrating solvent and side chains.

* Production: A molecular dynamics production run ( Dynamics (Production) ) generates the final simulation trajectory for analysis, starting from the equilibrated system. This stage supports both NVT (constant volume) and NPT (constant pressure) ensembles, with temperature control by means of Langevin dynamics using a configurable friction coefficient (default: 1.0 ps^-1). For NPT simulations, pressure is maintained using a Monte Carlo barostat at the specified reference pressure (default: 1.0 bar) with periodic pressure adjustments. The simulation runs for a configurable duration and time step (default: 2 fs), saving coordinates to a DCD trajectory file at specified intervals for subsequent analysis. Energy, temperature, density, and box volume data are logged throughout the simulation, along with performance metrics (ns/day) to monitor computational efficiency. The production trajectory captures the system's thermodynamic behavior and conformational sampling, providing the primary data for calculating structural properties, energetics, dynamics, and other observables of interest. You can apply position restraints if needed to maintain specific structural features while sampling the rest of the system.

* Load the input structure in the
Graphics View. All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield (charmm36 or CHARMm-MomanyRone).

All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield (charmm36 or CHARMm-MomanyRone).

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools and click Standard Dynamics Cascade (OpenMM)... to open the Standard Dynamics Cascade (OpenMM) dialog.

* Set the Input Typed Molecule .

* By default, the simulation time for the equilibration stage and production stage are specified to be 16 ps and 20 ps respectively, which is short for most 
input systems. Depending on the purpose of your simulation, you can increase the equilibration and production time by specifying the Simulation Time under the two corresponding parameter groups.

* If you increase the simulation time for the Production stage, evaluate and adjust
the Save Results Interval (ps) parameter accordingly to reduce the number of frames saved if needed.

* For details about the remaining parameters, see Standard Dynamics Cascade (OpenMM) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to the background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

You can inspect the individual output files that were generated in the Output directory of the run. The contents of this directory can be viewed by selecting the job in the Jobs Explorer, right-clicking and choosing Locate. The file names may differ from those listed here.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule with trajectory frames from the production phase in the simulation cascade stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order (that is, the first conformation corresponds to the first trajectory frame in the production phase saved by CHARMm). The time-dependent energy properties from the production phase are also stored with each conformation in this .dsv file. |
| <molecule>_noconfs.dsv | The output molecule without conformations. In this file, the molecule has the final coordinate of the dynamics simulation. This can be used together with the <molecule>.dcd file for trajectory analysis or input to restart another dynamics simulation. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule with the conformations of the production simulation, but with the solvent molecules removed for easy visualization. |
| heating.log | The log file from the heating stage, containing step-by-step information including potential energy, temperature, box volume, density, and simulation performance metrics (ns/day). Temperature increases linearly from the initial to target temperature during this phase. |
| equilibration.log | The log file from the equilibration stage, tracking system properties as thermal equilibration is achieved. Contains timestep data for potential energy, temperature, box volume, and density, showing stabilization of these properties around the target values. |
| production.log | The log file from the production run, containing the thermodynamic properties sampled during the main simulation. This data is used for calculating ensemble averages and analyzing system behavior. |
| combined_data_table.csv | A consolidated CSV file combining data from all simulation stages (heating, equilibration, and production). The file includes columns for Stage, Time, Potential Energy, Temperature, Box Volume, Density, and Speed, enabling easy visualization and analysis of the entire simulation workflow. |
| <molecule>_heating.dcd | The trajectory file from the heating stage in DCD format. Contains atomic coordinates sampled during the temperature ramp from initial to target temperature. Can be loaded using Structure \| Animation \| Load... to visualize the heating process. |
| <molecule>_equilibration.dcd | The trajectory file from the equilibration stage, capturing the system's structural evolution as it reaches thermal and (if NPT) pressure equilibrium. Import this file to analyze equilibration dynamics and verify system stability before production. |
| <molecule>_production.dcd | The main trajectory file from the production run that contains the conformational sampling used for analysis. This file can be imported using Structure \| Animation \| Load... or analyzed with the Analyze Trajectory protocol to extract structural and dynamic properties. |
| <molecule>_minimization.pdb | The energy-minimized structure in PDB format, representing the system after removal of unfavorable contacts and optimization to a local energy minimum. Serves as the starting point for the heating stage. |
| <molecule>_heating.pdb | The final structure from the heating stage in PDB format, showing the system configuration after reaching the target temperature. Used as input for the equilibration stage. |
| <molecule>_equilibration.pdb | The equilibrated structure in PDB format, representing the system after thermal and pressure equilibration. This well-equilibrated structure serves as the starting configuration for the production simulation. |
| <molecule>_production.pdb | The final structure from the production run in PDB format. Represents the last frame of the production trajectory and can be used as a restart point for extending the simulation. |

## Steered Molecular Dynamics - Parameters

### Performs steered molecular dynamics using CHARMm

Steered molecular dynamics speeds up conformational changes and provides insight into the transition mechanism of a molecule.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield.

* The molecule should be well equilibrated.

### Parameters

| --- | --- |

| Simulation Time (ps) | Time length (ps) to perform the dynamics simulation. |
| Save Results Interval (ps) | The time interval in picosecond (ps) to save coordinates, energies, and restart file during the simulation. Notes For consecutive runs, if you intend to combine the results, use the same value for Save Results Interval (ps) . At every specified time interval, the dcd, energy and restart files will be saved. Number of frames to be saved = Simulation Time (ps)/Save Results Interval (ps). |
| Pulling Atom Pair | Specify the two atoms to apply steering forces. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Steered Molecular Dynamics | Parameters related to steered molecular dynamics setup. |

| Steered Molecular Dynamics Target Temperature | Target temperature (K) for the dynamics simulation. |
| Steered Molecular Dynamics Target Pressure | Target pressure in atmospheres for running the simulation. |
| Steered Molecular Dynamics Force Constant | The force constant in pN/Å in restraining the steered atoms. |
| Steered Molecular Dynamics Pulling Speed | The speed of pulling the pair of atoms in Å/ps. The total pulling distance is equal to the product of the pulling speed and the simulation time. |

When Implicit Solvent Model is "Generalized Born" or "Generalized Born with Implicit Membrane (GBIM)", this parameter will be disabled and automatically set to the same value as the Nonbond Lower Cutoff Distance . # Steered Molecular Dynamics

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_steered_molecular_dynamics.htm

## Steered Molecular Dynamics

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Steered Molecular Dynamics protocol allows you to run molecular dynamics simulation while applying 
a steering force to a pair of selected atoms. The added steering force speeds up the dissociation processes and can be used to study the mechanisms of undocking of protein-ligand or protein-protein complexes. It can also be used to force the unfolding of a protein. However, it is not designed to dock a ligand into protein binding pocket. The pair of atoms is defined using the Create Pulling Atom Pair command,
and constant velocity is applied via a spring to those two atoms acting in opposite directions to pull them apart. The force profile of the simulation is saved, so that when you generate multiple trajectories, you can analyze them using the Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces protocol to obtain an averaged free energy as a function of separation distance using the Jarzynski's equality.

* It is assumed that a simulation system is generated, typed, and solvated. It is also recommended that the structure be properly equilibrated. The Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol could be used to accomplish this.

* Open Simulation | Run Simulation tools and use the Create Pulling Atom Pair command to specify the two atoms to which the pulling force will be applied.

* Open Simulation | Run Simulation tools and click Steered Molecular Dynamics dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule Choose the simulation system. Simulation Time (ps) Choose the length of the simulation. Together with the pulling speed (in Advanced > Steered Molecular Dynamics Pulling Speed), the length determines how far the two atoms will be moved during the simulation. For example, at the default pulling speed of 0.02 Å/ps, a pair of atoms will be displaced roughly 20 Angstrom in 1000 ps. Importantly, note that the planned pulling direction, speed and simulation time should ensure that none of the molecules being pulled exit the box. This may result in the simulation stalling. Save Results Interval Choose the frequency of saving the force values. Pulling Atom Pair Specify the atom pair on which to apply the external force. For details about the remaining parameters, see Steered Molecular Dynamics - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Choose the simulation system. |
| Simulation Time (ps) | Choose the length of the simulation. Together with the pulling speed (in Advanced > Steered Molecular Dynamics Pulling Speed), the length determines how far the two atoms will be moved during the simulation. For example, at the default pulling speed of 0.02 Å/ps, a pair of atoms will be displaced roughly 20 Angstrom in 1000 ps. Importantly, note that the planned pulling direction, speed and simulation time should ensure that none of the molecules being pulled exit the box. This may result in the simulation stalling. |
| Save Results Interval | Choose the frequency of saving the force values. |
| Pulling Atom Pair | Specify the atom pair on which to apply the external force. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Steered Molecular Dynamics - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation. It is recommended that you first run a pilot simulation with a rapid pulling schedule in order to test your choice of the pulling atom pair. A visual analysis of such a test SMD simulation (see below) would confirm if the transition of interest is being correctly planned.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

The summary section of the report shows the pulling force as a function of distance recorded during the simulation. The force profiles generated from multiple SMD simulations can be used to calculate the free energy as a function of the pulling distance using the Calculate Free Energy from Steering Forces protocol

Additionally, you can analyze the trajectories produced by the SMD run in various ways using the tools in the application to gain atomistic information about the molecular system. For example:

* Create a trajectory animation for a qualitative visualization of the molecular structure. See Structure | Animation | Create/Remove . As described above, it is helpful to run an initial test simulation and visually analyzing the trajectory to ensure that the desired transition is planned correctly. For example, if you want to simulate the unbinding of a ligand from a protein binding site, such a visual analysis would confirm that the chosen pulling pair atoms and the associated direction allow for the clear separation of the protein and ligand.

* Calculate RMS movement from a reference conformation to understand the extent of a conformational transition. See Analyze Trajectory .

* Apply non-bond monitors to trajectory frames for information on specific interactions within the molecular system during the course of the simulation. See Structure | Monitor .

* Calculate structural properties such as torsion, distance, and angle to study changes in certain regions of the molecule. See Analyze Trajectory .

* Calculate electrostatics solvation energies for specific trajectory frames to study the interaction between solute and solvent. See Solvation Energy.

* By default, the SHAKE constraints are applied to all bonds involving hydrogens, and the default time step is 2fs. 
In general, dynamics simulations may fail if the input structure has bad van der Waals clashes. Failures are typically more frequent when the SHAKE option is
enabled. The problem is not with the SHAKE option, but is an indication that the input structure is not properly minimized. 
If the simulation fails, check that the initial structure does not have bad clashes. You can extend the minimization steps in this protocol
to ensure the input structure is fully minimized before dynamics simulation starts.

* Running long dynamics simulation with large solvated molecular system requires a lot of memory. If the server does not have enough memory, the
protocol may fail in the post processing stage, but the main simulation results are available. When the report shows an error, first
check the charmm.log file to make sure that CHARMm run finished successfully. Then check that output DSV files exist. If the post processing step
failed to generate the output DSV files, do one of the following: Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory: From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_smd.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_smd.ene to each conformation. Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

* Load the trajectory in Discovery Studio client on a machine with adequate memory: From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder. Open Input/<molecule>.dsv . Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder. Select <molecule>_smd.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_smd.ene to each conformation.

* From the Jobs Explorer , right-click the finished job and choose Locate . 
This will open the Files Explorer and expand the job folder.

* Open Input/<molecule>.dsv .

* Choose Structure | Animation | Load.. from the menu bar and navigate to the Intermediate folder.

* Select <molecule>_smd.dcd to load. This will add the frames from the production stage as conformations to the input molecule and also adds the energy terms from <molecule>_smd.ene to each conformation.

* Sample the trajectory by running the Process Trajectory Files protocol with those files as input.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <molecule>.dsv | The output molecule. In this output molecule file, trajectory frames are stored as a collection of conformations in sequential order (i.e., the first conformation corresponds to the first trajectory frame saved by CHARMm). The time-dependent energy properties from the simulation are also stored with each conformation in this .dsv file. The trajectory can be sampled and analyzed using the Analyze Trajectory tool panel , or the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>_noconfs.dsv | The output molecule without conformations. In this file, the molecule has the final coordinate of the dynamics simulation. This can be used together with the <molecule>.dcd file for trajectory analysis. |
| <molecule>_nosolvent.dsv | The output molecule without solvent. This file has all of the conformations and solvent molecules removed for easy visualization. |
| <molecule>.dcd | The trajectory file generated by CHARMm. It saves the coordinates of each step for this dynamics simulation. You can import the trajectory frames to the molecule using Structure \| Animation \| Load... , or by sampling it with the Analyze Trajectory protocol . |
| <molecule>.ene | The energy file generated by CHARMm. It saves the time-dependent energy properties for this dynamics simulation. Its values will be loaded into the molecule when a corresponding dcd file is imported ( Structure \| Animation \| Load... from the menu bar). |
| Force-Profile.csv | Contains the Force as a function of pulling distance in CSV format. |
| <molecule>.ffml | A Forcefield Markup Language (FFML) file, used to store missing or estimated forcefield parameters. |
| charmm.log | Contains detailed log messages generated by the CHARMm simulation engine. |

# Trajectory Principal Component Analysis - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_trajectory_principal_component_analysis-para.htm

## Trajectory Principal Component Analysis - Parameters

### Calculates fundamental motions (Principal Components) of a trajectory using CHARMm

Calculates and diagonalizes the variance-covariance matrix of the atomic movements for a trajectory. The results are then used to create animations of the dominant motions. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is similar to quasi-harmonic analysis derived from vibrational modes. In quasi-harmonic analysis the mass weighted variance-covariance matrix is used, in PCA no mass weighting is performed.

Notes:

* The molecule must be typed with a supported forcefield and contain multiple conformations.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Selects a typed molecule with conformations for analysis. |
| Number of Principal Components | Specify how many principal components should be calculated. |
| Mode Temperature | Specifies the temperature (K) at which the mode amplitude is calculated according to equal partition of energy. The temperature is usually adjusted in order to produce a visible movement in each mode. |

Selects a typed molecule with conformations for analysis.

Specify how many principal components should be calculated.

Specifies the temperature (K) at which the mode amplitude is calculated according to equal partition of energy. The temperature is usually adjusted in order to produce a visible movement in each mode.

# Trajectory Principal Component Analysis

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/simulation_trajectory_principal_component_analysis.htm

## Trajectory Principal Component Analysis

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Trajectory Principal Component Analysis protocol performs a Principal Component
Analysis (PCA) on a set of molecular conformations (for example from an MD trajectory). Molecular
motions occur in a 3N-6 dimension conformational space. Thus even small molecules are associated with very large conformational space.

PCA is used to reduce the effective dimensions of molecular motions, by identifying a low-dimensional subspace that
captures most dominant fluctuations in conformational space.

The method takes the m-coordinate vectors, q, associated with the conformation sample and calculates the covariance matrix C, where

C = <(q - <q>)Tr(q - <q>)>

The covariance matrix C is diagonalized to obtain the eigenvectors that capture
most of the variance
in atomic fluctuations.

The notion behind PCA is that the essential dynamics space is much smaller than the full dimensionality. This assumption is found to be largely
valid for biomolecules. For example, for many systems, it was found that 70%-90% of the conformational fluctuation can be described in as few as
three dimensions [Caves, 1998] .

* Load a molecule that contains a set of conformations into the Molecule Window. For example, the output molecule from a dynamics simulation may be
used. The principal components are calculated using atomic fluctuation information contained in the trajectory frames.

* Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Trajectory Principal Component Analysis... to open the Trajectory Principal Component Analysis dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Typed Molecule Choose the loaded molecule. Number of Principal Components Specify number of principal components to be computed. Mode Temperature The temperature at which the amplitude of each component will be assigned.
The amplitude of a principal component is computed using equal partition theorem, which
states that each vibrational mode (quasiharmonic mode in our case) has an energy of kT.
The energy of each mode is 1/2 × ω 2 A 2 , where ω is the mode frequency, and A is the amplitude.
This means that A is proportional to 1/ω.
That is, the amplitude of the principal component decreases with its frequency and hence its mode
index. In PCA, the mode temperature is usually adjusted to illustrate the movement associated with each principal component. For details about the remaining parameters, see Trajectory Principal Component Analysis - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Typed Molecule | Choose the loaded molecule. |
| Number of Principal Components | Specify number of principal components to be computed. |
| Mode Temperature | The temperature at which the amplitude of each component will be assigned. The amplitude of a principal component is computed using equal partition theorem, which states that each vibrational mode (quasiharmonic mode in our case) has an energy of kT. The energy of each mode is 1/2 × ω 2 A 2 , where ω is the mode frequency, and A is the amplitude. This means that A is proportional to 1/ω. That is, the amplitude of the principal component decreases with its frequency and hence its mode index. In PCA, the mode temperature is usually adjusted to illustrate the movement associated with each principal component. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Trajectory Principal Component Analysis - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* All Simulation protocols require that the simulated system be typed using an appropriate forcefield. If a molecule is not typed when the protocol is launched, it will be automatically typed using the current forcefield selected in the Change Forcefield tools.

* If the automatic typing is unsuccessful, the protocol will not be launched. Use the Change Forcefield tools to investigate typing failures.

To view the illustrative principle components of motion:

* Open one of the .dsv files produced by the protocol.

* Ensure that the Graphics View is active (CTRL+G).

* Choose Structure | Animation | Play from the menu bar.

This shows the structure oscillating in
its principle component. At typical values for the temperature, this motion
is exaggerated, which results in a somewhat distorted animation, but allows
you to visualize the motion.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| charmm.log | The log file of the CHARMm Trajectory Principal Component Analysis calculation. |
| <molecule>_n.dsv | Contains the n th principal component projected onto Cartesian space as conformations. You can visualize these using the animation menu . |

## Type Ligands with MATCH - Parameters

### Forcefield typing using MATCH

Assigns the charmm36 forcefield to the input ligands by using the MATCH method. MATCH uses analogy to existing parameterized molecules in the CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF) to assign atomic partial charges and estimate bonded parameters.

See Also:

* Yesselman, J.D.; Price, D.J.; Knight, J.L.; Brooks III, C.L. MATCH: An atom-typing toolset for molecular mechanics force fields. J. Comput. Chem. 2011 , 33 , 189.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be typed. In Discovery Studio, select from all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. |

In Discovery Studio, select from all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window.

## Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype)

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) protocol allows a user to type a set of ligands with charmm36 forcefield using the Multipurpose Atom-Typer for CHARMM (MATCH) method [Yesselman et al., 2012] . The method implements a hierarchical atom typer and a chemical pattern-matching algorithm to assign molecular mechanics atom types, charges, and forcefield parameters as determined by analogy to existing molecules in the CHARMM General Forcefield (CGenFF), compatible with the charmm36 forcefield [Vanommeslaeghe et al., 2010] .

* Load the ligands you want to type into the Molecule Window.

* Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools and click Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype)... to open the dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameter: Parameter Description Input Ligands Choose the ligands to be typed. For details about the remaining parameters, see Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Choose the ligands to be typed. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Type Ligands with MATCH (Prototype) - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If the run is successful, open the Typed Ligands file to find the forcefield assignment information in its data table. You can use the typed molecule in subsequent simulation tasks. The ligands that failed typing can be found in the Failed Ligands file. Failure to type may happen if a closely matching template fragment or molecule is not found in CGenFF.

#### Troubleshooting

A typical run is expected to result in the following files. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Typed Ligands | File containing the ligands that could be successfully typed by MATCH. |
| Failed Ligands | File containing the ligands that could not be typed by MATCH. |

# Use a restart file

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tsk_restart-file.htm

## Use a restart file

When continuing a molecular dynamics (MD) simulation from a previous job, it is important to retain the atom velocities from one run to
the next. These velocities are stored in a restart ( .rst ) file, which you can save from one protocol and use in another. For each stage in the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol , this is done for you automatically and you only need the restart 
file if you wish to continue with Dynamics (Production) .

In the Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) protocol , the dynamics starts at a preset
temperature, and the initial velocities are assigned at this temperature. Restart files are not used in this protocol to specify initial
velocities.

To run Dynamics (Equilibration) and Dynamics (Production) protocols, 
follow these steps to set the restart file:

* Make sure that in the previous MD job, the restart file is saved. The Save Restart File parameter can be found in all the 
MD protocols: Standard Dynamics Cascade, Dynamics (Heating or Cooling), Dynamics (Equilibration), and Dynamics (Production) protocols.

* Open the protocol you want to run and set the Restart File parameter to the .rst file in the Output folder of the previous MD run.

* Specify other parameters necessary to run the MD protocol. In most cases, the same parameter setting used in the MD job that created the 
restart file should be used in the subsequent job.

You can start a Dynamics (NAMD) job from a previous CHARMm simulation job or a NAMD simulation job as follows:

* To restart from a previous CHARMm job, set the CHARMm Restart File parameter to the corresponding .rst file from the previous run.

* To restart from a previous NAMD job, set the following parameters under the NAMD Restart Files parameter group: Set Velocities Restart File to <molecule>_restart.vel in the Output folder of the previous run. Set Coordinates Restart File to <molecule>_restart.pdb in the Output folder of the previous run. Set Extended System to <molecule>_restart.xsc in the Output folder of the previous run.

* Set Velocities Restart File to <molecule>_restart.vel in the Output folder of the previous run.

* Set Coordinates Restart File to <molecule>_restart.pdb in the Output folder of the previous run.

* Set Extended System to <molecule>_restart.xsc in the Output folder of the previous run.

To use a restart file, you do not need to read in the previous job's output .dsv file, since 
the restart file contains not only the atomic velocities, but also the final coordinates of atoms in the molecule. You only need to read in the 
input .dsv file from the previous MD job. If you do use the output .dsv file from the previous MD job (which contains trajectory frames in the
conformation collections), the new conformations generated from the current job will be appended to existing ones and the resulting .dsv file
will have both the previously generated conformations and those from the restarted dynamics job.

# Prepare protein structure for simulation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tsk_simulation_prepare-for-simulation.htm

## Prepare protein structure for simulation

Simulating proteins with molecular mechanics requires accurate
representation of the structure. Proteins downloaded from the PDB may have
problems that should be corrected before running simulations.
Common problems and steps to correct them are discussed here. Some of the
problems must be corrected for the simulation to run. Other fixes are
optional, but are likely to improve results.

* Remove alternate conformations (Required): Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Clean . The first set of conformations is used by default.

* Patch missing atoms (Optional): Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Clean . If this step is not performed, hydrogen atoms may be added to fill valencies during typing. This may cause unknown residue
connectivities, which may not be typed successfully.

* Patch missing residues (Optional): See Identify missing residues in a protein structure and insert them for details.

* Type the molecule with a forcefield (Required): Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel. Choose a forcefield from the Forcefield menu. Click Apply Forcefield . Check the Status to make sure the molecule is typed.

* Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tool panel.

* Choose a forcefield from the Forcefield menu.

* Click Apply Forcefield .

* Check the Status to make sure the molecule is typed.

* Assign residue protonation states at given solution pH and optimize hydrogen positions (Optional):
Open the Macromolecules | Prepare Protein tools and click Calculating Protein Ionization and Residue pK to open the protocol dialog. Set the parameters as desired before running.

Alternatively, you can run the Prepare Proteins protocol to prepare the input for simulation.
