# Specify constraints and restraints

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tsk_simulation_restraints-constraints.htm

## Specify constraints and restraints

For some of the Run Simulations tools , you have the option of specifying constraints and restraints used in the simulation through an advanced parameter. For example, you can specify constraints in the Minimization tool with the Minimization Constraints parameter. Dynamics (NAMD) can also use these constraints in the Constraints parameter. They are converted to NAMD type constraints internally.

This parameter allows you to select one or more constraints and restraints that have been set up in the molecule system using the Setup Constraints tools . In addition, you can also specify a CHARMm stream file with constraints defined in standard CHARMm syntax.

A CHARMm stream file is a text file that contains standard CHARMm syntax. For example, you could create a file named fixed.stream with the following line in CHARMm syntax, which adds a fixed atom constraint to all hydrogen atoms:

CONS FIX SELECT TYPE H* END

When you set the Minimization Constraints parameter to point to this file, all hydrogen atoms will be fixed during the minimization.

For details on the standard CHARMm syntax, refer to the CHARMm documentation .

Please note that the CHARMm stream file option is provided for advanced users familiar with the CHARMm syntax. You should only use this option if you are familiar with CHARMm syntax. You will not be able to view the constraints on the molecule. For most commonly used constraints and restraints and visualization of the constraints, use the Setup Constraints tools .

#### Further information

Setup Constraints tools Minimization Standard Dynamics Cascade Dynamics (Production) Dynamics (Heating or Cooling) Dynamics (Equilibration)

# Save intermediate files

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tsk_simulation_saving-intermediate-files.htm

## Save intermediate files

To save intermediate files used in the Simulation protocols, check the Save intermediate files when 
running protocols option on the Protocols page of the Preferences dialog.

The Simulation protocols each return slightly different intermediate files, sometimes depending on which parameters have been specified. Advanced
users who are accustomed to running CHARMm from the command line may find these useful for performing further analysis and evaluation of results.

The following table describes several of the intermediate files that are commonly created by the Simulation protocols. These abbreviations are used
for parts of file names that are dependent on the input data or the protocol being run:

* molecule : The name of the user-specified input molecular system

* stage : An abbreviation of the protocol stage being run, for example, mini , heat , eq , or prod

| File Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| 1.crd(2.crd...) | Coordinate file generated during typing and used as input to CHARMm. Each CRD file corresponds to one chain in the molecular system. |
| molecule.crd | Coordinate file for the whole system generated during typing. |
| molecule.prm | Parameter file of the forcefield generated during typing and used as input to CHARMm. |
| molecule_custom.prm | Parameter file for any estimated parameters not in the forcefield. It was generated during typing for estimated parameters and used as input to CHARMm. |
| forcefield.rtf | Residue topology file generated during typing and used as input to CHARMm. |
| molecule_missing.rtf | Residue topology file for any new atom types generated during typing and used as input to CHARMm. |
| molecule_specific.rtf | Residue topology file for any new custom residues generated during typing and used as input to CHARMm. |
| molecule_stage.crd | Output coordinates for a specific CHARMm stage. |
| molecule_stage.dcd | Trajectory file for a specific CHARMm stage. |
| molecule_stage.ene | CHARMm energies for a specific CHARMm stage. |
| *.inp | The CHARMm input script that was run. This input script typically references several *.stream files. |
| *.stream | CHARMm stream files that perform the majority of the setup and calculations using CHARMm. |
| *_std*.txt | The STDOUT and STDERR of the various command-line processes that were run during execution of the protocol. |
| charmm.log | The CHARMm log file, which is also copied into the Output/ directory. |
| *.bat / *.sh | The batch files (Windows) or shell scripts (Linux) used to launch the various command-line processes that were run during execution of the protocol. |

# General simulation tasks

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tsk_simulations-general.htm

## General simulation tasks

The tasks below are basic tasks for working with simulations.
For a comprehensive list of simulation tasks that include basic tasks and tasks that involve working with the Simulation tool set, see Tasks - Simulations .

* Animate a dynamics trajectory

* Apply a forcefield with customized parameters

* Color an existing molecular surface by interpolated charges

* Color surfaces using electrostatic potential

* Create a single isocontour surface after Electrostatic Potential calculations

* Create multiple isocontour surfaces after Electrostatic Potential calculations

* Import a PSF file that was generated by CHARMm

* Monitor geometrical changes during a dynamics simulation

* Monitor the distance between the centroid of two sets of atoms during a dynamics animation

* Remove alternate conformers from the molecule

* Simulate the dynamic behavior of a peptide

* Stop, analyze partial results, and restart a long running dynamics simulation

To animate a dynamics trajectory

* Navigate to the output folder of a completed dynamics calculation
(see Simulate the dynamic behavior of a peptide ).
Depending on your preferences, you may be able to do this by double-clicking in the Jobs Explorer (a report on the calculation may also be
opened).

* Click the Output Molecule (a .dsv file) to open the calculation results.

* From the menu bar, choose, Structure | Animation | Play to cyclically display stored
frames from the dynamics calculation.

For information about using the animation toolbar, see Animation toolbar .

You can use animations of
dynamics calculations to explore the conformational flexibility of molecules.

To apply a forcefield with customized parameters

This example uses the 1aq1 structure for illustrative purposes. The steps can be
applied to any similar system:

* Open the file 1aq1.pdb from the Samples/Tutorials/Quick Start Tutorials folder. This
structure contains a protein and a ligand.

* Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools and set Forcefield to charmm27 .
Click Apply Forcefield . This forcefield has been
chosen because it does not perform automatic parameter estimation.

* A message dialog opens and indicate that the molecule cannot be typed by the forcefield. Click OK to close the dialog.

* Click More... on the tool panel to view the
missing parameters. Click the Atoms tab. This lists atoms which could
not be typed.

* Click on the row label "1" to select the atom that could not be
typed. Switch back to the Molecule Window by clicking its tab (if you click
in the window, you may reset the selection). Click Fit To Screen in the toolbar
to zoom in. The atom is an amide carbon in a ring.

* Click Modify Atom Type... on the tool panel 
to open the Choose a Forcefield Type dialog. From this dialog choose an appropriate atom type such as C .

* Click in the Molecule Window to deselect everything.

* Click Apply Forcefield again to use the new atom type. Now, when
you click More... there are tabs containing the missing Bond, Angle,
Torsion, and Improper terms with the estimated parameter values. 
This table is editable. Carefully review the parameters and set to appropriate values.

* This table is editable and you can type values into the corresponding cells to set the parameter values.
Clicking on the row label of the parameter will select the corresponding atoms and associated bond or angles, etc in the Molecule Window.
You can switch back to the Molecule Window by clicking its tab and click Fit To Screen in the toolbar
to zoom in to examine the selected atoms. Carefully review the parameters and reset the values if needed.

* Choose File | Save As... from the menu bar to save it as an FFML file. Close
the Forcefield window.

* Open the FFML file in Discovery Studio . It will appear in a new
Forcefield window. When you open an FFML file like this, you can make
changes and save the file again.

* Click Forcefield and choose Browse... from the
Forcefield dropdown menu and navigate to the FFML file you just saved.

* Click Apply Forcefield . The molecule is now typed
successfully without missing parameters. The parameters you supplied in
the FFML file are used to supplement the selected forcefield to
completely type the molecule.

To color an existing molecular surface by interpolated charges

Open a molecule and create a molecular surface using Surface | Add... command from Structure menu. 
In the Molecule window, open the Display Style dialog from the context menu, click the Surface tab, select the Color by: option in the Coloring group, and choose Interpolated Charge .
Click Apply or OK .

Details:

* The coordinates and partial charges of all atoms defining the molecular surface are collected. If the definition includes hidden terminal
hydrogen atoms, the charge distribution is updated as follows. If the hidden terminal hydrogen atom H is connected to an atom A which is also
part of the molecular surface definition, then the partial charge q (H) of the hydrogen atom is added to the partial charge q ( A ) of atom A , and
the partial charge of the hydrogen atom is ignored.

* The "electrostatic potential" is calculated at each mesh point P of the surface with 3D coordinates r ( P ) by considering the subset of atoms A with partial charges q ( A ) and 3D coordinates r ( A ) where the distance | r ( A ) - r ( P )| is less than a cutoff value of 12.5 Å. The
actual formula employed is V = [sum(i) q (A i )/d i ] / [sum(i) 1/d i ] where d i = ( r ( P ) - r ( A )) 2 and the sum runs over all atoms A that lie
within the cutoff distance from the mesh point P . Effectively, this calculates not the electrostatic potential, but interpolates a function
which assigns a partial charge q to each point in 3D space where only a finite set of data points { r ( A i ), q ( A i )} is given.
The interpolation employed has been described by Franke and Nielson [Franke and Nielson, 1980] .

To color surfaces using electrostatic potential

To color a molecular surface using the electrostatic potential created by the 
Electrostatic Potential, 
Electrostatic Potential with Focusing, or
Solvation Energy protocols:

* Open the output molecule containing the grid from one of the protocols into the Molecule Window.

* Choose the Structure | Surface | Add... from the menu bar to create the molecular surface.

* Open the Display Style dialog in the Molecule Window, click the Surface tab, select the By grid: option in the Coloring group, and choose the name of the grid. You can also adjust the coloring scheme and scale being used.

* Click Apply or OK .

To create a single isocontour surface after Electrostatic Potential calculations

* When the run finishes and the results open, expand the molecule in the Hierarchy View and check the Grid checkbox, which has the same name as the molecule.
This displays the first isosurface.

* Uncheck the <Solvent Grid Surface> checkbox to hide the solid surface display.

* Click on the Grid to select the first isosurface.

* Right-click in the Molecule Window and select Display Style... .

* On the Isosurface tab, set Isovalue to the desired value and
set the Custom color as desired to color the isosurface.

The potential values are in kT per one unit charge.

To create multiple isocontour surfaces after Electrostatic Potential calculations

* Uncheck the <SolidSurface> checkbox to hide the solid surface display.

* Right-click in the Molecule Window and choose Display Style... .

* To add a new isocontour, click the Grid object with the new isosurface to select it again.

* Choose Structure | Isosurface | New Contour... from the menu bar to open the Add Isosurface
Contour Level dialog.

* Type the desired isopotential value of the new isosurface into the Isovalue box.

* Repeat the last two steps for additional isopotential surfaces.

To import a PSF file that was generated by CHARMm

* Browse to a folder that contains a PSF file and a
CRD file associated with the same structure.

* If the forcefield is something other than CHARMm,
and the title line of the PSF file does not contain the forcefield name,
use a text editor to add the forcefield name to the title line which begins with an asterisk.
Valid forcefield names are: CHARMPLR, charmm19, charmm22, charmm27, charmm36 and XPROLIG.
If the forcefield name is not present, CHARMm will be used.

* Double-click the PSF file to load the structure and forcefield information for the structure.

To monitor geometrical changes during a dynamics simulation

* Load a molecule containing conformations into a Molecule Window. Typically,
this would be the result of a dynamics simulation.

* Set up monitors on geometrical properties of interest. From the menu bar,
choose Structure | Monitor or click the Measure button on the View toolbar. For
example, use the Distance monitor to check the CA-CA distance between
two residues.

* Open the Hierarchy View and expand the molecule. The monitors are updated as you click on the
conformations.

* For more detailed analysis, for example to plot a distance over the
time of the simulation, run the Analyze Trajectory protocol. Open the Simulation | Analyze Trajectory tools and click Analyze Trajectory to open the protocol dialog. Set the Input Molecule to the molecule of interest, make sure the Properties option is selected in the Analysis Type parameter and the desired monitors are selected in the Properties parameter, and then click Run.

* After the results open, click Create Plot... in the tool panel.
Choose Time for the X axis, and your monitors for the Y axis.

* Click OK to view the plot. Note that as you select points in the resulting plot,
the corresponding conformations are selected and displayed in the Molecule Window.

* For more advanced charting, such as creating 3D plots, use the options in the Chart menu.
Make the Data Table visible and select the Conformation tab before using these options.

To monitor the distance between the centroid of two sets of atoms during a dynamics animation

When investigating a dynamics calculation, you can monitor a range of
geometrical properties. For example, you can monitor the distance between two
centroids:

* Open a .dsv file from a dynamics calculations.

* Select a group of atoms and create a centroid monitor. Choose Structure | Monitor | Centroid from the menu bar.

* Select a different group of atoms and create another centroid monitor.
Choose Structure | Monitor | Centroid from the menu bar.

* Select the centroid monitors.

* Create a distance monitor between them.
Choose Structure | Monitor | Distance from the menu bar.

* Animate the frames of the trajectory stored for this structure to see how
this distance varied during the simulation. For details, see Animate a dynamics trajectory .

To remove alternate conformers from the molecule

* Select Edit | Preferences... and choose Protein Utilities | Clean Protein .

* In the Correct problems section, check the Alternate conformations (retain one set) checkbox.

* Load a molecule in Molecule Window that has alternate conformers.

* Open the Prepare Protein tool panel and click Clean Protein .

Forcefields other than XPROLIG
require any alternate conformers removed before typing.

To simulate the dynamic behavior of a peptide

* Choose File | New | Molecule Window from the menu bar.

* Open the Protein Modeling | Build and Edit Protein tools.

* Set Build Action to Create/Grow Chain .

* Set Conformation to Extended .

* Choose the following amino acids to create a simple tetra-peptide: Ala , Arg , Asn , and Asp .

* Open the Simulation | Change Forcefield tools and set Forcefield to CHARMm .

* Click Apply Forcefield . This sets up forcefield parameters for the dynamics simulation.

* Open the Simulation | Run Simulations tools, click Standard Dynamics Cascade to open the protocol dialog. Set the parameters as desired and click Run .

To stop, analyze partial results, and restart a long running dynamics simulation

* From the Jobs explorer, select the running job you want to stop.

* Right-click the job and choose Stop to open the Stop Job dialog, and then click Yes to retrieve files of the partially finished job.

* From the Analyze Trajectory tool panel, click Analyze Trajectory... and set Input Molecule to the same molecule you used to start the simulation.

* Click the button in the Trajectory File parameter and navigate to the stopped job, open the Intermediate folder, and select the .dcd file. Click OK to close the file Open dialog and focus on Trajectory File dialog. Move the scroll bar on the dialog and examine the basic information, such as simulation time, etc
of the DCD file listed in the dialog. Click OK to close the dialog. If you ran a Standard Dynamics Cascade job, the file will be located under subfolders corresponding to the steps
of the cascade in the Intermediate folder.

If you ran a Standard Dynamics Cascade job, the file will be located under subfolders corresponding to the steps
of the cascade in the Intermediate folder.

* Click the button in the Energy File parameter and select the .ene file 
from Intermediate folder.

* Check the RMSD option from the Analysis Type parameter, and then click Run .

* After the job finishes, with the output molecule opened, click Create Plot from the Analyze Trajectory tool panel.

* Choose Time for the X axis, 
and Total Energy for the Y axis to create the energy versus time plot.

* Create another chart with RMSD to conf 1 for the Y axis.

* To continue the dynamics simulation from where is was stopped, open the input molecule, and then click Dynamics (Production)... from the Run Simulations tool panel.

* Set the same parameter values used in the original simulation, and then set the Restart File as the .rst file in the Intermediate folder from
the previous job. Click Run to restart the simulation.

The status of the dynamics calculation is displayed on the Jobs Explorer. To display an animation of the calculation, Animate a dynamics trajectory .

# Type for bio-molecule and general forcefields

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tsk_type-biomolecule-forcefields.htm

## Type for bio-molecule and general forcefields

### Background

In molecular mechanical simulations, the energy of a molecular system is defined by atomic forcefield models. A forcefield typically has three 
elements: a functional form, a set of predefined atom types that covers certain groups of molecules (for example proteins, nucleic acids, and 
carbohydrates), and a set of parameters associated with those atom types (for example force constants, equilibrium values, partial charges, and van der 
Waals radii).

The concept of atom type is central to all forcefield based simulations. Every atom in a molecule is characterized by a specific atom type.

Preparing a molecular system for simulation involves three steps:

* Atom typing (including partial charge assignment)

* Parameter assignment

* Generation of simulation files

Typing atoms is the process of associating atoms with atom types and partial charges. A molecular system is said to be typed by a forcefield when 
all the atoms have been assigned a forcefield atom type and given a partial charge.

The total energy as a function of coordinates is well defined only after all the parameters for each of the potential 
energy terms such as bond or angle are assigned. You must supply the parameters, or with forcefields such as CHARMm, they can be estimated by the program.

In the last stage of forcefield typing, a set of files required by the simulation engine is generated. This stage is typically performed on the server.

### CHARMm Force fields in Discovery Studio

Discovery Studio supports a variety of forcefields. Refer to Select a forcefield for simulation for more information.

Because the CHARMm forcefield has the broadest coverage for organic molecules in
this application and is likely the most widely useful in 
pharmaceutical drug design, its atom typing procedures are detailed in the following section.

#### Atom typing

The CHARMm forcefield uses standard residue templates to type amino acids and nucleic acids, and a set of rules for typing general organic molecules. 
The residue template-based typing requires that both the atom and residue names match those in the residue template file.

In rule-based typing, the type of an atom is determined according to its local topology such as nearest neighbor connectivity, hybridization and 
aromaticity. Since it is difficult to detect delocalized structures such as conjugation with only local topology information, the logic for typing 
conjugated sub-structures is hardcoded, outside the typing rules stored in the data files.

If an atom fails both template-based typing and rule-based typing, then it is assigned a new atom type. In this case, the forcefield will not have 
parameters for any of the potential energy terms related to this missing atom, and these missing parameters will have to be supplied by you or 
estimated by the program.

Details on the parameter estimation in CHARMm forcefield are described in other sections. Refer to Parameter estimation for CHARMm forcefields for more information.

#### Partial charge assignment

If a residue is matched to a template in the CHARMm forcefield, partial charge is assigned according to the template. Otherwise use one of the following methods for assigning partial charge in the CHARMm forcefield:

* Use Momany-Rone bond charge increment rules to charge bonded atom pairs.

* Apply MMFF94 charges to atoms that are not part of a standard amino acid chain.

* Assign partial charges from CFF to atoms that are not part of a standard amino acid chain.

* Manually assign customized partial charge to an atom.

#### Further information

Parameter estimation for CHARMm forcefields Change Forcefield tools Choose a Forcefield Type dialog Forcefield Window How to select a forcefield

# Considerations for running simulations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssimulation

Source file: tssimulation/tssimulation_considerations.htm

## Considerations for running simulations

Consider the following when running simulation protocols.

### Nonbond cutoffs

Cutoff distances for nonbonded interaction shown as defaults in the
Simulations protocols should be consistent with forcefield
parameterization as shown in the following table.

| Forcefield | Cutoffs (Å) |
| --- | --- |
| CHARMm | 11, 14, 15 |
| charmm19 | 6.5, 7.5, 8.0 |
| charmm22 | 10, 12, 13 |
| charmm27 | 10, 12, 14 |
| charmm36 | 10, 12, 14 |
| cff | 8, 9, 9.5 |

### Temperature controls

Temperature controls for dynamics protocols are handled as follows:

* For both heating and equilibration, simple velocity re-assignment at the desired
temperature(s) is used to maintain thermal equilibration.

* In the Dynamics (Production) protocol, and for the production stage in the Standard Dynamics Cascade protocol,
Berendsen's weak coupling scheme [Berendsen, et al., 1984] is used to achieve constant
temperature dynamics in the NVT ensemble, while the Hoover's extended system constant pressure and
temperature algorithm is used for simulation in the NPT ensemble.

### Working with multiple molecules

When there are multiple molecules in a system, the simulation protocols
only take one molecule as the Input Typed Molecule parameter.

To run a multiple molecule simulation on a complex system, drag and drop the molecules
into a single molecule in the Hierarchy View ,
and run the simulation on this combined molecule.

### Running parallel Simulation protocols

Running Simulation protocols in parallel is supported on a multi-processor server.
To do this, you will need to set the advanced parameter Number of Processors to a number that is a power of 2. See Run a parallel calculation for further information.

## Simulation tool panels

The following tool panels are available in the Simulation tool set :

| Tool Panel | Tasks |
| --- | --- |
| Run Simulations tools | Prepare for and run dynamics calculations, calculate energy, minimize, and solvate molecules and complexes. |
| Run Free Energy Simulations tools | Set up and run free energy simulations. |
| Setup Constraints tools | Set up fixed atom and dihedral constraints, as well as harmonic, and distance restraints. |
| Change Forcefield tools | Apply and manage forcefields. |
| Analyze Trajectory | Analyze trajectories of a molecular system. |

# ADMET Descriptors - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/admet_admet_descriptors-para.htm

## ADMET Descriptors - Parameters

### Computes ADMET descriptors of ligands

Calculates the following Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) properties:

* Aqueous Solubility

* Blood Brain Barrier Penetration

* CYP2D6 Binding

* Hepatotoxicity

* Intestinal Absorption

* Plasma Protein Binding

Also calculates AlogP98 and PSA_2D, which are used in plotting the confidence ellipses.

Calculating ADMET descriptors early in the development of a drug is important to help avoid having to eliminate compounds with unfavorable ADMET characteristics later in the development process, preferably before synthesis.

The models used to predict the ADMET properties in this protocol are derived from a variety of experimental data sources and are 
catalogued in the product documentation.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| ADMET Descriptors | ADMET Descriptors include: Aqueous Solubility : Predicts the solubility of each compound in water at 25°C. Blood Brain Barrier Penetration : Predicts the blood brain barrier penetration of a molecule. CYP2D6 Binding : Predicts cytochrome P450 2D6 enzyme inhibition. Hepatotoxicity : Predicts the occurrence of dose-dependent human hepatotoxicity. Intestinal Absorption : Predicts Human Intestinal Absorption (HIA) after oral administration. Plasma Protein Binding : Predicts likelihood that a compound will be highly bound to carrier proteins in the blood. See Also: More details on the descriptors can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation and the ADMET Component Collection User Guide. Valid Values: Aqueous Solubility , Blood Brain Barrier Penetration , CYP2D6 Binding , Hepatotoxicity , Intestinal Absorption , Plasma Protein Binding |

# ADMET Descriptors

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/admet_admet_descriptors.htm

## ADMET Descriptors

* Description

* How to run ADMET Descriptors

* Analyzing results

The ADMET Descriptors protocol uses the QSAR models to estimate a range of ADMET related properties for small molecules.
The following properties, and classes of properties, can be computed:

* Aqueous solubility

* Blood brain barrier penetration (BBB)

* Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) 2D6 inhibition

* Hepatotoxicity

* Human intestinal absorption (HIA)

* Plasma protein binding

* Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click ADMET Descriptors to open the ADMET Descriptors dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . ADMET Descriptors Specify which descriptors to calculate. By default, all 6 descriptors are selected. At least one checkbox must remain checked.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| ADMET Descriptors | Specify which descriptors to calculate. By default, all 6 descriptors are selected. At least one checkbox must remain checked. |

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* When the job completes, the computed properties are added to the Data Table and 
a 2D ADMET Plot using AlogP98 and PSA_2D is displayed. If 
the Blood Brain Barrier checkbox or the Absorption checkbox are checked in the ADMET Plot subpage of the Preferences dialog, their 95% and 99% confidence ellipses are also added to 
the plot. If the job was sent to the background while running, view the results 
by clicking View Results in the Output Files section of the report.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <name>_ligands.sd | The calculated ADMET descriptors are in the property fields. The Input Ligands parameter determines the file name. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Script for viewing the results. |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

# Theory - Toxicity Prediction (Extensible)

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/admet_extensible_the.htm

## Theory - Toxicity Prediction (Extensible)

### Overview

TOPKAT models have been re-trained using updated training sets from the legacy TOPKAT
(Toxicity Prediction by Komputer Assisted Technology). The classification models are
built with Bayesian models, and the regression models are built with the partial least
squares (PLS) technique. All the Bayesian models were created using Modified Bayesian
learning (described in [Xia et al., 2004] ).

The following models are extensible and are derived using calculable properties in Pipeline Pilot Server :

* NTP Rodent Carcinogenicity

* FDA Rodent Carcinogenicity

* Weight of Evidence Carcinogenicity

* Carcinogenic Potency TD50

* Ames Mutagenicity

* Developmental Toxicity Potential

* Rat Oral LD50

* Rat Maximum Tolerated Dose

* Rat Inhalational LC50

* Rat Chronic LOAEL

* Skin Irritancy

* Skin Sensitization

* Ocular Irritancy

* Aerobic Biodegradability

* Fathead Minnow LC50

* Daphnia EC50

### Model applicability and usage

Every model has been validated using cross validation. Reported results are from leave-one-out cross validation for Bayesian models, 
and 10-fold cross validation (each time 10% are left as test set) for regression models. The prediction result can be further 
assessed with a wide range of model applicability and similarity search information:

* The univariate analysis examines each descriptor and reports any descriptor outside the range in the training set.

* The query structure is checked against the Optimum Prediction Space (OPS), a patented multivariate analysis technique.

* If any fingerprint is used as a training property, the presence of novel features will be reported in the applicability output.

* The Mahalanobis distance (MD) to the center of the training set is calculated for the query structure. MD is a generalization of the
Euclidean distance that accounts for correlation among the properties. An associated p-value is also calculated. The larger the MD and the
smaller the p-value, the less reliable the prediction.

* The prediction can be further examined by comparing the similar compounds in the training set returned by similarity search.

* The prediction report lists the structure features with the most significant contributions to toxicity and non-toxicity.

Descriptions of most of our toxicity predictors complying to the QSAR Model Reporting Format have been submitted to the OECD QSAR Model Database; 
once accepted, they will become available to the public at the Joint Research Centre Data Catalogue . 
To locate them, perform a free text search for the term BIOVIA.

### References for the training set compounds

The similarity search returns compounds that are similar to the input compound from the training set. The reference to the original test result 
is also included to help to verify the integrity of the data to validate the confidence of the model and the result. Some of the references came from sources
such as The Registry of Toxic Effects of Chemical Substances (RTECS). They might look cryptic to non-expert users. In general, the formats fall into one of 
the following categories:

| Category | Reference Format |
| --- | --- |
| Journal Articles | CODEN of the journal volume;page,year |
| PDR | Physicians' Desk Reference |
| NTP | US National Toxicology Program |
| TR | Technical Reports of the NTP |
| CPDB | Carcinogenic Potency Database |
| RTECS | The Registry of Toxic Effects of Chemical Substances |

The technical report can be found on the NTP website by searching the report number. For example, searching TR-120 returns https://ntp.niehs.nih.gov/ntp/htdocs/lt_rpts/tr312.pdf.

### Extending a model

All the models contained in the Toxicity Prediction (Extensible) protocol are extensible. The training
properties and all other necessary information are saved with the model components. You can extend them
by adding new training data using the Update TOPKAT Model example protocol. You can easily achieve this by using Pipeline Pilot Designer for Applications to modify the Extend Ames Model protocol in the Discovery Studio Example Protocols. 
See Customizing protocols for more information about modifying protocols.

### Detailed model information

NTP Rodent Carcinogenicity (Bayesian) models relate to a specific sex/species combination:

* TOPKAT_Rat_Male_NTP

* TOPKAT_Rat_Female_NTP

* TOPKAT_Mouse_Male_NTP

* TOPKAT_Mouse_Female_NTP

These discriminant models, which compute the probability of a submitted chemical structure being a 
carcinogen, are derived from uniform studies selected after critical review of technical reports on 
366 rodent carcinogenicity conducted by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the National Toxicology
Program (NTP) utilizing inbred rats and hybrid mice. By default, each model outputs a Bayesian score, 
a true/false prediction (true = carcinogen), an enrichment result compared with random chance, and an 
estimated probability that the sample is in the category.

According to the NTP protocol, a chemical's carcinogenicity is determined by testing it in both sexes 
of rat and mouse. The rodents are generally exposed to the chemical over the course of their lifetime. 
Pathological and other biological data are evaluated by a committee of experts, and on the basis of a 
majority rule, the chemical is assigned to one of four categories or carcinogenicity: Clear Evidence 
(CE), Some Evidence (SE), Equivocal Evidence (EE), and No Evidence (NE). In developing these models, 
only NE is treated as negative, and all three other categories are considered as positive results.

The following is the detailed information about each model:

###### Leave-one-out Cross-Validation Results

This model was built using 338 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

Best Split was calculated by picking the split that minimized the sum of the percent misclassified for category members and for category non-members, using the cross-validated score for each sample. Using that split, a contingency table is constructed, containing the number of true positives ( TP ), false negatives ( FN ), false positives ( FP ), and true negatives ( TN ).

| Output | XV ROC AUC | Best Split | TP/FN FP/TN | # in Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TOPKAT_Rat_Male_NTP | 0.765 | -0.423 | 121/51 45/121 | 172 |

###### Enrichment Results

This model was built using 338 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, an enrichment plot was generated, and the percentage of true category members captured at a particular percentage cutoff. For example, a column labeled "1%" would be the percentage of true category members (e.g., actives) that were found in the top 1% of the list when sorted by the model score.

The following table shows the output name, the percentage of samples that are in that particular category, the number of category members, and the percentage of true members found. Percentages that are less than 100% are displayed in bold .

###### Percentile Results

The following table shows the cutoff needed for each model to capture a particular percentage of the good samples. For each cutoff, it shows the estimated percentages of false positives and true negatives for the bad samples. The following table is designed to help you pick the cutoff value that best balances your desire to capture as many good samples as possible, while keeping the number of false positives to a minimum.

The rates are estimates derived from the cross-validated data. The rates for your own data may vary.

Cutoffs that lead to 10% or more false positives are displayed in bold .

###### Category Statistics Results

The following table shows for each category, the statistics derived from the cross-validated predictions of the model built for that category as applied to members of that category and non-members of that category. For each group, the following are given: the number of members/non-members (N), the mean prediction for each subset (Mean), and the estimate standard deviation of the predictions for each subset (StdDev).

Categories with one or no members do not have a mean and standard deviation, as there are too few predictions upon which to base them during cross-validation. Also, categories may occasionally contain many duplicate or highly-similar compounds that predict close or identical values, causing them to have unusually low standard deviation values. These low values may be adjusted at time of use of these standard deviations for predicting, for example, percentile results.

FDA Rodent Carcinogenicity (Bayesian) models relate to a specific sex/species combination: male rat, 
female rat, male mouse, and female mouse, each of which is further divided into carcinogen versus 
non-carcinogen, and multiple versus single site models:

* TOPKAT_Mouse_Female_FDA_None_vs_Carcinogen

* TOPKAT_Mouse_Female_FDA_Single_vs_Multiple

* TOPKAT_Mouse_Male_FDA_None_vs_Carcinogen

* TOPKAT_Mouse_Male_FDA_Single_vs_Multiple

* TOPKAT_Rat_Female_FDA_None_vs_Carcinogen

* TOPKAT_Rat_Female_FDA_Single_vs_Multiple

* TOPKAT_Rat_Male_FDA_None_vs_Carcinogen

* TOPKAT_Rat_Male_FDA_Single_vs_Multiple

These discriminant models, derived from data provided by the US FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and 
Research (CDER) under a material transfer agreement, compute the probability of a submitted chemical 
structure being a carcinogen. The first-stage model computes the probability of a chemical being a 
non-carcinogen versus a carcinogen. The second-stage model, multiple versus single-site, can then be 
applied to carcinogens.

This model was built using 312 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

The Weight-of-Evidence Rodent Carcinogenicity (Bayesian) model contains a single model: 
TOPKAT_Weight_of_Evidence_Rodent_Carcinogenicity.

This discriminant model, derived from data provided by the US FDA CDER and from uniform studies 
selected after critical review of technical reports on rodent carcinogenicity studies conducted by 
NCI and NTP, computes the probability of a submitted chemical structure being a carcinogen. The model 
scores the chemical using the FDA CDER weight-of evidence protocol, which scores the chemical as a 
carcinogen if one of the following is true:

* It is a multiple-site carcinogen in at least one sex/species combination (male or female/rat or 
mouse).

* It is a single-site carcinogen in at least two sex/species combinations.

This model was built using 470 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

A QMRF description of this model has been published at the JRC Inventory under QMRF number Q17-412-0049.

Carcinogenic Potency TD50 (Partial Least Squares) models predict the tumorigenic dose rate 50 (TD50)
of a chemical in a rodent chronic exposure toxicity test of carcinogenic potency:

* TOPKAT_Carcinogenic_Potency_TD50_Mouse

* TOPKAT_Carcinogenic_Potency_TD50_Rat

The property being modeled is the -log10(TD50) value (the unit of TD50 is mole/kg_body_weight/day). 
It is converted to weight/kg_body_weight/day unit (mg/kg_body_weight/day) using one of the following 
scripts before output:

TD50 := power(10, -TOPKAT_Carcinogenic_Potency_TD50_Mouse) * Molecular_Weight * 1000;

TD50 := power(10, -TOPKAT_Carcinogenic_Potency_TD50_Rat) * Molecular_Weight * 1000;

These models are trained using 530 mouse and 674 rat TD50 values from the Carcinogenic Potency Database. 
When there were multiple target sites, the TD50 were for all target sites.

This model was trained using 530 experimental Mouse TD50 values from the Carcinogenic Potency Database 
(http://potency.berkeley.edu/cpdb.html). When there were multiple target sites, the TD50 were for all target sites.

The method used to build the model was Partial-Least-Squares/NumberOfComponents=7.

The Ames Mutagenicity (Bayesian) model contains a single model: TOPKAT_Ames_Mutagenicity.

This model was trained using 6313 samples from six different mutagenicity datasets:

* TOPKAT version 6.2, BIOVIA , San Diego, CA 92121

* [Kazius et al., 2005]

* [Contrera et al., 2005]

* [Feng et al., 2003]

* [Helma et al., 2004]

* ISSCAN dataset, Instituto Superiore di Sanita (available at https://www.epa.gov/ ).

Duplicates were removed across the datasets. When there are conflicting results among different sources, 
positive result takes precedence. The compounds were assayed according to the OECD Guideline for Testing of 
Chemicals, Section 4 Test No. 471: Bacterial Reverse Mutation Test. According to the protocol, a chemical is 
tested using the Histidine Reversion Assay against at least the following five strains of Salmonella typhimurium or Escherichia coli :

* S. typhimurium TA 1535

* S. typhimurium TA 1537 or TA 97 or TA 97a

* S. typhimurium TA 98

* S. typhimurium TA 100

* S. typhimurium TA 102 or E. coli WP2 uvrA or WP2 uvrA (pKM101)

Tests are performed both with and without S9 activation. A chemical is considered a mutagen if a 
positive response (i.e., a significant increase in number of reversions compared to the background 
reversion) is observed for one or more strains, with or without S9 activation.

Early training set data are based on the US EPA GeneTox protocol, which did not include testing against the TA102 
strain of S.typhimurium . Newer guidelines like OECD 471 require to include TA 102 strain of S.typhimurium or an equivalent assay. Where available, however, such data were taken into account in the assessment of a compound as mutagen .

This model was built using 6313 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

| Output | XV ROC AUC | Best Split | TP/FN FP/TN | # in Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TOPKAT_Ames_Mutagenicity | 0.894 | -0.663 | 2779/746 403/2385 | 3525 |

The Developmental Toxicity Potential (Bayesian) model predicts whether a particular compound is 
likely to be toxic in a developmental toxicity potential assessment. It contains a single model:
TOPKAT_Developmental_Toxicity_Potential.

This model was trained using 270 samples in uniform experimental studies selected after critical
review of approximately 3000 open literature citations.

This model was built using 270 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, and a model built using the results of the samples, and that model used to predict the left-out sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

Best Split was calculated by picking the split that minimized the sum of the percent misclassified for category members and for category nonmembers, using the cross-validated score for each sample. Using that split, a contingency table is constructed, containing the number of true positives ( TP ), false negatives ( FN ), false positives ( FP ), and true negatives ( TN ).

| Output | XV ROC AUC | Best Split | TP/FN FP/TN | # in Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TOPKAT_Developmental_Toxicity_Potential | 0.750 | -0.312 | 95/47 33/95 | 142 |

(For example, in a column labeled "1%" would be the percentage of true category members (e.g., actives) that were found in the top 1% of the list, when sorted by the model score.)

For each group, the number of members/nonmembers (N) is given; the mean prediction for each subset (Mean); and the estimate standard deviation of the predictions for each subset (StdDev).

(Categories with one or no members do not have a mean and standard deviation, as there are too few predictions upon which to base them during cross-validation. Also, occasionally categories may contain many duplicate or highly-similar compounds which predict close or identical values, causing them to have unusually low standard deviation values. These low values may be adjusted at time of use of these standard deviations for predicting, for example, percentile results.)

The test to identify "good" samples is: Status is defined AND Status eq "Toxic"

An encrypted version of the training data has been saved with this model. You can extend this model by adding your own training data to it to create a new model. Use the New Model from Old component to do this. The new training samples must contain the properties as specified above (except that they need not contain properties that can be calculated on-demand). The "good" samples must be marked so that they can be identified by the above test.

A QMRF description of this model has been published at the JRC Inventory under QMRF number Q17-416-0041.

The Rat Oral LD50 (Partial Least Squares) model predicts the rat oral acute median lethal dose (LD50) 
in the toxicity test of a chemical. The model component name is TOPKAT_Oral_LD50. The property being 
modeled is the -log10(LD50) value (the unit of LD50 is mole/kg_body_weight). It is converted to 
weight/body_weight (g/kg_body_weight) by using the following script before output:

LD50 := power(10, -TOPKAT_Rat_Oral_LD50) * Molecular_Weight;

This model was trained using 3597 experimental rat oral LD50 values from open literature selected 
after critical review of experimental data. Most of the data were extracted from various editions 
of the Registry of Toxic Effects of Chemical Substances (RTECS).The following procedures were 
performed to minimize data errors from the source:

* A sample of data from RTECS was checked against the original literature. Deviations were found 
in less than 1% of the case.

* Those compounds found to be outliers during the modeling process were also checked against their 
literature values. A few inconsistencies were corrected.

The LD50 assay generally consists of a single administration of the chemical to several groups of 
rats at different dosages, followed by a 14-day observation period. The LD50 value is calculated from 
the number of deaths in the different dosage groups.

It is important to consider that RTECS lists the most toxic value when there are multiple values. 
For this reason, this model tends to overestimate the toxicity of a query structure.

A QMRF description of this model has been published at the JRC Inventory under QMRF number Q17-42-0038.

Rat Maximum Tolerated Dose (Partial Least Squares) models predict the rat maximum tolerated dose 
(MTD) of a chemical. Each model corresponds to a different route of dosing (water/feed or gavage):

* TOPKAT_Rat_Maximum_Tolerated_Dose_Feed

* TOPKAT_Rat_Maximum_Tolerated_Dose_Gavage

The property being modeled is the -log10(MTD) value (the unit of MTD is mole/kg body weight). 
It is converted to weight/body weight unit (g/kg body weight) using one of the following two scripts
before output:

MTD := power(10, -TOPKAT_Rat_Maximum_Tolerated_Dose_Feed) * Molecular_Weight;

MTD := power(10, -TOPKAT_Rat_Maximum_Tolerated_Dose_Gavage) * Molecular_Weight;

This water feed model is trained using 178 experimental MTD values from open literature selected 
after critical review of experimental data. Only water/feed dosing data are used in this model. 
The gavage model is trained using 96 experimental MTD values from open literature selected after 
critical review of experimental data. Only gastric gavage dosing data were used in this model.

The Rat Inhalational LC50 (Partial Least Squares) model predicts the median rat inhalational lethal 
concentration per hour (LC50) in an exposure toxicity test. The model component name is 
TOPKAT_Rat_Inhalational_LC50. The property being modeled internally is the -log10(LC50) value (the 
unit of LC50 is mole/m3/h). It is converted to weight/volume/hour unit (mg/m3/h) using the following 
script before output:

LC50 := power(10, -TOPKAT_Rat_Inhalational_LC50) * Molecular_Weight * 1000;

This model was trained using 666 experimental rat inhalational LC50 values from open literature 
selected after critical review of experimental data. Only exposure times in the range of 0.5 to 
14 hours were accepted. Endpoints were modeled as -log10(C/hours_of_exposure).

In order to normalize the data for different durations of exposure, it was assumed that within the 
range of adjustment, toxicity was proportional to duration. Thus, the units that were modeled were 
mole/m3/h. This normalization technique ignores the possibility that the slope at the observed time 
may not be the unit slope. However, since only a single time point was available, this information was 
lacking. The other possibility was to use data only for identical exposure durations (e.g., 2 or 4 
hours). But this alternative would severely limit the number of compounds in the training set, so 
the former normalization method was used.

A QMRF description of this model has been published at the JRC Inventory under QMRF number Q17-41-0005.

The Rat Chronic LOAEL (Partial Least Squares) model predicts the rat chronic lowest observed adverse 
effect level (LOAEL) value of a chemical. The model component name is TOPKAT_Chronic_LOAEL. The property
being modeled internally is the -log10(LOAEL) value (the unit of LOAEL is mole/kg body weight). It is 
converted to weight/body weight unit (g/kg body weight) using the following script before output:

LOAEL := power(10, -TOPKAT_Chronic_LOAEL) * Molecular_Weight;

This model was trained using 388 uniform experimental LOAEL values selected after critical review of 
open literature, NCI/NTP technical reports, and the US EPA databases.

A QMRF description of this model has been published at the JRC Inventory under QMRF number Q17-414-0006.

Three Skin Irritancy (Bayesian) models predict whether a particular compound is likely to be a skin 
irritant and how severe it is in a Rabbit Skin Irritancy test. 

Each model corresponds to a different
severity of the irritancy:

* TOPKAT_Skin_Irritancy_None_vs_Irritant

* TOPKAT_Skin_Irritancy_Mild_vs_Moderate_Severe

* TOPKAT_Skin_Irritancy_Moderate_vs_Severe

These models are used as follows:

* The None_vs_Irritant model is used to discover the irritants.

* The Mild_vs_Moderate_Severe model is applied to the identified irritants to find the moderate 
and severe irritants.

* The Moderate_vs_Severe model is applied to the moderate and severe irritants to differentiate them.

These models are trained using 1277 samples with Rabbit Skin Irritancy test result collected from
literature data. The sources of data include:

* Research Institute of Fragrance Materials

* U.S. Army Environmental Hygiene Agency

* Various other open literature sources

The classification of skin irritants is as follows:

| Category | Draize Scale ( Draize et al., 1944 ) | Primary Irritation Index ( Smyth and Carpenter, 1944 ) * |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | 0 | 0 |
| Mild | 1 | >0 - 2.0 |
| Moderate | 2 | 2.1 - 5.0 |
| Severe | 3 | > 5.0 |

* Primary (Dermal) Irritation Index is also known as 10-point score.

This model was built using 1277 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

| Output | XV ROC AUC | Best Split | TP/FN FP/TN | # in Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TOPKAT_Skin_Irritancy_None_vs_Irritant | 0.867 | -0.752 | 978/198 21/80 | 1176 |

Skin Sensitization (Bayesian) models predict whether a particular compound is likely to be a skin 
sensitizer and how severe it is in a guinea-pig maximization test (GPMT):

* TOPKAT_Skin_Sensitization_None_vs_Sensitizer

* TOPKAT_Skin_Sensitization_Weak_vs_Strong

* The None_vs_Sensitizer model is used to find out whether a chemical is a sensitizer.

* Sensitizers is passed to the Weak_vs_Strong model to determine the severity.

These models are trained using 392 samples collected from open literature after critical review.
The data, all based on the guinea-pig maximization test (GPMT) or minor modification of it, were
assembled from the following:

* A collection of published skin sensitization assays from 1985 and earlier.

* Later data published in Contact Dermatitis.

* [Cronin and Basketter, 1994]

* Augmented data from the 1999 RTEC CD for a total of 1300 chemicals.

The following table illustrates the classification of sensitization scales:

| Category | Animals Positive | Category in Magnusson and Kligman, 1969 | Category in Barratt et al. 1994 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| None | 0 | None | None |
| Weak | 1-70% | I,II,III | Weak or Moderate |
| Strong | 70-100% | IV,V | Strong |

This model was built using 392 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

| Output | XV ROC AUC | Best Split | TP/FN FP/TN | # in Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TOPKAT_Skin_Sensitization_None_vs_Sensitizer | 0.791 | -1.232 | 201/68 37/86 | 269 |

Three Ocular Irritancy (Bayesian) models predict whether a particular compound is likely to be an 
ocular irritant and how severe the irritation is in the Draize test:

* TOPKAT_Ocular_Irritancy_None_vs_Irritant

* TOPKAT_Ocular_Irritancy_Mild_vs_Moderate_Severe

* TOPKAT_Ocular_Irritancy_Moderate_vs_Severe

* The Mild_vs_Moderate_Severe model is applied to the irritants to find the moderate and severe 
irritants.

These models were trained using 1459 samples in the Draize test. The training set was selected from
1453 uniform studies after critical review of open literature.

The classification of irritants is according to the following scale ( Bruner et al., 1992 ):

| Maximum Average Score | Category |
| --- | --- |
| 0 - 5 | None |
| >5 - 15 | Mild |
| >15 - 50 | Moderate |
| >50 - 110 | Severe |

This model was built using 1459 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

The Aerobic Biodegradability (Bayesian) model predicts whether a particular compound is likely to 
be capable of aerobic biodegradation. The model component name is TOPKAT_Aerobic_Biodegradability.

This model was trained using 887 samples from a single study that reported the biodegradability of 
894 compounds. This was assessed by the Japanese Ministry of International Trade and Industry 
(MITI) 1 test protocol.

This model was built using 887 samples, and validated using a leave-one-out cross-validation. Each sample was left out one at a time, a model was built using the results of the samples, which was then used to predict the excluded sample. Once all the samples had predictions, a ROC plot was generated, and the area under the curve ( XV ROC AUC ) calculated.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

A QMRF description of this model has been published at the JRC Inventory under QMRF number Q17-23a-0009.

The Fathead Minnow LC50 (Partial Least Squares) model predicts the median lethal concentration (LC50) 
to Fathead minnows in an acute aquatic toxicity test. It contains a single model: TOPKAT_Fathead_Minnow_LC50.

The property being modeled internally is the -log10(LC50) value (the unit of LC50 is mole/l). It is 
converted to weight/volume unit (g/l) by using the following script before output:

LC50 := power(10, -TOPKAT_Fathead_Minnow_LC50) * Molecular_Weight;

This model was trained using 679 experimental Fathead minnow LC50 values from open literature selected
after critical review of experimental data. The source of data includes Geiger et al., 1984 [Geiger et al., 1984] . This collection reports on flow-through assays using carefully controlled and documented conditions.
Additional data were collected from USA EPA ECOTOX database. Only 96 hour data were used in this model.

The Daphnia EC50 (Partial Least Squares) model predicts the Daphnia magna EC50 value of a chemical 
in an aquatic toxicity test. It contains a single model: TOPKAT_Daphnia_EC50. The property being 
modeled in the model is the -log10(EC50) value (the unit of EC50 is mole/l). It is converted to 
weight/solution volume unit (g/l) by using the following script before output:

EC50 := power(10, -TOPKAT_Daphnia_EC50) * Molecular_Weight;

This model was trained using 654 Daphnia magna EC50 data collected from US EPA ECOTOX database 
(formerly AQUIRE database) and open literature after critical review of experimental data. Only 
48 hour assays were used. Results from assays on volatile chemicals that were performed in open 
beakers were not used. For those compounds with multiple assay values, the median of the available 
values was used.

# Theory - ADMET Descriptors

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/admet_the.htm

## Theory - ADMET Descriptors

### ADMET - Human Intestinal Absorption

This model predicts human intestinal absorption (HIA) after oral administration.
Intestinal absorption is defined as a percentage absorbed rather than as a ratio of concentrations (cf. blood-brain penetration).
A well-absorbed compound is one that is absorbed at least 90% into the bloodstream in humans.
The intestinal absorption model includes 95% and 99% confidence ellipses in the ADMET_PSA_2D,
ADMET_AlogP98 plane.

The ellipses define regions where well-absorbed compounds are expected to be found:
95% of well-absorbed compounds are expected to fall within the 95% ellipse,
while 99% of well-absorbed compounds should fall within the 99% ellipse.
Note that the location of any particular compound does not necessarily imply whether it will be well,
moderately, or poorly absorbed.
In general, however,
absorption tends to drop off quite rapidly outside the 95% ellipse.

There are four prediction levels:

* 0 (Good)

* 1 (Moderate)

* 2 (Poor)

* 3 (Very Poor)

These levels are defined by the 95% (blue line) and 99% (magenta line) confidence ellipsoids in Figure 1.
The upper limit of PSA_2D value for the 95% confidence ellipsoid is at 131.62,
while the upper limit of PSA_2D value for the 99% confidence ellipsoid is at 148.12.

#### Development of model

The model was developed using 182 compounds in the training set,
with descriptors that include AlogP98 and 2D polar surface area (PSA_2D) [Egan et al., 2000] , [Egan and Lauri, 2002] , and [Egan and Lauri 2006].
Well absorbed compounds have at least 90% absorption into human bloodstream,
and by this model will generally reside within the ellipse regions of 95% and 99% confidence levels.

Figure 1: The Development of Human Intestinal Absorption Model

The human absorption model was validated against several datasets.
Results showed that for drug-like compounds within the 99% absorption ellipsoid,
the following ratios were predicted correctly:

* Physicians Desk Reference (PDR): 87.4% of 438 orally delivered compounds

* World Drug Index: 82.9% of 8,504 with USAN or INN

* Comprehensive Medicinal Chemistry: 83.5% of 5,836 filtered by class

* Pharmacopeia's Caco-2 data (446 compounds with low, moderate, and high permeability (i.e., Papp),
used in many PCOP Labs collaborative projects): Moderate or High Papp: 91.5% of compounds lie within 99% ellipse Low Papp: 20.6% of compounds lie within 95% ellipse

* Moderate or High Papp: 91.5% of compounds lie within 99% ellipse

* Low Papp: 20.6% of compounds lie within 95% ellipse

#### Computed properties

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ADMET_PSA_2D | Fast polar surface area |
| ADMET_AlogP98 | ALogP |
| ADMET_Unknown_AlogP98 | The count of unknown AlogP atoms found in the molecule |
| ADMET_Absorption_Level | Categorical absorption level |

In calculating ADMET_AlogP98,
atoms with unknown AlogP98 types do not contribute to the AlogP98 calculation.

#### Key to human intestinal absorption (ADMET_Absorption_Level)

| Level | Value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | ADMET_Absorption_T2_2D < 6.1261 (inside 95%) | Good absorption |
| 1 | 6.1261 ≤ ADMET_Absorption_T2_2D < 9.6026 (inside 99%) | Moderate absorption |
| 2 | 9.6026 < ADMET_Absorption_T2_2D (outside 99%) | Low absorption |
| 3 | ADMET_PSA_2D ≥ 150.0 or ADMET_AlogP98 ≤ -2.0 or ADMET_AlogP98 ≥ 7.0 | Very low absorption |

ADMET_Absorption_T2_2D is the Mahalanobis distance for the compound in the ADMET_PSA_2D, ADMET_AlogP98 plane.
It is referenced from the center of the region of chemical space defined by well absorbed compounds

### ADMET - Aqueous Solubility

This model uses linear regression to predict the solubility of each compound in water at 25 o C.

Cheng and Merz reported a predictive model for aqueous solubility that was generated using a dataset containing 775 compounds
(molecular weight between 50 and 800) [Cheng and Merz, 2003] .
The training set compounds cover numerous classes,
including alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, halogens, amines, alcohols,
N-containing compounds, ketones, aldehydes, organic acids, etc.
A plot of the predicted versus experimental data gives a linear regression of LogSw (25 o C, pH=7.0) R 2 = 0.84, and standard deviation = 0.87.
The test set consisted of 34 compounds,
and the regression statistics are R 2 = 0.88 and standard deviation = 0.79 (see Figure 2).
A validation test consisting of 1,615 compounds from the PDR,
Comprehensive Medicinal Chemistry database (CMC),
and other sources was also performed.
Results yield an overall RMSE (SD) of 1.0.

Figure 2 shows the regression plots for the training set and test set applicable to the derivation and testing of this model

Figure 2: Development of Aqueous Solubility Model

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ADMET_Solubility | The base 10 logarithm of the molar solubility as predicted by the regression |
| ADMET_Solubility_Level | Categorical solubility level |

#### Key to aqueous solubility levels (ADMET_Solubility_Level)

| Level | Value | Drug-likeness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | log(Sw) < -8.0 | Extremely low |
| 1 | -8.0 < log(Sw) < -6.0 | No, very low, but possible |
| 2 | -6.0 < log(Sw) < -4.1 | Yes, low |
| 3 | -4.1 < log(Sw) < -2.0 | Yes, good |
| 4 | -2.0 < log(Sw) 0.0="" | Yes, optimal |
| 5 | 0.0 < log(Sw) | No, too soluble |
| 6 | -1000 | Warning: molecules with one or more unknown AlogP98 types |

In calculating aqueous solubility,
atoms with unknown AlogP98 types do not contribute to the AlogP98 calculation.

### ADMET - Blood Brain Barrier

This model predicts blood-brain penetration (blood brain barrier, BBB) after oral administration.
This model contains a quantitative linear regression model for the prediction of blood-brain penetration,
as well as 95% and 99% confidence ellipses in the ADMET_PSA_2D,
ADMET_AlogP98 plane.
These ellipses are not the same as those associated with the ADMET - Human intestinal absorption,
although they have an analogous interpretation.
They were derived from over 800 compounds that are known to enter the CNS after oral administration [Egan and Lauri, 2002] .

There are four prediction levels within the 95% and 99% confidence ellipsoids:

* 0 (Very high penetrant)

* 1 (High)

* 2 (Medium)

* 3 (Low)

* 4 (Undefined)

The plot depicts the five levels with logBB (ADMET_BBB) values as follows:

* Very high penetrants (logBB ≥ 0.7);

* High penetrants (0 ≤ logBB < 0.7),

* Medium penetrants (-0.52 < logBB < 0),

* Low penetrants (logBB ≤ -0.52).

No prediction is made for compounds outside the 95% and 99% confidence ellipsoids (undefined level = 4).

Scientists at BIOVIA recently developed two robust models for the prediction of BBB penetration.
A regression model to predict logBB values was derived from a training set of 102 compounds (R 2 = 0.7329, RMSE = 0.3638, N = 102),
and a test set of 86 compounds (R 2 = 0.8892, RMSE = 0.3064, N = 86).
The model was validated against 881 compounds designated as CNS compounds in the CMC database (Figure 3).
Further testing against a collection of 124 compounds with known logBB values yielded an R 2 = 0.889 and SD = 0.306.

Figure 3: Development of Blood-Brain Barrier Model

The plot highlights four BBB penetration levels:

* Very high penetrants (blue; logBB ≥ 0.7);

* High penetrants (green; 0 ≤ logBB < 0.7),

* Medium penetrants (cyan; -0.52 < logBB < 0),

* Low penetrants (orange; logBB ≤ -0.52).

No prediction is made for compounds outside the 95% and 99% confidence ellipsoids (gray triangles).

The regression is based on ADMET_PSA_2D and ADMET_AlogP98,
and the training set lies entirely within the 99% confidence ellipse.
This implies that predictions of ADMET_BBB are less reliable for compounds that lie outside the 99% ellipse.

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ADMET_PSA_2D | Fast polar surface area |
| ADMET_AlogP98 | Atom-based LogP |
| ADMET_Unknown_AlogP98 | The count of unknown AlogP atoms found in the molecule |
| ADMET_BBB | Base 10 logarithm of (brain concentration)/(blood concentration) as predicted by a robust (least-median-of-squares) regression derived from literature in vivo brain penetration data |
| ADMET_BBB_Level | Categorical level |

#### Key to BBB penetration levels (ADMET_BBB)

| Level | Value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Very High | Brain-Blood ratio greater than 5:1 |
| 1 | High | Brain-Blood ratio between 1:1 and 5:1 |
| 2 | Medium | Brain-Blood ratio between 0.3:1 and 1:1 |
| 3 | Low | Brain-Blood ratio less than 0.3:1 |
| 4 | Undefined | Outside 99% confidence ellipse |
| 5 | AlogP98 | Warning: molecules with one or more unknown AlogP98 types |

Atoms with unknown AlogP98 types do not contribute to the AlogP98 calculation.

### ADMET - Cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6)

The cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) model predicts CYP2D6 enzyme inhibition using 2D chemical structure as input. CYP2D6
is involved in the metabolism of a wide range of substrates in the liver and its inhibition by a drug constitutes a
majority cases of drug-drug interaction. Therefore, CYP2D6 inhibition experiment is required as part of the regulatory
procedures in the drug discovery and development process.

A computational model for compounds inhibiting the CYP2D6 enzyme was developed from a training set of 151 structurally diverse compounds with known CYP2D6 inhibition constants [Susnow and Dixon, 2003] .
However, the modeling methodology described in that paper was not used; instead, modified Bayesian
learning [Xia et al., 2004] was performed. A leave-one-out 
cross validation was conducted and the following table lists the performance of the model:

| Model Name | ROC Score | ROC Rating | True Positive | False Negative | False Positive | True Negative | Sensitivity | Specificity | Concordance Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6 | 0.877 | Good | 56 | 13 | 12 | 70 | 0.812 | 0.854 | 0.834 |

For definition of these terms, see Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Plot Analysis .

Figure 4: ROC Plot of model ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6 from Leave-One-Out Cross Validation

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6 | Bayesian score from the model |
| ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6#Prediction | The classification whether a compound is an CYP2D6 inhibitor using the cutoff Bayesian score of 0.161 (obtained by minimizing the total number of false positives and false negatives) |
| ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6_Applicability | The applicability of the model on the predicted compound |
| ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6#MD | The Mahalanobis distance (MD) to the center of the training data. MD is a generalization of the Euclidean distance that accounts for correlation among the properties. The larger the MD, the less reliable the prediction |
| ADMET_EXT_CYP2D6#MDpvalue | The p-value associated with the MD. The smaller the p-value, the less reliable the prediction |

### ADMET - Hepatotoxicity

The hepatotoxicity model predicts potential organ toxicity for a wide range of structurally diverse compounds.

The model was developed from available literature data of 436 compounds known to exhibit liver toxicity 
(i.e., positive dose-dependent hepatocellular, cholestatic, neoplastic, etc.), or trigger dose-related 
elevated aminotransferase levels in more than 10% of the human population [Cheng and Dixon, 2003] .
From this, a model was generated from a classification structure activity relationship (SAR) technique 
that uses a modified Bayesian learning [Xia et al., 2004] The model was validated using leave-one-out cross validation. The following table lists the performance
of the model:

| Model Name | ROC Score | ROC Rating | True Positive | False Negative | False Positive | True Negative | Sensitivity | Specificity | Concordance Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic | 0.888 | Good | 157 | 15 | 66 | 198 | 0.913 | 0.750 | 0.814 |

Figure 5: ROC Plot of model ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic from Leave-One-Out Cross Validation

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic | Bayesian score from the model |
| ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic#Prediction | The classification whether a compound is hepatotoxic using the cutoff Bayesian score of -4.154 (obtained by minimizing the total number of false positives and false negatives) |
| ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic_Applicability | The applicability of the model on the predicted compound |
| ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic#MD | The Mahalanobis distance (MD) to the center of the training data. MD is a generalization of the Euclidean distance that accounts for correlation among the properties. The larger the MD, the less reliable the prediction |
| ADMET_EXT_Hepatotoxic#MDpvalue | The p-value associated with the MD. The smaller the p-value, the less reliable the prediction |

### ADMET - Plasma Protein Binding

The plasma protein binding model predicts whether a compound is likely to be highly bound (>= 90% bound) to carrier 
proteins in the blood. Plasma protein binding of drug molecules can affect the efficiency of a drug, because the bound
fraction is temporarily shielded from metabolism. On the other hand, only the unbound fraction exhibits pharmacological
effects.

Two data sets with plasma protein binding level data [Dixon and Merz, 2001] [Votano et al., 2006] were combined and 
duplicates were removed to generate a training set of 854 compounds. Using a cutoff binding level of 90%, the training
set was divided into 329 binders and 525 non-binders. A modified Bayesian learning [Xia et al., 2004] was used to create a binary classification model.
The model was validated using leave-one-out cross validation. The following table lists the performance
of the model:

| Model Name | ROC Score | ROC Rating | True Positive | False Negative | False Positive | True Negative | Sensitivity | Specificity | Concordance Rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ADMET_EXT_PPB | 0.873 | Good | 285 | 44 | 121 | 404 | 0.866 | 0.770 | 0.807 |

Figure 6: ROC Plot of model ADMET_EXT_PPB from Leave-One-Out Cross Validation

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ADMET_EXT_PPB | Bayesian score from the model |
| ADMET_EXT_PPB#Prediction | The classification whether a compound is highly bounded (>= 90% bound) to plasma proteins using the cutoff Bayesian score of -2.209 (obtained by minimizing the total number of false positives and false negatives) |
| ADMET_EXT_PPB_Applicability | The applicability of the model on the predicted compound |
| ADMET_EXT_PPB#MD | The Mahalanobis distance (MD) to the center of the training data. MD is a generalization of the Euclidean distance that accounts for correlation among the properties. The larger the MD, the less reliable the prediction |
| ADMET_EXT_PPB#MDpvalue | The p-value associated with the MD. The smaller the p-value, the less reliable the prediction |
