# Search Small Molecule Conformations tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conf_sact.htm

## Search Small Molecule Conformations tools

The Search Small Molecule Conformations tools provide a quick way to generate conformations. For torsion based search methods, you can select the rotatable bonds to consider when generating the conformations.

### Conformation Search Setup

Add Rotatable Bonds: Adds Rotatable Bond Attributes to the selected 
bonds for each molecule, or all rotatable bonds if nothing is selected and updates the molecule property ROTBONDS. This property indicates which rotatable bonds will be modified during the torsion based search methods, including CAESAR, Systematic Search, Random Search, and Boltzmann Jump. If a user modifies the rotatable bond monitors in the 3D Windows (for example, deletes one of the rotatable bonds), this button should be used to update the molecule property ROTBONDS to reflect the changes prior to running the conformational search.

Torsion Kick: Alters the dihedral angles of all of selected bonds (apart from terminal bonds and bonds in rings) by a random increment that does not exceed +/- 45° .

Torsion Kick ignores terminal and ring bonds.
A terminal bond is a bond where at least one of the connected atoms has only one bond to other atoms.
A ring bond connects two atoms in a ring. For two atoms to be part of a ring, a bond path must 
exist that connects them after the bond between the two atoms has been removed.

### Conformation Search and Minimization

Generate Conformations: Opens the Generate Conformations protocol dialog. This protocol generates conformations for a set of input ligands.

### Analysis

Analyze Conformations: Opens the Analyze Conformations protocol dialog. This protocol computes several metrics to analyze conformational models.

Use Show All and Tile Molecules to visualize the conformations.

| Tool bar | Small Molecules \| Search Small Molecule Conformations |

# BEST conformation generation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conf_the_best-conf-gen.htm

## BEST conformation generation

In general, the best-quality conformation generation method provides improved conformational coverage relative to the fast method. It does this by performing a more rigorous energy minimization in both torsional and Cartesian space and by using poling. Use the best-quality method when conformational coverage is important (e.g., to build conformation models for automatic hypothesis-generation routines).

The following steps are performed by the BEST routine:

* Conjugate-gradient minimization in torsion space

* Conjugate-gradient minimization in Cartesian space

* Quasi-Newton minimization in Cartesian space

# FAST conformation generation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conf_the_fast-conf-gen.htm

## FAST conformation generation

The FAST conformation generation method uses one of three algorithms,
depending on the size of the molecule. The conformational space of small
molecules is generated using an efficient systematic search. If the 
molecule is too large, only one conformation is generated for each possible
combination of stereocenters. Conformations for molecules that are neither
too small nor too large, as measured by the flexibility of the molecule,
are generated with a random search method that uses poling. The following is covered here:

* FAST conformation generation for small molecules

* FAST conformation generation for medium-sized molecules

* FAST conformation generation for large molecules

A quasi-exhaustive systematic search is used to generate conformations for 
small molecules. The conformational space is composed of discretized rotations
about the rotatable bonds. The following table lists offsets and search increments for the 
hybridization types:

| Atom-Atom types | Offset | Search increment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sp 3 -sp 3 | 60.0° | 120.0° |
| sp 2 -sp 2 | 0.0° | 180.0° |
| sp 3 -sp 2 | 60.0° | 60.0° |

The conformational space is systematically searched and conformations that
have conformation energy above an energy threshold are removed.

A random search method with poling is used to generate conformations for 
medium-sized molecules if the estimated number of conformations is greater than
a threshold. This threshold is 750 by default, but can be modified via 
a Catalyst.cfg file. To generation conformations, the molecule is 
split into pieces, a systematic
search is performed on each piece, and the pieces are randomly reconnected.
Each new conformation is quickly optimized in the torsion space 
with poling penalty in order to maintain conformation diversity.

If the number of rotatable bonds is greater than 30, only one conformation is 
created for every possible stereocenter.

Theory - Ring Fragments

## Ring fragments

To reduce the time needed to generate conformations, ring conformations
are computed using distance geometry and the results are stored. When
the same ring is found in a new molecule, previously generated ring 
conformations are reused.

# Poling

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conf_the_poling.htm

## Poling

Poling is a mathematical method for achieving diverse conformer sampling [Smellie et al., 1995c
] . This is
achieved by adding a big penalty to a conformer when it is close to an
existing one. To disable poling, see Disable poling .

In conformation generation with poling, the energy function being minimized
is modified to force similar conformations away from each other. The poling term
in the total energy can be expressed as following:

Equation 1:

where, the generalized functional form of the poling function is:

Equation 2:

Equation 3:

D i = the root mean squared (RMS) difference between the
poling distances of the current conformation being poled and the corresponding
distances in the j th previous conformations d ij that are within a 
1.75 Å RMS computed over all N d poling distances.

The weight W controls the
amount of energy that the poling contributes to F total and is initially set to 20.0.
After a defined number of conformations are generated, the weight is
autoscaled so that the poling function contributes approximately the same
energy to F total . D i is raised to a
power of N , which controls the steepness of the poling function. By
default, N is set to 2.0.

Because choosing each interatomic distance as the poling distance
( N d in Equation 3) dramatically slows conformation generation,
a distribution of chemically significant features (hydrogen-bond
acceptors, hydrogen-bond donors, and hydrophobic groups) is therefore
selected and used. The most obvious set of poling distances would be all
combinations of interfeature distances. However, this causes a quadratic
increase in computation time as the number of features increase. To minimize
the computational expense, a maximum of 3 for each feature is randomly
selected. The combined distances are the total poling distances, N d .

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conf_the_topsym.htm

## Removing duplicate conformations

After the conformational models are generated using either the FAST or BEST
quality method, the conformations are analyzed to check for and eliminate
redundancy. This is done using a dual-level check. First, the conformations
are screened to see if any two conformations are within an
root-mean-square-displacement (RMSD) tolerance.

Topological symmetry is
considered during all RMSD calculations. By default, the first 1000 mappings 
are considered and only the non-hydrogen atoms are considered when
computing the RMSD values.

The RMSD tolerance is computed as:

Equation 1:

where, c is a scaling constant set to 0.02 by default, and N rot is the number of rotatable single bonds (allowing the
tolerance to scale with molecular flexibility).

Any two conformations that are within this threshold are then submitted to a
second level of checking, which is designed to identify conformations that have
local diversity (i.e., differ greatly by one chemical group). These
differences could be critical for database searching, pharmacophore
identification, etc., and therefore should not be removed. The check is
performed by computing distances between atoms in each atom pair. If no
distance is greater than a distance threshold, the higher-energy conformation
is removed. The distance threshold DIS tol is computed as:

# Torsion search methods

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conf_the_torsion-search-methods.htm

## Torsion search methods

The following three torsion search methods are available in the Generate Conformations protocol :

* Systematic Search

* Random Search

* Boltzmann Jump

This method systematically changes torsion angles on grids. The default 
torsion angle increments are 180° for Sp2-Sp2 rotatable bonds and 
120° for other rotatable bonds. All torsion increment values can be 
modified. The Dreiding forcefield is used for quick conformation 
minimization to avoid van der Waals clashes. Optionally, a more
exhaustive minimization can be used in the Generate 
Conformations protocol . Since the search is exhaustive, this 
option is prohibitive for molecules with a large number of rotatable 
bonds. You can either select a few rotatable bonds that are evenly 
distributed within the molecule using the Search Small Molecule Conformations tools or use the Random Search or Boltzmann Jump method.

This method randomly changes torsion angles on grids. The default 
torsion angle increments are 180° for Sp2-Sp2 rotatable bonds 
and 120° for other rotatable bonds. All the values can be modified. 
The Dreiding forcefield is used for quick conformation minimization 
and to avoid van der Waals clashes. The conformations are subject to 
conformation energy filtering using a user-defined energy threshold. 
The Random Search method can be used for molecules of any size, so
the number of maximum conformations must be provided. If the requested
number of conformations is greater than the number of estimated
conformations, the systematic search is automatically used. Note that 
the default values for the energy threshold and maximum conformations 
are used when using the tools.

Boltzmann Jump is also a random search method. However, instead 
of changing torsion angles on predefined grids, a sequence of 
perturbations using random torsion angle changes 
is performed for the generation of each conformation. Each random 
perturbation is either accepted or rejected according
to the Metropolis selection criterion with a ratio according to 
the Boltzmann distribution. If the change in energy (DE) resulting from 
the perturbation is negative, the move is selected. If DE is positive, 
the Boltzmann factor is computed and a random number from 0 to 1 is 
generated:

If the random number is greater than F, the move is selected. R is the 
Boltzmann gas constant and T is the temperature in Kelvin.

Perturbation is performed a specified number of times. If a new conformation 
is chosen in the previous perturbation, that conformation is perturbed in 
the next step. At the end of the perturbation sequence, the conformation is 
energy minimized and the minimized conformation is saved into a search output 
file. The perturbation sequence followed by the energy minimization is 
referred to as one cycle of the jump procedure. Each cycle results in a new 
conformation, which is subject to the final energy threshold filtering.

In the traditional implementation of Boltzmann Jump, only one seed conformation is 
used, and the diversity of conformation sampling largely depends on the 
Boltzmann temperature. For instance, to generate reasonably diverse 
conformations, you may need to use a temperature of a few thousand Kelvin. This
high temperature is probably not realistic if you want the conformation 
distribution to mimic the Boltzmann distribution. To solve this, this
implementation uses multiple starting conformations. The number of
seed conformations is set according to the number of the requested conformations 
and the number of selected rotatable bonds. The diversity of the conformations 
is controlled by the diverse multiple seeds, and the conformation sampling 
resolution is controlled by the number of requested conformations.

This method allows you to use sample conformational space with any resolution, 
which is controlled by the number of conformations and optionally by an RMSD 
filter. The number of perturbations for each new conformation is 20 in this 
implementation, and the torsion angle change window is set to 30°.
The final conformations are also subject to energy filtering using a 
user-specified conformation energy threshold. In the Search and Analyze 
Conformations tools, the Boltzmann temperature is set to 300 K. This is also
the default value in the Generate Conformations protocol. However, it 
can be modified in the Advanced parameters.

The following examples illustrate how the conformation search is affected by
different temperatures.

Figure 1: Conformation energy landscape of
a simple molecule

Figure 2: Conformations sampled with low temperature T = 100K.

Figure 3: Conformations sampled with room temperature T = 300 K.

Figure 4: Conformations sampled with very high temperature T = 5000 K.

# Analyze Conformations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conformations_analyze_conformations-para.htm

## Analyze Conformations - Parameters

### Computes several metrics to analyze conformational models

The calculated metrics are commonly used to assess conformational diversity and 
coverage. Use Basic Descriptors to compute descriptors typically used to measure 
the degree of extension or compactness of the conformational models (for example, the mean, minimum, 
and maximum of the radius of gyration, and the solvent accessible surface area).

Descriptors 
typically used to measure conformational diversity can also be computed. Use Fingerprints to compute all unique 3-point pharmacophore fingerprints and RMSD to compute the minimum, 
mean, and maximum of all pair-wise root mean squared deviations ( RMSD s) between the 
conformations.

Notes:

* Conformations are identified by name, therefore ensure that ligand conformations belonging together have identical names.

* Use Input 
Monitors to calculate distances, angles, or torsions across all conformations.

* Use Clustering by RMSD to create an interactive dendrogram of the pair-wise RMSD s between the conformations. The dendrogram can be viewed in Discovery Studio.

* Use Non-bond Interactions to compute the number intramolecular interactions.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Monitors | Computes distances, angles, or torsions across all conformations. In Discovery Studio, all appropriate monitors set on one of the input conformations in the Molecule Window are displayed in a drop down list. Select the monitors you wish to compute across all conformations of that ligand. The monitor objects can be atoms or centroid monitors. For example, to create a property on all conformations that measures the distance between two rings: Add a centroid monitor to each of the rings. Create a distance monitor between the two centroid monitors. Select the distance monitor from the drop down list. In Pipeline Pilot, select a comma separated text file that contains the following heading: Name , Type , Label , Group1 , Group2 , Group3, Group4 The rows under the headings are the monitors to be computed. Where: Name: is the name of the ligand. Type: is the type of monitor to compute (Distance, Torsion, or Angle). Label: is the name of the property created. Group1: is the atom index or indices of group 1. For example, "2" represents the single atom index 2, "1 2 3" represents the centroid of the three atoms with indices 1, 2, and 3. Group2, Group3, Group4: are the same format as Group1 or blank if not needed. |
| Basic Descriptors | Computes basic descriptors that estimate the degree of extension or compactness across the conformational models for each ligand. The descriptors include: Jurs_SASA_Mean: The mean solvent-accessible surface area. Jurs_SASA_StdDev: The standard deviation of the solvent-accessible surface area. Jurs_SASA_Min: The minimum solvent-accessible surface area. Jurs_SASA_Max: The maximum solvent-accessible surface area. RadOfGyration_Mean: The mean radius of gyration. The radius of gyration is defined as the mass weighted root-mean-square average distance of all atoms in the molecule from their center of mass: RadOfGyration = [Σm(x 2 +y 2 +z 2 )/Σm] 1/2 , where m is the mass of an atom and x, y, z are the atomic coordinates relative to the center of mass. RadOfGyration_StdDev: The standard deviation of the radius of gyration. RadOfGyration_Min: The minimum radius of gyration. RadOfGyration_Max: The maximum radius of gyration. See Also: Stanton, D.T., Jurs, P.C., "Development and Use of Charge Partial Surface Area Structural Descriptors in Computer-Assisted Quantitative Structure-Property Relationship Studies", Anal. Chem., 62, 2323-29 (1990). Valid Values: True , False |
| Non-bond Interactions | Computes intramolecular interactions of the conformations. The following properties are added: Hydrogen Bonds: The number of intramolecular hydrogen bonds. Electrostatic: The number of intramolecular electrostatic interactions. Hydrophobic: The number of intramolecular hydrophobic interactions. Halogen: The number of intramolecular halogen interactions. Miscellaneous: The number of intramolecular miscellaneous interactions (e.g. metal acceptors, Sulfur interactions, etc.) Unfavorable: The number of intramolecular unfavorable interactions (e.g. steric bumps, acceptor-acceptor interactions, etc.) Valid Values: True , False |
| Fingerprints | Computes the number of unique pharmacophore fingerprints ( Unique_Fingerprints ) across all conformations for each ligand. The pharmacophore features used as input are: Hydrogen Bond Acceptor - heavy atom Hydrogen Bond Donor - heavy atom Negative Ionizable Positive Ionizable Hydrophobic Valid Values: True , False |
| RMSD | Each conformer is aligned to the first pose or conformation, then all pair-wise root mean squared deviations (RMSDs) are calculated between the conformations. The algorithm used accounts for topological symmetry. Basic statistics such as the mean ( RMSD_Mean ), minimum ( RMSD_Min ), and maximum RMSD ( RMSD_Max ) values are computed for each ligand. Valid Values: True , False |
| Clustering by RMSD | Creates a script to display a dendrogram of the pair-wise root mean squared deviations between conformations in Discovery Studio. Valid Values: True, False |

# Analyze Conformations

Source type: HTML

## Analyze Conformations

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Analyze Conformations protocol computes several metrics to
analyze conformational models. The calculated metrics are
commonly used to assess conformational diversity and coverage.
Basic descriptors typically used to measure the degree of extension
or compactness of the conformational models (e.g., the mean, min, and
max of the radius of gyration and the solvent accessible surface area)
are computed. In addition, descriptors typically used to measure
conformational diversity can also be computed, including all unique
3-point pharmacophore fingerprints and the min, mean, and max of all
pair-wise root mean squared deviations (RMSDs) between the
conformations. It is also possible to create distance, angle, and
torsion monitors and quickly compute the values across all
conformations.

* Open the Small Molecules | Search Small Molecule Conformations tools tools and click Analyze Conformations... to open the Analyze Conformations dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands .

* You can compute distance, torsion, and angle constraints between
atoms or centroids of atoms across all conformations. Use
the Structure | Monitor menu to add Distance, Angle, Centroid, and Torsion
monitors on one of the ligand conformations. Once added, they will be listed in the Input Monitors parameter. When
the protocol runs, all selected monitors will be computed across all
conformations and exported as properties in the output .sd file. You
can then use the charting tools in Discovery Studio to visualize the results.

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Analyze Conformations - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>_analysis.sd | Contains a single conformation of each input ligand with the calculated properties. |
| <ligands>_analysis_all.sd | Contains all conformations of each input ligand with the calculated properties. |
| dendrogram.sd | Contains all the conformations of the ligand and contains all pair-wise RMSD values as properties. This file is only generated when a single ligand with multiple conformations is analyzed. It is used in conjunction with the ViewDendrogram.pl file to display a dendrogram for all the pair-wise RMSD values. |
| <ligands>_monitors.sd | Contains a measure of all input monitors for each conformation. |
| ViewDendrogram_<N>.pl | Plots a dendrogram view of all the pair-wise RMSD of the conformations of ligand <N>. This file is only created when the Clustering by RMSD parameter is set to True . |
| ViewResults_NumberOfFingerprints.pl | Plots the number of pharmacophore fingerprints per ligand. |
| ViewResults_RadOfGyration_Detailed.pl | Plots all the radius of gyration values. |
| ViewResults_RMSD.pl | Plots statistics of the RMSD values per ligand. |
| ViewResults_SASA_Detailed.pl | Plots all the solvent accessible surface area values. |
| ViewResults_Energy_Detailed.pl | Plots the absolute energy values. |

# Generate Conformations - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conformations_generate_conformations-para.htm

## Generate Conformations - Parameters

### Generates ligand conformations

Offers a selection of conformation and torsion search methods for creating diverse ligand conformations:

* FAST: Quickly generates diverse low-energy conformations. This can be used for general purpose conformation generation.

* BEST: Ensures the best coverage of conformational space (this requires more CPU time). This is recommended for conformation sampling for 3D pharmacophore generation.

* CAESAR: Very quickly generates conformations using CAESAR algorithm. It scales linearly with the number of conformations, and is highly efficient when a large number of conformations is required for very fine coverage of conformation space.

* Systematic Search: Systematically changed torsion angles. For ring compounds, the ring structures from input molecules are used.

* Random Search: Randomly change torsion angles. For ring compounds, the ring conformations of input molecules are used.

* Boltzmann Jump: Stochastic search with Metropolis selection criterion based on Boltzmann distribution. You can lower the temperature to focus the conformation sampling around different local minima.

If Conformational Method is set to: CAESAR, Systematic Search, Random Search or Boltzmann Jump, you can select a set of rotatable bonds which will be explored in conformation search. To do this, you need to prepare the ligands in the Discovery Studio Client. Add rotatable bond monitors for the selected bonds using the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel. In addition, you can minimize the conformations in solution or gas phase.

Properties added:

* AbsoluteEnergy : the conformational energy is calculated with the Catalyst forcefield when the Conformation Method is set to: FAST, BEST, or CAESAR, otherwise the Dreiding forcefield is used ( i.e. , Systematic Search, Random Search, and Boltzmann Jump).

* RelativeEnergy : calculated by finding the lowest energy conformation (AbsoluteEnergy min ) for each ligand and subtracting this value from the AbsoluteEnergy, i.e. , AbsoluteEnergy - AbsoluteEnergy min .

* ConfNumber : conformation are always sorted by energy, where ConfNumber 1 is the conformation with the lowest energy value.

* MolNumber : consecutive ligand numbering.

Notes:

* CAESAR : If partial rotatable bonds are selected and Discard Existing Conformations is set to False , then it is assumed that the geometric information of the input conformations is used for generating new conformations, and the torsion angles of the fixed rotatable bonds and conformations of all rings will be preserved. However, if Discard Existing Conformations is set to True (the default value), then no geometric information of input conformers will be used and conformations will be sampled for all rings and the standard torsion angles determined by CAESAR algorithm will be used for the fixed rotatable bonds.

* Systematic Search , Random Search , Boltzmann Jump : A property Angle# is added to specify the torsional angles.

* When enabling Conformation Minimization , conformations energies are re-evaluated and re-sorted with the energies from for the selected Minimization Forcefield; the forcefield name is also added to the AbsoluteEnergy property name.

See Also:

* Smellie, A.; Teig, S. L.; Towbin, P. Poling: Promoting conformational variation. J. Comp. Chem. 1995 , 16, 171-187.

* Smellie, A.; Kahn, S. D.; Teig, S. L. Analysis of conformational coverage. 1. Validation and estimation of coverage. J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. 1995 , 35, 285-294.

* Smellie, A.; Kahn, S. D.; Teig, S. L. Analysis of conformational coverage. 2. Applications of conformational models. J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. 1995 , 35, 295-304.

* Kirchmair, J.; Laggner, C.; Wolber, G.; Langer, T. Comparative Analysis of Protein-Bound Ligand Conformations with Respect to Catalyst's Conformational Space Subsampling Algorithms. J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2005 , 45 (2), 422-430.

* Li, J.; Ehlers, T.; Sutter, J.; Varma-OBrien, S.; Kirchmair, J. CAESAR: a new conformer generation algorithm based on recursive build-up and local rotational symmetry consideration. J. Chem. Inf. Model 2007 , 47, 1923-1932.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. Note: It is best to use a file when the atom and bond parity flags should be preserved. |
| Conformation Method | Algorithm for generating conformations: FAST: Quickly provides diverse low-energy conformations and can be used for general purpose conformation generation. BEST: Ensures the best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). This is recommended for conformation sampling for 3D pharmacophore generation CAESAR: Very quickly provides conformations using CAESAR algorithm. It scales linearly with the number of conformations, and is highly efficient when a large number of conformations is required for very fine coverage of conformation space. Systematic Search: Systematically change torsion angles. Random Search: Randomly change torsion angles. Boltzmann Jump: Stochastic search with Metropolis selection criterion based on Boltzmann distribution. By lowering temperature, one can focus the conformation sampling around different local minima. Valid Values: FAST , BEST, CAESAR, Systematic Search, Random Search, Boltzmann Jump |
| Maximum Conformations | Maximum number of conformations to be generated. |
| Energy Threshold | Conformations are created within this relative energy threshold (kcal/mol). For a molecule with stereo isomers, this threshold applies to conformations for each individual isomer. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Discard Existing Conformations | If True, discard existing conformations, otherwise keep all. Note : Set this option to False if you want to retain all input conformations in the output. Valid Values: True , False |
| Separate Conformations | If True, each record is treated separately (including enantiomers) and a set of conformations is generated for each record. If False, consecutive structures, which only differ in stereo-chemistry (e.g., enantiomers) are enumerated. Note : Set this option to True if you want to ensure that all ligands are enumerated, regardless of stereo-chemistry. Valid Values: True, False |
| Enumerate Unknown Stereocenters | The method used to enumerate stereo isomers when using BEST , FAST , or CAESAR . All: Enumerates all possible isomers and does not remove isomers that are mirror images. This method is useful when using algorithms that don't implicitly consider mirror images such as docking. Limited: Enumerates a reduced number of isomers. If an isomer is a mirror image of an existing isomer, it is not enumerated. This method is useful when using algorithms that implicitly consider mirror images such as pharmacophore analysis. Note: Only used for FAST , BEST , and CAESAR . The other algorithms ( Systematic Search , Boltzmann Jump , and Random Search ) only create conformations of the input isomer. Consider using a separate ligand preparation prior to using these algorithms if isomers should be enumerated for these methods. Valid Values: All , Limited |
| Ring Fragments File | File (fragments.data) that contains the ring conformations to use. The Catalyst Ring Fragment Writer component can be used to generate the file. Molecules that contain rings also found in the file will only use these ring conformations. Conformations for rings not found in the file are generated from scratch. Note: Only FAST and CAESAR will use this file. It have no effect on other methods. By default this parameter is blank and all ring conformations are generated from scratch. |
| Catalyst Parameter File | File containing .Catalyst parameter settings to define the default behavior of Catalyst programs. The file can be created using the Catalyst Parameter Settings component. This parameter is typically only changed by experts. A default .Catalyst parameter settings file can be created in the users directory on the server: $PipelinePilot_Install_Directory/public/users/ username /Catalyst.cfg If it exists, it is used when this parameter is left blank. |
| Initial Geometry | The initial 3D structure for conformation search. This option is only used for torsion search methods, including Systematic Search, Random Search and Boltzmann Jump. There are three options: Input: Use the input structure from the Molecule window. Standard 3D: Use Catalyst standard 3D structure. Minimization: Use forcefield minimized structure. Valid Values: Input , Standard 3D, Minimization |
| Input Forcefield | Forcefield to use for minimizing the initial structures of the input molecules: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF |
| Maximum Systematic Conformations | Maximum number for Systematic Search. If the number of estimated conformations for a molecule is greater than this limit, the Random Search is automatically used. |
| Boltzmann Temperature | Temperature for Boltzmann distribution. This is required only for the Boltzmann Jump method. |
| RMSD Cutoff | Conformations with an RMSD (Å) less than this value will be considered duplicates. Topological symmetry is taken into account. A higher specified RMSD value will reduce the generated conformations but increases the CPU time. Note: Filtering can be disabled by setting the value to 0 or leaving it blank. |
| Torsion Increment | Torsion angle increments (°). By default, torsion angle increments are pre-defined, and different algorithms have different settings. For a rule-based option, users can specify torsion increments for each type of rotatable bond, such as Sp3-Sp3, Sp3-Sp2 and Sp2-Sp2. This group of parameters applies to CAESAR and other torsion search methods. A user can select rotatable bonds for a conformational search using the Add Rotatable Bonds button in the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel. If you have removed some rotatable bond monitors in the 3D Window, make sure you click the Add Rotatable Bonds button to update the ROTBONDS property in the Data Table View. Alternatively, if you use the Add Rotatable Bond Monitors button in the Alignment toolbar, and you remove some rotatable bond monitors in the 3D Window, you may update the ROTBONDS property by clicking the Add Rotatable Bond Monitors button on that toolbar again. Valid Values: Default , Rules |
| Sp3-Sp3 | Torsion angle increment for a Sp3-Sp3 single bond. |
| Sp3-Sp2 | Torsion angle increment for a Sp3-Sp2 single bond. |
| Sp2-Sp2 | Torsion angle increment for a Sp2-Sp2 single bond. |
| Conformation Minimization | Minimization of conformation candidates. The minimization can be done either in gas phase or in solution using various solvation models, and forcefields. Valid Values: True, False |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR): Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent: In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient: An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell: This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not possible. Smart Minimizer: Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Smart Minimizer , Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell |
| Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit (kcal/mol-Å). For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Minimization Forcefield | Forcefield for the conformation minimization: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF |
| Minimization Partial Charge Estimation | Choose a method to assign partial charges. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . Generalized Born : A better approximation for the solvent effect. Effective Born radii in the Coulomb field approximation are calculated using pairwise sum of atomic volumes. About 4 times slower than None . Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV) : Effective Born radii are calculated by numerical integration of molecular volume. About 15 times slower than None . Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) : Similar to GBMV but replacing its computationally expensive molecular surface approximation with a van der Waals based surface with a smooth dielectric boundary. About 2-3 times faster than GBMV . See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Implicit Distance-Dependent Dielectrics, Implicit Generalized Born, Generalized Born with Molecular Volume (GBMV), Generalized Born with a simple SWitching (GBSW) |
| Minimization Dielectric Constant | Specifies the dielectric constant to use when Implicit Solvent Model is None or Distance-Dependent Dielectrics. When Implicit Solvent Model is set to Generalized Born, this value is fixed at 1.0. |
| Implicit Solvent Dielectric Constant | Specifies dielectric constant for bulk solvent. Used when Implicit Solvent Model is Generalized Born, GBMV, GBSW or PBSA. |
| Fast Minimization | Enable the fast minimization algorithm. Note: : This option is only available for the CHARMm forcefield and Implicit Solvent Model set to None or Implicit Distance-Dependent Dielectric Valid Values: True , False |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. | Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

# Generate Conformations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/conformations_generate_conformations.htm

## Generate Conformations

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Generate Conformations protocol generates conformations for a set of input ligands. The protocol also has several advanced options. For example,
it is possible to confine the search to specific rotatable bonds, or perform conformation optimization with various forcefields and solvation
models. The following conformation search algorithms are available:

| Algorithm | Description |
| --- | --- |
| FAST | Quickly generate diverse low-energy conformations. See FAST conformation generation . |
| BEST | Best coverage of conformational space (requires more CPU time). See BEST conformation generation . |
| CAESAR | Quickly generate conformations by sampling torsions. See CAESAR conformation generation . |
| Systematic Search | Systematically search torsion grids of user-defined rotatable bonds. See Systematic Search . |
| Random Search | Randomly change torsion angles of user-defined rotatable bonds. See Random Search . |
| Boltzmann Jump | Stochastically search for conformations and use the Metropolis selection criterion to accept or reject random changes in the specified torsion angles. See Boltzmann Jump . |

The Catalyst conformation search algorithms are not designed for searching for global energy minimums. Instead they are designed to generate a diverse sample of low energy conformations. However, when enough low energy conformations are sampled, it is often possible to find a conformation in the set that is very close to the energy minimum.

* Open the Small Molecules | Search Small Molecule Conformations tools tools and click Generate Conformations... to open the Generate Conformations dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Conformation Method Choose one of the following for Conformation Method : FAST BEST CAESAR Systematic Search Random Search Boltzmann Jump If you choose one of the three torsion search methods
(Systematic Search, Random Search and Boltzmann Jump) and the Input Ligands is displayed in a Molecule Window, you can select the rotatable
bonds in the Molecule Window to use for conformation sampling: Select the bonds in the Molecule Window. Open the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel in the Tools Explorer. Click Add Rotatable Bonds . If you remove some of the rotatable bond monitors, click Add Rotatable Bonds again to update the ROTBONDS property, which is passed to the Generate Conformation protocol for torsion search.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Conformation Method | Choose one of the following for Conformation Method : FAST BEST CAESAR Systematic Search Random Search Boltzmann Jump If you choose one of the three torsion search methods (Systematic Search, Random Search and Boltzmann Jump) and the Input Ligands is displayed in a Molecule Window, you can select the rotatable bonds in the Molecule Window to use for conformation sampling: Select the bonds in the Molecule Window. Open the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel in the Tools Explorer. Click Add Rotatable Bonds . If you remove some of the rotatable bond monitors, click Add Rotatable Bonds again to update the ROTBONDS property, which is passed to the Generate Conformation protocol for torsion search. |

* FAST

* BEST

* CAESAR

* Systematic Search

* Random Search

* Boltzmann Jump

If you choose one of the three torsion search methods
(Systematic Search, Random Search and Boltzmann Jump) and the Input Ligands is displayed in a Molecule Window, you can select the rotatable
bonds in the Molecule Window to use for conformation sampling:

* Select the bonds in the Molecule Window.

* Open the Search Small Molecule Conformations tool panel in the Tools Explorer.

* Click Add Rotatable Bonds . If you remove some of the rotatable bond monitors, click Add Rotatable Bonds again to update the ROTBONDS property, which is passed to the Generate Conformation protocol for torsion search.

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For instance, if you choose Systematic Search, Random Search, or Boltzmann Jump, you can adjust the RMSD filtering threshold. If the threshold is set to zero, the RMSD filtering is skipped for these conformation methods. You can also turn on conformation minimization, but one should be aware that this option can significantly increase the run time for a large set of ligands or conformations. For details about the remaining parameters, see Generate Conformations - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| input_fast.sd | Contains conformations of all input ligands in an .sd file. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opens the generated conformations in Discovery Studio (the conformations are not visible by default). |

# Build Fragment tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/fragmentbuildertools.htm

## Build Fragment tools

You can use the Build Fragment tool panel to build 3D molecules from existing fragments and create new fragments.
The tool panel includes a 3D display of the currently selected fragment
above a list of fragments organized by category. You can choose from
the following fragment categories:

* Aliphatics

* Aminoacids

* Aromatics

* Carbohydrates

* Groups

* PDB_Carbohydrates

* Rings

Add Fragment: Adds a fragment to the molecule in the Molecule Window. Each Fragment is added as a residue to the molecule.

Fuse Fragment: Intended for fusing carbohydrates, but also more generally applicable for joining fragments with the elimination of a water molecule. In a 3D Fragment View, a hydroxyl hydrogen should be selected. In a Molecule Window a hydrogen should be selected. The fusion of the fragment R-OH with the molecule H-M produces the molecule R-M. You can also select any atom attached to a hydrogen in the molecule window, in which case the fusion will use one of the attached hydrogen atoms.

Define Fragment: Defines the molecule selected in the Molecule Window as a new fragment that can be used
by Build Fragment tools. See Define Fragment dialog .

#### Further information

How to use the Build Fragment tools Define Fragment dialog

# How to use the Build Fragment tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/fragmentbuildertools_hw.htm

## How to use the Build Fragment tools

You can use the Build Fragment tool panel to build 3D molecules from existing fragments, and to and create new fragments.

On the Build Fragment tool panel, fragments are grouped into seven libraries by default. You can also add your own fragments and fragment
libraries. A 3D fragment view above the fragment list displays the currently selected fragment. This topic covers the following tasks:

* Build a molecule using fragments

* Build a carbohydrate using fragments

* Manipulate a fragment in the 3D fragment view

* Define a new fragment and create new fragment group

To build a molecule

* From the menu bar, choose File | New | Molecule Window .

* Open the Build Fragment tool panel.

* From the Tools Explorer, expand the desired fragment library, and then double-click the fragment to open it in the Molecule Window.

* From the fragment list, select another fragment by clicking the name.
The selected fragment is displayed in the 3D fragment view above
the list with one hydrogen atom highlighted in yellow. This hydrogen atom is the connection point and can be
changed by clicking a different hydrogen atom in the 3D fragment view.

* In the Molecule Window, select a hydrogen atom where the bond with the selected fragment
should be made.

* From the Build Fragment tool panel, click Add Fragment .
The second fragment is added to the first fragment in the Molecule Window.

* Repeat steps 3 and 4 to add more fragments to the molecule.

To build a carbohydrate molecule

Carbohydrate molecules are built as described above, but using the Fuse Fragment tool instead of Add Fragment . The appropriate hydroxyl hydrogen must be selected in the 3D fragment view.

Sugar fragments in different anomeric states are available in the Carbohydrate folder, and a selection of residues commonly found in glycosylated protein structures with PDB nomenclature under PDB_Carbohydrate , including some example multi-residue glycan moieties.

To manipulate a fragment in the 3D fragment view

You can manipulate the fragment directly in the 3D fragment view:

* Click a hydrogen atom on the fragment to select it as the connection point.

* Right-click and drag to rotate the fragment.

* Right-click in the view and choose Reset View to restore
the orientation and position of the fragment in the 3D fragment view.

* Press CTRL + to zoom in.

* Press CTRL - to zoom out.

* Press CTRL 0 to reset the zoom.

* Use the mouse wheel to zoom in and out.

* Press the HOME key to reset the rotation.

It is not possible to translate 
the fragment in the 3D fragment view.

To define a new fragment and create new fragment group

* Select a molecule from an open Molecule Window. The molecule can be created 
by any method (e.g., fragment building tools, sketching, or 
importing a file).

* From the Build Fragment tool panel, click Define Fragment to open
the Define Fragment dialog.

* Select an existing fragment library from the User fragment
library list, or type in a name to add a new fragment library.

* Type a Fragment name and then click OK . The new fragment library and fragment
appear in the fragment list on the Build Fragment tool panel.

Hydrogen atoms are automatically added to a newly defined fragment. Also, the fragment must be a single connected fragment, but can consist of multiple residues.

### Access methods

| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Build Fragment |
| --- | --- |

# Align to Selected Substructure - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_align_to_selected_substructure-para.htm

## Align to Selected Substructure - Parameters

### Aligns ligands to a specified substructure

Ligands are aligned to a selected substructure. The substructure can be a ligand, or a selection of atoms.

This is useful, for example, to quickly examine the core structures of conformations.

Note:

* Only heavy atoms are used for the substructure alignment.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Substructure | Substructure for the alignment. The file can be in DSV or SD file format. In Discovery Studio, select a set of atoms as the target substructure. Notes: If no atoms are selected, the complete molecule is considered for the substructure alignment. The file should only contain a single molecule. |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Additional Options | Contains less commonly used parameters |
| Return After First Alignment | When set to true, the substructure and ligands are aligned using only the first mapping found between the two molecules. Otherwise, the molecules are aligned using all the mappings (up to the maximum defined by Maximum Number of Alignments ) and the one with the best RMSD is selected. Valid Values: True , False |
| Maximum Number of Alignments | Maximum number of mappings between the substructure and ligands to try in the alignment. |
| Search Options | Options for substructure searching. For maximum ISIS compatibility, select the first six options. Substructure Search options: Use ISIS Aromaticity : Use aromaticity as done by ISIS, else use SciTegic 4n+2 Huckel aromaticity perception. Use Localized Aromatic Bonds : "Localized" aromatic bonds are bonds for which all kekule representations have the bond always the same type (single or double). For example, the single and double bonds in pyrrole are localized, while the bonds in pyridine are not. ISIS allows single or double bond queries to map onto localized aromatic bonds. Setting this option will make this component compatible with ISIS with respect to these bonds. Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms : Allow uncharged query atoms to map onto charged target atoms. NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers : Queries containing stereoatoms are considered as a mixture of enantiomers rather than absolute. Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets : A query marked Chiral can map only onto targets marked Chiral. Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms : Marked stereoatoms must map onto stereo-appropriate atoms in the targets, instead of being allowed to also map onto unknown or unmarked atoms. HFill if RAtoms Found : If RAtoms are found in the query, hydrogen-fill all other atoms; allow substituents only in the locations marked by the RAtoms. Check Bonds To RAtoms : Toggles the check of query features (e.g. order, Chain/Ring) on bonds to RAtoms. By default, this option is off to match ISIS behavior. Interpret RAtoms Literally : Treat R atoms as literal atoms, rather than as query types. Useful for searching and manipulating literal RAtoms in target molecules. Interpret ZAtoms Literally : Treat R atoms as literal atoms, rather than as attachment markers. Template (Z) atoms in queries are treated as A atoms attached by a bond which can be of any type (single, double, triple, or aromatic) Interpret StarAtoms Literally : Treat Star (*) atoms as literal atoms, rather than as query features. StarAtoms Can Map Hydrogens : Toggles whether Star (*) atoms can map hydrogen atoms. Exact Match : Return only targets that are an exact match to the query. That is, queries are required to match the entire target and not just a substructure of the target. Valid Values: Use ISIS Aromaticity, Use Localized Aromatic Bonds, Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms, NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers, Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets, Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms , HFill if RAtoms Found , Check Bonds To RAtoms, Interpret RAtoms Literally, Interpret ZAtoms Literally, Interpret StarAtoms Literally, StarAtoms Can Map Hydrogens, Exact Match |
| OutputAlignmentRMS | Output the calculated RMS Deviation between target and template atoms after the alignment is done. Valid Values: True , False |

Substructure for the alignment. The file can be in DSV or SD file format.

In Discovery Studio, select a set of atoms as the target substructure.

Notes:

* If no atoms are selected, the complete molecule is considered for the substructure alignment.

* The file should only contain a single molecule.

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

Contains less commonly used parameters

When set to true, the substructure and ligands are aligned using only the first mapping found between the two molecules. Otherwise, the molecules are aligned using all the mappings (up to the maximum defined by Maximum Number of Alignments ) and the one with the best RMSD is selected.

Valid Values: True , False

Maximum number of mappings between the substructure and ligands to try in the alignment.

* Use ISIS Aromaticity : Use aromaticity as done by ISIS, else use SciTegic 4n+2 Huckel aromaticity perception.

* Use Localized Aromatic Bonds : "Localized" aromatic bonds are bonds for which all kekule representations have the bond always the same type (single or double). For example, the single and double bonds in 
pyrrole are localized, while the bonds in pyridine are not. ISIS allows single or double bond queries to map onto localized aromatic bonds. Setting this option will make this component compatible with ISIS with respect to these bonds.

* Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms : Allow uncharged query atoms to map onto charged target atoms.

* NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers : Queries containing stereoatoms are considered as a mixture of enantiomers rather than absolute.

* Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets : A query marked Chiral can map only onto targets marked Chiral.

* Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms : Marked stereoatoms must map onto stereo-appropriate atoms in the targets, instead of being allowed to also map onto unknown or unmarked atoms.

* HFill if RAtoms Found : If RAtoms are found in the query, hydrogen-fill all other atoms; allow substituents only in the locations marked by the RAtoms.

* Check Bonds To RAtoms : Toggles the check of query features (e.g. order, Chain/Ring) on bonds to RAtoms. By default, this option is off to match ISIS behavior.

* Interpret RAtoms Literally : Treat R atoms as literal atoms, rather than as query types. Useful for searching and manipulating literal RAtoms in target molecules.

* Interpret ZAtoms Literally : Treat R atoms as literal atoms, rather than as attachment markers. Template (Z) atoms in queries are treated as A atoms attached by a bond which can be of any type (single, double, triple, or aromatic)

* Interpret StarAtoms Literally : Treat Star (*) atoms as literal atoms, rather than as query features.

* StarAtoms Can Map Hydrogens : Toggles whether Star (*) atoms can map hydrogen atoms.

* Exact Match : Return only targets that are an exact match to the query. That is, queries are required to match the entire target and not just a substructure of the target.

Valid Values: Use ISIS Aromaticity, Use Localized Aromatic Bonds, Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms, NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers, Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets, Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms , HFill if RAtoms Found , Check Bonds To RAtoms, Interpret RAtoms Literally, Interpret ZAtoms Literally, Interpret StarAtoms Literally, StarAtoms Can Map Hydrogens, Exact Match

# Align to Selected Substructure

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_align_to_selected_substructure.htm

## Align to Selected Substructure

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Align to Selected Substructure protocol allows you to quickly align
ligands to a common substructure. This is useful for examining ligands with a common core. The substructure can be the complete ligand or contiguous atom selection.

This protocol can be run from the Tool Panel (recommended) or Protocols Explorer.

* Open a Molecule Window with multiple visible ligands.

* Select a ligand or continuous ligand substructure.

* Open the Small Molecules | Align Small Molecules tools and click Align to Selected Substructure... to open the Align to Selected Substructure dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set Input Ligands to the name of the open Molecule window. For details about the remaining parameters, see Align to Selected Substructure - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed while the job is running. When the job finishes, the aligned ligands are updated automatically. You can double-click the job in the Jobs Explorer to open the report to get further information.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <ligands>.mol2 | The output .mol2 file containing the aligned ligands. |
| <ligands>_Core.sd | A .sd file with the reference substructure. |

# Basic Arithmetic - Parameters

Source type: HTML

## Basic Arithmetic - Parameters

### Performs basic math calculations

Derives a new property from an existing property or properties using basic math.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Property 1 | A numeric property to use in the math calculation. Or in the case of Avg or sum, a list of numeric properties. |
| Operation | Mathematical operation to apply. In the following expressions, "p1" represents the value of the first property (given by Property 1 ), and "p2" the value of the second (given by Property 2 ). The available options and the values they return are: Avg: the average of all properties in p1. Multiple properties should be specified in p1. sum: the sum of all properties in p1. Multiple properties should be specified in p1. +: p1 + p2. -: p1 - p2. *: p1 * p2. /: p1 / p2. bin: the bin number that p1 falls into, given a bin size of p2. E.g., bin(149, 100) yields 100. mod: the remainder when p1 is divided by p2. E.g., mod(22, 10) yields 2. power: p1 raised to the power p2. E.g., power(2,3) yields 8. 10^x: 10 raised to the power of p1. 10^-x: 10 raised to the power of -p1. abs: the absolute value of p1. ceiling: the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to p1. exp: the constant e raised to the p1 power. log: the natural logarithm of p1. log10: the base-10 logarithm of p1. -log10: the negative base-10 logarithm of p1. sqrt: the square root of p1. Valid Values: Avg , sum, +, -, *, /, bin, mod, power, 10^x, 10^-x, abs, ceiling, exp, log, log10, -log10, sqrt |
| Property 2 | Name of the second numeric property. If it is a constant value, use the Constant parameter to type it in. |
| Constant | Use this parameter to type in a value if Input Property 2 is a constant and can not be hand-typed in Discovery Studio Client. |
| New Property | Name of resulting property. |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

A numeric property to use in the math calculation. Or in the case of Avg or sum, a list of numeric properties.

Mathematical operation to apply.

In the following expressions, "p1" represents the value of the first property (given by Property 1 ), and "p2" the value of the second (given by Property 2 ). The available options and the values they return are:

* Avg: the average of all properties in p1. Multiple properties should be specified in p1.

* sum: the sum of all properties in p1. Multiple properties should be specified in p1.

* +: p1 + p2.

* -: p1 - p2.

* *: p1 * p2.

* /: p1 / p2.

* bin: the bin number that p1 falls into, given a bin size of p2. E.g., bin(149, 100) yields 100.

* mod: the remainder when p1 is divided by p2. E.g., mod(22, 10) yields 2.

* power: p1 raised to the power p2. E.g., power(2,3) yields 8.

* 10^x: 10 raised to the power of p1.

* 10^-x: 10 raised to the power of -p1.

* abs: the absolute value of p1.

* ceiling: the smallest integer that is greater than or equal to p1.

* exp: the constant e raised to the p1 power.

* log: the natural logarithm of p1.

* log10: the base-10 logarithm of p1.

* -log10: the negative base-10 logarithm of p1.

* sqrt: the square root of p1.

Valid Values: Avg , sum, +, -, *, /, bin, mod, power, 10^x, 10^-x, abs, ceiling, exp, log, log10, -log10, sqrt

Name of the second numeric property. If it is a constant value, use the Constant parameter to type it in.

Use this parameter to type in a value if Input Property 2 is a constant and can not be hand-typed in Discovery Studio Client.

## Basic Arithmetic

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Basic Arithmetic protocol implements functions to conduct basic math calculations such as 
addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, logarithm, power, etc.

This protocol requires a set of
ligand structures as input.

* Open a Molecule Window with one or more ligands.

* Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click Basic Arithmetic to open the Basic Arithmetic dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set Property 1 as the property to use. Note that for operators Avg and sum, multiple properties 
need to be selected.

* Set the desired choice for parameter Operation, and name the new property in parameter New Property. If the
operation is binary, parameter Property 2 is also required. To use a constant for parameter Property 2, 
expand parameter Property 2 and type in a value in parameter Constant.

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Basic Arithmetic - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

The new property is generated and inserted to the Data Table automatically. 

If the job ran in background mode, double-click on the job status in the Jobs Explorer to open the report.

# Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_calculate_ligand_efficiency-para.htm

## Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters

### Calculates ligand efficiency by normalizing activity with molecule size

Normalizes a selected set of numeric molecular properties by a measure of the molecule size. Typically activity measures (e.g., pKi, pIC50 ΔG) are normalized to generate a ligand efficiency.

Comparing the activity across a set of compounds is limited by the general trend that larger ligands have higher activities. For lead compounds or fragments, smaller compounds are more desirable so often the Ligand Efficiency is used. Ligand efficiency is an attempt to normalize the activity of a compound by its molecular size. This protocol allows normalization by a number of different measures.

See Also:

* Reynolds, C.H.; Tounge,B.A.; Bembenek, S.D. "Ligand Binding Efficiency: Trends, Physical Basis, and Implications" J. Med. Chem. 2008 , 51, 2432-2438.

* Congreve, M.; Chessari, G.; Tisi, D.; Woodhead, A.J. "Recent Developments in Fragment-Based Drug Discovery" J. Med. Chem. 2008 , 51, 3661-3680.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Properties | The names of the numeric properties which you wish to normalize. In Discovery Studio, when the ligands are selected from a Molecule Window, all numeric properties (those where the value for the first ligand is a number), are listed. |
| Normalization Method | The method to normalize the properties. Heavy Atom Count (LEHA) : Divide by the number of heavy atoms, traditionally used for Ligand Efficiency. All Atom Count (LEAA) : Divide by the total number of atoms, including hydrogen atoms. Molecular Weight (LEMW) : Divide Molecular Weight, based on average atomic weights. Surface Area (LESA) : Divide by Molecular Surface Area, a 2D approximation of the total surface area of the molecule. Polar Surface Area (LEPSA) : Divide by Molecular Polar Surface Area, a 2D approximation of the polar surface area of the molecule. Solvent Accessible Surface Area (LESASA) : Divide by Molecular SASA, a 2D approximation of the solvent accessible surface area modeled with a 1.4 Å probe. Polar Solvent Accessible Surface Area (LEPSASA) : Divide by Molecular Polar SASA, a 2D approximation of the solvent accessible polar surface area modeled with a 1.4 Å probe. Fit Quality (FQ) : Normalize using the number of heavy atoms and a regression equation that a FQ score above 1 for affinity measures (pKi/pIC50) reflects an exceptional efficiency. Ligand-Lipophilicity Efficiency (LLE) : Subtracts AlogP to account for non-specific lipophilic related activity. This method is only appropriate for log(10) values, e.g. pKi, pIC50. The method name (in parentheses) is used to generate the new property. For example if you select pKi as a numeric property and LEHA as the method, each data record will have a new property named 'pKi/LEHA'. See Also: Fit Quality: Reynolds et al. J. Med. Chem., 51 (8), 2432-2438, 2008. 10.1021/jm701255b Congreve et al. J. Med. Chem., 51 (13), 3661-3680, 2008. 10.1021/jm8000373 Valid Values: Heavy Atom Count (LEHA) , All Atom Count (LEAA), Molecular Weight (LEMW), Surface Area (LESA), Polar Surface Area (LEPSA), Solvent Accessible Surface Area (LESASA), Polar Solvent Accessible Surface Area (LEPSASA), Fit Quality (FQ), Ligand-Lipophilicity Efficiency (LLE) |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

The names of the numeric properties which you wish to normalize.

In Discovery Studio, when the ligands are selected from a Molecule Window, all numeric properties (those where the value for the first ligand is a number), are listed.

The method to normalize the properties.

* Heavy Atom Count (LEHA) : Divide by the number of heavy atoms, traditionally used for Ligand Efficiency.

* All Atom Count (LEAA) : Divide by the total number of atoms, including hydrogen atoms.

* Molecular Weight (LEMW) : Divide Molecular Weight, based on average atomic weights.

* Surface Area (LESA) : Divide by Molecular Surface Area, a 2D approximation of the total surface area of the molecule.

* Polar Surface Area (LEPSA) : Divide by Molecular Polar Surface Area, a 2D approximation of the polar surface area of the molecule.

* Solvent Accessible Surface Area (LESASA) : Divide by Molecular SASA, a 2D approximation of the solvent accessible surface area modeled with a 1.4 Å probe.

* Polar Solvent Accessible Surface Area (LEPSASA) : Divide by Molecular Polar SASA, a 2D approximation of the solvent accessible polar surface area modeled with a 1.4 Å probe.

* Fit Quality (FQ) : Normalize using the number of heavy atoms and a regression equation that a FQ score above 1 for affinity measures (pKi/pIC50) reflects an exceptional efficiency.

* Ligand-Lipophilicity Efficiency (LLE) : Subtracts AlogP to account for non-specific lipophilic related activity. This method is only appropriate for log(10) values, e.g. pKi, pIC50.

The method name (in parentheses) is used to generate the new property. For example if you select pKi as a numeric property and LEHA as the method, each data record will have a new property named 'pKi/LEHA'.

* Fit Quality: Reynolds et al. J. Med. Chem., 51 (8), 2432-2438, 2008. 10.1021/jm701255b

* Congreve et al. J. Med. Chem., 51 (13), 3661-3680, 2008. 10.1021/jm8000373

# Calculate Ligand Efficiency

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_calculate_ligand_efficiency.htm

## Calculate Ligand Efficiency

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

The Calculate Ligand Efficiency protocol normalizes a selected set of numeric molecular properties based on ligand size [ Reynolds et al., 2008 , Congreve et al., 2008 ]. For example, activity data (e.g., pKi, pIC50, ΔG) can be normalized to generate a ligand efficiency measure.

Comparing the activity across a set of compounds is limited by the general trend that larger ligands have higher activities. Ligand Efficiency is useful for lead compounds or fragments where smaller compounds are more desirable. The Ligand Efficiency protocol attempts to normalize the activity of a compound by its molecular size.

* Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click Calculate Ligand Efficiency to open the Calculate Ligand Efficiency dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Properties Select one or more property names to calculate the efficiency. Normalization Method Choose the method used to normalize the properties. For details, see Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters . For details about these and other parameters, see Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Properties | Select one or more property names to calculate the efficiency. |
| Normalization Method | Choose the method used to normalize the properties. For details, see Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters . |

For details about these and other parameters, see Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

New properties are inserted into the Data Table automatically.

If the job ran in background mode, double click on the job status in the Jobs Explorer to open the report.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <ligands>.sd | The output file containing the ligands with the efficiency values. The property names are created from the specified properties by appending the normalization method. For example, if the property Jain was selected with heavy atom count as the normalization method, the normalized values will have the name Jain/LEAH . |
| <ligands>_fail.sd | The output file containing the ligands that failed. |

#### Further information

Calculate Ligand Efficiency - Parameters . Receptor-Ligand Interactions Small Molecules tools
