# Calculate Molecular Properties - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_calculate_molecular_properties-para.htm

## Calculate Molecular Properties - Parameters

### Calculates ligand properties

A large number of properties such as traditional molecular descriptors, semiempirical QM descriptors, density functional QM descriptors, and predictions from user models can be calculated.

The calculated properties can be used in other protocols such as building QSAR models, library analysis and design, etc.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Molecular Properties | List of properties to calculate. These properties are classified into different categories. For more information about the properties, please see the documentation accessible through the help menu in Discovery Studio. Note: These properties are generally much faster to calculate than the QM properties. However, some fingerprint methods are memory intensive. Selecting all fingerprint properties at once can cause an "out of memory" error. |
| Model Input Files | Input model file or files (xml format) that contain Pipeline Pilot learners/models. Each model or models are applied to the dataset and the calculated properties are added. |
| Semiempirical QM Properties | Specifies which properties to calculate using VAMP. Total_Energy_VAMP: The total energy of the molecule. Electronic_Energy_VAMP: The electronic energy between all the atoms in the molecule. The total energy includes contributions from the electronic energy and the core-core repulsion energy. Heat_of_Formation_VAMP: The energy change that accompanies the formation of 1 mole of a substance in its standard state from its constituent elements in their standard states. HOMO_Eigenvalue_VAMP: The energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). LUMO_Eigenvalue_VAMP: The energy of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). Molecular_Surface_Area_VAMP: The solvent accessible surface area. Molecular_Point_Group_VAMP: The point group of the molecule. Dipole_Mag_VAMP: The magnitude of the dipole moment. Dipole_Components_VAMP: The components of the dipole moment along each of the axes. Three separate properties will be added: Dipole_X_VAMP , Dipole_Y_VAMP and Dipole_Z_VAMP . Quadrupole_Components_VAMP: The components of the quadrupole moment tensor. The quadrupole moment tensor has 9 components, but only 6 of them are independent and each of them is added as a separate property: Quadrupole_XX_VAMP , Quadrupole_XY_VAMP , Quadrupole_XZ_VAMP , Quadrupole_YY_VAMP , Quadrupole_YZ_VAMP and Quadrupole_XZ_VAMP . Octupole_Components_VAMP: The components of the octupole moment tensor. The octupole moment tensor has 27 components, but only 10 of them are independent. Each of them is added as a separate property. Mean_Polarizability_VAMP: The average polarizability over three rectilinear axes of the molecule. Polarizability is defined as the ratio of the induced dipole moment to the electric field that induces it. ESP_Charges_VAMP: The atomic charges derived from the electrostatic potential. Coulson_Charges_VAMP: The atomic charges derived from the Coulson method. Mulliken_Charges_VAMP: The atomic charges derived from the Mulliken method. Propgen_Outputs_VAMP: A number of molecular properties that are derived from the molecular orbitals. Notes: The atomic charges are returned as arrays of charges for each atom. The Propgen_Outputs_VAMP properties are described in the following articles: Goller, A.H., Hennemann, M., Keldenich, J., Clark, T. In Silico Prediction of Buffer Solubility Based on Quantum-Mechanical and HQSAR- and Topology-Based Descriptors. J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2006 , 46, 648-658. Cronce, D. T.; Famini, G. R.; DeSoto, J. A.; Wilson, L. Y. Using theoretical descriptors in quantitative structure-property relationships: Some distribution equilibria. J. Chem. Soc., Perkin Trans. 2, 1998 , 1293-1301. Valid Values: Total_Energy_VAMP, Electronic_Energy_VAMP, Heat_of_Formation_VAMP, HOMO_Eigenvalue_VAMP, LUMO_Eigenvalue_VAMP, Molecular_Surface_Area_VAMP, Molecular_Point_Group_VAMP, Dipole_Mag_VAMP, Dipole_Components_VAMP, Quadrupole_Components_VAMP, Octupole_Components_VAMP, Mean_Polarizability_VAMP, ESP_Charges_VAMP, Coulson_Charges_VAMP, Mulliken_Charges_VAMP, Propgen_Outputs_VAMP |
| VAMP Settings | The VAMP settings group allows you to select the type of calculation to be performed, and specify calculation-specific settings. |
| VAMP Settings Task | Specifies the type of calculation to be performed. Available options are: Energy : Performs a single-point energy calculation. Geometry Optimization : Searches for a minimum energy structure using the eigenvector following method. Valid Values: Energy , Geometry Optimization |
| Hamiltonian | Specifies the Hamiltonian to be used in the calculation: AM1 : Austin Model 1 AM1* : AM1 plus d-orbitals for transition metals MNDO : Modified Neglect of Differential Overlap MNDO/C : MNDO with explicit correlation effects MNDO/d : MNDO plus d-orbitals for transition metals PM3 : Parameterized Model 3 PM6 : Parameterized Model 6 Valid Values: AM1 , AM1*, MNDO, MNDO/C, MNDO/d, PM3, PM6 |
| Formalism | Specifies the spin state to be used in the calculation. UHF : Unrestricted Hartree-Fock. RHF : Restricted Hartree-Fock. A-UHF : Annihilated unrestricted Hartree-Fock (half-electron method). Valid Values: UHF, RHF , A-UHF |
| VAMP Settings Solvent | Specifies whether to include the effects of a solvent environment in the calculation, using the continuum screening model (COSMO) method. The solvent can be selected from the dropdown list. 'None' should be selected if no solvent effects are to be included in the calculation. Note: The COSMO model is not yet available with d-orbitals, i.e., when the Hamiltonian is set to AM1* or MNDO/d. Valid Values: None , Acetone, Acetonitrile, Benzene, Carbon tetrachloride, Chloroform, Diethyl ether, Dimethyl sulfoxide, Ethanol, Methanol, Methylene chloride, n-Hexane, n-Hexadecane, Nitrobenzene, Pyridine, Water |
| Use Internal Coordinates | Use the VAMP default of aligning the structure according to an internal Z-matrix representation. If False the VAMP keyword NOZ will be specified to avoid this alignment. Note: To get matching orientation of dipole and multipole components, you should set Use Internal Coordinates to True. Valid Values: True, False |
| Semiempirical QM Properties Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| VAMP Input File | Use VAMP Input File if you wish to provide your own input file containing the settings to be passed to the VAMP calculation engine. This will cause the other settings specified on the component to be ignored. |
| Density Functional QM Properties | Specifies which properties to calculate using DMol 3 . Total_Energy_DMol3: The total energy of the molecule. Binding_Energy_DMol3: The interaction energy between all the atoms in the molecule. Also known as cohesive energy. HOMO_Energy_DMol3: The energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). LUMO_Energy_DMol3: The energy of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). Band_Gap_Energy_DMol3: The energy difference between LUMO and HOMO. Dipole_Mag_DMol3: The magnitude of the dipole moment. Dipole_Components_DMol3: The components of the dipole moment along each of the axes. Three separate properties will be added: Dipole_X_DMol3 , Dipole_Y_DMol3 and Dipole_Z_DMol3 . Dielectric_Energy_DMol3: The energy stored in the dielectric in a solvated system. It is always equal to the solvation energy of the molecule. Solvation_Energy_DMol3: The solvation energy calculated as the difference of the total energy of the molecule in solvation and the total energy of the molecule in vacuum. Surface_Area_DMol3: The solvent accessible surface area of the molecule. Cavity_Volume_DMol3: The volume of cavities in the solvation calculation. ESP_Charges_DMol3: The atomic charges derived from the electrostatic potential. Mulliken_Charges_DMol3: The atomic charges derived from the Mulliken method. Hirshfeld_Charges_DMol3: The atomic charges derived from the Hirshfeld method. Notes: The atomic charges are returned as arrays of charges for each atom. The following properties are only available when the solvent is set to something other than None : Dielectric_Energy_DMol3 , Solvation_Energy_DMol3 , Surface_Area_DMol3 and Cavity_Volume_DMol3 . Valid Values: Total_Energy_DMol3, Binding_Energy_DMol3, HOMO_Energy_DMol3, LUMO_Energy_DMol3, Band_Gap_Energy_DMol3, Dipole_Mag_DMol3, Dipole_Components_DMol3, ESP_Charges_DMol3, Mulliken_Charges_DMol3, Hirshfeld_Charges_DMol3, Dielectric_Energy_DMol3, Solvation_Energy_DMol3, Surface_Area_DMol3, Cavity_Volume_DMol3 |
| DMol3 Settings | The DMol3 settings group allows you to select the type of calculation to be performed, and specify calculation-specific settings. |
| DMol3 Settings Task | Specifies the type of calculation to be performed: Energy : Performs a single-point energy calculation. Geometry Optimization : Searches for a minimum energy structure. Valid Values: Energy , Geometry Optimization |
| Functional | The exchange-correlation functional to be used in the quantum calculation. Local Density Approximation (LDA) functionals: PWC VWN Gradient corrected Generalized Gradient Approximations (GGA) functionals: PW91 BP PBE BLYP BOP VWN-BP RPBE HCTH Hybrid functional: B3LYP Notes : GGA provides a better overall description of the electronic subsystem than the LDA functionals. The LDA description tends to overbind atoms, so that the bond lengths and the cell volume are usually underestimated by a few percent and the bulk modulus is correspondingly overestimated. GGA corrects this error but may underbind instead, leading to slightly long bond lengths. B3LYP includes a portion of exact exchange from Hartree-Fock theory along with exchange and correlation contributions from other functionals with carefully chosen weights. The weights are obtained by fitting to experimental data. B3LYP gives better results but requires significantly more CPU time. Valid Values: PWC , VWN, PW91, BP, PBE, BLYP, BOP, RPBE, HCTH, VWN-BP, B3LYP |
| Add Dispersion Correction | Specify whether to add a dispersion correction to the DFT energy. This option is available when Functional is: "PBE", "PW91" "VWN", "PWC". Notes : The TS scheme is used when the Functional is "PBE" The OBS scheme is used when the Functional is "PWC", "VWN", "PW91". Valid Values: True, False |
| Quality | Specifies the overall quality for the DMol 3 calculation. This quality affects the basis set, k-point, and SCF convergence criteria. Available options are Coarse, Medium and Fine. These three levels offer progressively more accuracy at the expense of longer calculation times: Coarse : Uses DN basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-4. Medium : Uses DND basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-5. Fine : Uses DNP basis set with SCF density convergence of 1.0e-6. Valid Values: Coarse , Medium, Fine |
| DMol3 Settings Solvent | DMol3 allows you to simulate a solvent environment using the COSMO continuum solvation model. The default is None (Vacuum), i.e., no solvation is considered. Valid Values: None , Water, Acetone, Acetonitrile, Benzene, Carbon tetrachloride, Chloroform, Diethyl ether, Dimethyl sulfoxide, Ethanol, Methanol, Methylene chloride, n-Hexane, n-Hexadecane, Nitrobenzene, Pyridine, Perfect conductor |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |

This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |

| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

# Calculate Molecular Properties

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_calculate_molecular_properties.htm

## Calculate Molecular Properties

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Calculate Molecular Properties protocol can calculate many of the properties used to create a QSAR model. These range from the traditional
molecular descriptors, semiempirical QM descriptors, Density Functional QM descriptors, and properties that can be calculated from user-built QSAR 
models.

* Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click Calculate Molecular Properties... to open the Calculate Molecular Properties dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Molecular Properties List of traditional molecular properties to calculate. Properties calculable by user-built models also appear here. # Calculate RMSD - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_calculate_rmsd-para.htm

## Calculate RMSD - Parameters

### Calculates RMSD to assess pose similarity

Calculates the Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) of ligand poses (Å). RMSD values can be calculated with respect to the first pose or all poses. When the all poses option is selected, a dendrogram script is created (accessible from the report) that will display an interactive dendrogram in Discovery Studio.

Optionally, an RMSD filter can be applied.

A new property with the RMSD value is added to each pose.

Notes:

* The RMSD algorithm accounts for topological symmetry, returning the lowest RMSD of all symmetry mappings.

* The symmetry mappings also consider resonance stabilization for groups such as carboxylates, nitro, phosphates, guanidines, etc .

* RMSD values include only heavy atoms ( i.e. , excluding hydrogen atoms).

* Atom distances and mappings can be obtained by using the Calculate Pairwise Atom Distance option.

* If the RMSD Reference is set to "All Poses" an interactive dendrogram is displayed in Discovery Studio.

* Since resonance stabilization is accounted for in the atom mapping, the RMSD values may differ from the "Align to Selected Substructure" protocol (for some molecules).

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Reference Pose | The reference pose used for the RMSD calculation. The following options are available: First Pose : RMSD with respect to the first molecule with identical canonical SMILES. All Pose : RMSD between all poses, which can be useful for finding similar conformations (dendrogram scripts are created which are accessible through the report). Valid Values: First Pose , All Poses |
| RMSD Filter | Enable RMSD filter with respect to the reference pose (i.e., first input pose). The filter reduces the number of poses for each ligand. Notes: The poses order can be controlled with RMSD Filter Sort Property parameter. If the RMSD Filter Sort Property is not specified the original pose order is maintained. Valid Values: True, False |
| RMSD Filter Cutoff | Poses with an RMSD less than this value (Å) will be considered duplicates (with respect to the first ligand pose). A higher specified RMSD value will reduce the number of poses returned for each ligand. |
| RMSD Filter Sort Property | The name of the score property to maximize. The diverse pose with the highest value is kept. If a blank value is specified, no sorting is performed and the original order will be used. |
| RMSD Filter Maximum Number of Poses | If specified, limits the maximum number of poses returned for each ligand. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| RMSD Label | The prefix to be used for RMSD values property. |
| RMSD Label Add Name | Add molecule name to RMSD Label . Note : A pose counter is always appended to the RMSD Label if RMSD Reference is set to All Poses . Valid Values: True , False |
| Calculate Pairwise Atom Distance | Report pairwise atom distances from the RMSD calculation. The following properties are added: RMSD Pairwise Atom Distance : Pairwise atom distance for each mapped atom (Å) with respect to the reference pose. RMSD Query Map : Mapping indices for the pairwise atom distance with respect to the reference pose. Note : Hydrogen atoms are ignored in the calculation and have a query index of 0. Valid Values: True, False |
| Group Poses Options | Options for standardizing canonical SMILES for pose grouping. Poses with identical canonical SMILES are grouped together for the RMSD calculation. Valid Values: Kekulize , StandardizeStereo, StandardizeCharges, MakeAllAtomsCarbon, MakeAllBondsSingle, ClearStereo, ClearUnknownStereo , ClearCisTransBondStereo , ClearCharges, SetStereoFromCoordinates, RepositionStereoBonds, ClearQueryInfo , NeutralizeBondedZwitterions |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

## Calculate RMSD

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

This protocol allows you to analyze or filter a set of poses by Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD), for example, the results of a docking run.

* You may calculate the RMSD of the poses to each other or to a reference pose.

* Ligand poses can be filtered by RMSD to remove similar poses.

* Symmetry is taken into account to ensure that the lowest RMSD of symmetry related mappings is calculated (e.g., carboxylate ion).

* Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click Calculate RMSD to open the Calculate RMSD dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

# Calculate ROC Curve - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_calculate_roc_curve-para.htm

## Calculate ROC Curve - Parameters

### Calculates ROC curves for evaluating docking performance

Calculates a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve for quantitatively assessing High Throughput Screening (HTS) performance.

The ROC curve shows the fraction of true positive ligands versus the fraction of false positive ligands.

A docking/scoring method can be evaluated by the area of the ROC curve (AUC). A value closer to 1 indicates good selectivity, whereas a value closer to 0.5 indicates random selection.

See Also:

* http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Scores | The names of the numeric properties for generating ROC curves. In Discovery Studio, when the ligands are selected from a Molecule Window, all numeric properties (those where the value for the first ligand is a number), are listed. |
| Group Using | Set to a value(s) unique to each data point you wish to analyze. The data will be grouped by this value(s) and the maximum score for each group will be used in ROC analysis. For example, if you have a set of poses for each compound, you could specify the Name here and the best scoring pose for each Name will be used for the corresponding ROC analysis. |
| Control Property | This property will be used to categorize the data. Any data with this property defined and set to the Control Value will be considered "good". |
| Control Value | The Control Property must be set to this value to be considered "good". |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Total Records | Sometimes, the data set you are analyzing has been filtered in some way. In this case, the False Positive Rate will be truncated, leading to artificially bad ROC scores. If you set this value to the total number of original records then it will be used, in place of the number found in the data set. If the number is lower than the number of records in the data set then it will have no effect. |
| Total Positives | Sometimes, the data set you are analyzing has been filtered in some way, losing some "good" records. In this case, the True Positive Rate will be inflated, leading to artificially good ROC scores. If you set this value to the total number of original "good" records then it will be used, in place of the "good" records found in the data set. If the number is lower than the number of "good" records in the data set then it will have no effect. |
| Add Title to Chart | Add title to the chart, containing the area under the ROC curve for each property defined in Scores . Valid Values: True, False |
| Chart Width | Width (pixels) of the ROC chart. |
| Chart Height | Height (pixels) of the ROC chart. |
| Show Legend | Show a legend for the different scores in the chart. Valid Values: True , False |

## Calculate ROC Curve

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

This protocol calculates a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve of the ligands to distinguish "good" and "bad" samples. This is useful for analyzing a set of poses generated by a docking or scoring protocol.

ROC curves are used to analyze the enrichment based on the scores of a set of control poses. 
For example, if you have the results of a docking protocol with multiple poses per ligand where each ligand has a unique Name property, and the
control ligands have a value of one for their Control property, you
can generate a ROC curve for any score by setting Group Using to Name and Control Property to Control .

* Open the Small Molecules | Calculate Molecular Properties tools and click Calculate ROC Curve to open the Calculate ROC curve dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Scores Select one or more property names for calculating the ROC curves. Group Using Select a property name that is used to group poses. The highest scoring pose in each group will be used for analysis. Control Property Select a property name that is used to identify the control poses (i.e., the "good" poses). Control Value The value set for the Control Property that specifies a "good" pose. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate ROC Curve - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |

# Correlation and Statistics - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_correlation_and_statistics-para.htm

## Correlation and Statistics - Parameters

### Calculates correlation matrix and statistics

Calculate Pearson correlation matrix and statistics of a list of properties.

The correlation coefficient provides a measure of the interrelatedness of numeric properties. Values range from -1 (highly anticorrelated), through 0 (not correlated), to +1 (highly correlated).

The statistical quantities that can be calculated here include mean, sum, standard deviation, sum, min, max, etc.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Properties | A list of numeric properties to use. |
| Correlation Matrix | Whether to compute the correlation matrix for the properties listed in Input Properties. The correlation coefficient provides a measure of the interrelatedness of numeric properties. Values range from -1 (highly anticorrelated), through 0 (not correlated), to +1 (highly correlated). Notes: The type of correlation calculated here is Pearson correlation coefficient. When there are missing properties on an input ligand, only the correlation of the pairwise-complete values for each pair of properties is returned, that is, the samples for which both properties are defined and have valid numerical values. A correlation coefficient of zero is assigned for non-numeric properties. Valid Values: True , False |
| Statistics | The statistical quantities to calculate for the properties listed in Input Properties. You can choose any or all of the following: Mean: Sum of values divided by number of values. StdDev: Standard deviation if sample represents entire population. (Square-root of 1/N times sum of squared deviation from mean.) StdDevSample: Sample standard deviation. (Square-root of 1/(N-1) times sum of squared deviation from mean. This is the square-root of the unbiased estimator of the population variance if the sample is a subset of a larger population). N: Number of values. Variance: Variance of values if sample represents entire population; square of StdDev. Skew: Skew of values. Kurtosis: Kurtosis of values (excess kurtosis relative to a Gaussian). Sum: Sum of values. Min: Minimum value. Max: Maximum value. Median: Median value. Mode: Most common value. GeometricMean: The N-th root of the product of N values. MAD: Median Absolute Deviation, the median of the absolute value of the difference between each data point and the median of the data points. Percentile: Percentile values specified by Percentiles . Each property may have one or multiple values. Statistics are calculated over all values for all input ligands. For each statistic, a new property name is created by appending an underscore and the statistic name to the original property name. For percentiles, the number specifying the percentile level is appended to the name as well. Valid Values: Mean, StdDev , StdDevSample, N , Variance, Skew, Kurtosis, Sum, Min , Max , Median, Mode, GeometricMean, MAD, Percentile |
| Percentiles | Comma-separated list of the percentiles to output when Percentile is selected as one of the Statistics . Values are in percentages (as opposed to fractions). |
| Percentile Type | Method to use for computing percentiles. Options are: Excel: Method used by Excel. Equivalent to the R type 7 method (see link below), which is the default in R. NIST: Method recommended in the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook (see link below). Equivalent to the R type 6 method. Also used by Minitab and SPSS. Closest Value: Returns the value from the input data whose sorted index is the lowest index greater than or equal to N*p/100, where N is the number of data points and p is the percentile level. Equivalent to the R type 1 method. R Type 2: R type 2 method. Similar to "Closest Value" but with averaging at discontinuities. R Type 3: R type 3 method. Also used by SAS. R Type 4: R type 4 method. Linear interpolation of the empirical cumulative distribution function. R Type 5: R type 5 method. According to R documentation, "popular amongst hydrologists." R Type 8: R type 8 method. Recommended by Hyndman and Fan (see link below to R documentation). R Type 9: R type 9 method. According to R documentation, "resulting quantile estimates are approximately unbiased for the expected order statistics if x is normally distributed." Valid Values: Excel , NIST, Closest Value, R Type 2, R Type 3, R Type 4, R Type 5, R Type 8, R Type 9 |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

A list of numeric properties to use.

Whether to compute the correlation matrix for the properties listed in Input Properties.

Notes:

* The type of correlation calculated here is Pearson correlation coefficient.

* When there are missing properties on an input ligand, only the correlation of the pairwise-complete values for each pair of properties is returned, that is, the samples for which both properties are defined and have valid numerical values.

* A correlation coefficient of zero is assigned for non-numeric properties.

Valid Values: True , False

The statistical quantities to calculate for the properties listed in Input Properties. You can choose any or all of the following:

* Mean: Sum of values divided by number of values.

* StdDev: Standard deviation if sample represents entire population. (Square-root of 1/N times sum of squared deviation from mean.)

* StdDevSample: Sample standard deviation. (Square-root of 1/(N-1) times sum of squared deviation from mean. This is the square-root of the unbiased estimator of the population variance if the sample is a subset of a larger population).

* N: Number of values.

* Variance: Variance of values if sample represents entire population; square of StdDev.

* Skew: Skew of values.

* Kurtosis: Kurtosis of values (excess kurtosis relative to a Gaussian).

* Sum: Sum of values.

* Min: Minimum value.

* Max: Maximum value.

* Median: Median value.

* Mode: Most common value.

* GeometricMean: The N-th root of the product of N values.

* MAD: Median Absolute Deviation, the median of the absolute value of the difference between each data point and the median of the data points.

* Percentile: Percentile values specified by Percentiles .

Each property may have one or multiple values. Statistics are calculated over all values for all input ligands. For each statistic, a new property name is created by appending an underscore and the statistic name to the original property name. For percentiles, the number specifying the percentile level is appended to the name as well.

Valid Values: Mean, StdDev , StdDevSample, N , Variance, Skew, Kurtosis, Sum, Min , Max , Median, Mode, GeometricMean, MAD, Percentile

Comma-separated list of the percentiles to output when Percentile is selected as one of the Statistics . Values are in percentages (as opposed to fractions).

Method to use for computing percentiles. Options are:

* Excel: Method used by Excel. Equivalent to the R type 7 method (see link below), which is the default in R.

* NIST: Method recommended in the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook (see link below). Equivalent to the R type 6 method. Also used by Minitab and SPSS.

* Closest Value: Returns the value from the input data whose sorted index is the lowest index greater than or equal to N*p/100, where N is the number of data points and p is the percentile level. Equivalent to the R type 1 method.

* R Type 2: R type 2 method. Similar to "Closest Value" but with averaging at discontinuities.

* R Type 3: R type 3 method. Also used by SAS.

* R Type 4: R type 4 method. Linear interpolation of the empirical cumulative distribution function.

* R Type 5: R type 5 method. According to R documentation, "popular amongst hydrologists."

* R Type 8: R type 8 method. Recommended by Hyndman and Fan (see link below to R documentation).

* R Type 9: R type 9 method. According to R documentation, "resulting quantile estimates are approximately unbiased for the expected order statistics if x is normally distributed."

## Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules - Parameters

### Filters ligands using Lipinski and Veber rules

Selects drug-like ligands according to rules formulated by Lipinski (Rule of Five) and Veber. The ligands passing the filters have a higher probability of good oral bioavailability.

See also:

* Lipinski, C. A.; Lombardo, F.; Dominy, B. W.; Feeney, P. J. Experimental and computational approaches to estimate solubility and permeability in drug discovery and development settings. Adv. Drug Delivery Rev. 1997 , 23, 2-25.

* Veber, D. F.; Johnson, S. R.; Cheng, H-Y.; Smith, B. R.; Ward, K. W.; Kopple, K. D. Molecular properties that influence the oral bioavailability of drug candidates. J. Med. Chem. 2002 , 45, 2615-2623.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Rules | Choose one or two filter rules: Lipinski Rule of Five Veber Rule Note : The default values for the filters are set according to the published articles, but you can adjust them if desired. Valid Values: Lipinski Rule of Five , Veber Rule |
| Advanced | Contains advanced parameters. |
| Lipinski Rule of Five | Rule of Five settings formulated by Lipinski: Number of hydrogen bond donors is no more than 5. Number of hydrogen bond acceptors is no more than 10. Molecular weight is no more than 500. LogP is no more than 5. |
| Hydrogen Bond Donors | The upper limit for the number of hydrogen bond donors. Note : In the original Rule of Five, this is set to 5. |
| Hydrogen Bond Acceptors | The upper limit for the number of hydrogen bond acceptors. Note : In the original Rule of Five, this is set to 10. |
| Molecular Weight | The upper limit for the molecular weight. Note : In the original Rule of Five, this is set to 500. |
| AlogP | The upper limit for AlogP (the log value of octanol-water partition coefficient). Note : In the original Rule of Five, this is set to 5. |
| Number of Violations Allowed | How many violations can be tolerated, i.e., the ligand is still allowed to pass. Note : In Lipinski's original paper, this value is set to 1. Valid Values: 0, 1 , 2, 3 |
| Required Rules | Rules to be satisfied in order for a ligand to pass. This overrides the Number of Violations Allowed . For example, if you select AlogP ≤ 5 as required, then a ligand with AlogP of 6 will always fail even if the number of violations allowed is set to 1 or more. Valid Values: Hydrogen Bond Donors, Hydrogen Bond Acceptors, Molecular Weight, AlogP |
| Veber Rule | Veber rule settings: The number of rotatable bonds is no more than 10. The polar surface area is no more than 140 Å 2 or The sum of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors is no more than 12. |
| Rotatable Bonds | The upper limit of the number of rotatable bonds. Note : In Veber's original formulation, this is set to 10. |
| Polar Surface Area | The upper limit of polar surface area in Å 2 . Note: In Veber's original formulation, this is set to 140. This rule is in parallel of the sum of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors rule, i.e., only this or the sum of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors rule needs to be satisfied for the ligand to pass these two. |
| Hydrogen Bond Donors and Acceptors | The upper limit of the sum of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors. Note: In Veber's original formulation, this is set to 12. This rule is in parallel of the polar surface area rule, i.e., only this or the polar surface area rule needs to be satisfied for the ligand to pass these two. |

# Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_filter_by_lipinski_and_veber_rules.htm

## Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules

This topic discusses the Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules protocol. The following is covered:

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

Orally administered drugs should have good oral bioavailability in order to be effective. The pioneering research by
Lipinski et al. led to the well known "Rule of Five" for selecting drug-like molecules in 1997 [Lipinski et al., 1997] . According to the "Rule of Five", a drug-like molecule should have no more than one of the following violations:

* No more than 5 hydrogen bond donors

* No more than 10 hydrogen bond acceptors

* Molecular weight no more than 500

* LogP no more than 5

In 2002 Veber et al. published a different set of rules for selecting drug candidates with good oral bioavailability [Veber et al., 2002] :

* No more than 10 rotatable bonds

* Polar surface area no more than 1400 Å 2 or no more than 12 hydrogen bond donors and acceptors

These rules are implemented in this protocol to filter drug-like molecules in Discovery Studio .

* Open the Small Molecules | Prepare or Filter Ligands tools and click Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules... to open the Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters (for details, see Filter by Lipinski and Veber Rules - Parameters ): Parameter Description Input Ligands From the Parameters Explorer , set 
the Input Ligands . For details, see Specifying Ligands . For large data sets,
it may be easier to use the Browse... option rather than 
load the data into Discovery Studio . Rules Choose Lipinski Rule of Five and/or Veber Rule to apply the filter choice.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | From the Parameters Explorer , set the Input Ligands . For details, see Specifying Ligands . For large data sets, it may be easier to use the Browse... option rather than load the data into Discovery Studio . |
| Rules | Choose Lipinski Rule of Five and/or Veber Rule to apply the filter choice. |

* The default values for individual property thresholds are set according to the original publications. However, you can adjust each value if desired. Additionally, you can set a property as required in the "Rule of Five".
For details, see Filter by Property - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| filtered.sd | The output file containing the ligands that pass the filter. |
| failed.sd | The output file containing the ligands that failed to pass the filter. |

## Filter by Property - Parameters

### Filters ligands by property

Ligands that pass the filter are written to the output file. The following filter operations are available:

* Top (#) : Number of top molecules or poses.

* Top (%) : Percentage of top molecules or poses.

* Bottom (#) : Number of bottom molecules or poses.

* Bottom (%) : Percentage of top molecules or poses.

* Equals : Values that equal the specified string/number.

* Does not equal : Values that do not equal the specified number/string.

* Less than : Values that are less than the specified number/string.

* Less than or equal : Values that are less or equal than the specified number/string.

* Greater than : Values that are greater than the specified number/string.

* Greater than or equal : Values that are greater or equal than the specified number/string.

* Begins with : Values that begin with the specified number/string.

* Does not begin with : Values that do not begin with the specified number/string.

* Ends with : Values that end with the specified number/string.

* Does not end with : Values that do not end with the specified number/string.

* Contains : Values that contain the specified number/string.

* Does not contain : Values that do not contain the specified number/string.

Note:

* For determining the top or bottom scoring poses from a docking run, the molecules need to be grouped.

### Parameters

| Input Property | Property name to which the filter Choice will be applied to. |
| Choice | Ligand Input Property filter operator: Top (#) : Number of top molecules or poses. Top (%) : Percentage of top molecules or poses. Bottom (#) : Number of bottom molecules or poses. Bottom (%) : Percentage of top molecules or poses. Equals : Values that equal the specified number * /string. Does not equal : Values that do not equal the specified number/string. Begins with : Values that begin with the specified number/string. Does not begin with : Values that do not begin with the specified number/string. Ends with : Values that end with the specified number * /string. Does not end with : values that do not end with the specified number/string. # Filter by SMARTS - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_filter_by_smarts-para.htm

## Filter by SMARTS - Parameters

### Filters ligands by SMARTS substructures

Filters ligands through a series of substructure filters. The following filter options are available:

* SMARTS Each filter is a SMILES Arbitrary Target Specification (SMARTS) pattern, along with a minimum and maximum number of times it is allowed to map (specified in parentheses). This allows you, for example, to restrict ligands that contain a single reactive group (e.g. Alkyl-Halides 0-0), too many heteroatoms (e.g. N-O-S 0-9) or too few carbons (Carbons 1-30). Each Input Filter is applied to the molecules in turn. The molecule will pass a filter if the number of mappings for that substructure is within the allowed range. If a molecule fails one or more filters it is removed from the output.

SMARTS

Each filter is a SMILES Arbitrary Target Specification (SMARTS) pattern, along with a minimum and maximum number of times it is allowed to map (specified in parentheses). This allows you, for example, to restrict ligands that contain a single reactive group (e.g. Alkyl-Halides 0-0), too many heteroatoms (e.g. N-O-S 0-9) or too few carbons (Carbons 1-30). Each Input Filter is applied to the molecules in turn. The molecule will pass a filter if the number of mappings for that substructure is within the allowed range. If a molecule fails one or more filters it is removed from the output.

* PAINS Checks for PAINS (Pan Assay Interference Compounds) substructures in ligands with a number of undesirable substructures greater than the number specified in Max Number PAINS are filtered (see Baell et al., 2010).

PAINS

Checks for PAINS (Pan Assay Interference Compounds) substructures in ligands with a number of undesirable substructures greater than the number specified in Max Number PAINS are filtered (see Baell et al., 2010).

Notes:

* When selecting SMARTS , the substructure names of the Input Filters are generated from SMARTS Filters .

* The report contains information on the found substructures.

See Also:

* New Substructure Filters for Removal of Pan Assay Interference Compounds (PAINS) from Screening Libraries and for Their Exclusion in Bioassays, Jonathan B. Baell and Georgina A. Holloway. J. Med. Chem. 2010, 53, 7, 2719-2740.

* The PAINS structures were compiled from practicalcheminformatics.blogspot.com/2018/08/filtering-chemical-libraries.html

* For more information about SMARTS see www.daylight.com/dayhtml/doc/theory/theory.smarts.html

# Filter by SMARTS

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_filter_by_smarts.htm

## Filter by SMARTS

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Filter by SMARTS protocol allows you to filter ligands based on a set of substructures.
Each filter is applied to the ligands in turn. The ligand will pass a filter if the number of mappings for that substructure is within the allowed range. 
Any ligand that fails one or more filters is removed from the results.

The protocol supports the following filter options to remove ligands that are not likely to be "drug-like":

* SMARTS : Filters have been taken from the literature and are accessible using the Input Filters parameter.

For more information please see [Walters and Murcko, 2002] and [Hann et al, 1999] .
Optionally, one can also add a substructure filters using the SMARTS Filters parameter.

* PAINS : PAINS filter (Pan Assay Interference Compounds) [Baell and Holloway, 2010] . 
Substructures to remove frequent hitters (promiscuous compounds) in biochemical high throughput screens.

* Open the Small Molecules | Prepare or Filter Ligands tools tools and click Filter by SMARTS... to open the Filter by SMARTS dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Filter Method Select SMARTS or PAINS substructure filter. Input Filters The filters are named by a descriptive chemical group name
followed by a numerical representation of the acceptable ranges. For example, "Phosphonate ester (0-1)"
means that ligands can have a minimum of zero and a maximum of one phosphonate ester group. Filters
that have zero for the minimum and maximum value (e.g., "Peroxide (0 0)") indicates that this group
is not allowed. The Input Filters parameter is populated with filters
that assist with identifying "drug-like" [Walters and Murcko, 2002] and "lead-like" [Hann et al, 1999] molecules. You can add additional
filters to Input Filters using the SMARTS Filters parameter. You can also modify the minimum and maximum values for each SMARTS filter. For details, see Adding SMARTS Filters . Note : This option is only available when the SMARTS option was selected. Set the remaining parameters as desired. Parameters presented in red are required. For details, see Filter by SMARTS - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Filter Method | Select SMARTS or PAINS substructure filter. |
| Input Filters | The filters are named by a descriptive chemical group name followed by a numerical representation of the acceptable ranges. For example, "Phosphonate ester (0-1)" means that ligands can have a minimum of zero and a maximum of one phosphonate ester group. Filters that have zero for the minimum and maximum value (e.g., "Peroxide (0 0)") indicates that this group is not allowed. The Input Filters parameter is populated with filters that assist with identifying "drug-like" [Walters and Murcko, 2002] and "lead-like" [Hann et al, 1999] molecules. You can add additional filters to Input Filters using the SMARTS Filters parameter. You can also modify the minimum and maximum values for each SMARTS filter. For details, see Adding SMARTS Filters . Note : This option is only available when the SMARTS option was selected. |

Note : This option is only available when the SMARTS option was selected.

Set the remaining parameters as desired. Parameters presented in red are required. For details, see Filter by SMARTS - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

#### Adding SMARTS Filters

Add the following tab-delimited data to the Input Filters parameter (one row per filter):

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| SMARTS | The SMARTS pattern that defines the substructure filter. For information about SMARTS, see www.daylight.com/dayhtml/doc/theory/theory.smarts.html |
| NAME | The name for the pattern. This will form part of the output and will be used to identify the new filter in Input Filters . |
| MIN | The minimum number of times the substructure must map. |
| MAX | The maximum number of times the substructure can map. |

Updates to SMARTS Filters are automatically reflected in the Input Filters parameter and can
be selected as one of the filters. Make the following special considerations for the SMARTS Filters parameters:

* To specify a feature to be absent, set both MIN and MAX to zero.

* None of the fields can contain a tab, which are reserved for separating data. Spaces are allowed for NAME.

* Rows starting with # are considered comment lines.

* Blank rows are skipped.

* Duplicate names are supported.

* Recursive SMARTS (those containing "$" followed by "(" ) are not permitted
and cause problems generating the Input Filters.

* Commas in names are not allowed, though they are allowed in SMARTS.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Filtered.sd | Contains all the ligands that passed all the selected filters. |
| Failed.sd | Contains all the ligands that failed one or more of the filters. Two additional properties are added to this file: FilterPassed lists all the filters that the ligand passed, and FilterFailed lists all the filters the ligand failed. |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

#### Further information

SMARTS - A Language for Describing Molecular Patterns Small Molecules tools

# Minimize Ligands - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_minimize_ligands-para.htm

## Minimize Ligands - Parameters

### Minimizes a series of ligand poses using CHARMm

Uses CHARMm to minimize ligands.

This protocol adds several properties to the ligands including:

* Initial Potential Energy: The initial energy (kcal/mol) of the molecule before minimization.

* RMS Gradient: The final RMS gradient (kcal/molxÅ) of the minimized molecule.

* CHARMm Energy: The final energy (kcal/mol) of the minimized molecule.

* Minimization Criteria: The criteria used to stop the minimization. It can be the maximum steps, gradient, or energy tolerance has been met.

Note:

* If the ligands are not typed, they will be typed automatically by the forcefield specified by Input Forcefield . Any missing hydrogens will also be added during the typing.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MOL2 files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Forcefield | Forcefield for atom typing: CHARMm : General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules. MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions. Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF |
| Minimization | Parameters for minimization. |
| Minimization Algorithm | Algorithm to use for performing the minimization. Available options are: Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions. Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation. Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations. Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails. Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation. Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer |
| Minimization Max Steps | Maximum number of cycles for the minimization. |
| Minimization RMS Gradient | A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Angstrom). For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined. |
| Minimization Energy Change | A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase. |
| Minimization Save Results Frequency | When set to a number other than zero, the intermediate results are saved into a file every this number of steps. This will also enables reporting of intermediate progress. Setting to zero means do not save these intermediate results, speeding up the calculation, reducing the required disk space, and turning off progress reporting. |
| Implicit Solvent Model | Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation. Available options are: None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent. Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None . See Also: Discovery Studio documentation. Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224. Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics |
| Dielectric Constant | Dielectric constant used in Distance-Dependent Dielectrics implicit solvent model. |
| Nonbond List Radius | Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs. Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Partial Charge Estimation | Choose a method to assign partial charges when the input molecule is not typed. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported: Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. Existing: Uses existing atom partial charges. Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF, Existing |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. Valid Values: True, False |
| Parallel Processing Batch Size | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. |
| Parallel Processing Server | Comma separated list of servers (server-name:port-number) to be used for parallel processing. Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster). |
| Parallel Processing Server Processes | Comma separated list of the maximum batches that can be simultaneously executed on each server. Each value must correspond with an entry in the list of servers. The number of entries in this parameter must equal the number of servers. |
| Parallel Processing Preserve Order | Preserve the initial order of the data records. Valid Values: True , False |

Specify one or more MOL2 files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance.

Forcefield for atom typing:

* CHARMm : 
General-purpose all-atom forcefield with a wide coverage for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules.

* cff : Class II all-atom forcefield for proteins, nucleic acids and general organic molecules.

* MMFF : Like cff, MMFF is a class II forcefield derived from ab initio calculations and experimental data. It is designed to be a transferable forcefield for pharmaceutical compounds that accurately treats conformational energetics and nonbonded interactions.

Valid Values: CHARMm , cff, MMFF

Parameters for minimization.

* Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson (NR) : Uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm applied to a subspace of the coordinate vector spanned by the displacement coordinates of the last positions.

* Steepest Descent : In each step of this iterative procedure, the coordinates are adjusted in the negative direction of the gradient. It does not converge in general, but will rapidly improve a very poor conformation.

* Conjugate Gradient : An iterative method which makes use of the previous history of minimization steps as well as the current gradient to determine the next step. It has better convergence characteristics but is subject to numerical overflows when starting with very poor conformations.

* Powell : This algorithm is encouraged whenever ABNR is not effective or fails.

* Smart Minimizer : Performs 1000 steps of Steepest Descent with a RMS gradient tolerance of 3, followed by Conjugate Gradient minimization. Recommended for use when starting from a very poor conformation.

Valid Values: Adopted Basis NR, Steepest Descent, Conjugate Gradient, Powell, Smart Minimizer

Maximum number of cycles for the minimization.

A tolerance applied to the average gradient during a cycle of minimization. If the average gradient is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit. Unit: kcal/(mol x Angstrom).

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this controls only the last minimization phase since the others are pre-defined.

A tolerance applied to the change in total energy during a cycle of minimization. If the energy change is less than or equal to the tolerance, the minimization routine will exit.

For the Smart Minimizer algorithm, this only controls the last conjugate gradient minimization phase.

When set to a number other than zero, the intermediate results are saved into a file every this number of steps. This will also enables reporting of intermediate progress.
Setting to zero means do not save these intermediate results, speeding up the calculation, reducing the required disk space, and turning off progress reporting.

Implicit solvent model to use in the calculation.

Available options are:

* None : Do not use implicit solvent model. Use for modeling a system in vacuum or with explicit solvent.

* Distance-Dependent Dielectrics : A crude approximation of a polar solvent. About the same speed as None .

See Also:

* Discovery Studio documentation.

* Michael Feig, Charles L. Brooks III: Recent advances in the development and application of implicit solvent models in biomolecule simulations Current Opinion in Structural Biology (2004) 14, 217-224.

Valid Values: None , Distance-Dependent Dielectrics

Distance cutoff value (Å) to use for counting nonbonded interaction pairs.

Beyond this cutoff distance, nonbonded interactions between atom pairs are ignored.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Choose a method to assign partial charges when the input molecule is not typed. By default, these charges are only applied to atoms that do not match the residue templates, and only used when CHARMm forcefield is used. The following options are supported:

* Momany-Rone: Uses a set of bond-charge-increment rules for assigning atom partial charges.

* CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges.

* MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges.

* Existing: Uses existing atom partial charges.

Valid Values: Momany-Rone , CFF, MMFF, Existing

* Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size.

Add "localhost" to include the local server. This can be helpful on multi-CPU/multi-core systems (where the subprotocol jobs are spawned on the same machine) and Pipeline Pilot Linux clusters (where "localhost" requests spawning the subprotocol jobs on the same cluster).

# Prepare Ligands - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_prepare_ligands-para.htm

## Prepare Ligands - Parameters

### Creates tautomers, isomers, protomers and 3D coordinates

Prepare ligands for use in other applications, in particular those that require a 3D coordinates and biological ionization and tautomerization states.

When studying receptor-ligand interactions and other areas, it is important to correctly prepare the ligands. Different protonation states, isomers and tautomers typically have different 3D geometries and binding characteristics. If the known binding configuration is not known, one approach is to enumerate a number of likely configurations before running docking protocols. Ligand Preparation will help you with that task.

The following options are available:

* Standardize charges for common groups

* Retain only the largest fragment

* Add Hydrogens

* Represent in Kekule form

* Enumerate ionization states

* Ionize functional groups

* Generate tautomers and isomers

* Remove duplicates

* Fix bad valencies

* Calculate 3D coordinates using Catalyst

Depending on the setting, the following properties are added to the data stream:

* NumberOfIonizations : Number of ligand ionization states.

* NumberOfTautomers : Number of ligand tautomers.

* NumberOfStereoisomers : Number of stereoisomers.

* IonizationIndex : Ligand ionization number.

* StereoisomerIndex : Ligand stereoisomer number.

* TautomerIndex : Ligand tautomer number.

* Ionization pH : Ionization pH.

Notes:

* More options for ligand preparation are available in the Prepare Ligands protocol.

* If an input ligand contains multiple fragments, only the largest one is retained.

* These options often change the configuration of the ligands. It is important to include the 3D coordinate step even if the ligands start with 3D coordinates.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. Note: It is best to use a file when the atom and bond parity flags should be preserved. |
| NonStandard Name Property | Use a property other than "Name" to identify molecules. Setting to true will rename molecules using the Name Property . Any existing "Name" properties are renamed as "DSSaveName". Valid Values: True, False |
| Name Property | The property to be used in the place of Name to identify molecules. |
| Change Ionization | Whether to change the ionization state of the ligands. Several methods are available, controlled by the Ionization Method parameter. Note: If the ligands are not ionized in the correct state, as seen in a receptor-ligand complex, docking results may be unreliable. Valid Values: True , False |
| Ionization Method | The following methods are available for changing ionization state of the molecule: pH Based : Ionization states are predicted for the specified pH range using estimated pKa values for ligands. Rule Based : Ionization states are based on a set of rules for desired ionization states. Remove Charges : Neutralizes charges on acids and/or bases. Note: More details can be found in the parameter help. Valid Values: pH Based , Rule Based, Remove Charges |
| pH Based | Enumerate the ionization states of the molecule for the specified pH range. Finds pKa sites and calculates the corresponding pKa values. The ionization states of the molecule are enumerated based on the entered pH range. A new property, Ionization pH is calculated for each ionization state. This property has the form "pH_state", where "pH" is the pH at which the molecule was ionized, and "state" is a string of P and/or D values which indicate the protonation state of each pKa site, protonated or deprotonated. |
| Minimum pH | Minimum value of the pH range used to calculate ionization states |
| Maximum pH | Maximum value of the pH range used to calculate ionization states. |
| Rule Based | Ionization is based on a set of rules for how to protonate your ligands. Each rule is a SMIRKS transformation and is applied to the ligands in turn. You can select which of these rules you wish to apply. The set of Acid and Base rules are customizable using the advanced parameters. |
| Acid Ionization | Select from this list ionization templates. Molecules that match the groups are ionized. These filters are defined in the Advanced SMIRKS Acid Templates parameter. Valid Values: Amides, Carboxylate , Dithiocarboxylates, Hydroxamates, N-Acyl Amide, Phenol, Phosphate (1st ionization), Phosphate (2nd ionization), Phosphinates, Phosphonates (1st ionization), Phosphonates (2nd ionization), Sulfate, Sulfinic Acid, Sulfonamide (alkyl), Sulfonamides (aryl), Sulfonate, Tetrazolates 1, Tetrazolates 2, Thiocarboxylates, Thiol (aliphatic), Thiol (aryl) |
| Base Ionization | Select from this list ionization templates. Molecules that match the groups are ionized. These filters are defined in the Advanced SMIRKS Base Templates parameter. Valid Values: Amidine, Amine (aryl), Amine (primary) , Amine (secondary) , Amine (tertiary) , Guanidine, Hydrazide, Hydrazine (alkyl), Hydrazine (aryl), Imidazole |
| Ionization Enumeration | Determines the number of protomers generated for each ligand. One Protomer : only the protomer with the highest number of charged groups is returned. All Combinations : multiple ionization states are returned. Valid Values: One Protomer , All Combinations |
| Filter SMARTS | Choose undesired substructures which will be removed after ionization is performed. After enumeration, some protomers may have oppositely charged atoms in close proximity. You can use this filter to remove such undesirable protomers. Molecules that match any of the selected filters are discarded. These filters can be customized using the advanced SMARTS Charge Templates parameter. Valid Values: Negative 1-Bonds , Negative 2-Bonds , Negative 3-Bonds , Positive 1-Bond , Positive 2-Bonds , Positive 3-Bonds |
| Remove Charges | Specify what charges should be neutralized: Protonate Acids : Adds hydrogen atoms to acid functional groups in the molecule, adjusting the charges accordingly. Acid functional groups are defined as O, S, N, or C atoms with a negative formal charge, not attached to any charged atom. An implicit H atom is added to the oxygen or sulfur atom and the charge is set to zero. Deprotonate Bases : Removes hydrogen atoms from basic functional groups in the molecule, adjusting the charges accordingly. Basic functional groups are defined as nitrogen atoms with a positive formal charge and one or more attached hydrogen atoms. Valid Values: Protonate Acids , Deprotonate Bases |
| Generate Tautomers | Enumerate tautomeric forms for each structure, or generate a single canonical tautomer. Different tautomers have different charge and hydrogen bond distributions. If tautomers are not correct, you are likely to miss important binding modes in docking. Valid Values: True , False |
| Generate Tautomers Enumerate What | Enumerate all tautomers or only the canonical tautomer. The canonical tautomer is the tautomer with the best tautomer score. The tautomer score is calculated based on the count of specific substructures in the molecule, such as aromatic bonds, exocyclic double bonds, keto or enol forms, imine or enamine forms, etc. Valid Values: AllTautomers , CanonicalTautomer |
| Generate Tautomers Maximum Number of Tautomers | Maximum number of top scoring tautomers created (if blank or 0 all tautomers are returned). The tautomer score is calculated based on the count of specific substructures in the molecule, such as aromatic bonds, exocyclic double bonds, keto or enol forms, imine or enamine forms, etc. |
| Generate Tautomers ConsiderCarbonAsDonor | When to consider Carbon atoms as donors in a tautomeric fragment. The Carbon atom needs to be sp3 and have at least one Hydrogen that is implicit or explicit. Options include: Never : Never consider Carbon atoms as donors. BondedToTwoOrMoreTautomericAtoms : Carbon atom needs to be attached to at least two tautomeric atoms, either donor, acceptor, or sp2. BondedToOneOrMoreTautomericAtom : Carbon atom needs to be attached to at least one tautomeric atom, either donor, acceptor, or sp2. Valid Values: Never , BondedToTwoOrMoreTautomericAtoms, BondedToOneOrMoreTautomericAtom |
| Generate Tautomers MakeAllSp2AtomsAcceptors | Whether or not to consider sp2 hybridized atoms as acceptors when looking for tautomeric forms. Valid Values: True, False |

This is the default option. Tautomerize All Amides : tautomerize all amide groups Valid Values: Skip All Amides, Tautomerize Only Diamides , Tautomerize All Amides |
| Generate Tautomers Preserve Aromaticity | Reject any tautomers created that change the aromaticity are rejected. Valid Values: True, False |

MarkedStereoatoms : include stereo atoms with marked, known stereo (up or down). UnknownStereoatoms : include stereo atoms marked as unknown stereo, or not marked as stereo at all. MarkedStereobonds : include double bonds with known stereo (cis or trans) as determined from the coordinates. UnknownStereobonds : include double bonds marked as unknown stereo. Note : Enumerating Isomers will have the side effect of removing the coordinates from the molecule. These will be replaced if the Generate 3D parameter is set to True. Valid Values: True , False |

MarkedStereobonds : Include double bonds with known stereo (cis or trans) as determined from the coordinates. UnknownStereobonds : Include double bonds marked as unknown stereo. RepresentedStereoisomers : enumerates only the stereo isomers compatible with the molecular representation: The two enantiomers for molecules with one or more stereo atoms but without the 'chiral' flag. Only the configuration as drawn for molecules with one or more stereo atoms with the 'chiral' flag. The number of corresponding valid stereoisomers for molecules with BIOVIA Enhanced Stereochemical Representation. Valid Values: MarkedStereoatoms, UnknownStereoatoms , MarkedStereobonds, UnknownStereobonds , RepresentedStereoisomers |
| SkipStereoAtomsAtBridgeHeads | Specify whether or not to consider stereo atoms at bridge heads in the enumeration. Valid Values: True , False |
| AcceptInputStereoAsMarked | Toggles whether to accept atom and bond stereo as is marked in the input molecule. When set to false, the algorithm will check the marked stereocenters for connectivity and symmetry to see if the center is indeed stereo before enumeration proceeds. The property to be used in the place of Name to identify molecules.

Whether to change the ionization state of the ligands. Several methods are available, controlled by the Ionization Method parameter.

* If the ligands are not ionized in the correct state, as seen in a receptor-ligand complex, docking results may be unreliable.

Valid Values: True , False

The following methods are available for changing ionization state of the molecule:

* pH Based : Ionization states are predicted for the specified pH range using estimated pKa values for ligands.

* Rule Based : Ionization states are based on a set of rules for desired ionization states.

* Remove Charges : Neutralizes charges on acids and/or bases.

* More details can be found in the parameter help.

Valid Values: pH Based , Rule Based, Remove Charges

Enumerate the ionization states of the molecule for the specified pH range. Finds pKa sites and calculates the corresponding pKa values. The ionization states of the molecule are
enumerated based on the entered pH range. A new property, Ionization pH is calculated for each
ionization state. This property has the form "pH_state", where "pH" is the pH at which the molecule
was ionized, and "state" is a string of P and/or D values which indicate the protonation state of each pKa site, protonated or deprotonated.

Minimum value of the pH range used to calculate ionization states

Maximum value of the pH range used to calculate ionization states.

Ionization is based on a set of rules for how to protonate your ligands. Each rule is a SMIRKS transformation and is applied to the ligands in turn. You can select which of these rules you wish to apply. The set of Acid and Base rules are customizable using the advanced parameters.

Select from this list ionization templates. Molecules that match the groups are ionized.
These filters are defined in the Advanced SMIRKS Acid Templates parameter.
