Specify what charges should be neutralized:

* Protonate Acids : Adds hydrogen atoms to acid functional groups in the molecule, adjusting the charges accordingly. Acid functional groups are defined as O, S, N, or C atoms with a negative formal charge, not attached to any charged atom. An implicit H atom is added to the oxygen or sulfur atom and the charge is set to zero.

* Deprotonate Bases : Removes hydrogen atoms from basic functional groups in the molecule, adjusting the charges accordingly. Basic functional groups are defined as nitrogen atoms with a positive formal charge and one or more attached hydrogen atoms.

Valid Values: Protonate Acids , Deprotonate Bases

# Prepare Ligands

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_prepare_ligands.htm

## Prepare Ligands

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Prepare Ligands protocol helps to prepare ligands for input into
other protocols, performing tasks such as removing duplicates,
enumerating isomers and tautomers, and generating 3D conformations.

Many protocols (e.g., De Novo Library Generation), require
reasonable starting ligand structures to achieve good results. Protocols
may also benefit from enumerating valid ionization states, tautomers, and
isomers (e.g., the docking protocols). You can also save time by removing
duplicates or compounds with undesirable properties. This protocol accomplishes this by
performing the following steps, some of which can be
controlled by the protocol parameters:

* Generate canonical tautomers

* Keep only largest fragments

* Set standard formal charges on common functional groups

* Kekulize molecules

* Enumerate ionization states at a given pH range or set them according to pre-defined templates (optional)

* Enumerate tautomers (optional)

* Enumerate isomers (optional - by default, only unspecified bonds and atoms are enumerated)

* Remove duplicate structures (optional)

* Fix bad valencies (optional)

* Generate a reasonable 3D conformation using Catalyst (optional)

* Open the Small Molecules | Prepare or Filter Ligands tools and click Prepare Ligands... to open the Prepare Ligands dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . For details about the remaining parameters, see Prepare Ligands - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| prepared.sd | Contains the output ligands which have had the various selected preparation steps applied to them. |
| prepared_fail.sd | Contains ligands that were removed due to one of the filtering criteria. Each ligand in this file will have a property "FailureReason" that explains why the ligand was removed. Depending on the settings, ligands may be removed because they are duplicates, or because they failed to generate a 3D conformation. This file is created only if there are removed ligands. |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opens the prepared ligands in a Molecule Window. |

#### Further information

Run a parallel calculation Distributed grid computing Receptor-Ligand Interactions tools

## Split Ligands into Multiple Files - Parameters

### Splits large ligand SD files into multiple files

Creates several smaller ligand files from an input SD file. The number of files created, or the number of ligands per file can be controlled.

Optionally, ligands can be grouped to ensure similar poses are kept in the same file.

The output files are numbered consecutively (e.g., ligands_1.sd, ligands_2.sd)

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Maximum | The maximum number of data records to read (all if value is empty). |
| Split Into Files With Equal Numbers | If set to True, each file will contain equal number of ligands. The number of files to create can be specified in Number of SD Files . If set to False, Number of Ligands in Each Output SD File are saved to each file. Note : if Keep Poses Together is enabled, the number of ligands may be greater than the specified value to ensure similar poses are kept together. Valid Values: True , False |
| Number of SD Files | The molecules will be split into this number of files. |
| Number of Ligands in Each Output SD File | Number of ligands in each output SD file. Note : if Keep Poses Together is enabled, the number of ligands in each file may be larger. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Compress | Compress output files using gzip format. Valid Values: True, False |
| Keep Poses Together | If set to True, ligand poses ( i.e. , consecutive conformations) are kept together in the output SD file. Valid Values: True, False |

# Split Ligands into Multiple Files

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/general_purpose_split_ligands_into_multiple_files.htm

## Split Ligands into Multiple Files

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output and input files

The Split Ligands into Multiple Files protocol creates multiple smaller files from a large
input SD file. Optionally, docked poses can be kept together in the same file during splitting.
This can be useful, for example, when a large file with docked poses should be split into several smaller files for post-processing.

Output files are created sequentially by adding an index to the input ligand file name (e.g., ligands_1.sd, ligands_2.sd, etc.)

This protocol requires an input SD file or a set of ligand structures.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Small Molecules | Split Ligands into Multiple Files .

* In the Parameters Explorer, specify the ligand file to be used by the protocol. For details, see Split Ligands into Multiple Files - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

### Output files

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used and a table containing information about the generated files, such as name, number of ligands, and file size. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>_#.sd | Indexed output files with the ligands. The file can be compressed containing an additional .gz post fix. |

# Align Small Molecules tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_asmt.htm

## Align Small Molecules tools

The Align Small Molecules tools allow you to align ligands using various methods.

### Alignment

Molecular Overlay: Launches the Molecular Overlay dialog . The following actions are possible:

* Align by the field fit method. It is possible to set the desired percentages for steric and electrostatic contributions.

* Perform a consensus alignment. The molecules are aligned according to the best average overlay.

* Align to a target ligand.

* Add rotatable bonds for flexible alignments.

### Manual Alignment

These tools allow you to manually align the ligands.

Add Tether: Associates selected atoms to use when superimposing ligands. For details, see Add Tether .

Show/Hide Tether Lines: Shows or hides lines that connect the atoms.

Superimpose By Tether: Performs an RMS (Root Mean Squares) best fit on the objects connected by tethers. For details, see Superimpose By Tether .

### Substructure Alignment

Align to Selected Substructure: Opens the Align to Selected Substructure protocol dialog. This protocol aligns ligands that contain the specified substructure to the common substructure.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | Small Molecules \| Align Small Molecules |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| Small Molecules \| Align Small Molecules |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Align Small Molecules |

# Calculate Molecular Properties tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_cmpt.htm

## Calculate Molecular Properties tools

The Calculate Molecular Properties tools allow you to calculate various molecular properties.

### ADMET

ADMET Descriptors: Calculates the following Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) properties:

* Aqueous Solubility

* Blood Brain Barrier Penetration

* CYP2D6 Binding

* Hepatotoxicity

* Intestinal Absorption

* Plasma Protein Binding

Calculating ADMET descriptors early in the development of a drug is important to help avoid having to eliminate compounds with unfavorable ADMET characteristics later in the development process, preferably before synthesis.

# Create QSAR Model tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_cqmt.htm

## Create QSAR Model tools

The create QSAR Model tool panel provides a workflow for preparing the training and the test set, 
preparing the dependent property, and building various QSAR models, which can be shared with colleagues.

### Prepare Data

Prepare Ligands for QSAR: Opens the Prepare Ligands for QSAR protocol dialog. This protocol prepares ligands for building 
QSAR models. The following steps are performed:

* Standardize charges for common groups

* Retain only the largest fragment

* Add Hydrogens

* Represent in Kekulé form

* Enumerate ionization states (optional)

* Generate canonical tautomer (optional)

* Remove Duplicates

Prepare Dependent Property: Opens the Prepare Dependent Property protocol dialog. This protocol converts a raw property to a dependent or response property by scaling or binning the data.

Different QSAR protocols may require different types of data as the dependent property. 
For example, the Create Recursive Partitioning Model protocol requires categorical data. 
In some cases, the data may be better modeled when the response property is scaled to a
logarithm level. This utility protocol helps to achieve just that.

Generate Training and Test Data: Opens the Generate Training and Test Data protocol dialog. This protocol provides methods for splitting a data set into a training set and a test set. The training set can be used to build a QSAR model and the test set can be used to assess the performance of the model.

A report on the splitting analysis is given to evaluate the distribution of the two datasets in various chemical space using the first two principal components.

### Build Models

Create Bayesian Model: Opens the Create Bayesian Model protocol dialog. This protocol uses Bayesian categorization to build a model that distinguishes between good and bad ligands. Good ligands are indicated by a value of "1" for the property set by Property for Active . Bayesian models are created quickly and they have a built-in mechanism to guard against overfitting. There is also an option to use k-fold cross validation to assess the performance of the model.

Create Recursive Partitioning Model: Opens the Create Recursive Partitioning Model protocol dialog. This protocol uses the recursive partitioning method to build a QSAR or QSPR model, which can be a single tree or forest model.

A single tree model is less predictive, but more interpretable. There are options to use patented techniques developed by BIOVIA , such as lookahead and PUMP-RP. A lookahead model considers multiple alternative splits at each tree node to avoid getting stuck with a split that is locally optimal, but globally sub-optimal when splits further down the tree are considered. A multi-Y tree model using PUMP-RP supports predictions for two or more dependent (Y) classification properties using the same tree. Such a model can be useful in determining common features that affect the different Y properties (e.g., for selectivity studies).

A forest model contains multiple trees, each built using recursive partitioning. Forest models tend to be more accurate at prediction, but less directly interpretable than single-tree models. The enhanced accuracy comes from a cancellation of random errors when predictions of multiple trees in the forest are averaged together. The decreased interpretability is due to the relative ease of visually understanding the structure of a single tree compared to the structures of tens or hundreds of trees.

Create Multiple Linear Regression Model: Opens the Create Multiple Linear Regression Model protocol dialog. This protocol uses multiple linear regression to build a QSAR or QSPR user model. K-fold cross validation is available to assess the performance of the model.

Create Partial Least Squares Model: Opens the Create Partial Least Squares Model protocol dialog. This protocol uses partial least-squares (PLS) to build a QSAR or QSPR model. K-fold cross validation is available to assess the performance of the model. When cross validation is used, the number of components (also known as latent variables) is set automatically to the number that provides the best cross-validated coefficient of determination (q 2 ).

Create Genetic Function Approximation Model: Opens the Create Genetic Function Approximation Model protocol dialog. This protocol uses Genetic Function Approximation (GFA) to build a QSAR and/or QSPR models. GFA is a model-selection procedure analogous in some ways to stepwise regression, but with the key difference being that the GFA returns multiple models rather than a single "best" model.

However, some of the caveats that apply to other model-selection techniques also apply to GFA. In particular, reported quality-of-fit measures such as R 2 and p-values from statistical tests tend to give an overly-optimistic assessment of model quality. The reason is that the GFA creates a great number of trial models before arriving at a set of "best" models. The large number of models considered increases the likelihood of encountering spurious correlations specific to the training data that make a model appear better than it really is. In light of these issues, the GFA is best regarded as a technique for generating hypotheses rather than a technique for testing hypotheses. Testing of the resulting models should be done against a data set other than the one used to create the models.

Create 3D QSAR Model: Opens the Create 3D QSAR Model protocol dialog. This protocol uses molecular field analysis (MFA) technique to build a user QSAR model to predict activity. Drug design involves finding small molecules that are complementary in shape (steric) and charge (electrostatic) to a bio-molecular target. Regression models built from whole molecular steric and electrostatic fields can be useful for predicting activity and for visualizing favorable and unfavorable interactions. A Partial Least-Squares (PLS) model is built using energy grids as descriptors. The energy grids are computed using two probe types designed to measure electrostatic and steric effects.

K-fold cross validation is available to assess the performance of the model. When cross validation is used, the number of components in the PLS model is automatically set to the number that gave the best performance in cross validation.

### Delete Models

User-generated QSAR models cannot be manually removed because they are registered in the server component database. The Delete User Models protocol allows you to safely remove these models from the server. For details, see Delete User Models .

## Design and Analyze Libraries tools

The Design and Analyze Libraries tools allow you to perform tasks associated with designing and analyzing a library, such as

### Design and Enumerate

Enumerate Library from Ligands: Opens the Enumerate Library from Ligands protocol dialog. This protocol enumerates a combinatorial library from a set of molecules using the following:

* Core molecule

* List of attachment points in the core

* Set of ligands for each attachment point

* An attachment point definition for each set of ligands (e.g., Fluorine atoms)

To enumerate from an existing RG file, specify it using the Input RG File advanced parameter. Setting this will bypass the core and RG setup.

Enumerate Library by Reaction: Opens the Enumerate Library by Reaction protocol dialog. This protocol builds a combinatorial ligand library by enumerating all the input reactants according to the reaction rule specified in a reaction file.

### Fragments

Generate Novel Ligands: Opens the Generate Novel Ligands protocol dialog. This protocol uses the published BREED method, [Pierce et al., 2004] , for swapping matched bonds in a set of overlapping ligands to generate new hybrid ligands, which have combined structural features inherited from parent compounds. Because the original ligands are all good binders to the common receptor, the new ligands are certain to fit into the binding site of the receptor.

Generate RECAP Fragments: Opens the Generate RECAP Fragments protocol dialog. This protocol uses RECAP to generate a fragment library from a set of ligands.

### Cluster

Cluster Ligands: Opens the Cluster Ligands protocol dialog. This protocol groups a set of molecules into subsets (clusters) of molecules with similar properties. The clustering is based on the root mean square (RMS) difference of descriptor properties, the Tanimoto distance for fingerprints, or a combination of the two if numeric descriptors and fingerprints are used. The clustering method is based on maximal dissimilarity partitioning. You can perform cluster selection by size or by number. A property is added to each ligand to indicate cluster membership.

Ligand clustering is used for identifying common patterns shown by active compounds in high throughput screening, choosing a small subset that represents a large data set, and can be used with other protocols, such as Calculate Principal Components (i.e., using the first several principal components in clustering).

### Analyze

Calculate Diversity Metrics : Opens the Calculate Diversity Metrics protocol dialog. This protocol calculates a series of quantitative measures of diversity. The available metrics include:

* Number Fingerprint Features: The number of unique fingerprints normalized by the number of ligands.

* Number Assemblies: The number of unique assemblies normalized by the number of ligands. The type of assembly used is determined by the Fragments to Generate parameter.

* Fingerprint Distances: The minimum, maximum, and average distances between all pairs of fingerprints.

* Property Distances: The average Euclidean distance between all pairs of properties.

* Fraction Cells: The fraction of cells occupied by the binned space. The bins are determined based on the selected properties and binning parameters.

A diverse compound library covers more chemical space and potentially contains many different chemical classes. This improves chances for identifying enhanced compound specificity and efficacy in drug discovery.

Calculate Principal Components: Opens the Calculate Principal Components protocol dialog. This protocol conducts a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the input ligands and builds a model to calculate the principal components for any ligands. The principal components are ordered so that the first few principal components account for most of the variance.

Compare Libraries : Opens the Compare Libraries protocol dialog. This protocol compares two ligand libraries using the following methods:

* Assemblies: Breaks the ligands of each library into fragments determined by the Fragments to Generate parameter, then computes a Tanimoto similarity coefficient between the libraries based on the fragments that are common and unique to each library.

* Bayesian Model: Builds a Bayesian model to learn the library A ligands and one to learn the library B ligands. It then scores all ligands using both models. A distance is computed as: Distance = ScoreAA + ScoreBB - ScoreAB - ScoreBA where ScoreAA is the average score of the library A molecules scored by the Bayesian model that learned the library A ligands, etc. The greater the distance, the more dissimilar the libraries.

Distance = ScoreAA + ScoreBB - ScoreAB - ScoreBA

where ScoreAA is the average score of the library A molecules scored by the Bayesian model that learned the library A ligands, etc. The greater the distance, the more dissimilar the libraries.

* Cell Based: Assigns ligands in library A and B to cells of binned space. The bins are determined by the specified molecular properties and binning parameters. A similarity metric is then computed based on cell occupancy: Similarity = OC AB /OC Total where OC AB is the number of cells occupied by ligands from both library A and library B and OC Total is the total occupied cells.

Similarity = OC AB /OC Total

where OC AB is the number of cells occupied by ligands from both library A and library B and OC Total is the total occupied cells.

* Global Fingerprint: Generates a global fingerprint for all ligands in library A and B and then computes a Tanimoto similarity coefficient between the two.

The Prepare or Filter Ligands tools allow you to prepare ligands for other techniques such as docking. The tools can be used to prepare ligands in the following way:

* Standardize charges for common groups

* Retain only the largest fragment

* Add Hydrogens

* Represent in Kekulé form

* Generate tautomers and isomers

* Remove duplicates

These tools can also be used to refine a set of ligands by retaining ligands that match a certain criterion. For example, you can use the tools to:

* Find the ligands that have the top value of a certain property (e.g., a docking score)

* Find the top ligand poses for each unique molecule of a certain property

* Apply filtering options, such as equals, does not equal, less than, greater than, begins with, does not begin with, contains, etc.

* Remove ligands that contain a single reactive group

* Remove ligands that have too many heteroatoms or too few carbons

### Prepare

Prepare Ligands: Opens the Prepare Ligands protocol dialog. This protocol prepares ligands for input into
other protocols. It performs tasks such as removing duplicates,
enumerating isomers and tautomers, and generating 3D conformations.

Many protocols (e.g., De Novo Library Generation), require
reasonable starting ligand structures to achieve good results. Protocols
may also benefit from enumerating valid ionization states, tautomers, and
isomers (e.g., the docking protocols). You can also save time by removing
duplicates or compounds with undesirable properties. This protocol accomplishes this by
performing the following steps, some of which can be
controlled by the protocol parameters:

* Generate canonical tautomers.

* Keep the largest fragments.

* Set standard formal charges on common functional groups.

* Kekulize molecules.

* Enumerate ionization states at a given pH range or set them according to pre-defined templates (optional).

* Enumerate tautomers (optional).

* Enumerate isomers (optional). By default, only unspecified bonds and atoms are enumerated.

* Remove duplicate structures (optional).

* Filter structures that violate Lipinski rules (optional).

* Generate a reasonable 3D conformation using Catalyst (optional).

For details, see Prepare Ligands .

### Filter

Filter by Property: Opens the Filter by Property protocol dialog. This protocol filters ligands or ligand
poses by a specified property and operator. For example, you can return all
ligands greater than a certain molecular weight or extract the top
scoring ligands based on a docking score. You can also use the Filter by Group parameter to find the top scoring poses for each 
unique molecule name. This protocol can be useful for extracting relevant 
data from very large sets without loading them into Discovery Studio .

Filter by SMARTS: Opens the Filter by SMARTS protocol dialog. This protocol filters ligands based on a set of substructure filters.
Each filter is applied to the ligands in turn. The ligand will pass a filter
if the number of mappings for that substructure is within the allowed range.
Any ligand that fails one or more filters is removed from the results.

Many filters have been taken from the literature and are accessible using the Input Filters parameter.
These filters can be used to remove ligands from the inputs that are not likely to be "drug-like" [Walters and Murcko, 2002] or "lead-like" [Hann et al, 1999] , etc.

## Select Subset Libraries tools

The Select Subset Libraries tools allow you to use different techniques to find a subset of ligands from a larger library. You can find diverse or similar molecules or find several subsets from a large library using a Pareto Optimization method.

### Find Diverse

Find Diverse Molecules: Opens the Find Diverse Molecules protocol dialog. This protocol extracts a subset of ligands with diverse properties, which represents the original library well. This is useful in drug discovery when you want to conduct an experiment on a smaller data set.

### Find Similar

Find Similar Molecules by Numeric Properties: Opens the Find Similar Molecules by Numeric Properties protocol dialog. This protocol finds molecules in a library that have numeric properties similar to the reference ligands. Similarity is determined by a distance metric. When there are two or more reference ligands, the shortest distance to a reference ligand is used. The available distance metrics are:

* Euclidean

* Manhattan

* One Minus Correlation

* One Minus Correlation Squared

Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints: Opens the Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints protocol dialog. This protocol finds molecules in a library that have fingerprints similar to the reference ligands. The following similarity measures are available:

* Tanimoto: SA/(SA+SB+SC) - The number of "and" bits normalized by the number of "or" bits.

* Dice: 2*SA/(2*SA+SB+SC) - The number of "and" bits normalized by the arithmetic mean of the number of on bits in the target and reference.

* Cosine: SA/((SA+SB)*(SA+SC))^0.5 - The number of "and" bits normalized by the geometric mean of the number of on bits in the target and reference.

* Target: SA/(SA+SC) - The number of shared bits between the reference and target normalized by bits in the reference.

where:

* SA is the number of AND bits. Bits present in both the target and the reference.

* SB is the number of bits in the target but not the reference.

* SC is the number of bits in the reference but not the target.

### Find Subsets by Pareto

Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method: Opens the Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method protocol dialog. This protocol optimizes a specified number of subsets from a large library using the Pareto method. The coordinates in the subset library are in 2D.

Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method: Opens the Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method protocol dialog. This protocol optimizes a specified number of subset libraries from a combinatorial library
using the Pareto optimization method.

#### Pareto method

The Pareto method is useful for optimizing more than one property. Unlike other optimizations that generate a single solution, a Pareto optimization generates multiple solutions that indicate the best possible tradeoffs among the properties being optimized.

The optimum subset of samples is determined by the specified Optimization Properties . Each Optimization Property is a single-sample property used to compute the subset property to be optimized. What to Optimize specifies how to compute the subset property value from each of the single-sample property values (e.g., by taking the Mean). Goal specifies whether you want to Maximize or Minimize the result of What to Optimize . The most optimal subsets are those for which it is not possible to improve on one property without degrading at least one other.

# Applications theory

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_th_applications-theory.htm

## Applications theory

Semi-empirical programs should be used for molecules that are too large for geometry optimization at the Hartree-Fock split-valence 
level of ab initio theory or with comparable basis sets with DFT.

Currently, this means using semi-empirical programs for molecules in the range of 50 to 400 atoms, but these numbers may change as 
hardware and software become more powerful. Molecules larger than this range should be treated by forcefield methods or mixed QM/MM 
calculations, and smaller ones by ab initio or density functional theory.

Ab initio and density functional programs can handle molecules up to about 100 atoms, but for most problems the computation time 
needed to optimize geometries is prohibitive. Because of this, semi-empirical programs are often used in industry and application 
oriented research. Examples of their use include:

* Rapid calculation of optimized geometries and molecular orbitals

* Transition state searching and optimization

* Calculation of accurate and reliable molecular electrostatic properties, potentials, and fields

* Calculation of spectroscopic properties including ESR, NMR, IR, and Raman frequencies, together with hyperpolarizabilities for 
nonlinear optical studies

* Investigation of solvent effects and solvatochromic shifts

* Simulation of an environment using a mixed quantum mechanical and classical mechanical model

# Basic VAMP theory and approximations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_th_basic-vamp.htm

## Basic VAMP theory and approximations

VAMP is a semi-empirical molecular orbital method to determine a molecular wave function 
( [Pople and Beveridge, 1970] and [Stewart, 1990] ). 
This wave function can then be used to derive molecular 
properties, such as energy and dipole moments.

The molecular wave function, Ψ , is built by a Slater-determinant consisting of molecular spin orbitals, Ψ i . 
These are described by the usual LCAO method, in which the molecular orbitals are obtained as a linear combination of the atomic orbitals, Φ μ :

Equation 1:

In ab initio theory, these atomic orbitals are usually described by Gaussian functions, allowing an easier and faster calculation 
of the two-electron integrals ( [Pople et al., 1986] and [Szabo and Ostlund, 1989] ).

Semi-empirical MO theory uses Slater-type atomic orbitals rather than Gaussian functions. Slater functions are more difficult than
Gaussians to handle exactly, but are better at representing the electron density far from the nucleus. Semi-empirical methods can use
Slater functions by evaluating the two-electron integrals through a multipole approximation [Dewar and Thiel, 1977] , rather than an exact 
calculation. The so-called basis set of atomic orbitals are defined in the Vhamil.par file.

Molecular orbitals can then be built up by an iterative procedure that optimizes the LCAO (linear combination of atomic orbital) 
coefficients, c μi . This variable self-consistent field (SCF) method is based on Hartree-Fock-Roothaan-Hall theory, and constitutes the 
main part of most MO programs. It is also a part in which many approximations are implemented because of the very time consuming iterative procedure.

Once the wave function is determined, the program uses it to evaluate the energy of the molecule, the atomic forces, and many other 
electronic properties. The energy and the atomic forces are used to optimize the geometry of the molecule to a stationary point (usually 
a minimum or transition state) at which the atomic forces are ideally all zero.

MINDO/3 is a modification of Pople's INDO method, whereas MNDO, MNDO/d, AM1, AM1* and PM3 are based on NDDO. AM1 and PM3, which are 
quantum mechanically identical but vary in their parameterizations, are extensions of MNDO in which the nuclear repulsion energy function 
has been modified to provide better results, especially for hydrogen bonded systems.

The molecular wave function calculated depends on a number of variables, which are user defined and are stated explicitly in the 
input file to the VAMP calculation.

Descriptors Quantum mechanical theory related to descriptors

Source type: HTML

## COSMO solvent effects

DMol 3 includes certain COSMO controls, which allow for the treatment of solvation effects.

The COnductor-like Screening MOdel (COSMO - [Klamt and Schüürmann, 1993] and [Delley, 2006] ) is a continuum solvation model 
(CSM - [Tomasi and Persico, 1994] ) in which the solute molecule forms a cavity within the dielectric continuum of permittivity, ε, that represents the solvent:

The charge distribution of the solute polarizes the dielectric medium. The response of the dielectric medium is described by the generation of 
screening (or polarization) charges on the cavity surface. In contrast to other implementations of CSMs, COSMO does not require solution of the rather 
complicated boundary conditions for a dielectric in order to obtain screening charges, but instead calculates the screening charges using a much simpler 
boundary condition for a conductor. These charges are then scaled by a factor:

to obtain a good approximation for the screening charges in a dielectric medium.

The deviations of this COSMO approximation from the exact solution are small. For strong dielectrics like water, they are less than 1%, while for 
nonpolar solvents with ε ~ 2, they may reach 10% of the total screening effects. However, for weak dielectrics, screening effects are small, 
and the absolute error therefore amounts to less than 1 kcal/mol.

Altogether, COSMO is a considerable simplification of the CSM approach without significant loss of accuracy. Because of this simplification, COSMO provides a more efficient implementation of the CSM into quantum chemical programs and for accurate calculation of gradients, which allows geometry 
optimization of the solute within the dielectric continuum.

The screening charges are determined from the boundary condition of vanishing potential on the surface of a conductor. If we define q as a vector 
of the screening charges on the surface of the cavity, and

for the total solute charges such as electron density, ρ, and nuclear charges, Z , then the vector of potentials, V tot , on the surface is:

where BQ is the potential arising from the solute charges, Q , and Aq is the potential arising from 
surface charges, q . B and A are Coulomb matrices. For a conductor, the relation V tot = 0 must hold, which defines the screening charges as:

Equation 1:

For further details of the COSMO theory, see Klamt and Schüürmann [Klamt and Schüürmann, 1993] . COSMO provides 
the electrostatic contribution to the free energy of solvation. In addition, there are non-electrostatic contributions to the total free energy of 
solvation that describe the dispersion interactions and cavity formation effects.

### DMol 3 /COSMO

The COSMO electrostatic energy is analogous in form to the DMol 3 electrostatic energy, with the Coulombic operator replaced by the

Equation 2:

where ρ ~ represents the auxiliary density, which is introduced to solve the Poisson equation for the electrostatic potential of the 
solute. This total energy is minimized, resulting in the Kohn-Sham equations for the molecular orbitals. The Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian now includes an 
electrostatic COSMO potential:

Equation 3:

This potential is present in every SCF cycle. This direct incorporation of the solvent effects within the SCF procedure is a major computational 
advantage of the COSMO scheme. Since the DMol 3 /COSMO orbitals are obtained using the variational scheme, we can derive accurate analytic 
gradients with respect to the coordinates of the solute atoms. The complete theory is presented by Klamt and Schüürmann [Klamt and Schüürmann, 1993] and Andzelm et al. [Andzelm et al., 1995] . The gradients include 
the forces between the solute charges, Q , and the screening charges, q .

To summarize, a DMol 3 /COSMO calculation begins with the construction of the cavity surface. The screening charges are then evaluated 
using Equation 1 and the initial solute charges, Q . This allows for calculation of the electrostatic COSMO potential. The process is 
repeated until DMol 3 SCF convergence is achieved. The final total energy includes the DMol 3 /COSMO electrostatic energy (Equation 2).

If geometry optimization is requested, DMol 3 /COSMO gradients are evaluated and the new geometry is calculated. The next optimization 
cycle begins with reconstruction of the cavity surface and the process continues until the DMol 3 optimization convergence criteria are met.

The DMol 3 /COSMO method has been tested extensively 
( [Klamt and Schüürmann, 1993] and [Andzelm et al., 1995] ). The results depend mainly on the choice of the van der Waals radii used to 
evaluate the cavity surface. The other parameters defining the cavity surface (see below) are less important. Of course, solvation energies depend on 
the choice of DMol 3 parameters, such as the type of DFT functional, the basis set, and integration grid. Results obtained so far [Andzelm et al., 1995] suggest that the DMol 3 /COSMO model can predict solvation energies for 
neutral solutes with an accuracy of about 2 kcal/mol.

Recently, the DMol 3 /COSMO method has been generalized to the periodic boundary cases [Delley, 2006] . In this case, all the screening charge is localized at the cavity surface. This is achieved with the use of Lagrange constraints with a new 
integration scheme based on a larger number of integration mesh points [Delley, 1996] .

### Determination of the cavity surface (or solvent-accessible surface)

The surface is obtained as a superimposition of spheres centered at the atoms, discarding all parts lying on the interior part of the surface [Klamt and Schüürmann, 1993] . The spheres are represented by a discrete set of points, the 
so-called basic points. Eliminating the parts of the spheres that lie within the interior part of the molecule thus amounts to eliminating the basic 
grid points that lie in the interior of the molecule.

The radii of the spheres are determined as the sum of the van der Waals radii of the atoms of the molecule and of the probe radius. The surviving 
basic grid points are then scaled to lie on the surface generated by the spheres of van der Waals radii alone. The basic points are then collected into 
segments, which are also represented as discrete points on the surface. The screening charges are located at the segment points.

### Determination of non-electrostatic contributions to the free energy of solvation

The free energy of solvation is calculated as:

Equation 4:

where E o is the total DMol 3 energy of the molecule in vacuo, E is the total DMol 3 /COSMO energy of the molecule in 
solvent, and ΔG nonelectrostatic is the non-electrostatic contribution due to dispersion and cavity formation effects. The 
non-electrostatic contributions to the free energy of solvation are estimated from a linear interpolation of the free energies of hydration for 
linear-chain alkanes as a function of surface area:

Equation 5:

In the present implementation, the VWN potential, DNP basis set, and fine integration grid of DMol 3 were used to calculate energies of 
methane and octane (C 2h ). The experimental values of the free energy of solvation are 1.9 and 2.9 kcal/mol for methane and octane, 
respectively [Ben-Naim and Marcus, 1984] . The calculated surface areas, using the default COSMO parameters, 
were 38.4 and 104.1 Å 2 for methane and octane, respectively. The following values of A and B were used:

* A = 1.67274 (kcal/mol)

* B = 0.02052 (kcal/mol Å 2 )

The best A and B values to use depend on the choice of DMol 3 and COSMO input parameters. Our tests [Andzelm et al., 1995] indicate that selection of other parameters, such as the nonlocal BP potential and 
the van der Waals radii of atoms, can influence ΔG nonelectrostatic by as much as 0.5 kcal/mol.

# Electrostatics theory

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_th_electrostatics-theory.htm

## Electrostatics theory

VAMP allows the use of the natural atomic orbital/point charge (NAO-PC) model 
( [Rauhut and Clark, 1994] and [Rauhut and Clark, 1994] ) 
in conjunction with the Hamiltonian methods MNDO, AM1, and PM3. In the NAO-PC model, the electron cloud of the molecule is represented as an array 
of negative point charges (eight per non-hydrogen atom), which allows the fast and accurate calculation of a variety of one-electron molecular 
properties. Molecular electrostatic potentials, multipole moments, electrostatic fields, etc., can then be calculated from the model using classical 
electrostatics.

By default, VAMP creates a .vmp file that contains the NAO-PC model with the negative point charges defined as atoms of atomic number 
zero. Use the keyword COULSON to create an atom-centered point charge model using Coulson charges (the atomic charges normally given by the 
population analysis). User the keyword MULLIKEN create an atom-centered point charge model using Mulliken charges.

The model is analyzed to give molecular monopole, dipole, quadrupole, and octupole moments [Beck et al., 1994] and atomic monopole, dipole, and quadrupole moments for the non-hydrogen atoms. This simple type of distributed multipole analysis provides 
a more exact picture of the molecular electronics than the normal population analysis. The molecular quadrupoles calculated with the MNDO, AM1, or 
PM3 Hamiltonians agree with experimentally determined values at least as well as those calculated using ab initio theory at the MP2/6-31G* level [Beck et al., 1994] .

The NAO-PC atomic multipoles are also used as input descriptors for a neural net that estimates the 13 C chemical shift of carbon atoms 
in the calculated molecules [Clark et al., 1995] . The standard deviation of the calculated chemical 
shift from experimental values is about 7 ppm, but could be as high as 20 ppm. A warning is issued if the descriptors for a given carbon are out of 
the neural net's range. This usually suggests that the net was not trained on molecules containing carbons of this type.

The NAO-PC model is not currently available for the AM1*, MNDOD/d, and MNDO/C NDDO Hamiltonians 
or any of the ZINDO Hamiltonians.

# Energy gradients

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_th_energy-gradients.htm

## Energy gradients

### Predicting chemical structure

The ability to evaluate the derivative of the total energy with respect to geometric changes is critical for the study of chemical systems. 
Without the first derivatives, a laborious point-by-point procedure is required, which is taxing to both computer and human resources. The 
availability of analytic energy derivatives for Hartree-Fock [Pulay, 1969] , CI [Brooks et al., 1980] , and MBPT [Pople et al., 1979] theories (to name just a few) has made these remarkably successful methods for predicting chemical structures.

The energy gradient formulas for the Hartree-Fock-Slater method were first derived by Satako [Satako, 1981] and later implemented practically using Slater basis sets [Versluis and Ziegler, 1988] . Others have used Gaussian basis sets to compute derivatives of 
the DFT energy [Andzelm et al., 1989] .

### First derivative of total energy with respect to change in nuclear position

The derivative of the total energy in Equation 5 with respect to a nuclear perturbation in direction a (x, y, or z) of atom 
α may be written as:

Equation 6:

where the derivative density is defined as:

Equation 7:

with:

Equation 8:

### Derivative of the basis function

The derivative of the basis function χ m with respect to the perturbation a can be computed analytically 
because of the representation of the numerical basis sets. The angular portion of χ m is a spherical harmonic function, 
which is analytic and easily differentiated. The radial portion is represented by several cubic splines, each of which is also differentiable.

### Derivation of other terms

The derivatives of the eigenvalues can be obtained from Equation 3. Multiplying by θ i and integrating 
gives an expression for Ρ i :

Equation 9:

Differentiating and rearranging yields:

Equation 10:

The terms in Equations 10 and 14 involving Z α represent the Hellmann-Feynman force 
( [Hellmann, 1937] and [Feynman, 1939] ), which gives the 
derivative in the absence of any orbital relaxation.

Substituting Equation 10 into Equation 6 yields:

Equation 11:

Where E a t is the Hellmann-Feynman term. Now [Andzelm et al., 1989] :

Equation 12:

and recalling the definition in Equation 4, we can also write:

Equation 13:

### The final equation for the derivative of the energy

Therefore, the terms in Equation 11 involving ε xc cancel. In addition, if Equation 2 is used to construct the charge 
density, then the last two terms in Equation 11 also cancel, leaving:

Equation 14:

which is formally the same as the equation derived by other researchers ( [Andzelm et al., 1989] and [Versluis and Ziegler, 1988] ). In practice, however, it is necessary to compute both ρ V a /2 and ρ a V/2 , because the model density from Equation 4 is 
not exactly equal to the numerical charge density.

### Computational costs

The time required to evaluate all 3 N first derivatives for an N -atom system is typically the same as the time required for 
3-4 SCF iterations. For example, if convergence is achieved in 10-12 iterations, then 25-30% additional time is required to evaluate the 
derivatives. Others have obtained similar results [Versluis and Ziegler, 1988] .

### Potential problems

Because of numerical precision, two potential problems have been observed in evaluating gradients. First, the energy minimum does not 
correspond exactly to the point with zero derivative [Versluis and Ziegler, 1988] . 
The gradients are typically about 10 -4 at the energy minimum. A second important point is that the sum of the gradients is not 
always zero, as it must be for translational invariance. The sum can be as high as 10 -3 if the calculation is very poor. 
Increasing the quality of the integration mesh and the number of multipolar functions in the model density can reduce this to about 
3.0 × 10 -5 . This magnitude of error seems to be permissible for geometry optimizations: the error introduced in the geometry is 
typically on the order of 0.001 Å. Only for very flat potential energy surfaces should this be a problem.

### Minimization algorithms; molecular symmetry

Currently, the geometry is optimized using both Cartesian and internal coordinates. When the geometry is optimized under conditions of 
symmetry, only forces that maintain molecular symmetry are evaluated, resulting in considerable time savings. Even in the absence of symmetry, 
certain forces can be omitted from the calculation, resulting in faster calculations. For example, for a substrate adsorbed on a metal cluster, 
it is possible to compute gradients for the substrate only and perform no optimization on the metal.

# Density functional theory in DMol3

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

## Density functional theory in DMol3

Density functional theory begins with a theorem by Hohenberg and Kohn [Hohenberg and Kohn, 1964] , later
generalized by Levy [Levy, 1979] , which states that all ground-state properties are functionals of the 
electron density ρ . Specifically, the total energy E t may be written as:

Equation 1:

where T [ ρ ] is the kinetic energy of a system of noninteracting particles of density ρ , U [ ρ ]
is the classical electrostatic energy due to Coulombic interactions, and E xc [ ρ ] includes all
many-body contributions to the total energy, in particular the exchange and correlation energies. Equation 1 is
written to emphasize the explicit dependence of these quantities on [ ρ ] (in subsequent equations,
this dependence is not always indicated).

#### Common spin-density functionals

The simplest form of the exchange-correlation potential is the form derived by [Slater, 1951] , which
uses:

In this approximation, the correlation is not included. More sophisticated
approximations use the forms derived by Vosko et al. [Vosko et al., 1980] ,
denoted as VWN:

* BH [Von Barth and Hedin, 1972]

* JMW [Janak, Morruzi, and Williams, 1975]

* PW [Perdew and Wang, 1992]

#### Density gradient expansion

The next step to improve the local spin-density (LSD) model is to take into account
the inhomogeneity of the electron gas that naturally occurs in any molecular system.
This can be accomplished by a density gradient expansion, sometimes referred as the nonlocal
spin-density approximation (NLSD). It has been well documented that the gradient corrected
exchange-correlation energy E xc [ρ, d (ρ) /dr ]
is necessary for studying the thermochemistry of molecular processes
( [Ziegler, 1991] , [Labanowski and Andzelm, 1991] , and [Politzer and Seminario, 1995] ).

Commonly used NLSD functionals include the (PW) generalized gradient
approximation for the correlation functional [Perdew and Wang, 1992] , 
the (B) gradient corrected exchange functional [Becke, 1988] ,
and the gradient corrected correlation functional of (LYP)
is available [Lee et al., 1988] .

#### Total energy expression

The total energy can now be written as:

Equation 2:

To determine the actual energy, variations in E t must be optimized with respect to variations in ρ,
subject to orthonormality constraints [Kohn and Sham, 1965] :

Equation 3:

where ε ij are Lagrangian multipliers.

#### Kohn-Sham equations

This process leads to a set of coupled equations first proposed by 
Kohn and Sham [Kohn and Sham, 1965] :

Equation 4:

The term μ xc is the exchange-correlation potential, which results from differentiating E xc . For the local-spin density approximation, the potential μ xc is:

Equation 5:

Use of the eigenvalues of Equation 4 leads to a reformulation of the energy expression:

Equation 6:

#### Approximating the exchange-correlation energy

The final term in Equation 1, the exchange-correlation energy, requires some approximation for this method to be computationally 
tractable. A simple and surprisingly good approximation is the local density approximation, which is based on the known exchange-correlation 
energy of the uniform electron gas:

* [Ceperley and Alder, 1980]

* [Hedin and Lundqvist, 1971]

* [Lundqvist and March, 1983]

Analytical representations have been made by several researchers:

* [Perdew and Wang, 1992]

* [von Barth and Hedin, 1972]

* [Vosko et al., 1980]

The local density approximation assumes that the charge density varies slowly on an atomic scale (i.e., each region of a molecule 
actually looks like a uniform electron gas). The total exchange-correlation energy can be obtained by integrating the uniform electron gas result:

Equation 7:

where ε xc [ ρ ] is the exchange-correlation energy per particle in a uniform electron gas 
and ρ is the number of particles.

### Local functionals

For the exchange-correlation energy given by Equation 7, the specific local
functionals provided in DMol 3 are the VWN functional [Vosko et al., 1980] and PWC [Perdew and Wang, 1992] . The default is PWC.

### Nonlocal functionals

The so-called nonlocal or gradient-corrected functionals depend on dρ/dr as well as on ρ . 
This provides a considerable increase in the accuracy of predicted energies and structures, but with an additional cost. 
The NLSD functionals available in DMol 3 include:

| Name | Description | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PW91 | Perdew-Wang generalized-gradient approximation | [Perdew and Wang, 1992] |
| BP | Becke exchange plus Perdew correlation | [Becke, 1988] and [Perdew and Wang, 1992] |
| PBE | Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof correlation | [Perdew et al., 1996] |
| RPBE | Revised PBE functional by Hammer et al. | [Hammer et al., 1999] |
| HCTH | Hamprecht, Cohen, Tozer, and Handy functional | [Boese and Handy, 2001] |
| BLYP | Becke exchange plus Lee-Yang-Parr correlation | [Becke, 1988] and [Lee et al., 1988] |
| BOP | Becke One Parameter functional | [Tsuneda et al., 1999] |
| VWN-BP | BP functional with the local correlation replaced by the VWN functional. | [Vosko et al., 1980] , [Becke, 1988] , and [Perdew and Wang, 1992] |

These functionals can be specified in the DMol3 State section in the Parameters Explorer for the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol.

# Molecular properties

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/gp_th_molecular-properties.htm

## Molecular properties

The following categories of descriptors or molecular properties can be calculated by Discovery Studio :

* Other

* AlogP

* Molecular Formats

* Element Counts

* Molecular Property Counts

* Surface Area and Volume

* Topological Descriptors

* Fingerprints

* Estate Keys

* Dipole

* Jurs Descriptors

* Principal Moments of Inertia

* Shadow Indices

* Propgen Properties

This category includes all properties that can be calculated using user-built models. 
In addition, RandomNumber can give you a random number for
each molecule.

For some models (for example GFA and PCA 
models properties), you will find multiple entries added here
after the model is created because they can calculate multiple properties.

Discovery Studio uses the atom-based method published by Ghose and
Crippen [Ghose and Crippen, 1986] to calculate the octanol-water partition coefficient (LogP), and the molar
refractivity (MR). LogP provides a measure of the hydrophobicity of the molecule,
while MR contains information about molecular volume and polarizability.
The following properties are grouped in the AlogP category:

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| ALogP | Log of the octanol-water partition coefficient using Ghose and Crippen's method. |
| ALogP_MR | The Ghose and Crippen estimate of molar refractivity. |
| ALogP_Count | An array of 120 numbers that correspond to the 120 Ghose and Crippen atom types. The content of each array element is the number of times that particular atom type was seen in the molecule. |
| ALogP_AtomClass | Integer with the Ghose and Crippen atom type assigned to the atom, a number from 1 to 120. |
| ALogP_AtomClassName | String describing the Ghose and Crippen atom type assigned to the atom (example:"C in CH2R2"). |
| ALogP_AtomScore | Atomic contribution to the total value of ALogP. |
| ALogP_AtomMRScore | Atomic contribution to the total value of AlogP_MR. |

The following molecular formats can be obtained in this category:

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| SMILES | A terse textual representation of molecular data. |
| Canonical_SMILES | A form of SMILES that is independent of how the molecule is drawn and so can be used to compare whether two molecules are identical. |
| InChI | The IUPAC unique identifier. It is capable of uniquely representing a chemical substance. It is derived from a structural representation of that substance in a way designed to be independent of the way that the structure is drawn. |
| InChI_AuxInfo | Auxiliary information string, much more verbose than InChI in that it contains non-canonical information such as atom coordinates and explicit bond orders. |

The element counts properties are in the format of xx_Count, 
where the "xx" is the one- or two-character element type string.

You can query a 
number of nonstandard element symbols, such as "Z", "R", "X", "Q", "A", "AA", "NN" and 
"*". Depending on their source, they may represent unknown atom 
types, abstract atom types (for example, Q means non-hydrogen non-carbon atoms in MDL 
queries), or other features. For common data sources, these are not present.

This category contains the following properties:

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Energy | Gives the energy of the molecule's current 3D conformation evaluated using a variant of the published clean forcefield [Hahn, 1995] . It requires the molecules have 3D coordinates. |
| Minimized_Energy | Gives the energy after a fast minimization procedure using clean force field. |
| Strain_Energy | Gives the point strain energy. Strain_Energy is the difference between Energy and Minimized_Energy. |
| Molecular_Formula | The molecular formula is formatted according to the following rules (Hill System Order): Carbon first, Hydrogen second, all remaining elements, including Deuterium and Tritium, in alphabetical order. If no Carbon is present, all elements are listed in alphabetical order. |
| FormalCharge | The formal charge of the molecule. |
| CoordDimension | The dimension of the coordinates. Possible values are 0 (all coordinates are zero), 2 (2D structure, only X and Y coordinates are defined), and 3 (3D structure, X, Y and Z coordinates are defined). |
| IsChiral | Flag to indicate whether the molecule exists only in the represented absolute stereo configuration (value equals 1) or as a pair of enantiomers (value equals 0). This flag mirrors the Chiral flag in the MDL CTAB format. |
| BondDistance_Table | Calculates the number of bonds in the shortest path between each pairs of atoms in the molecule. The results are output as an array of strings representing the atom-atom distance matrix. |
| AverageBondLength | Calculates the average bond length for the molecule based on the atomic coordinates. |
| Molecular_Weight | The sum of the atomic masses. The isotope average is used for each atomic mass. |
| Molecular_Mass | The sum of the atomic masses. The most common isotope is used for each atomic mass. |
| Molecular_Solubility | Molecular solubility expressed as logS, where S is the solubility in mol/L. The method used to estimate the solubility is the published multiple linear regression model by Tetko et al. [Tetko et al., 2001] . |
| PhiAngle | The phi angle in a peptide. |
| PsiAngle | The psi angle in a peptide. |
| OmegaAngle | The omega angle in a peptide. |
| PhiAngle_Atoms | The atoms defining the phi angles in a peptide. |
| PsiAngle_Atoms | The atoms defining the psi angles in a peptide. |
| OmegaAngle_Atoms | The atoms defining the omega angles in a peptide. |
| VSA_AtomicAreas | Calculate the atomic surface area for each atom in the molecule. |
| VSA_AlogP | Calculate AlogP for each molecule and partition the atomic surface areas according to the specified AlogP ranges in -0.60, -0.33, -0.30, -0.08, 0.0, 0.20, 0.30, 0.65, 0.70 . |
| VSA_MR | Calculate Molar Refractivity for each molecule and partition the atomic surface areas according to the specified MR ranges 0.83, 0.85, 0.90, 1.00, 1.50, 3.50, 4.10 . The molar refractivity is calculated using the AlogP method. |
| VSA_PartialCharge | Calculate Gasteiger partial charges for each molecule and partition the atomic surface areas according to the specified partial charges ranges -0.30, -0.25, -0.20, -0.15, -0.10, -0.05, 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30 . |
| Gasteiger_Charges | The Gasteiger atomic partial charges. |
| logD | The octanol-water partition coefficient calculated taking into account the ionization states of the molecule. The default pH is 7.4 . This property is available only if you have installed the Advanced Chemistry component collection. |
| pKa | The pKa of all ionizable sites. This property is available only if you have installed the Advanced Chemistry component collection. |
| pKa_Atom | The atoms corresponding to the pKa calculation. This property is available only if you have installed the Advanced Chemistry component collection. |
| Apol | The polarizability descriptor, i.e., the sum of the atomic polarizabilities. |
| RadOfGyration | Radius of gyration, defined as the mass weighted root-mean-square average distance of all atoms in the molecular system from their center of mass. |
| SAscore | The Synthetic Accessibility Score is calculated based on [Ertl and Schuffenhauer, 2009] . It is calculated as the weighted contribution of the fragment score minus the complexity score: Note that the SAscore is normalized to [-1, +1] with higher values indicating easier to synthesize. |
| SAscore_Complexity | Complexity contribution to SAscore. The complexity of the molecule is estimated based on the molecule size (number of atoms), number of fused ring systems, number of macrocycles (rings of size 9 or larger), and number of stereo centers. For most molecules the score is normalized between 0 and 1, although it is possible for very complex or large molecules to have values greater than 1. |
| SAscore_Fragments | Fragment contribution to SAscore. The fragment score is calculated by analyzing the ECFP_4 fragments generated for the molecule in terms of the frequency of appearance in datasets of known synthesized molecules. The score is normalized between 0 and 1. |
| QESD | Quantitative Estimate of Drug-Likeness (QED) is calculated as described in [Bickerton et al., 2012] . The default weight factors for QED_MW, QED_ALOGP, QED_HBA, QED_HBD, QED_PSA, QED_ROTB, QED_AROM and QED_ALERTS are 0.66, 0.46, 0.05, 0.61, 0.06, 0.65, 0.48, and 0.95, respectively. |
| QED_Unweighted | Unweighted estimate of drug-likeness (or desirability) score. |
| QED_MW | Molecular weight contribution to the QED score. |
| QED_ALOGP | AlogP contribution to the QED score. |
| QED_HBA | Hydrogen bond acceptor contribution to the QED score. |
| QED_HBD | Hydrogen bond donor contribution to the QED score. |
| QED_PSA | Polar surface area contribution to the QED score. |
| QED_ROTB | Contribution to the QED score from the number of rotatable bonds. |
| QED_AROM | Contribution to the QED score from the number of aromatic rings. |
| QED_ALERTS | Contribution to the QED score from the number of undesirable substructures found in the molecule, which is calculated based on a list of 113 SMARTS queries. |

Radius of gyration, defined as the mass weighted root-mean-square average distance of all atoms in the molecular system from their center of mass.

The Synthetic Accessibility Score is calculated based on [Ertl and Schuffenhauer, 2009] . 
It is calculated as the weighted contribution of the fragment score minus the complexity score:

Note that the SAscore is normalized to [-1, +1] with higher values indicating easier to synthesize.

| Num_Macro_Residues | Residue records defined for macromolecules in .pdb files. |
| Num_TerminalRotomers | Terminal groups such as -CF3, -CCl3, -COO, and -NOO. A terminal rotomer is defined as either a non-terminal sp 3 atom connected to three-terminal atoms of the same type, or a non-terminal sp 2 atom connected to two-terminal atoms of the same type. Notice that groups such as -CH3 and -NH2 are not counted as terminal rotomers because the bond to the heavy atom is not considered terminal (the heavy atom is attached to only hydrogens). This property can be used to adjust the Num_RotatableBonds count, which includes bonds to terminal rotomers. For example, the Num_RotatableBonds count calculated for C6H5-CF3 is 1, and the Num_TerminalRotomers count is also 1. A modified number of rotatable bonds that excludes terminal rotomers can be calculated as Num_RotatableBonds - Num_TerminalRotomers. |
| Num_SpiroAtoms | A spiro atom is a linkage between two rings consisting of a single atom common to both. A free spiro atom is a linkage that constitutes the only union direct or indirect between the two rings. We count only free spiro atoms. |
| Num_BridgeHeadAtoms | A bridgehead atom connects a bridge to a ring. |
| Num_MetalAtoms | Atoms classified as metallic. |
| Num_H_Acceptors | Hydrogen Bond Acceptors are defined as heteroatoms (Oxygen, Nitrogen, Sulfur, or Phosphorus) with one or more lone pairs, excluding atoms with positive formal charges, amide and pyrrole-type Nitrogens, and aromatic Oxygen and Sulfur atoms in heterocyclic rings. |
| Num_H_Donors | Hydrogen Bond Donors are defined as heteroatoms (Oxygen, Nitrogen, Sulfur, or Phosphorus) with one or more attached Hydrogen atoms. |
| Num_H_Acceptors_Lipinski | Num_H_Acceptors_Lipinski is the equivalent of (N_Count + O_Count). |
| Num_H_Donors_Lipinski | Num_H_Donors_Lipinski more closely matches the convention used in Lipinski's paper that Num_H_Donors does in that it will count each primary amine as two donors. |
| HBA_Count | The number of hydrogen bond accepting groups in the molecule. It is calculated using substructure queries to count the number of times the queries match structural features in the molecule. |
| HBD_Count | Number of hydrogen bond donating groups in the molecule. It is calculated using substructure queries to count the number of times the queries match structural features in the molecule. |
| NPlusO_Count | The number of nitrogen and oxygen atoms in the molecule. |
| Organic_Count | The total number of the following atoms: O, C, N, S, P, F, Cl, Br, and I. |

Terminal groups such as -CF3, -CCl3, -COO, and -NOO.
A terminal rotomer is defined as either a non-terminal sp 3 atom connected to three-terminal atoms of the same type, or a non-terminal sp 2 atom connected to two-terminal atoms of the same type.

Notice that groups such as -CH3 and -NH2 are not counted as terminal rotomers because the bond to the heavy atom is not considered terminal (the heavy atom is attached to only hydrogens).

This property can be used to adjust the Num_RotatableBonds count, which includes bonds to terminal rotomers. For example, the Num_RotatableBonds count calculated for C6H5-CF3 is 1, and the Num_TerminalRotomers count is also 1. A modified number of rotatable bonds that excludes terminal rotomers can be calculated as Num_RotatableBonds - Num_TerminalRotomers.

Note: HBA_Count and HBD_Count are calculated differently for Num_H_Acceptors and Num_H_Donors. They are calculated
using substructure queries to count the number of times the queries match structural features in the molecule.
The substructure queries used to calculate these properties are present in the <pps_install> \apps\scitegic\chemistrydata\dataroot\data\Queries folder:

* Acceptors : HBA-Nitrogen.mol, HBA-Carboxylate.mol, HBA_Ester.mol, HBA-Ether.mol, HBA-Carbonyl.mol, 
HBA-Phenol.mol

* Donors : HBD-PrimaryAlcohol.mol, HBD-PrimaryAmine.mol, HBD-SecondaryAlcohol.mol, 
HBD-SecondaryAmine.mol, HBD-TertiaryAmine.mol

You can change the way hydrogen bond donors and acceptors are counted by adding your own definitions. 
The only constraint is that the file names should start with the prefix HBA- or HBD-.

The following properties are available in this category:

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Molecular_3D_SASA | Calculates the total solvent accessible surface area for each molecule using a 3D method. 3D coordinates are required. |
| Molecular_3D_PolarSASA | Calculates the polar solvent accessible surface area for each molecule using a 3D method. Atoms considered polar are N, O, P, S, hydrogens attached to them, and any atom with a formal charge. 3D coordinates are required. |
| Molecular_3D_SAVol | Calculates the solvent accessible volume for each molecule using a 3D method. 3D coordinates are required. |
| Molecular_SurfaceArea | Calculates the total surface area for each molecule using a 2D approximation. |
| Molecular_PolarSurfaceArea | Calculates the polar surface area for each molecule using a 2D approximation. |
| Molecular_FractionalPolarSurfaceArea | The ratio of the polar surface area divided by the total surface area. |
| Molecular_Volume | Calculates the 3D volume for each molecule using the current 3D coordinates. It will fail if there are no 3D coordinates for the molecule. |
| Molecular_SASA | Calculates the total solvent accessible surface area for each molecule using a 2D approximation. |
| Molecular_PolarSASA | Calculates the polar solvent accessible surface area for each molecule using a 2D approximation. The polar solvent accessible surface area is defined as the sum of the solvent accessible surface area of all the selected polar elements, which can include N, O, P, and S. |
| Molecular_FractionalPolarSASA | The ratio of the polar solvent accessible surface area divided by the total solvent accessible surface area. |
| Molecular_SAVol | Calculates the solvent accessible volume for each molecule using a 2D approximation. |

Solvent accessible surface area and solvent accessible volume are
calculated assuming a solvent probe radius of 1.4 angstroms.
The Molecular_SurfaceArea and Molecular_PolarSurfaceArea descriptors
are calculated using a method based on the published method in
Ertl et al. [Ertl et al., 2000] .
The solvent-accessible surface area descriptors measure the
surface area exposed to a solvent probe. This is based on a
2D approximation which uses models parameterized to reproduce
the results obtained with a full 3D calculation using a dot-based
procedure similar to the method originally described
by Shrake and Rupley [Shrake and Rupley, 1973] .

Topological descriptors are a special class of descriptors that do not 
rely on a three-dimensional model. All calculations are derived from the
two-dimensional topology of the molecule. In Discovery Studio there are 
several topological descriptors that fall into the following classes:

* Balaban Indices

* Wiener Index

* Zagreb Index

* Connectivity Indices

* Graph-Theoretical InfoContent descriptors

* Kappa Shape Indices

* Subgraph Counts

Before describing how these descriptors are calculated, it is useful 
to define a few terms that are commonly used to calculate many of the descriptors:

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Path | An alternating sequence of vertices v and edges e beginning and ending with vertices in which each edge is adjacent to the two vertices immediately preceding and following it. If there is a path in the following form: v 0 , e 0 , v 1 , e 1 , ..., v n-1 , e n-1 , v n , we say the vertices v 0 and v n are connected by this path. |
| Path length | The number of edges in the path. |
| Minimal path | A path of minimal length among all paths connecting a given vertex pair. |
| Cycle | A path v 0 , e 0 , ..., v n with v 0 = v n . |
| Connected graph | A graph is connected if, for any pair of vertices, there is a path connecting them. |
| Subgraph | A subset of the set of vertices and edges of the original graph which is itself a valid graph (namely, with each edge it contains the vertices adjacent to it). |
| Vertex valence | Number of edges adjacent to a vertex. Note that i th vertex valence equals the sum of matrix elements in the i th row (or column) of the A -matrix. It is denoted by d i |
| Adjacency matrix (A-matrix) | A symmetric N × N matrix { a ij }defined as: N = number of vertices, a ij = 1 if the vertices v i and v j are connected by an edge, a ij = 0 otherwise. |
| Edge adjacency matrix (E-matrix) | A symmetric M × M matrix { e kl } that is in a sense "complimentary" to the A -matrix and is defined as: M = number of edges, e kl = 1 if edges e k and e l share exactly one common vertex, e kl = 0 otherwise. |
| Distance matrix (D-matrix) | A symmetric N × N matrix a D ij ( N = number of vertices) where a D ij is the number of edges in a path of minimal length connecting v i to v j . |
| Edge distance matrix (ED-matrix) | A symmetric M × M matrix { e D kl },( M = number of edges) where e D kl is the number of vertices in a path of minimal length connecting e i to e j (not counting the terminal vertices of the path). |
