# Calculate Diversity Metrics

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_calculate_diversity_metrics.htm

## Calculate Diversity Metrics

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Calculate Diversity Metrics protocol computes diversity metrics for a set of ligands. The diversity
metric can be based on the number of fingerprint features, the number of assemblies, fingerprint distances,
property distances, or the fraction of populated cells.

The number of fingerprints is measured by the number of unique fingerprint features of the selected fingerprint property
normalized by the number of molecules.

The number of assemblies is the number of unique Ring, Chain, Bridge, or Murcko groups normalized by the number of
molecules. Murcko groups are contiguous ring systems plus chains that link two or more rings, as defined by Bemis and
Murcko [Bemis and Murcko, 1996] .

Fingerprint distances reports the minimum, maximum, and average fingerprint distance for all pairs of ligands in the set.

The property distance is computed as the average Euclidean property distance for all pairs of input ligands.

The fraction of cells is computed as occupied cells divided by the total number of possible cells using the selected
properties and bins.

* Open the Small Molecules | Design and Analyze Libraries tools and click Calculate Diversity Metrics to open the Calculate Diversity Metrics dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Diversity Metrics Select one or more diversity metrics to calculate. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Diversity Metrics - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Diversity Metrics | Select one or more diversity metrics to calculate. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Diversity Metrics - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. The summary section gives the result for each measure of diversity. The details section explains each term used in the diversity metrics. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

# Calculate Principal Components - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_calculate_principal_components-para.htm

## Calculate Principal Components - Parameters

### Conducts a principal component analysis on the molecular descriptors

Principal component analysis (PCA) is an orthogonal linear transformation technique that transforms the data into a new coordinate system such that the variance of the data is maximized on the first coordinate (called the first principal component), the rest of the variance maximized on the second coordinate, and so on. The first few principal components can normally explain most of the variance of the data; therefore PCA can be used to reduce the dimension of the data by keeping only the first few principal components.

To conduct a PCA calculation, set the minimum number of principal components to be produced and the minimum variance among the original descriptors that must be explained by the principal components. This analysis is saved as a learned model on the server. The model can be accessed using Calculate Molecular Properties in the QSAR collection.

Note :

* For more details about the generated PCA model, see the ModelDescription.html file in the Output directory.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |

Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for extending the model (Pipeline Pilot is required), but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component. Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model in order to establish the model's applicability domain. Track Fingerprint Features: Tracks features of the fingerprint specified by Model Domain Fingerprint , as well as any other fingerprint properties used to build your model. If you choose the modelname _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when a sample contains any fingerprint feature not seen in the training data, or lacks any feature appearing in all of the training samples. See Also: For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." ScaleToUnitVariance : Divides each column value by a factor to make the variance of the column equal to 1. MeanCenterAndScale : Performs both a mean centering and scaling to unit variance. Note : Generally, MeanCenterAndScale is the best choice. ## Calculate Principal Components

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Calculate Principal Components protocol conducts a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the selected molecular descriptors of the
input ligands.

* Open the Small Molecules | Design and Analyze Libraries tools and click Calculate Principle Components to open the Calculate Principal Components dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Model Name Name of the model to be created. For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Principal Components - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Model Name | Name of the model to be created. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Calculate Principal Components - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |

If more than three principal components are generated, the first three are used in a 3D Point Plot. This script is not present if only one principal component is generated. |
| <model name>.xml | This xml file contains the PCA model created in this protocol run. The name of this file is the value set in the Model Name parameter. The model can be later accessed through the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. This file can be imported into another server to allow model sharing. |
| ModelDescription.html | This html file contains more detailed information about the PCA model. |
| Input_Ligands_fail.sd | This .sd file contains the ligands with missing property values (thus not used in creating the PCA model). It is not present if there are no ligands with missing property values. |

# Calculate Property Profile Penalty - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_calculate_property_profile_penalty-para.htm

## Calculate Property Profile Penalty - Parameters

### Calculates the penalty score of a library according to a property profile

Given a property profile generated from a target library using Create Property Profile, a penalty score is calculated based on how the properties of a library deviate from the profile. You can use this to identify differences between libraries or determine which library is more (or less) similar to a target.

The penalty is based on binning a property into a histogram and comparing how the frequencies for each bin deviate from those in the target profile. For more details see Input Property Profile File .

### Parameters

| Name | Description | | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. | | | | | | | | |
| Molecular Property | The name of the property used in profile penalty calculation, for example, Molecular_Weight. | | | | | | | | |
| Input Property Profile File | The file that contains the property profile. Use "Create Property Profile" protocol to create a profile file from another library. The input property profile file must be a delimited text file containing the following columns: BinMin : The lower bound for each frequency bin. BinMax : The upper bound for each frequency bin. BinFreqMin : The minimum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction). BinFreqMax : The maximum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction). BinFreqWeight : The weight for this bin for deviations from the desired frequency range. Example: BinMin,BinMax,BinFreqMin,BinFreqMax,BinFreqWeight 0,100,0.1,0.1,1.0 100,200,0.2,0.2,1.0 200,300,0.4,0.4,1.0 300,400,0.2,0.2,1.0 400,1000,0.1,0.1,1.0 The penalty function is calculated as follows. If Freq i is the distribution value at bin i for an input library, the penalty function is defined as the average over all bins of: 100 * BinFreqWeight i * Delta i 2 Where Delta i is: Freq i Delta i Freq i < BinFreqMin i BinFreqMin i - Freq i BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i 0 BinFreqMax i < Freq i Freq i - BinFreqMax i | Freq i | Delta i | Freq i < BinFreqMin i | BinFreqMin i - Freq i | BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i | 0 | BinFreqMax i < Freq i | Freq i - BinFreqMax i |
| Freq i | Delta i | | | | | | | | |
| Freq i < BinFreqMin i | BinFreqMin i - Freq i | | | | | | | | |
| BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i | 0 | | | | | | | | |
| BinFreqMax i < Freq i | Freq i - BinFreqMax i | | | | | | | | |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. | | | | | | | | |
| Values Smaller Than Minimum | What to do with property values which are smaller than the lower boundary of the first bin. The options are to ignore these values or to include them in the first bin. Valid Values: Ignore , Add To First Bin | | | | | | | | |
| Values Greater Than Maximum | What to do with property values which are greater than the upper boundary of the last bin. The options are to ignore these values or to include them in the last bin. Valid Values: Ignore , Add To Last Bin | | | | | | | | |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

The name of the property used in profile penalty calculation, for example, Molecular_Weight.

The file that contains the property profile. Use "Create Property Profile" protocol to create a profile file from another library.

The input property profile file must be a delimited text file containing the following columns:

* BinMin : The lower bound for each frequency bin.

* BinMax : The upper bound for each frequency bin.

* BinFreqMin : The minimum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction).

* BinFreqMax : The maximum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction).

* BinFreqWeight : The weight for this bin for deviations from the desired frequency range.

Example: BinMin,BinMax,BinFreqMin,BinFreqMax,BinFreqWeight 0,100,0.1,0.1,1.0 100,200,0.2,0.2,1.0 200,300,0.4,0.4,1.0 300,400,0.2,0.2,1.0 400,1000,0.1,0.1,1.0

The penalty function is calculated as follows. If Freq i is the distribution value at bin i for an input library, the penalty function is defined as the average over all bins of:

100 * BinFreqWeight i * Delta i 2

Where Delta i is:

| Freq i | Delta i |
| --- | --- |
| Freq i < BinFreqMin i | BinFreqMin i - Freq i |
| BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i | 0 |
| BinFreqMax i < Freq i | Freq i - BinFreqMax i |

Contains less commonly used parameters.

What to do with property values which are smaller than the lower boundary of the first bin. The options are to ignore these values or to include them in the first bin.

Valid Values: Ignore , Add To First Bin

What to do with property values which are greater than the upper boundary of the last bin. The options are to ignore these values or to include them in the last bin.

Valid Values: Ignore , Add To Last Bin

# Calculate Property Range Penalty - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_calculate_property_range_penalty-para.htm

## Calculate Property Range Penalty - Parameters

### Calculates penalty score given a property range

Calculates a penalty score for each ligand according to a given property range. The penalty score is calculated based on how far the value lies outside a given range, and presented as property _RangePenalty, where property is the name of the property.

This can be useful in library selection when desirable compounds are known to have a property being in a certain range. For example, the drug-like compounds generally have their molecular weights between 100 and 500. The calculated penalty score can be used in other protocols, such as Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Molecular Property | The property that is used in property range penalty calculation. It must be either included in the input library ligands or calculable within Discovery Studio. |
| Minimum Value | Minimum value for the property without a penalty. |
| Maximum Value | Maximum value for the property without a penalty. |
| Standard Deviation | The standard deviation of the property range in penalty calculation. The raw penalty score is the square of the over-range property value divided by the standard deviation. |
| Penalty Cap Value | The penalty score to use if it is over this cap. This is done before applying the penalty weight. |
| Penalty Weight | A scaling factor to the final penalty score. |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

# Cluster Ligands - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_cluster_ligands-para.htm

## Cluster Ligands - Parameters

### Clusters ligands by a specified property or fingerprint

Clustering is the assignment of a set of molecules into subsets or clusters so that each molecule has similar properties in the same cluster. It is based on the root-mean-square (RMS) difference of descriptor properties or Tanimoto distance for fingerprints, or the combination of the two if both numeric descriptors and fingerprints are being used. The clustering is done by a relocation method based on maximal dissimilarity partitioning. Cluster selection can be performed by size or by number. A cluster membership property is added to each ligand.

Ligand clustering can be very useful in recognizing the common pattern shown by active compounds in a high throughput screening. Other usages include choosing a small subset to represent a large data set. It can be combined to use with other protocols, such as Calculate Principal Components, i.e., using the first several principal components in clustering.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Cluster Selection | Ligands can be clustered by: Fixed Number of Clusters : Number of cluster centers. Fixed Number of Molecules per Cluster : Average number of molecules per cluster. Valid Values: Fixed Number of Clusters , Fixed Number of Molecules per Cluster |
| Number of Clusters | Number of cluster centers. |
| Average Number of Molecules per Cluster | Average number of molecules per cluster. |
| Use Properties | The properties used for clustering: PredefinedSet : A property set selected from a list. UserSet : A user-defined property set. Valid Values: PredefinedSet , UserSet |
| Predefined Set | A predefined set of properties to use for clustering. Valid Values: FCFP_2, FCFP_4, FCFP_6 , ALogP, Molecular_Weight, Num_H_Donors, Num_H_Acceptors, Num_RotatableBonds, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6, MDLPublicKeys, Num_Atoms, Num_Rings, Num_AromaticRings, Num_Fragments, Molecular_PolarSurfaceArea, Molecular_PolarSASA, NPlusO_Count |
| User Set | A comma-separated list of properties to use for clustering |

# Create Property Profile - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_create_property_profile-para.htm

## Create Property Profile - Parameters

### Creates a profile from the property distribution

Creates a comma-separated text file containing the property distribution:

* BinMin : Minimum property value in the bin.

* BinMax : Maximum property value in the bin.

* BinFreqMin : Minimum fraction of ligands in the bin.

* BinFreqMax : Maximum fraction of ligands in the bin.

* BinFreqWeight : Weight of the bin.

Notes :

* The profile can be compared to that of another library with the Calculate Property Profile Penalty protocol.

* BinFreqMin and BinFreqMax defines a range of the fractions of ligands in the bin. Within the range there is no penalty. The created profile has a single value (the actual fraction) for both.

* The weights are 1 by default and can be changed before being used to calculate property profile penalty.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Property Name | The name of a numeric property for which to create the profile, for example, Molecular_Weight. |
| Minimum | The lower bound of the property range. |
| Maximum | The upper bound of the property range. |
| Number of Bins | Number of bins in the specified property range. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Values Smaller Than Minimum | How to count for property values below the lower bound: Ignore : To discard these ligands and do not count them in the profile. Add to First Bin : Count these ligands in the first bin. Valid Values: Ignore , Add To First Bin |
| Values Greater Than Maximum | How to count for property values above the upper bound: Ignore : To discard these ligands and do not count them in the profile. Add to Last Bin : Count these ligands in the last bin. Valid Values: Ignore , Add To Last Bin |

# Find Diverse Molecules - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_find_diverse_molecules-para.htm

## Find Diverse Molecules - Parameters

### Generates a subset of diverse ligands from a library

Extracts a subset of ligands with diverse properties. The selection is based on a maximum dissimilarity method using the same algorithm as the Cluster Ligands protocol.

The distance function between the molecules is a Euclidean distance (if numeric properties are used), Tanimoto distance (if fingerprints are used), or a combination of the two (if both types of properties are used). When a Euclidean distance is used,
each numeric property is first shifted and scaled so that each property has a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. The final distance is then scaled by the square root of the number of dimensions.

| Use Properties | The properties used for clustering: PredefinedSet : A predefined property set from a list. UserSet : A user-defined property set. Valid Values: PredefinedSet , UserSet |
| Predefined Set | A predefined set of properties used to determine molecular diversity. # Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_analysis_find_similar_molecules_by_fingerprints-para.htm

## Find Similar Molecules by Fingerprints - Parameters

### Finds molecules in a library with fingerprints similar to the reference ligands

Available similarity measures are:

* Tanimoto : SA/(SA+SB+SC) The number of "and" bits normalized by the number of "or" bits.

* Dice : 2*SA/(2*SA+SB+SC) The number of "and" bits normalized by the arithmetic mean of the number of on bits in the target and reference.

* Cosine : SA/((SA+SB)*(SA+SC))^0.5 The number of "and" bits normalized by the geometric mean of the number of on bits in the target and reference.

* Target : SA/(SA+SC) The number of shared bits between the reference and target normalized by bits in the reference.

Where SA , SB , and SC are defined as:

* SA : The number of AND bits. Bits present in both the target and the reference.

* SB : The number of bits in the target but not the reference.

* SC : The number of bits in the reference but not the target.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Reference Ligands | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the ligands as references for similarity selection. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| What To Find | Method to determine how many molecules to be selected. Valid Values: N Most Similar Molecules, Percentage Most Similar Molecules, All Molecules Within Minimum Similarity |
| Number of Similar Molecules | The number of the most similar molecules |
| Percentage of Similar Molecules | The percentage of molecules that are most similar to the reference. |
| Minimum Similarity | Molecules above the minimum similarity score |
| Similarity Coefficient | The function used to calculate the similarity between two fingerprints. The functions are defined as functions of their contributions. See the help for the OutputContributions parameter for definitions of the contributions. The following choices are available: Tanimoto : SA/(SA+SB+SC) The number of "and" bits normalized by the number of "or" bits. Dice : 2*SA/(2*SA+SB+SC) The number of "and" bits normalized by the arithmetic mean of the number of on bits in the target and reference. Cosine : SA/((SA+SB)*(SA+SC))^0.5 The number of "and" bits normalized by the geometric mean of the number of on bits in the target and reference. Target : SA/(SA+SC) The number of shared bits between the reference and target normalized by bits in the reference. Valid Values: Tanimoto , Dice, Cosine, Target |
| Output Contributions | Toggles the output of the contributions to the SimilarityCoefficient calculation. The contributions are defined as follows: SA : The number of AND bits. Bits present in both the target and the reference. SB : The number of bits in the target but not the reference. SC : The number of bits in the reference but not the target. Valid Values: True , False |
| Use Properties | Which fingerprint property to use in similarity check. There are two options: PredefinedSet : the fingerprint from a predefined list named Predefined Set. UserSet : the fingerprint from user supplied properties. Valid Values: PredefinedSet , UserSet |
| Predefined Set | A predefined set of fingerprints to use for similarities. Valid Values: FCFP_2, FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6, MDLPublicKeys, FCFC_2, FCFC_4, FCFC_6 , ECFC_2, ECFC_4, ECFC_6 |
| User Set | A user supplied fingerprint |

# Compare Libraries - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_compare_libraries-para.htm

## Compare Libraries - Parameters

### Compares two ligand libraries

Uses the following methods:

* Assemblies : Breaks the ligands of each library into fragments determined by the Fragments to Generate parameter, then computes a Tanimoto similarity coefficient between the libraries based on the fragments that are common and unique to each library.

* Bayesian Model : Builds a Bayesian model to learn the library A ligands and one to learn the library B ligands. Finally, it scores all ligands using both models. A distance is computed as: Distance = ScoreAA + ScoreBB - ScoreAB - ScoreBA where ScoreAA is the average score of the library A molecules scored by the Bayesian model
that learned the library A ligands, etc. The higher the distance, the more dissimilar the libraries.

Distance = ScoreAA + ScoreBB - ScoreAB - ScoreBA

where ScoreAA is the average score of the library A molecules scored by the Bayesian model
that learned the library A ligands, etc. The higher the distance, the more dissimilar the libraries.

* Cell Based : Assigns ligands in 
library A and B to cells of binned space. The
bins are determined by the specified molecular
properties and binning parameters. A similarity
metric is then computed based on cell occupancy: Similarity = OC AB /OC Total where OC AB are the number of cells
occupied by ligands from both library A and 
library B and OC Total are the total
occupied cells.

Similarity = OC AB /OC Total

where OC AB are the number of cells
occupied by ligands from both library A and 
library B and OC Total are the total
occupied cells.

* Global Fingerprint : Generates
a global fingerprint for all ligands in library A and all ligands in library B
and then computes a Tanimoto similarity coefficient between the two libraries.

### Parameters

| Input Library A | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the ligand library to be compared. Labeled as "Input Library A". In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| Input Library B | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the ligands in another library for comparison. Labeled as "Input Library B". In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| Comparison Methods | Methods for comparing the two libraries. Available methods are: Assemblies : Compute the similarity of two libraries from the number of unique assembly fragments in each library. In practice each unique library is hashed into a fingerprint, and the similarity score is calculated as the Tanimoto distance between the two libraries. Bayesian Model : Create two Bayesian classification models for the two libraries and calculate a Bayesian distance based on the Bayesian scores. Cell Based : Compute the similarity of the two libraries from cell occupancy in binned space of properties. # Compare Libraries

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_compare_libraries.htm

## Compare Libraries

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Compare Libraries protocol compares two ligand libraries using various methods. You can compare the libraries based on the following methods:
assemblies, a Bayesian model, a cell based method, or a global fingerprint.

* Assemblies

* Bayesian model

* Cell based

* Global fingerprint

When using the assembly method, each ligand library is decomposed into unique occurrences of molecular rings, ring assemblies, bridge
assemblies, chains, Murcko assemblies, or any combination of these. Murcko assemblies are contiguous ring systems plus chains that link
two or more rings, as defined by Bemis and Murcko [Bemis and Murcko, 1996] . The two libraries are compared using a
Tanimoto similarity of the assemblies.

When using the Bayesian method, a Bayesian model is created using ligands in Library A and another Bayesian model is created using
ligands in Library B. A score is computed for all ligands in both libraries using each model. The library comparison metric is measured
as the Bayesian distance:

Distance = ScoreAA + ScoreBB - ScoreAB - ScoreBA

where

* ScoreAA = average LibA score for the molecules in Library A

* ScoreBB = average LibB score for the molecules in Library B

* ScoreAB = average LibB score for the molecules in Library A

* ScoreBA = average LibA score for the molecules in Library B

The larger the distance, the more dissimilar the libraries.

When using the cell based method, each ligand in both libraries is assigned to a cell of binned space based on the specified numeric
properties. The library comparison metric is computed as:

Similarity = NC AB /NC total

where NC AB is the number of cells occupied by a ligand from Library A and a ligand from Library B, and NC total is the
total number of occupied cells.

When using the global fingerprint method, a global fingerprint is computed for all ligands in Library A and another global fingerprint is
computed for the ligands in Library B. The comparison metric is the Tanimoto similarity for the two fingerprints.

* Open the Small Molecules | Design and Analyze Libraries tools and click Compare Libraries to open the Compare Libraries dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Library A Specify the library source. Select all, visible, or selected ligands from a Molecule Window , or click Browse... to browse to a file. Input Library B Specify the source to compare. Comparison Methods Specify one or more methods for comparing the two libraries. Assemblies, Beyesian Model, Cell Based, and Global Fingerprint methods are available. For details about these and remaining parameters, see Compare Libraries - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Library A | Specify the library source. Select all, visible, or selected ligands from a Molecule Window , or click Browse... to browse to a file. |
| Input Library B | Specify the source to compare. |
| Comparison Methods | Specify one or more methods for comparing the two libraries. Assemblies, Beyesian Model, Cell Based, and Global Fingerprint methods are available. |

For details about these and remaining parameters, see Compare Libraries - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the comparison.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |

The remaining files are output based on the comparison method used:

* Output files for assemblies method

* Output files for bayesian model method

* Output files for cell-based method

* Output files for global fingerprint method

There is no extra output files when this method is invoked. The Tanimoto similarity score and its contributions
are reported in the summary section of Report.htm.

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Bayesian-Histogram-A.csv | .csv file containing the histogram data of both libraries scored by model "Library A". The histogram is created using a fixed bin setup: minimum 100, maximum 100, bin size 5. Score_LibraryA is the Bayesian score of the bin center, whereas LibraryA and LibraryB are the normalized frequency of ligands falling into this bin from the two input libraries. |
| Bayesian-Histogram-B.csv | .csv file containing the histogram data of both libraries scored by model "Library B". The histogram is created using a fixed bin setup: minimum 100, maximum 100, bin size 5. Score_LibraryB is the Bayesian score of the bin center, whereas LibraryA and LibraryB are the normalized frequency of ligands falling into this bin from the two input libraries. |
| ViewHistogram-LibA.ds_pl | Script that generates a plot using Bayesian-Histogram-A.csv . |
| ViewHistogram-LibB.ds_pl | Script that generates a plot using Bayesian-Histogram-B.csv . |
| Bayesian-MolsASimB.sd | Ligands in library A that are most similar to ligands in library B. |
| Bayesian-MolsADiffB.sd | Ligands in library A that are least similar to ligands in library B. |
| Bayesian-MolsBSimA.sd | Ligands in library B that are most similar to ligands in library A. |
| Bayesian-MolsBDiffA.sd | Ligands in library B that are least similar to ligands in library A. |
| LibA-ModelDescription.html | Model description for the Bayesian model built using ligands from library A. |
| LibB-ModelDescription.html | Model description for the Bayesian model built using ligands from library B. |

##### Output files for cell based method

Bin assignment for each property used in the comparison and library assignment based on cell population are added as new properties. The file name is a combination of two input library names, and may be different from the name here. |
| ViewCells.ds_pl | Script that opens Input_Library_A-Input_Library_B.sd in a table browser and generate a 3D point plot colored by library assignment for each ligand. This file is only present if three or more properties are used in cell-based comparison. The bin assignments of the first three properties are used as X, Y, and Z axes. |

# Enumerate Library by Reaction - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_enumerate_library_by_reaction-para.htm

## Enumerate Library by Reaction - Parameters

### Builds a ligand library based on a reaction

Builds a combinatorial ligand library by enumerating all the input reactants according to the reaction rule specified in a reaction file.

Note:

* Generated ligands have 2D coordinates

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Reactants | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the reactants used in the reaction to generate the library. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| Input Reaction File | The reaction file, in MDL reaction (.rxn) or Daylight SMIRKS (.smk) format. |
| If Multiple Mappings | What to do if more than one reactant maps, or if a single reactant maps more than once. Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings. Valid choices are: RejectStartingMaterial : Write the ligands to file Ligands-Reaction_fail.sd. UseFirstMapping : Uses the first encountered mapping for enumerating the reaction. UseEachMapping : Enumerates the reaction for all mappings of the reactant to the target. Note: Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings. Valid Values: RejectStartingMaterial, UseFirstMapping , UseEachMapping |
| Reject Symmetric Targets With Multiple Mappings | This parameter is enabled when If Multiple Mappings is set to RejectStartingMaterial . It toggles how to handle cases where the target multiply maps due to symmetry. To clarify this behavior, it is helpful to look at an example. Consider a simple reaction such as the following: F → I (change Fluorine to Iodine). The molecule FCCF will map twice due to symmetry. In some cases, the user may choose to accept this molecule because only one unique product will result from this reaction (FCCI). In other cases, the user may want to reject these inputs because the molecule may react twice. It is for these reasons that a special flag is present for handling the acceptance/rejection of symmetrical multiple mappings. Valid Values: True , False |
| If Multiple Reactions | What to do if a particular combination of reactants can be utilized by more than one reaction. UseFirstReaction : Uses the first reaction that works. UseEachReaction : Uses every reaction that works. Valid Values: UseFirstReaction , UseEachReaction |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Maximum | Maximum number of molecules to enumerate. If zero or left blank, it exhaustively enumerates. |
| Search Options | Options for substructure searching. For maximum ISIS compatibility, select the first six options. Substructure Search options: Use ISIS Aromaticity : Use aromaticity as done by ISIS, else use SciTegic 4n+2 Huckel aromaticity perception. Use Localized Aromatic Bonds : "Localized" aromatic bonds are bonds for which all Kekule representations have the bond always the same type (single or double). For example, the single and double bonds in pyrrole are localized, while the bonds in pyridine are not. ISIS allows single or double bond queries to map onto localized aromatic bonds. Setting this option will make this component compatible with ISIS with respect to these bonds. Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms : Allow uncharged query atoms to map onto charged target atoms. NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers : Queries containing stereoatoms are considered as a mixture of enantiomers rather than absolute. Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets : A query marked Chiral can map only onto targets marked Chiral. Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms : Marked stereoatoms must map onto stereo-appropriate atoms in the targets, instead of being allowed to also map onto unknown or unmarked atoms. HFill if RAtoms Found : If RAtoms are found in the query, hydrogen-fill all other atoms; allow substituents only in the locations marked by the RAtoms. Interpret RAtoms Literally : Treat RAtoms as literal atoms, rather than as query types. Useful for searching and manipulating literal RAtoms in target molecules. Interpret ZAtoms Literally : Treat ZAtoms as literal atoms, rather than as attachment markers. Check Bonds To RAtoms : Toggles the check of query features (e.g. order, Chain/Ring) on bonds to RAtoms. By default, this option is off to match ISIS behavior. Valid Values: Use ISIS Aromaticity, Use Localized Aromatic Bonds, Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms, NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers, Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets, Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms , HFill if RAtoms Found , Interpret RAtoms Literally, Interpret ZAtoms Literally, Check Bonds To RAtoms |
| Randomize | If True, enumerate random combinations. If False, enumerate systematically and exhaustively. Note: If you set this parameter to True, you must also set a value for the Maximum parameter so there is a maximum number to enumerate. Valid Values: True, False |
| Add Reaction Name | Adds the name of the reaction used to the enumerated molecules. Valid Values: True , False |

An MDL MOL/SD file containing the reactants used in the reaction to generate the library.

In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. 
If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file.

The reaction file, in MDL reaction (.rxn) or Daylight SMIRKS (.smk) format.

Valid choices are:

* RejectStartingMaterial : Write the ligands to file Ligands-Reaction_fail.sd.

* UseFirstMapping : Uses the first encountered mapping for enumerating the reaction.

* UseEachMapping : Enumerates the reaction for all mappings of the reactant to the target.

* Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings.

Valid Values: RejectStartingMaterial, UseFirstMapping , UseEachMapping

This parameter is enabled when If Multiple Mappings is set to RejectStartingMaterial . It toggles how to handle cases where the target multiply maps due to symmetry.

To clarify this behavior, it is helpful to look at an example. Consider a simple reaction such as the following: F → I (change Fluorine to Iodine). The molecule FCCF will map twice due to symmetry. In some cases, the user may choose to accept this molecule because only one unique product will result from this reaction (FCCI). In other cases, the user may want to reject these inputs because the molecule may react twice. It is for these reasons that a special flag is present for handling the acceptance/rejection of symmetrical multiple mappings.

Valid Values: True , False

* UseFirstReaction : Uses the first reaction that works.

* UseEachReaction : Uses every reaction that works.

Valid Values: UseFirstReaction , UseEachReaction

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Maximum number of molecules to enumerate. If zero or left blank, it exhaustively enumerates.

* Use ISIS Aromaticity : Use aromaticity as done by ISIS, else use SciTegic 4n+2 Huckel aromaticity perception.

* Use Localized Aromatic Bonds : "Localized" aromatic bonds are bonds for which all Kekule representations have the bond always the same type (single or double). For example, the single and double bonds in 
pyrrole are localized, while the bonds in pyridine are not. ISIS allows single or double bond queries to map onto localized aromatic bonds. Setting this option will make this component compatible with ISIS with respect to these bonds.

* Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms : Allow uncharged query atoms to map onto charged target atoms.

* NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers : Queries containing stereoatoms are considered as a mixture of enantiomers rather than absolute.

* Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets : A query marked Chiral can map only onto targets marked Chiral.

* Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms : Marked stereoatoms must map onto stereo-appropriate atoms in the targets, instead of being allowed to also map onto unknown or unmarked atoms.

* HFill if RAtoms Found : If RAtoms are found in the query, hydrogen-fill all other atoms; allow substituents only in the locations marked by the RAtoms.

* Interpret RAtoms Literally : Treat RAtoms as literal atoms, rather than as query types. Useful for searching and manipulating literal RAtoms in target molecules.

* Interpret ZAtoms Literally : Treat ZAtoms as literal atoms, rather than as attachment markers.

* Check Bonds To RAtoms : Toggles the check of query features (e.g. order, Chain/Ring) on bonds to RAtoms. By default, this option is off to match ISIS behavior.

Valid Values: Use ISIS Aromaticity, Use Localized Aromatic Bonds, Uncharged Atoms Can Map Charged Atoms, NonChiral Queries are Enantiomers, Chiral Queries Only Map Chiral Targets, Stereo Atoms Can Map Nonstereo Atoms , HFill if RAtoms Found , Interpret RAtoms Literally, Interpret ZAtoms Literally, Check Bonds To RAtoms

* If you set this parameter to True, you must also set a value for the Maximum parameter so there is a maximum number to enumerate.

Valid Values: True, False

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_enumerate_library_from_ligands-para.htm

## Enumerate Library from Ligands - Parameters

### Enumerates library from specified attachment points

Enumerates a combinatorial library from a set of molecules using:

* A core molecule

* A list of attachment points in the core

* A set of ligands for each attachment point

* An attachment point definition for each set of ligands (e.g. Fluorine atoms)

If enumeration from an existing RG file is desired, you can specify it using the Input RG File advanced parameter. This will bypass the core and RG setup.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Core Structure | The core structure for the library. |
| RGroups | The single-bonded attachment points on the core. In Discovery Studio, choose a Group containing the atoms to use as link points, or create a new Group from the current selection. In Pipeline Pilot, a space separated list of atom indices. Only the first 5 suitable atoms in the list will be used (e.g., 3 10 44). Note: Specified link points should have only one atom singly bonded, for example hydrogen or fluorine atoms. |
| Name Ligands Using | Generate a name for each ligand from: Sequential Numbers : A number starting from 1 is assigned to each ligand sequentially. R Group Indices : The indices of members in each R group are joined using the dash sign, e.g., 1-2-3. R Group Names : The names of members in each R group are joined using the dash sign, e.g., a1-b1-c1. Note: This protocol reads the R group names from the S group information of the properties block. The following two R group naming schemes are supported (att1 is the R group name): S SKP 1 S NAM att1 or M STY 1 1 DAT M SDT 1 MEMB_NAME T M SED 1 att1 Valid Values: Sequential Numbers, R Group Indices , R Group Names |
| R1 | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the ligands to attach at this attachment point. Ligands must contain a specified single-bonded attachment point, for example fluorine atoms. You can specify which atoms to use as the attachment point using the Attachment Point parameter. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| R1 Attachment Point | Choose how to identify attachment points in the ligands for this group. Attachment points are specified by the name of the reactions in SMIRKS Reactions . For example, choosing fluorine will attach the atom attached to fluorine in these ligands to the atom attached to the corresponding R group in the core. Valid Values: No reaction (Z group must be present), Fluoro, Chloro , Bromo, Iodo, Halides, Carboxylic Acid, Alcohols, Alcohols-Primary, Alcohols-Secondary, Alcohols-Tertiary, Thiols, Amines, Amines-Primary, Amines-Secondary, Amide, Nitrile, Aldehydes, Grignard, Suzuki, Hiyama RSiY, Negishi, Stille |
| R2 | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the ligands to attach at this attachment point. Ligands must contain a specified single-bonded attachment point, for example fluorine atoms. # Enumerate Library from Ligands

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_enumerate_library_from_ligands.htm

## Enumerate Library from Ligands

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Enumerate Library from Ligands protocol builds a combinatorial ligand library by enumerating all combinations of R groups attached to a core structure. You can perform this by specifying the core structure with attachment points and R group ligands. Alternatively, you can specify an MDL RG file that contains the core group and all the R groups.

The Enumerate Library from Ligands protocol enumerates a combinatorial library by attaching all combinations of R groups to a core structure.
You can run this protocol using one of the following methods:

* Specify the core structure with attachment points and R group ligands

* Use an RG file as input

* Open a core structure in a Molecule Window or sketch a molecule as the core structure.

* Select single bonded atoms as attachment points.

* Open the Small Molecules | Design and Analyze Libraries tools and click Enumerate Library from Ligands to open the Enumerate Library from Ligands dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Specify the Core Structure .

* Click the R Groups parameter and select Create New Group from Selection... . This defines the selected atoms as attachment points. If you have already defined a group of single-bonded atoms, you can select the group directly.

* Choose a method for naming the enumerated ligands.

* Specify the ligands for each R group and its attachment point according to instruction. The attachment point is specified by the name of the reactions in SMIRKS Reactions . For example, choosing fluorine will attach the atom attached to fluorine in these ligands to the atom attached to the corresponding R group in the core. You can also edit the ligands to match the selected attachment point. The number of R groups must match the number of attachment points in the core structure.

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Enumerate Library from Ligands - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

* The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

* Open the Advanced parameter group and specify the Input RG File .

Duplicate fragments within the same R group are automatically removed from the enumerated library.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Core-Fragments1-Fragments2.sd | The enumerated library in .sd file format. The name is derived from the core structure and fragments or the input RG file and may be different from the name listed here. |
| Core-Fragments1-Fragments2.rg | The pre-enumerated library in MDL RG file format. If an input RG file is used instead, this will carry the same file name, but the format is standardized. |
| Core-and-Fragments.sd | This .sd file contains the core and fragments from the core structure and fragments or the original input RG file. |

#### Further Information

Theory - Small Molecules Small Molecule tools tutorials

# Generate Novel Ligands - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_generate_novel_ligands-para.htm

## Generate Novel Ligands - Parameters

### Generates novel ligands from overlaid ligands

Generates new ligands from a set of overlaid ligands using the BREED method (Pierce et al. 2004). It first identifies overlapping bonds from a pair of the overlaid ligands, then breaks the matching bond and swaps the fragments on each side of each matching bond to generate new ligands.

If you have a few receptor-ligand complex structures, you can align these structures by superimposing the protein chains. This gives you a set of overlaid ligands in the same binding site. You can then use this protocol to generate more ligands.

See Also:

* Pierce, A. C.; Rao G.; Bemis G. W. BREED: Generating novel inhibitors through hybridization of known ligands. Application to CDK2, P38, and HIV protease. J. Med. Chem. 2004 , 47, 2768-2775.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | The file or URL source to read. The ligands should have been overlaid in order for this method to work. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| Property for Target | This is a property to identify target ligands. If this is set, only descendents from at least one target ligands are kept. A value of 1 for this property identifies a ligand as a target. |
| Maximum Distance | Distance threshold used in bond matching. If the distances between the atoms at each end of the bonds are greater than this value, the two bonds are not considered as matching. |
| Maximum Angle | Angle threshold used in bond matching. Two bonds with angle greater than this value are not considered as matching. |
| Generations | Number of generations of ligands to generate. The number of combinations increase exponentially with number of generations. Three generations usually give a very diverse library. A larger generation typically only adds very few new ligands, with most of the combined products being duplicate molecules. Valid Values: 1 , 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 |
| Minimize Ligands | Whether to run energy minimization on the output ligands. The Clean force-field (Hahn M. 1995) is used to generate minimized coordinates for the input molecules. The property Minimized_Energy , with the value of the energy at the end of the minimization, is added to the property list of each molecule. Notes: Minimization starts from the current 3D coordinates, if there are any present on the input molecule. If the molecule has no 3D coordinates, an initial 3D conformation is generated and minimized. See Also: Hahn, M. Receptor Surface Models. 1. Definition and Construction J. Med. Chem. 1995 , 38(12), 2080-2090. Valid Values: True, False |
| Maximum Number of Steps | The maximum number of minimization steps to perform. |
| Convergence Energy Difference | The energy difference between minimization steps required for convergence. |

In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. 
If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file.

# Generate Novel Ligands

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_generate_novel_ligands.htm

## Generate Novel Ligands

* Description

* Setting Up and Running

* Analyzing Results

The Generate Novel Ligands protocol uses the published BREED method [Pierce et al., 2004] for swapping matched bonds in a set of overlapping ligands to generate new hybrid ligands. This implementation extends the original method by allowing a target set to be specified and easily generate multiple sets of ligands. The new ligands have combined structural features inherited from parent compounds. Because the original ligands are all good binders to the common receptor, the new ligands are certain to fit into the binding site of the receptor.

This protocol requires a set of ligand structures as input.

* Load the ligand structures into the Graphics View .These ligands should have been properly aligned in order for this protocol to work.

* Open the Small Molecules | Design and Analyze Libraries tools and click Generate Novel Ligands to open the Generate Novel Ligands dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the Input Ligands parameter to the loaded ligands.

* To set a subset of ligands as targets (only offspring from these ligands are kept), expand the Input Ligands parameter and set Property for Target to identify these ligands.

* Set the remaining parameters as desired. For details, see Generate Novel Ligands - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Upon finishing, the new ligands will be opened in a new Molecule Window automatically. If the job ran in background mode, double click on the job status in the Jobs Explorer to open the report.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Generated new ligands. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Script to open the new ligands in a new Molecule Window. |

# Generate RECAP Fragments - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_generate_recap_fragments-para.htm

## Generate RECAP Fragments - Parameters

### Generates fragments using a retrosynthesis procedure

The RECAP (REtrosynthetic Combinatorial Analysis Procedure) algorithm is applied to identify building-block fragments rich in biologically recognized elements, privileged motifs, and structures. The fragments can be used for the design of building blocks, and the synthesis of libraries rich in biological motifs.

The following bond-type rules are used to cleave molecules:

* Amide

* Ester

* Amine

* Urea

* Ether

* Olefin

* Quaternary Nitrogen

* Aromatic nitrogen bonded to an aliphatic carbon

* Lactam nitrogen bonded to an aliphatic carbon

* Aromatic carbon bonded to an aromatic carbon

* Sulfonamide

See Also:

* Lewell, X. Q.; Judd, D. B.; Watson, S. P.; Hann, M. M. "RECAP--retrosynthetic combinatorial analysis procedure: a powerful new technique for identifying privileged molecular fragments with useful applications in combinatorial chemistry." J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. 1998, 38 ,511-522.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Rule Of Three Filters | Filters to apply for removing non-drug like structures. The filters available are: Molecular Weight ≤ 300 Hydrogen Bond Donors ≤ 3 Hydrogen Bond Acceptors ≤ 3 AlogP ≤ 3.0 Rotatable Bonds ≤ 3 Polar Surface Area ≤ 60 Å 2 The "Rule of Three" filters have been proposed for selecting molecules suitable for fragment based drug design. It uses simple rules analogous to the Lipinski (Rule of Five) filter. See Also: Congreve, M.; Carr, R.; Murray, C.; Jhoti, H. A 'Rule of Three' for fragment-based lead discovery?, Drug Discovery Today , 2003 8 , 876-877. Valid Values: Molecular Weight , Hydrogen Bond Donors , Hydrogen Bond Acceptors , AlogP , Rotatable Bonds, Polar Surface Area |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Atom to Add at Break Point | Type of atom to be added to the two atoms attached to each deleted bond. The atom type can be a regular element (C, N, Cl, ...) or a query atom (R, Z, A, ...). If left blank, no atoms are attached at the cleavage points. To keep the original atom types attached to the bond, enter 'Orig' as the atom type. |
| Remove Hydrogens | Remove hydrogens from fragments. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number of Heavy Atoms Filter | Only report fragments with a heavy atoms count more than the specified number. |
| Remove Duplicates | Remove duplicate fragments. Valid Values: True , False |

# Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_optimize_combinatorial_library_with_pareto_method-para.htm

## Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method - Parameters

### Optimizes a specified number of subset libraries from a combinatorial library

Uses Pareto optimization. This method is useful when you wish to optimize more than one property. Unlike other optimizations which generate a single solution, a Pareto optimization generates multiple solutions which give the best possible tradeoffs among the properties being optimized.

The optimum subset library is determined by the Optimization Properties . Each Optimization Property is the single-sample property that is used to compute the subset property to be optimized. What to Optimize specifies how to compute the subset property value from each of the single-sample property values (e.g., by taking the Mean). Goal specifies whether you wish to Maximize or Minimize the result of What to Optimize . The most optimal subsets are those for which it is not possible to improve on one property without degrading at least one other.

Note:

* The coordinates in the subset library are in 2D

### Parameters

| Name | Description | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input Library Type | Input type for combinatorial library to be generated. Valid Values: R Group , Reaction, Prebuilt | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Input RG File | The input MDL RG file to generate the combinatorial library by enumeration. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Maximum Attachments | The maximum number of attachments allowed. Prevents recursive enumeration from proceeding into infinity. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Options | RG Reader Options: Fill Equivalent RGroups with Same Fragment: forces all equivalent RGroups to be filled in with the same fragment. That is, if there are multiple instances of 'R1', then all 'R1' groups must be filled in with the same fragment. Use MDL Output Order: returns enumerated compounds in order of MDL R-Numbers. Valid Values: Fill Equivalent RGroups with Same Fragment, Use MDL Output Order | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Input Reactants | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the reactants to generate the combinatorial library using a reaction. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Input Reaction File | The file containing the reaction scheme in MDL reaction (.rxn) or Daylight SMIRKS (.smk) format. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| If Multiple Mappings | What to do if more than one reactant maps, or if a single reactant maps more than once. Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings. RejectStartingMaterial : Passes the reagent out the Fail port. UseFirstMapping : Uses the first encountered mapping for enumerating the reaction. UseEachMapping : Enumerates the reaction for all mappings of the reactant to the target. Note: Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings. Valid Values: RejectStartingMaterial, UseFirstMapping, UseEachMapping | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| If Multiple Reactions | What to do if a particular combination of reactants can be utilized by more than one reaction. UseFirstReaction : Uses the first reaction that works. UseEachReaction : Uses every reaction that works. Valid Values: UseFirstReaction , UseEachReaction | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Add Reaction Name | Adds the name of the reaction used to the enumerated molecules. Valid Values: True , False | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Input Prebuilt Library | An MDL MOL/SD file containing the pre-enumerated library either from Rgroup files or by reaction. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Group Index Property | Name of the property containing an array of indices of the R-groups or reactants corresponding to each enumerated ligand. This is used to identify the structure of the combinatorial library internally. For libraries from RGroups, this can be either RGroupIndices or AttachmentNames, while for libraries from reactions, this can be any array property identifying each original starting reactant uniquely. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Library Dimensions | A comma-separated list of the number of instances of each group type to be used to generate each subset library (e.g., the number of R1, R2, R3 fragments). For example, a list of 8,12,4 indicates an 8 x 12 x 4 subset of a library containing 3 different R group or reactant types. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Number of Libraries | Number of optimal libraries to be generated by the optimization. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Number of Iterations | Number of optimization iterations to perform. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 | Name of single-sample property to be used in optimization. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize | Specifies how to process the Optimization Property for each subset in order to compute a value to be optimized. Each option also results in the addition of a specific suffix to the Optimization Property name in the output. Options are: Mean : Mean value over the subset. Suffix: "_Mean". Minimum : Minimum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Minimum". Maximum : Maximum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Maximum". Standard Deviation : Standard deviation over the subset. Suffix: "_StdDev". Unique Value Count : Number of distinct values assumed by the property over all samples in the subset. Suffix: "_UniqueValueCount". Range Penalty : Mean range penalty over all samples in the subset. Use Range Minimum and Range Maximum to specify the desirable range. For a given sample, if the value of the Optimization Property is within this range, the penalty value is zero. For values outside the range, the penalty is proportional to the amount by which the value is greater than the Range Maximum or less than the Range Minimum . Suffix: "_RangePenalty". Distribution Penalty : Penalty value indicating the degree to which the distribution of Optimization Property values over the subset differs from a reference distribution specified in the Target Distribution Source file. Suffix: "_DistributionPenalty". Note: You will normally specify Minimize as the Goal for the "Range Penalty" and "Distribution Penalty" options. But you can choose Maximize if Range Maximum and Range Minimum define an un desirable range, or if you wish the distribution of values for your subsets to be as different as possible from the reference distribution. Valid Values: Mean , Minimum, Maximum, Standard Deviation, Unique Value Count, Range Penalty, Distribution Penalty | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize Range Minimum | Minimum desired value for property. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Range Penalty". | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize Range Maximum | Maximum desired value for property. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Range Penalty". | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize Target Distribution Source | Name of file containing the reference distribution for the property. Run Create property profile protocol to create such a file. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Distribution Penalty". The file must be a delimited text file containing the following columns: BinMin : The lower bound for each frequency bin (inclusive). BinMax : The upper bound for each frequency bin (exclusive). BinFreqMin : The minimum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction). BinFreqMax : The maximum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction). BinFreqWeight : The weight for this bin for deviations from the desired frequency range. Example: BinMin BinMax BinFreqMin BinFreqMax BinFreqWeight 0 100 0.1 0.1 1.0 100 200 0.2 0.2 1.0 200 300 0.4 0.4 1.0 300 400 0.2 0.2 1.0 400 1000 0.1 0.1 1.0 Note: If Freq i is the distribution value at bin i for a given subset, the penalty function is defined as the sum over all bins of: BinFreqWeight i * Delta i 2 where Delta i is: BinFreqMin i - Freq i , for Freq i < BinFreqMin i ; 0 , for BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i ; Freq i - BinFreqMax i , for BinFreqMax i < Freq i . See Also: For more on the use of penalty functions in optimizations, see "Tools for Designing Diverse, Druglike, Cost-Effective Combinatorial Libraries," by R.D. Brown, M. Hassan, and M. Waldman, in Combinatorial Library Design and Evaluation: Principles, Software Tools and Applications in Drug Discovery , A.K. Ghose and V.K. Viswanadhan, eds. (Marcel Dekker, 2001) | BinMin | BinMax | BinFreqMin | BinFreqMax | BinFreqWeight | 0 | 100 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 1.0 | 100 | 200 | 0.2 | 0.2 | 1.0 | 200 | 300 | 0.4 | 0.4 | 1.0 | 300 | 400 | 0.2 | 0.2 | 1.0 | 400 | 1000 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 1.0 |

| Optimization Property 1 Goal | Specifies whether the goal of the optimization is to Minimize or Maximize the value computed as specified by What to Optimize . Valid Values: Maximize , Minimize | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 Goal Weight | Optional weight value to be used to define a single objective function encompassing all Optimization Properties . Specifying weights allows you to rank the final Pareto-optimal subsets according to the relative importance you place on each of the properties. If you provide Weight values, an Objective property is added to the output data records. This property is defined as follows: Objective = W 1 * P 1 / SD 1 + W 2 * P 2 / SD 2 + ... where W i is the normalized weight for optimization property i . P i is the value of property i as computed according to the specified option for What to Optimize (with opposite sign if the value is to be maximized rather than minimized). SD i is the standard deviation of the property over all subsets in the initial population. Notes: The value of Objective does not affect the results of the optimization. The Objective property is only meaningful for ranking subsets within the same optimization run relative to each other. If no weights are specified, then no Objective property is computed. If weights are specified for some Optimization Properties but not others, the missing weights are assumed to be zero. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |

| Optimization Property 4 Goal | Specifies whether the goal of the optimization is to Minimize or Maximize the value computed as specified by What to Optimize . Valid Values: Maximize , Minimize | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 4 Goal Weight | Optional weight value to be used to define a single objective function encompassing all Optimization Properties . Specifying weights allows you to rank the final Pareto-optimal subsets according to the relative importance you place on each of the properties. If you provide Weight values, an Objective property is added to the output data records. This property is defined as follows: Objective = W 1 * P 1 / SD 1 + W 2 * P 2 / SD 2 + ... where W i is the normalized weight for optimization property i . P i is the value of property i as computed according to the specified option for What to Optimize (with opposite sign if the value is to be maximized rather than minimized). SD i is the standard deviation of the property over all subsets in the initial population. Notes: The value of Objective does not affect the results of the optimization. The Objective property is only meaningful for ranking subsets within the same optimization run relative to each other. If no weights are specified, then no Objective property is computed. If weights are specified for some Optimization Properties but not others, the missing weights are assumed to be zero. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |

Each option also results in the addition of a specific suffix to the Optimization Property name in the output. Options are: Mean : Mean value over the subset. Suffix: "_Mean". Minimum : Minimum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Minimum". Maximum : Maximum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Maximum". Standard Deviation : Standard deviation over the subset. Suffix: "_StdDev". Unique Value Count : Number of distinct values assumed by the property over all samples in the subset. Suffix: "_UniqueValueCount". Range Penalty : Mean range penalty over all samples in the subset. Use Range Minimum and Range Maximum to specify the desirable range. For a given sample, if the value of the Optimization Property is within this range, the penalty value is zero. For values outside the range, the penalty is proportional to the amount by which the value is greater than the Range Maximum or less than the Range Minimum . Suffix: "_RangePenalty". Distribution Penalty : Penalty value indicating the degree to which the distribution of Optimization Property values over the subset differs from a reference distribution specified in the Target Distribution Source file. Suffix: "_DistributionPenalty". Note: You will normally specify Minimize as the Goal for the "Range Penalty" and "Distribution Penalty" options. But you can choose Maximize if Range Maximum and Range Minimum define an un desirable range, or if you wish the distribution of values for your subsets to be as different as possible from the reference distribution.
