Input type for combinatorial library to be generated.

Valid Values: R Group , Reaction, Prebuilt

The input MDL RG file to generate the combinatorial library by enumeration.

The maximum number of attachments allowed. Prevents recursive enumeration from proceeding into infinity.

* Fill Equivalent RGroups with Same Fragment: forces all equivalent RGroups to be filled in with the same fragment. That is, if there are multiple instances of 'R1', then all 'R1' groups must be filled in with the same fragment.

* Use MDL Output Order: returns enumerated compounds in order of MDL R-Numbers.

Valid Values: Fill Equivalent RGroups with Same Fragment, Use MDL Output Order

An MDL MOL/SD file containing the reactants to generate the combinatorial library using a reaction.

In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. 
If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file.

The file containing the reaction scheme in MDL reaction (.rxn) or Daylight SMIRKS (.smk) format.

What to do if more than one reactant maps, or if a single reactant maps more than once. Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings.

* RejectStartingMaterial : Passes the reagent out the Fail port.

* UseFirstMapping : Uses the first encountered mapping for enumerating the reaction.

* UseEachMapping : Enumerates the reaction for all mappings of the reactant to the target.

* Only numbered atoms that are changed by the reaction are considered when performing the test for multiple mappings.

Valid Values: RejectStartingMaterial, UseFirstMapping, UseEachMapping

* UseFirstReaction : Uses the first reaction that works.

* UseEachReaction : Uses every reaction that works.

Valid Values: UseFirstReaction , UseEachReaction

Adds the name of the reaction used to the enumerated molecules.

Valid Values: True , False

An MDL MOL/SD file containing the pre-enumerated library either from Rgroup files or by reaction.

Name of the property containing an array of indices of the R-groups or reactants corresponding to each enumerated ligand. This is used to identify the structure of the combinatorial library internally.

For libraries from RGroups, this can be either RGroupIndices or AttachmentNames, while for libraries from reactions, this can be any array property identifying each original starting reactant uniquely.

For example, a list of 8,12,4 indicates an 8 x 12 x 4 subset of a library containing 3 different R group or reactant types.

Number of optimal libraries to be generated by the optimization.

Number of optimization iterations to perform.

Name of single-sample property to be used in optimization.

Specifies how to process the Optimization Property for each subset in order to compute a value to be optimized. Each option also results in the addition of a specific suffix to the Optimization Property name in the output.

Options are:

* Mean : Mean value over the subset. Suffix: "_Mean".

* Minimum : Minimum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Minimum".

* Maximum : Maximum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Maximum".

* Standard Deviation : Standard deviation over the subset. Suffix: "_StdDev".

* Unique Value Count : Number of distinct values assumed by the property over all samples in the subset. Suffix: "_UniqueValueCount".

* Range Penalty : Mean range penalty over all samples in the subset. Use Range Minimum and Range Maximum to specify the desirable range. For a given sample, if the value of the Optimization Property is within this range, the penalty value is zero. For values outside the range, the penalty is proportional to the amount by which the value is greater than the Range Maximum or less than the Range Minimum . Suffix: "_RangePenalty".

* Distribution Penalty : Penalty value indicating the degree to which the distribution of Optimization Property values over the subset differs from a reference distribution specified in the Target Distribution Source file. Suffix: "_DistributionPenalty".

* You will normally specify Minimize as the Goal for the "Range Penalty" and "Distribution Penalty" options. But you can choose Maximize if Range Maximum and Range Minimum define an un desirable range, or if you wish the distribution of values for your subsets to be as different as possible from the reference distribution.

Valid Values: Mean , Minimum, Maximum, Standard Deviation, Unique Value Count, Range Penalty, Distribution Penalty

Minimum desired value for property. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Range Penalty".

Maximum desired value for property. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Range Penalty".

Name of file containing the reference distribution for the property. Run Create property profile protocol to create such a file. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Distribution Penalty".

The file must be a delimited text file containing the following columns:

* BinMin : The lower bound for each frequency bin (inclusive).

* BinMax : The upper bound for each frequency bin (exclusive).

* BinFreqMin : The minimum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction).

* BinFreqMax : The maximum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction).

* BinFreqWeight : The weight for this bin for deviations from the desired frequency range.

Example:

| BinMin | BinMax | BinFreqMin | BinFreqMax | BinFreqWeight |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 100 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 1.0 |
| 100 | 200 | 0.2 | 0.2 | 1.0 |
| 200 | 300 | 0.4 | 0.4 | 1.0 |
| 300 | 400 | 0.2 | 0.2 | 1.0 |
| 400 | 1000 | 0.1 | 0.1 | 1.0 |

* If Freq i is the distribution value at bin i for a given subset,
the penalty function is defined as the sum over all bins of: BinFreqWeight i * Delta i 2 where Delta i is: BinFreqMin i - Freq i , for Freq i < BinFreqMin i ; 0 , for BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i ; Freq i - BinFreqMax i , for BinFreqMax i < Freq i .

* For more on the use of penalty functions in optimizations, see "Tools for Designing Diverse, Druglike, Cost-Effective Combinatorial Libraries," by R.D. Brown, M. Hassan, and M. Waldman, in Combinatorial Library Design and Evaluation: Principles, Software Tools and Applications in Drug Discovery , A.K. Ghose and V.K. Viswanadhan, eds. (Marcel Dekker, 2001)

Specifies whether the goal of the optimization is to Minimize or Maximize the value computed as specified by What to Optimize .

Valid Values: Maximize , Minimize

Optional weight value to be used to define a single objective function encompassing all Optimization Properties . Specifying weights allows you to rank the final Pareto-optimal subsets according to the relative importance you place on each of the properties.

If you provide Weight values, an Objective property is added to the output data records. This property is defined as follows:

Objective = W 1 * P 1 / SD 1 + W 2 * P 2 / SD 2 + ...

where W i is the normalized weight for optimization property i .

P i is the value of property i as computed according to the specified option for What to Optimize (with opposite sign if the value is to be maximized rather than minimized).

SD i is the standard deviation of the property over all subsets in the initial population.

Notes:

* The value of Objective does not affect the results of the optimization. The Objective property is only meaningful for ranking subsets within the same optimization run relative to each other.

* If no weights are specified, then no Objective property is computed. If weights are specified for some Optimization Properties but not others, the missing weights are assumed to be zero.

# Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_optimize_combinatorial_library_with_pareto_method.htm

## Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method protocol optimizes a specified number of subsets from a large, combinatorial
library using the multi-objective Pareto subset optimization method. The combinatorial library is enumerated from either an RG file or a
set of ligands and a Reaction file ( .rxn ).

Pareto optimization is useful when you have more than one property you wish to optimize. Unlike other optimizations, which generate a
single solution, a Pareto optimization generates multiple solutions that give the best possible tradeoffs among the properties being
optimized.

The optimality of a subset of samples is determined by the Optimization Properties that you specify.
Each Optimization Property is the single-sample property that is used to compute the subset property to be optimized.

* What to Optimize : Specifies how to compute the subset property value from each of the single-sample property
values (for example using the Mean).

* Goal : Specifies whether you wish the optimization to Maximize or Minimize the result of What to Optimize .

The most optimal subsets are those for which it is not possible to improve one property without degrading at least one other.

* Open the Small Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tools and click Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method to open the Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Library Choose R Group , Reaction , or Prebuilt . Input RG File The RG file source. Enabled if the Input Library is set to R Group . Input Reactants The library source. Select all, visible, or selected ligands from a Molecule Window , or
click Browse... to select a file. Browse to the Input Reaction File . Enabled if the Input Library is set to Reaction . Input Prebuilt Library The prebuilt library source. Enabled if the Input Library is set to Prebuilt . You must also specify a property to uniquely identify the source of each R Group or reactant. Library Dimensions Comma-separated numbers of R Groups or reactants. Optimization Property n Specify up to six properties in the optimization. At least two properties are required to run the optimization. Set What to Optimize and Goal for each. If What to Optimize is Range Penalty or Distribution Penalty , Range Maximum/Minimum or Target Distribution Source must be specified. Optionally, the Weight parameter can be specified to add an Objective property to each optimized library. Other optimization properties can be specified similarly. For details about the remaining parameters, see Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Library | Choose R Group , Reaction , or Prebuilt . |
| Input RG File | The RG file source. Enabled if the Input Library is set to R Group . |
| Input Reactants | The library source. Select all, visible, or selected ligands from a Molecule Window , or click Browse... to select a file. Browse to the Input Reaction File . Enabled if the Input Library is set to Reaction . |
| Input Prebuilt Library | The prebuilt library source. Enabled if the Input Library is set to Prebuilt . You must also specify a property to uniquely identify the source of each R Group or reactant. |
| Library Dimensions | Comma-separated numbers of R Groups or reactants. |
| Optimization Property n | Specify up to six properties in the optimization. At least two properties are required to run the optimization. Set What to Optimize and Goal for each. If What to Optimize is Range Penalty or Distribution Penalty , Range Maximum/Minimum or Target Distribution Source must be specified. Optionally, the Weight parameter can be specified to add an Objective property to each optimized library. Other optimization properties can be specified similarly. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Pareto.html | Contains the information for each optimized library and the point charts of the Pareto fronts for the properties used in Pareto optimization. |
| Pareto subdirectory | Contains the .sd files for the optimized libraries. The libraries are sequentially named as Subset-N.sd , where N is the library number. |
| Input_Reactants_fail.sd | An optional .sd file containing the reactants failed to react. This file is present only if the input library type is reaction and there are failed reactions. |

## Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method - Parameters

### Optimizes a specified number of subsets from a large library

Uses Pareto optimization. This method is useful when you wish to optimize more than one property. Unlike other optimizations which generate a single solution, a Pareto optimization generates multiple solutions which give the best possible tradeoffs among the properties being optimized.

The optimum subset of samples is determined by the Optimization Properties that you specify. Each Optimization Property is the single-sample property that is used to compute the subset property to be optimized. What to Optimize specifies how to compute the subset property value from each of the single-sample property values (e.g., by taking the Mean). Goal specifies whether you wish to Maximize or Minimize the result of What to Optimize . The most optimal subsets are those for which it is not possible to improve on one property without degrading at least one other.

### Parameters

| Name | Description | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Subset Size | Number of samples in each optimized subset. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Number of Subsets | Number of optimal subsets to be generated by the optimization. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Number of Iterations | Number of optimization iterations to perform. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 | Name of single-sample property to be used in optimization. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize | Specifies how to process the Optimization Property for each subset in order to compute a value to be optimized. Each option also results in the addition of a specific suffix to the Optimization Property name in the output. Options are: Mean : Mean value over the subset. Suffix: "_Mean". Minimum : Minimum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Minimum". Maximum : Maximum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Maximum". Standard Deviation : Standard deviation over the subset. Suffix: "_StdDev". Unique Value Count : Number of distinct values assumed by the property over all samples in the subset. Suffix: "_UniqueValueCount". Range Penalty : Mean range penalty over all samples in the subset. Use Range Minimum and Range Maximum to specify the desirable range. For a given sample, if the value of the Optimization Property is within this range, the penalty value is zero. For values outside the range, the penalty is proportional to the amount by which the value is greater than the Range Maximum or less than the Range Minimum . Suffix: "_RangePenalty". Distribution Penalty : Penalty value indicating the degree to which the distribution of Optimization Property values over the subset differs from a reference distribution specified in the Target Distribution Source file. Suffix: "_DistributionPenalty". Note: You will normally specify Minimize as the Goal for the "Range Penalty" and "Distribution Penalty" options. But you can choose Maximize if Range Maximum and Range Minimum define an un desirable range, or if you wish the distribution of values for your subsets to be as different as possible from the reference distribution. Valid Values: Mean , Minimum, Maximum, Standard Deviation, Unique Value Count, Range Penalty, Distribution Penalty | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize Range Minimum | Minimum desired value for property. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Range Penalty". | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize Range Maximum | Maximum desired value for property. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Range Penalty". | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 What to Optimize Target Distribution Source | Name of file containing the reference distribution for the property. Run Create property profile protocol to create such a file. Applies only when What to Optimize is set to "Distribution Penalty". The file must be a delimited text file containing the following columns: BinMin : The lower bound for each frequency bin (inclusive). BinMax : The upper bound for each frequency bin (exclusive). BinFreqMin : The minimum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction). BinFreqMax : The maximum desired frequency value for the bin (as a fraction). BinFreqWeight : The weight for this bin for deviations from the desired frequency range. Example: BinMin BinMax BinFreqMin BinFreqMax BinFreqWeight 0 100 0.1 0.1 1.0 100 200 0.2 0.2 1.0 200 300 0.4 0.4 1.0 300 400 0.2 0.2 1.0 400 1000 0.1 0.1 1.0 Note: If Freq i is the distribution value at bin i for a given subset, the penalty function is defined as the sum over all bins of: BinFreqWeight i * Delta i 2 where Delta i is: BinFreqMin i - Freq i , for Freq i < BinFreqMin i ; 0 , for BinFreqMin i < Freq i < BinFreqMax i ; Freq i - BinFreqMax i , for BinFreqMax i < Freq i . See Also: For more on the use of penalty functions in optimizations, see "Tools for Designing Diverse, Druglike, Cost-Effective Combinatorial Libraries," by R.D. Brown, M. Hassan, and M. Waldman, in Combinatorial Library Design and Evaluation: Principles, Software Tools and Applications in Drug Discovery , A.K. Ghose and V.K. Viswanadhan, eds. | Optimization Property 1 Goal | Specifies whether the goal of the optimization is to Minimize or Maximize the value computed as specified by What to Optimize . Valid Values: Maximize , Minimize | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Optimization Property 1 Goal Weight | Optional weight value to be used to define a single objective function encompassing all Optimization Properties . Specifying weights allows you to rank the final Pareto-optimal subsets according to the relative importance you place on each of the properties. If you provide Weight values, an Objective property is added to the output data records. This property is defined as follows: Objective = W 1 * P 1 / SD 1 + W 2 * P 2 / SD 2 + ... where W i is the normalized weight for optimization property i ; P i is the value of property i as computed according to the specified option for What to Optimize (with opposite sign if the value is to be maximized rather than minimized); SD i is the standard deviation of the property over all subsets in the initial population. Notes: The value of Objective does not affect the results of the optimization. The Objective property is only meaningful for ranking subsets within the same optimization run relative to each other. If no weights are specified, then no Objective property is computed. If weights are specified for some Optimization Properties but not others, the missing weights are assumed to be zero. | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |

Specifies how to process the Optimization Property for each subset in order to compute a value to be optimized. Each option also results in the addition of a specific suffix to the Optimization Property name in the output.

Options are:

* Mean : Mean value over the subset. Suffix: "_Mean".

* Minimum : Minimum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Minimum".

* Maximum : Maximum value within the subset. Suffix: "_Maximum".

* Standard Deviation : Standard deviation over the subset. Suffix: "_StdDev".

* Unique Value Count : Number of distinct values assumed by the property over all samples in the subset. Suffix: "_UniqueValueCount".

* Range Penalty : Mean range penalty over all samples in the subset. Use Range Minimum and Range Maximum to specify the desirable range. For a given sample, if the value of the Optimization Property is within this range, the penalty value is zero. For values outside the range, the penalty is proportional to the amount by which the value is greater than the Range Maximum or less than the Range Minimum . Suffix: "_RangePenalty".

But you can choose Maximize if Range Maximum and Range Minimum define an un desirable range, or if you wish the distribution of values for your subsets to be as different as possible from the reference distribution.

# Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_optimize_subset_library_with_pareto_method.htm

## Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method protocol optimizes a specified number of subsets from a large library using
multi-objective Pareto subset optimization method.

Pareto optimization is useful when you have more than one property you wish to optimize. Unlike other optimizations, which generate a single
solution, a Pareto optimization generates multiple solutions which give the best possible tradeoffs among the properties being optimized.

The optimality of a subset of samples is determined by the Optimization Properties that you specify. Each Optimization Property is the single-sample property that is used to compute the subset property to be optimized.

* What to Optimize : Specifies how to compute the subset property value from each of the single-sample property
values (for example using the mean).

* Goal : Specifies whether you wish the optimization to Maximize or Minimize the result of What to Optimize .

The most optimal subsets are those for which it is not possible to improve one property without degrading at least one other.

* Open the Small Molecules | Select Subset Libraries tools and click Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method to open the Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Optimization Property n Specify up to six properties in the optimization. At least two properties are required to run the optimization. Set What to Optimize and Goal for each. If What to Optimize is Range Penalty or Distribution Penalty , Range Maximum/Minimum , or Target Distribution Source must be set. Optionally, the Weight parameter can be specified to add an Objective property to each optimized library. Other optimization properties can be specified similarly. For details about the remaining parameters, see Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Optimization Property n | Specify up to six properties in the optimization. At least two properties are required to run the optimization. Set What to Optimize and Goal for each. If What to Optimize is Range Penalty or Distribution Penalty , Range Maximum/Minimum , or Target Distribution Source must be set. Optionally, the Weight parameter can be specified to add an Objective property to each optimized library. Other optimization properties can be specified similarly. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Pareto.html | Contains information on each optimized subset library and point charts of the Pareto fronts for the properties used in the Pareto optimization. |
| Pareto subdirectory | Contains the image file(s) used by Pareto.html . |
| Subset_Files subdirectory | Contains the .sd files for the optimized subset libraries. The libraries are sequentially named as Subset-N.sd , where N is the subset library number. |
| Library.csv | Comma separated value file of all the input ligands and the subsets they belong to. |

# Sort Data with Pareto Method - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_sort_data_with_pareto_method-para.htm

## Sort Data with Pareto Method - Parameters

### Sorts a library by multiple-objective Pareto method

The optimum sample is determined by the Optimization Properties that you specify. For each Optimization Property , Goal specifies whether you wish to maximize the value of the property or minimize it. The most optimal samples are those for which it is not possible to improve on one property without degrading at least one other (within the set of samples provided as input).

The samples are output in order from most to least optimal. The following two properties are added to each data record:

* ParetoFront : Indicates the front on which the sample lies. The most-optimal samples have a value of 1 for this property. The next most-optimal samples have a value of 2, and so on.

* CrowdingDistance : Indicates the relative distance (in terms of the optimization properties) to other samples on the same front. Samples at the extremes of the front are assigned an "infinite" crowding distance (1.0e99). Within a front, samples with greater values of CrowdingDistance are output before samples with lesser values.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Number of Fronts to Keep | Number of Pareto fronts to keep in output. If no value is given, all fronts will be kept. |
| Optimization Property 1 | Name of property to be used in Pareto-ranking of data records. In Discovery Studio, the choices will be populated with numeric properties in the molecular data if a Molecule window is specified in the Input Ligands parameter. Otherwise, if an SD file is specified, you can use any numeric property in the SD file or calculable properties available on the server. |
| Optimization Property 1 Goal | Specifies whether the goal of the sorting is to obtain samples with large values of the Optimization Property (Maximize) or small values of the property (Minimize). Valid Values: Maximize , Minimize |
| Optimization Property 1 Goal Weight | Optional weight value to be used to define a single objective function encompassing all Optimization Properties . Specifying weights allows you to rank the final Pareto-optimal samples according to the relative importance you place on each of the properties. If you provide Weight values, an Objective property is added to the output data records. This property is defined as follows: Objective = W 1 * P 1 / SD 1 + W 2 * P 2 / SD 2 + ... where W i is the normalized weight for optimization property i ; P i is the value of property i (with opposite sign if the property is to be maximized rather than minimized); SD i is the standard deviation of property i over all input samples. Notes: The value of Objective does not affect the order of data records output from the protocol. Records are sorted by ParetoFront and CrowdingDistance whether or not Weight values are specified. Specific values of Objective (including the sign) have no particular significance and are not comparable between data sets. The Objective property is only meaningful for ranking samples within the same data set relative to each other. If no weights are specified, then no Objective property is computed. If weights are specified for some Optimization Properties but not others, the missing weights are assumed to be zero. |
| Optimization Property 2 | Name of property to be used in Pareto-ranking of data records. In Discovery Studio, the choices will be populated with numeric properties in the molecular data if a Molecule window is specified in the Input Ligands parameter. Otherwise if an SD file is specified, you can use any numeric property in the SD file or calculable properties available on the server. |

# Sort Data with Pareto Method

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/library_design_sort_data_with_pareto_method.htm

## Sort Data with Pareto Method

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Output and input files

The Sort Data with Pareto Method protocol sorts the input samples according to their Pareto (multi-objective) optimality. The
optimality of a sample is determined by the Optimization Properties that you specify.
For each Optimization Property , Goal specifies whether
you wish to Maximize the value of the property or Minimize it. The most optimal
samples are those for which it is not possible to improve on
one property without degrading at least one other (within the set of samples provided as input).

The samples are output in order from most to least optimal. The following two properties are added to each data record:

* ParetoFront : Indicates the front on which the sample lies. The most-optimal samples have a
value of 1 for this property. The next most-optimal samples have a value of 2 , and so on.

* CrowdingDistance : Indicates the relative distance (in terms of the optimization properties) to
other samples on the same front. Samples at the extremes of the front are assigned an "infinite"
crowding distance (1.0e99). Within a front, samples with greater values of CrowdingDistance are
output before samples with lower values.

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Library Design | Sort Data with Pareto Method .

* In the Parameters Explorer, set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Optimization Property n Specify up to six properties for the Pareto sort. Set the Goal for each. Optionally, set Weight to add an Objective property to each
optimized library. Other optimization properties can be specified similarly. For details about the remaining parameters, see Sort Data with Pareto Method - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Optimization Property n | Specify up to six properties for the Pareto sort. Set the Goal for each. Optionally, set Weight to add an Objective property to each optimized library. Other optimization properties can be specified similarly. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Sort Data with Pareto Method - Parameters .

* In the Protocols menu bar, click the Run button.

* Monitor the status in the Jobs Explorer .

When the job finishes, double-click it in the Jobs Explorer to open the Output folder in the Files Explorer. See Output and input files for details about the files generated by this protocol. If the job did not run successfully, the Jobs Explorer will report an error. See Troubleshooting - Protocols for details.

There are no intermediate files generated by this protocol.

#### Output files

The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Input_Ligands-Pareto-Sort.sd | The output ligands after the Pareto sort. The file name may be different from the name listed here. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opening this file will plot the ligands using the optimized properties. If three or more properties are used in the optimization, the first three properties are used as X,Y,Z axes in a 3D plot. |

#### Input files

The following files are created in the Input directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| <ligands>.sd | The ligands used in the calculation. |
| Protocol.pr_xml | The saved protocol and job parameters. You can load this file at any time to re-run this protocol with the same settings. You can also share it with other users. For details see Discovery Studio Parameters (PR_XML) . |

## ADMET Plot

The ADMET Plot is a 2D plot using calculated PSA_2D and AlogP98 properties. 
The 95% and 99% confidence ellipses for the Human Intestinal Absorption model and the Blood Brain Barrier model
can be added to the plot to validate the predictions. 
Selecting a set of ligands either within or outside of the ellipses 
automatically highlights those ligands in the Molecule Window .

To control the ellipses, set the preferences for the ADMET Plot on the ADMET Plot subpage of the Preferences dialog.

# Create 3D QSAR Model - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_3d_qsar_model-para.htm

## Create 3D QSAR Model - Parameters

### Builds a 3D QSAR user model using partial least squares regression

Drug design involves finding small molecules that are complementary in shape (steric) and charge (electrostatic) to a bio-molecular target. Regression models built from whole molecular steric and electrostatic fields can be useful for predicting activity and for visualizing favorable and unfavorable interactions.

A Partial Least-Squares (PLS) model is built using energy grids as descriptors. The energy grids are computed using two probe types designed to measure electrostatic and steric effects. A user model is created, named according to Model Name , that can be used to predict the activity of unknown ligands.

Notes:

* The probe types used are steric (a van der Waals carbon) and electrostatic (a positive point charge H + ).

* The accuracy of the model depends on the activity range and the diversity of the ligands. Ligands with a narrow range of activity or that are highly diverse may give poor results.

* A good alignment is very important for the analysis of molecular fields. It is assumed that the molecules have been pre-aligned.

* The most uncorrelated descriptors are selected. A correlation threshold is applied for the selection. To avoid extremely large (or small) values of grid energy values, the grid points which are less than 1.5 Å or greater than 4.0 Å from any ligand atom are removed. An energy cutoff of 5.0 kcal is applied for the remaining grids.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. Note: To build a 3D QSAR model, the input ligands must have an activity property for each molecule. |
| Input Test Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Model Name | Name of the model to build. This also becomes the name of the property that can be calculated using the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. |
| Activity Property | The property name of the activity being learned. |
| Ligand Partial Charge Method | Specifies method for assigning partial charges to the ligands during forcefield assignment. The following options are supported: CHARMm: Uses Momany-Rone method (a set of bond-charge-increment rules) for assigning atom partial charges. CFF: Uses the charging rules used in the CFF forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. MMFF: Uses the charging rules used in the MMFF94 forcefield for assigning atom partial charges. VAMP ESP: Uses the partial charge derived from the electrostatic potential calculated by the semi-empirical quantum chemistry program VAMP. AM1 method is used with RHF wavefunctions. VAMP Mulliken: Uses the partial charge derived from Mulliken population analysis in VAMP. AM1 method is used with RHF wavefunctions. Existing: Uses existing atom partial charges specified in an array property. Valid Values: CHARMm , MMFF, CFF, VAMP ESP, VAMP Mulliken, Existing |
| Partial Charge Property | An array property specifying the partial charges for each atom. |
| Grid Spacing | Grid spacing (Å) for CHARMm energy grids. |
| Maximum Descriptor Correlation | The maximum correlation coefficient between two descriptors. Only the first descriptor is kept, if their correlation coefficient is greater than this value. The number of descriptors is also capped at 1000 in order to keep the run time reasonable. |
| Cross Validation | Whether to perform cross validation on the model. In a cross validation, the train set is split into a number of groups. Each group is left out in turn; a model is built with the remaining data, and the model is used to make predictions for the left-out data. Valid Values: True , False |
| Cross Validation Folds | The number of groups into which the data should be split for cross validation. Notes: The larger the folds, the longer it takes to perform the cross validation. To do a leave-one-out cross validation, set the folds to a number much larger than the number of samples. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Grid Extension | Grid extension beyond ligand bounds (Å). The algorithm first calculates the smallest containing box around the ligand. Each side of the box is then extended by this Grid Extension (Grid Extension / 2 in each direction). |
| Number of Components | Number of desired components (for Partial-Least-Squares). A higher number can improve the root-mean-square error for the training set, but has the potential to reduce the predictivity of the model. If cross validation is on, this number will be set according to the cross validation result to give the optimal performance. |
| Keep Grids in Output SD File | Keep CHARMm grid properties in the output SD file. If set true, this will also keep the grid properties when the model is applied. Valid Values: True, False |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance.

Note:

* To build a 3D QSAR model, the input ligands must have an activity property for each molecule.

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional.

# Create Bayesian Model - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_bayesian_model-para.htm

## Create Bayesian Model - Parameters

### Builds a user model using Bayesian categorization

Uses Bayesian categorization to build a model that distinguishes between "good" and "bad" ligands. "Good" ligands are defined by having a value of "1" for the property set by Property for Active .

A user model is created, named according to Model Name . The model can be used to predict how "good" ligands are using Calculate Molecular Properties.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Test Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Property for Active | This is used to identify ligands that are active or with "good" property. A unit (1) value for this property indicates that the ligand is active. Absence of this field or a value other than 1 indicates inactive. |
| Model Name | Name of the model to build. This also becomes the name of the property that can be calculated using the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. The model can be shared with your colleagues. See Also: More details on the model sharing can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation. |
| Independent Properties | List of properties to use as independent variables in building model. Both fingerprint and numeric properties can be used. |
| Calculable Properties | Add molecular properties that can be calculated on the fly to the list of independent properties so that you do not have to precompute them. |
| User Properties | Properties from a user specific source. For properties that can be calculated on the fly, use Calculable Properties . |
| Cross Validation | Whether to perform cross validation on the model. In a cross validation, the train set is split into a number of groups. Each group is left out in turn; a model is built with the remaining data, and the model is used to make predictions for the left-out data. Valid Values: True , False |
| Cross Validation Folds | The number of groups into which the data should be split for cross validation. Notes: The larger the folds, the longer it takes to perform the cross validation. To do a leave-one-out cross validation, set the folds to a number much larger than the number of samples. |
| Learn Options | Specifies additional preferences affecting the building of the model and information saved with the model. Options are: Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. This allows you to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data using Pipeline Pilot. In addition, you can determine the distance of a sample to the closest training samples when making predictions with the model. For identifying training samples, the model uses the Name property. If no such property exists in your training data, the names Train1 , Train2 , etc. are used. The "Save Training Properties" option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data. Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for rebuilding the model, but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component. Track Property Ranges: Tracks the ranges of property values seen in the input data in order to alert you to any out-of-range values found when you make predictions with the model. This helps indicate the model's domain of applicability and the degree to which you can trust the predicted values. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when the value of any property is outside the range of that property's values in the training data. If you wish to also track structural features of the data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking. Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model as an indicator of the model's applicability when making predictions. The OPS approach typically results in tighter boundaries around the training data than does simply tracking the property ranges. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions with the model on new data, the model output indicates whether each new sample lies within or outside the training data range for each principal component. If you wish to also track structural features of the data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking. If you select this option, you do not need to select "Track Property Ranges"; the property range tracking is done as part of the OPS analysis. Validate Models: Computes leave-one-out cross-validation statistics and add this information to the model component help. This is different from the k-fold cross validation, which is done separately. This option should be selected in order to generate the ROC score information. Remove Uninformative Bins: Removes bins that make only a small contribution to the model score (smaller in magnitude than 0.05). This decreases the amount of disk space required to save the model component. Ignore Uninformative Bins: Retains bins that make only a small contribution to the model score, but ignore these bins when making predictions. Scores obtained with this option are identical to those with "remove Uninformative Bins", but retaining the extra information allows formerly uninformative bins to become informative when adding new data to the model. Equipopulate Bins: Subdivides continuous variables so that each bin contains roughly the same number of samples. Notes: The Bayesian method used by this learner is highly efficient and can create a model from even hundreds of thousands of data records in a short time. By contrast, the PCA calculation required by the "Perform OPS Analysis" option is much slower and can increase the learning time by an order of magnitude or more for a large training set. It is best to use this option by re-training from the same data set after you have validated a model built with this learner and have decided to keep the model for later use. For models created by this learner, it is not strictly necessary to specify "Save Training Properties" in order to extend the model with new data in Pipeline Pilot. However, if you wish to obtain cross-validation statistics for the extended model, you must save the training properties. See Also: For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." You can find it at http://patft.uspto.gov/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm the US Patent Number Search site. Valid Values: Save Training Properties, Encrypt Data, Track Property Ranges, Perform OPS Analysis, Validate Models , Remove Uninformative Bins , Ignore Uninformative Bins, Equipopulate Bins |
| Model Domain Fingerprint | Name of fingerprint property to use in order to determine whether a test sample is within the applicability domain of the learned model. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model. Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6 |
| Additional Properties | Comma-separated list of properties to be saved with the model when "Save Training Properties" is selected as one of the Learn Options . These properties are in addition to those used to build the model, as specified by UseProperties . When making predictions with the model, the values of the Additional Properties are shown for the closest training samples when you select the "_ClosestSample" option from the list of available outputs on the model component. Notes: If you have selected "Encrypt Data" as one of the Learn Options for greater data security, make sure you do not subvert this security by including properties in the Additional Properties list that reveal more than you wish to about your training samples. In the model output with the "_ClosestSample" option, each property in Additional Properties is renamed to ModelName _Closest_ PropertyName where PropertyName is the original name of the property. If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Number of Bins | Number of bins to divide them into for continuous variables. |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional.

This is used to identify ligands that are active or with "good" property. A unit (1) value for this property indicates that the ligand is active. Absence of this field or a value other than 1 indicates inactive.

See Also:

* More details on the model sharing can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation.

List of properties to use as independent variables in building model. Both fingerprint and numeric properties can be used.

Add molecular properties that can be calculated on the fly to the list of independent properties so that you do not have to precompute them.

Properties from a user specific source. For properties that can be calculated on the fly, use Calculable Properties .

Whether to perform cross validation on the model.

In a cross validation, the train set is split into a number of groups. Each group is left out in turn; a model is built with the remaining data, and the model is used to make predictions for the left-out data.

Valid Values: True , False

Notes:

* The larger the folds, the longer it takes to perform the cross validation.

* To do a leave-one-out cross validation, set the folds to a number much larger than the number of samples.

* Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. This allows you to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data using Pipeline Pilot. In addition, you can determine the distance of a sample to the closest training samples when making predictions with the model. For identifying training samples, the model uses the Name property. If no such property exists in your training data, the names Train1 , Train2 , etc. are used. The "Save Training Properties" option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data.

* Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for rebuilding the model, but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component.

* Track Property Ranges: Tracks the ranges of property values seen in the input data in order to alert you to any out-of-range values found when you make predictions with the model. This helps indicate the model's domain of applicability and the degree to which you can trust the predicted values. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when the value of any property is outside the range of that property's values in the training data. If you wish to also track structural features of the data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking.

* Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model as an indicator of the model's applicability when making predictions. The OPS approach typically results in tighter boundaries around the training data than does simply tracking the property ranges. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions with the model on new data, the model output indicates whether each new sample lies within or outside the training data range for each principal component. If you wish to also track structural features of the data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking. If you select this option, you do not need to select "Track Property Ranges"; the property range tracking is done as part of the OPS analysis.

* Validate Models: Computes leave-one-out cross-validation statistics and add this information to the model component help. This is different from the k-fold cross validation, which is done separately. This option should be selected in order to generate the ROC score information.

* Remove Uninformative Bins: Removes bins that make only a small contribution to the model score (smaller in magnitude than 0.05). This decreases the amount of disk space required to save the model component.

* Ignore Uninformative Bins: Retains bins that make only a small contribution to the model score, but ignore these bins when making predictions. Scores obtained with this option are identical to those with "remove Uninformative Bins", but retaining the extra information allows formerly uninformative bins to become informative when adding new data to the model.

* Equipopulate Bins: Subdivides continuous variables so that each bin contains roughly the same number of samples.

* The Bayesian method used by this learner is highly efficient and can create a model from even hundreds of thousands of data records in a short time. By contrast, the PCA calculation required by the "Perform OPS Analysis" option is much slower and can increase the learning time by an order of magnitude or more for a large training set. It is best to use this option by re-training from the same data set after you have validated a model built with this learner and have decided to keep the model for later use.

* For models created by this learner, it is not strictly necessary to specify "Save Training Properties" in order to extend the model with new data in Pipeline Pilot. However, if you wish to obtain cross-validation statistics for the extended model, you must save the training properties.

* For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." You can find it at http://patft.uspto.gov/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm the US Patent Number Search site.

Valid Values: Save Training Properties, Encrypt Data, Track Property Ranges, Perform OPS Analysis, Validate Models , Remove Uninformative Bins , Ignore Uninformative Bins, Equipopulate Bins

Name of fingerprint property to use in order to determine whether a test sample is within the applicability domain of the learned model. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model.

Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6

* If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output.

# Create Bayesian Model

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_bayesian_model.htm

## Create Bayesian Model

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Create Bayesian Model protocol can build a Bayesian categorization model that distinguishes active ligands from baseline ligands. The model
may be based on numeric, fingerprint or textual properties. Once created, it appears in the Other group in the Molecular Properties dialog in the Calculate
Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands.

* Open the Small Molecules | Create QSAR Model tools and click Create Bayesian Model to open the Create Bayesian Model dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Property for Active Specify which ligands are active molecules. For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Bayesian Model - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Property for Active | Specify which ligands are active molecules. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Bayesian Model - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Cross validation is a good method for measuring the predictive performance of a statistical model. See Cross Validation .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| <ligands>.sd | Output ligands with additional properties added by the model generation. | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| ViewROCPlot.ds_pl | Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) plot of the input ligands. Information about the ROC plot, such as the area under the curve (XV ROC), can be found in the ModelDescription.html file. The value indicates how often the model correctly identifies the true positive and the true negative. It can be used to classify the accuracy of the model used to generate an ROC curve: XV ROC value Model rating 0.90-1 excellent (A) 0.80-0.90 good (B) 0.70-0.80 fair (C) 0.60-0.70 poor (D) 0.50-0.60 fail (F) | XV ROC value | Model rating | 0.90-1 | excellent (A) | 0.80-0.90 | good (B) | 0.70-0.80 | fair (C) | 0.60-0.70 | poor (D) | 0.50-0.60 | fail (F) |

| 0.90-1 | excellent (A) | | | | | | | | | | | | |

| ModelDescription.html | Contains important information about the model and training set including leave-one-out cross-validation, ROC plots, true/false positives, and true/false and negatives. | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| GoodAndBadFingerprints.html | This file is generated if the model used FCFP or ECFP fingerprints. The file contains images of the top 20 fingerprints that made the most positive contribution to the model as well as images of the top 20 that made the most negative contribution to the model. | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| Bayesian-Bin-Info.txt | Contains information of the feature statistics including which bins provided the most positive and negative information. | | | | | | | | | | | | |

# Create Genetic Function Approximation Model - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_genetic_function_approximation_model-para.htm

## Create Genetic Function Approximation Model - Parameters

### Builds a user model using genetic function approximation

Uses Genetic Function Approximation (GFA) to build QSAR or QSPR user model(s). GFA user models contain Number of Models equations. Each equation can be used separately to predict Dependent Property , or together in an ensemble prediction, using Calculate Molecular Properties.

A user model is created, named according to Model Name .

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Test Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Model Name | Name of the model to build. This also becomes the name of the property that can be calculated using the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. The model can be shared with your colleagues. If there are more than one model specified in the Number of Models parameter, the names of the properties calculable by these models are named with a suffix of ModelName_N , where N is the sequential number of the model. The ensemble from all models are called ModelName_AllNames and ModelName_AllValues . The applicability of these models is given in a property ModelName_Applicability . See Also: More details on the model sharing can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation. |
| Dependent Property | Name of the numerical property to be learned. Note: If the property specified by Dependent Property is an array, values in the array are treated as replicate measurements. If your experimental data contain replicates, this offers a concise way to represent the data, without the need for a separate data record for each replicate. |
| Independent Properties | List of properties to use as independent variables in building model. Both fingerprint and numeric properties can be used. |
| Calculable Properties | Add molecular properties that can be calculated on the fly to the list of independent properties so that you do not have to precompute them. |
| User Properties | Properties from a user specific source. For properties that can be calculated on the fly, use Calculable Properties . |
| Number of Models | Specifies the number of top models out of the entire population to be returned at the end of the model evolution process. This is different from the population size during the model evolution. |
| Model Options | Options controlling the types of terms that may appear in each model in the population |
| Model Form | Specifies the functional form of the model. Options are: Linear: Models contain only the original properties on the data stream, with no product terms. Binary Interaction: Models may contain (quadratic) products of different properties on the data stream in addition to linear terms. For N properties, this gives rise to N(N−1)/2 additional terms that may be included in the models. Simple Quadratic: Models may contain the product of each property with itself (but no products between different properties) in addition to linear terms. For N properties, this gives rise to N additional terms. Full Quadratic: Models may contain both binary interaction and simple quadratic terms in addition to linear terms. For N properties, this gives rise to N(N+1)/2 additional terms. Simple Cubic: Models may contain both the squares and cubes of each property in addition to linear terms. For N properties, this gives rise to 2N additional terms. Full Cubic: Models may contain any term consisting of the product of up to 3 properties in any combination. For example, for properties A, B, and C, the terms A, A 2 , AB, B 3 , ABC, A 2 B, etc. may be included in a model. For N properties, this gives rise to N(N+1)(N+5)/6 additional terms. Notes: Take care in choosing options other than Linear when you have a large number of properties in your data set, especially when the number of data records is also large. Some options can generate very large numbers of terms that may overwhelm your computer's memory or result in long calculation times. For example, with 50 independent properties, the Full Quadratic option yields 1275 extra terms, while the Full Cubic option yields 23375 extra terms. Apart from computer resource limitations, if the number of additional terms is many times larger than the population size, then many potential terms will never appear in the population, and so effectively will not be available for selection. For any array property used in model building, each array member is treated as a separate variable. For any fingerprint property, each distinct fingerprint feature or bit is treated as a separate variable with a value of 0 if the feature is absent on a given data record or 1 if it is present. For a fingerprint count property, the value for each feature is the same as its count. Valid Values: Linear , Binary Interaction, Simple Quadratic, Full Quadratic, Simple Cubic, Full Cubic |
| Additional Terms | Specifies additional terms to consider for inclusion in equations generated by the GFA. Options are: Linear Splines Quadratic Splines Valid Values: Linear Splines, Quadratic Splines |
| Initial Equation Length | Specifies the number of terms in each model for the first generation. (This number does not include the constant term.) |
| Maximum Equation Length | Specifies the maximum number of terms allowed in a model. (This number does not include the constant term, if present.) |
| Constant Equation Length | Specifies whether the number of terms in each model equation is fixed. If True, then all models in the population have the same number of terms, as specified by Initial Equation Length . If False, then the number of terms can vary. The learner can increase the equation length if the extra terms provide better accuracy, or decrease the equation length by eliminating terms that do not significantly improve the accuracy. Valid Values: True, False |
| GFA Options | Options controlling the learning process |
| Population Size | Specifies the total number of model equations in the evolving population |
| Maximum Generations | Specify the maximum number of evolutionary steps to perform in order to improve the quality of the models in the population. This should be set as large as possible, because the evolution stops once it reaches the convergence. |
| Scoring Method | Specifies the method to use for ranking the model equations in the population. In general, adding an extra term to an equation increases the accuracy of its fit to the training data, but makes the equation more complex and risks over-fitting-meaning the equation is less likely to have predictive accuracy for samples outside the training set. The following options provide alternative approaches for managing the tradeoff between equation size and fitting accuracy: Single Score: Uses a single score specified by the Score Function to rank the equations. Equations with high scores are carried forward to the next generation, while equations with low scores are dropped. Pareto (NSGA-II): Uses Pareto optimization of the entire population of equations to obtain a distribution of models ranging from those with fewer terms that fit the training data less-well to those with a greater number of terms that fit the data better (but at the risk of over-fitting). Score Function specifies the score used to determine the quality of fit. This option uses the NSGA-II algorithm for the Pareto optimization. Valid Values: Single Score , Pareto (NSGA-II) |
| Score Function | Specifies the scoring function used to rank model equations in the population when Scoring Method is set to "Single Score" or to determine the accuracy score when Scoring Method is set to a Pareto option. Options are: Friedman Lack-of-Fit: Uses a modified version of Friedman's lack-of-fit (LOF) measure. This scales the mean-squared error with a penalty factor based on the complexity of the model in order to reduce the risk of over-fitting. R-squared: Uses the coefficient of determination, R 2 . Beware that this option imposes no penalty for over-fitting. Thus, if you use this option, you should be sure to set Maximum Equation Length to a value much smaller than the number of samples. Adjusted R-squared: Uses R 2 adj . This option penalizes equations containing too many terms to justify their quality of fit. F Statistic: The F statistic is used to evaluate the statistical significance of a regression model. In general, the larger the value of F, the more statistically significant is the model equation. Notes: The equations used to calculate the various scoring functions are as follows: LOF = ∑(y i −ŷ i ) 2 / {N − 0.99[p + dC(N − p max ) / p max ]} 2 where the sum is over all training samples; y i is the value of the dependent variable for sample i; ŷ i is the value of y predicted by the model for sample i; N is the number of samples; p is the number of terms in the equation, excluding any constant term; d is the LOF Smoothness Parameter ; C is a measure equation complexity equal to the total number of features (variables) in the equation; and p max is the Maximum Equation Length . R 2 = 1 − ∑(y i −ŷ i ) 2 / ∑(y i − y ) 2 where y is the mean value of y. R 2 adj = 1 − (1 − R 2 ) (N − 1) / (N − p − 1) F = [∑(ŷ i − y ) 2 / p] / [∑(y i −ŷ i ) 2 / (N − p − 1)] No correction is applied to the scores to compensate for the fact that the GFA algorithm considers large numbers of potential models before arriving at the final set. This multiplicity increases the risk of accidental correlation between terms in a model equation and the response. Thus, any of the above scores is likely to be optimistic if used to assess the predictive performance of a model (as opposed to the purpose here of ranking potential models relative to one another). Predictive performance is best assessed with a test set of data separate from the training data. See Also: For the form of and justification for Friedman's original LOF measure, see "Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines," Annals of Statistics , 19 , pp. 1-141 (1991). For a modified version similar to the one used here, see "Application of Genetic Function Approximation to Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationships and Quantitative Structure-Property Relationships," by D. Rogers and A.J. Hopfinger, J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 34 , pp. 854-866 (1994). Valid Values: Friedman Lack-of-Fit , R-squared, Adjusted R-squared, F Statistic |
| LOF Smoothness Parameter | Smoothness parameter used in evaluating the Friedman lack-of-fit measure. Larger values cause larger models to be penalized to a greater degree. Valid range is between 0 and 1. |
| Additional Options | Contains less commonly used parameters |
| Random Seed | Seed for random number generator |
| Learn Options | Specifies additional preferences affecting the building of the model and information saved with the model. Options are: Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. If you have access to Pipeline Pilot, this allows you to use New Model from Old to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data. This option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data. Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for extending the model (Pipeline Pilot is required), but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component. Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model in order to establish the model's applicability domain. If you then choose the modelname _Applicability output when making predictions with the model on new data, the model output indicates whether each new sample is within or outside the training data range. Track Fingerprint Features: Tracks features of the fingerprint specified by Model Domain Fingerprint , as well as any other fingerprint properties used to build your model. If you choose the modelname _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when a sample contains any fingerprint feature not seen in the training data, or lacks any feature appearing in all of the training samples. See Also: For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." You can find it at http://patft.uspto.gov/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm , the US Patent Number Search site. Valid Values: Save Training Properties, Encrypt Data, Perform OPS Analysis , Track Fingerprint Features |
| Model Domain Fingerprint | Name of fingerprint property to use for indicating whether a test sample is within the applicability domain of the learned model. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model. Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6 |
| Additional Properties | Comma-separated list of properties to be saved with the model when "Save Training Properties" is selected as one of the Learn Options . These properties are in addition to those used to build the model, as specified by UseProperties . When making predictions with the model, the values of the Additional Properties are shown for the closest training samples when you select the "_ClosestSample" option from the list of available outputs on the model component. Notes: If you have selected "Encrypt Data" as one of the Learn Options for greater data security, make sure you do not subvert this security by including properties in the Additional Properties list that reveal more than you wish to about your training samples. In the model output with the "_ClosestSample" option, each property in Additional Properties is renamed to ModelName _Closest_ PropertyName where PropertyName is the original name of the property. If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output. |
| Minimum Samples Per Variable | Minimum number of samples that must have non-zero values for a property to be used in building the model. SqrtEstimate uses the square root of the number of samples. Valid Values: NoMinimum, OneSample, FourSamples, TenSamples, SqrtEstimate |
| Maximum Correlation | Maximum allowed magnitude of the correlation coefficient between any two variables in the input data. If the absolute value of the correlation is greater than or equal to this value, the second variable is not used for model building. |
| GFA Progress Interval | Interval in number of generations between which to write variable usage data to the progress file. |
| Number of Variables in GFA Progress | Number of variables for which variable usage data are to be reported. The variables chosen are those which occur in the most models in the final population. |
