* Apart from computer resource limitations, if the number of additional terms is many times larger than the population size, then many potential terms will never appear in the population, and so effectively will not be available for selection.

* For any array property used in model building, each array member is treated as a separate variable.

* For any fingerprint property, each distinct fingerprint feature or bit is treated as a separate variable with a value of 0 if the feature is absent on a given data record or 1 if it is present. For a fingerprint count property, the value for each feature is the same as its count.

Valid Values: Linear , Binary Interaction, Simple Quadratic, Full Quadratic, Simple Cubic, Full Cubic

Specifies additional terms to consider for inclusion in equations generated by the GFA.

Options are:

* Linear Splines

* Quadratic Splines

Valid Values: Linear Splines, Quadratic Splines

Specifies the number of terms in each model for the first generation. (This number does not include the constant term.)

Specifies the maximum number of terms allowed in a model. (This number does not include the constant term, if present.)

Specifies whether the number of terms in each model equation is fixed.

If True, then all models in the population have the same number of terms, as specified by Initial Equation Length .

If False, then the number of terms can vary. The learner can increase the equation length if the extra terms provide better accuracy, or decrease the equation length by eliminating terms that do not significantly improve the accuracy.

Valid Values: True, False

Options controlling the learning process

Specifies the total number of model equations in the evolving population

Specify the maximum number of evolutionary steps to perform in order to improve the quality of the models in the population. This should be set as large as possible, because the evolution stops once it reaches the convergence.

Specifies the method to use for ranking the model equations in the population. In general, adding an extra term to an equation increases the accuracy of its fit to the training data, but makes the equation more complex and risks over-fitting-meaning the equation is less likely to have predictive accuracy for samples outside the training set. The following options provide alternative approaches for managing the tradeoff between equation size and fitting accuracy:

* Single Score: Uses a single score specified by the Score Function to rank the equations. Equations with high scores are carried forward to the next generation, while equations with low scores are dropped.

* Pareto (NSGA-II): Uses Pareto optimization of the entire population of equations to obtain a distribution of models ranging from those with fewer terms that fit the training data less-well to those with a greater number of terms that fit the data better (but at the risk of over-fitting). Score Function specifies the score used to determine the quality of fit. This option uses the NSGA-II algorithm for the Pareto optimization.

Valid Values: Single Score , Pareto (NSGA-II)

Specifies the scoring function used to rank model equations in the population when Scoring Method is set to "Single Score" or to determine the accuracy score when Scoring Method is set to a Pareto option. Options are:

* Friedman Lack-of-Fit: Uses a modified version of Friedman's lack-of-fit (LOF) measure. This scales the mean-squared error with a penalty factor based on the complexity of the model in order to reduce the risk of over-fitting.

* R-squared: Uses the coefficient of determination, R 2 . Beware that this option imposes no penalty for over-fitting. Thus, if you use this option, you should be sure to set Maximum Equation Length to a value much smaller than the number of samples.

* Adjusted R-squared: Uses R 2 adj . This option penalizes equations containing too many terms to justify their quality of fit.

* F Statistic: The F statistic is used to evaluate the statistical significance of a regression model. In general, the larger the value of F, the more statistically significant is the model equation.

* The equations used to calculate the various scoring functions are as follows:

* LOF = ∑(y i −ŷ i ) 2 / {N − 0.99[p + dC(N − p max ) / p max ]} 2 where the sum is over all training samples; y i is the value of the dependent variable for sample i; ŷ i is the value of y predicted by the model for sample i; N is the number of samples; p is the number of terms in the equation, excluding any constant term; d is the LOF Smoothness Parameter ; C is a measure equation complexity equal to the total number of features (variables) in the equation; and p max is the Maximum Equation Length .

* R 2 = 1 − ∑(y i −ŷ i ) 2 / ∑(y i − y ) 2 where y is the mean value of y.

* R 2 adj = 1 − (1 − R 2 ) (N − 1) / (N − p − 1)

* F = [∑(ŷ i − y ) 2 / p] / 
[∑(y i −ŷ i ) 2 / (N − p − 1)]

* No correction is applied to the scores to compensate for the fact that the GFA algorithm considers large numbers of potential models before arriving at the final set. This multiplicity increases the risk of accidental correlation between terms in a model equation and the response. Thus, any of the above scores is likely to be optimistic if used to assess the predictive performance of a model (as opposed to the purpose here of ranking potential models relative to one another). Predictive performance is best assessed with a test set of data separate from the training data.

* For the form of and justification for Friedman's original LOF measure, see "Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines," Annals of Statistics , 19 , pp. 1-141 (1991). For a modified version similar to the one used here, see "Application of Genetic Function Approximation to Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationships and Quantitative Structure-Property Relationships," by D. Rogers and A.J. Hopfinger, J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 34 , pp. 854-866 (1994).

Valid Values: Friedman Lack-of-Fit , R-squared, Adjusted R-squared, F Statistic

Smoothness parameter used in evaluating the Friedman lack-of-fit measure. Larger values cause larger models to be penalized to a greater degree. Valid range is between 0 and 1.

Contains less commonly used parameters

Seed for random number generator

* Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. If you have access to Pipeline Pilot, this allows you to use New Model from Old to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data. This option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data.

* Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for extending the model (Pipeline Pilot is required), but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component.

* Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model in order to establish the model's applicability domain. If you then choose the modelname _Applicability output when making predictions with the model on new data, the model output indicates whether each new sample is within or outside the training data range.

* Track Fingerprint Features: Tracks features of the fingerprint specified by Model Domain Fingerprint , as well as any other fingerprint properties used to build your model. If you choose the modelname _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when a sample contains any fingerprint feature not seen in the training data, or lacks any feature appearing in all of the training samples.

* For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." You can find it at http://patft.uspto.gov/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm , the US Patent Number Search site.

Valid Values: Save Training Properties, Encrypt Data, Perform OPS Analysis , Track Fingerprint Features

Name of fingerprint property to use for indicating whether a test sample is within the applicability domain of the learned model. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model.

Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6

Comma-separated list of properties to be saved with the model when "Save Training Properties" is selected as one of the Learn Options . These properties are in addition to those used to build the model, as specified by UseProperties . When making predictions with the model, the values of the Additional Properties are shown for the closest training samples when you select the "_ClosestSample" option from the list of available outputs on the model component.

* If you have selected "Encrypt Data" as one of the Learn Options for greater data security, make sure you do not subvert this security by including properties in the Additional Properties list that reveal more than you wish to about your training samples.

* In the model output with the "_ClosestSample" option, each property in Additional Properties is renamed to ModelName _Closest_ PropertyName where PropertyName is the original name of the property.

* If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output.

Minimum number of samples that must have non-zero values for a property to be used in building the model. SqrtEstimate uses the square root of the number of samples.

Valid Values: NoMinimum, OneSample, FourSamples, TenSamples, SqrtEstimate

Maximum allowed magnitude of the correlation coefficient between any two variables in the input data. If the absolute value of the correlation is greater than or equal to this value, the second variable is not used for model building.

Interval in number of generations between which to write variable usage data to the progress file.

Number of variables for which variable usage data are to be reported. The variables chosen are those which occur in the most models in the final population.

* Setting up and running

The Create Genetic Function Approximation protocol will build a QSAR or QSPR model using the selected molecular descriptors. Once created, it
appears in the Other group in the Molecular Properties dialog in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future
ligands.

Model Name Once created, this model will appear under the Other category of the Molecular Properties parameter in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for
future ligands. For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Genetic Function Approximation Model - Parameters . If the Number Of Models parameter is set to a number greater than 1 (it is 10 by default), multiple GFA equations will be created. In this case, you will see multiple entries in the Molecular
Properties parameter, which is used in several protocols (e.g., Calculate Molecular Properties . Numbers are appended to the model name to differentiate them.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Model Name | Once created, this model will appear under the Other category of the Molecular Properties parameter in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Genetic Function Approximation Model - Parameters .

If the Number Of Models parameter is set to a number greater than 1 (it is 10 by default), multiple GFA equations will be created. In this case, you will see multiple entries in the Molecular
Properties parameter, which is used in several protocols (e.g., Calculate Molecular Properties . Numbers are appended to the model name to differentiate them.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Contains output ligands with additional properties added by the model generation. By default only the best model is applied to the ligands. Additional models can be accessed through the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. In addition to the prediction, the model also calculates an estimated error of the prediction result in a column Model_Name_error, where Model_Name is the name given in the Model Name parameter. |
| ModelDescription.html | Contains important information about the model and training set including model and input summaries, QSAR model equations, and model validation. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Compares the predicted property with the modeled property. |
| ViewVariableCounts.ds_pl | Plot of the occurrence of variables within the population against the generation. Only variables with the highest counts during the final generation are included. Also, the set of variables for the usage counts can only be determined at the end of the calculation. To alleviate these problems, the usage count information is collected for more variables than are plotted. |
| GFAVariableCounts.csv | The data file containing information about the occurrence of variables within the population against the generation. It is used by ViewVariableCounts.ds_pl . |
| GFATempModel.xml | Contains the built model which can be shared with colleagues, the name of this file is set in the Model Name parameter. |

### Builds a user model using multiple linear regression

Uses multiple linear regression to build a QSAR or QSPR user model.

A user model is created, named according to Model Name . The model can be used to predict the Dependent Property using Calculate Molecular Properties.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Test Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Model Name | Name of the model to build. This also becomes the name of the property that can be calculated using Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. The model can be shared with your colleagues. See Also: More details on the model sharing can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation. |

| Weight Property | Name of property containing weight of each molecule for constructing a weighted-least-squares model. If no Weight Property is specified, all samples are weighted equally. |
| Independent Properties | List of properties to use as independent variables in building model. Both fingerprint and numeric properties can be used. |
| Calculable Properties | Add molecular properties that can be calculated on the fly to the list of independent properties so that you do not have to precompute them. |

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Create Multiple Linear Regression Model protocol builds a Multiple Linear Regression model for a dependent property using the selected
molecular descriptors. Once created, it appears in the Other group in the Molecular Properties dialog in the Calculate
Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands.

Multiple Linear Regression requires at least as many molecules as independent variables.
Reliable results typically require 5 times as many molecules as independent variables.
Use Partial Least Squares when there are
a large number of independent variables.

For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Multiple Linear Regression Model - Parameters .

Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model. Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6 |
| Additional Properties | Comma-separated list of properties to be saved with the model when "Save Training Properties" is selected as one of the Learn Options . These properties are in addition to those used to build the model, as specified by UseProperties . When making predictions with the model, the values of the Additional Properties are shown for the closest training samples when you select the "_ClosestSample" option from the list of available outputs on the model component. Notes: If you have selected "Encrypt Data" as one of the Learn Options for greater data security, make sure you do not subvert this security by including properties in the Additional Properties list that reveal more than you wish to about your training samples. In the model output with the "_ClosestSample" option, each property in Additional Properties is renamed to ModelName _Closest_ PropertyName where PropertyName is the original name of the property. If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output. |
| Minimum Samples per Variable | Minimum number of samples that must have non-zero values so a property can be used in building the model. "SqrtEstimate" uses the square root of the number of samples. Valid Values: NoMinimum, OneSample, FourSamples, TenSamples, SqrtEstimate |
| Number of Components | The number of desired components (also known as latent variables) to use in PLS regression. If cross validation is on, this number will be set according to the cross validation result to give the optimal performance. |
| Maximum Correlation | Maximum allowed magnitude of the Pearson or Tanimoto correlation between any two variables in the input data. If the absolute value of the correlation is greater than or equal to this value, the second variable is not used for model building. |

In a cross validation, the train set is split into a number of groups. Each group is left out in turn; a model is built with the remaining data, and the model is used to make predictions for the left-out data.

In a PLS model, cross-validation is also used to select an optimal number of components to use in the final model built with all input ligands.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

* Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. If you have access to Pipeline Pilot, this allows you to use New Model from Old to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data. This option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data.

* Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model in order to establish the model's applicability domain. * Track Fingerprint Features: Tracks features of the fingerprint specified by Model Domain Fingerprint , as well as any other fingerprint properties used to build your model. If you choose the modelname _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when a sample contains any fingerprint feature not seen in the training data, or lacks any feature appearing in all of the training samples.

# Create Partial Least Squares Model

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_partial_least_squares_model.htm

## Create Partial Least Squares Model

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Create Partial Least Squares Model protocol will build a Partial Least Squares model for a dependent property using the selected molecular
descriptors. Once created, it appears in the Other group in the Molecular Properties dialog in the Calculate
Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands.

* Open the Small Molecules | Create QSAR Model tools and click Create Partial Least Squares Model to open the Create Partial Least Squares Model dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Model Name Once created, this model will appear under the Other
category of the Molecular Properties parameter in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property
for future ligands. For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Partial Least Squares Model - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Model Name | Once created, this model will appear under the Other category of the Molecular Properties parameter in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Partial Least Squares Model - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

Cross validation is a good method for measuring the predictive performance of a statistical model. See Cross Validation .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | The output ligands with additional properties added by the model generation. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opening this file allows you to compare the predicted property with the modeled property. |
| ModelDescription.html | Contains important information about the model and training set. |
| PLSTempModel.xml | Contains the built model which can be shared with colleagues. This file name is set in the Model Name parameter. |

#### Further information

Theory - Small Molecules Calculate Molecular Properties Share QSAR models
