# Create Recursive Partitioning Model - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_recursive_partitioning_model-para.htm

## Create Recursive Partitioning Model - Parameters

### Builds a user model using recursive partitioning

Uses recursive partitioning method to build a QSAR or QSPR user model.

A user model is created, named according to Model Name . The model can be used to predict the Dependent Property using the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Test Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Model Name | Name of the model to build. This also becomes the name of the property that can be calculated using Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. If there are multiple dependent properties, each dependent property is appended to the model name with an underscore to form the new property name calculable by this model. The model can be shared with your colleagues. See Also: More details on the model sharing can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation. |
| Dependent Property | Name of the categorical property to be learned. To learn multiple properties in the same model, select more than one property or enter a comma-separated list of property names. Only single RP tree model without cross-validation can be selected for multiple properties learning. |
| Independent Properties | List of properties to use as independent variables in building model. Both fingerprint and numeric properties can be used. |
| Calculable Properties | Add molecular properties that can be calculated on the fly to the list of independent properties so that you do not have to precompute them. |
| Keep Calculated Properties | Whether to add these properties to the output sd file. Valid Values: True, False |
| User Properties | Properties from a user specific source. For properties that can be calculated on the fly, use Calculable Properties . |
| Model Type | The type of recursive partitioning model to build. You can build either single tree models or forest models comprising multiple trees. Single-tree models tend to be less-accurate predictors but more interpretable compared to multi-tree Forest models. Each type has many different configurations. You can build single tree models of the following types: Traditional tree models as described in Classification and Regression Trees (full reference in notes below). The default parameter values with cross-validation set to false yield a model of this type. Lookahead models. A lookahead model considers multiple alternative splits at each tree node to avoid getting stuck with a split that is locally optimal, but globally sub-optimal when splits further down the tree are considered. To build a lookahead model, set Maximum Lookahead Depth under Advanced Tree Options to a value greater than 0. Multi-Y models. A multi-Y model supports predictions for two or more dependent (Y) classification properties using the same tree. Such a model can be useful in determining common features that affect the different Y properties-e.g., for selectivity studies. To build a multi-Y model, set Dependent Property to a comma-separated list of property names. Set Maximum Generic Depth under Advanced Tree Options to a number greater than 0. You can build forest models of the following types: Bagged Forest. Contains a relatively small number of trees (e.g., 10) using a separate bootstrap sample of the original data for each tree. All descriptors are considered as possible splitting criteria for each node. The default parameter values yield a model of this type. (Also, Weighting Method is set to "By Class" by default, in order to compensate for imbalanced data.) Forest of Random Trees. Contains a large number of trees (e.g., 500) using a separate bootstrap sample of the original data for each tree. A random subset of the descriptors is considered as splitting criteria for each node. For D descriptors, the default number selected is the square-root of D. (Set Number of Descriptors to Sqrt(D) to build a model of this type.) Weighted Forest of Random Trees. A variant of the above method which is appropriate for imbalanced data sets in which the number of members of the most-desirable class (the minority class ) is far fewer than the number of members of other classes. Members of the minority class are given a greater weight in determining the best splits and in determining the predicted class for each node in the tree. (Set Number of Descriptors to Sqrt(D), Weighting Method to "By Class", and Equalize Class Sizes to False for this method.) Balanced Forest of Random Trees. Another method appropriate for imbalanced data. In this method, the learner ensures that for each tree, the number of members of each class is equal to the number of members of the minority class. (Set Number of Descriptors to Sqrt(D), Weighting Method to "Uniform", and Equalize Class Sizes to True for this method.) Notes: Cross-validation is not supported for multi-Y models. Building cross-validated models is much slower than building models without cross-validation. E.g., if you use 5 cross-validation folds, it takes roughly 5-times longer to build a cross-validated model than one without cross-validation. An excellent introduction to recursive partitioning tree models is Classification and Regression Trees by Breiman, Friedman, Olshen, and Stone (Chapman & Hall, 1984). For a description of the patented PUMP-RP method for multi-Y tree models, see T.P. Stockfisch, "Partially Unified Multiple Property Recursive Partitioning (PUMP-RP): A New Method for Predicting and Understanding Drug Selectivity," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 43 , 1608-1613 (2003). The method used here differs from the one described in the paper in that "generic" splits are made whenever possible down to a node depth given by Maximum Generic Depth . See also U.S. patent number 7,016,887. For a description of the lookahead method, see U.S. patent number 7,269,597. Forest models do not require cross-validation because they are not pruned, and the out-of-bag (OOB) statistics reported by the learner provide an estimate of the models' predictive ability. Forest models tend to be more accurate at prediction but less directly interpretable than single-tree models. The enhanced accuracy comes from a cancellation of random errors when predictions of multiple trees in the forest are averaged together. The decreased interpretability is due to the relative ease of visually understanding the structure of a single tree compared to the structures of tens or hundreds of trees. However, one aid to interpretability available for forest models but not single-tree models is a set of descriptor importance measures, which indicate the relative importance of different properties or features in distinguishing among the different classes in the data. In most cases, a "descriptor" is the same as a property on the data record. However, in the case of fingerprints, each distinct fingerprint feature is treated as a separate descriptor for the purpose of descriptor sampling and for descriptor importance measures. Some of the importance measures reported for forest models are known to be biased in certain situations. See the reference below for more details. The lookahead and multi-Y methods available for single-tree models are not available for forest models. An excellent introduction to recursive partitioning tree models is Classification and Regression Trees by Breiman, Friedman, Olshen, and Stone (Chapman & Hall, 1984). For more on the bagging approach, see "Bagging Predictors" by L. Breiman at http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/breiman96bagging.html . The forest of random trees (a.k.a., Random Forest™) method for building multi-tree forest models is described at http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forest . (Random Forest is a trademark of Leo Breiman and Adele Cutler.) For the weighted and balanced forest of random trees methods, see "Using Random Forest to Learn Imbalanced Data" by C. Chen, A. Liaw, and L. Breiman (available on the internet at http://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/sdtr/ucb/text/666.pdf ). For issues of bias in descriptor importance measures, see "Bias in random forest variable importance measures: Illustrations, sources and a solution," by C. Strobl, A.-L. Boulesteix, A. Zeileis, and T. Hothorn, BMC Bioinformatics, 8 , p. 25 (2007), which can be found at http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2105/8/25 . Valid Values: Single Tree , Forest |
| Cross Validation | Whether to perform cross validation on the model. In a cross validation, the train set is split into a number of groups. Each group is left out in turn; a model is built with the remaining data, and the model is used to make predictions for the left-out data. This is only applicable to a single tree model. A forest model does cross validation intrinsically. Valid Values: True , False |
| Cross Validation Folds | The number of groups into which the data should be split for cross validation. The larger the folds, the longer it takes to perform the cross validation. |
| Tree Options | Options governing the building of individual trees in the model |
| Minimum Samples Per Node | The minimum number of samples that must be present in a new node for the node to be added to the tree |
| Maximum Tree Depth | The maximum number of levels in a tree. Larger values tend to increase accuracy on the training data and decrease the time required to build the model, but at the risk of over-fitting. Smaller values tend to increase the applicability of a tree to new data sets, but at the risk of decreased accuracy and of failing to identify important features in the training data. |
| Split Method | Method to be used for ranking the desirability of splits in the data. Options are: Gini: Uses the Gini index as a measure of the increase in node purity as the result of a split. Node purity is the degree to which a node contains members of only one class (i.e., category), as opposed to multiple classes. Splits that result in purer nodes are more desirable. Entropy: Uses the decrease in entropy as a measure of node purity as the result of a split. Twoing: Measures the degree to which a split results in two subsets of equal size while nevertheless separating different classes into separate nodes. This option is most useful for data sets with multiple (4 or more) classes. Valid Values: Gini , Entropy, Twoing |
| Weighting Method | Specifies the scheme to use in order to determine the relative importance of a sample in determining the predicted class for each node in the tree. Options are: Uniform: Each sample is weighted equally. The class for a node is simply the class represented by the greatest number of samples in the node. This is an appropriate option for balanced data sets-i.e., data sets in which the numbers of samples in each class is approximately the same. (For forest models, this is also the appropriate option for unbalanced data if you have set Equalize Class Sizes to True.) By Class: Each class is weighted equally. The class for a node is the class with the greatest weighted sum of samples in the node. This option is appropriate for unbalanced data sets, especially if the most-desirable class has far fewer samples than other classes. Example: A data set contains 100 members of class A and 200 members of class B. If "By Class" is specified, then each A sample is assigned a weight of 1.5 and each B sample a weight of 0.75. A node containing 10 A samples and 12 B samples has a predicted class of A because the weighted sum for class A (10×1.5 = 15) exceeds the weighted sum for class B (12×0.75 = 9). Valid Values: Uniform, By Class |
| Advanced Tree Options | Contains additional options governing the building of individual trees in the model. These include options for lookahead and multi-Y (PUMP-RP) models. |
| Maximum Knots Per Property | Specifies the maximum number of potential split points for each numerical property in the training data. Larger values increase the model building time, but may also increase the model accuracy. (For a property, X, a split point, S, is a value of X used to split the data in a tree node such that samples with X<S go to one child node, and samples with X≥S go to the other child node.) |
| Maximum Lookahead Depth | Maximum depth to which lookahead splits will be considered. Normally, a node is split by a single criterion (or not at all). In the lookahead case, multiple alternative splits are considered. The idea is that the "best" split criterion considering only the data in the current node might not be the best when considering the splits available to the child nodes. Lookahead allows alternative pathways to be explored, until the tree reaches Maximum Lookahead Depth . (Due to the computer memory and time consumed by the resulting "combinatorial explosion", this value should be kept fairly small.) The number of alternative splits at each point is given by Number of Lookahead Alternatives . After the tree is grown, the single best split is selected for each node based on the overall misclassification error. |
| Number of Lookahead Alternatives | If Maximum Lookahead Depth is greater than zero, the number of alternative splits to consider at each node above this depth |
| Maximum Generic Depth | In a tree model with multiple values for Dependent Property (i.e., a multi-Y model), the maximum depth for a "generic" node. A generic node is one whose split criterion considers all dependent (Y) variables. (This is by contrast with a "specific" node, for which a split criterion considers only a single dependent variable.) See Also: For more on multi-Y tree models, see T.P. Stockfisch, "Partially Unified Multiple Property Recursive Partitioning (PUMP-RP): A New Method for Predicting and Understanding Drug Selectivity," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 43 , 1608-1613 (2003). |
| Generic Node Weighting | Generality parameter (β) for a multi-Y tree. Gives the weight to assign a generic node when minimizing the following function during tree pruning: R = R 0 + α*(N leaves - β*N generic ) where R 0 is the misclassification error against the training data for the pruned tree; α is the complexity penalty factor; N leaves is the number of leaf nodes in the tree, and N generic is the number of generic nodes in the tree. |
| Forest Options | Options governing the building of forest (i.e., multi-tree) models. |
| Number of Trees | Total number of trees in the forest model. If set to 1, then a single-tree model is built, and the remaining Forest Options are ignored. |
| Ensemble Method | Method to use in constructing forest. Options are: Bagging: Short for "Bootstrap AGgregation". For each tree, a bootstrap sample of the original data is taken, and this sample is used to grow the tree. A bootstrap sample is a data set of the same size as the original one, but in which the same data record can be included multiple times. Excluding duplicates, a bootstrap sample on average contains about 63% of the original data records. Data excluded from the sample are called out-of-bag (OOB) data and can be used in model validation. Bagging with Duplicates Removed: Similar to Bagging except that duplicate data records are removed from each bootstrap sample. This may reduce bias. See Also: For information on bias in bootstrap sampling generally, see H. Steck and T.S. Jaakkola, "Bias-Corrected Bootstrap and Model Uncertainty" (Available online at http://people.csail.mit.edu/tommi/papers/SteJaa-nips03.pdf ). For information on bias in forest models, see C. Strobl et al., "Bias in random forest variable importance measures: Illustrations, sources and a solution" (Available online at http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2105/8/25 ). Valid Values: Bagging , Bagging with Duplicates Removed |
| Equalize Class Sizes | For the Bagging Ensemble Method , specifies whether to ensure that the number of samples for each class is equal in the data set used to train each tree. For forest models created from unbalanced training sets, this is generally a better alternative to the "By Class" Weighting Method , as it has the effect of both increasing the predictive accuracy and decreasing the time required for model building. Example: Suppose the input data contains 50 members of class A and 500 members of class B. If Equalize Class Sizes is set to True, then the data set used for each tree in the forest is a separate random sample containing 50 class A members and 50 class B members. As in the usual bootstrap sample, the sampling is done "with replacement"-i.e., duplicates are permitted for both the A and B class members. Valid Values: True, False |
| Number of Descriptors | Specifies the number of descriptor properties to consider for use as a split criterion within each tree. For options other than All, a separate random subset of the properties is selected at each node for which a split is possible. Options are: All: all properties are considered as possible split criteria. Sqrt(D): if the number of descriptors is D, then the number of descriptors considered at each node is the square root of D. Log2(D): the number of descriptors considered at each node is the base-2 logarithm of D. Fraction: a given proportion of descriptors, specified by Fraction , is considered at each node. Fixed Number: a fixed number of descriptors, specified by Fixed Number , is considered at each node. Notes: For fingerprint properties, each distinct fingerprint feature is considered a separate descriptor when counting the number of descriptors and selecting descriptor subsets. A forest model built with an Ensemble Method of Bagging and any of the above options other than All is a "random forest" model as defined by Breiman and Cutler. See https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ breiman/RandomForests/cc_home.htm . (Random Forests(TM) is a trademark of Leo Breiman and Adele Cutler.) Valid Values: All , Sqrt(D), Log2(D), Fraction, Fixed Number |
| Number of Descriptors Fraction | The fraction (between 0 and 1) of descriptors to consider at each potential split point when Number of Descriptors is set to Fraction. |
| Number of Descriptors Fixed Number | The number of descriptors to consider at each potential split point when Number of Descriptors is set to "Fixed Number". |
| Learn Options | Specifies additional preferences affecting the building of the model and information saved with the model. Options are: Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. This allows you to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data. In addition, you can determine the distance of a sample to the closest training samples when making predictions with the model. (Use Numeric Distance Function to specify the distance measure to use.) For identifying training samples, the model uses the Name property. If no such property exists in your training data, the names Train1 , Train2 , etc. are used. The "Save Training Properties" option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data. Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for rebuilding the model, but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component. Track Property Ranges: Tracks the ranges of property values seen in the input data in order to alert you to any out-of-range values found when you make predictions with the model. This helps indicate the model's domain of applicability and the degree to which you can trust the predicted values. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when the value of any property is outside the range of that property's values in the training data. If you wish to also track structural features of molecular data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking. Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model as an indicator of the model's applicability when making predictions. The OPS approach typically results in tighter boundaries around the training data than does simply tracking the property ranges. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions with the model on new data, the model output indicates whether each new sample lies within or outside the training data range for each principal component. If you wish to also track structural features of the data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking. If you select this option, you do not need to select "Track Property Ranges"; the property range tracking is done as part of the OPS analysis. See Also: For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." You can find it at http://patft.uspto.gov/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm the US Patent Number Search site. Valid Values: Save Training Properties, Encrypt Data, Track Property Ranges, Perform OPS Analysis |
| Numeric Distance Function | For numeric properties and categorical properties other than fingerprints, specifies the function to use for computing the distance between two data records. This distance is used by the built model to determine the closest training samples when you specify that the model should output the closest samples. The expressions for the following distance functions assume that each record has numerical properties x 1 , x 2 ,…, with x 1A , x 2A ,… the values for record A and x 1B , x 2B ,… the values for record B. Options and their mathematical definitions are: Euclidean: Distance (D) is the square-root of the sum of squared differences between corresponding property values: D = [∑(x iA − x iB ) 2 ] 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 upward. Manhattan: Distance is the sum of the absolute value of the differences between corresponding property values: D = ∑\|x iA − x iB \|. Possible values range from 0 upward. Mahalanobis: A generalization of the Euclidean distance that accounts for correlations between different properties. The distance is defined as: D = [∑(x iA − x iB )( S −1 ) ij (x jA − x jB )] 1/2 , where S −1 is the inverse of the covariance matrix for the entire data set. Possible values range from 0 upward. One Minus Correlation: Distance is 1 minus the Pearson correlation coefficient http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation between the vectors of property values for the two records. Possible values range from 0 to 2. (With two or fewer properties on each record, this is not a meaningful distance function.) One Minus Squared Correlation: Distance is 1 minus the square of the Pearson correlation coefficient between the vectors of property values for the two records. Use this function if you wish both strong correlation and strong anti-correlation to indicate that two records are "near". Possible values range from 0 to 1. (With two or fewer properties on each record, this is not a meaningful distance function.) Cosine: Distance is 1 minus the cosine of the angle between the vectors defined by the properties of the two records: D = 1 − ∑x iA x iB / [∑(x iA ) 2 ∑(x iB ) 2 ] 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 to 2. Dice: Distance is a generalization to continuous properties of the Dice distance for binary fingerprints: D = 1 − 2 ∑x iA x iB / [∑(x iA ) 2 + ∑(x iB ) 2 ]. Possible values range from 0 to 2. Tanimoto: Distance is a generalization to continuous properties of the Tanimoto distance for binary fingerprints: D = 1 − ∑x iA x iB / [∑(x iA ) 2 + ∑(x iB ) 2 − ∑x iA x iB ]. Possible values range from 0 to 1.3333. Notes: For Euclidean, Manhattan, and Mahalanobis distances, the difference between two string (categorical) values is considered 0 if the strings are identical, or 1 if they are not. For Cosine, Dice, and Tanimoto distances, the product of two string values is considered 1 if the strings are identical, or 0 if they are not. String properties are ignored for both correlation options. If a property is an array, then differences or products are taken element-by-element for the entire array. If the array on one record is shorter than on the other, unmatched elements of the longer array are ignored. For the Mahalanobis option, if the data are so highly-correlated that the covariance matrix is singular or nearly so, then the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse ( http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore-Penrose_pseudoinverse ) is used instead of the inverse. If even the pseudoinverse cannot be computed (due to SVD http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition non-convergence), an error occurs. In this case, you must use an alternative distance function. If you specify both numeric and fingerprint properties to use in the distance calculations, separate contributions to the distance are computed for the two types of property. The overall distance is the average of the two: D = 0.5(D numeric + D FP ). Take care to specify appropriate Numeric Scaling options for this case in order to prevent one or the other of these distance contributions from dominating. See Also: For more on several of the distance measures described here, see: P. Willett, J.M. Barnard, and G.M. Downs, "Chemical Similarity Searching," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 38 , 983 (1998), see http://www.dddc.ac.cn/embo04/material/Willett_1998.pdf For more on the Mahalanobis distance, see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalanobis_distance Valid Values: Euclidean , Manhattan, Mahalanobis, One Minus Correlation, One Minus Squared Correlation, Cosine, Dice, Tanimoto |
| Numeric Scaling | Settings controlling the scaling of numeric data when computing distances. Options are: Mean-Center and Scale: Shifts and scales each property to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. For Euclidean, Manhattan, Cosine, Dice, and Tanimoto distances, this is a recommended option, as it puts all numeric properties on equal footing. Without such scaling, properties with a large typical magnitude (e.g., 1000) dominate the calculated distance, while properties with a small typical magnitude (e.g., 1) have minimal effect. (For Mahalanobis and correlation distances, this option has no effect on the calculated distance.) Scale by Number of Dimensions: For Euclidean, Manhattan, and Mahalanobis distances only, divides the computed distance by P (Manhattan) or P 1/2 (Euclidean and Mahalanobis), where P is the number of properties (or total number of elements if some properties are arrays). This ensures that the typical magnitude of computed distances remains unchanged as you vary the number of properties in the calculation. Correct for Missing Values: For Euclidean and Manhattan distances only, multiplies the computed distance by P exp /P (Manhattan) or (P exp /P) 1/2 (Euclidean), where P exp is the expected number of properties (or expected total number of elements if some properties are arrays) in the absence of missing values. This ensures that the typical magnitude of computed distances remains unchanged when some properties are missing. Specifically, it ensures that distances to data records with missing properties are not unusually small as an artifact of the missing data. This option does not apply if "Scale by Number of Dimensions" is selected, as that option already corrects for missing properties implicitly. If none of the above options are selected, no rescaling is applied to the data. This is appropriate if all numeric properties already have the same characteristic scale or represent components of a vector in the same space (e.g., spatial x, y, z coordinates), and no properties are missing from any of the data records. Notes: If you specify more than one fingerprint property to use in the distance calculation, then the "Scale by Number of Dimensions" and "Correct for Missing Values" options apply to the fingerprint component of distance as well as to the numeric component. Specifically, Pfp and Pfp exp are used in the scaling of the summed fingerprint distances, where Pfp is the number of fingerprint properties and Pfp exp is the expected number. "Scale by Number of Dimensions" also applies to fingerprint distances when you specify Euclidean or Manhattan as the Fingerprint Distance Function . In this case, the distance for each fingerprint property is divided by C (Manhattan) or C 1/2 (Euclidean), where C is the total count of features over both data records (i.e., the "or" bit count). Valid Values: Mean-Center and Scale , Scale by Number of Dimensions , Correct for Missing Values |
| Fingerprint Distance Function | For fingerprint properties, specifies the function to use for computing the distance between two data records. This distance is used by the built model to determine the closest training samples when you specify that the model should output the closest samples. The expressions for the following distance functions assume that each record has a single fingerprint property, with quantities SA, SB, and SC defined as follows: SA: Number of fingerprint features common to both records. (Number of "and" bits.) SB: Number of features present in the first record but absent from the second. SC: Number of features present in the second record but absent from the first. Options and their mathematical definitions are: Cosine: Distance (D) is 1 minus the cosine of the angle between the two fingerprints when treated as binary vectors (vectors whose elements must be 0 or 1): D = 1 − SA / [(SA + SB)(SA + SC)] 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 to 1. Dice: Distance is 1 minus the number of "and" bits scaled by the mean number of "on" bits for both records: D = 1 − 2 SA / (2SA + SB + SC). Possible values range from 0 to 1. Tanimoto: Distance is 1 minus the number of "and" bits scaled by the number of "or" bits: D = 1 − SA / (SA + SB + SC). Possible values range from 0 to 1. Euclidean: Distance is the square-root of the number of "on" bits in the squared difference between the two fingerprints when treated as vectors. For a binary fingerprint, this can be expressed as: D = (SB + SC) 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 to the total number of features possible in a single fingerprint. Manhattan: Distance is the number of "on" bits in the absolute difference between the two fingerprints when treated as vectors. For a binary fingerprint, this can be expressed as: D = SB + SC. Possible values range from 0 to the total number of features possible in a single fingerprint. Notes: When more than one fingerprint property is present, a separate distance value is computed for each, and the results are summed or averaged (depending on the Numeric Scaling options). If you specify both numeric and fingerprint properties to use in the distance calculations, separate contributions to the distance are computed for the two types of property. The overall distance is the average of the two: D = 0.5(D numeric + D FP ). Take care to specify appropriate Numeric Scaling options for this case in order to prevent one or the other of these distance contributions from dominating. See Also: For more on the distance measures described here, see: http://www.dddc.ac.cn/embo04/material/Willett_1998.pdf P. Willett, J.M. Barnard, and G.M. Downs, "Chemical Similarity Searching," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 38 , 983 (1998). Also see: J.C. Gower, "Measures of Similarity, Dissimilarity, and Distance," in Encyclopedia of Statistical Sciences , S. Kotz, N.L. Johnson, Read C.B., eds., Vol. 5, p. 397 (1985). Valid Values: Cosine, Dice, Tanimoto , Euclidean, Manhattan |
| Model Domain Fingerprint | Name of fingerprint property to use in order to determine whether a test sample is within the applicability domain of the learned model. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model. Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6 |
| Additional Properties | Comma-separated list of properties to be saved with the model when "Save Training Properties" is selected as one of the Learn Options . These properties are in addition to those used to build the model, as specified by UseProperties . When making predictions with the model, the values of the Additional Properties are shown for the closest training samples when you select the "_ClosestSample" option from the list of available outputs on the model component Notes: If you have selected "Encrypt Data" as one of the Learn Options for greater data security, make sure you do not subvert this security by including properties in the Additional Properties list that reveal more than you wish to about your training samples. In the model output with the "_ClosestSample" option, each property in Additional Properties is renamed to ModelName _Closest_ PropertyName where PropertyName is the original name of the property. If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Random Seed | Seed for random number generator. |
| View Results | Option to view all trees or only the best tree. Not applicable for forest model. Valid Values: Best Tree, All Trees |

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files
that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation.

In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected,
or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file
offers the best performance.

Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. These ligands are used to test the performance of the model in the external validation step. This step is optional.

Name of the model to build. This also becomes the name of the property that can be calculated using Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. If there are multiple dependent properties, each dependent property is appended to the model name with an underscore to form the new property name calculable by this model. The model can be shared with your colleagues.

See Also:

* More details on the model sharing can be found in the Discovery Studio documentation.

Name of the categorical property to be learned. To learn multiple properties in the same model, select more than one property or enter a comma-separated list of property names. Only single RP tree model without cross-validation can be selected for multiple properties learning.

List of properties to use as independent variables in building model. Both fingerprint and numeric properties can be used.

Add molecular properties that can be calculated on the fly to the list of independent properties so that you do not have to precompute them.

Whether to add these properties to the output sd file.

Valid Values: True, False

Properties from a user specific source. For properties that can be calculated on the fly, use Calculable Properties .

The type of recursive partitioning model to build.

You can build either single tree models or forest models comprising multiple trees. Single-tree models tend to be less-accurate predictors but more interpretable compared to multi-tree Forest models. Each type has many different configurations.

You can build single tree models of the following types:

* Traditional tree models as described in Classification and Regression Trees (full reference in notes below). The default parameter values with cross-validation set to false yield a model of this type.

* Lookahead models. A lookahead model considers multiple alternative splits at each tree node to avoid getting stuck with a split that is locally optimal, but globally sub-optimal when splits further down the tree are considered.
To build a lookahead model, set Maximum Lookahead Depth under Advanced Tree Options to a value greater than 0.

* Multi-Y models. A multi-Y model supports predictions for two or more dependent (Y) classification properties using the same tree. Such a model can be useful in determining common features that affect the different Y properties-e.g., for selectivity studies.
To build a multi-Y model, set Dependent Property to a comma-separated list of property names. Set Maximum Generic Depth under Advanced Tree Options to a number greater than 0.

You can build forest models of the following types:

* Bagged Forest. Contains a relatively small number of trees (e.g., 10) using a separate bootstrap sample of the original data for each tree. All descriptors are considered as possible splitting criteria for each node. The default parameter values yield a model of this type. (Also, Weighting Method is set to "By Class" by default, in order to compensate for imbalanced data.)

* Forest of Random Trees. Contains a large number of trees (e.g., 500) using a separate bootstrap sample of the original data for each tree. A random subset of the descriptors is considered as splitting criteria for each node. For D descriptors, the default number selected is the square-root of D. (Set Number of Descriptors to Sqrt(D) to build a model of this type.)

* Weighted Forest of Random Trees. A variant of the above method which is appropriate for imbalanced data sets in which the number of members of the most-desirable class (the minority class ) is far fewer than the number of members of other classes. Members of the minority class are given a greater weight in determining the best splits and in determining the predicted class for each node in the tree. (Set Number of Descriptors to Sqrt(D), Weighting Method to "By Class", and Equalize Class Sizes to False for this method.)

* Balanced Forest of Random Trees. Another method appropriate for imbalanced data. In this method, the learner ensures that for each tree, the number of members of each class is equal to the number of members of the minority class. (Set Number of Descriptors to Sqrt(D), Weighting Method to "Uniform", and Equalize Class Sizes to True for this method.)

Notes:

* Cross-validation is not supported for multi-Y models.

* Building cross-validated models is much slower than building models without cross-validation. E.g., if you use 5 cross-validation folds, it takes roughly 5-times longer to build a cross-validated model than one without cross-validation.

* An excellent introduction to recursive partitioning tree models is Classification and Regression Trees by Breiman, Friedman, Olshen, and Stone (Chapman & Hall, 1984).

* For a description of the patented PUMP-RP method for multi-Y tree models, see T.P. Stockfisch, "Partially Unified Multiple Property Recursive Partitioning (PUMP-RP): A New Method for Predicting and Understanding Drug Selectivity," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 43 , 1608-1613 (2003). The method used here differs from the one described in the paper in that "generic" splits are made whenever possible down to a node depth given by Maximum Generic Depth . See also U.S. patent number 7,016,887.

* For a description of the lookahead method, see U.S. patent number 7,269,597.

* Forest models do not require cross-validation because they are not pruned, and the out-of-bag (OOB) statistics reported by the learner provide an estimate of the models' predictive ability.

* Forest models tend to be more accurate at prediction but less directly interpretable than single-tree models. The enhanced accuracy comes from a cancellation of random errors when predictions of multiple trees in the forest are averaged together. The decreased interpretability is due to the relative ease of visually understanding the structure of a single tree compared to the structures of tens or hundreds of trees. However, one aid to interpretability available for forest models but not single-tree models is a set of descriptor importance measures, which indicate the relative importance of different properties or features in distinguishing among the different classes in the data.

* In most cases, a "descriptor" is the same as a property on the data record. However, in the case of fingerprints, each distinct fingerprint feature is treated as a separate descriptor for the purpose of descriptor sampling and for descriptor importance measures.

* Some of the importance measures reported for forest models are known to be biased in certain situations. See the reference below for more details.

* The lookahead and multi-Y methods available for single-tree models are not available for forest models.

* For more on the bagging approach, see "Bagging Predictors" by L. Breiman at http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/breiman96bagging.html .

* The forest of random trees (a.k.a., Random Forest™) method for building multi-tree forest models is described at http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forest . (Random Forest is a trademark of Leo Breiman and Adele Cutler.)

* For the weighted and balanced forest of random trees methods, see "Using Random Forest to Learn Imbalanced Data" by C. Chen, A. Liaw, and L. Breiman (available on the internet at http://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/sdtr/ucb/text/666.pdf ).

* For issues of bias in descriptor importance measures, see "Bias in random forest variable importance measures: Illustrations, sources and a solution," by C. Strobl, A.-L. Boulesteix, A. Zeileis, and T. Hothorn, BMC Bioinformatics, 8 , p. 25 (2007), which can be found at http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2105/8/25 .

Valid Values: Single Tree , Forest

Whether to perform cross validation on the model.

In a cross validation, the train set is split into a number of groups. Each group is left out in turn; a model is built with the remaining data, and the model is used to make predictions for the left-out data.

This is only applicable to a single tree model. A forest model does cross validation intrinsically.

Valid Values: True , False

The number of groups into which the data should be split for cross validation. The larger the folds, the longer it takes to perform the cross validation.

Options governing the building of individual trees in the model

The minimum number of samples that must be present in a new node for the node to be added to the tree

The maximum number of levels in a tree. Larger values tend to increase accuracy on the training data and decrease the time required to build the model, but at the risk of over-fitting. Smaller values tend to increase the applicability of a tree to new data sets, but at the risk of decreased accuracy and of failing to identify important features in the training data.

Method to be used for ranking the desirability of splits in the data. Options are:

* Gini: Uses the Gini index as a measure of the increase in node purity as the result of a split. Node purity is the degree to which a node contains members of only one class (i.e., category), as opposed to multiple classes. Splits that result in purer nodes are more desirable.

* Entropy: Uses the decrease in entropy as a measure of node purity as the result of a split.

* Twoing: Measures the degree to which a split results in two subsets of equal size while nevertheless separating different classes into separate nodes. This option is most useful for data sets with multiple (4 or more) classes.

Valid Values: Gini , Entropy, Twoing

Specifies the scheme to use in order to determine the relative importance of a sample in determining the predicted class for each node in the tree. Options are:

* Uniform: Each sample is weighted equally. The class for a node is simply the class represented by the greatest number of samples in the node. This is an appropriate option for balanced data sets-i.e., data sets in which the numbers of samples in each class is approximately the same. (For forest models, this is also the appropriate option for unbalanced data if you have set Equalize Class Sizes to True.)

* By Class: Each class is weighted equally. The class for a node is the class with the greatest weighted sum of samples in the node. This option is appropriate for unbalanced data sets, especially if the most-desirable class has far fewer samples than other classes. Example: A data set contains 100 members of class A and 200 members of class B. If "By Class" is specified, then each A sample is assigned a weight of 1.5 and each B sample a weight of 0.75. A node containing 10 A samples and 12 B samples has a predicted class of A because the weighted sum for class A (10×1.5 = 15) exceeds the weighted sum for class B (12×0.75 = 9).

Valid Values: Uniform, By Class

Contains additional options governing the building of individual trees in the model. These include options for lookahead and multi-Y (PUMP-RP) models.

Specifies the maximum number of potential split points for each numerical property in the training data. Larger values increase the model building time, but may also increase the model accuracy.

(For a property, X, a split point, S, is a value of X used to split the data in a tree node such that samples with X<S go to one child node, and samples with X≥S go to the other child node.)

Maximum depth to which lookahead splits will be considered.

Normally, a node is split by a single criterion (or not at all). In the lookahead case, multiple alternative splits are considered. The idea is that the "best" split criterion considering only the data in the current node might not be the best when considering the splits available to the child nodes. Lookahead allows alternative pathways to be explored, until the tree reaches Maximum Lookahead Depth . (Due to the computer memory and time consumed by the resulting "combinatorial explosion", this value should be kept fairly small.)

The number of alternative splits at each point is given by Number of Lookahead Alternatives . After the tree is grown, the single best split is selected for each node based on the overall misclassification error.

If Maximum Lookahead Depth is greater than zero, the number of alternative splits to consider at each node above this depth

In a tree model with multiple values for Dependent Property (i.e., a multi-Y model), the maximum depth for a "generic" node. A generic node is one whose split criterion considers all dependent (Y) variables. (This is by contrast with a "specific" node, for which a split criterion considers only a single dependent variable.)

* For more on multi-Y tree models, see T.P. Stockfisch, "Partially Unified Multiple Property Recursive Partitioning (PUMP-RP): A New Method for Predicting and Understanding Drug Selectivity," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 43 , 1608-1613 (2003).

Generality parameter (β) for a multi-Y tree. Gives the weight to assign a generic node when minimizing the following function during tree pruning:

R = R 0 + α*(N leaves - β*N generic )

where R 0 is the misclassification error against the training data for the pruned tree; α is the complexity penalty factor; N leaves is the number of leaf nodes in the tree, and N generic is the number of generic nodes in the tree.

Options governing the building of forest (i.e., multi-tree) models.

Total number of trees in the forest model. If set to 1, then a single-tree model is built, and the remaining Forest Options are ignored.

Method to use in constructing forest. Options are:

* Bagging: Short for "Bootstrap AGgregation". For each tree, a bootstrap sample of the original data is taken, and this sample is used to grow the tree. A bootstrap sample is a data set of the same size as the original one, but in which the same data record can be included multiple times. Excluding duplicates, a bootstrap sample on average contains about 63% of the original data records. Data excluded from the sample are called out-of-bag (OOB) data and can be used in model validation.

* Bagging with Duplicates Removed: Similar to Bagging except that duplicate data records are removed from each bootstrap sample. This may reduce bias.

* For information on bias in bootstrap sampling generally, see H. Steck and T.S. Jaakkola, "Bias-Corrected Bootstrap and Model Uncertainty" (Available online at http://people.csail.mit.edu/tommi/papers/SteJaa-nips03.pdf ).

* For information on bias in forest models, see C. Strobl et al., "Bias in random forest variable importance measures: Illustrations, sources and a solution" (Available online at http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2105/8/25 ).

Valid Values: Bagging , Bagging with Duplicates Removed

For the Bagging Ensemble Method , specifies whether to ensure that the number of samples for each class is equal in the data set used to train each tree. For forest models created from unbalanced training sets, this is generally a better alternative to the "By Class" Weighting Method , as it has the effect of both increasing the predictive accuracy and decreasing the time required for model building.

Example:

Suppose the input data contains 50 members of class A and 500 members of class B. If Equalize Class Sizes is set to True, then the data set used for each tree in the forest is a separate random sample containing 50 class A members and 50 class B members. As in the usual bootstrap sample, the sampling is done "with replacement"-i.e., duplicates are permitted for both the A and B class members.

Specifies the number of descriptor properties to consider for use as a split criterion within each tree. For options other than All, a separate random subset of the properties is selected at each node for which a split is possible. Options are:

* All: all properties are considered as possible split criteria.

* Sqrt(D): if the number of descriptors is D, then the number of descriptors considered at each node is the square root of D.

* Log2(D): the number of descriptors considered at each node is the base-2 logarithm of D.

* Fraction: a given proportion of descriptors, specified by Fraction , is considered at each node.

* Fixed Number: a fixed number of descriptors, specified by Fixed Number , is considered at each node.

* For fingerprint properties, each distinct fingerprint feature is considered a separate descriptor when counting the number of descriptors and selecting descriptor subsets.

* A forest model built with an Ensemble Method of Bagging and any of the above options other than All is a "random forest" model as defined by Breiman and Cutler. See https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~ breiman/RandomForests/cc_home.htm . (Random Forests(TM) is a trademark of Leo Breiman and Adele Cutler.)

Valid Values: All , Sqrt(D), Log2(D), Fraction, Fixed Number

The fraction (between 0 and 1) of descriptors to consider at each potential split point when Number of Descriptors is set to Fraction.

The number of descriptors to consider at each potential split point when Number of Descriptors is set to "Fixed Number".

Specifies additional preferences affecting the building of the model and information saved with the model. Options are:

* Save Training Properties: Saves the properties of the training data in the model component for later use. This allows you to rebuild the model with new data added to the original data. In addition, you can determine the distance of a sample to the closest training samples when making predictions with the model. (Use Numeric Distance Function to specify the distance measure to use.) For identifying training samples, the model uses the Name property. If no such property exists in your training data, the names Train1 , Train2 , etc. are used. The "Save Training Properties" option increases the on-disk size of the model component in proportion to the quantity of training data.

* Encrypt Data: If saving training properties, specifies that the data are to be encrypted to prevent direct access. The data will still be available for rebuilding the model, but will not be recoverable in unencrypted form from the model component.

* Track Property Ranges: Tracks the ranges of property values seen in the input data in order to alert you to any out-of-range values found when you make predictions with the model. This helps indicate the model's domain of applicability and the degree to which you can trust the predicted values. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions, you are warned when the value of any property is outside the range of that property's values in the training data. If you wish to also track structural features of molecular data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking.

* Perform OPS Analysis: Performs a principal components analysis to determine the optimum prediction space (OPS) of the model as an indicator of the model's applicability when making predictions. The OPS approach typically results in tighter boundaries around the training data than does simply tracking the property ranges. If you choose the ModelName _Applicability output when making predictions with the model on new data, the model output indicates whether each new sample lies within or outside the training data range for each principal component. If you wish to also track structural features of the data, use Model Domain Fingerprint to specify the molecular fingerprint to use for feature tracking. If you select this option, you do not need to select "Track Property Ranges"; the property range tracking is done as part of the OPS analysis.

* For more on the optimum prediction space approach, see U.S. Patent 6,036,349, "Method and apparatus for validation of model-based predictions." You can find it at http://patft.uspto.gov/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm the US Patent Number Search site.

Valid Values: Save Training Properties, Encrypt Data, Track Property Ranges, Perform OPS Analysis

For numeric properties and categorical properties other than fingerprints, specifies the function to use for computing the distance between two data records. This distance is used by the built model to determine the closest training samples when you specify that the model should output the closest samples.

The expressions for the following distance functions assume that each record has numerical properties x 1 , x 2 ,…, with x 1A , x 2A ,… the values for record A and x 1B , x 2B ,… the values for record B.

Options and their mathematical definitions are:

* Euclidean: Distance (D) is the square-root of the sum of squared differences between corresponding property values: D = [∑(x iA − x iB ) 2 ] 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 upward.

* Manhattan: Distance is the sum of the absolute value of the differences between corresponding property values: D = ∑|x iA − x iB |. Possible values range from 0 upward.

* Mahalanobis: A generalization of the Euclidean distance that accounts for correlations between different properties. The distance is defined as: D = [∑(x iA − x iB )( S −1 ) ij (x jA − x jB )] 1/2 , where S −1 is the inverse of the covariance matrix for the entire data set. Possible values range from 0 upward.

* One Minus Correlation: Distance is 1 minus the Pearson correlation coefficient http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation between the vectors of property values for the two records. Possible values range from 0 to 2. (With two or fewer properties on each record, this is not a meaningful distance function.)

* One Minus Squared Correlation: Distance is 1 minus the square of the Pearson correlation coefficient between the vectors of property values for the two records. Use this function if you wish both strong correlation and strong anti-correlation to indicate that two records are "near". Possible values range from 0 to 1. (With two or fewer properties on each record, this is not a meaningful distance function.)

* Cosine: Distance is 1 minus the cosine of the angle between the vectors defined by the properties of the two records: D = 1 − ∑x iA x iB / [∑(x iA ) 2 ∑(x iB ) 2 ] 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 to 2.

* Dice: Distance is a generalization to continuous properties of the Dice distance for binary fingerprints: D = 1 − 2 ∑x iA x iB / [∑(x iA ) 2 + ∑(x iB ) 2 ]. Possible values range from 0 to 2.

* Tanimoto: Distance is a generalization to continuous properties of the Tanimoto distance for binary fingerprints: D = 1 − ∑x iA x iB / [∑(x iA ) 2 + ∑(x iB ) 2 − ∑x iA x iB ]. Possible values range from 0 to 1.3333.

* For Euclidean, Manhattan, and Mahalanobis distances, the difference between two string (categorical) values is considered 0 if the strings are identical, or 1 if they are not. For Cosine, Dice, and Tanimoto distances, the product of two string values is considered 1 if the strings are identical, or 0 if they are not. String properties are ignored for both correlation options.

* If a property is an array, then differences or products are taken element-by-element for the entire array. If the array on one record is shorter than on the other, unmatched elements of the longer array are ignored.

* For the Mahalanobis option, if the data are so highly-correlated that the covariance matrix is singular or nearly so, then the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse ( http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore-Penrose_pseudoinverse ) is used instead of the inverse. If even the pseudoinverse cannot be computed (due to SVD http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singular_value_decomposition non-convergence), an error occurs. In this case, you must use an alternative distance function.

* If you specify both numeric and fingerprint properties to use in the distance calculations, separate contributions to the distance are computed for the two types of property. The overall distance is the average of the two: D = 0.5(D numeric + D FP ). Take care to specify appropriate Numeric Scaling options for this case in order to prevent one or the other of these distance contributions from dominating.

* For more on several of the distance measures described here, see: P. Willett, J.M. Barnard, and G.M. Downs, "Chemical Similarity Searching," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 38 , 983 (1998), see http://www.dddc.ac.cn/embo04/material/Willett_1998.pdf

* For more on the Mahalanobis distance, see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalanobis_distance

Valid Values: Euclidean , Manhattan, Mahalanobis, One Minus Correlation, One Minus Squared Correlation, Cosine, Dice, Tanimoto

Settings controlling the scaling of numeric data when computing distances. Options are:

* Mean-Center and Scale: Shifts and scales each property to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. For Euclidean, Manhattan, Cosine, Dice, and Tanimoto distances, this is a recommended option, as it puts all numeric properties on equal footing. Without such scaling, properties with a large typical magnitude (e.g., 1000) dominate the calculated distance, while properties with a small typical magnitude (e.g., 1) have minimal effect. (For Mahalanobis and correlation distances, this option has no effect on the calculated distance.)

* Scale by Number of Dimensions: For Euclidean, Manhattan, and Mahalanobis distances only, divides the computed distance by P (Manhattan) or P 1/2 (Euclidean and Mahalanobis), where P is the number of properties (or total number of elements if some properties are arrays). This ensures that the typical magnitude of computed distances remains unchanged as you vary the number of properties in the calculation.

* Correct for Missing Values: For Euclidean and Manhattan distances only, multiplies the computed distance by P exp /P (Manhattan) or (P exp /P) 1/2 (Euclidean), where P exp is the expected number of properties (or expected total number of elements if some properties are arrays) in the absence of missing values. This ensures that the typical magnitude of computed distances remains unchanged when some properties are missing. Specifically, it ensures that distances to data records with missing properties are not unusually small as an artifact of the missing data. This option does not apply if "Scale by Number of Dimensions" is selected, as that option already corrects for missing properties implicitly.

If none of the above options are selected, no rescaling is applied to the data. This is appropriate if all numeric properties already have the same characteristic scale or represent components of a vector in the same space (e.g., spatial x, y, z coordinates), and no properties are missing from any of the data records.

* If you specify more than one fingerprint property to use in the distance calculation, then the "Scale by Number of Dimensions" and "Correct for Missing Values" options apply to the fingerprint component of distance as well as to the numeric component. Specifically, Pfp and Pfp exp are used in the scaling of the summed fingerprint distances, where Pfp is the number of fingerprint properties and Pfp exp is the expected number.

* "Scale by Number of Dimensions" also applies to fingerprint distances when you specify Euclidean or Manhattan as the Fingerprint Distance Function . In this case, the distance for each fingerprint property is divided by C (Manhattan) or C 1/2 (Euclidean), where C is the total count of features over both data records (i.e., the "or" bit count).

Valid Values: Mean-Center and Scale , Scale by Number of Dimensions , Correct for Missing Values

For fingerprint properties, specifies the function to use for computing the distance between two data records. This distance is used by the built model to determine the closest training samples when you specify that the model should output the closest samples.

The expressions for the following distance functions assume that each record has a single fingerprint property, with quantities SA, SB, and SC defined as follows:

SA: Number of fingerprint features common to both records. (Number of "and" bits.) SB: Number of features present in the first record but absent from the second. SC: Number of features present in the second record but absent from the first.

* Cosine: Distance (D) is 1 minus the cosine of the angle between the two fingerprints when treated as binary vectors (vectors whose elements must be 0 or 1): D = 1 − SA / [(SA + SB)(SA + SC)] 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 to 1.

* Dice: Distance is 1 minus the number of "and" bits scaled by the mean number of "on" bits for both records: D = 1 − 2 SA / (2SA + SB + SC). Possible values range from 0 to 1.

* Tanimoto: Distance is 1 minus the number of "and" bits scaled by the number of "or" bits: D = 1 − SA / (SA + SB + SC). Possible values range from 0 to 1.

* Euclidean: Distance is the square-root of the number of "on" bits in the squared difference between the two fingerprints when treated as vectors. For a binary fingerprint, this can be expressed as: D = (SB + SC) 1/2 . Possible values range from 0 to the total number of features possible in a single fingerprint.

* Manhattan: Distance is the number of "on" bits in the absolute difference between the two fingerprints when treated as vectors. For a binary fingerprint, this can be expressed as: D = SB + SC. Possible values range from 0 to the total number of features possible in a single fingerprint.

* When more than one fingerprint property is present, a separate distance value is computed for each, and the results are summed or averaged (depending on the Numeric Scaling options).

* For more on the distance measures described here, see: http://www.dddc.ac.cn/embo04/material/Willett_1998.pdf P. Willett, J.M. Barnard, and G.M. Downs, "Chemical Similarity Searching," J. Chem. Inf. Comput. Sci. , 38 , 983 (1998). Also see: J.C. Gower, "Measures of Similarity, Dissimilarity, and Distance," in Encyclopedia of Statistical Sciences , S. Kotz, N.L. Johnson, Read C.B., eds., Vol. 5, p. 397 (1985).

Valid Values: Cosine, Dice, Tanimoto , Euclidean, Manhattan

Name of fingerprint property to use in order to determine whether a test sample is within the applicability domain of the learned model. Any features seen in a test sample but not in any training sample will be noted in the ModelName _Applicability property when making predictions with the model.

Valid Values: FCFP_0, FCFP_2 , FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ECFP_0, ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6

Comma-separated list of properties to be saved with the model when "Save Training Properties" is selected as one of the Learn Options . These properties are in addition to those used to build the model, as specified by UseProperties . When making predictions with the model, the values of the Additional Properties are shown for the closest training samples when you select the "_ClosestSample" option from the list of available outputs on the model component

* If you have selected "Encrypt Data" as one of the Learn Options for greater data security, make sure you do not subvert this security by including properties in the Additional Properties list that reveal more than you wish to about your training samples.

* In the model output with the "_ClosestSample" option, each property in Additional Properties is renamed to ModelName _Closest_ PropertyName where PropertyName is the original name of the property.

* If you set Number of Closest on the model component to a value greater than 1, the additional property values are appended to form arrays if possible. If this is not possible (e.g., for a binary image property), only the property value for the single closest sample is output.

Contains less commonly used parameters.

Seed for random number generator.

Option to view all trees or only the best tree. Not applicable for forest model.

Valid Values: Best Tree, All Trees

# Create Recursive Partitioning Model

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_create_recursive_partitioning_model.htm

## Create Recursive Partitioning Model

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Create Recursive Partitioning Model protocol builds a recursive partitioning model to classify ligands into binary or multiclass categories. The model may be based on numeric, fingerprint, or textual properties. Once created, it appears in the Other group in the Molecular Properties dialog in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to make predictions on the classification of future ligands.

* Open the Small Molecules | Create QSAR Model tools and click Create Recursive Partitioning Model to open the Create Recursive Partitioning Model dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Input Test Ligands Optionally, specify a set of ligands to test the generated model. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Model Name Once created, this model will appear under the Other category of the Molecular Properties parameter in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands. Dependent Property Name of the categorical property to be calculated. Independent Properties List of properties to use as independent variables when building the model. For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Recursive Partitioning Model - Parameters . Cross validation is a good method for measuring the predictive performance of a statistical model. See Cross Validation . Cross validation is not supported for multi-Y models. Building cross-validated models is much slower than building models without cross-validation. For example, if you use five cross-validation folds, it takes roughly five times longer to build a cross-validated model than one without cross-validation. For building a multi-Y model, select more than one dependent property and set Maximum Generic Depth to a value greater than 0. Forest models do not require cross-validation because they are not pruned, and the out-of-bag (OOB) statistics reported by the learner provide an estimate of the model's predictive ability. The lookahead and multi-Y methods are only available for single-tree models; they are not available for forest models.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Input Test Ligands | Optionally, specify a set of ligands to test the generated model. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Model Name | Once created, this model will appear under the Other category of the Molecular Properties parameter in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol and can be used to compute the property for future ligands. |
| Dependent Property | Name of the categorical property to be calculated. |
| Independent Properties | List of properties to use as independent variables when building the model. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Create Recursive Partitioning Model - Parameters .

* Cross validation is a good method for measuring the predictive performance of a statistical model. See Cross Validation .

* Cross validation is not supported for multi-Y models.

* Building cross-validated models is much slower than building models without cross-validation. For example, if you use five cross-validation folds, it takes roughly five times longer to build a cross-validated model than one without cross-validation.

* For building a multi-Y model, select more than one dependent property and set Maximum Generic Depth to a value greater than 0.

* Forest models do not require cross-validation because they are not pruned, and the out-of-bag (OOB) statistics reported by the learner provide an estimate of the model's predictive ability.

* The lookahead and multi-Y methods are only available for single-tree models; they are not available for forest models.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| <ligands>.sd | Output ligands with additional properties added by the model generation. |
| <TestLigands>.sd | Output test ligands when using an external test set. |
| TestResults.html | Contains a confusion matrix of the test set members for each tree. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Script to open the output ligands file and display the recursive partitioning tree in a dendrogram. If the model uses multiple dependent properties (Y variables), each Y variable will have a script to view its specific tree. |
| ModelDescription.html | Contains important information about the model and training set including cross-validation, confusion matrix, and ROC score. |
| RPTempModel.xml | Contains the built model, which can be shared with colleagues. The file name is set by the Model Name parameter. |
| FingerprintFeatures.html | Shows the fingerprint features used for splitting the trees. |

#### Further information

Theory - Small Molecules Share QSAR models Viewing a Recursive Partitioning Tree in a Dendrogram Window [Gower, 1985] [Willet et al., 1992]

# Generate Training and Test Data - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_generate_training_and_test_data-para.htm

## Generate Training and Test Data - Parameters

### Splits data into a training and a test set

Provides various methods for splitting a data set into a training and test set. The training set can be used to build a QSAR model and the test set can be used to assess the performance of the model.

A report on the splitting analysis is generated to allow you to evaluate the distribution of the two datasets in various chemical space.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | The file or URL source to read. In Discovery Studio, you may also specify a Molecule Window. For large files, the fastest option is from a file. If a file is chosen, and the file is visible to the server, a link is created in the Input folder, rather than a copy of the entire file. |
| Split Method | The algorithm used to split data into training and test sets. Random : The full ligand set is sorted by a random index, the "Top N" ligands are then assigned to the training set based on the value of the Training Set Percentage parameter. Diverse Molecules : Selects a diverse subset of ligands using the molecular properties specified by Use Properties parameter. The training set will contain a Training Set Percentage of diverse molecules. Random Per Cluster : The ligands are first clustered according to the Clustering Options parameters, then a random percentage of ligands from each cluster is assigned to the training set based on the Training Set Percentage parameter. Individual Clusters (Pareto) : The ligands are first clustered according to the Clustering Options parameters, then entire clusters are assigned to the training set based on a pareto optimization scheme designed to achieve the desired Training Set Percentage Individual Clusters (Random) : The ligands are first clustered according to the Clustering Options parameters, then entire clusters are randomly assigned to the training set based the value of the Training Set Percentage parameter Valid Values: Random , Diverse Molecules, Random Per Cluster, Individual Clusters (Pareto), Individual Clusters (Random) |
| Random Number Seed | A user-specified number to initialize the random number generation to give repeatable random numbers. Leave this blank if you would like to get a different random series each time. |
| Training Set Percentage | The percentage of data that goes to the training set. The rest will be in the test set. |
| Use Properties | The properties to use when the splitting method is not random: PredefinedSet: A property set selected from a list. UserSet: A user-defined property set. Valid Values: PredefinedSet , UserSet |
| Predefined Set | A predefined set of properties to use for clustering. Valid Values: FCFP_2, FCFP_4, FCFP_6, ALogP , Molecular_Weight , Num_H_Donors , Num_H_Acceptors , Num_RotatableBonds , ECFP_2, ECFP_4, ECFP_6, MDLPublicKeys, Num_Atoms , Num_Rings , Num_AromaticRings , Num_Fragments , Molecular_PolarSurfaceArea , Molecular_PolarSASA, NPlusO_Count |
| User Set | A comma-separated list of properties to use for clustering. |
| Clustering Options | Parameters controlling the clustering process. You can force an input molecule to be used as a cluster center by defining a property named "ClusterCenter" on the data record and setting its value to any number greater than 0. |
| Average Number per Cluster | The average number of molecules per cluster. (Overrides Number of Clusters if both are specified.) |
| Number of Clusters | The number of initial cluster centers to select. You must leave Average Number per Cluster blank for the value of Number of Clusters to be used. |
| Maximum Distance | The maximum distance a cluster member can be from a cluster center. Note: When setting a value for Maximum Distance , you must still specify a value for Average Number per Cluster or Number of Clusters . These values are used in the initial clustering, after which the maximum distance criterion is applied. |
| Center Selection Method | The method to use for selecting new cluster centers. Valid Values: MaximumDissimilarity , NearestOutsideMaximum |
| Recenter Clusters | Whether to recenter clusters, that is, pick a new cluster center for each cluster rather than keep the original center. Valid Values: No , ToMinimizeMaximumDistance, ToMinimizeAverageDistance |
| Recenter Count | The number of times to recenter and recalculate the cluster members when recentering is used. |

The Generate Training and Test Data protocol offers several ways to split a data set into a training set and a test set. The training set can be used to create a QSAR model and the test set can then be used to assess the quality of the model.
