## Prepare Dependent Property - Parameters

### Prepares a dependent property for modeling

Convert a raw property to a dependent or response property by scaling and/or binning the data.

Some QSAR protocols require different types of data for the dependent property ( e.g. , the "Create Recursive Partitioning Model" protocol requires categorical data). In some cases, the data is better modeled when the response property is at the logarithmic scale.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Input Property | An existing numeric property to prepare. |
| Dependent Property | The name of the new property after scaling and/or binning. |
| Scale Data | Whether to scale the raw property in preparing the response. Valid Values: True , False |
| Scaling Type | Type of scaling methods: MeanCenterAndScaleToUnitVariance (Zscore): The data values are offset so their sum is zero (mean centering), and then divided by a factor so that the variance of the scaled data is one. ScaleToUnitRange: The data is scaled so that the lowest value becomes 0, the highest 1.0, and the remaining points linearly scaled into that range. ScaleBetweenMinusOneAndOne: The data is scaled so that the lowest value becomes -1.0, the highest 1.0, and the remaining points linearly scaled into that range. DivideByMean: The mean of the data samples is calculated and each value is divided by that mean. (If the mean is zero or negative, the values are left unchanged.) NaturalLog: All data members are replaced by the natural log of their absolute values. IC50(mM) to pIC50: Convert IC50 in millimolar to pIC50 using -log10(IC50) + 3. IC50(μM) to pIC50: Convert IC50 in micromolar to pIC50 using -log10(IC50) + 6. IC50(nM) to pIC50: Convert IC50 in nanomolar to pIC50 using -log10(IC50) + 9. Valid Values: MeanCenterAndScaleToUnitVariance , ScaleToUnitRange, ScaleBetweenMinusOneAndOne, DivideByMean, NaturalLog, IC50(mM) to pIC50, IC50(uM) to pIC50, IC50(nM) to pIC50 |
| Bin Data | Whether to convert a continuous property to categorical data that used by some QSAR protocols. Valid Values: True , False |
| Binning Method | The method to use in the binning operation. Uniform: divide into bins by evenly sized property value. Manual: manually specify the property value interval and its bin value. Population Weighted: divide the samples in variable property range so that they are populated equally in all bins. Standard Deviation based: divide the samples into either two or three bins specified by how many standard deviations from the center. Valid Values: Uniform , Manual, Population Weighted, Standard Deviation based |
| Number of Bins | The total number of bins to use in binning. It is used in uniform or population weighted binning. Alternatively, bin size (for uniform) or sample size (for population weighted) can be specified instead of number of bins. |
| Uniform Binning Setup | Setup for uniform binning scheme. |
| Minimum Value | The minimum value in range. If it is left blank, the minimum from all of the data is used. |
| Maximum Value | The maximum value in range. If it is left blank, the maximum from all of the data is used. |
| Bin Size | The size of each bin in property range. Specifying bin size will disable the number of bins parameter. If the range cannot be divided equally, the last bin will be smaller than others. |
| Options | How to deal with samples out of the range specified by the minimum and maximum. By default these samples are not assigned any bin value. |
| Lower Than Minimum | Options for samples with a property value lower than the minimum. Valid Values: Assign to First Bin , Assign Special Value |
| Lower Than Minimum Special Value | Special Value for samples with property value lower than the minimum. |
| Greater Than Maximum | Options for samples with property value greater than the maximum. Valid Values: Assign to Last Bin , Assign Special Value |
| Greater Than Maximum Special Value | Special Value for samples with property value greater than the maximum. |
| Manual Binning Setup | Manually specify the binning scheme. In this case you can assign non-numeric bin values. Each line specifies a bin value and a range (space-delimited), and the syntax is: Bin_Value Low_Range High_Range For example: None 0 0.3 Mild 0.3 0.6 Moderate 0.6 0.9 Severe 0.9 1.0 The ranges are inclusive on the left side with the exception of the last, which is inclusive on both sides. If your ranges overlap between two bins, the last takes precedence. |
| Population Weighted Setup | Options for population based binning. |
| Sample Size | Number of samples in each bin. |
| Standard Deviation Based Setup | Options for standard deviation based binning. |
| Number of Standard Deviations | This controls how many bins to create: Number of Standard Deviations = 0, two bins: [minimum, mean], and (mean, maximum]. Number of Standard Deviations = n, where n is > 0, three bins: [minimum, mean - n * stddev], (mean - n * stddev, mean + n * stddev], and (mean + n * stddev, maximum]. |

# Theory - 3D QSAR

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_3d_qsar_model.htm

## Theory - 3D QSAR

Most quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) methods do not consider the 3D structures of the ligands when creating a model. In a 3D QSAR method, the energy potentials calculated using the 3D structures of a set of ligands are used as descriptors to build a model that relates the biological activities to the 3D structures. In most cases, these ligands all bind into the same binding site of the same or similar receptors.

There are typically two separate steps in building a 3D QSAR model:

* The ligands are prealigned using a molecular overlay method and placed in a 3D grid space. The grid spacing is usually chosen to be between 1 Å and 2 Å. The extent of the grid
is often set to the bounding box of all the ligands plus a few Å of extension. The energy potentials on every grid point are then calculated using a forcefield. In Discovery Studio , the CHARMm force field is used and the electrostatic potential and the van der Waals potential are treated as separate terms. A +1e point charge is used as the electrostatic potential probe and distance-dependent dielectric constant is used to mimic the solvation effect. For the van der Waals potential a carbon atom with a 1.73 Å radius is used as a probe. Rather than the full potential, a soft-core potential suggested in CDOCKER [Wu et al., 2003] is used.

In Discovery Studio , the CHARMm force field is used and the electrostatic potential and the van der Waals potential are treated as separate terms. A +1e point charge is used as the electrostatic potential probe and distance-dependent dielectric constant is used to mimic the solvation effect. For the van der Waals potential a carbon atom with a 1.73 Å radius is used as a probe. Rather than the full potential, a soft-core potential suggested in CDOCKER [Wu et al., 2003] is used.

* The energy grid potentials are filtered to remove highly correlated descriptors.
A partial least squares (PLS) model is then built using these remaining descriptors. The model can then be used to make predictions on new ligands.

# Algorithms for selecting equations

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_algorithms-selecting-equations.htm

## Algorithms for selecting equations

The GFA model implements two algorithms for selecting equations from the current population to use as parents for the next 
generation, based on NSGA-II and SPEA-II.

### NSGA-II

The non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm [Deb et al., 2002] acts to find which 
Pareto front each model lies on. The Pareto-optimal equations all lie on the first front. The second front consists of all the equations 
that are dominated only by models that lie on the first front - this is the set of equations that would be Pareto-optimal if all the models 
on the first front were removed. Subsequent fronts are found in the same way by looking for models that are dominated only by equations on 
earlier fronts. The selection algorithm is based on choosing the equations from the fronts with the lowest indices.

### SPEA-II

The strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm [Zitzler et al., 2001] involves 
assigning a score to each model based on the number of other equations that dominate it. The score is equal to the number of equations 
that are dominated by all of the equations that dominate the given model. The selection algorithm then ranks the equations according 
to this score, which should be minimized. For example, if a particular model is dominated by two equations and those two equations in 
turn dominate 6 and 7 other equations, then the original model is assigned a score of 13.

The genetic function approximation results document shows the results of a Create Genetic Function Approximation protocol run. This document is 
automatically created. The results documents produced include a validation sheet, which summarizes the results statistics indicating the quality of the 
built model, including how well it fits the data, and the model's predictive power. For more information, refer to Create Genetic Function Approximation Model .

### Friedman LOF

and n is the total number of input data points.

The smoothing parameter, d, is defined as:

where p max is the maximum equation length (maximum allowable number of parameters in the equation) and α is the user-defined 
smoothing parameter, 0.0 < α < 1.0. The lower the value of Friedman LOF, the less likely it is that the genetic function approximation 
model is overfitting the data.

### R-squared

The fraction of the total variance of the Y variable that is explained by the genetic function approximation equation. r 2 is calculated as:

where SSR is the sum of squares of regression and SST is the total sum of squares. The closer the value is to 1.0 , the 
better the genetic function approximation equation explains the Y variable. However, the drawback of r 2 is that the size of the equation and 
the number of terms in the equation are not accounted for in this measure. r 2 always tends to increase, approaching 1, as the number of 
terms in the equation increase. r 2 alone does not indicate whether overfitting has occurred.

### Adjusted R-squared

An adjusted r 2 estimation is when the variance is reduced in proportion to the size of the estimated model. The adjusted r 2 is calculated as follows:

where p is the number of parameters in the regression equation. The adjusted r 2 is meaningful only when there are some degrees of freedom 
for lack-of-fit. For a model with an additional parameter to be considered an improvement, the addition of the parameter is required to decrease SSE at 
least proportionately to the reduction in the degrees of freedom. Compared to r 2 , this measure penalizes large equations.

### Cross validated R-squared

Cross-validated r 2 is derived from cross validation - it is the cross-validated equivalent of r 2 . The r 2 (CV) is 
calculated as follows:

where PRESS is the predictive sum of squares of a model.

The r 2 (CV) is also a key measure of the predictive power of a model. The closer the value is to 1.0 , the better 
the predictive power. For a good model, r 2 (CV) should be fairly close to r 2 . If r 2 (CV) is much less than r 2 , 
the model equation is probably overfitting the data. A model with an r 2 (CV) value of 0.0 or less has no predictive 
power at all, according to the cross-validation criterion.

### Significant regression

For an indication of whether or not the regression is statistically significant, the value is Yes if F > F cr is significant, and No if it is not. F is the significance-of-regression F value and F cr is the critical SOR F 
value (95%).

The F test is a standard statistical test for the equality of the variances of two populations having normal distributions. It is used to test 
whether the variance in the data which is explained by the regression is much larger than the variance remaining due to errors. If this is the case, 
then the model is said to be significant , rather than one which simply fits the noise.

The F test calculates:

* SST - The total sum of squares. This is the mean-corrected sum of squares of the responses over the entire data set.

* SSE - The sum of squares of errors. This is the sum of squared differences between measurements and model predictions over the entire data set.

* SSR - The sum of squares due to regression. SSR = SST - SSE.

* n - The number of data points from which the model is built.

* p - The number of parameters in a regression model (including the intercept, when present).

The ratio F = {SSR/(p - 1)}/{SSE/(n - p)} is then calculated and compared with tabulated values of the F distribution for different values of n and 
p. The regression is significant if F is greater than the tabulated value. In general, the larger the value of F, the better the model.

### Significance-of-regression F-value

The significance-of-regression F value is defined as:

This parameter is used to determine whether or not the regression is statistically significant.

### Critical SOR F-value (95%)

The critical significance-of-regression (SOR) F value is the critical point of the F distribution of degrees n - p and p - 1 evaluated for 
probability 0.05 (at 95% confidence level). In conjunction with the significance-of-regression F value, it is used to determine whether or not the 
regression is significant.

### Significance-of-regression p-value

The p-value is the probability that the regression is by chance and does not describe a real relationship. It corresponds to the part of the area under the tail of curve of an F distribution with the appropriate degrees of freedom.

This p-value is interpreted the same way as other p-values:

* The smaller the p-value, the stronger the evidence that the regression is significant.

* It is generally acceptable to consider regressions with a p-value of less than 0.05 as significant, though the only basis for this cutoff is convention.

### Replicate points

This is the number of replicated data points.

# Bayesian categorization

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_bayesian-categorization.htm

## Bayesian categorization

Bayesian categorization model is a simple probabilistic classification model. It is based on Bayes' theorem:

where

* h is the hypothesis or model

* d is the observed data

* p(h) is the prior belief (probability of hypothesis h before observing any data)

* p(d) is the data evidence (marginal probability of the data)

* p(d|h) is the likelihood (probability of data d if hypothesis h is true)

* p(h|d) is the posterior probability (probability of hypothesis h being true given the observed data d )

In the implementation of the Bayesian modeling in this application, the learned models are created with a learn-by-example paradigm:
the user marks the sample data that is of interest (good), and then the system learns to distinguish them from background data. 
No tuning parameters are required beyond the selection of the input descriptors from which to learn.

The learning process generates a large set of Boolean features from the input descriptors. It then collects the frequency of occurrence of 
each feature in the good subset and in all data samples. To apply the model to a particular sample, the features of the sample are generated,
and a weight is calculated for each feature using a Laplacian-adjusted probability estimate. The weights are summed to provide a probability 
estimate, which is a relative predictor of the likelihood of that sample being from the good subset.

Bayesian categorization can process large amounts of data, learns fast, and is tolerant of random noise.

### The Laplacian-corrected estimator

The Laplacian-corrected estimator is used to adjust the uncorrected probability estimate of a feature to account for the different sampling
frequencies of different features. The derivation is given below.

Assume that N samples are available for training, of which, M are active. An estimate of the baseline probability of 
a randomly chosen sample being active, P(Active) , is M/N .

Next, assume that feature F is contained in B samples, and that A of those samples are active. The 
uncorrected estimate of activity P(Active|F) is A/B . Unfortunately, as B becomes small, this
estimator tends to be less reliable.

For example, if A = 1 and B = 1, P(Active|F) would be 1 (active), which seems overconfident 
for a feature that has been seen once.

Most likely, the estimator is poor because the feature is not sampled adequately, and further sampling of that feature would improve the estimate.
It is possible to estimate the effect of further sampling by assuming that the vast majority of features have no relationship with activity. That is, if, for
most features, F i , P(Active|F i ) is expected to be equal to the baseline probability P(Active) .

If feature K is sampled additional times, P(Active)*K of those new samples are expected to be active. This provides 
the information needed to estimate the corrective effect of K additional samples:

For K = 1/P(Active), this is the Laplacian correction.

This correction stabilizes the estimator: as the number of samples, B , containing a feature approaches zero, the feature's probability 
contribution converges to P(Active) , which is the expected value for most features.

The final step is to make the estimator a relative estimate by dividing by P(Active) :

For most features, log P final ~ 0. For features more common in actives, log P final > 0. For features 
less common in actives, log P final < 0. The completed estimate for a particular sample is derived by adding together the 
log P final values for all the features present in that sample.

# Cross Validation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_cross-validation.htm

## Cross Validation

Cross validation is a method for assessing the statistical performance of the model when predicting an independent dataset. In general, the statistics of a model fit alone is not a reliable measurement of how well the model will perform on a different data set. For example, a high R 2 in a linear model does not necessarily indicate that the model will perform well on an external test set. The best method to assess the model quality is its performance on an external test set that was not part of the model generation process. It is easy to overfit the data by introducing too many degrees of freedom (parameters), thus inflating the R2 and other fit statistics. A model obtained from overfitting will likely perform poorly when used with a new data set.

A way to measure the predictive power of a model is to test it on a set of data that was not included in the fitting process. Such a data set is called the "test set", while the data set used to build the model is referred to as the "training set". In general, the Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the test set is larger than the MSE of the training set because the test set was excluded in the model building. However, there is a higher confidence that the model will perform better on a different data set.

Unfortunately, when a portion of the available data is excluded from testing, the amount of data to train the model decreases, which can lead to an inferior model. This is especially true when the amount of data is limited.

The cross validation method provides a way to overcome this problem and also helps in model selection. The performance estimation is performed as follows:

* The original data are split into a training set and a validation set.

* The training set is used to create a model using the same procedure as in the model training process described earlier.

* The validation set is used to assess the model created using the training set.

* The assessment is then extrapolated to the model using all data (i.e., cross validation is used to estimate the performance of the final model).

Multiple rounds of cross validation are usually performed using different partitions of data to reduce variability. The validation results are then averaged over all the rounds. Minimizing a cross validation statistic is useful in model selection (e.g., when choosing variables in a regression); it provides a nearly unbiased measure of the true MSE on the new data.

### Common types of cross validation

There are several varieties of cross validation:

* k-fold cross validation: The original data are randomly partitioned into k equal sized subsets. One of the subsets is kept as a validation set to assess the model, which is created using the rest of the subsets. This process is then repeated k times, with each subset used as the validation set in turn. This method has the advantage that all samples are used in the validation set.

* Leave-one-out cross validation: A single sample is used as the validation set, and the remaining N - 1 samples (N being the sample size) is the training set. This is a special case of k-fold cross validation, where k is equal to N.

* Random sampling cross validation: Data is split randomly into a training and validation set. Although the process is repeated many times, there is no guarantee that a sample will ever be selected in the validation set.

Each validation method has advantages and disadvantages. Leave-one-out cross validation is usually a good choice, but it can be very time-consuming if there are a large number of samples, or if the model building process is slow. Additionally, a small change in the data can lead to a large change in the model selected. Many statisticians have found that k-fold cross-validation performs better. In Discovery Studio , different validation methods are provided in the QSAR model creation protocols. Therefore, you should consider sample size and model type when choosing a validation method.

# Friedman LOF measure

Source type: HTML

## Friedman LOF measure

Various statistical measures can be adapted to measure the fitness of a GFA model during the evolution process. Use of the Friedman lack-of-fit 
(LOF ) measure has several advantages over the regular least squares error measure. According to Friedman [Friedman, 1991] , LOF is measured as:

where SSE is the sum of squares of errors, c is the number of basis functions (other than the constant term), d is a smoothing 
parameter, p is the total number of features contained in all the basis functions and M is the number of samples in the training set.

Unlike the commonly used least squares measure, the LOF measure cannot always be reduced by adding more terms to the regression model. 
While the new term may reduce the SSE, it also increases the values of c and p, which tends to increase the LOF score. Thus, adding a 
new term may reduce the SSE, but increase the LOF score. By limiting the tendency to simply add more terms, the LOF measure resists 
overfitting better than the SSE measure.

# Genetic Function Approximation

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_genetic-function-approximation.htm

## Genetic Function Approximation

The Genetic Function Approximation (GFA) algorithm [Rogers and Hopfinger, 1994] is designed to 
be applied to the problem of function approximation. When it receives a large number of potential factors influencing a response, including 
several powers and other functions of the raw inputs, it should find the subset of terms that correlates best with the response.

The following theory topics are available for GFA:

* Splines

* Friedman LOF measure

* Multiple object optimization

* Algorithms for selecting equations

* Stability and convergence

* Analysis equations

* Error estimate

### General GFA theory

The central concepts of genetic algorithms are simple. The region to be searched is coded into one or more strings. In the GFA, these 
strings are sets of terms - powers and splines of the raw inputs. Each string represents a location in the search space.

The algorithm works with a set of these strings, called a population. This population is evolved in a manner that leads it towards the 
objective of the search. This requires that a measure of the fitness of each string, corresponding to a model in the GFA, is available.

Following this, three operations are performed iteratively in succession: selection, crossover, and mutation. Newly added members are 
scored according to a fitness criterion. In the GFA, the scoring criteria for models are all related to the quality of the regression
fit to the data. The selection probabilities must be re-evaluated each time a new member is added to the population.

* Selection: Two parents are selected from the present population, with probabilities proportional to 
their fitness.

* Crossover: A crossover splices and rejoins the characters in the two parent strings to create a new 
child string. In conventional genetic algorithms, this is accomplished by selecting a crossover point along each of the parents and 
combining the first substring from the first parent with the second substring from the second parent: Parents x12, x2 | 3x4, x33 Child x12, x2, x4, x52
x1, x3 | x4, x52

```text
Parents x12, x2 | 3x4, x33 Child x12, x2, x4, x52
x1, x3 | x4, x52
```

* Mutation: In a mutation, a single term in a string (a model) is altered. This is a mechanism for 
continuously introducing a measure of diversity into the population, acting to prevent the algorithm from getting stuck within a 
suboptimal set of solutions. In the GFA algorithm, mutations are performed with a user-defined probability after each crossover.

The GFA procedure continues for a specified number of generations, unless convergence occurs in the interim. A generation is a number 
of attempted crossovers equal to the size of the population. Convergence is triggered by lack of progress in the highest and average 
scores of the population. Convergence is further discussed in stability and convergence .

## Error Estimate in Genetic Function Approximation

All experimental data points are subject to error ("experimental error"), of a variety of sources. This error 
then propagates into errors in the coefficients of any model derived from those data, and these propagate into 
errors in the model predictions. Models predict the mean value of a property of a given formulation (i.e., the 
mean of many property measurements on that formulation). The model prediction plus and minus the model errors 
gives the interval between which the mean property measurement could be expected to lie with a certain confidence.
It is reported as the Confidence Error in the output of a GFA model.

The error estimate in the GFA model follows the standard practice for methods based on least-squares minimization.
We assume that the data values are described by a population (probability distribution) of values with a constant 
variance (related to the second moment of the distribution). The variance is usually given the label σ 2 , and its value can be estimated using the residual sum of squares (also known as the sum of squares 
of errors SSE) once the model is built. It is reported as the Prediction Error in the output of a GFA model. The
prediction error is always greater than the confidence error.

## Multiple linear regression

In multiple linear regression analysis, there is a set of n observations of a dependent variable Y, each represented by p independent variables, 
X 1 , X 2 , ..., X p . The mathematical model that relates the Y values to the X values is assumed to be linear and 
of the form:

where the b 1 , b 2 ,...,b n are the regression coefficients and Y(pred) i is the predicted value of 
the i th observation. The values of the coefficients are found by the least-squares approach (i.e., minimizing the sum of the squared 
residuals). The residual is the difference between the observed and predicted values for the i th observation:

Multiple linear regression is very quick and easy to interpret, but it does not work when the number of independent variables (molecular 
descriptors) is larger than (or even comparable to) the number of observations (molecules). To produce reliable results, you typically need five times 
as many molecules as independent variables.

# Multiple object optimization

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_multiple-object-optimization.htm

## Multiple object optimization

The Friedman LOF measure uses a parameter, d, to choose a trade-off between complexity and accuracy. An alternative approach is to 
treat the model building process as an exercise in multiple objective optimization and to use Pareto dominance to compare the relative 
fitness of two equations.

In a multiple objective optimization, each equation is scored on a number of different criteria, each of which will be optimized. In 
the case of the GFA model, there are two criteria: accuracy (to be maximized) and complexity (to be minimized). One equation is said to 
be "Pareto dominant" over another if it is superior in at least one fitness measure and at least equal in all of the other criteria. The 
multiple objective optimization process attempts to find the Pareto-optimal models, that is, those with the highest possible accuracy for 
a given complexity and those with the lowest complexity for a given accuracy. An equation is Pareto optimal if there is no other equation 
which is Pareto dominant over it. For a given data set, there are likely to be a number of Pareto-optimal equations. These are the 
equations that have the highest accuracy for a given complexity.

Pareto optimality and Pareto dominance

In the figure above, the model labeled P is more accurate and less complex than all of the equations inside the area bounded by the 
dashed lines and so is Pareto dominant over them. All the other equations are either more accurate or less complex.

Multiple objective optimizations have two advantages over using a fitness measure based on a single score. First, the final 
population will contain a range of Pareto-optimal models, including both simple models, which are less accurate, and more complex 
models with greater accuracy. This allows you to choose the model that you consider most appropriate to the task in hand. Second, 
as the population evolves, it will contain models of varying complexity and this tends to encourage the population to maintain greater 
genetic diversity than is the case for models that have all made the same trade-off between complexity and accuracy.

The GFA model implements two algorithms for selecting equations from the current population to use as parents for the next generation, 
based on NSGA-II and SPEA-II , either of these can be specified in the Algorithm section in the Parameters Explorer for the Create 
GFA Model protocol.

## Partial least squares

Partial least squares (PLS) regression is an extension of the multiple linear regression model. Rather than using all the independent variables in the regression (as in multiple linear regression), a set of linear combinations of the original independent variables (X) are used. The linear combinations are called components or latent variables and are constructed in such a way that the covariance with the dependent variable (Y) is maximized. PLS bears some similarity to principal components regression. However, they differ in the way how the components are constructed, as explained below.

scaled by dividing by their standard deviations.

The true regression is done on a small number of latent variables in PLS regression. As a result,

# Recursive Partitioning

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_recursive-partitioning.htm

## Recursive Partitioning

Recursive partitioning (RP) is a data classification method used to uncover the relationship between a dependent property (Y variable) to a set of independent properties (X variables). Recursive partitioning creates a decision tree that strives to correctly classify members of the population based on a dichotomous splitting of a dependent property. Once a model is built, it can be used to make predictions about novel data.

When making a prediction with the model, a sample is assigned to a node of the tree according to the answers to the questions for that sample. The class predicted for that sample is the class to which a plurality of the training samples in the node belong.

### RP basic theory

To understand the RP process, there are a few concepts to understand:

* Splitting or partitioning criterion: During the process of decision tree induction, the questions for splitting the training set down the appropriate path must be considered. Only potential questions that have a true or false answer are considered so that any particular node will have exactly two child nodes in the next generation. This process is repeated for each child node recursively using only the independent variables in that child node.

* Purity measure: There are theoretically an indefinite number of splitting criteria that can be used to partition a node. For the purpose of choosing the most appropriate question, a "purity" measure is used to decide which split is the best possible split from the choices. There are many purity measures available. The simplest is Gini index, which is defined as the absolute purity of the most dominant class of a node. This measure is calculated for every possible split and the one that gives the highest possible value for one of the child nodes is the best one to use.

* Stopping criterion: If the splitting process is allowed to continue, a perfect tree would be created in which each leaf had a single sample. Most likely a tree of this sort is over-fitting for the training data and will not have any predictive power. Stopping criteria to halt the recursive partitioning process avoids over-fitting. Much like purity measures, stopping criteria come in many different forms, including: A maximum number of nodes in the tree. Once this maximum is reached, the process is halted. A maximum number of levels the tree can grow into. Once a node has been split a certain number of times down the path, the splitting is halted. A minimum number of samples in any particular node. If the number of samples in a node is less than or equal to a 
minimum value, partitioning of that node will not be attempted, and it becomes a leaf. A threshold for the purity measure. If a node has a purity value higher than the threshold, no partitioning will be 
attempted regardless of the number of samples.

* A maximum number of nodes in the tree. Once this maximum is reached, the process is halted.

* A maximum number of levels the tree can grow into. Once a node has been split a certain number of times down the path, the splitting is halted.

* A minimum number of samples in any particular node. If the number of samples in a node is less than or equal to a 
minimum value, partitioning of that node will not be attempted, and it becomes a leaf.

* A threshold for the purity measure. If a node has a purity value higher than the threshold, no partitioning will be 
attempted regardless of the number of samples.

* Pruning: Even with a stopping criterion, a tree can still overfit the training data, meaning that they capture not only the true relationships in the data, but also the noise. A consequence is that a tree model that appears to fit the training data extremely well (as measured by a confusion matrix or ROC score) may have poor performance when used to make predictions. To address this problem, a single-tree model should always be pruned using cross-validation or a test set before it is interpreted or used to make predictions. Pruning is the process of systematically removing branches of the initially grown tree to yield smaller trees. If too little pruning is 
done, predictions are poor due to overfitting. If too much pruning is done, predictions are poor due to the loss of branches containing 
real information (and not just noise). Pruning is done in stages by removing nodes in such a way that the following function is minimized [Breiman et al. 1984] : where: R 0 is the misclassification error against the training data for the pruned tree N leaves is the number of leaf nodes in the tree α is the complexity penalty, which varies from 0 for the unpruned tree to a maximum value for a tree
consisting of only the top node It is difficult or even impossible to determine the optimally-pruned tree by inspection. Therefore, it is important to use cross-validation or a test set to determine the best pruned tree to use for making predictions, or for drawing conclusions about relationships between descriptor values and class membership.

It is difficult or even impossible to determine the optimally-pruned tree by inspection. Therefore, it is important to use cross-validation or a test set to determine the best pruned tree to use for making predictions, or for drawing conclusions about relationships between descriptor values and class membership.

### Forest model

In a basic recursive partitioning model, only a single-tree is created. The two main virtues of RP models are that they are easily interpretable, while also providing a large degree of predictive accuracy. Even after using pruning to determine the optimum tree size, the predictive accuracy of a single-tree model might not be as good as desired. If none of the descriptors is strongly correlated with the class membership, single-tree models can be brittle, in that a relatively small change in the training data results in a large change in the structure of the tree, and thus in the tree's predictions.

A multiple tree, or forest, model can help address this problem, while having the added benefit that it eliminates the need for pruning. To build a forest model, the training data are randomly resampled multiple times. An RP tree is grown from each resampled dataset, using the algorithm described in the previous section (apart from pruning). For making predictions on a new sample, the sample is sent down each tree in turn until it reaches a leaf node. The leaf node probabilities from each tree are averaged together to yield a prediction for the forest as a whole.

The RP model in Discovery Studio uses bootstrap sampling as the resampling technique [Efron and Tibshirani, 1993] . For a training set containing N samples, a bootstrap sample is constructed by randomly selecting N samples with replacement from the training set. That is, a given sample can be selected any number of times with equal probability. On average, a bootstrap sample contains 63.2% of the original dataset samples at least once.

The process of averaging together the predictions of models built from bootstrap samples is known as bootstrap aggregation, or bagging [Breiman, 1996] . For a given tree, the roughly 63% of the original samples used to build the tree are known as in-bag samples. The roughly 37% of samples not considered in building the tree are known as out-of-bag (OOB) samples. Predictions made on the OOB samples provide an estimate of the predictive power of the model similar to cross-validation, but without the need to build separate cross-validation models.

Recall that the reason pruning is necessary for single-tree models is that such models tend to overfit the data, which is another way of saying that the models fit random noise in the data in addition to the signal in the data. The same problem applies to the individual trees in a forest model. However, because each tree in a forest uses a different random sample of the original data, the noise in the predictions of the individual tree tends to cancel out. Thus, even though each individual tree in a forest model tends to give worse predictions than a single-tree model built from all the data, the average prediction over all the trees in the forest can be significantly better than that for a single tree.

A forest model is less directly interpretable than a single-tree model in that there is not simply one tree to interpret, but depending on the type of forest, anywhere from ten to hundreds of trees. On the other hand, a forest model can provide statistical measures of the relative importance of the various descriptors in distinguishing among the different classes, which is not available with single-tree models.

#### Types of Forest Models

There are two broad types of forest model supported by BIOVIA . The first consists of a relatively small number of trees (10 to 20 typically) grown from bootstrap samples of the training data, without resampling of the descriptors. The second consists of a large number of trees (typically hundreds) also grown from bootstrap samples, but in which the descriptors are resampled as well. At each node of each tree for which a split may be possible, a separate random subset of descriptors is considered as possible splitting criteria. Typically, the size of this subset is the square-root of the number of descriptors.

Terminology: We refer to the first type of forest model as a "Bagged Forest". We use the term "Forest of Random Trees" for the second type of model [Breiman 2001] . Additional variants of this technique for imbalanced datasets is discussed in the next section.

For the purpose of counting and sampling descriptors, an ordinary numerical or categorical property counts as a single descriptor. However, for a fingerprint property, each separate fingerprint feature that is present in the training data counts as a separate descriptor.

### Variants of Single-tree Models

Besides the standard recursive partitioning algorithm described previously, two additional BIOVIA -patented techniques are available for building single-tree models. These methods are available for forest models as well, but are not as well-tested in this context.

#### Lookahead

The standard method for determining the best split criterion for a node does not consider the effect of the choice on future splits. Only the effect of the criterion on the purity of the node's immediate children is considered. Yet in some cases, a locally suboptimal choice of splitting criterion would turn out to be globally more optimal by allowing more effective splits further down the tree.

When using the lookahead method, an RP learner maintains a set of multiple tentative splitting criteria for each node down to a certain depth. The final choice of criteria is made only after the tree is grown to its full extent. To build a model with lookahead, set the Maximum Lookahead Depth parameter to a value greater than zero. The Lookahead algorithm is described in detail in U.S. patent 7,269,597 (owned 
by BIOVIA ).

#### Multi-Y (PUMP-RP)

The Partially-Unified Multiple Property Recursive Partitioning (PUMP-RP) method provides a way to consider multiple dependent (Y) 
classification properties in a single model ( [Stockfisch, 2003] and [Rao and Stockfisch, 2003] ). This is useful, for example, in attempting to 
identify features that enhance a desirable effect (e.g., activity) while reducing one or more undesirable effects (e.g., toxicity).

PUMP-RP is also covered by an BIOVIA patent (U.S. patent 7,016,887).

#### Imbalanced Training Data

Many datasets of practical interest are imbalanced in that the number of samples belonging to one class (often the class of interest) is much smaller than the number of members of other classes. For example, the number of active compounds in a dataset might be only 1% of the number of inactive compounds. The problem with such a dataset is that a model could be 99% accurate by predicting that every compound is inactive (i.e., it is a useless model for this dataset). An RP model built from such imbalanced data tends to have very few false positives (inactive compounds predicted to be active) and a large fraction of false negatives (active compounds predicted to be inactive).

To compensate, the samples can be reweighted. Ordinarily, in determining the winning class for a node, each sample is given uniform weight. A node with 2 active and 18 inactive samples is predicted to be an inactive node with 90% probability. With reweighting, the entire set of active samples can be given the same weight as the entire set of inactive samples. If the active class is weighted by a multiple of 99, the node with 2 active and 18 inactive samples now becomes an active node with 92% probability.

Empirically, reweighting improves the balance between the number of false positives and false negatives. To reweight the samples in an imbalanced dataset, change the Weighting Method parameter to By Class . More complex weighting schemes are possible, but for simplicity, this is the one supported by the Create Recursive Partitioning Model protocol.

The reweighting method is used for either single-tree or forest models. For forest models, an additional technique is possible for dealing with imbalanced data. The technique involves using an alternative to the bootstrap method for resampling the data. Due to the need to do sufficient resampling, it is more appropriate for large forests of random trees than for bagged forests.

In this technique, the dataset for each tree in the forest is constructed as follows [Chen et al., 2004] :

* A bootstrap sample is generated using only those samples in the minority class.

* For each of the other classes, a random sample of the same size is generated by sampling with replacement.

For example, suppose there are N A active compounds and N I inactive compounds in the original dataset, with N A < N I . The training data for each tree consists of a bootstrap sample of size N A , containing only active samples, added to a random sample of size N A , containing only inactive samples, for a total of 2N A samples. For highly imbalanced data, this sample size is much smaller than the original training dataset. Thus, in addition to compensating for the imbalance in the data, this method also increases the speed of tree construction.

### Determining the Best RP Model for Your Problem

The types of RP models available with the Create Recursive Partitioning Model protocol offer different tradeoffs between ease of interpretation, predictive performance, and speed of learning. The following table summarizes the strengths and weaknesses of the different types of models (see the note below regarding interpretability):

| Model Type | Typical Number of Trees | Interpretability | Predictive Performance | Speed of Learning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single-tree | 1 | Very Good | Good | Fast |
| Bagged Forest | 10 | Average | Very Good | Average |
| Forest of Random Trees | 500 | Direct: Poor Indirect: Good | Very Good | Slow |
| Balanced Forest of Random Trees | 1000 | Direct: Poor Indirect: Good | Very Good | Fairly Slow |

"direct" interpretability refers to the ease of interpretation by direct inspection of the tree structures. "Indirect" interpretability refers to the ease of interpreting the descriptor importance measures produced by the learning process.

For all model types other than the Balanced Forest of Random Trees, reweighting can be applied for imbalanced datasets without significantly affecting the speed. Reweighting is not appropriate for a balanced forest model because the data resampling already corrects for imbalance in the original dataset.

# Splines

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_splines.htm

## Splines

A key feature of the GFA algorithm is the use of splines. This feature draws inspiration from the MARS algorithm of Friedman [Friedman, 1991] . 
Splines allow for the data set to be classified into regions that display distinct behavior. Splines are denoted by angular brackets 
surrounding an algebraic expression and evaluate to zero when the enclosed expression is less than zero. For example, <x - α> 
evaluates to 0 when x is less than α and to (x - α) otherwise. Here, α is known as the knot of the spline.

The GFA model builder allows for the inclusion of both linear and quadratic splines. Splines allow interpolative models to be built 
for response surfaces of considerable complexity from simple building blocks. However, this added power comes at a cost: splines are
often difficult to associate with an underlying physical meaning and often do not lend themselves well to extrapolation. If having an 
accurate interpolative model is more important than having one that holds up to extrapolation, splines provide a simple but powerful 
way of obtaining such models.

# Stability and convergence

Source file: tssmallmolecules/qsar_th_stability-convergence.htm

## Stability and convergence

As with other iterative minimization algorithms, there are 
issues with the stability and convergence of the GFA algorithm.

You can obtain an indication of the stability of the GFA algorithm 
by generating a plot showing the evolution of variable 
usage with time. Such a plot shows the number of occurrences 
of each variable within the population for each generation of 
the evolution. For practical reasons, such as the reduction 
of the amount of data collected, such a plot should only be generated 
for those variables that occur most commonly in the final 
population and the data are not normally collected for every generation.

The GFA algorithm is assumed to have converged when no improvement 
is seen in the score of the population over a significant length 
of time, either that of the best model in each population or the 
average of all the models in each population. When this criterion has 
been satisfied, no further generations are calculated.

The criteria used to check for convergence depends on the filter 
algorithm that is being used. There are no user-adjustable parameters. 
The criteria are:

* Original algorithm : Count the number of generations for which the "score" of the best equation has not improved (A). Count the number of generations for which the average "score" of all the equations in the population have not improved (B). Convergence is assumed to have been achieved if: A * P > 60000 and B * P > 30000, where P is the population size.

* Count the number of generations for which the "score" of the best equation has not improved (A).

* Count the number of generations for which the average "score" of all the equations in the population have not improved (B).

* NSGA-II and SPEA-II : For both these algorithms, convergence is assumed to have been achieved if more than 25 generations have passed with exactly the same set of equations surviving in the population.

* For both these algorithms, convergence is assumed to have been achieved if more than 25 generations have passed with exactly the same set of equations surviving in the population.

## Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs - Parameters

### Analyzes the effect of fragment substitutions on activity in MMPs

Performs Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) transformations to explore changes in ligand activities. MMPs are pairs of ligands that differ by a single localized structural change. The two ligands belonging to an MMP can be interconverted by replacing the substructure in one of them with the different substructure in the other. The input ligands are fragmented and then analyzed to identify all the MMPs, and creates a table with the transformations and associated activity changes.

For each MMP, the activity change is classified as neutral, increased or decreased. The activity effects are tabulated and sorted to show which MMPs have the largest effects (15%) in each category. Tables and bar charts for the most frequent transformations are created based on:

* Most Frequent: Table with the most frequent transformations.

* Most Frequently Change Activity: Table with the most frequent transformations that changed the activity.

* Most Frequently Do Not Change Activity: Table with the most frequent transformations that did not change the activity

* All Transformations: Table with all transformations sorted by frequency.

# Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/sar_analyze_activity_effects_using_mmps.htm

## Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing Results

* Troubleshooting

This protocol performs Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) transformations to explore changes in ligand activities. MMPs are pairs of ligands that differ by a single localized structural change [Hussain and Rea, 2010] . The two ligands belonging to an MMP can be interconverted by replacing the substructure in one of them with the different substructure in the other [Leach et al., 2006] . The input ligands are fragmented and analyzed to identify MMPs with an activity change above the defined threshold.

For each MMP, the activity change is classified as neutral, increase, or decrease. The activity effects are tabulated and sorted to show which MMPs have the largest effects in each category [Papadatos et al., 2010] . 
Additionally, tables and bar charts are created for the most frequent transformations.

See the Understanding SAR Trends using Matched Molecular Pairs tutorial for an example showing how to use this protocol.

* Open the Small Molecules | Study SAR tools and click Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs to open the Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* In the Protocols Explorer , open Study SAR | Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Ligands Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. The ligands must contain activity data. For details, see Specifying Ligands . Activity Property Name Name of the property that contains the numeric activity values. Activity Change Threshold Threshold used to determine whether a change in activity is to be considered a decrease or increase. For details about these and other parameters, see Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs - Parameters .

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify the ligands to be used by the protocol. The ligands must contain activity data. For details, see Specifying Ligands . |
| Activity Property Name | Name of the property that contains the numeric activity values. |
| Activity Change Threshold | Threshold used to determine whether a change in activity is to be considered a decrease or increase. |

For details about these and other parameters, see Analyze Activity Effects using MMPs - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to the background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the job is done, click View Results in the report page to open a table with the following information about the MMPs transformations:

| Section | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Most Frequent | Contains a bar graph with the most frequent transformations. Each bar indicates a transformation and the color coding quantifies the activity increase (green), decrease (red), and neutral (yellow). A label on the right axis indicates the type and number. Additionally, a table on the right side contains the SMILES transformation and a sketch of the associated reaction. Note that you can click the SMILES link to load an SD file into the Table View to review the ligand cores. |
| Most Frequently Change Activity | Contains a bar graph of the transformations that most frequently changed the activity. The color coding is the same used in the Most Frequent section. |
| Most Frequent Do Not change Activity | Contains a bar graph of the transformations that most frequently did not change the activity. The color coding is the same used in the Most Frequent section. |
| All Transformations | A table containing statistical information for all MMPs transformations found. Note that you can sort the table by column. |

Full table functionality requires an active a Pipeline Pilot Server connection.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files and the parameters used. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| ViewResults.ds_pl | Opens the MMPs report. |
| <ligands>.html | MMPs report containing several tables. |

Find Activity Cliffs using MMPs Understanding SAR Trends using Matched Molecular Pairs

# Find Activity Cliffs using MMPs - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/sar_find_activity_cliffs_using_mmps-para.htm

## Find Activity Cliffs using MMPs - Parameters

### Identifies activity cliffs using MMPs

Performs Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) transformations to find ligand activity cliffs. MMPs are pairs of ligands that differ by a single localized structural change. The two ligands belonging to an MMP can be interconverted by replacing the substructure in one of them with the different substructure in the other.
Ligands with an activity change exceeding the value specified in Activity Change Threshold are considered activity cliffs.

The protocol annotates the input ligand file with activity cliff information, and a table is created with the activity cliff information.

See Also :

* Hussain, J. and Rea, C. "Computationally Efficient Algorithm to Identify Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) in Large Data Sets", J.Chem. Inf. Model. , 2010 , 50 (3), 339-348.

* Hu, X.; Hu, Y.; Vogt, M.; Stumpfe, D.; Bajorath, J. "MMP-Cliffs: Systematic Identification of Activity Cliffs on the Basis of Matched Molecular Pairs", J. Chem Inf Model. , 2012 , ASAP

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Ligands | Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. |
| Activity Property | Name of the numeric property containing the ligand activity. |
| Activity Change Threshold | Threshold used to determine whether a change in activity is considered an increase or a decrease. Changes in the activity between the negative of this value and this value are considered neutral. For example, if the activity scales logarithmically, and a change in activity of two orders of magnitude would be significant, then set this threshold to 2. However, if the activity scales linearly, a change in activity of two orders of magnitude would require a threshold value of 100. |
| Partner Activity Cutoff | At least one of the molecular pair needs to have an activity value equal or below this threshold. Leave blank to disable cutoff. |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Maximum Activity Cliffs to Display | Maximum number of activity cliffs in the HTML page (disabled if empty). A large number of activity cliffs may reduce performance when displaying the results. |
| Cliff Partner Indexing Method | Cliff partner indexing method for the annotated ligand file. You can chose between name or index based. Valid Values: Name , Index |
| Minimum Fragment Size | Minimum number of heavy atoms in the fragments that define an MMP (not including attachment points). MMPs with smaller fragments are not generated. Leave blank to allow any number of atoms as the lower limit. |

| Minimum Core Size | Minimum number of heavy atoms in the core that define an MMP (not including attachment points). MMPs with smaller cores are not generated. Leave blank to allow any number of atoms as the lower limit. |
| Maximum Core Size | Maximum number of heavy atoms in the core that define an MMP (not including attachment points). MMPs with bigger cores are not generated. Leave blank to allow any number of atoms as the upper limit. |

This protocol finds ligand activity cliffs by using Matched Molecular Pairs (MMPs) transformation. MMPs are pairs of ligands that differ by a single localized structural change [Hussain and Rea, 2010] . The two ligands belonging to an MMP can be interconverted by replacing the substructure in one of them with the different substructure in the other. Ligands with an activity change exceeding a specified value are considered activity cliffs [Hu et al., 2012] . The protocol annotates the input ligand file with activity cliff information and generates a table with the activity cliff information.

Activity Change Threshold Threshold used to determine whether a change in activity is to be considered an increase or a decrease. For details about these and other parameters, see Find Activity Cliffs using MMPs - Parameters .

For details about these and other parameters, see Find Activity Cliffs using MMPs - Parameters .

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. Sending a job to the background closes the status dialog and allows you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer .

When the job is done, click View Results in the report page to open the Activity cliffs.
Activity cliffs are grouped by cores and are sorted by the activity change; the group with the highest cliff are first. 
In addition, the table is interactive and the columns can be sorted. The following information is available in the table:

| Section | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Index | Counter for the activity cliff. |
| Core | Counter for the activity cliffs that belong to the same core. |
| Activity Change | Activity change of the transformation. The activity changes are always reported as positive value (i.e., negative activity changes are inverted). Hover the cursor over the value to display the activity values from before and after the transformation. |
| Reactant Name | Reactant ligand name. |
| Reactant | Depiction of the reactant with the transformation group highlighted in magenta. |
| Product | Product ligand name. |
| Product Name | Depiction of the product with the transformation group highlighted in magenta. |
| Reaction | Depiction of the transformation. |
| Transformation | SMILES representation of the transformation. |

The protocol also creates a file with the annotated input ligands. For each ligand, properties are added indicating 
if the ligand was part of an activity cliff and in how many transformations the ligand was found. Additionally, partners, transformations, and activity changes for each activity cliff are listed in separate columns.

# Sketch Molecules tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/sketch_analyze_guide.htm

## Sketch Molecules tools

The Sketch Molecules tools help you create new small molecules and perform simple edits to structures.

If a Molecule Window is not already open, use the Molecule Window action to create a new one.

Once you have sketched a molecule, you can minimize it using a fast Dreiding-like forcefield. See Clean Geometry .

### Sketching

Sketch: Sketches atoms and bonds. The cursor changes to indicate the Sketch tool is in use. To sketch atoms and bonds, click in the Molecule Window, move the cursor and click again. To change the bond order, click on the bond.

Chain: Draws chains of atoms. The cursor changes to a pencil and line to indicate the Chain tool is in use. An indicator appears to show how long the chain is.

Ring: Creates rings of any size.

* To draw a single six atom ring, click in the Molecule Window.

* To create a ring with more or fewer than six atoms, click while dragging.

* To create an aromatic ring, CTRL+click.

* To fuse a ring onto an existing ring, click a bond in an existing ring, and then drag the mouse to draw a new ring of the desired size.

* To spiro-fuse a ring onto an existing ring, click on an atom in the existing ring.

### Editing

Select: Allows you to selects one or more objects using the mouse. You can select multiple objects by using by either SHIFT+click additional objects, or by dragging a lasso around a set of objects.

Add: Adds hydrogen atoms to the selected atoms, or, if no selection is made, to any molecules in the active window.

Hide: Removes either the selected or all hydrogen atoms from the active window.

Torsion: Rotates atoms about a bond. The cursor 
changes to an arrow wrapping around a line to indicate the Torsion tool is in use.

* To rotate a torsion, click the bond to be rotated and drag. By default, the Torsion tool moves the part of the molecule containing
fewer atoms. To move the larger portion, use SHIFT+drag. If there is no torsion monitor for the bond being rotated, a temporary torsion monitor is created. The temporary torsion monitor is removed when releasing the mouse button.
See Structure | Monitor | Torsion for more information about the torsion monitor.

* To rotate the atoms of a peptide bond and all atoms immediately connected to them around the axis formed by the two C α atoms connected to the atoms of the peptide bond, use CTRL+drag.

* To rotate the carbonyl group around the axis formed by the C α and N atoms connected to the carbon atom of the carbonyl group, use CTRL+SHIFT+drag.

Table: Allows you to change the element of selected atoms by choosing from a periodic table. You can also use keyboard shortcuts for many common atoms such as C, H, N, O, P, F, S, I, B. See Change Element dialog .

Set: Changes the charge of selected atoms. You are prompted to enter a fractional charge as a numerator and denominator. For example, entering a value of 1 for each will set the charge to +1. See Set Formal Charge dialog .

There are several methods for modifying the bond order:

* Select a bond and type a number: 1 for single, 2 for double, and 3 for triple. To modify the bond order to aromatic or partial double bond, use one of the next two methods.

* Select the bond, and then right-click and choose an option from the Bond menu.

* Select the bond, choose Chemistry from the menu bar, and then choose an option from the Bond menu.

## Molecule Browser tools

The Molecule Browser tools allow you to use navigation arrows to step through molecules in the Data Table View , such as docking or scoring results. Additionally, you can filter molecules or group molecules by a property value, such as by name, and then display only molecules with that value.

Show First Molecule: Show the first molecule and hide the current one.

Show Previous Molecule: Show the previous molecule and hide the current one.

Show Next Molecule: Show the next molecule and hide the current one.

Show Last Molecule: Show the last molecule and hide the current one.

Group/Ungroup Ligands: Create or remove groups based on columns. You can browse the groups using the navigation arrows, or jump to a specific group using Current Group .

Current Group: Navigate to a specific group.

Filter: Opens the Filter dialog , which you can use to select molecules in the Data Table based on specific criteria.

Remove Filters: Removes filters and grouping.

Show First Group: Show the first group in the Data Table View.

Show Previous Group: Show the previous group in the Data Table View.

Show Next Group: Show the first next in the Data Table View.

Show Last Group: Show the last group in the Data Table View.

# Choose a QSAR model

Source type: HTML

Source section: tssmallmolecules

Source file: tssmallmolecules/tsk_qsar_choose-model.htm

## Choose a QSAR model

Choose a QSAR model based on the type of data:

| Model | Data | Advantages/Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bayesian | Binary classification (yes/no property), categorical, and fingerprint data | Intrinsically guards against overfitting Can handle a large amount of data Runs very fast Easy to interpret Cannot handle continuous data as a dependent property. |
| Multiple Linear Regression | Data with few descriptors; fingerprint data is treated as stepwise variables (1 if a feature is present, 0 if not) | Easy to interpret Prone to overfitting |
| Genetic Function Approximation | Data with many descriptors | Returns multiple models Selects variables automatically Prone to overfitting |
| Partial Least Squares | Data with few descriptors; fingerprint data is treated as stepwise variables (1 if a feature is present, 0 if not) | Often performs better than simple multiple linear regression Not easy to interpret |
| Recursive Partitioning | Data with many descriptors | Automatically selects variables for splitting Multiple ways to create a model (single tree, forest, multiple-Y, etc.) Single tree models are easy to interpret, but prone to overfitting and are less accurate Forest models are more accurate, but are not easy to interpret |

* Intrinsically guards against overfitting

* Can handle a large amount of data

* Runs very fast

* Easy to interpret

* Cannot handle continuous data as a dependent property.

* Prone to overfitting

* Returns multiple models

* Selects variables automatically

* Often performs better than simple multiple linear regression

* Not easy to interpret

* Automatically selects variables for splitting

* Multiple ways to create a model (single tree,
forest, multiple-Y, etc.)

* Single tree models are easy to interpret, but prone to overfitting and are less accurate

* Forest models are more accurate, but are not easy to interpret

## General small molecule tasks

The tasks below are basic tasks for working with small molecules.
For a comprehensive list of small molecule tasks that include basic tasks and tasks that involve working with the Small Molecules tool set, see Tasks - Small Molecules .

* Sketch a molecule

* Apply a QSAR model built within Discovery Studio

* Choose a training set

To apply a QSAR model built within Discovery Studio

Once a QSAR model is built, it adds the property or properties that this
model can calculate to the list of Molecular Properties under the "Other"
Category in the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. You can access these
properties by running a calculation using that protocol.

Calculable properties used in the model are calculated on the fly when applying the model, but external or non-calculable properties need to be precalculated for the compounds. Properties such as those calculated by DMol3 or VAMP must be calculated before applying the model because they cannot be calculated on the fly.

To build a carbohydrate

* Choose File | New | Molecule Window from the menu bar.

* Open the Small Molecules | Build Fragment tools.

* Expand the Carbohydrates fragment library and double-click the desired carbohydrate monomer.
This opens the first carbohydrate residue into the Molecule Window as a new molecule.

* Click another carbohydrate monomer, select the desired hydroxyl group hydrogen from the
3D Fragment View, and select the desired oxygen atom or the hydrogen atom of the
hydroxyl group that it will be attached to from the carbohydrate in the Molecule Window.

* Click Fuse Fragment .
The monomer in the 3D Fragment View is added to the carbohydrate in the Molecule Window
at the selection point.
The two hydroxyl groups have been replaced by a single oxygen atom.

* Repeat the last two steps to extend the carbohydrate chain.

* Check the quality; the predictive power of the QSAR model relies on the quality of the training data.

* Divide the data into a training set and a test set. Use the training set to build the model of choice, and use the test set to get an indication of how reliable the built model is. The splitting is often done randomly, and can be repeated multiple times. The Generate Training and Test Data protocol can be used to help accomplish this task.

To clean small molecules

Choose Structure | Clean Geometry menu.
A fast Dreiding-like forcefield geometry optimization is applied to the selection.

To create a tag property to use as the dependent property in the Create Bayesian Model protocol

Use the Add Attribute Dialog to create a new property.

To create an RG/RXN file

Discovery Studio client does not offer this capability. However, you can use a product such as BIOVIA Draw to accomplish this task.

To derive a new property

The Basic Arithmetic protocol allows you to derive a new property.

To disable poling

There are two Catalyst.cfg parameters that should be used to disable poling:

* confAnalysis.best.no.poling=true

* confGen.minTopPolingLength=10000 (or a large topological distance greater than any atom pair in a molecule)

Both the BEST and FAST conformation generation algorithms use poling. BEST applies poling to the 3D coordinate space, while FAST applies poling only to the torsion space. The CAESAR algorithm does not use poling to sample the torsion space. Both FAST and CAESAR use BEST to sample ring conformations.

To display error bars in the charts

Point plots support the display of an error bar. With the Data Window open, choose Chart | Point Plot from the menu
to open the Choose Plot Axes dialog. Select a column in the Error bars menu to choose the error bar property.

To distinguish between the two Pareto optimization protocols

The Optimize Combinatorial Library with Pareto Method protocol takes a pre-enumerated combinatorial library (either an RG or RXN file) as input. It then creates several smaller optimal combinatorial libraries, sampling each R group or reactant as specified by the input parameters. The output is essentially smaller combinatorial subset libraries with each R group or reactant sampled.

The Optimize Subset Library with Pareto Method protocol takes a set of ligands as input. It then creates several smaller optimal subsets. The protocol is designed to take any set of input ligands as input (e.g., a corporate collection, vendor ligands, etc.), not necessarily an enumerated combinatorial library. Even if your input is an enumerated combinatorial library, the subsets you get are unlikely combinatorial libraries (i.e., there is no guarantee that the R groups or reactants will be equally sampled).

To edit molecular properties

* The Molecule Window also provides a convenient way to edit molecule properties such as the activity data for HypoGen and HipHop. To do this,
first load molecules from a file into the Molecule Window. Open the Data Table by pressing CTRL+T .

* To modify the values of existing properties, select a cell and type in the new value.

* If a property does not exist, you can add the new property to all molecules by right clicking anywhere in the property table, and select Add Attributes... from the context menu. This will open the Attributes dialog, select Molecule in the Add to field, and type in new property name and value.
The same property and value will be added to all molecules in the Molecule Window.

* You can modify the values for each molecule if the values of all molecules are different. For HypoGen, the following properties are required:
activity (property name Activ ) and uncertainty (property name Uncert ).

* To run HypoGen , you can open the 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation protocol, and select Input Ligands from the Molecule Window for molecules with Activ and Uncert properties. See 3D QSAR Pharmacophore Generation for more details.

To minimize small molecules

Use the Minimize Ligands tool panel to minimize small molecules.

To perform a conformational search on small molecules

To remove a QSAR model from the server and from the Molecular Properties list

Use the Delete User Models protocol to remove a QSAR model. The protocol automatically finds the models you have permission to remove.

To share QSAR models

Each time you successfully build a QSAR model using any of the available methods, Name .xml and ModelDescription.html files are created in the Output folder. The base name of the .xml file is the value set by the Model Name parameter. The .xml file contains the actual model. ModelDescription.html contains
information about the model including how the model was built and what properties it can calculate. These files can be used to share the model with
other people. If you wish to share your model with colleagues, give these files to them. Your colleague can import this model into their server.

* In the Protocols Explorer , select the folder corresponding to the user's protocols.

* Right-click using the mouse and select Import .

* Select the .xml file that contains the built model. Since this is a component and not a protocol, it will not appear
in the users's protocol folder. However, it is imported into the database and can be accessed using the Calculate Molecular Properties protocol. It will appear under the Other category of the Molecular Properties parameter.

Use the Delete User Models protocol to delete one or more user-built QSAR models.

To use principal components

There are a number of ways to make use of these principal components:

* The Calculate Principal Components protocol generates a ViewResults.ds_pl script to allow you to visualize the first three principal components in 3D
plots. This usually gives you an idea how the molecules are distributed in the
principal components space.

* You can search for similar molecules from another library using these principal components,
to cluster molecules, to identify outliers or diverse set of molecules, etc.

* You can use these components to generate a regression model using Create Multiple Linear
Regression Model (Principal Components Regression).

To use the Minimum Number of Components parameter in the Calculate Principal Components protocol

In the Calculate Principal Components protocol, the number of components you get depends on two parameters: Minimum Variance Explained and Minimum Number of Components . The protocol will continue to add principal components until both criteria have been satisfied.
