# Validate Model Molecule

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/x-ray_validate_model_molecule.htm

## Validate Model Molecule

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Troubleshooting

The Validate Model Molecule protocol assesses the integrity of a protein structure by performing a
series of structural checks, and monitors the deviations from known values gathered from high-resolution crystal
structures. These structural tests are based on stereochemical and crystallographic benchmarks, such as bond lengths,
valence angles, Ramachandran plot violations, etc. This protocol is typically used during later stages of the
refinement process to check areas of the structure that need further adjustment.

Validate Model Molecule can be carried out with three available settings: refined, partially_refined, or high_resolution for high quality protein models.

The following structural checks are available:

* Bond Length Violations

* CA-CA Distance

* Valence Angle Violations

* Peptide Bold Planarity Violations

* Cis Peptide Bonds

* Ramachandran Map Violations

* Planarity Violations

* Chi1 Angle Violations

* Chi2 Angle Violations

* Chirality Violations

* Non-Bonded Clashes

* Residue B-factor Distribution

You can specify tolerances for the different tests when you set up the protocol run.
The default tolerances depend on the quality of the input structure. Three different rotamer libraries
are available for tests of preferred dihedral values: Ponder_Richards, Sutcliffe, and Oldfield.

After running the protocol, a summary report is created listing some of the violations. However a second report, which has greater detail of the tests performed, is named ModelStatistics.txt and can be found in the Output folder.

Values for R-work and R-free may differ from those reported by other programs. If comparing R-values from
other CNX refined structures, be sure to select the same bulk solvent correction method used for
the previous refinement.

* Load the structure you wish to validate into a Molecule Window.

* Open the X-ray | Edit X-ray Structure tools and click Validate Model Molecule... to open the Validate Model Molecule dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Protein Molecule Choose the loaded structure. Input Reflection Data Select a reflection data window or browse to the reflection file of
the molecule being validated. For details about the remaining parameters, see Validate Model Molecule - Parameters . The Validate Model Molecule protocol
performs the following 12 structure tests available from the Advanced | Structure Tests parameter: Bond Length Violations CA-CA Distances Valence Angles Violations Peptide Bond Planarity Violations Cis Peptide Bonds Ramachandran Map Violations Planarity Violations Chi1 Angle Violations Chi2 Angle Violations Chirality Violations Non-bonded Clashes Residue B-factor Distribution All of the above tests are selected by default, but can be individually deselected if
not required.

| Parameter | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecule | Choose the loaded structure. |
| Input Reflection Data | Select a reflection data window or browse to the reflection file of the molecule being validated. |

For details about the remaining parameters, see Validate Model Molecule - Parameters .

The Validate Model Molecule protocol
performs the following 12 structure tests available from the Advanced | Structure Tests parameter:

* CA-CA Distances

* Valence Angles Violations

* Peptide Bond Planarity Violations

All of the above tests are selected by default, but can be individually deselected if
not required.

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. If the job is sent to the background, the dialog window will close allowing you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can then monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer . If the job is not sent to the background, the job will then continue to completion and a report window will be displayed. You may then click on the "Model Statistics" link to retrieve the results of the validation run.

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Report.htm | Job summary including input and output files, summary of experiment information such as Unit Cell, Space Group, resolution limits used, and calculated values for R-factor and R-free. The report also indicates all of the parameters used in the calculation. |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| cnx_validate_stdout.txt | Raw CNX log file. |
| ModelStatistics.txt | Output file that contains detailed results of all the tests performed. |

# Pick Water - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/x-ray_water_picking-para.htm

## Pick Water - Parameters

### Picks water molecules from an electron density map

Detects water molecules in an electron density map of a fully or partially refined protein structure, and adds them to the initial structure.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecule | Selects a protein structure to read. |
| Input Reflection Data | Select a reflection data to read. |
| Field Mapping | Assigns field mapping for CNX/CNS format. |
| Amplitude Field | The field name for amplitude. |
| Amplitude Deviation Field | The field name for amplitude standard deviation. |
| Intensity Field | The field name for intensity. |
| Intensity Deviation Field | The field name for intensity standard deviation. |
| Minimum Peak Height | All electron density peaks with a maximum above this sigma level and containing no molecular coordinates are identified and sorted in descending order of peak magnitude. Water-deleting criteria are then applied to the selected peaks. |
| Water Picking Map Type | Specifies the type of map to generate. Note: Selection of a map of type Fo-Fc requires a minimum peak height of approximately 1.5 to 4 sigma units (with 3 sigma as default). A map of type 2Fo-Fc will require a minimum peak height closer to 1 sigma unit. Valid Values: Fo-Fc , 2Fo-Fc, 3Fo-2Fc |
| Advanced | Options for advanced users wanting to modify various default parameters related to: Pick and Refine Water Parameters Map Generation Refinement Target Resolution limits Forcefield selection Reflection Data Test Set definition |
| Water Picking | Water Picking parameter options related to: Maximum Number of Picked Peaks Water Picking Map Weighting Scheme Water Picking Map Grid Size Simulated Annealing Steps of Coordinate Minimization Steps of B-factor Minimization Distance Based Criteria |
| Maximum Number of Picked Peaks | Defines the Maximum Number of Peaks that can be picked. |
| Water Picking Map Weighting Scheme | Specifies the weighting scheme to use for map generation. Available weighting schemes: sigmaa : Weights calculated from sigmaA unweighted : No figure-of-merit weighting gradient : Gradient of the current crystallographic target with respect to Fc Note: Two additional weighting schemes are available from CNX standalone: combined : Combines model and experimental phases. observed : Uses observed phases and fom from phase probability distribution. Valid Values: sigmaa , unweighted, gradient |
| Water Picking Map Grid Size | Specifies the resolution of the grid for maps, relative to the high-resolution limit of the reflection data. In general, the resolution of the grid for maps is 1/3 to 1/4 of the high resolution in reciprocal space. For example, given a relative grid size of 0.33, if the high-resolution limit of the diffraction data is 3 Å, the grid spacing of the map is about 1 Å in each dimension. Valid Values: 0.33 , 0.25 |
| Steps of Coordinate Minimization | Number of steps to perform during coordinate minimization. |
| Steps of B-factor Minimization | Number of steps to perform during B-factor minimization using the Powell method. |
| Distance Based Criteria | Select picks based on distance criteria: none : all peaks greater than the minimum peak height and closer than the maximum distance are kept. distance : peaks greater than the minimum distance and less than maximum distance from any atom are kept. hbond : the above distance criterion is applied except that peaks further than the minimum hydrogen bonding distance from oxygen or nitrogen atoms are also kept. Valid Values: none, distance, hbond |
| Minimum Distance | Water molecules are rejected if the minimum distance between the water peak and any atom in the structure is greater than the maximum distance defined. |
| Maximum Distance | Water molecules are rejected if the minimum distance between the water peak and any atom in the structure is greater than the maximum distance defined. |
| Minimum H-Bond Distance Between HOH and N or O | Minimum H-Bond Distance Between HOH and N or O |
| Maximum H-Bond Distance Between HOH and N or O | Maximum H-Bond Distance Between HOH and N or O |
| Keep Only H-Bonded Waters | After the distance criteria are applied to the peaks, those Hydrogens farther than the maximum hydrogen bonding distance from nitrogen and oxygen atoms are rejected. Valid Values: True , False |
| B-factor Threshold | If coordinate and B-factor refinement are applied, then waters with a B-factor greater than this value are deleted. |
| Keep Waters at Special Positions | When this is turned on, waters at special positions are retained. Any atom which is within a Special Position Cutoff of itself after application of symmetry is considered to be in a special position. Valid Values: True, False |
| Generate Map | Specifies to generate maps at the end of refinement. Valid Values: True , False |
| Map Type | Specifies the type of map to generate. Valid Values: 2Fo-Fc , 3Fo-2Fc, Fo-Fc |
| Map Weighting Scheme | Specifies the weighting scheme to use for map generation. Available weighting schemes: sigmaA : Weights calculated from sigmaA unweighted : No figure-of-merit weighting. Valid Values: sigmaa , unweighted |
| Normalize Map | If this is turned on the map is normalized by dividing by the rms sigma of the map. Otherwise, the map is on an absolute scale. Valid Values: True , False |
| Relative Map Grid Size | Specifies the resolution of the grid for maps, relative to the high-resolution limit of the reflection data. In general, the resolution of the grid for maps is 1/3 to 1/4 of the high resolution in reciprocal space. For example, given a relative grid size of 0.33, if the high-resolution limit of the diffraction data is 3 Å, the grid spacing of the map is about 1 Å in each dimension. Valid Values: 0.33 , 0.25 |
| Extent | Defines how far the grid boundary points are from the solute as a percentage (%). Valid Values: molecule , asymmetric, unit, box, fractional |
| Map Cushion | Specifies size (in Å) of cushion around the molecule during map generation. |
| Refinement Target | When gradient weighting is selected, the map is weighted by the gradient of the crystallographic target with respect to Fc. Note: For this release of the collection, we will only support the mlf refinement target. However standalone CNX does supports a variety of refinement targets such as: mlf : Maximum likelihood target using amplitudes mli : Maximum likelihood target using intensities mlhl : Maximum likelihood target using amplitudes and phase probability distribution residual : Standard crystallographic residual vector : Vector residual mixed : (1-fom)*residual + fom*vector e2e2 : Correlation coefficient using normalized E2 1e1 : Correlation coefficient using normalized E f2f2 : Correlation coefficient using F2 f1f1 : Correlation coefficient using Fe Valid Values: mlf |
| Solvent Correction | Specifies solvent correction method to use. Valid Values: none, babinet, mask |
| Reflection Data Limits | Reflection Data resolution limits are automatically calculated and used by the protocol. These limits may be overwritten by providing values for these two parameters: High Resolution Limit Low Resolution Limit |
| High Resolution Limit | Limit on the reflection data that will be used for the individual coordinates and B-factors refinement. If left blank, values will be derived from the reflection data set. |
| Low Resolution Limit | Limit on the reflection data that will be used for the individual coordinates and B-factors refinement. If left blank, values will be derived from the reflection data set. |
| Forcefield Typing | Molecular Typing is performed automatically using forcefield based atom types and parameters provided by the XPROLIG forcefield. An alternate option for parameter and topology definition has been included using the third party algorithm XPLO2D for ligand atom typing, and the generate.inp script for protein typing. Setting the parameter Forcefield Name to XPLO2D will use the generate.inp molecular typing procedure. Please ensure that the XPLO2D executable has been properly installed as per the instructions provided in the Forcefield Name parameter help. Note: The XPLO2D code is licensed by the UPPSALA Software factory, and any inquiries should be made directly to: http://xray.bmc.uu.se/usf |
| Forcefield Name | Specifies which forcefield to assign. For XPLO2D , you need to have the lx_xplo2d executable installed, and set up the global property lx_xplo2d_exe to point to the executable, for example set lx_xplo2d_exe to /opt/xutil_linux/lx_xplo2d . You can use SciTegic Server Administration Portal to set up lx_xplo2d_exe for all users. Note: Currently only the Linux version of lx_xplo2d is available. See Also: http://xray.bmc.uu.se/usf Valid Values: XPROLIG , XPLO2D |
| Keep Existing | If True and the input data record already has the forcefield assigned as specified by Forcefield Name , the input data record is turned out of the pass port without any change. Valid Values: True , False |
| XPROLIG | The XPROLIG forcefield is a CHARMm based forcefield which has been designed to automate the process of molecular typing for X-ray refinement using CNX. Modifications to the estimated forcefield parameters can be easily made using the Discovery Studio Client. |
| Input FFML Filename | The FFML file which may contain customized parameters and atom types. When specified, this will override the Forcefield Name parameter. |
| Automatic Parameter Estimation | Specifies whether automatic parameter estimation is on or off. The default is true. Valid Values: True , False |
| Reflection Data Test Set | The following parameters allow the user to keep the existing selection of reflections to be used for the R-free calculation. The selection may be made anew, by setting the Keep Existing parameter to False . The percentage of reflections selected for the test set may also be defined by the Probability parameter. A threshold for the number of reflections selected for the test set is also provided to avoid nonsense refinement. |
| Reflection Data Test Set Keep Existing | Keep the existing test set unless its Test Set Percentage is zero or 1. Valid Values: True , False |
| Probability | Specified the probability that a reflection is to be selected into the test set. |
| Percentage Threshold | The data record is to be turned out of the Fail port if its TestSetPercentage is larger than the specified value. |

# HT-XPIPE - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/x-ray_xpipe-para.htm

## HT-XPIPE - Parameters

### Places and refines protein-ligand complexes in high-throughput mode

For each system, a reflection file, a model structure, and a set of ligands is used as input.

The following steps may be performed:

* Molecular Replacement: Performs the Rotation and Translation functions from CNX to find the best molecular replacement solution.

* Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization: Optimizes the model structure using rigid-body minimization.

* Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization: Optimizes the model structure using full model minimization.

* Pre-Placement Ligand Minimization: Optimizes ligand structures using CHARMm. Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson minimization algorithm is used. The maximum number of steps is 1000 and the RMS energy gradient convergence is set to 0.05 kcal/mol/Å.

* Ligand Placement: Flexibly fits ligands to the Fo-Fc electron density map using X-Ligand.

* Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization: Optimizes the complex using full model minimization.

* Water Picking: Adds water molecules to available density using a water selection heuristic.

* Final Refinement: Optimizes the complex in the final stage.

Notes:

* The final refined model is saved in a dsv file that contains the minimized protein structure with ligands and water placed.

* The density map is also included in the dsv file.

See Also:

* "Principles of Protein X-ray Crystallography" (2nd Edn.), by Jan Drenth, Springer, 1999 .

* Brunger et al., Crystallography & NMR System: A New Software Suite for Macromolecular Structure Determination, Acta Cryst. (1998), D54 , 905-921.

* Oldfield, T. J., X-LIGAND: an application for the automated addition of flexible ligands into electron density, Acta Cryst. (2001), D57 , 696-705.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Reflection Data | Reflection data files to use. Supported file formats include CNX/CNS (.cv), PDB sf-CIF (.cif, .ent), Scalepack (.sca), d*Trek (.hkl), SHELX (.hkl), and MTZ (.mtz). In Discovery Studio, you have the option to select the reflection data from active Reflection Data Window(s). Selection of a single or multiple files is also supported, and offers the best performance. |
| Input Model Structures | Structures to use as the starting model. Heavy metal atoms should be placed in the model structure manually prior to automatic placement of the ligand(s). In Discovery Studio, you can only select from Molecule Windows. |
| Input Ligands | The file or URL source to read. Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio, you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. Notes: When selecting from an active Molecule Window, only a single entry is allowed. If multiple sources are needed, you should use the file option. The ligands should contain a property ResName that will be used as the three-letter residue name in PDB format. If this property is missing, it will be generated from the acronym of the Name property. |
| File Mapping | Specify how the reflection data, model structures and ligands are grouped. Match by File Name: Match reflection data, model structures and ligands by file name. This option requires the number of files to match except that a single model structure can be used for all batches. Match Manually: Manually matching files. Input Mapping File: Use a spreadsheet file to specify the matching. Valid Values: Match by File Name , Match Manually, Input Mapping File |
| Manual File Mapping | Manually specify how to match data files. Each line should contain tab-delimited file names in order of reflection data, model structure and ligands file. For example: reflection1.cif protein1.pdb ligand1.sd reflection2.cif protein2.pdb ligand2.sd |
| Input Mapping File | A spreadsheet file with data files being matched. Each mapping should be in one line with the file names tab-delimited. For example: reflection1.cif protein1.pdb ligand1.sd reflection2.cif protein2.pdb ligand2.sd |
| Tasks | The following steps may be performed: Molecular Replacement: Performs the Rotation and Translation functions from CNX to find the best molecular replacement solution. Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization: Optimizes the model structure using rigid-body minimization. Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization: Optimizes the model structure using full model minimization. Pre-Placement Ligand Minimization: Optimizes ligand structures using CHARMm. Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson minimization algorithm is used. The maximum number of steps is 1000 and the RMS energy gradient convergence is set to 0.05 kcal/mol/Å. Ligand Placement: Flexibly fits ligands to the Fo-Fc electron density map using X-Ligand. Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization: Optimizes the complex using full model minimization. Water Picking: Adds water molecules to fit extra density. Final Refinement: Optimizes the complex in the final stage. Adjustable parameters of each task can be found in the Advanced parameter group. Valid Values: Molecular Replacement , Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization , Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization , Pre-Placement Ligand Minimization , Ligand Placement , Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization , Water Picking , Final Refinement |
| Advanced | Contains less commonly used parameters. |
| Molecular Replacement | Parameters used in Molecular Replacement . |
| Molecular Replacement Cross Rotation Reflection Data High Resolution Limit | High resolution limit. |
| Molecular Replacement Translation Reflection Data High Resolution Limit | High resolution limit. |
| Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization | Parameters used in Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization . |
| Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization Number of Cycles | Number of cycles of rigid-body minimization to perform. |
| Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization Number of Steps Per Cycle | Number of steps per cycle to use during rigid-body minimization. |
| Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization | Parameters used in Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization . |
| Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization Number of Cycles | Number of cycles of coordinate minimization to perform in post molecular replacement refinement. |
| Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization Number of Steps Per Cycle | Number of steps per cycle to use during coordinate minimization in post molecular replacement refinement. |
| Ligand Placement | Parameters used in Ligand Placement . |
| Ligand Placement Sigma Threshold | Specifies the map level (in sigma) at which the search for possible ligand sites is made. Higher thresholds result in more sites being found and also increase the extent of the volume of each site that does not overlap the protein. Lower thresholds often result in the overlap of sites, giving fewer, larger sites. In general, set the value to 1.5 for 2Fo-Fc density maps and 2.5 for Fo-Fc density maps. |
| Ligand Placement Rejection Threshold | A ligand placement is to be rejected if the best density fit score divided by the ligand's Molecular_Weight is less than the specified value. |
| Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization | Parameters used in Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization . |
| Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization Number of Cycles | Number of cycles of coordinate minimization to perform. |
| Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization Number of Steps Per Cycle | Number of steps per cycle to use during coordinate minimization. |
| Water Picking | Parameters used in Water Picking . |
| Water Picking Maximum Number of Picked Peaks | Defines the Maximum Number of Peaks that can be picked. |
| Water Picking Minimum Peak Height | All electron density peaks with a maximum above this sigma level and containing no molecular coordinates are identified and sorted in descending order of peak magnitude. Water-deleting criteria are then applied to the selected peaks. |
| Final Refinement | Refinement task you wish to perform. Available steps are: Coordinate Minimization Domain B-factor Minimization Group B-factor Minimization Individual B-factor Minimization Group Occupancy Minimization Individual Occupancy Minimization Note: Minimization steps should be selected depending on the task. Valid Values: Coordinate Minimization , Domain B-factor Minimization , Group B-factor Minimization , Individual B-factor Minimization , Group Occupancy Minimization , Individual Occupancy Minimization |
| Final Refinement Coordinate Minimization | Specifies the coordinate minimization settings for refinement. |
| Final Refinement Coordinate Minimization Number of Steps Per Cycle | Number of steps per cycle to use during coordinate minimization. |
| Final Refinement Coordinate Minimization Number of Cycles | Number of cycles of coordinate minimization to perform. |
| Final Refinement B-factor Minimization | B-factor Minimization Tasks to perform: Domain B-factor Minimization Group B-factor Minimization Individual B-factor Minimization All tasks may be selected or only a subset. |
| Final Refinement B-factor Minimization Domain Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during group B-factor minimization. |
| Final Refinement B-factor Minimization Group Number of Steps | Number of Steps for Residue B-factor Minimization. |
| Final Refinement B-factor Minimization Individual Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during individual B-factor minimization. |
| Final Refinement Occupancy Minimization | Occupancy minimization tasks to perform: Group Occupancy Minimization Individual Occupancy Minimization |
| Final Refinement Occupancy Minimization Group Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during group occupancy minimization. |
| Final Refinement Occupancy Minimization Individual Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during individual occupancy minimization. |
| Parallel Processing | Execute this protocol in parallel on Pipeline Pilot servers. You can set the number of data records sent in each process batch, the name of the servers, the number of protocol processes executed on each server, and whether to preserve the order of the processed data records. Notes : Not all parts of the protocol are run in parallel, which may affect scaling. In general, performance improves when the parallelization benefits outweigh the data transfer overhead for the specified batch size. By default, Pipeline Pilot servers are configured to allow a maximum of four processes per protocol. You can adjust this on the Pipeline Pilot Server Administration Portal. # HT-XPIPE

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/x-ray_xpipe.htm

## HT-XPIPE

* Description

* Setting up and running

* Analyzing results

High Throughput - X-ray crystallography PIPEline (HT-XPIPE) is a protocol that takes a reflection file, a model structure, and a set of ligands for each system and automatically places and refines protein-ligand complexes in high throughput mode. The following optional tasks can be performed by HT-XPIPE:

* Molecular Replacement: Conduct a round of molecular replacement using the traditional CNX Rotation and Translation routines. At this stage, the top orientation from the rotation search is used as input for the translation search query. The top solution from the translation search is then used as input for the next step in the pipeline. You can modify the high resolution limits, however, all other search parameters use sensible defaults.

* Post Molecular Replacement Rigid-Body Minimization: Perform rigid-body minimization using the Molecular Replacement solution or your initial input structure. Rigid body minimization is used to prepare the structure for further refinement. Options in this case allow you to modify the number of rigid body cycles and the number of steps.

* Post Molecular Replacement Coordinate Minimization: Minimize the coordinates of the solution from Molecular Replacement or your initial input structure. The number of cycles as well as the number of steps in the minimization can also be adjusted.

* Pre-Placement Ligand Minimization: Use the Adopted Basis Newton-Raphson method to minimize the ligands using the default CHARMm forcefield. This step will run until 1000 steps are completed or the RMS gradient converges to 0.05 kcal/mol/Å. Because of the routine nature of this method, no options are provided.

* Ligand Placement: Perform ligand placement for the input ligands. The ligand placement step follows the same methodology developed for X-Ligand [Oldfield, 2001] with several enhancements. The main steps of the ligand placement stage are: Site Search Ligand Conformational Search Scoring of the best conformers to the electron density Real space refinement The enhancements includes automated scanning of multiple sigma levels and the ability to place multiple ligands for a single receptor. To support the latter, automated sorting of the ligands based on molecular weight is necessary because larger ligands must be placed first followed by smaller ones. A final check to determine whether the ligand should be placed into the density involves a filter check with the threshold of the density fit score divided by the ligand's molecular weight. In cases where ligands do not bind to the receptor in the crystallization experiment, the check attempts to prevent the placement of ligands into areas of electron density where the ligand is not present.

* Site Search

* Ligand Conformational Search

* Scoring of the best conformers to the electron density

* Real space refinement

The enhancements includes automated scanning of multiple sigma levels and the ability to place multiple ligands for a single receptor. To support the latter, automated sorting of the ligands based on molecular weight is necessary because larger ligands must be placed first followed by smaller ones.

A final check to determine whether the ligand should be placed into the density involves a filter check with the threshold of the density fit score divided by the ligand's molecular weight. In cases where ligands do not bind to the receptor in the crystallization experiment, the check attempts to prevent the placement of ligands into areas of electron density where the ligand is not present.

* Post Ligand Placement Coordinate Minimization: After ligands have been placed, you can perform a round of minimization to refine the fit of the ligands into the electron density. This step is highly recommended given that initial placement of the ligand is typically not optimal.

* Water Picking: Add waters automatically using the water selection routine from CNX.

* Final Refinement: After the structure has been solved, initially refined, ligands and waters added, the model is ready for a final round of refinement. Coordinates, B-factors, and occupancies are refined at this stage to finalize the model.

* Load the structure you want to run the cascade on into a Molecule Window.

* Open the X-ray | Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools and click HT-XPIPE... to open the HT-XPIPE dialog. You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

You can also run this protocol using the Protocols Explorer .

* Set the following parameters: Parameter Description Input Reflection Data Reflection data files to use. Supported file formats include CNX/CNS (.cv), PDB sf-CIF (.sf, .cif, .ent), Scalepack (.sca), d*Trek (.hkl), SHELX (.hkl), and MTZ (.mtz). You have the option to select the reflection data from an active Reflection Data Window. Selection of a single or multiple files is also supported, and offers the best performance. Input Model Structures Structures to use as the starting model. Heavy metal atoms should be placed in the model structure manually prior to automatic placement of the ligands. You can only select from Molecule Windows. Input Ligands Specify one or more MDL MOL/SD files that contain the ligands to be used for the calculation. In Discovery Studio , you also have the option to specify all, selected, or visible ligands in an active Molecule Window. However, specifying a file offers the best performance. Ligands with greater than 10 rotatable bonds may cause problems during the conformer generation stage. Please limit the use of HT-XPIPE with ligands having less than 10 rotatable bonds. File Mapping Specify how the reflection data, model structures and ligands are grouped. The Match by File Name option can group them by sorting the file names and then group them sequentially. Generally the number of reflection data, model structures, and ligands should be the same to use this option. If there is a single model structure, it is duplicated to match the number of reflection data files. For other cases, use the Match Manually or Input Mapping File options, which allow you to specify the matching using a text box or spreadsheet file. For details regarding the remaining parameters, see HT-XPIPE - Parameters .

You have the option to select the reflection data from an active Reflection Data Window. Selection of a single or multiple files is also supported, and offers the best performance. |

For details regarding the remaining parameters, see HT-XPIPE - Parameters .

* Click Run to start the calculation.

The job status is displayed in a dialog that includes an option to send the job to background. If the job is sent to the background, the dialog window will close allowing you to continue using Discovery Studio while the job runs. You can then monitor the status of a background job and open the results from the Jobs Explorer . If the job is not sent to the background, the job will then continue to completion and a report window will be automatically displayed.

During the run, the protocol creates the following files and folders:

* Input folder: Contains the input data (reflection, mode and ligands) and the Protocol.pr_xml file that contains details from the run.

* Intermediate folder (optional): This folder contains all the files used at each step of the pipeline. The intermediate folder is only recommended in cases where an exhaustive analysis of the run is needed or for troubleshooting purposes.

* Output folder: Contains the refined structures holding the protein-ligand complex. The naming convention is: <reflection filename>_Complex.dsv.

* Report.htm Summarizes the information from the refined complex. The following information is included: General information of the overall run including name, status, user, etc. Summary table that includes the batch ID, inputs (reflection, model and ligands), refined model name, resolution, R-value and Free R-value, and the scoring information of the fit of the ligand to the electron density that was used for the final placement. Section with links to the results files are provided for further examination and analysis. Only systems that ran to completion are listed in this area. For any system that did not run to completion, an Error log file is created that provides additional information for troubleshooting.

* General information of the overall run including name, status, user, etc.

* Summary table that includes the batch ID, inputs (reflection, model and ligands), refined model name, resolution, R-value and Free R-value, and the scoring information of the fit of the ligand to the electron density that was used for the final placement.

* Section with links to the results files are provided for further examination and analysis. Only systems that ran to completion are listed in this area. For any system that did not run to completion, an Error log file is created that provides additional information for troubleshooting.

#### Troubleshooting

If there were problems with the results, you can inspect the individual output files that were generated by the run. The following files are created in the Output directory. The file names may differ from those listed here:

| File name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Output.log | Detailed messages generated by the protocol. If errors occur during the run, they are listed here. |
| Error.log | In rare cases a system may generate an error which forces the whole or part of the job to fail; in these cases an Error.log file is generated providing information on the origin of the error. |
| <ligand file>_<reflection file>_Failed.sd | Contains the ligands that failed to place. The reason for the failure is indicated by the ErrorText property. |

Alternatively, if problems persist or a greater level of detail is needed, save the Intermediate folder as described above.

# Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xligandtools.htm

## Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools

The Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools allow you to automatically fit ligand coordinates to electron density maps and make 
adjustments as needed.

### Binding Site

Search and Select Binding Sites: This button launches the Place and Refine X-ray Ligand Binding Site Search dialog . This dialog allows you to select the ligand and density 
map. You can also specify the Sigma threshold and specify a search volume.
The search finds sites around the receptor where the electron density is above the specified Sigma 
threshold value, but in which no model atoms occur. These 
sites are then sorted by size, with the largest region of density first. The ligand is placed at this largest site.

Adjust: This button adjusts the volume of the searched electron density so that it is the same as the volume of the ligand. 
This works by adjusting the specified Sigma threshold used in flood fill until the density volume found matches the 
volume of the ligand.

In general, setting the Sigma threshold to the default value of 2.5 is best when searching 
Fo-Fc density maps and 1.5 when searching 2Fo-Fc density maps. The Adjust button then 
searches down to find the correct extent of electron density for the ligand to fit into. If the initial value is set 
too low, the optimal volume is not found.

Ligand: <Ligand name>: This indicates the name of the structure considered the ligand, as specified in the Search... step.

Next Binding Site: This button moves the display to the next potential ligand site and places the ligand, in its current conformation, 
in the site in its best orientation.

Previous Binding Site: This button moves the display to the previous potential ligand site and places the ligand, in its current 
conformation, in the site in its best orientation.

### Search and View Conformations

Search...: This button launches the Place and Refine X-ray Ligand Conformation Search dialog which monitors the progress of your conformational 
search and dismisses when the search is complete or converged. If there are several internal degrees of freedom in 
the ligand, possible conformations are fitted to the density. The conformations are searched by changing the rotatable 
bonds. Twenty conformations are prepared in order of density fit.

Place and Refine X-ray Ligand automatically determines the precision at which rotatable 
bonds need to be searched to efficiently give good results.

Next Conformation: You can browse the ligand molecule conformations in this list. This button 
takes you to the next conformation on the list.

Previous Conformation: This button takes you to the previous ligand molecule conformation on the list.

Refine: This button performs a real space refinement of the current ligand conformation's torsion angles in the current site. 
The position, orientation, and all defined torsion angles are refined to the electron density by least squares.

Refine All: This button refines all 20 conformations found in the conformations search.

Accept: Deletes all conformations but the current one. Click this button when you 
have reached what you consider to be the best conformation.

Flip Torsion: Flips the currently selected torsion.

### Refine

Place Ligands: Opens the Place Ligands protocol dialog. This protocol automatically positions one or more ligands into 
unoccupied electron density.

HT-XPIPE: Opens the HT-XPIPE protocol dialog. This protocol automatically places and refines protein-ligand complexes in high throughput mode. For each system, a reflection file, a model structure, and a set of ligands is used as input.

### Access methods

| Tool bar | X-ray \| Place and Refine X-ray Ligand |
| --- | --- |
| Menu | Tools \| X-ray \| Place and Refine X-ray Ligand |
| Menu | View \| Tool Panels \| Place and Refine X-ray Ligand |

#### Further information

How to use the Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools Binding Site Search dialog Search Conformation dialog Place and Refine X-ray Ligand subpage - Preferences dialog

# How to use the Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xligandtools_hw.htm

## How to use the Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools

This topic discusses how to use the Place and 
Refine X-ray Ligand tools. The following tasks are covered:

* Search for sites

* Search conformations

To search for sites

The Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools require the 
presence of a receptor in a cell, an electron density map, and a ligand.

* To search for binding sites, load a structure, a density map,
and a ligand and click Search... from the Binding Site tools. 
This launches the Place and Refine X-ray Ligand Binding Site Search dialog.

* Specify the ligand under Select ligand molecule and the density map under Select electron density map . Unless you have multiple ligands and density maps open, these
should be automatically specified.

* Set the Sigma threshold . A good default value for Fo-Fc maps is 2.5 sigma. 
For 2Fo-Fc 1.5 sigma is recommended.

* Specify the Search volume . In most cases, you will want this to be equal to the receptor 
volume. However, you can specify a spherical volume to search with an origin at the Cartesian origin or about 
the selected atom(s).

* Click the OK button.

* Once the sites have been defined, you can navigate between them using the Next Binding Site and the Previous Binding Site buttons and adjust individual sites with the Adjust button.

To search conformations

* When you reach a likely binding site, you can generate twenty conformations in order of density fit by clicking 
the Search... button from the Conformation tools.

* Once the conformations have been defined, you can navigate between them using the Next Conformation and the Previous Conformation buttons and Refine individual 
sites or Refine All sites. The refinement method is a torsion-angle, real-space refinement, 
applying both linear and quadratic interpolation of the electron density. The final coordinates are within 0.01 of the refinement carried out with standard refinement procedures but the radius of 
convergence is much higher using this method.

* Once you have selected the best conformation, click the Accept button to delete all 
other conformations. You can save the result using the File | Save As... command.

### Access methods

| Tools explorer | View \| Tool Panels \| Place and Refine X-ray Ligand |
| --- | --- |

#### Further information

Place and Refine X-ray Ligand tools Binding Site Search dialog Search Conformation dialog Place and Refine X-ray Ligand subpage - Preferences dialog

# Refinement Cascade - Parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_model_refinement-para.htm

## Refinement Cascade - Parameters

### Refines crystal structures using multiple steps

Combines commonly used refinement steps into a single workflow:

* Rigid-body minimization.

* Simulated annealing.

* Coordinate minimization.

* Occupancy minimization (group and/or individual).

* B-factor minimization (group, residue and/or individual).

* Map generation.

Depending on the selected refinement tasks, different advanced options are available.

Note:

* The Refinement Cascade parameter uses a multi-selection dialog box for ease of selection of multiple tasks. Not all tasks need to be selected, and depending on the stage of refinement some tasks could be more appropriate than others.

### Parameters

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Input Protein Molecule | Select a protein structure to read. |
| Input Reflection Data | Select a reflection data to read. |
| Field Mapping | Assigns field mapping for CNX/CNS format. |
| Amplitude Field | The field name for amplitude. |
| Amplitude Deviation Field | The field name for amplitude standard deviation. |
| Intensity Field | The field name for intensity. |
| Intensity Deviation Field | The field name for intensity standard deviation. |
| Refinement Cascade | Select the refinement task you wish to perform. Available tasks are: Rigid-Body Minimization Simulated Annealing Coordinate Minimization Domain B-factor Minimization Group B-factor Minimization Individual B-factor Minimization Group Occupancy Minimization Individual Occupancy Minimization Map Generation Note: Parameters below are enabled depending on the selected task. Valid Values: Rigid-Body Minimization , Simulated Annealing, Coordinate Minimization, Domain B-factor Minimization, Group B-factor Minimization, Individual B-factor Minimization, Group Occupancy Minimization, Individual Occupancy Minimization, Generate Map |
| Rigid-Body Minimization | Specifies to perform rigid-body minimization during refinement. |
| Rigid-Body Minimization Number of Cycles | Number of cycles of rigid-body minimization to perform. |
| Rigid-Body Minimization Number of Steps Per Cycle | Number of steps per cycle to use during rigid-body minimization. |
| Rigid-Body Minimization High Resolution Limit | Limit on the reflection data that will be used for the individual coordinates refinement. |
| Rigid-Body Minimization Low Resolution Limit | Limit on the reflection data that will be used for the rigid-body minimization. |
| Simulated Annealing | Contains options for performing Simulated Annealing during refinement. |
| Simulated Annealing Number of Trials | Specifies number of trials to perform during Simulated Annealing. |
| Number of MD Steps | Number of molecular dynamics steps to run in case of Constant Temperature simulated annealing. |
| Coordinate Minimization | Specifies the coordinate minimization settings for refinement. |
| Coordinate Minimization Number of Cycles | Number of cycles of coordinate minimization to perform. |
| Coordinate Minimization Number of Steps Per Cycle | Number of steps per cycle to use during coordinate minimization. |
| B-factor Minimization | B-factor Minimization Tasks to perform: Domain B-factor Minimization Group B-factor Minimization Individual B-factor Minimization All tasks may be selected or only a subset. |
| B-factor Minimization Domain Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during group B-factor minimization. |
| B-factor Minimization Group Number of Steps | Number of Steps for Residue B-factor Minimization. |
| B-factor Minimization Individual Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during individual B-factor minimization. |
| Occupancy Minimization | Occupancy minimization tasks to perform: Group Occupancy Minimization Individual Occupancy Minimization |
| Occupancy Minimization Group Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during group occupancy minimization. |
| Occupancy Minimization Individual Number of Steps | Number of steps to perform during individual occupancy minimization. |
| Generate Map | Specifies to generate a map at the end of the refinement. |
| Map Type | Specifies the type of map to generate. Valid Values: 2Fo-Fc , Fo-Fc , 3Fo-2Fc |
| Advanced | Options for advanced users wanting to modify various default parameters related to: Simulated Annealing Occupancy Minimization B-factor Minimization Generate Map NCS Restraints Forcefield Typing |
| Solvent Correction | Specifies solvent correction method to use. Valid Values: none, babinet, mask |
| Reflection Data | Reflection Data Limits for the full Refinement Cascade (except for Rigid-Body Minimization) and Map Generation step. |
| High Resolution Limit | Limit on the reflection data that will be used for the Refinement Cascade and Map Generation. If left blank, values will be derived from the reflection data set. |
| Low Resolution Limit | Limit on the reflection data that will be used for the Refinement Cascade and Map Generation. If left blank, values will be derived from the reflection data set. |
| Advanced Simulated Annealing | Advanced options for performing Simulated Annealing calculations. |
| Advanced Simulated Annealing Type | Specifies the type of Simulated Annealing to use. torsion : Performs the molecular dynamics in torsion angle space. If selected, the default value of 2500.0 for Starting Temperature is the recommended starting temperature value. cartesian : Performs molecular dynamics in Cartesian space. If selected, the recommended value for Cartesian space dynamics for the Starting Temperature parameter is 500.0. Valid Values: torsion , cartesian |
| Annealing Schedule | Specifies the schedule that is used for Simulated Annealing. The annealing procedure begins at a defined Starting Temperature . This temperature can normally be higher for Torsion Angle Dynamics than for Cartesian Dynamics. slowcool : Cycles of annealing are run, with 6 steps of molecular dynamics per cycle. The temperature drops by the Temperature Drop per Cycle at each cycle. Cycles continue to be run until the last non-negative temperature has been reached. constant : The Number of MD Steps of annealing are run, all at the defined Starting Temperature . Valid Values: slowcool , constant |
| Starting Temperature | Starting temperature to use for Simulated Annealing procedure. The default of 2500.0 is appropriate for Torsion Angle Dynamics simulated annealing. The value 500.0 should be used as a default for Cartesian Dynamics. |
| Temperature Drop per Cycle | Specifies the temperature drop for each cycle when using slow cooling Simulated Annealing. |
| Maximum Unbranched Chain for Torsion Angle Dynamics | Used when torsion angle dynamics are being run, you need to increase this value if the CNX job fails and reports in the log file that this value has been exceeded. |
| Maximum Number of Distinct Bodies for Torsion Angle Dynamics | Used when torsion angle dynamics are being run. You will need to increase this value if the CNX job fails and reports in the log file that the "maxtree" value has been exceeded. |
| Advanced B-factor Minimization | Advanced options for performing B-factor Minimization calculations. |
| Preset B-factor Value | The B-factors are set to the specified value (for example: 25.0) prior to the first stage of B-factor refinement. Set the value to -1 for keeping the current atom B-factors. |
| B-factor Lower Limit | The minimum B-factor that is allowed during refinement. |
| B-factor Upper Limit | The maximum B-factor that is allowed during refinement. |
| Individual B-factor Minimization | Settings for Individual B-factor Minimization. |
| Weight for B-factor Restraints | Specifies the weight between the crystallographic target and the B-factor restraints (determined automatically if the value is -1 ). |
| Target Sigma for Bonds Main Chain | Specifies target sigma values during B-factor minimization for the distribution of B-factors for atoms that form main-chain bonds. |
| Target Sigma for Angles Main Chain | Specifies target sigma values during B-factor minimization for the distribution of B-factors for atoms that form main-chain angles. |
| Target Sigma for Bonds Side Chains | Specifies target sigma values during B-factor minimization for the distribution of B-factors for atoms that form side-chain bonds. |
| Target Sigma for Angles Side Chains | Specifies target sigma values during B-factor minimization for the distribution of B-factors for atoms that form side-chain angles. |
| Atoms Having Fixed B-factors | Selects atoms for which the B-factor should not be optimized. |
| Advanced Occupancy Minimization | Advanced options for Occupancy Minimization. |
| Group Occupancy Minimization | Options for Group occupancy minimization. |
| Preset Occupancies Value | The atom occupancies are set to the specified value (for example: 1.0) prior to the first stage of occupancy refinement. Set the value to -1 for keeping the current atom occupancies. |
| Individual Occupancy Minimization | Specifies to perform individual occupancy minimization during refinement. |
| Individual Occupancy Minimization Atoms to Refine | Atoms to refine during the individual occupancy minimization stage. |

# Refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_rfn.htm

## Refinement

The X-ray collection in Discovery Studio and Pipeline Pilot Server has been
built using CNX as its main refinement engine. Various commonly used
refinement tasks have been compiled and converted to Pipeline Pilot components
to provide easy access to refinement calculations used in the determination
of protein and nucleic acid crystal structures.

For many of the refinement calculations, CNX uses reciprocal-space refinement
methods commonly used in the determination of X-ray structures. The components
available from the Discovery Studio and Pipeline Pilot Client s, complement the
functionality available from other real-space crystal structure determination tools
such as:

* Build and Refine X-ray Structure

* Edit X-ray Structure

* Place and Refine X-ray Ligand

Macromolecular X-ray theory started with the methods used in the determination of the
first protein structure refined by Jensen and coworkers in the early 1970's [Watenpaugh et al., 1971] .
Since then, refinement of large biological crystal structures has evolved. X-ray theory has been modified and improved with the incorporation
of new methods and theoretical techniques. However, the basic concepts from
early work are still relevant to understanding calculations performed in CNX. The following concepts are covered here:

* Reciprocal-space refinement by least squares

* Restrained refinement

* Molecular mechanics in crystal structure refinement

* Cross-validation of refinement results

* Maximum likelihood refinement target

* Minimization methods

In the simplest case, reciprocal-space refinement is achieved by least squares
minimization of the crystallographic residual, D .

Equation 1:

The atomic parameters to be optimized
are χ j and B j , which
represent the positions and thermal vibrations of the atoms. These parameters
are related to the crystallographic residual as shown in the following equation:

Equation 2:

If F c (h) is expanded by Taylor's theorem, and assuming that changes
in atomic parameters are small, the quantity to be minimized in Equation 1 can be approximated
by a linear function as shown in Equation 3, where χ n are the individual
atomic parameters x 1 , y 1 , z 1 , B 1 , x 2 ,
y 2 , z 2 , B 2 , etc., with w h as a scale factor.

Equation 3:

The computational treatment for minimization of this equation leads to a square matrix
with n 2 elements. The diagonal terms of the matrix are often assumed
to be large with respect to the off-diagonal terms that describe the correlation between
structural changes. This assumption makes the computation more tractable, but further limits
the validity of the calculation to very small changes in structure. Thus, in practice, least
squares reciprocal-space refinement is applied in an iterative manner. Changes applied to
the atomic parameters lead to an improved calculation of F c that is used
in turn to calculate additional corrections to the atomic parameters. This cyclic process is
usually continued until convergence
( [Blundell and Johnson, 1976] , [Stout and Jensen, 1989] , and [Giacovazzo, 1992] ).

A central problem in macromolecular structure refinement at low to moderate
resolution is the low ratio of observations ( F o )
to the number of parameters being refined. Chemical knowledge about the nature
of the molecules being investigated may be applied in the form of restraints
to the changes in the structure during refinement. Added restraints increase
the amount of information incorporated into the calculation, and supplement the
direct experimental observations. The equation to be minimized then takes the
form of Equation 4:

Equation 4:

The variable E may be composed of multiple terms that describe
geometric knowledge of the molecular structure such as van der Waals distances,
bond lengths, bond angles, planarity, etc. These terms, in their simplest
form, will follow a pattern seen in Equation 5, where g eq is the ideal value for the restraint and w q is a weighting
factor.

Equation 5:

A number of schemes have been devised for restraints, and applied in refinement
programs such as PROLSQ [Hendrickson, 1985] and
TNT [Tronrud, 1997] .
The appropriate value for each weighting factor for restraints is not obvious.
These weights have often been adjusted to produce a molecular
model where the distribution of deviations of geometric measurements from ideal
is similar to that in very high-resolution X-ray crystal structures refined
without such restraints.

The molecular mechanics system employed in CHARMm [Brooks et al., 1983] was combined with reciprocal-space refinement in the program X-PLOR [Brünger et al., 1987] . CHARMm provides a sophisticated
system of restraints for refinement. This formulation also provides a means for the incorporation
of molecular dynamics operations, especially simulated annealing, as an adjunct to least squares
reciprocal-space refinement ( [Brünger et al., 1987] and [Brünger, 1991] .

The quantity E in Equation 4 now becomes the sum of the CHARMm empirical
energy terms. The factor w a performs an important
function in that it both scales the electron density, D , to the
empirical energy terms, and provides an overall weighting for the influence
of the X-ray term relative to the molecular mechanical energy terms. The
first four energy terms describe conformational energy, while the other
energy terms involve nonbonded interactions. The subscripts beginning
with p refer to interactions with symmetry-related molecules
in the crystal lattice.

Equation 6:

Although the CHARMm molecular mechanics scheme has been maintained in X-PLOR
and CNX, the full CHARMm parameter set is less than optimal for refinement restraints (e.g., the electrostatic terms are not evaluated,
nor are explicit H-bond terms used). Engh and Huber [Engh and Huber, 1991] have devised a parameter set for bond lengths and angles that has largely replaced
the use of those CHARMm parameters.

The program CNS [Brünger et al., 1998] updated and improved the molecular mechanics and reciprocal-space methods developed in X-PLOR.
CNX is the synthesis of the best functionality of X-PLOR and CNS, including elements discussed
below. Both CHARMm, and Engh and Huber parameter sets are provided for use with the complete CNX
program. The XPROLIG parameter set available in Discovery Studio is derived from the Engh and Huber
parameter set.

Due to the low ratio of data to adjustable parameters, and because of normal experimental errors,
multiple local minima appear to fit the data equally well during refinement. Thus, the traditional R -factor can be artificially decreased during refinement without any structure improvement in the
molecular model.

Equation 7:

If refinement is applied to a partial dataset containing 90 to 95 percent of the observations,
the remaining ten to five percent should show an improved fit if optimization of Equation 6 has
altered the molecular parameters to better agree with the true solution of the crystal structure.
Incorrect solutions may fit the working data set equally well, but the fit for the independent (free)
data set do not tend to improve. A reduction in both R -factor
and R -free is a good indication that the model correctly fits the experimental
observations, and true improvement occurs during refinement.

Cross-validation, an independent measure of the progress of crystal structure
refinement, was developed from work by Brünger [Brünger, 1992] . For cross-validation (Equation 7),
the R -free statistic is calculated from an independent subset of randomly
selected structure factors. Cross-validation first appeared in X-PLOR, but is integral to the workings of
CNS and CNX.

A more sophisticated approach to refinement has been developed
that depends on cross-validation [Pannu and
Read, 1996] . This maximum likelihood target uses a statistical analysis to account for the effects of
measurement errors, model errors, and data incompleteness encountered during the minimization process, and replaces Equation
6 with Equation 8.

Equation 8:

An important distinction from previous formulations is that F c in
Equation 2 is replaced with the expected values of | F o |, calculated
through the use of cross-validation. These values are more stable with respect to changes
in the structure than are F c , and lead to a larger radius of convergence
and less interference by false minima. When used with simulated annealing, the maximum
likelihood target can produce additional improved results from other refinement targets [Adams et al., 1997] .

Although the least squares methods are used extensively to minimize various
target equations, other algorithms are better suited for this goal. The original versions
of the X-PLOR program relied on the Powell routine [Powell, 1977] to perform energy
minimizations of macromolecular structures. The Powell algorithm is a gradient-based minimizer
that uses first derivative information to perform the optimization.

Theoretical reasons related to the large variation in atomic scattering factors within
protein structures suggest advantages for energy-minimization algorithms that make use of
second derivative information [Tronrud, 1992] .
Furthermore, the Powell energy-minimization routine sometimes terminates with a significantly
non-zero gradient for numerical reasons involving the step size used in the line search.
For these reasons, the ABNR energy-minimization routine [Brooks et al., 1983] is preferred and
has been implemented in CNX. Refinement trials with both crystallographic and NMR data confirm that
the ABNR minimization gives final refined models with lower energies than the Powell minimization
routine [Badger et al., 1999] .

# Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut.htm

## Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

The model building functionality in Build and Refine X-ray Structure is designed
to accelerate and simplify the process of model building and coordinate fitting to electron
density maps. The model building tools allow for real-space refinement in torsion angle space,
rigid body refinement, regularization, and manual editing of macromolecular coordinates.
These and other tools and protocols in Discovery Studio streamline the process of model building.

Build and Refine X-ray Structure supports three refinement techniques. Single residues can be fitted by:

* Grid searching about torsions.

* Torsion-angle real-space gradient refinement.

* Monte Carlo fitting.

The following links describe the implementation of real-space torsion angle refinement algorithms
as tools for model building with Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools:

* Density-fitting function

* Grid-refinement protocol

* Monte Carlo refinement

* Real-space refinement

* Refinement parameters

# Density-fitting function

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_density-fitting-function.htm

## Density-fitting function

Build and Refine X-ray Structure uses two forms of interpolation for the electron density: linear and quadratic.
Linear interpolation tends to produce poor approximations for a final atom position,
as an atom tends to move to the highest density point, but has the advantage that it results
in a continuous function with no false minima, which are often found with quadratic interpolation.
Hence, all refinement uses the linear interpolation until near convergence, then switches to the more
precise quadratic interpolation of the electron density and continues the refinement to tolerance
completion.

Since the electron density is stored as a grid map that is not necessarily orthogonal, it is
necessary to transform the atoms and map to the same axial system. It would not be efficient to
transform all or part of the map to an orthogonal grid, as this would be extremely computationally
expensive and could require large amounts of memory. Hence, the algorithm transforms the atomic positions
into map space during refinement and atom-fit values are determined by interpolation. Since the
torsion-angle parameters are defined in orthogonal "world" coordinates, while values and gradients
are defined from interpolated points defined from the torsion angle and thus the world coordinate
system, there is no xyz parameter dependence with nonorthogonal maps, which is the case for nonorthogonal
space groups. Such interpolations provide a greater degree of accuracy and efficiency when fitting
to electron density maps.

# Grid-refinement protocol

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_grid-refinement-protocol.htm

## Grid-refinement protocol

Grid-refinement performs real-space torsion-angle refinement of the grid. The principle of this type
of calculation is to find the best fit to density by systematically varying the torsion angle
parameters. This method of refinement always finds the same answer regardless of the starting
conformation and thus has an infinite radius of convergence. In practice, as the number
of torsion angles to fit increases, the number of density fits requiring evaluation quickly
reaches an impossibly large number. With a precision of 2°, n torsion angles require
180 n density-fit calculations (and nonbond calculations).

The grid refinement implemented in Discovery Studio offers shortcuts that allow four
torsion angles to be fitted (e.g., lysine/arginine side-chain) in approximately 0.3 s with a precision
of 2°. Hence, this method allows you to quickly and effectively fit side-chain atoms of amino acids, nucleic acids, and the
peptide planes of proteins.

For additional information choose one of the following:

* Fitting
main-chain atoms

* Fitting
amino-acid side-chains

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_grid-refinement-protocol_fitting-amino-acid-side-chains.htm

## Fitting amino-acid side-chains

All geometric terms are constrained to the initial values and are therefore unrefined. The algorithm
performs a two-stage tree search, progressively fitting each torsion angle. For each torsion angle fitted,
two open angles are defined about the second atom within the rotatable four atom set. For example, with
the chi1 torsion (N-Cα-Cβ-Cγ), the two opening angles are defined about the (N-Cα-Cβ)
triplet. The first opening-angle axis is defined as orthogonal to the three atoms set and through the
C α atom.

The second axis is coplanar with the three-atom set and orthogonal to the first
axis and runs through the Cα atom. These opening angles allow a greater convergence radius where there
is error in the Cα position or chiral volume. These errors can often prevent the placement of side-chain
atoms when changing torsion angles alone.

Starting with the first torsion angle in the side-chain (e.g.,
N-Cα-Cβ-Cγ), the torsion angle is varied with a precision of 10°. The opening angles are
searched at -8°, 0, and +8° about the initial value. The occupancy of the atoms further down a side-chain
is set to 0 . The best solution of this fit is then further refined by ±6°
with a precision of 3° about the opening angles and ±8° with a precision of 2° about the
torsion angle.

On completion of the fit of the first torsion angle, other torsion angles along the side-chain
(further from the Cα atom) are fitted in the same way.

Some covalent structures can prevent the determination of the correct torsion-angle
value because the solution to the tree search is ambiguous. This includes the amino acid isoleucine.
When χ 1 of isoleucine is fitted, the atoms Cγ 1 and Cγ 2 are
equivalent within the tree search. This is the case for any torsion angle followed by an atom with three or
more bonded atoms that are equivalent or nearly equivalent with regard to their interaction with X-rays.

To
resolve this problem, the algorithm revisits a χ angle. In the isoleucine example, χ 2 is fitted
for both alternative χ 1 values. The proline residue is fitted by rotating the five-member ring
about C(-1)-N-Cα-C and the pucker angle. The latter is searched within the range of ±30°.

# Fitting main-chain atoms

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_grid-refinement-protocol_fitting-main-chain-atoms.htm

## Fitting main-chain atoms

To fit peptide planes, an ideal trans-peptide plane is built and all combinations of the peptide plane
(rotated about the axis defined by the pseudo-bond Cα( n )-Cα( n +1)) are sampled
with 1° steps, plus variation of values between ±12° (also with 1° steps).

Modifying the Ω angle will likely distort the peptide plane and may
require redefinition of the peptide geometry after each main-chain refinement step. However, the
Cα - Cα separation is not redefined by this fitting procedure.

# Monte Carlo refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_monte-carlo-refinement.htm

## Monte Carlo refinement

Monte Carlo refinement samples the conformational space by setting the torsion angles search-parameter
to random values and then saving the best solutions identified by their fit to the electron
density. This refinement method is suitable for cases where a large radius of convergence is required, but
systematic grid searching would be too slow and inefficient. The Monte Carlo refinement method is
implemented for fitting main-chain protein atoms in loops or termini to electron density. For additional
information, see Loop fitting in proteins .

#### Further information

Density-fitting function Grid-refinement protocol Refinement parameters Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools theory

DOCUMENT 3198
==============================================================================================================

# Loop fitting in proteins

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_monte-carlo-refinement_loop-fitting-in-proteins.htm

## Loop fitting in proteins

Since the refinement proceeds in a driven random way, correlation between the torsion angles
does not prevent refinement, but does limit the number of simultaneously searched torsion angles. The
bonds, angles, improper angles (including chiral centers and coplanar groups of atoms), and torsion angles
are set to ideal values before starting and are constrained (i.e., not varied). The φ and ψ torsion
angles within the search zone are defined as search parameters. The nonbond interactions to the rest of the
model coordinates are required for each conformation. Since they are computationally expensive, these are
calculated once before beginning the search. The nonbond interactions with the moving atoms are calculated
for the fixed atoms at grid points within a suitable map volume about the starting loop conformation. That is,
a nonbond energy surface is generated on the map grid and this is used while exploring conformational space
of the loop under refinement to give a simultaneous energy term for nonbond clashes and map fit value.

The subtractive method for random numbers of Knuth [Knuth, 1981] is used to generate a satisfactory series of non-repeating random numbers. For each torsion-angle parameter,
a random value is generated between 0° and 359° in 1° steps, and the poly-alanine chain conformation
is set to reflect these. If a loop is to be fitted, then the length of the poly-alanine chain is determined
and checked to be within ±1 Å of the distance between the residues preceding and following
the loop. If this length is satisfied, then the first residue is superimposed on the original conformation.

Next, the intra-nonbond value is determined using the sum of all interactions of all the atoms in
the loop with themselves. This effectively determines whether the conformation has all residues lying approximately
within Ramachandran-allowed regions. If this restraint is satisfied, then the fit of the random conformation
to the electron density is determined in real space. Since the inter-nonbond interaction is encoded within this
electron density, the function calculated is a sum of intra-nonbonds and the fit to density. The
ten current best solutions are saved as the search progresses.

#### Further information

Monte Carlo refinement Refinement parameters Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools theory

# Real-space refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_real-space-refinement.htm

## Real-space refinement

The real-space refinement (RSR) methodology used in the algorithm is designed to quickly improve
the fit of coordinates to the electron density. Any map of the form nF o -
( n - 1) F c or any σ A -weighted map will show a gradient
in the neighborhood of incorrectly placed atoms. By improving the fit between the calculated atom
density and the map, this methodology allows you to quickly correct the model and allow visualize the action performed in real time.

RSR has the further advantage that sections of the model can be refined independently of others and
the underlying assumptions of structure and geometry can be temporarily relaxed during manual refinement
to arrive at the correct fit. This is particularly useful when using tools like Move Atom and Refine
Residue where you would interactively correct an atom position and the remaining residue coordinates
are automatically fit to electron density.

#### Further information

Density-fitting function Grid-refinement protocol Monte Carlo refinement Refinement parameters Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools theory

==============================================================================================================

# Refinement parameters

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_the_xbut_refinement-parameters.htm

## Refinement parameters

The refinement techniques applied use a mixed parameterization method to solve a number
of problems associated with both xyz(B) and torsion angle parameterization of macromolecular
structure. The refinement protocol carries out interspersed cycles of geometry refinement
using restraints on the stereochemistry followed by constrained torsion-angle refinement of
each separate amino acid. These cycles are entirely independent
and therefore require no weighting scheme.

During amino acid torsion-angle refinement, the additional degrees of freedom associated
with the rigid-body movement and rotation of each amino acid are also refined. Since the rigid-body
movement and rotation of each amino acid is defined along the principal components of the amino acid,
these six degrees of freedom are redefined at each step.

Although this appears to be inefficient, requiring the parameterization of both the geometrical
terms and rotatable bonds, it does allow large movements of the residues during the refinement to
experimental data while retaining the integrity of the polymer structure. The inclusion of cycles
of refinement where geometry is restrained also allows flexibility within the covalent structure
of the macromolecule. This is important during the initial stages of modeling, where significant
errors in the structure cannot be corrected by torsion-angle shifts alone.

To carry out torsion-angle refinement, a full description of rigid
units, rotatable bonds, and permissible limits is required. A highly optimized extensible template using the Engh and Huber
parameters [Engh and Huber, 1991] defines amino acids and nucleic acids. This file defines all rotatable bonds within each residue
construct and hence provides a full description of all geometrical and torsion angle parameters.
This allows the refinement of extremely distorted initial models where the close contacts have no
relation to the required connectivity.

All restraints on bond deviation (Equation 1), deviation in the open angle (Equation 2), and deviation
of the improper torsion angle (Equation 3) for chiral centers, prochiral centers, and planar atoms
are quadratic in form. Equation 4 represents the formulation of the torsion angle restraints with
multiple minima.

Equation 1:

Equation 2:

Equation 3:

Equation 4:

where:

* b [i] , θ [i] , and ζ [i] are the current values for the bond length, valence angle, improper angle, and torsion angle, respectively, for
the i th atom.

* b [i]o , θ [i]o , and
ζ [i]o are the optimal values for the bond length, angle, and improper torsion angle,
respectively, for the i th atom.

* n defines the number of minima about a torsion angle, δ 
is the phase shift in the torsion angle.

* W [i] is the weight used for
the energy term i .

Derivatives are calculated from these functions. The derivatives for nonbonding interactions are based on both
finite differences and on analytical derivatives for restraints.

There are three nonbond formulations. The first
is based on a Lennard-Jones 6-12 potential for van der Waals interactions plus an electrostatic term (using a radial
distant variation in dielectric (Equation 5), the second uses just the van der Waals term (Equation 6), and the third
uses a simple repulsive formulation (Equation 7).

Equation 5:

Equation 6:

Equation 7:

* σ ij is the equilibrium separation between atoms i and j .
This is estimated using the combination rules:
σ ij = (σ i /2 + σ j /2).

* ε ij is the minimum energy at the separation r = σ ij .
This is estimated using the combination rule
ε ij = ε i l/2 ε j 1/2 .

* q i and q j are the partial
changes for the atoms i and j .

* r ij is the separation
between the atoms i and j .

* W vdw , W elec , and W push are nonstandard
weights used to scale the nonbond terms with respect the other energy terms to soften the interaction.

During density-fitting of macromolecular structures, it is best to exclude electrostatic interactions when
the protein and solvent model is incomplete. The complete formulations for nonbonding are provided, but
their use is not recommended for crystallographic map interpretation. The simple repulsive formulation
results in fast minimization without loss of precision.
