# Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut.htm

## Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

Build and Refine X-ray Structure offers a suite of interactive and semi-automated tools to speed up
the model-building stage of crystallographic structure determination. Model
building constructs or adjusts the atomic coordinates of a molecular structure
to best interpret the electron density produced from previous steps.

The Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools include the following groups:

* Regularization

* Refinement

* Fitting

Regularize Selected Zone: Performs geometric regularization
of a selected residue or a selected zone of residues.

Move Atom and Regularize Zone: Refines a selected zone of
residue(s) with real space refinement and regularization.

Refine One Residue: Refines a selected residue using
real space refinement.

Move Atom and Refine Residue: Moves a selected atom while
regularizing a selected zone.

Fit Main-Chain by Real Space Refinement: Fits the peptide
plane of a selected C-N bond using real space refinement.

Fit Side-Chain by Real Space Refinement: Fits part of all
of the sidechain of a residue using real space refinement.

Refine Selected Zone: Refines a selected zone of
residue(s) with real space refinement and regularization.

Fit Rigid Body: Refines a selected zone
of residue(s) using rigid body refinement.

Fit Loop: Explores loop conformations in real space and
scores these conformations according to their fit to the electron density. Conformations are
listed in a table and these are ranked according to their electron density fit score.

Fit Terminal: Explores conformations of a terminal residue
segment in real space, and fits these to the electron density. A score of the fit is provided to
help sort conformations with the better fit to the electron density. Terminal residues can be
either N or C terminal.

Set Default Map: Sets the default density map for use with the commands.

Details about the use of these tools are covered in How to use the Build
and Refine X-ray Structure tools .

Prerequisites: The regularization tools ( Regularize
Selected Zone , Move Atom and Regularize Zone ,
and Refine Selected Zone ) require the molecule to be
typed using the XPROLIG forcefield. All of the tools except Regularize
Selected Zone , and Move
Atom and Regularize Zone require an electron density map.

### Advanced

Generate Electron Density Maps: Opens the Generate Electron Density Maps protocol dialog. This protocol generates one or more electron density 
maps from a molecular structure and its corresponding X-ray reflection data.

Refinement Cascade: Opens the Refinement Cascade protocol dialog. This protocol performs a series of refinement steps on a 
molecular structure and its corresponding X-ray reflection file.

Pick Water: Opens the Pick Water protocol dialog. This protocol generates a map (default: Fo - Fc; SigmaA), and then searches for unoccupied electron density.

# How to use the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut_hw.htm

## How to use the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools

The Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel contains interactive and 
semi-automated tools to speed up the model building stage of crystallographic 
structure determination. Model building involves the construction of a molecular 
structure and subsequent adjustment of its atomic coordinates to best interpret 
the electron density determined from previous steps, while maintaining the 
chemical validity of the structure. The topics below describe how to use Build and Refine X-ray Structure 
to accomplish various model building and refinement tasks:

* Building one residue

* Fitting loops

* Refining 
models with real-space refinement

* Refining structure 
segments

* Refining waters

* Using geometric 
regularization

* Using manual
editing functions

The remainder of this topic includes details that may be relevant to one or 
more of the tasks listed above.

### Using standard and nonstandard residues

Build and Refine X-ray Structure supports polypeptide chains that contain the 20 natural amino acids 
and 5 commonly appearing nonstandard amino acids, that is:

* Selenomethionine

* Phosphoserine

* Phosphothreonine

* Phosphotyrosine

* Sulfotyrosine

### Using electron density maps

You can import an external map file and manage the display properties of each 
electron density map using the application.

#### Managing maps and map display

The application allows multiple maps to be displayed; the display of maps is 
controlled through the Data Table View . Discovery Studio supports CNX ASCII map ( .map ) and QUANTA 
brick map ( .mbk ) files.

#### Default map

Because Build and Refine X-ray Structure uses an electron density map (default map) for real-space 
refinement (RSR), you must specify which map to use if more than one is 
associated with a molecule. To specify the default map, select the map in the 
Data Table View or the Graphics View, and then select the Set Default Map command in the 
Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel.

The ability to select density maps 
may be enabled or disabled from the X-ray page of the Preferences dialog.

### Using Build and Refine X-ray Structure when multiple structures exist

The application allows multiple structures to be loaded into and edited in 
the Graphics View. However, to ensure that Build and Refine X-ray Structure runs properly, it is 
recommended that you load only one molecular system at a time for model building 
with Build and Refine X-ray Structure.

### Using Ramachandran Plots

The interactive Ramachandran Plot can be used for guidance in model building 
because it provides a dynamically updated graphical representation of the local 
backbone conformation of each residue in a protein. It also includes a 
representation of the favorable and unfavorable regions for residues so that you 
can readily see whether individual residues are likely to be correctly built or 
not.

Refer to Ramachandran Plot for information on accessing this functionality.

# Building one residue

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut_hw_building-one-residue.htm

## Building one residue

For most residues, it is often only necessary to carry out RSR (real-space refinement) on the side-chain coordinates, followed by some regularization. This makes model building an easy process. Move Atom and Refine Residue on the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel is useful to adjust the Cα position while refining the whole side-chain so that the large portion of the residue can be simultaneously fit into the density. Once this Cα atom movement has been completed using the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools, use Fit Side-Chain by Real Space Refinement and Fit Main-Chain by Real Space Refinement to automatically place the other atoms.

Where the side-chain positions are indeterminate, Search Side-Chain Rotamers tools can generate a theoretical conformation based on the conformations observed from the protein databank.

Mutation can also be performed using Mutate Amino Acid on the Edit X-ray Structure tool panel, followed by automatic density fitting.

# Fitting loops and terminal segments

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut_hw_fitting-loops.htm

## Fitting loops and terminal segments

To fit a loop or a terminal segment, select three or more contiguous amino acid residues from the
active Molecule Window, then click Fit Loop or Fit
Terminal on the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tool panel.

The Molecule Window must contain a
density map for the commands to be accessible.

Loop fitting and terminal segment fitting are performed using a Monte Carlo sampling
method that can screen thousands of conformations against the electron density
while retaining the ten best current solutions during the search. The progress
of the search is displayed, and you can interrupt it when the solutions
have converged to a single solution, or when an obvious fit is observed.

# Refining models with real-space refinement

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut_hw_refining-models-with-real-space-refinement.htm

## Refining models with real-space refinement

Build and Refine X-ray Structure provides two forms of real-space refinement (RSR):

Refine One Residue is an algorithm that can optimize the position and orientation of any residue type, then a full 
torsion angle minimization can be accomplished.

Refine Selected Zone enables you to refine multiple
amino acid residues by real-space, torsion angle refinement while maintaining 
ideal covalent geometry by means of regularization.

Also specific to amino acids are Fit Side Chain by Real 
Space Refinement and Fit Main Chain by Real Space 
Refinement , which use an optimized grid-search algorithm on amino 
acid coordinates to refine them to completion. The specific amino acid 
refinement routine also searches all possible conformations available 
to the amino acid and so does not get into the nearest false minima. These 
specific routines are recommended for amino acid fitting to density. The specific amino acid routines are also fast enough to allow 
editing of atom positions in an amino acid while simultaneously refining the amino acid in real-time. 
This means that the effect of placing an atom at a position can be observed 
as a function of electron density fit.

Where the main-chain is not yet well fitted or a residue has a poor Cα 
chiral volume, the simple Fit Side Chain by Real Space 
Refinement tool sometimes seems to produce spurious results. Often, 
the geometry of the backbone interferes with fitting the side-chain. If 
this happens, you may want to pick up the Cα 
atom with the Move Atom and Refine Residue tool 
and move the atom until the side-chain snaps into the density. It is usually 
obvious when the side-chain has found the right density. Sometimes you 
only need to move the Cα atom a small distance.

Real-space refinement (RSR) 
tools cannot be applied to symmetry atoms.

# Refining structure segments

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut_hw_refining-structure-segments.htm

## Refining structure segments

The Fit Rigid Body command allows you to fit 
sections of a structure and to quickly find the nearest minima for all 
the atoms in a zone. The radius of convergence is not as great as in rigid 
body refinement in reciprocal space, so it may not be able to improve 
rotation or translation function solutions for a whole protein. It may be 
possible to refine each domain, or even secondary structure elements.

The Refine Selected Zone command includes rigid body refinement, full torsion angle refinement, and regularization 
for a selected region of the structure. Hence it is possible to rigid-body 
refine a domain, segments, or even just local folds to improve the initial 
fit to a map. The refinement protocol uses torsion angle refinement and 
rigid body refinement on a residue basis while retaining geometry with 
constraints on bonds, angles, and impropers. This results in 
a refinement method with a high radius of convergence (1.5 Å). This refinement 
protocol should not be used to replace normal XYZ refinement as it is 
only applied in real space and does not affect the map. It does provide 
a rapid method of refining regions using a powerful algorithm.

# Using geometric regularization

Source type: HTML

Source section: tsxray

Source file: tsxray/xray_xbut_hw_using-geometric-regularization.htm

## Using geometric regularization

The regularization tools correct bond, valence angle, dihedral angle and improper-torsion 
parameters. Before regularization, you must have assigned the proper atom types to the atoms 
using the XPROLIG forcefield.

The regularization implementation allows atom position editing while the regularization 
is active. This allows regions of atoms (for example, a loop in proteins) to 
be manually edited, with the program retaining the correct geometry during the 
editing process.

Real-space refinement (RSR) tools cannot be applied to symmetry atoms.

### Regularization compared to real-space refinement (RSR)

Regularization changes the bonds, angles, torsions, planes, and chiralities of
residues by optimizing the sum of their potential energies.

Real-space refinement changes the angles and adjusts some bond angles to help 
find density for side-chains. The algorithm rebuilds the residue first from 
the template, so after using the RSR side-chain tool, all bonds have the correct 
value regardless of the starting positions of the atoms. The bond angles and 
improper torsions may have a deviation of up to 12° from the parameter values 
to enable the algorithm to search density when the main-chain atoms are not 
in the correct positions (as judged from the density). Therefore, although the 
regularization and RSR algorithms are complementary and change different parameters, 
you should use real-space refinement on a residue first and regularize it after.

RSR in Build and Refine X-ray Structure is specifically designed to place atoms into electron 
density with some detriment to angles and improper torsions, the latter 
being easy to correct with the Regularize Selected Zone and Move Atom and Regularize Zone commands or 
with a general reciprocal-space refinement. The command Refine Selected Zone performs simultaneous refinement of the density and regularization.

#### Further information

How to use the Build and Refine X-ray Structure tools Refining structure segments

Edit torsion angle: Select the Torsion tool on the Sketching toolbar ). Position the mouse over a bond, then drag horizontally over the

Move 3D Pointer object: The 3D Pointer can be 
moved just like any other object (see Mouse and keyboard 
actions ).

Delete atom(s)/bond(s): Select atom(s) and/or 
bond(s), then press DELETE or select Delete from 
the Edit menu.
